summary: Captain Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, an encomendero of Cartago, granted general power of attorney to Gómez Arias. Gómez Arias was a legal procurator in the Audiencia of Guatemala.

people_involved: don Juan de Ocón y Trillo
summary: Gaspar Pereira Cardoso, the Alguacil Mayor, granted general power of attorney to Alonso Duarte, Jerónimo de Tovar, Manuel Rros., and Juan de Rosales. This power was for them to claim against Governor don Juan de Ocón y Trillo, who had removed Pereira Cardoso from his position.

Captain Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, an encomendero of Cartago, committed to pay Lucas de Espinoza, a perpetual councilman of Granada, 450 pesos. The debt included 200 pesos for 8 female mules and 250 pesos paid by Espinoza on Ocampo Golfín's behalf, to be settled in goods or reales de a ocho by June 1st.

people_involved: don Juan de Ocón y Trillo
summary: Don Juan Alvarez Pereira, aged between 18 and 25, sought permission to grant power of attorney to his father-in-law, Juan Cano, to claim his father's inheritance held by his brother-in-law, Bartolomé Sánchez. Governor don Juan de Ocón y Trillo appointed Juan Cano as his tutor and curator.
Juan Cano, acting as tutor for his son-in-law don Juan Alvarez Pereira, designated Captain Francisco de Ocampo Golfín as the guarantor for the tutelage. Ocampo Golfín accepted this responsibility.

people_involved: don Juan de Ocón y Trillo
summary: Juan Cano, a resident of Cartago, swore an oath before Governor Ocón y Trillo to accept his role as tutor for don Juan Alvarez Pereira. He was formally assigned the responsibility of tutelage.

Alonso Gutiérrez Sibaja, a sick resident and encomendero, granted power to Alonso Jiménez to make his will. He named his wife, María Alvarez del Pozo, and García de Quirós as executors, and his legitimate daughter, Catarina Gutiérrez de Sibaja, as the universal heir.
Captain Juan Solano, an encomendero, vouched for Leandro de Figueroa. Leandro de Figueroa was the King's Corregidor for the district of Pacaca.
Salvador de Torres, the Corregidor of the inland district of Chirripó, named Hernando Farfán as his guarantor.

García Ramiro Corajo, an encomendero, granted general power of attorney to several individuals, including himself, don Alonso de Sotomayor, a Knight of Santiago, Doctor Pedro Ramiro, a Canon of Badajos, and residents of Trujillo de Extremadura.

Diego, an indigenous person from Ujarraz and the legitimate son of Bre. Pici and Angelina, was handed over by his father to Baltasar García. Diego was to learn the carpentry trade from Baltasar García, an indigenous carpenter, for a period of three years.
Lucas Velázquez, an indigenous ladino, made a commitment. The details of this commitment are incomplete in the historical record.
An unnamed individual was obligated to serve Juan de los Ríos for one year in exchange for fourteen pesos.

people_involved: Don Gaspar de Quevedo y Torres
summary: Don Gaspar de Quevedo y Torres, a resident of Cartago, obligated himself to Andrés Alvarez, a resident of Granada, Nicaragua, for 220 pesos. This sum was given to Alvarez in Cartago by Cristóbal de Chaves on behalf of Capitán Juan Jiménez, representing part of the proceeds from papal bulls Alvarez had provided to Jiménez in Nicaragua.
Pedro, an indigenous man from Barba and part of García Ramiro's encomienda, was obligated to serve Alonso Hernández for one year for 12 pesos.
Sebastián and his wife Juana, indigenous people from the town of Pacaca, were obligated to serve Juan Bonilla for one year for 12 pesos.
Esteban Chiquirru, an indigenous man from Tobosi, was obligated to serve Francisco de Salas for one year for ten pesos.

Isabel, an indigenous woman from Tucurrique (of the Royal Crown), and Francisca, an indigenous woman from Atirro (from Alonso Jiménez's encomienda), both single, were obligated to serve Diego del Cubillo, the Royal Treasurer and Official Judge, for one year for six pesos each.

Luis de Rivera and his wife Magdalena Sánchez granted power of attorney to Pedro de Herrera and his wife Catalina Gómez. This power allowed them to collect tributes from their encomienda in the town of Adcerrí, including honey, wheat, corn, and mats.
Miguel de Villalobos sold a plot of land (solar) to Leandro de Figueroa for 40 pesos. The property bordered houses belonging to the seller and Beneficiado Lope de Chavarría.

Alonso Gutiérrez de Sibaja, a resident and encomendero of Cartago, made his will, requesting burial in the Main Church of Cartago. He declared his wife María Alvarez de Oviedo, his legitimate daughter Catalina de Zárate, and his natural children Francisca Gutiérrez de Sibaja and Cristóbal de Sibaja. He also detailed his encomienda in Buxibux and other properties, naming García de Quirós and his wife María Alvarez as executors.
Juan de Orozco, a resident of Cartago, granted power of attorney to Alonso Hernández.

Antón Prirritubi and his wife Ana, along with their natural son Simón Hidalgo (Alcalde of Ujarraz), were obligated to serve Miguel de Villalobos for one year. Antón and Ana would serve for 12 pesos, and Simón for 14 pesos.
Juan de Orozco designated Francisco de Ocampo Golfín as a guarantor in the execution proceedings he was pursuing against Alonso Ros. de Villegas.

Juan de Orozco granted power of attorney to Alonso Duarte, a procurador of the Royal Audiencia of Guatemala, to renounce his office as escribano of the Juzgador Mayor. Orozco, who had previously sold this office to Herdo. niño de Baragon, sought to obtain the vacant Treasurer of Costa Rica position, which became available due to the death of Alonso del Cubillo in April of the current year.
Miguel de Villalobos granted power of attorney to García de Quirós and Alonso Hernández.

Gobernador Ocón y Trillo entrusted Gaspar de Cáceres, a 15-year-old mestizo orphan whose mother was an indigenous woman from Curriraba, to Diego Rodríguez, a saddler official, for a period of four years.

Gaspar Pereira Cardoso, the Alguacil Mayor, and his wife Isabel de Acuña sold thatched houses to Juan de Lamas, Alcalde of the Santa Hermandad, for 346 pesos. These houses, previously purchased from Matías de Palacio, bordered properties belonging to Capitán Franc? Pavon, Inés Ampurro, Capitán Diego de Sojo, and Gaspar de Chinchilla.

Juan de Lamas and his wife Luisa Hernández obligated themselves to Gaspar Pereira Cardoso for 400 pesos. They committed to paying part of this debt in various goods, including fattened pigs, wheat, corn, honey, capirotes, and different types of pita from both local sources and Havana.

people_involved: Don Gaspar de Quevedo y Torres
summary: Don Gaspar de Quevedo y Torres, a resident of 'this city' (likely Cartago), obligated himself to Andrés Alvarez for 220 pesos. This sum was given to Alvarez in Cartago by Cristóbal de Chaves on behalf of Captain Juan Jiménez, and it represented part of the proceeds from 'bulas' that Alvarez had given to Jiménez in Nicaragua.
Pedro, an indigenous person from Barba and part of García Ramiro's encomienda, committed to serve Alonso Hernández for one year in exchange for 12 pesos.
Sebastián and his wife Juana, indigenous people from the town of Pacaca, committed to serve Juan Bonilla for one year in exchange for 12 pesos.
Esteban Chiquirru, an indigenous person from Tobosi, committed to serve Francisco de Salas for one year in exchange for ten pesos.

Isabel, an indigenous woman from Tucurrique under the Royal Crown, and Francisca, an indigenous woman from Atirro under Alonso Jiménez's encomienda, both single, committed to serve Diego del Cubillo, the Royal Treasurer Judge Official, for one year for six pesos each.

Luis de Rivera and his wife Magdalena Sánchez granted power of attorney to Pedro de Herrera and his wife Catalina Gómez to collect tributes from their encomienda in the town of Adcerrí, including honey, wheat, corn, and petates (mats).

Antón Prirritubi, his wife Ana, and their natural son Simón Hidalgo (who is also the Alcalde of Ujarraz from the Purapura parcialidad), committed to serve Miguel de Villalobos for one year. Antón and Ana would receive twelve pesos, and Simón would receive fourteen pesos.
Miguel de Villalobos sold a plot of land (solar) to Leandro de Figueroa for 40 pesos. The land bordered houses belonging to the seller and to Beneficiado Lope de Chavarría.

Alonso Gutiérrez de Sibaja, a resident and encomendero of Cartago, made his will. He requested burial in the Main Church of Cartago next to his wife, María Alvarez de Oviedo. He detailed his marriage, dowry (received over 24 years ago in León), and named his legitimate daughter Catalina de Zárate, and natural children Francisca Gutiérrez de Sibaja and Cristóbal de Sibaja. He also mentioned his encomienda of Buxibux in the Ujarraz valley, land near Cartago, and a cattle ranch occupied by Alonso Pérez Farfán. He appointed García de Quirós and his wife María Alvarez as executors, and his legitimate daughter as heir.
Juan de Orozco, a resident of 'this city', granted power of attorney to Alonso Hernández.
Miguel de Villalobos granted power of attorney to García de Quirós and Alonso Hernández.
Juan de Orozco provided Francisco de Ocampo Golfín as a guarantor for the outcome of an execution process against Alonso Ros. de Villegas.

Juan de Orozco granted power of attorney to Alonso Duarte, a procurador of the Royal Audiencia of Guatemala, to renounce his office as escribano of the Juzgador Mayor. Orozco had acquired this office from Juan Díaz de Guereño and had previously sold it to Herdo. niño de Baragon, but the King wanted Orozco to serve. Orozco now sought to obtain the vacant office of Treasurer of Costa Rica, which became available due to the death of Alonso del Cubillo in April of 'this year'.

Gaspar Pereira Cardoso, the Alguacil Mayor, and his wife Isabel de Acuña sold straw houses to Juan de Lamas, the Alcalde of the Santa Hermandad, for 346 pesos. These houses, originally bought from Matías de Palacio, bordered properties belonging to Captain Franc? Pavon, Inés Ampurro, Captain Diego de Sojo, and Gaspar de Chinchilla.

Juan de Lamas and his wife Luisa Hernández obligated themselves to Gaspar Pereira Cardoso for 400 pesos. They committed to pay part of this debt in local goods such as fattened pigs, and goods from Havana including wheat, corn, honey, capirotes, spun pita, thigh pita, and loose pita.
Governor Ocón y Trillo entrusted Gaspar de Cáceres, a 15-year-old mestizo orphan whose mother was an indigenous woman from Curriraba, to Diego Rodríguez, a saddle maker, for a period of four years.

Jn. Jerónimo de la Portilla sold the tributes from the pueblo of Caraquibi in Adcerrí, including goods and agricultural produce, to Francisco García for two years at 60 pesos per year. He also sold 100 cows and 12 mares, which he inherited from his father, P? de la Portilla, and were from his mother, Ana Gómez's, herd.
Juan Sánchez, the corregidor of Garavito, designated Juan Gutiérrez Jaramillo as his guarantor.

Mateo Cascante, an indigenous person from the encomienda of Alonso de Bonilla and his wife Catalina in Adcerrí, committed to serving Luis Cascante de Rojas for one year in exchange for fourteen pesos.
Diego, an indigenous person from the pueblo of Có, part of Felipe Diaz's encomienda, and his wife Ana, committed to serving Diego de Zúñiga for twelve pesos per year.
Juan de Enciso, appointed as corregidor of the Royal Crown's pueblo of Quepo for two years, designated Captain Juan Solano as his guarantor.
Captain Francisco de Ocampo Golfín committed to paying Antonio Fernández 100 pesos. This debt was noted as cancelled on June 1, 1608.

Juan de Orozco, a resident and notary of the High Court of Ciudad Real de Chiapas, granted special power to Gaspar Pereira Cardoso, a merchant and resident of Cartago, to demand payment from Alonso Rodríguez de Villegas or the person who acquires a ship. This demand relates to an execution against Gabriel Caballero, who is imprisoned for a principal debt of 996 pesos.
Juan de Orozco granted power to García de Quirós to demand 400 pesos from Alonso Rodríguez de Villegas, a resident of Cartago, for the price of an enslaved Black person.
Alonso, an indigenous person from Auyaque, and his wife committed to serving Ambrosio de Brenes for 18 months in exchange for 18 pesos.

Juan García Cordero, a resident of Cartago, granted power to Alonso Hernández to collect damages from Francisco Gutiérrez, Juan de Mobilla, and Juan López Santana, who are in Granada de Nicaragua. This stems from an incident where these individuals, along with Agustín Costancio and Pedro García Ruiz, were passengers on Cordero's frigate 'San Diego' traveling from Cartagena to Puerto de Suerre. They took the frigate without permission, sailed into the mouth of the Tarire River, and lost the ship and its cargo, valued at over 2000 pesos.
María, an indigenous widow from the pueblo of Ixtarú, committed to serving Juan Rodríguez for one year in exchange for six pesos.

Agustín Costanzo, a sailor from the frigate San Diego, which belonged to Juan García Cordero, recounted the loss of the ship. While sailing from Cartagena, they landed at Punta Blanca, and after Juan García Cordero went ashore, Costanzo and other passengers, believing García was dead, sailed the frigate, causing it to wreck and lose much cargo. Costanzo, acknowledging his fault, settled with Juan García Cordero by returning recovered items and agreeing to pay an additional 87.5 pesos.

Pedro García Ruiz, a passenger on the lost frigate San Diego owned by Juan García Cordero, was brought to Cartago and sued for damages. He agreed to pay Juan García Cordero 350 pesos, including 100 varas of pitch, for his role in the frigate's loss.
Miguel Calvo sold an enslaved Black man named Juan, from Angola, to Gaspar Pereira Cardoso, the Chief Constable of the Government, for 340 pesos.
Alonso Bagar, an indigenous man from the Royal Crown town of Quepo, committed to serve Manuel Farfán, a resident of Cartago, for one year in exchange for 8 pesos.

Francisca, an indigenous woman and daughter of Inés (a widow from Curriravá), committed to serve Juana de Cárdenas for one year. Captain Francisco de Ocampo Golfín obligated himself to pay Francisca a blanket and a new hood at the end of the year on behalf of Juana de Cárdenas.

Luisa, an indigenous woman from Atirro, committed to serve Francisca de Carbajal for one year. Luis Fernández Camelo obligated himself to pay Luisa six pesos at the end of the year on behalf of Francisca de Carbajal.
Ana, an orphan, committed to serve Juana Membreño, wife of Di? Ros. (Sánchez?), for two years in exchange for some skirts (naguas) and a new hood.
Juan, an indigenous man from Curriraba, committed to serve Juan Gutiérrez for one year in exchange for 6 pesos.

Juan Sánchez Terreros, Corregidor of Garavito, and his guarantor Juan de Segura, obligated themselves to Gaspar Pereira Cardoso for 100 pesos, which was given to Terreros in merchandise including 30 tribute cloths from Pacaca and 9 manta legs from Chiapa.
Gaspar Rodríguez, Ordinary Mayor of Cartago, granted a general power of attorney to Félix de Prendas, a perpetual alderman of the same city.

Catalina, an indigenous woman from Ujarraz, committed to serve Captain Bartolomé Sánchez for two years at six pesos per year. Doña Inés Alvarez Pereira, the Captain's wife, accepted the commitment in his absence.
Juan Tescato, an indigenous man from Aserrí under the encomienda of Domingo Jiménez, committed to serve Luis Cascante de Rojas, an ordinary mayor, for one year for twelve pesos.

Juan de Vargas, an 18-year-old Spaniard, with the consent of his appointed procurator Juan García Cordero, began an apprenticeship to learn the trade of river carpenter with Domingo López, who was a foreman and official in that trade.
Alonso Bueno, an indigenous man from Votos, and his wife Inés, committed to serve Francisco de Salas for one year in exchange for 18 pesos.
Juan de Lamas, Alcalde de la Santa Hermandad, owed Alonso Velázquez de Ortega 180 pesos for a portion of the price of mules, both male and female, of the Adelantado's breed, sold at 30 pesos each.
Alonso Velázquez de Ortega granted a general power of attorney to Juan de Lamas, Alcalde de la Santa Hermandad.
Don Diego de Sojo, an encomendero, obligated himself to pay Gaspar Pereira Cardoso 58 pesos.

Gaspar Rodríguez, an Ordinary Mayor, made a declaration and inventory of his assets. He stated he was first married to Inés Rodríguez, who died about a year and a half prior, and they had seven children. He then married María Ramírez, widow of Diego Romero, who had four children from her first marriage. He inventoried his assets from both marriages.
Pedro, an indigenous man from Tariaca (inland), committed to serve Mateo Cornejo, a resident of Cartago, for one year in exchange for 8 pesos.
The debt owed by Juan de Lamas to Alonso Velázquez de Ortega for mules was cancelled on January 11, 1610, by Cristobal de Chaves, who was the cessionary of Alonso Velázquez de Ortega.

Jerónimo Vanegas, a resident and encomendero, made his will, detailing his family, including his parents, wife Teresa Fernández, legitimate daughter María de Espinoza, and bastard daughter Isabel Gutiérrez. He also listed debts owed to him, including goods from Alvaro de Acuña and payments from indigenous governors of Tucurrique, Atirro, and Tiotique.

On February 11, 1608, the escribano certified the death of Jerónimo Vanegas. García de Quirós, Juan de Acuña, and Ambrosio de Brenes presented themselves to accept the role of executors for his estate.
Miguel de Villalobos granted general power of attorney to Baltasar de Grado, Francisco Solano, García de Quirós, and Sebastián Sánchez Holguín, who was the corregidor of Pacaca.
Captain Diego del Cubillo, the Royal Treasurer and Official Judge of the Treasury, granted general power of attorney to Sebastián Gudiel, a procurador of the Audiencia de Guatemala.

Encomdendero Gaspar de Chinchilla granted general power of attorney to Pedro de Villalobos, a procurador of the Audiencia de Guatemala. He also instructed Villalobos to audit Gome García, another procurador, for past business and revoked García's power.

Gaspar de Chinchilla agreed to pay Captain Bartolomé Sánchez, tutor of his brother-in-law Don Juan Alvarez Pereira, 80 pesos with annual interest. He guaranteed this payment with the tributes from his encomienda pueblos and mortgaged his cattle ranch and house in Cartago.
Captain Francisco de Ocampo Golfín granted general power of attorney to Alonso Sánchez de Figueroa, a resident of Guatemala, and Miguel de Villalobos, a resident of Cartago.
Leandro de Figueroa, the corregidor of the Aserrí district, granted general power of attorney to Antonio de Villalobos and Alonso Duarte, both procuradores of the Audiencia de Guatemala.

Gaspar Pereira Cardoso (Sr.), the Alguacil Mayor of the Gobernación, granted general power of attorney to Alonso Duarte, a procurador of the Audiencia de Guatemala, along with Manuel Rodríguez and Alonso Sánchez de Figueroa.

Gaspar Pereira Cardoso (Sr.), acting as the father of his son Gaspar Pereira Cardoso (Jr.), who held the Alguacil Mayor office, granted power to Pedro de Villalobos. The purpose was to request that Juan de Lamas temporarily serve as Alguacil Mayor until his son reached the necessary age, as the elder Cardoso was ill and needed to travel to the Royal Audiencia.

Pedro de Ribero obligated himself to Bachiller Lope de Chavarría, the Cura and Vicario of Cartago, for 127 pesos. This amount was paid by Chavarría on Ribero's behalf during an execution initiated by Bartolomé Sánchez, acting as tutor for Don Juan Alvarez Pereira.
Catalina, an indigenous woman from Curriravá, obligated herself to serve Miguel de Villalobos and his wife, Doña Isabel de Carvajal, for one year in exchange for 6 pesos.
Doctor Don Pedro de Villarreal, the Bishop of Nicaragua and Costa Rica, granted general power of attorney to Padre Luis Rodríguez, a presbyter and Chaplain of the Audiencia de Guatemala.

Isabel de Carvajal, a widow and tutora for her children and her deceased husband Luis Medina, granted power of attorney. The recipients included Sebastián Sánchez Holguín, corregidor of Pacaca, Sebastián Judice, and Pedro de Villalobos, a procurador of the Audiencia de Guatemala.
A fragment of a power of attorney granted by an unnamed woman to Francisco Arrieta was recorded on January 23, 1629.
Captain Pedro de Arce granted power of attorney in Esparza to Alférez Diego Peláez and Francisco de Arrieta.

Captain Francisco de Alfaro, Lieutenant Governor in Esparza, deposited an 8-year-old mulata girl named Catalina, from Nicaragua, in the house of Captain Don Juan Alvarez Pereira. Catalina had been stolen by a fugitive negro and was to remain there until she came of age and married.
Juan Bernabé de Vílchez, a resident of Esparza, granted power to Alonso de Sojo and Juan Delgado, residents of Cartago, to gather information about his merits and services.

Francisca López, widow of Alférez Felipe Monge, made her will in Cartago. She declared debts to Doctor Diego de Chavarría for masses said for her late husband and to the Cofradía de Ntra. Sra. de la Soledad for a cloak. She owned a house in Cartago and a cattle ranch in the Valle de Aserrí, mentioning her children Ana Martina and Juan Delgado, and her nephew Manuel de Plores.
Magdalena de la Portilla, widow of Captain Pedro de Arce, granted general power of attorney to Francisco de Arrieta.

A contract was established between Domingo, a boy of up to twelve years old from Curridaba and an encomienda of Alférez Diego de Ocampo Figueroa, and Mateo Díaz, a master blacksmith. The agreement stipulated that Mateo Díaz would teach Domingo the blacksmith trade for six years.

Nicolás López, Diego Quintero del Castillo, and María de Ayala, along with their absent brothers Juan López de Ascuñe and Hernando López, granted general power of attorney to their brother-in-law Hernando de Sibaja, who is married to Felipa de Ascuñe. The transaction took place in Esparza.

Captain Juan de las Alas, Alférez Luis Machado, Salvador de Torres, Francisco de Chavez, Andrés Jaimes, Francisco Rodríguez de Sosa, and Andrés Morillo, representing themselves and other farmers from the valleys of Barba and Mata Redonda, granted power to Francisco de Castro and Juan Martínez de Ferrera, procurators in the Audiencia of Guatemala. This was done in the town of Barba, within the corregimiento of Pacaca.
Andrés Aquizará, an indigenous man from Currirabá, committed to serving Antonio Rodríguez Moreno for one year as a miller in Moreno's mill in the town of Barba, for a payment of 25 pesos.
Captain Juan de las Alas granted power of attorney to Alférez Juan de Acuña and Francisco de Arrieta in Barba.

Andrés Morillo guaranteed Sebastián Pereira Cardoso, the corregidor of Pacaca, that royal tributes collected in Pacaca would be delivered to the royal official scribe of the province, with proper accounting, by Christmas and San Juan. This event took place in Barba.

Baltasar de Grado, a Presbyter and Commissary of the Holy Inquisition in Cartago, granted power to Diego Ruiz de Ocaña, a resident of Granada, Nicaragua, to accept censo imposition deeds. Grado also approved and ratified a censo deed previously imposed on the houses and possessions of Captain Cristóbal de Miranda, a resident of Granada.
Pablo Milanés granted general power of attorney to Juan Fernández.
Alférez Diego de Ocampo Figueroa granted general power of attorney to Bartolomé de Enciso Hita and Francisco de Arrieta.

Andrés Morillo obligated himself to Captain General Juan de Echauz, the Governor of the province, for 200 pesos. This money was borrowed to cancel a debt owed to Gil de Alvarado, the former corregidor of Pacaca.

Pedro de Córdova and his wife Catalina de Chaves granted a censo deed to Licenciado Baltasar de Grado, a presbyter and Commissary of the Holy Office, for 100 pesos at 5% annual interest. They mortgaged houses in Cartago as security.
Juana Solano, widow of Luis Cascante de Rojas, and her son Juan Cascante de Rojas, received a loan of 150 pesos from Padre Baltasar de Grado at a 5% interest rate.

people_involved: doña Ana Tomasina de Lermos y Salazar
summary: Juana Solano and Juan Cascante de Rojas mortgaged their adobe and straw-roofed houses in Cartago, which bordered properties of Captain Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, Juana de la Portilla, doña Ana Tomasina de Lermos y Salazar, and Diego de Escobar. They also mortgaged a cattle ranch in the valley on the royal road to Pacaca, including 150 cattle and 100 mares.

Luisa Hernández, widow of Captain Juan de Lamas, acknowledged a 100-peso mortgage on a mill, houses, and four plots of land that her husband had purchased in 1615 from Cristóbal García and Ana de los Ríos. The mortgage was held by the factory of the city's Main Church, and Luisa, as her husband's heir, committed to recognizing the capital and 5% interest.

Captain Juan Solano sold a 35-year-old 'negro criollo' named Luis, a 7-year-old 'negro' named Jusepe, 108 cattle, and 34 mares to his brother, Alférez Vasco Solano, for a total of 1100 pesos. This transaction settled a debt Juan Solano owed Vasco for mule freight and other goods.

Captain Juan Solano paid his brother Pedro Solano with three enslaved individuals: Lucía (48 years old), Luis (16 years old), and Andrés (2 years old), valued at 800 pesos. This payment was for 800 pesos that Pedro had paid to Pedro de Alarcón in Panamá on Juan's behalf for merchandise.
Isabel de Morales granted general power of attorney to her brother-in-law, Marcos de Herrera, though the transaction was not completed.

María de Alfaro, widow of Cristóbal de Chaves, created a closed will, naming her eight children, her mother Catalina Gutiérrez, and her brothers Francisco and Gómez de Alfaro. She declared ownership of estates in Mata Redonda and Pacaca la Vieja, and four enslaved individuals. The opening proceedings for the will began on December 30 but were incomplete.

Manuel de Flores, the escribano, granted power of attorney to Simón de Guzmán, King's escribano, and Pedro Mallen de Rueda, an official in don Fernando Ruiz de Contreras's Secretariat. This was done in the absence of another notary, allowing them to present a copy of his title to the Court and request its confirmation.

Isabel Jiménez, daughter of the late Sergeant Major Alonso Jiménez and widow of Francisco de Salas, made her will. She named her four daughters, two of whom were married to Juan López de Ortega and the late Jorge Sagasta. She also mentioned Hernando López de Aguilar, a debt from Alonso de Bonilla's estate, her late nephew Juan del Peso, and her absent brother Juan Jiménez, noting her father had died 19 years prior.

Juan López Bapta. became indebted to Captain Juan de las Alas for 110 pesos. He mortgaged a cornfield and two houses located on the road to the pastures, which bordered the cornfields of Gaspar Núñez and Juan Sánchez Crespo.

people_involved: doña Fabiana de Sojo y Peñaranda
summary: Doña Fabiana de Sojo y Peñaranda, a resident of Cartago and native of Talamanca (Archbishopric of Toledo, Spain), made her will. She identified herself as the legitimate daughter of the late Juan de Peñaranda and doña Fabiana de Sojo, and sister to Captain Juan de Peñaranda and don Diego de Sojo.

people_involved: Ana Tomasina de Lermos y Salazar
summary: Juana Solano, widow of Luis Cascante de Rojas, and her son Juan Cascante de Rojas, received a 150 pesos loan from Padre Baltasar de Grado. They mortgaged their adobe and straw-roofed houses in Cartago, along with a cattle ranch in the Pacaca valley, which included 150 cattle, 100 mares, donkeys, mules, and tame horses.

On December 5th, Luisa Hernández, widow of Capn. Juan de Lamas, recognized a 100 pesos mortgage on a mill. Her husband had purchased the mill, houses, and four lots from Cristóbal García and Ana de los Ríos in 1615, with the mill already mortgaged to the city's Main Church.

On December 8th, Capn. Juan Solano sold a 35-year-old Creole black man named Luis for 500 pesos, a 7-year-old black boy named Jusepe for 200 pesos, 108 cattle, and 34 mares to his brother, Alférez Vasco Solano. The total sum of 1100 pesos was owed by Juan to Vasco for mule freight and other goods.

On December 8th, Capn. Juan Solano gave three slaves – Lucía (48, 350 pesos), Luis (16, 350 pesos), and Andrés (2, 100 pesos) – to his brother Pedro Solano as payment. Pedro had paid 800 pesos in Panamá to Pedro de Alarcón on Juan's behalf for merchandise.
Isabel de Morales granted general power of attorney to her brother-in-law, Marcos de Herrera. However, this transaction did not proceed.

On December 29th, the closed will of María de Alfaro, widow of Cristóbal de Chaves, was recorded. She named her eight children, including doña Magdalena (married to Gaspar Abarca) and doña Catalina (married to don Pedro de Córdova). She owned estates in Mata Redonda and Pacaca la vieja, four slaves, and had common property with her brother Francisco de Alfaro.
Opening proceedings for the will of María de Alfaro began on December 30th, but were incomplete.

On April 5th, Escribano Manuel de Flores, lacking another official, granted power of attorney to Simón de Guzmán and Pedro Mallen de Rueda. They were tasked with presenting his title transfer in court and seeking confirmation of his office.

On March 28th, the will of Isabel Jiménez, widow of Francisco de Salas and daughter of the late Sargento Mayor Alonso Jiménez, was recorded. She named her children María Jiménez (married to Juan López de Ortega), Ana Martín Navarro (married to the late Jorge Sagasta), Isabel de Salas, and Catalina de Salas. She also mentioned her deceased father's passing 19 years prior, leaving her and her absent brother Juan Jiménez as heirs.

On June 22nd, Juan López Bapta. obligated himself to Capn. Juan de las Alas for 110 pesos. He mortgaged a cornfield and two houses located on the road to the pastures, bordering the cornfields of Gaspar Núñez and Juan Sánchez Crespo.

On April 30th, the will of doña Fabiana de Sojo y Peñaranda was recorded. A resident of this city (Cartago) and native of Talamanca (Archbishopric of Toledo, Spain), she was the daughter of the late Juan de Peñaranda and doña Fabiana de Sojo, and sister to Capn. Juan de Peñaranda and don Diego de Sojo.
The testadora mentions her aunt, Francisca de Peñaranda, who died in Talamanca, Spain, which was also the testadora's birthplace.
The testadora makes a provision for her niece, Juana de Sojo, to assist with her marriage.
Don Cristóbal Guajardo de Oses, a priest and resident of the city, makes a codicil.
Don Cristóbal Guajardo de Oses orders that a debt related to his deceased father, Alonso Guajardo de Oses, be collected from his sister, Doña María de Hoces, in Granada, Nicaragua.

Juan de Chavarría Navarro, Royal Treasury Treasurer, and his wife Doña María de Ocampo, sell a straw-roofed plot and house for 60 pesos to Licenciado Baltasar de Grado, Commissioner of the Holy Office. The property borders those of Doña Mayor de Benavides and Juan de Acuña.

Francisco de Chaves contracts with Blas de Acosta, attorney for Francisco García, to charter the fragata "Ntra. Sra. de la Candelaria" for the upcoming May. The ship, owned by Francisco García, will load flour, biscuits, capons, and chickens at Puerto de Suerre.

Sargento Jerónimo de Retes, chief constable of the government, grants power of attorney to Andrés de Escobar, chamber clerk of the Royal Audiencia of Guatemala, to purchase 200 pesos worth of clothing for him in Guatemala.

people_involved: Capn. don Pedro de Villarreal Salzedo
summary: Sargento Jerónimo de Retes grants power of attorney to Capn. don Pedro de Villarreal Salzedo, chief constable of the Holy Office in Nicaragua, and Capn. Pedro Velázquez, a resident of Granada.

people_involved: Don Cristóbal de Escobar Estrada y Medinilla
summary: Capn. Francisco de Ocampo Golfín obligates himself to pay 150 pesos to Don Cristóbal de Escobar Estrada y Medinilla upon confirmation of an encomienda in Nicaragua and Costa Rica for his son, Josepe de Sandoval. He had also sent 50 pesos to Licenciado don Gaspar Arias Hurtado, Don Cristóbal's brother.

people_involved: Doña Ana Tomasina de Lerma y Salazar
summary: Don Alonso Méndez de Sotomayor and his wife Doña María Calderón receive a 120-peso loan at 5% annual interest from Licenciado don Baltasar de Grado. They mortgage their straw-roofed houses, which include a bread oven and border properties of Doña Ana Tomasina de Lerma y Salazar and Capn. Francisco de Ocampo Golfín.
Baltasar de Grado, a priest and Commissioner of the Holy Office, grants power of attorney to Diego Ruiz de Ocaña, chief constable of Granada, Nicaragua, to invest funds at interest on real estate.

Juan Barboza grants power of attorney to Bartolomé de Enciso Hita to collect tributes for the year 1629 from the indigenous people in his encomienda in San Mateo de Chirripó, excluding those residing and serving Spaniards in the city.

people_involved: Gobernador frey don Juan de Echauz
summary: Licenciado Antonio de Fonseca, former beneficed priest of Cartago, commits to pay 362 pesos to Governor frey don Juan de Echauz for outstanding accounts, either in Cartago or Granada, Nicaragua, where he is traveling.

people_involved: Gobernador frey don Juan de Echauz
summary: Governor frey don Juan de Echauz, a Knight of the Order of St. John, grants power of attorney to Capn. don Juan de Agúero, Governor of Nicaragua province, to collect 300 pesos from the Royal Treasury of León for his salaries as Governor and Captain General.

people_involved: Gobernador frey don Juan de Echauz
Capn. don Pedro de Villarreal Salcedo
summary: Governor frey don Juan de Echauz grants power of attorney to Capn. don Pedro de Villarreal Salcedo and Capn. Pedro Velázquez to collect 200 pesos from the Royal Treasury of León for his salaries, for which he issued a draft in favor of Sargento Jerónimo de Retes.

Don Cristóbal Guajardo de Oses, unable to travel to Castilla due to illness, grants power of attorney to Agustín de Rojas el mozo to receive money and goods sent by his sister Doña María de Hoces and others from Granada. These items were intended for his journey and are on a ship in Puerto de Suerre bound for Tierra Firme.

An unnamed testadora, born in Talamanca, Spain, mentions her deceased aunt Francisca de Peñaranda, who also died in Talamanca. She also refers to her nephews Diego de Peñaranda and doña Francisca, her niece Juana de Sojo, and names her brother, don Diego de Sojo, as her heir.

Don Cristóbal Guajardo de Oses, a priest and resident of the city, made a codicil. He instructed that a debt owed to his deceased father, Alonso Guajardo de Oses, be collected in Granada, Nicaragua, from doña María de Hoces, who is Alonso's daughter and heir.

Juan de Chavarría Navarro, Royal Treasury Treasurer, and his wife, doña María de Ocampo, sold a straw-roofed house and lot in the city to Licenciado Baltasar de Grado, Commissioner of the Holy Office, for 60 pesos. The property was adjacent to houses owned by doña Mayor de Benavides and Juan de Acuña.

Francisco de Chaves entered into a contract with Blas de Acosta, acting as the agent for Francisco García, owner of the frigate 'Ntra. Sra. de la Candelaria.' The agreement was to charter the frigate for the upcoming May to transport 200 bales of flour and biscuit, 60 capons, and 200 chickens from the port of Suerre.

Sergeant Jerónimo de Retes, chief constable of this government, granted power of attorney to Andrés de Escobar, chamber scribe of the Royal Audiencia of Guatemala. This power authorized Escobar to purchase 200 pesos worth of clothing for Retes in Guatemala.

people_involved: Capn. don Pedro de Villarreal Salzedo
summary: Sergeant Jerónimo de Retes granted power of attorney to Captain don Pedro de Villarreal Salzedo, Chief Constable of the Holy Office in Nicaragua, and Captain Pedro Velázquez, a resident of Granada. The specific purpose of this power is not detailed in this entry but is later clarified as related to salary collection.

people_involved: don Cristóbal de Escobar Estrada y Medinilla
summary: Captain Francisco de Ocampo Golfín committed to pay 150 pesos to don Cristóbal de Escobar Estrada y Medinilla, a chamber scribe in the Royal Audiencia of Guatemala, upon the confirmation of an encomienda for his son, Josepe de Sandoval. This payment was in addition to 50 pesos previously sent to Licenciado don Gaspar Arias Hurtado, the beneficiary of Masaya and brother of don Cristóbal de Escobar.

people_involved: doña Ana Tomasina de Lerma y Salazar
Capn. don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Don Alonso Méndez de Sotomayor and his wife, doña María Calderón, received a 120-peso censo at 5% annual interest from Licenciado don Baltasar de Grado. They mortgaged their straw-roofed houses in the city, which included a bread oven and bordered properties belonging to doña Ana Tomasina de Lerma y Salazar and Captain don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín.

Baltasar de Grado, a priest and Commissioner of the Holy Office, granted power of attorney to Diego Ruiz de Ocaña, Chief Constable of Granada, Nicaragua. This power authorized Ocaña to invest funds at censo, secured by real estate mortgages.

locations: pueblo de San Mateo de Chirripó
summary: Juan Barboza granted power of attorney to Bartolomé de Enciso Hita to collect the 1629 tributes from the indigenous people in his encomienda in San Mateo de Chirripó. Barboza reserved the right to collect from indigenous people living outside the 'Tierra adentro' district and serving Spanish residents of the city, for his own sustenance.

people_involved: Gobernador frey don Juan de Echauz
summary: Licenciado Antonio de Fonseca, former beneficiary priest of Cartago, committed to pay 362 pesos, representing the balance of his accounts, to Governor frey don Juan de Echauz. The payment was to be made either in Cartago or in Granada, Nicaragua, where Fonseca was traveling.

people_involved: Gobernador frey don Juan de Echauz
summary: Governor frey don Juan de Echauz, a Knight of the Order of St. John, granted power of attorney to Captain don Juan de Agúero, Governor of Nicaragua province. This power authorized Agúero to collect 300 pesos from the Royal Treasury of León as partial payment for Echauz's salaries as Governor and Captain General.

people_involved: Gobernador frey don Juan de Echauz
Capn. don Pedro de Villarreal Salzedo
summary: Governor frey don Juan de Echauz granted power of attorney to Captain don Pedro de Villarreal Salzedo and Captain Pedro Velázquez to collect 200 pesos from the Royal Treasury of León. This sum was for Echauz's salaries as Governor and Captain General, for which he had previously issued a draft in favor of Sergeant Jerónimo de Retes.

Don Cristóbal Guajardo de Oses, a priest and native resident, explained that a severe illness prevented his planned journey to Tierra Firme, Puerto Belo, and Cartagena, from where he intended to sail to Castile. He granted power of attorney to Agustín de Rojas el mozo, owner and master of the frigate 'Nuestra Sra. de la Cabeza' in Suerre, to receive money and provisions sent by his sister, doña María de Hoces, and others from Granada, as the ship was departing for Tierra Firme.

María de Alfaro, widow of Cristobal de Chaves, committed to delivering 185 arrobas of flour and 40 chickens to Juan Ortiz Gómez in Cartago by June 20th at the port of Suerre. The agreed price was 10 reales per arroba and 3 reales per chicken.

Don Gil de Alvarado, corregidor of Pacaca, sold 20 mule beasts (14 mules and 6 males) to Andrés Morillo for 18 pesos each. The animals were to be delivered in Granada, Nicaragua, by the next Christmas, with Morillo paying in Cartago by October 1st. The transaction was granted in Barba.
Don Gil de Alvarado and Andrés Morillo declared that the payment for the previous obligation (the sale of mule beasts) had been completed.
Lorenzo de Ocampo, a free mulatto, committed to serving Alférez Diego de Ocampo Figueroa for two years in exchange for 70 pesos.

Luisa Hernández, widow of Captain Juan de Lamas, received 200 pesos from Padre Baltasar de Grado at a 5% annual interest rate. She mortgaged a mill in Cartago, adjacent to Juan de Echavarría Navarro's mill, and a tiled house with four plots of land.

María de Alfaro, widow of Cristobal de Chaves, settled a criminal case brought by Ayudante Pedro de Santiago Galindo against her son, Francisco de Chaves, for allegedly abducting Catalina Palacios, Santiago's stepdaughter. María agreed to pay Catalina 350 pesos for her dowry and marriage, with payments scheduled for May 1630, October 1630, and May 1631, in goods or silver coins.
Francisco de Chaves, encomendero of Barba, granted power of attorney to Padre Baltasar de Grado to collect tributes from the indigenous people for the current year.

Don Pedro de Córdova and his wife, Doña Catalina de Chaves, committed to paying 100 pesos to Alonso Gómez Macotela. The obligation was later cancelled on April 29, 1631, by the creditor's nephew, Juan Martín Macotela, a resident of Esparza.
Alférez Juan de Acuña, an encomendero, granted general power of attorney to Francisco de Castro and Juan Martínez de Ferreira, who was a Procurador of the Royal Audiencia of Guatemala.
Don Pedro de Córdova granted general power of attorney to his wife, Doña Catalina de Chaves, and to Alférez Juan López de Ortega and Juan de Acuña.

people_involved: Gobernador frey don Juan de Echauz
summary: Governor Frey Don Juan de Echauz granted general power of attorney to Bartolomé de Enciso Hita.

Alférez Juan de Acuña, acting as father and legal guardian for Juan de Alarcón Rabaneda, encomendero of Parragua, granted power of attorney to Gonzalo Romero of Madrid, or in his absence, to Don Andrés Criado de Castilla. Their task was to seek royal confirmation from the Council of the Indies for the encomienda, as previous titles were lost when ships were captured by the enemy.

Captain Juan de las Alas, an encomendero, received 180 pesos from the Confraternity of Nuestra Señora de la Concepción at a 5% annual interest rate. He mortgaged a cattle ranch named Nuestra Señora del Rosario in the Mata Redonda valley, which included two straw-roofed houses, 200 cattle, and 40 mares and tame horses.

Pedro Solano, who won the bid in Cartago for the office of general depositary of the province with a voice and vote in the Cabildo, granted power of attorney to Francisco de Castro and Juan Martínez de Ferrera, procurators in the Audiencia of Guatemala, to obtain confirmation of his title.
Alférez Vasco Solano was mentioned in relation to Pedro Solano having a public announcement (pregón) for the office of depositary.

María de Alfaro, widow of Cristobal de Chaves, committed to delivering 185 arrobas of flour and 40 chickens to Juan Ortiz Gómez in Suerre by June 20th. The goods were to be delivered at a price of 10 reales per arroba and 3 reales per chicken, with Juan Ortiz Gómez residing in Cartago.

Don Gil de Alvarado, the corregidor of Pacaca, sold 20 mules to Andrés Morillo for 18 pesos each. The animals were to be delivered in Granada, Nicaragua, by the upcoming Christmas, with Morillo scheduled to make the payment in Cartago by October 1st. The transaction was granted in Barba.
Don Gil de Alvarado and Andrés Morillo, the parties involved in the previous transaction, formally declared that the obligation regarding the sale of mules had been fully paid.
Lorenzo de Ocampo, identified as a free mulatto, entered into an agreement to serve Alférez Diego de Ocampo Figueroa for a period of two years. His service was contracted for a payment of 70 pesos.

Luisa Hernández, widow of Captain Juan de Lamas, received 200 pesos from Padre Baltasar de Grado, subject to a 5% annual censo. As collateral, she mortgaged a mill in Cartago, adjacent to Juan de Echavarría Navarro's mill, and a tiled house with four plots of land.

María de Alfaro, widow of Cristobal de Chaves, settled a criminal case brought by Ayudante Pedro de Santiago Galindo against her son, Francisco de Chaves, who was accused of abducting Catalina Palacios, Santiago's stepdaughter. María agreed to pay Catalina 350 pesos for her dowry and marriage, with payments scheduled in May 1630 (100 pesos in local goods at Caldera), October 1630 (50 pesos in Castilian clothing), and May 1631 (200 pesos in Castilian clothing or local goods at Caldera, or silver coins).
Francisco de Chaves, the encomendero of Barba, granted power to Padre Baltasar de Grado. This power allowed Padre de Grado to collect the tributes owed by the indigenous people for the current year.

Don Pedro de Córdova and his wife, Doña Catalina de Chaves, incurred a 100-peso obligation to Alonso Gómez Macotela. This debt was later cancelled on April 29, 1631, by Juan Martín Macotela, a resident of Esparza, acting on behalf of his uncle, the creditor.

Alférez Juan de Acuña, an encomendero, granted general power of attorney to Francisco de Castro and Juan Martínez de Ferreira. Juan Martínez de Ferreira is identified as a Procurator of the Royal Audiencia of Guatemala.
Don Pedro de Córdova granted general power of attorney to his wife, Doña Catalina de Chaves, and also to Alférez Juan López de Ortega and Alférez Juan de Acuña.

people_involved: Gobernador frey don Juan de Echauz
summary: Governor Frey Don Juan de Echauz granted general power of attorney to Bartolomé de Enciso Hita.

In 1630, Alférez Juan de Acuña, acting as father and legal guardian for his son Juan de Alarcón Rabaneda, encomendero of Parragua, granted power to Gonzalo Romero of Madrid, or alternatively to Don Andrés Criado de Castilla, a Knight of the Order of Santiago. Their mission was to seek royal confirmation of the encomienda in the Council of the Indies, as previous titles were lost when enemy forces captured ships.

people_involved: Cofradía de Ntra. Sra. de la Concepción
summary: Captain Juan de las Alas, an encomendero, received 180 pesos from the Confraternity of Nuestra Señora de la Concepción, subject to a 5% annual censo. He mortgaged his cattle ranch, Nuestra Señora del Rosario, located in the Mata Redonda valley, which included two straw-roofed houses, 200 cattle, and 40 mares and tame horses.

Pedro Solano, who won the auction in Cartago for the office of general depositary of the province, a position with voice and vote in the Cabildo, granted power to Francisco de Castro and Juan Martínez de Ferrera. These two, procurators in the Audiencia of Guatemala, were tasked with obtaining the confirmation of Solano's title.

Alférez Vasco Solano is mentioned in connection with Pedro Solano's public announcement (pregón) for the office of depositary. The text is incomplete, but suggests a relationship or involvement in the process of Pedro Solano securing his office.
An unnamed grantor guarantees Pedro Solano up to 1000 pesos to allow procuradores to bid for an office being auctioned. The payment for the office is offered in cash at the Royal Treasury of León.
Pedro Solano grants power of attorney to N.D. Ruiz de Ocaña, a resident of Granada.

Jerónimo de Retes and his wife María Vázquez Coronado receive 600 pesos at a 5% annual interest from Father Baltasar de Grado. They mortgage two city lots (previously bought from Captain Juan de las Alas) and a cattle/horse ranch in Ujarraz Valley.

Juan de Echavarría Navarro and his wife María de Sandoval receive 100 pesos at 5% annual interest from Alférez Mayor Francisco de Alfaro, patron of the Chaplaincy founded by Francisco de Paz. They mortgage a flour mill and a house near San Juan de Herrera, which was acquired from the estate of Catalina Vázquez de Grado, widow of Francisco de Paz.

Juana Solano and her son Juan Cascante de Rojas receive 100 pesos at 5% annual interest from Alférez Mayor Francisco de Alfaro, patron of the Chaplaincy founded by Francisco de Paz. They mortgage a cattle ranch, houses, and corrals in Cartago, which was purchased from the estate of Catalina de Grado, widow of Paz.

Juan de Morera, married to María de Bustamante, receives 350 pesos as part of her dowry. The sum is paid by Alonso Gómez Macotela (250 pesos) and Juan de Senabria Maldonado (100 pesos), the latter being the Steward of the Confraternity of the Conception in the San Francisco convent.
Alcalde Francisco de Ocampo Golfín delivers Ana Pereira, a mestiza woman aged 18-20, into the care of Ana del Cubillo, widow of Jerónimo de la Portilla, until Ana Pereira marries.

Diego de Mena de Escobar obligates himself to Governor Captain Fray Juan de Echauz for 500 pesos, for goods (sarsaparilla, biscuit, and flour) to be delivered by Captain Juan de Mendoza y Medrano at Suerre port by May 20. Mena de Escobar is to pay the 500 pesos in Puerto Belo.

Manuel Ruiz, owing 1538 pesos to the San Francisco Convent (related to goods from Father Fray Diego de Santiago and promissory notes), requested a reduction due to uncertainties. It was decided that Ruiz would pay Captain Juan Solano 400 pesos in four annual installments, a debt which Solano cancelled on January 12, 1638.

Captain Salvador de Torres makes his will, detailing his family. He mentions his deceased first wife Inés Farfán and their eight children, noting issues with sons Juan and Alonso Pérez Farfán, and Esteban. He also names his second wife, Isabel de Medina Cueto, who he suspects is pregnant.

An unnamed individual offers to pay 500 pesos for the general position of the province in the Royal Treasury of León. This individual also acts as a guarantor for Pedro up to 1000 pesos, enabling procurators to make offers for an office being auctioned.
Pedro Solano grants power of attorney to Ruyz de Ocaña, a resident of Granada.

Jerónimo de Retes and his wife, doña María Vázquez Coronado, receive 600 pesos at a 5% annual interest from Pe. Baltasar de Grado. They mortgage two city plots in Cartago, purchased from Capn. Juan de las Alas, and a cattle ranch in the Ujarraz valley.

Juan de Echavarría Navarro, Royal Treasurer Judge, and his wife, doña María de Sandoval, receive 100 pesos at a 5% annual interest from Alférez Mayor Francisco de Alfaro, patron of the Chaplaincy founded by Francisco de Paz. They mortgage a flour mill near San Juan de Herrera, purchased from the estate of doña Catalina Vázquez de Grado, and another house under construction.

Juana Solano, widow of Luis Cascante de Rojas, and her son Juan Cascante de Rojas, receive 100 pesos at a 5% annual interest from Alférez Mayor Fco. de Alfaro, patron of the Chaplaincy founded by Francisco de Paz. They mortgage a cattle ranch, houses, and corrals in Cartago, in the Puririsi area, which they acquired from the succession of doña Catalina de Grado.

Juan de Morera, married to María de Bustamante, receives 350 pesos as part of a dowry. 250 pesos come from Alonso Gómez Macotela of Esparza, and 100 pesos from don Júan de Senabria Maldonado, Steward of the Confraternity of the Conception in the San Francisco convent in Cartago.
Alcalde Frco. de Ocampo Golfín entrusts Ana Pereira, a mestiza aged 18-20, to doña Ana del Cubillo, widow of Jerónimo de la Portilla, until Ana Pereira marries.

people_involved: Gobr. Capn. Frey Juan de Echauz
Capn. don Juan de Mendoza y Medrano
summary: Diego de Mena de Escobar obligates himself to Gobernador Capitán Frey Juan de Echauz for 500 pesos, for goods including sarsaparilla, biscuits, and flour. These goods are to be delivered by Capitán don Juan de Mendoza y Medrano at the port of Suerre by May 20, and Mena will pay the 500 pesos in Puerto Belo.

people_involved: Rev. P. Fray Juan de S. José
P. definidor fr. Jnan de la Mota
P. predicador fr. Pedro Arista Guerrero
summary: Manuel Ruiz owed the San Francisco convent in Cartago 1538 pesos. Due to difficulties in collecting outstanding notes, he requested a reduction. A settlement was reached where Ruiz would pay 400 pesos to Capitán Juan Solano in four annual installments, which was later canceled on January 12, 1638.

Capitán Salvador de Torres, a comendero from Puerto Santa María, Spain, makes his will, detailing his two marriages and eight children from his first marriage to Inés Farfán. He mentions issues with his sons Juan, who dissipated funds in Mata Redonda while Salvador was in Guatemala, and Esteban, who became disobedient after his second marriage. His son Alonso Pérez Farfán left Cartago four years prior.

people_involved: Capn. Pedro Alonso de las Alas
summary: A person, identified as Juan de Torres (father of Juan de Torres, son), is described as being poor and indebted, having been involved in a dowry for Inés, owning land in Mata Redonda, and having a business partnership with Hernando de Luna for Cartago tithes in 1623. He managed funds for Juan Gómez de Bonilla's children, redeemed a census for Capn. Pedro Alonso de las Alas, and held an encomienda of indios de Có since 1625, which his son Juan de Torres was to inherit. He also had ongoing lawsuits with Pedro de Santiago Galindo and Capn. Alonso de Bonilla, and named Padre Baltasar de Grado and Capn. Juan Solano as his executors.

Diego de Mena de Escobar obligated himself to Governor don Juan de Echauz for 300 pesos. This sum was for the freight of 30 fully equipped mules, to be provided by Francisco de Chaves, for transporting goods from the city to the port of Suerre. The payment was due within five months in Puerto Belo.

people_involved: Capn. don Juan de Mendoza y Medrano
summary: Capn. don Juan de Mendoza y Medrano and his wife doña Isabel Méndez de Sotomayor acknowledged a debt of 1657 pesos 4 reales to Governor don Juan de Echauz, who was preparing to depart for Spain. They granted Echauz power to collect a similar sum in Sevilla from Francisco de Torre Blanca and Juan Jurado, owed to them for zarzaparrilla shipped by Mendoza and registered in Cartagena by Capn. Julio Evangelista. If this collection failed, Echauz was authorized to seek accounts in Madrid from doña Isabel's brother, Fernando Méndez de Ocampo, and other executors of her deceased parents, Fernando Méndez de Ocampo and doña Agustina Méndez de Sotomayor, to claim her inheritance.

people_involved: Alférez don Juan de Senabria Maldonado
summary: On April 29, Juan Delgado del Castillo and his wife Juana de la Cruz sold houses with two plots of land, bordering properties of Francisca de Bonilla and Diego Jiménez, to Alférez don Juan de Senabria Maldonado for 75 pesos. The payment was made with 48 pesos for the freight of 16 mules to Caldera and 27 pesos in Castilian clothes.

people_involved: Gobr. y Capn. Gral. Capn. y Sarg. Mayor Juan de Villalta
Juana (hija de Ana, india de Aserrí)
Maese de Campo don Diego de Sojo
summary: On April 31, Governor Juan de Villalta assigned Juan, an indigenous man from Orosi (encomienda of Maese de Campo don Diego de Sojo), and Ana and her daughter Juana, indigenous widows from Aserrí (encomienda of Pedro de Mora), to serve Capn. Frco. de Alfaro for one year. The agreed prices were 16 pesos for the man and 8 pesos for each woman. Due to Alfaro's absence, Alférez Franc? López de Ortega accepted as his guarantor.
On April 31, Agustín de Rojas, a resident, granted power to Juan Sánchez Crespo, Alcalde of the Santa Hermandad, to collect any debts owed to him.

Andrés de Miranda, legitimate son of Martín de Miranda and Inés Hidalgo, residents of León, gave a dowry receipt (a page is missing). Among the items received was a plot of land bordering Lázaro Pérez and María de Ortega, widow of García Quirós. Alférez Cristóbal de Marigal and Sargento Tomás Calvo acted as valuators for Miranda and his in-laws, respectively.

Don Alonso Méndez de Sotomayor, a resident and encomendero in Nicaragua (Masaya and Diriega parcialidad), granted power to Alférez don Francisco Valcarcel, a resident of Granada (Nic.), to collect the tributes owed to him by the indigenous people of Diriega.

people_involved: Maese de Campo don Diego de Sojo
don Juan de Mendoza y Medrano
summary: Juan Fernández, Maese de Campo don Diego de Sojo, Capn. Juan de las Alas, Alférez Francisco Román, and Andrés López de Céspedes, all residents and guarantors of the former Governor don Alonso de Guzmán, granted general power to Francisco de Castro Meléndez and Miguel Mateo, procurators of the Audiencia of Guatemala. This power was specifically to intervene in a lawsuit brought by don Juan de Mendoza y Medrano against Guzmán and his guarantors concerning the seizure of a frigate that don Alonso had effected in the Abangara shipyard, where Mendoza was building it with the deceased Capn. Pedro de Arce, in his capacity as Judge of Residence for don Juan de Mendoza y Medrano.

This entry details the testament of Catalina Martín, natural daughter of Alférez Juan de Acuña and Francisca Hernández, and widow of Juan de Vargas. She mentions her stepfather Esteban Martín and her children Francisco de Vargas (currently in Panamá) and Leonor (?). She declares Antonio and Juan as her natural children with Martín Peraza Ayala. Her executors are her father, Juan de Acuña, and Juan Solano.

Don Alonso Méndez de Sotomayor issued a libranza (draft) to Alférez Juan de Valverde Zárate, treasurer of the Santa Cruzada of this province, against Alférez don Francisco de Valcárcel, a resident of Granada (Nic.), for 216 pesos. This payment was for Castilian merchandise, and Valcárcel held funds from Sotomayor, derived from encomienda tributes in Diriega (part of Masaya).

people_involved: Alcalde Ord? Capn. Pedro de Artavia y Lisaum
summary: Alcalde Ordinario Capn. Pedro de Artavia y Lisaum assigned María, a free mulata, to Diego de Ocampo Sandoval for one year at a price of ten pesos.
On May 12, Francisco Melero, a resident departing for Puerto Belo on the frigate "San Nicolás de Tolentino" (mastered by Juan de Málaga), obligated himself to Juan de Echauz for 210 pesos.
Juan de Málaga is identified as the master of the frigate "San Nicolás de Tolentino," which is currently docked in the port of Suerre.
Inés received a dote of $600, although the original document stated $1200. This transaction is part of the affairs of the Unnamed Principal.
The Unnamed Principal formed a business partnership with Hernando de Luna in 1623 to manage the tithes of Cartago.

The Unnamed Principal is responsible for $108 belonging to the sons of Juan Gómez de Bonilla. This amount is to be offset by expenses incurred in two executions against the assets of Capitan Alonso de Bonilla.

people_involved: Capn. Pedro Alonso de las Alas
summary: The Unnamed Principal redeemed a censo (lien) that Capitan Pedro Alonso de las Alas owed to the Cofradía del Santísimo Sacramento. The redemption cost was $200 plus $26 in interest.

The Unnamed Principal holds an encomienda of indigenous people from Có. Due to a lack of confirmation, poverty, and illness, this encomienda is being managed by the Caja Real until confirmation is brought from San Juan in 1625. His eldest son, Juan de Torres, is designated to succeed him in this encomienda.
The Unnamed Principal appointed Padre Baltasar de Grado and his brother, Capitan Juan Solano, as his executors.
The Unnamed Principal is involved in a legal dispute with Pedro de Santiago Galindo concerning the ownership of the land where he is settled.
The Unnamed Principal has a lawsuit regarding $93 with the assets of Capitan Alonso de Bonilla.

Diego de Mena de Escobar committed to Gobernador don Juan de Echauz for $300. This payment is for the freight of 30 mules, provided by Francisco de Chaves, to transport goods from the city to Puerto de Suerre, with payment due in Puerto Belo within five months.

people_involved: Capn. don Juan de Mendoza y Medrano
summary: Capitan don Juan de Mendoza y Medrano and his wife, doña Isabel Méndez de Sotomayor, acknowledged a debt of $1657.4 reales to Gobernador don Juan de Echauz, who was preparing to depart for Spain. They empowered Echauz to collect this sum from Francisco de Torre Blanca and Juan Jurado in Sevilla, for zarzaparrilla shipped from Cartagena. If collection failed, Echauz was authorized to claim doña Isabel's inheritance in Madrid from her brother, Fernando Méndez de Ocampo, and the executors of her deceased parents.

people_involved: Alférez don Juan de Senabria Maldonado
summary: On April 29, Juan Delgado del Castillo and his wife, Juana de la Cruz, sold straw-roofed houses and two plots of land to Alférez don Juan de Senabria Maldonado for $75. The property bordered Francisca de Bonilla and Diego Jiménez, and payment was made partly in mule freight to Caldera and partly in Castilian clothes.

people_involved: Gobr. y Capn. Gral., Capn. y Sarg. Mayor Juan de Villalta
Maese de Campo don Diego de Sojo
summary: On April 31, Gobernador Juan de Villalta assigned Juan, an indigenous man from Orosi (encomienda of Maese de Campo don Diego de Sojo), and Ana and her daughter Juana, indigenous widows from Aserrí (encomienda of Pedro de Mora), to Capitan Frco. de Alfaro for one year of service. Alférez Franc? López de Ortega acted as guarantor for Alfaro, who was absent.
Agustín de Rojas, a resident, granted power to Juan Sánchez Crespo, Alcalde of the Santa Hermandad, to collect any debts owed to him.

On April 18, Andrés de Miranda, the legitimate son of Martín de Miranda and Inés Hidalgo of León, provided a dote receipt. The dote included a plot of land bordering Lázaro Pérez and María de Ortega. Alférez Cristóbal de Marigal and Sargento Tomás Calvo served as valuators for the transaction.

On April 20, Don Alonso Méndez de Sotomayor, an encomendero in Nicaragua and Masaya, empowered Alférez don Francisco Valcarcel of Granada, Nicaragua, to collect tributes from the indigenous people of Diriega.

people_involved: Maese de Campo don Diego de Sojo
Capn. don Juan de Mendoza y Medrano
summary: On April 21, several vecinos, acting as guarantors for former Gobernador don Alonso de Guzmán, empowered procuradores Francisco de Castro Meléndez and Miguel Mateo to intervene in a lawsuit. The suit was brought by don Juan de Mendoza y Medrano against Guzmán concerning the embargo of a frigate being built in Abangara by Mendoza and the deceased Capitan Pedro de Arce, during Guzmán's tenure as Juez de residencia.

Catalina Martín, natural daughter of Alférez Juan de Acuña and Francisca Hernández, and widow of Juan de Vargas, made her testament. She named her children Francisco de Vargas (currently in Panamá) and possibly Leonor, and declared Antonio and Juan as her natural children with Martín Peraza Ayala. Her father, Juan de Acuña, and Capitan Juan Solano were named as executors.

On April 25, Don Alonso Méndez de Sotomayor issued a libranza to Alférez Juan de Valverde Zárate, treasurer of the Santa Cruzada, against Alférez don Francisco Valcarcel of Granada, Nicaragua, for $216. This payment was for Castilian merchandise, and Valcarcel held funds from Don Alonso derived from encomienda tributes in Diriega.

people_involved: Alcalde Ord? Capn. Pedro de Artavia y Lisaum
summary: On April 27, Alcalde Ordinario Capitan Pedro de Artavia y Lisaum assigned María, a free mulata, to Diego de Ocampo Sandoval for one year of service at a price of $10.
On May 12, Francisco Melero, a resident departing for Puerto Belo on the fragata 'San Nicolás de Tolentino' (mastered by Juan de Málaga), obligated himself to Gobernador don Juan de Echauz for $210.

people_involved: Capn. frey don Juan de Echauz
summary: An incomplete document records an obligation to Captain Fray Don Juan de Echauz for 700 pesos. The payment for this obligation was to be made in Puerto Belo.

Juan de Málaga, acting with power from Captain Juan de Uriarte Araez, owner of the frigate San Nicolás de Tolentino, acknowledged receiving 450 pesos from Don Juan de Echauz. These funds were for the frigate's provisions and crew, with an obligation to repay them in Puerto Belo.
Diego de Mena Escobar, who was preparing to depart, granted a general power of attorney to Andrés Morillo. This power was for handling lawsuits and collections on his behalf.
Diego de Mena Escobar obligated himself to Don Juan de Echauz for a sum of 744 pesos and 4 reales.

Ensign Francisco de Alarcón Chacón obligated himself to Don Juan de Echauz for 420 pesos. Partial cancellations for this debt were later granted on May 3, 1633, and June 16, 1656, by Bartolomé de Enciso Hita, who was Echauz's attorney.

people_involved: Capn. frey don Juan de Echauz
summary: Captain Fray Don Juan de Echauz granted a general power of attorney for lawsuits and collections. This power was given to Captains Bartolomé de Enciso Hita and Don Juan de Salcedo Vallejo, who were residents of the area.

Don Juan de Echauz granted power to Miguel Calvo to collect 277 pesos from the estate of the deceased Pedro Arias, a former resident of this city. This amount was the remainder of a deed originally in favor of Don Diego Vázquez de Coronado of León, Nicaragua, which had been ceded to Echauz in 1626 and stemmed from a ranch Echauz purchased from Don Diego.

people_involved: Alférez Mayor y regidor Francisco de Alfaro
summary: Juan de Echavarría Navarro, the Treasurer, and his wife Doña María de Sandoval, received 100 pesos at an annual 5% interest from the Chaplaincy founded by Francisco Paz. They mortgaged a mill in the outskirts of this city, which had previously belonged to Doña Catalina de Grado, with Ensign Major and Alderman Francisco de Alfaro as patron and Licentiate Baltasar de Grado as chaplain.

Juana Solano, widow of Luis Cascante de Rojas, and her son Juan Cascante de Rojas, obligated themselves to the Chaplaincy of Francisco Paz for 100 pesos at 5% interest. They mortgaged a ranch called San Juan Bautista in the Poririse corner, about a league from this city, which included corrals, a house, and 300 cattle, and had previously belonged to Doña Catalina de Grado.

Captain Bartolomé de Enciso Hita, Corregidor of the interior, granted power to Don Juan de Echauz. This power allowed Echauz to obtain one thousand Castilian ducats for him in Madrid or any other location, and to obligate Enciso Hita for this amount.

people_involved: Licdo. don Antonio de Calatayud y Sandoval
summary: Captain Bartolomé de Enciso Hita also granted power to Licentiate Don Antonio de Calatayud y Sandoval, an Oidor in the Audiencia of Guatemala. This power was for obtaining one thousand Castilian ducats for Enciso Hita.

Ignacio de Artavia y Lisaum, legitimate son of Pedro Artavia and Isabel del Valle, residents of Guatemala, acknowledged receipt of his wife Doña Catalina de Jara's dowry. Doña Catalina is the legitimate daughter of Captain Miguel de Villalobos and Doña Isabel, and the dowry included various household and personal items.
An incomplete document records an obligation to Captain Fray Don Juan de Echauz for 700 pesos, which is to be paid in Puerto Belo.

An incomplete document states that Juan de Málaga, acting with power from Captain Juan de Uriarte Araez, acknowledged receiving 450 pesos from Don Juan de Echauz. These funds were for the outfitting and crew of the frigate San Nicolás de Tolentino, with an obligation to repay in Puerto Belo.
Diego de Mena Escobar, who was preparing to depart, granted general power of attorney for lawsuits and collections to Andrés Morillo.
Diego de Mena Escobar incurred an obligation to Don Juan de Echauz for 744 pesos and 4 reales.

Alférez Francisco de Alarcón Chacón became obligated to Don Juan de Echauz for 420 pesos. Partial cancellations for this debt were later granted on May 3, 1633, and June 16, 1656, by Bartolomé de Enciso Hita, acting as Echauz's attorney.
Captain Fray Don Juan de Echauz granted general power of attorney for lawsuits and collections to Captains Bartolomé de Enciso Hita and Don Juan de Salcedo Vallejo.

Captain Fray Don Juan de Echauz empowered Miguel Calvo to collect 277 pesos from the estate of the deceased Pedro Arias. This debt was the remainder of a document originally in favor of Don Diego Vázquez de Coronado of León, Nicaragua, which had been ceded to Echauz in 1626, stemming from a ranch Echauz bought from Don Diego.

Juan de Echavarría Navarro, Treasurer, and his wife Doña María de Sandoval, received 100 pesos annually at a 5% interest rate from the Chaplaincy founded by Francisco Paz. They mortgaged a mill in the city's outskirts, which previously belonged to Doña Catalina de Grado, with Francisco de Alfaro as patron and Licenciado Baltasar de Grado as chaplain.

Juana Solano, widow of Luis Cascante de Rojas, and her son Juan Cascante de Rojas, obligated themselves to the Chaplaincy of Francisco Paz for 100 pesos at 5% interest. They mortgaged a ranch named San Juan Bautista in Poririse, about a league from the city, which included corrals, a house, and 300 cattle, and had previously belonged to Doña Catalina de Grado.

Captain Bartolomé de Enciso Hita, corregidor of the interior, granted power to Don Juan de Echauz to obtain one thousand Castilian ducats (at eleven reales each) for him in Madrid or elsewhere, and to obligate Enciso Hita for the sum.
Captain Bartolomé de Enciso Hita also granted power to Licenciado Don Antonio de Calatayud y Sandoval, an Oidor in the Audiencia of Guatemala, to obtain one thousand Castilian ducats for him.

people_involved: Isabel, wife of Miguel de Villalobos
summary: Ignacio de Artavia y Lisaum, legitimate son of Pedro Artavia and Isabel del Valle, residents of Guatemala, acknowledged receipt of the dowry for his wife, Doña Catalina de Jara. Doña Catalina is the legitimate daughter of Captain Miguel de Villalobos and Doña Isabel, his wife. The dowry included various household items and clothing.

Experts Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado and Don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín were appointed for Pedro de Artavia Lisaum and his in-laws, respectively, regarding received assets. These assets included a solar bordering property of Pedro de Artavia Lisaum's father-in-law and María de la Portilla, 100 pesos worth of flour from the father-in-law, livestock, a farm with cattle, oxen, horses, a cart, pigs, a cornfield, a house in Barba, and a plantain grove. Pedro de Artavia Lisaum also offered 100 pesos as earnest money.

Diego Hernández, son of the deceased Manuel Hernández and María Fabiana, issued a dowry letter for his wife, María Sánchez. María Sánchez, an orphan raised by Gaspar de Rojas and María González, received 229 pesos in assets, including various livestock, as appraised by Jerónimo de Vera and Juan Sánchez Crespo.

Jusepe de Prendas, acting with power from Diego de Velazco (resident in Puerto Belo), sold an enslaved man named Pedro, of the Caravali nation and 40 years old, to Diego López de Ortega for 250 pesos. The payment was to be made in two installments, half by the next Christmas and the other half by the end of May, in local goods delivered to Caldera.

Pedro de Artavia Lisaum, acting as Alcalde, arranged for Jerónimo, a 14-year-old mestizo and son of María (an indigenous woman from Quircó married in Tucurrique), to be apprenticed to Marcos Martín, a master tailor, for four years to learn the trade.

people_involved: Licdo. Presbo. don Alonso de Sandoval
summary: Doña María de Sandoval, widow of Juan de Echavarría Navarro, granted power of attorney to Licdo. Presbo. don Alonso de Sandoval, Alférez Juan de Acuña, and Francisco de Arrieta to collect her dowry, which amounted to 4000 pesos.

Inés Pérez, widow of Francisco Hidalgo (a former perpetual councilman of the city), sold a piece of land she inherited from her husband to Luisa Hernández, widow of Juan de Lamas, for 50 pesos. The land was located at the source of the Toyocrix river, above the town of Co, near a lagoon called Los Potreros, with a title issued by Diego de Artieda.
On January 25th, Doña Antonia Vázquez de Coronado, widow of Sebastián Pereira Cardoso, granted power of attorney to Juan Fernández to reclaim her dowry assets.
On February 28th, Alférez Vazco Solano granted general power of attorney for lawsuits to Francisco de Arrieta.

On June 16th, Juan Gómez Rico, a native of Azuaga, Extremadura, made his will. He was the son of the deceased Pedro Gómez Rico and Franca Hernández, and was married to Doña María Pereira, daughter of the deceased Gaspar Pereira Cardoso and Isabel de Acuña. He listed their six children and stated he received 2685 pesos as his wife's dowry. His mother-in-law, Isabel de Acuña, died in Granada (Nicaragua) while he was established there with his family, and he took charge of his brothers-in-law's guardianship.

A valuation or transfer of various goods, including an estate with livestock, a house in Barba, and a solar, took place. Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado served as an expert for Artavia, while don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín served as an expert for Artavia's in-laws. The solar bordered properties of Artavia's father-in-law and María de la Portilla.

Diego Hernández, son of Manuel Hernández (deceased) and María Fabiana, issued a dowry letter in favor of his wife, María Sánchez. María Sánchez was an orphan raised by Gaspar de Rojas and María González. She received 229 pesos, and Jerónimo de Vera and Juan Sánchez Crespo were the appraisers.

Jusepe de Prendas, acting with power from Diego de Velazco (resident in Puerto Belo), sold an enslaved man named Pedro, of Caravali Nation and 40 years old, to Diego López de Ortega for 250 pesos. The payment was to be made in two installments, in local goods delivered to Caldera.

Pedro de Artavia Lisaum, acting as Alcalde, delivered Jerónimo, a 14-year-old mestizo and son of María (an indigenous woman from Quircó married in Tucurrique), to Marcos Martín, a tailor's official, for a four-year apprenticeship to learn the trade.

people_involved: Licdo. Presbo. don Alonso de Sandoval
summary: Doña María de Sandoval, widow of Juan de Echavarría Navarro, granted power of attorney to Licdo. Presbo. don Alonso de Sandoval, Alférez Juan de Acuña, and Francisco de Arrieta to collect her dowry of 4000 pesos.

Inés Pérez, widow of Francisco Hidalgo (a perpetual councilman of the city), sold a site at the source of the Toyocrix river, near the town of Co and a lagoon called Los Potreros, to Luisa Hernández, widow of Juan de Lamas, for 50 pesos. Inés Pérez had inherited the site from her husband, with a title issued by Diego de Artieda.
Doña Antonia Vázquez de Coronado, widow of Sebastián Pereira Cardoso, granted power of attorney to Juan Fernández to claim her dowry assets.
Alférez Vazco Solano granted a general power of attorney for lawsuits to Francisco de Arrieta.

Juan Gómez Rico, a native of Villa de Azuaga, Extremadura, and son of Pedro Gómez Rico and Franca. Hernández (both deceased), made his will. He was married to Doña María Pereira, daughter of Gaspar Pereira Cardoso and Isabel de Acuña (both deceased), and they had six children. His mother-in-law, Isabel de Acuña, died in Granada (Nicaragua) where he was established with his family, and he took charge of his brothers-in-law's guardianship.
Isabel Pereira, sister-in-law of an unnamed individual, married Alonso Yañes Vergara and received 1141 pesos as a dowry.
Doña Bartola, sister-in-law of an unnamed individual, married Luis de Villegas, a resident of Granada, and received an equal sum (1141 pesos) as Isabel Pereira.
Sebastián Pereira Cardoso, brother-in-law of an unnamed individual, received 506 pesos on account.
An unnamed individual paid Jerónimo de Retes 7000 tiles at 10 pesos each.

Diego de Herrera, a native of San Salvador, made his will. He was the natural son of Captain Gaspar González and the late María González, married to María González, and had two children, Sebastiána and Elena. His will details various debts owed by and to him, and mentions his service to Captain Juan de las Alas.
Captain Francisco de Alfaro, Alférez Mayor and Regidor of Cartago, renounced his offices in favor of his brother-in-law, Diego López de Ortega.

Antonio Rodríguez Moreno, Procurador Síndico, presented information about the poverty of the province and the services of its residents. He requested that Don Diego de Acuña, President of the Audiencia of Guatemala, instruct Florian Trujillo y Mendoza to suspend his commission for land composition and measurement, giving power to Francisco de Castro and Francisco de Carvajal to act as procurators.
Doña María Pereira Cardoso, widow of Juan Gómez Rico, granted power of attorney to Licenciado Presbítero Alvaro de Acuña and Alférez Francisco de Arrieta to claim payment of her dowry.

Alférez Juan de Senabria Maldonado and his wife, Doña Juana de Figueroa Moscoso, received 115 pesos as a censo from the Cofradía de la Limpia Concepción, founded in the Convento de San Francisco. They mortgaged houses in Cartago, which were later cancelled by Francisco de Arrieta, Mayordomo, on February 5, 1646.

Juan de Senabria Maldonado and his wife received 105 pesos as a censo from the Capellanía of Doña Ana de Medrano, part of the Cofradía de la Concepción. They mortgaged a mill near the Molinos river, adjacent to Captain Francisco de Alfaro's mill. This censo was cancelled on August 17, 1649, by Captain Pedro de Córdoba, Mayordomo.

Andrés López de Céspedes attempted to sell a 20-year-old Creole slave named Jerónimo to Francisco de Chaves for 320 pesos. The sale did not proceed because Chaves required Ana Gómez, the seller's wife, to also be obligated and requested a longer payment term.
Governor Juan de Villalta assigned Antonio, an indigenous person from Sufragua and part of María de Ortega's encomienda, to Alférez Miguel Calvo for one year at 16 pesos.

Don Diego Charles de Herrera, legitimate son and heir of the late Diego de Herrera and Doña Catalina de Godoy y Zárate, former residents of Guatemala, granted power of attorney to Francisco de Castro to claim his inheritance.
Francisco García Cordero obligated himself to Pablo Martín for 47 pesos, to be paid by the end of May in castrated animals and pigs.
Diego López de Ortega obligated himself to Pablo Martín for 74 pesos, to be paid by the end of May in castrated animals and pigs.
Diego López de Ortega granted general power of attorney to Francisco de Carvajal and Francisco de Castro, procurators in the Audiencia of Guatemala.

Juan Cascante de Rojas, legitimate son of the late Luis C. de R. and Juana Solano, acknowledged receipt of his wife María del Castillo's dowry, totaling 1087 pesos. María del Castillo was the legitimate daughter of the late Juan Gómez Rico and Doña María Pereira Cardoso. Juan Cascante de Rojas also offered 200 pesos in arras.

Lázaro de Guido, a resident of Puerto Belo, owed Pedro Solano, the general depositary of the province, 67 pesos and 7 reales. Guido obligated himself to pay this debt in January to Juan de Marmanillo, a resident of Panamá.

Alcalde Francisco de Ocompo Golfín, acting as the Chief Judge in the absence of Governor Juan de Villalta, assigned Pedro, an indigenous person from Turrialba of Juan Rodríguez's parcialidad, to Hernando Farfán for one year at 16 pesos.

Don Pedro de Córdoba and his wife Doña Catalina de Chaves obligated themselves to Don Gil de Alvarado, Corregidor of Turrialba, for 100 pesos, to be paid in April of the following year. This obligation was cancelled on May 15, 1633.

Alcalde Francisco de Ocampo Golfín assigned Pascual de Zúñiga, an indigenous naborío, and Ana, an indigenous widow from Pacaca, to Doña Ana del Cubillo, a widow, for one year. Pascual was to receive 16 pesos and Ana 8 pesos.
An unnamed individual arranged the marriage of his sister-in-law, Isabel Pereira, to Alonso Yañes Vergara and provided her with 1141 pesos.
An unnamed individual arranged the marriage of his sister-in-law, Doña Bartola, to Luis de Villegas, a resident of Granada, and provided her with 1141 pesos.
