An unnamed individual provided 506 pesos to his brother-in-law, Sebastián Pereira Cardoso, as an account payment.
An unnamed individual paid Jerónimo de Retes for 7000 tiles at a price of 10 pesos each.

people_involved: María González (mother of Diego de Herrera)
María González (wife of Diego de Herrera)
summary: Diego de Herrera, a native of San Salvador, made his will, detailing his family, debts owed to him, and debts he owed to others. He also noted his service to Capn. Juan de las Alas.
Capn. Francisco de Alfaro, Alférez Mayor and Regidor of Cartago, renounced his offices. He transferred these positions to his brother-in-law, Diego López de Ortega.

Antonio Rodríguez Moreno, Procurador Síndico, requested a copy of a report on the province's poverty and the services of its residents and conquistadors. He sought to present this to Don Diego de Acuña, President of the Audiencia de Guatemala, to halt Don Florian Trujillo y Mendoza's land measurement duties, granting power to Francisco de Castro and Francisco de Carvajal.

Doña María Pereira Cardoso, widow of Juan Gómez Rico, granted power of attorney to Lcdo. Presbítero Alvaro de Acuña and Alférez Francisco de Arrieta. This was to enable them to claim the payment of her dowry.

people_involved: Alférez Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado
summary: Alférez Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado and his wife Doña Juana de Figueroa Moscoso received a 115-peso loan at 5% interest from the Cofradía de la Limpia Concepción, mortgaging houses in Cartago. The debt was cancelled on February 5, 1646, by Mayordomo Francisco de Arrieta.

people_involved: Alférez Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado
summary: Alférez Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado and his wife Doña Juana de Figueroa Moscoso received a 105-peso loan from Doña Ana de Medrano's Capellanía, mortgaging a mill on the Río de los Molinos. This debt was cancelled on August 17, 1649, by Mayordomo Capn. Pedro de Córdoba.

Andrés López de Céspedes attempted to sell his 20-year-old criollo slave, Jerónimo, to Francisco de Chaves for 320 pesos. The sale failed because Chaves required the seller's wife, Ana Gómez, to also be obligated and desired a longer payment term.

Governor Don Juan de Villalta arranged a one-year labor contract for Antonio, an indigenous person from Sufragua under María de Ortega's encomienda. Antonio was to work for Alférez Miguel Calvo for 16 pesos.

people_involved: Don Diego de Herrera (father of Don Diego Charles)
Doña Catalina de Godoy y Zárate
summary: Don Diego Charles, legitimate son and heir of the deceased Don Diego de Herrera and Doña Catalina de Godoy y Zárate of Guatemala, granted power of attorney to Francisco de Castro. This was to claim his inheritance.
Francisco García Cordero obligated himself to Pablo Martín for 47 pesos. He committed to pay this amount by the end of May in castrated animals and pigs.
Diego López de Ortega obligated himself to Pablo Martín for 74 pesos. He committed to pay this amount by the end of May in castrated animals and pigs.
Diego López de Ortega granted general power of attorney to Francisco de Carvajal and Francisco de Castro, both procuradores in the Audiencia de Guatemala.

Juan Cascante de Rojas acknowledged receipt of his wife María del Castillo's dowry, totaling $1087-00. María del Castillo was the legitimate daughter of the deceased Juan Gómez Rico and Doña María Pereira Cardoso. Juan Cascante de Rojas also offered 200 pesos as arras.

Lázaro de Guido, a resident of Puerto Belo, owed Pedro Solano, the general depositary, 67 pesos and 7 reales. Guido obligated himself to pay this debt to Juan de Marmanillo, a resident of Panamá, in January.

Alcalde Francisco de Ocompo Golfín, acting in Governor Don Juan de Villalta's absence, arranged a one-year labor contract for Pedro, an indigenous person from Turrialba. Pedro, from Juan Rodríguez's parcialidad, was to work for Hernando Farfán for 16 pesos.

On December 6, Don Pedro de Córdoba and his wife Doña Catalina de Chaves obligated themselves to Don Gil de Alvarado, Corregidor of Turrialba, for 100 pesos, payable the following April. This debt was cancelled on May 15, 1633.

On December 11, Alcalde Francisco de Ocampo Golfín arranged one-year labor contracts for Pascual de Zúñiga, an indigenous naborío, and Ana, an indigenous widow from Pacaca. They were to work for Doña Ana del Cubillo, receiving 16 pesos and 8 pesos respectively.
Ana signs Alférez Francisco de Arrieta as her guarantor for an unspecified matter.

An orphan boy named Diego, 12 years old, from Ujarraci, is placed with Doña Ana del Cubillo to serve until he reaches tribute age or marries. Francisco de Arrieta accepts and guarantees this arrangement in Doña Ana's absence.
An orphan boy named Miguel, about 11 years old and a curero from Luisa Hernández's encomienda, is placed with Bernabé de Segura to serve until he reaches tribute age or marries.
An indigenous man named Juan from Aoyaque, part of Luisa Hernández's encomienda, is placed with Ignacio de Artavia for one year with a salary of 16 pesos.
Don Gil de Alvarado, Corregidor of Turrialba, grants general power of attorney to Don Pedro de Córdova, a resident of Cartago, and Francisco de Castro, a procurador of the Audiencia of Guatemala.

people_involved: Capn. Pedro de Artavia y Lisaum
summary: Captain Pedro de Artavia y Lisaum, as Alcalde Ordinario, issues a declaration acknowledging the severe damages resulting from guarantorships. He pledges, under penalty of 400 pesos, not to act as a guarantor for anyone in the future.

Juan Blasco, a resident of Cartago, receives a dowry of 1036 pesos and 4 reales for his upcoming marriage to María de Torres. The dowry includes livestock, grain, land, and various household items, appraised by Lope de Lumbides and Fco. Ocampo Gofín.
Don Alonso Méndez de Sotomayor issues a bill to Diego Ruiz de Ocaña, a resident of Granada, Nicaragua, for 364 and a half pesos owed to Juan de Valverde Zárate, Treasurer of the Santa Cruzada.
Alférez Juan de Valverde Zárate grants general power of attorney to his wife, Magdalena Gutiérrez, and Francisco de Arrieta, revoking a previous power of attorney given to Juan Fernández.
Antonio de Morales sells a 7-year-old mulatto slave named Nicolás, son of his enslaved black woman Sebastiana, to Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado for 150 pesos.
Pedro Solano, the general depositary, grants power to Juan de Valverde Zárate, who is traveling to Nicaragua, to sell a 20-year-old mulatto creole slave named María there.
Doña María de Sandoval, widow of Treasurer Juan de Echavarría Navarro, grants general power of attorney for lawsuits to Francisco de Castro, a Procurador of the Audiencia of Guatemala.

Governor Don Juan Villalta places an indigenous orphan girl named María, from Corroci (included in Tucurrique) and Jusepe de Sandoval's encomienda, with Alonso Pelaez to serve until she marries or pays tribute.
Magdalena de la Portilla, widow of Captain Pedro de Arce, grants general power of attorney to her father, Andrés López de Céspedes, and to Alférez Juan de Acuña and Alférez Juan López de Ortega.

Alonso López de Villademoros, Judge Commissioner of the General Court of Deceased Estates, grants general power of attorney to Juan Martínez de Ferrera and Juan de la Cruz Nuevo, residents of Guatemala.

The testament of Jerónimo de Vera, a native of Ariza, Spain, is recorded. He is married to Leonor de Ribera, has no children, and mentions having married his granddaughter, María de Ribera, to Andrés Jaimes.

An incomplete document records Miguel Calvo and his wife María Pereira receiving a 600-peso loan at 5% interest from Father Baltasar de Grado. They mortgage two adobe houses, bordering properties of Mariana Chinchilla and the heirs of Isabel Jiménez.
Juan Sánchez Valverde grants general power of attorney to García Ramiro Corajo.
An incomplete entry mentions Jusepe López, an indigenous man from the town of San Juan.
Ana signs a document, with Alférez Francisco de Arrieta acting as her guarantor.

An orphan boy named Diego, 12 years old and from Ujarraci, is placed with doña Ana del Cubillo until he reaches tribute age or marries. Francisco de Arrieta accepts and guarantees the arrangement in doña Ana's absence.
An orphan boy named Miguel, about eleven years old and from the encomienda of Luisa Hernández, is placed with Bernabé de Segura. Miguel is to serve Bernabé until he reaches tribute age or marries.
Juan, an indigenous man from Aoyaque and the encomienda of Luisa Hernández, is placed with Ignacio de Artavia for one year with a salary of 16 pesos.
Don Gil de Alvarado, Corregidor of Turrialba, grants general power of attorney to Don Pedro de Córdova, a resident of 'this city,' and Francisco de Castro, a procurator of the Audiencia of Guatemala.

people_involved: Capn. Pedro de Artavia y Lisaum
summary: Captain Pedro de Artavia y Lisaum, an Alcalde Ordinario, declares his intention to no longer act as a guarantor due to the significant financial losses and imprisonment experienced by guarantors. He obligates himself by this deed, under penalty of 200 pesos for the Santísimo Sacramento and 200 pesos for the Cofradía de la Concepción, which helps pay dowries for poor orphans.

Juan Blasco, a resident of Cartago and native of Granada, Spain, receives a dowry of 1036 pesos 4 reales for his upcoming marriage to María de Torres. The dowry includes various goods, livestock, land, and household items, with Lope de Lumbides and Fco. Ocampo Gofín acting as appraisers.
Don Alonso Méndez de Sotomayor paid 364.5 pesos to Juan de Valverde Zárate, Treasurer of the Santa Cruzada, through Diego Ruiz de Ocaña, a resident of Granada, Nicaragua, for an equal value received.
Alférez Juan de Valverde Zárate grants general power of attorney to his wife, Magdalena Gutiérrez, and to Francisco de Arrieta, while revoking a previous power of attorney granted to Juan Fernández.
Antonio de Morales sells Nicolás, a 7-year-old mulatto enslaved boy and son of his enslaved black woman Sebastiana, to Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado for 150 pesos.
Pedro Solano, the general depositary, grants power to Juan de Valverde Zárate, who is traveling to Nicaragua, to sell an enslaved mulatto woman named María, 20 years old, there.
Doña María de Sandoval, widow of Treasurer Juan de Echavarría Navarro, grants general power for lawsuits to Francisco de Castro, Procurator of the Audiencia of Guatemala.

Governor Don Juan Villalta places María, an indigenous orphan girl from Corroci (part of Tucurrique) and the encomienda of Jusepe de Sandoval, with Alonso Pelaez, for her to serve him until she marries or pays tribute.
Magdalena de la Portilla, widow of Captain Pedro de Arce, grants general power of attorney to her father, Andrés López de Céspedes, and to Alférez Juan de Acuña and Alférez Juan López de Ortega.

Alonso López de Villademoros, Judge Commissioner of the General Court of Deceased Estates in this province, grants general power of attorney to Juan Martínez de Ferrera and Juan de la Cruz Nuevo, residents of Guatemala.

This entry details the will of Jerónimo de Vera, son of the deceased Pedro Sánchez and María de Vera, originally from Ariza, Spain. He was married to Leonor de Ribera and had no children, and mentions having married his granddaughter, María de Ribera, to Andrés Jaimes.

Miguel Calvo and his wife María Pereira receive 600 pesos from Father Baltasar de Grado as a loan (censo del 5 ojo), mortgaging two adobe houses. The houses are adjacent to properties belonging to Mariana Chinchilla and the heirs of Isabel Jiménez.
Juan Sánchez Valverde, a resident, grants general power of attorney to García Ramiro Corajo.
Jusepe López, an indigenous man from the town of San Juan, is mentioned in an incomplete entry.

Herrera received seventy pesos from Alonso López de Villademoros, Judge Commissioner of deceased estates, to travel to Guatemala. His mission was to transport legal cases concerning the deaths of Juan de Mendoza Abaigar and Juan López de Sequeira, various testimonies, and letters for several officials in Guatemala.
Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado granted general power of attorney to Antonio Rodríguez Moreno, who held the title of lieutenant of cavalry captains.

people_involved: Capitán Pedro de Artavia y Lisaum
summary: Sargento Mayor García Ramiro Corajo, Captains Juan Solano and Pedro de Artavia y Lisaum, Alférez Vasco Solano, and don Alonso Méndez y Sotomayor, who were guarantors for the deceased Treasurer Juan de Echavarría Navarro, granted power to Captain Francisco de Ocampo Golfín. This power was to argue against a deficit declared by Governor Villalta during the account review.
On April 10th, Alférez Juan de Acuña granted general power of attorney to his sons, Licenciado Presbítero Alvarado de Acuña and José de Acuña, and also to Alférez Francisco de Arrieta.
On April 18th, Alcalde Juan Cascante de Rojas arranged for Luis Rodríguez, a 16-year-old mulatto, to be placed with José de Prendas, a master tailor, for a period of four years.

people_involved: Capn. don Juan de Salcedo Vallejo
summary: On April 18th, Captain don Juan de Salcedo Vallejo granted general power of attorney to Captain Bartolomé de Enciso Hita. This power was later substituted by Enciso to Pablo Milanés del Castillo on March 1st, 1635.

On April 24th, in the absence of the Governor who was visiting Esparza, Alcalde Lope de Lumbides placed Pedro, an orphan from Curriravá and part of Captain Diego de Ocampo Figueroa's encomienda, with Diego de Ocampo Sandoval. Pedro was to serve until he married or reached the age to pay tribute.

On April 25th, García Ramiro Corajo granted power to Juan de Marmanillo and Juanes de Echavarría, residents of Panamá, to charter a 500-piece frigate destined for Caldera. The frigate was expected to arrive the following February to load flour, biscuits, and lard.

On May 8th, Francisco Gómez el mozo, son of Alférez Francisco Gómez and recently married to Catalina García, made his will. He listed debts owed by Alonso Tuquerraba and Andrés, both indigenous people from Aserrí, and Cristóbal García Beltrán, and Catalina de Ortega, widow of Francisco de Alfaro. He also mentioned owning a farm near Captain Francisco de Ocampo's ranch, and named Pedro Solano and his uncle Cristobal de Madrigal as executors.

On May 11th, the Alcalde placed José, an indigenous person from Aserrí under the encomienda of Manuel de Flores, with Diego de Escobar. José was to serve until he married or reached the age to pay tribute.

On May 19th, Francisco de Aragoces, owner and master of the frigate 'Las Animas' docked in Suerre and destined for Puerto Bello, chartered the ship to don Pedro Gascón de Angulo. The purpose was to load flour, capons, and pork.

On May 19th, Manuel Ruiz granted power to Bartolomé de Enciso Hita to collect 245 pesos from Juan de Málaga, a resident of Cartagena. This debt was for chickens and other goods Ruiz had sold to Málaga in Suerre.

people_involved: Alférez don Juan del Castillo y Guzmán
summary: On May 19th, Alférez don Juan del Castillo y Guzmán granted general power of attorney to Bartolomé de Enciso Hita.

people_involved: Capn. Pedro de Artavia y Lisaum
summary: On May 30th, Doña Isabel de Herrera, wife of Captain Pedro de Artavia y Lisaum, granted power to Alférez Juan López de Ortega and Francisco de Arrieta. Their task was to reclaim a black slave named Tomás, owned by Doña Isabel, who had been embargoed from her husband due to a guarantee he provided for the former Treasurer, Juan de Echavarría Navarro.

people_involved: Capn. Pedro de Artavia y Lisaum
summary: On May 30th, Captain Pedro de Artavia y Lisaum confessed that his purchase of a black woman named Luisa and a black boy named Antonio for 400 pesos from Jerónimo de Retes, the Chief Constable, was a simulated transaction. Consequently, he transferred ownership of Luisa and Antonio back to Retes.

On June 4th, Padre Baltasar de Grado leased adobe houses, covered with tiles and bordering Andrés López de Céspedes' property, to Alonso López and his wife Ana de Zúñiga. The lease was for 500 pesos at an annual interest rate of 5%.
On June 9th, Andrés López de Céspedes and his wife Ana Gómez sold a 22-year-old Creole black slave named Jerónimo, son of their slave Violante, to don Juan de Senabria Maldonado for 300 pesos.

On June 16th, Ana Gómez, daughter of the deceased Román Benito and Juana Gómez, residents of Cartago, made her will. She was first married to Pedro de la Portilla, with whom she had several children, including the deceased Jerónimo, Ana, and Juan Matías, and the living María, Pedro, Diego Jacinto, Juana, Magdalena, Catalina, and Isabel. Ana was married to Juan de Segura, María to Juan de Mora, and Juana to Agustín Guerrero. Her daughter Magdalena was married to Pedro de Arce, and her son Jerónimo was married to doña Ana del Cubillo.

Herrera received seventy pesos from Alonso López de Villademoros, the Commissioner Judge of deceased estates, to travel to Guatemala. His mission was to transport legal documents concerning the deaths of Juan de Mendoza Abaigar and Juan López de Sequeira, along with various testimonies and letters for several officials in Guatemala.
Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado formally granted general power of attorney to Antonio Rodríguez Moreno. Moreno held the position of Lieutenant of Captain of horses.

people_involved: Capitán Pedro de Artavia y Lisaum
summary: Sergeant Major García Ramiro Corajo, Captains Juan Solano and Pedro de Artavia y Lisaum, Ensign Vasco Solano, and Don Alonso Méndez y Sotomayor, who were guarantors for the late Treasurer Juan de Echavarría Navarro, granted power of attorney to Captain Francisco de Ocampo Golfín. Their purpose was to challenge a deficit declared by Governor Villalta during the account review.

On April 10, Ensign Juan de Acuña granted general power of attorney to his two sons, Licentiate Presbyter Alvarado de Acuña and José de Acuña. He also extended this power to Ensign Francisco de Arrieta.

On April 18, Mayor Juan Cascante de Rojas arranged for Luis Rodríguez, a 16-year-old mulatto, to be apprenticed to José de Prendas, a tailor. The apprenticeship agreement was set for a duration of four years.

people_involved: Capn. don Juan de Salcedo Vallejo
summary: On April 18, Captain Don Juan de Salcedo Vallejo, a resident, granted general power of attorney to Captain Bartolomé de Enciso Hita. Subsequently, on March 1, 1635, Enciso transferred this power to Pablo Milanés del Castillo.

On April 24, Mayor Lope de Lumbides, acting in the absence of the Governor who was visiting Esparza, arranged for Pedro, an orphan from Curriravá, to be apprenticed to Diego de Ocampo Sandoval. Pedro, who belonged to Captain Diego de Ocampo Figueroa's encomienda, is to serve until he marries or reaches the age of tribute.

On April 25, Sergeant Major García Ramiro Corajo granted power of attorney to Juan de Marmanillo and Juanes de Echavarría, both residents of Panama. Their task was to charter a 500-piece frigate, destined for Caldera, to arrive the following February to load provisions such as flour, biscuits, and lard.

On May 8, Francisco Gómez el mozo, son of Ensign Francisco Gómez and a resident of the city, made his will. He had recently married Catalina García and listed several debtors, including Alonso Tuquerraba and Andrés, both indigenous people from Aserrí. His property included a chácara near Captain Fco. de Ocampo's hato, and his executors were Pedro Solano and his uncle, Cristóbal de Madrigal.

On May 11, the Mayor arranged for José, an indigenous person from Aserrí belonging to Manuel de Flores' encomienda, to be apprenticed to Diego de Escobar. José is to serve until he marries or reaches the age of tribute.

On May 19, Francisco de Aragoces, a resident and the owner and master of the frigate 'Las Animas' docked in Suerre, chartered his vessel to Don Pedro Gascón de Angulo. The frigate was destined for Puerto Bello and would be loaded with flour, capons, and pork.

On May 19, Manuel Ruiz, a resident, granted power of attorney to Captain Bartolomé de Enciso Hita. Enciso Hita's task was to collect 245 pesos from Juan de Málaga, a resident of Cartagena, which was owed for chickens and other goods sold in Suerre.

people_involved: Alferez don Juan del Castillo y Guzmán
summary: On May 19, Ensign Don Juan del Castillo y Guzmán granted general power of attorney to Captain Bartolomé de Enciso Hita.

people_involved: Capitán Pedro de Artavia y Lisaum
summary: On May 30, Doña Isabel de Herrera, wife of Captain Pedro de Artavia y Lisaum, granted power of attorney to Ensigns Juan López de Ortega and Francisco de Arrieta. Their mission was to reclaim Tomás, a black slave belonging to Doña Isabel, who had been embargoed from her husband due to a guarantee he provided for the former Treasurer, Juan de Echavarría Navarro.

people_involved: Capitán Pedro de Artavia y Lisaum
summary: On May 30, Captain Pedro de Artavia y Lisaum confessed that his 400-peso purchase of a black slave named Luisa and a black child named Antonio from Jerónimo de Retes, the Alguacil Mayor, was a simulated transaction. Consequently, he transferred ownership of Luisa and Antonio back to Retes.

On June 4, Father Baltasar de Grado granted a census, essentially a mortgage, on adobe houses to Alonso López and his wife Ana de Zúñiga for 500 pesos at a 5% annual interest rate. The houses were noted to border those belonging to Andrés López de Céspedes.

On June 9, Andrés López de Céspedes and his wife Ana Gómez sold a 22-year-old Creole black slave named Jerónimo to Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado for 300 pesos. Jerónimo was identified as the son of Violante, a slave owned by the sellers.

Ana Gómez, legitimate daughter of the deceased Román Benito and Juana Gómez of Cartago, made her will. She had been married to Pedro de la Portilla, with whom she had several children, some deceased and others still living, including María, Pedro, and Juana. Her will also details the marital status of some of her children, such as María being married to Juan de Mora and Juana to Agustín Guerrero, and mentions her son Pedro joined the Order of San Francisco.

Ana, now deceased, left her daughter Juana de Segura in the care of the testadora. After Ana's death, Juan de Segura remarried Ana del Cubillo. Juana de Segura is described as an orphan, alone, and unable to marry due to a severe throat injury.
The testadora, who raised Magdalena de Céspedes (a mestiza born in her house), bequeaths 12 tame cows and 6 colts to help with Magdalena's marriage.

The testadora married Andrés López de Céspedes in second nuptials approximately 28 years ago. She leaves him 100 cows, 50 mares, and 6 yokes of oxen, noting his need for sustenance due to his old age and weariness.

Andrés López de Céspedes had a lawsuit with Sebastián González, a former Corregidor of Pacacua. During this legal dispute, Andrés López de Céspedes spent two enslaved people, Juan Cascante and Jordán.
Lope de Lumbides grants general power of attorney for lawsuits to Captain Pedro de Artavia Lisaum and Alférez Francisco de Arrieta.

Alonso de Guido and Isabel Núñez agree to provide a dowry of 1,036 pesos for their daughter, Catalina de Guido, who is set to marry José de Prendas. The dowry includes flour, biscuits, and garlic to be delivered in Caldera.

Alcalde Pedro Solano arranges for Felipe Díaz (son), the 10-year-old son of the deceased Felipe Díaz (father) and Francisca de Flores, to be apprenticed to Lázaro Gutiérrez, an indigenous carpenter, for six years to learn the trade. This is due to the family's poverty and the son's vagrancy.

Doña Catalina de Ortega y Ribera, widow of Captain Francisco de Alfaro, grants general power of attorney for lawsuits to Captain Jerónimo de Retes. On September 26, 1633, Retes substitutes this power to Juan Fernández.

Juan Delgado appealed a decision by the Cofradía de la Concepción regarding a 100-peso dowry for his wife, Juana de la Cruz Alfaro. The Cofradía had conditioned the dowry on Juana appearing veiled. Br. Lope de Chavarría ordered the payment with a bond, and Alférez Pedro Enríquez acts as guarantor.

Francisca López, widow of Alférez Felipe Monge, and her son Juan Delgado del Castillo, offer a dowry for Ana Merino, widow of Juan Bautista Rodríguez, who is set to marry Juan Alonso Camacho. The dowry includes half of their livestock, houses, and corrals in the Aserrí valley, a yoke of oxen, and half of their houses, lots, and belongings in the city.

Juan de Monzón Quesada, son of the deceased Diego de Quesada and Francisca Gutiérrez, acknowledges receipt of the 650-peso dowry for his wife, Antonia Godoy y de Santiago, daughter of Ayudante Pedro de Santiago Galindo and María de Aguilar. He also acknowledges 200 pesos in arras.
Luisa Hernández, widow of Captain Juan de Lamas, donates her 10-year-old enslaved mulatilla named María to Domingo Hernández, whom she raised as her own son.
Domingo Hernández, recently married to Doña María de Carvajal (widow of Juan de Padilla with five children), makes an inventory of the 1547.3 reales in assets brought into their marriage.

Hernando Farfán, son of the deceased Captain Alonso Pérez Farfán and Marina de Anangas, makes his will. He was first married to Antonia de Trujillo (no children) and later married Catalina de Rueda in Cartago, with whom he has a 10-year-old son, Juan Gutiérrez Jaramillo. His nephew Juan Montero (nephew of Antonia) gave him 500 pesos for gananciales after he came to Costa Rica.

In the absence of Governor Villalta (who is in Quepo), the Alcalde arranges for Marcos, a 13-year-old orphan from Pacaca, to be apprenticed to Juan Hidalgo, an indigenous shoemaker, for 5 years to learn the trade.
The Alcalde arranges for Jusepe, an indigenous person, to be apprenticed.

Pedro de Artavia Lisaum was assigned to Pacaca de la Real Corona for one year with a salary of $16.00. He was responsible for retaining the tribute due to His Majesty and delivering it to the Treasurer.

Doña Leonor Chacón Narváez, a native of Antequera, made her will. She was the widow of Juan de Alarcón Rabaneda and Captain Francisco Pavón. Her first husband, Juan de Alarcón Rabaneda, died en route to 'esta provincia' from Trujillo, Honduras, while traveling with Governor Juan de Ocón y Trillo.

The Alcalde assigned Jerónimo de Mena, a mestizo, to Juan Pérez de Bonilla, a master tailor, for six years to learn the trade. This revoked a previous agreement with Marcos Martín, an indigenous tailor, as Marcos was deemed unqualified to teach and Jerónimo was found to be vagrant and causing trouble.

people_involved: Capn. Juan de Mendoza y Medrano
summary: Doña Ana del Cubillo, a widow, granted general power of attorney for lawsuits to Captain Juan de Mendoza y Medrano, a resident of 'esta ciudad' currently in Guatemala, and to Luis del Cubillo.

The Alcalde assigned Diego Hernández, son of the late Manuel Hernández and María Fabiana, to Franc? Merino, a master tanner, for four years to learn the trade. Diego was described as a vagrant and idler who had caused trouble and been imprisoned.
The Alcalde assigned Lucas Velazquez, an indigenous person from Aoyaque under the encomienda of Luisa Hernández, to Bartolomé Sánchez for one year with a salary of $16.00.

The Alcalde assigned Hernando, an indigenous person from the village of Corroci (included in Tucurrique) under the encomienda of José de Sandoval, to Alférez Franco. de Arrieta for one year with a salary of $16.00.

The Alcalde assigned Lucas and Alonso, sons of Isabel (a mestiza), to Ana Gómez, widow of Lucas Cordero, to serve her until they reach an age to support themselves or marry. Antonio Rodríguez Moreno acted as guarantor for Ana Gómez.

Andrés Jaimes, natural son of the late Alonso Jaimes and Franc* de Carvajal, made his will. He was married to María de Riba, with whom he had five children: Luis, María, Pedro, Clara, and Diego. His sister, Doña Melchora, was also mentioned.

Captain Salvador de Torres provided a receipt for the dowry of his wife, María Alvarez de Oviedo. Her parents were Gaspar Núñez de Oviedo and Beatriz Rodríguez, and the dowry amounted to $451 and 5 reales.
Captain Salvador de Torres granted general power of attorney for lawsuits to his father-in-law, Gaspar Núñez de Oviedo.

Presbítero Licenciado Baltasar de Grado donated a young enslaved girl named Isabel, approximately 10 years old, to his niece Doña Mayor de Benavides. The enslaved girl was the daughter of Isabel, an 'angola' slave belonging to Pedro Solano. Doña Mayor de Benavides was the daughter of Antonio Rodríguez Moreno and Doña Inés de Benavides.
The Alcalde assigned Juan Hernández, son of the late Manuel Hernández, to Melchor Carballo, a saddler, for four years. The entry is incomplete.

In March 1638, Luis Machado served as the escribano for Protocolo n° 5, Legajo 1. Juan Francisco Zambrano, acting with power from Captain Agustín de Rojas, a resident of Puerto Belo, initiated a sale (details incomplete).

A testadora details provisions for her granddaughter, Juana de Segura, who is an orphan and disabled, and for Magdalena de Céspedes, a mestiza raised in her house, to aid her marriage. The testadora also mentions her second marriage to Andrés López de Céspedes, who is old and in need, and recounts his past lawsuit with Corregidor Sebastián González, which involved two slaves.
Lope de Lumbides grants general power of attorney for lawsuits to Captain Pedro de Artavia Lisaum and Alférez Francisco de Arrieta.

Alonso de Guido and Isabel Núñez agree to provide a dowry of 1,036 pesos for their daughter Catalina de Guido's marriage to José de Prendas. The dowry includes specific goods like flour, biscuits, and garlic to be delivered to Caldera.

Alcalde Pedro Solano places Felipe Díaz hijo, a 10-year-old orphan whose father died long ago and whose mother is impoverished, with Lázaro Gutiérrez, an Indigenous carpenter, for six years to learn the trade. The boy is described as 'half wild and vagabond' due to his family's hardship.

Doña Catalina de Ortega y Ribera, widow of Captain France? de Alfaro, grants general power of attorney for lawsuits to Captain Jerónimo de Retes on July 28. On September 26, 1633, Retes substitutes this power to Juan Fernández.

Juan Delgado appealed a decision by the Cofradía de la Concepción regarding a 100-peso dowry for his wife, Juana de la Cruz Alfaro, which was conditional on her appearing veiled. Br. Lope de Chavarría ruled in favor of giving the dowry, provided a bond was given, which Alférez Pedro Enríquez then provided, guaranteeing repayment if the Bishop revoked the auto.

Francisca López and her son Juan Delgado del Castillo offer a dowry for Ana Merino, Francisca's daughter and Juan's sister, for her marriage to Juan Alonso Camacho. The dowry includes half of their livestock, houses, and corrals in the Aserrí valley, as well as half of their houses, lots, and belongings in the city.

Juan de Monzón Quesada, son of the deceased Diego de Quesada and Franc* Gutiérrez, acknowledges receipt of his wife Antonia Godoy y de Santiago's dowry. The dowry amounted to $650, with arras of $200.
Luisa Hernández, widow of Captain Juan de Lamas, donates her 10-year-old mulatilla slave named María to Domingo Hernández, whom she raised as if he were her own son.

Domingo Hernández, recently married to Doña María de Carvajal, widow of Juan de Padilla and mother of five children, creates an inventory of the assets brought into their marriage. The total value of the assets was 1547.3 reales.

people_involved: Juan Montero (father of Antonia de Trujillo)
Catalina de Trujillo (mother of Antonia de Trujillo)
Juan Montero (nephew of Antonia de Trujillo)
summary: Hernando Farfán, originally from Jerez, makes his testament. He recounts his first marriage to Antonia de Trujillo, leaving his estate to her when he came to Costa Rica to find his father, and later receiving $500 from his wife's nephew. He is now married to Catalina de Rueda in Cartago and has a 10-year-old son, Juan Gutiérrez Jaramillo.
In the absence of Gobernador Villalta, the Alcalde places Marcos, a 13-year-old orphan from Pacaca, with Juan Hidalgo, an Indigenous shoemaker, for five years to learn the trade.
The Alcalde places Jusepe, an Indigenous person, as an apprentice. Further details are not available due to the text cutoff.
Juan Alvarez Pereira, a resident of Esparza, purchased an enslaved Angolan man named Antón, who was between 18 and 20 years old, for $250.00.

Captain Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado granted power of attorney to Captain Andrés de Pedrosa and Pedro de Alarcón el mozo, the Chief Constable of Panama. The purpose was to charter a frigate capable of carrying 600 bales, which was to arrive at Caldera in January 1639 to load flour, garlic, hardtack, and chickens.

Mayor Alonso Peláez arranged for Nicolás and María, mestizo children aged 6 and 4, sons of Agustina de Rojas, to serve Doña Catalina de Ortega y Ribera. They were to serve until Catalina married and until Nicolás became a man, with Francisco de Chaves acting as guarantor for Doña Catalina.

Don Alonso Méndez de Sotomayor and his wife Doña María Calderón sold their adobe and straw-roofed dwelling to Captain Jerónimo de Retes for $200.00. The property, which bordered the public square, houses of Doña Antonia Vázquez de Coronado, and Captain Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, was also subject to a $125.00 mortgage to a census of Father Baltasar de Grado.

Ensign Manuel de Flores, public scribe, and his wife María Barboza, offered a dowry of $1884.00 for the marriage of their daughter Doña Isabel de Quiñones to Gabriel de Vargas Machuca, a resident of Madrid. The dowry included various goods such as clothing, jewelry, cash, flour, garlic, and castrated pigs.

Jerónimo de Retes sold an enslaved Creole woman named Juana Bohorques, approximately 25 years old, to Juan Francisco Zambrano, a resident of Granada (Nicaragua), for $400.00, with part of the payment on credit. Juana Bohorques had been previously purchased by Jerónimo de Retes from Captain Francisco de Obregón, also a resident of Granada.
The sale of Juana Bohorques from Jerónimo de Retes to Juan Francisco Zambrano, which occurred on May 10, 1639, was cancelled in April 1641.

Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado granted power of attorney to Lorenzo Sánchez, who was traveling to Panama, to collect a $400.00 debt from Juan Pérez de Guadamúz. This debt was for the price of an enslaved Creole man named Jerónimo, whom Senabria Maldonado had sold to Guadamúz.

Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado again granted power of attorney, this time to Alonso de Carvajal, a merchant, and Pedro de Alarcón el mozo, the Chief Constable of Panama. The purpose was to charter a frigate capable of carrying 600 to 700 bales, which was to arrive at Caldera the following January.

Governor Don Gregorio de Sandoval, a member of the War Council of the States of Flanders, granted power of attorney to his brothers, Licentiate Domingo Martínez de Anaya (a priest) and Don Juan Martínez de Anaya (Canon of Berlanga). He also included Juan de Aguirre, Secretary to Don Lorenzo Ramírez de Prado of the Royal Council of the Indies, and Pedro Marquina, his steward, to present capitulations to the Council of the Indies for the pacification of Talamanca province.

Ensigns Juan de Valverde Zárate and Don José de Sandoval y Ocampo provided surety for Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado. Senabria Maldonado had been awarded the office of Chief Ensign of the city, which became vacant upon the death of Francisco de Alfaro.
Ensign Sebastián de Guevara, a resident of Esparza, granted general power of attorney for lawsuits to Diego López de Ortega.

Diego de Esquivel, a native of Puerto Santa María, Spain, acknowledged receipt of his wife Juana Sánchez's dowry of $565.00 and arras of $200.00. Juana Sánchez was the legitimate daughter of Gaspar de Rojas and María González, and the dowry included a house bordering the estates of Juan Sánchez Crespo and Francisco Alvarez.

Gabriel de Aguilar sold an estate, located about a league from the city, to Governor Don Gregorio de Sandoval for $200.00. The estate, which included a house and 40 head of cattle, bordered properties of Catalina Palacios, Don Diego de Sojo, and Miguel Calvo, and was subject to a census debt to the Confraternity of the Conception.

Captain Jerónimo de Retes, the Chief Constable, granted power of attorney to Pedro de Retes Salazar (resident of Cartagena de Indias) and his brothers Diego de Retes and Pedro de Retes (residents of Seville). The purpose was to gather information regarding the nobility and hidalguía of his deceased father, Jerónimo de Retes (former Chief Constable), and his grandparents, Pedro de Retes and Doña Petronila de Lloredo, who were residents of Bilbao.

Ambrosio de Brenes el mozo sold an enslaved Creole man named Domingo Tiznado, 24 years old, to Juan Muñoz for $300.00. Domingo Tiznado had been acquired from Ambrosio de Brenes's father, Ambrosio de Brenes, and the payment was to be made in Cartagena de Indias during an upcoming trip.
Ambrosio de Brenes el mozo committed to travel with Juan Muñoz, assisting him, from Cartago to the port of Matina and then to Cartagena, and back, for $70.00.

Governor Don Gregorio de Sandoval and his wife Doña Gregoria de Escobar, widow of Marcos de Cortavarría (former Treasurer of Cartagena), granted power of attorney to Captain Juan de Somovilla y Tejada, Chief Engineer of Cartagena de Indias. This power was to assist in the audit of the late Treasurer's accounts and secure the release of funds held pending their finalization.

Juan Muñoz committed to deliver 150 castrated pigs and 20 bales of hardtack, garlic, and anise to the port of Punta Blanca by July 10th. These goods were for embarkation on the frigate chartered by Captain Jerónimo de Retes, the Chief Constable, which would arrive from Cartagena.
Esteban de Torres granted general power of attorney for lawsuits to Captain Salvador de Torres, his father.
Pedro de Artavia Lisaum was assigned to Pacaca de la Real Corona for one year, receiving a salary of 16 pesos and retaining the Crown's tribute to deliver to the Treasurer.

people_involved: Don Juan de Ocón y Trillo
summary: Doña Leonor Chacón Narváez, a native of Antequera, made her will. She was the widow of Juan de Alarcón Rabaneda and Captain Francisco Pavón. Her will details her children with Alarcón, the death of Alarcón during a journey to 'this province' via Trujillo, and mentions her grandson, a priest, and two servants to whom she bequeathed houses.

The Alcalde assigned Jerónimo de Mena, a mestizo, to Juan Pérez de Bonilla, a master tailor, for six years to learn the trade. This revoked a previous agreement with Marcos Martín, an indigenous tailor, who was deemed unqualified to teach and whose apprentice, Jerónimo, was vagrant.

people_involved: Capitán Juan de Mendoza y Medrano
summary: Doña Ana del Cubillo, a widow, granted general power of attorney for legal matters to Capitán Juan de Mendoza y Medrano, a resident of Cartago currently in Guatemala, and to Luis del Cubillo.
The Alcalde assigned Diego Hernández, who was a vagabond, idle, and had been imprisoned for mischief, to Francisco Merino, a master tanner, for four years to learn the trade.
The Alcalde assigned Lucas Velazquez, an indigenous person from Aoyaque and part of Luisa Hernández's encomienda, to Bartolomé Sánchez for one year with a salary of 16 pesos.

The Alcalde assigned Hernando, an indigenous person from Corroci (included in Tucurrique) and part of José de Sandoval's encomienda, to Alférez Francisco de Arrieta for one year with a salary of 16 pesos.

The Alcalde assigned Lucas and Alonso, sons of Isabel, a mestiza, to Ana Gómez, the widow of Lucas Cordero, to serve her until they could support themselves or marry. Antonio Rodríguez Moreno acted as guarantor for Ana Gómez.

Andrés Jaimes, the natural son of the deceased Alonso Jaimes and Francisca de Carvajal, made his will. He was married to María de Riba, with whom he had five children: Luis, María, Pedro, Clara, and Diego, and also mentioned his sister, Doña Melchora.

Capitán Salvador de Torres acknowledged receipt of the dowry for his wife, María Alvarez de Oviedo, which amounted to 451 pesos and 5 reales. María was the legitimate daughter of Gaspar Núñez de Oviedo and Beatriz Rodríguez.
Capitán Salvador de Torres granted general power of attorney for legal matters to his father-in-law, Gaspar Núñez de Oviedo.

Presbítero Licenciado Baltasar de Grado donated an enslaved black girl named Isabel, approximately 10 years old and daughter of Isabel (an enslaved Angolan woman belonging to Pedro Solano), to his niece Doña Mayor de Benavides. Doña Mayor was the legitimate daughter of Antonio Rodríguez Moreno and Doña Inés de Benavides.
The Alcalde assigned Juan Hernández, son of the deceased Manuel Hernández, to Melchor Carballo, a saddler, for four years. The entry is incomplete.
Juan Francisco Zambrano, acting on behalf of Capitán Agustín de Rojas, a resident of Puerto Belo, initiated a sale. The entry is incomplete.

Doña María de Sandoval, widow of Treasurer Juan de Echavarría Navarro, granted power of attorney to procurators Francisco de Castro and Miguel de Artavia in Guatemala. The purpose was to seek royal grants for herself and her children, citing the extensive services rendered to the province by her grandfather Juan Solano, father Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, and late husband Juan de Echavarría Navarro, who served as Treasurer for over 16 years.

Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado, the Procurador Síndico of Cartago, granted a general power of attorney for legal disputes. This power was given to Diego Ruiz de Ocaña, the Alguacil Mayor of Granada, Nicaragua, and Francisco de Salas, a resident of the same city.

Juan Muñoz and his wife, Magdalena Mauricia, incurred a debt of $467.00 to Father Baltasar de Grado, the Cura and Vicario of Cartago. As security for this obligation, they mortgaged an enslaved Black man named Domingo Tiznado.

Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado, the Alférez Mayor of Cartago, granted power of attorney to Don Diego Fernández de Córdova and his brother Juan Fernández de Córdova, who were business agents in the Consejo de Indias. Their task was to obtain royal confirmation for his office of Alférez Mayor and for an encomienda of indigenous people granted by the Audiencia president, based on his and his ancestors' services to the King, as well as those of his wife's ancestors.

Juan Muñoz incurred a debt of $144.00 to Captain Pedro de Retes, a resident of Cartagena de Indias. The loan was facilitated by Jerónimo de Retes, and Juan Muñoz committed to repaying the sum in Cartagena de Indias, where he was traveling.

José de Villalobos Jara, legitimate son of Captain Miguel de Villalobos and Doña Isabel de Carvajal, acknowledged receipt of his wife María de Murillo Campos's dowry, valued at $1412.00. The dowry included a cattle site near Barba, adjacent to lands of Juan Sánchez Saavedra and Ignacio de Artavia, and two hundred pesos in bizcocho to be delivered by his father-in-law in Granada.

Doña Ana de Guevara, widow of Francisco Rodríguez de Sosa, granted power of attorney to her father Juan de Acuña, Francisco de Arrieta, and her brother Francisco de Alarcón. The purpose of this power was to claim the payment of her dowry.

Alcalde Alonso Peláez arranged for Apolonia, a ten-year-old mestiza and daughter of Ana Jacinta, to be placed with Pedro Simón Ordoño. Apolonia's mother, Ana Jacinta, is described as a single mestiza of 'mal vivir'.

people_involved: Alférez Don José de Sandoval Ocampo
summary: Alcalde Alonso Peláez arranged for Pedro, an eleven-year-old mestizo and son of Beatriz, an indigenous woman from Aserrí, to be placed with Alférez Don José de Sandoval Ocampo for a period of nine years.

people_involved: Alcalde Capn. Diego de Ocampo Figueroa
summary: Alcalde Captain Diego de Ocampo Figueroa arranged for Jusepe, a mestizo boy of about ten years old, to be placed with Juan Alonso Hernández, a saddler official, for a period of five years.

people_involved: Alcalde Capn. Diego de Ocampo Figueroa
summary: Alcalde Captain Diego de Ocampo Figueroa arranged for Pedro, a fifteen-year-old indigenous orphan from Pacaca, to be placed with Francisco Rodríguez Merino, a master tanner, for a period of six years.

Juan Cascante de Rojas acted as a guarantor for Sebastián de Guevara, a resident of Esparza. This guarantee enabled Sebastián de Guevara to receive $100.00 from the estate of his deceased wife, Isabel de Medina, a sum he had contributed to their marriage.

Licenciado Presbítero Alvaro de Acuña, the Cura Beneficiado of Esparza, granted power of attorney to Bartolomé de Enciso Hita, Teniente de Contador y Tesorero. This power allowed Hita to collect 100 pesos from the Royal Treasury, which was owed to Acuña as salary for his offices of Sacristán Mayor and Cura Beneficiado for the year beginning Christmas 1637.
Lope de Lumbides issued a codicil, an amendment or addition, to his last will and testament. The original will had been granted in Teocigalpa, located in the province of Honduras.

Gobernador Sandoval assigned Inés, an indigenous widow from Barba with four children, to Leonor Jiménez, a widow, for a period of two years for $8.00. Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado acted as the guarantor for this arrangement.
Licenciado Presbítero Miguel de Arguedas, who served as a commissioner for the Holy Office, granted a general power of attorney for lawsuits to Cristóbal de Madrigal.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego Jiménez de Luna
summary: Father Baltasar de Grado, Commissioner of the Holy Office and the local Priest and Vicar, granted a general power of attorney for lawsuits to Licenciado Don Diego Jiménez de Luna, a priest residing in Granada, Nicaragua.

people_involved: Don Cristóbal de Argüello y Carvajal
summary: Don Cristóbal de Argüello y Carvajal, Corregidor of Quepo, made his will. He requested 100 masses, listed debts to several individuals, and made bequests to his servant Clara de Aguilar, Agustina Carrillo, Luisa de Fonseca, María Fabiana, and Clara de Aguilar's children. He named Pedro Enríquez and Juan Sánchez Crespo as executors, and the Cofradía del Rosario as his heir.

people_involved: Don Cristóbal de Argüello y Carvajal
summary: Don Cristóbal de Argüello y Carvajal issued a codicil to his will, which served to reduce the number of masses he had previously requested.
Alcalde Diego de Ocampo Figueroa assigned María, a mulata and daughter of Juan Estacio, to Jusepe de Prendas for a period of two years for $12.00.
Gabriel de Vargas Machuca, a native of Madrid, formally acknowledged the receipt of his wife Doña Isabel de Quiñones' dowry. This dowry was provided as per a promise made in May of the same year.

people_involved: Juan Pérez de Viguera y Andrada
summary: Juan Pérez de Viguera y Andrada committed to paying Cura Baltasar de Grado $18.00 annually. This payment was for the rent of his daughter Doña Ana de Guevara's house in Cartago, which was currently leased by Juan de Acuña.

Captain Diego de Ocampo Figueroa obligated himself to Alonso Gómez Macotela, a resident of Esparza, for $280.00. Additionally, he committed to purchasing two slaves (one male and one female, aged 18-20) in Panama for Macotela and transporting them to Caldera.
Juan Sánchez de Liñan provided a dowry of $810.00 and arras of $100.00 in favor of his wife, Eufrasia de Loría.

people_involved: Capn. don Juan de Senabria Maldonado
summary: Captain Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado, who held the title of Alférez Mayor, granted a general power of attorney for lawsuits. This power was given to Francisco de Castro, a procurator of the Audiencia de Guatemala, and to Diego de Escobar.

Alférez Vasco Solano received $300.00 from Cura Baltasar de Grado at a 5% interest rate. As collateral for this loan, Solano mortgaged a property that included a house made of adobe and tile, and a stable with a straw roof.
Juan Alvarez Pereira, a resident of Esparza, purchased an Angolan enslaved man named Antón, aged 18-20, for $250.

Captain Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado granted power to Captain Andrés de Pedrosa and Pedro de Alarcón el mozo, Alguacil Mayor of Panama, to charter a frigate. The frigate was intended to carry 600 tercios and arrive in Caldera in January 1639 to load flour, garlic, hardtack, and chickens.

people_involved: Doña Catalina de Ortega y Ribera
summary: Alcalde Alonso Peláez arranged for Nicolás (6 years old) and María (4 years old), mestizo children of Agustina de Rojas, to serve Doña Catalina de Ortega y Ribera. Nicolás would serve until he became a man, and María until she married, with Francisco de Chaves acting as Doña Catalina's guarantor.

Don Alonso Méndez de Sotomayor and his wife Doña María Calderón sold their adobe house, located near the public plaza and adjacent to properties of Doña Antonia Vázquez de Coronado and Capitán Frco. de Ocampo Golfín, to Capitán Jerónimo de Retes for $200. The sale included the responsibility for Retes to pay an additional $125 due to a mortgage held by P. Baltasar de Grado.

Alférez Manuel de Flores, public scribe, and his wife María Barboza, offered a dowry of $1884 for the marriage of their daughter Doña Isabel de Quiñones to Gabriel de Vargas Machuca. The dowry included various goods such as clothing, gold jewelry, cash, flour, garlic, anise, and pigs.

Jerónimo de Retes sold a 25-year-old Creole enslaved Black woman named Juana Bohorques to Juan Francisco Zambrano, a resident of Granada (Nicaragua), for $400, with part of the payment on credit. Retes had previously purchased Juana from Capitán Franc? de Obregón, also of Granada. The debt was cancelled in April 1641.

Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado granted power to Lorenzo Sánchez, who was traveling to Panama, to collect $400 from Juan Pérez de Guadamúz. This debt was the purchase price for a Creole enslaved man named Jerónimo, whom Maldonado had sold to Guadamúz.

Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado again granted power, this time to Alonso de Carvajal, a merchant, and Pedro de Alarcón el mozo, Alguacil Mayor of Panama. The power was to charter a frigate of 600 to 700 tercios capacity, which was to arrive in Caldera the following January.

Governor Don Gregorio de Sandoval, of the War Council of Flanders, granted power to his brothers, Licenciado Domingo Martínez de Anaya (a priest from Madrid) and Don Juan Martínez de Anaya (a Canon of Berlanga), along with Juan de Aguirre (Secretary to Don Lorenzo Ramírez de Prado) and Pedro Marquina (his steward). They were tasked with presenting capitulations to the Council of the Indies to pacify the province of Talamanca.

people_involved: Don José de Sandoval y Ocampo
summary: Alférez Juan de Valverde Zárate and Don José de Sandoval y Ocampo acted as guarantors for Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado, who had been awarded the office of Alférez Mayor of Cartago. The position had become vacant due to the death of Franc? de Alfaro.

Capitán Jerónimo de Retes, Alguacil Mayor, granted power to Pedro de Retes Salazar (resident of Cartagena de Indias) and his brothers Diego de Retes and Pedro de Retes (residents of Seville). The purpose was to gather information on the nobility and hidalguía of his deceased father, Jerónimo de Retes, and his grandparents, Pedro de Retes and Doña Petronila de Lloredo, who were residents of Bilbao.

Ambrosio de Brenes el mozo sold a 24-year-old Creole enslaved Black man named Domingo Tiznado to Juan Muñoz for $300, with payment to be made in Cartagena de Indias during an upcoming trip. Ambrosio de Brenes el mozo had acquired Domingo Tiznado from his father, Ambrosio de Brenes.
Ambrosio de Brenes el mozo committed to accompany Juan Muñoz, assisting him throughout a journey from Cartago to the port of Matina, then to Cartagena, and back, for a payment of $70.

people_involved: Capitán Juan de Somovilla y Tejada
summary: Governor Don Gregorio de Sandoval and his wife Doña Gregoria de Escobar (widow of Marcos de Cortavarría, former Treasurer of Cartagena) granted power to Capitán Juan de Somovilla y Tejada, Chief Engineer of Cartagena de Indias. This power was to enable him to attend the audit of the late Treasurer's accounts and secure the release of detained funds.

Juan Muñoz committed to deliver 150 castrated pigs and 20 tercios of hardtack, garlic, and anise to the port of Punta Blanca by July 10. These goods were for embarkation on a frigate chartered by Capitán Jerónimo de Retes, Alguacil Mayor, which would arrive from Cartagena.
Esteban de Torres granted general power of attorney for lawsuits to his father, Capitán Salvador de Torres.

Diego de Esquivel, a native of Puerto Santa María (Spain), acknowledged receipt of his wife Juana Sánchez's dowry, valued at $565, which included a house. Juana Sánchez was the legitimate daughter of Gaspar de Rojas and María González. Arras of $200 were also mentioned.

Gabriel de Aguilar sold a ranch (hato) located about a league from Cartago to Governor Don Gregorio de Sandoval for $200. The property, which included houses, corrals, and 40 cattle, bordered lands belonging to Catalina Palacios (a widow), Don Diego de Sojo, and Miguel Calvo. The purchase required the buyer to acknowledge a debt of this sum to the Cofradía de la Concepción.

Doña María de Sandoval, widow of Treasurer Juan de Echavarría Navarro, granted power of attorney to procurators Francisco de Castro and Miguel de Artavia in Guatemala. The purpose was to solicit royal grants for herself and her children, acknowledging the significant services of her late husband, father, and grandfather in the province. Her husband notably served as Treasurer for over 16 years.

Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado, the Procurador Síndico of Cartago, granted general power of attorney for legal disputes. This power was given to Diego Ruiz de Ocaña, the Alguacil Mayor of Granada, and Francisco de Salas, a resident of the same city.

Juan Muñoz and his wife, Magdalena Mauricia, incurred a debt of $467.00 to Father Baltasar de Grado, the Cura and Vicario of Cartago. As security for this obligation, they mortgaged an enslaved person named Domingo Tiznado.

Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado, the Alférez Mayor of Cartago, empowered Don Diego Fernández de Córdova and his brother Juan Fernández de Córdova, agents in the Council of the Indies. Their task was to secure royal confirmation for his office of Alférez Mayor and an encomienda of indigenous people, citing his and his wife's ancestors' services to the King.

Juan Muñoz committed to repay Captain Pedro de Retes, a resident of Cartagena de Indias, $144.00. This sum was a loan provided through Jerónimo de Retes, and Juan Muñoz intended to pay it back in Cartagena de Indias, where he was traveling.

José de Villalobos Jara, legitimate son of Captain Miguel de Villalobos and Doña Isabel de Carvajal, received his wife María de Murillo Campos's dowry. The dowry, totaling $1412.00, included a cattle site near Barba, adjacent to lands of Juan Sánchez Saavedra and Ignacio de Artavia, and $200.00 in "bizcocho" to be delivered by his father-in-law in Granada, plus $200.00 in arras.

Doña Ana de Guevara, widow of Francisco Rodríguez de Sosa, granted power of attorney to her father, Juan de Acuña, Francisco de Arrieta, and her brother, Francisco de Alarcón. The purpose of this power was to claim the payment of her dowry.

Alcalde Alonso Peláez arranged for Apolonia, a ten-year-old mestiza and daughter of Ana Jacinta, to be placed with Pedro Simón Ordoño. Apolonia's mother, Ana Jacinta, is described as a single mestiza of "mal vivir" (bad living).

people_involved: Alférez don José de Sandoval Ocampo
summary: Alcalde Alonso Peláez placed Pedro, an eleven-year-old mestizo and son of Beatriz, an indigenous woman from Aserrí, with Alférez Don José de Sandoval Ocampo. This arrangement was for a period of nine years.

people_involved: Alcalde, Capn. Diego de Ocampo Figueroa
summary: Alcalde Captain Diego de Ocampo Figueroa arranged for Jusepe, a mestizo of about ten years old, to be placed with Juan Alonso Hernández, a saddler. This placement was for a duration of five years.

people_involved: Alcalde, Capn. Diego de Ocampo Figueroa
summary: Alcalde Captain Diego de Ocampo Figueroa placed Pedro, a 15-year-old indigenous orphan from Pacaca, with Francisco Rodríguez Merino, a master tanner. This arrangement was for a period of six years.

Juan Cascante de Rojas provided a guarantee for Sebastián de Guevara, a resident of Esparza, concerning a claim of $100.00. This sum was part of the probate proceedings for Guevara's deceased wife, Isabel de Medina, and was intended to allow the judge to release the funds to him.

Licenciado Presbítero Alvaro de Acuña, the Cura Beneficiado of Esparza, authorized Bartolomé de Enciso Hita, Teniente de Contador y Tesorero, to collect 100 pesos from the Royal Treasury. This amount was due as part of his salary for the offices of Sacristán Mayor and Cura Beneficiado, covering the year that began at Christmas 1637.
A codicil was made by Lope de Lumbides, amending his previously granted will. The original will had been executed in Teocigalpa, located in the province of Honduras.

Alcalde Diego de Ocampo Figueroa arranged an 'asiento' (indentured service contract) for Catalina, a 12-year-old mulata and daughter of the late Juan Estacio, with Juan Delgado del Castillo. The contract was for 4 years or until Catalina's marriage, at a rate of $14 per year.
Alcalde Diego de Ocampo Figueroa arranged an 'asiento' for Luis, an orphaned mestizo approximately 12 years old, with Gabriel de Aguilar, a master tailor. The contract was for a period of 6 years.
Alcalde Diego de Ocampo Figueroa placed Juana de Bonilla in the service of Antonio González. She is to remain in his household until her absent husband, Juan de Santamaría, returns.
Alcalde Alonso Peláez arranged an 'asiento' for María, a mulata and daughter of Juana, with Pedro Simón Ordoño. The contract was for two years at $12 per year.

Alcalde Diego de Ocampo Figueroa arranged an 'asiento' for María, a mestiza approximately 12 years old and daughter of Beatriz, an indigenous woman from Barba, with Ana de las Alas. The contract is to last until María marries, with Juan Sánchez Crespo acting as guarantor.

Alcalde Diego de Ocampo Figueroa arranged an 'asiento' for Diego Chirraca, an indigenous carpenter from Curriravá, along with his son Alonso and son-in-law Jusepe. The contract is for six years, during which Diego Chirraca is to teach them his trade.

Alférez Tomás Calvo issued a dowry letter ('carta dote') for his wife, Eugenia Abarca, daughter of Alférez Gaspar Abarca de Latras and Magdalena de Chaves. The dowry amounted to $1270, including various valuable household and clothing items, along with 'arras' of $730.

Captains Diego de Ocampo Figueroa and Juan de Senabria Maldonado granted power to Pedro de Alarcón, Alguacil Mayor of Panamá, and Pedro Megía, a 'veinticuatro' and resident of Panamá. They are authorized to charter a 500-tercio frigate to arrive in Caldera by the end of the following March to load flour, biscuits, tobacco, garlic, and anise.

Juan Sánchez Crespo acted as guarantor for Cristóbal de Argúello y Carvajal, Corregidor of Quepo, who intended to take three indigenous men (Tomás, Benito, and Diego) as muleteers to Nicaragua. Sánchez Crespo guaranteed that if the indigenous men were not returned to their province, he would pay their tributes to their encomenderos and cover any resulting damages.

Licenciado Presbítero Miguel de Arguedas, Comisario of the Holy Office and retired Beneficed Priest of Esparza, residing in Cartago and a former resident of Santiago de Guatemala, made his will. He identified himself as the legitimate son of the late Licenciado Félix de Arguedas, a native of Valencia del Cid, and the late Leonor de Mármol, both former residents of Guatemala.

Miguel de Arguedas noted in his will that he receives an annual income of 183 pesos and 7 reales from the King. This income, which he previously collected as a beneficed priest of Esparza, is due by Christmas of this year.

Miguel de Arguedas recorded a debt of $50 owed by Captain Bartolomé de Enciso Hita. This debt included $30 from the 'casa excusada' of Esparza, which Enciso Hita failed to send from Juan de Salcedo Vallejo's hato, and $20 given by Antonio de Anabiscar for remittance to Guatemala with a report by Escribano Manuel de Flores, which also went unfulfilled.

In 1621, Francisco de Ocampo Golfín borrowed 110 pesos from Miguel de Arguedas for a trip to Guatemala and bought two mules for 30 pesos, promising to bring back black Mexican taffeta but failing to do so. Later, Ocampo's son-in-law, Juan de Echavarría Navarro, attempted to collect the debt, and Ocampo partially repaid with five baskets of biscuits, valued at $40.

Miguel de Arguedas recorded a $60 debt from Juan Alvarez Pereira for houses Arguedas had purchased from him. Pereira had intended to move to Orosi, but when his plans changed, the houses were transferred back to him.

Miguel de Arguedas, while serving as Cura of Esparza, buried Luis de Alfaro, son of Alférez Mayor Fco. de Alfaro. Esteban de Torres, Luis's brother-in-law and husband of Ana de Alfaro, owes $13 for the burial and mass services.

Alférez Juan de Válverde Zárare, Treasurer of the Santa Cruzada, granted a 'censo' (annuity/mortgage) on a house with an oven to Mateo de Sanabria and his wife Francisca de Brenes. The property, located in Cartago and described by its neighbors, was valued at $300 with a 3% annual interest.

The Cura Baltasar de Grado, Captain Diego de Ocampo Figueroa, Juan de Senabria Maldonado, and Mayordomo Jerónimo de Retes, as deputies of the Cofradía de las Benditas Animas in Cartago, granted power to Doctor Diego Fernández de Córdova and Juan Fernández de Córdova. These brothers, acting as business agents in the Council of the Indies in Madrid, are tasked with presenting the Cofradía's founding ordinances and seeking confirmation from the Holy Father in Rome.

Cristóbal Zapata y Salazar, as the legitimate son and heir of the late Juan Bautista Zapata and Antonia de Roa of Madrid, granted general power of attorney to his brothers, Licenciado Frco. de Zapata and Licenciado Juan Zapata, and to agents Doctor Diego Fernández de Córdova and Juan Fernández de Córdova. This power allows them to represent him in the liquidation of his parents' assets, remit collected funds to Agustín de Rojas in Puerto Belo, and donate 300 ducats to his sister Juana Zapata for her dowry or to his brother Juan Zapata if Juana is already married or in religion.

Cristóbal Zapata y Salazar granted power to the Fernández de Córdova brothers to petition the Royal Council of the Indies. The purpose is to request a government position, such as a governorship, corregimiento, or Alcaldía Mayor, or other favors in recognition of his ancestors' merits and services.
Alonso Díaz, a notary, is present for the recording of several transactions and legal documents around this date.

Gobernador Sandoval arranged for Inés, an indigenous widow from Barba with four children, to be placed with Leonor Jiménez, a widow, for two years for $8.00. Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado acted as guarantor for this arrangement.
Licenciado Presbítero Miguel de Arguedas, a commissioner of the Holy Office, granted general power of attorney for lawsuits to Cristóbal de Madrigal.

Father Baltasar de Grado, Commissioner of the Holy Office and Cura and Vicar of Cartago, granted general power of attorney for lawsuits to Licenciado Don Diego Jiménez de Luna, a Presbyter residing in Granada, Nicaragua.

Don Cristóbal de Argüello y Carvajal, Corregidor of Quepo, made his will. He requested 100 masses in Cartago's churches, listed debts to Martín del Castillo, Agustín Guerrero, and Jerónimo de Retes, and made bequests to his servant Clara de Aguilar, Agustina Carrillo, Luisa de Fonseca, and María Fabiana. He appointed Pedro Enríquez and Juan Sánchez Crespo as executors and named the Cofradía del Rosario as his heir.
Cristóbal de Argüello y Carvajal issued a codicil to his will, reducing the number of masses previously requested.
Alcalde Diego de Ocampo Figueroa arranged for María, a mulata and daughter of Juan Estacio, to be placed with Jusepe de Prendas for two years for $12.00.

Gabriel de Vargas Machuca, a native of Madrid, acknowledged receipt of the dowry for his wife, Isabel de Quiñones, as promised in May. Isabel is the daughter of public notary Manuel de Flores and María Barbosa.

people_involved: Juan Pérez de Viguera y Andrada
summary: Juan Pérez de Viguera y Andrada committed to pay $18.00 annually to Cura Baltasar de Grado, which is the rent for his daughter Ana de Guevara's house, leased from Juan de Acuña. The house in Cartago borders properties of Catalina de Zárate and Vasco Solano.

Captain Diego de Ocampo Figueroa obligated himself to Alonso Gómez Macotela, a resident of Esparza, for $280.00. He also committed to purchasing two slaves (male and female, 18-20 years old) in Panama for Macotela and bringing them to Caldera.
Juan Sánchez de Liñan established a dowry of $810.00 and arras of $100.00 for his wife, Eufrasia de Loría, who is the daughter of Antonio González and the late Ana de Loría.
Captain Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado, Alférez Mayor, granted general power of attorney for lawsuits to Francisco de Castro, a procurator of the Audiencia of Guatemala, and to Diego de Escobar.
Alférez Vasco Solano received $300.00 at a 5% censo from Cura Baltasar de Grado, mortgaging a property that included a house and a stable.
Doña Leonor Alvarez Pereira, widow of Lope de Lumbides, granted power of attorney to Juan Rodríguez to reclaim her dowry.

Diego López de Ortega, heir of the deceased Jerónimo Felipe, and Juan Fernández settled a lawsuit regarding two promissory notes. Fernández agreed to pay 80 pesos in flour delivered to Caldera, acknowledging the original debt stemmed from gambling over 15 years prior.

Alférez Miguel Calvo, son of Tomás Calvo and Benita García from Sevilla, made his will. He detailed his two marriages, first to Mariana Chinchilla (with children Juana, Mariana, and Alférez Tomás Calvo) and second to María Pereira Cardoso (with daughter Juana Benita), and listed his assets including slaves and property. The will also mentions his children's marriages and dowries, his executors, and debts owed to him.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan de Salcedo Vallejo
summary: Doña Magdalena de Chaves, whose husband Don Gaspar Abarca had been absent in Peru for many years and is now reported deceased there, granted power of attorney to Captain Don Juan de Salcedo Vallejo, a resident of Esparza, to investigate his death.
Doña Magdalena de Chaves also granted power of attorney to Jerónimo de Ocampo, a scribe in Panama, for the purpose of investigating her husband's death.

Alcalde Diego de Ocampo Figueroa placed Isabel (8 years old) and Francisca (3 years old), mulatto daughters of Ana, with Doña Isabel Pereira, a widow, until they reach marriageable age. Cristóbal Fernández Durán acted as guarantor.
Alcalde Diego de Ocampo Figueroa placed Francisco de Retes, an indigenous laborer and blacksmith, with Antonio González, a master blacksmith, for two years at a monthly wage of 6 pesos.
Alcalde Diego de Ocampo Figueroa deposited María Hernández, daughter of Juana (a mestiza), in Antonio González's house, as requested, until she marries.

Alcalde Alonso Peláez placed Juan, a mulatto boy about 10 years old, son of the deceased mulatto Lucas de Mayorga and Inés, an indigenous woman from Tucurrique, with Alférez Don Gil de Alvarado until he reaches the age of tribute.
Alcalde Alonso Peláez placed Isabel (about 7 years old) and Francisca (about 3 years old), mulatto daughters of Ana, with Alférez Francisco de Chaves until they marry or reach their age.
Magdalena Mauricia, widow of Juan Muñoz, granted power of attorney to Francisco de Arrieta to collect her dowry.

Gaspar Juárez, a resident of Esparza traveling to Panama, obligated himself to Pedro de Alarcón (or his son, Pedro de Alarcón el mozo) for a $100 debt lent by Father Baltasar de Grado, with payment due by the end of February or upon arrival in Panama.

Alcalde Diego de Ocampo Figueroa arranged for Catalina, a 12-year-old mulata and daughter of the late Juan Estacio, to serve Juan Delgado del Castillo for 4 years or until she marries, for $14 annually.
Alcalde Diego de Ocampo Figueroa arranged for Luis, a 12-year-old mestizo orphan, to serve Gabriel de Aguilar, a master tailor, for 6 years.
Alcalde Diego de Ocampo Figueroa placed Juana de Bonilla in Antonio González's service until her absent husband, Juan de Santamaría, returns.
Alcalde Alonso Peláez arranged for María, a mulata and daughter of Juana, to serve Pedro Simón Ordoño for two years at $12 annually.
Alcalde Diego de Ocampo Figueroa arranged for María, a 12-year-old mestiza daughter of Beatriz from Barba, to serve Ana de las Alas until she marries, with Juan Sánchez Crespo as guarantor.
Alcalde Diego de Ocampo Figueroa arranged for Diego Chirraca, an indigenous carpenter from Curriravá, along with his son Alonso and son-in-law Jusepe, to serve for six years to learn the trade.

Alférez Tomás Calvo provided a dowry of $1270 to his wife, Doña Eugenia Abarca, which included various household items and clothing. The dowry was given in favor of his wife, who is the legitimate daughter of Alférez Don Gaspar Abarca de Latras and Doña Magdalena de Chaves.

Captains Diego de Ocampo Figueroa and Juan de Senabria Maldonado granted power to Pedro de Alarcón, Alguacil Mayor of Panamá, and Pedro Megía, a veinticuatro and neighbor of Panamá, to charter a 500-tercio frigate to arrive at Caldera by late March to load various goods.

Juan Sánchez Crespo acted as guarantor for Cristóbal de Argúello y Carvajal, who was taking three indigenous men (Tomás, Benito, and Diego) as muleteers to Nicaragua. Sánchez Crespo guaranteed that if Argúello did not return the indigenous men, he would pay their tributes to their encomenderos and cover any resulting damages.

Licenciado Presbítero Miguel de Arguedas, a retired Beneficiado of Esparza residing in Cartago, made his will. He detailed various debts owed to him, including $50 from Captain Bartolomé de Enciso Hita, $110 from Francisco de Ocampo Golfín (plus 2 mules), and $60 from Juan Alvarez Pereira for a house transaction. He also mentioned burying Luis de Alfaro and being owed $13 for the service.

In 1621, Francisco de Ocampo Golfín borrowed 110 pesos from Miguel de Arguedas for a trip to Guatemala and bought two mules for 30 pesos. Ocampo Golfín failed to bring back Mexican taffeta as promised and later partially repaid the debt with 5 petacas of biscuits.

Alférez Juan de Válverde Zárare, Treasurer of the Santa Cruzada, granted a house with an oven to Mateo de Sanabria and his wife Francisca de Brenes for $300 at 3% annual interest. The house was located in the city, bordering Magdalena de Chaves's property and across the street from Pedro de Córdova and Juan López de Ortega's houses.

Cura Baltasar de Grado, Captain Diego de Ocampo Figueroa, Juan de Senabria Maldonado, and Jerónimo de Retes, as deputies of the Cofradía de las Benditas Animas, granted power to Doctor Diego Fernández de Córdova and Juan Fernández de Córdova in Madrid to present the founding ordinances and seek confirmation from the Pope in Rome.

Don Cristóbal Zapata y Salazar, as heir to his deceased parents Juan Bautista Zapata and Antonia de Roa, granted general power of attorney to his brothers Licenciado Frco. de Zapata and Licenciado Juan Zapata, and to Doctor Diego Fernández de Córdova and Juan Fernández de Córdova, to liquidate his parents' assets, remit funds to Puerto Belo, and donate 300 ducats to his sister Doña Juana Zapata for her dowry or to his brother Juan Zapata if she is already married or in religion.

On January 26, 1639, Cristóbal Zapata y Salazar granted power to the Fernández de Córdova brothers to petition the Royal Council of the Indies for a government, corregimiento, Alcaldía Mayor, or other position in the Indies, and to request other favors in recognition of his ancestors' merits and services.
Magdalena Mauricia, widow of Juan Muñoz, revoked the power she had previously conferred upon Francisco de Arrieta. She then granted this power to Juan Fernández.

Governor Gregorio de Sandoval, acting as tutor for the minor Ana de Cortavarría, granted power to Licenciado Domingo Martínez de Anaya and Canónigo Juan Martínez de Anaya, who are brothers and residents of Spain. Ana de Cortavarría is the legitimate daughter of Gregoria de Escobar (Sandoval's wife) and Marcos de Cortavarría, a former Treasurer of Cartagena.

Alcalde Gil de Alvarado placed Nicolás, an 8-year-old mestizo boy and son of María, an indigenous woman from Pacaca, with Pedro de la Portilla. This arrangement is to last until Nicolás reaches marriageable age.
Doña María de Carvajal, widow of Domingo Hernández and tutor of her son Antonio Hernández, who is the sole heir, granted power to Juan Ortíz Gómez. Juan Ortíz Gómez is a resident of Cartago.
Alférez Francisco de Arrieta granted general power to Alférez Juan del Castillo y Guzmán and Ayudante Jusepe de Echavarría. Both recipients are residents of León, Nicaragua.

Don Cristóbal de Zapata de Salazar sent proofs of service of his wife's ancestors (Juan de Echavarría Navarro, Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, and Juan Solano) to Doctor Diego Fernández de Córdova and his brother Juan Fernández de Córdoba in Madrid, seeking a royal office for himself. He also promised them 2000 ducats from his parents' inheritance (Juan Bautista Zapata and Antonia de Roa) if the negotiation was successful, for which he had previously empowered his brothers Francisco and Juan Zapata.

Don Cristóbal de Zapata de Salazar empowered his brothers, Francisco Zapata and Juan Zapata, to request a certificate of filiation from Alcocer, which was made in 1630. They are also to request a certificate of nobility from the Royal Chancellery of Granada, which his great-grandfather had won and left with his uncle, Juan Zapata.

Mateo de Saravia and Magdalena Mauricia, widow of Juan Muñoz, agreed that Saravia would travel to Cartagena to collect Mauricia's dowry, and in return, Mauricia would pay Saravia 300 pesos. However, this agreement was not carried out.

Governor Gregorio de Sandoval, along with Alcalde Diego de Ortega and other city officials including Captain Juan de Senabria Maldonado and Jerónimo de Retes, granted power to Doctor Diego Fernández de Córdova and his brother Juan Fernández de Córdoba. These agents, residents of Madrid, are to request royal grants for the city in recognition of their services.

Juana Benita, wife of Alonso de Bonilla, granted power to her husband and Alférez Pedro Enríquez and Francisco de Alarcón Chacón. This power is for collecting her inheritance as the sole heir of her deceased mother, María Pereira Cardoso, and the dowry goods given by her father, Miguel Calvo.

Catalina Palacios, a widow and legitimate daughter and heir of Luisa Hernández, granted power to Alférez Francisco de Arrieta. He is tasked with defending the estate left by her deceased mother against a lawsuit initiated by Doña María de Carvajal, widow of Domingo Hernández.
Doña Leonor Alvarez Pereira, widow of Lope de Lumbides, granted power of attorney to Juan Rodríguez. The purpose of this power was to reclaim her dowry.

Diego López de Ortega, heir of the deceased Jerónimo Felipe, and Juan Fernández settled a lawsuit concerning two promissory notes totaling 188 pesos. Fernández claimed the debt stemmed from gambling over 15 years prior, and they agreed he would pay 80 pesos in flour delivered to Caldera.

Alférez Miguel Calvo, a native of Sevilla, made his will in Cartago. He detailed his two marriages, first to Mariana Chinchilla in Trujillo de Honduras, and second to María Pereira Cardoso, outlining his children, dowries, properties, and various financial and familial relationships, including the sale of a slave and an emancipation for his son.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan de Salcedo Vallejo
summary: Doña Magdalena de Chaves, whose husband don Gaspar Abarca had been absent in Perú for many years and was reportedly killed there, granted power of attorney to Capitán don Juan de Salcedo Vallejo of Esparza. This power was for the purpose of investigating her husband's death.
Doña Magdalena de Chaves also granted power of attorney to Jerónimo de Ocampo, a scribe in Panamá. This was for the same objective of investigating the death of her husband, don Gaspar Abarca.

Alcalde Diego de Ocampo Figueroa placed Isabel, 8 years old, and Francisca, 3 years old, mulatto daughters of Ana, with Doña Isabel Pereira, a widow. This arrangement was to last until they reached marriageable age or married, with Cristóbal Fernández Durán acting as guarantor.

Alcalde Diego de Ocampo Figueroa indentured Francisco de Retes, an indigenous laborer and blacksmith's assistant, to Antonio González, a master blacksmith. The agreement was for a period of two years, with a monthly wage of 6 pesos.

Alcalde Diego de Ocampo Figueroa placed María Hernández, daughter of Juana (a mestiza), in the home of Antonio González. This placement was requested by María herself and was to last until she married.

Alcalde Alonso Peláez indentured Juan, a mulatto boy approximately 10 years old, son of the deceased mulatto Lucas de Mayorga and Inés, an indigenous woman from Tucurrique, to Alférez don Gil de Alvarado. This arrangement was to continue until Juan reached the age of tribute.

Alcalde Alonso Peláez indentured Isabel, about 7 years old, and Francisca, about 3 years old, mulatto daughters of Ana, to Alférez Francisco de Chaves. This placement was to last until they married or reached their age.
Magdalena Mauricia, widow of Juan Muñoz, granted power of attorney to Francisco de Arrieta. The purpose of this power was to collect her dowry.

Gaspar Juárez, a resident of Esparza traveling to Panamá, obligated himself to Pedro de Alarcón, a resident of Panamá and Receptor del Santo Oficio, or to Pedro de Alarcón el mozo, Alguacil Mayor, for a 100-peso debt. The money had been lent by P. Baltasar de Grado, and payment was due by the end of February or upon arrival in Panamá.

Alférez Juan de Valverde Zárate grants power to Captain Juan de Sanabria Maldonado, who is departing for Panamá, to demand an account from Baltasar de los Reyes regarding the proceeds of mules sent with Esteban de Mena.

Alcalde Diego López de Ortega obligates himself to Juan Ortíz Gómez for 42 pesos, covering the freight of six mules sent in 1630 to Puerto de Suerte. These mules were intended to transport cargo for the late Governor Juan de Villalta.
Alcalde Diego López de Ortega places Agustina de Rojas, a single mestiza, with Alférez Juan de Gamboa, a resident of the city, for a period of two years for 16 pesos.

Captain Jerónimo de Retes grants power to Diego and Juan Fernández de Córdova, residents of Madrid, to request confirmation of an encomienda. This encomienda was granted by the President of the Audiencia of Guatemala and became vacant upon the death of Luisa Hernández, serving as remuneration for Retes' services.
Francisco de Solís grants general power to Captain Jerónimo de Retes.

Captain don Juan de Sanabria Maldonado, Alférez Mayor and native of Alcántara, Extremadura, makes his testament. He is the legitimate son of the late Captain Gonzalo de Senabria Maldonado and doña Jerónima Bravo Barrantes, is married to doña Juana de Figueroa Moscoso with no children, and names her as his sole heir.

Doña Juana de Figueroa Moscoso makes her testament.
