She is the daughter of the late Captain Francisco de Ocampo Golfín and doña Inés de Benavides Solano, is married to don Juan de Sanabria Maldonado with no children, and names her husband as her sole heir. Her brother is don José de Sandoval y Ocampo.
Magdalena Mauricia de Espinoza, widow of Juan Muñoz, grants power to her brother Ambrosio de Brenes el mozo to collect her dowry assets.
Sebastián de Amores, residing in the Barba valley, grants general power to Licenciado Alvaro de Acuña, the priest of Esparza. This act was executed at the estate of Juan Sánchez Saavedra.

Sebastián de Amores, Vicente Rodríguez, and Inocencio Jorge, residing in the Barba valley and traveling with mules to Panamá, grant power to García Ramiro Corajo and Juan de Gamboa. This power allows them to reclaim any mules or male animals that become lost, tired, stolen, or injured in this province while en route to Panamá.

Antonio Rodríguez Moreno acts as a guarantor for Francisco Alonso, a resident of Esparza. Francisco Alonso, acting as agent for doña Ana Mejía, widow of Captain Juan de Leiva (?) of Granada (Nicaragua), had executed the assets of Francisco Merelo, formerly of Esparza, for 173 pesos. This transaction took place in the town of San Bartolomé de Barba.

A dowry letter is issued for Manuel Martínez, a native of Valencia, Castilla la Vieja, in favor of his wife Isidora Zambrano. The dowry, valued at $1558, includes various items of clothing, linens, and silver, with Isidora's father, Esteban Rodríguez Zambrano, stating that the funds were provided by his son, Fray Andrés Carlos, Isidora's brother.

Isidora Zambrano, wife of Manuel Martínez, grants power to Pedro de la Vega and Licencado Alonso de la Reguera to collect 100 ducats and their rents. These ducats were bequeathed to her 19 years prior by María de la O. in her will for her marriage, and are currently held at interest on a house and oven in Sevilla, for which Gregorio de Tinoco is responsible.
Governor Sandoval places Francisca, an indigenous widow from the pueblo of Curriravá, with Juan Sánchez Crespo for a period of two years for $8.

Governor don Gregorio de Sandoval and his wife doña Gregoria de Escobar grant general power to their brothers and brothers-in-law, Licenciado Domingo Martínez de Anaya, a Presbyter, and Juan Martínez de Anaya, a Canon of Berlanga.
Juan Martínez Lineros, departing for Panamá, grants power to García Ramiro Corajo to reclaim any animals lost from his current party and also gives him general power for lawsuits.

people_involved: Juan Pérez de Viguera y Andrada
summary: Juan Pérez de Viguera y Andrada grants power to his legitimate mother Andrea de Viguera and Pedro Pérez del Castillo, residents of Madrid. This power is for them to petition the King for an office in these parts, and for his mother to administer his estate and inheritance from his deceased father, Mateo Pérez.

Doña María de Sandoval Ocampo, widow of Juan de Echavarría Navarro and guardian of her legitimate children don Juan Solano and doña Ambrosia de Grado, grants power to Doctor don Diego Fernández de Córdova and Juan Fernández de Córdova, his brother, residents of Madrid. This power is to request confirmation of favors granted by the President of the Audiencia of Guatemala, including an encomienda of Indians and a pension for doña Ambrosia.

people_involved: Luis Calderón de Chaves y Paredes
summary: García Ramiro Corajo grants power to Miguel Ramiro Corajo and don Luis Calderón de Chaves y Paredes, a knight of the Order of Santiago.
Magdalena Mauricia, widow of Juan Muñoz, revoked the power previously given to Francisco de Arrieta. She then conferred this power to Juan Fernández.

Governor don Gregorio de Sandoval, acting as tutor for the minor doña Ana de Cortavarría, granted power to Licenciados Domingo Martínez de Anaya and don Juan Martínez de Anaya. Doña Ana is the legitimate daughter of Sandoval's wife, doña Gregoria de Escobar, and Marcos de Cortavarría.

Mayor don Gil de Alvarado arranged for Nicolás, an 8-year-old mestizo son of María (an indigenous woman from Pacaca), to be placed with Pedro de la Portilla. This arrangement is to last until Nicolás reaches marriageable age.
Doña María de Carvajal, widow of Domingo Hernández and tutor of her son Antonio Hernández (the sole heir), granted power to Juan Ortíz Gómez, who resides in Cartago.

people_involved: Don Juan del Castillo y Guzmán
summary: Ensign Franco. de Arrieta granted general power to Ensign don Juan del Castillo y Guzmán and Adjutant Jusepe de Echavarría, both residents of León (Nic).

people_involved: Don Cristóbal de Zapata de Salazar
Doctor don Diego Fernández de Córdova
Doña Ana de Echavarría y Ocampo
summary: Don Cristóbal de Zapata de Salazar sent proofs of service to S.M. by his father-in-law, Juan de Echavarría Navarro, and his wife's grandfather and great-grandfather, Captains Franc? de Ocampo Golfín and Juan Solano, to Doctor don Diego Fernández de Córdova and Juan Fernández de Córdoba in Madrid. This was to request a royal office for himself. He also granted them power to collect 2000 ducats from the inheritance of his deceased parents, Juan Bautista Zapata and Antonia de Roa, which he had previously entrusted to his brothers.

people_involved: Don Cristóbal de Zapata de Salazar
summary: Don Cristóbal de Zapata de Salazar granted power to his brothers, Licenciados Francisco Zapata and Juan Zapata, to request two certificates. One was for a filiation inquiry made in Alcocer in 1630, and the other for a nobility decree won by his great-grandfather in the Royal Chancellery of Granada, which was held by his uncle Juan Zapata.

Mateo de Saravia and Magdalena Mauricia, widow of Juan Muñoz, agreed that Saravia would travel to Cartagena to collect Magdalena's dowry. In return, Magdalena was to pay Saravia 300 pesos, though this agreement ultimately did not proceed.

people_involved: Doctor don Diego Fernández de Córdova
summary: Governor don Gregorio de Sandoval, Mayor Diego de Ortega, Ensign Major don Juan de Senabria Maldonado, Chief Constable Jerónimo de Retes, and other Regidores, acting on behalf of the city, granted power to Doctor don Diego Fernández de Córdova and Juan Fernández de Córdova. They were tasked with requesting royal properties for the city in recognition of their services.

Juana Benita, wife of Alonso de Bonilla, granted power to her husband and Ensigns Pedro Enríquez and Franco. de Alarcón Chacón. This power was for collecting her inheritance as the sole heir of her deceased mother, María Pereira Cardoso, and the dowry goods from her father, Miguel Calvo.

Catalina Palacios, widow and legitimate heir of Luisa Hernández, granted power to Ensign Francisco de Arrieta. This power was to defend the assets left by her deceased mother against a lawsuit initiated by doña María de Carvajal, widow of Domingo Hernández.

A son of Francisco Corajo Ramiro, originally from Trujillo in Extremadura, requested the King to grant him an office in the colonial kingdoms. This request was made in recognition of the services rendered by both him and his father in the province.
Diego de Ocampo Figueroa and José de Sandoval acted as guarantors for Juan de Valverde Zárate. Juan de Valverde Zárate had been appointed as the Treasurer of the Bulls of the Holy Crusade.

Pedro de Mora Salado, an Alcalde of the Santa Hermandad and encomendero in Aserrí and Barba, granted power to Antonio Rodríguez Moreno. The power allowed Rodríguez Moreno to collect 106 pesos in tributes owed to Salado for the current year.
The Governor, Don Gregorio de Sandoval, assigned José, an indigenous person from Ujarrás and son of Pedro Hernández, to Juan Sánchez Liñan, a tailor. This assignment was for a period of four years.

Jerónimo de Retes, the Alguacil Mayor, granted power to his uncle Martín de Erquiñigo and his cousin Martín de Erquiñigo, both residents of Bilbao. The purpose was to gather information regarding the quality and nobility of Jerónimo de Retes, his deceased father Jerónimo de Retes, and his grandparents Pedro de Retes and Petronila de Lloredo, along with other ancestors.

Cura Baltasar de Grado sold an adobe house with a tiled roof and a fenced lot to Francisco de Chaves for 450 pesos. The property, which bordered Andrés López de Céspedes's house, was subject to a 5% annual censo.

Cristóbal Fernández Durán acted as guarantor for María Cardoso, allowing her to send several indigenous people to Nicaragua with her pack train. The indigenous individuals included Tomás Payegua from Chiripó, Andrés de Céspedes from Aserrí, Andrés from Ujarrás, and Cristóbal from Ujarrás, who were from various encomiendas.
Clara de Flores granted general power of attorney to Us Fernández.
The Alcalde assigned Francisca de Iñiga, a single mestiza, to Josephe Méndez for a period of two years. The cost for this assignment was twelve pesos.

people_involved: Doña Isabel Sánchez de los Reyes
summary: Doña Gregoria de Escobar, daughter of deceased Madrid residents Cristóbal de Escobar and Doña Isabel Sánchez de los Reyes, made her will. She was first married to Marcos de Cortavarría, former Treasurer of Cartagena, and received 5500 reales from King Philip IV for her services to the Royal Palace, the Queen, Infantes, and previous Kings. She had one daughter, Doña Ana de Cortavarría, from her first marriage, and later married Don Gregorio de Sandoval, a Governor.

people_involved: Don Juan Domingo Martínez de Sandoval
summary: Don Gregorio de Sandoval, a member of the War Council of Flanders, Governor, and Captain General, and a resident of Cuenca, made his will. He was the legitimate son of the deceased Don Juan Domingo Martínez de Sandoval and Doña Agueda González de Alcalá, and was married to Doña Gregoria de Escobar, with no children. Vasco Solano and Juan Solano were named as his executors.
Antonio González and his wife, María de Zúñiga, obligated themselves to Governor Don Gregorio de Sandoval for 125 pesos. This obligation was later cancelled on June 16, 1640.
Alférez Francisco Román and Miguel Calvo obligated themselves to Catalina de Palacios for 166 pesos. Catalina de Palacios was the widow of Gaspar de Chinchilla.
Ayudante Baltasar de Ortega and his wife, Jerónima Gómez de San Miguel, obligated themselves to Governor Don Gregorio de Sandoval for 50 pesos. This obligation was later cancelled on June 16, 1640.

Ayudante Baltasar de Ortega and his wife, Jerónima Gómez de San Miguel, received 200 pesos from the Cofradía de la Concepción at a 5% annual censo. They mortgaged a hato named San José, located near the city, which included an adobe house, corrals, 300 cattle, and 30 mares, bordering properties of María de Ortega and Antonio Ramos.

Alférez Juan de Valverde Zárate granted power of attorney to Captain Juan de Sanabria Maldonado, who was departing for Panama, to demand an account from Baltasar de los Reyes regarding the proceeds from mules sent with Esteban de Mena.

Alcalde Diego López de Ortega obligated himself to Juan Ortíz Gómez for 42 pesos, representing the freight cost for six of Ortíz Gómez's mules. These mules were sent in 1630 to Puerto de Suerte with others to transport cargo for the deceased Governor of the province, Juan de Villalta.

Alcalde Diego López de Ortega arranged an indentured service agreement for Agustina de Rojas, a single mestiza, to serve Alférez Juan de Gamboa, a resident of 'this city,' for a period of two years at a cost of 16 pesos.

people_involved: Presidente de la Audiencia de Guatemala
summary: Captain Jerónimo de Retes granted power of attorney to Diego and Juan Fernández de Córdova, residents of Madrid, to petition for the confirmation of an encomienda. This encomienda was granted to Retes by the President of the Audiencia of Guatemala and became vacant upon the death of Luisa Hernández, serving as remuneration for Retes' services.
Francisco de Solís granted general power of attorney to Captain Jerónimo de Retes.

Captain don Juan de Sanabria Maldonado, Alférez Mayor and native of Alcántara, Extremadura, executed his testament. He declared himself the legitimate son of the deceased Captain Gonzalo de Senabria Maldonado and doña Jerónima Bravo Barrantes, and named his wife, doña Juana de Figueroa Moscoso, as his sole heir, noting they had no children.

Doña Juana de Figueroa Moscoso executed her testament. She declared herself the daughter of the deceased Captain Francisco de Ocampo Golfín and doña Inés de Benavides Solano, and named her husband, don Juan de Senabria Maldonado, as her sole heir, noting they had no children. Her brother, don José de Sandoval y Ocampo, was also mentioned.
Magdalena Mauricia de Espinoza, widow of Juan Muñoz, granted power of attorney to her brother, Ambrosio de Brenes el mozo, to collect her dowry assets.

Sebastián de Amores, residing in the Barba valley, granted general power of attorney to Licenciado Alvaro de Acuña, the priest of Esparza. This transaction took place at the estate of Juan Sánchez Saavedra.

Sebastián de Amores, Vicente Rodríguez, and Inocencio Jorge, currently in the Barba valley and traveling to Panama with mules, granted power of attorney to García Ramiro Corajo and Juan de Gamboa. This power allows them to reclaim any mules or male animals from their current expedition that may be lost, tired, stolen, or injured within 'this province'.

locations: pueblo de San Bartolomé de Barba
summary: Antonio Rodríguez Moreno acted as a guarantor for Francisco Alonso, a resident of Esparza. Alonso, acting as attorney for doña Ana Mejía (widow of Captain Juan de Leiva of Granada, Nicaragua), had seized the assets of the deceased Francisco Merelo, a former resident of Esparza, for a debt of 173 pesos. The guaranty was made in San Bartolomé de Barba.

Manuel Martínez, a native of Valencia, Castilla la Vieja, formalized a dowry letter for his wife, Isidora Zambrano, daughter of Esteban Rodríguez Zambrano and Juana Bautista. The dowry totaled 1558 pesos and included various valuable items. Isidora's father declared that the dowry was provided by his son, Fray Andrés Carlos, who is Isidora's brother.

Isidora Zambrano, wife of Manuel Martínez and native of Sevilla, granted power of attorney to Pedro de la Vega and Licenciado Alonso de la Reguera. This power enables them to collect 100 ducats and their rents, which were bequeathed to Isidora 19 years prior by María de la O for her marriage, and are currently secured by a house and oven in Sevilla owned by Gregorio de Tinoco.
Governor Sandoval arranged an indentured service agreement for Francisca, an indigenous widow from the pueblo of Curriravá, to serve Juan Sánchez Crespo for two years at a cost of 8 pesos.

Governor don Gregorio de Sandoval and his wife doña Gregoria de Escobar granted general power of attorney to their brothers and brothers-in-law, Licenciado Domingo Martínez de Anaya (Presbyter) and Juan Martínez de Anaya (Canon of Berlanga).
Juan Martínez Lineros, departing for Panama, granted power of attorney to García Ramiro Corajo to reclaim any animals lost from his current expedition and also granted him general power for lawsuits.

people_involved: Juan Pérez de Viguera y Andrada
summary: Juan Pérez de Viguera y Andrada granted power of attorney to his legitimate mother Andrea de Viguera and Pedro Pérez del Castillo, both residents of Madrid, to petition the King for an official position in 'these parts,' citing his satisfactory service as Lieutenant Governor and Captain General of the province. He also empowered his mother to administer the estate and inheritance due to him from his deceased father, Mateo Pérez.

people_involved: Presidente de la Audiencia de Guatemala
summary: Doña María de Sandoval Ocampo, widow of Juan de Echavarría Navarro and guardian of her children don Juan Solano and doña Ambrosia de Grado, granted power of attorney to Doctor don Diego Fernández de Córdova and his brother Juan Fernández de Córdova, residents of Madrid. This power is for requesting confirmation of grants from the President of the Audiencia of Guatemala, which include an encomienda of indigenous people in 'this province' and a lifetime pension of 100 tostones for doña Ambrosia.

people_involved: Luis Calderón de Chaves y Paredes
summary: García Ramiro Corajo granted power of attorney to Miguel Ramiro Corajo and don Luis Calderón de Chaves y Paredes, Knights of the Order of Santiago.
Felipe de Coto entered into an obligation to pay $100 to Governor Gregorio de Sandoval.

Juan Barbosa and his wife Beatriz Camelo, along with their guarantors Pedro de Mora Salado and Juan Fernández, became indebted to Governor Sandoval for $150. This money was lent to Barbosa to pay an equal sum to the Royal Treasury, as he was a guarantor for Captain Bartolomé de Enciso and had been imprisoned for this debt.

Juan de Válverde Zárate, Treasurer of the Santa Cruzada, granted power to Manuel Martínez, who was traveling to Granada. Martínez was authorized to receive bulls from Francisco de Obregón, Treasurer of the Santa Cruzada in that province and this one, for delivery to Cartago.

Bernabé de Segura became indebted to Governor Gregorio de Sandoval for $150, which Sandoval lent him to cover a guarantee Segura had made for Treasurer Bartolomé de Enciso. Cristóbal de Madrigal, Juan Sánchez Crespo, and Cristóbal de Araya served as guarantors, each for $50.
Alférez Pedro Enríquez and his wife Juana Chacón, as principals, along with Alonso de Bonilla, Juana's son, as guarantor, became indebted to Governor Sandoval for $50.
Captain José de Sandoval y Ocampo became indebted to Licenciado Presbítero Alonso de Sandoval, his brother, for $1350.

Governor Sandoval arranged for Juan, an orphaned indigenous boy from Aserrí, approximately twelve years old, to be placed with Francisco Solano, the Head Sacristan of the Parish Church, for a period of four years.
Esteban de Torres granted general power of attorney to Francisco de Chaves, who was traveling to Guatemala, and to Francisco de Castro, a procurator in the Audiencia of that city.

Governor Gregorio de Sandoval and his wife Gregoria de Escobar granted power to Juan de Somovilla Tejada and Pedro de Retes, residents of Cartagena, to demand a deed of recognition for a census (annuity) concerning money they had left with Fernando Gutiérrez and his son-in-law Miguel de Olmos.
The will of María Cardoso was recorded. She was the legitimate daughter of the late Juan Gómez Rico and María Cardoso, married to Juan Cascante de Rojas, and had three sons: Luis, Juan, and Gaspar.

Diego de Ortega granted general power of attorney for lawsuits to Francisco de Chaves, a resident of Cartago, Gregorio Martínez de Porta, a public scribe in Granada (Nicaragua), and Francisco de Castro, a procurator in the Audiencia of Guatemala.

The will of Father Miguel de Arguedas was recorded. He bequeathed a blanket to Antonia de Madrigal, the legitimate daughter of Alférez Cristóbal de Mena, and left his few furnishings to her in recognition of her many services, as she housed him. His father had established an income for him from the Jesuit haciendas in Guatemala, which his sister, Juana de San Francisco, a professed nun in Guatemala, managed in his absence.

Juan de Acuña declared that the ranch and estate he acquired for $170 at the death of Francisca de Bonilla, located in the Purires corner and including livestock, along with a site in La Candelaria, belonged to Isabel de Bonilla. He stated he purchased these properties for Isabel using her own money.
Esteban de Mena granted power of attorney to Francisco de Castro and Francisco de Carvajal, procurators in Guatemala, for all his lawsuits.
Sergeant Alonso de Sojo, a resident and Procurator Síndico of Esparza, granted general power of attorney to Alférez Manuel de Flores, who was a public scribe and scribe of this Governorship.

Juan de Válverde Zárate, acting as father and legitimate administrator for Martín Zárate and Esteban de Mena, ratified the power of attorney that Esteban de Mena had granted on the first of this month (November 1st) and conferred it to Francisco de Castro and Francisco de Carvajal.
Juan de Válverde Zárate granted general power of attorney to his wife, Magdalena Gutiérrez.
Juana de Vera, widow of García Ramiro Corajo, granted general power of attorney to Francisco de Arrieta.

Francisco Corajo Ramiro, originally from Trujillo in Extremadura, sought an office from the King in remuneration for services rendered by both himself and his father, Francisco Corajo Ramiro, in this province.
Diego de Ocampo Figueroa and José de Sandoval acted as guarantors for Juan de Valverde Zárate, who was appointed Treasurer of the Santa Cruzada bulls.

Pedro de Mora Salado, an Alcalde of the Santa Hermandad and encomendero in Aserrí and Barba, granted power to Antonio Rodríguez Moreno to collect 106 pesos in tributes owed to him for the current year.
The Governor arranged for José, an indigenous person from Ujarrás and son of Pedro Hernández, to be placed with Juan Sánchez Liñan, a tailor, for a period of four years.

Jerónimo de Retes, the Alguacil Mayor, granted power to his uncle Martín de Erquiñigo and his cousin Martín de Erquiñigo, both residents of Bilbao, to gather information on the quality and nobility of himself, his deceased father Jerónimo de Retes, and his grandparents Pedro de Retes and Petronila de Lloredo, as well as other ancestors.

Cura Baltasar de Grado sold an adobe house to Francisco de Chaves for 450 pesos, subject to a 5% annual censo. The rent is to be paid to Domingo de Chaves, his nephew, and served by Padre Alonso de Sandoval, also his nephew, until Domingo receives the order.

Cristóbal Fernández Durán acted as guarantor for María Cardoso to enable her to send several indigenous people, including Tomás Payegua, Andrés de Céspedes, Andrés, and Cristóbal, with her recua to Nicaragua.
Clara de Flores granted general power of attorney to Us Fernández.
The Alcalde arranged for Francisca de Iñiga, a single mestiza, to be placed with Josephe Méndez for two years at a cost of twelve pesos.

Doña Gregoria de Escobar, daughter of Cristóbal de Escobar and Isabel Sánchez de los Reyes from Madrid, made her testament. She was first married to Marcos de Cortavarría, former Treasurer of Cartagena, with whom she had a daughter, Ana de Cortavarría, and later married Governor Don Gregorio de Sandoval.

Don Gregorio de Sandoval, a member of the War Council of the States of Flanders, Governor, and Captain General from Cuenca, made his testament. He was the son of Juan Domingo Martínez de Sandoval and Agueda González de Alcalá, married to Gregoria de Escobar with no children, and named Vasco and Juan Solano as his executors.
Antonio González and his wife, María de Zúñiga, obligated themselves to Governor Don Gregorio de Sandoval for 125 pesos. This obligation was cancelled on June 16, 1640.
Alférez Francisco Román and Miguel Calvo obligated themselves to Catalina de Palacios, the widow of Gaspar de Chinchilla, for 166 pesos.
Ayudante Baltasar de Ortega and his wife, Jerónima Gómez de San Miguel, obligated themselves to Governor Don Gregorio de Sandoval for 50 pesos. This obligation was cancelled on June 16, 1640.

Baltasar de Ortega and Jerónima Gómez de San Miguel received 200 pesos from the Cofradía de la Concepción at a 5% annual censo. They mortgaged their hato named San José, located about a league from the city, which bordered properties of María de Ortega and Antonio Ramos.
Clara de Flores granted general power of attorney to Juan de Araya.
Alférez Gil de Alvarado, acting as ordinary Mayor and Lieutenant General Governor, arranged for Juan, a 3-year-old mestizo, to be seated with Isabel Jiménez de Salas.

Alférez Gil de Alvarado arranged for Cristóbal, a 10-year-old orphan indigenous person from San Mateo de Chirripó, under the encomienda of Juan Barbosa, to be seated with Francisco de Alarcón for four years.

Alférez Gil de Alvarado arranged for Juana, wife of Antonio (an indigenous person from Curriravá under Diego de Ocampo Figueroa's encomienda), to be seated with Alférez Juan Vázquez de Coronado until her husband Antonio returns from Guatemala.

Bartolomé Sánchez, son of the late Captain Bartolomé Sánchez and Inés Alvarez Pereira, established a dowry of $536.4 reales for his wife, Isabel de la Jara, daughter of Captain Miguel de Villalobos and Isabel de Carvajal. The dowry included a promissory note from Ignacio de Artavia, the wife's brother-in-law.

Alcalde Diego López de Ortega arranged for María, a mulata and daughter of an indigenous woman named María from Francisco de Chaves' encomienda in Barba, to be seated with Juan Blasco until she marries or comes of age.

Jerónimo de Retes granted general power of attorney to Gregorio Martínez de Porta, a scribe in Granada (Nicaragua), and Diego de Robles, also from Granada, specifically to charter a frigate to travel from Granada to Puerto Belo, Cartagena, and then to Punta Blanca and Matina.

Cura Baltasar de Grado, on behalf of his deceased brother Pedro Solano, founded a chaplaincy for 46 annual masses in the Main Church. Francisco de Rojas was designated as the first chaplain, with the grantor serving until Rojas is ordained. The chaplaincy was funded by credits against several individuals.
Alférez Juan Martín Macotela, a resident of Esparza and testamentary executor for Francisco Merelo, granted power of attorney to Juan de Acuña and Cristóbal Fernández Durán.

Luis González de Villalón, a resident of Antequera (Spain), established a dowry of $3665 for his wife, Catalina de Ortega, widow of Captain Francisco de Alfaro. The dowry included a hato in the Ujarraz valley, livestock, agricultural tools, a house in Cartago, and an enslaved Angolan man, an enslaved woman named Victoria, and their four children.
Cura Baltasar de Grado granted general power of attorney to Pedro de Alarcón, the Chief Constable of Panama.

Juan de Senabria Maldonado granted power of attorney to Pedro de Alarcón, Chief Constable of Panama, Contador Diego Rodríguez Grajeda, and Alonso de Carvajal, all from the same vicinity, to charter a 600-tercio frigate to come to Suerre.

Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado, encomendero of half the town of Boaco in Nicaragua, granted power of attorney to Diego de Ocampo Figueroa, who was en route to that province, to collect the tributes owed to him there.

Fernando de Salazar granted power of attorney to Francisco de Castro, a procurator in Guatemala, to seek an office or favor for him in recompense for the services rendered by his father, Captain Justo de Salazar (former Mayor of Nicoya), and the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather of his wife, Ambrosia de Echavarría Navarro.

Diego López de Ortega established a dowry of $1609 for his wife, Ana de Chaves, legitimate daughter of the late Cristóbal de Chaves and María de Alfaro. The dowry, delivered by her brother-in-law Francisco de Chaves, included an enslaved Angolan man named Gaspar.
Alférez Francisco de Chaves, Corregidor of the Chirripó district, granted general power of attorney to Diego López de Ortega and Francisco de Arrieta.
Felipe de Coto entered into an obligation with Governor Gregorio de Sandoval for the sum of $100. The nature of the obligation is not specified beyond the monetary amount.

Juan Barbosa and his wife Beatriz Camelo, along with guarantors Pedro de Mora Salado and Juan Fernández, became indebted to Governor Sandoval for $150. This loan was specifically to pay a debt Barbosa owed to the Royal Treasury as a guarantor for Captain Bartolomé de Enciso, a debt that had led to Barbosa's imprisonment.

Juan de Valverde Zárate, Treasurer of the Santa Cruzada, authorized Manuel Martínez to collect religious bulls from Francisco de Obregón, who was the Treasurer of the same institution in Granada. These bulls were intended for "this city," presumably Cartago.

Bernabé de Segura became indebted to Governor Gregorio de Sandoval for $150, which was a loan to cover a previous guarantee Bernabé had made for Treasurer Bartolomé de Enciso. Cristóbal de Madrigal, Juan Sánchez Crespo, and Cristóbal de Araya served as additional guarantors for Bernabé, each responsible for $50.

Alférez Pedro Enríquez and his wife Juana Chacón, along with Juana's son Alonso de Bonilla acting as guarantor, entered into an obligation with Governor Sandoval for $50. The specific reason for this obligation is not detailed.

Captain José de Sandoval y Ocampo entered into an obligation with his brother, Licenciado Presbítero Alonso de Sandoval, for the significant sum of $1350. The nature of this obligation is not specified.

Governor Sandoval arranged for Juan, an orphaned indigenous boy from Aserrí, approximately twelve years old, to be placed with Francisco Solano, the Sacristán Mayor of the Parish Church, for a period of four years. This arrangement likely served as an apprenticeship or form of indentured service.

Esteban de Torres granted general power of attorney to Francisco de Chaves, who was en route to Guatemala, and to Francisco de Castro, a procurator practicing in the Audiencia of Guatemala. This suggests Torres had legal or administrative matters requiring representation in Guatemala.

Governor Gregorio de Sandoval and his wife Gregoria de Escobar empowered Juan de Somovilla Tejada and Pedro de Retes, residents of Cartagena, to legally demand a recognition of census deed. This action concerned money they had previously entrusted to Fernando Gutiérrez and his son-in-law, Miguel de Olmos.

This entry records the testament of María Cardoso, who was the legitimate daughter of the late Juan Gómez Rico and Doña María Cardoso. She was married to Juan Cascante de Rojas and named her three sons, Luis, Juan, and Gaspar, in her will.

Diego de Ortega conferred general power of attorney for legal disputes to three individuals: Francisco de Chaves, a resident of Cartago; Gregorio Martínez de Porta, a public notary in Granada, Nicaragua; and Francisco de Castro, a procurator in the Audiencia of Guatemala. This indicates Ortega had legal interests spanning multiple locations.

Padre Miguel de Arguedas's testament details his bequests and financial arrangements. He left a blanket and his meager belongings to Antonia de Madrigal, daughter of Alférez Cristóbal de Mena, in gratitude for her services and providing him lodging. The will also describes an income from Jesuit haciendas in Guatemala, established by his father for his ordination, which his sister Juana de San Francisco managed in his absence, and stipulates a memorial of masses upon his death.

Juan de Acuña formally declared that a ranch and estate, which he had purchased for $170 from the estate of Francisca de Bonilla, actually belonged to Isabel de Bonilla. The property, located in Rincón de Purires and Candelaria, included livestock and was bought using Isabel's own funds.

Esteban de Mena granted power of attorney to Francisco de Castro and Francisco de Carvajal, both procurators in Guatemala, to handle all his legal cases. This indicates Mena had ongoing or anticipated legal proceedings requiring representation in Guatemala.

Sergeant Alonso de Sojo, a resident and procurator Síndico of Esparza, conferred general power of attorney upon Alférez Manuel de Flores. Flores held the roles of public notary and notary for the local Governorship, suggesting Sojo's need for broad legal and administrative representation.

Juan de Valverde Zárate, acting as the father and legal administrator for Martín Zárate and Esteban de Mena, ratified a power of attorney previously granted by Esteban earlier in the month. This power was specifically conferred to Francisco de Castro and Francisco de Carvajal, likely for legal matters.
Juan de Valverde Zárate granted general power of attorney to his wife, Magdalena Gutiérrez. This broad authorization would allow her to act on his behalf in various legal and administrative matters.

Juana de Vera, identified as the widow of García Ramiro Corajo, granted general power of attorney to Francisco de Arrieta. This legal authorization would enable Arrieta to act on her behalf in various affairs.

Gobernador don Gregorio de Sandoval arranged for Diego de Estrada, an indigenous person from Aserrí under Pedro de Mora's encomienda, to work for Cristóbal Fernández Durán for one year, earning 16 pesos.
Gobernador don Gregorio de Sandoval arranged for Miguel, an indigenous orphan from Pacaca, to work for Alonso Sánchez, an indigenous shoemaker from Tobosi, for three years.
Catalina de Palacios, widow of Gaspar de Chinchilla, and her legitimate son, Marcos de Chinchilla, granted general power of attorney to Juan Fernández.
Gobernador don Gregorio de Sandoval arranged for Jusepe, an indigenous person from Tucurrique under the Royal Crown, to work for Juan Sánchez Liñán for one year, earning 16 pesos.

Capitán Jerónimo de Retes granted power of attorney to Tomás de Fonseca and Lucas de Samudio, residents of Puerto Belo, to charter a frigate. The frigate was intended to sail to Punta Blanca to load various goods including capados, garlic, anise, and sarsaparilla.

Sargento Mayor Juan Solano granted power of attorney to Pedro de Retes Salazar and Juan de Uriarte Carvallo, residents of Cartagena, to sell 200 pigs. The sale was to take place at Punta Blanca, with each pig priced at 5 pesos.

Gobernador don Gregorio de Sandoval and his wife, doña Gregoria de Escobar, empowered Pedro de Retes Salazar, their son-in-law Diego Martínez Hidalgo, and Alonso de Espinoza, all residents of Cartagena, to request accounts from their agents, Juan de Tejada and Fernando Gutiérrez.

A dowry letter was issued for Roque Jacinto de la Fuente, a resident of León, Nicaragua, in favor of his wife, María Picado de Ortega. María, the legitimate daughter of Baltasar de Ortega and the late Catalina Picado, received a dowry of $680, with arras amounting to $600.

Esteban Rodríguez acted as a guarantor for Manuel Martínez, enabling him to transport a group of indigenous people to Nicaragua via his mule train. The indigenous individuals, including Diego, Gabriel, Francisco, Luis, and Lucas, were from various towns and encomiendas, indicating their labor was being relocated.

Licenciado Juan González Yañes, who previously served as the Beneficiado Priest of the city, granted power of attorney to Juan de Morales, a lieutenant of the Contador and treasurer. This authorization was for Morales to collect the tithes and first fruits that were due to Yañes from his tenure as priest.

Catalina de las Alas, the widow of Agustín de Rojas, granted power of attorney to Juan de Acuña to collect her dowry of 1000 pesos, which had been provided by her father, Capitán Juan de las Alas. Her husband, Agustín de Rojas, had died during a voyage to Panama while transporting a cargo of tobacco and other merchandise.

The Alcalde arranged for two young indigenous orphans, Ana (around 4 years old) and María (around 2 years old), daughters of Elena from Có, to be placed with Catalina de Rueda, a widow. Juan de Araya served as the guarantor for this arrangement.

Juan Fernández provided a guarantee of 33 pesos and 6 reales for Juan Díaz, an indigenous man from Có, to secure his release from prison. This amount covered thirteen years of tributes for Juan Díaz and his wife, Polonia, which had been embargoed from Salvador de Torres's encomienda due to a lack of confirmation.

people_involved: Sargento Pedro Alonso de las Alas
summary: María de Brenes, the widow of Sargento Pedro Alonso de las Alas, granted power of attorney to Francisco de Arrieta. This authorization was for Arrieta to collect her dowry.

The Alcalde arranged for María Dinarte, a mestiza widow of Juan Vanegas, to be placed with Diego de Ocampo Figueroa for a period of four years. Her annual salary for this arrangement was set at 9 pesos, totaling 18 pesos over the term.

Ambrosio de Brenes el mozo granted power of attorney to his brother-in-law, Lucas González, who was traveling to Panama. This authorization was for González to sell Ambrosio's 26-year-old black slave, Domingo Tiznado.
The testament of doña Magdalena de Chaves, the legitimate daughter of the late Cristóbal de Chaves and María de Alfaro, was recorded. She was married to don Gaspar Abarca.
Clara de Flores grants general power of attorney to Juan de Araya.
Alférez Gil de Alvarado, acting as ordinary Mayor and Lieutenant General Governor, places Juan, a 3-year-old mestizo, with Isabel Jiménez de Salas.
Gil de Alvarado places Cristóbal, a 10-year-old orphan indigenous person from San Mateo de Chirripó, who is under the encomienda of Juan Barbosa, with Francisco de Alarcón for 4 years.

Gil de Alvarado places Juana, wife of Antonio (an indigenous person from Curriravá under Diego de Ocampo Figueroa's encomienda), with Alférez Juan Vázquez de Coronado until her husband Antonio returns from Guatemala.

A dowry letter is issued by Bartolomé Sánchez (son of the late Captain Bartolomé Sánchez and Inés Alvarez Pereira) in favor of his wife, Isabel de la Jara (daughter of Captain Miguel de Villalobos and Isabel de Carvajal). The dowry is valued at $536.4 reales and includes a promissory note from Ignacio de Artavia, the wife's brother-in-law.
Alcalde Diego López de Ortega places María, a mulata daughter of María (an indigenous woman from Barba under Francisco de Chaves' encomienda), with Juan Blasco until she marries or comes of age.

Jerónimo de Retes grants general power of attorney to Gregorio Martínez de Porta, a scribe in Granada (Nicaragua), and Diego de Robles, also from Granada. The special power is to charter a frigate to travel from Granada to Puerto Belo, Cartagena, and then to Punta Blanca and Matina.

Cura Baltasar de Grado, on behalf of his deceased brother Pedro Solano, establishes a chaplaincy for 46 annual masses. Francisco de Rojas is designated as the first chaplain, with provisions for succession if he doesn't get ordained or dies, prioritizing relatives of Juan Solano (the Cura's father) who are priests. The chaplaincy is funded by 1050 pesos in credits against Francisco de Ocampo Geolffín (deceased), Cristóbal Zapata de Salazar and his wife Ana de Sandoval y Ocampo, and Vasco Solano, with Juan Cascante de Rojas and his descendants as patrons.
Alférez Juan Martín Macotela, a resident of Esparza and executor of Francisco Merelo's will, grants power of attorney to Juan de Acuña and Cristóbal Fernández Durán.

A dowry letter is issued by Luis González de Villalón, a resident of Antequera (Spain), in favor of his wife Catalina de Ortega, widow of Captain Francisco de Alfaro. The dowry, valued at $3665, includes a ranch in the Ujarraz valley, various livestock, farming tools, a house in Cartago, and an enslaved Angolan man with his wife Victoria and their four children. Diego López de Ortega, Catalina's brother, is to deliver these assets.
Cura Baltasar de Grado grants power of attorney to Pedro de Alarcón, the Chief Constable of Panama.

Juan de Senabria Maldonado grants power to Pedro de Alarcón (Chief Constable of Panama), Contador Diego Rodríguez Grajeda, and Alonso de Carvajal to charter a frigate of 600 tercios to come to Suerre.
Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado, encomendero of half the town of Boaco in Nicaragua, grants power to Diego de Ocampo Figueroa, who is en route to that province, to collect due tributes.

Fernando de Salazar grants power to Francisco de Castro, a procurator in Guatemala, to seek an office or favor for him. This request is in recompense for the services rendered by his father, Captain Justo de Salazar (former Mayor of Nicoya), and the ancestors of his wife, Ambrosia de Echavarría Navarro.

A dowry letter is issued by Diego López de Ortega in favor of his wife, Ana de Chaves (legitimate daughter of the late Cristóbal de Chaves and María de Alfaro). The dowry is $1609, delivered by her brother Francisco de Chaves, and includes an Angolan enslaved man named Gaspar ($400). The arras are $1000.
Alférez Francisco de Chaves, Corregidor of the Chirripó district, grants general power of attorney to Diego López de Ortega and Francisco de Arrieta.

An unnamed woman's husband left over 16 years ago for Peru. Her daughter, Doña Eugenia, married Alférez Tomás Calvo. The family's assets and debts include a fanega of potatoes, a gold Christ pledged to Francisco de Arrieta for 20 reales, a gold ring with an emerald pledged to Pe. Baltasar de Grado for six reales, and gold earrings pledged to Juan Sánchez Crespo.

The Alcalde arranged for Miguel, a mulato son of Inés, a meztiza, to be placed with Gabriel López, a black slave and blacksmith owned by María de Ortega, for a period of 6 years. Bernabé de Segura acted as guarantor for Gabriel López, who could not obligate himself.

Don José de Sandoval Ocampo and his wife Doña Isabel de Obando had obligated themselves to Licenciado Baltasar de Grado for 260 pesos, mortgaging a hato called San Antonio near Curriravá. Don José sold this hato to his brother and cuñado, Diego de Ocampo Figueroa, as payment for his inheritance from their father, Capitán Francisco de Ocampo Golfín. Consequently, the mortgage was transferred to two other hatos, San Juan Bautista and Santa Olalla, located across the Río Grande on the royal road to Esparza, near El Aguacate.
Juan López de Ortega committed to Valentín La Carnero for 308 pesos and 5 reales, which he agreed to pay in bizcocho delivered to Caldera.

Marcos de Arciniega Carrillo, a native of Córdova, Spain, and son of Bartolomé de Molina Arciniega and Doña Luisa Carrillo, provided a dowry of $430 to his wife, Doña Antonia Calvo, who is the legitimate daughter of Alférez Tomás Calvo, the depositario general.

Licenciado Baltasar de Castro, the priest of the Main Parish Church in this city, granted power of attorney to Marcos Machado, a deacon cleric, and Don Domingo de Echavarría, a subdeacon cleric, both residing in Nicaragua. This power was for them to collect one year's salary, amounting to 50,000 maravedís, from the Royal Treasury of León, which had become due last March.

people_involved: Padre predicador fray Martín de Guevara
summary: Doña Catalina de Chaves, the legitimate daughter of the deceased Cristóbal de Chaves and María de Alfaro, made her will. She is married to Capitán Pedro de Córdova, the Corregidor of the Tierra Adentro district, and named her children Doña Agustina, Doña Antonia, Don Fernando, and Don Jerónimo. She also bequeathed forty pesos in fideicomiso to Padre predicador fray Martín de Guevara, the guardian of the San Francisco convent.

Doña Gregoria de Escobar, the widow, executor, and sole heir of Gobernador Don Gregorio Sandoval, granted power of attorney to Juan de Morales, a Royal Official Judge. This power allowed him to collect 1300 pesos from the Royal Treasury of León, which were owed to her deceased husband as outstanding salaries.

Doña Gregoria de Escobar granted power of attorney to Juan de Morales, who was traveling to Nicaragua, to collect $200 from Licenciado Alvaro de Acuña. Acuña, who was the priest of Esparza and now of Masatepe, owed this amount to the estate of Doña Gregoria's deceased husband, Don Gregorio de Sandoval, as per a document dated September 18, 1645.
José de Moya granted power of attorney to Bartolomé Ruiz, a resident of Panamá, to charter a frigate. The frigate was intended to arrive in Caldera the following April.

Domingo Jiménez Maldonado, a merchant residing in this city, granted power of attorney to Bartolomé Ruiz López, a resident of Panamá. This power was to charter a frigate to arrive in Caldera by mid-June of the coming year.
Doña Gregoria de Escobar, the widow of Don Gregorio de Sandoval, granted general power of attorney for lawsuits to Juan García Vellido and Miguel de Artavia, who are procuradores in Guatemala.

people_involved: Pe. Fray Cristóbal de San Diego
Capitán Don José de Sandoval Ocampo
summary: Doña Antonia Vázquez de Coronado, widow of Sebastián Pereira Cardoso, made her will, requesting burial in the main church in her mother Doña Andrea Vázquez de Coronado's sepulchre. She owed 20 reales to Pe. Fray Cristóbal de San Diego. Her executors were her brother Ayudante Alonso Peláez, her cuñado Jerónimo de Retes, and Juan de Acuña. Having no living legitimate daughters, she named her grandchildren, Don Sebastián de Sandoval Ocampo and Doña Inés de Sandoval (children of Capitán Don José de Sandoval Ocampo and her deceased daughter Doña Isabel de Obando), as her heirs.
Doña Gregoria de Escobar, the widow of Don Gregorio de Sandoval, granted general power of attorney to Alonso de Bonilla.

Jerónimo de Retes granted power of attorney to Juan García Vellido, a procurador in Guatemala, to reclaim his runaway slave, Francisco Valeriano. Francisco, a 27-year-old criollo, was reportedly apprehended in Gracias a Dios under a false name, and the power also allowed for his sale.

Andrés López de Céspedes and Alonso Peláez, as Alcaldes, along with Jerónimo de Retes, the Alguacil mayor, and Tomás Calvo, the depositario general, acting on behalf of the Justice and Cabildo of Cartago, granted power of attorney to Juan García Vellido, a procurador in Guatemala.

Pedro de Campos Quirós, the legitimate son of Luis Campos Quirós and Doña Beatriz Gallardo, former residents of Medellín in Extremadura, provided a dowry of $3708 to his wife, Doña Bárbara Rodríguez Altamirano. Doña Bárbara is the legitimate daughter of the deceased Capitán Antonio Rodríguez Moreno and Doña Inés de Benavides Solano. A portion of this dowry, $500 in reales, 4 platters, and 1 jar, was a donation from Pe. Baltasar de Grado.
A power of attorney is granted to request the sale of adobe and tile houses that belonged to Captain Francisco de Alfaro, on which Catalina Gutiérrez, the grantor's grandmother, founded a chaplaincy.

Governor Sandoval arranges for Diego de Estrada, an indigenous person from Aserrí under the encomienda of Pedro de Mora, to be indentured to Cristóbal Fernández Durán for one year with a salary of 16 pesos.
Governor Sandoval arranges for Miguel, an indigenous orphan from Pacaca and son of Calixto de Salas, to be indentured to Alonso Sánchez, an indigenous shoemaker from Tobosi, for three years.
Catalina de Palacios, widow of Gaspar de Chinchilla, and her legitimate son Marcos de Chinchilla, grant general power of attorney to Juan Fernández.
Governor Sandoval arranges for Jusepe, an indigenous person from Tucurrique under the Royal Crown, to be indentured to Juan Sánchez Liñán for one year with a salary of 16 pesos.

Captain Jerónimo de Retes grants power of attorney to Tomás de Fonseca and Lucas de Samudio, residents of Puerto Belo, to charter a frigate to come to Punta Blanca to load capons, garlic, anise, sarsaparilla, and other goods.

Sergeant Major Juan Solano grants power of attorney to Pedro de Retes Salazar and Juan de Uriarte Carvallo, residents of Cartagena, to sell 200 heads of swine for him, located in Punta Blanca, at a price of 5 pesos each.

Governor Don Gregorio de Sandoval and his wife Doña Gregoria de Escobar grant power of attorney to Pedro de Retes Salazar, Diego Martínez Hidalgo (their son-in-law), and Alonso de Espinoza, residents of Cartagena, to demand accounts from Juan de Tejada and Fernando Gutiérrez, their previous attorneys.

Roque Jacinto de la Fuente, a resident of León (Nicaragua), issues a dowry letter in favor of his wife María Picado de Ortega, the legitimate daughter of Baltasar de Ortega and the deceased Catalina Picado, for $680, with a bridal gift (arras) of $600.

Esteban Rodríguez acts as a guarantor for Manuel Martínez, allowing him to transport a group of indigenous people to Nicaragua with his pack train. The indigenous individuals are Diego (from Guicase, encomienda of Juan Solano), Gabriel (from Corroci, encomienda of Don José de Sandoval Ocampo), Francisco (from Orosi, vacant from Don Diego de Sojo), Luis (from Quircó, encomienda of Francisco de Chaves), and Lucas (from Có, encomienda of Catalina Palacios).

Licenciado Juan González Yañes, former Beneficed Priest of Cartago, grants power of attorney to Juan de Morales, Lieutenant Accountant and Treasurer, to collect the tithes owed to him for the time he served as priest.

Catalina de las Alas, widow of Agustín de Rojas, grants power of attorney to Juan de Acuña to collect her dowry of 1000 pesos, which was given to her by her father, Captain Juan de las Alas. Agustín de Rojas died during a trip to Panamá, where he was transporting a cargo of tobacco and other goods.

The Mayor arranges for Ana (about 4 years old) and María (two years old), daughters of Elena, an indigenous woman from Có, and fatherless orphans, to be indentured to Catalina de Rueda, a widow. Juan de Araya acts as guarantor.

Juan Fernández acts as guarantor for the indigenous man Juan Díaz from the town of Có, for 33 pesos and 6 reales, which represent thirteen years of tributes for him and his wife Polonia, so that he can be released from prison. Their tributes, from the encomienda of Salvador de Torres, had been embargoed due to lack of confirmation.

people_involved: Sargento Pedro Alonso de las Alas
summary: María de Brenes, widow of Sergeant Pedro Alonso de las Alas, grants power of attorney to Francisco de Arrieta to collect her dowry.
The Mayor arranges for María Dinarte, a mestiza and widow of Juan Vanegas, to be indentured to Diego de Ocampo Figueroa for four years with an annual salary of 9 pesos and 18 reales.
Ambrosio de Brenes the younger grants power of attorney to his brother-in-law Lucas González, who is traveling to Panamá, to sell Domingo Tiznado, his 26-year-old enslaved Black man.
Doña Magdalena de Chaves, legitimate daughter of the deceased Cristóbal de Chaves and María de Alfaro, makes her will. She is married to Don Gaspar Abarca.
Vasco Solano made a donation of $96. Alonso de Sandoval donated animals and effects valued at $1360, which included houses where Father Baltasar de Grado currently resides.
The Alcalde arranged an 'asiento' (placement or indentured service) for Ana, a mestiza woman.
The Alcalde arranged an 'asiento' for Verónica, an indigenous woman.
Doña Antonia Vázquez de Coronado, a 52-year-old widow, was placed for 14 pesos, with Don José de Sandoval Ocampo serving as her guarantor.

people_involved: Capn. Antonio de Amaviscar y Loizaga
summary: Doña María de Lumbides discovered that her husband, Pedro Garay, was previously married in Guatemala to Ana de Orduña. Garay confessed and fled Cartago, prompting Doña María to grant power of attorney to Captain Antonio de Amaviscar y Loizaga and her brother Juan de Lumbides to pursue legal action.

Two indigenous orphans, a 17-year-old girl and Agustina (4 years old), daughters of the deceased Dierd Chique and Melchora from Atirro, were placed with Esteban Rodríguez. The elder was placed for three years, and Agustina until she marries or comes of age.
The Alcalde arranged an 'asiento' for María Estacio, a mulata and daughter of the deceased Juan Estacio and Luisa Flores, for one year and $14.

Juan de Olivar and his wife María de Brenes obligated themselves for 200 pesos at 5% interest to the Capellanía founded by Vasco Solano. They mortgaged a ranch with 200 cattle and 20 mares, located near Cartago and Barba, by the Río de la Bermuda, bordering the road and Diego Jiménez's house.

Juan de Herrera, with Juan de Morales as his guarantor, obligated himself to Don Pedro de Córdova for 100 pesos, borrowed for the dispatch of a frigate from Tierra Firme to Matina. This obligation was cancelled on January 6th of the following year by José de Moya, Córdova's attorney.

Salvador de Torres made a codicil, appointing his son Esteban de Torres as an executor in addition to his father-in-law, Gaspar Núñez de Oviedo. The codicil also noted that his daughter Elvira de Torres's husband, Juan de Aguilera, illegally sold half of the Mata Redonda ranch to Pedro de Santiago Galindo.

Don José de Sandoval Ocampo granted power of attorney to Don Diego de Escobar, a scribe of the Audiencia of Guatemala, to request an office or position for him, citing the services of his father and grandfather.

Lucas González and his wife Jerónima Tomasina de Brenes recognized a censo of 200 pesos in favor of the Confraternity of Nuestra Señora de la Concepción. They mortgaged an estate near Cartago, which was previously auctioned after Juan Pérez de Viguera's death and was subject to this sum due to an imposition made in 1613 by Diego de Aguilar and Leonor Jiménez.

A dowry letter was issued for Juan de Padilla, son of the late Juan de Padilla and Doña María de Carvajal, and his wife Doña Jerónima de Segura, daughter of Bernabé de Segura and Isabel de Morales. The dowry was $711, with arras (earnest money) of $300.

A dowry letter was issued for Alférez Don Francisco Ramiro Corajo, son of the late García Ramiro Corajo and Doña Juana de Vera, and his wife Doña María de Retes, daughter of Regidor Jerónimo de Retes and Doña María Vázquez de Coronado. The dowry was 7000 pesos, including various animals.
Doña Eugenia's husband had departed for Peru over 16 years prior to this record. It was known that he was residing there.
Doña Eugenia was married to Alférez Tomás Calvo. This relationship is noted in the context of her family and possessions.

Doña Eugenia pawned several valuable items: a gold Christ to Francisco de Arrieta for 20 reales, a gold ring with an emerald to Padre Baltasar de Grado for 6 reales, and gold earrings to Juan Sánchez Crespo.

An Alcalde arranged for Miguel, a mulato son of Inés, to serve as an asiento with Gabriel López, a black slave and blacksmith owned by María de Ortega, for a period of six years. Bernabé de Segura acted as guarantor for Gabriel López, who could not legally obligate himself.

Don José de Sandoval Ocampo and Doña Isabel de Obando changed the mortgage on a hato near Curriravá, originally securing a 260-peso debt to Licenciado Baltasar de Grado. The initial hato, sold to Diego de Ocampo Figueroa as part of his inheritance from Captain Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, was replaced with two new hatos, San Juan Bautista and Santa Olalla, located beyond the Río Grande on the royal road to Esparza.
Juan López de Ortega formally obligated himself to Valentín La Carnero for 308 pesos and 5 reales. This debt was to be paid in hardtack, delivered to Caldera.
A dowry letter was issued for Marcos de Arciniega Carrillo, a native of Córdova, Spain, and Doña Antonia Calvo, the legitimate daughter of Alférez Tomás Calvo. The dowry amounted to $430.00.

Licenciado Baltasar de Castro, the priest of the Main Parish Church in Cartago, granted power to Marcos Machado and Don Domingo de Echavarría, both clerics residing in Nicaragua. This power allowed them to collect a year's worth of his salary, totaling 50,000 maravedís, from the Royal Treasury of León.

people_involved: Padre predicador fray Martín de Guevara
summary: Doña Catalina de Chaves, daughter of the late Cristobal de Chaves and María de Alfaro, made her last will and testament. Married to Captain Pedro de Córdova, she named her children Agustina, Antonia, Fernando, and Jerónimo, and left 40 pesos in trust to Fray Martín de Guevara, guardian of the San Francisco convent.

Doña Gregoria de Escobar, widow and sole heir of Governor Don Gregorio Sandoval, granted power to Juan de Morales, a Royal Official Judge. This power authorized him to collect 1300 pesos owed to her late husband as outstanding salary from the Royal Treasury of León.

Doña Gregoria de Escobar empowered Juan de Morales, who was traveling to Nicaragua, to collect 200 pesos from Licenciado Alvaro de Acuña. This debt was owed to her late husband, Don Gregorio de Sandoval, as documented in an 18 September 1645 deed.
José de Moya granted power to Bartolomé Ruiz, a resident of Panamá, to charter a frigate. The frigate was intended to arrive in Caldera the following April.
Domingo Jiménez Maldonado, a merchant residing in Cartago, empowered Bartolomé Ruiz, a resident of Panamá, to charter a frigate. This frigate was to arrive in Caldera by mid-June.
Doña Gregoria de Escobar, widow of Don Gregorio de Sandoval, granted general power for legal proceedings to Juan García Vellido and Miguel de Artavia. Both individuals were procurators in Guatemala.

people_involved: Pe. Fray Cristóbal de San Diego
summary: Doña Antonia Vázquez de Coronado, widow of Sebastián Pereira Cardoso, made her will, requesting burial in the main church next to her mother, Doña Andrea Vázquez de Coronado. She named her grandchildren, Don Sebastián de Sandoval Ocampo and Doña Inés de Sandoval (children of Captain Don José de Sandoval Ocampo and the late Doña Isabel de Obando), as her heirs, and appointed Alonso Peláez, Jerónimo de Retes, and Juan de Acuña as executors.
Doña Gregoria de Escobar, widow of Don Gregorio de Sandoval, granted general power to Alonso de Bonilla. This power was likely for administrative or legal matters.

Jerónimo de Retes empowered Juan García Vellido, a procurator in Guatemala, to reclaim his runaway slave, Francisco Valeriano. Francisco, a 27-year-old creole, was reportedly captured in Gracias a Dios under a false name, and Vellido was also authorized to sell him.

Andrés López de Céspedes and Alonso Peláez (Alcaldes), Jerónimo de Retes (Alguacil mayor), and Alférez Tomás Calvo (depositario general), acting on behalf of the Justice and Cabildo of Cartago, granted power to Juan García Vellido, a procurator in Guatemala.

A dowry letter was issued for Pedro de Campos Quirós, son of Luis Campos Quirós and Doña Beatriz Gallardo from Medellín, Spain, and Doña Bárbara Rodríguez Altamirano, daughter of the late Captain Antonio Rodríguez Moreno and Doña Inés de Benavides Solano. The dowry included $3708.00, with $500.00 in reales, 4 plates, and 1 jar donated by Padre Baltasar de Grado.
Pedro Manzano, a free mulatto, committed to serving Sergeant Alonso de Vargas for one year in exchange for 16 pesos.

Jerónimo Leal and his guarantor, Doña Isabel Cardoso, a widow, committed to pay Sergeant Francisco Hurtado and his son Nicolás Hurtado, residents of Panama, 321 pesos and 5 reales. The payment would be made in various goods delivered to Caldera.
Jerónimo Leal and his wife María Yañes sold their 11-year-old Creole enslaved woman named Antonia to Captain Hernando de Carrión for 150 pesos.
Antonio de Orozco and his wife Ana Vázquez de Santiago incurred an obligation to Juan de Valverde Zárate for 145 pesos.

Diego de Ocampo granted a cattle ranch, including a house, corrals, 204 cattle, 5 horses, and land previously donated by Juan de Senabria Maldonado and Juana Moscoso, to Rodrigo Calderón de Anguas and his wife Isidora de Zambrano for 500 pesos. The property was located on the road to Aserrí, bordering Melchor Masís's ranch and the Aguacaliente river.

Francisco de Sosa, a resident of Cartago and native of Lisbon, made his will. He was the legitimate son of the late Franc? Díaz de Sosa and María Francisco, and was married in Lisbon to the late Luisa Francisca. Father Baltasar de Castro, a priest of Cartago, was named his executor.
Don Francisco Ramiro Corajo stood as guarantor for Don Francisco de Alvarado, who had been appointed by the King as Corregidor of the district of San Bernardino de Quepo.
Francisco de Sosa executed a codicil to his will, which was previously recorded on folio 8.

Hernando de Carrión and Don Gil de Alvarado stood as guarantors for Francisco de Chaves, to whom Gaspar Vidal, treasurer of the Santa Cruzada residing in El Realejo, had promised to send the Holy Bull for publication in the province.
Rodrigo Calderón granted general power of attorney for lawsuits and collections to Juan Fernández.
Ignacio de Aguilar and his wife Doña Agustina de Ulloa sold a plantain field in the Virilla River valley, behind Gaspar Núñez de Oviedo's ranch, to Don Diego de Ocampo Figueroa for 18 pesos.
Captain Gabriel de Vargas Machuca and his wife Doña Isabel de Flores Quiñones entered into an obligation.
Vasco Solano made a donation of $96, possibly related to a larger sum of $300 mentioned in the registry.
The Alcalde officially assigned Ana, a mestiza, to an unspecified party or service.
The Alcalde officially assigned Verónica, an indigenous woman, to an unspecified party or service.

Juan de Olivar and his wife María de Brenes pledged 200 pesos to the Capellanía founded by Vasco Solano. They mortgaged a ranch located about six leagues from Cartago and one league from Barba, near the Río de la Bermuda and adjacent to Diego Jiménez's house.
Alonso de Sandoval made a donation consisting of animals and other effects.
The houses where Father Baltasar de Grado currently resides were valued at $1360.
Doña Antonia Vázquez de Coronado, a 52-year-old widow, was involved in a transaction for 14 pesos, with Don José de Sandoval Ocampo acting as her guarantor.

people_involved: Capn. Antonio de Amaviscar y Loizaga
summary: Doña María de Lumbides granted power of attorney to Capn. Antonio de Amaviscar y Loizaga and her brother Juan de Lumbides. This action was taken because her husband, Pedro Garay, had married her five years prior while already married to Ana de Orduña in Guatemala, a fact Garay confessed before fleeing Cartago.

The Alcalde assigned Ana, 17, and Agustina, 4, who were orphans of the deceased indigenous couple Dierd Chique and Melchora from Atirro, to Esteban Rodríguez. Ana was assigned for three years, and Agustina until she marries or comes of age.
The Alcalde assigned María Estacio, a mulata and orphan of the deceased Juan Estacio and Luisa Flores, for one year for $14.

Juan de Herrera, with Juan de Morales as his guarantor, borrowed 100 pesos from Don Pedro de Córdova to dispatch a frigate from Tierra Firme to Puerto de Matina. The debt was later cancelled on January 6th of the following year by José de Moya, Córdova's attorney.

Salvador de Torres' codicil named his son Esteban de Torres as an executor alongside his father-in-law Gaspar Núñez de Oviedo. The codicil also noted that his daughter Elvira de Torres' husband, Juan de Aguilera, had illegally sold half of the Mata Redonda ranch to Pedro de Santiago Galindo.

Don José de Sandoval Ocampo granted power of attorney to Don Diego de Escobar, a notary of the Audiencia of Guatemala, to request an office or position for him based on the services of his father and grandfather.

Lucas González and his wife Jerónima Tomasina de Brenes acknowledged a 200-peso debt to the Cofradía de Ntra. Sra. de la Concepción, mortgaging a ranch near Cartago. This property, previously owned by Juan Pérez de Viguera, had been subject to this debt since an imposition made by Diego de Aguilar and Leonor Jiménez in 1613.

Juan de Padilla, a resident of Cartago and son of the deceased Juan de Padilla and Doña María de Carvajal, issued a dowry letter for his wife Doña Jerónima de Segura, daughter of Bernabé de Segura and Isabel de Morales, totaling $711, with an additional $300 in arras.

people_involved: El Alférez Don Francisco Ramiro Corajo
summary: Alférez Don Francisco Ramiro Corajo, son of the deceased García Ramiro Corajo and Doña Juana de Vera, issued a dowry letter for his wife Doña María de Retes, daughter of Regidor Jerónimo de Retes and Doña María Vázquez de Coronado, totaling 7000 pesos, including livestock.

A loan of 100 pesos was made to the Cofradía de Ntra. Sra. del Rosario, secured by straw houses in Cartago. These houses were originally owned by Hernando Farfán and Catalina de Rueda, sold in 1618 to Captain Antonio de Amabiscar and Alférez Juan de Gamboa, and later auctioned off due to Gamboa's death and Amabiscar's absence.

Antonio González provided a guarantee for don José de Sandoval Ocampo to transport four indigenous individuals (Tomás, Francisco, Diego, and Esteban) to Nicaragua. The agreement was formalized in the town of Barba, with the indigenous people originating from Ujarraci and Có.

Felipe de Coto acted as guarantor for María de Aguilar, a widow, to enable her to send the indigenous man Francisco Pinca from Curriravá to Nicaragua. Pinca's mission was to bring back mules for Antonio de Orozco, María de Aguilar's son-in-law, to travel on.

Juan Cascante de Rojas provided a guarantee for Captain Juan Solano to send four indigenous men to Nicaragua. The individuals included Juan Solano from Aserrí, Francisco Gutiérrez and Juan Matías from Curriravá, and Juan Cordero, a naborío.

María de la Portilla, widow of Sergeant Juan de Mora, sold her enslaved mulatto named Juan, approximately 14 years old, for 200 pesos. The buyers were her son, Alférez Pedro de Mora Salado, and his wife, doña Margarita de Flores.

Captain Diego de Ocampo Figueroa acted as guarantor for don Juan Solano de Echeverría to take three indigenous men to Nicaragua as muleteers. The individuals were Francisco Nicoya from Barba, Marcos (a naborío), and Andrés from Quircó.

Catalina de Mora, legitimate daughter of the late Sergeant Major Juan de Mora and María de la Portilla, granted power to her husband, Alférez Francisco García Cordero, to make her will. She named her eleven legitimate children as heirs and appointed her husband and her brother, Pedro de Mora Salado, as executors.
Luis Machado provided a guarantee for Juan de Morales Miranda to take the indigenous man Tomás Quirós, a 'payegua,' with mules by land to the city of Panama.

Juan de Morales Miranda and his wife, Beatriz Méndez, incurred a debt of 154 pesos to Captain Diego de Ocampo Figueroa. The debt was payable in August of the same year and was subsequently cancelled on August 30, 1648.
Juan de Vida Martell, residing in Cartago and en route to Panama, incurred a debt of 280 pesos to Rodrigo de Calderón. This debt was for the purchase price of 10 tame mules.
Pedro de Campos Quirós acted as guarantor for don José de Sandoval Ocampo to send two indigenous men, Francisco and Andrés from the town of Barba, to Nicaragua.
Pedro de Campos Quirós acted as guarantor for don Juan de Senabria Maldonado to send two indigenous men, Miguel from Curriravá and Jusepe from Tobosi, to Nicaragua.
José de Moya provided a guarantee for don Juan de Senabria Maldonado, who had been appointed as Corregidor for the district of Turrialba.

people_involved: Licdo. Presb? don Alonso de Sandoval
summary: Domingo Jiménez Maldonado and his wife, doña Juana de Sojo Pereira, sold their enslaved mulatto, Diego, approximately 20 years old, for 250 pesos. The buyer was Licenciado Presbítero don Alonso de Sandoval.

María de Ortega, widow of Jerónimo Felipe, donated her enslaved criolla named María, approximately 7 years old, to her granddaughter, doña Juana de Ortega. Doña Juana was the legitimate daughter of Alférez Diego López de Ortega and doña Ana de Chaves.
Alférez Francisco García Cordero granted general power for lawsuits to Francisco de Arrieta and Juan López de Ortega.
Tomás Calvo, the general depositary, incurred a debt of 100 pesos to don Gil de Alvarado. This debt was scheduled to be paid by January of the following year.
Pedro Manzano, a free mulatto, committed to serving Sergeant Alonso de Vargas for one year in exchange for 16 pesos.

Jerónimo Leal and his guarantor, Doña Isabel Cardoso, obligated themselves to Sergeant Francisco Hurtado and his son Nicolás Hurtado, residents of Panamá, for 321 pesos and 5 reales, to be paid in various goods delivered to Caldera.
Jerónimo Leal and his wife María Yañes sold their 11-year-old Creole enslaved woman named Antonia to Captain Hernando de Carrión for 150 pesos.
Antonio de Orozco and his wife Ana Vázquez de Santiago obligated themselves in favor of Juan de Valverde Zárate for 145 pesos.

Diego de Ocampo granted a cattle ranch, including a house, corrals, 204 cattle, and 5 horses, to Rodrigo Calderón de Anguas and his wife Isidora de Zambrano for 500 pesos. The property, originally a donation from Juan de Senabria Maldonado and Juana Moscoso, bordered Melchor Masís's ranch on the road to Aserrí near the Aguacaliente river.

Francisco de Sosa, a resident of Cartago and native of Lisbon, made his will. He was the legitimate son of the late Francisco Díaz de Sosa and María Francisco, and was married in Lisbon to the late Luisa Francisca, with whom he had no children. Father Baltasar de Castro was named his executor.
Don Francisco Ramiro Corajo vouched for Don Francisco de Alvarado, who had been appointed by the King as Corregidor of the district of San Bernardino de Quepo.
Francisco de Sosa made a codicil to his will, which was recorded on folio 8.

Hernando de Carrión and Don Gil de Alvarado vouched for Francisco de Chaves, to whom Gaspar Vidal, treasurer of the Santa Cruzada residing in El Realejo, had promised to send the Holy Bull of the latest preaching for publication in the province.
Rodrigo Calderón granted general power of attorney for lawsuits and collections to Juan Fernández.
Ignacio de Aguilar and his wife Doña Agustina de Ulloa sold a plantain field in the Virilla River valley, behind Gaspar Núñez de Oviedo's ranch, to Don Diego de Ocampo Figueroa for 18 pesos.
Captain Gabriel de Vargas Machuca and his wife Doña Isabel de Flores Quiñones obligated themselves to an unspecified agreement.
An unnamed grantor grants power of attorney for lawsuits to Juan Fernández. This is the first of two powers of attorney granted on this day by the same individual.

The same unnamed grantor grants general power of attorney to Licenciado Presbítero Alonso de Sandoval and to Doña Eugenia de Abarca, who is the grantor's wife. This grant is made without prejudice to the previous power of attorney issued earlier on the same day.
Doña Juana de Vera, the widow of García Ramiro Corajo, grants general power of attorney for lawsuits to Juan Fernández. This document formalizes her legal representation.

Juan de Vida Martell, a native of Sevilla, establishes a dowry of $2,297 for his wife, Doña Juana de Ortega, who is the daughter of Diego López de Ortega and Doña Ana de Chaves. The dowry includes an enslaved Creole woman named María, 10 years old, valued at $300, and a herd of cattle near Baltasar de Ortega's property, also valued at $300, along with arras of $500.

people_involved: Don Juan de Chaves y Mendoza
summary: Luis Machado, who has served as a public and Cabildo scribe for 18 years and is currently a lieutenant of the Royal Official Judges, resigns his office due to illness, age, and incapacitation. Despite being poor and burdened with a wife and children, he is unable to continue his duties. Governor Don Juan de Chaves y Mendoza forwards his resignation to the Fiscal of the Audiencia of Guatemala for review.

Diego de Peñaranda, a natural son of Juan de Peñaranda and a resident of Cartago, makes his will. He acknowledges debts from card games to Tomás Calvo ($50) and Juan Sánchez Crespo ($65), and leaves an enslaved mulatto blacksmith named Diego de Sojo, who is an official blacksmith. He also names his five natural daughters: Francisca de Peñaranda (married to Gaspar de los Ríos), Ana García, María de Sojo (married to Luis Vázquez), Andrea García (married to Cristobal López), and Jerónima de Avila, stipulating that Diego de Sojo's earnings should be distributed among them or that Diego can purchase his freedom for 500 pesos. His executors are Father Alonso de Sandoval and his brother, Sergeant Alonso de Sojo.

Juan Gómez de Bonilla establishes a dowry of $616 for his wife, Doña María de Villalobos Jara. Doña María is the legitimate daughter of the late Captain Miguel de Villalobos and Doña Isabel de Carvajal. The dowry funds are provided by Doña María's mother and her brother, José Villalobos Jara.

Gabriel de Vargas Machuca and his wife, Doña Isabel de Flores, obligate themselves to the Confraternity of the Conception for $200 at 5% annual interest. They mortgage their house in Cartago, which borders properties of Father Baltasar de Grado, Ana de Espinosa, and Gabriel de Aguilar, and already has a $100 mortgage to the Confraternity of the Rosario. They also mortgage a ranch with 80 cattle, corrals, and horses, previously owned by Luisa Hernández and near Catalina de Palacios's property. The funds were provided by the executors of Alférez Vasco Solano's will (Licenciado Baltasar de Grado, Don Alonso Sandoval, Capitán Juan Solano, and Capitán Diego de Ocampo Figueroa) as a legacy to the Confraternity to help marry orphans.
Ambrosio de Brenes makes a codicil to his will. He mentions his living wife, Francisca Jiménez, his son Mateo Jiménez (among others), and his son-in-law, Lucas González.

Don José Sandoval de Ocampo obligates himself to the estate, executors, and heirs of Vasco Solano for $100 at 5% annual interest. He mortgages a ranch across the Río Grande de la Hamaca, containing 500 mares, 9 stud donkeys, and 600 cattle, as well as his adobe and tile house in Cartago. His house is adjacent to Diego de Ocampo Sandoval's property and across the street from Alonso Peláez's, and already carries two mortgages: one for $260 whose interest is paid to Father Baltasar de Grado, and another for $300 to the Chaplaincy of Alonso Gómez Macotela.

Jerónimo de Retes, Diego de Ocampo Figueroa, Andrés López de Céspedes, Gabriel de Vargas Machuca, and Juan de Morales Miranda ratify their surety for Luis Machado, who serves as lieutenant accountant and royal official judge-treasurer, for a total of $1,400. This ratification is prompted by a new appointment following Andrés Gil de Palacios's assumption of the Treasurer position for Nicaragua and Costa Rica.

people_involved: Cofradía de Ntra. Sra. del Rosario
summary: A loan of 100 pesos at 5% annual interest was secured for the Confraternity of Our Lady of the Rosary, imposed on straw houses in Cartago. These houses, originally owned by the late Hernando Farfán and his wife Catalina de Rueda (according to a 1618 deed), were sold to Captain Antonio de Amabiscar and Alférez Juan de Gamboa. Following Gamboa's death and Amabiscar's absence, the houses were auctioned off, and the current grantor acquired them.

Antonio González provided a guarantee for José de Sandoval Ocampo to transport four indigenous individuals, Tomás (naborío), Francisco, Diego (from Ujarrás), and Esteban (from Có), to Nicaragua. This transaction was recorded in the town of Barba.

Felipe de Coto provided a guarantee for María de Aguilar, a widow, enabling her to send the indigenous man Francisco Pinca from Curriravá to Nicaragua. Pinca's mission was to transport mules for Antonio de Orozco, who is María de Aguilar's son-in-law.

Juan Cascante de Rojas acted as guarantor for Captain Juan Solano, allowing him to send four indigenous men, Juan Solano (from Aserrí), Francisco Gutiérrez, Juan Matías (from Curriravá), and Juan Cordero (naborío), to Nicaragua.
María de la Portilla, widow of Sergeant Mayor Juan de Mora, sold her 14-year-old mulatto slave named Juan to her son, Alférez Pedro de Mora Salado, and his wife, Margarita de Flores, for 200 pesos.

Captain Diego de Ocampo Figueroa provided a guarantee for Juan Solano de Echeverría to transport three indigenous men, Francisco Nicoya (from Barba), Marcos (naborío), and Andrés (from Quircó), to Nicaragua to work as muleteers.

Catalina de Mora, legitimate daughter of the late Sergeant Major Juan de Mora and María de la Portilla, granted power to her husband, Alférez Francisco García Cordero, to execute her will. She designated her numerous legitimate children as heirs and appointed her husband and her brother, Pedro de Mora Salado, as her executors.
Luis Machado provided a guarantee for Juan de Morales Miranda, enabling him to transport the indigenous man Tomás Quirós, along with mules, by land to the city of Panama.

Juan de Morales Miranda and his wife, Beatriz Méndez, incurred a debt of 154 pesos to Captain Diego de Ocampo Figueroa, with payment due in August of 1648. This debt was subsequently cancelled on August 30, 1648.
Juan de Vida Martell, currently in Cartago and traveling to Panama, committed to pay Rodrigo de Calderón 280 pesos. This payment was for the purchase of ten tame mules.
Pedro de Campos Quirós provided a guarantee for José de Sandoval Ocampo, allowing him to send two indigenous men, Francisco and Andrés from the town of Barba, to Nicaragua.
Pedro de Campos Quirós also acted as guarantor for Juan de Senabria Maldonado, enabling him to send two indigenous men, Miguel from Curriravá and Jusepe from Tobosi, to Nicaragua.
José de Moya provided a guarantee for Juan de Senabria Maldonado, who had recently been appointed as the Corregidor for the Turrialba district.
Domingo Jiménez Maldonado and his wife, Juana de Sojo Pereira, sold their 20-year-old mulatto creole slave named Diego to Licenciado Presbítero Don Alonso de Sandoval for 250 pesos.

María de Ortega, widow of Jerónimo Felipe, gifted a seven-year-old creole slave named María to her granddaughter, Juana de Ortega. Juana is the legitimate daughter of María's son, Alférez Diego López de Ortega, and Ana de Chaves.
Alférez Francisco García Cordero granted a general power of attorney for legal disputes to Francisco de Arrieta and Juan López de Ortega.
Tomás Calvo, acting as the general depositary, committed to pay Gil de Alvarado 100 pesos, with the payment due in January of the following year.

locations: rincón antiguo de los indios Tobosis
summary: Juan de Vida Martell and his wife, doña Juana de Ortega, obligated themselves to the Confraternity of the Santísimo Sacramento for $90 at 5% annual interest. They mortgaged an estate across the Pontezuela river, near the 'sabana grande' and Baltasar de Ortega's ranch in the old Tobosis Indian corner.

Juan de Morales Miranda and his wife, doña Beatriz Méndez, obligated themselves to Rodrigo Jurado, a resident of Esparza, for 421 pesos and 4 reales for 15 tame mules and 7 wild mules. They agreed to pay in July of the following year in Caldera.
Juan Cascante de Rojas ratified a bond of $200 that he had previously provided in favor of Luis Machado, who held the positions of lieutenant treasurer and accountant.
Antonio González ratified a bond of $200 that he had previously provided in favor of Luis Machado, who served as lieutenant accountant and treasurer.

Esteban de Torres obligated himself to the Chaplaincy founded by Francisco de Paz, with its Chaplain Licenciado don Alonso de Sandoval, for $100 at 5% annual interest. He mortgaged his adobe and straw houses in the city, bordering the hermitage of San Nicolás and the house of María de Aguilar, a widow, and an estate in the Mata Redonda valley, bordering Francisco de Chaves's property and the former property of his father, Salvador de Torres.
Hernando de Carrión Villasante, serving as Alcalde and Lieutenant General of the Governor, placed Francisca, a 7-year-old mulata orphan, with Captain Juan Solano for a period of 8 years.
Rodrigo Calderón ratified a bond of $20,000 that he had previously provided in favor of Luis Machado, who held the positions of lieutenant treasurer and accountant.
Don Francisco Solano sold an enslaved person named Pedro, of Congo origin and approximately 35 years old, to Don Gil de Alvarado for $150.

Doña Andrea Vázquez de Coronado, natural daughter of the former Adelantado don Gonzalo Vázquez de Coronado and widow of Alférez Diego Peláez for over 20 years, made her testament. Her children are Ayudante Alonso Peláez, Alférez Juan Vázquez de Coronado, doña Antonia Vázquez de Coronado, and doña María Vázquez de Coronado. Doña Antonia was married to the deceased Sebastián Pereira, and doña María is married to Captain Jerónimo de Retes, the Chief Constable. Her son Alonso owns a cattle ranch in the city's common lands near the Toyocris river, where she also has some livestock.
