Doña María de Peralta, widow of Captain Juan de Salazar, donated an enslaved person named Francisco, one year old and son of her enslaved woman Victoria (a black woman of Angola origin), to her granddaughter doña María de Peralta, who is the legitimate daughter of Captain Hernando de Carrión and doña María de Salazar, the donor's daughter.

Juan Solano, testamentary executor for Licenciado Baltasar de Grado and patron of the Chaplaincy founded by Grado, leased a bread mill for four years to doña María de Sandoval, widow of Juan de Echavarría Navarro. The mill, located below the city in its common lands near the former 'trapiche' house of Licenciado Baltasar de Grado, for an annual price of $25.

people_involved: Doña Francisca de Sojo y Peñaranda
summary: Doña Francisca de Sojo y Peñaranda granted freedom, effective after her death, to her enslaved mulato criollo, Hernando López, who was described as being of white and red complexion, around 40 years old, and inherited from her aunt doña Fabiana de Sojo.
Toribio La Vega, a resident of this city, granted general power of attorney to Sargento Mayor don José de Sandoval Ocampo.
Juan Catalán, a merchant trading in the provinces of Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and the Kingdom of Tierra Firme, granted general power of attorney to Captain Fernando de Carrión Villasante.
Captain Hernando de Carrión provided a bond for Sargento Mayor don José de Sandoval Ocampo, who was the Corregidor of the Pacacua district.

Pedro de Vargas, a native of Cuan, made a provision of $2,521 for his wife, María Estefanía de Aguilar, who was the widow of Juan de Herrera and the legitimate daughter of Francisco de Aguilar and doña Juana Chacón. The provision included a cattle and horse ranch named 'La Santa Cruz de Caravaca' near Cartago, along with livestock and other goods, and a dowry of $500.

Pedro de Vargas and his wife, María Estefanía de Aguilar, obligated themselves to the Chaplaincy of Alonso Gómez Macotela, whose first Chaplain is the presbyter Marcos Machado, for $150 at 5% annual interest. They mortgaged a ranch.
An unspecified person granted power of attorney for lawsuits to Juan Fernández.

An unnamed grantor gave general power of attorney to Licenciado Presbítero Alonso de Sandoval and Doña Eugenia de Abarca, who is identified as the grantor's wife. This power was granted without prejudice to the previous one.
Doña Juana de Vera, widow of García Ramiro Corajo, granted general power of attorney for lawsuits to Juan Fernández.

Juan de Vida Martell, a native of Sevilla, established a dowry of $2,297.00 for his wife, Doña Juana de Ortega. The dowry included an enslaved criolla woman named María, 10 years old, and a herd of cattle located near Baltasar de Ortega's property.

people_involved: Don Juan de Chaves y Mendoza
summary: Luis Machado, a public and Cabildo scribe for 18 years, resigned his office due to illness, old age, and inability to perform his duties. His resignation was forwarded by Governor Don Juan de Chaves y Mendoza to the Fiscal of the Audiencia of Guatemala.

Diego de Peñaranda made his will, acknowledging debts from card games and leaving an enslaved mulatto blacksmith, Diego de Sojo. He had five natural daughters, some of whom were married. His will stipulated that Diego de Sojo's earnings be distributed among his daughters and that Diego could purchase his freedom for 500 pesos. Alonso de Sandoval and Sargento Alonso de Sojo were named executors.

Juan Gómez de Bonilla established a dowry of $616.00 for his wife, Doña María de Villalobos Jara. The dowry was provided by Doña María's mother, Doña Isabel de Carvajal, and her brother, José Villalobos Jara.

Gabriel de Vargas Machuca and his wife, Doña Isabel de Flores, pledged $200.00 to the Confraternity of the Conception, mortgaging their city home and a ranch. The funds were a legacy from Alférez Vasco Solano, managed by his executors, to help marry orphans.
Ambrosio de Brenes made a codicil to his will, mentioning his living wife Francisca Jiménez, his son Mateo Jiménez, and his son-in-law Lucas González.

Don José Sandoval de Ocampo pledged $100.00 to the estate of Vasco Solano, mortgaging a ranch and his city home. The home already had existing mortgages, with interest paid to Baltasar de Grado and the Chaplaincy of Alonso Gómez Macotela.

Several individuals, including Jerónimo de Retes and Gabriel de Vargas Machuca, ratified their surety for Luis Machado, a lieutenant accountant and royal official judge treasurer, for up to $1,400.00. This was due to Andrés Gil de Palacios taking office as Treasurer of Nicaragua and Costa Rica.

Gaspar de Rojas and his wife, María González, pledged $100 to a Capellanía. They mortgaged their San Antonio estate and ranch, which included two houses, 200 cattle, and 50 mares, located near Cartago's common lands and bordering properties of Francisco Oviedo and Alonso de Mora Salado.

Nicolás Ramírez, a mestizo apprentice, left Francisco Hernández's saddler workshop, owing $26 and a horse. After refusing to work, he was imprisoned for over fifteen days. He then agreed to serve Pedro de Ocampos Quirós for two years, along with his wife Laureana, for 30 pesos annually, in exchange for Ocampos Quirós settling his debt.

Alonso de Bonilla and his wife, Juana Benita Pereira, pledged 100 pesos at 5% annual interest to the Capellanía founded by Father Baltasar de Grado. They mortgaged their adobe and tile houses, located across from the hermitage of San Juan Evangelista, and a cattle estate bordering the ranches of Catalina Palacios and Doña María de Aguilar, and the site of Juan Rodríguez. Father Domingo de Echavarría, the first Chaplain, provided the money.

Juana de Llanos, widow of Diego de Escobar, sold her adobe and straw houses to Juan Vázquez de Coronado for $100. The payment was made in flour and six mules. The houses were located across the street from Juan Cascante de Rojas's house and also across the street from María de Aguilar's house, who was also a widow.

Juan de Campos, a native of Ciudad Real, Spain, formally acknowledged receiving the dowry of $1,045 and arras of $200 for his wife, Inés del Castillo. The dowry was from Inés's parents, Juan Alonso Camacho and Ana Merina del Castillo, and the transaction took place at the San Juan Bautista estate in the Aserrí valley.
The Alcalde arranged for Luisa, an indigenous woman from Ujarraz, to serve Doña Ana de Guevara for one year. Salvador de Acuña provided the guarantee for this arrangement.

Francisco Ramiro Corajo and his wife, Doña María de Retes, pledged 50 pesos at 5% annual interest to the Cofradía de San Nicolás in Cartago. They mortgaged their adobe and tile houses in Cartago, which bordered the properties of Don José de Sandoval and Diego de Ocampo. Esteban Rodríguez, the mayordomo, delivered the money to them.

Juan Vázquez de Coronado exchanged the house he had previously purchased from Juana de Llanos for a house owned by Doña María de Carvajal, widow of Juan de Padilla. Vázquez's house was valued at $200, while Carvajal's was $100. Doña María de Carvajal guaranteed the $100 difference by offering her 20-year-old enslaved woman named María.
Diego de Ocampo Figueroa, acting as attorney for Captain Francisco de Obregón, a resident of Granada, sold a 28-year-old enslaved man named Juan Clemente to Don Gil de Alvarado for $200.

Esteban de Torres sold his 18-year-old enslaved Creole woman named María, along with her 2-year-old child named Luisa, to Don Gil de Alvarado for $300. This enslaved María was previously pledged to Esteban de Torres's son-in-law, Alonso Vázquez de Trejo.

Juan Bautista de Letona and his wife, María de los Angeles, initially pledged $120 at 5% annual interest to Isabel Bonilla, mortgaging a house. On November 15, 1657, Letona declared that his deceased mother-in-law, Isabel de Bonilla, had absolved them of this debt and its interest in her will, leading to the cancellation of the obligation, with Agustín Guerrero, the executor, being cited.

On November 15, 1657, the debt of Juan Bautista de Letona and María de los Angeles to Isabel Bonilla was cancelled. Juan Bautista de Letona stated that his deceased mother-in-law, Isabel Bonilla, had absolved them of the debt in her will. Agustín Guerrero, the executor, was cited for this cancellation.

Juan Pérez de Carmona, who had pursued legal action against his father-in-law, Juan de Valverde Zárate, for a 425-peso dowry debt owed for his daughter Doña Catalina de Valverde Zárate, accepted an enslaved Creole woman named Leonor, originally from Nicaragua, as full payment. The enslaved woman was received from Juan Gómez de Bonilla, the Lieutenant of the Chief Constable.

Don Francisco Ramiro Corajo and Don Fernando de Salazar guaranteed Juan de Echavarría, an encomendero, to receive a 'tercio' (tribute payment) that the Audiencia had ordered to be released. They committed that if the King later ruled that these retained payments should go to the Royal Treasury, Juan de Echavarría would make the payment.

Juan Alonso Camacho and his wife, Ana Merina del Castillo, pledged 105 pesos at 5% annual interest to the Cofradía de la Concepción and the Capellanía of Doña Ana de Medrano. They mortgaged two cattle estates, one named San Juan Bautista in the Aserrí valley, and another near the Turrubares river, along with livestock. Don Pedro de Córdova, the mayordomo, delivered the money.

Don Juan de Echavarría acted as guarantor for Don Fernando de Salazar, who was the Corregidor of the 'Tierra adentro' district and an encomendero in the province, concerning the receipt of a 'tercio' (tribute payment).

locations: Rincón antiguo de los indios Tobosis
summary: Juan de Vida Martell and his wife, Doña Juana de Ortega, committed to pay $90.00 annually at 5% interest to the Confraternity of the Most Holy Sacrament, founded in the parish church of this city. They mortgaged an estate located across the Pontezuela River, bordering the Sabana Grande and Baltasar de Ortega's ranch in the old corner of the Tobosis Indians.

Juan de Morales Miranda and his wife, Doña Beatriz Méndez, committed to pay Rodrigo Jurado, a resident of Esparza, 421 pesos and 4 reales. This payment was for 15 tame mules at 22.5 pesos each and 7 wild mules at 12 pesos each. The payment is due in July of the following year in Caldera.
Juan Cascante de Rojas ratified a bond of $200.00 that he had previously provided in favor of Luis Machado. Luis Machado held the positions of lieutenant treasurer and accountant.
Antonio González ratified a bond of $200.00 that he had previously provided in favor of Luis Machado. Luis Machado served as the lieutenant accountant and treasurer.

Esteban de Torres committed to pay $100.00 annually at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by Francisco de Paz, whose Chaplain was Licenciado don Alonso de Sandoval. He mortgaged his adobe and straw houses in this city, bordering the hermitage of San Nicolás and the house of María de Aguilar, a widow. Additionally, he mortgaged an estate in the Mata Redonda valley, bordering that of Francisco de Chaves and the former estate of his father, Salvador de Torres.

Hernando de Carrión Villasante, who served as Alcalde and Lieutenant General Governor, arranged an eight-year indentured service agreement for Francisca, a mulata orphan of about 7 years old, with Captain Juan Solano.
Rodrigo Calderón ratified a bond of $200.00 that he had previously provided in favor of Luis Machado. Luis Machado held the positions of lieutenant treasurer and accountant.
Don Francisco Solano sold an enslaved person named Pedro, of Congo origin and about 35 years old, to Don Gil de Alvarado for $150.00.

The will of Doña Andrea Vázquez de Coronado, natural daughter of the former Adelantado Don Gonzalo Vázquez de Coronado, was recorded. She was the widow of Alférez Diego Peláez for over 20 years and named her children: Ayudante Alonso Peláez, Alférez Juan Vázquez de Coronado, Doña Antonia Vázquez de Coronado, and Doña María Vázquez de Coronado. Her son Alonso had a cattle ranch in the city's common lands near the Toyocris River, where Doña Andrea also kept some cattle and mares.

Doña María de Peralta, widow of Captain Juan de Salazar, donated an enslaved person named Francisco to her granddaughter, Doña María de Peralta. The granddaughter was the legitimate daughter of Captain Hernando de Carrión and Doña María de Salazar, who was the donor's daughter. Francisco, one year old, was the son of Victoria, a black enslaved woman of Angola origin belonging to the donor.

Juan Solano, as the testamentary executor of Licenciado Baltasar de Grado and patron of the Chaplaincy founded by him, leased a flour mill to Doña María de Sandoval, widow of Juan de Echavarría Navarro, for four years at $25.00 annually. The mill, located below the city in its common lands, was fully equipped and bordered the house known as 'el trapiche' which formerly belonged to Licenciado Baltasar de Grado.

people_involved: Doña Francisca de Sojo y Peñaranda
summary: Doña Francisca de Sojo y Peñaranda granted freedom to her enslaved person, Hernando López, to take effect after her death. Hernando López, a mulato criollo from this city, described as white and red in complexion and about 40 years old, was inherited by Doña Francisca from her aunt, Doña Fabiana de Sojo.
Toribio La Vega, a resident of this city, granted general power of attorney to Don José de Sandoval Ocampo. Don José de Sandoval Ocampo held the rank of Sargento Mayor.
Juan Catalán, a merchant trading in the provinces of Nicaragua and Costa Rica and the kingdom of Tierra Firme, granted general power of attorney to Captain Fernando de Carrión Villasante.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don José de Sandoval Ocampo
summary: Captain Hernando de Carrión stood surety for Sargento Mayor Don José de Sandoval Ocampo. Don José de Sandoval Ocampo was also the Corregidor of the Pacacua district.

Pedro de Vargas, a native of Cuan, made an obligation in favor of his wife, María Estefanía de Aguilar, for $2,521.00. This included a cattle and horse ranch named Santa Cruz de Caravaca, located about a league from Cartago, which featured an adobe house with a tiled roof and a straw kitchen. The obligation also covered 150 corral cattle, 13 tame oxen, 8 tame horses, one wild horse, a cart, a turned wooden box, and a blue and white pavilion of local thread. The arras (dowry) amounted to $500.00.

Pedro de Vargas and his wife, María Estefanía de Aguilar, committed to pay $150.00 annually at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy of Alonso Gómez Macotela, whose first Chaplain was the priest Marcos Machado. They mortgaged a ranch (hato) as security for this obligation.

Gaspar de Rojas and his wife, María González, mortgaged an estate and ranch named San Antonio, located near Cartago, for $100 to a Chaplaincy. The property included two houses, 200 cattle, and 50 mares, bordering El Tejar, a river, and properties of Francisco Oviedo and Alonso de Mora Salado.

Nicolás Ramírez, a mestizo apprentice saddler, left Francisco Hernández's workshop, owing him $26 plus the cost of a horse. After refusing to work, Ramírez was jailed for over fifteen days. Pedro de Ocampos Quirós agreed to pay Ramírez's debt, and in return, Ramírez and his wife Laureana committed to serving Ocampos Quirós for two years for 30 pesos annually.

Alonso de Bonilla and his wife, Juana Benita Pereira, mortgaged their adobe and tile house and a cattle ranch for 100 pesos at 5% annual interest to a Chaplaincy founded by Father Baltasar de Grado. The properties bordered the hermitage of San Juan Evangelista, Catalina Palacios's ranch, María de Aguilar's ranch, and Juan Rodríguez's site. Father Domingo de Echavarría, the first Chaplain, provided the money.

Juana de Llanos, widow of Diego de Escobar, sold her adobe and straw house to Juan Vázquez de Coronado for $100, paid in flour and six mules. The house bordered properties owned by Juan Cascante de Rojas and María de Aguilar.

Juan de Campos, a native of Ciudad Real, Spain, acknowledged receipt of his wife Inés del Castillo's dowry of $1,045 and a bride-price (arras) of $200. The dowry was granted at the San Juan Bautista estate in the Aserrí valley. Inés del Castillo is identified as the legitimate daughter of Juan Alonso Camacho and Ana Merina del Castillo.
The Alcalde arranged for Luisa, an indigenous woman from Ujarraz, to serve Doña Ana de Guevara for one year. Salvador de Acuña acted as guarantor for the arrangement.

Francisco Ramiro Corajo and his wife, María de Retes, mortgaged their adobe and tile house in Cartago for 50 pesos at 5% annual interest to the Confraternity of San Nicolás. The property bordered houses belonging to José de Sandoval and Diego de Ocampo. Esteban Rodríguez, the steward, delivered the money.

Juan Vázquez de Coronado exchanged a house he had previously bought from Juana de Llanos for another house owned by María de Carvajal, widow of Juan de Padilla. The second house, valued at 100 pesos, bordered properties of Ambrosio de Brenes and Juan de Senabria Maldonado. Vázquez's house was valued at $200, and María de Carvajal guaranteed the $100 difference with her 20-year-old enslaved woman named María.
Diego de Ocampo Figueroa, acting as attorney for Captain Francisco de Obregón of Granada, sold an enslaved man named Juan Clemente, 28 years old, to Gil de Alvarado for $200.

Esteban de Torres sold an 18-year-old enslaved Creole woman named María and her 2-year-old child, Luisa, to Gil de Alvarado for $300. This enslaved woman had previously been mortgaged to Alonso Vázquez de Trejo, Torres's son-in-law.

Juan Bautista de Letona and his wife, María de los Angeles, mortgaged an adobe and tile house for $120 at 5% annual interest to Isabel Bonilla. The house bordered properties of Francisco de Chaves and Baltasar Muñoz.

The debt of Juan Bautista de Letona and María de los Angeles to Isabel Bonilla was cancelled on November 15, 1657. Juan Bautista de Letona stated that his deceased mother-in-law, Isabel Bonilla, had stipulated in her will that this debt and its interest should not be collected. Agustín Guerrero, the executor, was cited for this cancellation.

Juan Pérez de Carmona, who had pursued legal action against his father-in-law Juan de Valverde Zárate for a 425-peso dowry debt owed for his daughter Catalina de Valverde Zárate, accepted an enslaved Creole woman named Leonor from Nicaragua as payment. The enslaved woman was received from Juan Gómez de Bonilla, Lieutenant of the Chief Constable.

Francisco Ramiro Corajo and Fernando de Salazar guaranteed that Juan de Echavarría, an encomendero in the province, would pay back a 'tercio' (a third of tribute) that he was authorized to receive by the Audiencia, should the King decide that these retained tributes must be returned to the Royal Treasury.

Juan Alonso Camacho and his wife, Ana Merina, mortgaged two cattle ranches, including San Juan Bautista in the Aserrí valley, and livestock (200 cattle, 30 mares, 1 donkey) for 105 pesos at 5% interest to the Confraternity of La Concepción and the Chaplaincy of Ana de Medrano. The properties bordered Juan Delgado's estate and Juan de Chaves's ranch. Pedro de Córdova, the steward, provided the money.

Juan de Echavarría acted as guarantor for Fernando de Salazar, who was the Corregidor of the 'Tierra adentro' district and an encomendero in the province. The specific purpose of this guarantee is not fully detailed in the provided text.
Juan Pérez de Carmona and his wife, Doña Catalina de Valverde Zárate, sold a 30-year-old Creole slave named Leonor, originally from Nicaragua, to Rodrigo de Calderón for $200.00.
Don José de Sandoval Ocampo, Corregidor of Pacacua, provided a guarantee for Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado, Corregidor of Turrialba and encomendero, to receive retentions from his encomienda.
Don Gil de Alvarado and Don Francisco Ramiro provided a guarantee in favor of Don José de Alvarado, similar to a previous one.

Don Francisco Solano and Doña Isabel de Rosales pledged $200.00 at a 5% annual census to the Capellanía founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela. They mortgaged a house in the city and a ranch (hato) in the Aserrí valley, named Ntra. Sra. del Rosario de la buena Vista, which included livestock and property. Luis Machado delivered the money on behalf of the founder.

Antonio González sold his residence, consisting of two adobe-fenced plots, to Juan de Morales Miranda for 925 pesos. These houses, previously bought from Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado, carried a debt to the Capellanía founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela of Esparza, whose chaplain was Pe. Marcos Machado, and the buyer assumed this debt.
Antonio González granted power of attorney to Juan López de Ortega and Pedro de Mora Solado, though the document was incomplete.

Juan Bautista de Morales, a native and resident of Santiago de Alange, Veragua, and son of Capn. Pablo de Morales and Doña Juana Vaca de Castro, provided a dowry for his wife, Doña María de Lumbides, daughter of the late Lope de Lumbides and Doña Leonor Alvarez Pereira. The dowry included two mulatto slaves named Juana (one 40 years old for $500, another 8 years old for $250), and arras of $500, totaling $1436.5.

Lic. Baltasar de Castro, Provincial Vicar and Beneficiary Priest of Cartago, granted power to Luis Machado, Lieutenant Treasurer, and Don Pedro de Cordova. This power allowed them to sell the year's first fruits of wheat and honey, as well as his adobe and tile residence, which had a $300 census from the Confraternity of the Conception and Catalina Gutiérrez's Capellanía.

Francisco Gil de Quiñones Osorio, a native and resident of Villa de los Santos (Tierra Firme), and son of Fernando de Quiñones Osorio and Pascuala Megía, provided a dowry for his wife, Francisca Guerrero, daughter of Fernando Marín Guerrero and Francisca de Arrieta. The dowry was $516.00, with arras of $200.00.

Juan de Echavarría Navarro, Ordinary Mayor, pledged $100.00 at a 5% annual census to the Confraternity of the Rosary. He mortgaged his adobe and tile residence, which bordered houses of Lic. don Alonso de Sandoval and Pedro de Campos Quirós, and faced Alonso Peláez's house across the main street. Don José de Sandoval Ocampo, the Mayordomo, provided the money.

people_involved: Padre Fray Juan de la Concepción
summary: Juana de Llanos, natural daughter of Alférez Francisco Román and widow of Diego de Escobar, made her will. She mentioned a debt from Padre Fray Juan de la Concepción, bequeathed land from her ranch near Cartago to her niece Francisca Guerrero as a dowry, and livestock to her niece Juana Marín. She named Gaspar de los Ríos, Agustín de Arrieta, and Francisco de Arrieta as executors, and Francisco Solano (8), Pedro Solano (6-7), and Gregoria Benavides (4) as her heirs, whom she had raised.
Alonso Peláez provided a guarantee for Jerónimo de Retes, Corregidor of the town of Quepo.
Juan Bautista de Morales and his wife, María de Lumbides, pledged $100.00 in favor of Francisco Martínez.

Juan Hidalgo, a native and resident of Loja, Kingdom of Granada (Spain), provided a dowry for his wife, Doña María de Alfaro, daughter of the late Capn. Francisco de Alfaro and Doña Catalina de Ortega. The dowry included a 12-year-old black slave named Melchora, a plot with two adobe houses, and an 18-year-old Creole black slave named Juana, totaling $2085.00 with arras of $500. Doña Catalina de Ortega, María's mother, was married to the absent Luis González Villalón, and the assets were inherited from her father, Jerónimo Felipe.
Francisco de Oses, a resident of the city, owes Juan de Echavarría Navarro 90 pesos. This debt is to be paid in Panama in the upcoming month of May.

Doña María de Sandoval, widow of Juan de Echavarría Navarro, and Doña Inés de Benavides, widow of Capn. Antonio Rodríguez Moreno, as universal heirs of their uncle Pe. Baltasar de Grado, grant power of attorney to Juan de Echavarría Navarro. This power allows him to collect all sums owed to the estate in Panama.
Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro grants power of attorney to his uncle, Licenciado don Alonso de Sandoval, who is a Presbyter.

Rodrigo Calderón owes Juan de Echavarría Navarro 250 pesos. This loan was used to pay for Leonor, a black woman (criolla) from Granada, whom Calderón purchased from Juan Pérez de Carmona. Calderón is obligated to pay the debt in Panama, where he is currently traveling.
Francisco de Hoces, a resident, owes Juan de Echavarría 150 pesos. He is obligated to pay this amount in Panama in May.
Juan Solano grants general power of attorney to Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro. This document was executed in the place known as San Juan Bautista, located in the Curriravá valley.

Don Francisco Solano, the natural son and heir of Alférez Vasco Solano, grants power of attorney to Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro. This power enables Echavarría Navarro to collect all sums owed to his father in Panama. The document was granted in the same location as the previous entry.
Jerónimo de Retes, the Alguacil Mayor, grants general power of attorney for lawsuits to his brother, Diego López de Ortega.

José de Moya grants power of attorney to Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro. This power authorizes Echavarría Navarro to charter a frigate of 800 tercios capacity from Panama to Caldera in the upcoming June, for the purpose of loading flour, biscuits, and other goods from the province.
Juan de Valverde Zárate grants general power of attorney to Diego López de Ortega.
Francisco Martínez grants general power of attorney for lawsuits and collections to his wife, Francisca de Mendoza. This power of attorney is noted as incomplete.
Juan de Morales Miranda owes Toribio La Vega 100 pesos. This amount is to be paid in Panama by Christmas of the current year.

Juan de Morales Miranda and his wife, Doña Beatriz Méndez, acknowledge a debt of 925 pesos at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela, whose first Chaplain is Pro. Marcos Machado. This debt stems from their purchase of houses from Antonio González and María de Zúñiga, which carried this existing encumbrance.
Juan de Morales Miranda acts as guarantor for Diego Ramírez de Valdés. Valdés had been appointed as Corregidor and Alcalde Mayor for the district of Turrialba and its surrounding area.

Juan de Vida Martell and his wife Doña Juana de Ortega sell an estate named San Francisco to Juan Sánchez Crespo. The estate, located across the Portezuela river in the old site of Tobosi and near Baltasar de Ortega's estate, includes houses, corrals, and 90 cattle, for 90 pesos owed to the Cofradía del Santísimo Sacramento.

Juan Sánchez Crespo sells a cattle and horse ranch called San Bartolomé to Juan de Vida Martell. The property, located on the royal road to Pacacua, near estates of Andrés López de Céspedes and Juan de Chaves, beyond the Oro river and near the Cobre hill, includes houses, corrals, 122 cattle, and 63 breeding mares. The price is 360 pesos, owed to the Cofradía de la Soledad (200 pesos), a Chaplaincy patroned by Capn. Diego de Ocampo Figueroa (100 pesos), and another Chaplaincy patroned by Juan de Echavarría (60 pesos).
Juan de Vida Martell and his wife Doña Juana de Ortega obligate themselves to Juana Sanchez Crespo for 97 pesos. This amount is to be paid within one year.
Juan Pérez de Carmona and his wife Catalina de Valverde Zárate sold an enslaved woman named Leonor, a 30-year-old criolla from Nicaragua, to Rodrigo de Calderón for $200.
Don José de Sandoval Ocampo, Corregidor of Pacacua, provided a guarantee for Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado, Corregidor of Turrialba and encomendero, to receive retentions from his encomienda.
Don Gil de Alvarado and Don Francisco Ramiro provided a guarantee in favor of Don José de Alvarado.

locations: Ntra. Sra. del Rosario de la buena Vista
summary: Don Francisco Solano and his wife Doña Isabel de Rosales obligated themselves to the Capellanía founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela for $200 at a 5% annual census. They mortgaged a house in the city and a ranch in the Aserrí valley. Alonso Gómez Macotela delivered the money through Luis Machado.

Antonio González sold his dwelling houses to Juan de Morales Miranda for 925 pesos. These houses, previously bought from Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado, carried a debt to the Capellanía founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela, which Juan de Morales Miranda assumed.
Antonio González granted power of attorney to Juan López de Ortega and Pedro de Mora Solado. The document was incomplete.

A dowry letter was issued for Juan Bautista de Morales, native of Santiago de Alange, and Doña María de Lumbides. The dowry, totaling $1436.5, included two enslaved mulata women named Juana, aged 40 and 8, respectively, along with $500 in arras.

Lic. Baltasar de Castro, Provincial Vicar and Beneficiary Priest of Cartago, granted power to Luis Machado and Don Pedro de Cordova to sell the year's first fruits of wheat and honey, and his dwelling houses. The houses had a $300 census, with contributions from the Cofradía de la Concepción and the Capellanía de Catalina Gutiérrez.
A dowry letter was issued for Francisco Gil de Quiñones Osorio, native of Villa de los Santos, and Francisca Guerrero. The dowry amounted to $516, with $200 in arras.

Juan de Echavarría Navarro, Ordinary Mayor, obligated himself to the Cofradía del Rosario for $100 at a 5% annual census, mortgaging his dwelling houses. He received the money from Don José de Sandoval Ocampo, the Mayordomo.

people_involved: Padre Fray Juan de la Concepción
Francisca Guerrero (niece of Juana de Llanos)
summary: Juana de Llanos, natural daughter of Alférez Francisco Román and widow of Diego de Escobar, made her testament. She bequeathed the offspring of cows born in 1650 to her niece Juana Marín and named Francisco Solano (8), Pedro Solano (6-7), and Gregoria Benavides (4) as heirs, whom she had raised. She also mentioned a debt from Padre Fray Juan de la Concepción and a ranch in Ujarrás, part of which was given as dowry to her niece Francisca Guerrero.
Alonso Peláez provided a guarantee for Jerónimo de Retes, Corregidor of Quepo.
Juan Bautista de Morales and his wife María de Lumbides obligated themselves to Francisco Martínez for $100.

A dowry letter was issued for Juan Hidalgo, native of Loja, and Doña María de Alfaro. The dowry, totaling $2085, included two enslaved black women, Melchora (12) and Juana (18), and a solar with two houses. Doña Catalina de Ortega, mother of the bride, was married to Luis González Villalón, and the goods were inherited from her father, Jerónimo Felipe.
Francisco de Oses, a resident of Cartago, incurred a debt of 90 pesos to Juan de Echavarría Navarro. He is obligated to repay this amount in Panama by the upcoming month of May.

Doña María de Sandoval, widow of the deceased Juan de Echavarría Navarro, and Doña Inés de Benavides, widow of Captain Antonio Rodríguez Moreno, as universal heirs of their uncle Father Baltasar de Grado, granted power of attorney to Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro. This power authorizes him to collect all sums owed to the inheritance in Panama.
Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro granted power of attorney to his uncle, Licenciado Don Alonso de Sandoval, who is a Presbyter.

Rodrigo Calderón owes Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro 250 pesos, which was a loan to purchase Leonor, a Black creole woman from Granada, from Juan Pérez de Carmona. Calderón is obligated to repay the debt in Panama, where he is currently traveling.
Francisco de Hoces, a resident, owes Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro 150 pesos. He is obligated to pay this amount in Panama during the month of May.
Juan Solano granted general power of attorney to Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro. This document was executed at the site named San Juan Bautista, located in the valley of Curriravá.

Don Francisco Solano, the natural son and heir of Alférez Vasco Solano, granted power of attorney to Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro. This power enables Echavarría Navarro to collect all sums owed to Francisco's father in Panama, and the document was executed at the same location as the previous entry.
Jerónimo de Retes, the Alguacil Mayor, granted general power of attorney for lawsuits to his brother, Diego López de Ortega.

José de Moya granted power of attorney to Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro to charter a frigate with a capacity of 800 tercios. This frigate is intended to sail to Caldera in the upcoming June to load flour, biscuits, and other goods from the province.
Juan de Valverde Zárate granted general power of attorney to Diego López de Ortega.
Francisco Martínez granted general power of attorney for lawsuits and collections to his wife, Francisca de Mendoza. The document for this power is noted as incomplete.
Juan de Morales Miranda owes Toribio La Vega 100 pesos. He is obligated to pay this debt in Panama by Christmas of the current year.

Juan de Morales Miranda and his wife, Doña Beatriz Méndez, acknowledged a debt of 925 pesos at a 5% interest rate to the Chaplaincy founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela, whose first Chaplain is Father Marcos Machado. This debt originated from their purchase of houses from Antonio González and María de Zúñiga, which carried this existing encumbrance, referencing a previous deed from October 8, 1649.
Juan de Morales Miranda acted as a guarantor for Diego Ramírez de Valdés. Valdés had been appointed as Corregidor and Alcalde Mayor for the district of Turrialba and its surrounding area.

Juan de Vida Martell and his wife, Doña Juana de Ortega, sold an estate named San Francisco to Juan Sánchez Crespo. Located across the Portezuela River in the old site of Tobosi, near Baltasar de Ortega's estate, it included houses, corrals, and 90 head of cattle, with the sale price of 90 pesos owed to the Confraternity of the Most Holy Sacrament.

Juan Sánchez Crespo sold a cattle and horse ranch, including its site, houses, and corrals, named San Bartolomé, to Juan de Vida Martell. Located on the royal road to Pacacua, near the Gold River and Copper Hill, and adjacent to estates of Andrés López de Céspedes and Juan de Chaves, it included 122 cattle and 63 breeding mares for a price of 360 pesos, with existing debts to the Confraternity of Solitude, a Chaplaincy patroned by Captain Diego de Ocampo Figueroa, and another Chaplaincy patroned by Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro.
Juan de Vida Martell and his wife, Doña Juana de Ortega, obligated themselves to Juan Sánchez Crespo for 97 pesos. They are committed to paying this amount within one year.

Alonso de Sojo and Lucía de las Alas sold an estate with 200 cattle in Mata Redonda to Cristóbal Fernández Durán for 280 pesos. Of this amount, 180 pesos were owed to the Cofradía de Ntra. Sra. de la Concepción and 100 pesos to the Capellanía de Marcos Machado.
Alcalde Hernando de Carrión arranged an apprenticeship for Gaspar, a 12-year-old free mulatto, with Cristóbal Fernández Durán. Durán had raised Gaspar since he was two years old.

José de Moya and Mayor de Benavides Moreno sold a flour mill with three houses in the outskirts of San Bartolomé de Barba, Pacacua, to José de Sandoval for 600 pesos. Of this amount, 200 pesos were owed to Presbítero Domingo de Echavarría, the first chaplain of the chaplaincy founded by Padre Baltasar de Grado.

José de Sandoval y Ocampo acknowledged a debt of 200 pesos, at a 5% census, to the chaplaincy founded by Padre Baltasar de Grado and served by Presbítero Domingo de Echavarría. This debt was associated with the mill he purchased from José de Moya and Mayor de Benavides Moreno, located on the Río Segundo in the outskirts of Barba.

Cristóbal Fernández Durán and Ana Pereira Cardoso committed to the Cofradía de la Concepción for 180 pesos. This debt was for the estate they bought from Alonso de Sojo and Lucía de las Alas, originally imposed by Captain Juan de las Alas, the estate's first owner.

Cristóbal Fernández Durán and Ana Pereira Cardoso acknowledged a debt of 100 pesos to the Capellanía de Alonso Gómez Macotela, whose first chaplain was Padre Marcos Machado. This debt was imposed by Fabiama de Sojo.

Juan de Vida Martell and Juana de Ortega committed to the Cofradía de Ntra. Sra. de la Soledad for 200 pesos at a 5% annual census. They mortgaged an estate they had purchased with this encumbrance from Juan Sánchez Crespo.
Juan de Vida Martell and Juana de Ortega also acknowledged a debt of 100 pesos at a 5% annual census to the chaplaincy founded by Vasco Solano.
Juan de Quesada Monzón stood as guarantor for Baltasar de Rosales, the Corregidor of the San Mateo de Chirripó district in Tierra Adentro.
María de la Portilla, widow of Juan de Mora, made a codicil to her will, leaving a black woman named Leonor to her son, Alonso de Mora, as an inheritance improvement.

Juan Vázquez de Coronado committed to the Cofradía de Ntra. Sra. del Rosario for 50 pesos at a 5% annual census, mortgaging his residence which he bought from María de Carvajal. His property bordered houses of Francisca Jiménez and was across the street from houses of Juan de Senabria Maldonado, and he also had another 100 pesos census with the Cofradía de la Concepción.

Eugenia de Abarca Alatras granted power to her husband, Tomás Calvo, a regidor and general depositary, to make her will. She named her legitimate children Gaspar, Magdalena, Sebastiana, Juana, and Miguel as her heirs.

people_involved: Juan Fernández de Salinas y Cerda
summary: José de Sandoval y Ocampo of Cartago and Captain Juan Martín Macotela of Esparza provided a residency bond for Governor and Captain General Juan Fernández de Salinas y Cerda, a Knight of the Order of Calatrava. This was done before the Cabildo and Justice, including Sargento Mayor Juan Solano, Alcaldes Ordinarios Captain Hernando de Carrión, Alguacil Mayor Captain Jerónimo de Retes, Provincial of the Santa Hermandad and Regidor Captain Diego de Ocampo Figueroa, Regidor Fernando Salazar, and Alférez Tomás Calvo.

Inés Alvarez Pereira, natural daughter of the deceased Captain Antonio Pereira and widow of Captain Bartolomé Sánchez, made her will in 1654. She detailed her children and grandchildren, mentioned her brother Juan Pereira, and noted her role as executor for the will of Bachiller Lope de Chavarría, former priest of Cartago who died in Santiago de Guatemala. She also described her properties in the Valle de Landecho, near Cartago, and at Los tres Ríos.

An executor arranged for the founding of a Capellanía in the main church. Documents were delivered to the San Francisco convent by Juan Fernández and received by Fray Mateo de Miranda. Pe. José Lumbides was chosen as the first Capellán, and Pe. Alonso de Sandoval (or Domingo Jiménez Maldonado) as the patron. Luis González de Villalón and Teniente Juan Hidalgo were also named as executors.

Domingo Jiménez Maldonado and Bartolomé Sánchez settled a lawsuit concerning the division of a cattle ranch and land in Landecho valley. The dispute referenced a deed from August 1654 by Doña Inés Alvarez Pereira, Bartolomé Sánchez's widow, in favor of Jiménez. Jiménez ceded wild cattle and a claim to a young donkey to Sánchez, also permitting him to build a house.
Juan Clemente de Madrigal provided a dowry of $345.00 to his wife, Francisca Gutiérrez. This amount included $100.00 from the Cofradía de la Concepción.

Alonso de Bonilla committed to transport 50 cargas of flour, biscuits, sarsaparilla, or other merchandise belonging to Juan Bautista Capelaso to the port of Suerre or Punta Blanca. He received 500 pesos for this service, with a deadline of the upcoming January.

Following the death of Marcos de Chinchilla, Alcalde Ordinario Don Fernando de Salazar ordered an inventory of his estate. The inventory was conducted at the home of Catalina Palacios, the deceased's mother, and the goods were deposited with Alférez Tomás Calvo. Marcos de Chinchilla had two legitimate children with Doña Francisca del Castillo: Gaspar de Chinchilla and Doña Felipa de Chinchilla.
Juan de Chaves, an Alférez mayor and Regidor, granted a general power of attorney to Diego López de Ortega.
Juan Alonso Camacho granted a general power of attorney to Alférez Juan de Quesada Monzón.

On October 27, 1654, the Alcalde ordered an inventory of the assets left by María Rodríguez, widow of Juan Sánchez Crespo. Her children included Gaspar, Antonio, Francisca, Antonia, Ana María (a widow), and Leonor de Rivera (married). The inventory, including the San Francisco ranch, was deposited with Gaspar and Antonio Sánchez.

On October 27, 1654, the Alcalde ordered an inventory of the assets left by Juan Garro, who was married to Antonia María and had two children, Claudio and Ana. The inventory was conducted at the San Juan site, and the goods were deposited with Gaspar de Rojas, Antonia María's father.

people_involved: Licdo. don Diego de Obando y Espinosa
summary: On January 8, 1655, incomplete proceedings were held for the opening of the testament of Alférez Manuel de Flores, who died that day. His widow, Maria Barbosa, and Licdo. don Diego de Obando y Espinosa, the priest of Cartago, accepted the role of albaceas, but the testament was not present.

On October 6, 1654, Diego López de Ortega was recorded as a creditor of Alférez mayor Juan de Chaves for $563.00. Chaves settled the debt by giving Ortega 23 mules, 2 young donkeys, and 3 pesos in cash.

In 1654, Juan de Chaves sold an estancia called San Jerónimo to his sister, Doña Isabel de Chaves, for $600.00, including a $400.00 lien. The estancia, located near Pacaca, included livestock, houses, and plantations, and was subject to a lien in favor of the Capellanía of Vasco Solano and Juan Martín Macotela, and the Cofradía de la Concepción.

On April 24, 1656, Jerónimo Leal and his wife, Doña María Yáñez Cardosa, obligated themselves to the Cofradía de la Soledad for $960.00. This sum was for the purchase of the San Bartolomé cattle ranch from Juan de Vida Martell, which was mortgaged to the Cofradía.

On November 22, 1656, Captain Juan del Castillo received a dowry of $3878.00 for his wife, Doña Felipa de Chinchilla, from her grandmother Catalina Palacios. The dowry included a mill, land, a house, and four enslaved individuals: Juana, Cándida, Agustina, and Francisco. The dowry also included arras of $250.00.
In 1657, Juan Cascante de Rojas served as Alcalde.
Governor don Juan Fernández Salinas y Cerda granted a power of attorney. The fragment of this document was recorded.
Tomás Calvo, the general depositary, granted a general power of attorney to Francisco Fernández Miranda.

Nicolás Barrantes sold a cacao plantation with 160 fruit trees in the port of Matina to Governor Juan Fernández Salinas y Cerda for $100. The property was located on the banks of the Matina River and bordered another cacao plantation owned by Juan de la Cruz.

Francisco Gómez Rico obligated himself to the Cofradía del Rosario, founded in the parish church, for $50, which was delivered by Mayordomo Cristobal Durán. These funds were redeemed by Antonio González and belonged to the Capellanía of don Diego Charles. Gómez Rico mortgaged two plots, a house, adobe walls, and a 14-year-old slave named Luis, with the property bordering houses of don Juan de Senabria Maldonado and doña Margarita de Flores, for a term of two years at 5% interest.

Don José de Sandoval Ocampo sold a mill and several houses in the town of Barba to Antonio González for $500. The payment included $250 from two censos, one for the Capellanía of Baltasar de Grado (whose patron and chaplain was Licenciado don Domingo de Chavarría) and another for the Capellanía founded by don Diego Charles de Herrera in the Cofradía del Rosario. The remaining $250 was to be paid in the following May with flour and biscuits delivered to Caldera.

people_involved: don Diego de Obando y Espinoza
summary: Don Domingo de Chavarría, Cura of León de Nicaragua, and don Diego de Obando y Espinoza, Cura of Cartago, agreed to exchange their benefices. They requested approval for this exchange from the Most Illustrious Lord don Fray Tomás Manso, the Bishop-elect.

Doña Antonia Vázquez de Coronado made her testament. She was the legitimate daughter of Alférez Diego Peláez and doña Andrea Vázquez de Coronado, and the widow of Sebastián Pereira Cardoso. Her testament mentioned her deceased daughters, doña Isabel de Obando and doña Andrea Vázquez, and her grandchildren don Sebastián de Ocampo and doña Inés de Benavides Solano, children of doña Isabel and don José Sandoval Ocampo.

people_involved: doña Juana de Vera y Sotomayor
summary: Doña Juana de Vera y Sotomayor, widow of Sargento mayor García Ramiro Corajo, made her testament. She listed her eight children, their spouses, and her enslaved people: Margarita (pregnant), María, Gertrudis, Antonio, and Pedro. She also left legacies to several indigenous people, a free mulatto, Catalina del Peso and her daughter Leonor, and Isabel, daughter of Catalina Venegas. Her assets included an estate in Río de la Lajucla with livestock, a house in Barba, and goods in Caldera for her son don Diego, who was in Panama for business. Licdo. don Alonso de Sandoval, don Diego Ramiro, and don Fernando Ramiro were named as executors.
Doña Andrea Vázquez de Coronado made her testament, declaring that her son Alonso Peláez had supported her for over 28 years since the death of her husband.

people_involved: doña Juana de Vera y Sotomayor
summary: Doña Juana de Vera y Sotomayor emancipated her son, don Antonio Ramiro.
Captain don Rodrigo de Calderón granted power of attorney to Licenciado don Alonso de Sandoval, Alférez Juan de Quesada Monzón, and Agustín Guerrero.

people_involved: doña Juana de Sandoval y Olenzuela
summary: Pedro de la Portilla made his testament. He mentioned his wife, Magdalena de Loaiza, and stated that he had raised doña Juana de Sandoval y Olenzuela and Nicolás, a mestizo.
Nicolás de Guevara acted in favor of his wife, Ana María de Torres, who was the legitimate daughter of Salvador.

An executor disposes the foundation of a Capellanía (chaplaincy) in the main church, with documents held at the San Francisco convent. Juan Fernández, an executor appointed by Justice, delivered the documents to Fray Mateo de Miranda, the Guardian of the Convent. Pe. José Lumbides is chosen as the first Chaplain, and Pe. Alonso de Sandoval as the patron, with Domingo Jiménez as a substitute. Luis González de Villalón and Teniente Juan Hidalgo are also named as executors.

Domingo Jiménez Maldonado and Bartolomé Sánchez settled a dispute regarding the division of a cattle ranch and land in the Landecho valley. A document from August 1654 by doña Inés Alvarez Pereira, Bartolomé Sánchez's widow, was in favor of Jiménez. Jiménez ceded all wild cattle and rights to a young donkey in the Landecho ranch to Sánchez, also permitting him to build a house nearby.
Juan Clemente de Madrigal issued a dowry letter (carta dote) in favor of his wife, Francisca Gutiérrez, for $345.00. This sum included $100.00 from the alms of the Cofradía de la Concepción.

Alonso de Bonilla committed to deliver 50 cargas of flour, biscuits, sarsaparilla, or other merchandise belonging to Juan Bautista Capelaso to the port of Suerre or Punta Blanca. He received 500 pesos for this service, with a deadline of the entire upcoming January.

Following the death of Marcos de Chinchilla, who left two legitimate children with doña Francisca del Castillo (Gaspar de Chinchilla and Felipa de Chinchilla), the Ordinary Mayor don Fernando de Salazar ordered an inventory of his estate. The inventory was conducted at the house of Catalina Palacios, the deceased's mother, and the assets were deposited with Alférez Tomás Calvo.
Juan de Chaves, Alférez mayor and Regidor, granted a general power of attorney to Diego López de Ortega.
Juan Alonso Camacho granted a general power of attorney to Alférez Juan de Quesada Monzón.

The Alcalde ordered an inventory of the assets left by María Rodríguez, widow of Juan Sánchez Crespo. Her children included Gaspar Sánchez, Antonio Sánchez, Francisca Sánchez, Antonia González, Ana María (a widow), and Leonor de Rivera (married). The inventory included the San Francisco ranch, houses, corrals, and animals, which were deposited with Gaspar and Antonio Sánchez.

The Alcalde ordered an inventory of the assets left by Juan Garro, who was married to Antonia María and had two children, Claudio and Ana. The inventory included the San Juan site, and the assets were deposited with Gaspar de Rojas, the father of the widow Antonia María.

people_involved: Licdo. don Diego de Obando y Espinosa
summary: Incomplete proceedings for the opening of the will of Alférez Manuel de Flores, who died on this day. His widow, Maria Barbosa, and Licdo. don Diego de Obando y Espinosa, the priest and beneficiary of Cartago, accepted the executorship, but the will itself was not present.

Diego López de Ortega was a creditor of Alférez mayor Juan de Chaves for $563.00. This sum included $213.00 paid by Ortega for Chaves to Pedro Pereira, $250.00 that Chaves collected from Catalina de Guevara in 1651, and $100.00 given in fruit cloths and a towel. In payment, Ortega received 23 tame and wild mules, 2 young donkeys, and 3 pesos in cash.

Juan de Chaves sold an estate named San Jerónimo to his sister, doña Isabel de Chaves, for $600.00. The estate included 150 cattle, 50 mares, 6 tame horses, houses, corrals, a plantain and cacao plantation, and 10 yokes of oxen. It was located three leagues from Pacaca, bordering Alférez Juan Martell's ranch, Quebrada Honda, the Pacacas' ranch, and the Elvirilla River. The sale included a $400.00 lien in favor of the Capellanía of Vasco Solano and Juan Martín Macotela and the Cofradía de la Concepción.

Jerónimo Leal and his wife, doña María Yáñez Cardosa, who purchased the San Bartolomé cattle ranch from Juan de Vida Martell for $960.00, became obligated to the Cofradía de la Soledad for this sum at a 5% interest rate, as the ranch was mortgaged to them. The Alcalde at this time was don Francisco Ramiro Corajo.

Capn. Juan del Castillo, residing in Cartago, issued a dowry letter for his wife, Felipa de Chinchilla, daughter of the late Alférez Marcos de Chinchilla and doña Francisca del Castillo. He received $3878.00 from Catalina Palacios, the wife's grandmother, which included a mill, four plots, a tiled house, and several enslaved people: Juana (36-30 years old), Cándida (16 years old), Agustina (18 years old), and Francisco (18 years old). The arras (earnest money) was $250.00.
María Núñez delivers goods related to the deceased de Torres. Cristobal Núñez, doña Ana de Quesada, and Francisco de Arrieta are listed as appraisers for these goods.

people_involved: doña Juana de Ortega y Chaves
summary: Cristobal Durán, Mayordomo of the Cofradía del Rosario, along with deputies Cristobal de Araya, Pedro Simón de Ordoño, and Alonso de Mora, sell a solar in Cartago to Juan de Vida Martell and his wife, doña Juana de Ortega y Chaves, for 20 pesos as a censo. The solar, previously possessed by the deceased Gaspar Núñez, was abandoned by his widow after 15 years of unpaid interest.

people_involved: don Juan Fernández Salinas y Velasco
summary: Governor don Juan Fernández Salinas y Velasco grants general power for lawsuits to Juan de Escobar Guijarro, a resident of Cartago.
Don Rodrigo Calderón sells 25 mules and male animals of various colors to Comisario Licdo. don Alonso de Sandoval for 10 pesos each.
Don Rodrigo Calderón grants general power to his wife, doña Isidora Zambrano, for all his business affairs.

Jerónimo Leal and his wife, doña Ana María Yáñes, acknowledge a 100-peso debt to Licdo. don Alonso de Sandoval. This debt originated from the sale of the San Bartolomé estancia by Juan de Vida Martell to Leal, which was previously owned by Alférez Juan Sánchez Crespo and María Rodríguez, and carried several financial obligations.
Jerónimo Leal and doña Ana María Yáñes also acknowledge a debt to Pe. Domingo de Echavarría, the current Cura of Cartago, for the same reason related to the estancia purchase.

Governor and Captain General don Andrés Arias Maldonado y Velasco grants freedom to Felipe, an indigenous man from Auyaque, who was imprisoned for wounding Juan, an indigenous man from Ujarraz. Roque Jacinto de la Fuente provided the bail for Felipe's release.

The Governor, with Juan de Escobar Guijarro acting as defender of indigenous people, places Pascual, an indigenous man from Tobosi, for two years with Pascual Ramírez, a master tanner from the same village, to complete his training in the trade.

Juan de Morales, departing for Guatemala with two indigenous muleteers, Francisco de Cárdenas and Juan, names Sargento mayor José de Moya as his guarantor. Francisco is from Barba and encomienda of don José de Alvarado, while Juan is from Ujarraz and encomienda of don Juan de Salazar.

Don Fernando Ramiro Corajo, traveling to Panama with the indigenous man Matías, who is from Barba and encomienda of Sargento mayor José de Moya, names his brother, don Francisco Ramiro Corajo, as his guarantor.
The Alcalde places Juan Francisco, a mestizo and son of Andrea, as an apprentice for six years with Captain don Francisco Ramiro Corajo.
Captain Benito Díaz Bravo, a resident of Cartago departing for Panama, grants general power for lawsuits and collections to Sargento mayor José de Moya.
Sargento mayor José de Moya and his wife, doña Mayor de Benavides, sell Catalina, a 15-year-old enslaved black woman and criolla from Cartago, to Captain Benito Díaz Bravo for 200 pesos.
The general power granted by Captain Benito Díaz Bravo to Sargento mayor José de Moya on April 3, 1659, was substituted to Francisco de Arrieta.

people_involved: Don Juan Fernández Salinas y Cerda
summary: Governor Don Juan Fernández Salinas y Cerda granted a power of attorney. The specific details or recipient of this power are not provided in this fragment.
Tomás Calvo, acting as the general depositary, granted a general power of attorney to Francisco Fernández Miranda. The purpose or scope of this power is not detailed.

people_involved: Don Juan Fernández Salinas y Cerda
summary: Nicolás Barrantes sold a cacao plantation located in the port of Matina, featuring 160 fruit trees along the Matina River and bordering Juan de la Cruz's property, to Governor Don Juan Fernández Salinas y Cerda for $100.

Francisco Gómez Rico obligated himself for $50 to the Cofradía del Rosario, founded in the parochial church, receiving the money from Mayordomo Cristobal Durán. This sum, redeemed by Antonio González, belonged to the Chaplaincy of Don Diego Charles. Gómez Rico mortgaged two plots, a house, adobe walls, and a 14-year-old slave named Luis, with the property bordering houses of Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado and Doña Margarita de Flores, for a two-year term at 5% interest.

Don José de Sandoval Ocampo sold a mill in Barba, including a main house and three other structures, to Antonio González for $500. The payment included $250 from two censos (one for Baltasar de Grado's Chaplaincy, patroned by Licenciado don Domingo de Chavarría, and another for Don Diego Charles de Herrera's Chaplaincy in the Cofradía del Rosario), with the remaining $250 to be paid in flour and biscuits delivered to Caldera the following May.

people_involved: Don Diego de Obando y Espinoza
Illmo. señor don Fray Tomás Manso
summary: Don Domingo de Chavarría, Cura of León de Nicaragua, and Don Diego de Obando y Espinoza, Cura of Cartago, agreed to exchange their benefices. They sought approval for this change from the Most Illustrious Lord Don Fray Tomás Manso, the Bishop-elect.

Doña Antonia Vázquez de Coronado, daughter of Alférez Diego Peláez and Doña Andrea Vázquez de Coronado, and widow of Sebastián Pereira Cardoso, made her testament. She had two deceased daughters, Doña Isabel de Obando and Doña Andrea Vázquez. Doña Isabel was married to Don José Sandoval Ocampo and had two children, Don Sebastián de Ocampo and Doña Inés de Benavides Solano.

people_involved: Doña Juana de Vera y Sotomayor
summary: Doña Juana de Vera y Sotomayor, widow of Sargento mayor García Ramiro Corajo, made her testament, detailing her dote and listing her eight children and their spouses. Her assets included several mulatto slaves, an estancia on the Río de la Lajucla with livestock, a house in Barba with crops, and various household items. She left legacies to several indigenous people, a free mulatto, Catalina del Peso and her daughter Leonor, and Isabel, daughter of Catalina Venegas and Diego Hernández. Her son Don Diego was in Panamá for business, and she had flour and biscuits in Caldera to send to him. Her executors were Licenciado Don Alonso de Sandoval, Don Diego Ramiro, and Don Fernando Ramiro.
Doña Andrea Vázquez de Coronado made her testament, declaring that her son Alonso Peláez had maintained her for over 28 years since her husband's death.

people_involved: Doña Juana de Vera y Sotomayor
summary: Doña Juana de Vera y Sotomayor, widow of García Ramiro Corajo, formally emancipated her son Don Antonio Ramiro.
Captain Don Rodrigo de Calderón granted power of attorney to Licenciado Don Alonso de Sandoval, Alférez Juan de Quesada Monzón, and Agustín Guerrero.

people_involved: Doña Juana de Sandoval y Olenzuela
summary: Pedro de la Portilla made his testament, mentioning his wife Magdalena de Loaiza and stating that he had raised Doña Juana de Sandoval y Olenzuela and Nicolás, a mestizo.
Nicolás de Guevara acted in favor of his wife, Ana María de Torres, who is identified as the legitimate daughter of Salvador.
María Núñez delivers goods related to the deceased de Torres, which are appraised by Cristobal Núñez, doña Ana de Quesada, and Francisco de Arrieta.

people_involved: doña Juana de Ortega y Chaves
summary: Cristobal Durán, Mayordomo of the Cofradía del Rosario, and its deputies sell a solar in Cartago to Juan de Vida Martell and his wife, doña Juana de Ortega y Chaves, for 20 pesos at censo. The solar, previously owned by the deceased Gaspar Núñez, was abandoned by his widow after he failed to pay réditos for 15 years.
Governor don Juan Fernández Salinas grants general power of attorney for lawsuits to Juan de Escobar Guijarro, a resident of Cartago.
Don Rodrigo Calderón sells 25 mules and machos of various colors to Comisario Licdo. don Alonso de Sandoval for 10 pesos each.
Don Rodrigo Calderón grants general power of attorney for all his business affairs to his wife, doña Isidora Zambrano.

Jerónimo Leal and his wife, doña Ana María Yáñes, acknowledge a debt of 100 pesos to Licdo. don Alonso de Sandoval. This debt was originally imposed on the San Bartolomé estancia by Alférez Juan Sánchez Crespo and his wife, María Rodríguez, and was part of the sale of the estancia from Juan de Vida Martell to Jerónimo Leal.
Jerónimo Leal and his wife, doña Ana María Yáñes, acknowledge a debt to Pe. Domingo de Echavarría, the current Cura of Cartago, for the same reason as the previous debt acknowledgment.

people_involved: Don Andrés Arias Maldonado y Velasco
summary: Governor and Captain General don Andrés Arias Maldonado y Velasco grants freedom to Felipe, an indigenous man from Auyaque, who was imprisoned in Cartago for wounding Juan, an indigenous man from Ujarraz. Roque Jacinto de la Fuente provides bail for Felipe.

The Governor, through Juan de Escobar Guijarro, places Pascual, an indigenous man from Tobosi, with Pascual Ramírez, a master tanner from the same town, for two years to complete his training in the trade.

Juan de Morales, departing for Guatemala, provides don José de Moya as guarantor for two indigenous arrieros, Francisco de Cárdenas (from Barba, encomienda of don José de Alvarado) and Juan (from Ujarraz, encomienda of don Juan de Salazar), whom he is taking with him.

Don Fernando Ramiro Corajo, traveling to Panamá, provides his brother don Francisco Ramiro Corajo as guarantor for the indigenous man Matías (from Barba, encomienda of don José de Moya), whom he is taking with him.
The Alcalde places Juan Francisco, a mestizo and son of Andrea, with Captain don Francisco Ramiro Corajo for a period of 6 years.

Captain Benito Díaz Bravo, residing in Cartago and departing for Panamá, grants general power of attorney for lawsuits and collections to Sergeant Major José de Moya. This power was later substituted to Francisco de Arrieta on March 15, 1660.
José de Moya and his wife, doña Mayor de Benavides, sell Catalina, a 15-year-old enslaved black woman and criolla from Cartago, to Captain Benito Díaz Bravo for 200 pesos.

Don Juan de Senabria Moldonado, son of Capitán Gonzalo de Senabria Maldonado and doña Jerónima Bravo Barrantes, made his will. He was married to doña Juana Moscoso de Figueroa, had no legitimate children, but a natural son, Sargento Nicolás Barrantes. He was an encomendero and treasurer, owned several slaves, and left a solar intended for a church to San Sebastián, naming his wife and natural son as executors.

Capn. Francisco Fernández de Miranda and his wife, doña Magdalena Calvo de Abarca, obligated themselves for 100 pesos at 5% annual interest to the chaplaincy founded by Vasco Solano, whose patron and chaplain is Licdo. don Alonso de Sandoval. They mortgaged their house in Cartago, bordering that of Tomás Calvo, the grantor's father-in-law.

María de Brenes, authorized by the Justice, sold her 19-year-old mulatilla slave, Juana, for $400.00 to Alférez Tomás Calvo. This sale was made to pay a $200.00 census in favor of Vasco Solano's chaplaincy, as her husband Juan de Olivares had left for Tierra Firme over three years prior and not returned.

Doña Catalina de la Jara, widow of Ignacio Artavia, was appointed tutor for her four legitimate minor children: Miguel (20), Ignacio (16), doña Francisca (18), and doña Isabel (14). Capitán José de Villalobos Jara served as her guarantor, and her deceased husband had an inheritance in Guatemala from his parents.

Don Francisco Ramiro and doña María de Retes obligated themselves for $100.00 to the chaplaincy founded by the deceased Alférez Andrés López de Céspedes. They mortgaged their houses in Cartago and a cattle ranch called Santa Ana in the Aserrí valley, which they had bought from Céspedes' executors in 1655. The census was later cancelled in 1678 by Marcos Machado, as Dª Mayor de Benavides took it over.

Cristóbal Durán and his wife, doña Ana Cardoso, obligated themselves for $40.00 at 5% interest to the chaplaincy founded by Andrés López de Céspedes. They mortgaged the houses that previously belonged to Céspedes, which they had purchased for 300 pesos, bordering the hermitage of San Juan and the former house of Pedro de las Alas.

Alférez don Francisco Solano obligated himself for $200.00 at 5% annual interest to his sister-in-law, doña María Vázquez de Coronado, wife of Pedro Solano. He mortgaged a house in Cartago, bordering Pedro Simón's house and María de Guido's house.

Antonia López de Ortega, daughter of Francisco López de Ortaga and María, made her will. She requested masses from Pe. Fray Marcos for his assistance during her illness. She had been married first to Francisco Solís de Velazco, with whom she had four children, and had married Jerónimo Valeriano two months prior to the will.

people_involved: Pedro de Soto (father of Pedro de Soto)
summary: Pedro de Soto, a native of Orense, Galicia, and son of Pedro de Soto (father of Pedro de Soto) and Catalina de Sotelo, established a dowry letter for his wife, doña María de Chaves. She received goods worth 683 pesos, including 10 mules to be provided by Alférez don Francisco Enciso Hita, who was traveling to Nicaragua.
Unspecified sellers sold their mulato criollo slave, Juan, aged about 18, for $100.00 to an unspecified buyer.

Nicolás González, traveling to Nicaragua, provided Alférez Cristobal de Quesada as a guarantor to take the indigenous man Francisco, from the pueblo of Guicazí and encomienda of Juan de Echavarría, with him.

Sargento mayor Alonso de Bonilla sold a site and lands called La Granadilla, bordering the Tiribí and Orobres rivers, to the Cofradía de la Vera Cruz in San Luis de Aserrí for $1000.00. He inherited this land from his grandfather, Capn. Alonso de Bonilla, who had bought it from the minors of Juan Gómez de Bonilla, and had previously sold it to Alférez Alonso de Vargas, but that sale was rescinded.
Francisco Gómez Rico, on behalf of his mother doña María Cardoso, sold a mulato named Sebastián Pereira, aged about 24, to Capn. Benito Díaz Bravo, a resident of Panamá, for $300.00.
A mulato criollo slave named Juan, approximately 18 years old, was sold for $100. The transaction took place in Cartago.
Nicolás González, preparing for a trip to Nicaragua with the indigenous man Francisco from Guicazí (part of Juan de Echavarría's encomienda), provided Alférez Cristobal de Quesada as a guarantor.

Sargento mayor Alonso de Bonilla sold a site and lands called La Granadilla, bordering the Tiribí and Orobres rivers, to the Cofradía de la Vera Cruz in San Luis de Aserrí for $1000. Pedro Zambrano was the Mayordomo of the Cofradía. Alonso de Bonilla inherited the land from his grandfather, Capn. Alonso de Bonilla, who had purchased it from the minors of Juan Gómez de Bonilla, though a previous sale by the grandfather to Alférez Alonso de Vargas was rescinded.

Francisco Gómez Rico, acting on behalf of his mother doña María Cardoso, sold a mulato slave named Sebastián Pereira, approximately 24 years old, to Capn. Benito Díaz Bravo, a resident of Panamá, for $300.

A dowry letter was issued for Pedro de Soto, a native of Orense, Galicia, and his wife doña María de Chaves. María received goods worth 683 pesos, including 10 mules from Cristobal Guerrero, which Alférez Francisco Enciso Hita was to deliver within a year or upon his return from Nicaragua.

Capn. Francisco Fernández de Miranda and his wife doña Magdalena Calvo de Abarca obligated themselves for 100 pesos at 5% interest to the Capellanía founded by Vasco Solano, whose patron and chaplain was Licdo. don Alonso de Sandoval. They mortgaged their house in Cartago, which bordered the house of Tomás Calvo, the father-in-law of Francisco Fernández de Miranda.

María de Brenes, wife of Juan de Olivares (who had left for Tierra Firme over three years prior and not returned), was authorized by Justice to sell a 19-year-old mulatilla slave named Juana to Alférez Tomás Calvo for $400. This sale was made to pay a $200 censo owed to the Capellanía of Vasco Solano.

Don Francisco Ramiro and his wife doña María de Retes obligated themselves to the Capellanía founded by the deceased Alférez Andrés López de Céspedes, whose chaplain was Licenciado Marcos Machado and which belonged to Magdalena de la Portilla. They received $100 from Alférez Juan López de Ortega, Céspedes' executor, and mortgaged their houses in Cartago and a cattle ranch called Santa Ana in the Aserrí valley. The ranch had a $300 censo from Céspedes to endow the Capellanía, and Céspedes' executors had sold it to Ramiro and Retes for $200 in 1655. The censo was later cancelled in 1678 by Marcos Machado as D* Mayor de Benavides took it over.

Doña Catalina de la Jara, widow of Ignacio Artavia, was appointed guardian for her minor children: Miguel (20), Ignacio (16), doña Francisca (18), and doña Isabel (14). Her deceased husband, Ignacio Artavia, had an inheritance in Guatemala from his parents, Pedro de Artavia and Isabel del Valle. Capitán José de Villalobos Jara served as her guarantor.

Cristóbal Durán and his wife doña Ana Cardoso obligated themselves for $40 at 5% interest to the Capellanía founded by Andrés López de Céspedes. They mortgaged adobe and tile houses they had purchased for $300, which previously belonged to Céspedes and bordered the ermita de San Juan and the former house of Pedro de las Alas.

The will of don Juan de Senabria Maldonado was recorded, dated July 11, 1657, and legalized on July 13, 1657. He was the legitimate son of Capitán Gonzalo de Senabria Maldonado and doña Jerónima Bravo Barrantes, married to doña Juana Moscoso de Figueroa (who brought a 4000 pesos dowry), and had no legitimate children. He was an encomendero in Quircó and Granada, Nicaragua, with his wife as his successor. He had served as treasurer of stamped paper, rendering accounts to José de Moya. He owned several slaves and had a natural son, Sargento Nicolás Barrantes. He left a plot of land, intended for a church to San Sebastián, to the saint, and named his wife and natural son as executors.

Alférez don Francisco Solano obligated himself for $200 at 5% annual interest to his sister-in-law doña María Vázquez de Coronado, wife of Pedro Solano. He mortgaged a house in Cartago, which bordered the house of Pedro Simón (across the street) and the house of María de Guido.

The will of Antonia López de Ortega was recorded. She was the legitimate daughter of Francisco López de Ortega and María de _____. She requested masses for her soul from Pe. Fray Marcos of the Order of Mercedes, who had assisted her during her illness. She was first married to Francisco Solís de Velazco, with whom she had five children: Blas Cristóbal, Clara, Agustina, and Juana Paulina. Two months prior to the will, she had married Jerónimo Valeriano.
In 1659, Jerónimo Valerino was contracted by the testadora to administer her cacao plantation in Matina for six months, receiving an annual salary of $100.
Jerónimo Valerino traveled to Nicaragua to sell 200 pesos of cacao and 10 mules, and to purchase various goods.
Jerónimo Valerino owes Fray Juan de Medina, a preacher, $2.
The testadora owned a cacao plantation in Matina with over 800 cacao trees, a plantain grove, fruit trees, a house, and a canoe for transport.
The testadora bequeathed legacies to her mother, María Pérez, and her sister, Ana López, who is married to Gaspar Rodríguez.
The testadora appointed her father as the guardian for her minor children.
The testadora's testament was signed on the 28th, during which time her husband returned from Nicaragua with 135 pesos, mules, blankets, and cotton.

On March 28, the testadora made another testament, reducing the legacies for her mother and sister, and leaving the majority of her fifth to Jerónimo Valerino, whom she also named as tutor for her minor children. The cacao plantation in Matina is noted to have only 600 trees.

Former Governor Juan Fernández Salinas y Cerda sold a 20-year-old black slave named Juan to Captain Juan Bautista de Torres Capelazo for $540 on credit. The slave was originally purchased from Francisco Cortada Mendoza and María de Sandoval of Remedios. Juan Fernández Salinas y Cerda provided other slaves as collateral and Domingo de Echavarría Navarro as a guarantor.

Domingo de Otárola, son of Domingo de Otárola Sr. and María Gurciva y Arandia, provided a dowry of $4052 for his wife, María de Alvarado, daughter of Alférez Gil de Alvarado and Doña Juana de Vera. The dowry included two criollo slaves, Gregorio (11 years old) and María (26 years old), and a credit of $1100 against Don Diego de Ibarra.

On October 29, Depositario General Tomás Calvo, authorized by Presbítero Domingo de Echavarría Navarro, granted power of attorney to Presbítero Alonso de Sandoval, currently in Panama, to collect all sums and merchandise from Juan Alvarez de Valcárcel, who was Fray Arévalo's correspondent and agent. Merchandise was sent by Juan Capelaso, Aduanero of Caldera, via a frigate from San Juan de Bolívar, with all assets belonging to the R. P. Provincial de Andalucía.

On October 9, Cristóbal de Vargas and his wife Petronila de Grado Moreno undertook an obligation on behalf of the minor children Juan and Nicolás Jiménez, who are the sons of the deceased Antonio Jiménez and María de Araya.

On December 13, Captain Alonso de Bonilla and his wife Juana Benita de Calvo obligated themselves for one hundred pesos, the value of one hundred cattle auctioned from the estate of the Jiménez minors' parents. They mortgaged their house in Cartago, located near the hermitage of San Juan.

On January 10, Nicolás José de Céspedes, a native of Cartago, sought information to prove his legitimate birth and noble lineage, being the son of Fabián de Céspedes y Meneses and Elena de Alarcón Chacón, and grandson of Leonardo de Céspedes and María de Meneses of Madrid, and Alférez Francisco Alarcón Chacón. He also sought to confirm his single status and whether his mother was the natural daughter of Alférez Francisco Alarcón Chacón, with several notable individuals providing declarations.

On February 24, Doña Margarita de Flores, widow of Captain Pedro de Mora Salado, obligated herself to the Convent of San Francisco for $100 at 5% annual interest, mortgaging her houses and two slaves, Leonor (black) and Damiana (mulata, Leonor's daughter).

On February 26, Andrés de Esquivel and his wife Antonia de Madrigal obligated themselves to Depositario Tomás Calvo for $180 at 5% annual interest, mortgaging their house. This house already had a $100 encumbrance from two donations made by Martín and Nicolás de Madrigal to Francisca de Esquivel, daughter of the grantors.

On the 13th, Francisco López Serrano, a native of Ciudad de los Reyes, Peru, and son of Juan de Serrano and Marta de Gamboa, provided a dowry of $2000 for María de Sibaja, daughter of Baltasar de Ortega and Jerónima Gómez, whom he is marrying the next day. The dowry included some biscuits from Celidón de Ortega, her brother, and an arras of $500.

On the 7th, Cristóbal Durán and his wife Ana Pereira Cardoso obligated themselves to the Capellanía founded by Alférez Andrés López de Céspedes for $310 at 5% annual interest, representing the price of houses.

In 1659, the Testadora arranged for Jerónimo Valerino to manage her cacao plantation in Matina for six months at $100 annually. Valerino later traveled to Nicaragua to sell cacao and mules, returning with less money than expected. The Testadora's estate included a cacao plantation with over 800 trees, and she owed Fray Juan de Medina $2. She left legacies to her mother María Pérez and sister Ana López, and initially named her father as tutor for her minors.

On March 28, the Testadora made another will, stating her Matina cacao plantation now had only 600 trees. She reduced the legacies for her mother and sister, leaving the majority of the 'quinto' to Jerónimo Valerino, whom she also named as tutor for her minors.

people_involved: Don Juan Fernández Salinas y Cerda
Capitán Juan Bautista de Torres Capelazo
summary: Ex-Governor Don Juan Fernández Salinas y Cerda sold a 20-year-old black slave named Juan to Captain Juan Bautista de Torres Capelazo for $540 on credit. The slave had been purchased from Francisco Cortada Mendoza and María de Sandoval, residents of Remedios. Don Juan provided his mulatto slaves Juan de Regla and Francisca Herrador, and black slave Juan Francisco as collateral, and Pe. don Domingo de Echavarría as guarantor.

Domingo de Otárola, a native of Bilbao and legitimate son of Domingo de Otárola and María Gurciva y Arandia, provided a dowry for his wife Doña María de Alvarado, legitimate daughter of Alférez don Gil de Alvarado and Doña Juana de Vera. The dowry included $4052, an 11-year-old Creole black slave named Gregorio ($350), a 26-year-old Creole black slave named María ($550), and a credit of $1100 against Don Diego de Ibarra.

On October 29, Depositario General Tomás Calvo, authorized by Presbítero don Domingo de Echavarría Navarro, granted power of attorney to Presbítero don Alonso de Sandoval, currently in Panamá. This power was to collect sums and merchandise from Juan Alvarez de Valcárcel, Fray Agustín de Arévalo's correspondent, and from Juan Capelaso, the customs officer of Caldera. The commission, dated October 28, stated all goods belonged to the R. P. Provincial de Andalucía.

On October 9, Cristóbal de Vargas and his wife Petronila de Grado Moreno committed themselves to the minors Juan and Nicolás Jiménez, who were the children of the deceased Antonio Jiménez and María de Araya.

On December 13, Captain Alonso de Bonilla and his wife Juana Benita de Calvo committed themselves to Juan and Nicolás Jiménez for one hundred pesos, the value of one hundred cattle auctioned from their parents' estate. They mortgaged their house in Cartago, which included two plots and bordered the hermitage of San Juan.

On January 10, Nicolás José de Céspedes, a native of Cartago, sought information to prove his legitimate birth and noble lineage, and to confirm he was single. Witnesses, including Pe. don Domingo de Echavarría (35), Alférez Juan López de Ortega (72), Tomás Calvo (60), Capitán don Pedro de Córdova (63), Alférez Francisco Arrieta (over 84), and Capitán Juan de Vida Martell (37), were asked if Elena de Alarcón Chacón was the natural daughter of Alférez Francisco Alarcón Chacón.

On February 24, Doña Margarita de Flores, widow of Captain Pedro de Mora Salado, committed herself to the Convento de San Francisco for $100 at 5% annual interest. She mortgaged her houses and two slaves: a black woman named Leonor and her mulatto daughter, Damiana.

On February 26, Andrés de Esquivel and his wife Antonia de Madrigal committed themselves to Depositario Tomás Calvo for $180 at 5% annual interest. They mortgaged their house, which already had a $100 lien from two donations made by Martín and Nicolás de Madrigal to Francisca (?) de Esquivel, daughter of the grantors.

On the 13th, Francisco López Serrano, a native of Ciudad de los Reyes, Perú, and legitimate son of Juan de Serrano and Doña Marta de Gamboa, provided a dowry for Doña María de Sibaja, legitimate daughter of Baltasar de Ortega and Jerónima Gómez, whom he was to marry the next day. The dowry included $2000, with some biscuits to be delivered by Celidón de Ortega, her brother, and a 'arras' of $500.

On the 7th, Cristóbal Durán and his wife Doña Ana Pereira Cardoso committed themselves to the Chaplaincy founded by Alférez Andrés López de Céspedes for $310 at 5% annual interest, as payment for houses.

The executor, Alférez Juan López de Ortega, sold adobe and tile houses that had belonged to 'the founder' and were subsequently purchased by 'the grantors'. These properties bordered the land of Señor San Juan and Juan Bautista Letona.

Captain and Sargento Mayor José de Moya sold an enslaved Black man named Lázaro, who was one-eyed, to Captain Juan Bautista Torres Capelazo for $200. Moya had acquired Lázaro through a purchase from Catalina de Palacios.

Captain Juan Bautista de Torres Capelazo sold an adobe and straw house to Cristóbal de Vargas for $250. The house was originally purchased by Torres Capelazo from María Barboza, widow of Alférez Manuel de Florez, in 1657, and the sale included obligations to two chaplaincies.
The Mayor placed Jusepe de Mena, a 12-year-old son of the poor man Jerónimo de Mena, with tailor Juan de Liñan for 6 years to learn the trade.
Bernabé de Chaves committed to serving Captain Juan Bautista de Torres Capelazo for one year, working with his mule train to travel to Matina, Suerre, or Caldera, for a payment of $35.

The Mayor, having received notice of Lucas Cervantes, a mulatto from Los Angeles, severely beating his son Sebastián, placed Sebastián with tailor Diego Pérez for 6 years to learn the trade and prevent further abuse.

A dowry letter was issued for the marriage of Cristóbal de Vargas, a native of Seville, to Doña Petronila Moreno. Cristóbal received $3124 from Petronila's tutor, Sargento Mayor don José de Moya, which included four enslaved people and $1000 in arras.

Cristóbal de Vargas received an additional $2024 in assets from José de Moya on behalf of his wife, Doña Petronila Moreno. These assets included a cattle site in Barba, cattle, credit against Moya, and an inheritance from Licenciado Baltasar de Grado.
