Alférez Juan Vázquez de Coronado sold a wheat farm in the Aserrí valley, near the Río de las Cañas, with 18 fanegas of sown wheat, to Alférez don Fernando Ramiro for $150.

Sargento Mayor José de Moya and his wife, Doña Mayor de Benavides Moreno, committed to paying $150 at 5% annual interest to the legitimate sons and heirs of Antonio Jiménez and María de Araya, named Juan and Nicolás Jiménez. They mortgaged their house, which bordered properties of Tomás Calvo, Leonor Jiménez, and Juan de Echavarría Navarro.

Captain Sebastián de Quirós and his wife, Doña Isabel de Guevara, committed to paying $90 at 5% interest to the Cofradía de San Nicolás de Tolentino. They mortgaged a plantain and sugarcane field with two houses, located about two leagues from the Pez River and bordering the Orosi River.

Juan Vázquez de Coronado and his wife, Ana María de Mora, committed to paying $60 at 5% interest to the endowment for maidens and the Cofradía de la Concepción. They mortgaged a cattle ranch called San Alfonso in the Aserrí valley, which included two houses and bordered the ranch of Don Francisco Solano.
The Mayor arranged for Nicolás de Santiatiago, a 15-year-old native of Quircó, to apprentice with shoemaker Alonso Sánchez for 2 years.
Juana, an indigenous widow from Guaicasí, handed over her 9-year-old son Marcos to Alférez Juan López de Ortega for service.
The Mayor arranged for Lucas, son of the free mulatta Catalina Mayorga, to apprentice with tailor Diego Pérez de Medina for 4 years.
The Mayor arranged for Juan Alonso, an 11-year-old free mulatto orphan, to apprentice with master blacksmith Agustín González de Loría for 6 years.
A dowry letter was issued for the marriage of Alférez Sebastián de Zamora, a native of Marchena, Spain, to Doña Lucía de Ocampo Sandoval. The dowry amounted to $1021.
This entry mentions María Alvarez de Ochoa, widow of Juan Rodríguez, on April 5, 1661, likely in connection with a transaction or legal matter.

Alférez Juan López de Ortega, acting as executor, sold adobe and tile houses that originally belonged to the founder and were subsequently purchased by the grantors. These houses bordered properties of Señor San Juan and Juan Bautista Letona.

Captain and Sergeant Major José de Moya sold a one-eyed black slave named Lázaro to Captain Juan Bautista Torres Capelazo for $200. Moya had previously acquired Lázaro through purchase from Catalina de Palacios.

Captain Juan Bautista Torres Capelazo sold an adobe and straw house to Cristóbal de Vargas for $250. Torres Capelazo had purchased this house from María Barboza, widow of Alférez Manuel de Florez, in 1657. The sale included the obligation to pay $100 to Doña Ana de Medrano's chaplaincy and $150 to Licenciado Baltasar de Grado's chaplaincy.
The Alcalde arranged for Jusepe de Mena, a 12-year-old son of the poor Jerónimo de Mena, to be apprenticed to Juan de Liñan, a tailor, for a period of 6 years to learn the trade.
Bernabé de Chaves committed to serve Captain Juan Bautista Torres Capelazo for one year, working with his mule train on journeys to Matina, Suerre, or Caldera, for a payment of $35.

The Alcalde, after receiving notice of severe abuse, placed Sebastián, son of Lucas Cervantes, with Diego Pérez, a tailor, for 6 years. This action was taken because Lucas Cervantes, a mulatto from Los Angeles, had cruelly beaten his son, causing life-threatening injuries, and to prevent further such incidents.

A dowry letter was issued for the marriage of Cristóbal de Vargas, a native of Sevilla, to Doña Petronila Moreno. Doña Petronila received $3124 from her tutor, Sergeant Major Don José de Moya, which included four slaves and $1000 in arras.

Cristóbal de Vargas received an additional $2024 in assets from José de Moya on behalf of his wife, Doña Petronila Moreno. These assets included a cattle site in Barba, cattle, credit against Moya, and an inheritance from Licenciado Baltasar de Grado.

On December 18, 1674, Alférez Juan Vázquez de Coronado sold a wheat farm in the Aserrí valley, near the Río de las Cañas, to Alférez Don Fernando Ramiro for $150. The farm was estimated to have 18 fanegas of sown wheat.

On December 18, 1676, Sergeant Major José de Moya and his wife, Doña Mayor de Benavides Moreno, committed to pay $150 at 5% annual interest to the legitimate sons and heirs of Antonio Jiménez and María de Araya, named Juan and Nicolás Jiménez. They mortgaged their house, which bordered properties of Tomás Calvo, Leonor Jiménez, and Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro, a house previously owned by Pe. Alonso de Sandoval.

locations: Ermita de San Nicolás de Tolentino

They mortgaged a cattle ranch called San Alfonso in the Aserrí valley, which originated from a chaplaincy founded by Andrés López de Céspedes, whose executor was Juan López de Ortega.
On January 25, 1661, the Alcalde placed Nicolás de Santiatiago, a 15-year-old native of Quircó, with Alonso Sánchez, a shoemaker, for 2 years to learn the trade.
On January 25, 1661, Juana, an indigenous widow from Guaicasí, handed over her 9-year-old son Marcos to Alférez Juan López de Ortega for service.
On January 29, 1661, the Alcalde placed Lucas, son of the free mulatta Catalina Mayorga, with Diego Pérez, a tailor, for 4 years to learn the trade.

A father, whose name is partially recorded as 'guez', ceded a site to his daughter, María Alvarez de Ochoa, and her husband, Luis Gutiérrez. In exchange, the couple committed to pay $120 to the Cofradía de la Concepción.

people_involved: Don José de Guevara y Sandoval
summary: Don José de Guevara y Sandoval and his wife, Doña Inés Ocampo Golfín, committed to a $200, 5% annuity in favor of Alférez Tomás Calvo, the syndic of the San Francisco Convent, who founded a chaplaincy. They mortgaged their house in the city, which was part of Doña Inés's dowry from Don José de Sandoval Ocampo.

Catalina Palacios, widow of Gaspar de Chinchilla, committed to pay $100 to the Cofradía de la Concepción for a chaplaincy founded by Doña Ana de Medrano. Catalina's mother, Luisa Hernández, and stepfather, Juan de Lamas, were previously responsible for this chaplaincy. Catalina mortgaged her houses in the city.

A dowry letter was granted in the Valle de Barba by Francisco Hernández de Isido, son of Ambrosio Hernández de Isidro and Doña María de Silva, to his wife, Doña Juana de Añasco, for $466. Doña Juana is the natural daughter of Don Pedro Vázquez de Añasco and adopted daughter of Pedro de la Portilla and Magdalena de Loaiza, having married three years prior.

A dowry letter was granted by Jerónimo Valerino, widower of Antonia López, to his wife Francisca de Esquivel, for $1076, including a house and lot. Jerónimo is the son of Agustín Valerín and Batina Lozana, and Francisca is the daughter of Alférez Andrés de Esquivel and Antonia de Madrigal.
Manuel Agustín, a mulatto, was handed over to Juan Alonso Hernández, a master saddler, for four years to learn the trade.
Doña Inés Alvarez Pereira, widow of Capitán Bme. Sánchez, granted freedom to her enslaved criolla black woman named Luisa.

A dowry letter was granted by Feliciano Masís, son of Melchor Masís and Catalina Hernández, to his wife María de Madrigal, for $235. María is the legitimate daughter of Diego de Madrigal and Catalina de Guevara.

A dowry letter was granted by Andrés Jaimes, son of Esteban de las Alas and María de Rivera, to his wife Francisca de Mendoza, for $398. Francisca was raised by Isabel Jiménez and is reputed to be the natural daughter of the late Don Francisco de Mendoza.

A dowry letter was granted by Bernardo Torres Capelazo to his wife Doña Juana de Herrera for $3023. Doña Juana is the daughter of the late Juan de Herrera and Doña María Estefanía de Aguilar. The dowry included half of Doña María Estefanía's house and site called Santa Cruz de Caravaca. Juan Bautista Torres Capelazo stipulated that if the marriage was annulled, Doña María should receive aid to marry off a girl named Juana Bautista, whom she raised.
Teniente Pedro de Campos Quirós, preparing for a trip to Panamá, granted general power of attorney to his wife, Doña Bárbara Rodríguez Altamirano, and his brother-in-law, Sargento Mayor José de Moya.

people_involved: Doña Bárbara Altamirano Rodríguez y Moreno
Sargento Mayor don José de Moya
summary: Doña Bárbara Altamirano Rodríguez y Moreno, wife and attorney-in-fact for her husband Pedro de Campos Quirós, requested information to prove her legitimacy as the second of three legitimate daughters of Capitán Antonio Rodríguez Moreno and Doña Inés de Benavides. Witnesses, including Alférez Andrés de Esquivel and Alonso Peláez, provided testimonies regarding her family.

A dowry letter was granted by Nicolás de Brenes to his wife Inés Margarita for $487, including $100 from the Cofradía de la Concepción. Inés Margarita is the legitimate daughter of the deceased Baltasar Muñoz and Inés de Avalos, and her brother-in-law, Sargento Francisco Peláez, delivered the assets.

A dowry letter was granted by Luis de Fonseca to his wife Doña Jerónima de Retes for $5490. Doña Jerónima is the daughter of Capitán Jerónimo de Retes and Doña María Vazquez de Coronado. The dowry included three enslaved mulattoes (Beatriz with her two sons, Francisco (5) and Esteban Cecilio (1), and Juana (11)) and a sugar mill and site in Ujarrás.
The Alcalde delivered a mulatta girl named María, daughter of the poor woman Juana María and niece of Cristóbal García Beltrán, to Doña Mayor de Benavides, a widow.

people_involved: Doña María de Lara y Orozco
summary: A dowry letter was granted in the Valle de Aserrí by Sargento Antonio de Orozco to his wife Doña Isabel del Castillo for $1541. Doña Isabel is the daughter of the late Juan Gómez Rico and Doña María Cardoso. The dowry included a house and land, an enslaved mulatta named Ana, her daughter, and another enslaved infant.

Sargento Antonio de Orozco, who was to marry the next day, declared that he had been married a third time for 16 years to the deceased Ana López. They had four children: María de Orozco, Beatriz Agustina, Juan, and Francisco, and he declared the assets belonging to them.
José del Aya y Bolívar, a resident of Cartago, committed to pay Licenciado Don Domingo Echavarría Navarro, the city's priest, $236 that he had borrowed, with payment to be made in Bananía.
A father, identified as guez, ceded a site to his daughter, María Alvarez de Ochoa, and her husband, Luis Gutiérrez. In exchange, the couple committed to pay $120.00 to the Cofradía de la Concepción.

people_involved: Don José de Guevara y Sandoval
summary: Don José de Guevara y Sandoval and his wife, Doña Inés Ocampo Golfín, obligated themselves for a $200.00 annuity at 5% to Alférez Tomás Calvo, Syndic of the San Francisco Convent, who founded a chaplaincy. They mortgaged their city house, which was given to them as a dowry by Don José de Sandoval Ocampo and bordered properties of Don Francisco Ramiro, Diego de Ocampo, Alonso Peláez, and Esteban de Torres.

locations: calle que va á San Francisco
summary: Catalina Palacios, widow of Gaspar de Chinchilla, obligated herself to the Cofradía de la Concepción for $100.00 for a chaplaincy founded by Doña Ana de Medrano, previously managed by her mother Luisa Hernández and stepfather Juan de Lamas. Juan Vázquez de Coronado, Mayordomo of the Cofradía, was involved. Catalina mortgaged her houses in the city, on the street to San Francisco, bordering properties of Marcos de Herrera and Don José de Alvarado.

A dowry letter was issued in the Barba valley for Francisco Hernández de Isido, legitimate son of Ambrosio Hernández de Isidro and Doña María de Silva, residents of Pueblo Nuevo in Tierra Firme. The dowry of $466.00 was for his wife, Doña Juana de Añasco, natural daughter of Don Pedro Vázquez de Añasco and adopted daughter of Pedro de la Portilla and Magdalena de Loaiza, whom he married three years prior.

locations: calle que va de la plaza á la Soledad
summary: A dowry letter was issued for Jerónimo Valerino, a widower of Antonia López and native of Genoa, in favor of his wife, Francisca de Esquivel, legitimate daughter of Alférez Andrés de Esquivel and Antonia de Madrigal. The dowry was $1076.00, including a house and lot on the street from the plaza to La Soledad, bordering Doña Isabel Flores's houses. The arras was $500.00.
Manuel Agustín, a mulatto, was delivered to Juan Alonso Hernández, a master saddler, for a period of four years to learn the trade.
Doña Inés Alvarez Pereira, widow of Capitán Bme. Sánchez, granted freedom to her creole black slave, Luisa.

A dowry letter was issued for Feliciano Masís, legitimate son of Melchor Masís and Catalina Hernández, in favor of his wife, María de Madrigal, legitimate daughter of Diego de Madrigal and Catalina de Guevara. The dowry was $235.00, and the arras was $100.00.

A dowry letter was issued for Andrés Jaimes, legitimate son of Esteban de las Alas and María de Rivera, in favor of his wife, Francisca de Mendoza. Francisca was a young woman raised by Isabel Jiménez and was reputed to be the natural daughter of Don Francisco de Mendoza, a former resident of the city. The dowry was $398.00.

A dowry letter was issued for Bernardo Torres Capelazo, native of Genoa, legitimate son of Juan Bautista Monteproensia and Hortensia Monteproensa, in favor of his wife, Doña Juana de Herrera, legitimate daughter of the late Juan de Herrera and Doña María Estefanía de Aguilar. The dowry was $3023.00, including half of Doña María Estefanía's property, Santa Cruz de Caravaca, near Ujarrás. Juan Bautista Torres Capelazo contributed part of the dowry, stipulating that if the marriage was annulled, Doña María should receive aid to help marry Juana Bautista, a girl she raised.

Teniente Pedro de Campos Quirós, who was preparing for a trip to Panama, granted general power of attorney to his wife, Doña Bárbara Rodríguez Altamirano, and his brother-in-law, Sargento Mayor José de Moya.

people_involved: Doña Bárbara Altamirano Rodríguez y Moreno
Sargento Mayor don José de Moya
summary: Doña Bárbara Altamirano Rodríguez y Moreno, wife and attorney of Pedro de Campos Quirós, requested information to prove her legitimacy as the second of three daughters of Capitán Antonio Rodríguez Moreno and Doña Inés de Benavides. Witnesses, including Alférez Andrés de Esquivel and Alonso Peláez, testified about her family, identifying her sisters as Doña Mayor de Benavides (widow of Sargento Mayor don José de Moya), Doña Inés, and Doña Petronila.

A dowry letter was issued for Nicolás de Brenes in favor of his wife, Inés Margarita, legitimate daughter of the deceased Baltasar Muñoz and Inés de Avalos. Sargento Francisco Peláez, Inés Margarita's brother-in-law, delivered goods totaling $487.00, which included a $100.00 dowry from the Cofradía de la Concepción.

A dowry letter was issued for Luis de Fonseca, native of San Lúcar de Guardiana, legitimate son of Capitán Luis Alvarez and Doña María Gómez de Fonseca, in favor of his wife, Doña Jerónima de Retes, legitimate daughter of Capitán Jerónimo de Retes, Alguacil Mayor, and Doña María Vazquez de Coronado. The dowry was $5490.00, including three mulatto slaves (Beatriz and her two sons, Francisco and Esteban Cecilio, and Juana) and a sugar mill in Ujarrás, with an arras of $3000.00.
The Alcalde delivered a mulatto girl named Maria, daughter of the poor woman Juana María and niece of Cristóbal García Beltrán, to Doña Mayor de Benavides, a widow.

people_involved: Doña María de Lara y Orozco
summary: A dowry letter was issued in the Aserrí valley for Sargento Antonio de Orozco, native of Sevilla, legitimate son of Agustín de Rivera y Córdova and Doña María de Lara y Orozco, in favor of his wife, Doña Isabel del Castillo, legitimate daughter of the late Juan Gómez Rico and Doña María Cardoso. The dowry was $1541.00, including a house, lands, and three mulatto slaves (Ana, her daughter, and a baby), with an arras of $200.00.

An addition was made to Sargento Antonio de Orozco's dowry letter, stating that he was to marry the next day, May 7th. He declared his previous 16-year marriage to the deceased Ana López, a city resident, who brought a $1100.00 dowry, and acknowledged their four children: María de Orozco, Beatriz Agustina, Juan, and Francisco, detailing their inherited assets.
José del Aya y Bolívar, a resident of Cartago, obligated himself to Licenciado don Domingo Echavarría Navarro, the city's priest, for a $236.00 loan, which he promised to repay in Bananía.

Captain Alonso de Bonilla leased his share of a cacao plantation to Jerónimo Valerín for $100. This plantation was originally obtained from Maese de Campo Juan de Salinas and was previously co-leased with Captain Francisco Fernández de Miranda, who had already leased his portion to Valerín.

The will of Alférez Bartolomé de Aguilar, son of Pedro Hernández de Aguilar and María Calderón, was recorded. It detailed his two marriages, first to Luisa de Hogala with whom he had Margarita and Juan, and second to Catalina Palacios with whom he had Manuel. He also acknowledged a natural son, José, raised by María del Castillo, and named his brothers José and Antonio Calderón de Aguilar as executors.

Antonio Ramiro Corajo, son of García Romiro Corajo and Juana de Vera, took responsibility for a 220 pesos principal census. This debt was imposed on a cattle ranch in the Río Grande area, which he inherited from his parents, in favor of a chaplaincy founded by the deceased Juan Alonso.

Antonio Ramiro Corajo further obligated himself for $100 in favor of a chaplaincy founded by Vasco Solano. This obligation was secured with the same cattle ranch in the Río Grande area, for similar reasons as his previous commitment.

Following the death of Ana Merino, the Alcalde reassigned a mestizo boy named Juan, who had been under Merino's care, to Felipe Monge, Merino's son, for a term of one year. This event was recorded in the site of Nuestra Señora de la Concepción, located in the valley of Aserrí.

A dowry letter was issued for José del Aya y Bolívar, a native of Panama and son of Juan del Aya y Bolívar and Antonia de Llerena y Guzmán, and his wife María de Alfaro y Chaves, daughter of Alférez Diego López de Ortega and Ana de Chaves. The dowry amounted to $2000, with arras of $6000, and included an 11-year-old mulata slave named Lucía valued at $400.
Juan de Escobar Guijarro and his wife Catalina de Lumbides sold a 22-year-old mulata slave named Juana to the depositary Tomás Calvo for $300.

Don José de Guevara y Sandoval committed to providing the depositary Tomás Calvo with sufficient goods at the port of Caldera. These goods were intended to load a frigate that had arrived from Panama.

Captain Rodrigo Calderón and his wife Isidora Zambrano obligated themselves for $100 at a 5% census to the Confraternity of the Concepción's endowment fund for maidens. They mortgaged a flour mill in the valley of Aserrí, bordering Manuel Gómez's ranch and the town of Aserrí, receiving the funds from Juan López de Ortega, who acted as executor for Andrés López de Céspedes, the original donor.

A dowry letter was issued for Juan Ruiz Guillén, a native of Carmona and son of Sebastián Crespo and María Márquez, and his wife María de Santiago, daughter of Pedro de Santiago and Gertrudis de Escobar, natives of Cartago. The dowry totaled $1071, including a house with fruit trees in Potreros de Có ($200) and a cacao plantation in Jarro ($250), with arras of $500.

Alonso de Sibaja sold inherited properties, including two lots in Cartago bordering houses of Juana de Moscoso and Ana de Quesada, and a cattle ranch in the Barba valley at the confluence of the Elvirilla and Ciruelas rivers, to José de Sandoval Ocampo for $170. These properties, including 30 head of cattle and subject to a census for the Confraternity of the Concepción, were inherited from his deceased parents, Juan de Villarroel and Catalina de Zárate.

A dowry letter was issued for Juan Bantista Daniel, a native of Barati in the Lordship of Genoa and son of Francisco Daniel and Catalina Fava, and his wife Fabiana de Sojo y Peñaranda, daughter of Gaspar de los Ríos and Francisca de Peñaranda. The dowry amounted to $678, with arras of $200.

people_involved: Manuel Gómez de Ocón y Trillo
summary: Captain Manuel Gómez de Ocón y Trillo granted general power of attorney to Juan de Vida Martell.

A dowry letter was issued for Bartolomé Muñoz Hidalgo, a native of Montilla, Spain, and son of Andrés Muñoz Hidalgo and Catalina Sánchez de Ortega, and his wife Sebastiana Calvo Abarca, daughter of Alférez Tomás Calvo and Eugenia Abarca de Alatras. The dowry was $4332 and 4 reales, with arras of $2000, for their marriage scheduled for the 11th.

Captain Alonso de Bonilla leased his share of a cacao plantation, originally obtained from Maese de Campo Juan de Salinas, to Jerónimo Valerín for $100. This plantation was previously co-leased with Captain Francisco Fernández de Miranda, who had already leased his portion to Valerín.

Alférez Bartolomé de Aguilar's will details his family, including his parents Pedro Hernández de Aguilar and María Calderón. He was married twice, first to Luisa de Hogala, with whom he had Margarita (8 years old) and Juan (6 years old), and second to Catalina Palacios, with whom he had Manuel. He also acknowledged a natural son, José, raised by María del Castillo, and named his brothers José and Antonio Calderón de Aguilar as executors.

Antonio Ramiro Corajo took responsibility for a 220 pesos debt (censo) on a cattle ranch in Río Grande, which he inherited from his parents, García Romiro Corajo and Juana de Vera. This debt was in favor of a chaplaincy founded by the late Juan Alonso.
Antonio Ramiro Corajo obligated himself for another 100 pesos debt (censo) in favor of a chaplaincy founded by Vasco Solano. The same Río Grande site was used as collateral for this obligation.

Following the death of Ana Merino, the Alcalde reassigned a mestizo boy named Juan, who had been under Merino's care, to Felipe Monge, Merino's son, for a period of one year. This event took place in the valley of Aserrí.

José del Aya y Bolívar, a native of Panamá, provided a dowry of $2000 and arras of $6000 for his wife, María de Alfaro y Chaves. The dowry included an 11-year-old mulata slave named Lucía, valued at $400.
Juan de Escobar Guijarro and his wife, Catalina de Lumbides, sold a 22-year-old mulata slave named Juana to the depositary Tomás Calvo for $300.

Don José de Guevara y Sandoval obligated himself to the depositary Tomás Calvo to provide sufficient goods at the port of Caldera. These goods were intended to load a frigate that had arrived from Panamá.

Captain Rodrigo Calderón and his wife, Isidora Zambrano, obligated themselves for $100 at a 5% censo to the Cofradía de la Concepción's dowry fund for maidens. They mortgaged a flour mill in the valley of Aserrí, bordering Manuel Gómez's ranch and the town of Aserrí, receiving the funds from Juan López de Ortega, who was the executor for Andrés López de Céspedes, the original donor for this foundation.

Juan Ruiz Guillén, a native of Carmona, provided a dowry of $1071 for his wife, María de Santiago, whose parents were from Cartago. The dowry included a house with 43 peach and 6 quince trees in the Có pastures valued at $200, and a cacao plantation in Jarro with 100 flowering trees valued at $250, along with arras of $500.

Alonso de Sibaja sold two inherited solars in Cartago and a cattle ranch in the valley of Barba, located at the confluence of the Elvirilla and Ciruelas rivers, to Don José de Sandoval Ocampo for $170. These properties were inherited from his deceased parents, Juan de Villarroel and Catalina de Zárate, and the ranch included 30 head of cattle and was subject to a censo in favor of the Cofradía de la Concepción.
Juan Bantista Daniel, a native of Barati in the Lordship of Genoa, provided a dowry of $678 for his wife, Fabiana de Sojo y Peñaranda. He also provided arras of $200.

people_involved: Manuel Gómez de Ocón y Trillo
summary: Captain Manuel Gómez de Ocón y Trillo granted general power of attorney to Juan de Vida Martell.

Bartolomé Muñoz Hidalgo, a native of Montilla, Spain, provided a dowry of $4332 and 4 reales for his wife, Sebastiana Calvo Abarca. Their marriage was scheduled for the 11th, two days after the document's creation.

Esteban de Hoces Navarro, son of Esteban de Hoces Navarro and Gracia Retano, established a dowry of $3922-4 reales and an 'arras' of $1000-00 for his wife, doña Juana Calvo de Abarca, daughter of Tomás Calvo and doña Eugenia de Abarca Alatras.

Don Juan del Castillo and his wife, doña Felipa de Santiago, sold an 18-year-old enslaved mulata named Agustina to Licenciado don Domingo de Echavarría, the Cura of Cartago, for $300-00. Agustina had been part of doña Felipa's dowry.
Tomás Calvo, acting as the general depositary, cancelled a census (debt) of $100-00 for which Don Juan del Castillo and his wife, doña Felipa Chinchilla, were responsible.

Nicolás Camacho and his wife, Catalina López, took on an obligation of $105-00 to the Cofradía de la Concepción, a debt previously owed by Ana Merino, Nicolás Camacho's deceased mother. They secured this obligation with a mortgage on a cattle ranch.
Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado and his wife, doña Juana Moscoso y Figueroa, granted freedom to their enslaved mulato, Nicolás de Figueroa.

Catalina de Alarcón, widow of Diego de Madrigal, forgave don Francisco de Linares for her husband's death, acknowledging that Madrigal had provoked Linares to self-defense. Linares offered $100-00 for the sustenance of Madrigal's children.
Cristóbal de Vargas delivered his enslaved criollo, Juan, to Diego Pérez, a master tailor, for six months. The purpose was for Pérez to complete Juan's training in the tailoring trade.

El Presbítero don Domingo de Echavarría, Cura and Vicar of Cartago, granted power of attorney to Cristóbal de Vargas to collect 400 pesos from Amaro López de Lozada in Panamá, based on a written agreement.

people_involved: Don Rodrigo Arias Maldonado y Velasco
summary: Don Salvador Jirón de Alvarado, acting as agent for Juan Tercero de Montalvo, sold an enslaved mulato named Juan de Herrera, 36 years old, to Don Rodrigo Arias Maldonado y Velasco, the Governor and Captain General of Cartago province, for $300-00. This transaction referenced an earlier sale of the same enslaved person (then named Juan Díaz) from José Méndez de Sierra to Tercero in León in 1661.
Lucas Cervantes agreed with Diego de Santiago, a blacksmith, to apprentice his son, Sebastián, to him for four years to learn the trade.

people_involved: El Capitán don José Pérez de Luna
don José de Guevara y Sandoval
summary: Capitán don José Pérez de Luna, expecting a frigate in June at Caldera to load 600 tercios as agreed with Captains Ascensio Ruiz and Nicolás Hurtado of Panamá, made an agreement with don José de Guevara y Sandoval for the latter to load 300 tercios.
Capitán Diego de Zúñiga agreed with Agustín González de Loría, a blacksmith, to apprentice his grandson, Esteban, to him to learn the trade.
Andrés Alvarez, son of Andrés Alvarez and Juana de los Reyes, established a dowry of $454-00 for his wife, Francisca de Madrigal, daughter of Domingo Carbonero and Catalina Rodríguez.

Esteban de Hoces Navarro, originally from Andosilla, Navarra, established a dowry for his wife, Juana Calvo de Abarca. The dowry amounted to 3922 reales and 1000 pesos in arras, which included a gold Santo Cristo valued at 25 pesos.

Don Juan del Castillo and his wife, Doña Felipa de Santiago, sold Agustina, an 18-year-old mulata slave, to Licenciado don Domingo de Chavarría, the Cura of the city. Agustina had been part of Doña Felipa's dowry, and the sale was for 300 pesos.
Tomás Calvo, the general depositary, cancelled a census (debt) of 100 pesos for which Don Juan del Castillo and his wife, Doña Felipa Chinchilla, were responsible.

Nicolás Camacho and his wife, Catalina López, assumed an obligation of 105 pesos to the Cofradía de la Concepción. This debt was originally owed by Ana Merino, Nicolás's deceased mother, and was secured with a mortgage on a cattle ranch.
Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado and his wife, Doña Juana Moscoso y Figueroa, granted freedom to their mulato slave, Nicolás de Figueroa.

Catalina de Alarcón, widow of Diego de Madrigal, forgave Don Francisco de Linares for her husband's death. She acknowledged that Madrigal had provoked Linares, who acted in self-defense, and Linares offered 100 pesos for the sustenance of Madrigal's children.
Cristóbal de Vargas entrusted his creole slave, Juan, to Diego Pérez, a master tailor, for six months. The purpose was for Juan to complete his training in the tailoring trade.

Presbítero don Domingo de Echavarría, the Cura and Vicario of the city, granted power of attorney to Cristóbal de Vargas. This power allowed Vargas to collect a 400-peso debt from Amaro López de Lozada in Panamá, based on a previous document.

people_involved: Don Rodrigo Arias Maldonado y Velasco
summary: Don Salvador Jirón de Alvarado, acting as agent for Juan Tercero de Montalvo, sold a 36-year-old mulato slave named Juan de Herrera to Don Rodrigo Arias Maldonado y Velasco, the Governor and Captain General of the province, for 300 pesos. This transaction referenced a prior sale of the same slave (then called Juan Díaz) from José Méndez de Sierra to Tercero in León in 1661, and Tercero's power of attorney to Alvarado from Nueva Segovia in 1661.
Lucas Cervantes arranged for his son, Sebastián, to be apprenticed to Diego de Santiago, a blacksmith, for four years to learn the trade.

people_involved: Capitán don José Pérez de Luna
don José de Guevara y Sandoval
summary: Capitán don José Pérez de Luna, expecting a frigate in June to load 600 tercios at Caldera as per an agreement with Capitanes Ascensio Ruiz and Nicolás Hurtado from Panamá, arranged with don José de Guevara y Sandoval for the latter to load 300 tercios.
Capitán Diego de Zúñiga arranged for his grandson, Esteban, to be apprenticed to Agustín González de Loría, a blacksmith, to learn the trade.
Andrés Alvarez, originally from Granada, Nicaragua, established a dowry of 454 pesos for his wife, Francisca de Madrigal.

Captain Juan Bautista Torres Capelazo, preparing for a journey to the Urinamas Indians in the province of Talamanca, executed a codicil to his will. He appointed his cousin, Bernardo Torres Capelazo, as his executor.

Captain Alonso de Bonilla and his wife, Juana Benita, obligated themselves for $100 to the Chaplaincy of Licenciado Marcos Machado, whose patron was Alonso Gómez Macotela of Esparza. They mortgaged their house, located near Mayor de Benavides's house, the San Juan hermitage, and Xpbal de Araya's house, along with a cattle ranch called San Mateo, situated near Cartago and the royal road to Ujarráz.

Jerónimo Valerino and his wife, Francisca de as!, committed to pay the lease of a cacao plantation to the estate of Antonia López. Francisco López de Ortega, who served as the tutor for Antonia's minor children, accepted this obligation on their behalf.

Captain Cristóbal de Vargas granted general power of attorney to Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro. This power was specifically for Echavarría Navarro to bid for the office of Treasurer of the Santa Cruzada in the province, which had become vacant due to the death of Luis González Villalón.

Don José de Guevara y Sandoval and his wife, Doña Inés de Sandoval y Ocampo, obligated themselves for $250 to the Cofradía de la Concepción. They mortgaged their house, located on the street leading to the plaza and Cabildo houses, adjacent to the houses of Don Francisco Ramiro, Diego de Ocampo, and Alonso Peláez.
Don Miguel de Herrera Cid, a resident of Panamá, granted general power of attorney to Gaspar González Guillarte, who was also from Panamá. The document does not specify the purpose of this power.

Licenciado Don Alonso de Sandoval, Commissary of the Holy Office and Provincial Vicar, granted power to Don José de Guevara y Sandoval. This power authorized Guevara y Sandoval to reclaim mules and male donkeys found in Nicaragua, specifically a black mule held by the Prior of the Convent of San Juan de Dios in Granada and a male donkey held by Lieutenant Pedro de Campos Quirós.

Juan de la Estrella and his wife, María Jiménez de Aguilar, sold a plot of land and a house in the city for $70. The property was purchased by Doña Jerónima de Retes, who is identified as the wife of Luis de Fonseca.

people_involved: Ana de Retes Vázquez de Coronado
summary: Captain Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro, Provincial Mayor of the Santa Hermandad, and his wife, Doña Ana de Retes Vázquez de Coronado, obligated themselves for $300 to the Chaplaincy founded by Doña María de Sandoval, whose first chaplain was Licenciado Don Francisco de Echavarría Navarro. They mortgaged their house with a walled plot of land, adjacent to Alonso Peláez's plot, Mayor de Benavides Moreno's house, Esteban Torres's plot, and the San Nicolás hermitage.

Doña Leonor Pereira made her will, detailing her family and possessions. She was married twice, first to Juan de Velastiguí, with whom she had a son Diego who died at age 3, and then to Lope de Lumbide, with whom she had José and María de Lumbides. She mentioned giving two slaves, Lucas and Mónica, as a dowry to her granddaughter Catalina, and owned three other slaves: Catalina and her children Clemente and Lorenzo. Licenciados Marcos Machado and José de Lumbides were named as her executors, and the will was visited by M. Don Juan Zapata on April 7, 1664, regarding pious works.

Doña Margarita de Flores, widow of Captain Pedro de Mora and current wife of Pedro Galindo, requested and was granted permission by the Alcalde to sell a slave. She stated that she was awarded a slave named Leonor, who had two children (Damiana and another unnamed), from Mora's estate, and sought to sell her to fund a divorce suit against her absent husband, Pedro Galindo.

Captain Juan Bautista Torres Capelazo, preparing for a journey to the Urinamas Indians in Talamanca, executed a codicil. In this document, he appointed his cousin, Bernardo Torres Capelazo, as his executor.

Captain Alonso de Bonilla and his wife Juana Benita committed to pay $100 to the Chaplaincy of Licenciado Marcos Machado, whose patron was Alonso Gómez Macotela of Esparza. They mortgaged their house in Cartago, bordering Mayor de Benavides, the San Juan hermitage, and Xpbal de Araya's house, along with a cattle ranch named San Mateo near Ujarráz.

Jerónimo Valerino and his wife Francisca de as! obligated themselves to the estate of Antonia López to pay the rent for a cacao plantation. Francisco López de Ortega, acting as tutor for Antonia's minor children, accepted this obligation.

Captain Cristóbal de Vargas granted general power of attorney to Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro. This power was specifically for bidding on the office of Treasurer of the Santa Cruzada in the province, which became vacant following the death of Luis González Villalón.

Don José de Guevara y Sandoval and his wife Doña Inés de Sandoval y Ocampo obligated themselves to the Cofradía de la Concepción for $250. They mortgaged their house, located on the street leading to the plaza and Cabildo houses, bordering the properties of Francisco Ramiro, Diego de Ocampo, and Alonso Peláez.
Don Miguel de Herrera Cid, a resident of Panamá, granted general power of attorney to Gaspar González Guillarte, who was also from Panamá.

Licenciado Don Alonso de Sandoval, Commissary of the Holy Office and provincial Vicar, granted power to Don José de Guevara y Sandoval. This power was to reclaim mules and male donkeys found in Nicaragua, specifically a black mule held by the Prior of the Convent of San Juan de Dios in Granada and a male donkey held by Lieutenant Pedro de Campos Quirós.
Juan de la Estrella and his wife María Jiménez de Aguilar sold a lot and house in this city for $70. The property was purchased by Doña Jerónima de Retes, who is the wife of Luis de Fonseca.

people_involved: Ana de Retes Vázquez de Coronado
summary: Captain Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro, Provincial Mayor of the Santa Hermandad, and his wife Doña Ana de Retes Vázquez de Coronado, obligated themselves for $300 to a Chaplaincy. This Chaplaincy was founded by Doña María de Sandoval, and its first Chaplain was Licenciado Don Francisco de Echavarría Navarro. They mortgaged their house and walled lot, bordering Alonso Peláez's lot, Doña Mayor de Benavides Moreno's house, and Esteban Torres's lot and the San Nicolás hermitage.

Doña Leonor Pereira made her will, detailing her family and possessions. She was the daughter of Bartolomé Sánchez and Inés Pereira, and had been married twice, first to Juan de Velastiguí and then to Lope de Lumbide, having children from both marriages. Her will also mentioned several slaves and named Licenciado Marcos Machado and José de Lumbides as executors, with a later visit by M. Don Juan Zapata on April 7, 1664, regarding pious works.

Doña Margarita de Flores, widow of Captain Pedro de Mora and current wife of Pedro Galindo, sought permission to sell a slave to fund a lawsuit and free her house. She stated that she was awarded a black slave named Leonor, who had two children, Damiana and another unnamed child, from Mora's estate. Galindo was absent, and she was pursuing a divorce from him for 'just causes,' a request which the Alcalde granted.

people_involved: Licenciado don Domingo de Echavarría Navarro
summary: Doña Margarita, with judicial license and as the wife of Pedro Fernández Galindo, sold her 6-year-old enslaved mulata named Damiana to Licenciado don Domingo de Echavarría Navarro, who was the Cura and Vicario provincial of the city, for $150.

people_involved: Licenciado don Domingo de Echavarría Navarro
summary: Licenciado don Domingo de Echavarría Navarro granted power of attorney to Capitán don Juan Echavarría Navarro, who was preparing to depart for Panamá.

people_involved: Licenciado don Domingo de Echavarría Navarro
summary: Capitán don Rodrigo Calderón became obligated to Licenciado don Domingo de Echavarría Navarro for $230.

people_involved: Don Rodrigo Arias Maldonado y Velasco
Maese de Campo don Andrés Arias Maldonado
summary: Don Rodrigo Arias Maldonado y Velasco, Governor and Captain General of Costa Rica, sold a cacao plantation in the Matina valley to Capitán don Rodrigo Calderón, Alguacil Mayor, for $130. This plantation, with 230 fruitful cacao trees, was part of the estate of the deceased Maese de Campo don Andrés Arias Maldonado, who was a former Governor and the father of Don Rodrigo Arias Maldonado y Velasco.

Sargento Gaspar de los Ríos and his wife Francisca de Peñaranda, along with Juan Bautista Daniel and his wife Fabiana de Sojo, became obligated for $100 to the Chaplaincy founded by Alférez Vasco Solano, of which Licenciado don Alonso de Sandoval is the patron. They mortgaged a house in the city and a hato called San Pedro, located one league from Cartago.

people_involved: Don José de Guevara y Sandoval
Maestre de Campo don José de Sandoval Ocampo
summary: Don José de Guevara y Sandoval granted general power of attorney to Maestre de Campo don José de Sandoval Ocampo and Capitán Cristóbal de Vargas.
Catalina de Palacios, a widow, committed to pay $150 in fruits from the next harvest to Baltasara de Chinchilla, an orphan she had raised in her home, who was preparing for marriage.

people_involved: Doña María de Sandoval y Ocampo
summary: Doña María de Sandoval y Ocampo, widow of Tesorero Juan de Echavarría Navarro, donated a 100-peso credit to Doña Isabel and Doña Baltasara, legitimate daughters of Francisco García Cordero and Catalina de Mora Salado. This credit was inherited from Licenciado Baltasar de Grado and was secured by a cattle ranch in the Aserrí valley and a house in Cartago; Ayudante Esteban de Torres, tutor of the donees, accepted the deed.
Juana de la Portilla donated her 22-year-old enslaved black woman named Ursula to her son Agustín Guerrero, in recognition of his service to her for over 20 years.

people_involved: Don Rodrigo Arias Maldonado y Velasco
summary: Gobernador don Rodrigo Arias Maldonado y Velasco sold a 38-year-old enslaved mulato named Juan de Herrera to Alférez Sebastián de Zamora for $400. The Governor had previously purchased Juan de Herrera from don Salvador Jirón de Alvarado.

people_involved: R. P. Fray Marcos de Talavera
summary: R. P. Fray Marcos de Talavera, a Mercedarian friar, sold his 50-year-old enslaved black woman named Juana to Alférez Sebastián de Zamora for $230. Fray Marcos had acquired Juana from doña Francisca del Castillo, a resident of the city and mother and legitimate heir of the deceased doña Felipa de Chinchilla, in exchange for a certain number of masses he committed to say for doña Felipa's soul.

Antonio Camelo, a native and resident of the city, provided a dowry letter for his wife María de Sibaja, legitimate daughter of the deceased Alférez Juan de Quesada and Antonia Galindo, totaling $430, which included $100 from the Confraternity of the Concepción. He also provided $100 in arras.

people_involved: Licenciado don Domingo de Echavarría Navarro
summary: Licenciado don Domingo de Echavarría Navarro, Cura of the city, granted power of attorney to his brothers, Licenciado don Francisco Echavarría Navarro and Capitán don Juan Echavarría Navarro.

Juan Delgado del Castillo, legitimate son of the deceased Alférez Felipe Monje and Francisca López, made his will. He was married to Juana de la Cruz and had several children: María del Castillo (wife of Rodrigo de Cabrera), Isabel Suárez, Andrés López, Francisca del Castillo, Bernardo García, Nicolás López, and Catalina de la Concepción.

people_involved: Licenciado don Domingo de Echavarría Navarro
summary: Doña Margarita, with judicial license, sold her 6-year-old mulata slave named Damiana to Licenciado don Domingo de Echavarría Navarro, the city's priest and provincial vicar, for $150.00. Doña Margarita is identified as the wife of Pedro Fernández Galindo.

people_involved: Licenciado don Domingo de Echavarría Navarro
summary: Licenciado don Domingo de Echavarría Navarro granted power of attorney to don Juan de Echavarría Navarro, who was preparing to depart for Panamá.

people_involved: Licenciado don Domingo de Echavarría Navarro
summary: Capitán don Rodrigo Calderón became obligated to Licenciado don Domingo de Echavarría Navarro for the sum of $230.00.

They mortgaged a house in Cartago and a hato named San Pedro, located a league from Cartago, as collateral.

people_involved: Don José de Guevara y Sandoval
Maestre de Campo don José de Sandoval Ocampo
summary: Don José de Guevara y Sandoval granted general power of attorney to Maestre de Campo don José de Sandoval Ocampo and Capitán Cristóbal de Vargas.

Catalina de Palacios, a widow, obligated herself to pay $150.00 in fruits from the upcoming harvest to Baltasara de Chinchilla. Baltasara was an orphan whom Catalina had raised in her home and who was preparing for marriage.

people_involved: Doña María de Sandoval y Ocampo
summary: Doña María de Sandoval y Ocampo, widow of Tesorero Juan de Echavarría Navarro, donated a credit of one hundred pesos to Doña Isabel and Doña Baltasara, legitimate daughters of the deceased Francisco García Cordero and Catalina de Mora Salado. This credit, inherited from Licenciado Baltasar de Grado, was secured by a mortgage on a cattle ranch in the Aserrí valley and a house in Cartago, and was accepted by their tutor, Ayudante Esteban de Torres.
Juana de la Portilla donated her 22-year-old black slave, Ursula, to her son Agustín Guerrero. This donation was made in recognition of Agustín's service to his mother for over 20 years.

people_involved: R. P. Fray Marcos de Talavera
summary: The Reverend Father Fray Marcos de Talavera, a Mercedarian friar, sold a 50-year-old black slave named Juana to Sebastián de Zamora for $230.00. Fray Marcos had acquired Juana from Doña Francisca del Castillo, a city resident and mother of the deceased Doña Felipa de Chinchilla, in exchange for masses for Felipa's soul.

Antonio Camelo, a native and resident of Cartago, established a dowry of $430.00 for his wife María de Sibaja, the legitimate daughter of the deceased Alférez Juan de Quesada and Antonia Galindo. This amount included $100.00 from the Confraternity of the Conception, and he also provided $100.00 in arras.

people_involved: Licenciado don Domingo de Echavarría Navarro
summary: Licenciado don Domingo de Echavarría Navarro, the city's priest, granted power of attorney to his brothers, Licenciado don Francisco Echavarría Navarro and Capitán don Juan Echavarría Navarro.

Juan Delgado del Castillo, legitimate son of the deceased Alférez Felipe Monje and Francisca López, made his will. He was married to Juana de la Cruz and had seven children: María del Castillo (wife of Rodrigo de Cabrera), Isabel Suárez, Andrés López, Francisca del Castillo, Bernardo García, Nicolás López, and Catalina de la Concepción.

Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro, corregidor of Turrialba, granted power to Toribio de la Vega, a resident of Panamá, to charter a frigate of 600 tercios capacity to arrive in Caldera by the upcoming June.

Doña Catalina de la Jara, widow of Ignacio de Artavia and administrator of her children's assets, granted power to Capitán Fernando de Carrión Villasante in León to collect her deceased husband's inheritance from José de Artavia, her brother-in-law.

A dowry letter was issued by Bartolomé de Benavente, son of Capitán Bartolomé de Benavente and Doña Francisca de Obando, in favor of his wife Antonia de Vargas Machuca, daughter of Alférez Alonso de Vargas and María del Pueyo, for $1224.00, including a property that once belonged to Juan Gómez de Bonilla.

Doña María de Sandoval, widow of Juan de Echavarría Navarro, donated 1300 pesos in various goods, including a 16-year-old mulata slave named Luisa, to her granddaughter Doña Antonia Zapata, the legitimate daughter of Don Cristóbal Zapata and the deceased Doña Ana de Echavarría.

A dowry letter was issued by Matías de Aguilar, son of Gabriel de Aguilar and Ana de Espinoza, in favor of his wife María del Cubillo, daughter of Alférez Bernabé de Segura and Isabel de Morales, for $2095.00.

Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro granted power to Toribio de la Vega and Don Gómez de Cárdenas, residents of Panamá, to charter a frigate of 800 to 900 tercios capacity to arrive in Caldera in December to load goods.

Juan Bautista Torres Capelazo obligated himself to Licenciado Don Alfonso de Oviedo for $500.00, representing the value of 100 loads he is to deliver to the port of Punta Blanca on the North Sea, payable in Puerto Belo.
Juan Bautista Torres Capelazo granted general power to Capitán Jorge Calvo Minucho, Alcalde Mayor of San Felipe de Puerto Belo.

Doña Inés Alvarez Pereira, widow of Capitán Bartolomé Sánchez and natural daughter of Capitán Antonio Pereira, divided an estate inherited from her father in the valley of Landecho among her heirs, giving portions to her granddaughter Doña Juana de Sojo and her son Bartolomé Sánchez.

María Rodríguez, widow of Alférez Juan Sánchez Crespo, made a will, listing her deceased parents Gaspar and Inés Rodríguez, and her children: Gaspar Sánchez, Leonor de Rivera (married to Alonso de Mora), Antonio Sánchez, Ana María Sánchez (married to Gregorio Alvarez), Francisca Sánchez, and Antonia González.

María de Ortega, widow of Jerónimo Felipe, donated a 6-year-old black creole slave named Juana to her granddaughter Doña Gregoria de Ortega, the legitimate daughter of her son Alférez Diego López de Ortega and Doña Ana de Chaves.
Ayudante Alonso Peláez provided surety for Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro, who was appointed corregidor of Turrialba and Alcalde Mayor of the Port.

Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro, corregidor of Turrialba, granted power of attorney to Toribio de la Vega, a resident of Panama, to charter a frigate of 600 tercios. The frigate was intended to arrive in Caldera by the following June.

Doña Catalina de la Jara, widow of Ignacio de Artavia and administrator of her children's assets, granted power of attorney to Capitán Fernando de Carrión Villasante, a Royal Official Judge in León. This power was for collecting her deceased husband's inheritance from José de Artavia, her brother-in-law.

A dowry letter was issued for Bartolomé de Benavente, son of Capitán Bartolomé de Benavente and Doña Francisca de Obando, in favor of his wife Antonia de Vargas Machuca. The dowry amounted to $1224.00, including a property that previously belonged to Juan Gómez de Bonilla, and the arras were $600.00.

Doña María de Sandoval, widow of Juan de Echavarría Navarro, donated 1300 pesos in various goods to her granddaughter Doña Antonia Zapata. The donation included a 16-year-old mulata slave named Luisa. Doña Antonia Zapata is the legitimate daughter of Don Cristóbal Zapata and the deceased Doña Ana de Echavarría.

A dowry letter was issued for Matías de Aguilar, son of Gabriel de Aguilar and Ana de Espinoza, in favor of his wife María del Cubillo. María del Cubillo is the legitimate daughter of Alférez Bernabé de Segura and Isabel de Morales. The dowry amounted to $2095.00, with arras of $100.00.

Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro granted power of attorney to Toribio de la Vega and Don Gómez de Cárdenas, both residents of Panama. This power was to charter a frigate of 800 to 900 tercios to arrive in Caldera in December to load goods.

Juan Bautista Torres Capelazo obligated himself to Licenciado don Alfonso de Oviedo for $500.00. This amount represented the value of 100 loads that Torres Capelazo was to deliver to the port of Punta Blanca in the North Sea, with payment due in Puerto Belo.
Juan Bautista Torres Capelazo granted general power of attorney to Capitán Jorge Calvo Minucho. Capitán Jorge Calvo Minucho held the position of Mayor of San Felipe de Puerto Belo.

Doña Inés Alvarez Pereira, widow of Capitán Bartolomé Sánchez and natural daughter of Capitán Antonio Pereira, divided an estate inherited from her father in the Landecho valley among her heirs. Her granddaughter Doña Juana de Sojo received half of the livestock and a property called 'del cacaotal', while her son Bartolomé Sánchez received the other half of the animals and a property called 'el Guayabal'.

The will of María Rodríguez, legitimate daughter of the deceased Gaspar and Inés Rodríguez and widow of Alférez Juan Sánchez Crespo, was recorded. Her children were named as Gaspar Sánchez, Leonor de Rivera (married to Alonso de Mora), Antonio Sánchez, Ana María Sánchez (married to Gregorio Alvarez), Francisca Sánchez, and Antonia González.

María de Ortega, widow of Jerónimo Felipe, donated a 6-year-old black creole slave named Juana to her granddaughter Doña Gregoria de Ortega. Doña Gregoria is the legitimate daughter of María's son, Alférez Diego López de Ortega, and Doña Ana de Chaves.
Ayudante Alonso Peláez acted as surety for Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro. Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro had been appointed corregidor of Turrialba and Mayor of the Port.
Capitán José de Moya acted as a guarantor for don Pedro de Córdova, who was the corregidor of the Pacacua district.

people_involved: Padre Fray Juan Tomás de Coto
summary: María de Ortega, daughter of the deceased Juan López and Catalina de Ortega, made her will. She ordered masses for her deceased daughter doña Isabel de Herrera, Pablo Muñoz, and Magdalena de Alfaro. She detailed her two marriages to Capitán Jerónimo de Retes and Jerónimo Felipe, listing her children and their spouses, and made provisions for her grandchildren, including land, cattle, and slaves. She also inherited the encomienda of Cayagua and Sucagrua from her father and owned land in Cartago near Quircó, establishing a chaplaincy with her grandson Cristóbal López as the first chaplain. Her executors were don Pedro Córdova, Al? Peláez, and her brother Jn. López de Ortega.
Licenciado don Alfonso de Oviedo granted power of attorney to Contador don Ignacio de Oyarsabal, a resident of Panamá.
Licenciado don Alfonso de Oviedo granted power of attorney to Jerónimo de Segovia, a resident of Puerto Belo.

people_involved: M. de Campo don Juan Fernández Salinas y Cerda
summary: Licenciado don Alfonso de Oviedo and M. de Campo don Juan Fernández Salinas y Cerda, Captain General of the province, granted power of attorney to Juan Bautista de Letona. This power allowed Letona to recover and sell a black slave in Panamá, which had been adjudicated from the assets of Francisco Tojeano, a resident of Pueblo Nuevo, in an executive lawsuit.

A codicil to María de Ortega's will was made, noting that her son Diego López de Ortega had passed away. His children, doña Gregoria de Ortega, Agustín de Chaves, Cristóbal de Chaves, doña María de Alfaro, doña Luisa, doña Isabel, and doña Laureana, entered into the inheritance in his place.

Ana de Espinosa, widow of Gabriel de Aguilar, sold a plot of land in Cartago to Sargento Francisco Hernández Barquero for $30. The land was located on the street leading from the plaza to the ermita de la Soledad, bordering the buyer's houses and houses belonging to María de Espinosa, her daughter, and Cristóbal de Vargas.
Antonio Orozco and his wife, doña Isabel del Castillo, sold a 21-year-old mulatto slave named Lorenza to Francisco Hernández Barquero for $100.

Don Miguel Ortiz de Chaves and his wife, doña Agustina Fernández de Córdova, pledged $100 to a chaplaincy founded by Tomás Calvo for one of his sons. They mortgaged a house they had inherited upon the death of don Pedro de Córdova, who was doña Agustina's father and don Miguel's father-in-law.

people_involved: doña María González y Ru Mayor
doña Luisa de Ortega y Chaves
Alférez Diego López de Ortega y Chaves
summary: Alférez Francisco Ramírez y Rumayor, a native of Sevilla and son of Alférez Agustín Ramírez and doña María González y Ru Mayor, made a provision of $2020 in favor of his wife, doña Luisa de Ortega y Chaves. Doña Luisa was the legitimate daughter of Alférez Diego López de Ortega y Chaves, who was the legitimate son of Alférez Diego López de Ortega and doña Ana de Chaves. Juan Patricio Vázquez, legitimate son of the deceased Alonso de Avila and Ana López de Ortega, made a dowry agreement in favor of his wife Inés de Rojas, legitimate daughter of Sargento Franco de Rojas and Magdalena de Oñate, for $560, with arras of $300.

Captain García de Alvarado, legitimate son of Alférez Gil de Alvarado (native of Santiago de Guatemala) and Juana de Vera y Sotomayor (native of Cartago), made a dowry agreement in favor of his wife Juana de Echavarría y Salazar, legitimate daughter of Treasurer Fernando de Salazar and Ambrosia de Echavarría Navarro, for $4446, including half a house and slaves, with arras of $1000.

Juan Núñez Suárez, a native of Puerto Santa María, Spain, legitimate son of Juan Núñez and María Suárez, made a dowry agreement in favor of his wife Juana Calderón, legitimate daughter of Captain Rodrigo Calderón and Isidora Zambrano, for $2648, with arras of $2000.
Adriano de Figueroa agreed with Diego Pérez de Medina, a tailor, to entrust his son Nicolás de Figueroa to him for 7 years to learn the trade.

Domingo de Esquivel, legitimate son of Andrés de Esquivel and María de Hinojosa (all natives of Cartago), made a dowry agreement in favor of his wife Felipa de Morales, legitimate daughter of Jerónimo Coronel and Isabel de Ortega, for $674. This included a house valued at $150, bordering the San Francisco convent and Catalina Palacios' house.

Sebastián de Zamora and his wife Lucía de Ocampo sold the houses they had purchased in June from Domingo Jiménez Maldonado and Juana de Sojo to Manuel Pérez and his wife María Arias for $300, with the obligation to pay Licenciado Alonso de Sandoval.
Captain José de Villalobos Jara sold an unspecified item to Bartolomé Benavente and his wife Margarita Vázquez.

An unnamed woman sold a cattle ranch in the city's valley, on the road to Có, for $200. The property bordered land owned by Catalina Palacios, Esteban Rodríguez, and Francisca de Brenes, and was subject to an existing lien.

people_involved: Padre Guardián del Convento de San Francisco
summary: Catalina de Palacios, widow of encomendero Gaspar de Chinchilla, founded a chaplaincy for masses for her soul, her parents, husband, and relatives. She designated $500 as capital, charged on her houses in Cartago, which bordered Jerónimo Coronel and don Gil de Alvarado. Her grandson, Gaspar de Chinchilla, was named the patron.

Juan de Vida Martell, Mayordomo of the Cofradía de la Concepción, sold a cattle ranch and a caballeria of land near the Taras river to Manuel Pérez and his wife, María Arias Maldonado y Velasco, for $100. The Cofradía had acquired this land from the deceased couple Diego de Aguilar and Leonor Jiménez.
Catalina de Palacios ratified the sale of a 5-year-old slave named José to Licdo. don Francisco de Ocampo for $100. This sale had originally taken place the previous year.

In the valley of Barba, Domingo Jiménez Maldonado granted power of attorney to his wife, doña Juana de Sojo, to sell a 4-year-old mulatto slave named Juana. The purpose of the sale was to redeem a $200 debt owed to the Cofradía del Rosario.
Using the power of attorney from her husband, doña Juana de Sojo sold the mulatto slave, Juana, to don Alonso de Sandoval, a presbítero and Comisario del Santo Oficio, for $200.

Capn. José de Alvarado and his wife, doña Perronila de Retes, committed to delivering 100 fanegas of wheat (valued at $2 each) to doña María de Retes by April of 1665. This agreement was made because doña María de Retes, widow of Capn. don Francisco Ramiro, had charged $200 on her houses in favor of the Capellanía founded by Depositario Pedro Solano.

Doña Francisca del Castillo, widow of Marcos de Chinchilla, founded a chaplaincy for masses for her soul, her parents, her daughter Felipa de Chinchilla, and her mother-in-law Catalina de Palacios. The masses were to be said in the Convento de San Francisco. She designated $450 as capital, charged on a flour mill she owned on the Río del Molino, which bordered the indigenous settlement of San Juan de Herrera. Her son, don Gaspar de Chinchilla, was named the patron.

As part of her chaplaincy foundation, doña Francisca del Castillo immediately sold her flour mill to Jerónimo Leal and his wife, doña María Yañes, for $450. This amount was then left as a 5% lien (censo) on the property, serving as the capital for the chaplaincy.

Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro paid a $100 debt to the Cofradía del Rosario. The payment was received by Mayordomo Cristobal Durán, and the debt was subsequently canceled by Durán and the Deputies don Rodrigo Calderón, don Fernando Ramiro, and Bartolomé Muñoz Hidalgo.

A dowry letter was issued for Pedro Jiménez, son of Domingo Jiménez and doña Francisca de Ochoa, in favor of his wife, María Calderón. The dowry included $103 from the Cofradía de la Concepción, half a plot of land where María Calderón's grandmother's houses stood, and 100 pesos in cacao from Matina, which Alférez Bartolomé Calderón was obligated to deliver. Arras amounted to $100.

Sargento Nicolás Barrantes and his wife, doña Juana Moscoso, obligated themselves for $100 in favor of the Cofradía del Rosario. Nicolás Barrantes mortgaged a mill located in the city's vicinity on the Río de los Molinos, which already had a $200 lien for the Cofradía de la Concepción from a previous deed with his former wife, María Sagaste.

Juan de Austúa and his wife, doña María de Chaves, obligated themselves for $100 in favor of the Capellanía founded by Depositario Pedro Solano. They mortgaged half of a house in Cartago, which already had a $100 lien for the Cofradía de los Angeles. This transaction was executed in the valley of Barba.

people_involved: Licdo. don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Licdo. don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, through a letter written from Granada where he was studying, acknowledged that Alférez Cristobal Durán had sold something in his name to don Juan de Echavarría Navarro in 1661.

An unnamed woman sold a cattle site in the valley of the city, on the road to Có, for $200. The property bordered sites belonging to Catalina Palacios, Esteban Rodríguez, and Francisca de Brenes, with a river separating it from Catalina Palacios' land. The sale included a charge to pay a census on the site.

people_involved: Padre Guardián del Convento de San Francisco
summary: Catalina de Palacios, widow of encomendero Gaspar de Chinchilla, founded a Chaplaincy of masses for the repose of her soul, her parents' souls (Matías de Palacios and Luisa Hernández), her husband's, and other relatives, as well as souls in Purgatory. She designated $500 as capital, charged to her houses in Cartago, which bordered those of Jerónimo Coronel and don Gil de Alvarado. Her grandson, Gaspar de Chinchilla, was named the patron.

Juan de Vida Martell, Mayordomo of the Cofradía de la Concepción, sold a cattle site and a caballeria of land to Manuel Pérez and his wife María Arias Maldonado y Velasco for $100. The land, bordering the Taras river, had been acquired by the Cofradía from the deceased Diego de Aguilar and Leonor Jiménez.
Catalina de Palacios, a widow, ratified the sale of a 5-year-old slave named José to Licdo. don Francisco de Ocampo for $100. This sale had originally taken place the previous year.

In the valley of Barba, Domingo Jiménez Maldonado granted power of attorney to his wife, Juana de Sojo, to sell a 4-year-old mulatto slave named Juana. The purpose of the sale was to use the proceeds to redeem a $200 debt owed to the Cofradía del Rosario.
Juana de Sojo, acting under the power of attorney from her husband, sold the mulatto slave named Juana to don Alonso de Sandoval, a presbyter and Comisario del Santo Oficio, for $200.

Capn. José de Alvarado and his wife doña Perronila de Retes committed to deliver one hundred fanegas of wheat, valued at two pesos each, to doña María de Retes by April of that year. This agreement was made because doña María de Retes, widow of Capn. don Francisco Ramiro, had charged her houses with two hundred pesos in favor of the Chaplaincy founded by Depositario Pedro Solano.

Doña Francisca del Castillo, widow of Marcos de Chinchilla, founded a Chaplaincy of masses for her soul, her parents', her daughter Felipa de Chinchilla's, and her mother-in-law Catalina de Palacios'. The Chaplaincy, to be held at the Convento de San Francisco, involved 16 masses annually for 20 pesos, with a capital of $450. She also sold a tile and stone mill, inherited from her daughter Felipa, to Jerónimo Leal and doña María Yañes for $450, which they left as a 5% census.

Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro paid his $100 debt to the Cofradía del Rosario to Mayordomo Cristobal Durán. Durán, along with Deputies don Rodrigo Calderón, don Fernando Ramiro, and Bartolomé Muñoz Hidalgo, then canceled the debt.

Pedro Jiménez, son of Domingo Jiménez and doña Francisca de Ochoa, provided a dowry letter for his wife, María Calderón. The dowry included $103 from the Cofradía de la Concepción, half a plot of land where his wife's grandmother María Calderón's houses stood, and 100 pesos in Matina cacao from Alférez Bartolomé Calderón.

Sargento Nicolás Barrantes and his wife doña Juana Moscoso obligated themselves for $100 in favor of the Cofradía del Rosario. Nicolás Barrantes mortgaged a mill on the river called de los Molinos, which already had a $200 charge in favor of the Cofradía de la Concepción from a previous deed with his former wife María Sagaste.

Juan de Austúa and his wife doña María de Chaves obligated themselves for $100 in favor of the Chaplaincy founded by Depositario Pedro Solano. They mortgaged half a house in Cartago, which already had another $100 charge in favor of the Cofradía de los Angeles. The deed was granted in the valley of Barba.

people_involved: Licdo. don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Licdo. don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas acknowledged that Alférez Cristobal Durán had sold property in his name to don Juan de Echavarría Navarro in 1661. This acknowledgement was based on a letter from Cascante, written from Granada where he was studying.

Alférez Manuel Pérez and his wife, María Arias Maldonado, purchased a house in Cartago from Sebastián de Zamora and Lucía de Ocampo for $300. They obligated themselves to the Chaplaincy founded by Alférez Vasco Solano for this amount and left the house, which bordered properties of María de Sandoval, Juan Solano, and Inés Velázquez, as collateral.

Antonio García, a native of Mexico, provided a dowry of $581 to his wife, Tomasina Pereira. The dowry included a Seville cloak that Tomasina's brother, Diego de Arroyo, was obligated to provide within six months or sooner if he returned from Panama.
The Alcalde arranged for Francisco, a ten-year-old mulato son of Mariana de Porres (a free mulata), to be placed with Pedro Sánchez Navarrete, a tailor, for six years.

Sergeant Francisco Hernández Barquero and his wife, Ana de Espinosa de Aguilar, obligated themselves for $300 to the Confraternity of the Holy Vera Cruz. They mortgaged a house and two plots in Cartago, bordering properties of Isabel de Flores, María de Zúñiga, Petronila de Grado, and Agustín González de Loría, as well as a cattle ranch on the royal road to Ujarraz. Payments were made in 1668 by Hernández Barquero, who was a Mayordomo.

Captain Bartolomé Muñoz Hidalgo and his wife, Sebastiana Calvo, obligated themselves for $150 to the Chaplaincy founded by Alférez Pedro Solano. They mortgaged a house in the San Juan street of the city, which Sebastiana Calvo had received as a dowry from Depositary Tomás Calvo.

Catalina de Palacios, widow of Gaspar de Chinchilla, donated four slaves (Luis, Marcos, Ana, and Francisca) and a cattle site in Cartago to her granddaughter, Catalina Palacios. The granddaughter, daughter of the deceased Marcos de Chinchilla, had been married for five years to Alférez Bartolomé de Aguilar Calderón.

Doña María de Retes, widow of Captain Francisco Ramiro, obligated herself for $200 to the Chaplaincy founded by Pedro Solano. She mortgaged a house in Cartago, bordering her mother María Vázquez's house. The obligation was cancelled in 1676 by Lic. Francisco de Echavarría Navarro.

people_involved: Juan Fernández de Salinas y Cerda
summary: Luis de Fonseca, acting as agent for Lucas de Zamudio of Panama, chartered Zamudio's ship, "Ntra. Sra. de la Concepción y Santiago," to Juan Fernández de Salinas y Cerda, Adelantado of Costa Rica, and García de Alvarado. The ship was to sail to Caldera to transport goods to Panama.
The Alcalde placed Pablo de Salazar, a ten-year-old mestizo son of Alonso Zapata and Catalina (an indigenous woman from Aserrí), with Agustín González de Loría, a master blacksmith, for six years.
Alonso Ruiz de Pasillas sold a forge to Andrés Gómez, a free mulato, for $110.
The Alcalde placed Juan de Vargas, a ten-year-old son of the deceased Cristobal de Vargas and Isabel de Araya, with Diego de Santiago, a master blacksmith, for eight years.

This entry details the will of Alférez Juan López de Ortega. He was married to María Jiménez, and their deceased daughter, Juana Martínez Navarro, was married to Domingo López of Esparza, with whom she had a son, Alonso López. His sister-in-law was Isabel Jiménez, and his brother was Francisco López de Ortega. He was also an executor for Francisco de Bonilla.

This entry details the will of Alférez Andrés Morillo de Campos, a native of Hinojosa, Extremadura. He was married to Magdalena de Guido and had ten children. His deceased daughter María was married to Captain José de Villalobos Jara. His daughter Juana's marriage to Sebastián de Rivera was annulled because Rivera was already married in La Granja, Extremadura. His deceased daughter Margarita was married first to Captain Diego Quintero del Castillo and then to Alvaro de Nava, leaving no succession. His daughter Lucrecia married Matías de Madrigal. His assets included a mill in Barba and a site in Cartago, bordering María Sagaste's property, which he bought from the estate of Alférez Mayor Francisco de Alfaro.
Gaspar de Chinchilla sold his 34-year-old Creole slave, Antonia, to his uncle, Alférez Tomás Calvo, for $360. Antonia was inherited by Gaspar from his grandmother, Catalina de Palacios.

Don José Pérez de Muro, a native of Miranda de Arga, Navarra, provided a dowry of $3200 and "arras" of $1000 to his wife, Mariana de Echavarría Navarro. The dowry included a house in Cartago valued at $1000.

locations: San Juan de Herrera de los Naboríos
summary: Francisca de Bonilla, an indigenous woman from Cartago and resident of San Juan de Herrera de los Naboríos, delivered her legitimate mulata daughter, Bernarda, to María de Sandoval. Bernarda's father, Diego de Rojas, was absent from the province.

Alférez Manuel Pérez and María Arias Maldonado purchased a house in Cartago from Sebastián de Zamora and Lucía de Ocampo for $300. The house, bordering properties of María de Sandoval and the deceased Captain Juan Solano, and across the street from Inés Velázquez, was left encumbered in favor of a Chaplaincy founded by Alférez Vasco Solano.

Antonio García, a native of Mexico, provided a dowry of $581 to his wife, Tomasina Pereira. The dowry included a Seville cloak that Tomasina's brother, Diego de Arroyo, was obligated to provide within six months or upon his earlier return from Panama.
The Alcalde arranged for Francisco, a mulato boy of about ten years old and the natural son of Mariana de Porres, a free mulata, to be placed with Pedro Sánchez Navarrete, a tailor, for six years.

Sergeant Francisco Hernández Barquero and his wife, Ana de Espinosa de Aguilar, committed to the Confraternity of the Santa Vera Cruz for $300, mortgaging a house and two plots in Cartago and a cattle ranch near Ujarraz. Payments were recorded on Dec 11, 1668, to Mayordomo Alonso de Bonilla, and on Feb 4, 1688, to deputies Andrés Torres Capelazo, Gregorio de Arrieta, Sebastián de Fonseca, and Juan González Ochoa, with Hernández Barquero serving as Mayordomo.

Captain Bartolomé Muñoz Hidalgo and his wife, Sebastiana Calvo, committed to the Chaplaincy founded by Alférez Pedro Solano for $150. They mortgaged a house in the San Juan street of the city, which Sebastiana Calvo had received as a dowry from Depositario Tomás Calvo.

Catalina de Palacios, widow of Gaspar de Chinchilla, donated four slaves (Luis, Marcos, Ana, and Francisca) and a cattle site in Có to her granddaughter, Catalina Palacios. Catalina Palacios, the natural daughter of her deceased son Marcos de Chinchilla, had been married for five years to Alférez Bartolomé de Aguilar Calderón.

Doña María de Retes, widow of Captain Don Francisco Ramiro, committed to the Chaplaincy founded by Pedro Solano for $200, mortgaging a house in Cartago bordering her mother Doña María Vázquez's house. The obligation was cancelled on June 12, 1676, by Licenciado Don Francisco de Echavarría Navarro, the patron and Chaplain.

people_involved: Juan Fernández de Salinas y Cerda
summary: Luis de Fonseca, acting as agent for Lucas de Zamudio of Panama, chartered Zamudio's ship, 'Ntra. Sra. de la Concepción y Santiago,' to Don Juan Fernández de Salinas y Cerda, Adelantado of Costa Rica, and Don García de Alvarado. The ship was to sail to Caldera to transport goods to Panama, and the charter was rescinded on April 2, 1665.

The Alcalde arranged for Pablo de Salazar, a ten-year-old mestizo boy and natural son of Alonso Zapata and Catalina, an indigenous woman from Aserrí, to be placed with Agustín González de Loría, a master blacksmith, for six years.
Alonso Ruiz de Pasillas sold a forge to Andrés Gómez, a free mulato, for $110.

The Alcalde arranged for Juan de Vargas, a ten-year-old boy and legitimate son of the deceased Cristobal de Vargas and Isabel de Araya, to be placed with Diego de Santiago, a master blacksmith, for eight years.

This entry details the will of Alférez Juan López de Ortega, son of the deceased Juan López de Ortega, and married to María Jiménez. His deceased daughter, Juana Martínez Navarro, was married to Domingo López of Esparza, and they had a son, Alonso López. His sister-in-law Isabel Jiménez and brother Francisco López de Ortega are mentioned, and he was an executor for Francisco de Bonilla.

This entry details the will of Alférez Andrés Morillo de Campos, a native of Hinojosa, Extremadura, and husband of Magdalena de Guido. They had ten children, with details provided for the marriages of María, Juana, Margarita, and Lucrecia. His assets included a mill in Barba and a property in Cartago, acquired from the estate of Alférez Mayor Francisco de Alfaro.
Gaspar de Chinchilla sold his 34-year-old Creole slave, Antonia, to his uncle, Alférez Tomás Calvo, for $360. Gaspar had inherited Antonia from his grandmother, Catalina de Palacios.

Don José Pérez de Muro, a native of Miranda de Arga, Navarra, provided a dowry of $3200 and arras of $1000 to his wife, Doña Mariana de Echavarría Navarro. The dowry included a house in Cartago valued at $1000, and their parents' names were also recorded.

locations: San Juan de Herrera de los Naboríos
summary: Francisca de Bonilla, an indigenous woman from Cartago and resident of San Juan de Herrera de los Naboríos, delivered her legitimate mulata daughter, Bernarda, to María de Sandoval. Bernarda's father, Diego de Rojas, was absent from the province.
Captain Antonio Cuaresma, a resident of the villa of... (entry incomplete).

people_involved: don Juan López de la Flor
summary: Jerez de la Choluteca committed to pay $260.00 to Gobernador don Juan López de la Flor. The payment was to be made in Panamá.

people_involved: Juan de la Cruz (brother of Mateo)
summary: Mateo de Madrigal, natural son of Alférez Cristobal de Madrigal, made his testament. He mentioned his natural daughter María de Madrigal, his brother Juan de la Cruz, and his nephew José de Prendas.
Andrés Morillo de Campos executed a codicil to his will.
Don Rodrigo Calderón committed to pay $170.00 to María Jiménez, the widow of Alférez Juan López de Ortega. This money belonged to the children of Fc? de Solís and Anta. López.

Asisclo López Torralbo and his wife doña Micaela Vázquez de Coronado sold a ranch site with one 'caballería' of land to Juan Ricardo, a resident of the city. The land, located across the Agua Caliente river, had previously belonged to Ambrosio de Brenes, then his son Juan de Vinda, and was purchased by Alférez Juan Vázquez de Coronado, who was doña Micaela's father. The sale price was $20.00.

people_involved: Gobernador don Juan López de la Flor
summary: Gobernador don Juan López de la Flor granted general power of attorney to Captain Antonio de Siero, a resident of León, Nicaragua.

people_involved: Juan de la Cruz (father of Agustín)
don Miguel Ortiz de Chaves y Aldana
summary: Agustín Rodríguez Betancourt, legitimate son of Juan de la Cruz and Isabel de Betancourt (former residents of Guatemala), provided a dowry letter for his wife Isabel de Chaves, legitimate daughter of Pedro de Valerio and Ana de Chaves (residents of this city). The dowry was $400.00, with 'arras' of $200.00, and José de Uros and don Miguel Ortiz de Chaves y Aldana served as appraisers.

Sebastián de Zamora and his wife doña Lucía de Sandoval Ocampo committed to pay $100.00 to the 'Dotación de doncellas' established by Alonso Hernández and affiliated with the Cofradía de la Concepción. They mortgaged a ranch located about half a league from the city, across the Pontezuela river, bordering Isabel de Ortega's property.

Don José de Alvarado and his wife doña Petronila de Retes committed to pay $100.00 to the Cofradía de la Vera Cruz. They mortgaged a property in Ujarraz called Sta. Gertrudis, which previously belonged to Jerónimo Felipe, then to Captain Jerónimo de Retes (doña Petronila's father), and subsequently to doña Jerónima de Retes (doña Petronila's sister).

people_involved: Ayudante Fernando López de los Santos
summary: Captain José Pérez de Luna and his wife doña Josefa de Chaves exchanged enslaved people with Ayudante Fernando López de los Santos, a resident of Esparza. Pérez de Luna and Chaves gave Juan Narváez, a 24-year-old mulatto, in exchange for Juan Cascante, a 20-year-old mulatto whom López de los Santos had purchased from don Luis Cascante de Rojas.

people_involved: Gobernador don Juan López de la Flor
summary: Jerónimo Valerino and his wife Francisca de Esquivel committed to pay $300.00 to Gobernador don Juan López de la Flor, payable 15 days after Valerino's return from Guatemala. They mortgaged a house, co-owned by themselves and their guarantor Andrés de Sandoval, and a cacao plantation in Matina.

José Marín de Laguna, a native of Soto, Castilla la Vieja, and legitimate son of Franc? Marín and Cecilia Laguna, provided a dowry letter for his wife doña Catalina de Moya Colmenero, legitimate daughter of the deceased don José de Moya and doña Mayor de Benavides Moreno. The dowry was $2411.00, with 'arras' of $500.00.
In the town of San Bartolomé de Barba, the Alcalde delivered a 14-year-old orphan boy named José Jiménez to Agustín González de Loría, a blacksmith.

Francisca Jiménez, natural daughter of Domingo Jimenez and Gracial, and widow of Ambrosio de Brenes, made her testament. She named her children: María, Francisca, Jerónima, Catalina, Gregorio, Mateo, Marcos, and Andrés de Brenes, and Antonio and Juan de Vinda, and Domingo Jiménez.

Alférez Francisco López, legitimate son of the deceased Antonio Hernández and Lucía de Madrigal, made his testament. He mentioned a property given to Elvira Gómez for service and his marriage to the deceased Juana de Ortega, with whom he had a daughter, doña María Gómez, who later married Alférez Juan Vázquez de Coronado and had three children.

people_involved: Capn. Manuel Gómez de Ocón y Trillo
summary: Captain Manuel Gómez de Ocón y Trillo, a resident of this city, sold a half-site for cattle in the Aserrí valley to Alférez Gaspar Arias. This property, acquired in 1661 from the estate of don Franc? Solano, bordered land owned by Pedro Solano and included a house and two 'caballerías' of land, sold for $500.00.
María Sagaste, widow of Sergeant Nicolás de Barrantes, sold property to Alférez Juan Alvarez de Ulate, a trader in this province and the province of Panamá.

A dowry letter was granted in Barba. Doña Juana Moscoso donated an enslaved person, Diego Barrantes (23 years old), valued at $400, to her husband. Juan Ruiz de Villegas, son of Francisco Ruiz and María de Villegas from Puebla de los Angeles, made a grant in favor of his wife Juana de Zúñiga, daughter of the late Juan de Ortega and María de Zúñiga, who is currently married to Agustín de Arrieta. The entry is incomplete.

people_involved: Capn. Manuel Gómez de Ocón y Trillo
summary: Captain don Benito Díaz Bravo, a resident of Panamá, sold an enslaved mulato named Pedro, 30 years old, to Captain Manuel Gómez de Ocón y Trillo for $300. Díaz Bravo had purchased Pedro from don Salvador Jirón, a resident of León, Nicaragua. Manuel Gómez de Ocón y Trillo was unable to sign the document.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Francisco de Obregón
summary: Sergeant Major Agustín Corleto, a resident of Guatemala, obligated himself to Sergeant Major don Francisco de Obregón, a resident of Granada, Nicaragua, for 1142 pesos and 4 reales. This money was a loan for Corleto's provisions, which he promised to repay in Panamá within one month.
Sebastián de Zamora granted a general power of attorney to Licenciado don Alonso de Sandoval, who was the Commissioner of the Holy Office.
