Pedro Fernández Galindo, a river carpenter, committed to Alférez Manuel Pérez and Jerónimo Valerino to build a boat in the port of Matina. The boat would be 16 varas long at the keel, 10 tercias wide, 10 tercias flat, and 4 tercias deep, made entirely of cedar planks and shored up. Delivery was expected within approximately 4 months for a price of 250 pesos.

people_involved: Adelantado don Juan Fernández de Salinas y Cerda
summary: Adelantado don Juan Fernández de Salinas y Cerda leased a cacao plantation with 266 fruit-bearing trees on the banks of the Matina River to Jerónimo Valerino for 5 years. The annual rent was 150 pesos, payable in cacao at a rate of 70 grains per real, delivered in Cartago.

This entry details the will of María de Aguilar. She was married a second time to Ayudante Pedro de Santiago Galindo, and their children were Antonia Godoy Morán, Juana Morán Crespo, Agustina de Aguilar, Ana López de Santiago, and María Vázquez de Rosa. From her third marriage, her children were the late Diego de Aguilar, the late Pedro del Pueyo, Isabel María, María del Pueyo, and Catalina Palacios (the only single living child).
María de Aguilar, a widow, donated a portion of a house to her daughter María Vázquez de Rosa and to Francisco de Vergara, her daughter's husband.

people_involved: General don Rodrigo Arias Maldonado y Velazco
summary: Sebastián de Zamora sold an enslaved mulato named Juan de Herrera, branded between the eyebrows, to General don Rodrigo Arias Maldonado y Velazco, the Mayor Alcalde of Nicoya province. This was the same enslaved person Zamora had bought from don Rodrigo in 1663 for $400. Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro accepted on behalf of don Rodrigo, using a power of attorney granted in Nicoya on the 8th of this month.
Catalina de Palacios, a widow, sold her enslaved mulatilla, Laos María, approximately 7 years old, to Ana Torrente de Obregón for $180.
Tomás Calvo, as the Depositary and Syndic of the Convent of San Francisco, granted power of attorney to Simón Pleites de Figueroa, a procurator in the Audiencia of Guatemala.

Licenciado don Alonso de Sandoval, Commissioner of the Holy Office, founded a chaplaincy for ten recited masses annually to be said for his soul, his parents, and those under his obligation. These masses would be held at the Convent of San Francisco, or in the parish church by the poorest priest if the convent was unavailable. The endowment included $250 at 5% interest, $150 owed by Alvaro de Nava and Margarita Morillo (secured by a cattle site called San Jerónimo in the Landecho valley), and $100 owed by Fernando López de los Santos and Catalina Ruiz (secured by a site called Santa Lucía). The Syndic of the Convent was designated as the patron.

This entry details the will of don Francisco de Enciso Hita, a native of this city (likely Cartago) and a resident of Nicaragua. He was married to doña Ursula de Molina, who was previously widowed twice (first from Marcos de Umanes, second from Pedro de Angulo). The children from her first marriage was doña Catalina de Umanes, and from her second marriage were don Alonso, don Francisco, don Pedro, don Diego, and doña María, all of whom lived in Enciso Hita's house while their mother was alive. He had assets in both Cartago and Nicaragua. His brother-in-law was Cristóbal Guerrero, and his uncle was Cristóbal de Chaves. His sister, doña Gertrudis, wife of Cristóbal Guerrero, was named his heir.
Alonso Ruiz de Pasillas, a resident, obligated himself to Captain Pedro Venegas for $100, which Venegas had lent him.

people_involved: don Juan López de la Flor
summary: An unnamed individual from Jerez de la Choluteca obligates themselves to Governor don Juan López de la Flor for $260.00. This sum is to be repaid in Panamá.

The will of Mateo de Madrigal, natural son of Alférez Cristobal de Madrigal, is recorded. His natural daughter, María de Madrigal (a widow), his brother Juan de la Cruz, and his nephew José de Prendas are mentioned in the testament.
A codicil (an amendment to a will) for Andrés Morillo de Campos is recorded.
Don Rodrigo Calderón obligates himself to María Jiménez, the widow of Alférez Juan López de Ortega, for $170.00. This money is specified as belonging to the children of Fc? de Solís and Anta. López.

Asisclo López Torralbo and his wife doña Micaela Vázquez de Coronado sell a ranch site with one caballería of land to Juan Ricardo for $20.00. The property, located across the Agua Caliente river, previously belonged to Ambrosio de Brenes, then his son Juan de Vinda, and was purchased by Alférez Juan Vázquez de Coronado, who is the father of doña Micaela and father-in-law of Asisclo.

people_involved: don Juan López de la Flor
summary: Governor don Juan López de la Flor grants general power of attorney to Captain Antonio de Siero, a resident of León, Nicaragua.

people_involved: don Miguel Ortiz de Chaves y Aldana
summary: A dowry letter is issued for Agustín Rodríguez Betancourt, legitimate son of Juan de la Cruz and Isabel de Betancourt (formerly of Guatemala), in favor of his wife Isabel de Chaves, legitimate daughter of Pedro de Valerio and Ana de Chaves (residents of this city). The dowry is $400.00, with an additional $200.00 in arras, and José de Uros and don Miguel Ortiz de Chaves y Aldana are the appraisers.

Sebastián de Zamora and his wife doña Lucía de Sandoval Ocampo obligate themselves for $100.00 to the 'Dotación de doncellas,' an endowment established by Alonso Hernández and affiliated with the Cofradía de la Concepción. They mortgage a ranch located about half a league from the city, across the Pontezuela river, bordering Isabel de Ortega's property.

Don José de Alvarado and his wife doña Petronila de Retes obligate themselves for $100.00 to the Cofradía de la Vera Cruz. They mortgage a property in Ujarraz, named Sta. Gertrudis, which previously belonged to Jerónimo Felipe, then to Captain Jerónimo de Retes (father of doña Petronila and father-in-law of don José), and subsequently to doña Jerónima de Retes (sister of doña Petronila and sister-in-law of don José).

people_involved: Ayudante Fernando López de los Santos
summary: Captain José Pérez de Luna and his wife doña Josefa de Chaves exchange slaves with Ayudante Fernando López de los Santos, a resident of Esparza. Pérez de Luna and Chaves give Juan Narváez, a 24-year-old mulatto, while López de los Santos gives Juan Cascante, a 20-year-old mulatto he purchased from don Luis Cascante de Rojas.

people_involved: don Juan López de la Flor
summary: Jerónimo Valerino and his wife Francisca de Esquivel obligate themselves to Governor don Juan López de la Flor for $300.00, payable 15 days after Valerino's return from Guatemala. They mortgage a house in this city, bordering the Barbozas street, the Church, and Juan de Vida Martell's house, and also a cacao plantation in Matina, with Andrés de Sandoval acting as guarantor.

locations: villa de Soto, Castilla la Vieja
summary: A dowry is established for José Marín de Laguna, legitimate son of Franc? Marín and Cecilia Laguna, native of Soto, Castilla la Vieja, in favor of his wife doña Catalina de Moya Colmenero, legitimate daughter of the deceased don José de Moya and doña Mayor de Benavides Moreno. The dowry is $2411.00, with an additional $500.00 in arras.
In the town of San Bartolomé de Barba, the Alcalde delivers a 14-year-old orphan boy named José Jiménez to Agustín González de Loría, a blacksmith.

The will of Francisca Jiménez is recorded. She is the natural daughter of Domingo Jimenez and EGracial 1 e, and the widow of Ambrosio de Brenes. Her will lists her children: María, Francisca, Jerónima, Catalina, Gregorio, Mateo, Marcos, and Andrés de Brenes, along with Antonio de Vinda, Domingo Jiménez, and Juan de Vinda.

The will of Alférez Francisco López is recorded. He was the legitimate son of the deceased Antonio Hernández and Lucía de Madrigal, and was married to the deceased Juana de Ortega for about 70 years. He had given a property in La Laguna de Orris to Elvira Gómez over ten years prior for personal service. His daughter, doña María Gómez, married Alférez Juan Vázquez de Coronado, and they had three children: doña María, Antonio, and Diego Vázquez.

people_involved: Capn. Manuel Gómez de Ocón y Trillo
summary: Captain Manuel Gómez de Ocón y Trillo, a resident of this city, sells half a cattle ranch in the Aserrí valley to Alférez Gaspar Arias for $500.00. The property, bordering Pedro Solano's land, includes a house and two caballerías of land, which Gómez de Ocón y Trillo acquired in 1661 from the estate of don Franc? Solano.
María Sagaste, widow of Sergeant Nicolás de Barrantes, sells an unspecified item to Alférez Juan Alvarez de Ulate, a trader active in this province and Panamá.

Doña Juana de Moscoso, widow of Capitán don Juan de Senabria, donates an enslaved woman named María, 33 years old, and her three children (María, Gregorio, and Juliana) to Nicolás Barrantes. This donation is made in recognition of the many services rendered by Nicolás, his wife María de Sagaste, and his daughter Jerónima Barrantes.
Alonso Ruiz de Pasillas obligates himself to Ayudante Francisco Ramírez for $460, which he borrowed and promises to return in Panamá.

people_involved: Capitán Pedro Alonso de las Alas
summary: María de Guido, widow of the late escribano Alférez Luis Machado, sells a cattle site to Cristóbal Durán de Chaves. This site was inherited from her father, Pedro de las Alas, who in turn inherited it from Capitán Pedro Alonso de las Alas, her grandfather. The property carries a $50 charge in favor of the Chaplaincy founded by Doña Ana de Medrano, which is attached to the Cofradía del Rosario, and the buyer will pay this amount to the Cofradía.

people_involved: Capitán Pedro Alonso de las Alas
summary: María de Guido, widow of Alférez Luis Machado, seeks information to prove her inheritance of a large cattle ranch in Mata Redonda from her father, Alférez Pedro de las Alas. This ranch is located near another one currently owned by Cristóbal Durán de Chaves, which belonged to her late uncle, Capitán Juan de las Alas. She references a past lawsuit between Juan Gutiérrez Jaramillo and her grandfather, Capitán Pedro Alonso de las Alas, regarding the relocation of the ranch.

people_involved: Capitán Pedro Alonso de las Alas
summary: Cristóbal Durán de Chaves and his wife, Doña Ana Pereira Cardoso, obligate themselves to the Cofradía del Rosario for $50, representing a lien on the Mata Redonda site they purchased from María de Guido. This $50 is part of an original $200 debt incurred in 1615 by Capitán Pedro Alonso de las Alas and his wife, María de Guido (grandmother), with $150 of that sum having been redeemed in 1641 by Alférez Luis Machado, the former husband of the current María de Guido.

Luis de Salas, a native of Jerez, Spain, son of Diego Salas and Inés López, makes his testament. He states he has been married to Beatriz de Sosa for 18 years and has two sons, Luis and Pedro, aged 9-11, and a stepson, Juan Domínguez. A marginal note indicates he died on the same day.

Domingo Jiménez Maldonado and his wife, Doña Juana de Sojo, sell a 22-year-old mulata enslaved woman named Francisca, described as 'cuarentona' (around forty), to Licenciado don Domingo de Echavarría, Cura and Vicario of Cartago, for $400. The transaction was executed in Barba.
Bartolomé Muñoz Hidalgo and Nicolás Barrantes act as sureties for Capitán Benito Díaz Bravo, who has been appointed as the Lieutenant Governor of Esparza.
Capitán Benito Díaz Bravo and his surety, Ayudante Juan de Morales, obligate themselves to Tesorero don Fernando de Salazar for $144.

people_involved: Doña María Arias Maldonado y Velazco
Mre. de Campo don Andrés Arias Maldonado y Velazco
summary: Doña María Arias Maldonado y Velazco, daughter of the late Governor Mre. de Campo don Andrés Arias Maldonado y Velazco, grants power of attorney to Capitán Juan López del Alburuz and Andrés de Castro. This is to represent her in a dispute over her deceased father's estate, which her brother, Capitán don Rodrigo Arias Maldonado, seeks to send to Spain, despite her claim as the eldest child entitled to her legitimate inheritance from wealth acquired in the Indias through her father's role as Governor and Captain General.

Capitán Alonso Pérez Merchán, owner and master of the frigate 'La Concepción y Santiago' docked in Caldera, charters his vessel to Licenciado don Domingo de Echavarría to transport goods to Panamá. This charter was subsequently annulled.

A dowry letter was granted in Barba, detailing Juana Moscoso's donation of a 23-year-old slave named Diego Barrantes to her husband. The document also mentions Juan Ruiz de Villegas, a vecino of Puebla de los Angeles, making a dowry in favor of his wife, Juana de Zúñiga, who is also noted as being married to Agustín de Arrieta.

people_involved: Manuel Gómez de Ocón y Trillo
summary: Captain Benito Díaz Bravo, a vecino of Panamá, sold a 30-year-old mulato slave named Pedro to Captain Manuel Gómez de Ocón y Trillo for $300. Pedro had been previously purchased by Díaz Bravo from Salvador Jirón, a vecino of León. Manuel Gómez de Ocón y Trillo was noted as being unable to sign the document.

Sargento Mayor Agustín Corleto, a vecino of Guatemala, became indebted to Sargento Mayor Francisco de Obregón, a vecino of Granada, for 1142 pesos and 4 reales. This money was a loan for Corleto's provisions, which he committed to repay in Panamá within one month.
Sebastián de Zamora granted general power of attorney to Licenciado Alonso de Sandoval, who held the position of Comisario del Santo Oficio.

Pedro Fernández Galindo, a river carpenter, contracted with Alférez Manuel Pérez and Jerónimo Valerino to build a cedar boat at the port of Matina. The boat was specified to be 16 varas long at the keel and was to be delivered within approximately four months for a price of 250 pesos.

people_involved: Juan Fernández de Salinas y Cerda
summary: Adelantado Juan Fernández de Salinas y Cerda leased a cacao plantation with 266 fruit trees along the Matina River to Jerónimo Valerino for five years. The annual rent was 150 pesos, payable in cacao at a rate of 70 grains per real, delivered in Cartago.

María de Aguilar's will was recorded, detailing her two marriages and her children. She was married second to Ayudante Pedro de Santiago Galindo, with whom she had five children, and from her third marriage, she had five children, including the deceased Diego de Aguilar and Pedro del Pueyo, and Catalina Palacios, noted as her only living unmarried child.
María de Aguilar, a widow, donated a portion of her house to her daughter, María Vázquez de Rosa, and to María's husband, Francisco de Vergara.

Sebastián de Zamora sold a mulato slave named Juan de Herrera to General Rodrigo Arias Maldonado y Velazco, the Alcalde Mayor of Nicoya. This slave had previously been purchased by Zamora from Rodrigo Arias Maldonado y Velazco in 1663 for $400, indicating a re-sale. Juan de Echavarría Navarro accepted the purchase on behalf of Rodrigo Arias Maldonado y Velazco.
Catalina de Palacios, a widow, sold her mulatilla slave, Laos María, who was approximately 7 years old, to Ana Torrente de Obregón for $180.
Tomás Calvo, acting as the Depositario and Síndico of the Convento de San Francisco, granted power of attorney to Simón Pleites de Figueroa, a procurador in the Audiencia of Guatemala.

Licenciado Alonso de Sandoval, Comisario del Santo Oficio, founded a Chaplaincy for ten annual masses to be said for his soul, his parents, and those under his obligation, primarily at the Convento de San Francisco. The chaplaincy was endowed with $250 at 5% interest, plus debts owed by Alvaro de Nava and Margarita Morillo, and Fernando López de los Santos and Catalina Ruiz, secured by properties in Valle de Landecho and Santa Lucía.

Francisco de Enciso Hita, a native of this city (likely Cartago) and vecino of Nicaragua, made his will. He was married to Ursula de Molina, who had children from two previous marriages. His will named his sister, Gertrudis, married to Cristóbal Guerrero, as his heir, and also mentioned his uncle, Cristóbal de Chaves.
Alonso Ruiz de Pasillas, a resident, became indebted to Captain Pedro Venegas for $100, which Venegas had lent him.

Artavia, acting as the tutor for her children, granted power of attorney to Captain José de Aguilar and Antonio Delgado, residents of Guatemala. This power was for them to collect her children's inheritance from the succession of their deceased grandparents, Pedro de Artaviz and Isabel del Valle.

Esteban Lorenzo, a native of Marsella, established a dowry of $635.00 and arras of $200.00 in favor of his wife, Gregoria de Sojo. Gregoria is identified as the legitimate daughter of Sergeant Gaspar de los Ríos and Francisca de Peñaranda, and the dowry was granted at Gaspar de los Ríos's property.
General don Juan de Obregón granted general power of attorney to Captain don Antonio de Campuzano. Campuzano is described as a knight of the Order of Santiago and a resident of Guatemala.

people_involved: Capitán Sargento Mayor Juan de Vida Martell
Capitán don Juan de Echavarría Navarro
summary: General don Juan de Obregón, having been appointed Alcalde Mayor of Nicoya by the Audiencia of Guatemala, was unable to attend his residency review for his previous role as Governor and Captain General of the province. He therefore granted power to Captain Sergeant Major Juan de Vida Martell and Captain Juan de Echavarría Navarro to represent him in the judgment of residency.
General don Juan de Obregón granted general power of attorney to Licenciado don Alonso de Sandoval, Commissary of the Holy Office, Ensign Manuel Pérez, and Depositary Tomás Calvo.

Antonia Sánchez, widow of Jerónimo Vanegas, received $300.00 as paternal inheritance for her minor children. Captain Bartolomé Muñoz Fidalgo and Captain Francisco Fernández de Miranda served as guarantors for this transaction.

Ensign Sebastián de Aguirre, husband of Doña Petronila de Grado Moreno, requested that guarantors be admitted to allow his wife to receive her dowry assets. These assets were due from the estate of her deceased first husband, Cristóbal de Vargas, and the Alcalde approved the request.

Jerónimo Leal, Domingo de Otárola, and Esteban de Hoses Navarro acted as guarantors for Doña Petronila de Grado, widow of Captain Cristóbal de Vargas. This allowed her to receive her dowry assets, with the condition that she would return them if a claimant with a better right emerged.
Juan López de Ortega's codicil mandated the founding of a Chaplaincy of masses. He also served as the executor for his brother, Baltasar de Ortega, and his wife was María Jiménez.

people_involved: General don Rodrigo Arias Maldonado y Velazco
summary: Doña Juana de Moscoso, widow of don Juan de Senabria Maldonado, granted freedom to María de la Natividad, a 3-year-old zamba daughter of her black slave Francisca, for $225.00. The payment was made by Juan Pérez de Carmona, agent for Ensign Bartolomé de la Cerda of Nicoya, whose power of attorney, granted on June 30, 1665, also mentioned the freedom of Antonia and María, daughters of Francisca.
Gaspar de Rojas's codicil revoked a previous testament's foundation of a Chaplaincy. This decision was made due to his many children, and his wife was María González.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Juan de Vida Martell
summary: Juan de la Cruz and Mateo de Madrigal, who are brothers, granted power of attorney to Sergeant Major Juan de Vida Martell.

Juana de Llanos, widow of Diego de Escobar, made her testament. She named Francisco and Pedro Solano, whom she had raised as her own children, as her heirs and co-executors, along with Diego de Santiago and Gaspar de los Ríos.

people_involved: Licenciado don Domingo de Echavaría Navarro
summary: Licenciado don Domingo de Echavaría Navarro, as Chaplain and patron of the Chaplaincy founded by Commissary Baltasar de Grado, sold houses in Cartago. These houses, previously given as a censo in 1631 for $370.00 to the deceased Francisco Rodríguez de Sosa and his wife Doña Ana de Guevara, were being sold because Doña Ana, now poor and with children, could not pay the censos. The properties bordered those of Ensign Vasco Solano and Sergeant Juan de Villarroel.
Domingo de Otárola was the highest bidder for a piece of land that had been held for over 15 years. He purchased it with his wife, María de Alvarado, for $260, which they left as a 5% annuity.
Francisco de Rojas requested that the closed will of his father, Gaspar de Rojas, be opened.

The closed will of Gaspar de Rojas, granted in Cartago, was recorded. He was married to María González and had several children: Lucía, Francisco, Antonio (deceased), Miguel, Antonia, José, Juan, and Juana (deceased). His granddaughter, Ana Francisca, was also mentioned.

people_involved: Don Rodrigo Arias Maldonado y Velazco
Don Juan López de la Flor
summary: Don Rodrigo Arias Maldonado y Velazco granted power to Captain Juan de Acosta. Acosta was to represent Maldonado y Velazco before Governor Don Juan López de la Flor regarding the residency he needed to render for his time in office.
Doña Juana Moscoso, a widow, sold her 7-8 year old mulatto slave named Juan Luis to Captain Don García de Alvarado for $250.

A dowry letter was issued for Juan Dominguez, natural son of Pedro Domínguez and Beatriz de Sosa, in favor of his wife Victoria Chacón. Victoria was the legitimate daughter of Diego Chacón and Jerónima de Peñaranda, and the dowry amounted to $478.

people_involved: Doña Petronila de Grado y Moreno
summary: Alférez Sebastián de Aguirre and his wife, Doña Petronila de Grado y Moreno, obligated themselves to Domingo Jiménez Maldonado and his wife, Doña Juana de Sojo, for $350. Aguirre committed to buying a female slave in Panamá for that sum and bringing her to his creditors as payment.

Alférez Luis de Fonseca ratified the sale of a cattle ranch near the town of Ujarráz, which his wife Doña Jerónima de Retes had made to Don José de Alvarado. The price was $500, with $100 reserved by the buyer to cover an annuity on the property in favor of the Cofradía de la Vera Cruz.

Sargento Juan Solano sold a house in Cartago to Diego Pérez, a tailor. The house bordered a lot belonging to the seller and a house owned by Juana de la Portilla, with a street in between, for a price of $25.
Doña Juana de Moscoso requested that the will of her son, Sargento Nicolás Barrantes, be opened.
Gaspar de Chinchilla provided bail for Antonio de Acosta in a lawsuit brought against him by Juan de la Cruz and Mateo de Madrigal.

The will of Sargento Nicolás Barrantes was recorded. He was the son of the deceased Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado and was married to María Sagaste, the legitimate daughter of Jorge Sagaste and Ana Martín Navarro. Their children were Jerónima, Benito, and Juana Barrantes.

people_involved: Don Juan López de la Flor
summary: Governor Don Juan López de la Flor granted power to his cousin, Captain Don Francisco Zapata, to collect two thousand ducats of his salary from the Royal Treasury in León.
Sargento Francisco Hernández Barquero and Juan de Padilla provided bail for Pedro Sánchez Navarrete, who was imprisoned in the public jail due to a legal case against him.

Captain Don José de Alvarado and his wife, Petronila de Retes, obligated themselves to the Cofradía de la Vera Cruz for $100. They mortgaged a property called Santa Gertrudis, located in the rocky area of Ujarráz, though the document was not signed.
Depositario Tomás Calvo provided bail for Juan de la Cruz and Mateo de Madrigal in the execution they were pursuing against Alférez Antonio de Acosta.
Alférez Manuel Pérez and Jerónimo Valerino rescinded a contract they had previously made to construct a ship, which they had already begun building.

Doña Juana de Moscoso, widow of Capitán don Juan de Senabria, donates an enslaved woman named María, aged 33, and her three children, María (5-6 years), Gregorio (3 years), and Juliana (1 year), to Nicolás Barrantes. This donation is made in recognition of the many services rendered by Nicolás Barrantes, his wife María de Sagaste, and their daughter Jerónima Barrantes.
Alonso Ruiz de Pasillas obligates himself to Ayudante Francisco Ramírez for a debt of $460.00. This amount was a loan from Ramírez, and Pasillas commits to repaying it in Panamá.

people_involved: Capitán Pedro Alonso de las Alas
summary: María de Guido, widow of the late escribano Luis Machado, sells a cattle site to Cristóbal Durán de Chaves. This site was inherited by María from her father, Pedro de las Alas, who in turn inherited it from his father, Capitán Pedro Alonso de las Alas, the seller's grandfather. The property carries a $50.00 charge in favor of the Chaplaincy founded by doña Ana de Medrano, which is attached to the Cofradía del Rosario, and the buyer will pay this amount to the Cofradía.

people_involved: Capitán Pedro Alonso de las Alas
summary: María de Guido, widow of Alférez Luis Machado, requests information to prove her inheritance of a large cattle ranch in Mata Redonda from her father, Alférez Pedro de las Alas. This ranch is located near the main Mata Redonda ranch currently owned by Cristóbal Durán de Chaves, which belonged to her deceased uncle, Capitán Juan de las Alas. She states that the two ranches were divided between the brothers after their parents' deaths, and her grandparents held title from Capitán Diego de Artieda Chirinos, as evidenced by a lawsuit Juan Gutiérrez Jaramillo filed against her grandfather, Capitán Pedro Alonso de las Alas, regarding moving the ranch, though the original title is lost.

people_involved: Capitán Pedro Alonso de las Alas
summary: Cristóbal Durán de Chaves and his wife, doña Ana Pereira Cardoso, obligate themselves to the Cofradía del Rosario for $50.00, which is a lien on the Mata Redonda site they purchased from María de Guido. The original debt of $200.00 was received in 1615 by Capitán Pedro Alonso de las Alas and his wife María de Guido, but $150.00 of this sum was redeemed in 1641 by Alférez Luis Machado, the husband of the current María de Guido.

Luis de Salas, a native of Jerez, Spain, and legitimate son of Diego Salas and Inés López, makes his testament. He states he has been married to Beatriz de Sosa for 18 years and has two sons, Luis and Pedro de Salas, aged 9-11 years, as well as a stepson, Juan Domínguez. A marginal note indicates he died on the same day.

Domingo Jiménez Maldonado and his wife, doña Juana de Sojo, sell a 22-year-old mulata enslaved woman named Francisca to Licenciado don Domingo de Echavarría, who serves as the Cura and Vicario of Cartago, for $400.00. The transaction was granted in Barba.

Bartolomé Muñoz Hidalgo and Nicolás Barrantes act as sureties for Capitán Benito Díaz Bravo. Capitán Díaz Bravo has been appointed as the Teniente de Gobernador (Lieutenant Governor) of the city of Esparza.
Capitán Benito Díaz Bravo and his surety, Ayudante Juan de Morales, obligate themselves to Tesorero don Fernando de Salazar for $144.00.

people_involved: Doña María Arias Maldonado y Velazco
Mre. de Campo don Andrés Arias Maldonado y Velazco
summary: Doña María Arias Maldonado y Velazco, legitimate daughter of the deceased Governor Mre. de Campo don Andrés Arias Maldonado y Velazco, and with permission from her husband Alférez Manuel Pérez, grants power of attorney to Capitán Juan López del Alburuz and Andrés de Castro. This is to represent her in a pending case concerning the estate of her father, which her brother Capitán don Rodrigo Arias Maldonado is attempting to claim for remittance to Spain. Doña María asserts her right as the eldest surviving child who came to the Indias with her father, stating he brought no assets but gained them through his role as Governor and Captain General, and she is entitled to her legitimate inheritance.

Capitán Alonso Pérez Merchán, owner and master of the frigate 'La Concepción y Santiago' docked in Caldera, charters it to Licenciado don Domingo de Echavarría to transport goods to Panamá. This entry was subsequently annulled.
Doña Catalina de la Jara is mentioned as the widow of Ignacio de [name cut off].

Artavia, acting as a widow and tutor for her children, granted power of attorney to Captain José de Aguilar and Antonio Delgado, residents of Guatemala. This power was for collecting her children's inheritance from the succession of their grandparents, Pedro de Artaviz and Isabel del Valle.

Esteban Lorenzo, a native of Marsella, established a dowry of $635.00 and arras of $200.00 in favor of his wife, Gregoria de Sojo. Gregoria is the legitimate daughter of Sergeant Gaspar de los Ríos and Francisca de Peñaranda, and the document was granted at Gaspar de los Ríos' property.
General don Juan de Obregón granted general power of attorney to Captain don Antonio de Campuzano, a knight of the Order of Santiago and a resident of Guatemala.

people_involved: Capitán Sargento Mayor Juan de Vida Martell
Capitán don Juan de Echavarría Navarro
summary: General don Juan de Obregón, appointed Alcalde Mayor of Nicoya by the Audiencia of Guatemala, granted power of attorney to Captain Sergeant Major Juan de Vida Martell and Captain Juan de Echavarría Navarro. This was to represent him in the juicio de residencia for his previous role as Governor and Captain General of the province, as his new appointment prevented him from attending personally.
General don Juan de Obregón granted general power of attorney to Licenciado don Alonso de Sandoval, Commissioner of the Holy Office, Ensign Manuel Pérez, and Depositary Tomás Calvo.

Antonia Sánchez, widow of Jerónimo Vanegas, received $300.00 as paternal inheritance for her minor children. Captain Bartolomé Muñoz Fidalgo and Captain Francisco Fernández de Miranda served as guarantors for this transaction.

Ensign Sebastián de Aguirre, husband of Doña Petronila de Grado Moreno, requested the admission of guarantors to receive the dowry goods belonging to his wife from the estate of her deceased first husband, Cristóbal de Vargas. The Alcalde approved this request.

Jerónimo Leal, Domingo de Otárola, and Esteban de Hoses Navarro acted as guarantors for Doña Petronila de Grado, widow of Captain Cristóbal de Vargas, enabling her to receive her dowry goods. They guaranteed that she would return the goods if a creditor with a better claim appeared.
Juan López de Ortega's codicil mandated the founding of a Chaplaincy for masses. His wife was María Jiménez, and Baltasar de Ortega, his brother, was his executor.

people_involved: General don Rodrigo Arias Maldonado y Velazco
summary: Doña Juana de Moscoso granted freedom to María de la Natividad, a 3-year-old zamba daughter of her slave Francisca, for $225.00. This payment was made by Juan Pérez de Carmona, acting as attorney for Ensign Bartolomé de la Cerda, based on a power of attorney granted in Nicoya on June 30, 1665, which also mentioned the freedom of Antonia, another daughter of Francisca.
Garpar de Rojas' codicil revoked a previous testament's foundation of a Chaplaincy due to his many children. His wife was María González.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Juan de Vida Martell
summary: Juan de la Cruz and Mateo de Madrigal, who are brothers, granted power of attorney to Sergeant Major Juan de Vida Martell.

Juana de Llanos, widow of Diego de Escobar, made her testament, stating she had no children with him. She named Francisco and Pedro Solano, whom she raised as her own, as her heirs and co-executors, along with Diego de Santiago and Gaspar de los Ríos.

people_involved: Licenciado don Domingo de Echavaría Navarro
summary: Licenciado don Domingo de Echavaría Navarro, as Chaplain and patron of the Chaplaincy founded by Commissioner Baltasar de Grado, sold houses in Cartago. These houses, originally given in censo to the deceased Francisco Rodríguez de Sosa and his wife Doña Ana de Guevara in 1631 for $370.00, bordered properties of Ensign Vasco Solano and Sergeant Juan de Villarroel. Doña Ana, now poor and with children, had not paid the censos.
Pérez agreed to pay Valerino for expenses incurred and would become the owner of the work started in the Matina river.
Juana de la Portilla, a widow, issued a codicil revoking a previously established chaplaincy foundation. Her children, María and Agustín Guerrero, were mentioned in the document.

Juana de la Portilla founded a chaplaincy for masses, endowed with $200 owed to her by Manuel Gómez and his wife Juana de Mora. One of Gómez's sons was designated as the chaplain, with Padre José de Lumbides serving until then, and Agustín Guerrero as the patron.

Manuel Gómez and Juana de Mora mortgaged a site and ranch in the Aserrí valley, which they had purchased from Francisco Solano. This property already carried a $100 lien, with interest collected by María Vázquez, wife of Pedro Solano.
A marginal note indicates that in 1707, José Hidalgo, who owned the mortgaged site in the Aserrí valley, made a payment related to the property.

Licenciado José de Lumbides, a priest, sold his enslaved woman named Luisa, approximately 24 years old, to his nephew Juan Guijarro de Escobar, a scribe, for $400. Luisa was inherited by Lumbides from his deceased mother, Leonor Pereira.

Leandro Pérez, originally from Pueblo Nuevo and son of Diego Pérez de Zúñiga and María de Espinoza, provided a dowry of $1327 to his wife, María Manuela de Loría. María Manuela is the daughter of Agustín González de Loría and Leonor Núñez de Leredo.

Domingo de Vargas, son of the deceased Alonso de Vargas and María del Pueyo, made an obligation of $766 to his wife, Margarita Méndez. Margarita is the daughter of the deceased José Méndez and Juana de Zúñiga, and the obligation included $60 for a house to be built by her brother, Diego Méndez.

María de Zúñiga, a widow, obligated herself for $250 to the chaplaincy founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela, whose patron and chaplain is Licenciado Marcos Machado. She mortgaged a house and a mill she owned in Barba as security.
Agustín González de Loría obligated himself for $250 in favor of María de Zúñiga, who is identified as his mother-in-law.

Alférez Manuel Gómez and his wife Juana de Mora sold houses in Cartago to Licenciado Alonso de Sandoval, a priest, for $500. The properties, which they had acquired from Francisco Solano, bordered houses belonging to María de Guido (widow of Luis Machado), Domingo de Otárola, and Ana de Quesada, and were subject to a $250 lien for the chaplaincy founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela.

Ambrosia de Echavarría Navarro made her will. She was the legitimate daughter of Juan de Echavarría Navarro, a former provincial treasurer, and María de Sandoval Ocampo, and was married to Treasurer Fernando de Salazar. Her children were Juana (married to García de Alvarado), Ana, Manuela, Marcos, Francisco, Agustín, and Francisco de Padua.

Antonio Ramiro Corajo sold an enslaved mulatto named Pedro, approximately 17 years old, to Juan de Echavarría Navarro for $400. Pedro was inherited by Antonio from his parents, García Ramiro and Juana de Vera.
Catalina de Palacios, a widow, sold an enslaved mulatto girl named Luisa, about 4 years old, to the Depositary Tomás Calvo for $100.
Rodrigo Calderón and his wife Isidora Zambrano obligated themselves for $200 to the chaplaincy founded by Baltasar de Grado. They mortgaged a house and a mill in the Aserrí valley as security.

Felipe Gómez Macotela made his will. He was the legitimate son of the deceased Captain Juan Martin Macotela and Luisa de Figueroa (a resident of Esparza), and was married to Tomasina de Ocampo, daughter of Lieutenant Diego de Ocampo and María de Mora. He had a 3-month-old son, Miguel Gómez, and a brother, Juan Romero Macotela.

The estate of an unnamed deceased person included livestock in various locations such as Palomo, Landecho, and Asiento Viejo. Fray Diego de Macotela, Francisco de Ocampo (the deceased's brother-in-law), and doña Tomasina (the deceased's wife) were named as executors of the estate.
Don José de Guevara Sandoval and his wife, doña Inés de Sandoval Ocampo, committed to pay $200.00 to Tomás Calvo, who served as the Depositary and Síndico for the Convent of San Francisco.

people_involved: Gobernador don Juan López de la Flor
summary: Gobernador don Juan López de la Flor conferred general power of attorney to Capitán don Rodrigo Arias Maldonado.

Domingo de Otárola provided surety for Juan de Gamboa, enabling him to transport two indigenous men, Lorenzo (from Aserrí) and Francisco (from Guicasí), to Nicaragua as arrieros. Lorenzo's encomienda was vacant due to Manuel de Flores' death, while Francisco was from don Juan de Chaves' encomienda.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Bartolomé Arias Maldonado
Mtre. de Campo don Andrés Arias Maldonado
doña Melchora de Góngora y Córdoba
summary: Sargento Mayor don Bartolomé Arias Maldonado provided a dowry of $3641.00 to his wife, doña Sebastiana de Alvarado. The dowry included $500 in reales and two enslaved mulatto individuals, Felipe (17) and Antonia (16), valued at $1100. The document was granted in Barba at the house of don Gil, who was unable to sign due to impaired vision.

people_involved: Licenciado Presbítero don Alonso de Sandoval
Sargento Mayor don José de Sandoval
summary: Licenciado Presbítero don Alonso de Sandoval, out of affection and gratitude for her services, donated an enslaved Creole man named Francisco (15 years old) and an enslaved woman named Justa, along with 30 marks of silver, to María de Sandoval. The donation was conditional on María not selling the enslaved people and living honorably, with any marriage requiring the consent of don José de Sandoval and don Juan de Echavarría Navarro; otherwise, the assets would pass to doña María Ramiro and her children.

people_involved: Licenciado Presbítero don Alonso de Sandoval
summary: Licenciado Presbítero don Alonso de Sandoval donated houses in Cartago to doña María Ramiro, wife of his brother don José de Sandoval. These houses, acquired from Capitán Manuel Gómez, were located near properties of Domingo de Otárola and don Fernando de Salazar. He also donated an enslaved Angolan woman named María (over 60) and an enslaved man named Andrés (17), who was currently a fugitive. The houses were eventually to pass from the donee's children to the Cofradía del Santísimo Sacramento.

people_involved: Licenciado Presbítero don Alonso de Sandoval
summary: Licenciado Presbítero don Alonso de Sandoval donated a 5-year-old mulatto girl named Juana Gregoria, whom he had purchased from Domingo Jiménez Maldonado and his wife doña Juana de Sojo, to his niece doña Mariana de Ocampo Golfín. In the event that doña Mariana could not be the beneficiary, her sister doña Nicolasa de Ocampo Golfín would receive the donation.

people_involved: Licenciado Presbítero don Alonso de Sandoval
summary: Licenciado Presbítero don Alonso de Sandoval granted power of attorney to his brother don José de Sandoval and his nephew don Juan de Echavarría Navarro.

Capitán José de Villalobos Jara sold an estate and cattle ranch, including a house and furniture, in the city's ejidos to Asisclo López Torralbo and his wife doña Micaela Vázquez for $100.00. The property, bordering ranches of Alonso Peláez and Mateo de Sanabria, was subject to a Capellanía founded by Vasco Solano.

Capitán José de Villalobos Jara granted power to Asisclo López Torralbo to collect tributes from the indigenous people under his encomienda. Additionally, José de Villalobos Jara and his wife doña Catalina Arias obligated themselves to López Torralbo for $50.00.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan de Echavarría Navarro
summary: Sargento Mayor Alonso de Bonilla committed to deliver 160 cedar scissors, 20 cedar chains, 70 cedar canaletes, and 10 cedar corridor pillars to Capitán don Juan de Echavarría Navarro by the following April. The items were priced individually.

people_involved: Licenciado Presbítero don Alonso de Sandoval
summary: Sebastián de Zamora owed Licenciado Presbítero don Alonso de Sandoval 108 pesos 4 reales as a final balance, with payment due by the end of June 1666. A cancellation document for this debt was issued on June 16, 1666, by don Juan de Echavarría Navarro, acting as Sandoval's attorney.

Mateo de Madrigal, representing himself and his brother Juan de la Cruz, granted power of attorney to Capitán Juan López del Alburo, the Treasurer of stamped paper and a resident of Guatemala, to represent them in a lawsuit against Antonio de Acosta.
An unnamed grantor sold a property, which they had possessed for over 15 years, to Domingo de Otárola and his wife María de Alvarado for $260, leaving it under a 5% lien.
Francisco de Rojas requested the opening of his father, Gaspar de Rojas's, will.

The closed will of Gaspar de Rojas, executed in Cartago on August 25, 1665, was opened. It revealed his marriage to María González and listed their children and their spouses, as well as his granddaughter Ana Francisca.

people_involved: Don Rodrigo Arias Maldonado y Velazco
Don Juan López de la Flor
summary: Don Rodrigo Arias Maldonado y Velazco granted power of attorney to Captain Juan de Acosta to represent him before Governor Don Juan López de la Flor. This was for the residency review of Don Rodrigo's previous term as Governor.
Doña Juana Moscoso, a widow, sold her enslaved mulatto boy, Juan Luis, aged 7 or 8, to Captain Dn. García de Alvarado for $250.

A dowry letter was issued for Juan Dominguez, natural son of Pedro Domínguez and Beatriz de Sosa, in favor of his wife Victoria Chacón, legitimate daughter of Diego Chacón and Jerónima de Peñaranda, for $478.

people_involved: Doña Petronila de Grado y Moreno
summary: Alférez Sebastián de Aguirre and his wife Doña Petronila de Grado y Moreno obligated themselves to Domingo Jiménez Maldonado and his wife Doña Juana de Sojo for $350. Aguirre committed to buying an enslaved Black woman in Panamá for that sum and bringing her to his creditors as payment.

Alférez Luis de Fonseca ratified the sale of a cattle ranch near Ujarráz, which his wife Doña Jerónima de Retes had sold to Don José de Alvarado for $500. The buyer reserved $100 to cover a lien on the property in favor of the Cofradía de la Vera Cruz.
Sargento Juan Solano sold a house in Cartago to Diego Pérez, a tailor, for $25. The house bordered a lot belonging to the seller and a house of Juana de la Portilla, with a street in between.
Doña Juana de Moscoso requested the opening of the will of her son, Sargento Nicolás Barrantes.
Gaspar de Chinchilla provided a guarantee for Antonio de Acosta in a lawsuit brought against him by Juan de la Cruz and Mateo de Madrigal.

The will of Sargento Nicolás Barrantes, son of the deceased Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado, was recorded. He was married to María Sagaste, and they had three children: Jerónima, Benito, and Juana Barrantes.

people_involved: Don Juan López de la Flor
summary: Governor Don Juan López de la Flor granted power of attorney to his cousin, Captain Don Francisco Zapata, to collect two thousand ducats of his salary from the Royal Treasury in León.
Sargento Francisco Hernández Barquero and Juan de Padilla provided bail for Pedro Sánchez Navarrete, who was imprisoned in the public jail due to a legal case against him.

Captain Don José de Alvarado and his wife Petronila de Retes obligated themselves to the Cofradía de la Vera Cruz for $100, mortgaging a site called Santa Gertrudis in the rocky area of Ujarráz. The document was not signed.
Depositario Tomás Calvo provided a guarantee for Juan de la Cruz and Mateo de Madrigal in the execution proceedings they were pursuing against Alférez Antonio de Acosta.
Alférez Manuel Pérez and Jerónimo Valerino rescinded a contract they had made to build a ship, which they had already begun constructing.

Francisco de Fama, a resident of Cartago, sold his 18-year-old mulatto slave, Juan de Vergara, to Francisco García for $400. Fama had previously acquired Juan de Vergara through purchase from Diego Ruiz de Ocaña.

Catalina de Palacios, a widow, sold her 19-year-old mulatto slave named Ana to Padre Mro. fr. Carlos Vitorino for $400. This sale required the Governor's license due to a court ruling concerning a donation she made to her natural granddaughter, Catalina de Palacios, and her husband, Bartolomé de Aguilar.

Jerónimo Valerino and his wife, Francisca de Esquivel, made an obligation in favor of the children of Antonia López de Ortega, who was Jerónimo Valerino's first wife. Juan de Morales Miranda and Francisco de Quirós served as guarantors for this obligation.

José de la Cruz, a 'pardo', sold a cacao plantation in Matina containing 300 trees to Francisco de Quirós for $100. The property bordered cacao plantations owned by Mateo de Madrigal and Juan de la Cruz, as well as a river.

On April 28, an open Cabildo meeting in Cartago addressed an enemy invasion, which saw 700 men march to Turrialba, 7 leagues from the city, after capturing 25 people. The enemy was repelled due to warnings and preparations by the Governor and Captain General of the province, and aid from Juan Pérez de Guzmán, Governor of Panama. The Cabildo resolved to send a deputy to Panama to request arms and ammunition.

The Cabildo, Justicia y Regimiento of Cartago granted power to Padre Mro. fr. Carlos Vitorino to travel to Panama. He was tasked with representing the province's urgent need for arms and requesting 100 arquebuses and 25 muskets with all necessary supplies.

María Jiménez, widow of Alférez Juan López de Ortega, made an obligation of $400 at 5% interest in favor of the minor children of the deceased Francisco de Solís and Antonia López de Ortega. She mortgaged her house and a cattle ranch near Agua Caliente as security for this debt.

A ratification of María Jiménez's obligation was attempted on September 17, 1666, but it was deemed invalid. This was because the notary, Juan Guijarro, had traveled to Panama and was unavailable to complete the legal process.

On March 5, 1668, Basilio de Coto, husband of Agustina de Solís and buyer of the mortgaged houses, cancelled $300 of the debt related to María Jiménez's obligation. This action partially settled the financial arrangement.

The Cabildo, Justicia y Regimiento of Cartago granted power to fr. Carlos Vitorino to purchase 80 arquebuses and 20 muskets along with their necessary supplies. Payment for these arms would be made in flour and biscuits, delivered either to Caldera or Panama.

The Cabildo granted power to Alférez Antonio Machado to travel to Guatemala and present the province's recent dangers and needs to the Audiencia. He was to request aid, including a garrison and paid troops (two infantry and one cavalry company), to staff three watchtowers at Portete, La Reventazón, and the San Juan river/Votos road, and to seek reimbursement for expenses incurred in repelling the English enemy who disembarked at Portete.
Sebastián de Zamora sold a 60-year-old Mandinga black slave named Juana to Juan Ruiz Guillén for $200. This transaction transferred ownership of the enslaved woman.
Juan Ruiz Guillén made an obligation of $1460 in favor of Juan de Echavarría Navarro. This financial commitment was later cancelled on July 15, 1668, indicating the debt was settled.

An obligation of $1460 made by Juan Ruiz Guillén in favor of Juan de Echavarría Navarro was officially cancelled on July 15, 1668. This cancellation signifies the resolution of the financial agreement between the two parties.
Pérez agreed to pay Valerino's expenses and take ownership of a project that Valerino had started in the Matina river.
Juana de la Portilla, a widow, executed a codicil to her will, revoking a previously established chaplaincy foundation. Her children, María and Agustín Guerrero, are mentioned.

Juana de la Portilla founded a chaplaincy for masses with 200 pesos, owed by Manuel Gómez and Juana de Mora. Agustín Guerrero was named patron, and Padre José de Lumbides was designated as a temporary chaplain. Manuel Gómez and Juana de Mora mortgaged property in Aserrí, acquired from Francisco Solano, which had a 100 peso lien payable to María Vázquez, wife of Pedro Solano. A 1707 note indicates José Hidalgo, the current owner, made a payment on the mortgaged site.

On November 13, Licenciado José de Lumbides, a priest, sold his enslaved black woman named Luisa, approximately 24 years old, to his nephew, Juan Guijarro de Escobar, a scribe, for 400 pesos. Luisa had been inherited by Lumbides from his deceased mother, Leonor Pereira.

On September 25, a dowry letter was issued for Leandro Pérez, a native of Pueblo Nuevo and son of Diego Pérez de Zúñiga and María de Espinoza, in favor of his wife, María Manuela de Loría. María Manuela is the daughter of Agustín González de Loría and Leonor Núñez de Leredo, and the dowry amounted to 1327 pesos.

On September 25, Domingo de Vargas, son of the late Alonso de Vargas and María del Pueyo, provided a dowry of 766 pesos for his wife, Margarita Méndez. Margarita is the daughter of the late José Méndez and Juana de Zúñiga, with 60 pesos of the dowry allocated for a house to be built by her brother, Diego Méndez.

On November 2, the widow María de Zúñiga committed to a 250-peso obligation to the chaplaincy established by Alonso Gómez Macotela, whose patron and chaplain is Licenciado Marcos Machado. She secured this obligation by mortgaging a house and a mill she owns in Barba.
On November 2, Agustín González de Loría committed to a 250-peso obligation in favor of his mother-in-law, María de Zúñiga.

On November 3, Alférez Manuel Gómez and his wife, Juana de Mora, sold houses in Cartago to Licenciado don Alonso de Sandoval, a priest, for 500 pesos. These properties, originally purchased from Francisco Solano, were subject to a 250-peso lien for the chaplaincy founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela.

On November 2, Doña Ambrosia de Echavarría Navarro, daughter of the former provincial treasurer Juan de Echavarría Navarro and María de Sandoval Ocampo, made her will. She is married to Treasurer don Fernando de Salazar, and their children include Juana (married to D? García de Alvarado), Ana, Manuela, Marcos, Francisco, Agustín, and Francisco de Padua.

On November 3, Don Antonio Ramiro Corajo sold an enslaved mulatto man named Pedro, approximately 17 years old, to don Juan de Echavarría Navarro for 400 pesos. Antonio Ramiro Corajo had inherited Pedro from his parents, García Ramiro and Juana de Vera.
On November 17, Catalina de Palacios, a widow, sold an enslaved mulatto girl named Luisa, approximately 4 years old, to Depositario Tomás Calvo for 100 pesos.

On December 3, Don Rodrigo Calderón and his wife, Doña Isidora Zambrano, committed to a 200-peso obligation to the chaplaincy founded by Baltasar de Grado. They secured this debt by mortgaging a house and a mill located in the valley of Aserrí.

On December 7, Felipe Gómez Macotela, a resident of Esparza and son of the late Captain Juan Martin Macotela and Luisa de Figueroa, made his will. He is married to Doña Tomasina de Ocampo, daughter of Lieutenant Diego de Ocampo and María de Mora, and they have a three-month-old son named Miguel Gómez. His brother, Juan Romero Macotela, is also mentioned.

Comisario Presbítero Alonso de Sandoval, gravely ill, decided to renounce secular life and join the Order of San Francisco. He made arrangements with Provincial Fray Juan Montero de Espinoza and Guardian Fray Pedro Fernández de Aragón to be received into the convent. Sandoval also revoked prior testaments, ratified donations, and granted power of attorney to his nephew, Juan de Echavarría Navarro, to manage his assets and fulfill his final wishes, effectively ceding his property to him.

Captain José de Guevara y Sandoval granted power of attorney to Nicolás de Maeda, an Escribano de Cámara, and Andrés de Castro, a procurador, both from the Audiencia de Guatemala. Their task was to solicit a favor on his behalf and to finalize the auction of the office of Alguacil Mayor of "this city," which Guevara y Sandoval had valued at $500.

On July 28th, Gaspar de Chinchilla requested the opening of his grandmother Catalina de Palacios's will, who had passed away that day. Catalina de Palacios's will, dated October 20, 1665, identified her deceased son Marcos de Chinchilla, who had a legitimate son named Gaspar de Chinchilla and a natural daughter named Catalina de Palacios (wife of Bartolomé de Aguilar Calderón). The will also ratified a donation of four slaves to her granddaughter Catalina, mentioned her nephew Tomás Calvo, and noted her deceased granddaughter Felipa de Chinchilla, who died without issue.

On August 7th, Fernando de Salazar, Lieutenant Accountant and Judge Official of the Royal Treasury, received a shipment of military supplies from Juan de Zepeda, Lieutenant Alguacil Mayor of the Court of Guatemala. The shipment included 50 arcabuses, 20 muskets, gunpowder, bullets, and iron for forks, sent by the Audiencia de Guatemala. Some items required repair and were given to master armorer Agustín de Loría. Additionally, Salazar received 4139 pesos, 30 arcabuses, and two boxes of bullets from the President of Guatemala, delivered by Antonio de los Reyes.

On August 14th, Rodrigo Calderón leased a cacao plantation in Matina for four years from the minor children of the late Francisco de Solís and Antonia López de Ortega. The plantation had been abandoned by Jerónimo Valerino due to damages inflicted by English enemies. Calderón agreed to an annual payment of $437 and 4 reales, with Sargento Francisco Carrillo and Antonio de la Vega acting as guarantors, and further mortgaged another cacao plantation in Matina with 700 trees and a mill.

On August 22nd, Bartolomé de Aguilar Calderón and his wife, Catalina de Palacios, committed to a $200 obligation in favor of the minor children of Francisco de Solís and Antonia López de Ortega. To secure this obligation, they mortgaged a cacao plantation in Matina, which contained 500 trees.

On August 22nd, Alférez Francisco Solano, by order of the Royal Audiencia, received the mortuary file of his father, Alférez Vasco Solano. He was tasked with delivering this document to one of the offices within the Audiencia.

On August 28th, Juan Cascante de Rojas, who was over 26 years old, sold his 20-year-old mulatto slave named Luis to Hernando de los Santos, a resident of Esparza. The transaction was completed for a sum of $300.
On August 28th, Jerónimo Valerino granted power of attorney to Sargento Nicolás de Céspedes.

On June 2nd, a dowry letter was issued for Francisco Salguero, son of Felipe Salguero and María de Aldana from Guatemala, in favor of his wife, María Magdalena de Peláez. María Magdalena is the legitimate daughter of Alférez Francisco Peláez and Ana de Flores, residents of "this city." The dowry amounted to $939, which included half of Peláez's house, bordering properties of Matías Jacinto and Cristóbal de Araya.

On August 23rd, the Mayor arranged for Cristóbal de Cárdenas, a 20-year-old native of Pacacua of the Royal Crown, to be apprenticed to Diego Blas, a master carpenter from Aserrí. The apprenticeship is set for three years, during which Diego Blas will teach Cristóbal de Cárdenas the carpentry trade.
Don José de Guevara Sandoval and his wife, Doña Inés de Sandoval Ocampo, obligated themselves to pay $200.00 to Tomás Calvo, who served as the Syndic for the Convent of San Francisco.

people_involved: Don Juan López de la Flor
summary: Governor Don Juan López de la Flor conferred general power of attorney to Captain Don Rodrigo Arias Maldonado.

Domingo de Otárola vouched for Juan de Gamboa, enabling him to transport two indigenous men, Lorenzo (from Aserrí) and Francisco (from Guicasí), to Nicaragua as muleteers. Lorenzo's encomienda was vacant due to Manuel de Flores' death, while Francisco belonged to Don Juan de Chaves' encomienda.

people_involved: Doña Melchora de Góngora y Córdoba
summary: Sergeant Major Don Bartolomé Arias Maldonado, son of former Governor Don Andrés Arias Maldonado and Doña Melchora de Góngora y Córdoba, granted a dowry of $3641.00 to his wife, Doña Sebastiana de Alvarado. The dowry also included a 17-year-old mulato named Felipe and a 16-year-old mulata named Antonia, valued at $1100.00. The document was executed in Barba at the home of Don Gil de Alvarado, Doña Sebastiana's father, who was unable to sign due to impaired vision.

Licenciado Presbítero Don Alonso de Sandoval, out of affection and gratitude for María de Sandoval's care during his illnesses, donated a 15-year-old criollo negro named Francisco, a negra named Justa, and 30 marks of silver household objects to her. The donation was conditional on her not selling the slaves and living honorably, with any marriage requiring the consent of Don José de Sandoval and Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro; otherwise, the donation would pass to Doña María Ramiro and her children.

Don Alonso de Sandoval donated houses in Cartago, previously purchased from Captain Manuel Gómez and bordering properties of Domingo de Otárola and Don Fernando de Salazar, to Doña María Ramiro, wife of his brother Don José de Sandoval. He also donated an Angola negra named María, over 60 years old, and a 17-year-old negro named Andrés, who was currently a fugitive. The houses were stipulated to pass from Doña María Ramiro's children to the Cofradía del Santísimo Sacramento.

Don Alonso de Sandoval donated a 5-year-old mulatilla named Juana Gregoria, whom he had purchased from Domingo Jiménez Maldonado and Doña Juana de Sojo, to his niece Doña Mariana de Ocampo Golfín. If Doña Mariana could not receive the benefit, it would pass to her sister, Doña Nicolasa de Ocampo Golfín.
Don Alonso de Sandoval granted power of attorney to his brother Don José de Sandoval and his nephew Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro.

Captain José de Villalobos Jara sold a ranch and cattle farm, including a house and furniture, in the city's ejidos to Asisclo López Torralbo and his wife Doña Micaela Vázquez for $100.00. The property, which bordered lands of Alonso Peláez and Mateo de Sanabria, was subject to a chaplaincy founded by Vasco Solano.

Captain José de Villalobos Jara granted power to Asisclo López Torralbo to collect tributes from the indigenous people under his encomienda. Additionally, Captain Villalobos Jara and his wife, Doña Catalina Arias, obligated themselves to López Torralbo for $50.00.

Sergeant Major Alonso de Bonilla obligated himself to deliver 160 scissors, 20 chains, 70 canaletes, and 10 corridor pillars, all made of cedar wood cut during a waning moon, to Captain Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro by the following April.

Sebastián de Zamora owed Licenciado Presbítero Don Alonso de Sandoval 108 pesos and 4 reales as a balance of accounts, with payment due by the end of June. The debt was subsequently cancelled on June 16, 1666, by Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro, acting as Sandoval's attorney.

Mateo de Madrigal, acting for himself and his brother Juan de la Cruz, granted power of attorney to Captain Juan López del Alburo, Treasurer of stamped paper and a resident of Guatemala, to represent them in a lawsuit against Antonio de Acosta.

Francisco de Fama, a resident of Cartago, sold a mulatto slave named Juan de Vergara, 18 years old, to Francisco García, also a resident. Fama had previously acquired Juan de Vergara through purchase from Diego Ruiz de Ocaña. The sale price was $400.

Catalina de Palacios, a widow, sold her mulatto slave named Ana, about 19 years old, to Padre Mro. fr. Carlos Vitorino for $400. This sale required and obtained the Governor's license, as a previous court ruling stipulated she could not sell slaves without informing the Governor, following a donation she made to her natural granddaughter, Catalina de Palacios, and her husband, Bartolomé de Aguilar.

Jerónimo Valerino and his wife, Francisca de Esquivel, made an obligation in favor of the children of Antonia López de Ortega, who was Jerónimo Valerino's first wife. Juan de Morales Miranda and Francisco de Quirós served as guarantors for this obligation.

José de la Cruz, described as pardo, sold a cacao plantation in Matina with 300 trees to Francisco de Quirós for $100. The property bordered cacao plantations belonging to Mateo de Madrigal and Juan de la Cruz, as well as a river.

people_involved: Don Juan López de la Flor
summary: On May 12, the Cabildo of Cartago, including Governor Juan López de la Flor and other officials, met to address the urgent need for arms and munitions following an enemy attack. An enemy force of 700 men disembarked on April 8, marched over 40 leagues, captured 25 people, and reached Turrialba by April 15, but retreated after warnings from an indigenous woman and intelligence from Panamá's Governor, Don Juan Pérez de Guzmán. The Cabildo resolved to send Padre Mro. fr. Carlos Vitorino to Panamá to request 100 arquebuses and 25 muskets, and later empowered Alférez Antonio Machado to go to Guatemala to request further aid and reimbursement for expenses incurred in repelling the English enemy who disembarked at Portete.

María Jiménez, widow of Alférez Juan López de Ortega, made an obligation for $400 at 5% interest in favor of the minor children of the deceased Francisco de Solís and Antonia López de Ortega (Agustina, Paula, Blas, and Cristóbal de Solís). She mortgaged her house and a ranch near Agua Caliente with 300 cattle. Later, in 1668, Basilio de Coto, husband of Agustina López de Solís and buyer of the mortgaged houses, cancelled 300 pesos of the debt.
Sebastián de Zamora sold a 60-year-old Mandinga black slave named Juana to Juan Ruiz Guillén for $200.
Juan Ruiz Guillén made an obligation in favor of Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro for $1460. A cancellation document for this obligation was recorded on July 15, 1668.

Comisario Presbítero Alonso de Sandoval, being ill, decides to leave secular life and enter the Order of San Francisco. He makes arrangements with Provincial Fray Juan Montero de Espinoza and Guardian Fray Pedro Fernández de Aragón. He revokes previous testaments, ratifies donations, and grants power of attorney to his nephew, Juan de Echavarría Navarro, to manage his assets and fulfill his wishes.

Captain José de Guevara y Sandoval grants power of attorney to Nicolás de Maeda, an Escribano de Cámara, and Andrés de Castro, a procurador, both from the Audiencia de Guatemala. Their task is to seek a favor for Guevara y Sandoval and to auction the office of Alguacil Mayor of Cartago for $500.
Gaspar de Chinchilla requests the opening of the testament of his grandmother, Catalina de Palacios, who passed away on this day.

The testament of Catalina de Palacios, widow of Gaspar de Chinchilla, is recorded. It mentions her deceased son Marcos de Chinchilla, who had a legitimate son, Gaspar de Chinchilla, and a natural daughter, Catalina de Palacios (wife of Bartolomé de Aguilar Calderón). The testament ratifies a donation of four slaves to her granddaughter Catalina and mentions her nephew Tomás Calvo and deceased granddaughter Felipa de Chinchilla.

Fernando de Salazar, Teniente de Contador, receives 50 arcabuses, 20 mosquetes, 4 powder jars, 2 qq. of bullets, and 20 iron forks from Juan de Zepeda, sent by the Audiencia de Guatemala. These arms are then given to master armorer Agustín de Loría for repairs. Additionally, Salazar receives 4139 pesos, 30 arcabuses, and two boxes of bullets from the President of Guatemala, delivered by Antonio de los Reyes.

Rodrigo Calderón leases a cacao plantation in Matina for four years from the minor children of Francisco de Solís and Antonia López de Ortega. The plantation was previously abandoned by Jerónimo Valerino due to damages from English enemies. Calderón pays $437 and 4 reales annually and provides Sargento Francisco Carrillo and Antonio de la Vega as guarantors, also mortgaging another cacao plantation.

Bartolomé de Aguilar Calderón and his wife Catalina de Palacios obligate themselves for $200 in favor of the minor children of Francisco de Solís and Antonia López de Ortega. As security, they mortgage a cacao plantation in Matina with 500 trees.
Alférez Francisco Solano receives the mortuary file of his deceased father, Alférez Vasco Solano, by order of the Real Audiencia. He is to deliver the file to one of the Audiencia's offices.
Juan Cascante de Rojas, who is over 26 years old, sells his 20-year-old mulatto slave named Luis to Hernando de los Santos, a resident of Esparza, for $300.
Jerónimo Valerino grants power of attorney to Sargento Nicolás de Céspedes.

A dowry letter is issued for María Magdalena de Peláez, daughter of Alférez Francisco Peláez and Ana de Flores, for $939. Her husband is Francisco Salguero, son of Felipe Salguero and María de Aldana, residents of Guatemala. The dowry includes half of the house where Peláez lives, which borders properties of Matías Jacinto and Cristóbal de Araya.
The Alcalde arranges a three-year apprenticeship for Cristóbal de Cárdenas, a 20-year-old from Pacacua, with Diego Blas, a master carpenter from Aserrí, to teach him the trade.

Juan de Morales Miranda and his wife Beatriz Méndez obligated themselves to Antonio Domínguez Lozano, a resident of Cartago, for $383. This debt was for 25 mules Morales purchased from Lozano, and they agreed to pay in local goods (flour and biscuits) delivered to Caldera.

Juan de Morales Miranda obligated himself to Juan Pérez de Guadamuz for $2362 and 5 reales. This debt was originally owed to Marcos Gallardo, a neighbor of Los Santos, who transferred it to Pérez. Morales agreed to pay with goods (flour and biscuits) delivered to Caldera and Granada.

Alférez Gaspar Arias, Alcalde of the Santa Hermandad, and his wife María de Monterroso, obligated themselves to Depositario Tomás Calvo for $180. This obligation was later cancelled on December 6, 1659.

The children of the late Sargento Mayor García Ramiro Corajo and Juana de Vera (Francisco, Diego, Fernando, Micaela, and Antonio Ramiro Corajo) agreed to arbitration to resolve a dispute over their mother's assets. They appointed Tomás Calvo and Tesorero Fernando de Salazar as arbitrators, with the Franciscan preacher fr. Antonio Gregorio de Francia as the third party in case of disagreement.
Matías Jacinto and his wife Isabel de Benavides sold an enslaved Black man named Francisco, aged 7, to Sargento Mayor José de Moya for $10.

Antonio Ramiro Corajo acted as a guarantor for his brother Diego, who was preparing to travel to Granada. This guarantee was for any amount Diego might be condemned to return by the arbitrators in the dispute over the assets of their mother, Juana de Vera.

people_involved: Juan Fernández de Salinas y Cerda
José de la Torre y Escandón
summary: Governor Juan Fernández de Salinas y Cerda granted power of attorney to José de la Torre, a resident of León (Nicaragua), to collect $400 from the Royal Treasury on account of his outstanding salaries.

people_involved: José de la Torre y Escandón
Juan Fernández de Salinas y Cerda
summary: José de la Torre y Escandón received $50 from Governor Juan Fernández de Salinas y Cerda. This payment was part of the power of attorney granted to him to collect $400 from the Royal Treasury in León.

Catalina Tuia, a poor indigenous widow from Curriravá, made her will with the help of interpreters Luis Rodríguez and Gabriel. She declared her children and noted that Captain Juan de Senabria and his wife Juana Moscoso owed her for the service of her deceased daughter, Ana de Senabria, whose will stipulated Catalina's care, which had not been fulfilled, leaving her son Gaspar de Rojas to provide for her.
Juan del Castillo reconciled with his wife, Felipa de Chinchilla, and committed to attending to her as required.

Margarita de Flores y Quiñones, widow of Captain Pedro de Mora Salado, sold a ranch and cattle herd to Captain Francisco Fernández de Miranda and his wife Magdalena Calvo de Abarca for $500. The property, previously owned by Rodrigo Calderón and Isidora Zambrano (1652) and Diego de Ocampo Figueroa (1647), was mortgaged to Ocampo Figueroa, and the buyers assumed this obligation to his widow, Inés Velázquez, who agreed to reduce the debt by $100.
Antonio González executed a codicil to his will, improving the inheritance for his daughter María de Zúñiga and ratifying a bequest for his son Nicolás González.

José de Alvarado, son of Alférez Gil de Alvarado and Juana de Vera, provided a dowry of $4300 to his wife Petronila de Retes, daughter of Capitán Jerónimo de Retes and María Vázquez. The dowry included various assets such as money, livestock, a city plaza solar, and a portion of the Santa Ana site.

Jerónimo Vanegas, natural son of Baltasar de Espinosa and Ana Rodríguez, made his will. He had been married for two years to Antonia Sánchez, with whom he was expecting a child. His wife's dowry of $100 came from the Cofradía de la Concepción, and he named Agn. Guerrero and his brother Juan Martín as executors.

María de Zúñiga, widow of Antonio González, was granted guardianship of her children Nicolás González, María González de Zúñiga, and Juan. She obligated herself to them and provided Juan de Echavarría Navarro and Fernando Ramiro Corajo as guarantors.

Francisco Hernández de Madrigal, son of Juan Hernández de Madrigal and Juana Gómez de Herrera, provided a dowry of $400.00 to his wife, Mariana Hernández. Mariana is the daughter of Francisco Hernández and Ana de los Santos.

people_involved: Capitán Juan de Salamanca y Alarcón
summary: Captain Juan de Salamanca y Alarcón, a resident of Cartago, granted power of attorney to don José de Alvarado and Juan Martínez de Ahumada, who were departing for Panamá. They were authorized to collect from Ayudante Francisco Ramos de Aguiar and Juan Alvarez, residents of Panamá, for 134 chicubites of flour, 50 petacas of biscuits, a gold band, and $15.00 delivered by Alférez Juan Calvo.

Nicolás Barrantes and his wife, María Sagaste, committed to pay $200.00 at 5% interest to the Cofradía de la Concepción. They mortgaged a house and the first mill on the Molino River, located in the common lands of Cartago.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan de Echavarría Navarro
summary: Captain don Juan de Echavarría Navarro granted power of attorney to don José de Alvarado and don Fernando Ramiro Corajo, who were departing for Panamá. Their purpose was to collect a debt of $1221.00 from Sergeant Juan de Chiquillejo and his guarantor, Alonso Rodríguez Bucuro.

people_involved: ex-Gobernador don Juan Fernández de Salinas
summary: Ayudante Alonso de Mora, don José de Alvarado, Nicolás Barrantes, and Gaspar de Rojas posted bail for Agustín de Rojas, an indigenous man imprisoned by order of the Governor. Agustín was in debt for $105.00 to the ex-Gobernador don Juan Fernández de Salinas, and the guarantors committed to ensure payment by the end of May.

locations: Nuestra Señora de la Limpia Concepción
summary: Juan Gómez Rico, son of the deceased Juan Gómez Rico and doña María Cardoso, made his will. He was married to doña María de Castellón, a resident of Nueva Segovia, and had a 15-month-old daughter named Isabel. The will was granted at Francisco Gómez Rico's estancia, Nuestra Señora de la Limpia Concepción, before don Rodrigo Calderón, Corregidor of Pacacua.

Doña Inés Pereira, widow of Captain Bartolomé Sánchez, made her will, mentioning her deceased sons Antonio, Jerónimo, and Alférez Lorenzo Sánchez, and living children Lorenzo, Bartolomé Sánchez, and doña Leonor Pereira. She noted that her deceased son, Alférez Lorenzo Sánchez, had dissipated the Landecho ranch. She also mentioned her granddaughter doña Juana de Sojo, married to Domingo Jiménez Maldonado, and her great-granddaughter doña Catalina de Lumbides.

people_involved: Presbítero Licenciado don Domingo de Echavarria
summary: Sargento Mayor Alonso de Bonilla and his wife, Juana Benita, committed to pay $175.00 at 5% interest to Presbítero Licenciado don Domingo de Echavarria, the priest of Cartago. They mortgaged their house in Cartago, which borders Cristóbal de Araya's house and the hermitage of San Juan de Herrera de los naboríos, and already has a $100.00 lien from a chaplaincy founded by Comisario Baltasar de Grado, for which Padre don Domingo is the chaplain.

Juan Vázquez de Coronado and his wife, Ana María de Mora Salado, committed to pay $100.00 at 5% interest to the Cofradía de la Vera Cruz. They mortgaged their house, which is located near the Main Church and don Juan de Senabria Maldonado's house, with streets in between.

Pedro de Campos Quirós and his wife, doña Bárbara de Rodríguez Altamirano, committed to pay $150.00 at 5% interest to a chaplaincy founded by Vasco Solano, with Padre Alonso de Sandoval serving as its patron and chaplain. They mortgaged a house they had purchased from Francisca Jiménez, the widow of Ambrosia de Brenes.

Don Antonio Ramiro Corajo donated a ranch in Río Grande to his sister, doña Francisca de Zúñiga. This ranch was part of their mother doña Juana de Vera's estate and came with the condition that doña Francisca acknowledge a $500.00 lien on it for various chaplaincies.

Captain José de Luna provided a dowry of $2480.00 and $500.00 in arras to his wife, doña Josefa Gertrudis de Chaves. Doña Josefa is the legitimate daughter of the deceased Alférez Mayor Francisco de Chaves and doña Francisca de Zúñiga.

people_involved: Doctor don Diego Fernández de Córdoba
Padre fray Gabriel de la Torre
summary: Tomás Calvo, the depositary and syndic of the Convent of San Francisco, granted power of attorney to Doctor don Diego Fernández de Córdoba and don Diego Ignacio de Córdoba, agents in Madrid. They were tasked with requesting the incorporation of Padre fray Gabriel de la Torre, current president of the Convents of Aserrí and Curridavá, into the province of San Jorge de Nicaragua, as his ailments prevented his return to Florida.

Juan Gómez de Bonilla, natural son of Román Benito, made his will. He had been married to Juana de Aguilar and listed his children: Clara Gómez (deceased, married to Marcos de Esquivel), Francisca Gómez, Ana de Aguilar, Juan Gómez (deceased), Catalina Gómez, and Francisco Carrillo (absent from the city).

Captain Jerónimo de Retes, the Alguacil Mayor, granted power to Francisco de Castro, a procurator in the Audiencia of Guatemala, and Nicolás de Maeda, a scribe. This power was for them to defend Retes in a residency trial. The trial was conducted by Judge Juan de Balarte (?, y Sotomayor, appointed by the Audiencia, concerning Retes's past role as corregidor of Quepo.

Cristóbal de Oviedo, husband of Ana de la Portilla, sold two 'caballerías' of land in the Aserrí valley to Nicolás Camacho for $30.00. The land, bordered by the La Lajuela and Tiribí rivers and Los Naranjos stream, was originally given as a dowry to Ana by her mother-in-law, Isabel de la Portilla, who had possessed it for over 70 years. Catalina de la Portilla previously owned an adjacent 'caballería'.

Presbyter Tomás de Colina Ruiz, a resident of Realejo and Cartago, granted power to Francisco de Guido, also from Realejo and residing in Cartago, who was departing for Panamá. Guido was authorized to transport and sell a shipment of mules and four enslaved individuals (Francisco, Bartolo, Benito - criollos, and Antón - angola). Guido could also substitute this power to Toribio de la Vega in Panamá.

Doña Catalina de la Jara, widow of Ignacio Artavia, granted power to Captain Sebastián de Quirós, who was traveling to Guatemala. Quirós was tasked with collecting the inheritance due to Catalina's deceased husband from the executors of her parents-in-law, Pedro de Artavia and Isabel del Valle.

Cristóbal Durán de Chaves, acting on behalf of his owner Gaspar Cascante de Rojas (who was in Nicaragua studying for ordination), sold a 3-year-old enslaved girl named Petrona to Juan de Echavarría Navarro for $190.00. Petrona was inherited by Gaspar from his father, Lieutenant Juan Cascante de Rojas, and is the daughter of Catalina, a mulatto enslaved woman also owned by Gaspar.

Agustín Dabrío de Lopas, a resident of Cartago traveling to Panamá, obligated himself to Juan de Echavarría Navarro for $1083.00, payable in Panamá by the end of July of the current year. Captain Manuel Gómez of Cartago acted as his guarantor.

Juan de Echavarría Navarro granted power to Presbyter Alonso de Sandoval, currently in Panamá, and Captain Juan García de Avila, a resident of Panamá. This power was to receive the $1038.00 owed to him by Agustín Dabrío de Lopas.

locations: San Juan de Herrera de los Naboríos
summary: Juan del Castillo and his wife Felipa de Chinchilla obligated themselves to Depositary Tomás Calvo for $100.00 at 5% interest. They mortgaged a mill on the Río de los Molinos, near the town of San Juan de Herrera de los Naboríos, which Felipa had received as a dowry from her grandmother, Catalina de Palacios.

Cristóbal de Vargas granted power to Cristóbal Carreño and Nicolás Hurtado, residents of Panamá, to charter a frigate. The frigate was to arrive in Caldera by the end of June to transport goods to Panamá.

A dowry letter was issued for Francisco de Morales Meléndez, son of Pedro Díaz de Morales Delencalvo and Catalina de Gallegos Meléndez, a native of Jerez de la Frontera. The dowry, valued at $2427.00, was in favor of his wife, Gregoria López de Chaves, daughter of Alférez Diego Lopez de Ortega and Ana de Chaves.

A dowry letter was issued for José de Guevara y Sandoval, son of José de Sandoval (from Valladolid) and Luisa Maldonado (from Mérida), and a native of Mérida. The dowry, valued at $3175.00, was in favor of his wife, Inés de Ocampo Golfín, daughter of José de Sandoval Ocampo and Isabel de Obando.
A dowry letter was issued for Juan Francisco Michel, son of Francisco Michel, a native of the islands of Ireland.
A dowry of $785.00 was established in favor of Clara de las Alas, the legitimate daughter of Sargento Pedro de las Alas and María de Brenes, from Michel and Catalina Morfa.

A dowry of $623 and 4 reales was established for Juana Rodríguez, the legitimate daughter of Diego de Santiago and Gertrudis de Escobar, from Gregorio de Arrieta, the natural son of Fernando Marín Guerrero and Francisca de Arrieta.

Capitán Pedro Venegas Hurtado de Mendoza, a native of Sevilla, established a dowry or transferred property worth $8565.00 to his wife, Antonia de Ocampo Golfín. The property included a mill near Curriravá, a house and lot in Cartago, flour and biscuits, and a 17-year-old enslaved woman named Lucía.

Capitán Benito Díaz Bravo, a resident of Panamá, granted power of attorney to Luis González de Villalón to collect debts from the estate of Sargento Mayor José de Moya and to continue a lawsuit against the estate of the deceased Adelantado Diego Vázquez de Coronado. González also received a substituted power from Capitán Manuel Noble Clanchas.

Capitanes Benito Díaz Bravo (from Panamá) and Juan Bautista Torres Capelazo (from Cartago) submitted their disputes to the arbitral decision of Licenciado Presbítero Alfonso de Oviedo and Fernando de Salazar.

Alférez Francisco Solano sold a house in Cartago and a half-site of cattle land in the Aserrí valley, along with some cattle, to Capitán Manuel Gómez for $1205.00. The property, inherited from his father Vazco Solano, had a $550.00 lien, and in partial payment, Gómez ceded a $650.00 credit against Cristóbal de Vargas to Solano.

people_involved: Manuel Gómez de Ocón y Trillo
summary: Capitán Manuel Gómez de Ocón y Trillo granted power of attorney to Capitán Cristóbal de Vargas, who was traveling to Panamá, to collect 47 mules. These mules had been sent to Panamá for sale with Domingo Carbonero and were to be collected from Juan Gónzález of Granada or Juan Alvarez of Panamá.
