Cristóbal de Vargas, who was traveling to Panamá, obligated himself to Francisco Solano, also departing for Panamá, for $435.00 lent by Solano. Additionally, Vargas assumed a $665.00 debt that Manuel Gómez owed and had transferred to Solano.

Capitán Jerónimo Leal and his wife María Yañez sold a 28-year-old mulatto enslaved man named Diego to Rodrigo Calderón, Corregidor of Pacacua, for $300.00. The transaction took place at Leal's estancia, Nuestra Señora del Rosario, in the Aserrí valley.

people_involved: Juan Fernández de Salinas y Cerda
summary: General Juan Fernández de Salinas y Cerda, Adelantado of Costa Rica, granted power of attorney to procurators Francisco de Castro and Pedro de San Juan in Guatemala to defend his claim to the Adelantamiento. He asserted his right through his marriage to María de Vega Núñez Coronado, the eldest granddaughter of the deceased Adelantado Diego Vásquez Coronado, who had renounced the title in his favor.

Alférez Diego Ruiz, a native of Panamá, made his will. He was the legitimate son of Juan de Escarraman and Ana Ruiz, married to Juana Jacinta Rodríguez for ten years, and had two daughters, Juana Pérez and María Ruiz.

Doña María de Aguilar, a widow, presented a title for confirmation of her cattle estancia on the Ujarráz road, which Alcalde Juan de Vida Martell approved. The original title, issued by Governor Diego de Artieda Chirinos and countersigned by escribano Francisco Pavon on February 13, 1587, was granted to Pedro Ribero, who had requested the site in the Guarco valley from Capitán Juan Solano seven years prior.

Capitán Juan Bautista Torres Capelazo obligated himself to Alvaro de Nava to deliver 78 tercios of flour, each weighing 156 lbs, to Caldera by the following May, having received 351 pesos for the goods.

A dowry of $554.00 was established for Ana de Loría, the legitimate daughter of Juan de Liñán and Eufrasia de Loría, from Agustín Hernández, the legitimate son of Francisco Hernández and Ana de los Santos.
Beatriz Camelo, widow of Juan Barboza, is mentioned as the owner of something (details incomplete in text).

A house in front of the Convento de San Francisco was mortgaged in 1631 to the Cofradía de la Concepción. Juan de Escobar Guijarro, as Mayordomo, demanded payment from Juan de Senabria Maldonado. After Senabria Maldonado paid the Cofradía, the grantor obligated herself to Juana Moscoso y Figueroa, Senabria's widow, for $123.00 with the same mortgage.

people_involved: Capitán Manuel Gómez de Ocón y Trillo
summary: Capitán Manuel Gómez de Ocón y Trillo obligated himself to Alvaro de Nava for $150.00. This sum was to be paid in flour by the upcoming June.

people_involved: Cristóbal Fernández de Salinas y Cerda
summary: Luis González de Villalón granted power of attorney to Cristóbal Fernández de Salinas y Cerda, Doctor Diego Fernández de Córdova, and Ignacio Fernández de Córdova in Madrid. The purpose was to present his Treasurer of the Santa Cruzada title to the Consejo de Indias for confirmation after a Royal decree dispossessed him, and to collect 100 ducats from his brother Rodrigo González Villalón in Antequera, left by their uncle Domingo de Villalón, plus his mother's legitimate inheritance.

Capitán Francisco Fernández de Miranda, who was leasing a 300-foot cacao plantation on the Matina River with Sargento Mayor Alonso de Bonilla from Juan de Salinas y Cerda, transferred his lease rights to Jerónimo Valerino.

Ambrosio de Brenes obligated himself to Juana Moscoso y Figueroa for a sum related to a house and lot she sold him. This property had a 35-peso charge for the Cofradía de la Concepción, which Gaspar Rodríguez, a former owner, paid. The Cofradía had previously obligated Juana's late husband, Juan de Senabria Maldonado, to pay this sum for unauthorized actions as Mayordomo.
Capitán Juan Bautista Torres Capelazo obligated himself to Gaspar González Guillarte, a resident of Panamá, for $517.144. The payment was due in Panamá by the upcoming February 2nd.

Doña Mayor de Benavides, widow of José de Moya, sold a mulata slave named Margarita to Juan Bautista Torres Capelazo for $300.00. Margarita had originally been purchased by José de Moya from Juan Cascante de Rojas.
María de Ochoa, widow of Luis Gutiérrez, formally requested the approval of her late husband's nuncupative will.

Luis Gutiérrez granted his will in the valley of Aserrí. He was married to María de Ochoa and had two children, Francisco and Inés, the latter married to Antonio de la Vega. His will also mentioned his granddaughter Josefa, daughter of Juan González.

Pablo Sánchez, the legitimate son of Lorenzo Sánchez and Isabel Jiménez, provided a dowry letter for $544.00. This dowry was in favor of his wife, María Rodríguez, who was the legitimate daughter of Manuel Rodríguez and Gertrudis de Alarcón.

Juan de la Estrella, a native of Dunkerque in Flandes and legitimate son of Juan de la Estrella and Isabel Flores, provided a dowry letter for $500 and R. 4. This dowry was in favor of his wife, María de la O., who was the daughter of Magdalena de Acuña.

people_involved: Capitán Don José del Aya y Bolívar
summary: Doña Francisca de Peñaranda sold a lot, inherited from Doña Fabiana de Sojo with a $50.00 charge for the Capellanía of Doña Ana de Medrano, to Capitán Don José del Aya y Bolívar and his wife Doña María de Ortega for $50.00 plus $12.50 in back interest. The lot bordered her house, Don Rodrigo Calderón's lot, and a street leading from the plaza to the Sabana, crossing San Francisco street by Juan López de Ortega's house. Diego Chacón had previously redeemed $50.00 of the original charge.

Doña María de Aguilar Estefanía sold a titled land site called 'La Cruz de Caravaca,' located about a league from Cartago, to Capitán Juan Bautista Torres Capelazo for $150.00. The land was encumbered since 1649 for a Capellanía founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela, with Pe. Marcos Machado as Chaplain. The buyer also added a lot and house in Cartago as guarantee, bordering properties of Melchor de los Reyes, Doña María Cardoso, and Joaquín Vásquez de Coronado.

people_involved: Gobernador Don Juan López de la Flor
summary: Don Juan Ruiz de Velazco, a merchant from Panamá, obligated himself to Gobernador Don Juan López de la Flor for $350.00. As a guarantee, he committed not to dispose of 50 mules he was transporting to Panamá until this debt was fully covered.

people_involved: Gobernador Don Juan López de la Flor
summary: Sebastián Gutiérrez, a trader in Panamá, obligated himself to Gobernador Don Juan López de la Flor for $300.00. This sum was to be paid in Panamá to the Reverend Father Fray Carlos, a Carmelite friar.
An unspecified payment is made for biscuits transported on Captain Benito Díaz Bravo's frigate and for mules sent by land with Alférez Francisco Fernández Barquero.

Gobernador don Juan López de la Flor grants power to Captains Francisco González Carrasco and Jn. Jiménez Salvatierra, Alonso Fernández Tovar, Alférez Juan Hidalgo (who manages Tovar's business in Panamá), and Alférez Francisco Fernández Barquero (from Cartago), to sell mules he is sending to Panamá with Barquero.
Doña Juana Moscoso, a widow, sells a house in the city for $800 to Ayudante Esteban de Torres and his wife, Doña Catalina. The sale involves a responsibility to the Convento de San Francisco.
Doña María Arias Maldonado, wife of Alférez Manuel Pérez (who is currently in Matina as a lookout chief), obligates herself to Antonio Manterola, a merchant in Panamá, for $107.
Don García de Alvarado entrusts his ten-year-old slave, Juan Luis, to Pablo Sánchez, a tailor, for three years to teach him the trade.
Antonio Manterola and Juan Alvarez de Ulate, merchants operating in Panamá and Puerto Belo, obligate themselves to Gobernador don Juan López de la Flor for $50.
Antonio Manterola grants power to Gobernador don Juan López de la Flor to collect $107 owed to him by Alférez Manuel Pérez and his wife, doña María Arias Maldonado.

María Jiménez, widow of Alférez Juan López de Ortega, sells a house in Cartago to Alférez Antonio Machado for $600. The house is bordered by properties belonging to don Gil de Alvarado, Blas de Solís, and the heirs of doña Francisca de Zúñiga.

A dowry letter is issued for Alberto de Rivera y Orozco, son of Agustín de Rivera and doña María de Lara from Sevilla, in favor of his wife Catalina Hernández, daughter of Alférez Francisco Hernández Barquero and Ana de Espinoza, for $1344.

Alférez Francisco López de Ortega sells one-third of a cacao plantation on the Matina River to Depositario Tomás Calvo for $400. This portion was inherited by Ortega from his granddaughter Clara de Solís, and it is incorporated with two other thirds belonging to his granddaughters Agustina and Juana Paulina, who are daughters of Francisco de Solís and Antonia López (Ortega's daughter).

A dowry letter is issued for Ignacio de Loinaz, native of Tolosa, in favor of his wife doña Francisca Calvo, daughter of Depositario Tomás Calvo, for $4026. The dowry includes a house on San Francisco street valued at $700 and a 16-year-old mulatto slave named Juana valued at $500.
The Alcalde places Matías Calvo, a 16-year-old indigenous person from Guicasí, with Bernabé de la Cerda, a Spanish shoemaker, for a three-year apprenticeship.

people_involved: Pe. Guardián del Convento de San Francisco
summary: Doña Francisca del Castillo, widow of Marcos de Chinchilla, revokes a previous chaplaincy foundation of $450 on a mill she sold to Jerónimo Leal and doña María Yáñez. This mill was inherited from her daughter doña Felipa de Chinchilla, who received it as a dowry from her grandmother Catalina de Palacios. Castillo aggregates this foundation to another $500 chaplaincy established by Catalina Palacios on her house, with Pe. Gaspar Cascante de Rojas designated as the first chaplain for both.
Francisco Calderón requests the opening of his father, don Rodrigo Calderón's, will, as his father passed away on this day.
The will of Capitán don Rodrigo Calderón, a native of Donbenito, Extremadura, is recorded.

Details about Francisco Calderón's family are provided, including his parents, his wife Isidora Zambrano, and their children: Juana (deceased), Francisco, Antonia, María, and Sebastiana. Isidora had a previous marriage and a son named Pedro de Colina. His daughter Juana was married to Juan Núñez Suárez, and their assets included houses rented by the Governor and a mill in the valley of Aserrí.
The Alcalde arranged for Isidro, a 12-year-old free mulato orphan, to be apprenticed to Diego Pérez, a tailor, for a period of 5 years.

Licenciado Presbítero José de Lumbides, expressing affection for Juana Núñez de Trujira, natural daughter of María del Pou, donated two slaves, José (4 years) and María Manuela (7 months), to her. Juana, who was 12 years old and had served him since age 5, received this donation to help her marry or enter a convent in Guatemala.
The Alcalde arranged for Santiago, a 12-year-old orphan who had been raised by Ana Rodríguez, to be apprenticed to Sergeant Juan Bautista Bonifasio, a carpenter, for 4 years.

Alférez Mayor Juan de Chaves provided 14 mules to Ayudante Francisco Hernández Barquero for sale in Panamá. Hernández sold the mules and delivered $380 in Castilian clothing, leading Chaves to obligate himself to respond for Hernández in case of any claims related to the sale.
Mateo Sánchez Castañeda, a native of Villigal, provided a dowry letter of $1904 to his fiancée, Ana de Olivares. Their marriage was scheduled for the following day, September 12.

Asisclo López Torralbo, originally from Lucena, Andalucía, made his will. He was married to Micaela Vázquez Coronado, daughter of Alférez Juan Vásquez Coronado and Ana María de Mora Salado, and they had no children.
Jerónimo Valerino ceded the lease of a cacaotal in Matina, which belonged to the heirs of Francisco de Solís and Antonia López, to Sargento Mayor Alonso de Bonilla for a period of two years.

Nicolás Solano and his wife Antonia Sánchez obligated themselves for $100 in favor of Antonia's children from her first marriage to Jerónimo Vanegas. They mortgaged a cattle ranch located in San Francisco, within the city's jurisdiction.

Sebastián de Benavides and his wife Ana María Crespo obligated themselves for $90 in favor of the heirs of Jerónimo Vanegas and Antonia Sánchez. They mortgaged a cattle ranch located in San Francisco, behind the brickyard, within the city's jurisdiction.

Juana de Murillo, daughter of the deceased Alférez Andrés Morillo de Campos and Magdalena de Guido, made her will. She was married to Sebastián de Rivera, with whom she had two sons, Sebastián and Lucas. It was later discovered that her husband had been married in Spain two years into their marriage. Her brothers Juan and Jerónimo Morilo, along with her son Sebastián, were named as executors.

Juan González Romero sold a cacaotal in Matina, containing 400 trees, to Juan de Mesa for $300. Cristóbal de Aguilar was to pay part of the price with 8 gentle mules, and Roque Jacinto de la Fuente was to pay the remaining portion.
Juan de Mesa sold a cacaotal to Cristóbal de Aguilar.
A chácara (farm) located outside the city limits of Cartago, about a league away on royal land, with a house, was sold for $130.00.
Jerónimo Valerino granted power of attorney to his brother, Benito Valerino, and his wife, Francisca de Esquivel.

A dowry letter was issued for Lorenzo de Mora, son of Capitán Pedro de Mora and doña Margarita de Flores, in favor of his wife, María Bernabela, daughter of Francisco Hernández Barquero and Ana de Espinosa, for $1011.00. The document was granted in San Francisco, within Cartago's common lands.

people_involved: Capitán don José de Guevara y Sandoval
summary: Juan de Morales Miranda granted general power of attorney to Juan López de Artiaga, a Procurator of the Audiencia of Guatemala. This power was specifically to bid for the office of Alguacil Mayor and Regidor of Cartago, an office held by Capitán don José de Guevara y Sandoval, valued at $525.00.

Ayudante Esteban de Torres, having frequently gambled and lost money, pledged to pay $50.00 to the Cofradía del Santísimo Sacramento if he gambled again, with increasing penalties for subsequent offenses. He acknowledged the harm caused to his conscience and his family's assets by his gambling.

Sargento Francisco Carrillo and his wife, Ana de Aguilar, pledged $90.00 to the Cofradía de San Nicolás de Tolentino. They mortgaged a property, including a plantain and sugarcane field, a house, and livestock, which previously belonged to the deceased Sebastián de Quirós and his wife, doña Isabel de Acuña.
Lucas Cervantes apprenticed his 16-year-old son, Sebastián de Cervantes, to Agustín de Loría, a master locksmith, for a period of four years.

A dowry letter was issued for Juan Fernández de la Fuente, son of Juan Fernández and María de la O., natives of Villaseca, Spain, in favor of his wife, doña María de Chaves, daughter of Alférez Cristóbal Durán and doña Ana Pereira Cardoso, for $2487.00.

people_involved: Gobernador don Juan López de la Flor
summary: Alférez Juan Alvarez de Ulate sold a 23-year-old Creole black man named Diego Barrantes to Gobernador don Juan López de la Flor for $400.00. Ulate had previously acquired Diego Barrantes from Alférez Nicolás Barrantes.

people_involved: Gobernador don Juan López de la Flor
summary: Juan Ruiz de Velazco, from Tierra Firme, became obligated to Gobernador don Juan López de la Flor for 50 pesos. He also received 27 mules to sell in Panama with the involvement of the Gobernador's agents.

Francisca Jiménez, widow of Ambrosio de Brenes, sold a house and lot in Cartago to her daughter, Francisca de Brenes, for $35.00. The property bordered houses belonging to doña Bárbara de Altamirano and Pedro de Campos Quirós, and Juan Vásquez de Coronado, as well as a street.

people_involved: José de Vega Laso Ponce de León
summary: Pedro de Altamirano, a resident of Panama, granted general power of attorney to José de Vega Laso Ponce de León, also from Panama.

Capitán don Juan de Guzmán, a resident of Panama, became obligated to Esteban de Hoces of Cartago for $300.00, a debt inherited from his father, Capitán don Luis de Guzmán. The agreement was granted in Esparta before Alcalde don Fernando de Luján.
Capitán Benito Díaz Bravo, a resident of Panama and married to doña Ana María González, emancipated his sons, Manuel Díaz Bravo and Benito Díaz Bravo.

people_involved: Licenciado don Francisco de Echavarría Navarro
summary: Juan Vázquez de Coronado issued a codicil, granting power to Licenciado don Francisco de Echavarría Navarro to modify his will.
Basilio de Coto, son of Felipe de Coto and Isabel Alvarez, provided a dowry of $1565.00 to his wife, Agustina de Solís, daughter of the late Francisco Solís and Antonia Lopez.

Alférez Tomás Calvo, a general depositary and son of Alférez Miguel Calvo and Mariana de Chinchilla (formerly of Trujillo, Honduras), made his will. He was married to doña Eugenia Abarca, daughter of don Gaspar Abarca and doña Magdalena de Chaves, and they had eight children. The will also detailed the marriages of some of his children and mentioned his granddaughter Eugenia Gertrudis and brother-in-law Alonso de Bonilla.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco Fernández de Miranda
summary: Capitán don Francisco Fernández de Miranda provided a dowry of $5253.00, including $2000.00 in cash, to his wife, doña Magdalena Calvo Abarca. Magdalena was the legitimate daughter of Depositario Tomás Calvo and doña Eugenia Abarca.

Tomás Calvo added a codicil to his will, declaring Mariana Calvo as his natural daughter and bequeathing her 100 cattle and 100 mares. He also noted that his nephew, Gaspar Arias, owed him $25.00 for his mother's burial expenses.

The Alcalde arranged an apprenticeship for Francisco, a 12-year-old free mulatto and son of Paula, a free black woman. Francisco was apprenticed to Nicolás de Arce, a free mulatto carpenter, for six years.

Doña Isidora Zambrano, widow of don Rodrigo Calderón, granted power of attorney to her son, don Pedro de Colina. This power authorized him to apprehend and secure her mulatto slave, Diego Leal, in Granada, Nicaragua, and subsequently sell him. The document was granted at the mill of Capitán don Rodrigo Calderón in the valley of Aserrí.

Salvador de Acuña, who inherited a $1150.00 debt to the Cofradía del Santísimo Sacramento from his father, Alférez Juan de Acuña, requested that Felipe and Basilio de Coto and their wives be admitted as new debtors. They offered a cacao plantation in Matina and livestock as collateral. The Cofradía's deputies accepted, releasing Acuña from the debt.

Salvador de Acuña sold a large cattle site in the valley of Cartago for $1170.00 to Felipe de Coto and Basilio de Coto. The land, previously owned by his father Juan de Acuña and titled by Artieda Chirinos, had a $150.00 mortgage to the Cofradía del Santísimo Sacramento. The buyers and their wives, Isabel Vázquez de Oviedo and Agustina de Solís, assumed the mortgage and offered a cacao plantation in Matina and livestock as additional collateral, while Acuña reserved a portion for his dwelling.

Francisco López de Ortega, natural son of the late Juan López de Ortega and Juana Pavón, made his will. He was married twice, first to María Pérez, with whom he had Ana de López, Antonia de López, and Melchor de los Reyes. His second marriage was to Ana María, with whom he had a daughter named Margarita. The will also mentions his granddaughter Margarita (daughter of Ana López), his deceased granddaughter Clara de Solís, and other grandchildren Agustina and Juana Paulina Solís.

Juana de Llanos made a codicil, stating that the house and livestock at Hato de la Concepción belonged to her sons, Francisco and Pedro Solano. She specified that they had built, manufactured, and purchased these assets at their own expense.

people_involved: Ayudante don José de Vega Laso Ponce de León
summary: Ayudante don José de Vega Laso Ponce de León from Panamá granted power of attorney to Antonio Machado, a resident of Cartago, and Juan Bautista Fernández, a resident of Esparza.

Jerónima de Brenes, widow of Lucas González, sold a plot of land in Cartago for $20.00 to Juan Bautista Torres Capelazo. The plot bordered the buyer's house, a plot belonging to María de Barboza, and was across a street from doña María de Cardoso's house.

locations: ermita de Nuestra Señora de los Angeles
summary: In 1660, the Cabildo, under Alcalde Juan de Echavarría Navarro, granted a solar to Jerónima de Brenes. This solar was located near the ermita de Nuestra Señora de los Angeles and adjacent to the former house of Margarita de Flores.
On October 28, a dowry letter was issued for Juan de Aguilar and Eugenia Vásquez, legitimate daughter of Luis Vásquez and María de Sojo. The dowry amounted to $402.00.

On October 10, Juan de Echavarría Navarro, acting as the former Alcalde from 1660, issued a certification. This document confirmed that the Cabildo had granted a solar to Jerónima de Brenes in 1660, located near the ermita de Nuestra Señora de los Angeles and Margarita de Flores' former house.

On November 25, a dowry letter was issued for Andrés de Valverde, a native of Ecija and legitimate son of Francisco de Valverde and María de Carmona. The dowry was in favor of his wife, Ana de Vílchez y Figueroa, legitimate daughter of Mateo de Sanabria and Francisca de Brenes, and amounted to $1175.00.

On December 4, Sargento Francisco Carrillo sold two cacao plantations in Matina to Jerónimo Valerino for $500.00. One plantation had a thousand trees already in production, while the other had nine hundred trees not yet bearing fruit.

On October 14, Teniente Pedro de Campos Quirós obligated himself to Capitán Juan Bautista Torres Capelazo for $213.4 reales. This amount represented the balance of their accounts, which Quirós agreed to pay with two mules and wheat.

On November 2, Mateo de Madrigal and Juan de la Cruz agreed to settle a lawsuit concerning the division of a cacao plantation and other assets. They established the terms for their separation of these properties.
On November 2, Antonio de Acosta, a Greek national and creditor of Mateo de Madrigal, granted Madrigal an extension for the payment of his debt.

On November 20, Alférez Fernando de Córdova, legitimate son of Capitán Pedro de Córdova and Catalina de Chaves, made his testament. He named his sister Antonia as his heir and mentioned his brother-in-law Miguel Ortiz de Chaves, his disabled brother Jerónimo de Córdoba, and his natural sister Nicolasa.
On November 21, Fernando de Córdova issued a codicil, which is an amendment or supplement to his will made the previous day.
Juan de la Cruz, natural son of the deceased Cristóbal de Madrigal and María de Fonseca, made his testament. The document is noted as incomplete.

On December 16, Clara de las Alas, widow and heir of Juan Francisco Michel, obligated herself to Capitán Juan de Echavarría Navarro for $500.00, payable by next June. She mortgaged her slave Lucía and Lucía's two daughters as collateral.

On February 3, Capitán Pedro Ortiz de Mendoza, a resident of Guatemala, obligated himself to Presbítero Domingo de Echavarría, Cura and Vicario of the city, for $500.00. He committed to paying this sum in Panamá by the end of June to Capitán García de Alvarado or Matías González Camino.

On February 14, Matías González Camino obligated himself to Gobernador Juan López de la Flor for $3000.00. He committed to paying this sum in Panamá to Capitán Francisco González Carrasco, with Ayudante Juan Mateos Ramírez, a resident of Panamá, acting as guarantor.

On February 20, Alférez Juan Bta. Fernández, a resident of Esparza, acting for himself and as attorney for Francisco Daniel and his wife Ana de Ortuño, obligated himself to Gobernador Juan López de la Flor for 1200 pesos. This obligation, secured by their ship 'Vuestra Señora de la Merced' which was preparing for a voyage to Panamá, was due by June of that year and was later cancelled. The power of attorney was granted in Esparza on December 6, 1670, before Escribano José Núñez de Figueroa.

On April 7, Bernardo Cortés, a resident of Panamá traveling to that city with his mules, obligated himself to Matías González Camino for $533.00. He agreed to pay this amount in Panamá by April 30 to García de Alvarado.

Doña Mayor de Benavides Solano, widow of Sargento Mayor José de Moya, sold a 16-year-old enslaved Black man named Francisco to Licenciado don Domingo de Echavarría, the city's priest. Francisco had previously belonged to Matías Jacinto, and the sale was for $200.
Cura Domingo de Echavarría declared that the previous purchase of the enslaved man, Francisco, was made on behalf of Capn. Pedro Ortiz de Mendoza, a resident of Guatemala.

Sargento Mor. Alonso de Bonilla and his wife, Juana Benita Calvo, committed to pay $150 to the Chaplaincy founded by Vasco Solano, for which Cura Domingo de Echavarría served as patron and chaplain. They mortgaged a cacao plantation with 1000 trees in La Reventazón.

Doña María Ramiro, widow of don José de Sandoval Ocampo, committed to pay $50 to the Chaplaincy of the Blessed Souls, located in the Convento de San Francisco. She mortgaged a large cattle ranch in Río Grande, including 450 cattle, 200 mares, a breeding donkey, and a colt, along with a house, sugar mill, and cane fields at another location.

Capn. Franco. Fernández de Miranda, a native of Utrera, Spain, made his will. He was the legitimate son of the deceased Domingo González Fernández and Doña Dominga de Miranda, and was married to Doña Magdalena Calvo Abarca, legitimate daughter of Tomás Calvo and Doña Eugenia Abarca. He had no children.

Don José Pérez de Muro granted power of attorney to don García de Alvarado and Antonio Machado, who were traveling to Panamá, to collect 94 petacas of biscuits and two zurrones of tobacco from the Royal Treasury officials. He also authorized them to investigate the disappearance of his servant, Juan de Mora, an Indigenous person from the province, who vanished with a desk containing money, jewels, and important documents while Pérez de Muro was leaving for a campaign, presumed to have been robbed and killed.

people_involved: Capn. José del Aya y Bolivar
summary: Capn. José del Aya y Bolivar and his wife, doña María de Ortega, committed to pay $100 to the estate of Jerónimo Murillo. They mortgaged a sugar mill with cane fields, a house, and an oven on two caballerias of land in the Aserrí valley, bordering the lands of Cristobal Durán de Chaves, which they had purchased at an auction from the estate of Alférez Mayor Juan de Chaves.

people_involved: Capn. Juan Bta. de Tarres Capelazo
summary: Capn. Juan Bta. de Tarres Capelazo, who purchased 16 mules at $25 each from the auction of Jerónimo Murillo's estate, named Tomás Calvo, the general depositary, and Jerónimo Valerino as his guarantors.

Francisco Hernández Barquero and his wife, Ana de Espinosa, committed to pay $240 to the estate of Jerónimo Murillo, who was imprisoned due to mental illness. They mortgaged a country estate in the city's valley, a house in Cartago near the hermitage of La Soledad bordering Doña Isabel de Flores's property, and an enslaved girl named Florencia, about 8 years old.

people_involved: Sarg. Mor. Juan García de Avila
summary: Sarg. Mor. Juan García de Avila, a resident of Panamá, granted power of attorney to Jerónimo Sánchez de Angulo, don Pedro de Vergara, and Fco. Gómez Vázquez, a resident of the Villa de los Santos.

people_involved: Pe. don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Doña Francisca del Castillo, legitimate daughter of the deceased Juan Gómez Rico and Doña María de Cardoso, made her will. She founded a chaplaincy for a sung mass with the value of an enslaved person, naming her cousin, Padre Durán de Chaves (son of Cristobal Durán de Chaves and Doña Ana Cardoso), as chaplain, and her nephew, Pe. don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, until her cousin was ordained. Her son, don Gaspar de Chinchilla, was named patron. She was the widow of Marcos de Chinchilla and left bequests to Catalina de Palacios (her husband's natural daughter), Doña Micaela Durán (her niece), Pe. Fr. Juan Pereira, and Domingo de Chinchilla (her husband's son). She mentioned her deceased daughter Doña Felipa, and her sister Doña Isabel Cardoso and cousin Doña María Yáñez.
Juana Paulina Solís, daughter of Francisco de Solís and Antonia Pérez, made her will. She named her siblings and Doña Juana Vida Martell as heirs and mandated the founding of a chaplaincy.

Alférez Mayor Juan de Chaves, son of deceased Cristóbal de Chaves and María de Alfaro, made his will in the valley of Aserrí. He owed money to Leonor, left 200 pesos to the San Francisco convent, and divided his Pacacua estate between his daughters María and Gregoria. He also made provisions for masses for Juana María, left money to Padre fray Juan Pereira for a trip to Panamá, and mandated a chaplaincy with the remainder of his assets, noting he was blind and unable to sign.
Alonso de Bonilla, Alcalde Ordinario, confirmed seeing the body of Juan de Chaves at Juan de Vida Martell's house. He ordered an inventory and summoned the executors for the estate of Juan de Chaves.

Don José de Escalante Paniagua, a native of Jerena, Extremadura, and son of Don Pedro del Villar and Doña Juana de Escalante Paniagua, provided a dowry of 1765 pesos and 500 pesos in arras to his wife, Doña Manuela de Vida Martell. Manuela was the daughter of Captain and Sergeant Major Juan de Vida Martell and Doña Juana de Ortega.

A fragment of Félix de Coto's will named his son Juan Bautista and a posthumous child from his daughter-in-law (Juan Bautista's widow) as heirs. He appointed his wife as the guardian for both children.

Juan Gómez de Bonilla, widower of Juana de Aguilar, made his will in Rincón de Purires. He named his children: Franco. Gómez (deceased), Clara (deceased), Fca. de la Fe, Juan (deceased), Ana Josefa, and Catalina Cecilia. Fca. and Josefa were married, with Fca. married to Domingo Jiménez Brenes.
Doña Juana Moscoso, widow of Don Juan Senabria Maldonado, sold a ten-month-old mulata slave named Juana, daughter of her other mulata slave María, to Licenciado Don Miguel Calvo for 80 pesos.
Alférez Alonso de Quesada, a native of Cartago and son of Diego de Quesada and Francisca Gutiérrez de Sibaja, made his will.

Governor Don Juan López de la Flor added a codicil to his will. He mentioned his children Elena and Juan Anselmo in Flandes, and Pedro José and Carlos in 'this city.' He also mentioned his deceased wife Margarita Vatecant and his mother-in-law Margarita de Lebron in Tournay, and left 100 pesos to the San Francisco convent for the main altar's altarpiece.

Alférez Bartolomé Calderón and his wife Catalina de Palacios obligated themselves for $240.00 to a Capellanía founded by Alférez Tomás Calvo, with his son Miguel Calvo as the first chaplain. They mortgaged a cacao plantation with 1000 trees located on the Matina riverbank.
Sergeant Juan González granted power of attorney to Alférez Antonio Machado to collect one hundred pesos from Jerónimo Valerino.
Alcalde Alonso de Bonilla arranged an apprenticeship for Diego de Sojo, son of Alonso de Sojo and Ana de Arrieta, with Pedro de Alvarado, a weaver, for a period of two years.

Ignacio de Artavia, son of Ignacio de Artavia and Doña Catalina dela Jara, issued a dowry letter for $782.00 in favor of his wife, Ana de Murillo, daughter of Andrés Murillo and Magdalena de Guido. Juan Murillo de Campos was to deliver $200.00 of this amount.

Procurador Licenciado José de Lumbides sold a 28-year-old mulatto slave named Timoteo to Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro for $300.00. Lumbides had previously purchased Timoteo from Bartolomé Sánchez, who is the seller's uncle.
The Alcalde, Alonso de Bonilla, arranged an apprenticeship for Antonio, a 16-year-old mulatto orphan (fatherless), with Andrés Gómez, a blacksmith, for four years.
The Alcalde, Alonso de Bonilla, arranged an apprenticeship for Nicolás Figueroa, 16 years old and son of Adriano de Figueroa, with Andrés Gómez, a blacksmith, for four years.

The Alcalde, Alonso de Bonilla, arranged an apprenticeship for Bernabé de Sandoval, an orphan about 12 years old from the town of Co and son of Ambrosio Sánchez, with his uncle Ventura Sánchez, a master shoemaker, for four years to learn the trade.
The Alcalde, Alonso de Bonilla, arranged an apprenticeship for Marcos Calvo, an orphan about 12 years old and son of Juan Calvo, with his brother Francisco Calvo, a shoemaker, for four years.
The Alcalde, Alonso de Bonilla, arranged an apprenticeship for Andrés Sánchez, an orphan 12 years old and son of Ambrosio Sánchez, with his uncle Ventura Sánchez, a shoemaker, for four years.
The Alcalde, Alonso de Bonilla, arranged an apprenticeship for Valerio, an orphan 12 years old, with Francisco Rodríguez, a shoemaker, for four years.

The Governor Juan López de la Flor, Alcalde Alonso de Bonilla, Provincial Juan de Echavarría Navarro, Treasurer Fernando de Salazar, and Depositario Tomás Calvo, all perpetual regidores of Cartago, granted power of attorney to Alférez Antonio Machado, who was departing for Guatemala. This power allowed him to represent them in matters concerning the well-being and growth of the province and its residents.

Juan de Echavarría Navarro and José de Alvarado, representing their wives Ana and Petronila de Retes, along with María de Retes (widow of Francisco Ramiro) and Jerónima de Retes (acting for her absent husband Luis de Fonseca), all daughters of the late Captain Jerónimo de Retes, granted power of attorney to procurators José de Aguilar and Juan López de Astiaga in Guatemala. This was for a pending case to revoke a sentence by Captain Juan de Balcázar y Sotomayor during the residencia of Captain Retes as Corregidor of Quepo, and to collect $900.00.

Captain García de Alvarado and his wife Juana de Salazar obligated themselves for $100.00 at 5% interest to the Confraternity of the Most Holy Sacrament, founded in the parish church of Cartago. They mortgaged a stone and lime house, adjacent to Matías González Camino's house, which they received as part of a dowry from Fernando de Salazar, Juana's father. This obligation was cancelled on October 21, 1676.

Captain García de Alvarado and his wife Juana de Salazar obligated themselves for $1000.00 at 5% interest to the Capellanía founded by Alférez Vasco Solano, with Cura Domingo de Echavarría as its patron and chaplain. They mortgaged the same house mentioned in the previous obligation. This obligation was cancelled on October 21, 1676.

Juana de Aguilar, daughter of the late Francisco Carrillo and Ana de Aguilar, and widow of Juan Gómez de Bonilla, made her will. Her deceased children were Francisco, Juana, and Clara, while her living children were Francisca de la Fé, Ana Josefa, and Catalina Cecilia (the first and third being married). Her son-in-law was Domingo Jiménez Brenes.

Margarita Vatecant, a native of Tournay in Flanders and daughter of the late Gabriel Vatecant and Doña Margarita Lebron, granted power to her husband, Don Juan López de la Flor (Governor of the province), to make her will. Her executors were Juan de Vida Martell and Tomás Calvo, and her heirs were her children Doña María Elena, Don Pedro José, Don Juan Anselmo, and Don Carlos López.

people_involved: Don Juan López de la Flor
summary: Gobernador Don Juan López de la Flor granted general power for lawsuits to Captains José Agustín de Estrada and Don José de Aguilar, both residents of Guatemala.

A dowry letter was issued for Juan de Alfaro, a native of Cartago, and his wife Juana Sánchez de Oviedo. Juan's father-in-law, Franc? de Oviedo, committed to supporting the couple for two years, providing food, drink, and clean clothes without charge.

Alférez Juan Bta. Fernández, a resident of Esparza, obligated himself to Licdo. Don Domingo de Echavarría, the priest of Cartago, for $247.00. This money was intended to complete a frigate that Fernández had in the shipyard.
Juan Francisco Michel, a native of Hibernia, Ireland, made his will. He was married to Clara de las Alas and had no children, and declared 20 fanegas of wheat in his house in the Valle de Barba.

Juan de Mesa and his wife Andrea Rodríguez obligated themselves for $100.00 to the children of the deceased Fe? Solís and Antonia López, whose tutor was Jerónimo Valerino. They mortgaged a cacao plantation with 800 trees in Matina.

people_involved: Capn. Manuel Gómez de Ocón y Trillo
summary: Captain Manuel Gómez de Ocón y Trillo obligated himself to María Guerrero for $300.00. This obligation was later cancelled.
Alcalde Alonso de Bonilla arranged for Nicolás Calvo, an indigenous person from Co, to be placed with José Falcon, a master carpenter, for a period of four years.

Alférez Juan de Gamboa obligated himself to Captain Don Deodoro de Castro and Tomás Pereyra, both residents of Cartago, for $101.00. This sum was owed to Juan Francisco Valenzuela, a resident of Granada, and was to be paid within two months or sooner if Captain José de Ollo's frigate arrived at the port of Caldera.

Captain José France? del Ollo, owner and master of the frigate Jesús María, currently docked in Caldera, chartered his frigate to Don José Pérez de Muro, the ordinary mayor of Cartago, for September of this year. The purpose was to transport flour and biscuits to Panamá.

Clara de las Alas, widow and heir of Juan Francisco Michel, obligated herself to Captain Juan Bautista Torres Capelaso for $247.00. This amount was the remaining balance of a larger sum that Torres Capelaso had lent to Michel for a trip to Nicaragua and Nicoya to buy mules. This obligation was later cancelled.

Doña Juana Calvo, daughter of Alférez Tomás Calvo and Doña Eugenia de Abarca, made her will. She was married to Alférez Esteban de Oses Navarro and had four children: Josefa, Sebastián, Félix, and Fermín.

people_involved: Señor Cura Don Domingo de Echavarría
summary: Ayudante Franc? Hernández Barquero, Mayor of the Santa Hermandad, obligated himself to Señor Cura Don Domingo de Echavarría for $260.00. This sum was to be paid next January or sooner if Barquero returned from Nicaragua. This obligation was later cancelled.

Sergeant Salvador de Acuña stated that he inherited a cattle site from his father, Alférez Juan de Acuña, with a title from Don Diego de Artieda Chirinos. To discharge encumbrances, he sold part of it to Felipe de Coto and his son Basilio de Coto, reserving a portion. He now sells this reserved portion to Ignacio de Loinaz, a resident of Cartago, for 50 pesos.

Juana de la Portilla, widow of Agustín Guerrero, donated her 15-year-old mulatto slave, Leonor (daughter of her black slave Mónica), to her granddaughter Juana de la Portilla Solano. Leonor had been previously bequeathed in a will to the children of Juan Solano.
José de Vargas Machuca obligated himself to Don José Pérez de Muro for $360.00, to be paid in Panamá within one year.

people_involved: Capn. Don José de Guevara y Sandoval
summary: Doña María Ramiro, widow of Don José de Sandoval, along with other parties, agreed that she would take all the deceased's assets and assume all debts, as the estate was insufficient to cover her dowry. Doña María also committed to paying Don Sebastián, son of Don José's first wife, his maternal inheritance.

Doña Micaela Vázquez Coronado, widow of Asisclo López Torralbo, sold a cattle ranch with a house and corrals in the common lands of Cartago to Antonio de Acosta and his wife Juana de la Cruz Fonseca for $200.00. She had acquired this property from José de Villalobos Jara.
A donation was made to the Chaplaincy that Alférez Vasco Solano had founded. The details of the donation or the recipient are not specified beyond the Chaplaincy itself.
Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro acted as a guarantor for Doña María Ramiro to ensure the payment of a debt she owed to Don Sebastián de Ocampo Golfín, as stipulated in a transaction deed.

The Alcalde arranged an apprenticeship for Cristóbal de Chinchilla, son of Nicolás de Chinchilla, with Andrés Méndez, a blacksmith, for a period of five years. However, this agreement was ultimately not finalized.

people_involved: Gobernador Don Juan López de la Flor
Doña Ana del Cubillo y Sojo
summary: Alférez Tomás Calvo and his wife Doña Eugenia de Abarca obligated themselves to Gobernador Don Juan López de la Flor for $1194.00. This sum was from a draft against the Royal Treasury of León, intended to pay Fernando de Cuellar Centeno for a debt originally owed by the deceased Capitán Francisco de Matos, and subsequently by Capitán Don Gaspar Faustino Calvo and Doña Ana del Cubillo y Sojo.
The Alcalde arranged an apprenticeship for Alonso, an apprentice shoemaker, with Francisco Rodríguez, a master of the trade, for two years.
The Alcalde arranged an apprenticeship for Nicolás de Figueroa, 16 years old and son of Adriano de Figueroa, with Andrés Gómez, a blacksmith, for four years.
The Alcalde arranged an apprenticeship for Antonio, a 16-year-old mulato, with Andrés Gómez, a blacksmith, for four years.

people_involved: Licenciado Don Francisco de Ocampo Figueroa
summary: Antonio de Acosta Arévalo sold a cattle ranch near the Toyogres river to Doña Jerónima de Abarca for $200.00, a property he had acquired from Doña Micaela Vázquez de Coronado. Doña Jerónima then mortgaged a house near the San Francisco convent to secure a Chaplaincy, for which Licenciado Don Francisco de Ocampo Figueroa served as patron and chaplain.

Doña Juana de Ortega, a widow, obligated herself to the minor children of the deceased Sargento Francisco Carrillo and Ana de Aguilar for $121.00. This amount represented a portion of the $221.00 for which she had acquired their property, including a site, houses, cattle, and horses. Fco. Ramírez and Domingo López de Ortega served as guarantors for this obligation.

people_involved: Gobernador Don Juan López de la Flor
Capitán Don Antonio de Sequeira y Valdés
summary: Nicolás de Céspedes, acting on behalf of María Bella, a widow from León, sold an enslaved mulato named Alonso, 20 years old and imprisoned, to Gobernador Don Juan López de la Flor for $400.00. The power of attorney for this sale was originally granted by María Bella in León on February 5, 1672, to José Núñez de Figueroa, an escribano from Esparza, and later substituted to Céspedes in Esparza on May 27, before Capitán Marcos de Ledezma.

Domingo Otárola, Mayordomo of the Cofradía de la Concepción, sold two plots of land to Isabel Carrillo. These plots, previously sold to Sargento Francisco Carrillo and Ana de Aguilar, were returned by their succession and are located next to the Ermita de la Soledad, sold for $20.00 with a 5% annuity.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don José de Sandoval Ocampo
Licenciado Don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Doña Juana de Figueroa Moscoso, widow of Capitán Juan de Senabria, added a codicil to her will. She designated Don José de Sandoval Ocampo, legitimate son of her deceased brother Sargento Mayor Don José de Sandoval Ocampo, as the chaplain for her established Chaplaincy. Licenciado Don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas was appointed to serve as interim chaplain until Don José de Sandoval Ocampo could be ordained.

Capitán Pedro Lorenzo Venegas, the senior Alcalde Ordinario, arranged an apprenticeship for Pedro Hernández, aged 10-12 and son of the deceased Juan Alonso Hernández, with Tomás Meléndez, a carpenter, for four years.

people_involved: Doña Catalina de Carvajal y Castillera
Sargento Mayor Don José de Sandoval Ocampo
summary: Capitán Alonso Arias Romero, a native of Carmona, Spain, and legitimate son of Don Antonio Arias Romero and Doña Catalina de Carvajal y Castillera, provided a dowry letter for his wife, Doña Mariana de Ocampo Golfín. Doña Mariana was the legitimate daughter of the deceased Sargento Mayor Don José de Sandoval Ocampo and Doña María Ramiro Corajo. The dowry amounted to $3364.00, including $1000.00 in earnest money, a house, and a site on the Ciruelas river.

Doña María de Chaves Alfaro, widow of Juan de Astúa (who died en route to Panama), initially granted power of attorney to Don Francisco Hita and Don José Pérez de Luna to sell 25 mules her husband was transporting. She later transferred this power to Don García de Alvarado and José de Vargas Machuca, who were residing in Panama.

Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro granted power of attorney to Don García de Alvarado and Don Matías González Camino, who were in Panama, to sell an enslaved mulato named Cristobal, 26 years old. Echavarría Navarro had purchased Cristobal from the representative of Doña Ana Pereira de Castro, a resident of Mompós.

Doña Ana de Arias, a native of Marbella, Spain, and legitimate daughter of the deceased Martín Las Fuentes and Antonia González, made her will. She was the widow of Francisco Rodríguez Tarifa, had no children, and had been married in Spain and endowed in this location by Don Manuel Pérez and Doña María Arias Maldonado.

María de Guido, natural daughter of the late Pedro de las Alas and Juana Sánchez, and widow of Alférez Luis Machado, made her will. She named her children Agustín, Fernando, Padre Marcos, doña Beatriz, Antonio, and Francisco, and mentioned her sister Ana de las Alas. Her daughter doña Beatriz was married to Ayudante Juan de Morales Miranda.

people_involved: doña Juana de Vera y Sotomayor
Capn. y S. Mor. Juan de Vida Martel
summary: Don Pedro de Alvarado, legitimate son of Alférez don Gil de Alvarado and doña Juana de Vera y Sotomayor, granted a dowry to his wife doña Catalina de Vida Martell. Doña Catalina is the legitimate daughter of the late Captain and Sargento Mayor Juan de Vida Martel and doña Juana de Ortega. The dowry included $1758, with 500 cacao trees in Bonilla, and arras of $500.
José María Laguna and his wife doña Catalina de Moya entered into an obligation in favor of some minors. The first part of this document is missing.

people_involved: Don Pedro José López de la Flor
Gobernador don Juan López de la Flor
summary: Don Pedro José López de la Flor, a native of Tournay in Flanders and legitimate son of Gobernador don Juan López de la Flor and the late doña Margarita Vaticant, granted a dowry to his wife doña Ambrosia de Echavarría Navarro. Doña Ambrosia is the legitimate daughter of don Juan de Echavarría Navarro and doña Ana de Retes. The marriage was scheduled for October 11th, and the dowry included $3338, with two slaves and cash to be paid by his father-in-law upon the arrival of the galleon fleet from Peru. A marginal note from April 29, 1676, acknowledges receipt of the $1000 paid by don José Pérez de Muro, executor of don Juan.

Doña Gregoria López de Ortega, widow of Francisco Morales Meléndez, sold a house she and her late husband bought from Catalina de Rueda to don José Escalante Paniagua and his wife doña Manuela de Vida Martel. Doña Gregoria was a debtor of one hundred pesos to the Cofradía de la Concepción, with the house mortgaged, and the buyers assumed the debt. The house bordered doña Catalina de Chaves's house and the plaza.
Alférez don Francisco Enciso Hita made a codicil, naming his sister doña Gertrudis de Enciso Hita and her husband Alférez Cristobal Guerrero as his executors.

people_involved: Gobernador don Juan López de la Flor
summary: Pro. Lic. José de Lumbides sold his six-year-old mulato slave named José, who was born in his house to another of his slaves, to Gobernador don Juan López de la Flor for $200.

Jerónimo Valerino and his wife Francisca de Esquivel entered into an obligation for $200 in favor of the Capellanía founded by Alférez Antonio Machado, of which Licdo. Pro. Marcos Machado is patron and chaplain. They mortgaged a house in the city and a cacao plantation of 5000 trees on the Matina riverbank. The house bordered doña Juana de Ortega's solar, Alférez Gaspar Arias's house, and doña Isabel Flores's house.

people_involved: Cura don Domingo de Echavarría Navarro
Licdo. don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Alférez Manuel Pérez and his wife doña María Arias Maldonado entered into an obligation for $100 in favor of the Capellanía founded by Diego Quintero del Castillo and Francisca Hernández, former residents of Esparza. They mortgaged their house in the city, which bordered doña María de Sandoval's house (where Cura don Domingo de Echavarría Navarro lives) and Licdo. don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín's house. The Cura is the patron and chaplain, and these $100 were redeemed by doña Margarita de Betancur, widow of Alférez Diego López de Santana, residents of Esparza.

people_involved: Capn. Manuel Gómez de Ocón y Trillo
summary: Captain Manuel Gómez de Ocón y Trillo, a resident of Esparza and legitimate son of Pedro Gómez de Sandoval and Catalina de Ocón (former residents of Figuera de Vargas, Spain), made his will. He left 25 pesos to Sebastián de Benavides. He married Juana de Mora around 1649, who died in 1660 and was the widow of Pedro de Estanda. With Juana, he had children José, Francisco (22 years old), Manuel (deceased), and Sebastián (15 years old). He married a second time to Isabel Alvarez.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Juan de Balcazar y Sotomayor
summary: Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro (representing his wife doña Ana de Retes), don José Alvarado (representing his wife doña Petronila de Retes), doña María de Retes (widow of Captain don Francisco Ramiro), and doña Jerónima de Retes, all legitimate daughters and heirs of the late Captain Jerónimo de Retes and doña Maria Vázquez de Caronado, granted power of attorney to Diego de Escobar and Nicolás de Maeda, residents of Santiago de Guatemala. This was to recover a 1000-peso fine imposed on Jerónimo de Retes during his residency as Corregidor and Captain of War of San Bernardino de Quepo, which was taken by Sargento Mayor don Juan de Balcazar y Sotomayor. The Audiencia of Guatemala ordered a new residency to be taken by Gobernador don Juan de Obregón or his commissioner, which was done by Captain Francisco Fernández.

people_involved: Capn. Lorenzo de la Madriz Paniagua
Gobernador don Juan López de la Flor
summary: Don José de Escalante Paniagua reported that Captain Lorenzo de la Madriz Paniagua, a resident of Realejo, had a Creole slave named Salvador escape. Salvador was found in a place called El Salto within this jurisdiction and was delivered as a fugitive to Gobernador don Juan López de la Flor, who brought him to the city.

A black slave, belonging to Don Lorenzo, stole $209 from the Gobernador's house after the Gobernador had provided him with clothes worth $28. The slave was jailed, and an agreement was reached for his return to Don Lorenzo, who would pay the Gobernador $237. Don Lorenzo's attorney committed to covering this sum in El Realejo upon the slave's delivery.

Diego de Chaves obligated himself to the Cofradía de Ntra. Sra. de la Soledad for $100, the price of 50 head of cattle. He mortgaged a cattle site named San Nicolás de Tolentino, located on the road to Pacacua.
Antonio de Acosta Arévalo obligated himself to the Cofradía de Ntra. Sra. de la Soledad for $50 at a 5% interest rate. He mortgaged his cacao plantation situated on the banks of the Matina River.

Captain Francisco Fernández Miranda and his wife Doña Magdalena Calvo obligated themselves to the heirs of Sergeant Francisco Carrillo for $200. This sum was for a cacao plantation of 500 new trees from the succession, located on the banks of the Reventazón River, which Captain Fernández Miranda had auctioned.

A dowry letter was issued for Captain Antonio Vázquez Coronado, son of the late Alférez Juan Vázquez de Coronado and María de Madrigal, in favor of his wife Doña Gertrudis Hidalgo y Alfaro, daughter of Lieutenant Juan Hidalgo and the late Doña María de Alfaro. The dowry amounted to $754, with arras of $500.

Captain Don García de Alvarado granted power of attorney to Andrés de Castro and José de Aguilar, attorneys of the Real Audiencia of Guatemala, to bid for the office of Alférez Mayor and perpetual Regidor of 'this city' for $300, payable over three years.

people_involved: Reverend Licentiate Don Domingo de Echavarría Navarro
summary: Reverend Licentiate Don Domingo de Echavarría Navarro, the parish priest, sold his mulatto slave named Beatriz, approximately 22 years old, to Bernardo Cortés for $300. Beatriz had previously been purchased from Captain Fernando Luján, a resident of Esparza.

Captain Don Pedro Lorenzo Venegas obligated himself to the Convent of San Francisco for an unspecified sum (implied $500) at 5% annual interest, delivered by Syndic Captain Bartolomé Muñoz Hidalgo. He mortgaged his house in the city, adjacent to Licentiate Don Francisco de Ocampo's, and another property in the Curriravá valley, which included a house, mill, sugarcane field, sugar mill, and land. The funds originated from a chaplaincy founded by Luisa Hernández and offered by Assistant Esteban de Torres.

people_involved: Sergeant Major Don José de Moya
summary: A dowry letter was issued for Don Antonio de Moya, son of the late Sergeant Major Don José de Moya and Doña Mayor de Benavides, in favor of his wife Doña Isabel de Alvarado, daughter of Captain Don José de Alvarado and Doña Petronila de Retes. The dowry was $2183, with arras of $500, for a marriage scheduled for the following day.

Captain Francisco Fernández de Miranda and his wife Doña Magdalena Calvo obligated themselves to the heirs of Sergeant Francisco Carrillo for $200, for a cacao plantation of 560 new trees on the La Reventazón river that Fernández de Miranda had auctioned. They also mortgaged their house in the city on the street leading to San Francisco. This entry is noted as a testimony of a previous deed (folio 34).
A dowry letter was issued in favor of Isabel Alvarez, whose husband's name was not legible. The dowry amounted to $1018, with arras of $1000.

people_involved: Gobernador Don Juan López de la Flor
summary: Captain Don García de Alvarado and Don Matías González Camino obligated themselves to Gobernador Don Juan López de la Flor for $4000, payable within one year in Portobelo.

people_involved: Captain Manuel Gómez de Ocón y Trillo
summary: Captain Juan Alvarez de Ulate, a resident of Esparza and testamentary executor of the late Captain Manuel Gómez de Ocón y Trillo, sold a 36-year-old slave named Juan to Alférez Don Francisco Enciso Hita for $500.

Doña Beatriz Méndez Machado, widow of Assistant Juan de Morales Miranda, sold a house in 'this city' to Matías Jacinto de los Reyes for $925. The house, adjacent to the parish church and the Cabildo house, was mortgaged to a chaplaincy founded by Alonso Gómez Maco.

Matías Jacinto de los Reyes and his wife Isabel de Bonilla assumed a $925 debt to the Capellanía founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela, which was tied to a house they purchased from Beatriz Méndez Machado.
Captain García de Alvarado and his wife Juana de Salazar pledged $800 to the Capellanía of Antonio Machado, mortgaging their house of residence.

A document from 1685 records that the house previously mortgaged by Captain García de Alvarado and Juana de Salazar was sold to Pro. Agustín de Torres, who then took responsibility for the associated debt.

A dowry letter was issued for José Maroto, native of Villalón, and his fiancée Luisa Calvo, daughter of the late Tomás Calvo and Eugenia de Abarca. They were scheduled to marry on March 1st, with a dowry of $5436 and a bridal gift of $100.
A dowry letter was issued for Lázaro de Ortiz, native of Ecija, and his wife Tomasina de Ocampo, daughter of Lieutenant Diego de Ocampo Sandoval and María de Mora Salado, for $2242.
Captain Pedro Ortiz de Mendoza, a resident of Santiago de Guatemala, granted power of attorney to Esteban de Hoces Navarro and Cristobal Durán de Chaves.

Luis Tamayo, a native of Bornos and resident of Panamá, made his will. He was the legitimate son of Andrés Tamayo and Ana María, married to Juana Martínez in Panamá, and had a 9-year-old son also named Andrés. His brother, Juan de Tamayo, was also mentioned.
Captain Alonso Arias Romero and his wife Mariana de Ocampo Sandoval sold a mulata named Antonia, approximately eleven years old, to Lorenzo Romero de Sousa, a resident of Guatemala, for $460.
Pedro Ortiz de Mendoza, a resident of Guatemala, became obligated to Governor Juan López de la Flor for $1800.

Captain José de Guevara y Sandoval sold an estate near Curriravá, including houses, cornfields, and wheat fields on royal lands, to Carlos Ambrosio del Arca and his wife Isabel de Ortega for $200, to be paid in Panamá.
Pedro Ortiz de Mendoza sold a 26-year-old black man named Andrés to Captain José de Alvarado for $250.

Jerónimo Valerino, tutor of the minor natural children of the deceased Alférez Antonio Machado, issued a receipt to Assistant Sebastián Aguirre, the executor, for $400 in assets belonging to the children.
A 1685 document states that Juan González Ochoa received the assets of Antonio Machado's minor children for administration and guardianship.
Pedro Ortiz de Mendoza sold a 30-year-old Conga black woman named Lucía to Alférez Esteban de Oses de Navarro for $200.
A dowry letter was issued for Andrés de Irula, native of Mundaca, and his wife Magdalena de Chaves, daughter of Juan de Caro and Jerónima de Abarca, for $1296.
Pedro Ortiz de Mendoza sold three enslaved black individuals, to be chosen from a group of 47 he owned in the Landecho Valley, to Captain Juan de Echavarría Navarro for $900.
A dowry letter was issued for Jorge de Alvarado, son of Gil de Alvarado and Juana de Vera, and his wife Gertrudis de Sandoval, daughter of Juan de Echavarría Navarro and María de Retes, for $335.
An incomplete dowry letter was issued for Jacinto de Mora in favor of Francisca Hernández Barquero. Francisco Hernández Barquero and Ana de Espinoza were present during the proceedings.

Legal proceedings were initiated to confirm the death of Presbyter Domingo de Echavarría Navarro, who served as the Cura and Vicario of Cartago. The purpose was also to open his last will and testament.

The will of Presbyter Domingo de Echavarría Navarro was opened. He left 400 pesos for an altarpiece in the main chapel and several slaves, and named his brother, Captain Juan de Echavarría Navarro, as the perpetual patron of the Chapel of Nuestra Señora del Rosario, which he built in the parish church of Cartago and where he wished to be buried. His mother, María de Sandoval Ocampo, was named his heir, and Gobernador Juan Fco. Sáenz Vázquez owed him approximately 2000 pesos.
Pedro de Elguea, a trader in the province, granted general power of attorney to Ayudante Sebastián de Aguirre for the purpose of collecting debts.

people_involved: Ambrosia de Echavarría (wife of José López de la Flor)
summary: Captain José López de la Flor and his wife Ambrosia de Echavarría obligated themselves for 500 pesos in favor of the minor children Francisco and Pedro de Moya. This obligation stemmed from the auction of certain goods from the estate of their mother, Mayor de Benavides. This obligation was later cancelled in 1684.

Ayudante José Marín Laguna requested and was granted permission to transfer a 110-peso mortgage, owed to the minor children of Francisco Carrillo, from a portion of his house to a cattle ranch he owned. He then sold his part of the house, which he had received as a dowry from his deceased mother-in-law Mayor de Benavides, to Captain José López de la Flor for 200 pesos, with his wife Catalina de Moya also participating in the new mortgage.

Magdalena de Guido requested authorization to withdraw 550 pesos from a capital placed at interest and an additional 200 pesos, secured by a mill in Barba, to provide for her son Jerónimo Murillo, who was mentally ill and imprisoned. The permission was granted, and Salvador Murillo received the 200 pesos in 1675.

Captain Francisco de Bonilla obligated himself to Magdalena de Guido for 1100 pesos, which belonged to her son Jerónimo Murillo. As security for this obligation, he mortgaged a cacao plantation with 500 trees located on the banks of the La Reventazón river.

The will of Presbyter Licentiate Pedro de la Hoz, a native of Spain from the archbishopric of Burgos and an apostolic missionary, was opened. He named his niece, Luisa de Quintana, as his heir and Sebastián de Zamora as his executor.

Captain Jerónimo Leal sold an 18-year-old mulata slave named Victoria for 300 pesos. The buyer was Captain Juan Romero y Tamaris, acting as the attorney for Margarita de Villegas, the widow and heir of Diego López de Cabrera, a resident of Granada, Nicaragua.

Gaspar de Chinchilla and his wife Sebastiana de Vargas ratified the sale of a 20-year-old one-eyed slave named Juan for 300 pesos. This sale had originally been made six months prior to the deceased Diego López de Cabrera, a resident of Granada, and was now ratified to Juan Romero y Tamaris, attorney for Cabrera's widow and heir.

Captain Francisco de Bonilla obligated himself for four years not to play any card games of chance in Cartago and its jurisdiction. Should he break this pledge, he would pay 50 pesos to the Cofradía de las Animas for the first offense and 100 pesos for the second.

Antonio de Moya and his wife Isabel de Alvarado obligated themselves for 1000 pesos in favor of their minor brothers Francisco and Pedro de Moya, sons of Sergeant Major José de Moya and Mayor de Benavides. They mortgaged their house, which bordered that of José de Alvarado, the father and father-in-law of the grantors. This obligation was cancelled in 1685.

The will of Maestre de Campo Agustín Sáenz Vázquez, a resident of Madrid, was opened. He had been married to Antonia María Gil for 13.5 years and had a 13-year-old son, Captain Juan Sáenz Vázquez. His executors were his brother, Gobernador Juan Fco. Sáenz Vázquez, and his wife Antonia María Gil.
Salvador Murillo obligated himself for 200 pesos in favor of his brother, Jerónimo Murillo.

people_involved: Ambrosia de Echavarría (daughter of María de Sandoval Ocampo)
summary: The will of María de Sandoval Ocampo, widow of Treasurer Juan de Echavarría Navarro, was opened. She was the daughter of Captain Francisco de Ocampo Golfín and Inés de Benavides Solano. Her children included Domingo (presbyter), Ana (married to Cristobal Zapata with a 4000 peso dowry), Ambrosia (married to Regidor Fernando de Salazar with a 3400 peso dowry), Francisco (presbyter), and Juan. Her granddaughter Manuela de Salazar was also mentioned.
An incomplete dowry letter was issued in favor of Clara de Esquivel.
Sargento Mayor Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín granted general power of attorney for lawsuits to Captain José de Guevara y Sandoval.

José Maroto and his wife Luisa Calvo obligated themselves for $450 to a Chaplaincy founded by Alférez Antonio Machado, represented by Presbítero Marcos Machado. They mortgaged their house located on the street from Naboríos to the Convent of San Francisco.

Doña María de Sandoval Ocampo, widow of Treasurer Juan de Echavarría Navarro, confirmed and approved the distribution of assets as stipulated in the will of her son, the Beneficiado Domingo de Echavarría Navarro.

Don José López de la Flor pledged to abstain from playing various card games, including "envite," "pinta," "tabaco primera," and "penchingonga," under a 50-peso fine for the souls in Purgatory. He reserved the right to play "ombrecientos" and "sanga."

people_involved: Sebastián Alvarez Alfonso Rosica de Caldas
summary: Captain Bartolomé Muñoz Hidalgo empowered former Governor Juan López de la Flor, who was traveling to Spain, to present a grievance to the King. Muñoz Hidalgo had been unjustly imprisoned for over 22 months in Granada by Sebastián Alvarez Alfonso Rosica de Caldas for refusing to give false testimony against Maese de Campo Juan Fernández Salinas y Cerda. He also sought to recover 3600 pesos for eight drafts taken from him by Alvarez Alfonso.

On April 10, Maese de Campo Juan López de la Flor donated a 500-tree cacao plantation on the Matina River to his son, José López de la Flor. The donation was conditional on José funding an altarpiece and railing for the Santa Vera Cruz chapel in the San Francisco convent, and arranging annual masses for the soul of his deceased wife, Margarita Vetecant, who was buried there.

On May 1, Juan de Montaño, a resident, granted power of attorney to Captain Juan Alvarez de Ulate to pay Antonio Mata, a resident of Nicoya, $628. The payment was to be made in tallow and other local goods, settling a debt for clothing.

On May 13, Doña María de Sandoval Ocampo, widow and universal heir of her son Domingo de Echavarría Navarro, granted power of attorney to Captains Francisco Navarrete and Jerónimo de Villegas, residents of Granada, to recover a runaway slave.

On June 14, Captains Alfonso Sáenz Vázquez and Juan Flores, owner of the ship "Ntra. Sra. de las Mercedes," formed a partnership. Sáenz Vázquez committed to preparing wood for loading, while Flores agreed to transport the cargo to Callao for sale, with profits divided after costs.
On January 17, brothers Gaspar and Alférez Juan Cascante de Rojas sold a house in Cartago, inherited from their father Juan Cascante de Rojas, to Alférez Sebastián de Zamora for $800.

On June 19, Ayudante Sebastián de Aguirre, the city's Steward and Procurator, granted power of attorney to Diego Ignacio de Córdova, a business agent in Madrid. The purpose was to petition for the incorporation of "this province" into the Reino de Tierra Firme and its separation from the Audiencia de Santiago de Guatemala, citing various inconveniences.
On June 19, Diego López de Cabrera, a resident of Cartago, provided a receipt for $250 to Juan Fernández de la Fuente.

On June 20, Alférez Sebastián de Zamora sold a cacao plantation on the Matina River to Juan de la Cruz Fonseca for $1200 in cacao. The land was inherited by their wives from Mateo de Madrigal Fonseca, Juan de la Cruz's brother, with Zamora's portion being his wife Luisa de Quintana's dowry from 1673. A related debt was cancelled in 1677.

On June 23, Juan de la Cruz Fonseca, son of the late María de Fonseca, made his will. He established a Chaplaincy in the hermitage of Soledad and mentioned his niece Luisa de Quintana, his natural daughter Juana de la Cruz (married to Antonio de Acosta), and his wife Ana López, to whom he had been married for 20 years.

On June 26, Presbítero Marcos Machado, Chaplain of the Chaplaincy founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela, was granted permission by the late Bishop Fray Alonso Bravo de Laguna and ratified by the Venerable Dean to travel to Peru for four years.
The Cabildo, in a vacant seat, appointed Pro. don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas as a substitute chaplain. This appointment was made for a sum up to $3500-00.

María de Sagaste, widow of Sergeant Nicolás Barrantes and guardian of their children Jerónima and Benito Barrantes, granted freedom to Juana de Moscoso, a Black enslaved woman. This enslaved woman had been previously donated to Nicolás Barrantes by Doña Juana de Moscoso, widow of Captain Juan de Senabria Maldonado.

Doña Juana de Moscoso, widow of Captain Juan de Senabria Maldonado, granted freedom to an enslaved girl named Juana. This enslaved girl was approximately two years old and was the daughter of another enslaved woman named María.

Don Fernando de Salazar, a perpetual councilman, and Captain Juan de Echavarría Navarro, provincial of the Santa Hermandad, settled a dispute. Salazar had sued Doña María de Sandoval, his mother-in-law and mother of the deceased Domingo de Echavarría Navarro and Juan de Echavarría Navarro, concerning sales she made after Domingo's death. Captain Echavarría represented his mother in resolving the matter.

On September 16, 1646, Fernando de Salazar conducted an extensive interrogation of his mother-in-law, María de Sandoval, regarding various financial transactions and properties involving the deceased Domingo de Echavarría Navarro. The inquiry covered items given to Domingo, goods he requested or disposed of, and outstanding debts, including a capellanía for Salazar's son Francisco and a balance from a house sale in Cartago. María de Sandoval clarified that their departure for León occurred in early 1646.

On September 18, María de Espinosa, daughter of the deceased Juan Muñoz and Magdalena Mauricia, made her will. She had been married to Tomás de las Salas for 37 years and named their five children, including Magdalena, who was married to Cristobal Tenorio and had a 4-year-old son José, and Juana, married to Alférez Francisco Solano. Her executors were her husband Tomás de las Salas and her brother Alférez Andrés de Esquivel.

On October 25, Juana Solano, widow of Bernabé de Segura, sold a 7-year-old enslaved girl named Leonor to Don Pedro de Alvarado and his wife Doña Catalina de Vida Martell for $250. Leonor had originally been a donation from María de la Portilla to Juana Solano.

On November 6, Don Fernando de Salazar, a perpetual councilman, committed to pay $200 at 5% interest to the Confraternity of Nuestra Señora de la Soledad, whose steward was Alférez Esteban de Hoces Navarro. He mortgaged a house and an attached sugarcane field with a sugar mill in Cartago, bordering property owned by Doña María de Sandoval. This obligation was later cancelled in 1685.

On December 13, Diego Francisco de Chaves sold a large cattle ranch, including houses and corrals, in the valley of Pueblo Viejo de Pacacua to the town of Nuestra Señora de la Asunción de Pacacua. He had acquired this property through an auction of the assets of Alférez Mayor Juan de Chaves.

The Cabildo, represented by Captain Juan de León, Bartolomé de Avalos, Diego Martínez, and Juan Cosme, accepted the sale of pastures, watering holes, and 80 head of branded cattle for $340.00 on behalf of the town. This transaction was approved with the license of Governor don Juan Francisco Sáenz.

Salvador Morillo de Campos, son of the late Alférez Andrés Morillo de Campos and María de Guido, established a dowry in favor of his wife, Clara de Esquivel. Clara is the daughter of the late Alférez Andrés de Esquivel and Antonia de Madrigal. The document is incomplete.
An incomplete agreement was made between Captain Bartolomé Muñoz y Hidalgo and Alonso de Porras.

people_involved: Pro. don Francisco de Echavarría Navarro
Capn. don Juan de Echavarría Navarro
summary: Don Francisco de Echavarría Navarro, acting as executor for his deceased family members, declared the will regarding two enslaved women. Don Domingo de Echavarría Navarro had left a 14-year-old 'negra' named Paula and a 30-year-old 'mulata blanca' named Francisca to his nieces, doña Juana de Salazar and doña Ana de Salazar. Doña Juana is the daughter of don Fernando de Salazar and doña Ambrosia de Echavarría, and doña Ana is married to don Matías González del Camino.

Ayudante José de Rojas, son of the late Gaspar de Rojas and María González, established a dowry of $321.00 in favor of his wife, Isabel de los Santos. The dowry was provided by Jacinto Fernández, his brother, and Sargento Juan de Rojas, his brother-in-law.

Captain of Cavalry don Alfonso Sáenz Vázquez granted power of attorney to Captains don Alonso Lanini and Francisco Ramírez de Rumayor. This power allowed them to sell timber in Callao, which was shipped on the frigate 'Ntra. Sra. de la Concepción' on behalf of Sáenz Vázquez and Captains Juan López Mundo and Manuel de los Santos.

Captain Francisco de Bonilla obligated himself to the Cofradía de la Soledad for $100.00. He mortgaged a cacao plantation of 500 trees located on the banks of the Reventazón river. The Cofradía's officials involved were Treasurer Esteban de Hoces Navarro and deputies Juan de la Cruz, Jerónimo de Mena, and Antonio de Bonilla.

people_involved: Capn. don José de Guevara y Sandoval
summary: Captain don José de Guevara y Sandoval granted general power of attorney to Sergeants Major Pedro Lorenzo Venegas and don Sebastián de Sandoval Ocampo.

Don Alfonso Sáenz Vázquez obligated himself to the Cofradía de los Angeles for $426.00. He mortgaged a cacao plantation of approximately 10,000 trees in the Matina valley, at a place called Cuchicuchi, next to a river.

Francisco de Araya, on behalf of his daughter Francisca de Araya, settled a lawsuit against Jusepe de Loría, son of Agustín González de Loría. Francisca had sued Jusepe for breach of promise of marriage. The dispute was resolved with a payment of $200.00, in exchange for which Francisca would withdraw her demand.

This entry details the will of the late Alférez Salvador de Contreras, a bachelor born in Marchena, Spain, son of Francisco Rodríguez de Contreras and Inés de las Nieves. He bequeathed a pair of breeches to Juan de Flores, a poor man, and a coyol rosary to doña Josefa de Aguilar, daughter of doña María Estefanía.

Captain Bartolomé Muñoz Hidalgo granted power of attorney to Pedro Roldán Abarca, a Procurador in the Audiencia of Guatemala. The purpose was to collect over $3000.00 owed to Muñoz Hidalgo by the Royal Treasurer through various drafts.

people_involved: Juez del Santo Tribunal de León
summary: Pedro de Otálora and don José Escalante Paniagua settled a lawsuit. Otálora had criminally accused Escalante, the Treasurer of the Santa Cruzada. The case was initially decided by the Ordinary Mayor, then sent to the Judge of the Holy Tribunal of León, and Otálora appealed to the Audiencia. Escalante then approached don Ginés Recio, Maestrescuela of León and Commissary Judge of the Santa Cruzada, who annulled the case and ordered it to be re-tried before don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, the local priest, provincial Vicar, and Commissary of the Santa Cruzada. The parties ultimately desisted.

Juan and Salvador Murillo, along with their sisters Isabel and Lucía, heirs of the late Alférez Andrés Murillo de Campos and Magdalena de Guido, settled a dispute with Lucas Murillo de Rivera and his brother Sebastián. The dispute concerned a mill in Barba, which Andrés Murillo had given as a dowry to his daughter Juana (mother of Lucas and Sebastián) but later recovered. The mill and other dowry assets were awarded to Isabel and Lucía, who were to pay $250.00 to the Riveras.

José de Vargas Machuca and his wife, doña Gertrudis de Alvarado, acknowledged a debt of $1169.50 to the succession of the late Pro. don Domingo de Echavarría Navarro, representing a balance of accounts. The debt was later cancelled.

Captain Manuel Pérez sold a pasture known as 'potrero de Felipe Díaz' to Captain Jerónimo Valerino for $100.00. The pasture is located in the cordillera of the city and a valley descending from the volcano. This land was originally granted to Andrés Benito, a conquistador, by Governor Artieda de Chirinos in 1579, and Pérez purchased it from Sargento Celidón de Ortega, an heir of Benito.

people_involved: Capn. don José Pérez de Muro
summary: Doña Ana de Retes, widow of Juan de Echavarría Navarro, clandestinely married Captain Don Diego de Ibarra. She subsequently granted general power of attorney to her new husband and Captain Don José Pérez de Muro.

people_involved: Maese de Campo don Agustín Sáenz
summary: Alférez Francisco Fernández established a dowry for his wife, Eugenia Rodrigues, which included goods from Doña Antonia María Gil, who raised Eugenia, and $600 from Governor Don Juan Francisco Sáenz, totaling $2518.

people_involved: Pro. don Francisco de Echavarría Navarro
Capn. don Juan de Echavarría Navarro
summary: A legal transaction was made to settle a lawsuit, involving Don Fernando de Salazar and Don Fernando Ramiro Corajo, who were to receive $3000. The agreement involved multiple parties, including executors of Captain Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro and a curator for his minor children, but was not signed by all.

Domingo de Alvarado's will named his wife, Juana de Carvajal, and their four children: Mariana, Manuel, Pedro, and Gregoria. It also mentioned his brother, Pedro de Alvarado, and his wife's parents, Bartolomé Sánchez and Isabel de Carvajal.

people_involved: Pro. don Francisco de Echavarría Navarro
summary: A transaction was conducted involving Captain Don Diego de Ibarra and the same parties who participated in the legal agreement recorded on folio 89 (Nov 19).
Don Fernando Ramiro Corajo received one thousand pesos from Captain Diego de Ibarra as part of the settlement from the earlier transaction.
Don Fernando Ramiro Corajo acquired a two-year-old mulatto girl named Brígida from Captain Diego de Ibarra for $100.
Captain Diego de Ibarra committed to paying Don Fernando Ramiro Corajo $900 as part of the previously agreed-upon transaction.
Don Fernando de Salazar received $500 from Captain Diego de Ibarra, also in connection with the same transaction.
Jerónimo Valerino and his wife, Francisca de Esquivel, incurred a $100 debt to the Cofradía de la Soledad, securing it with a mortgage on their cacao plantation in the Matina valley.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín
summary: Doña Juana Moscoso de Figueroa, widow of Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado, granted power of attorney to Sergeant Major Don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín to sell any of her assets.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín
summary: Doña Juana Moscoso de Figueroa granted general power of attorney for lawsuits to Sergeant Major Don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín, though the document was not signed.

A complex legal dispute was settled between Francisco de Araya and Agustín González de Loría concerning a broken marriage promise between their children, Francisca de Araya and José de Loría. Agustín had accused Francisca of using witchcraft, but the parties ultimately agreed to drop all charges, free the young couple to marry others, and Francisco de Araya would receive $100 in local goods.

people_involved: Presbítero don Domingo de Echavarría Navarro
summary: Don Matías González Camino and Doña Ana de Peralta granted freedom to their slave, Francisca de Montoya, who had been given to them by Presbítero Don Domingo de Echavarría Navarro. Francisca paid $325 upfront and still owed $150 for her freedom.

people_involved: Capitán don José de Guevara y Sandoval
summary: Captain Nicolás Serrano, a resident of Panama, incurred a debt of $199 to Captain Don José de Guevara y Sandoval.
Don Fernando de Salazar incurred a debt of $100 to Doña Inés de Benavides.

people_involved: Gobernador don Juan Francisco Sáenz Vásquez
summary: Governor Don Juan Francisco Sáenz Vásquez granted power of attorney to Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes, who was traveling to León de Nicaragua, to settle his salary accounts and collect any outstanding balance from the Treasury there.

people_involved: Capitán don Carlos Eugenio de Lisaun y Suescun
summary: Licenciado José de Lumbides, the interim priest of Cartago, sold a mulatto slave to Captain Don Carlos Eugenio de Lisaun y Suescun, a resident and Ordinary Mayor of Esparza.

An enslaved person named Clemente, about 18 years old and described as tall, curly-haired, and light-skinned, who is the son of an enslaved woman named Catalina, was involved in a transaction. In exchange for Clemente, 100 head of cattle (up to 2 years old), 200 fillies, and two donkeys are to be given in the valley of Landecho.

Captain Jerónimo Leal obligated himself to the Cofradía del Santísimo Sacramento for $1000 at 5% interest. He mortgaged a mill located in the common lands (ejidos) of Cartago as collateral for this debt.
Benito Valerino incurred a debt of $250 at 5% interest to the Convento de San Francisco. He used a cacao plantation located on the Matina riverbank as collateral for this obligation.
