A dowry letter was issued for the marriage of Alférez don Fernando Núñez Bejarano, originally from Valladolid de Comayagua, and doña Baltasara Vásquez de Coronado. The dowry was $1254 and the arras (earnest money) was $1500.
Juan de Castro Rodríguez and his wife, doña Petronila Arias de Monterroso, sold an 11-year-old enslaved girl named Rufina to Teniente Alonso de Sibaja for $250. Rufina was part of Petronila's dowry.

Cristóbal López, Mayordomo of the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora de los Angeles, with the consent of cofradía deputies and Vicario Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, leased cacao haciendas on the Matina riverbank to his son Salvador López. The five-year lease, starting May 1st, for 247 cacao trees, costs $500 annually, and Salvador also committed to caring for an adjacent hacienda with 2,500 small trees.

Don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, Cura propietario and Vicario Juez Eclesiástico, obligated himself to Captain don García de Alvarado, Mayordomo of the Cofradía del Santísimo Sacramento, for $50 received at 5% censo. He mortgaged a cattle ranch in the Barba valley, near the Segundo river, which included 400 cattle and two houses.

Captain don Juan Francisco Sáenz, in Cartago, granted power of attorney to Maestre de Campo don Juan de Valtierra Ribadeneira of Ciudad Real de Chiapa. This was to pursue the collection and confirmation of an encomienda of indigenous people in Chiapa province, which had been granted four years prior by the President of the Real Audiencia de Guatemala, Fernando Francisco de Escobedo, and became vacant upon the death of Sargento Mayor don Antonio de Aguilar.

Captain don José de Alvarado and Alférez Esteban de Hoces Navarro, Mayordomos of two Cofradías based in the Convento de San Francisco, sold two caballerías of land to the pueblo of Tobosi for $40. The land, originally donated by the deceased Luis González de Estrada, was located near Tobosi and bordered a ditch, the Candelaria road, and the Purire river.

On November 29, José de Vargas Machuca obligated himself to doña Beatriz de Guido y Machado, the widow of Juan de Morales Miranda and a resident of Cartago, for $460. This money was provided for him to purchase Castilian and Peruvian clothing/textiles in Puertobelo and Panamá, where he was departing.

On December 7, a dowry letter was issued for the marriage of Sargento Francisco Hernández Isidro, widower of doña Juana de Añasco, and María de Sandoval. The dowry was $1487, including an enslaved Creole woman named Justa Rufina (26 years old), her 6-year-old mulato son Alfonso, and her 4-year-old enslaved daughter. The arras was $200.

On December 17, an inventory was made of the goods contributed by Sargento Francisco Hernández Isidro to his marriage with María de Sandoval, totaling $2029. He declared having three children from his first marriage, and the inventory included 26 mules.

On December 29, a dowry letter was issued for the marriage of Baltasar de Segura, legitimate son of the deceased Faustino de Segura and Margarita de Espinoza, and María de Aguilar, an orphan girl raised by Alférez José Calderón. The dowry was $908 and the arras was $1000.
On November 28, doña Beatriz de Guido y Machado, widow of Juan de Morales Miranda, sold a 24-year-old enslaved Zambo man to José de Vargas Machuca.

Matías González Camino obligated himself to Captain José Pérez de Muro for $1238. He agreed to pay $619 in January 1678 in mule trains, with the remaining balance to be paid in cash in Panama. This obligation was later cancelled.

Captain José Francisco del Hoyo, a resident of Panama, committed to bringing his ship or a chartered vessel to the port of Caldera by the following May. The purpose was to load fifteen bales of mora for Sargento Mayor Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín, for which he would receive $500.
In the year 1678, Captain Francisco de Bonilla held the position of Alcalde Ordinario in Cartago.

Alférez Jerónimo de Guzmán sold a 900-tree cacao plantation in La Reventazón to Matías Jacinto de los Reyes for $230. As partial payment, Guzmán received a straw and pole house, acquired through his wife Isabel de Bonilla's dowry, which bordered properties of Francisco Peláez and Inés Solano.

Captain Miguel Calvo granted power of attorney to Lorenzo Pérez de Rivera, a royal scribe in Guatemala, and Captain Juan Sáenz, a Cartago resident traveling to Guatemala. This was to manage the confirmation of his brother, Captain Gaspar Faustino Calvo's, renunciation of the perpetual Depositary and Regidor office in Cartago in favor of Miguel Calvo.

Tomás de Umaña and his wife, Isabel de Chaves, sold their enslaved mulata, María, who was approximately 15 years old and quince-colored, to Juan de la Cruz Fonseca. The sale price was $450, paid in cacao at a rate of 100 grains per real.

Alférez José Calderón obligated himself for $100 at a 5% interest rate to Alférez Esteban de Hoces Navarro, who was the tutor of Francisco Carrillo's minor children. Calderón mortgaged a cacao plantation on the Matina River, bordering properties of Bartolomé Calderón's minors and Antonio de Amaviscar, an indigenous person.

people_involved: Francisco de Padua de Salazar y Peralta
summary: Captain Fernando de Salazar, a perpetual regidor of Cartago, made his will, detailing his family, including his deceased parents, wife, and children, and their spouses. He also mentioned his roles as Mayordomo and Encomendero, and mandated the collection of the value of his enslaved mulato, Segundo, from Captain José de Alvarado, who had executed Segundo in 1677.
Andrés de Vinda apprenticed his 15-year-old son, Sebastián de Vinda, to master blacksmith Esteban de Zúñiga for a period of four years to learn the trade.

Jorge de Alvarado initiated legal proceedings concerning the execution of Segundo, an enslaved mulato formerly owned by Fernando de Salazar. Segundo had been prosecuted and given the death penalty by Jorge's brother, Captain José de Alvarado, who was Lieutenant Governor in 1677.

Sargento Mayor Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín sold 240 mules, both tame and wild, for saddle and cargo, to Alférez Juan Patricio de Sandoval for $7680. The mules were to be delivered and paid for in Panama two months after the arrival of the next galleons from Spain, expected from the ports of San Felipe and Puerto Belo.
Sargento Mayor Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín granted general power of attorney to Santiago Vásquez, a procurator of the Audiencia of Guatemala.

Juan Fernández Chacón's testamentary memory was recorded, detailing his parentage (Eugenio Fernández Chacón and María Núñez, natives of Extremadura), his marriage to Ana Solano, and his children: Gaspar de los Reyes, Cristóbal Fernández, Salvador Silvestre, and Margarita de la Rosa.

Don José requested the original legal case document to defend himself before the King and the Audiencia of Guatemala. An unnamed guarantor committed that his brother, Don José, would appear before the Audiencia with the original case within six months.

Alférez don Francisco Enciso Hita, natural son of the late Captain Bartolomé de Enciso Hita and widower of Doña Ursula de Ortega, made his will. He bequeathed three mule beasts to Pedro de Soto to complete a dowry for his niece Doña María de Hita, and one hundred pesos to his niece Gregoria Guerrero for her dowry. He also founded a Chaplaincy, naming his nephew Francisco Guerrero as the first Chaplain if ordained.

Francisco Antonio Castrejón, acting as attorney for Bachiller don Luis Lovato, sold two fugitive slaves apprehended in Cartago. He sold Francisco (18 years old) to Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes for $300 and Tomás (21 years old) to don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín for $400.

Don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín committed to pay Francisco Antonio Castrejón $700 in Panamá by the end of October. This obligation was made under the power of attorney granted by Bachiller don Luis Lovato.

Don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, the Beneficed Priest of Cartago, granted power of attorney to Captain don José de Alvarado, who was traveling to Guatemala. The purpose was to collect the full Synod payment, which had been unpaid due to the curacy being divided between two beneficed priests despite a large number of parishioners.

Captain Jerónimo Leal, a native of Cuéllar, Castilla la Vieja, established a dowry for Doña María Vázquez de Coronado, daughter of the late Alférez Juan Vásquez de Coronado and Ana María de Mora Salado. The dowry included a 20-year-old mulata slave named Antonia, six mule beasts, and fifty head of cattle, totaling $1157, with an additional $750 in arras.
Don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín granted general power of attorney to don Matías González Camino and don José de Guevara Sandoval.

Licenciado José de Lumbides, a Cleric, sold a mulato slave named Clemente, approximately 18 years old and son of his deceased slave Catarina, to Captain Francisco de Obregón, a resident of Nicoya, for $200.

people_involved: Capitán don Carlos Eugenío de Lisaun y Suescum
summary: Captain don Carlos Eugenío de Lisaun y Suescum, Ordinary Mayor of Esparza, and Captain don Juan Alonso Lanini, Captain of the paid Company, formed a partnership for a large cattle ranch. The ranch, located in TZacacongo within Esparza's jurisdiction, included 200 head of cattle, 500 breeding mares, and 4 breeding donkeys, with an investment of $2060.

Antonio de Acosta Arévalo established a dowry of $688 for his wife, Doña Josefa de Santiago, an orphan girl raised by Doña María de Aguilar. Their marriage was scheduled for the following day, March 27, with an additional $2500 in arras.
Don Matías González Camino committed to repay don García de Alvarado $1350, which was lent in Nicaragua to help purchase mules for sale in Panamá. This obligation was later canceled.

Captain Alonso Arias Romero and his wife, Doña Mariana de Sandoval Ocampo, committed to pay the Cofradía de la Concepción $110 at 5% interest. This obligation was secured by a mortgage on solars in Cartago and lands in Río Segundo, which they had received from Doña Mariana's father, don José de Sandoval Ocampo, with this existing encumbrance.

people_involved: Don Juan Antonio Ruiz de Velazco
Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
summary: Doña Lucía de Abarca, widow of don Juan Antonio Ruiz de Velazco (who died intestate in Veragua province), acting for herself and as guardian of her son Juan de Velazco, granted power of attorney. The power was given to Captains don José Pérez de Muro and José de Vargas Machuca, who were in Panamá, and to Alférez Andrés de Yrula, who was traveling to Panamá.
Sargento Mayor Jerónimo Valerino guaranteed the debt of Pedro García, a resident of Panamá, who owed don García de Alvarado $93 and four reales.

Melchora de los Reyes, natural daughter of Alonso Martín Macotela and María Lobo, made her will. She inherited a solar in partnership with her deceased sister, Inés Maria, who had left four children: fray Nicolás Peláez, Gregoria Josefa de Chaves, and María de Jesús y Chaves.
Fray Nicolás was married and had a son named Francisco Nicasio Peláez.

people_involved: Doña Ana de Salazar y Peralta
summary: Don Matías González Camino granted general power of attorney to his wife, Doña Ana de Salazar y Peralta, and to Captain Don García de Alvarado.

Captain Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, perpetual Regidor of Cartago, granted power to Bernardo de Aparicio, his son Juan Antonio de Aparicio, and his son-in-law Agustín de Cevallos, to seek confirmation of his regidor title in Madrid.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín
Doña Angela María de la Paz y Salgado
summary: Sergeant Major Don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín and his wife Doña Angela María de la Paz y Salgado obligated themselves to Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes for 1872 pesos and 4 reales, which Céspedes had lent them from the Santa Cruzada alms. This obligation was cancelled on August 20, 1679.
Alonso García, a trader in the province, granted general power of attorney for lawsuits to Captain Francisco Fernández de Miranda.
This entry records the testament of Juan Arias, a resident of Panamá, who was the legitimate son of Jerónimo Arias and Ana de la Laguna.
Juan Arias, a resident of Panamá, granted general power of attorney to Diego de Pesquera and Diego de la Trinidad, also residents of Panamá.

people_involved: Capitán don José de Guevara y Sandoval
summary: Captain Don José de Guevara y Sandoval and his wife Doña Inés de Sandoval Ocampo obligated themselves to Salvador Murillo, acting as tutor for his incapacitated brother Jerónimo, for 100 pesos at a 5% interest rate, mortgaging a house in Cartago.

people_involved: Doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar
summary: Manuel de Mora Salado and his wife Doña Juana Bautista sold a farm and land site in the valley of Cartago, on the road to Ujarrás, with a straw house, for 150 pesos to Antonio de Acosta Arévalo and his wife Doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar. An existing mortgage was transferred to the house of Doña María de Aguilar, who was the mother and mother-in-law of the sellers.

people_involved: Presbítero don Francisco de Echavarría Navarro
summary: Antonio de Acosta Arévalo, who purchased the slaves Mateo and Manuel from the estate of the deceased Presbyter Don Francisco de Echavarría Navarro, acknowledged a debt of 600 pesos for the auction price, with Captain Don García de Alvarado serving as his guarantor.

people_involved: Presbítero don Francisco de Echavarría Navarro
summary: Proceedings were initiated for the opening of the will of the recently deceased Presbyter Don Francisco de Echavarría Navarro, at the request of Fray Ambrosio Salado de Ordiales and Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes.

people_involved: Presbítero don Francisco de Echavarría Navarro
summary: This entry details the testament of Presbyter Don Francisco de Echavarría Navarro, legitimate son of the deceased Treasurer Juan de Echavarría Navarro and Doña María de Sandoval. He made bequests to his nephew Miguel de Echavarría and 100 pesos to Doña Catalina de Aguirre, daughter of Captain Sebastián de Aguirre, due to affection and kinship.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Captain Don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, perpetual Regidor, granted general power of attorney to Santiago Vásquez, a procurator in the Audiencia of Guatemala.
Doña Petronila de Retes, with judicial license, granted general power of attorney to her husband Don José de Alvarado, who was absent in Guatemala.
This entry records the testament of Clara Montero de Espinoza, legitimate daughter of Andrés Montero de Espinoza and Catalina López, and wife of Alférez Antonio Calderón for about 20 years.
Ambrosio Ricardo, legitimate son of Juan Ricardo and María de Esquivel, and widower of Antonia Masís, made his will. He had a 5-year-old daughter named Manuela.
Fernando de Tapia, a resident of Cartago and departing for Panama, incurred an obligation of $464.00 in favor of Captain Antonio Pacheco.

Captain García de Alvarado, acting as general attorney for Matías González Camino, who acquired an enslaved woman named María de la O from the estate of Presbyter Francisco de Echavarría Navarro, incurred an obligation of $400.00 in favor of the estate.

Captain García de Alvarado, acting in the same capacity as before, incurred another obligation of $400.00 to the same estate for the purchase of an enslaved Creole man named Baltasar, acquired in auction.

Alférez Sebastián de Ribera, legitimate son of Sebastián de Rivera and Juana Murillo de Campos, provided a dowry of $1031.00 and 'arras' of $500.00 to his wife, Isabel de Porras y Estrada, legitimate daughter of Alonso de Porras and Magdalena de Torres.

people_involved: Diego de Ocampo Figueroa y Golfín
summary: Licenciado Francisco de Ocampo Golfín granted power of attorney to Governor Juan Francisco Sáenz y Vásquez, who was departing for Guatemala. The power allowed Sáenz y Vásquez to sell an enslaved mulatto named Josepe, inherited from Francisco's father, and to request payment of the full synod from the Royal Treasury in Cartago.

people_involved: Toribio de la Riva y Agúero
summary: Sergeant Major Toribio de la Riva y Agúero, originally from Navajea, Burgos, made his will. He was the legitimate son of Captain Mateo de la Riva and Francisca de Agüero, married to Inés de Chaves, and had three children: Francisca, Antonio, and Fernando.
Francisca de Peñaranda, natural daughter of Juan de Peñaranda, made her will. Cristóbal López was named her executor, and Sofía de Flores was named her heir.

Alférez Antonio Calderón, legitimate son of the deceased Diego Hernández de Aguilar and María Calderón, and widower of Clara de Espinoza y Montero, made his will. He listed his children, mentioned his niece Margarita (wife of Bernardo Sarmiento), and his brother José Calderón.

María de Sagaste, widow of Sergeant Nicolás Barrantes and guardian of their children, sold an enslaved woman named María (daughter of another enslaved María) to Sebastiana Calvo for $250.00. This sale was due to poverty amidst a lawsuit with Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín, heir of Juana Moscoso, concerning a donation of enslaved people to Nicolás Barrantes, with the appeal going to the Audiencia of Guatemala.

Juan Masís leased a cacao plantation for 5 years. The plantation, located on the Matina River in Barbilla and containing 420 trees, belonged to the minor Manuela, daughter of the deceased Ambrosio Ricardo.
Antonio de Acosta Arévalo granted general power of attorney to Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes.
Proceedings were initiated for the opening of the will of Beneficiado don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, who passed away on the day of the document.

The will of Beneficiado Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, the oldest rector priest of Cartago parish and Commissary of the Holy Office of the Inquisition in Mexico, was recorded. He was the legitimate son of Captain Diego de Ocampo Figueroa Golfín and Doña Inés Velázquez, and his cousin Don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín and his mother Doña Inés were mentioned.

The will of Alférez Francisco Enciso Hita, a widower of Doña Ursula de Ortega and former resident of Nicaragua, was recorded. He established a Chaplaincy, naming his 6-7 year old nephew, Francisco Guerrero Hita, as the first Chaplain, and Alférez Esteban de Hoces Navarro as the first patron. A previous will from June 7, 1676, was also noted.
The Justice system placed Nicolás, a 16-year-old mestizo married to María, a zamba, as an apprentice carpenter with master José de Rivera for a period of four years.

people_involved: Francisco Antonio de Rivas y Contreras
summary: Don Francisco Antonio de Rivas y Contreras, former Governor and Captain General, granted power to Captains Juan de Andueza and Juan Rodríguez to collect a debt of $5664.50 from Governor Don Luis de Berrío. This debt was for supplies and dispatch of Berrío's frigate in Granada de Nicaragua.

people_involved: Toribio de la Riva y Agüero
summary: Doña Inés de Chaves, widow of Sergeant Major Toribio de la Riva y Agüero, sold a house in Cartago to Captain José Marín and his wife Doña Catalina de Moya for $400. The house, which had multiple mortgages and was damaged by earthquakes in 1678, was sold with the buyers assuming the existing encumbrances.

On November 17, 1685, the mortgages on the house previously sold by Inés de Chaves were cancelled. Alférez Don Sebastián de Garita, steward of the Cofradía de la Concepción, Cristóbal López, steward of the Cofradía de los Angeles, and Sergeant Major Don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín, as patron of the Chaplaincy founded by Comisario Baltasar de Grado, executed the cancellation.

Doña Catalina Monterroso, widow of Ayudante Esteban de Torres, ratified a $100 debt at 5% interest that her husband owed to the Cofradía de la Concepción. The debt was secured by a mortgage on a plot of land in Cartago, which Esteban de Torres had inherited with the same encumbrance from his father, Salvador de Torres.
Agustín Guerrero sold an enslaved black woman named Ursula, whom he had inherited from his mother Juana de la Portilla, to Captain Don Matías González Camino for $500.

A dowry letter was issued on November 20 for Juan Antonio de Guevara and Doña Clara Eugenia de Echavarría Navarro, detailing a dowry of $5421 and a bride price of $1000. The dowry included enslaved persons (María, 26; Leocadia, 3; José, 11), jewelry, and 100 mules. Doña Ana de Retes, mother of Clara Eugenia, appeared with her new husband, Captain Don Diego de Ibarra.

On November 22, Doña María Arias Maldonado Velazco, widow of Captain Manuel Pérez, ratified her husband's sale of a pasture known as 'Felipe Díaz's pasture' to Captain Jerónimo Valerino. The pasture was originally acquired from Celidón, Leonor, and Baltasar de Ortega, with a title issued by Diego de Artieda Chirinos in 1579 to Andrés Benito.

A copy of a land title, issued in Cartago on August 4, 1579, by Diego de Artieda Chirinos, was included. This title granted two 'caballerías' of land in Quercua and an additional 'caballería' near a cattle ranch and pasture to Andrés Benito, one of the first conquistadors and settlers.

A dowry letter was issued on December 5 for Simón Muñoz, son of Juan Muñoz and María de Espinoza, and Agueda de Santiago, daughter of Manuel Rodríguez and Gertrudis de Alarcón. The dowry amounted to $658, with a bride price of $300.

Alonso García, a resident of this city and native of Villa del Banco, Asturias, son of Medero and Marina García, issues a dowry letter for Doña Eugenia Gertrudis Muñoz. Doña Eugenia is the legitimate daughter of Captain Bartolomé Muñoz Hidalgo and Doña Sebastiana Calvo. The dowry is valued at $3539.00, with an additional $1000.00 for arras.

Nicolás de Bonilla and his wife, Doña María de Flores, obligate themselves for $100.00 at 5% interest to the Capellanía founded by Alférez Antonio Machado. They mortgage a cacao plantation with 200 trees in the Reventazón valley, which borders the haciendas of Alférez Antonio de Bonilla and Captain Francisco de Bonilla. This transaction is made with the consent of Doña Beatriz Machado, widow and mother of Agustín de Morales, the Capellán.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín
summary: María Sagaste, widow of Nicolás Barrantes and mother of Benito, Jerónima, and Juana Barrantes, settles a lawsuit with Sargento Mayor Don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín. The dispute concerned the ownership of the enslaved woman María and her children Gregorio, Juliana, Salvador, María Manuela, and María, who were originally donated to Barrantes by Doña Juana Moscoso. Sandoval Golfín desists from his claim and, in exchange for $250.00 spent on the litigation, receives ownership of Salvador.

people_involved: Capitán Don José López de la Flor
summary: Captain Don José López de la Flor and Doña Ambrosia Echavarría Navarro obligate themselves for $100.00 at 5% interest to the Cofradía del Santo Rosario, founded in the parish church of Cartago. Captain José Marín, the Mayordomo, provided the funds. They mortgage a cacao plantation with 400 fruit trees on the Matina river and houses in Cartago, which were purchased from the heirs of Doña Mayor de Benavides.

people_involved: Capitán Don José López de la Flor
summary: Captain Don José López de la Flor and Doña Ambrosia Echavarría Navarro obligate themselves for $200.00 at 5% interest to the Cofradía de la Concepción, founded in the Convento de San Francisco. They use the same cacao plantation on the Matina river and houses in Cartago as collateral for this new obligation.

Juan de la Cruz Fonseca, married to Ana López for over 24 years, donates an enslaved Creole woman named María to his wife in recognition of her many good services. María, who is about fifteen years old, was originally purchased by Fonseca from Tomás de Umaña and his wife Doña Laurena de Ortega.

people_involved: Doña Angela de Paz y Flores
summary: Doña Catalina de Monterroso, widow of Ayudante Esteban de Torres and tutor of their minor children, sells a house in Cartago to Don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín and his wife Doña Angela de Paz y Flores for $800.00. This house was originally purchased from Doña Juana Moscoso, widow of Don Juan de Senabria Maldonado, and half of its value was owed to the Capellanía of Luisa Hernández.

people_involved: Doña Angela de Paz y Flores
summary: Don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín and his wife Doña Angela de Paz y Flores obligate themselves for $100.00 at 5% interest to the Cofradía de la Concepción. They mortgage the house in Cartago that they recently purchased from Doña Catalina de Monterroso as collateral for this new debt.

people_involved: Doña Angela de Paz y Flores
summary: Don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín and his wife Doña Angela de Paz y Flores obligate themselves for $400.00 at 5% interest to the Capellanía founded by Luisa Hernández. They use the same house in Cartago, which they recently acquired, as collateral for this obligation.

locations: calle que va de los naboríos al Convento de San Francisco
summary: José de Vargas Machuca and his wife Doña Gertrudis de Alvarado obligate themselves for $1000.00 to the Capellanía founded by Francisco Enciso Hita. They mortgage their residence in Cartago, located on the street from the naboríos to the Convento de San Francisco. The property borders lands of Doña Sebastiana de Alvarado, Gaspar de Chinchilla, and the heirs of Don García de Alvarado. This obligation was later cancelled on April 4, 1690.

Doña Juana de Salazar, widow of Captain Don García de Alvarado, protests against Sargento Benito de Acuña, owner of the frigate 'Nuestra Señora de la Concepción.' Her deceased husband had verbally agreed to relieve Acuña of an obligation to the Royal Official Treasurer of Esparza for wine duties from Panama. Acuña and his agent, Juan López Mundo, demand Salazar guarantee the payment, which she refuses, leading Acuña to withhold a receipt for $508.00 she paid him for other debts of her husband.

Don José de Alvarado and Doña Petronila de Herrera acknowledge a $1000 debt, originally incurred by José de Vargas Machuca and Doña Gertrudis de Alvarado, for a Chaplaincy founded by Francisco de Enciso Hita. To guarantee the debt, they hypothecate properties including houses in Cartago, a cattle ranch in La Lajuela, a horse and mule ranch in Tenorio, and a house, sugar mill, and cane fields in Ujarrás. These properties include some acquired from Doña Juana de Salazar, widow of Don García de Alvarado.

Benito Valerino, a native of Utre in Genoa and son of Agustín Valerino and Betina Bosana, grants power to testate to his brother, Capitán Jerónimo Valerino. He names his mother as his heir, or his brother if his mother is deceased, and appoints Andrés de Esquivel and Sebastián de Zamora as executors.

Benito Valerino reiterates his power to testate to his brother, Capitán Jerónimo Valerino. He declares he was married to Magdalena Vigo and had no children with her before coming to these parts, and states that half of his properties in the Matina valley belong to his brother Jerónimo.

people_involved: Capitán Don Juan de Echeverría Navarro
summary: Juan Antonio de Guevara and Doña Clara de Echavarria Navarro sell a ten-year-old dark-skinned mulato named José to Don Pedro de Alvarado for $150. The mulato was part of the dowry given to Doña Clara by her parents, Doña Ana de Retes and Capitán Don Juan de Echeverría Navarro.

Juan Murillo de Campos, son of the deceased Alférez Andrés Murillo de Campos and Magdalena de Guido, and widower of Doña Lucrecia de Quirós, makes his will. He names his legitimate children Agueda, Gil, Gabriel, Ambrosio, and Catalina, and his natural daughter Luisa Murillo, and appoints Matías de Madrigal (his brother), Nicolás González, and Agustín Guerrero as executors.

Juan Martín de Viegas, a former resident of Cartago, established a Chaplaincy of fifty recited masses in his will dated June 16, 1677, to be funded by a 750-foot cacao plantation. He named Pablo de Otárola Alvarado as the first chaplain, followed by his brothers Francisco and Antonio de Otárola, but due to their youth, Presbítero Don Gaspar Cascante was chosen. Cristóbal López was named patron, and his executors, Cristóbal and Salvador López, carried out the foundation.

José de Pro, a native of Santiago de Chile and son of Antonio de Pro and Catalina de Morales, provides a dowry of $5541 (including a $4700 cacao plantation) and arras of $500 for his wife, Gregoria de Acosta Arévalo. Gregoria is the legitimate daughter of Antonio de Acosta Arévalo and Juana de la Cruz, whose marriage had been annulled.

The closed will of Benito Valerino, executed on day 9, was opened, reiterating previous declarations. Benito declares significant debts to his brother Jerónimo, whom he names as his heir. He details a debt of over $1800 from a failed venture to Puerto Belo with Antonio de Acosta Arévalo, and another $1000 for Jerónimo's expenses in Guatemala pursuing an appeal in a lawsuit against Antonio de Acosta Arévalo.

Matías de Madrigal and his wife Lucrecia de Murillo commit to pay $50 to the Cofradía del Santísimo, having acquired a mill and its site on the river of San Bartolomé de Barba. This obligation carries a 5% annual interest.

On August 31, Matías de Madrigal and Lucrecia de Murillo undertake another obligation, this time to the Cofradía del Rosario, for $150 at 5% annual interest. This obligation is related to the same mill that previously belonged to Juan Murillo de Campos and Doña Lucrecia de Quirós.

On September 2, Matías de Madrigal and Lucrecia de Murillo commit to pay $300 to Jerónimo (described as mentally ill), Luisa, and Isabel Murillo. This sum represents their inheritance share from a mill left by the parents of the grantors, Alférez Andrés Murillo and Magdalena de Guido.

On November 3, Alférez Gregorio de Torres, son of the deceased Ayudante Esteban de Torres and Doña Catalina Monterroso, provides a dowry for his wife, Doña Catalina de Escobar Guijarro. Doña Catalina is the legitimate daughter of the deceased Secretario Juan de Escobar Guijarro and Doña Catalina de Lumbides. Her brother-in-law and tutor, Teniente Juan de Saborío, delivers assets totaling $1013, including a 36-year-old Creole black woman named Luisa valued at $400, and arras of $1000.

On November 9, José García de Quirós, legitimate son of the deceased Capitán Sebastián de Quirós and Doña Isabel de Acuña, provides a dowry for his wife, Josefa. The details of the dowry and Josefa's full name are incomplete in the provided text.

María Machado, the natural daughter of Alférez Antonio Machado and Magdalena Milanés, is recorded with a dote of $578 and arras of $100. This entry likely pertains to her marriage or a related financial arrangement.

Gregorio Matínez, a native of Mairena, Spain, and legitimate son of Francisco Martínez and Ana Dominguez, provides a dote for his wife, María Machado. María is identified as the natural daughter of Alférez Antonio Machado and Magdalena Milanés, with the dote valued at $496 and arras at $600.

Alférez Esteban de Hoces Navarro, acting as Mayordomo of the Cofradía de la Concepción, sells a plot of land to Doña Inés Cerrato de Chaves for $15. The land previously belonged to Francisco López de Ortega and was located next to Margarita Milanés' property.

people_involved: Teniente general don José Pérez de Muro
summary: Antonio Guembe de Villanueva, treasurer of the Santa Bula de la Cruzada for this province and Nicoya, grants power to Teniente general don José Pérez de Muro and Capitán don Matías González Camino. They are authorized to sell approximately 200 mules in Panamá, which Guembe de Villanueva had previously sent there via Capitán don Juan Casco and Sargento Juan Arias.

Doña María de Alvarado, widow of Domingo de Otárola, leases two black slaves (Gregorio and Antonio Caravolt) and two mulatto slaves (Sebastián and Antonio) to Bernardo Cortés for four years. The annual payment for this lease is fifty fanegas of wheat and fifty fanegas of dry corn.

Capitán don Antonio Pacheco, tutor of the minor Don Juan Ruiz de Velazco (son of the deceased Don Juan Ruiz de Velazco), grants power to Capitán don Juan González Camino. Camino is authorized to collect over 7,400 pesos in Panamá from Capitán Juan Tamayo and Capitán Andrés Jaramillo de Andrade.

people_involved: Teniente general don José Pérez de Muro
summary: Capitán Juan Francisco Valenzuela, a resident of Granada, Nicaragua, grants power to Capitanes don Matías and don Juan González Camino, and Teniente general don José Pérez de Muro. The specific purpose of this power is not detailed in this entry.

people_involved: Capitán don Diego Vásquez de Montiel
Capitán don García de Alvarado y Benavides
summary: Capitán Juan Francisco Valenzuela requests the preservation of a receipt issued by Capitán Francisco de Obregón and a legalized testimony. The receipt confirms that Obregón, a resident of Nicoya, sent 153 mules and male animals to Panamá in 1577 under Valenzuela's care, which Valenzuela sold for $52 each. Accounts were settled in Granada in 1579 with the involvement of Capitán don Diego Vásquez de Montiel and Capitán don García de Alvarado y Benavides.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín
summary: Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín grants power to Don Tomás Ponce de León, Capitán don Juan González Camino, and Don José de Alvarado. This power enables them to collect various sums in Panamá and to receive any amounts already collected on his behalf by Don Simón Gonzáles.

Capitán don Matías González Camino commits to repay Capitán don Isidro de Pineda, or in his absence Don Felipe del Castillo, or in their absence Capitán Francisco González Carrasco, the sum of $6464 lent by Pineda. The payment is scheduled 15 days after the arrival of the first fleet from Callao de Lima, carrying royal and private treasure, at the port of Perico in Panamá.

Silvestre Gallegos, currently in this city, assigns and transfers a credit of one thousand pesos to Capitán Juan Francisco Valenzuela. This credit is against Ayudante Juan de Barrientos, a resident of León, Nicaragua, and is payable in Panamá.

Capitán don Antonio de Moya, lieutenant of the Royal Officials' Judge, grants power to Capitán don Matías González Camino, who is traveling to Panamá. Camino is authorized to collect $1531.09 on behalf of the Royal Treasury of Cartago for provisions requested by Don Juan de Gomendia Urrutia, Factor of the Royal Official Judge of San Felipe de Puerto Belo and Panamá, and delivered to the port of Matina.

Don Francisco de Castro, a resident of Cartago departing for Panamá, sells 220 tame pack and cavalry mules to Capitán don Matías González Camino. These mules were sent to Panamá with Pedro del Pozo for a total price of $7480, with $2333 already received and the remainder due five months after the Spanish fleet leaves Panamá.

Alférez Juan Jines de Hinojosa, a resident of Guatemala and natural son of the deceased Juan Jines de Hinojosa, provides a dote for his wife, Gertrudis Guillén Ruiz. Her dotal goods, valued at $950, are delivered by her mother María de Santiago (and her husband Antonio Varela) and her grandfather Pedro de Santiago.

people_involved: Maese de Campo don Alfonso Sáenz
Maestre de Campo don Juan Francisco Sáenz
summary: Maese de Campo don Alfonso Sáenz agrees to pay Alférez Sebastián de Zamora $750, which was embargoed by Royal Justice at Zamora's request. This amount is part of a larger debt owed to Juan Flores, a resident of Villa de los Santos, from the sale of a frigate. Zamora holds a draft on the Royal Treasury of León for this sum, against the accrued salaries of Maestre de Campo don Juan Francisco Sáenz during his governorship.

people_involved: Capitán don Diego Sendín de Sotomayor
summary: Capitán don Diego Sendín de Sotomayor, a native of Madrid and legitimate son of Don Francisco Sendín de Sotomayor and Doña Felipa Sáenz de Quintanilla, provides a dote of $1542 for his wife, Doña Catalina Ortiz. Doña Catalina is the legitimate daughter of Don Miguel Ortiz and Doña Agustina de Córdoba, residents of Cartago.

people_involved: Doña María Arias Maldonado y Velazco
Maestre de Campo don Andrés Arias Maldonado y Velazco
Doña Melchora de Góngora y Córdoba
summary: This entry records the will of Doña María Arias Maldonado y Velazco, widow of Capitán Manuel Pérez. She was a native of Marbella, Spain, and the legitimate daughter of the deceased Maestre de Campo don Andrés Arias Maldonado y Velazco and Doña Melchora de Góngora y Córdoba. She states that she has no children.
Ayudante Juan de Piedra leased a cacaotal with 400 fruit trees in the Matina Valley to Ayudante Antonio de Castro for three years, at a price of $200.

Captain Francisco de Bonilla committed to pay $30 to Manuela, the minor daughter of Ambrosio Ricardo, for a loan provided by her tutor Andrés Méndez. Bonilla mortgaged a cacaotal with 100 trees in the Reventazón Valley as security.

An incomplete dowry letter from Alonso Romero to his wife Ana Micaela detailed assets worth $2558. The dowry included a mulata slave named María (8 years old), various livestock, and a piece of agricultural land in Aserrí Valley, adjacent to land owned by Cristóbal Durán de Chaves.

The Cabildo of Cartago, including Sargento Mayor Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín, Captain Francisco de Bonilla, Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes, Captain Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, and Alférez Cristóbal Durán de Chaves, granted power of attorney to Captain Alonso Arias Romero Murillo. He was authorized to appear before His Majesty and the Council of the Indies to request favors and honors for the city of Cartago.

Nicolás de Céspedes, a perpetual Regidor of Cartago, granted power of attorney to Bernardo de Aparicio, his son Juan Antonio de Aparicio, and his son-in-law Agustín de Ceballos. Their mission was to seek confirmation of his Regidor title, which had been issued by the Royal Audiencia, in the Court of Madrid.

The Cabildo of Cartago, comprising Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín, Francisco de Bonilla, Alonso Arias Romero Murillo, Fernando de Salazar, Nicolás de Céspedes, Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, and Cristóbal Durán de Chaves, granted power of attorney to Santiago Vásquez, a Procurador before the Audiencia of Guatemala.

people_involved: Manuel Gómez de Ocón y Trillo
Francisco Gómez de Ocón y Trillo
summary: Captain Juan Alvarez de Ulate, acting as executor for the deceased Captain Manuel Gómez de Ocón y Trillo, ratified a public auction sale of a cattle ranch in La Ciruela. He then resold the ranch, which Captain Miguel de Omonte y Robledo had initially purchased for $700, back to Omonte y Robledo for $1100, thereby fulfilling the deceased's will and paying the maternal inheritance to Francisco Gómez de Ocón y Trillo.

Diego de Ibarra and his wife Ana de Retes sold a 24-year-old Acara slave named Martín to Captain José de Alvarado for $350. Martín was part of the estate of Ana de Retes' first husband, Juan de Echavarría Navarro, who had inherited him from his mother María de Sandoval Ocampo. Ana de Retes herself inherited Martín from Beneficiado Domingo de Echavartía, a former priest of Cartago.

A dowry letter was issued from Tomás Mazedo Ponce de León, a native of Cádiz and son of the late Diego Mazedo Ponce de León and Ana Núñez Francisco, in favor of his wife Fabiana de Sandoval y Guevara, daughter of Captain José de Guevara Sandoval and Inés de Sandoval Ocampo, for a total of $2044.
Andrés Calvo committed to pay $535 to José de Vargas Machuca.
An incomplete record from 1677 mentions Alférez Antonio de Urrutia residing in the city.
Benito Valerino is granted power to transport 100 mules to Panama and sell them as he sees fit.
Benito Valerino grants power to Antonio de Urrutia to administer a cacao hacienda owned by Valerino on the Matina riverbank.
Antonio de Urrutia and Benito Valerino form a partnership for the sale of mules and cacao.

Don Juan Francisco Valenzuela, as heir to the deceased Don Francisco de Castro, empowers Don Juan González Camino, Don José Pérez de Muro, and Don José de Vargas Machuca to collect debts owed to Castro in Panama.

Doña Juana Sánchez, widow of Sargento Domingo de Alvarado, grants power to Domingo de Otárola to collect any amounts due to her from the succession of her father, Bartolomé Sánchez, and to claim any assets her father received as dowry and arras when he married her deceased mother, Doña Isabel de Caravajal.

people_involved: Don José Sáenz de las Cubillas
summary: Domingo de Otárola, acting on behalf of Doña Juana Sánchez, requests that the death records of Bartolomé Sánchez be brought before the Governor. Governor Sáenz instructs his Lieutenant of Esparza, Don José Sáenz de las Cubillas, to remit these documents.
Don Matías González Camino obligates himself to pay Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes $2000, which Céspedes had lent him. This obligation was later cancelled.

Don Juan Francisco Valenzuela sells 967 mules to Capitanes Don Matías González Camino and Don José Pérez de Muro for $34086.75, payable within two years or upon the arrival of the first galleons from Spain at Puerto Belo. He also sells two slaves, Simón de la Torre (approx. 20, bought from Doña Ana Jirón de Alvarado of Granada) and Francisco de Acevedo (approx. 20, bought from José de Acevedo of Segovia), for $900. A marginal note from October 10, 1700, indicates the obligation was cancelled after Cristóbal Martín de Cubero, representing Valenzuela's widow's executor, claimed $10199 from Matías's estate, embargoing $8850 owed by Diego Bernal of Panama, and a cacao plantation in Matina. It also notes satisfaction for $1907 Matías owed Francisco Castro, for whom Valenzuela was executor.

Antonio Guembe de Villanueva, a resident of León, obligates himself to pay $728.3 reales to Teniente Juan de Balmaceda, a resident of Realejo and treasurer of the Santa Bula de la Cruzada in Nicaragua and Costa Rica, or to his brother Simón de Balmaceda, who holds the same position in Segovia.
Don Diego de Ibarra grants power to Don Matías González Camino to collect $2033 from Antonio de Andrade.

people_involved: Maese de Campo don Lorenzo González Calderón
summary: Antonio Guembe de Villanueva obligates himself to Maese de Campo Don Lorenzo González Calderón, a resident of León, for $1387, mortgaging 50 mules as security.

people_involved: Alférez Antonio López de San Román Ladrón de Guevara
summary: Don Matías González Camino owes Alférez Antonio López de San Román Ladrón de Guevara, a resident of Cartago, $500, which he is to pay in Panama.

people_involved: Teniente General don José Pérez de Muro
Capitán don José López de la Flor
Capitán don Miguel de Echavarría Navarro
summary: Capitán Don Antonio de Moya, appointed Lieutenant of Royal Official Judge in Cartago, names several individuals as guarantors for up to $2000, with each person responsible for $200.

Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín, holding the titles of Alférez Mayor and Alcalde ordinario, and encomendero in Tucurrique and Diriá, renounced his encomienda in Diriá. This action followed the confirmation of his Alférez Mayor position by S.M., with the proceeds (caídos) from the encomienda, collected and deposited in the Royal Treasury of Granada, designated for the fortification of the province or other Royal service expenses.

Alférez Antonio de Urrutia and Benito Valerino entered into an agreement. Valerino acted as guarantor for Urrutia's $3700-00 debt to Luis de Abarca Paniagua, a resident of Guatemala, and received 100 mules to sell in Panama to cover this credit. Additionally, Valerino owed Urrutia $1074-00 as a balance of accounts, which he committed to pay.

Doña Inés Velásquez y Rosales sold a 28-year-old mulato slave named José de Ocampo to don Pedro Lorenzo Venegas for $250-00. She had previously acquired José de Ocampo through purchase from Catalina de Palacios, who was the widow of Marcos de Chinchilla.
Juan de Ugalde, a resident of Panama, sold two enslaved black men, Antonio, aged 21, and Andrés, aged 23, to Alférez Alonso Mateo Hurtado, a resident of Esparza. The transaction was for $800-00.

locations: San Francisco del pueblo de los Naboríos
summary: Alférez José Maroto and his wife, doña Luisa Calvo, obligated themselves for $400-00 to a Capellanía founded by don Francisco Enciso Hita. They mortgaged houses in the new street to San Francisco del pueblo de los Naboríos, which already had existing mortgages of $400-00 to a Capellanía founded by Licenciado Marcos Machado and $200-00 to the minor children of Antonio Machado and Gregoria de Abarca.

Don Antonio de Moya, Teniente Juez Oficial de la Real Hacienda, was required to provide an additional $750-00 in bond. He named don Antonio Pacheco, don Alonso García, and don José Calderón as his guarantors for this obligation.

Capitán don Antonio Pacheco, acting as tutor for the minor Juan Ruiz de Velazco, obligated himself to pay $200-oo to don José Pérez de Muro, who was representing Maese de Campo don Lorenzo González Calderón. This payment was for mules that the deceased don Juan Ruiz de Velazco had transported to Panama on behalf of the also deceased don Francisco de Herrera, whose executor and heir was González Calderón.

Doña Eugenia de Abarca, widow of Alférez Tomás Calvo, donated a cacao hacienda to her son, Capitán Miguel Calvo. The hacienda, located on the Suerre river in a place called La Reventazón, comprised about 500 trees and bordered a cacao plantation belonging to the heirs of Alonso de Bonilla.

Don Matías González Camino granted power of attorney to don José Pérez de Muro and don José de Vargas Machuca. This authorization allowed them to sell consignments of mules he had sent to Panama and to invest the proceeds in Castilian or local clothing, slaves, jewels, or gold and silver.
An existing chaplaincy, patroned by Alférez Esteban de Oses Navarro, is mentioned, involving cacao in Matina and a 5% census.

Capitán Francisco de Bonilla issued a dowry letter to his wife, Leonor María de Vargas, detailing a dowry of $1274, which included an enslaved 15-year-old criollo named Manuel, and a marriage portion of $1500. The document also mentions their parents and Leonor's current marriage to Sebastián de Aguirre.

An inventory was made of the $8850 worth of goods Capitán Francisco de Bonilla brought to his marriage with Leonor María de Vargas. These assets included old cacao plantations located along the Reventazón River and in Matina, near the haciendas of Iscaris and Santa Rosa.
In 1680, Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes, a councilman of Cartago, granted power of attorney to Sebastián de Zamora, a Procurador Síndico, and to Esteban de Oses Navarro.

In 1681, Antonio Guembe de Villanueva, Treasurer Receiver of the Santa Cruzada and a resident of León de Nicaragua, became indebted to Juan de Balmaceda, Treasurer General and also a resident of León, for 728 pesos and 3 reales related to the administration of the Holy Bull, mortgaging 30 mules.

In January 1680, Isabel Alvarez, widow of Capitán Manuel Gómez, donated 12 breeding mares, 3 head of cattle, and a silver salt shaker to her sister, Ambrosia de Benavides. The document also identifies their parents as Sebastián de Benavides and Ana María Sánchez.

In July 1680, Alférez Antonio Calderón issued a dowry letter for $355 to his wife, Isabel Alvarez, who is identified as the widow of Capitán Manuel Gómez and the legitimate daughter of Gregorio Alvarez and Ana María Sánchez.

In August 1680, Doña Josefa de Moya donated a 5-year-old enslaved mulata named Gertrudis, daughter of enslaved mulata Paula, to her niece, also named Doña Josefa de Moya. The niece is the legitimate daughter of Capitán Antonio de Moya and Doña Isabel de Alvarado.
In September 1680, Capitán Jerónimo Valerino granted power of attorney to Alférez Sebastián de Zamora.

In October 1680, Alférez Antonio de Urrutia, a native of Orrio, Vizcaya, made his will in "this city." He had financial dealings with Capitán Luis Abarca Paniagua and his wife Magdalena de Sierra from Guatemala, and was owed goods from the deceased Benito Valerino and Capitán Juan Sáenz of Granada. His parents, Domingo de Urrutia and María de Ibarra, were designated as his heirs.

In November 1680, Teniente Juan de Bonilla obligated himself for $1000 to the chaplaincy established by Alférez Francisco de Enciso Hita. He mortgaged a cacao plantation along the Reventazón River, which he inherited from his parents, Sargento Mayor Alonso de Bonilla and Juana Benita Calvo, and which bordered the cacao plantations of his siblings, Alonso and Josefa Sebastiana de Bonilla.

In December 1680, Don José de Escalante Paniagua, acting as substitute attorney for Francisco de Velzunegui, a merchant from Guatemala, sold a 24-year-old enslaved mulato named Domingo de la Trinidad to Don Juan Alonso Lanini.

An unnamed ayudante purchased an enslaved person from Bachiller don Tomás de Revalorio, Beneficiado del partido de Mita, for $350, payable in Panamá. Lanini declared that the enslaved person belongs to don Juan Francisco Sáenz, the Governor of the province. A power of attorney from Velzunegui, issued in Antequera de Nueva España, was attached to the transaction.

Nicolás Chacón, the legitimate son of Martín Chacón and Luisa Hernández, residents of Cartago, provided a dowry of $573 to his wife, Josefa González. Josefa is the legitimate daughter of Juan González and María de Espinosa.

people_involved: Capitán Antonio López de San Román Ladrón de Guevara
summary: Capitán Antonio López de San Román Ladrón de Guevara granted a general power of attorney for collections to Capitanes Tomás Martínez de Urizar and Juan Antonio de Guevara. Both recipients of the power of attorney were residents of Panamá.
Juan Antonio de Guevara and his wife, doña Clara de Echavarría, committed to an obligation of $2000 in favor of Capitán Juan González Vesa. Capitán Vesa was a resident of Granada, Nicaragua.
Antonio Guembe de Villunueva entered into an obligation to Bartolomé López Morillo, a resident of Panamá, for the sum of $2125.

Capitán Francisco Ramírez de Ruimayor, who was involved in a lawsuit against the estate of don Juan Ruiz de Velasco and against don Antonio Pacheco, agreed to a settlement. Pacheco was the husband of doña Luisa de Abarca, the former wife of Ruiz Velasco and tutor of their son Juan Ruiz, and the settlement was for $230 regarding 8 mule beasts.

people_involved: Teniente general don José Pérez de Muro
summary: Capitán don Francisco de Obregón, a resident of Nicoya, granted power of attorney to don Jorge de Alvarado and Teniente general don José Pérez de Muro. Both Alvarado and Pérez de Muro were preparing to depart for the city of Panamá.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don Juan López de la Flor
summary: Capitán don Francisco de Obregón, as the debtor, and don Jorge de Alvarado, as the guarantor, committed to pay Maestre de Campo don Juan López de la Flor, who resided in Panamá, $500. This payment was for a loan that Juan Martín Lovato, a resident of Cartago, had previously extended to Obregón.

people_involved: Doña Juana de Vera y Sotomayor
summary: Doña Juana de Vera y Sotomayor, widow of Capitán don Gil de Alvarado, sold an 8-year-old Creole enslaved boy named Francisco to her son, Capitán don José de Alvarado, for $250. The payment was structured as an annual 5% censo, and she mortgaged houses in Cartago, near the plaza and the street leading from the Cabildo to San Nicolás, bordering property of her sister-in-law, Jerónima de Retes.

people_involved: Doña Juana de Vera y Sotomayor
summary: Doña Juana de Vera y Sotomayor sold a 5-year-old enslaved girl named Bartola to her son, don Pedro de Alvarado, for $250, with the payment structured as an annual 5% censo. She mortgaged a cacao plantation in the Barbilla valley, which bordered the Barbilla river and another cacao plantation belonging to her mother-in-law, doña Juana de Ortega.

people_involved: Doña Juana de Vera y Sotomayor
summary: Doña Juana de Vera y Sotomayor established a Chaplaincy for recited masses with a capital of $500, owed by her sons don José and don Pedro de Alvarado at 5% annual interest. She designated her grandson, Pablo de Otárola, son of the late don Domingo de Otárola and doña María de Alvarado, as the first Chaplain, with a succession plan for her other descendants. Padre don Gregorio de Moya was named interim Chaplain until Pablo's ordination, and don Pedro de Alvarado was appointed patron.

Don Matías González Camino, the senior ordinary Alcalde and Teniente de Gobernador, arranged for Juan de Moro, an orphan, to be apprenticed to Francisco de Rojas, a master tailor. The apprenticeship was set for five years, during which Rojas was obligated to train Moro to become a skilled tailor.

people_involved: Capitán don Fernando de Carrión Villasante
summary: Presbítero Agustín de Torres, the Cura of Cartago, sold a plot of land in León de Nicaragua to Capitán don Fernando de Carrión Villasante for $100, at a 5% censo. The solar, located at the corner facing the Main Church and Cabildo, belonged to the Chaplaincy founded by Juan de Morales Dávila, of which Torres was both patron and Chaplain.

people_involved: doña María Josefa Ponce de León
summary: Bernardo Sarmiento de Sotomayor, a native of Peru and son of don Francisco Sarmiento Sotomayor and doña María Josefa Ponce de León, provided a dowry of $7211 to his wife, doña Antonia María Venegas. Doña Antonia is the legitimate daughter of Sargento Mayor don Lorenzo Venegas and doña Antonia de Ocampo Golfín, and the dowry was delivered by her grandmother and doña Jerónima de Retes, the widow of Sargento Mayor Venegas.
Alférez Francisco Fernández and his wife, Eugenia Rodríguez, obligated themselves to the Chaplaincy of Las Animas for $100. As security for this obligation, they mortgaged some houses.

people_involved: doña Juana de Villar y el Pino
summary: Alférez don Fernando Núñez Bejarano, a native of Comayagua, made his will. He was the son of don Juan de Medina Bejarano and doña Inés de Lara, married to doña Baltasara Vásquez Coronado with minor children Juan and Inés. He had a previous marriage to doña Juana de Villar y el Pino, a native of Segovia, with whom he had a son, don Feliciano Núñez Bejarano.
Baltasar Gómez provided a dowry of $574 to his wife, Antonia de Aguilar. Antonia is the legitimate daughter of Juan de Aguilar and Eugenia Vásquez.

Francisco de Quirós, the legitimate son of the deceased Capitán García de Quirós and Juana de Chinchilla, made his will. He was married to doña María Angulo Gascón and had three daughters, doña María, doña Petronila, and doña Manuela, with another child expected. He owned a cattle ranch located on the Segundo River.

people_involved: Juan Ruiz de Velazco (father of minor)
summary: Capitán Antonio Pacheco and his wife, Luisa de Abarca, obligated themselves to Juan Ruiz de Velazco (minor) for $2175.50 from his inheritance. They mortgaged a cacao plantation in Matina as collateral for this obligation.

José Narváez, a native of Antequera, granted a dowry of $1793 to his wife, Juana de Sojo, a widow. The dowry included a country house in the Barba valley, previously owned by Diego de Artieda Chirinos, and five enslaved mulatos: Magdalena (50 years), Francisco (20 years), Agustín (16 years), Ana (12 years), and Antonio (8 years).
Luis Cascante de Rojas sold an 8-year-old mulato named Juan to Capitán Rodrigo Vásquez Coronado, a resident of Esparza, for $100.

An incomplete dowry letter was recorded for Alonso Romero, a native of Paterna del Campo, Spain, son of Alonso Romero (father) and Ana de Baza. The dowry was in favor of his wife, Micaela Durán de Chaves, daughter of Alférez Cristóbal Durán de Chaves and Ana Cardoso.

Juan Muñoz Bermúdez, residing in Cartago, granted a dowry of $2143 to his wife, Jerónima López, daughter of Sargento Francisco López Serrano and María de Sibaja. Francisco González served as the escribano for this transaction.
Gabriel Rodríguez, a native of Ayamonte, Spain, son of the deceased Miguel Rodríguez and Ana Rodríguez, made his will. Capitán Juan López Mundo, from Panama, was named as his heir.

Capitán Esteban de la Mata, a resident of Esparza, granted power of attorney to Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes. This power was for Céspedes to conclude a lawsuit that Mata was pursuing as the guardian of the minor Francisco Clanches.

Don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín, Alférez Mayor and ordinary Alcalde, placed Pascual de León, a 12-year-old orphan, with Mateo Hernández, a master saddler. This arrangement was for a period of 4 years.

Manuel de Santillán, a resident of Cartago traveling to Guatemala, and his wife Eugenia Gertrudis Muñoz Hidalgo, granted power of attorney to Licenciado Diego de Angulo Gascón, the parish priest. The power was to collect sums owed to Capitán Alonso García, the grantor's first husband, and to establish a chaplaincy for recited masses.

Manuel de Santillán and Eugenia Gertrudis Muñoz Hidalgo sold a plot of land on the royal street in Cartago to Capitán José Pérez de Muro for $100. The land belonged to Eugenia as part of her dowry when she married her deceased first husband, Capitán Alonso García.
Manuel de Santillán and Eugenia Gertrudis Muñoz Hidalgo sold a cacao plantation in Matina, containing a thousand trees and a cleared area, to Sebastiana Calvo, the mother of Eugenia, for $800.

Alférez Juan Cascante de Rojas made his will, naming his brother, Presbítero Licenciado Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, as his heir. He was the legitimate son of the deceased Alférez Juan Cascante de Rojas (father) and María del Castillo.

Antonio Varela, a native of Chantada, Galicia, son of Antonio Varela (father) and Dominga, made his will. He had been married for 14 years to María de Santiago, daughter of Diego Santiago and widow of Juan Guillén. María had three children from her first marriage (Domingo, María, Sebastián) and five children with Antonio (Francisco, Diego, Blas, Julián, Angela).

Alférez Juan Patricio de Sandoval obligated himself for $50 to the minor children of the deceased María de Zamora and José de Gallegos. He provided a cattle ranch in Esparza, at Corroscobí, with 250 cattle, 50 mares, a breeding donkey, houses, and corrals as guarantee. The money was received from Francisco de Rojas, María de Zamora's executor. This obligation was cancelled on December 4, 1715, by Pedro de Arroyo, husband of Manuela Gallegos.

Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes obligated himself for $50 (at 5% annual interest) to the minor children of the deceased María de Zamora and José de Gallegos. He provided a cattle ranch with houses, corrals, and 200 cattle in La Lajuela, Barba valley, as guarantee.

Juan de Ibarra and his wife Francisca Calvo obligated themselves for $100 (at 5% interest) to the Confraternity of Nuestra Señora del Rosario in Cartago, which included the chaplaincy founded by Ana de Medrano. They provided houses in Cartago as guarantee, which Francisca had received as dowry from her father, Tomás Calvo, when she married her first husband, Ignacio Loynaz. Capitán José Marín Laguna, Mayordomo of the Confraternity, delivered the money.

Teniente José de Escalante Paniagua and his wife Manuela de Vida Martel obligated themselves for $200 (at 3% annual interest) to the chaplaincy founded by Andrés López de Céspedes and Magdalena de la Portilla. They provided a house behind the main church, acquired from María de Mora, widow of Alférez Juan Vásquez de Coronado, as guarantee. Padre Gaspar Cascante de Rojas was the chaplain.
Juana de Figueroa Moscoso, widow of Capitán Juan de Senabria Maldonado, sold a mulata to Miguel Calvo, a cleric for minors. The record of this transaction is incomplete.

A mulata named María, 21 years old, with her infant son Miguel, was sold for $550. Eugenia de Abarca, widow of Tomás Calvo and mother of the buyer, paid $350 upfront and committed to pay the remaining $200.
José de Rivera, a master carpenter and turner, took Gaspar Gallegos, a 9-year-old minor and son of the deceased María de Zamora, as an apprentice for seven years to teach him the trade.

people_involved: Gobernador don Francisco Antonio de Rivas y Contreras
summary: Capitán don Matías González Camino recognized a debt to Gobernador don Francisco Antonio de Rivas y Contreras. This debt originated from Capitán Juan Francisco Valenzuela owing Sargento Mayor Diego de Almendares $1239, which González Camino had agreed to pay, and Rivas y Contreras had paid on his behalf. González Camino committed to repay Rivas y Contreras in Panamá.

Don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín, patron of the Chaplaincy founded by his grandfather Capitán Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, appointed his nephew, don Francisco de Salazar, a minor cleric, as Chaplain, enabling him to be ordained as a priest.

Alférez Valentín de Garay, a resident of León and departing for Panamá, incurred a debt of $304.5 to Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes for provisions like hardtack, meat, and other supplies for a mule shipment.
Alférez Cristóbal Durán de Chaves committed to repay Juan de Vega $150 that he had borrowed, with the repayment to be made in Panamá.

people_involved: Doña Ana de Salazar y Peralta
summary: Capitán don Matías González Camino sold a large cattle site in the valley of this city, specifically in the Agua Caliente area, to Sargento Juan González for $529. The property, which González Camino received as a dowry from his father-in-law Regidor don Fernando de Salazar upon marrying doña Ana de Salazar y Peralta, included a house, a cattle pen, a plantain grove, 133 cattle, and 4 tame horses.

Lorenzo de Mora, son of Sargento Luis Rodríguez, made his will. He had been married for 17 years to Elena de las Alas, daughter of Tomás de las Alas, and they had nine children: Juan, Diego, Cristóbal, Lúcas, Bartolomé, Ventura, Manuela, Juana, and Clara.
Alférez Cristóbal Durán de Chaves committed to pay Juan de Vega $255 in Panamá.
Alférez Cristóbal Durán de Chaves committed to pay Diego de la Trinidad, a resident of Panamá, or his representative Capitán Juan López Mundo, $100 that he owed.

Capitán Jerónimo Valerino, as executor and heir of his brother Benito Valerino, granted power of attorney to don Matías González Camino to claim payment from Juan Bracamonte, a resident of Panamá, for a debt related to mules sold on credit by Benito Valerino.
José Falcón, a master carpenter, took Juan Fonseca, a minor boy and son of Dionisio de Fonseca, as an apprentice.

people_involved: Ana de Espinoza (wife of Ayudante F.H.B.)
Ana de Espinoza (mother of Ana de Espinoza wife)
summary: Ayudante Francisco Hernández Barquero, the oldest Alcalde of the Santa Hermandad, made his will. He was a native of Fresnedos, Extremadura, son of Francisco Hernández and Catalina Alonso. He had been married for 35 years to Ana de Espinoza, daughter of the late Gabriel de Aguilar and Ana de Espinoza, and they had eight children. He also raised his granddaughter Margarita Mora and an orphan named Antonio, 7 years old.

Alférez don Francisco de Espinoza and his wife doña Sebastiana de Bonilla committed to an obligation in favor of the Chaplaincy founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela, whose first Chaplain was the Licenciado.

people_involved: Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: An unnamed grantor, who inherited from Alonso de Bonilla and Juana Benita Calvo, mortgaged a 500-tree cacao plantation on the Reventazón river and a house in Cartago. The mortgage was granted to Marcos Machado and Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas for $150 at a 5% annual census. The cacao plantation was adjacent to those of her sisters, doña María, doña Juana, and doña Josefa de Bonilla.

Nicolás de Bonilla leased a 500-tree cacao plantation, known as 'el cacaotal viejo,' in the Reventazón valley to Jacinto de Mora Salado for four years. The annual rent was $120 in cacao, with $100 paid in the valley and $20 in Cartago. The plantation was located near those of his brothers, Capitán Francisco de Bonilla and Alférez Antonio de Bonilla, as well as those of don Francisco de Espinoza and doña Josefa de Bonilla.

people_involved: doña Juana de Vera y Sotomayor
doña Juana de Vera y Sotomayor (the elder)
Sargento Mayor don Bartolomé Arias Maldonado
summary: Doña Juana de Vera y Sotomayor, legitimate daughter of the deceased Sargento Mayor García Ramiro Corajo and doña Juana de Vera y Sotomayor, made her testament. She was the widow of Capitán don Gil de Alvarado, whom she married over 50 years ago, and listed their eight legitimate children and their spouses. She also mentioned her granddaughter, doña Isabel de Alvarado, and Isabel, a mulata she raised and married to Antonio de la O.

locations: Vega del río que llaman de la Lajuela
people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Miguel Gómez de Lara
summary: Capitán don José de Alvarado obligated himself for $200 to a Chaplaincy founded by Capitán don Matías González Camino for the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora del Rosario, a sum previously charged to Capitán don Diego de Ibarra. He mortgaged a cattle ranch in the Lajuela river valley in Barba, which he had purchased from doña Juana de Salazar, widow of Capitán don García de Alvarado. This obligation was later cancelled on November 8, 1687, before Sargento Mayor don Miguel Gómez de Lara.

locations: Ciudad del Espíritu Santo de Esparza
people_involved: Capitán José de la Aya y Bolívar
summary: José de Quesada and doña Francisca Sánchez de Orozco, his wife, added an obligation to a census deed they granted on February 5 of this year, related to the auction of the deceased Francisco Rodríguez de Sosa's rural estates. The new obligation stipulated that they must deliver the principal and interest to the minor heirs as they come of age. This was granted before Capitán José de la Aya y Bolívar in Esparza, with Alcalde González Camino noting the main deed was accumulated with inventory records.

people_involved: Capitán don José López de la Flor
Sargento Mayor don Juan Alonso Lanini
summary: Sargento Diego de Quesada and Alférez Alonso de Quesada, brothers, resolved a dispute over the partition of a cacao plantation they established in the Matina valley. Alférez Alonso became the owner of the main plantation, while Sargento Diego received 600 fruit-bearing cacao trees from the downstream side, bordering Capitán Juan Antonio de Castro's property. The partition was to be overseen by Sargento Mayor don Juan Alonso Lanini and Capitán don Antonio Pacheco.

On October 24, Lorenzo de Villarreal, legitimate son of José de Villarreal and Ana José de Aguilar, provided a dowry letter for his future wife, Luisa González. Luisa is the legitimate daughter of Sargento Juan González Ochoa and María de Espinoza. Their marriage was scheduled for the following day, October 25, with a dowry of $1124 and arras of $300.

locations: Pueblo de San Juan de Herrera de los Naboríos
people_involved: Capitán José de la Aya y Bolívar
summary: On November 6, Juana de Salazar, widow of Capitán don García de Alvarado, sold adobe and tile houses in Cartago to Licenciado Agustín de Torres. The houses, inherited from Antonio Machado's heirs, were located on the street leading from San Juan de Herrera de los Naboríos to the San Francisco Convent, bordering properties of doña Gertrudis de Alvarado, Capitán José Marín Laguna, Sebastián de Benavides, and Capitán José de la Aya y Bolívar. The property was encumbered by a Chaplaincy founded by Licenciado Marcos Machado, whose patron was Alférez Esteban de Oses Navarro, and sold for $1300.

On November 9, Antonio de Acosta Arévalo and doña Josefa de Santiago Aguilar, his wife, sold an estate and land for cattle in the valley of Cartago, on the road to Ujarraz, to Alférez Francisco de Salas and Leonor Chacón, his wife. The property, which included straw houses, was originally purchased from Manuel de Mora Salado and doña Juana Bautista Torres Capelaso. The sale price was $150, and the existing mortgage on the property was transferred to the houses of doña María de Aguilar, mother of doña Josefa.

people_involved: Doña Juana de Vera y Sotomayor
summary: Don Jorge de Alvarado and his wife, Doña Gertrudis de Echavarría Navarro, sold a 20-year-old mulato slave named José to Captain and Sergeant Major Don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín for $500. Don Jorge had inherited José from his deceased mother, Doña Juana de Vera y Sotomayor.

José de Quesada and his wife, Doña Francisca Sánchez de Orozco, residents of Espíritu Santo de Esparza, transferred a cattle ranch to Don Jorge de Alvarado and Doña Gertrudis de Echavarría Navarro. The ranch, located near the Gamalotal river in Esparza, included 15 cows, 130 mares and foals, a breeding donkey, 7 mule beasts, and houses/corrals. This property was originally sold at public auction after the deaths of Francisco Rodríguez de Sosa and Ana de Santiago, with the proceeds benefiting their minor children, for whom Don Jorge and his wife assumed the principal and annual interest.

Captain Don Esteban de Moya and his wife, Doña Rafaela de Alvarado, obligated themselves for $1000 at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by Doña Inés Pereira, with Lic. José de Lumbides serving as Chaplain. They mortgaged three-quarters of a house and lot in the main plaza of Cartago, adjacent to the homes of Doña Jerónima de Retes and Doña María de Retes.

people_involved: Teniente de Caballos Juan de Gamboa
summary: Francisco Falla, a native of Cádiz and son of Jacinto Falla and Antonia de Rivera, provided a dowry for his wife, Doña Mariana Solano, daughter of the deceased Lieutenant Pedro Solano and Doña María Vásquez de Coronado. The dowry, received from Doña Mariana's stepfather Juan de Gamboa, totaled $935 and included a 6-year-old mulata slave named Dominga, a house and land in Aserrí, and a half lot in the Soledad neighborhood. Francisco López de Astorga and Alférez Francisco Solano served as valuators.

Pedro Jaimes de las Salas, son of the deceased Andrés Jaimes de las Salas and Francisca de Mendoza, provided a dowry of $359 for his fiancée Leonor de Alvarado. Leonor, an orphan, was raised by Captain José de Vargas Machuca, who provided the dowry goods. Their marriage was scheduled for the following day.

Alférez Pedro Martínez de Colina sold a flour mill in the Aserrí valley to Alférez Juan Vázquez de Coronado for $200. Pedro had acquired the mill in the auction of his deceased mother Doña Isidora Sambrano's assets. $100 of the price was a lien on the mill for the Cofradía de la Concepción, and the buyer was obligated for the other $100 to a Chaplaincy founded by the seller, with Don Diego Campos de Quirós as its patron and chaplain.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don José de Sandoval Ocampo
summary: Juan de Villalobos sold a straw-roofed house with a lot in Cartago to Lic. Don Diego de Angulo, the city's priest, for $224. Villalobos had purchased the property from Alférez Cristóbal de Quesada, a resident of Esparza. The property bordered houses and lots belonging to Captain Don Matías González Camino, Doña María Ramiro (widow of Sergeant Major Don José de Sandoval Ocampo), and Doña María de Sandoval Ocampo (widow of Captain Alonso Arias).

Alférez Juan Vázquez de Coronado obligated himself for $100 at 5% interest to the Cofradía de la Concepción. This obligation was secured by a mill he had purchased from Alférez Pedro Martínez de Colina for $200. Alférez Sebastián de Garita, the confraternity's steward, accepted the obligation.

Alférez Juan Vázquez de Coronado obligated himself for $100 at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by Pedro Martínez Colina, with Presbítero Don Diego Campos de Quirós as the Chaplain. This obligation was imposed on the mill he had purchased from Colina.

Alférez Francisco Solano and his wife, Juana de las Alas, obligated themselves for $100 at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by Luisa Hernández in the San Francisco convent. They received the funds from Juan Antonio de Guevara, the convent's syndic, and secured the obligation on a house they owned.

An obligation of $100 at 5% was made in favor of the Capellanía founded by Catalina Gutiérrez in the San Francisco convent. Juan Ant. de Guevara, the syndic, received the funds, and a house was mortgaged, located near Ujarrás.

people_involved: Doña Juana de Vera y Soto Mayor
summary: Capitán José de Vargas Machuca, Alguacil Mayor of the Holy Office of the Inquisition and native of Cádiz, made his will. He listed debts owed to him by several individuals in Panama and 'esta ciudad', acknowledged a debt to his wife Doña Gertrudis de Alvarado, and named his sister Doña Sebastiana de Alvarado. He also listed his enslaved people and their children, and founded a Capellanía, naming his 13-year-old son, Don Antonio de Vargas Machuca, as the first chaplain, with provisions for his grandchildren (specifically Pablo de Otálora) if Antonio did not get ordained. His executors were Capitán don Matías González Camino, don José Pérez de Muro, and Alférez don Sebastián de Garita.

Ana López, daughter of deceased Juan López Rubio and María de Herrera, made her will. She mentioned her sisters Juana Gómez and María de las Nieves, and her adopted son Luis de la Cruz, whom she and her husband Juan de la Cruz Fonseca raised. She founded a Capellanía, naming Sebastián de Oses Navarro as the chaplain, with Luis de la Cruz as the successor if he studied, otherwise the poorest priest.

Capitán José de Vargas Machuca made a codicil to his will while traveling to Panama for medical treatment. He appointed Don Jorge de Alvarado and Don José de Guzmán as his executors in case he died during the journey, as they were also traveling to Panama.

people_involved: Doña Juana de Vera y Soto Mayor
summary: Capitán don Matías González Camino, as an executor of the deceased Capitán José de Vargas Machuca, founded a Capellanía for recited masses as per the will. The capital was $500, and Don Antonio de Vargas Machuca, son of the deceased, was named chaplain, with similar conditions regarding the grandchildren of don Gil de Alvarado and Doña Juana de Vera y Soto Mayor.

people_involved: Mtre. de Campo don Alfonso Sáenz Vázquez
Sargento Mayor don Juan Alonso Lanini
Capitán don Alonso de la Vega Cabral
summary: Mtre. de Campo don Alfonso Sáenz Vázquez and Sargento Mayor don Juan Alonso Lanini obligated themselves for $500 at 5% to the Capellanía. Sáenz Vázquez mortgaged a cacao plantation in Matina, and Lanini mortgaged a house in 'esta ciudad'. A marginal note from June 16, 1705, indicates that Licenciado Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, the current chaplain, canceled this obligation as it was transferred to Manuel García de Hergueta and Doña Antonia Loinaz y Istueta on October 22, 1704.

Doña Gertrudis de Alvarado, widow of Capitán José de Vargas Machuca, and on behalf of her minor son Don Antonio de Vargas Machuca (under 14), granted general power of attorney to Capitán don Matías González Camino, who was departing for Panama. In his absence, the power would go to Capitán don Juan González Camino, also traveling to Panama.

A dowry letter was issued for Miguel de Brenes, son of Mateo de Brenes and Agustina Fernández del Pueyo, in favor of Mariana Aguilar Calderón, daughter of Alférez Antonio Aguilar Calderón and the deceased Clara Montero de Espinosa. Their marriage was scheduled for the following day, October 8, with a dowry of $700 and a bridal gift (arras) of $200.

Juan de Meza and Jerónimo Valerino settled a lawsuit regarding the ownership of a cacao plantation in the Matina valley, specifically in the area called 'de las Carreras'. Valerino became the owner of the cacaotal and paid Meza $200.

locations: costa de la mar del Norte
summary: Antonio de Acosta Arévalo sold a cacao plantation of 2000 trees located on the Matina riverbank, on the North Sea coast, to Don Pedro de Alvarado. The property bordered a cacaotal owned by Domingo.

locations: Ciudad de los Reyes del Perú
people_involved: doña Catalina de Torres y Portugal
summary: Francisco Gutiérrez de Velazco, native of Ciudad de los Reyes del Perú, established a dowry of $580-00 and arras of $500-00 for his wife, Baltasara de los Reyes Falcón, following their marriage. He is the son of Francisco Gutiérrez de Velazco and doña Catalina de Torres y Portugal, and she is the daughter of Ayudante José Falcón and Ana María Romero.

Lieutenant of Cavalry don Gil de Alvarado sold an 18-year-old enslaved Black woman named Juana to his sister, doña Gertrudis de Alvarado, a widow, for $500-00. Juana was inherited from their mother, doña Juana de Vera.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don José de Sandoval Ocampo
Lic. don Diego Campos de Quirós
summary: Sergeant Major don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín, Alférez Mayor, acknowledged censos on a cattle ranch in Esparza, inherited from his parents, Sargento Mayor don José de Sandoval Ocampo and doña Isabel de Obando. These included $270-00 and $100-00 for a Chaplaincy founded by Baltasar de Grado, served by Lic. don Diego Campos de Quirós. On May 2, 1684, Lic. don Diego cancelled $200-00 of the debt, leaving $170-00 valid.

Alférez don Francisco de Moya and his wife, doña Manuela de Alvarado, pledged $100-00 to the Cofradía de la Vera Cruz, located in the Convento de San Francisco. They mortgaged a property named Santa Gertrudis, which included houses, corrals, cattle, and cane fields. The obligation was later cancelled.

locations: Valle y ribera del río de Matina
summary: Alférez Esteban de Oses Navarro, as executor of the deceased Ana López, founded a Chaplaincy based on her will dated May 4. The Chaplaincy was endowed with 2,100 cacao trees owned by her husband, Juan de la Cruz Fonseca, in the Matina river valley. Sebastián de Oses Navarro, Esteban's 20-year-old son, was named the first chaplain, with Luis de la Cruz as a successor, and Lic. don Gregorio de Moya serving temporarily.

Alférez Rafael Vázquez Trejo, son of Alonso Vázquez Trejo and doña Mariana de la Paz, established a dowry of $2,610-00 and arras of $1,000-00 for his wife, Gregoria de Aguilar Calderón. They had married on July 27; she is the daughter of Alférez José de Aguilar Calderón and Juana Jiménez.

Captain José Marín Laguna sold a country estate and cattle ranch, located near the city's ejidos, the Agua Caliente river, and the Tejar, to Sergeant Francisco López Serrano for $300-00. The property included cattle, oxen, mares, and horses, and the payment was to be pledged to two cofradías.

Francisco López Serrano and his wife, María de Sibaja, pledged $100-00 to the Cofradía del Santísimo Sacramento and $200-00 to the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora de la Concepción. They mortgaged the cattle ranch that Francisco had purchased the previous day.

Juan de la Cruz Fonseca granted freedom to his enslaved mulatto woman, Juana, aged 2 to 3 years. Juana was the daughter of his enslaved mulatto woman, María, whom he had purchased from Tomás de Umaña. Juana was born in his house and treated like a daughter, a sentiment shared by his deceased wife, Ana López.
Francisco de las Alas established a dowry of $800-00 and arras of $500-00 for María de Madrigal, daughter of Matías de Madrigal and Lucrecia Morillo, whom he was to marry on January 21.

Captain Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, perpetual Regidor, granted power of attorney to Bernardo de Aparicio, his son don Juan Antonio de Aparicio, his son-in-law Agustín de Ceballos (Agents in Madrid), and don Esteban Casa Rebollo to seek confirmation of his Regidor title.
Captain don Juan González Camino, who was departing for Panamá, owed Juan Alvo González $700-00. This debt was later cancelled on October 30, 1688.
