Nicolás de Quirós established a dowry of $635-00 and arras of $500-00 for María de Chaves, daughter of the deceased Pedro Valerio and Ana de Chaves. He was to marry her on February 14, and the dowry was received from Alférez Tomás de Chaves, María's brother.

Manuel de Chaves established a dowry of $173-00 and arras of $100-00 for Baltasara de los Reyes, an orphan girl raised by María de Sibaja, widow of Sergeant Antonio Camelo. Their marriage was scheduled for March 4.

Alférez don Sebastián de Garita leased a 750-tree cacao plantation on the Matina riverbanks, which funded a Chaplaincy founded by Juan Martin de Viegas. The lease was for two years, requiring payment for 50 masses annually and church dues. Cristóbal López, the patron, sought a new arrangement due to uncertainties, and doña María de Alvarado, tutor of the minor Pablo de Otárola, agreed to find a suitable tenant, leading to the suspension of an auction and López's removal from patronage.
Doña María de Alvarado, a widow, made an obligation (details incomplete).

Alférez Sebastián de Garita rented a cacao plantation for two years. This rental was connected to a chaplaincy for his son, Pablo de Garita, who was the true Chaplain. After the two years, Sebastián was obligated to pay for any surplus masses and church rights.

Doña Inés Velásquez y Rosales, widow of Capitán Diego de Ocampo Figueroa, granted general power of attorney to her grandson, don Bernardo Sarmiento de Sotomayor. This power was specifically for a lawsuit.

Sargento Ambrosio de Brenes, legitimate son of the deceased Ambrosio de Brenes and María de Espinosa, made his will. He was married to María Camelo and had one deceased legitimate daughter, Isabel de Brenes, who was married to Francisco Estaban. His heirs were his wife and his granddaughter, María de los Angeles, daughter of Isabel and Francisco Estaban, and he also raised an orphan named Josefa.

people_involved: Beneficiado don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Capitán Jerónimo Valerino sold a mulatto criollo slave named José, estimated to be 30 years old, to Licenciado Agustín de Torres, the parish priest. Valerino had purchased José from the executors of the deceased Beneficiado don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín for $450.00.

locations: San Juan de Herrera de los naboríos
summary: Licenciado Agustín de Torres, serving as Cura rector, Vicario Juez eclesiástico, and comisario subdelegado of the Santa Cruzada and Santo Oficio of the Inquisition, obligated himself to the Cofradía de la Soledad for $300.00. This amount was redeemed by Capitán Jerónimo Valerino, and Torres imposed the obligation on his residence and plot of land in Cartago, located on the street leading from the San Francisco Convent to the town of San Juan de Herrera de los naboríos.

Cristóbal López sold 220 cacao trees, which were beginning to bear fruit, to Alférez don Sebastián de Garita. The sale also included a cleared piece of land adjacent to the cacao plantation, both located on the banks of the Matina River, for a total price of $220.00.
Alcalde Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes arranged for Agustín Español, an orphan boy without parents, to be placed with Ayudante José Falcon. This placement was for a period of six years.

Alcalde Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes placed Felipe de Vindas, a 10-year-old boy and son of the widow María Rosales, with Pedro Martínez. Pedro Martínez, a master weaver, would take Felipe for four years to teach him the trade.
Sargento Francisco Hernández Isidro, a resident of Esparza, sold a 12-year-old mulatto criolla slave girl to Sargento Francisco Gutiérrez for $250.00.

Ayudante Francisco Hernández Barquero acted as a guarantor for Sargento Francisco Gutiérrez, who was indebted to Sargento Francisco Hernández Isidro for $325.00. A margin note indicates that Hernández Isidro canceled the debt on April 26, 1686.
Doña Margarita Flores de Quiñones, a widow, sold a 20-year-old mulatto slave named Pedro to don Pedro de Alvarado for $300.00.

Francisco de Araya, a native of Cartago and resident of Espíritu Santo de Esparza, made his will. He was the legitimate son of the deceased Jn. de Araya and Jerónima Bustos. He married Lucía de Castro (deceased) and later Beatriz de Orozco, detailing his children, their spouses, and his granddaughter.

locations: San Juan de Herrera de los Naboríos
summary: Licenciado Agustín de Torres, Cura and Vicario, obligated himself to the Cofradía del Santísimo Sacramento for $50.00 at 5% interest. This amount was redeemed by Capitán Jerónimo Valerino, and Torres imposed the obligation on his residence, located on the street from the San Francisco Convent to San Juan de Herrera de los Naboríos.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín
Licenciado don Diego Campos de Quirós
summary: Licenciado Agustín de Torres obligated himself to the Capellanía founded by the deceased Vasco Solano for $100.00. Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín was the patron and Licenciado don Diego Campos de Quirós was the Chaplain of this Capellanía, and the amount was redeemed by Capitán Jerónimo Valerino. Torres imposed the obligation on his previously mentioned residence in Cartago.

people_involved: Capitán don José de Guevara Sandoval
summary: Alférez Francisco de Arleguí and his wife, doña Juana de Echavarría Navarro, obligated themselves to the Convento de San Francisco for $200.00. Alférez Esteban de Oses Navarro was the Síndico of the convent, and the obligation was secured by the former residence of the deceased Capitán don José de Guevara Sandoval and his wife doña Inés de Sandoval Golfín, which had been put up for auction.

Lorenzo de Arburola, the Síndico del Convento, cancelled a debt of $100, which was part of a $200 payment received from Francisco Arleguí. This transaction likely relates to a larger obligation involving censos.

Francisco Arleguí and Juana de Echavarría Navarro obligated themselves for $250 to the Cofradía de la Concepción, whose Mayordomo was Alférez Sebastián de Garita. This obligation was for the same reason as a previous, unspecified transaction.
Alférez Sebastián de Garita cancelled a debt of $100 after receiving payment from Francisco Arleguí.

Juan de Villalobos, a native of Nata in Tierra Firme, made his will. He was the natural son of the deceased don Baltasar de Villalobos and doña Luisa del Castillo, and was married to Francisca de Torres, with whom he had eight living children.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín
Licenciado don Diego Campos de Quirós
summary: Alférez Diego de los Ríos obligated himself to pay $200 annually at 5% interest to the Capellanía founded by the deceased Licenciado Baltasar de Grado. This obligation was secured by a 2000-cacao tree plantation in Reventazón, near Matina, named Nuestra Señora de Uxarrase, with Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín as patron and Licenciado don Diego Campos de Quirós as chaplain.

people_involved: Capitán don José de Guevara y Sandoval
summary: Alférez Francisco Arleguí and his wife, doña Juana de Echavarría Navarro, obligated themselves for $100 to the Cofradía de la Concepción in Esparza, whose Mayordomo was Capitán don Gaspar Faustino Calvo. This debt was secured by the former residence of the deceased Capitán don José de Guevara y Sandoval and his wife, doña Inés de Sandoval Golfín, which Arleguí had acquired.

Alférez Juan Ginés de Hinojosa and Diego Chacón acted as fiduciaries for doña Ana Sandí, the widow of José de Rivera, to manage the assets of her minor children, Josefa Ventura, Juana Gertrudis, and Juan José, following the division of Rivera's estate.

Andrés de Esquivel, legitimate son of Alférez Andrés de Esquivel and Antonia de Madrigal, provided a dowry of $633 and arras of $400 to his wife, María de Segura, who was the legitimate daughter of Capitán Bernabé de Segura and Francisca de Aguilar.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín
summary: Doña Juana de Sojo, widow of Domingo Jiménez Maldonado, sold a piece of land in the Barba valley to Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín for $60. The land, where Sandoval Golfín resided, was originally acquired by Diego de Artieda Chirinos from his deceased father Lorenzo Sánchez, who had purchased it from Capitán Alonso de Bonilla. The transaction was notarized at the home of Capitán Bernabé de Segura in Barba.

Antonio de la Jara, Isidora de Aguilar Calderón, and Margarita Montero de Aguilar (representing herself, her absent husband Bernardo Sarmiento, and Catalina Palacios, the second wife of their deceased father/father-in-law Bartolomé Calderón de Aguilar) obligated themselves to Agustina de Solís for $200. This debt was secured by a cacao plantation in Matina, part of Bartolomé Calderón de Aguilar's estate, which Jerónimo Valerino had declared belonged to Agustina de Solís.

Teniente Juan de Gamboa, acting as the executor for the deceased Capitán Francisco de Vergara Alcoba, sold a mulatto slave named Antonio Román, approximately one year old and son of María de la Rosa (Vergara's slave), to doña Sebastiana Calvo, the widow of Capitán Bartolomé Muñoz Hidalgo, for $100.

Domingo de Ballesteros, legitimate son of Capitán Matías de Ballesteros Saavedra and Inés Solano, both residents of Esparza, made his will. He stated he had been married to Ana de Ortuño for about 8 years and had no children.

Doña Ana Sendín, a widow, and her sister doña Sebastiana Sendín, granted power of attorney to don Matías González Camino, who was in Panama, to collect assets from their deceased father, Alférez Diego Núñez Sendín Zavaleta. Their father, a former resident of Cartago, had died in the Kingdoms of Peru many years prior, leaving behind some assets.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín
summary: Capitán y Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín, who was also Alférez Mayor and ordinary Mayor of Cartago, sold a city lot to Ayudante José Falcón. The lot had been inherited by Sandoval Golfín.

Doña Ana de Peralta, legitimate daughter of the deceased Capitán don Fernando de Salazar and Doña Ambrosia de Echavarría Navarro, made her will. She was married to don Matías González Camino, with whom she had three minor children: don Jn., doña Ambrosia, and doña Catalina González Camino. She also mentioned her sister Doña Juana de Salazar, her aunt Doña Bárbara Rodríguez Altamirano, and her brother Don Francisco de Salazar.

María de Vargas, legitimate daughter of the deceased Cristóbal de Vargas and Isabel de Araya, and widow of Manuel de Arroyo, made her will. She had several children including José, Juana Gregoria, Clara Manuela, María, Diego, Ana, Francisca, and Francisco. Her daughter Juana was married to Diego Chacón, and her daughter Francisca was entrusted to Sargento Juan González to be raised. She also mentioned her brother Lorenzo de Vargas.

A dowry letter was issued for Lucas Hernández Llora, a native of Tenerife, son of Francisco Hernández Llora and Clara Francisca Sardana, in favor of Juana Mauricia de Bonilla, legitimate daughter of Nicolás de Bonilla and María de Rojas. The dowry amounted to $489 and 4 reales, with arras of $300.

A dowry letter was issued for Juan Matías de Campos, legitimate son of the deceased Alférez Juan de Campos and Inés del Castillo, in favor of his wife Isabel de Bonilla. Isabel is the legitimate daughter of Nicolás de Bonilla and María de Rojas. The dowry was $481 and 4 reales, with arras of $300.

A dowry letter was issued for Alférez Juan de Ballesteros, a native of Esparza, in favor of his wife Doña Juana de Torres. Doña Juana is the legitimate daughter of the deceased Ayudante Esteban de Torres and Doña Catalina de Monterroso. The dowry was $893, with arras of $500.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego Campos de Quirós
Maestre de Campo don Juan Francisco Sáenz
summary: Licenciado don Diego Campos de Quirós, a Presbyter Cleric, obligated himself to the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora de la Concepción for $100, a debt previously owed by Alférez Francisco de Arleguí. He secured this obligation with his houses in Cartago, which he inherited from Doña Inés de Benavides, and which bordered properties of Doña Bárbara Lanini, Don Pedro de Alvarado, Capitán don Juan González Camino, and Don Jorge de Alvarado.

A dowry letter was issued for Pedro de Campos, legitimate son of the deceased Alférez Juan de Campos and Inés del Castillo, in favor of his wife Micaela Méndez. Micaela is the legitimate daughter of Andrés Méndez and Juana Masís. The dowry was $998, with arras of $200.

Doña Gertrudis de Alvarado, a widow, sold a 20-year-old Creole black slave named Juana to Capitán Juan Antonio de Castro for $500. Doña Gertrudis had originally purchased the slave from her brother, Capitán don José de Alvarado.

Capitán Juan Antonio de Castro and his wife Doña Petronila Valerino obligated themselves for $500 to the Capellanía founded by the deceased Alférez Francisco de Enciso Hita, of which Esteban de Oses Navarro was the patron and chaplain. This obligation was secured by 2000 fruit-bearing cacao trees they owned in the Matina valley and was cancelled on July 4, 1691.

Capitán Francisco de Chaves made his will, entrusting a document containing his affairs and disposition of goods to Beneficiado Agustín de Torres, the parish priest. Agustín de Torres was named as his heir and executor.

A dowry letter was issued for Juan Ramírez, a native of Córdoba, Spain, son of Alonso Ramírez and Francisca de Ortega, in favor of his wife Francisca Serrano. Francisca is the legitimate daughter of the deceased Francisco Serrano and Ambrosia de Sanabria. Their marriage was scheduled for May 8, with a dowry of $1127 and arras of $500.

Teniente Alonso de Sibaja, legitimate son of Jn. de Villarroel and Catalina de Zárate, made his will. He was first married to Margarita de Ortega Picado, with whom he had children Luis, Doña Catalina, Doña María, and Doña Manuela de Sibaja. Doña Catalina was married to Juan de Villalobos, and Doña María to Juan Rodríguez. He was subsequently married a second time to Doña Baltasara Monterroso, with whom he had Martina, Juana, María, Pablo, and Francisco de Sibaja.

Don Bernardo Sarmiento de Sotomayor and his wife Doña Antonia María Venegas sold a large and small cattle ranch, including houses and corrals, located in the Barba valley by the Segundo river, along with 124 head of cattle, to Capitán Bernabé de Segura.
Captain José de Alvarado sold an enslaved 12-year-old Creole Black man named Francisco to Nicolás González for $250.
Juan García de Ortigosa, a resident of Esparza, sold a 5-year-old Creole Black boy named Francisco to Alférez Francisco Solano for $100.
Juan García de Ortigosa, acting as executor for the deceased Captain Fernando de los Santos, sold an enslaved mulatto man named Marcos to Pedro de Alvarado for $200.

Captain José de Alvarado donated half a plot of land in Cartago to his daughter Manuela de Alvarado, who is also the daughter of his deceased wife Petronila de Retes and wife of Alférez Francisco de Moya. The property borders lands of Captain José Pérez de Muro, Jerónima de Retes, and Captain Esteban de Moya.
María de Brenes, a widow, sold an enslaved 40-year-old Creole mulatto man named Pedro to Francisco de las Alas for $200.

Antonio de la Vega incurred a debt of $100 to Antonia de Rojas, a widow, to be paid in May of the following year with wheat, corn, and mules. This obligation was made in exchange for Antonia de Rojas dropping a lawsuit against Juan de Piedra. The obligation was granted in Barba and cancelled on December 12, 1687, before Alcalde Bernardo Sarmiento de Sotomayor.

Francisco de las Alas and his wife María de Madrigal incurred a debt of $200 to María de Brenes, a widow, to be paid by the end of next May in the Barba valley with cotton and mules. The obligation was granted in Barba at Matías de Madrigal's residence and mill.

people_involved: Francisco Gregorio de Govantes y Zúñiga
summary: A dowry agreement was made for the upcoming marriage of Francisco Gregorio de Govantes y Zúñiga, son of Ventura de Govantes and María de Cañas más Caureguz, and Andrea González, daughter of Nicolás González and Magdalena González. The dowry was $4145 and the arras $800. The agreement was granted in Barba at María de Zúñiga's property.
Benito Barrantes sold an enslaved Creole mulatto girl, aged 9-10 years, to Nicolás González for $200. The transaction took place in Barba at María de Zúñiga's property.

A dowry agreement was made for the upcoming marriage of Juan Bautista Retana, son of Mateo Fernández de Retana and María González de Urune, and Bernarda de Sandoval, daughter of Alférez Juan Patricio de Sandoval and Inés de Rojas. The dowry was $35 and the arras $500. The agreement was granted in Cartago at Alférez Juan Patricio de Sandoval's residence.

Captain Miguel Calvo exchanged an enslaved 15-year-old white mulatto man named Francisco, son of his enslaved woman Ana Cardoso and inherited from his deceased father Tomás Calvo, with his mother Eugenia de Abarca for an enslaved 22-year-old Creole Black woman named Ramona, daughter of the enslaved woman Paula de Arce.
Eugenia de Abarca, widow of Depositario Tomás Calvo, granted freedom to her enslaved man Francisco, the same one she acquired in the previous exchange.

Pedro de Alvarado granted power of attorney to Captain José Pérez de Muro to collect $1180 from Captain Pedro de Trejos, a mule train owner residing in Panama, for 20 mules purchased on Alvarado's behalf in Panama.

Juana Torres Capelazo made her will, detailing her marriage to Manuel de Mora Salado and their three children: Juana Damiana (11), Ambrosio (10), and Miguel (0). Her assets included an enslaved mulatto woman named María (24) and her three children: Juan (7), Antonia (4), and Josefa (2). She also mentioned her sister Josefa and two orphans, Mariana and Jacinto, who are to be given to Alférez Sebastián de Garita. Her executors are her brother Andrés Torres Capelazo, Lieutenant Francisco de Bonilla, and Licenciado Agustín de Torres.
Juan de Fonseca, legitimate son of the deceased Francisco de Fonseca and Catalina de Aguilar, made his will.

Juan de Fonseca (senior), married to the late Ana de Aguilar y Siria and without children of his own, had raised an orphan girl. He designated his son, Alférez Juan de Fonseca, as his heir and executor, entrusting him with the care of the orphan girl.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan de Echavarría Navarro
Licenciado don Diego Campos y Quirós
Capitán Martín de Ordeñana y Goiri
summary: On Feb 11, 1636, Licenciado Baltasar de Grados imposed a $200 censo on properties in Granada (Nic.) owned by Antonio de la Cerda. This censo was inherited by various parties, including the heirs of Capitán Antonio Rodríguez Moreno, doña Inés de Benavides, and doña María de Sandoval. Capitán don Diego de Ibarra and doña Ana de Retes paid off part of the censo to the heirs, including the Moya brothers, and transferred the obligation for the remaining $100 to Capitán Martín de Ordeñana y Goiri, who paid it on behalf of Diego de la Cerda.

people_involved: Capitán Martín de Ordeñana y Goiri
summary: On March 4, Capitán Martín de Ordeñana y Goiri, a resident of Granada, granted general judicial power to Juan Antonio de Guevara and Alférez Esteban de Oses Navarro.

On March 24, Antonio de Acosta Arévelo committed to pay Ayudante Juan Mallén de Barrientos $335 in cacao from Matina by June. This debt was later cancelled on February 28, 1689, by Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes, acting as the attorney for Juan Mallén de Barrientos.

On April 10, Alférez don Lope de Alcarazo and his wife doña Ana de Echavarría Navarro sold a 14-year-old mulato slave named José, who was part of doña Ana's dowry, to Alférez Pedro de Araujo for $250.
On April 1, master blacksmith Roque López agreed to teach his trade to Diego de Arroyo, an orphan boy under 14, over a six-year period during which Diego would live under his care.

On June 19, doña Luisa Calvo, legitimate daughter of the late Depositario Tomás Calvo and doña Eugenia de Abarca, made her testament. She was the widow of Alférez José Maroto and had six living children: Gertrudis, José, Gabriel, Miguel, Ana María, and María Magdalena.

On June 21, Capitán Sebastián de Aguirre, a native of the Bastan valley in Navarra, Spain, made his testament. He was the legitimate son of the late Pedro de Aguirre and Catalina de Saldarriaga, and was married to doña Petronila de Grados, daughter of the late Antonio Rodríguez and doña Inés de Benavides. Doña Petronila was previously married to Cristobal de Vargas, with whom she had Nicolás and doña María Leonor. With Sebastián, she had Catalina, Sebastiana, Jerónimo, Juana, Claudio, and Miguel Cayetano.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego de Angulo Gascón
Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: On July 3, Licenciado don Diego de Angulo Gascón, the priest of Cartago, obligated himself to the Chaplaincy founded by doña Francisca del Castillo for $100 at 5% annual interest. The patron of the Chaplaincy was Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, and the obligation was secured by houses and a lot near the San Francisco Convent.

On July 3, Ayudante José Falcon, a native of Santiago de Guatemala, made his testament. He was the legitimate son of the late Juan Falcon and Luisa Juárez, and was married to doña Ana María Romero, natural daughter of Catalina de las Alas. They had eight children: Baltasara (married to Francisco Gutiérrez Velazco), Antonio, Gertrudis, María de la Rosa, Catalina, María, Petronila, and Josefa.

Alférez José Calderón leased a cacao plantation of 700 trees in the Matina river valley from Isidora Calderón, his niece and daughter of the deceased Bartolomé Calderón. The annual price was $101. This lease was initiated by Alférez Esteban de Oses, syndic of the San Francisco Convent, due to a $140 debt on the plantation to the Convent, imposed by Bartolomé Calderón, and its abandoned state. Isidora agreed to the lease to settle the debt.

Lieutenant Juan de Bonilla leased a cacao plantation of 2000 trees on the Matina riverbank from Cristóbal López, the Mayordomo of the Confraternity of Nuestra Señora de los Angeles. The lease was for 4 years at $100 per year.

A dowry letter was prepared for Don José Carvajal Gutiérrez, a native of Plasencia, Extremadura, Spain, and his future wife Doña Clara de Vida Martel. José is the legitimate son of Captain Don Rodrigo Carvajal Gutiérrez and Doña Nicolasa de Mayorga, while Clara is the legitimate daughter of the deceased Sergeant Major Don Juan de Vida Martel and Doña Juana López y Chaves. The marriage is scheduled for the following day, with a dowry of $2,801 and arras of $1,000.

Doña María Estefanía de Aguilar (whose name was corrected to Josefa but signed as María Estefanía) sold houses in this city to Antonio de Acosta Arévalo for $150. The houses, made of horcones and covered with straw, bordered properties of the seller, María de Chaves, and a street. The buyer acknowledged a lien on the houses for a Capellanía founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela, whose principal is Licenciado Marcos Machado.
Diego de Espinosa, a master shoemaker, committed to teaching his trade to Manuel Solano, an orphan under 12 years old. Manuel will remain under his care for 7 years.

Alférez Andrés Torres Capelazo obligated himself for $1,173 to the minor children Juana Damiana, Ambrosio, and Miguel de Mora Salado, representing their legitimate inheritance from their parents Manuel de Mora Salado and the deceased Juana Bautista Torres Capelazo. He mortgaged three mulatto slaves and some houses, with Alférez José Calderón, Antonio de Acosta Arévalo, and Lieutenant Juan de Bonilla acting as guarantors. A marginal note indicates the obligation was cancelled on May 7, 1691, as Doña Josefa de Aguilar took charge of it.

Sergeant Diego de Cárdenas, a master tailor, committed to teaching his trade to Juan de Alvarado, a 16-year-old orphan (father deceased) and son of Antonia de Cárdenas. Juan will be under his care for one year.
Sergeant Diego de Cárdenas also committed to teaching his trade to Esteban de Padilla, an orphan under 10 years old. Esteban will remain under his care for 8 years.

Juan Antonio de Guevara and his wife Doña Clara de Echavarría Navarro obligated themselves for $200 at 5% interest to a Capellanía. This Capellanía was founded by Captain Don Matías González Camino, who was also the executor of Licenciado Don Francisco de Echavarría Navarro, and Licenciado Don Francisco de Salazar is its Capellán. They mortgaged houses in this city.

A dowry letter was issued for Ramón de la Cruz, a natural son of the deceased María de la Cruz, and his wife Gregoria de Acuña, the legitimate daughter of the deceased Juan de Acuña and Clara de Morera. Their marriage took place on this day. Ramón received goods from Bernardo Cortés, who was Clara de Morera's second husband, as part of the dowry totaling $808.

Doña Eugenia de Abarca, widow of the Depositario Tomás Calvo and owner of a cattle ranch (hato) in the Las Cañas river area, jurisdiction of Esparza, formed a partnership with Tomás de Aquino, a free mulatto from Granada, Nicaragua. The partnership aims to exploit the said ranch, which includes livestock and a dwelling house.

Alférez José Calderón sold a plot of land in this city to Doña Eugenia Muñoz Hidalgo, widow of Don Manuel de Santillán, for $100. José Calderón had acquired this plot from Isabel Jiménez, who had previously given it to Gregoria and Gertrudis Calderón, daughters of José Calderón and granddaughters of Isabel Jiménez. The plot bordered properties of Captain Don José Pérez de Muro, Doña Sebastiana Calvo, and Ayudante José Falcón.

Captain Don Diego de Ibarra and his wife Doña Ana de Retes obligated themselves for $700 at 5% annual interest to a Capellanía. This Capellanía was founded by Lorenzo de Arburola, with Alférez Esteban de Oses Navarro as its patron and Sebastián de Oses Navarro as its Capellán.

Lorenzo de Arburola cancels an obligation before Captain José Pérez de Muro, Lieutenant Governor. This cancellation concerns houses in 'this city' that were originally built by the late Captain Juan de Echavarría Navarro, who was the first husband of Doña Ana.

Juan Antonio de Guevara and his wife Clara de Echavarría Navarro obligate themselves for $250 at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by Doña Juana de Vera y Sotomayor. Don Pedro de Alvarado is the patron and Licenciado Don Gregorio de Moya is the interim chaplain, with the obligation secured by their houses in 'this city' purchased from Captain Don Esteban de Moya.

Sergeant Jerónimo de Arrieta provides a dowry letter for his fiancée, Feliciana Carbonero, the legitimate daughter of Don Domingo Carbonero and Catalina Carballo. Their marriage is scheduled for the following day, with a dowry of $4109 and arras of $100.

Luis Peláez, legitimate son of Alférez Francisco Peláez and Ana de Flores, provides a dowry letter for his future wife, María de los Santos Solano, legitimate daughter of Nicolás Solano and Antonia Sánchez. Their marriage is scheduled for the 30th, with a dowry of $979 and arras of $200.

Miguel de Aguilar, legitimate son of Mateo de Aguilar and María del Cubillo, provides a dowry letter for his future wife, Manuela Solano, legitimate daughter of Nicolás Solano and Antonia Sánchez. Their marriage is scheduled for the upcoming 30th, with a dowry of $979 and arras of $200.

Captain Don Esteban de Moya and his wife Doña Rafaela de Alvarado sell one and a half adobe houses in 'this city' to Juan Antonio de Guevara and his wife Doña Clara de Echavarría for $200. The property borders those of Doña Jerónima de Retes, Captain Don Antonio de Moya, Doña María de Retes, and the public square.

Doña Ana Sendín, widow of José de Rivera, sells a ranch and farm with a house, plantain grove, and cultivated land, located about a league from 'this city' across the Purisis and La Pontezuela river towards Tobosi. The sale, including livestock, is for $150, and the buyer obligates himself to the minor children of Ana Sendín and her late husband, who own the property.

Lieutenant Don José Escalante Paniagua and his wife Doña Manuela de Vida Martel obligate themselves for $150 at 5% interest to the minor children of the late José de Rivera and Doña Ana Sendín. This obligation is secured by the same ranch they purchased in the previous transaction.
Sergeant Major Don Miguel Gómez de Lara, Governor and Captain General of 'this province,' grants general judicial power to Sergeant Major Don Manuel Gómez de Lara.

Captain Don Matías González Camino requests testimony of a cancellation granted in his favor by Agustín de Morales, patron, and Vicar Agustín de Torres, chaplain of the Chaplaincy founded by Antonio Machado, for $600 redeemed from a $1000 obligation. Alcalde Sarmiento orders the testimony to be provided on April 23.

Alférez Don Sebastián de Garita obligates himself for $600 at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by the late Alférez Antonio Machado. Agustín de Morales Miranda is the patron and Licenciado Agustín de Torres, Cura of 'this city,' is the chaplain. The obligation is secured by 2,000 fruiting cacao trees on the Matina riverbanks, inherited from the late Sergeant Major Don Juan Antonio Lanini.
Captain Don Esteban de Moya entrusts Don Pedro de Alvarado to collect $129 from the assets of Manuel Sanz, who died intestate in Puertobelo and owed the money.

Captain Don Juan Plaza, from Santiago de Guayaquil, provides a dowry letter for Doña Juana de Salazar, widow of Captain Don García de Alvarado, whom he is to marry the next day. The dowry includes houses, paintings, and several enslaved people. Deductions are made for a debt to Sergeant Major Don Manuel Gómez de Lara and for the guardianship of her minor children, Gertrudis and Miguel de Alvarado, which includes an enslaved boy Sebastián inherited from their grandmother, Doña Juana de Vera y Sotomayor.

Don Francisco López Conejo, originally from Málaga, Spain, provides a dowry letter for his fiancée Doña María de Quirós, legitimate daughter of the late Francisco de Quirós and Doña María de Angulo Gascón. Their marriage is scheduled for the next day, with a dowry of $1674 and arras of $1000.

Juan de Artieda, acting with power of attorney for Francisca de Peñaranda, obligates himself to the Chaplaincy founded by Licenciado Baltasar de Grado. Alférez Don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín was the patron, and Licenciado Don Diego was the chaplain.

Juan Teodor de Artieda recognized a debt of $200 at 5% interest to Francisca de Campos Quirós. This debt was originally the responsibility of the deceased Alférez Diego de los Ríos, who was Artieda's brother and Francisca's son. The debt was imposed on a 2,000-tree cacao plantation in the Reventazón valley, named Santa Juana and Nuestra Señora de Ujarraz, which Francisca inherited from Diego.

The will of Alférez Cristóbal Durán de Chaves, a native of Santa Fé de Bogotá, was recorded. He was the legitimate son of the deceased Captain Alonso Durán de Chaves and Lucía Ruiz, and was married to Ana Pereira Cardoso. His children were María, Cristóbal (also an Alférez), Ana Micaela, Pedro, and the deceased Ana Manuela, with María married to Juan Fernández de la Fuente and Ana Micaela married to the deceased Sergeant Alonso Romero.

Alférez Antonio Calderón and his wife Isabel Alvarez, along with Alférez José Calderón and Antonio de Acosta Arévalo, obligated themselves to Juana de Rojas, a minor. This obligation was for $300, representing her paternal inheritance from her deceased father Francisco de Rojas and mother María de Ortega. A cattle ranch across the Purisis river, one league from the city, was mortgaged, with José Calderón and Antonio de Acosta Arévalo acting as guarantors.

Gregoria de Figueroa, widow of Miguel López, obligated herself to her minor children for $1920, with $640 for each as their paternal inheritance. A productive cacao plantation in the Matina valley was mortgaged for this purpose. Alférez Antonio Calderón served as the guarantor for this obligation.

Alférez Cristóbal Durán de Chaves (son) and Pedro Durán de Chaves, as universal heirs of their deceased father Alférez Cristóbal Durán de Chaves and mother Ana Pereira Cardoso, acknowledged existing censos (liens). These censos were imposed on their family home in the city, a large cattle ranch, and an estate in the Aserrí valley.

people_involved: Angela María de la Paz y Salgado
summary: A dowry letter was prepared by Lieutenant Gil de Alvarado for his future wife, Inés de Sandoval Golfín, daughter of Captain and Sergeant Major Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín and Angela María de la Paz y Salgado. The marriage was scheduled for May 4. The dowry, totaling $5115 with $1000 arras, included several enslaved mulatos: José ($500), two named Francisca ($500 and $400), two named Nicolasa ($350 each), and Sebastián ($350).

locations: Villa de la Puente de la Reina
summary: A dowry letter was prepared by Francisco de Arleguí y Armendares for his future wife, Juana de Echavarría. Francisco, from Villa de la Puente de la Reina, was the son of Felipe de Arleguí and Graciosa de Armendares. Juana was the legitimate daughter of the deceased Captain Juan de Echavarría Navarro and Ama de Retes. The marriage was set for two days later, with a dowry of $5107 and arras of $1000.

A dowry letter was prepared by Nicolás de Quirós (son) for his future wife, María Víctor de Peñaranda. Nicolás was the legitimate son of the deceased Nicolás de Quirós (father) and María de Guevara. María Víctor was the legitimate daughter of Cristóbal López and Andrea de Peñaranda. The dowry was $9500 with $100 arras, overseen by Alcaldes Captain José Pérez de Muro and Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín, and Escribano Francisco Ramírez Rodado.

Lieutenant Pedro de Campos Quirós and his wife Bárbara Rodríguez Altamirano sold a plot of land and part of another, including their former residence, to the widow Ana Micaela Durán de Chaves for $150. They had purchased these properties from Francisca Jiménez, widow of Ambrosio de Brenes. The property was subject to a lien for a Capellanía instituted by Vasco Solano, with Licenciado Diego Campos de Quirós as Chaplain. Ana Micaela Durán de Chaves assumed this obligation, which was later cancelled on September 4, 1698, by Licenciado Diego Campos de Quirós before Captain Francisco de Bonilla, Lieutenant Governor.

The will of Alférez Esteban de Oses Navarro, a native of Andosilla, Navarra, Spain, was recorded. He was the son of Esteban de Oses Navarro and Gracia Resana, and was married to Juana Calvo, daughter of Depositario Tomás Calvo and Eugenia de Abarca. He listed his sister Sebastiana Calvo and his children: Josefa, Sebastián, Fermín, Andrés, Antonia, Teresa, Gracia, Petronila, and Félix. His daughter Josefa, married to Lorenzo de Arburola Iribaren, had pledged the mulata María Bergara and her son Mariano for $150.
Alférez Manuel Prieto de Tobar, a resident of Santiago de Alanje, obligated himself to Gertrudis de Alvarado, a widow, for $200. This amount represented the value of 17 mule beasts.

Captain Rodrigo Vázquez Coronado, a resident of Esparza, acting on behalf of his sister Isabel Vásquez Coronado, widow of Alonso Mateos Hurtado, granted power of attorney to Captain Fernando Pérez de Vera, residing in Granada. This power allowed Fernando Pérez de Vera to sell an enslaved black man named Miguel, of Congo origin.

people_involved: Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín
summary: The Cabildo, Justicia y Regimiento of Cartago, including several officials, granted general power of attorney for lawsuits. This power was given to Francisco Somosa and Antonio Rodríguez Menéndez, who were Procuradores of the Royal Chancellery in Santiago de Guatemala.
Teniente Bernardo de Abarca sold a straw house and its plot in Cartago for $100 to Alférez Pedro de Soto. The property had been inherited by Bernardo from his mother, doña Jerónima de Abarca.

A dowry letter was issued for the upcoming marriage between Juan Antonio de Soto and Juana de Acosta Arévalo, scheduled for the following day. Juan Antonio's parents were from Escopero, Greece, and the dowry was valued at $3771 with arras of $1000.
A dowry letter was issued for the upcoming marriage between Blas Solís and María de la Candelaria, scheduled for the following day. The dowry was $355 and arras were $200.

Licenciado don Diego Angulo Gascón, the city's Cura, committed to pay $100 at 5% annual interest to the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora del Rosario. Don Pedro de Moya served as Mayordomo of the Cofradía, and the obligation was secured by houses Angulo Gascón was constructing.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don José de Sandoval Ocampo
summary: Doña María Ramiro Corajo, widow of Maestre de Campo don José de Sandoval Ocampo, made her testament. She named her seven children, her brothers don Diego and don Antonio Ramiro, and her grandson don José Arias, also listing six slaves.

people_involved: Capitán de caballos corazas don Antonio Pacheco
summary: Teniente don Gil de Alvarado and his wife, doña Inés de Sandoval, sold a 14-year-old mulata slave named Francisca to Capitán de caballos corazas don Antonio Pacheco for $250.
Doña María Ramiro added a codicil to her testament, specifically mentioning that her daughter, doña Juana de Sandoval, was blind.
Capitán Rodrigo Vázquez Coronado was indebted to don Pedro de Alvarado for the sum of $425.

Capitán Francisco de Bonilla provided a guarantee for Capitán Lorenzo de Arburola, who had secured the tithes of the province for two years for $3050. Capitán don Antonio de Moya, Teniente de Jueces oficiales reales of the Royal Treasury, accepted the guarantee.
Alférez don Sebastián de Garita and his wife, doña Margarita de Aguiar, committed to an obligation of $3000 at 5% interest to Gregoria de Figueroa, the widow of Miguel López.
Juana de Aguilar, widow of José de Peñalosa and daughter of Isidro de Aguilar and the late María de Cárdenas, made her testament. She named her son Bernardo de Peñalosa as her sole heir.

people_involved: María de la O de Guevara
summary: A dowry letter was issued for the upcoming marriage between Domingo Rodríguez and Petronila de la Estrella, scheduled for the following day. The dowry was $378 and arras were $200.

Doña Juana Calvo, acting as guardian for her children, sold two mulato slaves, María and her son Mariano, to Alférez Felipe Bermúdez Velázquez for $148 as a pledge. The agreement stipulated that the slaves would be freed upon repayment of the sum.
Pedro Jorge Bontt represented Capitán Antonio Garrido, who was a resident of Chichigalpa, within the jurisdiction of León.
A ship named San Juan de Alba, docked in Caldera, was sold to Captain Miguel Rodríguez Camilo for $500.00. The seller is not explicitly named in this fragment.
Captain Miguel Rodríguez Camilo became obligated to Captain Antonio Garrido for $500.00, which he committed to pay in cacao delivered to León.
Lieutenant Juan Pérez de Gamboa granted general judicial power to Ensign Sebastián de Zamora.

Doña Eugenia Gertrudis de Muñoz, widow of Alonso de García and Manuel de Santillana, attempted to grant freedom to her slave, Gaspar Rodríguez, a Congo black man over 25 years old. This act was not finalized.

Doña Eugenia Gertrudis Muñoz Hidalgo, widow of her first husband Alonso García, granted power to Captain Francisco Astolabeitia, Martín de Artieda, and Miguel Emporen, residents of Villa del Realejo, to sell a Cape Verdean slave named Gaspar, over 25 years old, in the kingdoms of Peru.
Captain Jerónimo de Leal donated a mulatto named Nicolás de Villegas to his wife, Doña María Vázquez Coronado.

Captain Jerónimo Leal, a native of Cuellar, made his will. He was the legitimate son of deceased Manuel Leal and Isabel Ruiz, and was married first to the deceased María Núñez, and currently to María Vázquez Coronado. He mentions having raised two orphans, Andrea Calderón and Victoria.
Pedro Alvarado sold a piece of cacao plantation in the Barbilla valley to Ensign Domingo Vásquez for $50.00. This transaction was not finalized.
Ensign Domingo Vásquez sold a piece of cacao plantation in Matina to Don Pedro de Alvarado for $50.00. This transaction was not finalized.
Captain Miguel Rodríguez Camilo granted judicial power to Captain Juan de Contreras (absent) and Domingo Correo, both residents of San Felipe de Puerto Belo.

Doña Bárbara Lanini, widow of Maestre de Campo Don Juan Francisco Sáenz Vásquez, founded a Chaplaincy for six sung masses. This was established on a cacao plantation in Matina, which her late husband had previously donated to his nephew, Don Diego Sendín de Sotomayor, with this specific encumbrance.

Isabel Alvarez made her will, identifying herself as the legitimate daughter of deceased Gregorio Alvarez and Ana Sánchez, and wife of Antonio de Aguilar Calderón, with children Juan and María. She also mentions her stepfather Sebastián de Benavides and a significant inheritance from her father in New Spain that she has not received.
Adjutant Francisco Hernández Barquero became obligated to Lieutenant of Cavalry Felipe Bermúdez Velázquez, who was acting as attorney for Captain Don Francisco Xabriel del Folgar, for $473.00.
Gregoria de Figueroa, acting as guardian for her minor children, leased a cacao plantation of 2000 trees in Matina to Ensign Antonio Calderón for four years, at an annual price of $200.00.

María de Sibaja made her will. She is the legitimate daughter of deceased Juan de Quesada and Antonia de Galindo, and the widow of Antonio Camilo, with no children. She mentions her sisters Mariana, Francisca, and Juana, her niece María (daughter of Juana), her cousin Cristóbal de Quesada, and an orphan named Baltasara whom she raised and married off.

Antonio de Espinosa made his will. He is the legitimate son of the deceased Gabriel de Aguilar and Ana de Espinosa. He was widowed twice, first from María del Cubillo, with whom he had four children living in Nicaragua, and second from Catalina Azofeifa, with whom he had two children, Andrés and Francisca.

Antonio de Acosta Arévalo, preparing to depart for Puerto Belo from Matina in his boat, received 82 sacks of flour from Alférez Francisco Fernández. He is tasked with transporting and delivering these to Captain Juan de Contreras in Puerto Belo.
Antonio de Acosta Arévalo granted judicial power to his brother, Antonio de Soto, who was traveling to the city of San Felipe de Puerto Belo.
Francisca Calvo, widow of Juan de Ibarra, granted general power for lawsuits to Alférez Sebastián Garita.
Diego Luis granted judicial power to an unnamed Alférez.
Lorenzo de Arburola granted judicial power to Alférez Andrés Torres Capelazo and Captain Miguel Calvo.

Captain Diego de Ibarra and his wife Ana de Retes committed to a chaplaincy, founded by Alférez Francisco Enciso Hita, for $100 at 5%, secured by houses in the city. A marginal note indicates that on February 15, 1701, Lorenzo de Arburola Iribaren, the patron of the chaplaincy, cancelled this obligation before José Perez, the Lieutenant Governor.

Juan López de Soto and his wife Antonia de Sandoval sold an 8-year-old mulata slave named Martina to Francisco de Ocampo Golfín for $250. Antonia de Sandoval had inherited Martina from her mother, María Ramiro.
Francisco de Brito, a 'pardo' resident of León, Nicaragua, committed to Eugenia Gertrudis de Abarca for $300.
Eugenia Gertrudis de Abarca granted freedom to her 16-year-old 'pardo' slave, Margarita de Alvarado, who was born and raised in her house.
Alférez Alonso de Quesada leased a 1500-tree cacao plantation in the Matina valley to Ayudante Antonio de Castro for three years at $175 per year.

Alférez Jerónimo de Gúzmán and his wife Juana de Bonilla acknowledged an obligation to a chaplaincy, whose chaplain was Licenciado Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, for $150 at 5%. This obligation was secured by two cacao plots in the Reventazón river lands, originally imposed by Alférez Alonso de Bonilla, whose plots were auctioned to the current obligors.

Sebastián de Contreras, as debtor, and Teniente Felipe Bermúdez Velázquez, as guarantor, committed to María Vázquez Coronado for $225. This sum represented the value of a mulata slave named María, who was auctioned to Sebastián de Contreras.

María Guerrero granted freedom to Jacinto de Arcía Guerrero, a 'pardo' slave over 30 years old, born and raised in her house. Jacinto is the son of Magdalena, a living black slave still in María Guerrero's possession.
Alcalde Antonio Pacheco apprenticed 13-year-old Nicolás Sibaja, a 'pardo' son of free mulata Francisca, to Pedro de Alvarado, a master weaver, for five years.

Francisca Calvo, widow of Juan de Ibarra, committed to the Cofradía del Santísimo Sacramento for $1500 at 5%. This obligation stems from her possession for over 15 years of a cattle ranch in the city's valley, bordering the Río de las Amoladeras, which belongs to the Cofradía and was acquired from Salvador de Acuña.
Juan Idiarte granted general power to Alférez Juan de Alfaro.

Captain Matías González Camino, acting on behalf of Licenciado Francisco de Echavarría Navarro, founded a chaplaincy for masses for the souls of Francisco and his brother, Licenciado Domingo de Echavarría Navarro, with a principal of $500. This sum was secured by houses belonging to Captain Antonio de Moya ($300) and Juan Antonio de Guevara ($200). Matías González Camino was the patron, and Licenciado Francisco de Salazar, a Presbyter Cleric and Sacristan Mayor, was the chaplain.

Captain Miguel Rodríguez Camilo owed Captain Sebastián Díaz de Avecillas, a resident of Panamá, $1340 and 4 reales. He agreed to pay $600 by constructing and delivering a lanchón (boat) in Granada, Nicaragua, by May or July of the next year, and the remaining $740 and 4 reales in achiote, tallow, and pitch, loaded onto the lanchón and transported to Granada.

Captain Esteban de la Mata, a resident of Esparza, acting on behalf of Benita de Guzmán from Chame, Panamá, sold a 30-year-old black slave named Pedro to Captain Matías González Camino for $480. The power of attorney for this sale was granted in Chame on July 2.

Doña Benita de Guzmán, acting as the widow and executor of Capitán Pedro García Romero, sold a slave to Capitán Esteban de la Mata. The transaction was overseen by Sargento Jn. Ramón, the ordinary mayor of the town.
Capitán don Matías González Camino became obligated to Doña Benita de Guzmán for $480.00, representing the price of a slave he had purchased from her in a prior transaction.
Domingo Rodríguez, the legitimate son of the late Domingo Rodríguez and Catalina Riveras, and a native of Santiago de Veragua, drafted an incomplete will that was not finalized.

Teniente don José Escalante Paniagua sold a small farm, a labor and cattle ranch, a straw house, and a plantain grove, located about a league from Cartago across the Purises River towards Tobosi, to Juan Martin de la Mata for $150.00. This transaction was incomplete due to missing pages.
Teniente don José Escalante Paniagua, the grantor, cancelled the previously initiated sale of property to Juan Martin de la Mata.

Doña María Vásquez Coronado, widow of Jerónimo Leal, sold a bread mill with its tiled house, another dwelling, and four plots of land to Lorenzo de Arburola for $550.00. The payment included funds from a chaplaincy founded in the San Francisco Convent and the Brotherhood of the Blessed Sacrament.

Capitán Nicolás Gutiérrez Jaramillo, a resident of Esparza, granted general judicial power to Manuel de Zamora and Alférez Patricio de Sandoval, or to Sebastián Díaz de Avecillas of Panamá in their absence. This power also authorized them to sell a shipment of mules in Panamá.

Capitán Nicolás Gutiérrez Jaramillo obligated himself for $250.00 to a Chaplaincy founded by the late Manuel García, a former resident of Nicaragua, imposing the sum on his old cattle ranch 'Sam José' in Esparza. Andrés González and his wife María Núñez García later redeemed this obligation, with Licenciado don Diego Angulo Gascón serving as Chaplain.

Alférez Jacinto de Pasos y Porta, a resident of Granada, Nicaragua, obligated himself to Capitán Juan López de Soto Mayor of Panamá for $420.00. Payment was due within a year, 15 days after the Royal Armada arrived at the port of Perico from Peru, with a shipment of beasts mortgaged as security.

Diego de Mayorga, a resident and Regidor of León, Nicaragua, obligated himself to Capitán Juan López de Soto Mayor for $228.00. This sum was to be paid in Panamá under the same conditions as the previous obligation, tied to the arrival of the Royal Armada.

Diego de Mayorga granted power to Capitán Juan López de Soto Mayor, who was traveling to Panamá, to collect debts. Specifically, he was authorized to collect $762 and 4 reales from Juan Allallen de Barrientos, a resident of León currently in Panamá.

Capitán Rodrigo Vázquez Coronado, a resident of Esparza departing for Tierra Firme, owed Capitán Juan López de Soto Mayor of Panamá $350.00. This debt was payable in Panamá within a year or sooner if the Royal Armada arrived, and was secured by mortgaging two slaves named Juan and Francisco.

people_involved: Juan López Esteban de Soto Mayor
summary: Juan Antonio de Guevara, acting with power from Capitán Martín de Ordeñana y Goiri of Granada, Nicaragua, owed Juan López Esteban de Soto Mayor of Panamá $1190.00. This sum was for the outfitting and transport of 250 mules to Panamá on Ordeñana y Goiri's account, with the mules mortgaged and payment due upon the armada's arrival.
Capitán don Matías González Camino, who was departing for Panamá, owed Antonio de Acosta Arévalo $1400.00. This transaction was not finalized.

Doña Gertrudis de Alvarado, widow of Capitán José de Vargas Machuca, acting for herself and her minor son Antonio de Vargas, granted general judicial power to Alférez Jacinto de Pasos y Porta and Sargento Mayor don Juan de Betancourt, both residents of Granada, Nicaragua.

people_involved: Juan López Esteban de Soto Mayor
summary: Dionisio de Rocha, a resident of Panamá who was traveling there, owed Capitán Juan López Esteban de Soto Mayor $420.00. This debt was payable within a year or sooner if the Royal Armada arrived earlier.

Alférez don Lope de Alcarazo, as the debtor, and Capitán don José Pérez de Muro, as the guarantor, owed Capitán Juan López de Soto Mayor $350.00. The payment terms were the same as a previous obligation, and this debt was later cancelled.

Capitán y Sargento Mayor don Manuel Gómez de Lara obligated himself for $250.00 at 5% interest to a Chaplaincy instituted by Doña Francisca del Castillo in the San Francisco Convent, imposing the debt on his dwelling houses. This transaction was not finalized.

Captain Juan Rodríguez Plaza and his wife Juana de Salazar obligated themselves for $300 to a Chaplaincy founded by Captain Matías González Camino, acting as executor for Domingo de Echavarría Navarro. The obligation, which was redeemed by Captain Antonio de Moya, was imposed on houses in Cartago. The Chaplaincy's chaplain was Francisco de Salazar, and its patron was Captain José de Mier Ceballos.
Lorenzo de Arburola Iribaren sold an enslaved Angolan Creole man named Juan García, 20 years old, to Captain Pedro de Vergara for $250.

Doña Tomasa de Ocampo, a widow, obligated herself for $250 to a Chaplaincy instituted by Doña Francisca del Castillo, imposing the debt on her houses in Cartago. She also mortgaged two enslaved people, Hipólito (27 years old) and María (12 years old). The obligation was later canceled by Francisco Fernández, Síndico.

Captain and Sergeant Major Manuel Gómez de Lara, a 'Melero' of Costa Rica, granted power of attorney to Ayudante Cristóbal López and Captain Juan Rodríguez Plaza before traveling to Panama. In the event of his death, they were instructed to take possession of his assets and remit them to his father, Maestre de Campo Miguel Gómez de Lara, his universal heir.

Maestre de Campo Miguel Gómez de Lara, Governor and Captain General of Costa Rica, granted power of attorney to Captain and Sergeant Major Manuel Gómez de Lara, who was traveling to Panama. Manuel was tasked with requesting the remittance of $1335 owed to the Royal Coffers, which had been used to pay Antonio Martín for services against pirates in 1687, for the construction of a fort on the Matina coast.
Captain Matías González Camino, preparing for a trip to Panama, acknowledged a debt of $1492 to Antonio de Acosta Arévalo, promising to pay within a year or sooner if the Spanish armada arrived.

Sergeant Major Juan de Betancourt y Castrillo, a resident of Granada, Nicaragua, granted general judicial power of attorney to Captain Alonso de Castillo Guzmán (regidor and ordinary mayor of Granada), Captain Juan Bernabé Sagredo y Saavedra, Captain Juan Antonio Pérez de Noboa, and Miguel de Gresar, all identified as his brothers and residents of Granada.

Licenciado Diego de Angulo Gascón, Cura and Rector of the Holy Parish Church, obligated himself for $100 to the Confraternity of the Most Holy Sacrament, whose Mayordomo was Alférez Cristóbal Durán de Chaves. This debt, redeemed by Lorenzo de Arburola, was imposed on Angulo Gascón's houses in Cartago and others under construction near the Convent of San Francisco.

Alférez Isidro González Correa and his wife Doña Juana Ramiro Corajo obligated themselves for $100 to the Convent of San Francisco, receiving the money from Brother Lorenzo de Arburola, the General Síndico of the Convent. The debt was imposed on their houses in Cartago.

Captain José de Alvarado and Captain Juan González Camino posted bail for Captain Matías González Camino, who had been imprisoned in Cartago's Cabildo for over a year and a half by order of the Governor for a civil cause. This allowed Matías González Camino to travel to Panama.
Captain Matías González Camino granted general judicial power of attorney to his brother, Captain Juan González Camino, and to Alférez Nicolás de N.
Captain Juan González Camino granted judicial power to his brother, Captain Matías González Camino, who was traveling to Panama.
José Hidalgo, Alcalde de la Santa Hermandad, with power from his wife Juana Arias, sold an enslaved woman named Juana, 40 years old, to Sergeant Francisco Gutiérrez for $1350.

In the valley of Aserrí, at the home of María de Monterroso, Juana Arias granted power of attorney to her husband, José Hidalgo, for the sale of an enslaved woman. This act was witnessed by four people.

Sergeant Major Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín arranged for Agustín de Morales, a 14-year-old pardo boy and son of free mulata Isabel de Morales, to apprentice with shoemaker Carlos de Umaña for three years. This arrangement was not finalized.

Ensign Nicolás de Céspedes arranged for Nicolás del Monte, an 11-year-old pardo boy, son of free mulata María de Torres and fatherless, to apprentice with carpenter Ensign Juan de Fonseca for five years.

Sergeant Major Juan de Betancourt, a resident of Granada, Nicaragua, traveling to Panama, owed $400 to the Royal Coffers of Cartago. He received this amount from Captain Antonio de Moya, Lieutenant of Royal Treasury officials, and was to repay it within one year.

Captains José de Alvarado and Pedro de Alvarado posted bail for Sergeant Major Juan de Betancourt, who was imprisoned in the Cartago Cabildo. He was accused by Ensign Antonio de Rivera of owing royal sales taxes on a sale of mules to Captain Antonio de Pucheta and had to provide proof of delivery within one year.
Sergeant Major Juan de Betancourt, traveling to Panama, owed Lieutenant Felipe Bermúdez Velásquez $200. He was to pay this debt one month after his arrival in Panama.

Sergeant Major Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín arranged for Manuel Rodríguez, a 14-year-old criollo black boy, son of enslaved Mateo Rodríguez and free mulata Ana de Salazar, to apprentice with stonemason Ensign Sebastián de Contreras for five years.

Pedro de Alvarado and his wife Catalina de Vida Martel pledged $500 at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela. This debt, previously redeemed by Ana del Cubillo (widow of Captain Gaspar Faustino Calvo), was received by interim Chaplain Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, and they mortgaged a cacao plantation in Matina. The debt was cancelled on February 25, 1690.

locations: Real y Supremo Consejo de Indias
summary: Bernardo Sarmiento de Sotomayor, Regidor and General Depositary of Cartago, granted power of attorney to Captain José Barón de Berrieza, a Knight of Calatrava and Treasurer General of the Santa Cruzada residing in Santiago de Guatemala. Berrieza was tasked with requesting royal confirmation of Sarmiento de Sotomayor's positions from the Royal and Supreme Council of the Indies.

Juan de la Cruz, son of the deceased María de Fonseca and widower of Ana López, made his will. He declared his natural daughter, Juana de Madrigal (married to Antonio de Acosta), as his heir. He freed his enslaved woman Juana (daughter of María de Ortega) and left her brother Francisco to Luis de la Cruz, with the condition that Francisco could not be sold. He bequeathed María de Ortega to Nuestra Señora de la Soledad to serve in her hermitage, also without being sold, and mentioned another enslaved person, Mateo Rodríguez.
Eugenia Gertrudis de Abarca granted freedom to her 40-year-old pardo enslaved woman, Ana Cardoso, whom she had purchased 20 years prior from Catalina de Palacios.

Captain Miguel de Echavarría Navarro received $1903 as his inheritance from his deceased father, Captain Juan de Echavarría Navarro, from Captain Diego de Ibarra, who is married to Miguel's mother, Ana de Retes.

Francisco de Aguirre was authorized to collect his outstanding salary from the Royal Coffers for his service to His Majesty in the city's Plaza de Armas. He had served as a Sergeant, Alférez, and Captain of the paid company stationed there.

Captain Matías González Camino obligated himself to the Convento de San Francisco for $150 at 5% interest. This obligation was secured by a cacao hacienda with over 1000 trees located in Matina, and Lorenzo de Arburola, the Síndico general, received it.

On March 16, 1703, the $150 debt obligation previously made by Matías González Camino to the Convento de San Francisco was redeemed. Captain Antonio de la Vega Cabral took over this debt under the same terms.

people_involved: Diego de San Martín y Soto
summary: A dowry letter was issued for Diego de San Martín y Soto and his wife, Doña Josefa de los Reyes, for $1829. Doña Josefa is the legitimate daughter of Captain Matías Jacinto de los Reyes and Doña Isabel de Bonilla. Additionally, $200 was provided as arras.

A dowry letter was issued for Bartolomé Lizondo, a resident of Puerto de Santa María, Spain, and his future wife, Margarita de Halhavilla, for $739. Margarita is the legitimate daughter of Ayudante Antonio de Castro and María de Arrieta. Arras amounted to $300.

A dowry letter was issued for Captain Francisco Alvarez and his wife, Doña María de Vargas, for $638. Doña María is the legitimate daughter of the deceased Vargas and Doña Petronila de Granados Moreno. Arras amounted to $1000.

Captain Francisco de Bonilla donated a cacao plantation of 1000 trees in the Matina valley to his brother-in-law, Captain Francisco Alvarez, and his wife, Doña María de Vargas. Bonilla committed to planting and cultivating the trees, delivering the plantation within a year to aid their marriage.

Captain Don Esteban de Moya, legitimate son of the deceased Sargento Mayor José de Moya and Doña Mayor de Benavides, made his will. His debts and credits were detailed in a signed and written memorandum by his brother, Alférez Don Pedro de Moya. He had been married for nine years to Doña Rafaela de Alvarado, legitimate daughter of Captain José de Alvarado and Doña Petronila de Retes, and they had three children: Gregorio Cayetano, Bernarda, and Petronila. His wife and brothers, Captain Don Antonio and Alférez Don Pedro de Moya, were named as executors.

Captains Miguel Calvo, Miguel de Echeverría Navarro, Gil de Alvarado, and Nicolás González acted as guarantors for Captain Pedro de Vergara, who was sentenced by the court. Vergara was required to present an improvement of his slave, Simón Francisco de Herrera, within six months, as they had a pending lawsuit regarding Simón Francisco's freedom. Simón Francisco had been ordered to be sent to Panamá.

Captain Pedro de Vergara granted power of attorney to Captain Matías González Camino and Sargento Mayor Juan de Betancourt, who were traveling to Panamá. This power allowed them to handle lawsuits on his behalf and to sell his enslaved black man, Simón Francisco, who was over 15 years old and being sent to Panamá.

Doña Eugenia Gertrudis de Abarca donated a young enslaved girl to her son, Captain Miguel Calvo. The girl, who was paid for by Francisco de Brito, was to be brought from Panamá the following year (1690) and would be twelve years old, or her value would be provided if she wasn't brought. Additionally, Doña Eugenia donated 300 breeding mares located in San Antonio de las Cañas, within the jurisdiction of Esparza.

A dowry letter was issued for Lieutenant Juan de Bonilla and his wife, Doña Francisca de Astúa, whom he had married 15 days prior, for $775. Doña Francisca is the legitimate daughter of the deceased Juan de Astúa and Doña María de Chaves, who is currently in her third marriage with Alférez Andrés de Solís. Arras amounted to $1000. The document was granted at La Concepción, a hacienda and sugar mill on the city's common lands, about a league away, belonging to Alférez Andrés de Solís.

Captain Lucas Cervantes, legitimate son of the deceased Bartolomé de Zúñiga and Catalina de Ortega, made his will. He was first married to María Jiménez, with whom he had children María, Sebastián, and Felipa. Sebastián left home years ago, taking over $70, and is now married in Nicaragua. Felipa was disinherited for disrespect and disobedience, and the other two children were also disinherited. After his daughter María married, his house burned down, leaving him poor. He married María Núñez 20 years ago, who is his living heir.

Don Pedro de Alvarado sold a cacao hacienda of 4000 trees in the Matina valley to Francisco López Conejo and his wife, Doña María de Quirós, for $850. The hacienda bordered Captain Pedro García's property to the west and the Río Grande and mountains to the east. The price included existing encumbrances: $250 to the Chaplaincy established by Doña Juana de Vera y Sotomayor, $100 to the one by Doña Inés Pereira, and $500 to Licenciado Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, who was the patron and interim chaplain of the chaplaincy founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela for Licenciado Marcos Machado.
Cristóbal López offered to lease a cacao plantation with 1800 trees in the Matina valley to Manuel de Mena for four years. However, this agreement did not proceed.

A dowry letter was issued for José de Chinchilla and his promised wife, María Gertrudis Ricardo, for $500. María Gertrudis is the legitimate daughter of Leonardo Ricardo and Josefa Rogates. Arras amounted to $100.
A dowry letter was issued for Nicolás de Segura.
Juana Ricardo, legitimate daughter of Leonardo Ricardo and Josefa Rogates, is promised in marriage with a dowry of $500 and arras of $200.

Alférez Pedro de Moya provides a dowry for his future wife, Doña Angela Sáenz, legitimate daughter of the late Maestre de Campo Don Juan Francisco Sáenz and Doña Bárbara Lanini. The dowry totals $5375, with arras of $1000, including 2000 cacao trees in Matina and $1000 held by Don Sebastián Garita, left by Angela's uncle Sargento Mayor Don Juan Alonso Lanini.
Pedro de Moya and Angela Sáenz were married on Christmas Day, the 8th of the current month.
Capitán Diego Sendín de Sotomayor leases a cacao hacienda with 1500 trees in the Matina valley to Alférez Domingo Vásquez for four years at a price of $50 per year.

Capitán Don Juan Sáenz provides a dowry for his future wife, Doña Ana Margarita Escalante Paniagua, legitimate daughter of Teniente Don José Escalante Paniagua and Doña Manuela de Vida Martel. The dowry totals $3352, with arras of $1000, including a cacao hacienda across the Barbilla river, two slaves, mules, and clothing.

Diego Chacón, legitimate son of the late Francisco Chacón and Juliana de Acuña, makes his testament. He has been married to Jerónima de Peñaranda for over 40 years and lists their eleven children. He notes that his current residence, San Francisco, located about 1.5 leagues from Cartago, belongs to his son-in-law Francisco de Salas.

Nicolás de Bonilla and his wife María de Flores sell a straw house on stilts with its lot in Cartago to Alférez Domingo Vásquez for $50. The property was originally given to María de Flores as a dowry by her mother, María Barboza.

Doña Ana Pereira Cardoso, widow of Alférez Cristóbal Durán de Chaves and legitimate daughter of the late Gaspar Pereira and Isabel de Acuña, makes her testament. She was married to Durán de Chaves for over 50 years and lists her children and a granddaughter.
Doña Bárbara Lanini, widow of Maestre de Campo Don Juan Francisco Sáenz, grants general judicial power to her son, Don Juan Sáenz.

Capitán Don Miguel Calvo obliges himself to Don Bernardo Sarmiento de Sotomayor, Depositario General, for $400, payable on San Juan's Day of the next year in cattle from the jurisdiction of Esparza, delivered to Cartago at a rate of eleven reales per head.
Teniente de caballos Felipe Bermúdez Velásquez grants general judicial power to his brother-in-law, Alférez Sebastián Garita.

Capitán de caballos corazas Don Antonio Pacheco, acting as tutor and curator for the minor Don Juan Ruiz de Velazco (legitimate son of the late Don Juan Ruiz de Velazco and Doña Luisa de Abarca), grants power to Capitán Juan Rubio de Amutio and Comisario General Don Francisco de Peralta Rincón, both residents of Panamá, for collections from debtors including Sargento Mayor Andrés Jaramillo de Andrada and the late Capitanes Miguel and Juan Tamayo.

Alférez Juan Vásquez de Coronado obliges himself for $400 at 5% interest to the Capellanía to be founded by Doña María Vásquez Coronado for the souls of Doña María Yáñez and Capitán Jerónimo Leal. The Capellanía's patron is Licenciado Don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, and the obligation is secured by an estancia named San Ildefonso near Aserrí, which also carries charges from the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora de la Concepción and a Capellanía recited by Licenciado Don Diego de Campos.
Don Alonso de Aranda y Acevedo and Capitán Miguel Rodríguez Camilo settle their ongoing lawsuits and differences concerning company and partnership accounts that have been pending since 1983.

Capitán Juan Gómez grants power to Teniente Felipe Bermúdez Velásquez, who is traveling to Panamá, to collect $800 from Juan Núñez and his wife Leonarda de Mora (owed since April 7, 1889, per a public deed in Santiago de Veragua) and $80 from Alonso Gómez, a resident of Pueblo Nuevo.

Capitán Miguel Rodríguez Camilo and Capitán Juan Gómez settle their differences and accounts. Rodríguez Camilo gives Gómez $250 in cacao, to be collected in Matina by Capitán Don Antonio Pacheco. In return, Gómez gives Rodríguez Camilo an $800 deed and an $80 promissory note with power and cession for collection.

Doña María Vásquez Coronado, widow of Capitán Jerónimo Leal, founds a perpetual Capellanía of masses for the soul of Doña María Yáñez, her husband's first wife, for Leal's soul, and for those under her obligation. This fulfills María Yáñez's will, which left her goods to Leal with this condition, which he failed to meet during his lifetime. The principal of $400 is charged on a large cattle hacienda near Aserrí, for which Alférez Juan Vásquez Coronado is obligated.

people_involved: Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: An unnamed individual (referred to as 'ésta') appointed Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, her nephew, as the first Chaplain and patron.
Doña María Vásquez Coronado, a widow, sold a 25-year-old mulatto creole slave named Salvador to her brother, Alférez Juan Vásquez Coronado, for $250.
Capitán Miguel Rodríguez Camilo became obligated to Capitán Miguel de Echavarría Navarro for $154. However, this transaction did not proceed.

José de Aguilar established a dowry for his future wife, María de Ochoa, the legitimate daughter of Sargento Juan González and María de Espinosa. The dowry, valued at $1718, included a cacao plantation, a plot of land, cacao, two mule beasts, a horse, clothing, and $200 in earnest money.

Alférez Sebastián de Contreras sold a 50-year-old brown-skinned slave named María to Ayudante Alonso de Mora for $225. This slave had been acquired from the estate of Doña María Vásquez Coronado's deceased husband, Capitán Jerónimo Leal.

Juan Gómez established a dowry for his wife, Manuela Ricardo, the legitimate daughter of the deceased Ambrosio Ricardo and Antonia Masís. He received the dowry assets, totaling $1413 and 6 reales, from Andrés Méndez, Manuela's tutor and curator, which included cacao trees, a plot in San Francisco, and land near Agua Caliente.

Sebastián de Benavides sold a 50-vara square vacant lot in the city to Licenciado Agustín de Torres, the local Cura and Vicario, for $50. The lot was bordered by houses belonging to Sebastiana de Alvarado, the buyer's houses, and two royal roads.

María Pereira, legitimate daughter of Francisco de Arroyo and Mariana Cardoso, made her will. She had been married to Juan de Astorga for 3 years, with whom she had a daughter, Mariana, now married to Sebastián de Cárdenas. She was then married to Juan de Madrigal for over 17 years. Her will named her daughter Mariana Astorga as her heir and mentioned her siblings, granddaughter, and goddaughter. The will was granted in Nuestra Señora de la Concepción, within the common lands of Cartago.

Bernarda Velásquez, widow of Teniente Juan García de Ortigoza, granted power of attorney to Alférez Sebastián de Zamora. She authorized him to claim Gregorio, a 14 or 15-year-old mulatto slave, as her property, as he was bequeathed to her by her deceased uncle, Capitán Fernando López de Ascuña. The power was granted in the valley of Barba, before Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes, a perpetual Regidor and Ordinary Mayor of Cartago.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín
Capitán Matías Jacidto de los Reyes
summary: The Cabildo, Justice, and Regiment of Cartago, including Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín, Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes, Capitán don Francisco de Ocampo, and Bernardo Sarmiento de Sotomayor, granted general judicial power to Capitán Jerónimo Valerino, Manuel de Fariñas, Alférez Antonio Rodríguez Meléndez (procurators of Santiago de Guatemala), and Capitán Matías Jacidto de los Reyes. This transaction was not finalized.

Alcalde don Pedro de Alvarado placed Francisco Madrigal, son of María de Coto and over 10 years old, as an apprentice with Juan de Villavicencio, a master tailor, for a term of 7 years. This arrangement did not proceed.

Don Jorge de Alvarado obligated himself to Alférez Tomás Chaves for $1000, payable in Panama within six months or sooner if the fleet from Peru arrived. Capitán don José de Alvarado and Alférez Francisco de Arley served as guarantors for this obligation.

Teniente don Gil de Alvarado and his wife, Doña Inés de Sandoval Golfín, obligated themselves to Capitán Lucas González de Ledezma, a resident of Esparza, for $380. The payment was due in Cartago one month after Don Gil's return from Tierra Firme. This obligation was later cancelled on July 23, 1691.

Doña Bárbara Lanini, a widow, donated $3000 worth of 1500 cacao trees from her hacienda in the Matina valley to her son, Licenciado don P? Sáenz, a minor cleric. The donation was intended to fund his studies, facilitate his ordination, and establish a chaplaincy using the income from the trees.

people_involved: doña Juana de Vera y Sotomayor
summary: Capitán Francisco López Conejo and doña María de Quirós obligated themselves for $250 at 5% to a chaplaincy founded by doña Juana de Vera y Sotomayor. This obligation was secured by a cacao hacienda in Matina, which they had purchased from don Pedro de Alvarado in 1689.

Capitán Francisco López Conejo and doña María de Quirós placed another $100 at 5% obligation on the same hacienda. This was for a chaplaincy established by doña Inés Pereira, with Licenciado don José de Lumbides serving as chaplain.

people_involved: Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Capitán Francisco López Conejo and doña María de Quirós imposed a third obligation of $500 on the same hacienda. This was for a chaplaincy founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela for Licenciado Marcos Machado, with Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas as patron and interim chaplain.

Lorenzo de Arburola Iribaren transferred two Congo slaves, Francisco and Juana (aged 18-20), to Capitán don Antonio Pacheco. Arburola had purchased these slaves, along with five others, in Portobelo from don Francisco de Casaus, the Factor of slave introduction, for $2850.

Lorenzo de Arburola Iribaren sold a Creole slave named Juan de Acevedo, over 22 years old and from Portobelo, to Capitán don Antonio Pacheco for $300. Juan de Acevedo had been the slave of doña Ana de Acevedo, who had entrusted Arburola with his sale.

Capitán don Antonio de Moya and his wife, doña Isabel de Alvarado, obligated themselves for $400 at 5% to a chaplaincy founded by the late doña Josefa de Moya. This obligation was secured by their residential houses in Cartago.

Doña Rafaela de Alvarado, a widow, obligated herself for $100 at 5% to the chaplaincy founded by the late doña Josefa de Moya. Capitán don Antonio de Moya was the patron and executor, and Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya was the chaplain. The obligation was secured by a house and land in Ujarráz.

Lorenzo de Arburola transferred a Congo slave named Sebastiana, over 16 years old, to doña Juana Calvo. Arburola had purchased Sebastiana on Calvo's behalf in Portobelo, as part of a group of seven slaves mentioned previously.

Teniente Juan de Bonilla, as the successful bidder for a cacao hacienda in Matina, acknowledged a $600 at 5% lien on the property. This lien was in favor of a chaplaincy for which Licenciado José de Lumbides served as patron and chaplain, and the hacienda had previously belonged to Juan de la Cruz.

Teniente Juan de Bonilla acknowledged another $500 at 5% lien on the same cacao hacienda in Matina. This lien was in favor of a chaplaincy where Lorenzo de Arburola was the patron and Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya was the interim chaplain.

Capitán Jerónimo Valerino obligated himself for $100 at 5% to a chaplaincy founded by Francisco de Paz, with Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya as interim chaplain. This obligation was secured by Valerino's houses in Cartago, and was part of a $450 debt received in '85 from Capitán José Marín, executor of Comisario don Francisco de Ocampo.

Capitán don Antonio de Moya, as executor for his deceased sister doña Josefa de Moya, founded a chaplaincy for recited masses with a principal of $3500. The principal included funds from Antonio de Moya's houses in Cartago and doña Rafaela de Alvarado's property in Ujarráz. Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya was named the first chaplain, with a succession plan involving family members.
María Madrigal arranged for her 13-year-old son, Juan de Madrigal, to be apprenticed to Andrés de Lobo, a master shoemaker. This arrangement was recorded but did not proceed.

people_involved: Alcalde, Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín
summary: Alcalde, Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín apprenticed Antonio Ramiro, a Pardo-colored son of mestiza Josessía Ramiro, to Francisco de Umaña, a master shoemaker, for five years.

people_involved: Capitán y Sargento Mayor don Miguel Gómez de Lara
Licenciado don Diego de Campos Quirós
summary: Capitán y Sargento Mayor don Miguel Gómez de Lara founded a chaplaincy for an annual recited mass in the parish church on Ascension Day, for the souls of himself, his parents, and grandparents. Licenciado don Diego de Campos Quirós was named the chaplain.
An unnamed grantor establishes Licenciado don Diego as the Patrón, effective upon the grantor's death or absence, with a principal of $100 secured by houses in the city.

Doña Inés de Sandoval Ocampo, acting as tutor for her minor children, sells her dwelling house and an adjacent stone-fenced plot in San Antonio, located in the city's ejidos, to Juan Antonio de Soto for $400. The property was originally built by her and her deceased husband, don José de Guevara.

Juan Antonio de Soto and his wife, Juana de Acosta, commit to pay don Agustín González $750. The payment schedule includes $200 by the end of the upcoming May and the remaining $550 by November of the current year.
Alférez Juan Ginés de Hinojosa pledged $100 at 5% to the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora de Ujarraz, secured by 2000 cacao trees in Matina, a debt previously redeemed by Capitán Jerónimo Valerino.

people_involved: Capitán Diego de Barros y Carvajal
Wife of Alférez Juan Ginés de Hinojosa
summary: On October 20, 1719, Capitán Juan Guerrero, Mayordomo of the Cofradía, officially canceled the $100 debt owed by Alférez Juan Ginés de Hinojosa. This cancellation occurred before Capitán Diego de Barros y Carvajal, with the payment received from Capitán Francisco Gutiérrez and the wife of Alférez Juan Ginés de Hinojosa.

Basilio de Mora, son of Ayudante Alonso de Mora and the late Leonor de Rivera, executes his will. He has been married to Lorenza Villanes for over six years and they have a two-year-old daughter named Leonor.

Alférez don Pedro de Moya and his wife, doña Angela Sáenz, commit to pay $100 at 5% to the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora del Rosario, a debt previously redeemed by doña Juana Calvo. They secure this obligation with a portion of a house in the city and a cacao hacienda, which doña Angela received as a dowry from her mother, doña Bárbara Lanini.

people_involved: Ilustrísimo y Reverendísimo señor don Francisco Nicolás Delgado
summary: Tomás Meléndez, a master carpenter and architect, agrees to construct a cedar altarpiece for the Virgin Santísima de Ujarraz, matching the main altar's dimensions and a specific design. He received $200 from Bishop don Francisco Nicolás Delgado and is obligated to complete the work within six months, with Capitán don Antonio Pacheco and Lorenzo de Arburola serving as guarantors.

María de Leitón, daughter of the late Juan Bautista Leitón and doña María de los Angeles, executes her will. She has been married to Francisco de Oviedo for more than 14 years and they have no children.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Capitán don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín commits to pay $100 at 5% to the Convento de San Francisco, receiving the funds from Lorenzo de Arburola, the Síndico general. This obligation, previously redeemed by Francisca de Brenes, is secured by a sugar mill, straw houses, and 100 cattle on his hacienda in the Barba valley, near the Segundo river.

Juana Guerrero donates a straw-covered house and its plot in the city to doña Juana de Torres, who is married to Juan de Ballesteros. Juana Guerrero had inherited this property from her father, Agustín Guerrero.
Doña Casilda Núñez, the legitimate daughter of the late Juan Núñez Juárez and doña Juana Calderón, executes her will.

people_involved: Unnamed wife of Juan de Abarca
summary: An unnamed woman, mother of the deceased Josefa de Abarca, was married to Alférez Juan de Abarca for over 6 years. Her husband is designated as her heir.
