In 1687, Francisco de Flores purchased a cacao hacienda in Matina with 700 trees for $700. This amount is tied to a Capellanía founded by Juan Martín de Villegas, for which Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas is the interim Chaplain.

Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes, an Ordinary Mayor, arranged for Antonio de Arrieta, a 14-year-old orphan and son of Juana de Arrieta, to apprentice with Andrés de Casasola, a master mason, for five years. This apprenticeship, however, did not proceed.

A dowry letter was issued by Don Gabriel de Echavarría Navarro in favor of his future spouse, Doña Antonia María de Otálora. She is the legitimate daughter of the deceased Capitán Domingo de Otálora and Doña María de Alvarado, with a dowry of $1660 and arras of $1000.

Lorenzo de Arburola Iribaren transferred the 12-year-old black slave Sebastiana to Capitán y Sargento Mayor don Manuel Gómez de Lara. Sebastiana was one of seven slaves bought by Arburola in Portobelo on commission for Gómez de Lara.

Doña María Guijarro, a widow, sold a 7-year-old mulato slave named Pedro, born in her house and son of her mulata slave Mónica, to Licenciado don Francisco de Salazar, the Sacristán Mayor in Cartago, for $200.
Licenciado don Francisco de Salazar, the Sacristán Mayor, granted freedom to his slave Pedro, the same one he had just purchased in the previous transaction.
Doña María Guijarro granted freedom to Esteban, a 16-year-old mulato, who is the son of her slave Mónica.

people_involved: Diego de San Martín y Soto
summary: Francisco de los Reyes and his wife Doña Josefa de Bolívar, who purchased houses and two plots in Cartago that belonged to his parents, Capitán Matías Jacinto de los Reyes and Doña Isabel de Benavides, recognized a censo of $300 at 5% on these properties. The censo is in favor of the Capellanía founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela, for which Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas is the patron and chaplain. Francisco acquired the houses jointly with Don Diego de San Martín, with each couple obligated to recognize half the censo.

Cristóbal López, natural son of the deceased Antonio de Ramírez and Leonor López, made his testament. He is married to Andrea de Peñaranda and has children Domingo, Juana, María Víctor, and Claudia López. María Víctor is married to Nicolás de Quirós, and Juana is married to Cristóbal de Mena. Bernardo, Pedro, and Agustín are his grandchildren.

people_involved: Diego de San Martín y Soto
summary: Diego de San Martín y Soto and his wife Doña Josefa de los Reyes, who purchased houses and plots that belonged to her parents, Capitán Matías Jacinto de los Reyes and Doña Isabel de Benavides, jointly with Francisco de los Reyes and his wife, recognized a censo of $200 at 5% in favor of the Capellanía of Alonso Gómez Macotela, whose patron and chaplain is Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas.

Blas González Coronel and his wife Doña Bernarda de Retes sold a 14-year-old pardo slave named María Nicolasa to Sargento Juan González for $325. María Nicolasa is the daughter of Juana, a mulata slave, and was born in the house of Doña Jerónima de Retes, who gave her to Bernarda as a dowry.
Diego Miguel Algarín sold a cacao hacienda in the Reventazón valley, which he had purchased from Jacinto de Mena, to Bartolomé Lizano for $200.
On September 6, María Guerrero, who is ill and losing her sight, granted freedom to her slave María de Arce, effective upon Guerrero's death, in recognition of her extensive service.

On September 28, Capitán don Diego de Ibarra sold a 25-year-old black creole slave named José García, originally from Panama, for $500. Capitán don Juan González Camino made the purchase on behalf of Alférez José Gómez de los Elgueros, a resident of Panama, using a power of attorney granted in Panama on July 18 of the same year before Escribano de S. M. Juan Montero de Espinosa.

On October 15, Sargento Mayor don Manuel Gómez de Lara sold houses with a kitchen and fenced plot to Don Pedro de Alvarado for $1400. Gómez de Lara had previously sold these houses to Don Matías González Camino in '84, but they were returned due to non-payment. Gómez de Lara also declared a previous obligation of $100 for a mass on Ascension Day null, promising to fulfill this obligation in Spain.

On November 2, Licenciado Agustín de Torres, the Cura and Vicario of Cartago, being ill in bed, granted power to testate to Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, a cleric. The executors are Bachiller don Diego de Angulo Gascen, Cura Rector, and don Gaspar. His heirs are his sister Francisca de Torres and his niece Juana Ruiz, who are currently with him.
On November 2, Don Pedro de Alvarado sold a dwelling house with a fence to Ayudante Antonio de Castro.

An unnamed grantor purchased a property in Cartago, consisting of adobe and tile houses with a straw-covered kitchen on four plots, from Licenciado don José de Lumbides for $400. One plot was reserved for Lumbides for life, to revert to the grantor upon his death.

Alférez Francisco Fernández, originally from Avila de los Caballeros, and his wife Eugenia Rodríguez, from San Martín, Oviedo, made their testament. They had been married for over 13 years with no biological children but had raised Josefa Fernández (3 years old) and María Fernández (7 years old, 'de Color pardo', orphan).

Alférez Juan Ginés de Hinojosa leased a cacao hacienda with 2000 fruit trees in the Matina valley to Juan de Vida Martel for one year. The rent was $130 in cacao, with Teniente don José Escalante Paniagua acting as guarantor.
Alférez Juan Ginés de Hinojosa cancelled the lease agreement for the cacao hacienda in Matina.

Salvador Ramírez and Nicolasa de Castillo exchanged plots of land in Cartago. Nicolasa had built adobe and tile houses on Salvador's original plot and paid him $12 for the improvements, receiving in return a plot she owned from her aunt, María de Castillo.

María Sagaste, widow of Nicolás Barrantes, made her testament, mentioning her children Jerónima, Benito, and Juana. She detailed a donation made by Doña Juana Moscoso and Capitán don Juan de Senabria to her late husband, Nicolás Barrantes, which included an enslaved woman named María and her children, some of whom were later freed or involved in a legal dispute.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego de Angulo Gascón
summary: Juana Barrantes, daughter of Nicolás Barrantes and María Sagaste, made her testament at 21 years old while ill and single. She named her soul as heir and appointed Licenciado don Diego de Angulo Gascón as her executor.

people_involved: Doña Ana Micaela Durán de Chaves
Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Doña Ana Micaela Durán de Chaves, widow of Sargento Alonso Romero, made her testament, designating $4130 for her 9-year-old son, Alonso Romero. She also arranged for a perpetual chaplaincy of $500 for recited masses, with Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas as patron and chaplain.

Capitán José Pérez de Luna, originally from Utrera, Spain, made his testament. He was the widower of Doña Josefa de Chaves and had two daughters, Doña Micaela and Doña María Magdalena, with Doña Micaela having been married to Ayudante Eugenio Martínez for over 7 years.

people_involved: Alférez Juan Fernández de la Fuente
Doña Ana Josefa Fernández de la Fuente
summary: Alférez Juan Fernández de la Fuente, originally from Villa Seca, made his testament. He had been married for over 20 years to Doña María Durán de Chaves, and their daughter, Doña Ana Josefa Fernández de la Fuente, was named heir. Licenciado Gaspar Cascante de Rojas and Doña María's brothers, Alférez Cristóbal and Pedro Durán de Chaves, were appointed as executors.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don Juan Francisco Sáenz Vásquez
Maestre de Campo José Agustín de Estrada
summary: Doña Bárbara Lanini, originally from Madrid, made her testament. She was the widow of Maestre de Campo don Juan Francisco Sáenz Vásquez and had six children. Her assets included houses in Cartago and a cacao hacienda in Matina, which was embargoed due to a debt her late husband guaranteed for don Alonso Sáenz, with payments being made to Maestre de Campo José Agustín de Estrada.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego de Campos Quirós
summary: Licenciado don Diego de Campos Quirós, a Presbyter Cleric, made his testament. He named his mother, Doña Bárbara Rodríguez Altamirano, who lived with him and his father, Teniente Pedro de Campos Quirós, as his heir and executor.

Agustín de Torres, a priest and tutor, granted power to the de la Cerda brothers in Nicaragua to collect the estate of his deceased sister, María de Torres, who died intestate in Nicaragua. The estate belongs to María's minor children, Juana and Francisco Ruiz, who were also children of the deceased Bernardino Ruiz.

Alférez Jerónimo Guzmán leased a cacao plantation, consisting of four large plots and a straw house in the Reventazón valley, to Baltasar de Leitona and Francisca de los Reyes for a period of four years. The lease agreement specified varying payments in cacao and money for each year.

This entry records the incomplete testament of José de Rojas, who was the legitimate son of José de Rojas and Isabel María Ruiz, residents of Lima. He was widowed from María de la Portilla and listed his living children as Juan, Francisca, José, Tomasina, Gertrudis, and possibly Bonifacio.

Capitán Antonio Vásquez Coronado, son of the deceased Alférez Juan Vásquez de Coronado and María de Madrigal, made his testament in Barba. He was married to doña Gertrudis Hidalgo, daughter of Teniente Juan Hidalgo and the deceased María de Alfaro, and they had no children yet.

Doña Gertrudis Hidalgo, legitimate daughter of Teniente Juan Hidalgo and the deceased María de Alfaro, made her testament in Barba. She was married to Capitán Antonio Vásquez Coronado, whom she named as her heir and executor.
Salvador Murillo made his testament in Barba. He was married to Clara de Esquivel and they had no children.

Luis Vásquez made his testament in Barba. He was married to María de Sojo and had six children: Juan Vásquez de Solera, Atanasio Vásquez, Jorge Vásquez, Eugenia María, Luisa, and Andrea Vásquez, with the latter three being married. His wife and son Juan de Solera were named as executors.

Juan Ruiz de Villegas, a native of Puebla de los Angeles in Cartago and son of the deceased Francisco Ruiz and María Villegas, made his testament in Barba. He was married to the deceased Juana de Zúñiga, daughter of the deceased Francisco de Ortega and María Picón, and had one son, Francisco Ruiz de Villegas. He also mentioned that Juan Matías de Mores owed him payment for teaching his son to read.
María de Zúñiga, a resident of Cartago and the valley of Barba, made her testament in Barba. She was the widow of Antonio González and had three children: the deceased María, Nicolás, and Juan.

Capitán Juan García de Ortigosa, a native of Pedroso, Spain, and son of the deceased Juan García de Ortigosa and Francisca Pascuala, made his testament in Barba. He was married to Bernarda Velásquez and had a deceased daughter named Francisca García, naming his wife as his heir.

María de Brenes made her testament in Barba. She was the widow of Pedro Alonso de las Salas, with whom she had a daughter, Clara de las Salas. She was also formerly married to Juan de Olivares, with whom she had two married daughters, Ana and Inés de Olivares. Her son-in-law, Mateo Sánchez, was named as her executor.

Alférez Fernando Tapia, a native of Pliego, Andalucía, Spain, and son of Martín Jiménez de Tapia and Magdalena de Ortega, made his testament in Barba. He was married to doña Juana de la Jara and had two children, Fernando and María de Tapia.
This entry records an incomplete dowry letter concerning Matías Calderón, who is identified as the legitimate son of Alférez Antonio Calderón and Clara Montero.

A marriage contract was established between Espinosa and Mauricia González, the legitimate daughter of Juan González and Petronila de Acuña. The agreement stipulated marriage within four months, with a dowry of $530 and a dower of $300. The contract was granted in Barba.

Gregorio de Segura issued a dowry letter for his wife, Josefa de Sandoval, whom he had married six days prior. He received $900 in goods from his father-in-law, Alférez Juan Patricio de Sandoval, and a dower of $200. The document was granted in the countryside near Cartago.

Sargento Pedro de Leitona, married to Margarita Milanés and without children, made his will in Cartago. He named his mother, Doña María de los Angeles, as his universal heir. His brothers, Sargento Francisco de Oviedo and Baltasar, were appointed as executors.

On March 7, 1693, Escribano real Francisco Ramírez Rodado issued a testimony regarding a 1688 document. In the original document, Capitán Rodrigo Vásquez Coronado had obligated himself to don Pedro de Alvarado for $425.
Fernando de Tapia, a resident of Barba, sold an 8-year-old enslaved boy named Andrés, son of his enslaved woman Lucía, to Juan Gregorio Ramírez for $210. The transaction was recorded in Barba.

Salvador Murillo de Campos, a resident of Barba and legitimate son of the deceased Andrés Murillo Velarde and Magdalena de Guido, made his will. He was married to Clara de Esquivel and had no children. The will was granted in Barba.
Juan Gregorio Ramírez was recorded as owing Alférez Fernando de Tapia $100, which was part of the $200 price for the enslaved person named Andrés. This debt was later cancelled by Tapia in Barba.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego Campos de Quirós
summary: Licenciado don Gregorio Moya, a priest and chaplain for 13.5 years, made his will. He served chaplaincies founded by his deceased uncles Baltasar de Grado, Vasco Solano, Pedro Solano, and Francisco de Paz, sharing duties with his cousin Licenciado don Diego Campos de Quirós. He also served chaplaincies founded by his deceased sister doña Josefa de Moya, doña Juana de Vera, and Ana López, naming his brother Capitán don Antonio de Moya as heir.

Doña Eugenia Gertrudis de Abarca granted freedom to her enslaved women, María (19 years old) and Feliciana (6 years old), both of "pardo" complexion. They are the daughters of Ana Cardoso, a free "pardo" woman currently in service.

people_involved: Capitán don Miguel de Echavarría Navarro
Licenciado don Diego Campos de Quirós
summary: Capitán don Miguel de Echavarría Navarro and his wife, Doña Eugenia Gertrudis de Abarca, as patrons and chaplains of a chaplaincy founded by Licenciado Baltasar de Grado, obligated themselves for its principal and interest. They received $385 at 5% from doña Ana de Retes, imposing it on a cacao plantation in Matina with 2000 trees and three enslaved persons: Juan García, Clemente Muños, and Gaspar García.

Alférez Sebastián de Zamora granted power of attorney to Secretary Esteban de la Fuente and Manuel de Farinas, attorneys of the Royal Audiencia of Santiago de Guatemala. Their purpose was to bid for the office of Provincial of the Santa Hermandad in this province, which became vacant due to Capitán don José de Alvarado's lack of confirmation.

people_involved: Capitán de caballos don Antonio Salmón y Pacheco
summary: Capitán de caballos don Antonio Salmón y Pacheco granted power of attorney to Esteban de la Fuente and Manuel de Farinas to bid for the office of General Depositary of this city. The office became vacant upon the death of don Bernardo Sarmiento de Sotomayor and had been announced for auction at the request of Alférez Andrés Muñoz Hidalgo, with an initial bid of $300.

Doña María de Monterroso, widow of Alférez Gaspar Arias and legitimate daughter of the deceased Francisco García Cordero and Catalina de Mora, made her will. Her living children include doña Juana, doña Petronila, Andrés, Pedro, Bartolomé, and José Arias. Doña Petronila is married to Juan de Castro, and her son-in-law is José Hidalgo.

Ayudante Alonso de Mora, legitimate son of the deceased Sargento Mayor Juan de Mora and María de la Portilla, and widower of Leonor de Rivera, made his will. His children include the deceased Juan de Mora, María de Mora, Jerónima de la Portilla, Bárbara, the deceased Basilio, and Margarita de Mora. Jerónima is married to Sargento Juan Cristóbal Coronado.
Doña Petronila Valerino, a widow, sold an enslaved man named Francisco, 25 years old, to Capitán don Antonio de Moya for 500 pesos.

Luis Cascante de Rojas sold a vacant pasture land named el Guachipelín, located in Aserrí, to Alcaldes Jacinto Sánchez and Domingo Sáenz, and Regidores Salvador Gaitán and Miguel Sánchez of Pacaca, for 1000 pesos. The land, inherited from his father Juan Cascante de Rojas, bordered lands of his brother don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas.

Alférez Sebastián de Zamora, the senior Alcalde Ordinario, arranged for José Mejía, 514 years old, son of Antonio Mejía and Lucía Picado, to apprentice with master carpenter Ayudante José Falcón for four years. The arrangement did not proceed.
Capitán Miguel Calvo, Alcalde Ordinario, arranged for Domingo de Araya, a 13-year-old orphan, to apprentice with Carlos de Umaña, a master shoemaker. The arrangement did not proceed.

Teniente Manuel de Zamora, representing Lucrecia Murillo, and Alférez Francisco Jiménez, executor for Matías de Madrigal, sold a bread mill in San Bartolomé de Barba to Capitán Bernabé de Segura for 960 pesos. The proceeds were distributed among various entities and individuals, including the minor children of Juan Murillo (Gabriel, Gil Ambrosio, Catalina) and Jerónimo, Lucía, and Isabel Murillo.

Alférez Mayor Marcos de Ledezma, a resident of Esparza, re-acknowledged a 200-peso obligation at 5% interest on his properties in Esparza, in favor of a Capellanía founded by Margarita de Murillo. This re-acknowledgment was necessary because the original deed was destroyed during a pirate attack that burned the city.

Alférez Francisco de Salas, son of the deceased Luis de Salas and Beatriz de Sosa, and widower of Leonor Chacón, made his will, listing his living children: Juan, Pedro, Pablo, Juana, Miguel, and José de Salas.

Francisca de Torres, daughter of the deceased Gaspar de los Ríos and Ana Merina, and widow of Juan de Villalobos, made her will, listing her living children: Antonio (who is married), Juan, Cristóbal, Juana, María, Magdalena, Dorotea, and Margarita de Villalobos.

people_involved: Capitán de caballos don Miguel de Echavarría Navarro
Capitán don Luis Antonio Avellán Fernández
summary: Capitán de caballos don Miguel de Echavarría Navarro granted power of attorney to Capitán don Luis Antonio Avellán Fernández, a resident and Alcalde Ordinario of Granada, Nicaragua, to bid for the office of Alcalde Provincial de la Santa Hermandad of this province in Guatemala, an office vacant due to lack of confirmation for Capitán don José de Alvarado.

people_involved: Doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar
summary: Doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar, wife of the absent Antonio de Acosta Arévalo, granted general judicial power of attorney to Capitán don Antonio Pacheco.

Licenciado Agustín de Torres, Cura Rector and Vicario, acting as tutor and curator for doña Juana and Francisco Ruiz (legitimate children of the deceased Bernardino Ruiz and doña María de Torres, his sister, formerly of Granada), granted power of attorney to Capitán Mateo Hurtado de Mendoza, Capitán Bernardo Gutiérrez, and Capitán Juan Vázquez de Lemos to collect the intestate inheritance of doña María de Torres in Nicaragua, which included 5 enslaved persons and other valuables worth over 1500 pesos.

Doña Juana de Echavarría Navarro, legitimate daughter of the late Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro and Doña Ana de Retes, made her testament. She is married to the absent Alférez Francisco de Arley and has two living children, Angela María and Manuel Antonio. She also mentions her aunt, Doña María de Retes, and several enslaved individuals: Victoria, Gabriel, José, Manuela Josefa, and María Nicolasa.

A dowry letter was issued for Juan Gómez Rico in favor of his future wife, Claudia López de Peñaranda. Claudia is the legitimate daughter of Cristóbal López and Andrea de Peñaranda. The dowry amounted to $737.144, with an additional $250.00 in arras.

people_involved: Doña María Magdalena Pérez de Luna
summary: Capitán José Pérez de Luna issued a codicil to his testament from November 22, 1690. He changed his burial location from the Church of Nuestro Padre San Francisco to the Parochial Church and redirected a portion of his assets, previously for his daughter Doña María Magdalena Pérez de Luna, to be used for masses for his soul and that of his late wife, Doña Josefa de Chaves.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
Doña María Magdalena Pérez de Luna
summary: A dowry letter was issued for Capitán don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín in favor of Doña María Magdalena Pérez de Luna, whom he is to marry tomorrow. Doña María Magdalena is the legitimate daughter of Capitán José Pérez de Luna and the late Doña Josefa de Chaves. The dowry included two parda enslaved women, Juana (18 years old) and Josefa (12 years old), valued at $900.00, contributing to a total dowry of $1761.00 and arras of $1000.00.

Alférez Andrés Torres Capelazo sold five enslaved individuals to Doña Josefa de Aguilar for $1000.00. The group included María, a parda woman over 32 years old, and her four pardo children: Juan (8 years), Josefa (4 years), Cayetano (2 years), and José (10 months). Andrés Torres Capelazo had acquired these enslaved people from the estate of his deceased sister, Doña Juana Bautista Torres Capelazo.

Doña Josefa de Aguilar received $1149.00 from Alférez Andrés Torres Capelazo, who renounced his guardianship, for her minor nephews and niece, Juana Damiana, Ambrosio, and Miguel, children of the late Doña Juana Bautista Torres Capelazo. Doña Josefa pledged her houses and a flour mill in the city, along with 8000 cacao trees in the Matina valley, as security, with Alférez José de Proa and Juan Antonio de Soto acting as guarantors.

Capitán Jerómimo Valerino leased a cacao hacienda named Nuestra Señora del Carmen, with 4000 cacao trees in Matina, to Manuel de Mena for four years. Manuel de Mena is obligated to maintain the hacienda, replant missing trees, build a house, live there, and share the annual produce equally.

Francisco de las Alas sold a cattle ranch site with two caballerías of land and a thatched house to Pedro de la Fuente for $200.00. The property, previously bought from Antonio de Acosta Arévalo, is located more than a league and a half from the city and borders lands of Doña Luisa Calvo, Esteban de Mena, and Sargento Francisco Gutiérrez, and a hill and lagoon towards Ujarraz.

Several cacao hacienda owners from Cartago, with properties in Matina, Barbilla, and Reventazón, granted power of attorney to Capitán Jerómimo Valerino. He is to petition the King and the Real Audiencia in Santiago de Guatemala for indigenous labor from Urimanas pueblo for their haciendas, funds for road repair to Matina and building shelters, and the construction of a fortification on the Matina river with assigned infantry to protect the province from pirate attacks.
Doña Margarita de Flores, a widow, sold an enslaved criolla woman named Leonor, 50 years old, to her niece, Doña Margarita de Aguiar, for $200.00.

Doña Margarita de Flores sold her parda enslaved woman, Felipa, 25 years old, along with Felipa's infant daughter (over one year old), to her son Francisco de Flores for $550.00. Felipa is described as the daughter and the child as the granddaughter of Leonor, the previously mentioned negra criolla.

people_involved: Doña Eugenia Urbana Laínez y Histueta
summary: A dowry letter was issued for Gaspar de Bazterrica y Narbaiza, a native of Vergara, Guipúzcoa, Spain, and legitimate son of Andrés de Bazterrica and Doña Mariana de Narbaiza. The dowry is in favor of his fiancée, Doña Eugenia Urbana Laínez y Histueta, legitimate daughter of Ignacio Laínez y Histueta and Doña Francisca Calvo, whom he is to marry tomorrow. He also receives assets from Doña Eugenia de Abarca.

Doña Francisca Calvo is involved in a transaction concerning a dowry or arras. This includes a zamba named Paula, 16 years old, a mulato named Diego, 15 years old, and a negro named Andrés, who is located in Guatemala. Various goods like mules and cattle are also part of the transaction.

A dowry letter was issued by Cristóbal de Quesada in favor of his wife, Dorotea de la Rosa. Dorotea is identified as the legitimate daughter of Cristóbal de Solís and Gregoria de Chaves, with the dowry valued at $5109 and arras at $100.

Alférez Domingo Vásquez obligated himself to Capitán don Diego de Ibarra for $250 at 5% interest. The debt is to be paid within two years in cacao, and a cacao hacienda in Matina was hypothecated as collateral.

Doña Margarita de Flores, widow of Capitán Pedro de Mora Salado, made her will. She named her children: Onofre, Manuel (married to Doña Juana Bautista Torres Capelazo), Jacinto, and three deceased sons, Lorenzo, José, and Juan.

Doña Antonia María Venegas, widow of Don Bernardo Sarmiento de Sotomayor who died in Nicaragua the previous year (90), granted power of attorney to Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes. This power was given to collect the assets left by her deceased husband on behalf of their children: María Gregoria, Gertrudis, José, Manuela, and Manuel Melchor.

A dowry letter was drafted for Marcos de la Cruz in favor of his wife, Sebastiana de Chaves, daughter of Andrés Delgado and Gregoria de Chaves. The dowry was $250 with $100 in arras, but the document was not signed.

people_involved: Doña Isabel de Guevara y Sandoval
Capitán don Miguel de Echavarría Navarro
summary: Doña Isabel de Guevara y Sandoval, whose husband Agustín González Villalobos was absent, granted general judicial power to Capitán don Miguel de Echavarría Navarro.

Alférez Juan González Correa made his will. He identified himself as the legitimate son of Juan González Correa and Ana de los Angeles, natives and residents of San Lúcar de Barrameda in Castile. He is married to Doña Juana Ramíro Corajo and has two living children, Catalina and Manuel Martín.

Alférez Antonio Calderón, as a debtor, and Alférez Rafael Vásquez, as a guarantor, obligated themselves to the heirs of José de Rojas for $200. The payment is to be made in cacao at a rate of $25 per tercio.

A dowry letter was prepared for Juan de Segura in favor of his future wife, Juana de Rojas, the legitimate daughter of a deceased father and María de Ortega. Juana received over $500 in clothing and $300 held at interest by Antonio, but the document was not signed.

Capitán don Antonio de Moya and his wife, Doña Táabals de Alvarado, obligated themselves to a chaplaincy founded by Alférez don Francisco Enciso Hita, of which Lorenzo de Arburola is the patron. They pledged their houses in the city as collateral for $500 at 5% interest.
Doña María de Retes, a widow, sold an undeveloped lot located behind her dwelling houses in Cartago to don Pedro José Sáenz for $100.

Alférez Antonio Calderón made his will, identifying his deceased parents as Diego Hernández de Aguilar and M.S. Calderón. He detailed his three marriages: first to Clara Montero de Espinosa, with whom he had Matías, Gil, Mariana, Antonia, Inés, and Juana; second to Isabel Alvarez, with whom he had Juan and María; and currently to Margarita de Quesada, with whom he has Ramón Antonio.
Sargento Francisco Gutiérrez initiated a sale transaction, though the details of what was sold are incomplete in the provided text.
A black creole slave named Juana, 40 years old, was sold to Juan Ballesteros for $100.00. The transaction details were recorded on this date.

Doña Josefa de Aguilar, widow of Antonio Acosta, sold a 25-year-old black creole slave named Luisa to Alférez Tomás de Chaves for $300.00. Doña Josefa had previously acquired Luisa from Doña María de Monterroso.

Capitán Jerónimo Valerino, acting as representative for the cacao hacienda owners of Matina, Barbilla, and Reventazón valleys, borrowed $1040.00 from Don Jorge de Alvarado for a trip to Guatemala. Valerino and his constituents committed to repaying the loan in cacao the following May.

Alférez Pedro de la Fuente sold two plots of savanna land, each 100 varas square and with a poró fence, to Francisco Granados for $20.00 each. The land, located over a league from the city in a cattle area, had been previously purchased by de la Fuente from Alférez Francisco de Salas.

José de Chinchilla, legitimate son of Gaspar de Chinchilla and Sebastiana de Vargas, made his will. He was married to María Gertrudis Ricardo and had a 6-month-old daughter, Manuela de Chinchilla. His brother Marcos de Chinchilla, his wife, and Leonardo Ricardo were named as executors.

Alférez Sebastián de Zamora and his wife, Doña Luisa de Quintana, obligated themselves to the Cofradía de la Concepción for $105.00 at 5% interest. They received this sum from Alférez Francisco Fernández, the Mayordomo, and secured the obligation with their houses and plots in the city.

Sargento Juan Matías Bautista Lizondro, legitimate son of Juan Matías Bautista and Ana José de Aguilar, made his will. He was married to Doña Francisca Guzmán y Benavente and had nine living children. His wife and son Miguel were named as executors.

Licenciado Agustín de Torres, Cura Rector and Vicario of the city, obligated himself to the Chaplaincy founded by the late Agustín Guerrero for $500.00 at 5% interest. Torres, who is the Chaplain and an heir of Guerrero, received the funds from Guerrero's estate and secured the obligation with his houses in the city.

people_involved: Alférez Don Jacinto de los Reyes Solano
summary: Alférez Francisco Solano, natural son of the late Alférez Don Jacinto de los Reyes Solano, made his will. He was married to Juana de las Salas and had six living children. His wife and his brother, Alférez Pedro Solano, were named as executors.

people_involved: Licenciado Don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Capitán Don José de Alvarado granted power to Licenciado Don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, a clergyman, to make his will on his behalf.

people_involved: Capitán Don Diego Sendín de Sotomayor
summary: Capitán Don Diego Sendín de Sotomayor leased a cacao hacienda with 1200 fruit-bearing trees in the Matina valley to Juan de Vida Martel for two years. The rent for the first year was two sacks of cacao, and for the second year (93), three sacks of cacao, with specific payment schedules.

Jacinto Sánchez, Domingo Sáenz, Salvador Gaitán, and Domingo Sánchez, acting as Alcaldes and Regidores of Pacaca, sold a vacant pasture site named El Guachipelín in the Aserrí valley to Sargento Laureano Guerrero for $100.00. This land, suitable for planting corn and wheat, had been previously purchased by Pacaca from Luis Cascante.

people_involved: Diego de San Martín y Soto
Capitán Don Miguel de Echavarría Navarro
summary: Diego de San Martín y Soto and his wife, Doña Josefa de los Reyes, sold half a house made of adobe to Capitán Don Miguel de Echavarría Navarro.

people_involved: Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: An unnamed party and Francisco de los Reyes jointly purchased a house, half a kitchen, and a lot in Cartago through a public auction. The property carries a $300 lien belonging to a Chaplaincy, of which Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas is the patron. The new owner is obligated to acknowledge this existing debt.
Don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín, Alférez Mayor, sold a vacant lot in Cartago to Ayudante José Falcón for $25.00. The lot was inherited by Sandoval Golfín from his aunt, Doña Juana Moscoso.

Laureano Guerrero and Ana de Vargas Machuca, his wife, obligated themselves to the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora de la Soledad for $100 at 5% interest. This debt was secured by a pasture called El Guachipelín, which they bought with the existing encumbrance from the natives of Pacaca. The debt was later cancelled on April 18, 1695, by Mayordomo Capitán José Antonio de Moya.

Capitán Bernabé de Segura and his wife, Francisca de Aguilar, obligated themselves to the Cofradía del Santísimo Sacramento of Cartago for $50 at 5% interest. This obligation was placed on a flour mill they purchased from Lucrecia Murillo, which already carried a $960 lien. The debt was cancelled on August 24, 1693, by Mayordomo Juan Antonio de Guevara.

Capitán Bernabé de Segura and Francisca de Aguilar incurred another obligation of $360 at 5% interest to Jerónimo, Lucía, and Isabel Murillo, also secured by their flour mill. Isabel Murillo de Campos cancelled $100 of this debt on December 21, 1694. The remaining $270 was cancelled on November 8, 1702, by Salvador, who received the payment from Francisco Javier de Segura, the depositary of the deceased couple's assets.

Capitán Bernabé de Segura and Francisca de Aguilar took on a further obligation of $400 at 5% interest to Agueda, Gil, Ambrosio, and Catalina Murillo, also secured by the same flour mill. Gil Murillo de Campos cancelled $100 of this debt on December 20, 1694.

Cristóbal Solís and Gregoria de Chaves, his wife, obligated themselves for $100 at 5% interest to Salvador Murillo, who was acting as tutor for Jerónimo Murillo. The debt, which was redeemed by Capitán Francisco de Bonilla, was secured by a large cattle ranch with 200 cattle, located near the Montanes pass by the Virilla river.

people_involved: Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
summary: Doña Catalina de Monterroso, a widow, sold a lot in the city of Cartago to Doña Mariana de Echavarría Navarro, wife of Capitán don José Pérez de Muro, for $50. The transaction was granted at her residence in San Antonio, Curridabá valley.

people_involved: Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca
summary: Don Pedro de Alvarado and his wife, Doña Catalina de Vida Martel, obligated themselves for $500 at 5% interest to a Chaplaincy that Doña Gertrudis de Alvarado intended to fund for her son, Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca. This obligation was secured by their residential houses in Cartago. The debt was cancelled on January 7, 1697, by Comisario Agustín de Torres, acting as attorney for Vargas Machuca, who was in Nicaragua.
Capitán Jerónimo Valerino granted general judicial power to Alférez Francisco Fernández on October 10.

Leonardo Ricardo, natural son of the deceased Inés de Ortega, made his testament on November 28. He was married to Josefa Rosales and had five children: María Gertrudis, Juana, Antonio, Tomasa, and Alfonsa, with the first two being married. He also mentioned his nephews, the children of his deceased sister María Ricardo, and named his wife and Alférez Juan Ginés de Hinojosa as his executors.

Doña Gertrudis de Alvarado, widow of Capitán José de Vargas Machuca, founded a perpetual Chaplaincy on December 14. This Chaplaincy provides for 7 annual recited masses for her soul, her husband's, and other obligated persons, to be celebrated on specific Marian and saint's feast days.

A Capellanía is described with a principal of $500 secured on Pedro de Alvarado's houses. Antonio de Vargas Machuca is the first Chaplain and patron, currently studying in Guatemala. While he prepares for priesthood, Licenciado Gregorio de Moya is named interim Chaplain and patron.

Captain Miguel Calvo, Ordinary Mayor of Cartago, arranged for Pablo Severino, a 12-year-old mulatto and son of the deceased free black woman Melchora de los Reyes, to be apprenticed to master blacksmith Francisco Calvo for 8 years. Francisco Calvo has a shop in the city.

Licenciado Agustín de Torres, the oldest Rector Priest of Cartago and heir to the deceased Agustín Guerrero, founded a perpetual Capellanía for 7 recited masses, as per Guerrero's will. The Capellanía has a principal of $500, secured on Torres' residential houses. Agustín de Torres is named Chaplain and patron, with his nephew Francisco Ruiz as successor, followed by a son of his niece Juana de Torres, then Antonio de Vargas Machuca, and finally the city's priests.
This entry marks the beginning of records for the year 1692, with Francisco Ramírez Rodado serving as the Royal Scribe for Expediente 25.

Sergeant Major Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín and his wife Angela María de la Paz committed to pay $50 at 5% interest to the Cofradía of Nuestra Señora del Rosario, whose Mayordomo is Alférez Pedro de Moya. This sum, which Captain Bernabé Segura redeemed, is secured on their residential houses.
In 1690, Captain Diego de Vida Martel purchased the San Francisco de Buenaventura cattle hacienda in the jurisdiction of Esparza from Captain Antonio Ramiro Corajo for $500.

On January 3, 1692, Captain Diego de Vida Martel recognized an obligation of $180 at 5% interest, part of the hacienda's cost, which belongs to the Capellanía founded by Licenciado Baltasar de Grados and served by Licenciado Diego de Campos Quirós.

On January 5, 1692, Diego de Vida Martel committed to an obligation of $100 at 5% interest, secured on the San Francisco de Buenaventura hacienda. This obligation is for the Capellanía founded by Vasco Solano, of which Licenciado Gregorio de Moya is the patron and Chaplain. Diego de Vida Martel purchased the hacienda with this existing obligation.

On January 7, 1692, Diego de Vida Martel committed to another obligation of $220 at 5% interest, secured on the San Francisco de Buenaventura hacienda. This obligation is for the Capellanía founded by Juan Alonso, of which Licenciado Gregorio de Moya is the patron and Chaplain.
On January 8, 1692, Licenciado Diego de Campos Quirós committed to an obligation of $100 at 5% interest to the Cofradía del Rosario, secured on his houses in Cartago.
In 1692, the will of Gertrudis de las Salas, daughter of Esteban de las Salas and María de Rivera, was recorded. The entry is only an encabezado (heading).

In May 1690, Francisco de los Reyes Benavides and his brother Diego de San Martín purchased a house (each buying half) at a public auction of Matías Jacinto de los Reyes's assets. The total price for both halves was $600, which corresponded to a Capellanía founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela.

On January 12, 1692, Francisco de los Reyes Benavides sold half a house, including its lot and half a kitchen, to Captain Miguel de Echavarría Navarro for $300. This amount is to be recognized by the buyer as an obligation to the Capellanía founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela, of which Licenciado Gaspar Cascante de Rojas is the patron and Chaplain.
On February 16, 1692, Alférez José de Quesada and his wife Francisca Sánchez granted freedom to their 25-year-old pardo-colored slave, Simón Sánchez. This act was granted in San Bartolomé de Barba.
On March 17, 1692, Simón Sánchez committed to pay $150 to Doña Francisca Sánchez, wife of Alférez José de Quesada, within two years. This obligation was granted in Barba.
On March 26, 1692, Nicolasa del Castillo sold adobe houses with a tiled roof and a 50-vara square lot in Cartago to Sergeant Juan Matías Bautista for $400.

In 1692, Captain Francisco Alvarez and his wife María de Vargas sold a plot of new cacao trees, over two years old, in the Matina valley to Juan Antonio de Soto for $300. These trees were originally given to them by Captain Francisco de Bonilla as a dowry payment.

On March 27, 1692, the will of Maestre de Campo Miguel Gómez de Lara was recorded. He was the Governor and Captain General of the province, legitimate son of the deceased Francisco Gómez de Lara and Quiínterza Brocal, who were residents of Cartagena de Levante in the kingdoms of Castile, and he was a native of Murcia.

An order was issued for the burial of a widower, who was previously married to Isabel Ana de Torres in Lérida, Spain, to take place in the Church of Ujarraz. His son, Sargento Mayor don Manuel Gómez Lara, along with Capitán Cristóbal López and Francisco de Aguirre, were named as executors.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Gaspar de Chinchilla sold an adobe and tile house with two plots of land in Cartago to Capitán don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín for $400. Of this amount, $50 was designated for the Capellanía founded by doña Francisca del Castillo, for which the buyer was obligated.

people_involved: doña Isabel de Guevara y Sandoval
summary: Ayudante Antonio de Castro sold his adobe and tile house with a straw kitchen and plot of land to doña Isabel de Guevara y Sandoval, wife of Agustín González, for $400. Castro had previously purchased this house from don Pedro de Alvarado.

A dowry letter was issued for Matías Arias in favor of doña María de Puello, whom he was to marry the following day. Doña María was the legitimate daughter of Sargento Juan de Vargas and the deceased doña Quirós. The dowry was $235, and the arras was $1100.

Doña Josefa de Santiago, a widow, sold two enslaved persons, María (25 years old, pardo) and her son José (1.5 years old, pardo), to Capitán Francisco de Bonilla for $275. Doña Josefa had previously purchased them from her brother, Alférez Andrés Torres Capelazo.

people_involved: Capitán don Gabriel de Echavarría Navarro
summary: Alférez Francisco de Arleguí, acting as tutor and curator for his minor children, doña Angela María and Manuel Antonio, whose mother (his deceased wife doña Juana de Echavarría Navarro) left them $4085 and 4 reales, provided several guarantors to administer their assets. The guarantors included Capitán don Diego de Ibarra and his wife doña Ana de Retes, Juan Antonio de Guevara, don Jorge de Alvarado, don José de Guzmán, Capitán don Gabriel de Echavarría Navarro, and Alférez don Pedro de Moya.

A dowry letter was issued for Capitán Domingo de Pus Mariño, a native of Galicia, in favor of doña Leonor Muñoz Hidalgo, whom he was to marry the following day. Doña Leonor was the legitimate daughter of Bartolomé Muñoz Hidalgo and doña Sebastiana Calvo. The dowry was $1162, and the arras was $1000.

people_involved: doña Magdalena de Luque y Leal
summary: A dowry letter was issued for Blas González Coronel, a native of Seville and legitimate son of Manuel González Coronel and doña Magdalena de Luque y Leal, in favor of his wife doña Bernarda de Fonseca, legitimate daughter of Capitán Luis de Fonseca and doña Jerónima de Retes. The dowry was $2693, and the arras was $1000.

Doña Margarita de Flores, paternal grandmother, tutor, and curator of the minor children Ambrosio and Miguel Salado, received their assets totaling $766 from doña Josefa de Santiago. Capitán Francisco de Bonilla, Alférez don Pedro de Moya, Alférez Juan Ginés de Hinojosa, and José Hidalgo served as guarantors.

Don Pablo José de Alvarado received 100 pregnant mares, valued at 8 reales each, from his father, Capitán don José de Alvarado, in the Bagaces valley. This transfer was made on account of his paternal and maternal inheritance, and the transaction was granted in Barba.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego de Campos Quirós
summary: Alférez Juan Vázquez sold a flour mill with straw houses and a caballeria of land in Aserrí to Ayudante Antonio de Castro for $200. Vázquez had bought it from Alférez Pedro Martínez de Colina for the same price. Of the sale price, $100 was for a Capellanía established by Martínez de Colina, administered by Licenciado don Diego de Campos Quirós, and the other $100 was for the Cofradía de la Concepción, with Castro obligated to acknowledge these terms.

Doña Lucía de Chaves, widow of Capitán don Francisco Ramírez, sold adobe and tile houses she received as a dowry from her parents to Alférez Diego de Cárdenas for $350. The houses were located in Cartago, bordering the hermitage of San Nicolás to the east, and the sale involved obligations to various Cofradías.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego de Campos Quirós
summary: Sargento Juan Matías Bautista and his wife doña Francisca Guzmán y Benavente obligated themselves for $100 at 5% interest, secured by their houses in Cartago, in favor of the Capellanía founded by Capitán y Sargento Mayor don Manuel Gómez de Lara, which was administered by Licenciado don Diego de Campos Quirós. This obligation was cancelled by Licenciado Campos Quirós on August 27, 1698.

Francisco de Sandoval's will was recorded. He was married to María de la Candelaria, and his aunt was Dorotea. His nephews were Francisco and Agustín de Robres. Licenciado don Diego Angulo Gascón and Lázaro de Robres were named as executors.
Alférez Francisco de Arleguí obligated himself for $669 at 5% interest, secured by his houses in Cartago, in favor of the Capellanía instituted by his deceased wife, doña Juana de Echavarría Navarro.

Alférez Diego de Cárdenas and his wife Andrea Barbosa purchased houses with two plots of land in Cartago from doña Lucía de Chaves for $350. They recognized an existing obligation of $100 at 3% interest on the property to the Cofradía de la Vera Cruz. This obligation was cancelled on January 12, 1697, by Alférez José Calderón, Mayordomo of the Cofradía.

Doña Juana Núñez de Trupira, a widow, acting for herself and her minor children, sold an enslaved woman named María Manuela, described as pardo and over 30 years old, to Juan Hidalgo for $400. María Manuela had been a donation to doña Juana from the deceased Licenciado José de Lumbides.

people_involved: Capitán y Sargento Mayor Juan de Vida Martel
summary: A testimony was recorded regarding a donation made by Licenciado José de Lumbides to doña Juana Núñez de Trupira, his natural daughter with María del Puello. The donation, granted in Cartago on July 18, 1668, before Alcalde Ordinario Capitán y Sargento Mayor Juan de Vida Martel, included two enslaved persons: José, 4 years old, and María Manuela, 7 months old. Doña Juana had served Lumbides from age 5 to 12.

A mother of four children requests permission to sell her slave. The slave is described as having a bad nature, being a fugitive for over a year, and having run away again after being brought back home, rendering her unprofitable.

Alcalde and Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes arranges for Juan Martínez, a 12-year-old orphan, to be apprenticed to his brother, Sargento Pedro Martínez. Pedro Martínez is a master weaver of skirts and other textiles, and the apprenticeship is set for five years.

Alférez Diego Santiago de Cárdenas obligates himself to the Cofradía de la Concepción for $100 at 5% interest, secured by houses he purchased from doña Lucía de Chaves. This obligation was later cancelled on January 27, 1698, by Capitán don Miguel Calvo, the Síndico for the Franciscans.

Alférez Diego Santiago de Cárdenas obligates himself to the Cofradía del Santísimo Sacramento for $1000 at 5% interest, also secured by the same houses. This obligation was cancelled on November 26, 1699, by Juan Antonio de Guevara, the Mayordomo.

Alférez Diego Santiago de Cárdenas makes a third obligation for $50 at 5% interest to the Cofradía del Rosario, also secured by the same houses. This obligation was cancelled on January 27, 1698, by don José de Guzmán, the Mayordomo.

Alférez don Sebastián de Garita and his wife, doña Margarita de Aguiar, obligate themselves to the minor children of the deceased José de Rojas for $300. This sum was previously owed to Gregoria de Figueroa, who transferred the obligation to them, stemming from the cattle and houses they bought at a public auction of José de Rojas's assets, with the condition to formalize the deed for the minors.
Capitán don José de Alvarado sells a vacant lot in Cartago to don Francisco de Moya for $50.

Felipe de Mesa, who won the bid for the lease of a cacao plantation belonging to his minor brother-in-law Juan López for four years at $50 per year, provides Teniente Juan de Alfaro as a guarantor for the agreement.

people_involved: José de la Aya y Bolívar
summary: Capitán don José de la Aya y Bolívar sells two 'caballerías' of land, a house, kitchen, sugar mill, and a plot of sugarcane in the Aserrí valley to Alférez don Pedro Durán de Chaves for $100. This property was acquired by don José de la Aya y Bolívar at a public auction of Alférez Mayor Juan de Chaves's assets, and the $100 belongs to Jerónimo Murillo, an obligation that Chaves must acknowledge.

Doña María Ramírez grants power of attorney to her husband, Alférez Juan Albo, to purchase slaves in the jurisdiction of Esparza. These slaves are from the assets left by the deceased Capitán Marcos de Ledezma, which belong to his daughter doña Rufina de Ledezma, and Juan Albo is authorized to obligate himself for their value.

Teniente don José Escalante Paniagua obligates himself to the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora del Carmen for $250. This sum was originally owed by doña Gertrudis de Alvarado, who donated it to the Cofradía.

Doña Antonia María de Venegas, a widow, sells houses in Cartago, inherited from her grandmother doña Inés Velázquez, to Alférez don Lope de Alcarazo for $1000. The sale includes obligations to three chaplaincies: $500 to the one founded by Capitán Francisco de Ocampo Golfín (Capellán: Licenciado don Francisco de Salazar), $400 to the one founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela (Capellán: Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas), and $100 to the one founded by Comisario Baltasar de Grados (Capellán: Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya), all at 5% interest, which the buyer and his wife must acknowledge.

Doña Antonia María de Venegas, widow of don Bernardo Sarmiento de Sotomayor, requests and receives permission from the interested chaplains (Licenciado don Francisco de Salazar, Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, and Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya) to proceed with the previously mentioned sale of her houses.
Capitán don Gabriel de Echavarría Navarro sells a 22-year-old pardo slave named Juan de Echavarría, son of Isabel Cardoso, to Bernardo Cortés for $300.

Alférez don Lope de Alcarazo and his wife, doña Ana de Echavarría Navarro, fulfill an obligation from a previous deed by obligating themselves to the chaplaincy founded by Capitán Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, with Licenciado don Francisco de Salazar as Capellán, for $500 at 5% interest, secured by the houses they purchased.

Alférez don Lope de Alcarazo and his wife, doña Ana de Echavarría Navarro, similarly obligate themselves to the chaplaincy founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela, with Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas as Capellán, for $400 at 5% interest, secured by the same houses.

Alférez don Lope de Alcarazo and his wife, doña Ana de Echavarría Navarro, also obligate themselves to the chaplaincy founded by Comisario Baltasar de Grados, with Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya as Capellán, for $100 at 5% interest, secured by the same houses.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín
summary: Capitán don Matías González Camino, acting on behalf of Alférez José Gómez Eigueros of Panamá, sold a 28-year-old 'negro criollo' slave named José de Ibarra to Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín for $500. The power of attorney for this sale was granted in Panamá on September 4, 1691.

Capitán Francisco de Bonilla and his wife, doña Leonor María de Vargas, obligated themselves to the Convento de San Francisco for $100 at 5% interest. This obligation was secured by their residential houses in Cartago.

Sargento Juan Matías Lizondo obligated himself for $273 to the minor children of Nicolás Camacho and María de Ortega (Juana, María de la Rosa, María, Angela, Nicolasa, Isabel, and José Camacho). This sum represented their inheritance from their deceased father, adjudicated in livestock held by Juan and Bartolomé Camacho, who had renounced their guardianship.

This entry records the testament of Teniente Felipe Bermúdez Velásquez, legitimate son of the deceased Francisco Bermúdez Delgado and Francisca Velásquez Conejo, residents of Antequera in the kingdoms of Castilla. He declared himself married to doña Juana de Aguiar for over 10 years and listed his living sons as Miguel, José, and José Felipe.

people_involved: Doña María de Córdoba y López
summary: Alférez Ignacio de Artavia and his wife, doña María de Córdoba y López, sold half a house and its corresponding half lot in Cartago to Capitán don Juan Sáenz for $300. The property, received as a dowry, carried a $100 obligation at 5% to the Cofradía de la Soledad, which the buyer was to acknowledge.

María de Aguilar sold 435 cacao trees in the Matina valley, inherited from her deceased grandson Tomás López, to her grandson Felipe de Mesa. The sale also included 53 cattle and 15 breeding mares, totaling $318.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Manuel Gómez de Lara
summary: Sargento Mayor don Manuel Gómez de Lara, serving in the plaza de armas of Cartago, sold a productive cacao hacienda with over 1000 trees in the Matina valley to Capitán José Pérez de Muro for $600.

This entry is an incomplete testament of Capitán don Juan González Camino, who declared himself the legitimate son of the deceased Pedro González Camino and doña Catalina Jiménez, residents of Villa Nueva de la Sirena in Extremadura.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego de Angulo Gascón
summary: This entry details the testament of Cristóbal López, natural son of Antonio de Ramos and Leonor López. He was widowed from Andrea de Peñaranda, with whom he had deceased sons Salvador and Domingo, and living daughters Juana, María, and Claudia. He was remarried to Mariana de Quirós and had in his care Bernardo, Eugenia, Agustín, and Juliana. His executors included Nicolás de Quirós, Alférez don Sebastián de Garita, and Licenciado don Diego de Angulo Gascón.

On November 1, the opening of Capitán don Juan González Camino's testament was requested by his widow, doña Manuela de Salazar. The will, granted in Cartago on October 25, 1692, identified him as the legitimate son of the deceased Pedro González Camino and doña Catalina Jiménez from Villa Nueva de la Sirena, Spain. He was married to doña Manuela de Salazar, had two living daughters (Catalina and Josefa), and owned eight slaves. His executors were his wife, his brother Capitán don Matías González Camino, and Capitán Juan Rodríguez Plaza.

Juan Camacho purchased 22 cattle, 51 mares, 3 horses, and 2 mules at a public auction for a total of $125 and 6 reales. He obligated himself for this amount, which belonged to Felipe Camacho, the minor son of Lucas Camacho and Sebastiana Masís, as his paternal inheritance. Sargento Juan Matías Lizondo served as the guarantor.

Capitán don Juan Rodríguez Plaza obligated himself for $397 to Pedro Antonio and Diego, the minor sons of the deceased Domingo Vásquez and María de Salazar y Vargas. This sum represented their paternal and maternal inheritance, which was the price of a cacao hacienda in Matina that was auctioned off to Capitán Rodríguez Plaza after Domingo's death, and which he now encumbered with this obligation.
Teniente Juan de Bonilla owed Alférez don Lope de Alcarazo $154 and 7 reales. This debt was officially cancelled on January 6, 1693.

Alférez Juan de Abarca sold a house made of adobe and covered with tiles, including a straw kitchen and a fenced adobe lot, in Cartago to Sargento Juan González for $200. The property bordered the plaza to the North.

A dowry letter was prepared for Miguel Angel Lizondo and his wife Gertrudis Falcon, legitimate daughter of Ayudante José Falcon and Ana María, for $503 in dowry and $500 in arras. However, this dowry transaction was not completed.

Alférez Sebastián de Zamora and his wife, doña Luisa de Quintana, obligated themselves for $130 to Domingo Camacho, the minor son of the deceased Lucas Camacho and Sebastiana Masís. This amount represented the value of a donkey and a small chest of clothes that arrived from Panamá, which had been adjudicated to Domingo as part of his inheritance.

Tomasina, Gertrudis, Miguel, and Bonifasia de Rojas, legitimate children of José de Rojas, obligated themselves for 110 pesos to Juan (name incomplete) for ten tercios of cacao received from Alférez Antonio Calderón. They mortgaged their city houses and country estate.

people_involved: Diego de San Martín y Soto
summary: Francisca de Rojas canceled the obligation related to the Rojas children, receiving 110 pesos from Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto. Zamora, who was involved in the original transaction, was deceased.

Francisco Ramírez Rodado and his wife Jerónima de Retes (acting as executrix and heir of her second husband, Sargento Mayor Pedro Lorenzo Venegas) attempted to sell a 20-year-old 'negro bozal' slave named Francisco from Cabo Verde to Manuela de Salazar, widow of Capitán don Juan González Camino, for 400 pesos. The transaction was incomplete and not passed.

Doña Juana Josefa de Aguiar, widow of Lieutenant Felipe Bermúdez Velázquez and guardian of her three minor sons (Miguel, José Antonio, and José Felipe), appointed Alférez don Sebastián de Garita and his wife doña Margarita de Aguiar as guarantors for the paternal inheritance of 488 reales and 4 maravedíes held by her for each son.
Proceedings were initiated for the opening of the sealed will and codicil of doña Gertrudis de Alvarado, at the request of her brother, Capitán don José de Alvarado.

Sargento Gil de Morales, a resident of Panamá, obligated himself to Capitán don Juan de Oreamuno for 280 pesos, received from Luis de Iturbide (Oreamuno's agent), for the outfitting and transport of 100 mule beasts to Panamá, which he mortgaged.

Doña Gertrudis de Alvarado, daughter of Capitán don Gil de Alvarado and doña Juana de Vera, and widow of Capitán José de Vargas Machuca, made her sealed will in Cartago. She declared herself healthy and fulfilled the requirement of the Third Order of Saint Francis to make a will within three months of taking the habit. She mentioned her son, Antonio de Vargas Machuca, who inherited 5000 pesos from his father, to be collected from various debtors in Panamá. She also ordered a Chaplaincy of 1000 pesos and named her sister Sebastiana de Alvarado, Capitán don José Pérez de Muro, José de Guzmán, and Juan Antonio de Guevara as executors.

Doña Gertrudis de Alvarado, while ill in bed in Cartago, made a sealed codicil. She had recently received a letter from her son, Antonio de Vargas Machuca, in Guatemala, informing her of his intention to be ordained as a Subdeacon. Due to his capacity, she ordered her estate to be delivered to him upon his return, or to her sister Sebastiana in the interim, and if Sebastiana died, to Licenciado Agustín de Torres.

Sargento Gil de Morales, a resident of Panamá, obligated himself again to Capitán don Juan de Oreamuno, a Knight of the Order of Santiago and resident of Panamá, for 70 pesos received from Luis de Iturbide (Oreamuno's agent). He mortgaged the same 100 mule beasts he was transporting to Panamá.
Doña Sebastiana Calvo pawned a 7-year-old 'pardo' slave named Antonio Cubillo to Capitán don Miguel Calvo for 150 pesos, with a one-year term.

Capitán don José de la Haya Bolívar sold a pasture site with some cacao trees, located in Palmar and the Barranca river area near Aranjuez, about two leagues from Esparza, to Teniente Juan de Gamboa, a resident of Esparza, for 200 pesos. Gamboa was obligated to pay 5% interest to the current or future Cura of Esparza, as this encumbrance was on the property.

Catalina Murillo, legitimate daughter of the deceased Andrés Murillo de Campos and Magdalena de Guido, made her will. She was married to Andrés Calvo, who was absent, and had an 18-year-old daughter named Antonia María Calvo. Her brother, Salvador Murillo, was also mentioned.

Alférez don Pedro Durán de Chaves and his wife doña María Vásquez Coronado bought a plot of land with two 'caballerías,' a straw house and kitchen, and a sugar mill with a cane field in Aserrí, from Capitán don José de la Haya y Bolívar for 100 pesos. They obligated themselves to Jerónimo Murillo for this amount at 5% interest.

Licenciado don Diego de Angulo Gascon, the Cura of this city, obligated himself to the Confraternity of the Conception for 100 pesos at 5% interest, imposing this charge on his residential houses in the city.

Alférez Pedro de Torres, acting on behalf of Salvador de Torres and his wife doña Cecilia Vásquez Coronado, residents of Esparza, obligated himself for 1000 pesos at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by Vasco Solano, and for 220 pesos at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by Juan Alonso. Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya was the Chaplain for these foundations.

people_involved: Capitán don Diego de Vida Martel
summary: Land with livestock in the jurisdiction of Esparza was purchased at a public auction of Capitán don Diego de Vida Martel's assets. The buyers, represented by Pedro de Torres, were obligated to recognize existing censos on the property.
Licenciado don Gregorio performed a cancellation on July 17, 1699, likely related to the land transaction or associated obligations.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego de Campos Quirós
summary: An obligation of $180 at 5% was placed on the hacienda in favor of a Chaplaincy founded by Baltasar de Grado, with Licenciado don Diego de Campos Quirós serving as Chaplain. This obligation was also assumed by the buyers of the hacienda.
Doña Cecilia Vásquez Coronado, wife of Salvador de Torres and a resident of Esparza, granted power of attorney to her brother-in-law, Pedro de Torres, to execute the two preceding deeds.

In 1685, during the pirate Lorencillo's presence in the Matina valley, two enslaved men, Pedro Blanco and Domingo, escaped. Pedro Blanco, originally from Martinica, was declared free by Domingo and Simón Blenac, who stated Pedro and his parents were free before Pedro was forcibly taken by the pirate from his master, Juan, a convoy captain from Puerto Belo.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Miguel Gómez de Lara
summary: On March 15, 1687, Sargento Mayor don Miguel Gómez de Lara, Governor and Captain General, issued a certification at Pedro Blanco's request. This certification confirmed Pedro Blanco's and his parents' free status, based on declarations from Domingo and Simón Blenac.

Pedro Antonio Blanco, a free black man from Martinica, requested witness information to confirm the freedom and whereabouts of his brother, Juan Blanco. Witnesses, including don Luis de Castilla, testified that Juan Blanco was known in Panamá, served as a sailor, and possessed a certification of freedom from the Conde del Palmar.

In 1683, Juan Blanco served as a soldier on a galley in Panamá under the Conde del Palmar and later on a convoy brigantine from Puerto Belo under Antonio Martín. He was recognized as free and held a certification from the Conde del Palmar.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don Manuel de Bustamante y Vivero
Maestre de Campo don Lorenzo Calderón
summary: Maestre de Campo don Manuel de Bustamante y Vivero, Governor and Captain General, granted general judicial power to Maestre de Campo don Lorenzo Calderón, a resident of León. This power of attorney was not executed.

Capitán don Juan Rodríguez Plaza sold a cacao hacienda with 1500 trees in the Matina valley to Blas González Coronel for $600. Of this amount, $397 at 5% was to be obligated by the buyer to Pedro and Diego, minor children of the deceased Alférez Domingo Vásquez and María de Salazar.

Blas González Coronel and his wife, doña Bernarda de Fonseca, obligated themselves to the minors Pedro and Diego for $397 at 3%, as stipulated in the previous hacienda sale. This obligation was not executed.
Nicolás de Arce, as debtor, and Miguel de Arce, as guarantor, obligated themselves to Capitán Nicolás Gutiérrez Jaramillo, a resident of Esparza, for $254.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don Manuel de Bustamante y Vivero
Capitán Matías Jacinto de los Reyes
summary: Maestre de Campo don Manuel de Bustamante y Vivero, Governor and Captain General, granted general judicial power to Capitanes Esteban de la Fuente and Matías Jacinto de los Reyes, who are procurators in the Audiencia de Guatemala.
Sargento Juan González sold houses in Cartago, which Alférez Juan de Abarca had previously purchased from doña Antonia de Bustamante, for $200.
Capitán Nicolás Gutiérrez Jaramillo, a resident of Esparza, granted general power for lawsuits to Capitán don Francisco Castrajón and Alférez don Sebastián de Garita.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don José Sandoval Golfín
summary: Doña Nicolasa de Sandoval Golfín made her will, identifying her deceased parents, her uncle, her brothers (one of whom died intestate in Nicaragua), and her niece María de la Rosa, whose parents reside in León. She also ordered the establishment of a Chaplaincy, naming don Teodomiro Arias as a future Chaplain.
Capitán Eugenio Martínez, son of Benito Martínez and Juana Félix González (both deceased and from Cartagena de las Indias), began drafting his will. The document was barely started.

Capitán don Matías González Camino obligated himself to Francisco de Paula Salazar for $800 at 5%, an amount Francisco inherited from his deceased father, Capitán don Francisco de Salazar. This debt was previously charged against the houses and mill of Doña Josefa de Santiago, widow of Antonio de Acosta Arévalo, who was embargoed and requested the charge be moved. Matías González Camino then imposed the debt on his own houses in Cartago and a cacao plantation in Matina, with Capitanes don Antonio Pacheco and Jerónimo Valerino as guarantors.

Capitán don Matías González Camino obligated himself to Ambrosio and Miguel, minor sons of the deceased Manuel de Mora Salado and Doña Juana de Torres Capelazo, for $216 at 5%. The funds were received from their grandmother and tutor, Doña Margarita de Flores. Miguel de Mora Salado later cancelled this obligation in October 1698.

Gregoria de Abarca, natural daughter of Don Antonio de Abarca and Magdalena de Acuña (both living), made a will. She is married to Don José de Prado Balcázar, who is currently in Nicaragua, and has a natural daughter named Jerónima, who is about 25 years old.

Juan Martín de Flores, legitimate son of the deceased Martín de Flores and Petrona Pérez (natives of Gira de Grecia, kingdoms of Castile), made a will. He is single, and Capitán don Antonio Pacheco is designated as his heir.

people_involved: Alférez don Diego de Cuitiño Masariego
summary: Capitán don Juan Sáenz and his wife, Doña Ana de Escalante Paniagua, granted power of attorney to Alférez don Diego de Cuitiño Masariego to sell a 30-year-old Congo slave named Juan. This slave had been given to them as a dowry by Doña Ana's father, Don José de Escalante Paniagua.
Juan López Guerrero, married to Lorenza Rodríguez (a resident of León), made a will. He had no children, but the will was not finalized or executed.

Sebastián de Benavides, legitimate son of the deceased Alonso Cordero and Francisca de Benavides, made a will. He is the widower of Ana María Sánchez and has children: Francisco, María (married to Juan de Alcaina), Ambrosia, and Nicolasa (married). His stepdaughter is married to Antonio Calderón, and Matías de Monestel is his son-in-law.

Doña Josefa de Aguilar, widow of Antonio de Acosta Arévalo and tutor/curator of their minor children (Gaspar, Miguel, Cayetano, Antonio, José, Manuel, and Francisca), obligated herself to them for $475 and 6 reales, representing their paternal inheritance. Alférez José Calderón and Alférez Nicolás Calderón served as guarantors.

Juan Martín de la Mata, legitimate son of Francisco Martín de la Mata and Luisa Muñoz de Rojas (residents of Cazalla in the kingdoms of Castile), made a will. He is married to Clara de Rojas and has two living sons, Juan and Miguel.

people_involved: Capitán don Diego Sendín de Soto Mayor
Don Francisco Sendín de Soto Mayor
Doña Catalina Ortiz de Chaves y Aldana
Don Miguel Ortiz de Chaves y Aldana
summary: Capitán don Diego Sendín de Soto Mayor, a native of Madrid and legitimate son of the deceased Don Francisco Sendín de Soto Mayor and Doña Francisca de Quintanilla, made a will. He is married to Doña Catalina Ortiz de Chaves y Aldana, legitimate daughter of Don Miguel Ortiz de Chaves y Aldana and Doña Agustina Fernández de Córdova. They have six children: Agustina, Felipa, Manuel, Raimundo, Rosalía, and Josefa Tomasina de Soto Mayor. His wife and Don Miguel Ortiz de Chaves y Aldana are his executors.
Doña Sebastiana Calvo, widow of Capitán Bartolomé Muñoz Hidalgo, granted general judicial power of attorney to Capitán Domingo del Puerto Mariño.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don José de Sandoval Golfín
summary: A dowry letter was issued by Don Manuel de Sandoval Golfín, legitimate son of the deceased Maestre de Campo don José de Sandoval Golfín and Doña María Corajo, in favor of his wife, Doña Petronila de Quirós. Doña Petronila is the legitimate daughter of the deceased Alférez Francisco de Quirós and Doña María de Angulo Gascón. The dowry was $1792, with a separate arras of $1000.

people_involved: Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
Capitán don Gabriel de Echavarría Navarro
summary: Capitán don José Pérez de Muro, Don José de Guzmán, and Don Jorge de Alvarado, acting as executors for the deceased Alférez Francisco de Arleguí, sold Arleguí's dwelling houses in Cartago to Capitán don Gabriel de Echavarría Navarro for $869. The sale included existing charges: $669 for the Chaplaincy founded by Doña Juana de Echavarría (whose chaplain is Licenciado don Francisco de Salazar), $100 for the Confraternity of the Concepción, and $100 for Jerónimo Murillo, which the buyer must assume.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don Manuel de Bustamante y Vivero
summary: Maestre de Campo don Manuel de Bustamante y Vivero is mentioned as a Knight of the Order of Santiago, and the Governor and Captain General of the province of Costa Rica.

Captain Pedro Santos de la Madriz, a resident of Panama, was granted power of attorney to request the remittance of $1335 owed to the Royal Treasury of the province. This sum was part of $2000 originally designated for constructing fortifications in Matina. The document also references $500 worth of biscuits provided to Antonio Martín, commander of war vessels, in 1687, for operations against pirates in the South Sea near Amapala and Isla de la Conchagua.

On October 6, Captain Gabriel de Echavarría Navarro and his wife, Antonia María de Otálora, committed to an obligation of $669 at 5% interest. This obligation was made in favor of a chaplaincy established by Juana de Echavarría, for which Licenciado Francisco de Salazar served as chaplain, and was secured by houses they had previously acquired.

On October 6, Captain Gabriel de Echavarría Navarro and Antonia María de Otálora acknowledged a lien of $100 at 5% interest on their houses. This lien was in favor of the Confraternity of the Conception located in the city of Esparza.

On October 7, Alférez José de Prado issued a dowry letter for his wife, Juana Damiana de Mora Salado. The dowry comprised goods inherited from her aunt, Josefa de Aguilar, valued at $913 and 4 reales, along with a bridal gift (arras) of $800. Juana Damiana was the legitimate daughter of the deceased Manuel de Mora Salado and Juana Torres Capelazo.

On October 7, Captain Gabriel de Echavarría Navarro and his wife, Antonia María de Otálora, acknowledged a lien of $100 at 5% interest on the houses they had purchased. This specific lien was established in favor of Jerónimo Murillo.

On October 7, Doña Sebastiana Calvo, a widow, committed to an obligation of $200 at 5% interest. This obligation was made in favor of a chaplaincy founded by Doña Francisca del Castillo at the Convent of San Francisco, and it was secured by Sebastiana Calvo's houses in the city.

On October 15, Doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar, widow of Antonio de Acosta Arévalo, committed to an obligation of $1490 at 5% interest for a chaplaincy she was to establish, as directed by her late husband. As the patroness, she secured this obligation with her residence, a flour mill in the city's common lands, and 600 cacao trees located in Matina.

On November 3, Doña Sebastiana Calvo, widow of Captain Bartolomé Muñoz Hidalgo, committed to an obligation of $100 at 5% interest for a chaplaincy founded by Vasco Solano, with Licenciado Gregorio de Moya serving as its patron and chaplain. She secured this with her houses and noted that she and her late husband received this sum over 20 years prior from Cristóbal de Araya, who redeemed it. The deed was not granted then because her husband was traveling to Peru, and Comisario Alonso de Sandoval was the patron and chaplain at that time.

On November 26, Captain Miguel Calvo committed to an obligation of $290 at 5% interest in favor of the minor children of the late Francisco Gómez Oconitrillo, having received the sum from Francisco de Aguirre, a depositary who had resigned. A marginal note indicates that Doña María Vásquez received and canceled this obligation on February 18, 1696.

On November 29, Captain Matías González Camino, Alférez Mayor Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín (Ordinary Mayors), Captain Gabriel de Echavarría Navarro (Chief Constable), Maestre de Campo Miguel de Echavarría Navarro (Provincial Mayor), Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes, and Captain Francisco de Ocampo (Perpetual Councilmen) obligated themselves to Captain Miguel Calvo for $290 at 5%. This payment was contingent on an order to return the sum to the heir of the late Francisco Gómez Oconitrillo, who resided in Guatemala. A marginal note indicates this obligation was canceled on August 18, 1714.

On November 4, José de Rojas committed to an obligation of $100. This sum was divided, with $68 and 4 reales designated for his minor nephews, Juan and Miguel de Rojas, as their paternal inheritance. The remaining portion of the $100 was to be paid to Clara de Rojas, the mother of the minor children and wife of Juan Martín de la Mata.
On November 4, Captains Antonio Pacheco and Juan Sáenz provided a guarantee for Governor Maestre de Campo Manuel de Bustamante.
A fianza (bond) was required from the Gobernador to ensure proper administration of the estates of deceased persons during his term in office.
The same individuals who provided the previous bond also guaranteed the Gobernador for the rights related to "penas de cámara" (chamber penalties) during his government.
Alférez Juan Vásquez sold Salvador Leal, a 30-year-old "pardo" creole enslaved person, to Alférez Tomás de Chaves for $300.00.
Doña Juana Pérez, widow of Bernardo Chacón, sold María, a 20-year-old "parda" enslaved person, to Juan Gregorio Ramírez for $300.00.
Juan Gregorio Ramírez incurred a debt of $300.00 to Doña Juana Pérez, payable over three years. This debt was later cancelled by Doña Juana Pereira on February 18, 1696.

Doña Ana de Retes, representing herself and her husband Capitán don Diego de Ibarra, committed to pay $4085.4 reales to their grandchildren, Doña Angela María and Manuel Antonio, as their inheritance from their deceased parents, Alférez Francisco de Arleguí and Juana de Echavarría Navarro. Several individuals acted as guarantors for this obligation.

people_involved: Capitán don Gabriel de Echavarría Navarro
summary: Capitán don Diego de Ibarra, due to illness preventing travel to Cartago, granted power of attorney to his wife, Doña Ana de Retes. This was formalized in Santa Ana, within the jurisdiction of Cartago, before Capitán don Gabriel de Echavarría Navarro, the Alguacil Mayor.

people_involved: Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
summary: Doña Ana de Retes, acting as tutor and curator for her grandchildren (children of the late Alférez Francisco de Arleguí), sold Gabriel, a 20-year-old "negro" of Congo nation enslaved person, to Capitán don José Pérez de Muro for $350.00.

people_involved: Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
Capitán don Juan López de la Flor
Capitán don José López de la Flor
summary: Capitán don José Pérez de Muro, don José de Guzmán, and don Jorge de Alvarado, as executors for Alférez Francisco de Arleguí, established a Capellanía for masses as directed by the late Doña Juana de Echavarría Navarro. The principal was charged to the houses of don Gabriel de Echavarría Navarro, and an interim chaplain was named with a succession plan for future chaplains from specific family lines.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don José de Prado
summary: Sargento Mayor don José de Prado obligated himself to Jerónima de Abarca for $1100.00 at a 5% interest rate.

Doña Manuela de Salazar, widow of Capitán don Juan González Camino and tutor for her minor daughters Doña Catalina and Doña Josefa González Camino, received $3077 and 1 real as their paternal inheritance, for which she assumed an obligation.
Francisco de Benavides obligated himself to Mateo de Campos for $150.00, to be paid in two installments of tame wild mules and cattle: $50.00 within 20 days and $100.00 within a year.

people_involved: Alférez don Pedro Durán de Chaves
summary: A dowry letter was issued on November 12 for the marriage of Alonso Ruiz Arroyo and Isabel Durán de Castro, scheduled for November 14. The dowry was $3163.00, and the arras was $1000.00. Alonso's parents were José Ruiz Arroyo and Doña Juana Berrocal from Cádiz, and Isabel's parents were Alférez don Pedro Durán de Chaves and the late Doña Francisca Rodríguez de Castro.

people_involved: Doña Ana Josefa Fernández de la Fuente
Alférez Juan Fernández de la Fuente
summary: A dowry letter was issued on November 12 for the marriage of Juan Fernández de Serralonga and Doña Ana Josefa Fernández de la Fuente, scheduled for November 14. The dowry was $3030.00, and the arras was $6000.00. Juan's parents were José Fernández de Serralonga and Doña Juana Nuño y Colón from Sevilla, and Ana Josefa's parents were Alférez Juan Fernández de la Fuente and Doña María Durán de Chaves.
Juan Matías de Mores sold Feliciana, a Black enslaved woman he had purchased from Captain Jorge de Alvarado, to Treasurer Juan Alvarez de Pedrosa for $450. The transaction was executed in Barba.

Alférez José de Quesada received $250 from his mulatto slave, Francisco, as a down payment towards his agreed-upon freedom price of $400. The formal deed for Francisco's liberty will be issued once the remaining balance is paid.

Juan Matías de Mores obligated himself to Treasurer Juan Alvarez de Pedrosa for $541, which included $200 for the Cofradías de la Concepción in Cartago and Esparza, for which Doña Francisca de Ascuña had a prior obligation. The debt was later cancelled on April 6, 1695, by Captain Domingo Guerrero, acting as executor for the deceased Alvarez Pedrosa, upon receiving the full amount from Mores.

Treasurer Juan Alvarez de Pedrosa sold a hacienda and cattle ranch in the Landecho valley to Juan Matías de Mores for $1341. The property, which Pedroza had acquired from Lucas de Ledezma, included various livestock, houses, corrals, and cultivated cacao, plantains, and fruit trees.

Lieutenant Francisco Montero de Espinosa, a resident of Cartago and Barba, obligated himself to Alférez José de Quesada for $150, to be paid in cacao the following February. This obligation was later cancelled by Quesada in Cartago on July 16, 1707.

Dionisio de Fonseca, legitimate son of Francisco de Fonseca and Catalina de Aguilar, executed his testament in Barba. He was married to Doña Mariana de Paz, and they had four children: Manuel, Miguel, Gertrudis, and Manuela.

people_involved: Capitán don Gabriel de Echavarría Navarro
summary: Captain Don Gabriel de Echavarría Navarro and Doña Antonia María de Otálora sold an 18-year-old mulatto criollo enslaved person to Captain Don Miguel Calvo for $200.

Doña Isabel de Guevara, whose husband Don Agustín González was absent in Tierra Firme, obligated herself for $100 at 5% to a Capellanía. This Capellanía was instituted by the late Doña Josefa de Moya and is patronized by Captain Don Antonio de Moya, with the obligation secured against houses she purchased from Ayudante Antonio de Castro.

people_involved: Doña Nicolasa de Vargas y Machuca
Alférez Francisco de Vargas y Machuca
