summary: A dowry letter was issued for Lieutenant Francisco Montero de Espinosa, a native of Panamá, in favor of his wife, Doña Nicolasa de Vargas y Machuca. She is the legitimate daughter of Alférez Francisco de Vargas y Machuca and Doña María de Ocampo, with a dowry of $554 and arras of $1000.

Lieutenant Francisco Montero de Espinosa and his wife, Doña Nicolasa de Vargas Machuca, obligated themselves to Domingo Guerrero, executor of the late Juan Alvarez de Pedrosa, for $400. This sum represented the remaining balance for 80 mules Pedrosa had sold them, with payments scheduled for Panamá and 'this city' upon their return.
Doña Juana Arias granted power of attorney to her husband, José Hidalgo, who was absent in Nicaragua, authorizing him to sell a criolla Black enslaved woman named Antonia.
Clara de Rojas is identified as the widow of Juan Martín de la Mata in an incomplete registry entry.

Lucas Hernández Iraola was granted power to collect funds in Panama from Sargento Bartolomé Morillo, who previously acted as a representative for 'la Mata'. The funds are related to credits of 'la Mata', whose documents are currently held by Morillo.

people_involved: Jerónimo Morales (son of Beatriz Méndez Machado)
summary: Jerónimo Morales, who as a minor donated his inheritance from his deceased mother, Beatriz Méndez Machado, to his sisters, now seeks to annul this donation. Being married with children, he aims to reclaim his inheritance and has granted power of attorney to his brother, Captain Agustín de Morales, to pursue this claim.

Juan Matías de Mores is obligated to Alférez Domingo Guerrero, a resident of Esparza, for $217.00 and 50 mares. Additionally, he must pay $68.00, distributed among Juan Moreno, Seneríno de Aguilar, Captain Sebastián de Zamora, and the Gobernador y Capitán General, with the entire debt originating from $541.00 owed to the late Juan Alvarez Pedrosa, whose executor is Domingo Guerrero.
On April 6, 1695, Captain Domingo Guerrero officially cancelled the obligation previously established with Juan Matías de Mores.

people_involved: Pedro Alonso de Rodas y Salgado
María Gómez de Ocón y Trillo
Francisco Gómez de Ocón y Trillo
summary: A dowry letter was issued for Pedro Alonso de Rodas y Salgado, a native of Santiago de Guatemala, and his wife, María Gómez de Ocón y Trillo, with a dowry of $419.00 and arras of $500.00. María is identified as the legitimate daughter of Francisco Gómez de Ocón y Trillo and María Vásquez de Trejos.

On November 6, 1692, Blas Solís, the legitimate son of the late Francisco Solís and Antonia López, executed his testament. He had eight children from his first marriage to Isabel de Salazar, including Francisca, who was married to Jerónimo Morales, and two children from his second marriage to María de la Candelaria. His brothers, Alférez Tomás de Chaves and Sargento Cristóbal Solís, were named as his executors.

Captain don Gabriel de Echavarría Navarro requested testimony of an arrest warrant issued by Gobernador Manuel de Bustamante y Vivero, which ordered Echavarría to imprison Francisco Ramírez Rodado. This request followed an incident where the Gobernador questioned Echavarría's authority for the arrest and then denied issuing the order, despite Echavarría's insistence.

On February 27, 1687, Alférez Andrés de Irula and his wife, doña Magdalena de Abarca, became indebted to Alférez Esteban de Oses Navarro for $291.7 reales at 5% interest. This debt compensated Oses Navarro for acting as Irula's guarantor in a lawsuit against Captain don Antonio Pacheco, who was the tutor of the minor Juan Ruiz de Velazco, concerning goods collected by Irula in Panama. The obligation was formalized before Alcalde don Miguel de Echavarría Navarro.

On March 22, 1694, doña Juana Calvo, acting as tutor and curator for her children, requested testimony of the previous document that established an obligation in favor of her husband, Alférez Esteban de Oses Navarro.

people_involved: Jerónimo Morales (son of Beatriz Méndez Machado)
summary: On April 14, Captain Agustín de Morales, representing himself and Jerónimo de Morales as heirs of Beatriz Méndez Machado, sought to reclaim a mulatto slave named Antonio from Alférez José Calderón, who had taken him seven months prior. The slave had been entrusted to Agustín by his deceased sister, María de Morales, over six years ago. An Alcalde ordered Antonio to be deposited with Morales, secured by a bond from Juan de Vida Martel and Francisco Fallas.
On April 3, doña Juana de Salazar, the legitimate daughter of the late don Fernando de Salazar and doña Ambrosia de Echavarría Navarro, executed a closed testament.
Capitán don Juan Rodríguez Plaza requested the opening proceedings for the will of his deceased wife, Doña Juana de Salazar.
María de la Candelaria, widow of Blas Solís, granted power of attorney to Juan López de Soto to collect $300 from her husband's estate as her dote. This transaction took place in Barba.

Doña Manuela de Salazar, acting as tutor and curator for her minor children, sold a cacao hacienda with 1500 fruit-bearing trees in the Matina valley to Capitán don Juan Sáenz for $200. Her deceased husband, Capitán don Juan González Camino, had originally purchased this hacienda from Capitán don Esteban de Moya.
Capitán don Matías González Camino, as executor for Doña Juana de Salazar and tutor for her minor children, sold a 12-year-old black slave named Salvador to Capitán don Antonio de Moya for $300.

Capitán don Antonio de Moya obligated himself to Capitán don Matías González Camino, acting as executor for Doña Juana de Salazar and curator for her minor children, for $300 at 5% interest. This money belonged to the minor don Miguel de Alvarado. Moya hypothecated his slaves Salvador (12, negro), Paula (40), and Petronila (14).

Capitán don Matías González Camino, as executor for Doña Juana de Salazar and tutor for her minor children, sold a mulata slave named Juana, described as 'color pardo' and over 40 years old, to Doña Juana de Aguiar for $300.

Doña Juana de Aguiar obligated herself to Capitán don Matías González Camino, as executor for Doña Juana de Salazar and tutor for her minor children (of her and Capitán don García de Alvarado), for $300 at 5% interest. She hypothecated her dwelling houses in Cartago and her slave Juana (mulata, color pardo, over 40 years old).

Capitán don Matías González Camino, as executor for Doña Juana de Salazar and tutor for her minor children, sold a black slave named Isabel, over 40 years old, to Licenciado Agustín de Torres, the city's priest, for $425.

Doña Manuela de Salazar, widow of Capitán don Juan González Camino, acted as guarantor for her niece Doña Gertrudis de Alvarado, legitimate daughter of the deceased Capitán don García de Alvarado and Doña Juana de Salazar. This allowed Doña Gertrudis to receive $5351 from don José Guzmán, her curator ad litem, as part of her legitimate inheritance.
Manuel de Mena owed Victoria Chacón $144.50, which was the price for the lease of a cacao plantation.

A dote letter was issued for Blas Suárez, a native of the island of Tenerife and son of Juan Suárez and María Tristán, and his fiancée María de Chaves, daughter of Alférez Tomás de Chaves and Juana de Solís. Their marriage was set for the upcoming July 10th, with a dote of $1300 and arras of $500.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don Miguel de Echavarría
Capitán don José Pérez del Muro
summary: Capitán Miguel Calvo provided bail for Tomás Ruiz, a 'color pardo' prisoner. Tomás Ruiz had been arrested by Maestre de Campo don Miguel de Echavarría, Provincial of the Santa Hermandad, under orders from Capitán don José Pérez del Muro, for claiming to have power from a resident of Nata city. Tomás Ruiz was to be delivered when he legitimized his right.

A dote letter was issued for Juan de Dios Aguilar, son of the deceased Sargento Agustín de Aguilar and Catalina Méndez, and his fiancée Margarita Fernández, daughter of the deceased Juan Fernández and Ana Solano. Their marriage was set for Sunday, November 29th, with a dote of $1028 and arras of $1000.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego de Angulo Gascón
summary: Capitán don Matías González Camino, while traveling to Panama, granted general power of attorney to Doña Manuela de Salazar, Licenciado don Diego de Angulo Gascón (the Beneficed Priest of the parish church in Cartago), and don Francisco.

Francisco de Salazar, Sacristán Mayor, and Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes are granted power of attorney to act as tutors and curators for Miguel de Alvarado. They are tasked with pursuing a legal case concerning Miguel's inheritance, following the deaths of his parents, Captain García de Alvarado and Juana de Salazar, and his sister Gertrudis de Alvarado.

Captain Agustín de Morales, son of the deceased Ayudante Juan de Morales and Beatriz Machado, executes his will. He is married to Rodulfa Salguero and names their children Beatriz, Salomona, and Bernardo Morales. He also mentions his deceased uncle, Alférez Antonio Machado, who founded a chaplaincy of which Agustín is the patron, and his brothers Isidoro, Pedro, and Jerónimo de Morales.

Jerónimo de Morales obligates himself to José de Prado, who is the curator for the minor children Antonia Clemencia and Francisca. The obligation is for $162.00, representing the value of 54 cattle purchased by Morales that belong to the minors, children of the deceased Sergeant Blas de Solís and Isabel de Salazar. Morales mortgages an estate in the Barba valley, by the Virilla river, as security.

Juan Gómez, a native of Sevilla and son of Juan Gómez and María Maderos, makes his will. He instructs that his assets be delivered to Captain Alonso de Aranda y Acevedo upon his return from Granada, Nicaragua, so that Aranda, along with his executors, can manage them according to Gómez's instructions.

Doña María de Retes, widow of Captain Francisco Ramiro Corajo, along with Captain Pedro José Sáenz and his wife Doña María de la Rosa (who is María de Retes' daughter), obligate themselves to the Cofradía de la Concepción for $200.00 at 5% interest. This debt was originally owed by the deceased Sergeant Francisco López Serrano, and they mortgage a house in the city as collateral.
Manuel de Bonilla is recorded as owing Captain Francisco de Castrejón, a trader in the province, 209 reales.

Doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar, a widow, sells a 38-year-old mulatto slave named Benito to Don José de Prado y Valcázar for $300.00. This amount is owed by the seller to the buyer, as evidenced by a dowry letter granted by José de Prado y Valcázar to his wife, Doña Juana Damiana de Mora, who is Josefa's niece.

Licenciado Don Francisco de Salazar, Presbítero and Sacristán Mayor of the city, requests testimony of the will granted by the deceased Alférez Don Pedro Durán de Chaves, for whom Salazar serves as an executor.

The testament of Alférez Pedro Durán de Chaves details his family. He was first married to Francisca de Castro, with whom he had a daughter, Isabel Durán de Castro, who married Alférez Alonso Ruiz Arroyo. He was married a second time to María Vásquez Coronado. His sister is Micaela Durán, and his brother-in-law is Juan Fernández de la Fuente. His heirs are his wife and daughter, and his executors are Licenciado Francisco de Salazar, Micaela Durán de Chaves, and Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes.

Juan Antonio de Guevara, attorney for Captain Martín de Ordeñana y Goiri of Granada, Nicaragua, obligates himself to Captain Juan de Oriamuno, a knight of the Order of Santiago and resident of Panama, for $1400.00. This sum was received from Captain José Pérez de Muro. Guevara mortgages 200 mule beasts located in Panama, belonging to Ordeñana and under the care of Alférez Juan Patricio de Sandoval.
The Beneficiado Agustín de Torres, Cura of the city, sells a lot within the city to Don Antonio de Bustamante for $50.00.

Alférez Alvaro de Guevara y Sandoval, son of Captain José de Guevara and Inés de Sandoval Golfín, makes his will. He mentions his cousin Sebastiana de Aguirre, his uncle Sebastián Golfín, and his sister Isabel de Guevara. His executors are his sister Isabel, Captain Antonio de Moya, and Alférez Francisco de Moya, with his mother, Doña Inés, named as his universal heir.

Captain Francisco López Conejo, acting on behalf of Ayudante Juan de Torres, a resident of Granada, Nicaragua, obligates himself to Captain Juan de Oriamuno, a resident of Panama, for $420.00. He mortgages a lot of one hundred mule beasts as security for this obligation.

Doña Juana de Sandoval, daughter of the deceased Maestre de Campo José de Sandoval and María Ramiro, makes her will. Her heirs are her nephews Juan, José, Manuel, and niece Ana, who are the children of her sister Doña Antonia de Sandoval. Juan López de Soto, identified as her brother or brother-in-law, is named as her executor.

Gregoria de Acosta, daughter of the deceased Antonio de Acosta and Juana Madrigal, makes her will. She is the widow of José de Proa and names her three children, Luisa, Juana, and Francisco, as her heirs. Juan Antonio de Soto is appointed as her executor.

locations: ribera del río de la Reventazón
summary: Cristóbal Alvarez de Oviedo sold a cocoa plantation with 1000 fruit-bearing trees on the Reventazón riverbank to Jerónimo Muñoz for $200. The plantation belonged to Juana de Oviedo, Cristóbal's 4-year-old granddaughter, who resided with him.

Captain Gabriel de Echavarría Navarro, Alguacil Mayor and Regidor of Cartago, made his will. He was the legitimate son of the late Captain Juan de Echavarría Navarro and Ana de Rites, married to Antonia María de Otálora, and had two living daughters, Juana Josefa and Juana María, with another child expected. He was also a professed son of the Third Order of San Francisco.

Maestre de Campo Miguel de Echavarría Navarro, Alcalde Mayor provincial of the Santa Hermandad, attempted to lease a cocoa plantation of 1000 trees in the Matina valley to Bernardo Delgado for 2 years. The rent was set at 7 zurrones of cocoa annually, but the transaction did not proceed.

Captain Juan Sáenz and his wife, Ana de Escalante Paniagua, obligated themselves for $100 at 5% interest to the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora de la Soledad. This obligation was secured by half a house and half a plot in Cartago, which they had purchased with this existing encumbrance from Alférez Ignacio de Artavia and his wife, María de Córdova.

Captain Francisco de Bonilla obligated himself for $50 at 5% interest to the Convento de San Francisco, for which Captain Miguel Calvo served as Syndic. This amount, redeemed by Lorenzo de Arburola, pertained to a Chaplaincy established by Francisco del Castillo and was secured by Bonilla's houses in Cartago.

Captain Juan de Bonilla made his will. He was the legitimate son of the late Sergeant Major Alonso de Bonilla and Juana Benita Pereira, married to Francisca de Astúa, and had two living daughters named María and Francisca.

Blas González Coronel, the Escribano, and his wife Bernarda de Fonseca, sold a cocoa plantation of 1,500 trees in the Matina valley to Juan de Vida Martell for $600. The sale included an existing $397 obligation at 5% interest on the hacienda, owed to Pedro and Diego, minor sons of Domingo Vázquez and María de Salazar, whose tutor was Juan Plaza. The buyer was required to acknowledge this obligation.

Juan de Vida Martell formally obligated himself for $397 at 5% interest to Pedro and Diego, minor sons of Domingo Vázquez and María de Salazar, as agreed in the previous sale. He secured this obligation on the purchased hacienda and provided Lieutenant José de Escalante Paniagua as a guarantor.

Alférez Antonio de Bonilla, the natural son of Captain Francisco de Bonilla, issued a dowry letter for María Solano, the legitimate daughter of Alférez Francisco Solano and Juana de las Salas. Antonio and María were scheduled to marry on the upcoming Monday, May 2nd, with a dowry of $1254 and earnest money (arras) of $500.
Maestre de Campo Miguel de Echavarría Navarro granted general judicial power to Captain Zelidón de Barraondo, a procurator residing in the city of Santiago de Guatemala.
Alférez Juan Matías Baptista Lizondo sold a 32-year-old Conga black woman named Paula to Alférez Tomás de Chaves for $300.

locations: Nápoli de Romania en la Grecia
summary: Juan Salvador Mauricio, a native of Naples in Romania (Greece), made a closed will. He declared he was unmarried, had no children, siblings, or living ascendants/descendants, as his parents had died 48 years prior. He named Captain Antonio Pacheco as his universal heir and appointed Captain Antonio Pacheco and Licenciado Gaspar Cascante de Rojas as his executors.

Doña Isabel de Guevara, wife of Agustín González de Villalobos (absent for over 5 years), obligated herself to the Cofradía del Rosario for $500 at 5%. This debt, which she redeemed from Alférez Diego de Cárdenas, pertained to a chaplaincy established by Doña Josefa de Moya, with Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya as chaplain. The obligation was secured by her house in Cartago.

Sargento Francisco Gutiérrez made a donation of $100 to his niece, Juana de Oviedo, the legitimate daughter of deceased Juan de Oviedo and Juana de la Vega. Juana de Oviedo was born in his house over four years ago and he had raised her. This transaction was not finalized.

Doña Micaela Durán de Chaves sold an enslaved person named Juan Toribio, described as Pardo and 28 years old, to Alférez Francisco Fernández for $300. Juan Toribio had been acquired by her deceased husband, Alonso Romero, in Cartagena.

Don Antonio de Bustamante sold a house of adobes with a tiled roof and a fenced lot, along with six chairs, a wooden estrado, and a wooden bed, to Capitán don Juan Sáenz for $300. The property, previously bought from Sargento Juan González, was located in Cartago, bordering properties of Capitán Antonio Pacheco, Capitán José Pérez de Muro, and the Governor and Captain General.

people_involved: Capitán don Diego Sendín de Sotomayor
summary: Don Antonio de Bustamante sold houses of adobes with tiled roofs, a kitchen quarter, and a fenced lot to Capitán don Pedro José Sáenz for $3200. The property was located in Cartago, bordering properties of Juan Antonio de Guevara, Capitán don Juan Sáenz, Doña Catalina Ortiz de Aldana (widow of Capitán don Diego Sendín de Sotomayor), and Comisario Agustín de Torres.

Capitán don Pedro José Sáenz, as principal, and Capitán don Juan Sáenz, as guarantor, obligated themselves to don Antonio de Bustamante for $1500, payable within two years. This obligation was cancelled on March 8, 1697, in Cartago, as Bustamante received the payment from the principal debtor.

Capitán don Juan Sáenz and his wife, Doña Ana de Escalante Paniagua, sold an enslaved Black man, about 30 years old and of Congo caste, to Sargento Juan González for $300. The enslaved man was part of Doña Ana's dowry from her parents, Teniente don José Escalante Paniagua and Doña Manuela de Vida Martel.

people_involved: Alcalde Alférez Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín
summary: Ambrosio de Mora Salado, between 14 and 25 years old, sought to receive and administer his inheritance from his deceased parents, Manuel de Mora Salado and Doña Juana Torres Capelazo, which was under Capitán Francisco de Bonilla's care. Alcalde Alférez Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín required a guarantor, and Alférez don José del Prado served as such.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Juan de Vida Martel
summary: This is the will of Doña Manuela de Vida Martel, daughter of deceased Sargento Mayor don Juan de Vida Martel and Doña Juana de Ortega, and wife of Teniente don José Escalante Paniagua. She listed her seven children: don José, Doña Ana (married to Capitán don Juan Sáenz), don Juan, don Manuel (absent), doña Baltasara, don Antonio, and doña Francisca. She also owned four enslaved Black men: José, Manuel, Antonio, and Felipe.

Capitán Domingo del Puerto Mariño and Gaspar de Basterrica y Narbaiza, who were acquitted in a criminal lawsuit against Capitán don Antonio Pacheco regarding the death of Alférez don Luis de Castillos in Santiago de Guatemala, agreed to desist from claiming damages from Pacheco to avoid further disputes. They imposed a $500 fine on themselves, payable to the Cofradía del Santísimo Sacramento, if they violated the agreement. This transaction was not finalized.

This is a dowry letter for Andrés de Salazar, a merchant from Santiago de Guatemala, legitimate son of don Pedro de Salazar and doña Josefa Suárez, in favor of Gregoria de Flores, daughter of Catalina de Flores. They were to marry on Sunday, the 21st of the current month. The dowry was $1179 and 4 reales, with arras of $200.

Andrés Arias and his wife, Doña Isabel de Alfaro Hidalgo, sold a Creole enslaved Black man, about 18 years old, to Alférez Tomás de Chaves for $400. The enslaved man was part of Doña Isabel's dowry from her parents.

Blas González Coronel, the scribe, and his wife, Doña Bernarda de Fonseca, obligated themselves to the Convento de San Francisco, represented by its Syndic Capitán don Miguel Calvo, for $400 at 5%. This obligation was secured by half a house and lot in Cartago, which they had bought with this obligation from Francisco Ramírez Rodado and Doña Jerónima de Retes, who were also their parents. The obligation was cancelled on December 20, 1707, in Cartago.

This is a dowry letter for Juan Camacho, legitimate son of deceased Nicolás Camacho and Catalina López, in favor of his wife Doña Beatriz de Morales, legitimate daughter of deceased Juan de Morales and Doña Beatriz Méndez Machado. He received the assets of Doña Josefa de Morales, Doña Beatriz's sister, totaling $470, with arras of $300.

This is a dowry letter for Miguel Damián de Lizondo, legitimate son of Alférez Juan Matías Baptista Lizondo and Doña Francisca Guzmán de Benavente, in favor of his wife Doña Antonia de Morales Miranda, legitimate daughter of deceased Juan de Morales and Doña Beatriz Méndez Machado. He received the assets of Doña Josefa de Morales, Doña Antonia's sister, totaling $635 and 4 reales, with arras of $400.

Andrés de Salazar and his wife, Gregoria de Flores, sold an enslaved mulata named Juana, about 20 years old, to Sargento Juan Masís for $250. Juana was part of Gregoria de Flores's dowry from her mother.

Alférez Tomás de Chaves committed to pay Jerónimo Murillo $100 at 5% interest for a house, kitchen, trapiche, and two caballerías of land in the valley of Aserrí. These properties were purchased at a public auction of the late Alférez Pedro Durán de Chaves's estate. Due to Jerónimo Murillo's illness, the payment is to be made to his brother and tutor, Salvador Murillo.

Sergeant Juan González and his wife María de Espinosa obligated themselves to their minor grandson, Manuel Antonio, for $520, which constituted his inheritance. Manuel Antonio is the son of their deceased son, Felipe Romero, and Lucía Picón. They committed to pay 5% interest on this sum.

Maestre de Campo Miguel de Echavarría Navarro and his wife Eugenia Gertrudis de Abarca attempted to sell an enslaved Black man named Gaspar García, aged 30, to Alférez José Calderón for $200. However, the transaction did not pass or complete.

Captain Juan Sáenz sold half a house of adobe and tile with half a plot of land to Doña Catalina Ortiz de Aldana for $200. This property had been acquired by Juan Sáenz from Alférez Ignacio de Artavia and his wife María de Córdoba. The sale was burdened with two encumbrances of $100 each, one for the Cofradía de la Soledad and another for Chaplain Licenciado Gregorio de Moya, which the buyer was required to recognize.

Sergeant Juan González, son of the late Lorenzo Domínguez Romero and María de Ochoa, made his will. He stated he had been married to María de Espinosa for approximately 50 years and listed their children: Felipe Romero (deceased, married to Lucía Picón), Mariana (married to Teniente José de Quirós), Josefa (married to Nicolás Chacón), Luisa (married to Lorenzo de Villarreal), María (married to José de Aguilar), and single children Antonia, Jorge, and Miguel. He also mentioned his enslaved people Nicolasa María and Juan (negro congo), his grandson Manuel Antonio (also referred to as Antonio José), and Ana, a 14-year-old he had raised, along with his grandson Juan Miguel de Quirós.

Maestre de Campo Miguel de Echavarría Navarro and his wife Doña Eugenia Gertrudis Abarca sold an enslaved Black man named Gaspar Rodríguez, approximately 36 years old, to Alférez Francisco Fernández for $200.

Maestre de Campo Miguel de Echavarría Navarro and his wife Doña Eugenia Gertrudis de Abarca, whose residential houses were mortgaged for $600 to a chaplaincy, were required to rebuild due to deterioration and partial collapse. They obligated themselves to reconstruct the property and further mortgaged 500 cattle in the common lands of Cartago and 1000 cacao trees in Matina. The chaplaincy's patron and chaplain was Licenciado Gaspar Cascante de Rojas.

Doña Sebastiana Calvo, widow of Captain Bartolomé Muñoz Hidalgo, granted general power of attorney to Secretario Zeledón de Barraondo, a Procurador in the Audiencia de Guatemala. This power was for a lawsuit against Maestre de Campo José Agustín de Estrada, a resident of Guatemala, concerning a debt his deceased father, also named José Agustín de Estrada, allegedly owed her late husband. She also authorized him for other legal matters.

Alférez Juan Ginés de Hinojosa, a native of Santiago de Guatemala and legitimate son of the late Captain Juan Ginés de Hinojosa and María Orduño, made his will. He stated he had been married to Gertrudis Ruiz Guillén for 15 or 16 years and listed their children: Francisca (11), Gertrudis (8), Juan (5), and Josefa (5 months). He also named his wife's parents, Juan Ruiz Guillén and María Rodríguez, and appointed Beneficiado Diego de Anguda Gascón and Captain Antonio Pacheco as his executors.
The Alcaldes for the year 1695 were listed as Captain Domingo del Puerto Mariño, Captain Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, and Captain Francisco López Conejo.

Alférez Bartolomé Torralba, a trader in the province and traveling to Panama, obligated himself to Captain Juan de Oriamuno, a Knight of the Order of Santiago and resident of Panama, for $280. This sum was received from Captain José Pérez de Muro for outfitting a mule train, and Torralba mortgaged 50 of the mules he was transporting.

Licenciado Antonio de Vargas Machuca, as the legitimate son and heir of his deceased parents Captain José de Vargas Machuca and Doña Gertrudis de Alvarado, granted power of attorney. He authorized Captain Jacinto de Pasos y Porta, a resident of Granada, Jorge de Alvarado, a resident of Cartago, and Francisco de Cosio Mier, a trader traveling to Panama, to sell a quantity of mules and collect debts owed to his late father.
Francisco Vélez de Guevara, a trader in Cartago and traveling to Panama, granted power of attorney to Captain Martín de Ordeñana Goiri, a resident of Cartago.

Captain Matías Delgado de Aguilar, a resident of Granada, Nicaragua, granted power of attorney to an unnamed individual in the same city. This power was for the purpose of collecting his cattle and handling all his legal disputes.

Francisco Vélez de Guevara, a trader traveling to Panamá, became indebted to Captain Juan de Oriamuno for $700. This loan, facilitated by Captain José Pérez de Muro, was intended for outfitting a herd of 150 mules, which Vélez de Guevara hypothecated as security.

people_involved: Gil de Morales de la Torre
summary: Sergeant Gil de Morales de la Torre, a resident of Panamá, incurred a debt of $980 to Captain Juan de Oriamuno. The loan, arranged by Captain José Pérez de Muro, was for outfitting 170 mules and was to be repaid in Panamá within a year, with the mule herd serving as collateral.
Matías Masís, a master blacksmith, took an 11-year-old orphan boy named Pablo de Sandoval into his care. Masís committed to teaching Sandoval his trade over a period of six years.

Juan Fernández de la Fuente and his wife, María Durán de Chaves, sold houses with four lots in Cartago to Roque López and his wife, Gregoria Ricardo, for $300. The property was encumbered by a 5% chaplaincy instituted by Andrés López de Céspedes, and the buyers assumed this obligation.

Juan Fernández de la Fuente, a native of Sagra de Toledo, Spain, made his will. He was married to María Durán de Chaves and had a daughter, Ana Fernández de la Fuente, who was married to Juan Fernández de Serralonga. The will also mentioned his nephew Alonso Ruiz Arroyo and four slaves, with Catalina, aged 2, to be freed after the testators' deaths.
Juan Fernández de la Fuente and his wife, María Durán de Chaves, sold a 7-year-old mulatto slave named Petronila, daughter of their slave María, to José Hidalgo for $200.

María de Monterroso, widow of Alférez Gaspar Arias, made a codicil to her will in José Hidalgo's home in Valle de Aserrí. She noted that her son Pedro Arias had died intestate in San Vicente de Austria, and his paternal inheritance reverted to her. She also revoked instructions for masses for her deceased slave Ventura and mentioned her son José Arias, who was tasked with fulfilling that disposition. Her son Bartolomé Arias had married María de Porras, died childless, and his inheritance returned to her. She also mentioned selling a solar in Cartago to María de Alvarado.
Licenciado Antonio de Vargas Machuca, while traveling to León on orders, granted power of attorney for his affairs in the local province to Licenciado Agustín de Torres.
Juan Fernández de la Fuente and his wife, María Durán de Chaves, granted general power of attorney to their nephew, Alférez Alonso Ruiz Arroyo.

Antonio Jiménez Maldonado sold a 20-year-old mulatto slave named Agustín de Sojo, who had been donated to him by his mother Juana Jiménez, to Captain Domingo Guerrero, a resident of Esparta, for $250.

people_involved: Josefa Antonia de Barrientos y Orellana
summary: Captain Cristóbal Díaz de Orellana Barrientos, a native of Moron de la Frontera, made his will. He was first married to María Ruiz de Corpas, with whom he had a son, Francisco Ruiz de Corpas Barrientos, aged 26 and married in Havana. His second marriage was to Isabel Josefa de Cote from Cádiz, with whom he had two daughters, Andrea (21) and Josefa Antonia (8). Captain Antonio de Moya and Alférez Sebastián de Garita were named as executors.
Ana de los Santos, a widow and legitimate daughter of Felipe de Coto and Juana Jilera, made her will. She was the widow of Francisco Hernández Ferreto and mentioned her children.

Juan Monge, acting for himself and as tutor for his minor siblings (children of the late Felipe Monge), sold a piece of pasture land in the jurisdiction of Aserrí to José de Rojas for $100. The land was bordered by the Tiribí River and properties belonging to Francisco Grómez.
Lieutenant Sebastián de Contreras formally obligated himself to Juan Moreno, a merchant in the city, for a sum of $243. Contreras committed to paying this debt in Panamá.

people_involved: Juan López de la Rea y Soto
summary: Captain Francisco de Cabrera, a native of Trujillo, Honduras, executed his will. He was married to Mariana de Sandoval for eight years and had no children with her, though his wife had two sons, Antonio and José Arias. His executors were his brother-in-law, Juan López de la Rea y Soto, and his wife, who was also named his sole heir.

Doña Manuela de Salazar, widow of Captain Juan González Camino and mother of Catalina and Josefa, granted a general power of attorney. This power was given to Pedro de Alvarado and Captain José Pérez de Muro (residing in Panamá) to collect debts owed to her late husband.

people_involved: Angela de la Paz y Flores
summary: Sergeant Major Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín and his wife Angela de la Paz y Flores attempted to sell a cattle pasture with a house and kitchen, located 14 leagues from the city across the Río Grande, along with cattle, to Alférez Tomás de Chaves for $510. The buyer was to recognize obligations to the Cofradía de las Animas de San Francisco and the Capellanía of Licenciado Diego de Campos Quirós, but this transaction was incomplete and did not pass.

people_involved: Angela de la Paz y Flores
summary: Sergeant Major Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín and his wife Angela de la Paz y Flores sold a cattle pasture and other items to Alférez Tomás de Chaves for $510. The buyer was to recognize obligations to the Convento de San Francisco, the Capellanía of Diego de Campos Quirós, the Capellanía of the beneficed priests of the Parish Church, and the Cofradía de la Concepción, all at 5% interest.

Alférez Tomás de Chaves sold an enslaved Black woman named Pura, 32 years old, to Sergeant Major Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín for $250. Chaves had previously acquired Pura through a purchase from Josefa de Aguilar.

The Cabildo, Justice, and Regiment, including Captain Francisco de Bonilla, Alférez Sebastián de Garita, Sergeant Major Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín, Maestre de Campo Miguel de Echavarría Navarro, Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes, and Captain Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, revoked a power of attorney previously granted to Captain Diego Rodríguez Menéndez, a Procurador in Santiago de Guatemala. They then conferred general power to Zeledón de Barraondo and Francisco de Amezquita, both Procuradores in Santiago de Guatemala. This document was not signed or passed.

Alférez Mayor Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín, who was the auctioneer for movable goods from the estate of the deceased Basilio de Mora, became obligated for $176. This sum belonged to Leonor de Mora, the legitimate daughter of Basilio de Mora and Lorenza Millanés. Sandoval Golfín mortgaged his residential houses in the city at 5% interest to secure this obligation.

Captain of Cavalry Antonio Pacheco, acting as tutor and curator for his stepson Juan Ruiz de Velazco (son of the late Juan Ruiz de Velazco and Luisa de Abarca, who is now Pacheco's wife), granted general power of attorney to Captain Pedro Santos de la Madriz, a resident of Panamá. This power was for collecting debts, specifically $2170 from Captain Juan Tamayo and his son Miguel Tamayo, and $1000 from Sergeant Major Andrés Jaramillo.

people_involved: Angela de la Paz y Flores
summary: Alférez Tomás de Chaves and his wife Juana Paula Solís purchased a cattle ranch from Sergeant Major Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín and his wife Angela de la Paz y Flores for $500. They recognized an obligation of $100 at 5% interest to the Capellanía administered by the beneficed priests of the city. This obligation was later cancelled on April 9, 1701, by Licenciado Diego de Angulo Gascón, the oldest Rector Priest.
Alférez Tomás de Chaves and his wife Juana Paula Solís obligated themselves to the Convento de San Francisco for $50 at 5% interest, likely related to their recent purchase of a cattle ranch.
On April 9, 1701, Alférez Francisco Fernández, the Síndico of the San Francisco Religious, performed a cancellation. The specific nature of the cancellation is not detailed in the record.

The Cabildo, including Captain Francisco de Bonilla and other officials, revoked the power of attorney previously granted to Captain Diego Rodríguez Menéndez, Procurador of the Real Audiencia of Santiago de Guatemala. They then conferred general power to Gaspar de Basterrica y Narbaiza, Procurador Síndico of 'this city,' to represent them before the Real Audiencia for all their affairs.

Alférez Tomás de Chaves and his wife Juana Paula Solís committed to an obligation of $160.00 at 5% interest in favor of the Chaplaincy managed by Don Diego de Campos Quirós. This obligation was later cancelled on January 21, 1704.

Don Miguel de Alvarado attempted to sell a 12-year-old Creole slave named Salvador to Captain Don Antonio de Moya for $400.00. Salvador was inherited by Miguel from his deceased mother, Doña Juana de Salazar, but the sale did not go through.

Don Miguel de Alvarado sold an 8-9 year old enslaved girl named María to Doña Mariana de Echavarría Navarro for $250.00. María was inherited by Miguel from his deceased sister, Doña Gertrudis de Alvarado.

Don Miguel de Alvarado sold a 7-year-old enslaved mulatto girl named Manuela to Doña Mariana de Echavarría Navarro for $250.00. Manuela was also inherited by Miguel from his deceased sister, Doña Gertrudis de Alvarado.

Doña Antonia María de Otárola, widow of Don Gabriel de Echavarría Navarro, sold houses and goods in 'this city' to Don José de Guzmán for $869.00. The payment was allocated to a Chaplaincy founded by Doña Juana de Echavarría Navarro (with Licenciado Francisco de Salazar as chaplain and Maestre de Campo Miguel de Echavarría Navarro as patron), the Cofradía de la Concepción de Esparza, and Jerónimo Murillo. A marginal note from July 26, 1696, confirms José de Guzmán redeemed $100.00 for the Chaplaincy.

people_involved: Juan López de la Rea y Soto
summary: Alférez Tomás de Chaves and his wife Juana Paula Solís committed to an obligation of $200.00 at 5% interest to the Cofradía de la Concepción of 'this city,' mortgaging property she had purchased. This obligation was cancelled on November 14, 1607, by Juan López de la Rea y Soto, Mayordomo of the Cofradía.

Don Miguel de Alvarado attempted to sell a 40-year-old pardo slave named Juana and her 1-year and 5-month-old daughter Josefa to Alférez Diego de Cárdenas for $300.00. Juana was inherited by Miguel from his deceased mother, Doña Juana de Salazar, but the sale did not go through.

Doña Antonia María de Otárola, a widow, committed to an obligation of $169.00 at 5% interest to Don José de Guzmán. She clarified that the previous sale of houses to Guzmán was for $700.00, not $869.00, and she would pay the remaining $169.00 from assets she has in Panama. This obligation was cancelled on February 14, 1698.

Don Miguel de Alvarado sold a 40-year-old pardo slave named Juana and her 1-year and 5-month-old daughter Josefa to Alférez Diego de Cárdenas for $500.00. Juana was inherited by Miguel from his deceased mother, Doña Juana de Salazar.
Don Miguel de Alvarado sold a 12-13 year old Creole slave named Salvador to Captain Don Antonio de Moya for $100.00.

Don Antonio, Don Pablo José, and Don Salvador de Alvarado, legitimate sons of Captain Don José de Alvarado and the deceased Doña Petronila de Retes, received their maternal inheritance totaling $5439.00. Each son received $1813.00, with Antonio and Salvador receiving livestock and property in Santa Rosa, and Pablo José receiving a 30-year-old mulatto slave named José and the remainder in livestock.

Don Miguel de Alvarado granted freedom to his slave Domingo, who had been inherited from his parents, Don García de Alvarado and Doña Juana de Salazar. The freedom was granted as per a disposition made when Miguel turned 20 years old.

Captain Don Alonso de Aranda y Acevedo, a merchant traveling between 'this province' and Nicaragua, granted general power of attorney to Captain de Caballos Corazas Don Antonio Pacheco and Don Juan Ruiz de Velazco.

On April 7, Don José de Guzmán sold a house and lot in 'this city' to Don Juan de Vida Martel for $600.00. The property, previously owned by Doña María Arias, was bordered by properties belonging to Don Jorge de Alvarado, Doña Manuela de Salazar, and Captain Don Lope de Alcarazo.
Don Gregorio de Moya is identified as the Chaplain of a Chaplaincy founded by Pedro Solano. This Chaplaincy pays $100 at 5% to the Beneficiary Priests of the city.

people_involved: don Manuel de Bustamante y Vivero
Capitán Pedro Santos de la Madriz
summary: Maestre de Campo don Manuel de Bustamante y Vivero, Governor and Captain General of the province, grants general power of attorney to Captain don Juan de Oriamuno and Captain Juan Bracho de la Madriz, residents of Panama. This power is specifically for collecting assets from the estate of the deceased Captain Pedro Santos de la Madriz, who was Bustamante y Vivero's agent and administrator.

people_involved: doña Juana de Vera y Soto Mayor
Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Captain don José de Alvarado's testament outlines his family, including his deceased parents, wife doña Petronila de Retes, and eight children. He establishes a Chaplaincy of $1000, naming Licenciado Esteban Marín Laguna as interim Chaplain, to be succeeded by his grandsons don Juan Antonio de Moya and don Gregorio de Moya. His son don Pablo José is the patron, and Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas and Capitán don Antonio de Moya are the executors.

Luisa de Quintana, widow of Captain Sebastián de Zamora and guardian of their minor children, grants special power of attorney to Captain Miguel Rodríguez Camilo, who is traveling to Guatemala. The purpose is to collect $60 from Captain Diego Rodríguez Menéndez, a Procurator in the Royal Audiencia, which her late husband had sent for a pending legal case that had not been acted upon.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan de Vida Martel
Sargento Mayor don Juan de Vida Martel
summary: Captain don Juan de Vida Martel provides a dowry letter for his wife, Clara de Quirós. The dowry amounts to $1659, with a bridal gift (arras) of $1400, and identifies their respective parents.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín
don Diego de San Martín y Soto
summary: Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín sells a 26-year-old black slave named Luisa to don Diego de San Martín y Soto for $300. Luisa was previously purchased from Alférez Tomás de Chaves.

Doña María Vázquez Coronado sells a 40-year-old brown-skinned slave named Nicolás Villegas to Captain don Gregorio de Chaves for $250. Nicolás Villegas was inherited by doña María from her husband, Jerónimo Leal.

Juan Antonio de Guevara and doña Clara de Echavarría Navarro sell half a house and lot in the city to Teniente José de Quirós for $500. The property, previously acquired from don Esteban de Moya and doña Rafaela de Alvarado, is subject to payments to three chaplaincies: one founded by doña Juana de Vera (chaplain Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya), one by Licenciado don Domingo de Echavarría (chaplain Licenciado don Francisco de Salazar), with the remaining $50 going to the sellers.

Captain don Antonio de Moya provides a dowry letter for his future wife, doña Juana Ruiz, including $3900 (with $900 designated for her brother Francisco Ruiz) and a bridal gift of $600. The dowry also includes several enslaved individuals: Agustín (18, $450), Isabel (28, $500), José (12, $350), Nicolás (8, $300), María (mulata, $200), Juana (mulata, 22, $500), and Rafaela (mulata, $250). Doña Juana also receives assets from her uncle, Beneficiado E de Torres.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don José de Sandoval
Licenciado don Diego de Angulo Gascón
summary: Don Manuel de Sandoval's testament identifies his deceased parents, his wife doña Petronila de Quirós (married for 3 years), and their one-year-old daughter María Teresa. Licenciado don Diego de Angulo Gascón and Juan López de Soto are named as executors.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan de Vida Martel
Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Captain don Lope de Alcarazo sells adobe houses in the city to Juan Antonio de Guevara for $1000. The property, previously bought from doña Antonia María Venegas, is subject to payments to three chaplaincies: one founded by Capitán Francisco de Ocampo Golfín (chaplain Licenciado don Francisco de Salazar), one by Alonso Gómez Macotela (chaplain Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas), and one by Baltasar de Grados (chaplain Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya).

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don José de Sandoval Golfín
summary: Doña Nicolasa de Sandoval Golfín's testament identifies her deceased parents, states she is over 25 and single, and mentions her brothers Capitán Francisco de Cabrera and don Manuel de Sandoval Golfín, and her niece María de la Rosa.

Captain Pedro José Sáenz and his wife María de la Rosa pledged their houses in Cartago as security for a $100 loan at 5% interest from the Cofradía de la Vera Cruz, whose Mayordomo was Alférez José Calderón.
On April 8, 1699, Alférez José Calderón, the Mayordomo of the Cofradía de la Vera Cruz, cancelled the obligation made by Captain Pedro José Sáenz and María de la Rosa.

On July 23, Captain Pedro José Sáenz and his wife María de la Rosa pledged their houses in Cartago for a $100 loan at 5% interest to the Capellanía established by Catalina Gutiérrez in the Convento de San Francisco.
On April 8, 1699, Captain Miguel Calvo, the Síndico of the Convento de San Francisco, cancelled the obligation made by Pedro José Sáenz and María de la Rosa.

people_involved: Presidente de la Real Audiencia de Santiago de Guatemala
summary: On July 23, several Maestres de Campo and Captains of Spanish Infantry from Cartago, including Miguel de Echavarría Navarro and Lope de Alcarazo, granted power of attorney to Captain Pedro José Sáenz. This was in response to a dispatch from the President of the Real Audiencia of Santiago de Guatemala, requiring military officers to present their titles and patents.

On July 24, María Sagaste, the widow of Sergeant Nicolás Barrante and mother of the late Juana Barrantes, empowered her grandson, Lieutenant Juan Alvarez de Ulate, to collect the assets left by her deceased daughter.
On July 26, Captain Lope de Alcarazo sold a 20-year-old Congo slave named Juan Antonio, inherited from his late wife Ana de Echavarría Navarro, to Sergeant Juan González for $300.

On July 26, Captain Pedro José Sáenz and his wife María de la Rosa pledged their houses in Cartago as security for a $100 loan at 5% interest to the Capellanía established by Juana de Echavarría Navarro.

On July 27, the executors of the late Ana de Echavarría Navarro – Licenciado Diego de Angulo Gascón, Maestre de Campo Miguel de Echavarría Navarro, and Captain Lope de Alcarazo – established a perpetual Capellanía of masses for Ana's soul at the Convento de San Francisco, as directed by her will. The Capellanía was funded with $525 from the sale of the slave María, with Gertrudis de Echavarría Navarro and her husband Jorge de Alvarado to be obligated, and Ana's nephew Juan López de la Flor named as the first chaplain.

On July 28, Captain Pedro José Sáenz and his wife María de la Rosa pledged their houses in Cartago as security for a $50 loan at 5% interest to the Cofradía del Rosario, an amount previously redeemed by Isabel de Guevara.
On April 8, 1699, Jorge de Alvarado, the Mayordomo of the Cofradía del Rosario, cancelled the obligation made by Pedro José Sáenz and María de la Rosa.

On May 30, Ana de Echavarría Navarro, daughter of the late Juan de Echavarría Navarro and Ana de Retes, and wife of Captain Lope de Alcarazo, made her will. She named her slaves Juan Antonio and María, her niece Angela María, and ordered the establishment of a Capellanía to be funded by the sale of her slave María. The will was executed before Captain Francisco de Bonilla.

On July 8, the executors of Ana de Echavarría Navarro's will, including Licenciado Diego de Angulo Gascón, requested Ana de Retes, the deceased's mother, to confirm she had granted her daughter permission to dispose of her assets.

On July 13, at Captain Diego de Ibarra's home in Valle de Santana, Ana de Retes confirmed she had given her daughter Ana de Echavarría Navarro permission to dispose of her assets after the will was read to her.

On August 27, Captain Pedro José Sáenz and his wife María de la Rosa pledged their houses in Cartago as security for a $50 loan at 5% interest to the Capellanía established by Lorenzo Morera, an amount previously redeemed by Eugenia Lainés.
On May 8, 1699, Captain Miguel Calvo, as Síndico of the San Francisco Religious, cancelled the obligation made by Pedro José Sáenz and María de la Rosa.

On July 27, the executors of Ana de Echavarría Navarro's will, including Licenciado Diego de Angulo Gascón, sold a 25-year-old Arara slave named María to Gertrudis de Echavarría Navarro, wife of Jorge de Alvarado, as per Ana's instructions.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don Miguel de Echavarría Navarro
summary: Doña Gertrudis de Echavarría Navarro, wife of don Jorge de Alvarado (who is absent in Panamá), obligated herself to her brother, Maestre de Campo don Miguel de Echavarría Navarro, for $525.00 at 5%. The document was neither signed nor passed.

people_involved: El Capitán don Pedro José Sáenz
summary: Captain don Pedro José Sáenz and his wife doña María de la Rosa sold a house and kitchen, built with posts and covered with straw, along with its plot of land in Cartago, to Jacinto de Rivera for $100.00. They had acquired this property by purchase from doña María de Retes, doña María de la Rosa's mother.

people_involved: Beneficiado don Diego de Angulo Gascón
Maestre de Campo don Miguel de Echavarría Navarro
summary: Doña Gertrudis de Echavarría Navarro, wife of don Jorge de Alvarado (absent in Panamá), obligated herself for $525.00 at 5% to Beneficiado don Diego de Angulo Gascón, Maestre de Campo don Miguel de Echavarría Navarro, and Capitán don Lope de Alcarazo. She committed to pay them upon her husband's return.

people_involved: El Capitán don Miguel de Alvarado
summary: Captain don Miguel de Alvarado founded a perpetual chaplaincy of recited masses for his soul and the souls of his parents and grandparents. His uncle, Licenciado don Francisco de Salazar, was named as the patron and chaplain. The principal of $150.00 was charged upon his dwelling houses in Cartago, which he inherited from his deceased mother, doña Juana de Salazar.

people_involved: El Capitán don Miguel de Alvarado
summary: Captain don Miguel de Alvarado sold his adobe and tile-roofed dwelling houses in Cartago, which he inherited from his deceased mother doña Juana de Salazar, to Licenciado don Francisco de Salazar for $450.00. Of this amount, $300.00 corresponded to the buyer, and $150.00 was allocated to the chaplaincy established by the seller in the previous deed, for which Licenciado don Francisco was the chaplain.

Juan Antonio de Guevara and his wife doña Clara de Echavarría Navarro obligated themselves for $500.00 at 5% to the chaplaincy founded by Captain Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, with Licenciado don Francisco de Salazar serving as its chaplain. This obligation was imposed on houses they had purchased, with this existing encumbrance, from Captain don Lope de Alcarazo.

people_involved: Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Juan Antonio de Guevara and doña Clara de Echavarría Navarro obligated themselves for $400.00 at 5% to the chaplaincy founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela, for which Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas was the chaplain. This obligation was imposed on the same houses referenced in the previous deed.

This entry records the will of María Sagaste, legitimate daughter of deceased Jorge Sagaste and Ana Martínez Navarro, and widow of deceased Sergeant Nicolás Barrantes. She had children Jerónima, Benito, and the deceased Juana Barrantes. The will details a donation of a slave named María and her children (Juana, Gregorio, Juliana) by the deceased Doña Juana Moscoso to Barrantes, and lists additional children born to María (María, Baltasar, Juana, Manuela, Salvador). Her executors were her brother don Pedro de Sagaste and Alférez José Calderón.

Juan Antonio de Guevara and his wife doña Clara de Echavarría Navarro obligated themselves for $100.00 at 5% to the chaplaincy founded by Comisario Baltasar de Grado, with Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya serving as its chaplain. This obligation was imposed on the houses they had purchased with this existing encumbrance, as detailed in the deed on folio 75 vuelto.

people_involved: Diego de San Martín y Soto
Maestre de Campo don Manuel de Bustamante
summary: Captain don Miguel Calvo and Diego de San Martín y Soto acted as guarantors for Captain Bernabé de Segura, his son Francisco de Segura, and Nicolás Carbajal. This guarantee was related to the outcome of a criminal case initiated against them by Maestre de Campo don Manuel de Bustamante, the Governor and Captain General of the province. This document was not passed.

people_involved: Diego de San Martín y Soto
Maestre de Campo don Manuel de Bustamante
summary: Captain don Miguel Calvo and Diego de San Martín y Soto acted as guarantors for Captain Bernabé de Segura, his son Francisco de Segura, and Nicolás Carbajal. This was in connection with a criminal case by Maestre de Campo don Manuel de Bustamante, where the Seguras appealed to the Real Audiencia de Guatemala. The Audiencia ordered the case documents to be delivered to the Seguras, with a bond, for presentation to the Audiencia, and the guarantors ensured this delivery.
Juan Moreno granted general judicial power to Captain don Antonio Pacheco.

This is a dowry letter from Francisco de Flores in favor of María Magdalena, the legitimate daughter of Sergeant Francisco López Serrano and María de Sibaja. Their marriage was scheduled for the following day, with a dowry of $1221.00 and arras of $200.00.

Josefa Rosales, widow of Leonardo Ricardo, obligated herself to her children Antonio, Pomasa, and Alfonsa Ricardo for $457.7 reales at 5%. This amount represented $152.5 reales for each child as their legitimate paternal inheritance.
Doña Josefa de Santiago, a widow, sold a dark-skinned slave named Cayetano to Sergeant Juan Masís for $150.00. Cayetano was described as being 'de gaños'.
This entry records a codicil made by Cristóbal López to his existing will.

Doña Margarita de Flores revoked a clause in her will that left a fifth of her assets to her deceased wife and daughters, as they had already received their share. She now leaves it to her grandsons Eugenio and Bernardo. She also changed the disposition of a piece of land, originally for all heirs, to be given specifically to her daughter Juana.
Jaime Fuerte, a bachelor from Palma, Spain, made his will. He named Capitán Miguel Calvo as his universal heir and executor.

Alférez Blas González Coronel and his wife Bernarda de Fonseca obligated themselves for $100 at 5% interest to the minors Beatriz and Bernardo de Morales, who are the legitimate children of the deceased Capitán Agustín de Morales and Rodulfa Salguero, and grandchildren of Sargento Juan González, from whom they received the $100. They mortgaged their homes in this city.

Capitán Francisco de Bonilla and his wife Margarita de Bolívar obligated themselves for $100 at 5% interest to the minors Beatriz and Bernardo de Morales, who are the legitimate children of the deceased Capitán Agustín de Morales and Rodulfa Salguero, and grandchildren of Sargento Juan González. They mortgaged their homes in this city.

Capitán don Miguel Calvo made a donation to his niece, doña Antonia de Oses Navarro, of a 6-month-old 'pardo' slave named Josefa. Josefa is the daughter of Juana, another slave owned by Miguel Calvo, whom he bought from doña Juana Moscoso. Antonia is the legitimate daughter of Esteban de Oses Navarro and Juana Calvo (Miguel Calvo's sister).
Alférez José Calderón obligated himself to Sargento Juan González for $150 at 5%, payable in cacao during the upcoming January. The obligation was cancelled by Sargento González on May 15, 1709.

Doña Margarita de Flores made a codicil to her will, mentioning her son Jacinto de Mora, to whom she had given three mules, and her son Onofre de Mora. The codicil was granted before Francisco Ramírez Rodado, Royal Scribe.

Rodulfa Salguero, widow of Capitán Agustín de Morales and guardian of her minor children Beatriz and Bernardo de Morales, obligated herself to them for $97 and 3 reales at 5%. Sargento Juan González acted as guarantor.

people_involved: Alcalde Gaspar de Bastarrica y Narbaiza
summary: Alcalde Gaspar de Bastarrica y Narbaiza placed Francisco de León, an orphan of about 16 years old, as an apprentice with Alférez Esteban de Zúñiga, a master blacksmith, for 5 years.

Don José de Guzmán and his wife doña Antonia de Echavarría Navarro obligated themselves for $569 at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by the deceased doña Juana de Echavarría Navarro, for which Licenciado don Francisco de Moya was the interim Chaplain. They imposed this obligation on a house and lot in this city that they bought from doña Antonia María de Otárola. The obligation was cancelled on April 10, 1752, by Licenciado José Hermenegildo de Arleguí, who was the patron and proprietary Chaplain of the Chaplaincy, and grandson of the founder.

Alférez Blas González Coronel and his wife doña Bernarda de Fonseca obligated themselves for $200 at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by the deceased Licenciado don Domingo de Echavarría, for which Licenciado don Francisco de Salazar was the Chaplain. They imposed this obligation on half a house and lot in this city.

Jerónima Barrantes, a single woman, made her will. She named her natural children and listed her slaves, granting freedom to Juana (a black woman) upon her death. Don Pedro de Azofeifa and Benito Barrantes (her brother) were named executors.

Alférez Blas González Coronel and his wife doña Bernarda de Fonseca obligated themselves for $250 at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by the deceased doña Juana de Vera, for which Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya was the Chaplain.
Don Pablo José de Alvarado, who was traveling to León, Nicaragua, granted a general power of attorney to Capitán don Antonio de Moya.

Capitán don Pedro José Sáenz and his wife doña María de la Rosa obligated themselves for $331 at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by the deceased Lorenzo de Morera, for which Sargento Pedro de Loría was the executor. They imposed this obligation on their homes in this city. The obligation was cancelled on April 8, 1700, by Capitán don Miguel Calvo, the Syndic of the Convent of San Francisco.
Nicolasa de Benavides, widow of Matías de Monáster and guardian of her children María and Francisco de Monáster, granted power of attorney to don Jorge.

Alférez Antonio de Angulo, as the auction buyer of assets from the deceased Juan Camacho's estate, obligates himself to Domingo José, minor son of Lucas Camacho and Sebastiana Masís, for $120 at 5% interest. This obligation was originally a charge against Juan Camacho's estate. The obligation was later cancelled by Domingo José on February 6, 1709.

Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín, Alférez Mayor and regidor of Cartago, being ill, renounces his offices. He designates his nephew, Alférez don Alvaro de Guevara, and his son-in-law, Teniente don Gil de Alvarado (absent in Panama), as successors. Don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín died on March 27, 1697.

Jaime Fuerte, a bachelor from Palma, Mallorca, Spain, and son of the deceased Jaime Fuerte and Catalina de la Cruz, executes his testament. He names Teniente Diego Isidro as his universal executor and heir.

people_involved: Doña Juana de Vera y Soto Mayor
summary: Capitán Francisco López Conejo sells a cacao hacienda with 2,500 trees in the Matina valley to don Andrés Salazar for $850. The hacienda carries existing obligations totaling $850 at 5% interest, which the buyer must assume, including payments to Capellanías established by doña Juana de Vera y Soto Mayor, doña Inés Pereira, and Alonso Gómez Macotela. The hacienda was originally purchased from don Pedro de Alvarado.

people_involved: Doña Angela de Paz y Flores
summary: Don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín, Alférez Mayor and Regidor perpétuo, executes his testament, detailing his family, including his wife doña Angela de Paz y Flores and daughters. He establishes a Capellanía and names his wife, Capitán don Matías González Camino, regidor Nicolás de Céspedes, and Alférez don Sebastián de Garita as executors. His daughter doña Inés de Sandoval Golfín is named universal heir.

José de Chavarría, a resident of León, Nicaragua, and son of Cristóbal de Chavarría and Sebastiana Díaz, provides a dowry of $769 and arras of $500 to his wife, María Calvo, natural daughter of Ana Palacios.

people_involved: Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
summary: Capitán don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín grants general power of attorney to don Jorge de Alvarado, Capitán don José Pérez de Muro, and Alférez Pedro Martínez Colina, all in Panama. The power is specifically to recover 110 mule beasts and other goods from the estate of his deceased agent, José Arias, who died intestate in Panama.

people_involved: Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca
summary: Doña Sebastiana de Alvarado, a widow, sells a house in Cartago to Alférez Francisco de Moya for $300. The house is situated on a plot of land that Sebastiana had acquired from her nephew, Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca.

people_involved: Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca
summary: Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca obligates himself to his aunt, Doña Sebastiana de Alvarado, for $600 at 3% interest. This obligation is secured by his houses located in the city.

people_involved: Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca
summary: Doña Sebastiana de Alvarado, a widow, establishes a perpetual chaplaincy for masses. Her nephew, Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca, a Presbyter Cleric, is designated as the patron and chaplain. The chaplaincy is funded by a $600 principal, which is under Don Antonio's charge at 5% interest, with each mass costing $3.

people_involved: Doña Juana de Vera y Soto Mayor
Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca
summary: Doña Sebastiana de Alvarado, legitimate daughter of the deceased Alférez don Gil de Alvarado and Doña Juana de Vera y Soto Mayor, and widow of don Bartolomé Arias, makes her will. She mentions her nephews Alférez don Francisco de Moya and Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca, her niece Juana María (daughter of Capitán don Gabriel de Echavarría and Doña Antonia María de Otárola), and Francisca, an orphan she raised. Her executors are Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca and her brother don Pedro de Alvarado.
Teniente don José Escalante Paniagua sells a 6-year-old mulatto slave named Felipe José, son of Lorenza, to Bernardo Cortés for $100.

Doña Juana de Otárola sells a 10-year-old mulatto slave named Gaspar Cayetano to Sargento Francisco Gutiérrez for $150. Gaspar Cayetano was inherited by Doña Juana from her deceased mother, Doña María de Alvarado.

Doña Juana Bautista Calvo and Capitán don Miguel Calvo obligate themselves to the absent don Francisco de Otárola for $100 at 5% interest, representing the value of the slave Diego, who was adjudicated to Francisco upon the death of his mother, Doña María de Alvarado. A marginal note confirms Francisco de Otárola received the $100 from Lorenzo de Arburola in Cartago on June 20, 1698, and Doña Juana Bautista is deceased.

Doña Antonia María de Otárola, a widow, and Alférez José Calderón, as guarantor, obligate themselves to Don Francisco de Otárola for $200. This sum represents the value of María Nicolasa, a 10-year-old mulatto slave, who was adjudicated to Otárola as part of his maternal inheritance.

locations: río del Molino de esta ciudad
summary: Antonio and Francisco Alvarez de Ulate, with Alférez José Calderón as guarantor, obligate themselves to Juan and José Alvarez de Ulate, who are in Panama, for $510. This amount is the value of a mulatto slave named Francisca and half a house by the Molino river in the city, which they inherited upon the death of their mother, Jerónima Barrantes.

people_involved: Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto
summary: Juan Antonio de Guevara obligates himself to Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto for $150, to be paid in cacao. A marginal note indicates the debt was cancelled by the creditor on November 13, 1697.

people_involved: Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca
summary: Doña Juana Aguiar, a widow and debtor of Don Pablo José de Alvarado for $300, assumes his debt of the same amount to the chaplaincy founded by Doña Gertrudis de Alvarado. Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca is the patron and chaplain of this chaplaincy, and Doña Juana mortgages her houses in the city as security.

Don Pablo José de Alvarado obligates himself to the chaplaincy founded by his deceased father, Capitán don José de Alvarado, for $1000 at 5% interest. This obligation is secured by a house, a sugar mill, two cauldrons, and a sugarcane plot in the Ujarraz valley, which he inherited from his father with the condition of recognizing this $1000 principal for the chaplaincy.

locations: ermita de San Juan de esta ciudad
summary: Capitán don Antonio de Moya, as the testamentary executor of the deceased Capitán don José de Alvarado, establishes a chaplaincy for masses to be said in the hermitage of San Juan in the city, with a principal of $1000 and each mass costing $3. Licenciado don Esteban Marín Laguna is named interim chaplain until don Juan Antonio de Moya, son of the grantor and Doña Isabel de Alvarado, and grandson of the deceased don José, is ordained. Don Pablo José de Alvarado is named the patron.

people_involved: Doña Juana de Vera y Soto Mayor
summary: Andrés de Salazar and his wife Gregoria de Flores obligate themselves for $250 at 5% interest to the chaplaincy established by Doña Juana de Vera y Soto Mayor. This obligation is secured by a cacao plantation in the Matina valley, which they purchased from Capitán Francisco López Conejo with this existing encumbrance.

Andrés de Salazar and Gregoria de Flores incur another obligation for $100 at 5% interest to the chaplaincy established by Doña Inés Pereira. This obligation is also secured by the same cacao plantation mentioned in the previous entry.

Andrés de Salazar and Gregoria de Flores incur a third obligation for $500 at 5% interest to the chaplaincy founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela. This new encumbrance also burdens the same cacao plantation.

people_involved: Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto
summary: Don José del Prado sells a 30-year-old mulatto slave named Benito Barrantes to Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto for $250. Don José del Prado had previously acquired Benito Barrantes from Doña Josefa de Santiago.

Gertrudis Guillén, a widow, leased a cacao plantation with 2,000 fruit trees in the Matina valley to Alférez Marcelo Blasco for four years. The lease agreement stipulated an annual payment of seven zurrones of cacao, and the property bordered land belonging to Alférez Francisco Fernández, the Río Grande, and the mountains.

Nicolás González acted as a guarantor, and Antonio González as the principal, obligating themselves to Alférez Salvador Morillo for $90.00 at 5% interest. This agreement was formally granted in Barba.

Alférez Andrés de Siles and his wife, María de Chaves, granted general power of attorney to their son, Vicente Andrés Polo, who was traveling to León, Nicaragua. The purpose was for Vicente to collect the assets of the deceased Alférez Antonio de Astúa, who was the son of María de Chaves and her late husband, Juan de Astúa.

Doña Eugenia de Abarca, a widow, granted freedom to her 50-year-old enslaved woman, Clara Calvo, who was described as 'pardo' (brown-skinned). Clara Calvo was the daughter of Paula de Arce, also an enslaved woman belonging to Eugenia de Abarca.

Doña Inés de Sandoval Golfín, wife of the absent Lieutenant Gil de Alvarado, attempted to sell an enslaved man named Sebastián, described as 'pardo' and 22 years old, to Doña Mariana de Echavarría for $300.00. However, this transaction did not proceed.
Following a failed attempt, Doña Inés de Sandoval Golfín successfully sold the enslaved man Sebastián, previously mentioned, to Captain Antonio Pacheco for $300.00.

Sergeant Alonso de Porras, acting as the guardian for the minor José Arias, obligated himself to the minor for $421.00, representing the minor's paternal and maternal inheritance. Alférez Pedro de Torres and Juan de Torres served as guarantors for this obligation.

Captain Diego de Barros y Carbajal, Lieutenant General of Cartago, canceled the obligation made by Alonso de Porras to the minor José Arias. This cancellation was due to Alonso de Porras presenting a testamentary memory from the minor José Arias, in which the minor named Porras as his heir.

Alférez Francisco de Moya and his wife, Manuela de Alvarado, obligated themselves for $300.00 at 5% interest to their minor nephews and nieces, Gregorio and Petronila, who were the children of Francisco's deceased sister, Rafaela de Alvarado. They mortgaged their houses in Cartago and a sugar cane plantation with a house and mill in Ujarraz.

Alférez Juan Matías Baptista Lizondo and his wife, Francisca de Benavente, obligated themselves for $200.00 at 5% interest to the minor children Gregorio and Petronila, offspring of the deceased Captain Esteban de Moya and Rafaela de Alvarado. This money was received from Alférez Francisco de Moya, the minors' guardian, and they mortgaged houses in Cartago and a cacao plantation in the Barbilla valley.

people_involved: María de la Rosa Echavarría Navarro
summary: A dowry letter was issued for José de Armaola, a native of Marquina, Spain, son of Francisco de Armaola and Magdalena de Uriburu, in favor of his fiancée, María de la Rosa Echavarría Navarro. María was the legitimate daughter of the deceased Captain Juan de Echavarría Navarro and Ana de Retes, and José received assets from the estate of Captain Diego de Ibarra, Ana de Retes's second husband, including enslaved people, land, and livestock, totaling $5938.00 with a pledge of $1000.00.

Lieutenant Diego Francisco de Chaves, a single man, made his will, naming his 16-year-old natural daughter, Eugenia, as his sole heir. Captain Miguel Calvo and Alférez Pedro de Torres were appointed as his executors.

A dowry letter was issued for Manuel de Herrera, a native of San Lúcar de Barrameda, Spain, son of Captain Bartolomé Díaz and Juada de Herrera, in favor of his fiancée, Gertrudis Maroto. Gertrudis was the legitimate daughter of Alférez José Maroto and Luisa Calvo, and the granddaughter of Eugenia Gertrudis Abarca, with their marriage scheduled for December 26. The dowry included enslaved women Francisca and Ursula, and twenty mules, totaling $2817.00 with a pledge of $500.00.

Sergeant Major Antonio de Moya and Pablo José de Alvarado provided a residency bond for Captain Blas González Coronel, the Public Scribe of the Cabildo and Government. Blas González Coronel was traveling to Santiago de Guatemala to seek confirmation of his title, and the bond was for $100.00 related to his judicial and sentencing responsibilities.
Captain Blas González Coronel and his wife, Bernarda de Fonseca, entered into an obligation. The details of the obligation are incomplete in the record.

A Capellanía founded by Licenciado Domingo de Chavarría, with Licenciado Francisco de Salazar as its Chaplain, holds a lien of $200 at 5% interest on half a house and lot in Cartago. This property was previously purchased from Teniente José de Quirós by unnamed parties.

Unnamed parties (referred to as 'Los mismos') obligated themselves for $250 at 5% interest to a Capellanía founded by Doña Juana de Vera, with Licenciado Don Gregorio de Moya as its Chaplain. This obligation is secured by the same half house and lot mentioned in the previous entry.

Unnamed parties obligated themselves for $100 at 5% interest to Beatriz and Bernardo de Morales, legitimate children of the late Captain Agustín de Morales and Rodulfa Salguero. The funds were received from Sergeant Juan González, the children's grandfather. The obligation was cancelled on December 1, 1905, by Eugenio Solís, Beatriz de Morales' husband.
Ayudante Francisco Hernández Barquero and his wife, Ana de Espinosa, sold a 12-year-old mulato slave named Esteban, son of Juana (a mulata slave), to Sergeant Juan González de Ochoa for $225.

Ayudante Francisco Hernández Barquero, a native of Tresneroniso, Estremadura, Spain, made his will. He was married to Ana de Espinosa and had eight children, and two granddaughters under his care. His executors were Alférez Francisco Fernández, Sergeant Francisco Gutiérrez, and his son, Sergeant Francisco Barquero.
Licenciado Don Diego de Angulo Gascón, Cura Rector of Cartago, obligated himself for $100 at 5% interest to the Convento de San Francisco. He mortgaged his residential houses in the city as security.
Doña Micaela Durán de Chaves, a widow, sold a 20-year-old negro slave named Raimundo to Alférez Marcelo Blasco for $200. Raimundo was inherited by Doña Micaela from her late husband, Alonso Romero.

Doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar, a widow and guardian of her minor children, obligated herself for $100 at 5% interest to Magdalena Solano, who was between 14 and 25 years old and the legitimate daughter of the late Sergeant Juan Solano and Josefa Machado. The obligation was secured by her houses in Cartago and a cacao hacienda in the Matina valley, and was cancelled on July 19, 1709, by José del Castillo, Magdalena Solano's husband.

Alférez Vicente Andrés Polo, legitimate son of the late Tomás Andrés Polo and Doña María de Chaves, issued a dowry letter for his fiancée, Doña Alfonsa de Bonilla. Alfonsa is the legitimate daughter of the late Alférez Antonio de Bonilla and Doña María de Grados. The dowry amounted to $1381 and 4 reales, with an additional $500 in arras.

locations: Ribera del río de la Reventazón
summary: Alférez Don Francisco de Espinosa and his wife, Doña Sebastiana de Bonilla, obligated themselves for $150 at 5% interest to a Capellanía founded by the late Alférez Vasco Solano, with Licenciado Don Diego de Campos Quirós as its Chaplain. This obligation was secured by a 100-foot cacao hacienda on the Reventazón riverbank, which they had purchased for the same price.

Captain Don Juan de Vida Martel and his wife, Clara de Quirós, sold adobe houses with a 50-vara lot in Cartago to Francisco Pérez de Cote for $600. The property's boundaries included houses of Don Jorge de Alvarado, Doña Manuela de Salazar, and Juan Antonio de Guevara. The sellers had acquired the property from Captain Don José de Guzmán. The payment included $300 for a Capellanía founded by the late Pedro Solano (Capellán: Licenciado Don Gregorio de Moya), $100 for the city's beneficed priests, and $200 directly to the sellers.

people_involved: Angela de la Paz y Flores
summary: Teniente Don José Escalante Paniagua sold adobe houses, four new chairs, a cedar wood estrado, and a lot with two tapia walls to his son-in-law, Captain Don Juan Sáenz, for $710. The buyer was to recognize obligations including payments to the Cofradía de la Concepción, Capellanías founded by Vasco Solano and Magdalena de la Portilla, and the minor children of the late José de Rivera and Doña Ana de Quesada.

Captain Don Juan Sáenz and his wife, Doña Ana de Escalante Paniagua, sold adobe houses with four chairs and a wooden estrado to Alférez Vicente Andrés Polo. The description of the property is cut off.

José de Prado y Valcázar and Juana Damiana de Flores obligate themselves for $100 at 5% to the minor children of the deceased Capitán don Esteban de Moya and Rafaela de Alvarado. Alférez don Francisco de Moya, the children's tutor, receives the money. They mortgage their houses in Cartago, a 14-year-old slave named Josefa, and a cacao hacienda in Matina, with Alférez Juan Vicente Godoy as guarantor.

Juan Antonio de Soto and Juana de Acosta Arévalo obligate themselves for $100 at 5% to Alférez don Francisco de Moya, tutor of the minor children of the deceased Capitán don Esteban de Moya and Rafaela de Alvarado. They mortgage a cacao hacienda with 2000 trees in Matina. Don Pablo José de Alvarado acts as guarantor.

people_involved: Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
summary: Capitán Alonso Ruiz Arroyo acts as guarantor for doña Antonia Solano, widow of Juan Muñoz de la Calle, enabling her to receive an inheritance of $518.5 reales. This inheritance was previously renounced by Capitán don José Pérez de Muro in the contested estate of Juan Muñoz de la Calle.

Alférez Vicente Andrés Polo and doña Alfonsa de Bonilla obligate themselves to Capitán don Juan Sáenz for $500 at 3%. This debt stems from the sale of houses in Cartago by Capitán don Juan Sáenz to them.

A dowry letter is issued for the upcoming marriage of Teniente Manuel de Zamora, son of the deceased Capitán Sebastián de Zamora and doña Lucía de Ocompo Sandoval, to doña Baltasara de Escalante Paniagua, daughter of Teniente don José Escalante Paniagua and the deceased doña Manuela de Vida Martel. The marriage is scheduled for the following Sunday, with a dowry of $1515 and arras of $1000.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego de Campos Quirós
summary: Capitán don Juan Sáenz and doña Ana de Escalante Paniagua obligate themselves for $200 at 5% to the Capellanía founded by Magdalena de la Portilla, with Licenciado don Diego de Campos Quirós as interim Chaplain. This obligation is imposed on houses the grantor purchased from his father-in-law, Teniente don José Escalante Paniagua, which already carried this encumbrance.

people_involved: Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca
summary: Capitán Francisco de Bonilla, acting as Lieutenant Governor, grants freedom to Luis, a black slave. This manumission was ordered in the closed will of the deceased Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca, Luis's former owner.

Capitán don Juan Sáenz and doña Ana Escalante Paniagua obligate themselves for $200 at 5% to the Capellanía imposed by Vasco Solano, with Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya as Chaplain. This obligation is charged on houses the grantor bought from his father-in-law, Teniente don José Escalante Paniagua.
Capitán Jerónimo Valerino acts as guarantor for Capitán don Matías González Camino, who is a creditor with a better right in the contested estate of Juan Muñoz de la Calle, for a credit of $570.
Capitán Jerónimo Valerino acts as guarantor for Capitán Nicolás Gutiérrez Jaramillo, a resident of Esparza, in the same contested estate of Juan Muñoz de la Calle, for a credit of $201.6 reales.

people_involved: Capitán don José Antonio de Viva
Sargento Mayor don Antonio de Moya
summary: A dowry letter is issued for the upcoming marriage of Capitán don José Antonio de Viva, a native of León, Spain, to doña Josefa de Moya. The marriage is set for December 8, with a dowry of $2100 and arras of the same amount, including a mulata slave named Gertrudis with a small child and cacao.

Capitán Juan de Bonilla and doña Francisca de Astúa obligate themselves to the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora de los Angeles, whose Mayordomo is Sargento Pedro de Alvarado, for $100 annually for 5 years. This is for the lease of a cacao hacienda with 2000 fruit-bearing trees belonging to the Cofradía, located on the banks of the Matina river.
An entry mentions Francisco Gregorio de Govantes and Andrea Gon, but the details of the event are incomplete in the provided text.
González and his wife sold a 26-year-old black slave named Marcela to Alférez Marcelo Blasco for $200. Marcela was inherited by González's wife from her father, Nicolás González.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan de Vida Martel
summary: Doña Catalina Ortiz de Aldana leased a productive cacao hacienda called 'el Santo Cristo' in the Matina valley to Alférez Marcelo Blasco. The lease was for 24 years, with an annual payment of 6.5 zurrones of cacao, and bordered properties of Capitán don Juan de Vida Martel and Capitán don Matías González Camino.

people_involved: Doña Juana de Alvarado Vera y Sotomayor
summary: Don Pedro Ortiz de Rosas provided a dowry of $5375 and arras of $2000 for his future wife, Doña Juana de Alvarado Vera y Sotomayor, the legitimate daughter of Don Pedro de Alvarado and Doña Catalina de Vida Martel.
