The dowry included 1000 cacao trees in Matina, two 20-year-old black slaves named Agustina and Nicolasa, and silver. Their marriage was scheduled for February 2nd.

people_involved: Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto
summary: Teniente Antonio de Zamora committed to Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto for $153 and 1 real of cacao, to be delivered in Matina. This obligation was later cancelled on July 14, 1799.

Capitán Antonio de Rojas Miranda, as the principal, and Alférez Diego de Cárdenas, as guarantor, committed to Capitán don Miguel Calvo for $100 at 5% interest. This obligation was cancelled by Capitán Calvo on February 22, 1706.

people_involved: Doña Angela de la Paz y Flores
Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín
summary: Doña Angela de la Paz y Flores, widow of Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín, founded a Capellanía for recited masses. The curates would serve as chaplains and patrons until Miguel de Céspedes or don Antonio de Guevara, nephew of Sandoval Golfín, were ordained priests. The Capellanía's principal of $500 was charged on houses, a sugar mill, and cane fields in the Barba valley.

people_involved: Doña Angela de la Paz y Flores
Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín
summary: Doña Angela de la Paz y Flores, widow of Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín, sold a sugar mill hacienda and cane fields in the Barba valley to Alférez Juan de Ballesteros Saavedra for $500. The buyer and his wife were required to recognize this amount in favor of the Capellanía founded by Doña Angela.

people_involved: Doña Angela de la Paz y Flores
summary: Alférez Juan de Ballesteros Saavedra and his wife, Doña Juana de Torres, fulfilled their previous obligation by recognizing the imposition of $500 as principal and 5% annual interest on the hacienda they purchased from Doña Angela de la Paz y Flores. This recognition was made in favor of the Capellanía founded by Doña Angela.

people_involved: Illmo. señor don Diego Ladrón de Guevara
summary: Licenciado don Alonso Berrocal, a priest from Medina Sidonia, Spain, currently residing in Aserrí, made his will. He bequeathed three slaves (Juana, Esperanza, Atanasio) to the Conception Convent in Panama, to be held by Doña Micaela Durán de Chaves and his nephew Alférez Alonso Ruiz Arroyo until Bishop Diego Ladrón de Guevara's promotion or death. He also detailed donations of property in Panama and funds in Portobelo, naming his nephew, Alférez Alonso Ruiz Arroyo, as his heir.

people_involved: Curas de la Iglesia parroquial de Santago de la ciudad de Medina Sidonia
summary: Licenciado Don Alonso Berrocal, a Presbyter Cleric, granted power to his brother, Captain Pedro Lozano de Piña, and the Curas of the parish church of Santiago in Medina Sidonia, Spain. This power was for establishing a chaplaincy of sung masses in that church, with a principal of $2250.00. His nephew, Licenciado Don Antonio Lozano Berrocal, was also authorized to use this power in the absence or death of Captain Pedro Lozano.

Alonso Berrocal granted power to his brother, Captain Pedro Lozano de Piña, and his nephew, Licenciado Don Antonio Lozano Berrocal, both residents of Cádiz. This power was to establish two chaplaincies of recited masses in Cádiz for $4400.00. His other nephew, Don Juan Lozano Berrocal, was also to be included in these patronages and chaplaincy.

Alonso Berrocal granted power to Pedro Lozano de Piña and Antonio Lozano Berrocal to found and establish two chaplaincies of recited masses in Cádiz for $4000.00. The patrons were designated as the Bishop of Cádiz and Captain Pedro Lozano de Piña, or Antonio Lozano Berrocal in case of impediment. Don Francisco Lozano Berrocal, another nephew, was named perpetual chaplain, with provisions for two students from the Colegio de San Bartolomé if he did not get ordained.

people_involved: Cura más antiguo de la iglesia parroquial de Chiclana
summary: Alonso Berrocal empowered Pedro Lozano de Piña and Antonio Lozano Berrocal to establish a chaplaincy of recited masses in Chiclana, Spain, for $2000.00. These annual masses were to be said in the church where his mother, Doña Leonor Benites, was buried, for her soul. The oldest priest of the parish church in Chiclana was designated as the patron and chaplain.

This entry records the will of Ayudante Alonso de Mora, a resident and native of Cartago, executed in Sar Bartolomé de Barba. He was the legitimate son of the deceased Juan de Mora and María de la Portilla, and widower of Leonor de Rivera. His children were listed as Juan de Mora (deceased), María de Mora, Jerónima, Bárbula, Margarita, and Basilio (also deceased).

This entry mentions the will of Captain Don Gregorio de Chaves, legitimate son of the deceased Francisco de Chaves and Doña Francisca de Zúñiga y Sotomayor. The will was noted as 'No pasó' (did not pass/was not executed).

people_involved: Antonio de la Riva y Agüero
summary: Don Antonio de la Riva y Agüero sold a 30-year-old brown-skinned slave named Juan de Chaves to Captain Don Gregorio de Chaves for $200.00. Juan de Chaves was born and raised in the house of Doña Inés de Chaves, the deceased mother of the seller.

people_involved: Antonio de la Riva y Agüero
summary: Don Antonio de la Riva y Agüero obligated himself to his sisters, Doña Francisca and Doña Jerónima de la Riva Agüero, for $225.00. This money was received from their uncle, Captain Don Gregorio de Chaves, and constituted their inheritance from their deceased mother, Doña Inés de Chaves.
Ayudante Alonso de Mora, a resident of Cartago and currently residing in the Barba valley, granted general power to Captain Bernabé de Segura.

people_involved: Angela María de la Paz y Flores
summary: Doña Angela María de la Paz y Flores sold a 40-year-old black Creole slave named José Ibarra to Alférez Juan de Ballesteros for $200.00.

This is a dowry letter from Manuel García de Ergueta in favor of his future wife, Doña Antonia Lainez de Iztueta. Antonia is the legitimate daughter of the deceased Ignacio Lainez de Iztueta and Doña Francisca Calvo. The dowry amounted to $2233.00, with arras of $500.00, and included a mulata named María ($300.00) and a mulato named José ($200.00).

people_involved: Angela María de la Paz y Flores
summary: Alférez Juan de Ballesteros Saavedra obligated himself to Doña Angela María de la Paz y Flores for $574.00. A marginal note indicates that Doña Angela cancelled this obligation on July 28, 1699.

Domingo Guerrero, a resident of Esparza, sold a brown-skinned slave named Francisco Jorge, approximately 25 years old, to Alférez José Calderón, a resident of Cartago. Guerrero had previously acquired Francisco Jorge by purchase from Alférez Marcelo Blasco. The price was $250.00.

people_involved: Diego de San Martín y Soto
summary: Captains Don Matías González Camino, Don José Pérez de Muro, Diego de San Martín y Soto, and Don Jorge de Alvarado acted as guarantors for Don Francisco Serrano de Reina, who held the titles of Governor and Captain General.

people_involved: Diego de San Martín y Soto
summary: Capitanes Don Matías González Camino, Don José Pérez de Muro, Don Jorge de Alvarado, and Diego de San Martín y Soto acted as guarantors for Gobernador y Capitán General Don Francisco Serrano de Reina. They guaranteed the payment of his first "media anata" within six months.

people_involved: Diego de San Martín y Soto
summary: The same four captains (Don Matías González Camino, Don José Pérez de Muro, Don Jorge de Alvarado, and Diego de San Martín y Soto) again guaranteed Gobernador y Capitán General Don Francisco Serrano de Reina. This guarantee covered the payment of his first "media anata" within six months, his second "media anata" in the first month of his second year in office, and a third of emoluments, freight, and averages.

Capitán Francisco de Bonilla, Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes, Capitán Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, Capitán Don Miguel Calvo, and Alférez Don Pedro de Moya provided a 3000-peso guarantee for Gobernador y Capitán General Don Francisco Serrano de Reina. This fianza covered his judicial review (residencia juzgado y sentenciado) and the collection of royal tributes from the indigenous population.

people_involved: Capitanes Esteban de la Fuente y Zeledón de Berraondo
summary: Don Francisco Serrano de Reina, Gobernador y Capitán General of the province, granted general power of attorney to Capitanes Esteban de la Fuente y Zeledón de Berraondo. These captains were residents of Santiago de Guatemala and procurators of the Royal Audiencia there.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo Don Lorenzo González Calderón
summary: Don Francisco Serrano de Reina granted special power of attorney to Maestre de Campo Don Lorenzo González Calderón, a resident of León (Nicaragua). This power allowed him to collect Don Francisco's annual salary from the Royal Treasury and Accounting Office in León for his role as Gobernador y Capitán General.

Doña Catalina de Moya, a widow, obligated herself to the Capellanía of the late Doña Rafaela de Alvarado for 300 pesos at 5% interest. This money was received from Alférez Don Pedro de Moya, Doña Rafaela's executor, and was secured by Doña Catalina's residence in the city.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Antonio de Moya
summary: Juan Antonio de Guevara, as principal, and Sargento Mayor Don Antonio de Moya, as guarantor, obligated themselves to the Royal Treasury for 2910 pesos. This amount represented the value of the auction of the tithes of the city and its jurisdiction, which Juan Antonio de Guevara had won.

A dowry letter was issued for Doña Angela de Arlegui, the legitimate daughter of the late Doña Juana de Echavarría Navarro and Alférez Francisco de Arleguí, upon her marriage to Juan Antonio Serrano y Ayarra. The dowry, totaling 3080 pesos and 4 reales, included assets from her grandparents Capitán Don Diego de Ibarra and Doña Ana de Retes, such as enslaved persons (Victoria, Manuela Josefa, María Josefa), two city lots, and 1000 pesos in cash, with an additional 1000 pesos in arras.

Capitán Blas González Coronel, acting as a notary, and his wife Doña Bernarda de Fonseca, sold Juan José, a 14-year-old enslaved Black man, to Bdo. Cortés for 200 pesos. Doña Bernarda had inherited Juan José from her mother, Doña Jerónima de Retes.

people_involved: Don Antonio de la Riva Agüero
Doña Francisca de la Riva Agüero
Doña Jerónima de la Riva Agüero
summary: Don Antonio de la Riva Agüero, as principal, and Alférez Don Alvaro de Guevara, as guarantor, obligated themselves to Don Antonio's sisters, Doña Francisca and Doña Jerónima de la Riva Agüero, for 225 pesos. This money, representing their maternal inheritance, was received by Don Antonio from Capitán Don Gregorio de Chaves.

Alférez José Calderón and his wife Juana de las Alas obligated themselves to the Capellanía founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela for 100 pesos at 5% interest. This amount was redeemed by Capitán Domingo Guerrero, a resident of Esparza, and was secured by their residence in the city, adjacent to the hermitage of Nuestra Señora de la Soledad.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Antonio de Moya
summary: Alférez Don Pedro de Moya, as executor of the late Doña Rafaela de Alvarado, founded a Capellanía for her soul, requiring 10 recited masses per year. Licenciado Don Esteban Marín Laguna was named interim patron and chaplain, with Gregorio de Moya (son of Don Esteban and Doña Rafaela) as the designated future chaplain, followed by Don Juan Antonio de Moya (son of Sargento Mayor Don Antonio de Moya and Doña Isabel de Alvarado) if Gregorio fails. The Capellanía's 460-peso principal was secured by Doña Catalina de Moya's residence and a debt from Don Pablo José de Alvarado, with the 5% interest funding masses and church maintenance.

people_involved: Capitán Don Juan Ruiz de Velazco
summary: Capitán Don Juan Ruiz de Velazco received 1064 pesos and 4 reales as inheritance from his late father, also Capitán Don Juan Ruiz de Velazco, from his tutor and curator, Capitán Don Antonio Pacheco. Don Juan Ruiz de Velazco then donated 3172 pesos (half of which was his) to Don Antonio Pacheco, which he held in Panama as paternal inheritance. In return, Don Antonio Pacheco renounced and transferred to Don Juan Ruiz de Velazco any pending amounts against Alférez Andrés de Irula, a resident of León (Nicaragua).

people_involved: Licenciado Don Antonio de Vargas Machuca
summary: Licenciado Don Antonio de Vargas Machuca, a Presbyter Cleric, made his will. He was chaplain of three Capellanías, founded by his deceased father José de Vargas Machuca, his deceased mother Doña Gertrudis de Alvarado, and his aunt Doña Sebastiana de Alvarado. Among his assets, he listed and bequeathed several enslaved persons, including Luis (negro), Tiburcio (mulato), José (mulato), Gil, Nicolás, Francisco, Luisa, Jerónima, and Gertrudis (all mulatos).

An unnamed testator makes several bequests, including $500 to his godchild Juana, $500 to his cousin Doña Antonia de Alvarado, $300 each to his cousin's daughters Juana Josefa and Juana María de Echavarría, $300 to Josefa Clemencia, and $300 to his godchild María Antonia Lorenza. The Cofradía del Carmen also receives religious artworks. Don Jorge de Alvarado, Don Pedro de Alvarado, and Lorenzo de Arburola are named as executors.

people_involved: Capitán don Rodrigo de Gadea y Marrufo
Capitán de Caballos y Corazas don Antonio Salmón y Pacheco
summary: Capitán don Rodrigo de Gadea y Marrufo provides a dowry of $3396 and arras of $500 to Doña Antonia Salmón y Pacheco, the legitimate daughter of Capitán de Caballos y Corazas don Antonio Salmón y Pacheco and Doña Luisa Abarca. The dowry includes $500 in reales, a 22-year-old mulato slave named Sebastián valued at $430, and 80 sacks of cacao or $2000 in silver.

Doña Eugenia de Abarca, a widow, donates a 5-month-old white mulato slave named Manuel, son of her slave Francisca, to her grandson, Licenciado don Tomás Muñoz Hidalgo, a Presbyter. Tomás is the legitimate son of Capitán Bartolomé Muñoz Hidalgo and Doña Sebastiana Calvo.
Licenciado don Tomás Muñoz Hidalgo, a Presbyter, confers general power of attorney to Capitán don Miguel Calvo.

Doña Isabel de Estrada grants power to Capitán Martín de la Pinilla, a resident of Panamá, to collect a debt from Nicolás de Bochelo, also a resident of Panamá. The debt includes the proceeds from a 10-year-old 'negrita' that Bochelo was supposed to send, for which Isabel had given six mules.

Doña Eugenia de Abarca, a widow, donates a 3-year-old mulata slave named Marcela, daughter of her slave Francisca, to Doña María Antonia García. Doña María Antonia García is the legitimate daughter of Alonso García and Doña Eugenia Gertrudis Núñez Hidalgo.

people_involved: Gobernador y Capitán General don Francisco Serrano de Reina
Capitán de Caballos y Corazas don Fernando de Carrión Villasante
Capitán don Justo de Salazar y Carrión
Maestre de Campo don Lorenzo González Calderón
summary: Gobernador y Capitán General don Francisco Serrano de Reina grants power to Capitán de Caballos y Corazas don Fernando de Carrión Villasante and Capitán don Justo de Salazar y Carrión (residents of León, Nicaragua) to collect his salary from the Royal Treasury officials in León. This covers his current and future earnings during his governorship, starting from the last payment made to the deceased Maestre de Campo don Lorenzo González Calderón.

people_involved: Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto
summary: Bartolomé Lizano incurs an obligation to Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto for $75 in cacao. This document was not signed.

Doña Ana de Retes, ill at her country estate in the Santa Ana valley, grants power to her husband, Capitán don Diego de Ibarra (who is also ill in Cartago), to sell three of their zambo slaves—Manuela (15), Ambrosia (8), and Pedro (7), all children of their slave Alfonsa—for $900.

Juan Fernández Martínez provides a dowry of $3265 and arras of $500 to Doña Cayetana de Acosta Arévalo, the legitimate daughter of the deceased Antonio de Arévalo and Doña Josefa de Aguilar. The dowry includes 1000 fruit-bearing cacao trees in the Matina valley ($2000), 16 sacks of cacao ($400), and a plot of land ($60).
The document mentions Capitán don Diego de Ibarra at the beginning of an entry, but the rest of the details are missing.

people_involved: Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
summary: Doña Ana de Retes, acting through her power, sold three slaves named Manuela (15 years old), Ambrosia (8 years old), and Pedro (7 years old) to Captain Don José Pérez de Muro, the Lieutenant Governor, for $900.

Don Pablo José de Alvarado incurred a debt of $133 at 5% interest to Captain Don Miguel Calvo. On April 9, 1701, Captain Don Miguel Calvo received the $133 from Don José de Vivas, who was the executor of the deceased Don Pablo José de Alvarado.

people_involved: Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
Capitán don Juan de Echavarría Navarro
summary: Doña Ana de Retes, gravely ill and unable to obtain her husband's permission due to his absence in Cartago, granted power to Captain Don José Pérez de Muro to make her will. Her heirs were her children from her first marriage to Captain Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro, with Doña Petronila receiving an improved share of her assets. This act was granted in Santa Ana, at her estate.

people_involved: Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Licenciado Agustín de Torres, the oldest parish priest and commissary of the Holy Office, being ill in bed, granted power to Licenciado Don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, a priest and consultant of the Holy Office, to make his will. His soul was named as the heir.

people_involved: Capitán de Caballos y Corazas don Álvaro de Guevara
Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca
summary: Captain Don Álvaro de Guevara and Doña María de Sáenz, his wife, who acquired two houses from the estate of the deceased Licenciado Don Antonio de Vargas, acknowledged a $600, 5% lien on these properties. This lien was in favor of the Chaplaincy founded by Doña Sebastiana de Alvarado.

people_involved: Capitán de Caballos y Corazas don Álvaro de Guevara
Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca
summary: Captain Don Álvaro de Guevara and Doña María de Sáenz incurred a new $500, 5% obligation to the Chaplaincy founded by the deceased Licenciado Don Antonio de Vargas Machuca, receiving the funds from executor Lorenzo de Arburola. This obligation was placed on their adobe and tile houses in this city, which already carried a $600 lien for Doña Sebastiana de Alvarado's Chaplaincy.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Antonio de Moya
Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Licenciado Agustín de Torres's closed will detailed bequests to his niece Doña Juana Ruiz, her husband Sargento Mayor Don Antonio de Moya (to whom he owed cacao), his nephew Francisco Ruiz (who had funds held by Don Antonio de Moya), and an orphan named María. He also mentioned his role as executor for the deceased Francisco Chaves for over 10 years, and named Licenciado Don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, Captain Don José de Vivas, and Sargento Mayor Don Antonio de Moya as his executors.

Ayudante Francisco Hernández Barquero, a native of Fresnedoso de Estremadura, made his will, naming his deceased parents, his wife Ana de Espinosa, and his children as beneficiaries. He also mentioned his grandchildren Cayetana, Josefa, and Antonio Solano, and bequeathed four slaves to his unmarried daughter Margarita.

people_involved: Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca
Capitán de Caballos y Corazas don Álvaro de Guevara
summary: Lorenzo Arburola Iribarren, acting as executor for the deceased Licenciado Don Antonio de Vargas Machuca, established a perpetual chaplaincy for 7 annual masses, as per Vargas Machuca's will. Don Esteban Marín Laguna was named the perpetual patron and chaplain, with a principal of $500 secured by houses in this city that were purchased from Captain Don Álvaro de Guevara.
Doña María de Escobar Guijarro, a widow, granted power of attorney to Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes, a perpetual councilman, to represent her in the division of assets and property.
Pedro de Azofeifa died, leaving behind his wife.
Capitán Francisco de Bonilla obligates himself to the executors of Comisario Agustín de Torres for 13 sacks of cacao, to be delivered in Cartago.

Isidro de Aguilar's testament names his deceased parents Diego de Aguilar and Leonor Jiménez, his wife Ana Velázquez, and his ten children (some deceased, some married). Sargento Juan González Brenes is named as his executor.

Capitán José de Vivas, as executor for the deceased Comisario Agustín de Torres, grants power of attorney to Capitán Juan de Osejo and Capitán Simón de Balmaceda to collect money owed to Pe. Torres from the Royal Treasury officials in León, Nicaragua, up to the date of his death on March 24.

Sargento Mayor Pedro José Sáenz sells his house in Cartago, previously bought from Antonio de Bustamante, to Manuel García Ergueta for $931.00. The property carries obligations to Chaplaincies and Confraternities, which the buyer and his wife must recognize.

Licenciado Alonso Berrocal, a priest domiciled in Panama and residing in Cartago, grants general power of attorney to Capitán Gabriel de Urriola, a resident of Panama, to collect 5 enslaved people he left in Panama.

Licenciado Alonso Berrocal's testament lists eight enslaved people and details a prior donation of these enslaved people and $60,000 to the Convento de la Concepción in Panama. Bishop Diego Ladrón de Guevara had nullified a previous donation to a daughter of Francisca Ranjel due to her scandalous life. Berrocal ratifies the $60,000 donation (held by Francisca Ranjel and her children) but reserves the enslaved people. His assets are to be sold and proceeds sent to his brother, Capitán Pedro Lozano de Piña, in Cádiz.

locations: Ciudad de los Reyes del Perú
summary: Capitán Domingo del Puerto Mariño's testament details his two marriages: first to María Ortiz de la Torre (deceased, with six children, three deceased), and second to Leonor Muñoz Hidalgo (with three children and one unborn). His executors are Capitán Jorge de Alvarado and Lorenzo de Arburola.
Manuel de Chaves sells an enslaved woman named Luisa, 30 years old and of brown complexion, to Capitán José Pérez de Muro for $400.00.

Ayudante Francisco Hernández Barquero and his wife Ana de Espinosa sell a house in Cartago to Sargento Juan Masís for $300.00. Masís is obligated to pay $100 to Jerónimo Morillo and $200 to the sellers.
On January 16, 1701, Ana de Espinosa, now a widow of Francisco Hernández Barquero, receives the $200 owed to her and her deceased husband from Sargento Juan Masís.

Rafael Mogeizmes Fajardo issues a dowry letter for $2,053.00, with $500.00 earnest money, in favor of doña Josefa Sáenz Vásquez, daughter of the deceased Maestre de Campo Juan Francisco Sáenz Vásquez and doña Bárbara Lancini, for their upcoming marriage.
Sargento Juan Masís obligates himself to Ayudante Francisco Hernández Barquero for $550.00.
Martín de Sivitola issues a dowry letter for $3,000.00, with $100.00 earnest money, in favor of his wife María Calderón, daughter of Alfonso José Calderón and Juana de las Alas.

locations: Convento de San Bartolomé de Barba
summary: Manuel García de Ergueta and his wife Antonia Lainez de Iztueta acknowledge a 5% lien of $381.00 on the house they bought from Sargento Mayor Pedro José Sáenz, in favor of a Chaplaincy founded by the deceased Lorenzo Morera at the Convento de San Bartolomé de Barba.
On January 26, 1704, Francisco Fernández, General Syndic of the San Francisco Convents, acknowledges receipt of $381.00 in favor of García Ergueta, likely related to the lien.
Manuel García de Ergueta and Antonia Lainez de Iztueta acknowledge a second 5% lien of $100.00 on the same houses, in favor of a Chaplaincy at the Church of San Francisco.
Catalina Gutiérrez founded 'this city', which is inferred to be Cartago based on the document context.
An unspecified group acknowledged a lien (censos) of $200 at 5% on certain houses. This lien was in favor of the Cofradía de la Concepción, which was located in the San Francisco Convent in Cartago.
Doña Sebastiana de Alvarado, a widow, sold an enslaved mulatto woman named María Micaela, aged 16 and daughter of her enslaved woman Antonia, to her brother Don Pedro de Alvarado for $200.

Sergeant Rodrigo de la Fuente, as the principal, and Don Antonio de Alvarado, as guarantor, committed to pay Francisca González, the minor daughter of the deceased Juan González, $58 and 1 real as her paternal inheritance.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan de Echavarría Navarro
Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
summary: Doña Ana de Retes made her will, detailing her lineage, her deceased first husband, and her current husband. She listed her numerous children, both living and deceased, and specified inheritances including enslaved people and a sugarcane field. She also named her grandchildren, sons-in-law, and executors.
Doña Eugenia de Abarca, a widow, made a donation to Francisco Calvo. The donation consisted of a 3-year-old mulatto enslaved boy named Antonio, who was the son of Manuela.

Sebastián de Rojas, as the principal, and Francisco de Rojas, as guarantor, committed to pay Juan and Miguel de la Mata, minor sons of the deceased Juan Martín de la Mata and Clara de Rojas, $183 and 1/2 real as their paternal inheritance.

Doña Sebastiana de Alvarado, a widow, established a chaplaincy for 9 recited masses for her soul and her parents' souls. Licenciado don Francisco de Salazar was appointed interim chaplain, and her brother Don Pedro de Alvarado was named the first patron. The endowment of $600 at 5% was secured on the residence of Captain Don Alvaro de Guevara in Cartago.

Andrea de Aguilar, a widow and principal, along with Juan de Rojas as guarantor, committed to pay Luis de Rojas, her son with her deceased husband José de Rojas, $177, 7 reales, and 6.5 maravedís as his paternal inheritance.

Juan de Astúa and Martín de Sivitola, as principal and guarantor respectively, committed to pay Cayetana, the minor daughter of Tonmias de la Cruz and Juana Barquero, $151 and 6 reales as her maternal inheritance. This inheritance had previously been under the care of the deceased Francisco Hernández Barquero.

Doña Eugenia de Abarca and her son, Captain Don Miguel Calvo, attempted to sell a cattle and horse ranch named San Antonio de las Cañas, located in royal lands near the city of Esparza, to Gaspar de Basterrica for $2,156 and 4 reales. The transaction ultimately did not proceed.

people_involved: Capitán don Rodrigo Gadea y Marrufo
summary: Captain Don Rodrigo Gadea y Marrufo committed to pay Don Miguel Ichazo y Redín $1675 for Castilian clothing he had received. A marginal note from January 25, 1700, indicates that Captain Manuel Antonio de Lima, as executor for the deceased Don Miguel Ichazo y Redín, was involved in this matter.

people_involved: Capitán don Miguel de Ichazo y Redín
summary: Captain Don Miguel de Ichazo y Redín, a resident of Quito and native of Pamplona, Spain, made his will. He detailed his parents, his first marriage in Tunja to the deceased Doña Lucía de Arellano, and mentioned his daughter, Doña Luisa Ichazo y Redín.

people_involved: Doña Andrea de Aro y Vinuesa
summary: Miguel de Ichazo y Redín married for the second time in San Francisco de Quito to Doña Isabel González de Escobedo, the legitimate daughter of Juan González de Escobedo and Doña Andrea de Aro y Vinuesa. This marriage produced no children. Capitán Miguel de Lima was named as the executor.
A codicil was added to the previous testament of Ichazo y Redín. This codicil served to include some assets that had been forgotten in the original testament.

Alférez don Francisco de Espinosa, a native of Granada, Nicaragua, made his testament. He was the legitimate son of the deceased Capitán don Juan de Espinosa and Ana María de Caraballo, and was married to Doña Sebastiana de Bonilla. Of their six children, only María Nicolasa, aged 5, was still alive, and Capitán don Miguel Calvo and Lorenzo de Arb. rola were named as executors.

Doña Eugenia de Abarca, a widow, and her son, Capitán don Miguel Calvo, sold a cattle and horse ranch named San Antonio de las Cañas to Manuel García de Ergueta. The property, located in royal lands within the jurisdiction of Esparza, was inherited by them after the death of Don Gregorio Calvo, who was Doña Eugenia's son and Capitán don Miguel Calvo's brother. The sale price was $2156 and 4 reales.

Licenciado don Francisco de Salazar, the Ecclesiastical Judge Vicar of Cartago, obligated himself for $100 at 5% in favor of the Capellanía founded by Vasco Solano. He received these funds from the Patron and Chaplain, Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya, and from those redeemed by Capitán Salvador de Torres, imposing the obligation on his dwelling houses in the city.

Licenciado don Francisco de Salazar obligated himself for $220 at 5% in favor of the Capellanía founded by the deceased Juan Alonso. He received these funds from Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya, the Patron and Chaplain, and from those redeemed by Capitán Salvador de Torres, a resident of Esparza, imposing the obligation on his dwelling houses.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan de Echavarría Navarro
summary: A dowry letter was issued by Francisco de Otárola, the legitimate son of the deceased Domingo de Otárola and Doña María de Alvarado, in favor of his wife, Doña Petronila de Echavarría Navarro. Doña Petronila was the legitimate daughter of the deceased Capitán don Juan de Echavarría Navarro and Doña Aya de Retes. The dowry amounted to $4347, with arras of $1000.

Alférez don Francisco de Moya, as principal, and Alférez don Pedro de Moya, as guarantor, obligated themselves for $80 at 5% in favor of the Capellanía founded by the deceased Depositario Tomás Calvo. The principal obligor received the funds from Capitán don Miguel Calvo.
Capitán don Miguel Calvo cancelled an obligation related to the Capellanía founded by Depositario Tomás Calvo.

Leonor Moreno, a widow, as principal, and Capitán don Gregorio de Chaves, as guarantor, obligated themselves for $165 and 1 real. This obligation was in favor of José, Francisca, Juan, and Nicolasa, who were the minor children of Leonor and the deceased Sargento Faustino de Segura, for their paternal inheritance.

people_involved: Don Miguel de Ichazo y Redín
summary: Capitán Miguel Antonio de Lima, acting as the testamentary executor for the deceased Don Miguel de Ichazo y Redín, sold an enslaved person named Juan Pascual to Don Francisco Serrano de Reyna. Juan Pascual was a 20-year-old criollo who had belonged to Ichazo y Redín, and the sale price was $450.

A dowry letter was issued for Don Cristóbal Martínez Cubero, a native of Segovia, Spain, and legitimate son of Don Diego Martín Cubero and Doña María Díaz, in favor of his future wife, Doña Catalina González del Camino. Doña Catalina was the legitimate daughter of the deceased Capitán don Juan González Camino and Doña Manuela de Salazar. The dowry amounted to $6059, with arras of $2000, and included assets such as half of Doña Manuela's houses, 1000 cacao trees in Matina, and enslaved persons Mónica (a mulata with a 4-year-old daughter) and Gil (a mulato).

Matías Calderón, as principal, and Juan Hidalgo, as guarantor, obligated themselves for $116 and 2 reales. This obligation was in favor of Gabriela and Isidora González, who were the minor daughters of the deceased Juan González, for their paternal inheritance.
Francisco de los Reyes Benavides, a resident of Esparza, attempted to sell an enslaved mulato named Pedro de las Alas, aged 20, to Juan de Ovares for $250. However, the sale did not proceed.

Francisco de Flores and his wife, Magdalena López, leased a productive cacao hacienda in the Matina valley, consisting of 500 trees, to Alonso Camacho for a period of four years. The hacienda bordered land belonging to Francisco López, Magdalena's father, as well as the mountain and the Río Grande of the valley. The annual rent was set at 3 zurrones of cacao.

people_involved: Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
summary: Capitanes don José Pérez de Muro (Lieutenant Governor in political matters), don Miguel Calvo (Chief Constable of the Holy Office), don Gregorio de Chaves, Francisco de Bonilla, don José de Guzmán, and Luis Cascante de Rojas acted on their own behalf and in the name of the deceased Capitán Antonio Vásquez in an unspecified transaction.

Capitán don Lope de Alcarazo and Juan Antonio de Guevara, as guarantors, are owed $3000 from a judgment against ex-Gobernador Manuel de Bustamante. Bustamante's salary was previously unembargoed by the Real Audiencia of Guatemala despite charges from the Cabildo of Cartago. Alcarazo and Guevara granted power to procurators Zeledón de Berraondo and Francisco de Amesqueta to request a new embargo on Bustamante's salary until he fulfills his residency review obligations.

Ana Solano, widow of Juan Fernández, executed her will, naming her children Gaspar, Cristóbal, Salvador, and Margarita (the latter two deceased). She also mentioned her grandchildren María Fernández, Ana Fernández, and Juana Fernández, and an orphan she raised, Antonio Fernández. Provisions were made for Juan Lucas Solano, her indigenous servant Tomás, and her sister María Solano, with Alférez Francisco Fernández and Lorenzo de Arburola appointed as executors.

Doña María de Escobar y Guijarro, along with guarantors Capitán Antonio Aurelio de Zamora and Alférez Pedro Martínez de Colina, committed to pay $313-211 reales to Ana and María de Azofeifa. This payment represents their paternal inheritance from their deceased father, don Pedro de Azofeifa.

people_involved: Dese López de la Rea y Soto
summary: Doña Josefa Rosales, widow of Leonardo Ricardo, made her will, listing her children María Gertrudis, Juana, Antonio, Tomasa, Alfonsa, Catalina, and Josefa (the latter two deceased). She also named her sons-in-law Manuel de Araya, Juan de Villalobos, Domingo de Araya, and Nicolás de Segura. Alférez Francisco Fernández and Dese López de la Rea y Soto were appointed executors, and Josefa transferred $27 held for orphans Eugenia, Clara, Juana, and Esteban to Alférez Diego de Cárdenas for investment.

A dowry letter was issued for the marriage of Domingo de Inza, a native of Hernani, Spain, and Doña Alfonsa Muñoz Hidalgo. Domingo, son of Juan López de Inza and Francisca de Zesueta, provided a dowry of $1694 and an 'arras' of $500 to Alfonsa, daughter of the deceased Capitán Bartolomé Muñoz Hidalgo and Doña Sebastiana Calvo.

Juan Antonio de Foto, originally from Escopelos, Greece, made his will. He was married to Doña Juana de Acosta Arévalo and had three minor children: Josefa Elena, Cayetana, and Ferdando de Foto. He also declared responsibility for 900 cacao trees in Matina belonging to the minor children of the deceased Gregoria de Acosta and José de Proa: Luisa Bartola, Francisco, and Juana.

Licenciado don Francisco de Salazar and Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes, as executors for Alférez don Pedro Durán de Chaves, established a chaplaincy. This fulfilled a testamentary disposition by Pedro, honoring a request from his deceased mother, Doña Ana Pereira, for eight recited masses. The chaplaincy, with a principal of $200, was located on properties in La Lata Redonda, Curridabat, and named Bachiller Pedro Meléndez as the perpetual chaplain.

Capitán don Gregorio de Chaves issued a codicil to his closed will, previously granted on March 6th of the preceding year. He acknowledged a debt of over $300 to his natural son, Juan de Chaves, and directed it be paid with his mulatto slave, Nicolás Villegas. He also bequeathed his mulatto slave, Juan de Chaves, to Mateo and Francisco de Chaves, to be shared equally by value.

Licenciado don Diego de Angulo Gascón, the senior parish priest, committed to the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora de la Pura y Limpia Concepción for $150 at 5% interest. He received this money from the Mayordomo, Alférez Francisco Fernández, and imposed it on his houses.

Domingo Tomás Guillén and his wife Juana Calderón obligate themselves to Josefa Guillén, minor daughter of Domingo and his first deceased wife Juana Barquero, for $151-6 reales as her maternal inheritance.

Doña Antonia María Venegas, a widow, obligates herself to the Chaplaincy founded by the deceased Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas for $320-00 at 5%, which she received from his executor Lorenzo de Arburola. The obligation is secured by her houses in "esta ciudad".
Capitán don Alvaro de Guevara and his wife doña María Sáenz obligate themselves for $100-000 at 5% to the Parish Church factory. This obligation was not completed.
José de Prado sells a 40-year-old Creole enslaved man named Mateo to doña Jerónima de Retes for $230-00.

people_involved: Juan López de la Rea y Soto
summary: Sargento Francisco Gutiérrez makes his will, detailing his legitimate parents, deceased wife Nicolasa de Flores and their seven children, a natural son with his wife before marriage, and three orphaned children he raised. He names Alférez Francisco Fernández and Juan López de la Rea y Soto as executors.

Alférez Marcelo Blasco, a native of Granada, Spain, makes his will, identifying his legitimate parents Lucas Marcelo and doña Catalina Blasco, his wife doña Clara de Vida Martel, and their two sons, Lucas and Marcelo. The will was not completed.

people_involved: Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca
summary: Lorenzo de Arburola, as executor of the deceased Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca, establishes a Chaplaincy for four masses with a principal of $320-00, secured by houses in "esta ciudad". His son Manuel Antonio is named the first Chaplain, with Licenciado don Esteban Marín serving until Manuel Antonio's ordination, and don Pedro de Alvarado as patron.
Pedro Rodríguez Palacio issues a dowry letter for his future wife doña Teresa de Oses Navarro, legitimate daughter of deceased Esteban de Oses Navarro and doña Juana Baptista Calvo, for $1932-00.

people_involved: Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
summary: Doña María Durán de Chaves sells an enslaved woman named Nicolasa to José Hidalgo. The transaction was granted before Capitán don José Pérez de Muro, the Lieutenant Governor.

people_involved: Don Alvaro de Guevara y Sandoval
Capitán don José de Guevara y Sandoval
Maestre de Campo don Juan Francisco Sáenz Vásquez
summary: Don Alvaro de Guevara y Sandoval issues a dowry letter for his future wife doña María Sáenz Vásquez for their upcoming marriage. The dowry is $2552-00 and arras $1500-00, including 1000 cacao trees in Matina. The document was granted before Capitán don Antonio Pacheco.

people_involved: Capitán don Gabriel de Echavarría Navarro
Maestre de Campo don Miguel de Echavarría Navarro
B? don Diego de Angulo Gascón
summary: Doña Antonia María de Otálora makes her will, identifying her deceased parents, deceased husband, three minor children, mother-in-law, brother, cousin, and sister. She names her sister, doña Juana de Otálora, as tutor for her children, and B? don Diego de Angulo Gascón and Alférez don Sebastián de Garita as executors.

people_involved: Juan López de la Rea y Soto
summary: Sebastián de Benavides makes his will, identifying his deceased parents, deceased wife Ana Sánchez, and their four children. The will was granted before Juan López de la Rea y Soto, Judge of the Countryside.

people_involved: Diego de San Martín y Soto
summary: Toribio Valverde and Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto initially obligated themselves for $111 and 10 maravedíes from the paternal inheritance of minors Jerónimo and María de Trejos. Following Toribio Valverde's death, San Martín y Soto was exempted, and the minors' grandfather, Juan de Valonena, assumed guardianship on December 21, 1701.

Alférez Francisco Pérez de Cote and his wife María de Zamora recognized a 5% censo of $300 in favor of the Capellanía founded by the deceased Pedro Solano, whose chaplain is Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya. This censo burdens houses they purchased from Capitán Juan de Vida Martel and Clara de Quirós on October 16, 1698.
Alférez Francisco Pérez de Cote and his wife María de Zamora also recognized another 5% censo of $100 on the same houses, this time in favor of the beneficed priests of the city.

Calixto de Segura posted bail for his son, Juan José de Segura, who was imprisoned at the request of Francisca de Prendas for breaking a promise. The Gobernador y Capitán General ordered Juan José's release on bail for 30 days, starting from the eve of Easter.

Ambrosio de Mora Salado, a brother of the 3rd order of San Francisco, made his will. He left his mulata slave María and her 3-year-old son to his cousin Claudia Enríquez de Matamoros, and named his grandmother Margarita de Flores as his universal heir. Capitanes Juan de Bonilla and Manuel de Zamora were appointed as albaceas.

people_involved: Diego de San Martín y Soto
summary: Luisa de Quintana, widow of Capitán Sebastián de Zamora, made her will. She listed her children, including María de Zamora, who married Alférez Francisco Pérez de Cote, and Feliciana, who married Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto. Diego de San Martín y Soto and Gregorio Gordiano de Zamora were named as albaceas.

Doña Gertrudis de Alfaro Hidalgo, a widow, sold 200 head of cattle to Andrés Arias for $500, which she left as a 5% censo. On May 16, 1703, Doña Gertrudis, identified as the widow of Capitán Antonio Vásquez, received the $500 from Arias, cancelling the censo.
Alférez Pedro Martínez Colina obligated himself to Alférez Salvador Murillo for $200 at 5% annual interest. Murillo later cancelled this obligation on December 29, 1707.

Gaspar de los Reyes sold a house with a straw roof and a wooden fence, including a plantain patch, in the Valle de Aserrí at La Lajuela, to Marcos de Zamora for $18. Gaspar de los Reyes had previously purchased this property from the deceased Juan Monje.

Margarita de Flores, widow of Capitán Pedro de Mora Salado, made her will, listing her deceased sons and a son born after her widowhood, Francisco de Flores. Her deceased grandson, Ambrosio de Mora (son of Manuel), and her niece Margarita Aguiar, wife of Alférez Sebastián de Garita, were also mentioned. Her grandchildren were named as heirs.

Don Pablo José de Alvarado made his will, listing his slaves and various bequests. He left $600 to his nephew Fernando de Moya, whom he raised, and $100 to his aunt Doña Sebastiana de Alvarado to help raise Francisca, an orphan. He also left $400 in trust with his uncle Pedro de Alvarado for his nephews and nieces, children of Antonio de Alvarado, and $100 each to his nieces Juana and Polonia de Moya.
Pedro de Alvarado's inheritance was divided, with half designated for his soul and the other half for his nephew, José Fernando de Moya.
Alférez José Calderón and his wife Juana de las Alas committed to an obligation of $100 at 5% interest to the Cofradía de la Vera Cruz, but this transaction did not proceed.

people_involved: Ambrosia María de Santilla y Zúñiga
summary: Sargento Mayor Gregorio de Caamaño, a native of Noya, Galicia, made his will. He was married to Ambrosia María de Santilla y Zúñiga, who was previously widowed from Sebastián López de Cárdenas, and they had no children. He named Francisco Serrano de Reina as his heir and, along with others, as an executor depending on his place of death.
Manuel de Moya y Alvarado provided a dowry of $3015, including $500 in arras, to his wife Manuela Sáenz Vásquez. The dowry included 1360 cacao trees in Matina and other goods.

Fermín de Oses Navarro, who was single, made his will. He named his brother Lorenzo de Arburola as executor and his siblings Antonia, Juana Gertrudis, Petronila, and Félix de Oses Navarro as his heirs.

Sebastiana Calvo, widow of Captain Bartolomé Muñoz Hidalgo, granted her sealed will on November 1, 1700. Her will was opened on November 4, naming her children Andrés, Tomás, María, and Bárbara Muñoz Hidalgo as heirs, and her brother Miguel Calvo, Miguel de Echavarría Navarro, and Lorenzo de Arburola as executors.

Juana de Acosta Arévalo, a widow, leased a cacao plantation of 1670 trees on the Matina riverbanks, along with tools and three mules, to Alférez Francisco Pérez de Cote for four years. The annual rent was 8 sacks of cacao, delivered to Alajuela.

Alférez Francisco de Moya and his wife Manuela de Alvarado sold a house and lot in Cartago to Captain Pedro Ortiz de Rosas for $620. The property was bordered by houses belonging to Alvaro de Guevara, Juan Matías Baptista Lizondo, Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, and Rodrigo Gadea y Marrufo.

Captain Pedro Ortiz de Rosas and his wife Juana de Alvarado acknowledged a lien of $85 at 5% interest on the houses he purchased. This lien was in favor of the Chaplaincy founded by Depositario Tomás Calvo.

Pedro Ortiz de Rosas and Juana de Alvarado acknowledged another lien of $300 at 5% interest on the same houses. This lien was in favor of the minor children of the deceased Captain Esteban de Moya and Rafaela de Alvarado, whose guardian was Francisco de Moya.
On September 28, 1701, Francisco de Moya, acting as guardian, canceled $200 of the $300 lien on the houses, with the remaining balance still active.
A will was made by an unnamed Captain of Cuirassier Cavalry.

Details of Blas González Coronel, a native of Sevilla, Spain, including his parentage, marriage to Bernarda de Fonseca, his 8-year-old son Manuel, and his 40-year-old mulata slave Juana. His will names his wife, José de Guzmán, and Lorenzo de Arburola as executors, and mentions Lorenza Venegas as his son's aunt.
Don José de Guzmán and his wife Doña Antonia de Echavarría Navarro sold a 40-year-old black slave named Isabel to Manuel García de Ergueta for $420.00.
A power of attorney document was signed by Francisco Solano, Gaspar P? Cardoso, Luis Cascante de Rojas, and Francisco de Ocampo y Golfín. The heading of the document is missing.
Doña Magdalena de Chaves granted power of attorney to Juan Fernández. The document is torn and incomplete.

A certification was issued on November 3, 1662, regarding diligences from June 22, 1640. In 1640, Captain Juan de Senabria Maldonado declared the San Antonio cattle estate, including 300 cattle, houses, corral, two 'caballerías' of land, and an Angolan black man named Pedro, as property of Juana Benita Pereira, wife of Alonso de Bonilla and universal heir of Alférez Miguel Calvo and María Pereira Cardoso. This declaration was made despite opposition from Alférez Tomás Calvo, legitimate son of Miguel Calvo and stepson of María, who claimed the assets belonged to him and were donated to his stepmother.

Alférez Juan de Vida Martel stood surety for the royal tributes and 'media anata' for Alférez Juan Vázquez de Coronado, who was appointed Corregidor of the Quepo party. The ordinary Alcalde was Fernando de Salazar.

Alférez Tomás Calvo, the General Depositary of the city, stood surety for the royal tributes for Bartolomé de Marzana, who was appointed Corregidor of the San Mateo de Chirripó party. The ordinary Alcalde was Fernando de Salazar.

Alférez Juan Cascante de Rojas stood surety for the royal tributes and 'media anata' for Captain Matías de Ballesteros, who was appointed Corregidor of the Pacacua party. The Alcalde was Fernando de Salazar.
Captain Juan de Echavarría Navarro stood surety for the royal tributes and 'media anata' for Captain Juan Valcárcel Soto Mayor, who was Corregidor of the Turrialba party.
Sargento Mayor José de Moya stood surety for Ayudante Juan de Morales Miranda, who was appointed Corregidor of the San Mateo de Chirripó party.

Captain Francisco Fernández de Miranda stood surety for Francisco de Hitapor for the delivery of an indigenous person within a year, or proof of their death, acknowledging their value. The heading is missing.

A dowry letter was issued by Juan González in favor of his future wife, Isabel de Oviedo Alvarez, the legitimate daughter of Francisco de Oviedo and Lucía de Tapia, for their marriage scheduled for the next day. The document was granted before Francisco Fernández de Miranda, the ordinary Alcalde, and is torn.

people_involved: Don Juan López de la Flor
summary: Alférez Bartolomé Calderón became obligated to Gaspar de Chinchilla for 12 breeding mares or their value, which Catalina de Palacios (deceased) had donated to him, but this donation was declared null. The obligation was granted before Don Juan López de la Flor, Governor and Captain General.

people_involved: Captain and Sargento Mayor Alonso de Bonilla
summary: Captain and Sargento Mayor Alonso de Bonilla, the oldest ordinary Alcalde, apprenticed Antonio, a mulato orphan of his father and son of Juana de Acuña (naboría) and Andrés Gómez, to the blacksmith trade for a period of 4 years.

Alférez Tomás Calvo and Jerónimo Valerino stood surety for Ayudante Sebastián de Aguirre for $910.00, the value for which the city's tithes were auctioned to him for a term of one year. This was granted before Don Fernando de Salazar, Lieutenant Accountant and Treasurer, Official Judge of the Royal Treasury of this city.
A fragment of a will mentions a marriage to Isabel Alvarez, who is identified as the legitimate daughter of Gaspar Núñez and Beatriz.

Agustín Guerrero acted as a guarantor for Captain Don García de Alvarado, the auctioneer for the silver and royal papers of the royal treasury's administration for the year 1670. This guarantee was for the delivery of these items to the Royal Accounting Office in León, and the transaction was witnessed by Don Fernando de Salazar.

Esteban Rodríguez and Ana de Santiago, married for over 40 years, created a sealed will, naming their legitimate children Diego de Santiago and Manuel Rodríguez. Esteban's parents were Diego Rodríguez and María de Uriarte (both deceased), and Ana's parents were Juan de Araya and Isabel de Rojas (both deceased). The will was opened on May 20, 1672, at the request of Diego de Santiago, following Ana de Santiago's death on that day, before Captain Lorenzo Venegas.

Agustín Guerrero acted as a guarantor for Captain Don Matías González Camino, the auctioneer for the silver and papers of the Royal Treasury's administration for the year 1671. This guarantee was for their delivery to the Royal Accounting Office in León, and the transaction was witnessed by Don Fernando de Salazar.

José Marín Laguna and his wife, Doña Catalina de Moya, committed to pay $110 at 5% interest to the minor children of the late Sergeant Francisco Carrillo and Juana del Pueyo: Nicolás María, Juana Antonia, Tomás, and Manuel Carrillo. The transaction was incomplete, but Alférez Esteban de Oses, the minors' guardian, cancelled the obligation on August 19, 1676. The document was witnessed by Don José Pérez de Muro.

Don Matías González Camino and Lieutenant Juan de Gamboa acted as guarantors for Alférez Gregorio de Urquiza, who was the auctioneer for the tithes of Cartago for the year 1673, for the sum of $700. The transaction was witnessed by Don Fernando de Salazar.

Doña Mariana Flores de Miranda granted power of attorney to her husband, Diego Romero, to sell a 20-year-old mulatto slave named José. José was given to Doña Mariana as a dowry by her parents, Juan de Morales and Doña Beatriz Méndez Machado. The document was witnessed by Don José Pérez de Muro.

people_involved: doña María de Lara y Orozco
summary: Antonio de Orozco, a native of Spain and son of the late Agustín de Rivera and Doña María de Lara y Orozco of Seville, made his will. He was first married to Ana López de Santiago, whose mother, María de Aguilar, gave him $780, and they had four children: María de Orozco (married to Bartolomé Sánchez), Beatriz Agustina, Juan de Orozco, and Francisco. He was married a second time to Doña Isabel de Castillo, who, along with Luis Gómez Rico, were named as executors. The will was witnessed by Jerónimo Leal.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don Juan López de la Flor
summary: Don García de Alvarado committed to pay $660 to Maestre de Campo Don Juan López de la Flor, the Governor and Captain General of the province. Don Juan de Echavarría Navarto delivered the money on López de la Flor's order. The obligation was cancelled on June 27, 1674, by López de la Flor. The document was witnessed by Don José Pérez de Muro.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don Juan López de la Flor
summary: Don Matías González Camino committed to pay $660 to Maestre de Campo Don Juan López de la Flor, the Governor and Captain General. Don Juan de Echavarría Navarro delivered the money on López de la Flor's order. The obligation was cancelled on June 27, 1674, by López de la Flor. The document was witnessed by Don José Pérez de Muro.

Doña Juana de Ortega acknowledged a lien (censo) of $90 in favor of the Cofradía de San Nicolás, encumbering a property within Cartago. This property previously belonged to the deceased spouses Francisco Carrillo and Ana de Aguilar and was auctioned to Doña Juana for $211. The document is incomplete.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín
summary: Alférez Sebastián de Zamora acted as a guarantor for Sargento Mayor Don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín, who was a bidder for the office of Alférez Mayor and Regidor of Cartago, for the sum of $210. The transaction was witnessed by Alférez Nicolás de Céspedés.
Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín acted as guarantor for Capitán Alonso Arias Romero, who was bidding for the office of Alguacil Mayor of Cartago. The guarantee was for $450.
Benito Valerino acted as guarantor for Sargento Mayor Jerónimo Valerino, who was bidding for the office of Regidor perpétuo of Cartago. The guarantee was for $200.

A dowry letter was issued for the marriage of Francisco Peláez, natural son of Alférez Francisco Peláez, and Francisca Barboza, legitimate daughter of a deceased father and Juana Velázquez de Ortega. The dowry was $338, with $100 in arras.

people_involved: José de la Haya y Bolívar
summary: Teniente Juan de Gamboa, Claudio de la Mata, and Alvaro de Nava, residents of Esparza, provided a $1000 guarantee for Francisco de los Reyes. This allowed Francisco de los Reyes to assume the administration of the royal treasury as Teniente de Jueces Oficiales reales. The document was granted in Esparza before Capitán don José de la Haya y Bolívar, Teniente de Gobernador.

Francisco González de Ledezma and Sargento Andrés Clavijo provided a $500 guarantee for Juan Antonio de Bogarín. This allowed Bogarín to enter the administration of the royal treasury as Teniente de Jueces y Oficiales reales. The document was granted in Esparza before Capitán don José de Rojas y Miranda, Teniente de Gobernador.

Capitán don Andrés de Salazar sold a cacao plantation with 2500 trees in the Matina valley to Martín de Civitola for 1500 pesos. The sale involved recognizing existing liens (censos) of 500 pesos to Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, 250 pesos to Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya, and 100 pesos to Licenciado don Tomás Muñoz Hidalgo, all at 5% interest.

Martín de Civitola and his wife María Calderón formally acknowledged a 250-peso censo (lien/annuity) in favor of Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya. This censo was situated on the hacienda they had recently purchased.

Martín de Civitola and his wife María Calderón formally acknowledged a 100-peso censo at 5% on their hacienda. This censo was in favor of Licenciado don Tomás Muñoz Hidalgo, who was the Sacristán Mayor of the parish in Granada, Nicaragua.
Martín de Civitola and his wife María Calderón formally acknowledged a 500-peso censo at 5% on their hacienda. This censo was in favor of Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas.

Capitán don Juan de Vida Martel and his wife Clara de Quirós sold a fruiting cacao hacienda with 1300 trees to Capitán don José de Guzmán for 1300 pesos. The payment included 400 pesos cash, 397 pesos charged on the hacienda for Domingo Vázquez's minor children, 350 pesos in cacao for the next San Juan, and 152 pesos and 5 reales for Christmas. The hacienda had originally been purchased by Martel from Capitán Blas González Coronel.

locations: Ermita de la Cofradía de San Juan
summary: Alférez Esteban de Zúñiga, as Mayordomo of the Cofradía de San Juan and perpetual patron, appointed a new chaplain for the chaplaincy of masses in the Cofradía's hermitage. This chaplaincy was founded by Sargento Mayor don Antonio de Moya as executor for the late Capitán don José de Alvarado, and the position was vacant due to the death of Licenciado don Esteban Marín Laguna.

Capitán don José de Vivas and doña Josefa de Moya received a house, kitchen, sugar mill, two cauldrons, and a sugar cane plot in Ujarrás from Esteban de Zúñiga. They are obligated to recognize 1000 pesos on these assets at 5% interest for a Chaplaincy founded by Capitán don José de Alvarado.

Doña Luisa Calvo, widow of José Maroto and daughter of Tomás Calvo and doña Eugenia de Abarca, made her will. She named her children Gertrudis, José Gabriel, Ana María, Miguel, and María Magdalena, and listed several slaves. Her brother, Capitán don Miguel Calvo, and Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribarén were named as executors.

people_involved: María (slave, owned by Jorge de Alvarado)
summary: Doña Gertrudis de Echavarría Navarro, acting as attorney for her husband Capitán don Jorge de Alvarado, sold a 30-year-old 'negra casia arara' slave named María to Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribarén for 525 pesos. The slave was purchased from the estate of doña Ana de Echavarría Navarro, sister of the seller. The power of attorney for Capitán don Jorge was granted in León, Nicaragua on May 6, 1700, before Escribano José de Guzmán.

Licenciado don Tomás Muñoz Hidalgo, Sacristán Mayor of Granada, Nicaragua, obligated himself for 300 pesos at 5% interest to a Chaplaincy founded by the late don Francisco de Enciso Hita, for which he is the Chaplain. This obligation is secured by houses in 'esta ciudad' inherited from his deceased mother, doña Sebastiana Calvo.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan Esteban de Munarris
summary: Sarjento Juan Fernández granted power of attorney to Capitán don Juan Esteban de Munarris, don Gabriel de Borda, and Capitán Martín de Artieda, all residents of 'ciudad de los Reyes' in Peru, to judicially collect 1000 pesos from the estate of the late Capitán Juan Ibáñez. This money was left in Ibáñez's will to Manuel Fernández, who was Juan Fernández's son and servant, and who died without other heirs, making Juan Fernández the rightful claimant. Manuel Fernández was the legitimate son of Juan Fernández and María de Espinoza.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan de Vida Martel
summary: Doña Catalina Ortiz de Aldana leased a productive cacao plantation named 'el Santo Cristo de la Victoria' in the Matina valley, consisting of 700 trees, to Capitán don Juan de Vida Martel for two years. The rent for the first year was 6 zurrones of first-grade cacao and one of second-grade, and for the second year, 7 of first-grade and 1 of second-grade.

Licenciado don Tomás Muñoz Hidalgo, as principal, and Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribarén, as guarantor, obligated themselves for 690 pesos at 5% interest to Alférez Andrés Muñoz Hidalgo, who is absent from the province. This sum represents Andrés's inheritance from the late doña Sebastiana Calvo, who was the mother of don Tomás.

people_involved: Mtre. de Campo don Miguel de Echavarría Navarro
Capitán don Juan de Echavarría Navarro
summary: Capitán don Diego de Ibarra and his wife doña Ana de Retes obligated themselves for 525 pesos at 5% interest to a Chaplaincy founded by the late doña Ana de Echavarría Navarro. The Master of Camp don Miguel de Echavarría Navarro is the patron of this Chaplaincy. The obligation is secured by houses in 'esta ciudad' that were released by the late Capitán don Juan de Echavarría Navarro, who was doña Ana de Retes's first husband.

Doña Ambrosia de Echavarría Navarro, a widow, obligated herself to Juan Moreno, a merchant in the province, for 202 pesos. This sum included 102 pesos for various Castilian and local clothes bought on credit from his shop, and 100 pesos that Juan Moreno paid on her behalf (50 pesos to José de Armada and 50 pesos to Gaspar de los Reyes).

people_involved: Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
summary: Alférez don Francisco de Moya sold a plot of land to Capitán don José Pérez de Muro for 38 pesos. This plot, which borders the royal plaza to the North, was originally acquired by Moya from the late Capitán don José de Alvarado.

people_involved: María Magdalena (daughter of Francisco López Serrano)
summary: Sarjento Francisco López Serrano, a native of 'ciudad de los Reyes' in Peru, made his will. He was the legitimate son of the late Juan López Serrano and doña María de Gamboa, and was married to María de Sibaja, daughter of the late Ayudante Baltasar de Ortega and Jerónima Gómez. He named his children Jerónima (deceased), María Magdalena (widow of Francisco de Flores), and Francisca Victoria. His wife and Sarjento Francisco Gutiérrez were named as executors.

Antonio de Flores, residing in 'esta ciudad' and a resident of San Miguel, obligated himself to Capitán Rodrigo Nieto for 499 pesos and 5 reales, representing the remaining balance from their accounts and contracts. He committed to pay within four months.

people_involved: Alférez Juan Francisco de Puerto Marino
Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto
summary: Doña Sebastiana Calvo and Alférez Juan Francisco de Puerto Marino obligated themselves to Capitán Juan de Quirós of León, Nicaragua. A debt of 592 pesos and 4 reales was owed from the estate of the late Capitán Domingo de Puerto Marino, father of Juan Francisco and husband of doña Leonor Muñoz Hidalgo (daughter of doña Sebastiana). Quirós, through his attorney Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto, forgave 92 pesos and 4 reales, with doña Sebastiana obligating for 300 pesos and Alférez Juan Francisco for 200 pesos, to be paid by July of the next year.

Juan Moreno, acting with power from Capitán Juan de Quirós, received 300 pesos from Capitán don Miguel Calvo, who was acting as attorney for Licenciado don Tomás Muñoz Hidalgo. This payment settled the obligation of the late doña Sebastiana Calvo, mother of don Tomás.

people_involved: Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto
summary: Alférez Vicente Andrés Polo, as principal, and Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto began an obligation (details incomplete).

Soto, acting as a guarantor, obligated himself to Salvador de Berroterán for 408 pesos, 1/2 real, and 8 maravedíes. This amount was determined in a lawsuit initiated by Soto against José de Echavarría, who was Berroterán's attorney. The agreement stipulated that 185 pesos were to be paid in León, and Berroterán would cover this amount from his own funds if it couldn't be collected.

Francisco Fernández executed his will, naming his wife Eugenia Rodríguez and their 12-13 year old daughter Josefa. He also left legacies to Bernardo, son of his servant Feliciana; Manuela, an orphan they raised; and María, another servant. Captain Antonio Pacheco and Alférez Francisco Solano were appointed as executors.

Licenciado Esteban Marín Laguna, a Cleric Presbyter, made his will. He was the legitimate son of the late Captain José Marín Laguna and Catalina de Moya. His brother, Alférez Antonio Marín, and his mother, Catalina de Moya, were named as executors, with his mother also being the heir.

Doña Micaela Duran de Chaves issued a codicil to her sealed will, originally made on December 23, 1697, before Notary Captain Blas González Coronel. She declared that she had sold most of her previously declared assets and distributed the rest, instructing that her sister María Duran de Chaves and her servants not be held accountable for household items. She also ordered that her mulatto slave, Tomás, approximately ten months old and son of her slave María, be freed upon her death.

Captain Don Diego de Ibarra and his wife Doña Ana de Retes sold a 15-year-old mulatto slave named Antonio, born and raised in their household and son of Isabel, to Captain Don José Pérez de Muro for 300 pesos.

Don Pedro de Alvarado, son of the late Alférez Gil de Alvarado and Juana de Vera y Sotomayor, made his will. He was married to Catalina de Vida Martel and had eight children. He named his sister Sebastiana, niece Antonia, and granddaughters María Catalina and Josefa Ortiz de Rosas. He bequeathed 1000 pesos for two chaplaincies and appointed Captain José Ponce as executor if he died in Panama, or his brother Jorge de Alvarado, son-in-law Captain Pedro Ortiz de Rosas, and Captain José de Vivas if he died in Cartago.

Gaspar de Bastarrica y Narvaiza and his wife Eugenia Urbana Láinez de Iztueta, as principals, along with Manuel García de Argueta and his wife Antonia Láinez de Iztueta, as guarantors, obligated themselves to Eugenia de Abarca Alatras and her son Captain Miguel Calvo for 700 pesos. This debt was secured by half a cattle and horse ranch named San Antonio de las Cañas in Esparza. A marginal note indicates that Captain Miguel Calvo, acting for himself and as his deceased mother Eugenia's heir, cancelled the debt in favor of Bastarrica on March 26, 1703.

Don Pedro de Alvarado and Doña Catalina de Vida Martel donated their cacao plantation in the Matina valley to their granddaughters, María Catalina and Josefa Ortiz de Rosas, daughters of Captain Pedro Ortiz de Rosas and Juana de Alvarado. They excluded 1000 trees previously given as a dowry to Juana de Alvarado. Additionally, they gifted a mulatto slave named Juan, about a year and a half old and son of their slave Micaela, to María Catalina.

Captain Francisco de Bonilla sold a cacao hacienda named "las calles y San Silvestre," located in the Reventazón valley and comprising 400 fruit-bearing trees, to his son, Alférez Antonio de Bonilla, for 75 pesos. The hacienda bordered the Reventazón River.

Don Francisco Serrano de Reina, Governor and Captain General, sold a 21-year-old Creole black slave named Juan Pascual to Captain Don José Pérez de Muro for 450 pesos. Serrano de Reina had acquired Juan Pascual from Captain Miguel Antonio de Lima, a resident of Nata de los Caballeros, who was the executor of Don Miguel de Ichazo y Redín.

Don Cristóbal Martín Cubero, acting on behalf of Licenciado Don Francisco Lozano, the Parish Rector of Granada, Nicaragua, opposed the assets left by the deceased Captain Don Matías González Camino. The claim was for 11,296 pesos, comprising 10,199 pesos from a joint obligation with Captain José Pérez de Muro to the late Captain Juan Francisco Valenzuela, and 1,097 pesos from a debt Matías González Camino owed to the late Francisco de Castro, whose heir was Juan Francisco Valenzuela. Francisco Lozano was the testamentary executor for these claims.

A legal process concerning a debt owed to Lozano, possibly by the estate of Juana de Eguizabal, widow of Captain Juan Francisco Valenzuela. The debt involved a cession of 8450 pesos against Diego Bernal. Lozano received 8573 pesos, which he declared were in his possession as 4839 cacao trees in Matina valley and five enslaved individuals.

Captain José Pérez de Muro, acting with power from Lozano, declared that an obligation for 11,296 pesos was cancelled. This cancellation occurred because Captain Antonio de la Vega Cabral, Doña Ambrosia, and Doña Catalina González Camino (his wife and sister-in-law) agreed to pay Lozano this sum within 6 years, despite a previous cession of 8450 pesos made by the deceased Captain Matías González Camino to Lozano against Diego Bernal.

Captain José de Casasola y Córdoba established a dowry (carta dote) of 6500 pesos in favor of Doña Águeda Pérez de Muro, whom he was scheduled to marry on December 26th. The dowry included various assets such as enslaved individuals, a vacant lot, gold chain, silver, shirts, cacao, and coined silver. Águeda is identified as the legitimate daughter of Captain José Pérez de Muro and Doña Mariana de Echavarría Navarro.

Francisco de los Santos and his wife María de Solís agreed with Licenciado Tomás Muñoz Hidalgo to transfer their claim on a cacao plantation in Matina valley. The plantation, part of María's dowry, had fallen into disrepair after the death of Antonio de la Jara and they were unable to maintain it or pay a 140-peso charge belonging to a chaplaincy founded by Tomás Calvo, of which Tomás Muñoz Hidalgo was the chaplain.
Captain José de Vivas obligated himself to pay 100 pesos at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy of the deceased Inés Alvarez, for which Licenciado Tomás Muñoz Hidalgo served as chaplain.
Captain Miguel Calvo, acting as the attorney for Licenciado Tomás Muñoz Hidalgo, cancelled the obligation made by Captain José de Vivas to the Chaplaincy of Inés Alvarez.

Doña Juana Damiana de Mora Salado, a widow, sold a cacao plantation in Matina valley, inherited from her deceased husband José de Prado, to Captain Rodrigo Gadea y Marrufo for 900 pesos. The payment terms included 100 pesos obligated to the minor children of the deceased Doña Rafaela de Alvarado, with the remainder used to pay her late husband's debts and the balance paid in two installments tied to cacao harvests.
Doña Juana Damiana de Mora Salado cancelled the sale agreement of the cacao plantation.

Doña Ambrosia González Camino, wife of Antonio de la Vega Cabral, and her sister Doña Catalina González Camino, granted power of attorney to Antonio de la Vega Cabral to collect their paternal and maternal inheritances due to the death of their parents, Captain Matías González Camino and Doña Ana de Peralta.

locations: Ciudad del Espíritu Santo de Esparza
summary: Sergeant Major Gregorio de Camaño, Lieutenant Governor and Captain General of Ciudad del Espíritu Santo de Esparza, granted general power of attorney to Captain Juan Ordóñez, a procurator of the Royal Audiencia of Santiago de Guatemala.
Captain José de Vivas obligated himself to Captain Miguel Calvo for 146 pesos and 5 reales at 5% interest.

Captain Alvaro de Guevara y Sandoval and his wife Doña María Sáenz Vázquez obligated themselves to Pedro Romero, a trader, for 377 pesos and 4 reales. They agreed to pay 223 pesos in cacao in Matina valley and the remaining 154 pesos and 3 reales in 'this city,' mortgaging a cacao plantation of 1,400 trees in Matina.

Captain Juan Sáenz and his wife Doña Ana de Escalante Paniagua received 500 pesos at 5% interest from Captain Rodrigo de Gadea y Marrufo. In exchange, they transferred to him an equal obligation that Alférez Vicente Andrés Polo and his wife Doña Alfonsa de Bonilla had granted to them on November 3, 1698.

Sergeant Juan González and his wife María de Espinoza made their will, listing their parents and their nine children. The will also noted the marital status of some children and named Sergeant Francisco Gutiérrez and José de Aguilar as executors.
Doña Juana de Vida Martel and Doña María de Vida Martel leased something (implied property or assets) for three years to their brother, Captain Juan de Vida Martel.

An unnamed individual or individuals inherited a cacao hacienda consisting of 500 trees in the Barbilla valley, following the death of Doña Juana de Ortega. The hacienda was valued at twelve zurrones of first-quality cacao per year.

people_involved: Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
Doña Ana de Peralta y Salazar
summary: A dowry letter was issued for the upcoming marriage of Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral, a native of Fresno, Portugal, and Doña Ambrosia González Camino. The dowry included 3,528 pesos, 2,000 pesos in arras, several enslaved individuals (Águeda, Juana, Juana's 2-year-old daughter, Petronila, Catalina), and 46 marcos of worked silver.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Gregorio de Camaño
Doña María Pérez de la Cruz
Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Gregorio de Camaño, Teniente de Gobernador and Capitán General of Espíritusanto de Esparza, issued a codicil to his testament, which was originally dated October 22, 1700. In this codicil, he acknowledged a debt to Don Francisco de Montezer, ordered 100 pesos to be paid to the heirs of Sebastián de Villa Real, and instructed Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya to distribute 500 pesos. He also appointed Capitán don José Pérez de Muro and Jacinto de Pasos as additional executors.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego Campos de Quirós
Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Moya
summary: Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya, a Presbyter Cleric, made his testament. He was chaplain of several chaplaincies founded by his deceased uncles Baltasar de Grado, Vasco Solano, Pedro Solano, and Francisco de Paz, as well as those founded by his deceased sister Doña Josefa de Moya, Doña Juana de Vera, and Ana López. He also cared for an orphaned boy, Pedro de Moya, and named his brothers Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Moya and Alférez don Francisco de Moya, along with Alférez Diego de Cárdenas, as executors.

José, a 12-year-old zambo boy and son of the deceased Manuel de Córdoba and Pascuala Morillo, was delivered to Sarjento Pedro de Alvarado, a master weaver and resident of Cartago, for a 6-year apprenticeship.

Capitán don Gregorio de Chaves, a single man, made his testament. He owned an enslaved mulato named Juan and acknowledged seven natural children: Francisca (married to Alférez Miguel de Salazar), Juan, Ana (married to Francisco de Salazar), María, Mateo, Antonia (married to Juan Pérez), and Francisco. He also ordered the establishment of a chaplaincy and named Don Pedro de Alvarado, Capitán Juan de Ballesteros, and Lorenzo de Arburola as his executors.

A dowry letter was issued for the marriage of Alférez Nicolás de Madrigal, son of Matías de Madrigal and Lucrecia Murillo, and Doña Micaela Rodríguez, daughter of Capitán Juan Rodríguez and Doña María de Sibaja. The dowry amounted to 936 pesos, with 500 pesos in arras.
Capitán don Cristóbal Martín Cubero and his wife Doña Catalina González Camino sold an enslaved mulato criollo named Gil, 27 years old, to Alférez Diego Santiago de Cárdenas for 400 pesos.

Don Francisco Serrano de Reina, Governor and Captain General, granted general power of attorney to Juan Ordóñez, a procurator of the Audiencia de Guatemala. This act revoked previous powers given to Capitán Esteban de la Fuente and Zeledón de Barraondo.

people_involved: Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
Don José de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Capitán don José Pérez de Muro, Don Jorge de Alvarado, and Don José de Casasola y Córdoba jointly granted general power of attorney to Capitán Esteban de la Fuente, a procurator of the Royal Audiencia de Guatemala.
Doña Ambrosia de Echavarría Navarro granted general power of attorney to Capitán Esteban de la Fuente, a procurator of the Audiencia de Guatemala.

Teniente Diego de Aguilar became obligated for 320 pesos to Manuel Antonio, a minor, which he had received from the deceased Capitán don Matías González Camino on January 22, 1700. These funds were part of 520 pesos redeemed by Sarjento Juan González Ochoa, the minor's tutor and grandfather, and were imposed on a ranch in the city's common lands.

José de Aguilar and his wife María de Ochoa became obligated for 200 pesos to the minor Manuel Antonio. These funds were imposed on 500 trees in the Barbilla valley and the obligation was granted before Teniente de Gobernador Matías González Camino on January 22, 1700.

Alférez Vicente Izaguirre, a single man, made his testament. He bequeathed 100 pesos to his minor nephew Joaquín de Izaguirre (with his sister María as an alternate heir) and 50 pesos each to his natural children, José and María. He named Alférez José Calderón and Juan de la Madriz as his executors.

Francisco Ruiz, a soldier preparing to travel to Talamanca with 30 other soldiers to guard missionaries for the reduction of indigenous people, granted freedom to his enslaved mulato criollo, José de Ocampo, who was over 40 years old.
Francisco de Noguera Moncada, a merchant in Cartago, sold an enslaved congo named José Miguel, who was over 30 years old, to Alférez Tomás de Chaves for 200 pesos.

people_involved: Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral, his wife Doña Ambrosia González Camino, and Doña Catalina González Camino became obligated to Licenciado don Francisco Lozano, the Cura Rector of the Granada parish in Nicaragua, who was acting as a testamentary executor and fiduciary.

An obligation was made to the estate of Juana de Equizabal, widow of Capitán Juan Francisco Valenzuela, for 11,296 pesos. This amount covered a debt owed by the deceased Capitán Don Matías González Camino to Capitán Valenzuela. The payment was to be made within 6 years, with a prior obligation by Capitán Don Cristóbal Martín Cubero from 1700, and contingent on the collection of an 8,850 peso cession made by Capitán Don Matías González Camino to Lozano in Diego Bernal. A cacao plantation in Malina and five enslaved individuals were mortgaged as collateral.

people_involved: Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
General Don Francisco de Rivas y Contreras
summary: Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral and his wife Doña Ambrosia González Camino obligated themselves to General Don Francisco de Rivas y Contreras for 1,400 pesos. This debt originated from Doña Ambrosia's deceased father, Capitán Don Matías González Camino, and Capitán Don Cristóbal Martín Cubero was also obligated. The payment schedule was 280 pesos in one month and the remaining 1,120 pesos within four years. The obligation was later cancelled on August 1, 1711, by Capitán Don Juan López Coronado acting as attorney for Alférez Alonso Aldana de Meneses, the executor of the deceased General Don Francisco de Rivas y Contreras.

Juan Fernández Martínez and his wife Doña Cayetana de Acosta Arévalo, with Alférez José Calderón as guarantor, obligated themselves to the three minor children of the deceased Gregoria de Acosta (Francisco, Luisa Bartola, and Juana) for 1,083.5 pesos as their maternal inheritance. Each minor was due 361 pesos, 1 real, and 12 maravedíes. They mortgaged 1,000 cacao trees in Matina. The obligation was partially cancelled on August 20, 1709, by Fermín de Prendas (husband of Juana de Proa) and Luisa Bartola de Proa, and fully cancelled by Francisco de Proa on January 22, 1712.

Don Tomás Muñoz Hidalgo, a Presbítero and Sacristán Mayor of Granada, sold houses, corrals, fences, and all cattle and horses he inherited from his deceased mother, Doña Sebastiana Calvo, to Sarjento Juan Masís for 3,600 pesos.

people_involved: Licenciado Don José Miguel de Echavarría
summary: Sarjento Juan Masís and his wife Francisca Barbosa obligated themselves to Licenciado Don Tomás Muñoz Hidalgo for 3,400 pesos. The payment was to be made over 6 years in Matina cacao, with 600 pesos for the first 5 years and 400 pesos for the last. On December 14, 1709, Licenciado Don José Miguel de Echavarría, acting as attorney for his mother Doña Eugenia Muñoz Hidalgo, received the 3,400 pesos from Masís, as Licenciado Don Tomás had passed away.

Alférez Diego Santiago de Cárdenas and his wife Andrea Barbosa obligated themselves to Capitán Don Miguel Calvo for 200 pesos at 5% interest. Capitán Don Miguel Calvo later cancelled this obligation on February 22, 1706.

Alférez Tomás de Chaves sold a 'negrita bozal, conga' named Juana Josefa to Don José de Guzmán for 200 pesos. Juana Josefa had been acquired at a public auction in Espíritu Santo de Esparza, having been brought from Panamá on the frigate 'Nuestra Señora de la Soledad y Santa Isabel' as confiscated goods.

Capitán Don José de Vivas and his wife Doña Josefa de Moya obligated themselves to Gregorio and Petronila, minor legitimate children of the deceased Capitán Don Esteban de Moya and Doña Rafaela de Alvarado, for 800 pesos.
