Alférez Don Francisco de Moya, their uncle, was their tutor. The debt was originally owed by the deceased Don Pablo José de Alvarado. They mortgaged a rural estate in San José de Tenorio, within the jurisdiction of Esparza. The obligation was cancelled on August 29, 1710, by Don Gregorio de Moya and Don Francisco de Ibarra, husband of Doña Petronila.

people_involved: Capitán Francisco de los Reyes Benavides
Capitán Don Antonio de Utrera y Medina
summary: Capitán Don José de Vivas and his wife Doña Josefa de Moya obligated themselves to María, Julián, and Nicolasa, minor children of the deceased Juana de Villalobos, for 149 pesos and 1 real at 5% interest. On June 28, 1710, Capitán Francisco de los Reyes Benavides received 71 pesos from Doña Josefa de Moya, now a widow, for María de Villalobos, who was under his care. On August 25, 1710, Alférez Francisco Solano, as tutor for the other two minors, received 111 pesos from Capitán Don Antonio de Utrera y Medina, who had married Doña Josefa de Moya.

Capitán Don José de Vivas and his wife Doña Josefa de Moya obligated themselves to Juan and Francisco, minor legitimate children of the deceased Juan de Villalobos and Gertrudis Ricardo, for 166 pesos 5 reales at 5% interest.

Luisa González, widow of Sarjento Lorenzo de Villarreal, as principal, and Jorge González as guarantor, obligated themselves to Andrés, Ana, Blas, Gertrudis, and Gregoria, minor daughters of Luisa González and her deceased husband, for 143 pesos, 3 reales, and 7 maravedíes.

Catalina Milanés, a widow, made a donation to her granddaughters Gertrudis, Catalina, María, and María de la Rosa, who were the legitimate daughters of the deceased Ayudante José Falcon and Ana. The donation consisted of a plot of land in the city where their parents had lived, which included a house built with posts and a straw roof.

A dowry letter (carta dote) was issued for Alférez Alonso de Porras, legitimate son of the deceased Al" de Porras and Doña Magdalena de Torres, in favor of his wife Doña Ana de Castro Rodríguez, legitimate daughter of Juan de Castro Rodríguez and Doña Petronila Arias Monterroso. The dowry amounted to 271 pesos, with arras (earnest money) of 800 pesos.

people_involved: Licenciado Don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Capitán Don José de Vivas and his wife Doña Josefa de Moya obligated themselves to the Capellanía founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela, for which Licenciado Don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas served as patron and chaplain. The obligation was for 200 pesos at 5% interest, secured by a cattle ranch located in Tenorio, within the jurisdiction of Esparza.

people_involved: Capitán Don José Pérez de Muro
summary: Doña Ana de Retes, a widow, sold a 12-year-old 'negrito' named Pablo, who was the son of her slave Alfonsa, to Capitán Don José Pérez de Muro for 200 pesos.

people_involved: Doña Antonia María de Acosta Arévalo
summary: A dowry letter (carta dote) was issued for Don Agustín de Alvarado, natural son of Don Pedro de Alvarado, in favor of his future wife Doña Antonia María de Acosta Arévalo, who was the legitimate daughter of Antonio de Acosta Arévalo.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco Vélez de Guevara
summary: Capitán don Francisco Vélez de Guevara obligated himself to don Francisco Simón for 130 pesos. The payment was to be made in indigo ink at 2.5 reales per pound, upon don Francisco Simón's arrival in León, Nicaragua.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
summary: Capitán Pedro Ibáñez, a native of San Lúcar de Barrameda, entered into a marriage contract with doña Manuela de Quirós. The dote amounted to 4,614 pesos, including a 15-year-old mulata slave named Juana, 20 mules, and pearls, with arras of 1,000 pesos. The assets were received from doña Manuela's uncle, Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón.

Doña María de Escobar Guijarro, widow of don Pedro de Azofeifa and guardian of their minor daughters Ana and María, granted power of attorney. She authorized Secretario Juan Montero de Espinosa, Agustín Romero, and Capitán Juan de Ballesteros Savedra to collect debts owed to her deceased husband in the kingdom of Tierra Firme.

people_involved: doña Josefa López de la Flor
Capitán don José López de la Flor
summary: Alférez Tomás Andrés Polo, son of the deceased Tomás Andrés Polo and María de Chaves, entered into a marriage contract with doña Josefa López de la Flor. The dote was 857 pesos, with arras of 1,000 pesos, including a mulato named Juan Manuel valued at 250 pesos. The marriage was scheduled for two days later.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don Miguel Echavarría Navarro
Capitán don Juan de Vida Martel
doña Angela María de la Paz y Flores
Beneficiado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
summary: Alférez don Sebastián de Garita, acting as attorney for doña Eugenia Gertrudis Muñoz Hidalgo, sold adobe houses in Cartago to Capitán don Juan de Vida Martel for 400 pesos. The property was adjacent to the Parish Church, Cabildo houses, and properties of doña Angela María de la Paz y Flores and Beneficiado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón. Capitán don Juan de Vida Martel and his wife Clara de Quirós obligated themselves to the Capellanía founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela for the same amount, at 5% annual interest, with Capitán don Alvaro de Guevara and Alférez Jacinto de Rivera as guarantors.
María de Sibaja, a widow, leased a cacao plantation in the Matina valley to Alférez Bartolomé de Meneses for five years. The annual rent for the property was 125 pesos of cacao.

María Magdalena López, a widow, leased a 500-tree cacao plantation in the Matina valley to Alférez Bartolomé de Meneses for five years. This plantation was incorporated into her mother María de Sibaja's hacienda, with an annual rent of 50 pesos of cacao.
Sebastiana de Quirós leased a cacao plantation in the Matina valley to Capitán Blas González Toronel for four years. The annual rent for this property was 80 pesos of cacao.

people_involved: don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: Capitán Bernabé de Segura, son of the deceased Alférez Bernabé de Segura and Isabel de Morales, made his will. He was married to Francisca de Espinosa and had seven children: Margarita, María, Petronila, Francisco, Bernabé, Josefa, and Juana. His wife, son Francisco, and don Antonio de la Vega Cabral were named as executors.

people_involved: Capitán Pedro Santos de la Madriz
summary: María Calderón, widow of Martín de Civitola, and her brother Juan de Astúa as guarantor, obligated themselves to don Cristóbal Martín Cubero, attorney for Capitán Pedro Santos de la Madriz, for 719 pesos 4 reales. This amount represented the remaining balance of a larger debt Civitola owed to Santos de la Madriz, and María Calderón mortgaged cacao plantations in Matina as security.

Alférez Juan de la Madriz and his wife Juana Calderón obligated themselves to Manuel García de Argueta for 200 pesos at 5% interest. They mortgaged 500 fruit-bearing cacao trees in the Matina valley as security for this obligation.

Roque López and his wife Gregoria Ricardo sold a house and kitchen on four lots in Cartago, near the Ermita de San Juan, to Capitán Juan de Bonilla for 300 pesos. The property was previously owned by Juan Fernández de la Fuente and his wife doña María Duran de Chaves. The buyers, Juan de Bonilla and his wife, were obligated to recognize a 5% annual interest payment on the 300 pesos to the Capellanía founded by Magdalena de la Portilla.

Ambrosia de Sanabria, a widow originally from Spain, made her will. Her children were Mateo Serrano, living in Esparza, and Francisca Serrano, who lived with her and was married to Juan Ramírez. She also mentioned her granddaughter Catalina. Her son-in-law Juan Ramírez and Sarjento Juan González were named as executors.

people_involved: Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
summary: Alférez Jacinto de Rivera obligated himself to Capitán don José Pérez de Muro for 321 pesos. The payment was to be made in cacao.

Capitán Juan de Bonilla, cabo gobernador for Talamanca, and his wife doña Francisca de Astúa, obligated themselves to the Capellanía founded by Andrés López de Céspedes (as executor for Magdalena de la Portilla) for 300 pesos at 5% interest. This obligation was imposed on the houses and lots they had purchased from Roque López and Gregoria Ricardo, acknowledging the existing encumbrance.
Capitán Pedro Ibáñez, a native of San Lúcar de Barrameda, began to make his will.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
summary: A Capellanía of 4,000 pesos is established in memory of Alonso Ibáñez and María de Ayadra. Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón and Capitán don Francisco López Conejo are designated as patrons, with the first chaplains to be the founder's sons or his brother-in-law's sons. The executors include the founder's wife, Manuela de Quirós, Licenciado don Diego, and Capitán don José Pérez de Muro.

Capitán Alonso de Porras and his wife doña Ana de Castro Rodríguez obligate themselves to Salvador Murillo for 100 pesos at 5% interest. This sum belongs to Salvador's brother, Jerónimo Murillo, for whom Salvador is a tutor. The obligation was cancelled on July 17, 1703.

people_involved: doña Isabel de Guevara y Sandoval
summary: Capitán don Juan Sáenz and his wife doña Ana Escalante Paniagua sell a house and furniture in Cartago to doña Isabel de Guevara y Sandoval for 710 pesos. The payment is distributed among the Cofradía de la Concepción, two Capellanías (one founded by Magdalena de la Portilla and another by Vasco Solano), the minor children of José de Rivera and doña Ana Sendín, and the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora del Rosario.

people_involved: Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
summary: doña Jerónima de Retes, with permission from the Royal Justice due to her husband Francisco Ramírez Rodado's absence, sells houses and a sugar mill in the outskirts of Cartago to Capitán don José Pérez de Muro for 1200 pesos. The buyer is obligated to pay 200 pesos of this amount to Capitán don Miguel Calvo, who later confirmed receipt on December 25 of the same year.

doña Jerónima de Retes, widow of Sarjento Mayor Pedro Lorenzo Venegas, requests and receives authorization to sell houses she inherited from her deceased husband. Her current husband, Francisco Ramírez Rodado, has been absent in Granada, Nicaragua, for over three years.

people_involved: doña Isabel de Guevara y Sandoval
summary: doña Isabel de Guevara y Sandoval, with judicial license due to her husband don Agustín González de Villalobos's absence, sells houses in Cartago to Capitán Rafael Fajardo for 460 pesos. The payment is distributed among the Cofradía de La Concepción, the Capellanía of Vasco Solano (managed by Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya), and the Cofradía del Rosario. Fajardo's wife, doña Josefa Sáenz Vásquez, accepts the deed on his behalf as he is in Matina.

doña Luisa de Abarca, as the principal, and Alférez Francisco Fernández, as guarantor, commit to pay 2868 pesos and 4 reales to the minor children of doña Luisa and her deceased husband, Capitán don Antonio Pacheco. This sum represents their paternal inheritance, with each child receiving 573 pesos, 5 reales, and 22 maravedíes.

people_involved: Sárjente Mayor don Antonio de Moya
Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
summary: This is the will of Sárjente Mayor don Antonio de Moya, son of José de Moya and Mayor de Benavides. He details his two marriages: first to Isabel de Alvarado (with whom he had eight children, two deceased), and second to Juana Ruiz (with whom he has a five-year-old daughter, María de Moya). The will also mentions his siblings, in-laws, and names Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón, don José de Guzmán, and Capitán don José de Vivas as his executors.

This is the closed will of doña Eugenia de Abarca Alatras, daughter of Capitán don Gaspar de Abarca and doña Magdalena de Chaves. She was the widow of Depositario Tomás Calvo, with whom she had eight children, two of whom (Capitán don Gaspar Calvo and Capitán don Gregorio Calvo) are deceased. The will also lists her children's spouses and her seven slaves.

The will of an unnamed deceased person, who was married but left no children, was executed. Don Miguel (her son), Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes, and Lorenzo de Arburo-la (her grandson) were named as executors.
Legal proceedings were initiated at the request of Capitán Miguel Calvo.

Doña Magdalena Calvo, widow of Capitán Francisco Fernández de Miranda, legally bound herself not to claim ten varas of land that her nephew, Don Tomás Muñoz Hidalgo, had incorporated into his property. This obligation was made at the request of her brother, Capitán Miguel Calvo, who was selling Muñoz Hidalgo's houses to Doña Jerónima de Retes.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego Campos de Quirós
Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Capitán don Miguel Calvo, acting on behalf of Don Tomás Muñoz Hidalgo, a priest and Sacristán Mayor of Granada, sold a house to Doña Jerónima de Retes for 850 pesos. The house, inherited by Muñoz Hidalgo from his deceased mother Doña Sebastiana Calvo, included a high room with a street balcony. The proceeds were distributed among various chaplaincies and a convent.

Ana Solano, legitimate daughter of deceased Juan Solano and Magdalena Guerrero, and widow of Juan Fernández, made her will. She named her living sons Gaspar and Cristóbal, and mentioned deceased children Salvador and Margarita. She left bequests to Antonio Solano, Juan Lucas, and Tomasina, all of whom she had raised, and named Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes and her son Gaspar Solano as executors.

Doña Francisca Calvo, a widow, committed to an obligation of 140 pesos at 5% interest for a chaplaincy founded by her deceased father, Alférez Tomás Calvo. She received the funds from Capitán don Miguel Calvo, the patron of the chaplaincy, and secured the obligation with her houses in the city.

locations: costa de la mar del Sur
summary: Gaspar de Basterrica y Narvaiza provided a guarantee for Diego Casillas de la Vega, who represented Luis Antonio de Castro, as a preferred creditor in a case against Juan Bautista Plaza. The debt, totaling 726.5 pesos, involved a canoe named San José, which was auctioned to Capitán Jerónimo Valerino for 750 pesos, with an obligation to recognize the debt.

Capitán Francisco de Bonilla obligated himself for 110 pesos at 5% interest to the minor children of the deceased Sarjento Baltasar de Letona. He received the funds from Capitán Manuel de Zamora, the depositary of Letona's assets, and mortgaged a cacao plantation of 2500 trees in Matina as security.

Capitán José de Vivas obligated himself for 100 pesos at 5% interest to a chaplaincy founded by Doña Juana Moscoso. Capitán don Miguel Calvo had redeemed these funds. Vivas secured the obligation with a stone enclosure and a cane field he owned in Ujarrás.

Alférez José Calderón and his wife Juana de las Alas obligated themselves for 220 pesos at 5% interest to the minor children of the deceased Sarjento Baltasar de Letona. They mortgaged a cacao plantation of 2000 trees in Matina as security.

people_involved: Doña Petronila de Grado y Benavides
summary: Capitán Francisco Alvarez, widower of Doña María de Vargas, sold a 30-year-old mulato slave named José to Alférez Diego Santiago de Cárdenas for 500 pesos. José, son of Lorenza de Vargas, was originally a slave of Doña Petronila de Grado y Benavides, who had gifted him to her daughter Doña María upon her marriage. The sale proceeds were designated for Alvarez's minor children.

Alférez Diego Santiago de Cárdenas and his wife Andrea Barbosa obligated themselves for 500 pesos at 5% interest to the minor children of Capitán Francisco Alvarez and the deceased Doña María de Vargas. This sum represented the price of the slave José, purchased in the previous transaction. They guaranteed the obligation with houses, five other slaves, and cattle.

Alférez Agustín Valerino provided a guarantee for his father, Capitán Jerónimo Valerino, in a debt case against Juan Bautista Plaza. Plaza's canoe, "San José," had been auctioned to Jerónimo Valerino for 750 pesos, with an obligation to pay 241.5 pesos to Diego de Casillas (representing Luis Antonio de Castro). Agustín Valerino's guarantee ensured his father could collect the remaining credit after fulfilling this payment.

people_involved: Capitán don José de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Capitán Jerónimo Valerino and Alférez Agustín Valerino obligated themselves for 390 pesos to Capitán don José de Casasola y Córdoba. This loan was for provisions, equipment, wages, and other necessities for a canoe owned by Jerónimo Valerino, located in Puerto de la Caldera.
Hermano Andrés Peláez, natural son of the deceased Nicolás Peláez and Rodríguez, made his will. He was married to Catalina Rosales and had children.
Gertrudis Peláez married Sarjento Gregorio Picado over twelve years ago.
Gertrudis Peláez and Capitán Miguel Calvo were appointed as executors for an unnamed person's will.

people_involved: Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto
summary: The Royal Justice ordered the delivery of Juan Fernández de Rivera, a mulatto slave from the deceased Capitán Juan de Ballestero Saavedra's estate, to Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto, who committed to return him upon request.
Capitán Juan de Bonilla and his wife Doña Francisca de Astúa obligated themselves to Pedro Rosales for 450 pesos for 225 cattle, agreeing to pay in Matina cacao by February of the following year.
Francisco Montero de Espinosa, acting as Pedro Rosales's attorney, cancelled the obligation for Doña Francisca de Astúa, who was by then the widow of Capitán Juan de Bonilla.

A dowry letter was established for Francisco Martínez and his wife Doña Lorenza Venegas, detailing a dowry of 3101 pesos and 1 real, 1000 pesos in arras, and assets including houses and three enslaved mulatto women: Josefa (19), Eugenia (25), and María Magdalena (23). They had married two months prior.

people_involved: Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto
Alférez Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín
summary: Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto and his wife Doña Feliciana de Zamora acknowledged a 500-peso, 5% interest census on properties they acquired from the intestate estate of Capitán Juan de Ballesteros Saavedra, which was established for a chaplaincy founded by the deceased Alférez Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín.

Francisco Martínez and his wife Doña Lorenza Venegas obligated themselves to pay 200 pesos at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy of Vasco Solano, with Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya as Patron and Chaplain, securing the debt against their city residence.

Francisco Martínez and his wife Doña Lorenza Venegas obligated themselves to pay 75 pesos at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy of Depostiario Pedro Solano, with Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya as Patron and Chaplain, securing the debt against their city residence.

Capitán don José de Arrieta, a native of Sevilla, made his will, stating his wife Doña Juana Josefa Pachardo was deceased and mentioning a daughter, Doña Ana de Arrieta, aged about 17, whose status he was unsure of. He appointed Gaspar de Bazterrica y Narvaiza and Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribarén as executors.

Capitán don José de Arrieta issued a clarification to his previous will, retracting his statement about having a daughter, explaining it was made under duress from his illness and the crowd, and declared he had no children.

Doña Baltasara de Escalante Paniagua, widow of Capitán Manuel de Zamora, obligated herself to Diego Miguel de Algarín, her deceased husband's brother-in-law, for 500 pesos for goods her husband had sent him to sell before his death.
Diego Miguel de Algarín, residing in Cartago, cancelled the obligation owed by Doña Baltasara de Escalante Paniagua.

people_involved: Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto
summary: Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto and his wife Doña Feliciana de Zamora acknowledged a 100-peso, 5% interest census on properties in Valle de Barba, including the San Juan site, which they acquired from the intestate estate of Capitán Juan de Ballesteros Saavedra, and which was burdened by a chaplaincy for the deceased Laureano Ballesteros.

people_involved: Alférez don Antonio López del Corral
summary: Alférez José de Echavarría obligated himself to Alférez don Antonio López del Corral for 125 pesos, to be paid by the following February.
Andrea Barbosa made her will, naming her husband Diego Santiago de Cárdenas as universal heir and co-executor with Alférez don Pedro de Moya, and stating they had one son who died at four months old.

Francisca de Benavente, widow of Alférez Juan Matías Bautista Lizondo, obligated herself to her minor granddaughter Josefa Lizondo for 170 pesos at 5% interest, representing Josefa's inheritance from her deceased father, Miguel Damián Lizondo, which originated from his father's estate.

Hermano Juan Ramírez, a native of Córdoba, Spain, made his will, listing his wife Francisca Serrano and their six children: Alfonso, Catalina, José, Antonio, Agustín, and Juan Ramírez. His wife and Capitán Pedro José Sáenz were named as executors.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Moya
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Moya added a codicil to his will, which had been originally granted on June 28, more than two months prior. The specific content of the codicil is incomplete in the provided text.

An unnamed father/testator instructs that his legitimate children, Juana, Juan Antonio, and Mariana Polonia, who are between 14 and 25 years old, should receive their paternal and maternal inheritance from his first wife, Isabel de Alvarado. He also mentions other minor children from his current wife, referring to a clause in his will regarding them.

Alférez Antonio de Ángulo, a native of Granada, Nicaragua, issues a dowry letter for his wife, doña Josefa Rodríguez, who is the adopted daughter of Alférez Francisco Fernández and doña Eugenia Rodríguez. The dowry includes 1702 pesos, 400 pesos in arras, a 15-16 year old enslaved black man named Pedro valued at 500 pesos, and 500 pesos worth of high-quality cacao.

Silvestre Mesa, legitimate son of the late Juan de Mesa and Andrea de Ortega, issues a dowry letter for his wife, Josefa Elena de Solo. Josefa is the legitimate daughter of the late Juan Antonio de Soto and Juana de Acosta Arévalo. The dowry amounts to 2,064 pesos, with 300 pesos in arras, and includes a cacao plantation with 1000 trees adjacent to the Matina river, valued at 1,750 pesos.
Capitán Lorenzo de Arbnrola y Ribarén sells a 46-year-old enslaved creole woman named Justa to Capitán Juan Antonio de Bogarín, a resident of Esparza. The sale price is 250 pesos.

Doña Francisca and doña Luisa Calvo, both widows, along with Fermín de Hoces Navarro (acting for himself and his siblings doña Antonia, doña Gracia, doña Petronila, and Félix Agustín), grant general power of attorney to Gaspar de Bazterrica y Narvaiza. These individuals are the legitimate children of the late Depositario General Tomás Calvo and doña Eugenia de Abarca, and of the late Alférez Esteban de Hoces Navarro and doña Juana Bautista Calvo. Doña Francisca also revokes a previous power of attorney given to Alférez don Sebastián de Garita.

Alonso Godoy, a native of Málaga, son of Juan López and Florencia de Espinosa, makes his will. He is a widower of ... Carballo, with whom he married on the island of San An... and had a daughter named María. He leaves clothing to María de la Rosa and Francisca Valverde, his sword and dagger to Francisco Valverde, and 10 pesos of cacao to Antonio the shoemaker. His executors are his brother Juan Ramírez and fray Francisco Sánchez.

Doña Micaela Duran de Chaves, a widow, grants power to Capitán Andrés de Salazar to collect 175 pesos from Juan de Salas, her runaway enslaved mulato. This amount represents the remaining balance for Juan de Salas's freedom. The collection did not proceed.

Francisco Martínez and his wife doña Lorenza Venegas obligate themselves to the Capellanía of the late Pedro Solano, whose patron and chaplain is Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya, for 75 pesos at 5% interest. This obligation is secured by their residential houses in the city. A marginal note indicates that on December 11 of the same year, the same parties made another identical deed before José de Prado, rendering this one void.

Francisco Javier de Segura obligates himself for 220 pesos at 5% interest to Jerónimo Morillo, for whom he is a tutor due to Jerónimo's brother Salvador Morillo being insane, and also to Lucía Morillo. The obligation is secured by a straw-roofed flour mill on stilts and adobe and tile houses located in Barba.

Rafael Fajardo and his wife doña Josefa Sáenz obligate themselves to the Capellanía of Vasco Solano, whose patron and chaplain is Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya, for 200 pesos at 5% interest. This obligation is secured by their residential houses.

Teniente Rafael Fajardo and his wife doña Josefa Sáenz obligate themselves to the Cofradía de la Concepción, whose steward is Hermano Francisco Fernández, for 210 pesos at 5% interest. This obligation is secured by their residential houses and was granted before Escribano José de Prado. The document is incomplete.

Alférez don Sebastián de Garita obligates himself to the Convento de San Francisco, whose syndic is Hermano Francisco Fernández, for 50 pesos at 5% interest. The obligation is secured by adobe houses with a tile roof and a straw kitchen on stilts in the city.

Alférez Bartolomé Lizano obligates himself to Alférez don Antonio López del Corral to transport eight loads of cacao from the Matina valley using his mule train. The freight cost has been received as payment towards a larger debt Lizano owes to doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco, López del Corral's wife, stemming from accounts Lizano had with Antonia's first husband, the late Capitán don Rodrigo Marrufo.

Doña Micaela Duran de Chaves, widow of Alonso Romero and daughter of the late Alférez Cristóbal Duran de Chaves and doña Ana Cardoso, makes her will. She details her enslaved people, including Juan (left to her sister María Duran de Chaves) and Tomás (to be freed upon her death). She also mentions her runaway enslaved mulato, Juan Toribio, from Cartagena, whose freedom was arranged by her nephew Capitán Alonso Ruiz Arroyo, with a remaining debt. Her will also names her cousin Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, her deceased niece doña Isabel Duran de Chaves, an orphan Agustina she raised, and her compadre Sárjenlo Francisco Barquero.

people_involved: Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
Juan López de la Rea y Soto
summary: An unnamed testator ordered the establishment of a Chaplaincy, naming Licenciado don Gaspar as the first Chaplain and also as an executor, along with Alférez don Sebastián de Garita and Juan López de la Rea y Soto. The testator's soul was named as the heir.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Moya
summary: The executors of the deceased Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Moya's will, including Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón, Capitán don José de Vivas, and don José de Guzmán, sold an enslaved woman named María, approximately 16 years old, to Juan Gregorio de Ramírez for 300 pesos.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don José Agustín de Estrada y Aspeitia
summary: Capitán Blas González Coronel granted general power of attorney to Maestre de Campo don José Agustín de Estrada y Aspeitia, a resident of Santiago de Guatemala.

people_involved: Capitán don José de Casasola y Córdoba
Maestre de Campo don José Agustín de Estrada y Aspeitia
summary: Capitán don José de Casasola y Córdoba, Alférez Mayor and perpetual Regidor, granted general power of attorney to Maestre de Campo don José Agustín de Estrada y Aspeitia, a resident and Alguacil Mayor of the Holy Office in Santiago de Guatemala and Correo Mayor in his district.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don José Agustín de Estrada y Aspeitia
summary: Capitán don José de Vivas, Alguacil Mayor, granted general power of attorney to Maestre de Campo don José Agustín de Estrada y Aspeitia.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don José Agustín de Estrada y Aspeitia
summary: Don Cristóbal Martín Cubero, Regidor and Depositario General, granted general power of attorney to Maestre de Campo don José Agustín de Estrada y Aspeitia.

people_involved: Capitán don P" Ortiz de Rosas
Capitán don José de Casasola y Córdoba
Maestre de Campo don José Agustín de Estrada Aspeitia y Sierra
summary: The Cabildo, Justicia y Regimiento of the city, including Alcaldes ordinarios Capitán don Miguel Calvo and Capitán don P" Ortiz de Rosas, Alférez Mayor Capitán don José de Casasola y Córdoba, Alguacil Mayor don José de Vivas, Alcalde Mayor provincial Blas González Coronel, Regidor Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes, and Regidor and Depositario General Capitán don Cristóbal Martín Cubero, granted general power of attorney to Maestre de Campo don José Agustín de Estrada Aspeitia y Sierra, a resident and perpetual Regidor of Santiago de Guatemala.

Juan Jacobo Regazio, originally from Burgo de Poschiabo in the state of Milan, provided a dowry of 4697 pesos 4 reales, including 2200 cacao trees in Matina, to his wife Francisca Victoria López Serrano. The dowry also included 300 pesos as arras.

people_involved: Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Luis Cascante, a bachelor, made his will, freeing his enslaved mulatos Inés, Juan, and Isabel upon his death and bequeathing them a site in Santana. He also established a Chaplaincy of masses with a principal of 300 pesos, naming his brother Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas as Patron and Chaplain. His executors were his brother, Alférez don Sebastián de Garita, and Capitán Alonso Ruiz Arroyo.

people_involved: Alférez Juan de la Madriz Linares
summary: Capitán don Cristóbal Martín Cubero, Depositario General of the city, presented several individuals as guarantors for a 2000-peso bond required for his office.

people_involved: Alférez don Francisco de Enciso Hita
summary: Alférez Tomás de Chaves and his wife Juana de Solís committed 300 pesos at 5% interest, secured by houses and a sugar mill in Curriravá valley, to a Chaplaincy founded by the deceased Alférez don Francisco de Enciso Hita, whose Capellán was the deceased Licenciado don Tomás Muñoz Hidalgo.

people_involved: Sindico del Convento de San Francisco
summary: The Sindico of the Convent of San Francisco, who inherited the Chaplaincy after the death of Licenciado Muñoz Hidalgo, cancelled an obligation related to the Chaplaincy.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Gregorio de Caamaño
summary: Juan Antonio de Bogarín, a resident of Esparza, sold an enslaved Creole Black man named José de Ibarra to Alférez Tomás de Chaves for 350 pesos. Bogarín had originally purchased José from Sarjento Mayor don Gregorio de Caamaño, who was the Lieutenant Governor and Captain General of Esparza.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Capitán Francisco de Bonilla sold a cacao plantation in the Matina valley to Maestre de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba for 3500 pesos. The payment included three enslaved Black people valued at 500 pesos each, 600 pesos in cacao, and the remainder due within a year. The transaction was incomplete due to a missing page in the protocol.
Capitán Francisco de Bonilla, the seller, cancelled the sale of a cacao plantation.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don ...rizio de Morales
doña María de la O de Céspedes
Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
summary: José de Morales, originally from Santiago de Chile, made an agreement in favor of his future wife, doña María de la O de Céspedes, two days before their marriage. The agreement involved 2401 pesos, with 500 pesos as arras, and included various assets like cattle and two enslaved mulatos, Antonio (donated by doña Tomasa de Ocampo) and José Ventura (3 years old), and cattle donated by Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín.

people_involved: Capitán Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribarén
summary: Alférez Esteban de Zúñiga made his will, naming his wife Bárbula Corzo as his heir. He mentioned his deceased parents, his deceased children, his stepfather Luis Chacón, and two boys, Diego (his nephew) and Pedro (an orphan he raised). Capitán Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribarén was named as his executor.

Ventura Ramírez undertook an obligation for 201 pesos and one real, derived from the inheritance of the deceased Alférez Juan Albo and doña María Ramírez, on behalf of their minor children Francisca, José, and Gregoria. José Hidalgo and Capitán Alonso de Porras served as guarantors.

In San Antonio de Currirabá, Alférez José de Morales, acting as Alcalde Ordinario of Cartago and Lieutenant Governor, witnessed José Hidalgo and Capitán Alonso de Porras present 141 pesos and one real as payment for their obligation as guarantors for the deceased Ventura Ramírez.

people_involved: Capitán don Rodrigo Gadea y Marrufo
summary: A document details the assets of doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco, wife of Capitán don Antonio del Corral and widow of Capitán don Rodrigo Gadea y Marrufo. She receives 3466 pesos in goods, including houses in the city plaza and a cacao hacienda in Matina, with 600 pesos in arras.

people_involved: Beneficiado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
summary: Doña Catalina de Moya, widow of Capitán José Marín Laguna, executes her will. She names her deceased parents, her deceased and living children, her brother Licenciado Gregorio de Moya, her servant Isabel, and appoints Beneficiado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón and her brother don Pedro de Moya as executors.

Alférez Felipe de Mesa leases 2360 fruiting cacao trees in the Matina valley to Alférez Bartolomé de Meneses for four years. The annual rent is seven zurrones of first-quality cacao delivered to Cartago and one zurrón of second-quality cacao delivered in Matina.

people_involved: Doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar
summary: Doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar, widow of Antonio de Acosta Arévalo, donates 450 fruiting cacao trees and an adjacent plot for planting in her Matina hacienda to her son, Miguel de Acosta.

Francisco Medal, a native of Sevilla and married to Juana Cordero of Cartago, executes his will. He mentions his deceased father, living mother, his wife's parents, his cousins Domingo Medal and Isabel Ponce, and his nephew Francisco Medal. Alférez Pedro de Torres and Sárjenlo Juan Masís are named as executors.

José Francisco de Quirós, a native of Puerto de Santa María, provides a dowry for his wife María de la Rosa. The dowry totals 1288 pesos 4 reales, including 500 pesos in arras, 100 cattle, a plot of land by the Río Grande, and cacao from Matina.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Sargento Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín grants freedom to his 43-year-old mulata slave, María de Aguilar, for 305 pesos. He had acquired her from the estate of the deceased Ambrosio de Mora Salado with the condition that she would be freed upon payment of the purchase price.
Alférez Francisco Fernández obligates himself for 100 pesos at 5% interest, secured by his houses in Cartago, in favor of María Jerónima, a minor orphan being raised by Alférez Cristóbal Guevara.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Moya
summary: Doña Juana Ruiz, widow of Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Moya, obligates herself to her minor daughter doña María de Moya for 324 pesos, 5 reales, and 13 maravedíes, representing her paternal inheritance. She pledges two slaves, Juana (35 years old) and her daughter Rafaela (12 years old).

people_involved: Capitán don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: Alférez Pedro de Torres, acting as tutor for the minor daughters doña María and doña Francisca de Ballesteros, sells a 30-year-old mulato slave named Juan de Rivera to Capitán don Antonio de la Vega Cabral for 350 pesos. The buyer and his wife, doña Ambrosia González Camino, are obligated for this sum.

people_involved: Capitán don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: Capitán don Antonio de la Vega Cabral and his wife doña Ambrosia González Camino obligate themselves to the minor daughters doña María and doña Francisca de Ballesteros for 350 pesos at 5% interest, representing the value of the slave purchased in the previous deed.

Doña Tomasa de Ocampo, a widow, obligates herself to care for the minor doña María Antonia de Ballesteros until her marriage. Doña Tomasa receives María Antonia's paternal and maternal inheritance of 415 pesos and 2 reales, securing this obligation with a mortgage on her houses in Cartago. María Antonia's parents were the deceased nephew and niece of Doña Tomasa.

people_involved: Doña Catalina de Ortiz de Aldana
summary: Doña Catalina de Ortiz de Aldana, a widow, leases a cacao hacienda in Matina to Capitán Vicente Andrés Pulo for two years. The annual rent is 200 pesos, payable in eight installments of first-quality cacao delivered to Cartago.
Gregorio de Vargas provides a dowry for Lorenza de Sandoval, whom he is scheduled to marry on the 28th of the current month. The document is incomplete.

people_involved: doña Eugenia Gertrudis Urbana Leináz de Iztueta
summary: Doña Eugenia Gertrudis Urbana Leináz de Iztueta, married to Gaspar de Bastardea y Narvaiza for about twelve years, executes her will. She names her deceased father, partially named mother, her husband, and their five living children. Her husband and Lorenzo de Arburo-la y Ribarén are appointed as executors.
Antonio de Soto y Barahona provides a dowry for his fiancée doña Petronila de Hoces Navarro. Petronila is the legitimate daughter of Alférez Esteban de Hoces Navarro and doña Juana Bautista.
The goods of Alférez Fermín de Hoces Navarro, brother of doña Petronila, are received. The total value is 1438 pesos, including 500 pesos in arras.

Capitán Francisco de Bonilla leases a cacao plantation named 'La Santísima Trinidad' in the Matina valley to Diego Martínez Pinteño for five years. The plantation, initially planted with 5000 trees, is leased for 200 pesos in first-grade cacao annually, plus a zurrón of second-grade cacao.

Gaspar de Bastarrica y Narvaiza, representing doña Francisca and doña Luisa Calvo, and Fermín de Hoces (as heirs of doña Juana Bautista Calvo), settles a lawsuit with Capitán don Miguel Calvo. The dispute concerned a claim against the estate of doña Eugenia de Abarca Alatras, which don Miguel opposed based on her will. They reached a settlement, with a 500-peso fine for anyone who insists on the demand, payable to the Cofradía del Santísimo Sacramento.

people_involved: Don Diego de Barros y Carvajal
Capitán don Andrés de Barros y Carvajal
Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
summary: A dowry letter is issued for doña Josefa Pérez de Muro, who is to marry don Diego de Barros y Carvajal. The dowry amounts to 6667 pesos, with 2000 pesos in arras, including enslaved people, silver, a gold chain, gold and emerald rings, coined silver, and cacao.

José de Prado, a native of Mexico City, makes his will. He is married to Francisca Méndez for about 15 years and has four living children: Juan José, Antonio Clemente, Catalina, and Manuel Joaquín. Capitán Francisco Alvarez and Juan Moreno are named as his executors.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan de Vida Martel
Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Clara de Quirós, widow of Capitán don Juan de Vida Martel, sells her adobe and tile houses in Cartago to Alférez Jacinto de Rivera for 400 pesos. The buyer and his wife are obligated to pay this amount to the Capellanía founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela, whose Patron and Chaplain is Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas.

people_involved: Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Alférez Jacinto de Rivera and his wife, Ana del Camino, acknowledge a 400-peso censo at 5% interest on the houses Rivera previously bought from Clara de Quirós. This censo is in favor of the Capellanía of Alonso Gómez Macotela, with Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas serving as its Patron and Chaplain.

people_involved: Juan de Guevara de la Cerda
Alférez Juan de Guevara de la Cerda
Capitán don Antonio de Abarca Alatras
summary: Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes and Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribarén, executors of the late doña Eugenia de Abarca Alatras, establish a Capellanía of recited masses with an 800-peso principal. Juan de Guevara de la Cerda is appointed as the first Chaplain, replacing Licenciado don Tomás Muñoz Hidalgo who died. While Juan de Guevara prepares for ordination, masses will be recited at the Convento de San Francisco.

people_involved: Don Alonso de Bersabé Cabeza de Vaca
Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Moya
summary: A dowry letter is issued for doña Juana de Moya, who marries don Alonso de Bersabé Cabeza de Vaca on the same day. The dowry is 1863 pesos, with 500 pesos in arras.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Maestre de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba grants general power of attorney to Capitán don Francisco Noguera Moncada.

Capitán don Miguel Calvo, as Alcalde ordinario, places José de Santiago and Sebastián de Santiago, brothers and sons of María de Santiago, as apprentices with master shoemaker José de Molina for five years.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Doña Petronila Valerino provides surety through her father, Capitán Jerónimo Valerino, and her brother, Alférez Agustín Valerino, for a 390-peso debt owed to Maestre de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba. The debt, for which Casasola y Córdoba had sued them, is due in the upcoming December.

people_involved: doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar
summary: Miguel de Acosta Arévalo receives a cacao plantation named 'La de arriba' in the Matina valley, consisting of 450 fruit-bearing trees. This inheritance comes from his deceased father, Antonio de Acosta Arévalo, via his mother, doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar.

people_involved: doña Eugenia de Abarca y Alatras
summary: Doña Luisa de Abarca, widow of Capitán don Antonio Pacheco, obligates herself to Capitán don Miguel Calvo, Patron of the Capellanía founded by the late doña Eugenia de Abarca y Alatras (with Juan de Guevara as Chaplain), for 200 pesos at 5% interest. This obligation is charged on her houses in the city.

Doña Josefa de Morales, widow of Francisco Peláez, makes her will. She is the legitimate daughter of the late Juan de Morales and doña Beatriz Machado. She has a 14-year-old son named Cayetano and an enslaved mulato also named Cayetano.
Capitán don Miguel Calvo, as the senior ordinary mayor, apprentices Manuel Flores, a 15-year-old boy and son of Magdalena García, to Roque López, a master blacksmith, for a period of 5 years.

Don Francisco de Moya and his wife Doña Manuela de Alvarado obligate themselves for 336 pesos at 5% interest to Don Gregorio and Doña Petronila, minor children of the deceased Alférez don Esteban de Moya and Doña Rafaela de Alvarado. They mortgage a house, kitchen, a stone enclosure with sugarcane, a plantain field, 100 cattle, and a 40-year-old enslaved man named Andrés, located near Ujarraz.

Don Pedro de Moya and his wife Doña Angela Sáenz obligate themselves for 100 pesos at 5% interest to the same minors (Don Gregorio and Doña Petronila) mentioned in the previous deed. They mortgage a stone room in the house of Doña Bárbara Lanini (Angela's mother) and a cacao plantation in Matina.
Capitán don Miguel Calvo, acting as attorney for don Gregorio de Moya, cancels the obligation made by Don Pedro de Moya and Doña Angela Sáenz on August 31.
Capitán don José de Vivas obligates himself for 200 pesos at 5% interest to the same minors (Don Gregorio and Doña Petronila). He mortgages a sugarcane plot and a plantain field.

people_involved: Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
summary: Roque López obligates himself to Capitán don José Pérez de Muro for 210 pesos.

Capitán Jerónimo Valerino grants power of attorney to his son, Alférez Agustín Valerino, who is traveling to Tierra Firme, to sell a canoe and its equipment and cargo that makes voyages to that Kingdom.

people_involved: Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
Maestre de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Doña Mariana de Echavarría, gravely ill, grants power of attorney to her husband, Capitán don José Pérez de Muro, to make her will. She names him executor and guardian of their minor daughter, Doña María. Her heirs are her three daughters: Doña Josefa (married to don Diego de Barros Carvajal), Doña Águeda (married to Maestre de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba), and Doña María.

people_involved: Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto
Capitán don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto obligates himself to Capitán don Antonio de la Vega Cabral for 374 pesos. He will pay this amount by transporting all of Cabral's cacao from Matina in the coming year at a rate of 10 pesos per load, pledging 30 tame mules for the fulfillment of this obligation.

people_involved: Capitán don José de Viveros Escalante Panlagua
Capitán don Pedro Ortiz de Rosas
summary: Capitán don José de Viveros Escalante Panlagua, a native of Sevilla, makes his will. He was married to Doña Manuela de Vida Martel, with whom he had several children. He names Capitán don Pedro Ortiz de Rosas and his daughter Doña Baltasara as executors.

people_involved: Teniente de Capitán Antonio de Barahona
summary: Capitán Rafael Mogeimes Fajardo and his wife Doña Josefa Sáenz Vásquez sell a cacao plantation in Matina named Nuestra Señora de la Soledad to Teniente de Capitán Antonio de Barahona for 1000 pesos. Doña Josefa received this plantation as a dowry from her mother, Doña Bárbara Lanini.
Capitán Rafael Mogeimes Fajardo cancels the 1000 pesos obligation related to the sale of the cacao plantation.

Doña Manuela Sáenz Vásquez, a widow, sells a cacao plantation in Matina to Antonio de Barahona for 1000 pesos. This plantation was given to her by Doña Bárbara Lanini when she married Don Manuel de Moya.
Doña Manuela Sáenz Vásquez cancels the obligation related to the sale of the cacao plantation.

people_involved: Capitán don Pedro Ortiz de Rosas
Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
summary: Capitán Francisco Pérez de Cote and his wife Doña María Zamora sell houses and a plot in this city to Capitán don Pedro Ortiz de Rosas for 400 pesos. The buyer agrees to recognize 300 pesos for a chaplaincy founded by Pedro Solano (chaplain Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya) and 100 pesos for another chaplaincy served by the curates of the Parish Church, all at 5% interest.

people_involved: Capitán don Pedro Ortiz de Rosas
summary: Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya receives 300 pesos from Doña Juana de Alvarado, wife of the absent Capitán don Pedro Ortiz de Rosas, as part of the obligation from the sale of houses.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
summary: Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón, the senior curate, receives 100 pesos from Doña Juana de Alvarado, as part of the obligation from the sale of houses.

people_involved: Capitán don Pedro Ortiz de Rosas
summary: Capitán don Pedro Ortiz de Rosas sells houses and a fenced plot in this city to Doña Baltasara de Escalante Panlagua, widow of Capitán Manuel de Zamora, for 441 pesos and 4 reales. The buyer must recognize 300 pesos for the minor children of the deceased Alférez don Esteban de Moya and Doña Rafaela de Alvarado, 85 pesos for a chaplaincy of the deceased Tomás Calvo, and the rest in cash.

Juan Jacobo Regazzio and his wife Francisca Victoria López obligate themselves for 100 pesos to Doña María and Doña Francisca de Ballesteros Saavedra, minor daughters of Capitán Juan de Ballesteros Saavedra. This amount represents the value of an enslaved Creole woman named Juana.

people_involved: Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Doña Bárbara Lanini, widow of Gobernador don Juan Sáenz Vásquez, cedes houses in this city and a cacao plantation of 1500 trees in Matina to her sons, Capitán don Juan Sáenz Vásquez and don Pedro Sáenz Vásquez. These properties are subject to existing liens, including 500 pesos for a chaplaincy served by Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas and 300 pesos for the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego de Campos y Quirós
summary: An obligation of 1350 pesos was established, with specific amounts designated for various cofradías and a chaplaincy. The Cofradía de Nuestra Señora de los Angeles and Cofradía de la Concepción each received 150 pesos, the Capellanía of Licenciado don Diego de Campos y Quirós received 350 pesos, and the Cofradía del Rosario received 50 pesos. The cessionaries are bound by these obligations.

Alférez Juan Vicente Godoy obligated himself to his legitimate daughters, Catalina and Petrona, for 500 pesos. This sum represents their maternal inheritance from his first, deceased wife, Josefa de Esquivel, with each daughter receiving 250 pesos.

Gobernador don Juan de Bonilla, Capitán Francisco de Bonilla, Alférez don Francisco de Moya, Capitán don Alvaro de Guevara, Francisco Martínez, and Francisco Solano provided a guarantee for Capitán Blas González Coronel. Coronel, who was appointed Lieutenant of Royal Officials for the province, was required to post a 1500 peso bond for his position.

Capitán don Alvaro de Guevara and his wife, doña María Sáenz Vásquez, sold a cacao plantation located on the Matina riverbank to Manuel García de Argueta for 1150 pesos. Doña María Sáenz Vásquez had originally received this property as a dowry from her mother, doña Bárbara Lanini.

people_involved: Capitán Juan de la Madriz Linares
summary: Capitán Juan de la Madriz Linares, a native of Lastres in Asturias and son of Antonio de la Madriz Linares and María Barrero, established a dowry of 3000 pesos and arras of 500 pesos for his wife, Juana Calderón. Juana is the daughter of Alférez Jogé Calderón and Juana de las Salas. The dowry included 500 cacao trees in Matina, a 24-year-old mulata slave named María, 50 cattle, 4 mules, and additional cacao.

people_involved: Alférez don Diego Santiago de Cárdenas
summary: Domingo de Inza and his wife, doña Alfonsa Muñoz Hidalgo, obligated themselves to the Convento de San Francisco for 200 pesos at 5% interest. These funds belonged to a chaplaincy founded by the deceased don Francisco de Enciso Hita, which is recited in the convent until a relative of Enciso is ordained. They mortgaged a country house in the city's outskirts, with Alférez don Diego Santiago de Cárdenas acting as guarantor.

people_involved: Don José de Vargas y Ulloa
Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Don José de Vargas y Ulloa, as principal, and Alférez José Calderón, as guarantor, obligated themselves to Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona for 756 pesos. Vargas received this amount in the value of 36 mules, which he intended to sell in Santiago de Alanje by July, or in Santiago de Veragua, Nata, and other parts of Tierra Firme by September, with payment in silver reales. The obligation was cancelled by Barahona on June 15, 1705.

Capitán don Juan Sáenz obligated himself for 100 pesos at 5% interest to the chaplaincy founded by Catalina Gutiérrez in the Convento de San Francisco, funds which Capitán Manuel García de Argueta had redeemed. Sáenz mortgaged a portion of his stone and mortar houses in Cartago and 1500 cacao trees on the Matina riverbank.

Juana de Acosta Arévalo, a widow, leased a cacao plantation with over a thousand fruit-bearing trees on the Matina riverbank to Sarjento Manuel Lascares for five years. The annual rent was 100 pesos in cacao, equivalent to four zurrones, to be delivered in Cartago.
Francisco Loria established a dowry of 306 pesos and arras of 200 pesos for his wife, Angela María. Angela María was an orphan who had been raised in the household of doña Ana de Retes.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don Miguel de Echavarría
Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
summary: Doña Ana de Retes, legitimate daughter of the deceased Jerónimo de Retes and doña María Vásquez Coronado, and widow of don Juan de Echavarría Navarro, made her will. She named her thirteen children, six slaves, and appointed her sons-in-law, Capitán don José Pérez de Muro and don José de Guzmár, as executors. Her universal heirs were her grandchildren: José Miguel and Sebastiana de Echavarría (children of Maestre de Campo don Miguel de Echavarría and doña Eugenia Gertrudis Muñoz), and Juana María de Echavarría (daughter of the deceased don Gabriel de Echavarría and doña Antonia María de Otórola), with instructions for them to be notified of their inheritance.

Juana de Acosta Arévalo leased a cacao plantation on the Matina riverbank to Alférez Luis Gutiérrez for three years. The rent was set at three zurrones of prime cacao for the first year and four zurrones for each of the subsequent two years, to be delivered in Cartago. The document was not signed.

Manuela Hernández, widow of Andrés de Morera, obligated herself to her minor daughters, Josefa Petronila and Micaela, for 125 pesos and 2 reales, representing their paternal inheritance. Alférez Tomás de Chaves and Tomás de Morera served as guarantors for this obligation.

Juana de Acosta Arévalo, a widow, leased a cacao plantation on the Matina riverbank to Sarjento Manuel Lascares for three years. The rent for the first year was three zurrones of prime cacao, and for each of the subsequent two years, it was four zurrones of prime cacao.

Sebastián Vásquez established a dowry of 1000 pesos and arras of 500 pesos for his future wife, Josefa Rodríguez. Josefa is the legitimate daughter of the deceased Domingo Rodríguez and Petronila de la Estrella.

Miguel de Acosta Arévalo, legitimate son of the deceased Antonio de Acosta Arévalo and doña Josefa de Aguilar, established a dowry of 1041 pesos and arras of 1000 pesos for his wife, doña María Mayor Marín. Doña María is the legitimate daughter of the deceased Capitán José Marín Laguna and doña Catalina de Moya. The dowry included a house.

Ayudante Lázaro de Robles, a native of Comayagua, Honduras, and son of the deceased Blas de Robles and María Díaz, made his will. He was married to Andrea de Sandoval and had three sons: Francisco, Manuel, and Diego. He also owned a 24-year-old 'negro bozal' slave named José. Ayudante General Esteban was named as an executor.

Juan de Ugalde, a native of Cádiz and son of Pedro de Ugalde and Luisa de Ochoa, established a dowry of 916.5 pesos and 200 pesos in arras for his future wife, María de la Rosa. María is the legitimate daughter of Capitán Juan Rodríguez and the deceased María de Sibaja.

Doña Gertrudis Hidalgo, daughter of Teniente Juan Hidalgo and Doña María de Alfaro, and widow of Capitán Antonio Vásquez, made her will. She had no children and named her brother José Hidalgo and brother-in-law Andrés Arias as executors. She also mentioned her sister Doña Isabel, her nephew Miguel (Isabel's son), and her niece Francisca (daughter of her brother Juan Hidalgo).

Clara de las Alas, daughter of deceased P. de las Alas and María de Brenes, made her will. She was married first to Juan Francisco Michel (deceased) and then to Sarjento Antonio de la Vega, having no children with either. She owned three slaves (Lucía, Ambrosio, Bernardino), granting Lucía freedom upon her death and the others two years later, and named Miguel de la Vega and Antonio de la Vega, whom she raised, as her executors.

people_involved: Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
summary: Doña Ana de Retes, a widow, made a donation to her son-in-law, Capitán don José Pérez de Muro. The donation included land and houses in Valle de Santana, livestock, household items, a city lot near her residence and facing Ermita de San Nicolás, and three slaves: Rosa (26, mulata), her 6-year-old pardo son José, and Cayetano (19, negro).

people_involved: Doña María de Escobar y Guijarro
summary: Capitán Antonio de Zamora, son of Capitán Sebastián de Zamora and Doña Luisa de Ocampo Golfín, established a dowry of 965 pesos and 800 pesos in arras for his wife, Doña Francisca Saborido. Doña Francisca is the legitimate daughter of Teniente Juan de Saborido and Doña María de Escobar y Guijarro. The document is incomplete.

people_involved: María de la Candelaria de Mora
summary: Salvador Murillo, a resident of Cartago living in Valle de Barba, made his will. He was married to Clara de Esquivel, had no children, and was the guardian of his mentally incapacitated brother, Jerónimo Murillo. He mentioned his sisters Lucía and Isabel Murillo, María de Acuña (a person of his affection), and his goddaughter María de la Candelaria de Mora, naming his wife and Capitán Juan Rodríguez as executors.

María de Mora, daughter of deceased Ayudante Alonso de Mora and Leonor de Rivera, made her will. She was unmarried and had no legitimate heirs, naming her nephew Juan de Mora as her executor and sole heir.

Capitán Juan Rodríguez, son of Andrés Rodríguez and María de Espinoza, established a dowry of 1121 pesos and 300 pesos in arras for his wife, Doña Elena de Umaña. Doña Elena is the legitimate daughter of Tomás de Umaña and Doña Laureana de Chaves. The document was granted at Doña Laureana's residence.

people_involved: Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto
summary: Luisa de Quintana, widow of Capitán Sebastián de Zamora, sold houses and a lot in the city to Doña Manuela de Quirós for 635 pesos. The payment was structured to cover various obligations, including to the Cofradía de la Concepción, a chaplaincy served by Don Diego Campos de Quirós, the Convento de San Francisco, the guardianship of Domingo José (minor son of deceased Lucas Camacho and Sebastiana Masís), and Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto (Luisa's son-in-law).

people_involved: General don Francisco Serrano de Reina
summary: General don Francisco Serrano de Reina, former Governor and Captain General of the province, granted general power of attorney to Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes before departing for Santiago de Guatemala.

people_involved: Capitán Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina
General don Francisco Serrano de Reina
summary: Capitán Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina, a native of Seville and son of General don Francisco Serrano de Reina and Doña Luisa Lisalde, established a dowry of 4931 pesos and 1000 pesos in arras for his wife, Doña María Leocadia Pacheco. The dowry included 1500 cacao trees in Matina, valued at 3000 pesos, and a half-house and lot for 500 pesos.

people_involved: Mtre. de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba
Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca
summary: Capitán don Alvaro de Guevara and his wife Doña María Sáenz sold houses in the city to Mtre. de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba for 1100 pesos. The houses were acquired by Guevara through public auction of the assets of Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca, who was the sole heir of his deceased mother, Doña Gertrudis de Alvarado. The sale involved obligations to two chaplaincies, one founded by Doña Sebastiana de Alvarado and another by Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca.
Doña Sebastiana de Alvarado received 600 pesos from her chaplaincy, as noted in the margin of a property sale document from April 19, 1704.

Capitán don Cristóbal Martín Cubero, as Alcalde Ordinario, arranged an apprenticeship for Miguel Gómez, a 12-year-old orphan, with Jerónimo Sánchez, a master shoemaker from Tobosi. The agreement was for three years. Miguel Gómez is the son of the deceased Juan Gómez and María de Laguna.

locations: Ciudad del Espíritu Santo de Esparza
people_involved: Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
summary: Juan Antonio Bogarín, a resident of Esparza, sold two enslaved individuals, Tomás and Cristóbal (Congos, 15-16 years old), to Capitán don José Pérez de Muro for 600 pesos. Bogarín had acquired them from Capitán Juan de Escobar, who obtained them at a public auction in Esparza from a confiscated ship named "Nuestra Señora de la Soledad y Santa Isabel."

people_involved: Capitán don Juan de Echavarría Navarro
Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
Capitán don Diego de Barros Carvajal
Mtre. de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Doña Mariana de Echavarría Navarro, daughter of the late Capitán don Juan de Echavarría Navarro and doña Ana de Retes, granted power to her husband, Capitán don José Pérez de Muro, to make her will. She named him executor and guardian of their minor daughter, doña María. Her other daughters, doña Josefa (wife of Capitán don Diego de Barros Carvajal) and doña Águeda (wife of Mtre. de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba), were also mentioned as heirs.

Capitán don José de Vivas committed to pay 100 pesos at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by the late doña Josefa de Moya, an amount previously redeemed by doña Isabel de Guevara. This obligation was secured by a stone enclosure and a plot of sugarcane owned by Vivas in the Ujarras valley.

people_involved: Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
summary: Capitán Vicente Andrés Polo, acting as attorney for Licenciado don Francisco Lozano, Cura Rector of the Parish of Granada, Nicaragua, sold an enslaved "negra bozal" named Catalina, approximately 14 years old and of Arara caste, to Capitán don José Pérez de Muro for 400 pesos.

This entry records the will of Capitán Juan de Bonilla, legitimate son of the late Sargento Mayor Alonso de Bonilla and Juana Benita Calvo. He was married to doña Francisca de Astúa and had six children: María, Francisca, Josefa, Juan, Juana Benita, and José. His executors were his wife and Alférez Juan Marín.

Capitán don Cristóbal Martín Cubero, as Alcalde Ordinario, arranged an apprenticeship for Nicolás de Sanabria, a 15-year-old boy and legitimate son of the late Nicolás de Sanabria and Juana de Quirós, with Alférez Diego Santiago de Cárdenas, a master tailor, for three years.

people_involved: Mtre. de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Juana de Acosta Arévalo, widow of Juan Antonio de Soto, sold a productive cacao plantation with a cleared area in Matina to Mtre. de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba for 675 pesos.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Antonio de Moya
summary: This entry records the will of doña Juana Ruiz, legitimate daughter of the late Capitán Bernardino Ruiz and María de Torres, and widow of Sargento Mayor don Antonio de Moya. Her sole heir was her 7-year-old daughter, doña María de Moya. Her assets included several enslaved individuals. Her executors were don Diego de Herrera Campuzano (Governor and Captain General), don Pedro Ortiz de Rosas, and Alférez don Sebastián de Garita, with a fifth of her assets left to the Governor.

people_involved: Mtre. de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba
Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
Capitán de Caballos don Alvaro de Guevara
Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca
summary: Mtre. de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba and his wife doña Águeda Pérez de Muro committed to pay 600 pesos at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by doña Sebastiana de Alvarado, secured by houses they bought in Cartago. These houses also carried a previous 500-peso obligation to a Chaplaincy founded by the late Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca. Margin notes indicate the 600-peso obligation was cancelled, and 150 pesos of the 500-peso obligation were redeemed by doña Juana Ramiro Corajo, with the remaining 350 pesos redeemed on March 11, 1713, by Alférez Tomás de Chaves and his son Tomás de Chaves for the Holy Church of Cartago.

people_involved: Doña Eugenia Urbana Láinez de Iztueta
summary: Gaspar de Basterrica y Narvaiza and his wife doña Eugenia Urbana Láinez de Iztueta committed to pay 100 pesos at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by doña Juana de Echavarría Navarro. This amount was previously redeemed by Manuel García de Argueta. The obligation was secured by a rural property they own in the Ujarrás valley.

people_involved: Doña Eugenia Urbana Láinez de Iztueta
summary: Gaspar de Basterrica y Narvaiza and his wife doña Eugenia Urbana Láinez de Iztueta committed to pay 200 pesos at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by Catalina Gutiérrez, which is prayed for in the Convento de San Francisco. This obligation was secured by a ranch, farm, houses, and corrals they own in the Ujarrás valley. A margin note from May 12, 1714, indicates that Capitán José Antonio Bermúdez, Mayordomo of the Cofradía de la Concepción, cancelled this obligation.

people_involved: Doña Eugenia Urbana Láinez de Iztueta
summary: Gaspar de Basterrica y Narvaiza and his wife doña Eugenia Urbana Láinez de Iztueta committed to Manuel García de Argueta for 580 pesos, which was the price of a ranch called San Antonio de las Cañas, located in the jurisdiction of Esparza, that Argueta sold to them. They mortgaged the ranch. A margin note indicates cancellation by Argueta on July 31, 1711.

people_involved: Mtre. de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: This entry records the will of the late doña Mariana de Echavarría Navarro, granted by her husband don José Pérez de Muro. They had three children: doña Josefa (married to don Diego de Barros), doña Águeda (married to Mtre. de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba), and doña María, who was approximately 15 years old.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
Licenciado don Diego de Campos Quirós
summary: María de Mora, a resident of Valle de Pacaca, sold a large cattle site and farmland named San Bmé. to Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón for 60 pesos. The property, inherited from her father Ayudante Alonso de Mora, bordered Río del Oro and lands of doña Ana de Retes. The 60 pesos were charged to the property in favor of the Chaplaincy founded by Licenciado don Baltasar de Grado, for which Licenciado don Diego de Campos Quirós is the Chaplain.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
summary: Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón, the parish priest of Cartago, obligates himself to a Chaplaincy founded by Licenciado don Baltasar de Grado for 60 pesos. This obligation is secured by a property he previously purchased from María de Mora.

people_involved: Capitán don Pedro Ortiz de Rosas
summary: Lorenzo de Rivas and Juana Barrantes sell an overgrown cacao plantation in Matina to Capitán don Pedro Ortiz de Rosas for 100 pesos. They inherited this land after the death of Antonio Arara, who was Juana's husband and Lorenzo's father.

Sarjento Francisco Barquero, as Mayordomo of the Cofradía de la Vera Cruz, along with deputies Juan Francisco Marín, Juan Marcelo Gutiérrez, Matías Masís, and Lucas de Jesús, sell 14 head of cattle to Sarjento Francisco Gutiérrez. The cattle were located in a small ranch within the common lands of Cartago, sold for 385 pesos.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego de Campos Quirós
summary: H° don Pedro José Sáenz sells a productive cacao plantation in the Valle de Matina to Manuel García de Argueta for 850 pesos. This hacienda was originally acquired by Pedro José and his deceased brother, don Juan Sáenz, through a cession from their mother, doña Bárbara Lanini, and carries obligations to several Chaplaincies.

people_involved: Capitán don Pedro Ortiz de Rosas
summary: Capitán Vicente Andrés Polo, as the principal, and Capitán don Pedro Ortiz de Rosas, as guarantor, obligate themselves to the Cofradía de los Angeles for 150 pesos. This sum represents the value of the lease for a cacao plantation owned by the Cofradía on the banks of the Matina river.

Sarjento Francisco Gutiérrez obligates himself to the Cofradía de la Vera Cruz for 385 pesos, which he received from Mayordomo Francisco Barquero. This obligation is secured by a productive cacao plantation he owns in Barbilla, located in the Matina valley, and was later cancelled in 1713 by don Gil de Alvarado.

people_involved: Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Manuel García de Argueta and his wife, doña Antonia Láinez de Iztueta, obligate themselves for 500 pesos to the Chaplaincy founded by the deceased Capitán José de Vargas Machuca. This obligation is secured by the hacienda that Manuel García de Argueta purchased from H° don Pedro José Sáenz, with a partial payment received in 1711.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego de Campos Quirós
summary: Manuel García de Argueta and doña Antonia Láinez de Iztueta acknowledge a 250-peso annuity (censo) to the Chaplaincy founded by Comisario Baltasar de Grado. This obligation is secured by the same hacienda mentioned previously and was later transferred to Alférez don Sebastián de Garita and Sarjento Mayor Francisco López Conejo.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego de Campos Quirós
summary: Manuel García de Argueta and doña Antonia Láinez de Iztueta obligate themselves for 100 pesos to the Chaplaincy founded by the deceased Alférez Andrés López. This obligation is also secured by the same hacienda, which they acquired with this existing encumbrance.

Hermano don Pedro José Sáenz and his wife, doña María Rosa Vásques, having sold their Matina cacao hacienda, now obligate their houses in Cartago for 100 pesos to the Cofradía de la Vera Cruz. This action was necessary because the buyer of the hacienda assumed some obligations, but 100 pesos remained to be recognized on their separate city houses.
Hermano don Pedro José Sáenz and doña María Rosa Vásques obligate their houses for 100 pesos to the Chaplaincy founded by the deceased Catalina Gutiérrez.
Hermano don Pedro José Sáenz and doña María Rosa Vásques obligate their houses for 381 pesos to the Convento de San Francisco in the Pueblo de Barba.
Hermano don Pedro José Sáenz and doña María Rosa Vásques obligate their houses for 400 pesos to the Cofradía de los Angeles.

Doña Francisca de Astúa obligates herself for 300 pesos to the Chaplaincy founded by the deceased Magdalena de la Portilla. Her husband, Capitán Juan de Bonilla, was also obligated to this Chaplaincy, and she mortgages her houses as security.

people_involved: Mtre. de Campo don Diego de Herrera Campuzano
Mtre. de Campo don José Agustín de Estrada Aspeitia y Sierra
summary: Mtre. de Campo don Diego de Herrera Campuzano, Governor and Captain General of the province, grants general power of attorney to Mtre. de Campo don José Agustín de Estrada Aspeitia y Sierra, Alguacil Mayor of the Holy Inquisition in Guatemala, and secondarily to Capitán don Diego Rodríguez Menéndez.

people_involved: Capitán don Pedro Ortiz de Rosas
Mtre. de Campo don Diego de Herrera Campuzano
summary: Capitán don Pedro Ortiz de Rosas and Alférez don Sebastián de Garita, acting as executors for doña Juana Ruiz, sell a 20-year-old mulato named Agustín to Governor Mtre. de Campo don Diego de Herrera Campuzano for 300 pesos.

people_involved: Capitán don Pedro Ortiz de Rosas
Mtre. de Campo don Diego de Herrera Campuzano
summary: Capitán don Pedro Ortiz de Rosas and Alférez don Sebastián de Garita, in their capacity as executors, sell a 10-year-old mulata named María to Governor Mtre. de Campo don Diego de Herrera Campuzano for 250 pesos.
Francisco Martínez and his wife, doña Lorenza Venegas, obligate their houses for 100 pesos to the Chaplaincy founded by the deceased doña Eugenia de Abarca Alatras.

Pedro Santos de la Madriz sent a letter from Panama to Francisco de Cossio Mier in Cartago, instructing him to receive his slave Pedro (a Congo negro) and two pearl boxes from Diego de Ángulo. Cossio Mier was also to receive another slave, Pedro Rodríguez, and was authorized to sell Pedro (Congo) for 500 pesos if a buyer was found.
Captain Francisco de Cossio Mier, acting on behalf of Captain Pedro Santos de la Madriz, sold Pedro, a 24-year-old Congo negro slave, to Beneficiado Diego de Ángulo Gascón for 500 pesos.

Doña Catalina de Vida Martel, widow of Captain Pedro de Alvarado, granted general power of attorney to her son-in-law, Captain Pedro Ortiz de Rosas. She acted as mother and guardian for her seven legitimate sons, including Gil, José, Miguel, Pedro, Hermenegildo, Juan Manuel, and Antonio de Alvarado.

Maestre de Campo José de Cásasela y Córdoba granted power of attorney to Captains Pedro Ortiz de Rosas and Francisco de Cossio Mier, who were traveling to Panama, to reclaim two runaway Arara negro slaves named Juan and Miguel.

José de Guzmán and his wife Antonia de Echavarría Navarro obligated themselves to Maestre de Campo José de Cásasela y Córdoba for 300 pesos, payable in cacao by August. A marginal note indicates that Águeda Pérez de Muro, widow of Casasola y Córdoba, received the 300 pesos from Guzmán on February 14, 1720.

Doña Clara de Vida Martel, widow of Alférez Marcelo Blasco, granted power of attorney to Captain Pedro Ortiz de Rosas, who was traveling to Panama. This power allowed him to collect 400 pesos owed by Juan Cordero to her deceased husband, Marcelo Blasco, from Cordero's estate, acting as guardian for her sons Marcelo José and Lucas Blasco.

Manuel Fernández, a bachelor from Chinchón de la Mancha, Spain, made his will. He bequeathed one-third of his assets to his 3-year-old natural son, José Faustino Fernández, born with Juana Mejías of Granada. Captain Francisco de Cossio Mier was named an executor, and the Souls in Purgatory were designated as his heirs.

Licenciado Diego de Ángulo Gascón and Doña Manuela de Quirós, as executors of the deceased Captain Pedro Ibáñez, granted power of attorney to Captains Francisco López Conejo, Pedro Ortiz de Rosas, and Jorge de Alvarado. This power allowed them to sell pearls previously sent to Panama and to collect any debt or remaining pearls from Captain Pedro Santos de la Madriz owed to the late Ibáñez, with proceeds intended for a chaplaincy.

Alonso Rodríguez Bellido, a priest residing in Cartago but currently in the Barba valley, granted freedom to his 30-year-old black Arara slave, Nicolasa Avaria. This act was performed in the town of San Bartolomé de Barba before Governor Diego de Herrera Campuzano.
Alférez José de Echavarría and his wife, María Calvo, obligated themselves to Captain Manuel García de Argueta for a debt of 663 pesos.

Captain Blas González Coronel and his wife, Bernarda de Fonseca, provided a new obligation for 1500 pesos as security for Blas's role as Lieutenant of the Royal Coffers in Cartago and Esparza, appointed by Juan Martínez Vaquero. They mortgaged 1000 cacao trees in Matina and pledged several enslaved individuals as collateral.

Captains Cristóbal Martín Cubero and Antonio de la Vega Cabral acted as guarantors for Sergeant Major Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina. Serrano de Reina was mandated to pay or secure 850 pesos to the Royal Treasury for goods brought from Panama in 1703 by Master Alonso Rodríguez de Alfaro on the ship 'Nuestra Señora del Pópulo y las Animas'.

Luis Cascante de Rojas, a bachelor, made his will, naming his brother Gaspar as Capellán and an executor. He freed his mulata slave Inés and her children Juan and Isabel upon his death, bequeathed 100 pesos to his servants Isabel and Alberto, and gave land to Juan Delgado. He also appointed Sebastián de Garita and Alonso Ruiz Arroyo as co-executors.
Francisca López, widow of Juan Jacobo Regazzio, sold a 50-year-old black slave named Juana Arias to Francisca Calvo, a widow, for 100 pesos.

Gertrudis Ruiz, a widow, leased a cacao hacienda in the Matina valley to Bartolomé Meneses for three years. The rent was 200 pesos of first-quality cacao per year, to be delivered in Cartago. The hacienda bordered properties of the late Antonio de Moya and Alférez Francisco Fernández.

Ana de Retes, widow of Juan de Echavarría Navarro, donated a 'caballería de tierra' and two cane fields in the Santa Ana hacienda to her son-in-law, Captain José Pérez de Muro. This donation was in recompense for his continued support and for paying 1312 pesos to her grandson Manuel Antonio de Arleguí, which she owed for his legitimate inheritance. She also referenced a previous donation to him on November 25, 1704.

Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, Alonso Ruiz Arroyo, and Sebastián de Garita, acting as executors of the late Luis Cascante de Rojas, sold a 16-year-old 'mulata blanca' slave named Petronila to Alférez Tomás de Chaves for 400 pesos.
Alonso Ruiz Arroyo and Sebastián de Garita, as executors of Luis Cascante de Rojas, sold a one-year-old 'mulata' slave named María to Licenciado Gaspar Cascante de Rojas for 100 pesos.

Alférez Tomás de Chaves, as principal, and Captain Miguel Calvo, as guarantor, obligated themselves for 100 pesos at 5% interest to the Capellanía founded by Luis Cascante de Rojas, of which Gaspar Cascante de Rojas was Patron and Capellán. The obligation was cancelled on July 9, 1706, when Gaspar Cascante de Rojas received the 100 pesos from Calvo.
Licenciado Gaspar Cascante de Rojas obligated himself for 100 pesos at 5% interest to the Capellanía founded by Luis Cascante de Rojas. This debt was imposed on a herd of cattle in the Aserrí valley.

Captain José de Vivas and his wife Josefa de Moya obligated themselves for 380 pesos at 5% interest to the Capellanía founded by Captain Pedro de Ibáñez. This debt was imposed on a large cattle ranch in the Bagaces valley, including houses, corrals, 600 cows, 600 mares, and four donkeys. The obligation was cancelled on December 20, 1725, by Diego de Ángulo Gascón, as the principal had been transferred to another tenant and imposed on houses built by Sergeant Major Antonio de Moya.

Miguel de Acosta leased a cacao hacienda in the Matina valley, consisting of 450 fruit-bearing trees, to his brother Alférez Gaspar de Acosta for two years. The rent was 150 pesos of first-quality cacao and a 25-peso 'zurrón' of second-quality cacao annually. The hacienda bordered Josefa de Aguilar's property and the Río Grande.

Manuel Antonio de Arleguí issued a dowry letter in favor of his wife, Gracia Gertrudis de Hoces Navarro. Captain Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribarén, as executor for Gracia's deceased parents Esteban de Hoces Navarro and Juana Bautista Calvo, delivered 1416 pesos in assets to Gracia, which included 1000 pesos in 'arras'.

Licenciado Diego de Ángulo Gascón and Doña Manuela de Quirós obligated themselves for 175 pesos at 5% interest to the Capellanía founded by the late Captain Pedro Ibáñez, who was Manuela's husband. This debt was charged against two houses in the city and eight named slaves of various castes.

Maestro de Campo José de Cásasela y Córdoba sold two slaves, Diego (24, 'cabo verde') and Carlos (24, 'arara'), to Manuel García de Argueta for 800 pesos. These slaves were purchased from the 'asiento de negros' in Panama, administered by Manuel de Paiba.

Captain Alonso Ruiz Arroyo and his wife Antonia Solano renewed an obligation for 100 pesos to the Capellanía of Alonso Gómez Mácatela, of which Gaspar Cascante de Rojas was Patron and Capellán. This debt, originally left by Antonia's deceased father Cristóbal Duran, was charged against a herd of cattle in 'la Mata Redonda'. Gaspar Cascante de Rojas later received the 100 pesos from José de Gamboa, who bought the cattle from Antonia Solano after Alonso Ruiz Arroyo's death.

people_involved: Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
Wife of Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas and his wife grant a new obligation for 200 pesos at 5% interest, belonging to the Chaplaincy founded by doña Ana Pereira.

people_involved: Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas cancels an obligation in favor of José de Gamboa, who had purchased an estate from doña Antonia Solano, the widow of Ruiz Arroyo.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
