summary: Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón sells an estate of livestock, including 285 cattle, 119 mares, 2 donkeys, and 5 tame horses, along with houses and corrals, in La Candelaria to Capitán don Cristóbal Martín Cubero for 937 pesos 4 reales. The property borders an estate belonging to Aserríes and another owned by Miguel Lizondo.

people_involved: Mtre. de Campo don Manuel de Bustamante
Capitán Antonio de Rojas y Miranda
summary: María de Zarate makes her will, declaring her legitimate daughters Mariana, Rosa, and Petronila, born out of wedlock. She details unpaid service to Mtre. de Campo don Manuel de Bustamante, who promised her an estate and goods in Cartago, to be delivered by his attorney, Capitán don Cristóbal Martín Cubero, but some items were not delivered. Her son-in-law, Matías Masís, husband of Antonia, is named as an executor.

Alférez Cristóbal Guerrero, a resident of Ujarrás and native of Marbella, Spain, makes his will. He is the widower of doña Gertrudis de Enciso Hita and names his children and executors, including his son Sárjente Juan Guerrero and son-in-law Andrés Chacón.

Antonio de Miranda, a native of Santiago de Alange, grants a dowry of 1360 pesos and arras of 1000 pesos to his wife, Ana María Maroto Ruiz, daughter of the deceased Alférez José Maroto and doña Luisa Calvo.
Alférez José de Segura grants a dowry of 1558 pesos and arras of 500 pesos to his future wife, Antonia Cartín, daughter of the deceased José Daniel Cartín and María de la O. Guevara.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego Campos de Quirós
summary: Alférez Antonio de Ángulo and his wife Josefa Fernández obligate themselves for 260 pesos at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by the deceased Comisario Baltasar de Grado. This obligation is secured by a house and plot in Cartago, which they purchased from doña Petronila de Quirós, widow of don Manuel de Sandoval.

Doña Ana de Escalante Paniagua leases a cacao plantation in the Barbilla valley to Alférez Antonio de Ángulo for three years. The price is 75 pesos in cacao for the first year and 100 pesos for each subsequent year.
Andrés Chacón grants a dowry of 1489 pesos 4 reales and arras of 500 pesos to his wife, doña Gertrudis Guerrero, daughter of the deceased Alférez Cristóbal Guerrero and doña Gertrudis Enciso Hita.
Doña Juana de Aguilar obligates herself for 600 pesos at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by doña Sebastiana de Alvarado, securing the amount with a house and kitchen in Cartago.

Capitanes Francisco de Bonilla, Vicente Andrés Polo, Alonso de Porras, and Alférez Diego Santiago de Cárdenas, along with other guarantors, are ordered to pay 670 pesos for tithes from 1704 and 1705. Lacking funds, they obligate themselves to Capitán Manuel García de Argueta for 300 pesos he lent them, to be paid in cacao within a month, pledging Francisco, a 30-year-old Congo enslaved person belonging to Bonilla, as collateral.
Capitán Manuel García de Argueta receives the 300 pesos from Capitán Francisco de Bonilla, canceling the obligation.

people_involved: Juan López de la Rea y Soto
doña Angela María de la Paz y Flores
Comisario don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
summary: Juan López de la Rea y Soto, as executor for the deceased doña Mariana de Sandoval, sells houses and two plots in Cartago to Capitán don Alvaro de Guevara for 110 pesos. The property borders Alférez Antonio de Ángulo, Simón Muñiz, doña Angela María de la Paz y Flores, Juan Fernández Martínez, the heirs of Catalina de Flores, and Comisario don Diego de Ángulo Gascón. The buyer must recognize a lien of 110 pesos on the property in favor of the Cofradía de la Concepción.
Capitán don Alvaro de Guevara and his wife doña María Sáenz recognize the 110-peso lien at 5% interest on the previously purchased property, in favor of the Cofradía de la Concepción.

Doña Mariana Vásquez Coronado, a widow, sold a piece of land in Patarra, near Aserrí, to Baltasar de Mora for 50 pesos. This land was inherited from her deceased parents, Alférez Juan Vásquez Coronado and Ana María de Mora Salado, who had received it as a dowry from Juan de Mora. The property bordered land previously adjudicated to her deceased brother, Alférez Juan Vásquez.

Francisco Montero de Espinosa and his wife Doña Nicolasa de Vargas obligated themselves to Salvador Murillo, tutor of his brother Jerónimo Murillo, for 100 pesos at 5% interest, a sum redeemed from 200 pesos by Pedro Martínez de Colina. The obligation was secured by a house, a sugar mill, and four cane fields in the Barba valley. Capitán don José de Morales later certified the payment of the 100 pesos, with 20 pesos received by the deceased Salvador Murillo and the remaining 80 pesos adjudicated by Morales as judge.

Clara de las Alas made her will, identifying herself as the legitimate daughter of deceased Pedro de las Alas and María de Brenes. She had no children from her first marriage to the deceased Juan Francisco Michel, nor from her second marriage to the deceased Sarjento Antonio de la Vega. She granted freedom to her three mulatto slaves, Lucía and her sons Ambrosio and Bernardino, upon her death, with the condition that Ambrosio and Bernardino serve Miguel and Antonio de la Vega for one year each, as she had raised them. She also mentioned providing dowries for her nieces, Jerónima Jiménez and Margarita de las Alas, and named Miguel and Antonio de la Vega as her executors.

Doña Manuela de Quirós, a widow, recognized a 105-peso lien at 5% interest in favor of the Cofradía de la Concepción, which encumbered her dwelling houses in Cartago. She had purchased these houses with this gravamen from Luisa de Quintana, widow of Capitán Sebastián de Zamora, on December 3, 1704, before Alcalde Ordinario Francisco de Bonilla.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego Campos de Quirós
summary: Doña Manuela de Quirós recognized a 90-peso lien at 5% interest on the same houses, in favor of the Chaplaincy founded by the deceased Doña Inés de Benavides. Licenciado don Diego Campos de Quirós served as the Patron and Chaplain of this Chaplaincy.

Doña Manuela de Quirós recognized a 200-peso lien at 5% interest on the same houses, in favor of the Chaplaincy founded by the deceased Alférez don Francisco Enciso Hita. This chaplaincy's prayers were recited in the Convento de San Francisco.

people_involved: Juan López de la Rea y Soto
summary: Capitanes Francisco de Bonilla, don Miguel Calvo, and Juan López de la Rea y Soto provided bail for Manuel Venegas, who was imprisoned for a criminal cause and was ill. The Governor agreed to release Venegas to his home for recovery, contingent on the provided bail.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
Licenciado don Diego Campos de Quirós
summary: Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón, the oldest Cura Rector, recognized a 60-peso lien at 5% interest in favor of the Chaplaincy founded by the deceased Comisario Baltasar de Grado, of which Licenciado don Diego Campos de Quirós was Chaplain. This lien was on a cattle ranch and farmlands named San Bartolomé in the Pacacua valley, which Gascón had purchased with this encumbrance from María de Mora on August 27, 1704, before Alcalde don Cristóbal Martín Cubero.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
summary: Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón obligated himself for 160 pesos at 5% interest to the same Chaplaincy (founded by Comisario Baltasar de Grado), charging this sum on his dwelling houses in Cartago.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Félix Malo de Molina
Capitán don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: Doña Luisa de Abarca, a widow, obligated herself to Sarjento Mayor don Félix Malo de Molina for 600 pesos, payable in prime cacao at 20 pesos per zurrón in the upcoming August, delivered in the Matina valley. She mortgaged a hacienda with 2000 cacao trees in Matina and provided Capitanes Antonio de Soto Barahona, don Antonio de la Vega Cabral, and Francisco López Conejo as guarantors.
Agustín Pérez, a resident of León, Nicaragua, obligated himself to Andrea de Sandoval for 220 pesos at 5% interest, payable within five years. He pledged 20 mules and pack mules as collateral.

Alférez don Pedro de Moya and his wife Doña Angela Sáenz obligated themselves for 100 pesos at 5% interest in favor of the Chaplaincy founded by the deceased Doña Rafaela de Alvarado. This sum was charged on a hacienda with 2000 cacao trees located on the banks of the Matina river.

Alférez don Sebastián de Garita, as Mayordomo of the Cofradía de las Animas, sold a piece of land in the Aserrí valley to Capitán Blas González Coronel for 25 pesos. This land had belonged to the deceased Luis Cascante de Rojas, who inherited it from his deceased father, Alférez Juan Cascante de Rojas, and had left it, along with other goods, to the blessed Souls (Animas).

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco de Noguera y Moncada
Sarjento Mayor don Gregorio de Camaño
summary: Capitán don Francisco de Noguera y Moncada, head recruiter for Talamanca, sold a 23-year-old Creole black slave named Lorenzo, originally from Santo Domingo, to Capitán Diego Miguel González Algarín, a resident of León, Nicaragua, for 415 pesos. Noguera y Moncada had acquired Lorenzo from the seized assets of Sarjento Mayor don Gregorio de Camaño, who was formerly the Lieutenant Governor and Captain General of Esparza.

Doña Catalina Ortiz de Aldana recognized a 100-peso lien at 5% interest in favor of the Chaplaincy founded by the deceased Comisario Baltasar de Grado, of which Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya was Patron and Chaplain. This lien was on half a house and lot in Cartago, which Aldana had purchased with this encumbrance from the deceased Capitán don Juan Sáenz on October 12, 1695, before the public scribe of the Cabildo and Government, Capitán Blas González Coronel.

Doña Josefa Santiago de Aguilar, widow of Antonio de Acosta Arévalo, recognized a 100-peso lien at 5% interest in favor of the Chaplaincy of Alférez Vasco Solano. Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya was the Patron and Chaplain of this Chaplaincy, and the lien was placed on some houses.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don Juan Francisco Sáenz Vásquez
summary: An unnamed widow and her late husband purchased properties, including houses, a bread mill, and a sugar mill, for 2290 pesos from Licenciado don Francisco de Salazar on February 22, 1681. The transaction was witnessed by Maestre de Campo don Juan Francisco Sáenz Vásquez, then Governor and Captain General of the province.

An unnamed widow recognized a 500-peso censo at 5% interest on her properties. This censo was in favor of a Chaplaincy founded by the deceased Comisario Baltasar de Grado, with Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya serving as its Patron and Chaplain.

Capitán don Pedro José Sáenz and his wife doña María de la Rosa obligated themselves to pay 700 pesos to doña Manuela Sáenz Vásquez, a widow, by the following January. They mortgaged houses and half a plot of land in Cartago as security.
On March 21, 1707, Capitán don José de Bonilla, husband of doña Manuela Sáenz Vásquez, cancelled the obligation previously made to his wife.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan de Echavarría Navarro
Licenciado don Diego Campos de Quirós
summary: Doña Ana de Retes, a widow, transacted censos totaling 720 pesos on her properties in the Valle de Santana, originally for a Chaplaincy founded by the deceased Comisario Baltasar de Grado. She transferred this obligation to her city houses, which already held a 525-peso censo for a Chaplaincy founded by her deceased daughter, doña Ana de Echavarría Navarro. All involved parties, including the Patrons and Chaplains Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya and Licenciado don Diego Campos de Quirós, and Capitán don Miguel Calvo, consented to the transaction.

people_involved: Alférez don Antonio de la Riva Agüero
summary: Capitanes Vicente Andrés Polo and Juan de Astúa posted bail for Alférez don Antonio de la Riva Agüero, who was imprisoned for a criminal case. The complaint, filed by doña Luisa de Quintana, alleged that Agüero had promised marriage to her daughter, doña Gertrudis de Zamora. Due to illness, Agüero was granted house arrest with the provided bail.

A dowry letter was issued for Pablo Peraza, son of Andrés Peraza and Juana de Sandoval, in favor of his wife Petronila de Salazar, daughter of Francisco de Salazar and Ana de Chaves. The dowry amounted to 340 pesos, with an additional 300 pesos in arras.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Félix Malo de Molina
summary: Capitán Blas González Coronel granted general power of attorney to Sargento Mayor don Félix Malo de Molina, who was departing for Santiago de Guatemala.

A dowry letter was issued for Tomás de Chaves, son of Alférez Tomás de Chaves and Juana Paulina de Solís, in favor of his future wife Francisca Masís, daughter of Sarjento Juan Masís and Francisca Barbosa. The dowry was 1405 pesos, with an additional 500 pesos in arras.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco de Noguera y Moncada
summary: Doña Ana de Retes, a widow, sold a 'caballería de tierra' in the Valle de Santana, known as El Hato Viejo, to Capitán don Francisco de Noguera y Moncada for 50 pesos. The sale included a condition ensuring her right to draw water from nearby houses.
Alférez Antonio Rodríguez sold a 'chacra' and country houses with a fenced ditch in the common lands of Cartago, along the Reventado River, to Blas de Ancheta for 250 pesos.

people_involved: Capitán Juan de la Madriz Linares
summary: Capitán Juan de la Madriz Linares granted general power of attorney to his brother, Francisco de la Madriz Linares.

people_involved: Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Capitán Francisco López Conejo obligated himself to pay 100 pesos at 5% interest in favor of a Chaplaincy founded by Luis Cascante de Rojas, for which Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas served as Patron and Chaplain.

people_involved: Capitán don Antonio López del Corral
Capitán don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina
summary: Capitán don Antonio López del Corral granted general power of attorney to Capitán don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina
summary: Capitán don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina and his wife doña María Leocadia Salmón Pacheco obligated themselves to pay 100 pesos at 5% interest for a Chaplaincy founded by the deceased Alférez don Francisco Enciso Hita. This Chaplaincy was observed in the Convento de San Francisco following the death of its former Chaplain, Licenciado don Tomás Muñoz Hidalgo, and they mortgaged a cacao plantation in Matina.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina
summary: Alférez Francisco Fernández sold an enslaved Creole black man named Miguel, approximately 20 years old and born in his house, to Capitán don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina for 325 pesos.
Gabriel de Trejo obligated himself to pay 200 pesos to Capitán don Alvaro de Guevara by the following October. The payment was to be made in Matina cacao at a rate of 25 pesos per zurrón.

Alférez José Calderón obligated himself to pay 350 pesos to Alférez Gerardo Azofeifa as the remainder of a dowry. This dowry was given when Azofeifa married Francisca Calderón, a girl raised by José Calderón, and the payment was to be made in first-quality Matina cacao delivered in Cartago.

people_involved: Visitador don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
summary: On May 19, 1705, in Granada, Capitán Carlos Francisco de Sifuentes, a resident of Panama and merchant in Nicaragua, granted power of attorney to Visitador don Diego de Ángulo Gascón, the oldest Beneficiary Priest of Cartago. This power allowed Gascón to apprehend and sell Sifuentes' enslaved mulatto, Victorino, who was about 30 years old and imprisoned in Cartago. Sifuentes had purchased Victorino from Atanasio de Saavedra, a resident of Villa de los Santos.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
summary: Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón, acting as agent for Capitán Carlos Francisco de Sifuentes, sold an enslaved mulatto named Victorino López to Capitán Blas González Coronel for 350 pesos. Victorino was imprisoned in Cartago at the time.

Juan Lucas Solano provided a dowry letter for his future wife, Gertrudis de Chaves, daughter of the deceased Manuel de Chaves and Josefa de Benavente. The dowry amounted to 540 pesos, with 200 pesos designated as arras.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan Agustín Ruiz de Mesa
Capitán Diego Miguel González de Algarín
summary: Capitán don Juan Agustín Ruiz de Mesa, a resident of Nata, had sold a 20-year-old Congo slave named Domingo to Capitán Diego Miguel González de Algarín for 450 pesos. Due to reasons from the buyer, Domingo was returned, and in exchange, Ruiz de Mesa provided a different slave, Francisco, an 18-20 year old Creole black, for the same price.

people_involved: Juan López de la Rea y Soto
Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Alférez Antonio de Ángulo and his wife Josefa Fernández sold houses with a kitchen and lot in Cartago to Juan López de la Rea y Soto. The property bordered those of Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, Capitán Francisco de Bonilla, and Capitán don Alvaro de Guevara. The 260-peso price included a lien on the property for a chaplaincy founded by the deceased Comisario Baltasar de Grado, which the buyer and his wife, doña Antonia de Sandoval, were required to acknowledge.

people_involved: Juan López de la Rea y Soto
summary: Juan López de la Rea y Soto and his wife doña Antonia de Sandoval formally acknowledged the lien on their property, as referenced in the previous deed.

people_involved: Juan López de la Rea y Soto
summary: Alférez don Pedro de Moya, acting as Ordinary Mayor, ordered the cancellation of the October 5 deed. This decision was made following a definitive ruling in a lawsuit between Juan López de la Rea y Soto and doña Antonia María Acosta, which mandated Acosta to assume the obligation, thereby releasing Soto.

people_involved: Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca
summary: Doña Antonia María Venegas sold houses in Cartago to Alférez Antonio Ángulo, with the property bordering those of doña Clara de Echavarría, doña Manuela de Quirós, María Guerro, doña Manuela de Salazar, and the Cartago stony area. The 600-peso price included two liens: 320 pesos for a chaplaincy founded by the deceased Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca, and 170 pesos for a chaplaincy founded by Comisario Baltasar de Grado (whose patron and chaplain was Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya), which was charged on a mill and houses two leagues from the city. The remaining amount covered outstanding interest on both liens, all of which the buyer and his wife, Josefa Fernández, were to acknowledge.

people_involved: Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca
summary: Alférez Antonio de Ángulo and his wife Josefa Fernández acknowledged a 320-peso lien at 5% interest on the houses they purchased. This lien belonged to the chaplaincy founded by the deceased Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca, which was managed by the Beneficiary Priests of Cartago.

Alférez Antonio de Ángulo and his wife Josefa Fernández acknowledged a 170-peso lien at 5% interest, previously charged to doña Antonia María Venegas. This lien was for the chaplaincy founded by Comisario Baltasar de Grado, with Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya as its patron and chaplain, an obligation they had committed to recognize in the October 8 deed.

Don José, don Juan, and don Antonio Escalante Paniagua sold a 55-year-old slave named José, who belonged to their deceased father Teniente don José Escalante Paniagua, and 1300 cacao trees in the Barbilla valley, next to Matina, to Tomás Alvarez de Villanueva for 500 pesos. The buyer agreed to pay don Manuel Escalante Paniagua, brother of the sellers, the amount adjudicated to him from his legitimate inheritance in the slave and estate.
Doña Tomasa de Ocampo Golfín, a widow, sold a 23-year-old white mulatto woman named Antonia to Capitán Alonso de Porras for 300 pesos.

people_involved: Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
summary: Tomás Alvarez de Villanueva and his wife doña Baltasara Escalante Paniagua obligated themselves to Capitán don José Pérez de Muro, acting as agent for don Manuel Escalante Paniagua, for 155 pesos. This amount represented the remaining balance of don Manuel's paternal and maternal inheritance, to be paid in cacao within eight months, unless Capitán Simón de Balmaceda of León, Nicaragua, was not satisfied with another sum the grantor ordered to be delivered to him.

people_involved: Capitán don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
Alférez don Antonio de la Riba Agüero
summary: Capitanes don Antonio de la Vega Cabral and don Alvaro de Guevara provided a new bond for Alférez don Antonio de la Riba Agüero. Agüero had been imprisoned and then released on bail following a criminal complaint by doña Luisa de Quintana, who alleged he had promised marriage to and then enjoyed her maiden daughter, doña Gertrudis de Zamora. The case was remitted to Guatemala for legal advice, and Agüero requested release while awaiting the decision.
Capitán Alonso de Porras and his wife doña Ana de Castro Rodríguez obligated themselves to doña Tomasa de Ocampo Golfín, a widow, for 400 pesos.

Tomás Alvarez de Villanueva and his wife doña Baltasara Escalante Paniagua obligated themselves to the minor doña Francisca Escalante Paniagua for 279 pesos and 7 reales, representing her paternal and maternal inheritance.

Alférez Teodomiro Arias, as the husband of doña Francisca Escalante Paniagua, cancelled the obligation from November 23 in favor of Capitán José Antonio Bermúdez, who was the husband of doña Baltasara Escalante Paniagua.
Felipe Monge sold a piece of land in the Aserrí valley to Pedro Martín for 20 pesos. This land was part of his paternal inheritance after the death of his father, Felipe Monge.

Isabel María Chacón, acting as guardian for her legitimate daughters María, Ana, Antonia, and Francisca (children of her deceased husband Felipe Monge), sold a piece of land in the Aserrí valley to Marcos de Zamora for 15 pesos.
Isabel María Chacón, acting in her capacity as guardian, sold a piece of land in Aserrí to Miguel Delgado for 30 pesos.
Capitán Francisco López Conejo and his wife doña María de Quirós obligated themselves for 120 pesos at 5% interest to the chaplaincy founded by the deceased Capitán Pedro Ibáñez.

Licenciado don Diego Ángulo Gascón is identified as the Patron and Chaplain of a Capellanía. A ranch and estate in Candelaria, including houses, a corral, 200 cattle, 150 mares, and two donkeys, are mortgaged.

people_involved: Juan López de la Rea y Soto
summary: Capitán Francisco López Conejo, who is departing for Panamá, grants general power of attorney to Juan López de la Rea y Soto.

Sarjento Jerónimo Morales and his wife Francisca de Solís undertake an obligation to Juan Solís, who is absent. This obligation is for 58 pesos and 1 real, representing Juan Solís's paternal inheritance from his deceased father, Blas Solís, who was also Francisca de Solís's father.

A dowry letter is issued by José de Acuña, son of Ventura de Acuña and Marcela Jiménez, for his future wife, Felipa Gutiérrez. Felipa, a Spanish maiden, was raised in the home of Sarjento Francisco Gutiérrez. Their marriage is scheduled for December 21st, with a dowry of 425 pesos and 4 reales, and arras of 200 pesos.

people_involved: Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Alférez don Sebastián de Garita, acting as the testamentary executor for the deceased Luis Cascante de Rojas, establishes a Capellanía for masses with a principal of 200 pesos. The will names Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, brother of Luis, as the Patron and Chaplain.

people_involved: Capitán don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
Capitán don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina
summary: In 1705, Capitán don Antonio de la Vega Cabral and Capitán don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina served as Alcaldes Ordinarios.

Juan Gregorio Ramírez's will, dated 1705, mentions his slave Andrés and 200 pesos held by his mother-in-law. He entrusted a house in Mineral del Corpus to his countryman Juan de Urtecho Vosava. His executors are Capitán Miguel Calvo and his father-in-law Antonio Jiménez.

Doña Mariana de Sandoval's will, dated March 13, 1705, reveals she was the widow of Capitán Alonso Arias Romero and had a second marriage to Capitán Francisco de Cabrera. She mentions her son José and a debt of 60 pesos owed to her niece, doña María de Sandoval of León, which had been left by the deceased doña Nicolasa de Sandoval. The will was granted in the home of doña Sebastiana de Alvarado.

On March 17, 1705, José Jiménez sold a mulatta named Ana Jiménez to Sargento Francisco Alvarez de Oviedo for 300 pesos. José Jiménez had acquired Ana Jiménez as a donation from his mother, doña Juana de Sojo Polido.

On April 16, 1705, María de Sibaja and María Magdalena López leased a cacao plantation with 2,000 fruit-bearing trees in the Malina valley to Francisco Rodríguez for four years. The rent was set at 32 sacks of prime cacao annually, with payments due during the San Juan and Christmas harvests.

people_involved: doña María de Ballesteros y Saavedra
summary: On April 19, 1705, Ventura Ramírez, son of the deceased Capitán Francisco Ramírez and doña Lucía de Chaves, issued a dowry letter for his future wife, doña María de Ballesteros y Saavedra. The marriage is set for April 21st, with a dowry of 940 pesos and arras of 1000 pesos, including 193 pesos to be paid to Alférez Pedro de Torres as doña María's tutor, and a 6-year-old Creole black girl named Josefa valued at 200 pesos.

people_involved: doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar
summary: Miguel de Acosta Arévalo's will, dated April 24, 1705, identifies him as the son of the deceased Antonio de Acosta Arévalo and doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar. He is married to doña Josefa Marín Laguna, with whom he has no children, and co-owns houses with his mother-in-law doña Catalina de Moya and her son Juan Marín. His brother is Andrés de Acosta, and his wife is named as his heir, with Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes and don Pedro de Moya as executors.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina
Mtre. de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: On May 8, 1705, Capitán don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina incurred a debt of 600 pesos to Mtre. de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba, Alférez Mayor, with a one-year repayment term. This obligation was cancelled by don José de Casasola y Córdoba on October 14, 1706.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina
summary: On May 8, 1705, doña Luisa de Abarca committed to pay her son-in-law, Capitán don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina, 253 pesos in cacao by the upcoming Christmas harvest, delivered in the city.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina
Mtre. de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: On May 12, 1705, Capitán don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina transferred the 253-peso obligation from his mother-in-law, doña Luisa de Abarca, to Mtre. de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba, to whom he owed 200 pesos. This 200-peso debt was cancelled by Casasola in favor of Capitán Serrano de Reina on October 14, 1706.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego Campos de Quirós
summary: On June 1, 1705, Licenciado don Diego Campos de Quirós acknowledged a 200-peso, 5% census (lien) in favor of the Capellanía founded by the deceased Alférez Vasco Solano, for which Quirós is partly Chaplain and Patron. This lien is on houses and a corral in the city's common lands, along with 80 cattle, which Quirós bought from the deceased doña Jerónima de Abarca. Quirós also mortgaged his own residence in the city.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego Campos de Quirós
summary: On June 2, 1705, Licenciado don Diego Campos de Quirós undertook an obligation for 180 pesos at 5% interest to the Capellanía founded by the deceased Comisario Baltasar de Grado, for which Quirós is Chaplain and Patron. This obligation is secured by houses in the city, bordered by properties of Capitán Rafael Fajardo, don Jorge de Alvarado, Capitán don Pedro José Sáenz, and doña Manuela de Salazar.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego Campos de Quirós
summary: On June 3, 1705, Licenciado don Diego Campos de Quirós, as Patron and Chaplain, undertook another obligation for 150 pesos at 5% interest to the Capellanía founded by the deceased Alférez Vasco Solano. This amount was redeemed by doña Micaela Duran de Chaves, a widow.

An unnamed grantor, who is the patron and chaplain, made an obligation for 100 pesos at 5% interest in favor of a chaplaincy founded by Sarjento Mayor Manuel Gómez de Lara. This obligation is charged against the grantor's dwelling houses in Cartago.

An unnamed grantor, one of the chaplains and patron, made an obligation for 75 pesos at 5% interest in favor of a chaplaincy founded by the late Depositario Pedro Solano. This sum is part of 150 pesos redeemed by Capitán Miguel Calvo, acting as attorney for the late Licenciado Tomás Muñoz Hidalgo, who was the son and heir of the late Sebastiana Calvo. The obligation is charged against the grantor's dwelling houses in Cartago.

Capitán Vicente Andrés Polo made an obligation for 150 pesos at 5% interest in favor of a chaplaincy instituted by the late Alférez Vasco Solano. Licenciado Diego Campos de Quirós is the patron and chaplain of this chaplaincy. The obligation is charged against 100 cacao trees in 'El Coco' in the Reventazón valley, which Polo purchased with this encumbrance from Sebastiana de Bonilla, widow of the late Alférez Francisco de Espinosa.

locations: Valle y Río de la Reventazón
summary: Capitán Francisco de Bonilla made an obligation for 300 pesos at 5% interest in favor of a chaplaincy founded by the late Baltasar de Grado. Licenciado Diego Campos de Quirós is the patron and chaplain. This sum is charged against a cacao plantation in the Reventazón valley, which previously had an equal sum charged by the late Alférez Diego de los Ríos.

Isabel de Guevara y Sandoval, wife of the absent Agustín González de Villalobos, made an obligation for 200 pesos at 5% interest in favor of a chaplaincy founded by Alférez Andrés López de Céspedes for the soul of the late Magdalena de la Portilla. Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes is the patron, and Licenciado Diego Campos de Quirós is the interim chaplain. This sum is charged against houses in Cartago that Isabel purchased from Capitán Juan Sáenz and his wife Ana de Escalante Panlagua for 710 pesos, with the sale documented on May 28, 1702, before Escribano público José de Prado.

Alférez Pedro de Torres, as executor of the late Capitán Juan de Ballesteros Saavedra and guardian of his minor daughters María and Francisca de Ballesteros (from his marriage to Juana de Torres), sold a cattle ranch named San Juan in the Bagaces valley to Alférez José de Saborido and Ventura Ramírez for 630 pesos and 4 reales. The payment was distributed among Juana Josefa (wife of José de Saborido), María de Ballesteros (wife of Ventura Ramírez), and funds for masses for the deceased and other payments, with the remaining 90 pesos to be paid to the minor Francisca de Ballesteros.

Alférez José de Saborido and Ventura Ramírez made an obligation for 90 pesos at 5% interest in favor of the minor Francisca de Ballesteros. This obligation was made in accordance with the agreement from the previous sale of the San Juan ranch.

The testament of Juana de Vida Martel, single daughter of the late Sarjento Mayor Juan de Vida Martel and Juana López de Ortega, was recorded. She appointed Capitanes Miguel Calvo and Lorenzo de Arburola as her executors and established a chaplaincy, naming Félix de Hoces Navarro as chaplain, or the Guardian of the San Francisco Convent until he is ordained.

The testament of Manuel de Espinoza, a brother of the Third Order of San Francisco, resident of León, Nicaragua, and native of Madrid, Spain, was recorded. He was the legitimate son of the late Simón Pérez de Espinoza and María de Torredana, married to Clara Meléndez de Cuenca, and had children Juan Manuel and María de Espinoza. He listed several debts to captains and other individuals in Guatemala and mentioned a loss of 5000 pesos in the Corpus fire. Pedro José Sáenz and Francisco Fernández were named as executors.

Alférez Bartolomé de Meneses made an obligation to Manuel de Espinoza, a resident of León and currently in Cartago, for fifteen bales of first-quality cacao. Nine bales were for a payment Meneses owed to Felipe de Mesa, which Espinoza paid, and the other six were for 150 pesos Espinoza gave him. Payment is due next December.

The testament of Capitán Jerónimo Valerino, a native of Otre del señorío de Genova, was recorded. He was the legitimate son of Agustín Valerino and Francisca Basano. He was first married to Antonia de Ortega (no children) and then to Francisca de Esquivel, daughter of Andrés de Esquivel and Antonia de Madrigal, with whom he had ten children. His daughters Petronila, María, Manuela, and Gertrudis were married to Capitán Juan Antonio de Castro, Bernardo Pacheco, Alférez Diego de Cárdenas, and Alférez Gaspar de Acosta, respectively. His sons-in-law Bernardo Pacheco, Alférez Gaspar de Acosta Arévalo, and Alférez Diego de Cárdenas were named as executors.

Capitán Vicente Andrés Polo made an obligation for 550 pesos to María Manuela Varón de Virriera, widow of the late Maestre de Campo Francisco Navarro de Mendoza, and Comisario Bartolomé de Gálvez Corral, both residents of Santiago de Guatemala. This sum originated from a 775-peso payment ordered against Polo in a lawsuit brought by Alférez José de Chavarría, acting as attorney for the late Salvador de Berroterán. Paula del Real, Berroterán's widow, ceded this amount to María Manuela and Bartolomé in payment of her husband's debt to them.
The testament of Alférez José Calderón and his wife Juana de las Salas was recorded.

Felipe de Mesa guaranteed a debt of Alférez Bartolomé de Meneses to Hermano Manuel de Sabanas for fifteen sacks of cacao. Nine of these sacks were used by Meneses to pay a debt to Capitán Manuel García de Argueta. A note clarifies that the original obligation was to Manuel de Espinoza, not Sabanas.
Ana de Espinoza sold her 3-year-old mulatto slave, Micaela, to her son, Pablo Barquero, for 150 pesos. Micaela was born in Ana's house and is the daughter of Juana, Ana's slave.

Juan de Sosa established a dowry of 490 pesos and arras of 500 pesos for his wife, doña Catalina Godoy. The document details their parentage, noting that both sets of parents are deceased, except for Alférez Juan Vicente Godoy.

people_involved: doña María de Escobar y Guijarro
summary: Alférez José de Saborido established a dowry of 727 pesos 4 reales and arras of 500 pesos for his wife, doña Juana Josefa de Ballesteros, whom he married three years prior. The document details their parentage, including his parents Teniente Juan de Saborido and doña María de Escobar y Guijarro, and her parents Capitán Juan de Ballesteros Saavedra and doña Juana de Torres.

Francisca de Chaves, widow of Alférez Miguel de Salazar, obligated herself to Salvador Murillo, tutor of his demented brother Jerónimo Murillo, for 100 pesos at 5% interest, secured by houses in the valley of Curriravá. A marginal note indicates that Capitán Francisco Montero de Espinoza, as executor for the deceased Salvador Murillo, cancelled this obligation on March 20, 1710.

people_involved: Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
Capitán don Andrés López del Corral
summary: José de Ocampo obligated himself to Sarjento Francisco Alvarez de Oviedo for 173 pesos 4 reales, which Oviedo paid on Ocampo's behalf to Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona, Capitán don Andrés López del Corral, and Alférez Bartolomé de Meneses. Ocampo will repay the debt through personal labor at a rate of 4 pesos per month.

Doña Catalina Ortiz de Aldana leased a cacao plantation in the Matina valley to Alférez Blas de Ancheta for three years. The rent is 200 pesos per year, payable in eight thirds of prime cacao delivered to the city. The property borders land owned by don José de Guzmán, mountains, and a river.
Capitán don Miguel Calvo granted freedom to his one-year-old mulatto blanco slave, Antonio Nicolás, who was born in his house and is the son of his mulatto slave, Juana Calvo.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don José Agustín de Estrada y Aspeitia
summary: Licenciado don Diego Ángulo Gascón, the senior Cura Rector of the Parroquial, and Licenciado don Cosme Damián Suárez, Cura of the other half-benefice, granted general judicial power to Maestre de Campo don José Agustín de Estrada y Aspeitia, who is the Correo Mayor of this Kingdom and Alguacil Mayor of the Holy Office in Santiago de Guatemala.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don Diego de Herrera Campuzano
summary: Capitán Rafael Fajardo and his wife doña Josefa Sáenz Vásquez sold a 15-year-old black slave named María, born and raised in their house, to Maestre de Campo don Diego de Herrera Campuzano, the Governor and Captain General of the province, for 400 pesos. The entry is incomplete.

people_involved: Capitán don Antonio López del Corral
summary: Don José de Vargas Ulloa granted general power of attorney to Capitán don Antonio López del Corral.

people_involved: Capitán don Antonio López del Corral
Licenciado don Diego Campos de Quirós
summary: Capitán don Antonio López del Corral and his wife doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco acknowledged a 100-peso, 5% interest lien on their houses, favoring the Chaplaincy founded by Alférez Vasco Solano, whose Chaplain and Patron is Licenciado don Diego Campos de Quirós. These houses were previously owned by Comisario Agustín de Torres and later acquired by Capitán don Rodrigo Gadea Marrufo, doña Antonia's first husband, with the obligation to recognize existing liens.

people_involved: Capitán don Antonio López del Corral
Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Capitán don Antonio López del Corral and doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco acknowledged another 100-peso, 5% interest lien on the same houses, this time favoring the Chaplaincy founded by doña María de Yáñez, whose Patron and Chaplain is Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas.

people_involved: Capitán don Antonio López del Corral
Comisario don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
summary: Capitán don Antonio López del Corral and doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco acknowledged an 800-peso, 5% interest lien on the same houses, belonging to the Chaplaincy founded by Alférez Antonio Machado. The Patron is a 'blanco Morales' and the interim Chaplain is Comisario don Diego de Ángulo Gascón.

people_involved: Capitán don Antonio López del Corral
summary: Capitán don Antonio López del Corral and doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco acknowledged a 50-peso lien on the same houses, favoring the Confraternity of the Holy Sacrament, whose Mayordomo is Capitán don Cristóbal Martín Cubero.

people_involved: Capitán don Antonio López del Corral
Maestre de Campo don José de Cásasela y Córdoba
summary: Capitán don Antonio López del Corral and doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco acknowledged a 50-peso, 5% interest lien on the same houses, favoring the Confraternity of the Rosary, whose Mayordomo is Maestre de Campo don José de Cásasela y Córdoba.

people_involved: Capitán don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: Capitán don Antonio de la Vega Cabral and his wife doña Ambrosia González Camino sold a plantain patch with some cacao trees to Capitán Alvaro de Nava, a resident of Esparza and its political lieutenant. The land, inherited by doña Ambrosia from her father Capitán don Matías González Camino, is located in El Toris and borders lands that belonged to doña Mariana, the buyer's mother, for 60 pesos.
Captain Diego Miguel González de Algarín, a resident of León, Nicaragua, granted general power of attorney to Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes and Captain don Antonio de la Vega Cabral.

Miguel de Acosta, son of the late Antonio de Acosta and Josefa de Aguilar, made his testament. He was married to María Mayor Marín and named his unborn child as heir, or his mother Josefa de Aguilar if the child did not survive. His brother was Alférez Gaspar de Acosta, and his executors were Pedro de Moya and Captain Esteban Nieto.

Juan Fernández Martínez and his wife Cayetana de Acosta leased three cacao plots in the Matina valley, named 'la Loma', 'el Chileno', and 'el Riachuelo', to Francisco Martínez for four years at a price of 200 pesos in cacao annually. A marginal note indicates that on March 3, 1708, the lessors received the leased property.

Doña Francisca Calvo, daughter of the late Tomás Calvo and Eugenia de Abarca Alatras, made her testament. She was a widow of Ignacio Láinez de Iztueta and Alonso Gómez Mácetela, and married to Captain Juan de Ibarra. Her children were Eugenia Urbana, Andrés, Antonia, and Juan Francisco de Ibarra, and she mentioned her brother Captain Miguel Calvo, her servant Pedro, her granddaughter Lucía, and a child she raised, Juan Calvo. Her executors were Captain Blas González Coronel, her son-in-law Gaspar de Bastarrica, and her son Juan Francisco de Ibarra.
Doña Francisca Calvo made a codicil to her testament, leaving 20 cattle to her son-in-law Manuel García and ordering the payment of some debts.

Don Pedro José Sáenz and his wife Doña María Rosa Vásquez obligated themselves to the Cofradía de la Vera Cruz for 100 pesos at 5% interest, which was redeemed by brother José Calderón. They mortgaged their houses in Cartago. Don Pedro de Moya was the Mayordomo, and Miguel González, Marcelo Gutiérrez, and José de Coto were his deputies.

Captain don José de Vivas obligated himself to the Chaplaincy founded by the late Agustín Guerrero for 200 pesos at 5% interest. The Licenciado don Agustín de Torres redeemed these funds, which were charged against a stone enclosure and two new cane plots in the Ujurrás valley.

Captain don José de Vivas obligated himself to the Chaplaincy founded by the late Doña Gertrudis de Alvarado for 50 pesos at 5% interest. Don Pedro de Alvarado, also deceased, had redeemed these funds, which were imposed on the same properties mentioned in the previous entry in the Ujurrás valley.

Doña Clara de Vida Martel, a widow, sold an enslaved woman named Marcela, 30 years old, to Captain Antonio Gamboa, a resident of León, Nicaragua. Marcela had been purchased by Clara's late husband, Marcelo Velazco, from Francisco Bogantes.

Alférez Pedro de Torres, who had received a solar from the late Juana Guerrero with conditions he failed to meet, ceded his right to the solar to Mateo Guerrero. Juana Guerrero, in her dying declaration, stated that Mateo Guerrero had provided her care and burial, thus making him the rightful beneficiary.
Don José de Escalante Paniagua and Pedro de Alvarado posted bail for Francisco de Alvarado, who was imprisoned for a criminal cause.

Captain don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina sold an enslaved man named Miguel, 20 years old, to José de Quirós for 350 pesos. Miguel had been acquired by Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina from brother Francisco Fernández.

Doña Catalina Ortiz de Aldana, a widow, leased a cacao hacienda in the Matina valley to Alférez don Antonio de la Riva Agüero for two years. The hacienda bordered land belonging to don José de Guzmán, the mountains, and a river, with an annual rent of 150 pesos in cacao.

Alférez don Pedro Somoza y Lozada, as principal, and Captain don Diego de Barros y Carvajal, as guarantor, obligated themselves to Captain don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina for 680 pesos. The principal was to pay in Panamá, pledging 33 tame mules as security.

Maestre de Campo don José de Casásela y Córdoba, Alférez Real and senior Alcalde Ordinario, placed Antonio, a 9-year-old mulatto boy, son of free mulatto Salvador Padilla and María de Ocampo, into apprenticeship with Alférez Blas de Ancheta, a master silversmith, for a period of eight years.

Captain don Juan Agustín Ruiz de Meza sold an enslaved man named Domingo, a 21-year-old 'bozal' of Congo origin, to Captain Manuel García de Argueta for 310 pesos. Domingo had been previously sold by Ruiz de Meza to Captain Diego Miguel González Algarín the previous year, but was returned by mutual agreement in exchange for another enslaved person.

Captain Juan Rodríguez and his wife Doña Elena de Umaña sold a solar with adobe walls and a tiled roof in Cartago to Manuel Antonio de Arleguí. The property bordered the royal street, houses of Alférez Diego de Cárdenas, Alférez Jerónimo Guzmán, and Doña Sebastiana and Doña Josefa.

Doña Margarita de Aguiar, wife of Alférez don Sebastián de Garita and legitimate daughter of the late Alférez Gabriel Sanjurjo de Aguiar and doña Isabel de Flores, granted power to her husband to make her will.

Francisco Fernández, a native of Avila, Castilla la Vieja, and a brother of the Third Order of San Francisco, made his will. He was married first to the late doña Eugenia Rodríguez and then to Feliciana Chinchilla, having no biological children with either. He and his first wife had declared Josefa Fernández, now wife of Alférez Antonio Ángulo, as their legitimate daughter, having adopted her as an orphan. His executors were Capitán don Miguel Calvo and Alférez don Pedro de Moya, and his wife was named as his heir.

people_involved: Capitán don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
Maestre de Campo don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín
summary: Capitanes don Antonio de la Vega Cabral, Juan de Astúa, Juan de la Madriz Linares, don Antonio López del Corral, Antonio de Barahona y Soto, Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribarén, and Sargento Francisco Gutiérrez provided a residency bond for Maestre de Campo don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín. He had arrived in the province as the newly appointed Governor and Captain General.

people_involved: Don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín
summary: Don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín, serving as Governor and Captain General, granted general power of attorney to Capitán Zeledón de Barraondo. Capitán Zeledón de Barraondo was a Royal Scribe and procurator of the Audiencia of Santiago de Guatemala.

people_involved: Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Doña Antonia Solano, widow of Capitán Alonso Ruiz Arroyo and custodian of his assets, sold a cattle ranch in 'Mata Redonda' in the Curriravá valley to José de Gamboa for 800 pesos. The sale included a house, corrals, 300 cattle, 30 mares/foals, a yoke of oxen, and 9 tame horses, with payment structured as a censo to various religious entities and chaplaincies, and outstanding interest.

people_involved: Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: A marginal note, dated March 22, 1715, provides testimony from Juan López de la Rea, Public Scribe of the Cabildo. It confirms that in the will of the late Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, it was recorded that José de Gamboa owed 250 pesos of a 300-peso censo and tribute, having already satisfied the remaining 50 pesos to the executors of the deceased.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina
summary: Sargento Mayor don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina, departing for Santiago de Guatemala, granted general power of attorney to his wife, doña María Leocadia Salmón Pecheco.

Alférez Blas de Ancheta and his wife Manuela de Madrigal obligated themselves for 300 pesos at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by the late Depositario Pedro Solano. This obligation was secured by a rural estate in the common lands of the city, by the 'Reventado' river, with Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya serving as the Patron and Chaplain.

Miguel de Acosta Arévalo leased a cacao plantation with 450 fruit-bearing trees in the Matina valley to Gabriel de Trejos for two years. The rent was 250 pesos per year, payable in ten sacks of cacao delivered to 'this city.' Additionally, the lessee was required to plant 600 cacao trees in an adjacent clearing belonging to the lessor.

Nicolás de Quirós obligated himself to Tomás de Chaves for 333 pesos, to be paid in first-grade Matina cacao. The cacao was to be delivered to 'this city' in sacks of twenty thousand units, each valued at 25 pesos.

people_involved: Capitán Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribarén
summary: Sargento Mayor Juan de Zavaleta, a widower from Fuenterrabía, Spain, and son of the late Capitán Martín de Zavaleta and doña María de Arániva, entered into a marriage contract with doña Antonia de Hoces Navarro. Doña Antonia is the daughter of the late Alférez Esteban de Hoces Navarro and doña Juana Bautista Calvo. The marriage was scheduled for August 15th, with doña Antonia's brother-in-law, Capitán Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribarén, delivering the assets totaling 2074 pesos, and arras set at 1000 pesos.
Alférez Gaspar de Acosta Arévalo obligated himself to Capitán Manuel García de Argueta for 300 pesos at 5% interest. This obligation was secured by a cacao plantation in Matina.
A marginal note indicates that on December 4, 1709, Capitán Manuel García de Argueta cancelled the obligation made by Alférez Gaspar de Acosta Arévalo.

Capitán Nicolás de Madrigal, son of Matías de Madrigal and Lucrecia Murillo, made his will. He was married to doña Micaela Rodríguez and had two children, Juana Teodora and José, who were named as his heirs. His executors were his father-in-law, Capitán Juan Rodríguez, and Alférez Salvador Murillo.
Doña Juana Pulido de Sojo, a widow, sold a mulatto slave named Teodoro, son of her slave Ana, to Sargento Francisco Alvarez de Oviedo for 150 pesos. Teodoro was estimated to be 6 to 7 years old.

Domingo Bernardo de Puerta, a native of Cádiz, Spain, and son of Francisco de Puerta and Isabel de Avila, entered into a marriage contract with his wife, doña Ana de Quesada. Doña Ana is the daughter of Alférez José de Quesada and the late doña Francisca Sánchez Alvarez Pereira. The dowry was 3500 pesos, and arras were 1000 pesos.

José Lorenzo de Viera, a native of Cádiz, Spain, and son of Manuel de Viera and doña Juliana Florencia de León, entered into a marriage contract with his wife, doña Leonor Jiménez Maldonado. Doña Leonor is a native of 'this city' and daughter of Antonio Jiménez and doña Mariana Hidalgo. The dowry was 643 pesos, and arras were 500 pesos.
Matías Calderón and his wife Mauricia González obligated themselves to Gabriela and Isidora González, who are Mauricia's sisters, for 120 pesos.

An obligation from 1700 or 1701, originally made before Captain José Pérez de Muro with Juan Hidalgo as guarantor, was renewed. Juan Hidalgo requested to be released from his surety, leading to a new obligation where Gregorio de Vargas and his wife Lorenza de Sandoval became the new guarantors.

Alférez José de Quesada, a native of Málaga, Spain, established a dowry of 485 pesos and arras of 500 pesos for his wife, Ana Jiménez Maldonado. Ana is the legitimate daughter of Antonio Jiménez Maldonado and Mariana Hidalgo.

people_involved: Francisco Gómez de Ocón y Trillo
summary: Lázaro de Acosta, a native of Genova, Spain, and son of Carlos de Acosta and María Magdalena de Amonte, established a dowry of 846 pesos and an equal sum in arras for his future wife, Felipa de Ocón y Trillo. Felipa is the legitimate daughter of Francisco Gómez de Ocón y Trillo and María Vásquez de Trejo.

Captain Francisco de Bonilla made an obligation in favor of the minor legitimate children of the deceased Sergeant Baltasar de Letona: Juan, Alejandro, Catalina, and Agustín. Sergeant Francisco Hernández Barquero is their tutor, and the obligation is secured by a mortgage of 1800 cacao trees in the Reventazón valley.

Sergeant Major Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, Ordinary Mayor, arranged a five-year apprenticeship for Antonio de Salazar, a boy aged 12 to 14 and son of Petronila Masís, with his stepfather, Alférez Juan de Fonseca, who is a master carpenter.

Sergeant Major Blas González Coronel made an obligation for 300 pesos at 5% interest in favor of Francisca Josefa, the minor daughter of the widow Antonia Cartín. This sum was provided by a benefactor to help Francisca Josefa enter into marriage.

Maestre de Campo Francisco Serrano de Reina, former Governor and Captain General of the province, who is departing for Spain, granted general power of attorney to his son, Sergeant Major Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina.

Sergeant Major Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina granted power of attorney to his father, Maestre de Campo Francisco Serrano de Reina, who is departing for Spain. The purpose is for the father to petition the Royal and Supreme Council of the Indies for a position for his son in the Indies, specifically in New Spain or Peru, in recognition of his services.
Sergeant Major Juan de Zavaleta, who is departing for Panama, left general power of attorney to his wife, Antonia de Hoces Navarro.

Sergeant Major Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina and his wife, María Leocadia Salmón Pacheco, made an obligation for 400 pesos at 5% interest in favor of the Convento de San Francisco. The funds, redeemed by Sergeant Major Blas González Coronel, were delivered by Captain Miguel Calvo, and the obligation is secured by a hacienda with 1500 cacao trees on the Matina riverbank.

Juan Cayetano Jiménez, a native of Roda, Spain, and son of Cristóbal Jiménez Carrasco and María Jurada Villafuerte, established a dowry of 1391 pesos and arras of 1000 pesos for his wife, Josefa Martínez de Herrera. Josefa is the legitimate daughter of the deceased Captain Eugenio Martínez de Herrera and Micaela Pérez de Luna.

María Duran de Chaves, a widow, founded a Chaplaincy of masses for her soul, her deceased husband Juan Fernández de la Fuente, her parents, and her deceased sister Ana Fernández de la Fuente. The principal of 300 pesos is charged on a property in Curridavá, which was her dowry from her deceased father, Alférez Cristóbal Duran de Chaves. Licenciado Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, her cousin, was named the patron and chaplain.

Clara de Vida Martel sold a 10-month-old Creole enslaved boy named Alfonso to Captain Antonio Gamboa for 125 pesos. Alfonso was born and raised in her house and is the son of Marcela, her enslaved woman.

Mariana González, a widow and mother of José, Juan Miguel, and Nicolás de Quirós (children of her deceased husband José de Quirós), sold a new cacao hacienda in the Matina valley to Maestre de Campo José de Casasola y Córdoba for 400 pesos.

Ana de Retes sold a 20-year-old Creole enslaved man named Cayetano to Maestre de Campo Diego de Herrera Campuzano for 350 pesos. Cayetano was born in her house and is the son of Catalina, her enslaved woman.

Ana de Retes also sold a 9-year-old Creole enslaved boy named José, described as 'zambo', to Maestre de Campo Diego de Herrera Campuzano for 150 pesos. José is the son of her enslaved mulatta woman, Rosa.
Josefa de Aguilar, a widow, made an obligation to Juan Vicente de Herrera for 238 pesos, to be paid by the first of July. This obligation was later cancelled by Herrera on September 3, 1707.

Captain José Pérez de Muro founded a Chaplaincy of 25 annual masses for his soul, his deceased wife Mariana de Echavarría, his parents, and others. The principal of 1500 pesos is charged on his main houses in the city. His nephew, Captain José de Velazco Jiménez, was named the first perpetual chaplain, with succession planned for the children of José de Casasola and Agueda Pérez de Muro, and the children of Diego de Barros Carvajal and Josefa Pérez de Muro.
Feliciana Chinchilla, the widow of Francisco Fernández, granted general power of attorney to Captain Francisco Alvarez.

people_involved: Don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín
summary: Don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín, the Governor and Captain General of the province, granted general power of attorney to Captain Simón de Balmaceda, a resident of León, Nicaragua.

Alférez Antonio de Ángulo and his wife Josefa Fernández granted power to Lieutenant Pedro Rodríguez Palacios to represent them in the estate of Alférez Francisco Fernández, Josefa's father and Antonio's father-in-law, and to accept their inheritance, which also included a portion from Doña Eugenia Rodríguez, Francisco Fernández's deceased wife.

people_involved: Capitán don Diego de Barros y Carvajal
summary: Captain Don Diego de Barros y Carvajal, the Ordinary Mayor, officially apprenticed Agustín de Arroyo, the 12-13 year old son of the absent Nicolás de Arroyo, to Captain Blas Ancheta, a master silversmith, for a period of 8 years.

A dowry letter was issued for the upcoming marriage of Don Gil de Alvarado and Doña Josefa González Camino, scheduled for October 30. The dowry, totaling 3911 pesos with arras of 2500 pesos, included half a house where Don Cristóbal Martín Cubero lived, 600 cacao trees in Matina, a 28-year-old mulata slave named Juana, a 12-year-old negro slave named Baltasar, and silver.

people_involved: Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
Capitán don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: Capitán don Cristóbal Martín Cubero, a native of Segovia, Spain, made his testament. He was married to Doña Catalina González Camino and had a son named Manuel, along with several slaves including Tomás, Felipe, Diego, José, Miguel, Mónica and her daughters Cayetana, María, Antonia, and Victoria. Capitán don José Pérez de Muro and Capitán don Antonio de la Vega Cabral were named as his executors.

Tomás Alvarez de Villanueva, a native of Santiago de Guatemala and natural son of the deceased Antonia Alvarez de Miranda, made his testament. He was married to Doña Baltasara Escalante Paniagua, daughter of Teniente don José Escalante Paniagua and Doña Manuela de Vida Martel, and named his wife as his sole heir and executor, as they had no children.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don Francisco Serrano de Reina
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina and his wife Doña María Leocadia Salmón Pacheco obligated themselves to the Cofradía de la Concepción for 200 pesos at 5%, a sum previously redeemed by Alférez Tomás de Chaves. They secured this obligation with a cacao plantation of 1000 trees located on the banks of the Matina river.

people_involved: Capitán Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribarén
Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
summary: Doña Juana Ramiro Corajo, a widow, obligated herself for 150 pesos at 5% to a Chaplaincy founded by the deceased Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas and established by his executor, Capitán Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribarén. She mortgaged half of a house she owned in the city, with the other half belonging to her mother, Doña María de Retes.
Capitán don Miguel Calvo granted freedom to Catalina Calvo, his 36-year-old mulata slave of pardo color, who was raised in his parents' house and was the daughter of his negra slave, Paula de Arce.

locations: Consejo de Vimenes del Principado de Asturias
summary: A dowry letter was issued for Domingo García de Estrada, a native of Consejo de Vimenes del Principado de Asturias, in favor of his future wife Doña Catalina González Correa, the legitimate daughter of the deceased Alférez Isidro González Correa and Doña Juana Ramiro Corajo. The dowry amounted to 1247 pesos, with arras of 300 pesos.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Antonio López del Corral
Maestre de Campo don Francisco Serrano de Reina
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Antonio López del Corral granted power to Maestre de Campo don Francisco Serrano de Reina, who was departing for Spain, to request a position from His Majesty in the kingdoms of Spain or Peru as remuneration for his services.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Capitán Juan Francisco de Ibarra obligated himself to the absent Andrés Láinez de Iztueta for 1188 pesos at 5%, which Andrés received due to the death of his mother Doña Francisca Calvo. Juan Francisco mortgaged a block of houses and a cattle ranch. The obligation was cancelled on July 6, 1735, by Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra as attorney for his brother, having remitted the amount.

people_involved: Capitán Gaspar de Bastarrica y Narvaiza
Maestre de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba
Don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín
summary: The officials for the year 1708 included Sarjento Mayor Blas González Coronel, Capitán Gaspar de Bastarrica y Narvaiza, and Maestre de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba, all serving as Alcaldes Ordinarios, along with Don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín as Gobernador y Capitán General, and Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes as Alcalde Ordinario.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz
summary: Manuel de Espinoza, a brother of the 3rd order of San Francisco, resident of León, Nicaragua, and native of Madrid, Spain, made his testament. He was a widower of Doña Clara Meléndez and had children Juan and María, and a deceased daughter also named María. He learned his daughter María was to marry Gregorio Zamora in Cartago. His brother, Reverendo Padre Fray Francisco Meléndez, held his jewels in León. His executors included Sarjento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz and Capitán Francisco Alvarez from Cartago, and Capitán Juan de Osejo and Capitán Julián Larios from León, Nicaragua.

people_involved: Licenciado don Juan Antonio de Moya
summary: Capitán don José de Vivas and his wife Doña Josefa de Moya obligated themselves for 1000 pesos at 5% to a Chaplaincy founded by the deceased don José de Alvarado, with Licenciado don Juan Antonio de Moya serving as Chaplain. They secured this lien on a sweet cane plantation, house, kitchen, and sugar mill in the valley of Ujarrás, bordering haciendas owned by Alférez don Francisco de Moya and don Antonio de Alvarado.

people_involved: Licenciado Don Juan Antonio de Moya
Sarjento Mayor Don Antonio de Utrera
summary: Capitán Don Pedro de Moya, acting as attorney for Licenciado Don Juan Antonio de Moya, cancelled a 1000 peso debt owed by Sarjento Mayor Don Antonio de Utrera. This debt was related to the purchase of assets left by the deceased Don Pablo José de Alvarado, which included land near Don Alonso Bersabé's estate and the Agua Caliente river. Don Antonio de Utrera was married to Doña Josefa de Moya, who was previously married to Capitán Don José de Vivas.

people_involved: Licenciado Don Juan Antonio de Moya
Sarjento Mayor Don Antonio de Moya
summary: Licenciado Don Juan Antonio de Moya recognized a 500 peso, 5% annuity (censo) on his houses in the city, in favor of a Chaplaincy founded by Doña Josefa de Moya. He had inherited these houses with this encumbrance from his deceased father, Sarjento Mayor Don Antonio de Moya.

people_involved: Licenciado Don Juan Antonio de Moya
Licenciado Don Francisco de Rivas y Velazco
summary: Licenciado Don Juan Antonio de Moya, acting as Patron and Chaplain of the Chaplaincy, declared that he had transferred the 500 peso annuity (censo) to Licenciado Don Francisco de Rivas y Velazco.

people_involved: Don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín
summary: Don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín, serving as Governor and Captain General, granted general power of attorney to Capitanes Don Juan de Aspur, Juan Luis, and Pedro Martínez, who were residents of Panama City in the Kingdom of Tierra Firme.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Don Pedro José Sáenz
summary: Sarjento Mayor Don Pedro José Sáenz and his wife Doña María de la Rosa obligated themselves for a 250 peso, 5% annuity (censo) to a Chaplaincy founded by the late Comisario Baltasar de Grado. This censo was imposed on their lime and stone houses in the city, which they had purchased from Doña Bárbara Lanini, and the amount was supposedly redeemed by Capitán Manuel García de Argueta.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Don Pedro José Sáenz
summary: Licenciado Don Gregorio de Moya, Patron and Chaplain of the Chaplaincy, declared that the 250 pesos from the obligation remained with Manuel García de Argueta, who had not delivered them to Don Pedro José Sáenz despite the redemption. Argueta had paid the interest, and Sáenz was consequently released from the obligation.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Don Pedro José Sáenz
summary: Sarjento Mayor Don Pedro José Sáenz and his wife Doña María de la Rosa obligated themselves for a 100 peso, 5% annuity (censo) to a Chaplaincy founded by the late Alférez Andrés López de Céspedes. This censo was imposed on their previously mentioned houses, and the amount was redeemed by Capitán Manuel García de Argueta.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Don Pedro José Sáenz
summary: Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes made a declaration similar to that of Licenciado Don Gregorio de Moya, releasing Sarjento Mayor Don Pedro José Sáenz and his wife Doña María de la Rosa from their obligation regarding the 100 peso annuity.

Capitán Juan Francisco de Ibarra sold a 26-year-old male slave named Pedro, of 'mina' caste, to Doña Catalina de Vida Martel, a widow. Ibarra had inherited Pedro from his deceased mother, Doña Francisca Calvo, and the sale price was 300 pesos.

people_involved: Capitán Don Francisco de Noguera y Moncada
Doña Margarita López de la Flor
Don Francisco López de la Flor
summary: Capitán Don Francisco de Noguera y Moncada, Governor of Talamanca, and his wife Doña Margarita López de la Flor, granted power of attorney to Don Francisco López de la Flor, and alternatively to Don Bernardo de Roca, both of Panama City. The purpose of this power was to sell their 26-year-old mulata slave named Mariana for 500 pesos.

Capitán José de Saborido and his wife Doña Juana Josefa de Ballesteros sold a 'caballería' of land in the Curriravá valley to Sarjente Juan Manuel and Francisco de Palma for 50 pesos. The land was bordered by the Torres river, Boca del Monte, and the mountain.

José de Gamboa and his wife Doña Petronila Vélez recognized a 50 peso, 5% annuity (censo) in favor of the Cofradía del Rosario. This censo was imposed on a cattle ranch they had purchased from Doña Antonia Solano, widow of Alonso Ruiz Arroyo, located in the Curriravá valley at Mata Redonda. This transaction was not registered.

people_involved: Licenciado Don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: José de Gamboa and Doña Petronila Vélez obligated themselves for a 200 peso, 5% annuity (censo) to a Chaplaincy founded by Doña Ana Pereira, for which Licenciado Don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas was the Patron and Chaplain. This censo was imposed on their cattle ranch, but the transaction was not registered.
José de Gamboa and Doña Petronila Vélez recognized a 100 peso annuity (censo) on their cattle ranch in favor of a Chaplaincy founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela. This transaction was not registered.

Licenciado Don Cosme Damián Juárez, the Parish Priest of the Sagrario in the city, granted power of attorney to Don Francisco Henguel, a resident of Cádiz, Spain. This power was for Henguel to petition His Majesty for favors as remuneration for Juárez's services in the bishopric of Nicaragua and Costa Rica.

Andrea González, widow of Francisco Gregorio de Bogantes, granted power of attorney to Licenciado Don Pedro Meléndez of Santiago de Guatemala. This power was to represent her in her deceased husband's probate case and to collect 1400 pesos from his assets, which constituted her dowry and for which Bogantes had provided a receipt upon their marriage.
Ana de Espinoza, a widow, sold a 3-year-old mulata slave named Juana Josefa, described as 'pardo' in color and the daughter of her other mulata slave, Juana, to Gaspar Solano for 150 pesos.

Doña Gertrudis Maroto, legitimate daughter of Alférez José Maroto and Doña Luisa Calvo, made her will. She was the widow of Manuel Díaz de Herrera and had three sons: Juan, José Antonio, and Pedro Manuel, who died as a minor. Her executors were Capitán Miguel Calvo and her brother, Alférez Gabriel Maroto.

Diego de Vargas and his wife Juana de Chavarría obligated themselves for a 100 peso, 5% annuity (censo) to the Chaplaincy of Diego Quintero, which was administered by the city's priests. This censo was imposed on their newly built houses of posts and adobe in the city, with specific neighboring properties.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Don Manuel Antonio Arleguí
Comisario Don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
summary: Sarjento Mayor Don Manuel Antonio Arleguí declared that he had acquired the houses previously owned by Diego de Vargas and Juana de Chavarría from Pascual Salguedo, with the condition of recognizing the 100 peso censo and another 200 pesos. As he had redeemed these amounts to Comisario Don Diego de Ángulo Gascón, the debt was cancelled.

Doña María de Retes, a widow, donated half of an adobe house and its corresponding lot in the city to her son, Don Francisco Ramiro. This property was adjacent to the other half of the house that she had previously given as a dowry to her daughter, Doña Juana Ramiro.

people_involved: Licenciado Don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
summary: Licenciado Don Diego de Ángulo Gascón acted as the executor for the deceased Capitán Pedro Ibá.

A Capellanía of 45 annual masses is founded with a principal of 4000 pesos, generating 200 pesos in income. The grantor and Captain Francisco López Conejo are patrons, with López Conejo's sons designated as perpetual chaplains. The principal is secured on properties belonging to Captain don José de Vivas, Captain Francisco López Conejo, the testator, and doña Manuela de Quirós.

Miguel de Acosta Arévalo and his wife, doña María Marín, obligate themselves for 300 pesos at 5% interest to the Capellanía of the deceased doña Rafaela de Alvarado. This sum was redeemed by doña Catalina de Moya, who is the mother of doña María Marín and mother-in-law of Miguel de Acosta Arévalo, and who gave them the houses and solar as a dowry.

Alférez Manuel Antonio de Arleguí grants power of attorney to Maestre de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba to reclaim a 22-year-old mulatto creole slave named José de Arlegui. The slave, described with specific physical features, has run away and is believed to be in Santiago de Guatemala.

Marcos Gutiérrez, a resident of Valle de Barba, as principal, and don Antonio de Alvarado, as guarantor, obligate themselves to doña Lucrecia Murillo, a resident of Birba, for 100 pesos at 5% interest.
Alférez José Calderón owes Juan Gregorio Ramírez 400 pesos, which he was to pay by August. The debt was subsequently cancelled on November 15, 1709.

Sarjento Mayor don Antonio López del Corral leases a productive cacao hacienda in the Matina valley, comprising over 1000 trees, to Alférez Gaspar de Acosta for three years at 200 pesos per year. The hacienda borders properties of don Agustín de Azofeifa and Capitán don José de Vivas, as well as a river and mountain.
José Gamboa sells a 28-year-old Conga slave named María Gamboa to Basilio Picado, a resident of León, Nicaragua, for 400 pesos.
Capitán Juan Francisco de Ibarra, captain of the cavalry company in this city, grants general power of attorney to Maestre de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba, who is currently in Guatemala.

Capitán Juan Francisco de Ibarra sells an estate (hato) with livestock, horses, lands, and houses, along with a mulatto slave named Juan, to Capitán Manuel García de Argueta for 1188 pesos and 6 reales. This property was inherited from his deceased mother, doña Francisca Calvo, and carries an obligation to Andrés Láinez de Iztueta, his brother, as part of doña Francisca's inheritance.

Doña Antonia Láinez de Iztueta, legitimate daughter of the deceased Ignacio Láinez de Iztueta and doña Francisca Calvo, makes her testament. She is married to Capitán Manuel García de Argueta and has seven minor children, also listing eight slaves. Her husband and her uncle, Capitán don Miguel Calvo, are named as executors.

Pedro de Alvarado, illegitimate son of the deceased don Gil de Alvarado, makes his testament. He is married to Felipa de Palma, daughter of the deceased María Lucrecia de Palma, and has no children with her, but had a natural daughter, Juana de Alvarado, who married the deceased Matías Mayorga. His executors are Sarjento Juan Fernández and his wife, Felipa.
Juana Moreno, acting as executor for the deceased widow Antonia Cartín, sells a 17-year-old Conga slave named María to Sarjento Mayor don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina for 400 pesos.
Francisco Granados sells a 20-year-old Conga slave named María Granados to Capitán Manuel García de Argueta for 350 pesos.

The testament of Capitán don José de Vivas is granted by power of attorney through Licenciado don Juan Antonio de Moya and doña Josefa de Moya, his widow, as they had no children. The power of attorney was originally granted before Capitán don José del Aya y Bolívar, Lieutenant Governor and Captain General of Esparza, on July 10, 1708.

Don Gregorio de Alvarado provides a dowry of 3098 pesos and arras of 300 pesos to his wife, doña Francisca Lorenza de Acosta, legitimate daughter of the deceased Antonio de Acosta Arévalo and doña Josefa Santiago de Aguilar. The dowry includes a bread mill and 1000 cacao trees in the Matina valley.

Sarjento Mayor don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina and his wife, doña María Leocadia de Pacheco, obligate themselves for 400 pesos at 5% interest to Francisca Josefa, the minor daughter of the deceased widow Antonia Cartín. This sum comes from the sale of a slave they bought from Juan Moreno, Antonia's executor, with this obligation attached, and Capitán don Diego de Barros y Carvajal acts as guarantor.

Martín de Avellaneda, a native of Portugalete, Vizcaya, Spain, and legitimate son of the deceased Martín de Avellaneda and Luisa de Pucheta, is married to Rosa Viterbo, legitimate daughter of Alférez Tomás de Chaves and Juana Paula de Solís.

Alférez Tomás de Chaves made his will, detailing his family, including his wife Juana Paula de Solís, seven children, and their spouses. He also mentioned his nephew and several slaves. His wife and several captains were named as executors.

Diego Rangel, a native of Panamá, obligated himself to Captain Manuel García de Argueta for 300 pesos, to be paid upon his return from Panamá. Rangel was traveling to Panamá to acquire goods for Argueta, pledging 30 mule beasts held by Francisco de Aguilar as security.
Captains Gregorio de Chaves and Juan de Chaves initiated proceedings for the opening of the will of the deceased Diego de Chaves.

Diego de Chaves's will, granted in Valle de Barba, stated he was married to Juana de Benavente with no children. He had possession of goods belonging to María de Alvarado and Casilda de Esquivel, legitimate daughters of deceased individuals. His wife was named his heir, and Captains Gregorio de Chaves and Juan de Chaves were his executors.

Doña Josefa de Aguilar y Santiago obligated herself for 500 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Comisario Baltasar de Grado, with Licenciado Gregorio de Moya as chaplain. This obligation was secured by houses she owned in the city's common lands, with an exception for a flour mill belonging to her son-in-law, Gregorio de Alvarado.

Doña Josefa de Aguilar y Santiago, a widow, further obligated herself for 100 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Alférez Vasco Solano, secured by the same houses and with the same mill exception as her previous obligation.
Doña Josefa de Aguilar y Santiago acknowledged a 150-peso lien on her houses in favor of the chaplaincy founded by Don Alonso Gómez Macotela, whose patron was Licenciado Don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas.

Juan Ramírez, as executor for the deceased Ambrosia de Brenes, sold adobe walls and a plot of land in Cartago to Doña Petronila Valerín for 75 pesos. The property bordered lands owned by María de Chaves, Juan Masís, Doña Micaela Duran, and Feliciana de Chaves.

Doña Luisa Calvo, grandmother and guardian of the minor children Juan and José Antonio Díaz de Herrera (whose parents were deceased), obligated herself for 1464 pesos and 3 reales, representing their maternal inheritance. Alférez Gabriel Maroto served as her guarantor.

Sarjento Mayor Blas González Coronel granted general power of attorney to Maestre de Campo Don Francisco Serrano de Reina, with the document continuing before Maestre de Campo Don José de Cásasela y Córdoba.

Teniente Juan de la Madriz Linares and his wife Juana Calderón acknowledged a 100-peso obligation to the Cofradía del Santísimo Sacramento. This obligation, stemming from a chaplaincy founded by Doña Juana López de Ortega, was imposed on houses they purchased from the estate of Doña Juana de Vida Martel near the city plaza.
Francisco Rodríguez and his wife Juana de Salas obligated themselves to Sarjento Mayor Don Pedro José Sáenz for 275 pesos, payable in cacao. They mortgaged a cacao plantation in Matina as security.

Sarjento Domingo García de Estrada and his wife Doña Catalina Correa obligated themselves for 375 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela, with Licenciado Don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas as patron and chaplain. This amount, redeemed by Captain Don José de Vivas, was secured by a house in Cartago bordering the Cabildo's houses.

Don Francisco Ramiro Corajo and his wife Doña Ramona de Canales obligated themselves for 100 pesos to the Cofradía de la Concepción. This sum, redeemed by Captain Don Alvaro de Guevara, was charged against half an adobe and tile house in Cartago.

Doña Gertrudis de Sandoval, widow of Don Jorge de Alvarado (who died in Panamá), granted power of attorney to Don Antonio Barraza and Sarjento Mayor Francisco Cosió, both residents of Panamá. They were tasked with representing her in her husband's estate to claim her dowry and community property.

Juan López, a resident of Tuis, sold a mountain clearing and a plantain grove in Atirro to Sarjento Mayor Blas González Coronel for 65 pesos. The property bordered lands owned by Blas González Coronel, Captain Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral, the Reventazón river, and Francisco Martínez.
Captain Francisco Alvarez, identified as the defender of the natives of the province, submitted a petition. The content of the petition is not fully described.

Juan López, principal and Governor of the town of luis, sold a cleared field and plantain plantation. The Governor and Captain General granted permission for the sale, provided López executed it in person.

people_involved: Capitán Don Francisco de Cosío Mier
Capitán Don Pedro Ortiz de Rosas
summary: Doña Catalina de Vida Martel, widow of Don Pedro de Alvarado, granted power of attorney to her son Don José de Alvarado, Captain Don Francisco de Cosío Mier, Captain Don Antonio de Barraza, and Lieutenant Pedro Rodríguez Palacios. This power was to collect from the estate of her son-in-law, Captain Don Pedro Ortiz de Rosas, who died in Panamá, what she would have collected from her deceased husband's assets.

people_involved: Capitán Don Francisco de Cosío Mier
summary: Doña Juana de Alvarado, widow of Don Pedro Ortiz de Rosas, who died intestate in Panamá, granted power of attorney to the same individuals as in the previous entry. This was to claim the assets remaining from her deceased husband.

people_involved: Capitán Don Pedro Ortiz de Rosas
Capitán Jacinto de Pasos y Porta
summary: Doña Clara de Vida Martel granted power of attorney to Don José de Alvarado, who was departing for Panamá. This was to collect 350 pesos from the estate of Captain Don Pedro Ortiz de Rosas, which had been collected by Captain Jacinto de Pasos y Porta from the estate of Captain Juan Cordero in Panamá, and were adjudicated as dowry assets to Doña Clara's two minor children, for whom she is guardian.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo Don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín
Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto
summary: Maestre de Campo Don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín, Governor and Captain General, ordered Captain Diego de San Martín y Soto, Lieutenant of Barba, to visit Juan Bautista in the Barba valley, who was gravely ill.
