The Lieutenant was to instruct Juan Bautista to make his will, and was authorized to notarize it due to the absence of a scribe or competent judge.

Juan Bautista Ricardo, a bachelor from Balvino residing in Barba, made his will. He was the legitimate son of the deceased Bernardo Ricardo and María Raimundo. He appointed Captain Diego Rangel and Alférez Francisco Javier Segura as executors, ordered a chaplaincy, and named his soul as heir.

Marcos de Chinchilla, with verbal permission from his bedridden father Gaspar de Chinchilla, sold a piece of farmland (about three plots) belonging to his father to Francisco Granados for 30 pesos. The sale was made in the presence of Captain Juan de Astúa and other city residents, as Gaspar could not appear before a judge. The land was located near Juan Gómez's property and extended to the Paz River, where Francisco Granados lived.
Marcos de Chinchilla sold a site named "las lagunillas del potrero," suitable for livestock, to Captain Juan de Astúa for 100 pesos.

Marcos de Chinchilla, with permission from his bedridden father Gaspar de Chinchilla, sold a dwelling site to María Chacón for 30 pesos. The property was located near the Paz River, extending from a path towards Ujarrás, along Quebrada Seca, and bordered by Diego Chacón's fences.

Marcos de Chinchilla sold a piece of land, where Diego Chacón lived and had his fences, to Diego Chacón for 25 pesos. The property was located one league from the city, with the Paz River serving as a boundary.

people_involved: Don Claudio de la Chapela Briart
summary: Captain Miguel Antonio de Lima, a resident of Villa de los Santos, acted as guarantor in a dispute over payments to the royal treasury. The dispute involved 58 "piezas de indias" (likely enslaved people) from the Malina valley, which were to be delivered to Don Francisco Paloe under a power of attorney from Don Claudio de la Chapela Briart, Administrator General for the introduction of enslaved people in America. The assessed amount was 3867 pesos 7.5 reales, but Paloe claimed it was only half, offering to provide certification from Panamá officials regarding currency differences and to guarantee payment if the amount was higher.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo Don José de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Maestre de Campo Don José de Casasola y Córdoba leased two cacao haciendas, each with 2000 trees, on the Matina River to Marcos Daniel and Juan Miguel de Quirós for three years. The annual rent was 450 pesos, to be paid in first-quality cacao in "this city".

people_involved: Maestre de Campo Don José de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: In Cartago on February 15, 1714, Doña Águeda Pérez de Muro, widow of Maestre de Campo Don José de Casasola y Córdoba, received 450 pesos from Marcos Daniel, representing the outstanding payment for the last year of the lease.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Sarjento Mayor Don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín granted general power of attorney to Captain Domingo García Moscoso and Captain Don Juan del Río, residents of Santiago de Guatemala. (The entry is incomplete).

Don Diego Campos de Quirós, a Cleric Presbyter and legitimate son of the deceased Lieutenant Pedro Campos de Quirós and Doña Bárbara Rodríguez, made his will. He was the Patron and Chaplain of the Chaplaincies of Doña Inés de Benavides, Vasco Solano, and an incomplete "Pedro".
Alférez Diego Sosa Hurtado, a native of Cádiz, provided a dote of 924 pesos and arras of 500 pesos to his wife, doña María Josefa Alvarez de Oviedo. The dote letter details their parentage.

Margarita de las Alas, natural daughter of the deceased Onofre de las Alas, made her testament. She named her husband, Hermano Tomás de Céspedes, and her daughter, Juana, as heirs, with Francisco de las Alas appointed as albacea.

Andrés Chacón, legitimate son of Diego Chacón and the deceased Jerónima de Peñaranda, made his testament. He named his wife, doña Gertrudis Guerrero, and their four children as heirs, with Capitán Lorenzo de Arburola and Alférez Gabriel Maroto as albaceas.

people_involved: Juan López de la Rea y Soto
summary: Juan López de la Rea y Soto, as Mayordomo of the Cofradía de la Concepción, sold a solar and guachipelín posts for 50 pesos to Capitán don Antonio de la Vega Cabral. The Cofradía had acquired the property through a lawsuit against the deceased doña Petronila Rodríguez Moreno, widow of Capitán Sebastián de Aguirre, for a 150-peso debt.

Nicolás de Quirós, as Mayordomo of the Cofradía de los Angeles, leased a cacao hacienda of 2000 trees in the Matina valley to Capitán don José de Bonilla for three years. The lease price was 250 pesos in first-grade cacao.

Sarjento Juan González Ochoa and his wife María de Espinoza made their testament, detailing their parentage and ten children, some deceased. Their daughter Antonia, over 25, had received an enslaved person named Juan Antonio as part of her inheritance. Capitán Francisco Gutiérrez and José de Aguilar were named as albaceas.

Capitán Francisco de Benavides and his wife Verónica Jiménez sold an enslaved mulato named Mateo, approximately 26 years old, to Sarjento Mayor Antonio Aurelio de Zamora for 300 pesos. Mateo had been part of Verónica Jiménez's dote from her aunt, Clara de las Alas.

Capitán Pedro de Torres, acting as depositary for the assets of his deceased parents doña Catalina Monterroso and Ayudante Esteban de Torres, sold an enslaved criollo negro named Juan to Sarjento Mayor Antonio Aurelio de Zamora for 380 pesos. The sale was formalized with a deed after some time.
Sarjento Juan González Ochoa and his wife María de Espinoza granted freedom to their enslaved mulato, Cayetano, who was approximately 9 years old.
Sarjento Juan González Ochoa and his wife María de Espinoza granted freedom to their enslaved mulato, Nicolas, who was 8 years old and the son of their enslaved mulata, María Nicolasa.

Doña Micaela Duran de Chaves, a widow, sold various building materials and a house in Cartago to Juan Cayetano Jiménez for 700 pesos. The property bordered solares of Juan Ramírez, doña Isabel de Guevara, and across the street, Alférez don Sebastián de Garita and the parish church. Doña Micaela retained the right to live in the houses until her death.

Isabel Murillo, single and legitimate daughter of the deceased Alférez Andrés Murillo de Campos and Magdalena de Guido, made her testament. She mentioned her sister Lucía Murillo and an orphan she raised, Juan José, who had a daughter Gracia Gertrudis with Eugenia Elizondo. Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón was named albacea.

Alférez Pedro Martínez de Colina made a codicil to his testament, which was originally made on July 12, 1701, before Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes. He declared himself married to doña Andrea Calderón, having been single at the time of his original testament, and named additional albaceas in Panamá for his journey.

Doña Micaela Duran de Chaves, a widow, founded a Capellanía for 8 masses for her soul, her deceased husband Alonso Romero, her parents, and her deceased son Alonso Romero, with a principal of 300 pesos owed by Juan Cayetano Jiménez. Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas was named Patron and Chaplain, with child Juan de Bonilla (son of her cousin Capitán Juan de Bonilla and doña Francisca de Astúa) as his successor.

Feliciana de Chinchilla, widow of Alférez Francisco Fernández, and Alférez Pedro de Moya as guarantor, obligate themselves to María Francisca, Feliciana's minor daughter, for 1239 pesos 5 reales as her legitimate inheritance.
Alférez Antonio de Ángulo and his wife Josefa Fernández obligate themselves to Basilio Picado, a resident of León de Nicaragua currently residing in Cartago, for 116 pesos to be paid next March.

people_involved: Juan López de la Rea y Soto
summary: Don Francisco Ramiro Corajo and his wife Doña Ramona Canales obligate themselves to the Cofradía de la Concepción, whose Mayordomo is Juan López de la Rea y Soto, for 100 pesos at 5% interest. This obligation is secured by half of their houses in Cartago, which were donated to Francisco by his mother, Doña María de Retes.

Feliciana de Chinchilla, widow of Alférez Francisco Fernández, obligates herself to María Jerónima, an orphan girl raised in the house of the late Alférez Cristóbal Guerrero, for 100 pesos at 5% interest. This debt is secured by the houses that belonged to her late husband, located in Cartago and bordering properties of Juan Fernández Martínez, Juan Ramírez, Doña Josefa de Aguilar, and Doña Isabel de Guevara.
Feliciana de Chinchilla recognizes a lien (censo) of 80 pesos at 5% interest on her houses in Cartago, in favor of the Chaplaincy founded by the late Alférez Antonio Machado.
Feliciana de Chinchilla recognizes a lien (censo) of 200 pesos at 5% interest on her houses in Cartago, this time in favor of the Convento de San Francisco.

Feliciana de Chinchilla obligates herself to Basilio Picado, a resident of León de Nicaragua, for 450 pesos. The payment will be made in 'cacao de Malina' of first quality, in installments of twenty thousand units, at a rate of 25 pesos each.

A dowry letter is issued for the upcoming marriage of Don Juan García Adán, originally from Villa del Alcocer, Spain, and Doña Josefa de Ocampo Golfín. The dowry includes 4202 pesos 4 reales, with arras of 1800 pesos, comprising four enslaved individuals and 600 heads of cattle located in the Higuerón ranch within Esparza's jurisdiction. The marriage is scheduled for the following Saturday, December 1st.

Clara de las Alas, a widow, issues a codicil to her will, granting immediate freedom to her mulatto slaves Luisa and her sons Ambrosio and Bernardino. She also changes her executors, appointing only Sargento Mayor Antonio Aurelio de Zamora instead of Miguel and Antonio de la Vega. The codicil was granted in Barba.
Don Alonso Bersabé Cabeza de Vaca and his wife Doña Juana de Moya sell a 2-year-old mulatto boy named Nicolás, son of their Creole slave Laureana, to Alférez Antonio Rodríguez for 100 pesos.
An apprenticeship agreement is made between a boy named Sebastián and the master Antonio de Umaña. The document is partially illegible.

Captain Don Diego de Barros y Carvajal and his wife Doña Josefa Pérez de Muro obligate themselves to the Chaplaincy founded by Captain Pedro Ibanez for 450 pesos, with funds provided by the chaplain Diego de Ángulo y Gascón and Ibanez's widow Manuela de Quirós. They hypothecate a cacao plantation in Malina. The obligation was later partially paid and then cancelled by Manuel López Conejo in 1717.

Captain Don José Mier Cevallos and his wife Doña Catalina González Camino obligate themselves to the same Chaplaincy for 250 pesos. They hypothecate their house in Cartago, which they co-own with Don Gil de Alvarado and his wife Doña Josefa González Camino. The obligation was later cancelled by Padre Ángulo Gascón.
Alférez Juan de Torres owes Alférez Tomás de Chaves 300 pesos. The debt was later cancelled by Chaves on February 9, 1712.

Captain Francisco de Bonilla sells a 40-year-old Congo slave named Francisco Canela to Tomás de Chaves for 300 pesos. Bonilla had previously purchased Francisco Canela, along with other slaves, from Maese de Campo Don José de Casasola y Córdoba.

people_involved: Ana Josefa de la Vega Celi
summary: Alférez Juan Moreno, a native of Villafranca de Arverza, France, and resident of Cartago, makes his will. He is married to Doña Ana Josefa de la Vega Celi, daughter of Captain Domingo de la Vega Celi and Isabel Gutiérrez from Seville, and they have no children. He names Don Sebastián de Garita and Jerónimo Remigio de Aguirre as executors, and instructs that his assets be sent to Captain Simón de Balmaceda in Granada, Nicaragua, to fulfill his instructions.
Captain Alonso del Cantillo and his wife Doña María Antonia García sell all their cattle to Francisco Martínez for 512 pesos. The document is unsigned.

Captain Juan de Astúa and his wife Gertrudis Calderón obligate themselves to the Chaplaincy founded by Pedro Ibanez for 200 pesos. They hypothecate their labor estancia, located one league from Cartago, which includes fences and a house made of straw and wood.

people_involved: Antonio de la Riba y Agüero
summary: Doña Francisca de Benavente y Guzmán, a widow, leases a hacienda to Alférez Don Antonio de la Riba y Agüero.
The justice system apprenticed José de los Reyes, an 11-year-old zambo son of María de Chaves, to Sarjento Juan Fernández, a master tailor, for five years.
Capitán don Alvaro de Guevara and his wife, doña María Sáenz, pledged 200 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Pedro Ibanez, mortgaging a house and lot in Cartago.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz and his wife, doña María de la Rosa, pledged 300 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Pedro Ibanez. They mortgaged a tiled house in the countryside beyond Río Seco and Los Angeles, and three of their slaves: Manuela and her two sons, Francisco and Pedro.

people_involved: doña Ana de Escalante y Paniagua
summary: Doña Ana de Escalante y Paniagua, a widow, leased a cacao hacienda in Barbilla to Marcos Daniel for an annual rent of 3 zurrones of cacao. Marcos Daniel's wife, Clara de Quirós, also obligated herself.

The justice system apprenticed Juan Manuel, a 12-year-old zambo, legitimate son of Juan Manuel (a black man) and Manuela de Salazar (an indigenous woman from Ujarraz), to Capitán Esteban de Zúñiga, a master blacksmith, for six years.

Capitán Blas de Ancheta and his wife, Manuela de Quirós (who also signed as Manuela de Madrigal y Quirós), pledged 150 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Pedro Ibanez, mortgaging a house and enclosure by the Reventado River. This debt was cancelled in 1716 by Licenciado don Manuel López Conejo.
Alférez don Sebastián de Garita and his wife, doña Margarita de Aguiar, pledged 100 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Pedro Ibanez, mortgaging an adobe and tiled house on Cartago's main street.

people_involved: Capitán don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
summary: Capitán don Antonio de la Vega Cabral and his wife, doña Ambrosia González Camino, acknowledged a debt of 540 pesos to the Cabildo of León. This debt stemmed from a larger obligation of 11,296 pesos to doña Catarina González Camino, which was originally owed by Capitán don Matías González Camino to Capitán Valenzuela. They mortgaged a cacao hacienda with 4800 fruit-bearing trees in Matina.
Doña Manuela de Quirós, a widow, pledged 242 pesos to doña Potenciana and doña Nicolasa Guerrero, to be paid in pearls, silver, or Matina cacao of specific quality and price, delivered to Cartago.

The justice system apprenticed Juan de Seas, a 12-year-old zambo, legitimate son of Sebastián de Seas and Margarita de Mora (both zambos and residents of Cartago), to Sárjenlo Juan de Villavicencio, a master tailor, for four years.

people_involved: Maese de Campo don Manuel de Bustamante y Vivero
summary: Sárjenlo Francisco Hernández Barquero sold a site and labor estancia with a house and stone fences, located a quarter league from Cartago, to doña Manuela de Quirós, a widow, for 200 pesos. This property was originally purchased at a public auction of the assets of Maese de Campo don Manuel de Bustamante y Vivero, a former Governor, to pay his residency debt.

people_involved: Presbítero Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
Juan Cascante de Rojas (vecino de Aserrí)
Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
summary: Presbítero Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas made his will, owning a house in Cartago, mulatto slaves, livestock, and mules. He owed 400 pesos to the soul of his aunt, doña María Yañez, and ordered the founding of a chaplaincy. He bequeathed specific items to relatives and granted freedom to his slave Catarina, naming several executors and heirs.

people_involved: doña María Ramona de la Canal
summary: Don Francisco Ramiro Corajo and his wife, doña María Ramona de la Canal, pledged 60 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by doña Rafaela de Alvarado, whose patron was don Gregorio de Moya. They mortgaged half of an adobe house; the other half belonged to Domingo García and his wife, doña Catarina Correa.

Alférez don Pedro de Moya, as executor for the deceased Alférez Francisco Fernández and his first wife doña Eugenia Rodríguez, founded a chaplaincy with 500 pesos in the Convento de San Francisco in Cartago. The funds came from the sale of houses to Feliciana de Chinchilla, who was also Fernández's wife.
Don José de Guzmán leased a cacao plantation with 20 trees in Matina to Juan Bautista Retana for two years, at an annual rent of 150 pesos.

people_involved: Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos
summary: Don Gil de Alvarado and his wife, doña Josefa González Camino, sold a part of a tiled adobe house, which was given to her as a dowry, to Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos and his wife, doña Catarina González Camino, for 500 pesos.
María de Grados, legitimate daughter of Jacinto de Grados and doña María, made her will.

Don José de Alvarado provided a dowry of 2050 pesos, largely in clothing and jewelry, along with mules and cattle, for his upcoming marriage to Doña Úrsula Josefa López Conejo. The wedding was scheduled for the 23rd of the month. Don José is the son of Don Pedro de Alvarado and Doña Catarina de Vida Martel, while Doña Úrsula is the daughter of Capitán Francisco López Conejo and Doña María de Quirós.

people_involved: Doña Catarina Martínez de la Barrera
Capitán Don Diego Sendín de Sotomayor
Sarjento Mayor Don Francisco de Ocampo
Juan López de la Rea y Soto
summary: Alférez Manuel de Castro, a native of Lugo, Galicia, made his will. He is the son of Simón de Navas de Castro and Doña Catarina Martínez de la Barrera, and is married to Doña Felipa Sendín de Sotomayor, with whom he has a son, José Manuel, and another child expected. He noted debts to Capitán Francisco López Conejo and Sarjento Mayor Don Francisco de Ocampo for the education of their children, and named Juan López de la Rea y Soto and his wife Doña Felipa as executors.

Ana de Aguilar, a widow, sold an enslaved woman named Antonia, approximately 20 years old, to Capitán Diego de Aguilar for 300 pesos. Ana had inherited Antonia from her deceased son, Gabriel de Trejo.
Doña Catarina de Vida Martel, widow of Don Pedro de Alvarado, received 2389 pesos. This money belonged to her minor sons, Don Hermenegildo, Don Juan Manuel, and Don Antonio de Alvarado.

Capitán José de Mier Cevallos and his wife, Doña Catarina González Camino, committed to an obligation of 450 pesos for chaplaincies. These chaplaincies were founded by Don Matías González Camino for the souls of Licenciados Don Domingo and Don Francisco de Echavarría, and Capitán Don Miguel de Alvarado, with Don Manuel Martín Cubero serving as chaplain. They mortgaged half of a house they had purchased from Don Gil de Alvarado.

people_involved: Capitán Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: Capitán José de Mier Cevallos and Doña Catarina González Camino committed to an obligation of 823 pesos to Capitán Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral. Cabral was acting as the executor for the deceased Capitán Don Cristóbal Martín Cubero, who had been the city's general depositary and had endowed Doña Catarina with 2000 pesos.

Feliciana de Chinchilla, widow of Alférez Francisco Fernández, committed to an obligation of 500 pesos to the Confraternity of the Limpia Concepción. This amount was left by her deceased husband, and she took possession of his houses in exchange for the obligation.

Alférez Luis Peláez and his wife, María de los Santos, committed to an obligation of 200 pesos for a chaplaincy founded by Don Francisco de Hita Enciso. Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribarén was the patron and Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro was the chaplain. This obligation was previously held by Alférez Domingo Inza, and the couple mortgaged a country house near the Taras river.

Capitán Fermín de Hoces Navarro made his will, identifying himself as the son of the deceased Alférez Esteban de Hoces Navarro and Doña Juana Calvo. He owned a cacao plantation in the Reventazón valley, where his brother Félix Esteban owned 300 trees. He was owed 100 pesos by Andrés de Irula, a trader in Nicaragua currently in Perú, and named Sarjento Mayor Juan de Zavaleta and Teniente Pedro Rodríguez Palacio as executors. His niece, Doña Catarina de Arburola, daughter of Lorenzo, was also mentioned.

Bartolomé de Aguilar, a native of Antequera, Spain, and son of Matías de Aguilar and Catarina de León, provided a dowry of 1650 pesos for his marriage to Catarina Ramírez. Catarina is the daughter of Juan Ramírez and Francisca Serrano, and their wedding was scheduled for the 24th of the month.
In a codicil to his will, Capitán Fermín de Hoces Navarro clarified that the 100-peso credit owed by Andrés de Irula belonged to his brother-in-law, Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribarén.

Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribarén, as executor for the deceased Doña Juana de Vida Martel, founded a chaplaincy of masses in the Convent with a capital of 150 pesos. Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro or a close relative was designated as the chaplain once ordained, with the Padre Guardián serving in the interim. Don José Escalante Paniagua, son of Don José Escalante Paniagua and Doña Manuela de Vida Martel, was named as the patron.

people_involved: Capitán Don Francisco Duque de Estrada
summary: Capitán Don Francisco Duque de Estrada, a resident of Granada, Nicaragua, and native of Onís, Spain, made his will. He is the son of the deceased Don Antonio Duque de Estrada and Doña María Suárez de Sevos, and is married to Doña Catarina Hurtado de Mendoza, a native of Granada and daughter of the deceased Capitán Mateo Hurtado de Mendoza and Doña Agustina de Orozco. He listed his sons as Bernardo, Francisco, and Miguel, and noted having debts in Nicaragua and Guatemala.

Francisco Granados committed to an obligation of 400 pesos for a chaplaincy founded by Don Pedro de Alvarado, with the funds provided by Doña Catarina de Vida Martel, the founder's widow. Granados mortgaged his house, located more than a league from Cartago, near Chircagres and the Río de Paz. This obligation was later cancelled in 1717 by Don Gil de Alvarado, the patron.

Doña Manuela de Salazar, a widow, sold a house made of adobe and tile to Don Gil de Alvarado for 770 pesos. She had inherited the property from her deceased brother, Licenciado Don Francisco de Salazar, and the house bordered the city jail.

people_involved: Don Alonso Bersabé Cabeza de Vaca
summary: Don Alonso Bersabé Cabeza de Vaca and his wife, Doña Juana de Moya, committed to an obligation of 150 pesos for a chaplaincy founded by Doña Gertrudis de Alvarado. They mortgaged a country property in the Ujarraz valley, near Santiago, which included a house, a sugar mill, a copper pot, a stone fence, two plots of sugarcane, and three enslaved people named Juana Josefa, Laureana, and Pablo Cayetano.

Ayudante Nicolás de Estrada leased a cacao plantation with 700 trees in the Reventazón valley to José Felipe Bermúdez for two years. The annual rent was 100 pesos, and the lease was cancelled in 1711.

Doña Francisca de Astúa, a widow, sold a house made of posts and tiles in the common lands to Captain Tomás Andrés Polo for 300 pesos. She had acquired the house through the death of her husband, Captain Juan de Bonilla.

people_involved: Doña Josefa López de la Flor
summary: Captain Tomás Andrés Polo and his wife, Doña Josefa López de la Flor, committed to pay 300 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Magdalena de la Portilla. This sum was related to the house they purchased from Doña Francisca de Astúa, and Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes was the current patron of the chaplaincy.

people_involved: Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: José Hidalgo sold a 17-year-old mulatto slave named Nicolás to Captain Antonio de Soto y Barahona for 200 pesos. Hidalgo had previously purchased Nicolás from Doña María Duran de Chaves, a widow, in 1701.
The justice system handed over a white boy, approximately 11 years old and son of Gregoria de Villarreal, to Sergeant Pedro de Alvarado, a master weaver, for a period of 5 years.

A dowry letter was issued for Captain Juan Francisco de Ibarra, son of Juan de Ibarra and Doña Francisca Calvo, in favor of his wife Doña Petronila de Moya. Doña Petronila is the daughter of Captain don Esteban de Moya and Doña Rafaela de Alvarado, and her brother Don Gregorio de Moya provided goods worth 1724 pesos.

people_involved: María de la O de Guevara
summary: A dowry letter was issued for Francisco Cartín, son of the deceased José Daniel Cartín and María de la O de Guevara, in favor of his wife Isabel de Quirós. Isabel is the daughter of the deceased Captain José de Quirós and Mariana González, with a dowry value of 719 pesos.
Alférez Manuel Antonio Arleguí leased a cacao plantation in the Reventazón valley to José Felipe Bermúdez for two years at 45 pesos per year. This lease was later cancelled in 1717.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz
summary: Sergeant Major don Pedro José Sáenz and his wife Doña María de la Rosa sold a house made of posts with a fence, located across the Dry River, to Captain Juan Sancho de Castañeda for 100 pesos.

José Antonio Bermúdez and his wife Doña Baltasara de Escalante Paniagua committed to pay 300 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Don Pedro de Alvarado, a sum delivered by the founder's widow, Doña Catarina de Vida Martel. They mortgaged a house on the royal street that Doña Baltasara had purchased from Don Pedro Ortiz de Rosas.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz
Capitán don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: Sergeant Major don Pedro José Sáenz and his wife Doña María de la Rosa sold a 5-6 year old black boy named Francisco, son of their black slave Manuela, to Captain don Antonio de la Vega Cabral for 100 pesos.

Doña Francisca de Astúa, daughter of Juan de Astúa and Doña María de Chaves and widow of Captain Juan de Bonilla, made her will. She named her seven children, her son-in-law Alférez Juan Marín, her sisters-in-law Doña Sebastiana and Doña Josefa de Bonilla, and her brother Captain Juan de Astúa. Her executors were her son-in-law and Captain Tomás Andrés Polo.

Alférez José Calderón sold a 25-year-old Creole black man named José Tomás de Herrera, a native of San Lucar de Barrameda, Spain, to Captain Juan Gregorio Ramírez for 400 pesos. José Calderón had inherited José Tomás from his deceased son, Alférez Nicolás Calderón.

people_involved: Capitán don Pablo José de Alvarado
Licenciado don Juan Antonio de Moya
summary: Doña Josefa de Moya, widow of Captain don José de Vivas, bought a hacienda in Ujarrás from the deceased Captain don Pablo José de Alvarado. She acknowledged owing 1000 pesos for this purchase, which belonged to the chaplaincy founded by Don José de Alvarado, with Licenciado don Juan Antonio de Moya as the current chaplain.

people_involved: Juan López de la Rea y Soto
Capitán don Alonso de Aranda y Acevedo
summary: Ayudante José de Manzanillo, a resident of Esparza, sold a 23-year-old Creole black man named Miguel López, a native of Cartago, to Juan López de la Rea y Soto for 440 pesos. Manzanillo had previously bought Miguel López from the same Juan López de la Rea y Soto in 1708, before Captain don Alonso de Aranda y Acevedo, Lieutenant Governor.

people_involved: Capitán don Antonio de Soto Barahona
Maese de Campo don José de Cáscasela y Córdoba
summary: Captain don Antonio de Soto Barahona sold a 17-year-old mulatto named Nicolás to Maese de Campo don José de Cáscasela y Córdoba for 200 pesos. Soto Barahona had previously acquired Nicolás from José Hidalgo.

Ayudante Nicolás de Estrada and his wife Doña Lorenza Muñoz owed Doña Nicolasa Guerrero 100 pesos, which belonged to the orphan María Jerónima. They mortgaged a cacao plantation in the Reventazón valley, and a payment confirmation was signed by Fray Diego Caballero, the priest in Ujarrás. The debt was cancelled in 1717.
The justice system handed over the minor Sebastián Carrillo, a white orphan boy about 11 years old, to Sergeant Gregorio de Umaña, a master shoemaker, for 5 years.

people_involved: R. P. fray Andrés Torres Cápelazo
summary: Doña Magdalena Calvo, daughter of the deceased Tomás Calvo and Doña Eugenia de Abarca Alatras and widow of Captain Francisco Fernández de Miranda, made her will. She had no children, owned a house in Chircagres, and bequeathed 50 pesos to Fray Andrés Torres Cápelazo. Her executors were Captain Gabriel Maroto and Lieutenant Pedro Rodríguez Palacio, and she mentioned María de la Rosa and José Agustín de Espinosa, whom she had raised.

people_involved: Don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín
summary: Don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín, Governor of the province, committed to a chaplaincy founded by Baltasar de Grado. By his order, Alférez Diego Santiago de Cárdenas purchased an adobe house from the assets of the deceased Doña Ana de Retes for 1500 pesos, with portions allocated to chaplaincies founded by Baltasar de Grado and Doña Ana de Echavarría Navarro, whose patrons included Licenciado don Gregorio Moya and Licenciado don Manuel de Guzmán.

people_involved: Don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín
summary: Don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín acknowledged owing 525 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Doña Ana de Echavarría Navarro, for the same reasons as the previous day's transaction.

people_involved: Presbítero don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Captain Francisco López Conejo and his wife Doña María de Quirós committed to pay 100 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Luis Caspante de Rojas. Presbítero don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, a consultant of the Holy Office, served as the chaplain and patron of this chaplaincy.
A ranch named La Candelaria, located 6 leagues from Cartago, was mortgaged. The mortgage included 200 cattle, 2 donkeys, 100 mares, and an 18-year-old Mina slave named Juan.

Sarjento Mayor Pedro José Sáenz and his wife María de la Rosa borrowed 300 pesos from the chaplaincy founded by Pedro Ibáñez. They mortgaged their house in Cartago, which was already encumbered with debts to several religious entities, and two slaves, Manuela and her son Pedro Manuel.
Pedro José Sáenz and María de la Rosa took an additional 100 pesos from the chaplaincy founded by Andrés López de Céspedes. They used the same guarantees as the previous day's transaction.

Sarjento Mayor Francisco López Conejo and his wife María de Quirós obligated themselves for 100 pesos to a chaplaincy founded by Capitán José Pérez de Muro, whose patron and chaplain was Licenciado José de Velazco. They mortgaged a house and site in the area called La Candelaria.

Francisco López Conejo, acting as attorney for Teniente Juan García Sanabria of Panamá, sold a 50-year-old Zambo slave named Baltasar to Licenciado Diego de Ángulo Gascón for 200 pesos. Baltasar had been previously purchased from Felipe Gabriel de Moya, and the power of attorney was executed in Panamá before notary Cristóbal de Madina Veitía.

Alférez Nicolás de Guevara sold a 23-year-old black slave named María de la Candelaria to Capitán Francisco Gutiérrez for 300 pesos. María de la Candelaria was inherited by Nicolás from his mother, Clara de Echavarría Navarro.

Alférez José Antonio Bermúdez and his wife Baltasara Escalante Paniagua obligated themselves for 120 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Comisario Baltasar de Grado. The funds were provided by Licenciado Gregorio de Moya, who served as the patron and chaplain of the chaplaincy, and they mortgaged their house.

Capitán Francisco Alvarez de Oviedo, a resident of the Barba valley, obligated himself for 100 pesos to the minor Francisco de Acuña. Francisco de Acuña was the legitimate son of Baltasar de Acuña and Martina de Alvarado, and the money was delivered by Capitán Juan Rodríguez de Segura.

Gregorio de Vargas, a resident of Barba, and Andrés Arias, a field judge of the same valley acting as guarantor, obligated themselves for 100 pesos to José de Bonilla. This sum represented José de Bonilla's paternal inheritance as the legitimate minor son of the deceased Juan de Bonilla.

Alférez Tomás de Chaves, from the Barba valley, founded a chaplaincy for masses for his soul, his wife Juana Paula's soul, and his parents' souls, with a capital of 1000 pesos. The chaplaincy was based on his house, sugar mill, and pasture in the Aserrí valley, and his son José de Chaves, currently in Guatemala, was named as the chaplain.
The justice delivered Diego, a 10-year-old mestizo orphan, to Juan Salvador Hernández, a master shoemaker, for a period of 5 years.

The will of María de Grados was opened. She was the legitimate daughter of the deceased Jacinto de Grados and María de Ocampo Golfín, and the widow of Alférez Antonio de Bonilla. She had three children: Ildefonsa (married to Capitán Vicente Andrés Polo), Juan (deceased, father of José Antonio de Bonilla), and Gertrudis (deceased).

Josefa de Santiago de Aguilar, a widow, leased a cacao plantation in Matina with 1300 trees to Capitán Juan Francisco de Ibarra. The annual rent was 14 zurrones of 20,000 cacao beans, with 12 of them being of first quality.

Miguel de Acosta Arévalo leased a cacao plantation in Matina with 400 trees to Alférez Bernabé de Segura for 90 pesos per year. The plantation bordered that of Josefa de Santiago de Aguilar, who was the mother of Miguel de Acosta Arévalo.

Nicolás de Alfaro and his wife María de Mojera, residents of the Barba valley, obligated themselves for 400 pesos to Lucrecia de Murillo, a widow and resident of the same valley. They provided a cattle ranch with a house and corrals in the Barba valley, which they had purchased from Gregorio de Chaves, as a guarantee.

Proceedings for the opening of the sealed will of Alférez Pedro Martínez de Colina, granted on July 12, 1701, were conducted. He recognized four natural daughters and mandated the founding of a chaplaincy with 400 pesos, naming Licenciado Diego de Campos Quirós as the first patron and chaplain.

Capitán José de Mier Cevallos, Lieutenant Governor, granted general power of attorney to Maese de Campo Sebastián de Arancivia y Zazi, who was the Governor and Lieutenant Captain General of Granada, Nicaragua.

The will of Juan Gómez, a native of Málaga, was opened. He was the legitimate son of Francisco Gómez and María Rodríguez del Castillo, and was widowed from María de los Angeles, also from Málaga. He had two sons, Nicolás and Antonio María, who had fled due to a plague.

people_involved: Juan López de la Rea y Soto
summary: Capitán don Alvaro de Guevara sold a house, which he had previously acquired from Juan López de la Rea y Soto, to Capitán Francisco Gutiérrez for 200 pesos. This amount was designated to a chaplaincy founded by Pedro Ibañez.

people_involved: Padre don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
summary: The sale of the house between Alvaro de Guevara and Francisco Gutiérrez, which was tied to Pedro Ibañez's chaplaincy, was cancelled in 1715. The cancellation was performed by Padre don Diego de Ángulo Gascón, who served as the priest of Cartago and chaplain of the institution.

people_involved: Capitán Juan de la Madriz Linares
summary: Juana Calderón, a widow, made an obligation of 300 pesos to the Cofradía del Santísimo Sacramento, a debt she shared with her deceased husband, Capitán Juan de la Madriz Linares. She mortgaged a cacao plantation in Matina, bordering her father Alférez José Calderón's property, along with two slaves, Lorenzo and María Leocadia.

Doña María Duran de Chaves, widow of Juan Fernández de la Fuente, made a codicil to her will, which was originally granted on February 20, 1695, before don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, jointly with her husband. Her slave, Cristóbal, was obligated to cover her burial expenses for a year and arrange solemn suffrages, with any remaining funds from 80 pesos to be used for masses. Upon completion and payment, Cristóbal was to receive his letter of freedom.

Sargento Juan Fernández Bulagai, a native of Mexico, made his will. He was the legitimate son of Francisco Fernández de Bulagai and Mónica de Aldana, and widower of María de Espinoza (daughter of Ana Rodríguez). He listed nine children, including Manuel who died in Tierra Firme and Josefa who was married to José Damián de Molina. Manuel was to receive 1000 pesos from Capitán Juan de Ibañez's will, which his albaceas in Panama had not yet delivered. His granddaughter was Manuela de Mora, and his albaceas were Jerónimo Remigio de Aguirre and his son Juan.

people_involved: Capitán Francisco de la Madriz Linares
Capitán don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
Juan López de la Rea y Soto
summary: Capitán Francisco de la Madriz Linares and his wife doña Manuela de Quirós obligated themselves to Capitán don Antonio de la Vega Cabral and Juan López de la Rea y Soto for 1181 pesos and 7.5 reales. This sum covered the cost of maintaining slaves apprehended in the Matina valley, as ordered by the provincial governor. The payment was to be made in silver reales in the city upon the arrival of the ship "San Juan Bautista," owned by Antonio de León Navarro, from Caldera to Panama.
The obligation made by Capitán Francisco de la Madriz Linares and doña Manuela de Quirós to Capitán don Antonio de la Vega Cabral and Juan López de la Rea y Soto was cancelled in 1711.

people_involved: doña Magdalena de Luque y Ceas
R. P. fray Antonio de Escurra
summary: Sargento Mayor Blas González Coronel, Alcalde provincial of the Santa Hermandad and lieutenant of royal treasury officials, made his will. He owned various properties and slaves, and ordered the foundation of a chaplaincy with his 18-year-old son, Manuel González Coronel, as patron. He renounced his office of Alcalde Mayor provincial in favor of his brother-in-law Francisco Martínez, and left legacies to his nieces and goddaughter.

people_involved: Doña Angela de la Paz y Flores
Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Doña Angela de la Paz y Flores, widow of Sargento Mayor don Sebastián de Ocampo Golfín, sold an adobe and tile house on the royal street to Alférez José de Morales for 350 pesos. The house was encumbered with a debt to the Cofradía del Rosario, which José de Morales assumed.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz
Beneficiado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
summary: Sargento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz and his wife doña María de la Rosa sold a 26-year-old enslaved woman named Manuela and her 4-year-old son, Pedro Manuel, to Sargento Mayor Antonio Aurelio Zamora for 200 pesos. This sale was made with the license of Beneficiado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón, who was the priest and patron of the chaplaincy founded by Capitán Pedro Ibáñez, and with the license of Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes, perpetual councilman and patron of the chaplaincy founded by Magdalena de la Portilla.
Cristóbal Alberto Cascante, a resident of the Aserrí valley and natural son of the deceased Luis Cascante, made his will. He was married to María Guerrero and had no children.

José de Gamboa, a resident of Valle de Aserrí, made his will. He was the legitimate son of Juan de Gamboa and María Vásquez, and was married to Petronila Vélez de Guevara, daughter of Bernardino Vélez and Francisca Muñoz, all deceased residents of Cartago. They had no children, and he named his wife and Esteban, a child he raised, as his heirs.

Doña Antonia María Venegas, a widow, obligated herself for 300 pesos in favor of the chaplaincy founded by Don Pedro de Alvarado. She mortgaged a house and a mill located about 4 leagues from Cartago near the road to Urriravá, along with two caballeries of land.
In 1720, Don José de Alvarado took over the debt owed by Doña Antonia María Venegas to the chaplaincy founded by Don Pedro de Alvarado.

people_involved: Guardián del Convento de San Francisco
summary: Don Pedro José Sáenz, as the dative executor of Don Pedro de Alvarado, founded a chaplaincy for recited masses with a capital of 1000 pesos. The capital was secured by a house and enclosures across the Río de Paz, about one league from Cartago, and various credits. The guardian of the Convent of San Francisco was named as the chaplain.

people_involved: Capitán Don Miguel de Santiago y Alvear
Don José de Toledo y Gudiño
summary: Doña Inés de Sandoval Golfín, widow of Don Gil de Alvarado (who died in Panamá), granted general power of attorney to Capitán Don Miguel de Santiago y Alvear, castellano of the Castillo de Chagres. In his absence, the power would go to Don José de Toledo y Gudiño, a resident of Panamá.

Francisco de Aguilar acted as a guarantor for Cristóbal Duran, an enslaved person of the deceased Doña María Duran de Chaves. This was for the fulfillment of conditions in Doña María's codicil to grant Cristóbal his freedom.

The justice system granted freedom to Catalina, an enslaved woman who belonged to Doña María Duran de Chaves. Doña María had died on July 6th of the previous year and was the widow of Juan Fernández de la Fuente. Catalina, described as 'pardo' (brown-skinned), was granted freedom based on a testamentary clause.

people_involved: Don Claudio de la Chapela Briart
summary: Don Claudio de la Chapela Briart, Inspector Director and General Administrator of the Royal Asiento and Company for the introduction of enslaved Africans in America, granted power to Don Francisco Palos. This power, originally made in Panamá on June 2, 1710, authorized Palos to manage all 'negros bozales' (newly arrived enslaved Africans) transported to Nicaragua and Costa Rica via Matina or other locations, and to claim any excess funds from those sold by S.M. beyond 33 and 1/3 pesos per 'pieza de indias'. He was also empowered to claim any confiscated enslaved people not yet sold and transport them to Cartago.

As an authorized agent, Don Francisco Palos obligated himself to Capitán Miguel Antonio de Lima, a resident of Villa de los Santos in Tierra Firme, for 5604 pesos. This money was borrowed to pay individuals who apprehended 105 enslaved men and women in the Matina valley. The debt was cancelled in 1711.

people_involved: Capitán Francisco de la Madriz Linares
Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
Juan López de la Rea y Soto
summary: Don Francisco Palos obligated himself to Capitán Francisco de la Madriz Linares for 1182 pesos. This money was borrowed to pay Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral and Juan López de la Rea y Soto for the maintenance expenses of enslaved people deposited in their homes in Matina. The debt was cancelled.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Don Pedro José Sáenz
Capitán Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
Sarjento Mayor Don Antonio López del Corral
Sarjento Mayor Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reyna
summary: A group of individuals, including Sarjento Mayor Don Pedro José Sáenz and Capitán Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral, acted as guarantors for Sarjento Mayor Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reyna. He was appointed as lieutenant of the official judges of the Royal Treasury in Cartago and its Royal Box. The first eight guarantors pledged 250 pesos each, and the last two (Don Antonio López del Corral and Doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco) pledged 2000 pesos, mortgaging their house near the Plaza and their cacao plantation with 2400 trees in Matina.
Juana de Salas, widow of Francisco Rodríguez, leased a cacao plantation in Matina with 1000 trees to Sarjento Mayor Antonio Aurelio Zamora for three years at an annual price of 150 pesos.
Doña Luisa de Abarca, a widow, leased a cacao plantation in Matina with 2000 trees to Alférez Bartolomé Meneses for four years at an annual price of 225 pesos.

Capitán Manuel García Argueta leased two cacao plantations in Matina, named 'Nuestra Señora de la Soledad' and 'Las Setenta Calles,' to Sarjento Mayor Rafael Fajardo for three years at an annual price of 225 pesos.

people_involved: Licenciado Don Juan Antonio de Moya
summary: Licenciado Don Juan Antonio de Moya, a presbyter, leased a cacao plantation in Matina, along with an enslaved man named Francisco (of Mina caste), to Alférez Luis Gutiérrez for four years at a price of 250 pesos. The agreement was rescinded in 1713.

Capitán Don José de Bonilla and his wife Doña Manuela Sáenz obligated themselves for 100 pesos in favor of the chaplaincy founded by Juan Fernández de la Fuente and Doña María Duran de Chaves. They mortgaged a house of posts and tiles on this side of the Río de Toyogres.

Don José de Guzmán and his wife Doña Antonia de Echavarría Navarro obligated themselves to Capitán Manuel García Argueta for 100 pesos. This was a settlement for a lawsuit García had pursued against Cayetana, a mulatto enslaved woman belonging to Guzmán and Echavarría Navarro. The debt was cancelled in 1721.

people_involved: Capitán Francisco de la Madriz Linares
Don Pedro Rodríguez de San Martín
summary: Domingo García de Estrada, with Capitán Francisco de la Madriz Linares as guarantor, obligated themselves to Don Pedro Rodríguez de San Martín for 460 pesos. This amount was to be paid the following year in Santiago de Alanje with 22 tame mules, some for saddle, valued at 21 pesos each. Don Pedro Rodríguez de San Martín was a resident of Cartago and a resident of Panamá.

people_involved: Licenciado Don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
Licenciado Don Juan de Guevara de la Cerda
summary: Licenciado Don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, a presbyter and Consultor of the Holy Office for the Supreme Court of Mexico, sold three enslaved people to Licenciado Don Juan de Guevara de la Cerda, a resident of the town of Nicaragua.

A transaction occurred involving María, aged 50, and her children Ventura, 12, and Baltasara, 7, who were owned by Juan Fernández de la Fuente and the deceased María Duran de Chaves. Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, acting as María Duran de Chaves's executor, was the grantor in this transaction, which was valued at 600 pesos.
On October 7, 1711, Guevara de la Cerda entered into an obligation with Gaspar Cascante de Rojas for 400 pesos.

On October 11, 1711, Alférez Pedro de Moya attempted to lease a cacao plantation in Matina with 1600 trees to Teodomiro Arias for three years at 220 pesos. The transaction did not proceed because the guarantor, Don Alvaro de Guevara, refused to sign due to a dispute.

On October 13, 1711, the will of Ana Velásquez, originally granted on January 22, 1701, was opened at the request of her son, Captain Diego de Aguilar. The will revealed details about her family and a past legal issue involving her son Severino, who was imprisoned by Alcalde Sebastián de Zamora.

On October 18, 1711, a dowry letter was prepared for Alférez Antonio de la Riva Agüero and his fiancée, Catarina de Arburola y Ribarén, ahead of their marriage on the 19th. The dowry, totaling 2187 pesos, included 50 head of cattle and 600 cacao trees located in Matina.

On October 23, 1711, Alférez Pedro de Moya, José Antonio Bermúdez, and Antonio de Ángulo each guaranteed 250 pesos for Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina. Serrano de Reina had been appointed treasurer to replace three previous guarantors who were deemed insolvent.
On November 4, 1711, Ayudante José de Chavarría and his guarantor, José Murillo, committed to pay Captain Alvaro de Guevara 100 pesos. This payment was to be made in cacao.

On November 7, 1711, Antonio de Alvarado's will was recorded. He was the legitimate son of José de Alvarado and Petronila Retes, married to Juana de Aguirre, and had nine children. His executors were Jerónimo Remigio de Aguirre and his wife, Juana de Aguirre.

On November 8, 1711, the will of Gertrudis de Chavarría Navarro was recorded. She was the legitimate daughter of Captain Juan de Chavarría Navarro and Ana de Retes, and the widow of Jorge de Alvarado. Her will listed her three daughters and mentioned her brother-in-law, José Pérez de Muro, who was married to her deceased sister Mariana.

people_involved: Juan López de la Rea y Soto
summary: On November 10, 1711, Juan López de la Rea y Soto, majordomo of the Cofradía de la Pura y Limpia Concepción, sold a cacao plantation in Matina to Sargento Francisco de Loaiza for 100 pesos. The Cofradía had acquired the plantation from the deceased Ayudante Juan de Piedra due to a debt, and the sale was carried out under the order of Visitador Licenciado Cosme Damián Suárez.

On November 10, 1711, the justice system placed the minor Francisco de Grado, aged 12-14 and son of María Méndez, with José de Vanegas, a master shoemaker. Francisco was to be apprenticed for a year and a half to learn the shoemaking trade.

On November 12, 1711, Simón Muñiz's will was recorded. He was the legitimate son of Juan Muñiz and María de Espinosa, and married to Águeda Rodríguez, daughter of Sargento Manuel Rodríguez and Gertrudis de Alarcón, with no direct heirs. His will mentioned his niece Juana de la Fuente, a child he raised named Manuel Muñiz, and his niece María Méndez.

On November 13, 1711, Licenciado Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, acting as the executor for María Duran de Chaves, sold a cattle ranch to Captain Alvaro de Guevara for 300 pesos. The property, located in the Curriravá valley at Mata Redonda, included a house, corrals, and 100 head of cattle.
On November 15, 1711, Don Alvaro de Guevara obligated himself to Don Gregorio de Moya for 200 pesos. He used the Mata Redonda site, which he had recently acquired, as collateral for this debt.

locations: Nuestra Señora de la Soledad hermitage
people_involved: Juan López de la Rea y Soto
summary: On November 20, 1711, Juan López de la Rea y Soto, majordomo of the Cofradía de la Concepción, sold two plots of land to Mateo de Quirós for 400 pesos. The plots, previously belonging to Isabel Carillo and mortgaged to the Cofradía, were sold because her co-heirs, Alférez Antonio Calderón and Juana Carrillo, refused to pay the annuity, and the sale was ordered by Visitador Juárez.

On November 22, 1711, Alférez Tomás de Chaves sold an enslaved 38-year-old Creole man named José de Ibarra, originally from Panama, to Fernando Faro for 200 pesos. José de Ibarra had previously been purchased by Tomás de Chaves from Captain Juan Antonio Bogarín, a resident of Esparza.

On November 22, 1711, Mateo de Quirós and his wife Antonia López obligated themselves to the Cofradía de la Concepción for 400 pesos. They mortgaged the plots of land they had purchased from the Cofradía on November 20th as security for this obligation.

people_involved: Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balón
summary: On November 22, 1711, Captain Antonio de la Vega Cabral sold two enslaved Mina-caste women, Manuela and Josefa (both 12 years old), and a 7-year-old enslaved boy named Francisco to his sister, Catarina González Camino, for 750 pesos. He had acquired Manuela and Josefa from Governor Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balón, and Francisco from Pedro José Sáenz.

On November 23, 1711, María del Camino, widow of Alférez Juan de Rojas, along with Captain Pedro de Torres as guarantor, obligated themselves to her minor son, Pedro de Rojas, for 292 pesos. This sum represented his paternal inheritance.

people_involved: Angela de la Paz y Flores
summary: On November 23, 1711, Doña Angela de la Paz y Flores, a widow, sold some houses to Don Alvaro de Guevara for 350 pesos, to be paid as an annuity and tribute. The record of this transaction is incomplete.

people_involved: Padre Guardián del Convento de San Francisco
summary: Sargento Mayor Blas González Coronel, widower of Doña Bernarda de Fonseca, founded a chaplaincy for recited masses. The endowment of 2200 pesos was secured by two cacao plantations in Matina and Tuis. His son, Manuel González Coronel, was named the first chaplain and patron, with the children of Francisco Martínez and Lorenza Venegas designated as future chaplains.

people_involved: Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín
summary: Lieutenant Domingo García de Estrada and his wife, Doña Catarina González Correa, committed to an obligation of 190 pesos in favor of the provincial Governor, Don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín.

Alférez Teodomiro Arias, son of Captain Alonso Arias and Doña Mariana de Sandoval, established a dowry letter for his wife, Doña Francisca Escalante Paniagua. The dowry, totaling 776 pesos, was delivered by Doña Francisca's brother, Licenciado Don Manuel de Escalante Paniagua.

people_involved: Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín
summary: Lieutenant Don Antonio de Utrera y Medina and his wife Doña Josefa de Moya sold a house inherited by Josefa from her father, Don Antonio de Moya, to Licenciado Don Francisco de Rivas y Velazco for 1130 pesos. The sale involved settling various debts owed to several chaplaincies, which Josefa had been obligated to with her first husband, Captain Don José de Vivas.

people_involved: Padre Guardián del Convento de San Francisco
summary: Doña Micaela Duran de Chaves, widow of Captain Alonso Romero, made her will, bequeathing freedom to her slaves María and her son Tomás upon her death, and offering freedom to Juan Toribio for 450 pesos. She also left a cattle ranch and houses in Mata Redonda to Juan Duran, and mandated the founding of a chaplaincy at the altar of Nuestra Señora del Trono in the Convento de San Francisco.

Don Antonio de Utrera y Medina and his wife Doña Josefa de Moya committed to an obligation of 99 pesos 3 reales and 3/4 in favor of the minor children of Juana de Villalobos, Juan and Nicolasa. This debt originated from Josefa's obligations with her first husband, Don José de Vivas, as per a 1701 document.

Don Antonio de Utrera y Medina and Doña Josefa de Moya undertook an obligation of 166 pesos 5 reales to the minor children of the deceased Juan de Villalobos and Gertrudis Ricardo. This debt was also from Josefa's time with her first husband, Don José Vivas.

Don Antonio de Utrera y Medina and Doña Josefa de Moya became obligated for 478 pesos to Don José Fernando, minor son of Sargento Mayor Don Antonio de Moya and Doña Isabel de Alvarado. This debt, which Josefa owed with her first husband Don José de Vivas, was cancelled by the creditor in 1720.

Don Antonio de Utrera y Medina and Doña Josefa de Moya committed to an obligation of 500 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Doña Josefa de Moya, with Licenciado Don Juan Antonio de Moya as patron and chaplain. This debt, which Josefa owed with her first husband Don José de Vivas, was secured by a house, corrals, and livestock in San José de Tenorio.

Don Antonio de Utrera y Medina and Doña Josefa de Moya undertook an obligation of 300 pesos to the heirs of Francisco de Chaves, a merchant from Spain. This money, originally charged to Presbítero Licenciado Don Juan Antonio de Moya, was later transferred to Captain Juan Sancho de Castañeda.
Feliciana de Chinchilla, a widow, leased a cacao plantation in Matina to Francisco Cordero for 165 pesos per year for a period of three years.

Sargento Mayor Don Antonio López del Corral leased a cacao plantation in Matina to Captain Gaspar de Acosta Arévalo for an additional two years, extending a previous agreement from 1708. Doña Josefa de Aguilar acted as guarantor for the lessee.
Mariajia González, a widow, incurred an obligation of 181 pesos in favor of Don Alvaro de Guevara, though the document was not signed.

Captain Don Alvaro de Guevara sold a cattle ranch in Mata Redonda, which he had acquired from the estate of Doña Micaela Duran de Chaves, to Licenciado Don Diego de Ángulo Gascón for 300 pesos. The buyer was to use 200 pesos to cover a debt to Don Gregorio de Moya.

Captain Don José de Mier Cevallos and his wife Doña Catarina González Camino sold a 24-year-old Fulupo slave named Felipe to Sargento Mayor Don Blas González Coronel for 400 pesos. Catarina had inherited Felipe from her first husband, Captain Don Cristóbal Martín Cubero, and the sale was applied to her dowry.

Alférez don Sebastián de Garita leased a cacao plantation with 2000 trees in Matina to Francisco Martínez for four years. The rent was set at 50 pesos for the first year, 100 for the second, and 125 for the remaining two years.

Licenciado don Diego Ángulo Gascón assumed a 200-peso obligation to don Gregorio de Moya, a debt previously held by don Antonio de Guevara. This obligation was later cancelled in 1722 by don Juan Francisco de Ibarra, acting as the executor for Br. don Gregorio de Moya.

Don Gil de Alvarado and his wife, doña Josefa González Camino, obligated themselves for 220 pesos to the capellanía founded by Juan Alonso. This debt was associated with a house donated to them by doña Manuela de Salazar, their mother, located south of the Convent and Royal Jail.

people_involved: Licenciado don Juan Antonio de Moya
summary: Don Gil de Alvarado and doña Josefa González Camino acknowledged a 100-peso debt to the capellanía founded by Vasco Solano. Licenciado don Juan Antonio de Moya was serving as the interim chaplain for this capellanía.

people_involved: Don Alonso Bernabé Cabeza de Vaca
summary: Alférez Antonio Rodríguez sold a three-year-old mulatto slave named Nicolás to Francisco Cartín for 100 pesos. Rodríguez had previously purchased Nicolás from don Alonso Bernabé Cabeza de Vaca and his wife, doña Juana de Moya.

Cura Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón and Sarjento Mayor Francisco López Conejo appointed Licenciado don Manuel López Conejo as chaplain for the capellanía founded by Pedro Ibáñez. Don Manuel López Conejo is the legitimate son of Francisco López Conejo and doña María de Quirós.

A dowry letter was issued for Lorenzo Martínez, a native of Huelva, Spain, son of Blas López and Catarina Real, in favor of his wife, Josefa de Chaves. Josefa is the legitimate daughter of Alférez Tomás de Chaves and Juana Paula Solís, and their marriage was scheduled for May 18th with a dowry of 1263 pesos.

people_involved: Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reyna
Don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reyna sold a cacao plantation in Matina, which was part of his deceased wife's dowry, to Capitán don José de Bonilla for 700 pesos. The property was encumbered with debts to various entities, which Don José de Bonilla and his wife doña Manuela Sáenz agreed to assume.

Capitán José de Bonilla and his wife, doña Manuela Sáenz, committed to a 100-peso obligation to the capellanía of Francisco Enciso Hita. They mortgaged their house, located immediately next to the Toyogres river, as collateral.
Capitán José de Bonilla and doña Manuela Sáenz further obligated themselves for 200 pesos to the Cofradía de la Concepción. This obligation was secured with the same guarantee as their previous debt.

On the same day, José de Bonilla and doña Manuela Sáenz incurred a 400-peso obligation to the Convento de San Francisco in Cartago. They used the same house as collateral for this debt as for their previous obligations.

Juan de Quesada, son of the late Alférez Alonso de Quesada and María López Rubio, made his will. He was a widower of Juana Román, with whom he had a son, Manuel de Quesada, and was currently married to Margarita Solano without children. He named his nephew, Alférez Luis Gutiérrez, as an executor and directed that the remainder of his estate be given to Fray Andrés Torres Capelazo.

Sarjento Mayor Blas González Coronel took on a 250-peso obligation to the capellanía founded by Pedro Ibáñez. This debt was tied to a house he had purchased from don José de Mier Cevallos and his wife, doña Catarina González Camino.
The following day, Blas González Coronel incurred another obligation, this time for 150 pesos, to the capellanía founded by don Miguel de Alvarado.

Don Agustín de Alvarado, natural son of Capitán don Pedro de Alvarado, made his will. He was married to doña Antonia de Acosta Arévalo, with whom he had two children, Antonia Josefa and Pedro. His estate included a cacao plantation in Matina and two 15-year-old slaves, Manuel and Magdalena, and he also mentioned his brother, don Gregorio de Alvarado, and an orphan he raised, José de Alvarado.

people_involved: Doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar
summary: Doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar, natural daughter of the late doña María de Aguilar and widow of Antonio de Acosta Arévalo, made her will. She listed her seven children, noting their paternal inheritance, and specified that her daughters Cayetana, Antonia, and Francisca were married to Juan Fernández Martínez, don Agustín de Alvarado, and don Gregorio de Alvarado, respectively. She also requested freedom for her pardo slave, Juan, and addressed an unfulfilled obligation to found a capellanía from her deceased husband's estate.

people_involved: Doña Inés de Sandoval Ocampo Golfín
Don Miguel de Santiago y Alvear
Don José de Toledo y Gudiño
summary: Doña Inés de Sandoval Ocampo Golfín, widow of Gil de Alvarado who died in Panama, granted power of attorney to don Miguel de Santiago y Alvear and don José de Toledo y Gudiño. Their task was to collect 5115 pesos from her deceased husband's estate, representing her dowry brought into the marriage.

people_involved: Licenciado don Juan Antonio de Moya
summary: Alférez don Francisco de Moya, along with Manuel de Soto and his wife Nicolasa Cayetana de Moya as heirs, obligated themselves for 300 pesos to don Gregorio de Moya. This sum represented don Francisco's inheritance from his deceased parents, don Esteban de Moya and doña Rafaela de Alvarado. They mortgaged property in Ujarrás, including a house, trapiche, and cattle, with Licenciado don Juan Antonio de Moya and Capitán don Pedro de Moya as guarantors.
Sarjento Mayor don Antonio began the process of writing his testament. The provided text ends before the testament's full details are revealed.
López del Corral, a native of Madrid, owns a cacaotal in Matina and has two slaves, Sebastiana (pardo) and Miguel (negro). His house is burdened with 1400 pesos for various capellanías.

people_involved: Capitán Juan de Noarbe y Osejo
summary: López del Corral is owed 244 pesos by don Francisco Gabriel de Bustamante, Alcalde Mayor of San Bartolomé de Nicoya, and 74 pesos by Marcela, widow of Bonifacio de Luna. He also has accounts with don Francisco Duque de Estrada of Esparza and Capitán Juan de Noarbe y Osejo of León, Nicaragua.

people_involved: don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina
summary: López del Corral names don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina and his wife, doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco, as his executors (albaceas).
Don Pedro de Moya leases a cacaotal with 1600 trees in Matina to Alférez Teodomiro Arias for two years at 220 pesos annually.

Doña Antonia de Acosta Arévalo, widow of don Agustín de Alvarado, sells a cacaotal in Matina with a thousand trees, bordering Madre de Dios, to don Gregorio de Alvarado for 900 pesos. Don Agustín had owed the buyer 800 pesos, and the remaining amount was received by Doña Antonia.

people_involved: Capitán don Alonso de Aranda y Acevedo
summary: Capitán don Alonso de Aranda y Acevedo, a bachelor and native of Zamora (Castilla la Vieja), son of Santiago de Aranda and doña Beatriz de Acevedo, makes his will. He designates Alférez Basilio Picado as his executor to distribute his assets according to his instructions.

Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya, a minor cleric, grants general power of attorney to Capitán Juan Francisco de Ibarra for lawsuits and administration. Moya states he is preparing to travel to León de Nicaragua to continue his studies for the priesthood, and may also need to go to Santiago de Guatemala or other places, thus also empowering Ibarra to make a will on his behalf.

people_involved: Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Capitán Juan Francisco de Ibarra obligates himself for 400 pesos to a capellanía founded by Capitán José de Vargas Machuca, whose patron is don Gil de Alvarado and interim Capellán is Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas. Ibarra mortgages a cacaotal in Matina that he purchased from Capitán Gaspar de Acosta.

people_involved: Teniente Juan López de la Rea y Soto
Licenciado don Manuel López de la Rea y Soto
summary: Alférez don Sebastián de Garita and his wife doña Margarita de Aguiar obligate themselves for 120 pesos to a capellanía founded by Comisario Baltasar de Grado. The capellanía's patron is Teniente Juan López de la Rea y Soto, and its Capellán is Licenciado don Manuel López de la Rea y Soto. They mortgage their house on the calle real, which already has other encumbrances.

people_involved: Capitán don Antonio de Soto Barahona
summary: Sarjento Mayor Juan de Zavaleta and his wife doña Antonia de Hoces Navarro sell their right to a house and solar in Cartago to Capitán don Antonio de Soto Barahona for 250 pesos.

people_involved: Capitán don Antonio de Soto Barahona
summary: Capitán don Antonio de Soto Barahona purchases a right in a house and solar from don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí and his wife doña Gracia de Hoces Navarro for 250 pesos.

Doña Gertrudis de Chavarría Navarro, widow of don Jorge de Alvarado (who died in Panamá), grants power of attorney to Capitán don José de Quesada. This power enables him to represent her in the division of assets among her deceased husband's creditors and to assert her dower rights.

people_involved: Capitán don Diego Vásquez Montiel y Coronado
R. P. Predicador fray Fernando Ortiz de Aldana
summary: Bernardo Cortés gives power of attorney to Capitán don Diego Vásquez Montiel y Coronado of Granada, Nicaragua, to reclaim 85 pesos from Capitán Francisco de Vargas, also from Granada. Vargas had received this money in Panamá from Capitanes don Jacinto de Pasos and don Francisco Duque de Estrada. The collected sum is to be delivered to R. P. Predicador fray Fernando Ortiz de Aldana, Síndico General of the Franciscans in Nicaragua, to whom Cortés owes money.
Capitán don Miguel Calvo donates a 5-year-old mulato blanco slave named Blas, son of his mulata slave Catalina, to his natural daughter Feliciana Calvo.

people_involved: Maese de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdova
Capitán don Diego de Barros y Carvajal
Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
summary: Maese de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdova and his wife doña Águeda Pérez de Muro, along with Capitán don Diego de Barros y Carvajal and his wife doña Josefa Pérez de Muro, receive their inheritance from Capitán don José Pérez de Muro, their father/father-in-law. The Casasola couple receives 7454 pesos, and the Barros couple receives 6432 pesos, as part of their paternal and maternal inheritance following the death of doña Mariana de Chavarría Navarro, wife of Pérez de Muro.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego de Campos Quirós
summary: Doña Bárbara Rodríguez Altamirano, daughter of the deceased Capitán Antonio Rodríguez Moreno and doña Inés de Benavides, and widow of Teniente Pedro de Campos Quirós, makes her will. She names her children doña Agustina, the deceased Licenciado don Diego de Campos Quirós, and doña María de Campos Quirós. She also grants freedom to her negra slave Isabel due to her age and services, along with Isabel's children and grandchildren: Manuel, Dionisia, Juana, Miguel, Cayetano, María, José Manuel, and Francisco.

people_involved: Presbítero Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Francisco Martínez provides a bond for costs to Sarjento Mayor Blas González Coronel in a lawsuit against Presbítero Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas concerning certain lands located in the valley of Aserrí.
José Gamboa sells a 12-year-old negra slave named Teresa, who was raised in his household, to hermano José Hidalgo for 100 pesos.

people_involved: Licenciado Presbítero don Juan Antonio de Moya
Licenciado Presbítero don Manuel de Guzmán
summary: Licenciado Presbítero don Juan Antonio de Moya grants general power of attorney for lawsuits and administration to Licenciado Presbítero don Manuel de Guzmán.

people_involved: Licenciado Presbítero don Juan Antonio de Moya
Licenciado Presbítero don Manuel de Guzmán
summary: Licenciado Presbítero don Juan Antonio de Moya, being close to a trip to Nicaragua, grants power to Licenciado Presbítero don Manuel de Guzmán to make his will, naming his sister doña Polonia de Moya as his heir.

people_involved: Licenciado Presbítero don Manuel de Guzmán
summary: Doña Laureana López de Chaves's dowry from her first marriage to Alférez Tomás de Umaña included a site in Curridavá with houses, burdened by a chaplaincy founded by Francisco de Paz, currently served by Licenciado Presbítero don Manuel de Guzmán. An obligation of 80 pesos was made in her favor, related to a deed by the deceased Francisco de Alfaro, previously managed by her deceased parents, Alférez Diego López de Ortega and Doña Ana de Chaves.

Doña Nicolasa de Morales Miranda granted power of attorney to Capitán Miguel Antonio de Luna, who was residing in Cartago and departing for Villa de los Santos in Tierra Firme. The purpose was to sell her 24-year-old mulatto slave, Ignacio, a shoemaker born in the house of her deceased mother, Doña Beatriz Méndez Machado, widow of Ayudante Juan de Morales Miranda.
Doña Angela María de Arleguí donated a slave named Diego José, son of her slave Victoria, to her natural son, José Antonio de Arleguí.
Doña Angela María de Arleguí sold a one-year-old slave named Antonia Josefa, daughter of her slave María and born in her own house, to Capitán Gabriel Maroto for 100 pesos.

people_involved: Doña Francisca de Guzmán y Benavente
Capitán Juan Gómez de Ocón y Trillo
summary: Doña Francisca de Guzmán y Benavente, widow of Alférez Juan Bautista Lizondo, sold 900 cacao trees in Barvilla, near the Matina valley, to Capitán Juan Gómez de Ocón y Trillo for 1350 pesos.

people_involved: Capitán Juan Gómez de Ocón y Trillo
Doña Francisca de Guzmán y Benavente
summary: Capitán Juan Gómez de Ocón y Trillo obligated himself to Doña Francisca de Guzmán y Benavente for 1350 pesos. This included payments to her daughters Eugenia, Francisca Lizondo, Catarina Lizondo, and her grandson Nicolás Camacho, with the remainder for Doña Francisca's lifetime support, clothing, and funeral expenses.

Manuel Padilla, a natural of Esparza, son of José de Padilla and María de Mendoza, and widower of Juana de Brenes, made his will. He named his daughter María Padilla as his heir and noted that 100 pesos, left by his father with Capitán Gutiérrez Jaramillo and later passed to Francisco Gutiérrez Jaramillo, were owed to him with 18 years of interest.

Doña Ana de Escalante Paniagua, a widow, leased a cacao plantation in Barvilla to Alférez Bernabé de Segura for three years at 125 pesos annually. Segura's wife, Doña Juana Damiana de Flores, also obligated herself for the payment.
The Justice assigned Francisco, a 12-year-old mestizo minor and son of Gregoria de Villarreal, to master Gregorio de Umaña for six years as an apprentice.

people_involved: Licenciado Presbítero don Manuel de Escalante Paniagua
summary: Alférez José Antonio Bermúdez and his wife, Doña Baltasara de Escalante Paniagua, sold an adobe house with a tiled roof for 505 pesos to Licenciado Presbítero don Manuel de Escalante Paniagua and Alférez Teodomiro Arias. The sale covered obligations to various chaplaincies, including those of Tomás Calvo, Don Pedro de Alvarado (chaplain Don Hermenegildo de Alvarado), and Vasco Solano (chaplain Manuel López).

people_involved: Doña Josefa de los Santos y Torres
summary: Antonio de Chapuí, a native of Genoa, Spain, and son of the deceased Bartolomé de Chapuí and Magdalena Cosido, issued a dowry letter for his wife, Doña Josefa de los Santos y Torres. She is the legitimate daughter of Capitán Pedro de Torres and Doña María Meléndez, residents of Cartago. The dowry totaled 901 pesos 4 reales and included livestock, horses, land, and various personal items, with the marriage scheduled for the following Sunday.

Alférez José de Murillo, a native of Málaga and son of the deceased Don Manuel Murillo and Doña Ana de Espinoza, issued a dowry letter for his wife, Doña María de Quesada. She is the legitimate daughter of Alférez José de Quesada and the deceased Doña Francisca Sánchez, with a dowry of 1500 pesos.

people_involved: Maestro de sastre José de Salas
summary: The Justice assigned Antonio, a 12-year-old orphan minor, to master tailor José de Salas for six years as an apprentice.
Francisco de Proa, legitimate son of José de Proa and Gregoria de Acosta, and a bachelor, made his will. He named his soul as his heir and mandated the founding of a chaplaincy for masses.
Doña Juana de Aguilar, a widow, sold a cacao plantation with 300 trees in the Reventazón valley to Ayudante Nicolás de Estrada for 100 pesos.
Juana de Proa, wife of Atanasio de Oviedo (who was incapacitated in bed), leased a cacao plantation in Matina to Nicolás de Briones for two years at 75 pesos annually.

Doña Andrea Calderón, widow of Alférez Pedro Martínez de Colina, obligated herself for 800 pesos to Ana, Josefa, María, and Isidora, her husband's minor natural daughters. Her attorney, Don Sebastián de Garita, successfully requested the adjudication of the family home, sugar mill, and cane fields in Barba valley to Doña Andrea, contingent on her fulfilling this obligation.

Doña Andrea Calderón acknowledges a debt of 500 pesos to the Capellanía founded by her deceased husband, Pedro Martínez de Colina. This debt is likely part of a larger sum of 1300 pesos (800 + 500) for which Captain Francisco Javier de Segura and Alférez Luis Morera acted as guarantors.

Juana Calderón, a widow, obligates herself for 150 pesos to the capellanía founded by doña Juana de Vida Martel. The money was delivered by the capellanía's executor, Captain Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribaren, and Juana hypothecates her house in Cartago as collateral.

Alférez don Pedro Florencio del Aguilla and his wife doña Margarita López de la Flor obligate themselves for 739 pesos to don José Ramón. This sum represents José Ramón's paternal inheritance from his legitimate father, Captain don Francisco de Nogüera y Moncada, who was doña Margarita's first husband.

Hermano Francisco de Aguirre, as the dative executor of Alférez Pedro Martínez de Colina, formally establishes a capellanía for masses with a capital of 500 pesos, as per Colina's will. Licenciado don Gregorio de Moya is named as the first chaplain, replacing the deceased don Diego de Campos Quirós, and the 500 pesos are those previously acknowledged by doña Andrea Calderón.

Alférez José de Morillo, a native of Málaga, makes his will. He is the legitimate son of the deceased don Manuel Morillo and doña Ana de Espinoza, and is married to doña María de Quesada, daughter of Alférez José de Quesada and the deceased doña Francisca Sánchez, with no children yet.

Doña Catarina de Vida Martel, a widow, sells a 20-year-old 'negro bozal' slave named Pedro, of Mina ethnicity, to Alférez José Antonio Bermúdez for 400 pesos. She had previously acquired Pedro from Captain Juan Francisco de Ibarra.

Diego Chacón, natural son of the deceased Alférez Francisco Alarcón Chacón, makes his will, listing his deceased wife Jerónima de Peñaranda and their numerous children, some also deceased. His daughters Francisca and Ana are named as heirs, and his son-in-law Gaspar Solano and grandson Pedro de Salas are appointed as executors.

Alférez José Antonio Bermúdez and his wife doña Baltasara Escalante Paniagua obligate themselves for 400 pesos to doña Catarina de Vida Martel. They hypothecate a cacao plantation in Barbilla, containing 2000 trees, as collateral for this debt.
Doña Margarita López de la Flor grants general power of attorney to her husband, don Pedro Florencio del Águila, for legal and administrative matters.

Alférez Baltasar Ramírez, legitimate son of Teniente Salvador Ramírez and Magdalena Milanés, makes his will. He is married to Manuela de Segura, lists their five children, and mentions his brother Antonio de Segura, noting he owns livestock in Chomes.

people_involved: Juan López de la Rea y Soto
summary: The Cabildo, justice, and Regiment of Cartago, including several prominent officials like Sarjento Mayor Blas González Coronel and Maese de campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba, grant general power of attorney for lawsuits to Juan López de la Rea y Soto.

Doña Magdalena Pérez de Luna, residing in the valley of Barba, makes her will. She is married to Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín and lists their children, including her deceased son José and her daughter Josefa, who is married to Juan García de Adán.

locations: ermita de San Nicolás de Tolentino
summary: Don Manuel Sendín de Sotomayor and his wife doña Ana Josefa de Guevara sell a plot of land to Ayudante Nicolás de Estrada for 50 pesos. The land is located bordering the hermitage of San Nicolás de Tolentino to the North.
Gabriel Lobo and his wife Micaela de Echavarría sell a house constructed of posts and mud, with a straw roof, along with half of its solar, to Jerónimo Pacheco for 50 pesos.

people_involved: Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín
summary: Captain Manuel García de Argueta grants power of attorney to Captain Pedro Castilla, who is departing for Panamá, to sell two enslaved men named Juan and Antonio, both appearing to be over 19 years old. These slaves were previously purchased from the former governor, don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín.

Sarjento Baltasar de Mora, natural son of the deceased Juan de Mora, makes his will. He is married to Lucrecia Martínez Enríquez and lists his numerous children, including Inés, María, and Simona, who are married, along with several other unmarried children.

Alférez Tomás de Chaves clarifies the terms of a capellanía he founded on August 28, 1710, with 1000 pesos secured by properties near Cartago. He reiterates that his son, José de Chaves, is the first chaplain, but adds a stipulation that if his son is not ordained, the capellanía should pass to the local convent.
Juana Paula de Solís, legitimate daughter of the deceased Francisco de Solís and Antonia López, makes her will. She is married to an Alférez whose name is incomplete in the record.

Alférez Salvador Morillo and his wife Clara de Esquivel made their testament. They declared no children and Salvador was the tutor of his brother Jerónimo Murillo, holding 400 pesos for him. They bequeathed half a house in Cartago to their niece Juana Valerino, or to María Josefa if Juana died before marriage, and mandated the founding of a capellanía.

Gonzalo Martín and his wife Josefa de Chaves sold a piece of land, which was part of Josefa's dowry from her father Alférez Tomás de Chaves, to José de Quirós for 150 pesos. The land, located in Río Grande, Esparza, included 100 cattle.

Doña Sebastiana de Bonilla, a widow, sold a room in her adobe and tile house in Cartago to Doña Francisca de Astúa, also a widow, for 150 pesos. The house, which Doña Francisca de Astúa and Doña Josefa de Bonilla already possessed parts of, bordered the Ermita del Señor San Juan Evangelista.

Doña Francisca de Astúa, a widow, obligated herself for 150 pesos to the capellanía founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela, for which Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas served as patron and chaplain. This obligation was secured by the house she had purchased from Doña Sebastiana de Bonilla.

María de Inarte, a widow, sold her share in a cattle ranch in Río Segundo, Valle de Barba, to Pedro de Arroyo for 70 pesos. This land had been previously acquired by María and her deceased husband, Salvador Cordero, from Agustín de Arrieta, and bordered properties belonging to Doña Catalina de Inarte and Doña Ana de Guevara, as well as the royal road from Cartago to Esparza. She was responsible to the Cofradía del Santísimo Sacramento for this amount.
Pedro de Arroyo and his wife Manuela Gallegos obligated themselves for 70 pesos to the Cofradía del Santísimo Sacramento in Cartago, referencing the terms of the previous land sale.

people_involved: Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín
