summary: Maese de Campo don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín, serving as Governor and Captain General, granted general power of attorney to Capitán don Diego Rodríguez Meléndez, who was a royal treasury official in Santiago de Guatemala.

Doña Josefa de Aguilar, a widow, leased a cacao plantation in Matina to Capitán Juan Francisco de Ibarra for one year at a price of 265 pesos. This document was executed before don Francisco López Conejo, the Lieutenant Governor for political affairs.

Basilio Picado, a resident of León, sold an enslaved man named Francisco de Santiago, a 30-year-old Congo, to Capitán Juan Francisco de Ibarra for 400 pesos. Francisco de Santiago was part of the estate of the deceased Capitán don Alonso de Aranda y Acevedo, for whom Basilio Picado was the executor. The transaction was notarized by don Francisco López Conejo.

Sarjento Juan Masís made his testament, identifying his deceased parents, wife Francisca Barbosa, and children: José, Miguel, Francisca, and Juan. He noted his deceased daughter Francisca was married to Alférez Tomás de Chaves. His assets included houses in Cartago, a cacao plantation in Barbilla with 1200 trees, and several enslaved individuals. He mandated the founding of a capellanía with his Cartago house, naming his son José Masís as patron and his grandson José Felipe as future chaplain.

Doña Gertrudis de Chavarría Navarro, widow of don Jorge de Alvarado who died in Panamá, made her testament. She listed her deceased parents, her three daughters, her brother-in-law Don José Pérez de Muro, and nephews Manuel Antonio Arleguí and Don José de Alvarado. Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral was appointed as tutor for her daughter Doña Gertrudis.

Capitán Nicolás de Guevara sold an enslaved man named Manuel Antonio to Alférez Juan José Vásquez de Aguilar, a resident of Nicaragua, for 200 pesos. Manuel Antonio had been inherited by Nicolás from his mother, Doña Clara de Chavarría Navarro.

people_involved: Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín
summary: Maese de Campo don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín, Governor and Captain General, made his testament. He declared various debts to individuals in Pacaca, Cádiz, Santa Fe, Mompox, and Granada, and stated that the Royal Coffers of León owed him 3 years and 6 months of salary. He also declared holding the judicial review he conducted for don Manuel de Bustamante Vivero, don Francisco Serrano de Reina, don Diego de Herrera Campuzano, and other justices.

people_involved: Coronel don Francisco Serrano de Reina
Sárjenlo Mayor Francisco de la Madrid Linares
Francisco Antonio de Granda y Matta
summary: Juan González de Ochoa's will declares his assets, including three black slaves (Tomás, Antonio, Pedro), luxury clothing, weapons, furniture, and a house in Cartago bought from Doña Ana de Retes' succession. He mandates the freedom of his slave Juan upon his death and pledges 800 pesos and a pearl jewel to Nuestra Señora de Covadonga in Asturias. The will names Francisco de la Madrid Linares and Juan Sancho de Castañeda as executors, and his natural daughter, Antonia de Granda y Balvín, as his universal heir, and was granted in Ujarrás with several witnesses.

Lucrecia Martínez Enríquez, widow of Sárjenlo Baltasar de Mora, along with sureties Manuel de Mora and Juan Julián, obligates herself to her minor children Manuela, Juana, Juan, and Gertrudis. This obligation is for 161 pesos and 2 reales each, representing their paternal inheritance.

Capitán Manuel García de Argueta sells a 21-year-old black slave named Antonio, of Mina caste, to Gonzalo Martín for 300 pesos. García de Argueta had previously acquired the slave from Gobernador Granda y Balvín.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco Javier de Bustamante
summary: Alférez Tomás de Chaves, acting on behalf of Capitán don Francisco Javier de Bustamante, Alcalde Mayor of Nicoya, provides surety as a preferred creditor. This action pertains to the estate of Manuel de la Peña Muñoz, a deceased and intestate merchant in the province, and was granted before Blas González Coronel.

Juan Manuel Pérez de Espinoza and his surety, Alférez José Antonio Bermúdez, obligate themselves to Inés de Herrera for 100 pesos. The document was granted before Blas González Coronel, Teniente de Gobernador.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco Bruno Serrano da Reina
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco Bruno Serrano da Reina grants power to Alférez Melchor Toruno de Figueroa, a resident of León, Nicaragua, to sell an 18-year-old 'bozal' slave named Miguel, of Mina caste. Serrano da Reina had acquired this slave from Gobernador Granda y Balvín.

people_involved: Doña Micaela de Arburola y Ribaren
Capitán Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribaren
summary: Don Pedro Manuel de Moya grants a dowry (carta dote) of 2180 pesos to his wife, Doña Micaela de Arburola y Ribaren, the legitimate daughter of Capitán Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribaren and Doña Josefa de Hoces Navarro. The dowry includes 500 cacao trees, 16 sacks of cacao, and a solar in Cartago.

Capitán Juan Francisco de Ibarra sells a cacao plantation in Matina, containing 500 trees, to Francisco Morales for 140 pesos. Ibarra had inherited this plantation from his deceased mother, Doña Francisca Calvo.

Juana de Acosta, a widow, sells a solar in Cartago, located on the Alameda street leading to Los Angeles, to Francisco Granados for 12 pesos. This solar was part of her dowry when she married Juan Antonio de Soto.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina
Capitán don José Mauricio Serrano de Reina
Coronel don Francisco Serrano de Reina
Doña Luisa Marina Serrano de Reina
Maese de Campo don Melchor de Acuña
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina and Capitán don José Mauricio Serrano de Reina, sons, executors, and heirs of the deceased Coronel don Francisco Serrano de Reina (former Governor and Captain General) and Doña Luisa Lizalde, grant power to Maese de Campo don Melchor de Acuña and Isidro Antonio Pranduna in Guatemala. This power is to collect three years of half-salary owed to their deceased father as governor, also acting on behalf of their sister, Doña Luisa Marina Serrano de Reina, who is in Sevilla.

An obligation for 150 pesos was made in favor of don Alvaro de Guevara, secured by a mortgage on mule beasts. The document was made before José de Morales, but the debtor's identity is missing due to torn pages.

people_involved: Don José de Casasola y Córdova
Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: A power of attorney, which was not concluded or signed, was granted by don José de Casasola y Córdova, Blas González Coronel, don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, and don Antonio de la Vega Cabral to Juan de Aspur of Panamá.

An unnamed individual declared their parentage as Lorenzo Domínguez and María de Espinoza. They also stated ownership of land in Agua Caliente and identified two of their children as Mariana and Miguel.

Gregorio de Alvarado's will was recorded. It clarified that he was the natural son of Pedro de Alvarado, brother of the deceased Agustín de Alvarado, and brother-in-law of Antonia de Acosta, leaving his son as his heir.

Sarjento Mayor Francisco de la Madriz Linares and his wife Manuela de Quirós incurred a debt of 646 pesos 4 reales to José de Mier Ceballos, with a four-month repayment period. This obligation was later cancelled in April 1713.

people_involved: Juan Matías (son of Francisca de Benavente)
Juan (deceased son of Francisca de Benavente)
Catalina (deceased daughter of Francisca de Benavente)
Juana (deceased daughter of Francisca de Benavente)
María (deceased daughter of Francisca de Benavente)
Juan Gómez de Ocón y Trillo
summary: Doña Francisca de Benavente, legitimate daughter of deceased Bartolomé de Benavente and Agustina de Quesada, and widow of Alférez Juan Matías Lizondo, made her will. She named her numerous children, including some who died young, and her son-in-law Captain Juan Gómez de Ocón y Trillo. She also bequeathed 23 pesos to Fray Antonio Espejo and mandated the founding of a chaplaincy with 1000 pesos.

José Masís and his wife Teodora de Molina obligated themselves to Gertrudis and Gregoria Ramírez, minor legitimate children of the deceased Alférez Baltasar Ramírez and Manuela de Segura, for 200 pesos given by their grandfather Salvador Ramírez. They mortgaged a cacao plantation in Barbilla with 600 trees as security.

people_involved: Manuel (son of Josefa de Hoces Navarro)
Catarina (daughter of Josefa de Hoces Navarro)
María (daughter of Josefa de Hoces Navarro)
Francisca (daughter of Josefa de Hoces Navarro)
Antonio de la Riva y Agüero
María (enslaved by Josefa de Hoces Navarro)
Juana (enslaved by Josefa de Hoces Navarro)
Magdalena (enslaved by Josefa de Hoces Navarro)
Salvador (enslaved by Josefa de Hoces Navarro)
Pedro (enslaved by Josefa de Hoces Navarro)
Francisco (enslaved by Josefa de Hoces Navarro)
Juan José (enslaved by Josefa de Hoces Navarro)
Antonio (enslaved by Josefa de Hoces Navarro)
summary: Doña Josefa de Hoces Navarro, legitimate daughter of deceased Alférez Esteban de Hoces Navarro and Juana Caho, and wife of Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribaren, made her will. She listed her eight children and mentioned that two of her daughters, Catarina and Rosa Micaela, were married to Antonio de la Riva y Agüero and Pedro Manuel de Moya, respectively. She also listed several enslaved people.

Eusebio Jiménez, acting as executor for Captain Juan Gregorio Ramírez of León, sold an enslaved man named José Tomás, 25 years old, to Captain Antonio de la Vega Cabral for 300 pesos. José Tomás had previously been purchased by Ramírez from Alférez José Calderón of Cartago.

Benito Várela, a native of Villagarcía in Galicia, Spain, made his will. He was the legitimate son of Alonso Várela and María de Villanra, and was married to Tomasina de Quirós, daughter of García de Quirós and Josefa Machado, with whom he had no children.

Bernardo Cortés, a resident of the Barba valley and native of Panamá, made his will. He was the natural son of deceased Juan Cortés and Magdalena García, and was widowed from Clara Morera, with whom he had no children. Clara had two daughters, María and Gregoria, from a previous relationship; María died leaving children Juan, Lucía, and Nicolasa, with Lucía married to Juan de la Falca and Nicolasa to Dionisio Hernández. Bernardo disinherited his grandson Juan for disobedience. He was remarried to Juana de Herrera, with whom he also had no surviving children. He listed several enslaved people, including Felipe, whom he ordered sold to fund a chaplaincy, with Licenciado José Nicolás de Guzmán as the first chaplain and his brother Licenciado Manuel de Guzmán as interim.

people_involved: María de Quirós (wife of Francisco López Conejo)
summary: Licenciado Manuel López Conejo, a cleric and chaplain of a chaplaincy founded by Comisario Baltasar de Grado, sold a house with its plot to Sarjento Mayor Francisco López Conejo, Lieutenant Governor. The house had a 260-peso lien in favor of the chaplaincy, and Francisco López Conejo, with his wife María de Quirós, obligated themselves to pay this sum as a perpetual annuity.

Alférez Andrés de Siles, legitimate son of Andrés de Siles and Isabel de Siles, natives of Córdoba, Spain, made his will. He was married to María de Chaves and listed their six children. His daughter Isabel was married to José de Ulloa, and Catalina to Domingo de Casares. He also mentioned his stepson, Captain Juan de Astúa.

Alférez José Antonio Bermúdez sold an enslaved man named Pedro, 26 years old, of 'mma' caste, to Captain Juan Francisco de Ibarra for 300 pesos. Bermúdez had previously acquired Pedro from Doña Catalina de Vida Martel.

Licenciado Juan Antonio de Moya, a presbyter, obligated himself for 449 pesos to Alférez Manuel de Selva Mayor, a resident of Granada and tutor of Doña María de Moya. María was the legitimate daughter of the deceased Sarjento Mayor Antonio de Moya and Juana Ruiz, former residents of Cartago. Juan Antonio de Moya mortgaged a cacao plantation in Matina with 2000 trees, which he inherited from his father, Sarjento Mayor Antonio de Moya.

people_involved: Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín
Antonio (enslaved by Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín)
summary: Captain Juan Sancho de Castañeda and his wife Juana de Alvarado obligated themselves to pay for an enslaved man named Antonio, 30 years old, of Angola caste, whom Castañeda acquired for 350 pesos from the estate of the deceased Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín. They also purchased clothing from the estate for 130 pesos 4.5 reales, totaling 480 pesos 4.5 reales, to be paid in cash and cacao respectively. The obligation was cancelled in 1716.
Captain Antonio de la Vega Cabral granted general power of attorney for lawsuits to Captain Sebastián Hurtado de Betancour, a resident of Guatemala and procurator of the Royal Audiencia.
Captain Gaspar de Acosta Arévalo sold a cacao plantation in Matina, containing 2000 trees, to Captain Juan Francisco de Ibarra.

A property with 300 fruit trees, adjacent to land owned by Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar, mother of the seller, was sold for 800 pesos. Of this amount, 400 pesos were designated for the chaplaincy of José de Vargas Machuca, which the buyer was obligated to acknowledge.

people_involved: Maese de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: The Cabildo, Justicia y Regimiento of the city, including Maese de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba (Alférez Mayor), Sarjentos Mayores Blas González Coronel (Alcalde Mayor Provincial de la Santa Hermandad), and don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín (Regidor), granted general judicial power to Alférez José de Morales.

Mateo Sánchez de Castañeda, a native of Billigar, Montañas de Burgos, and his wife Ana de Olivares, executed their testament. They listed their children: María, Catarina, Micaela, Gertrudis, Francisca, and Juan Sánchez, noting the marriages of María and Catalina. The testament also detailed their property, including a house near La Bermuda stream, and their slaves: Isabel (50, parda, to be freed upon their deaths), Gregorio (36), Baltasara (20), José (13), and Manuel (24, negro).

Capitán Juan Francisco de Ibarra granted power to Capitán don José de Castellano, a resident of Panamá, to sell a 30-year-old Congo slave named Francisco de Santiago. This slave had previously been sold to Ibarra by Alférez Basilio Picado.

people_involved: Capitán don Rodrigo de Gádea y Marrufo
summary: Doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco, a widow, leased a cacao plantation in Matina, containing over a thousand trees, to Alférez Luis Gutiérrez. This plantation was inherited from her deceased husband, Capitán don Rodrigo de Gádea y Marrufo, and the lease was for three years at an annual rent of 200 pesos.

people_involved: doña Francisca de Zúñiga y Sotomayor
summary: Capitán don Gregorio de Chaves executed his testament, detailing his parents, spouse Juana Hernández, and their seven children, including their spouses. He listed his property, which included a house, enclosures, and a sugar mill in Valle de Aserrí, along with a cattle ranch of 50 head in San Pablo. He also mentioned his slaves, Juan (pardo, 40) and Maximiliano (negro, criollo, 12), and appointed his son Juan de Chaves and Alférez Tomás de Chaves as executors.

Capitán Juan de Chaves, Mateo de Chaves, and Francisco de Chaves, sons of Capitán Gregorio de Chaves, obligated themselves to the Cofradía de la Vera Cruz for 385 pesos. They mortgaged their share of a house and enclosures in Valle de Aserrí, which their father had designated for them.

Alférez Antonio de Ángulo and his wife Josefa Fernández obligated themselves to the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora del Rosario, located in the parish church, for 50 pesos. They mortgaged their house on the main street, with Alférez don Pedro de Moya serving as the current mayordomo of the Cofradía.

people_involved: Síndico general del Convento de San Francisco
summary: Alférez Tomás de Chaves (son) acknowledged receiving 100 pesos from his father, Capitán Tomás de Chaves. In return, he was obligated to deliver 5 pesos annually in lard to the Síndico general del Convento de San Francisco, to be used for continuously lighting the lamp of the Santísimo Sacramento.

Capitán Tomás de Chaves (father) and his wife Juana Solís donated a cattle ranch (hato) in the jurisdiction of Esparza, beyond the Río Grande, to their son Alférez Tomás de Chaves. This donation was in gratitude for 300 pesos and other assistance, with the condition that the parents could extract 400 cattle from the hato and 25 large cattle annually for their sustenance. They also mentioned previous donations to other children and a later donation to their granddaughter María del Carmen.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco Javier de Bustamante y Melgar
summary: Capitán Tomás de Chaves (father) and his wife Juana Solís executed their testament, listing their children and their spouses, including María (married to Blas Suárez), Tomás (Alférez), María de la Rosa (married to José de Quirós), Rosa de Viterbo (married to Martín de Villaneda, then Pedro Lascares), Josefa (married to Martín González), José (studying in Guatemala), and Cristóbal. They detailed their assets, including a house, sugar mill, cane fields near Río Virilla, 300 cattle, mules, oxen, and a pasture in Tibás, as well as their slaves. They also declared a chaplaincy for their son José's studies in Guatemala and noted that the husband was preparing for a trip to León de Nicaragua, holding effects belonging to Capitán don Francisco Javier de Bustamante y Melgar, Alcalde Mayor of Nicoya.

people_involved: Maese de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Capitán Tomás de Chaves (father) and his son Alférez Tomás de Chaves obligated themselves to pay 350 pesos to the city's priests, a debt redeemed by Maese de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdova. The obligation was cancelled in 1721 after Pedro Rodríguez Palacio and his wife doña Teresa de Hoces Navarro took over the debt, leading to its cancellation by Licenciados Diego de Ángulo Gascón and Juan Antonio de Moya.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: Sarjento Mayor Francisco de la Madriz Linares and his wife doña Manuela de Quirós became depositaries of 600 pesos after purchasing two 'bozal' (newly arrived) slaves from the assets of Gobernador Granda y Balvín. The slaves were Tomás, a 30-year-old Angola negro, purchased for 300 pesos, and Pedro José, a 16-year-old Mina negro, also purchased for 300 pesos. A cancellation related to payments in a 'juicio de residencia' was noted in 1716.

Captain Antonio de Soto y Barahona and his wife, Doña Petronila de Hoces Navarro, committed to pay 150 pesos to the San Francisco Convent. This sum was provided to them by Captain Miguel Calvo, who served as the general syndic for the religious order.

people_involved: Josefa de los Santos y Torres
summary: Captain Pedro de Torres and his wife, Doña María Meléndez, made a commitment in favor of their minor grandson, Jose Antonio Chapuí. This obligation was for 596 pesos, representing his inheritance from his deceased father, Antonio Chapuí, and his mother, Doña Josefa de los Santos y Torres.

Captain Juan de Chaves granted freedom to his enslaved man, Nicolás de Villegas. Nicolás was described as a "pardo" (dark-skinned) man over 50 years old, whom Juan had inherited from his deceased father, Don Gregorio de Chaves.

Sergeant Major Francisco de la Madriz Linares and his wife, Doña Manuela de Quirós, exchanged haciendas with Captain Don José de Mier Cevallos and his wife, Doña Catarina González Camino. The Madriz couple traded an estancia near the Agua Caliente river and an enslaved mulato named Manuel Cedeño, while the Mier Cevallos couple traded an estancia in La Candelaria.

Alférez José Antonio Bermúdez leased a cacao plantation in the Barvilla valley to Captain Manuel García de Argueta for three years. Bermúdez owned the plantation jointly with his wife, Doña Baltasara Escalante Paniagua, who had acquired it from the estate of her second husband, Tomás Alvarez. The annual rent was 12 zurrones of prime cacao, to be delivered in Cartago.

Francisca Nicasia, widow of Atanasio de la Cruz, and Captain Antonio Solórzano as guarantor, obligated themselves to the minor children of Atanasio de la Cruz. This obligation was for 266 pesos, representing the paternal inheritance for each of the seven children, delivered by the estate's depositary, Captain Francisco Javier de Segura.

Don José de Baeza, a native of Antequera in New Spain, provided a dowry letter for his wife, Doña María Magdalena Maroto. The dowry, valued at 1624 pesos, included a plot of land, two enslaved women (Gertrudis and María Candelaria), 100 head of cattle, and a saddled mule.

Captain Don José de Mier Cevallos, who had successfully bid on an enslaved "negro bozal" named Antonio, ceded the auction to Maese de Campo Don Diego de Herrera y Campuzano for 250 pesos. Mier Cevallos had made the bid on commission for Herrera y Campuzano, for the enslaved man who was confiscated after being found lost in Matina.

Sergeant Miguel González leased a cacao plantation with 2000 trees in Barvilla to Alférez Manuel Antonio de Arleguí for two years at an annual price of 200 pesos. Miguel had received this plantation as a donation from his father, Sergeant Juan González de Ochoa. A marginal note from 1717 indicates Antonia González, as heir, acknowledged receipt of the cacaotal and rents.

people_involved: Josefa (daughter of José Pérez de Muro)
summary: Diligences for the opening of Captain José Pérez de Muro's testament, dated May 2, 1713, were conducted on May 11. The testament detailed his origins in Miranda de Arga, Navarra, his family (including deceased wife Mariana de Echavarría Navarro and daughters Josefa and Águeda), and his extensive estate, which included enslaved people, cacao plantations in Matina, and properties in "this city." He also mentioned his agent in Panamá, a pepper shipment from León, and a cacao grove established for his nephew, José de Velazco.
The testament of Simón Muñiz was recorded. Simón Muñiz was the legitimate son of Juan Muñiz and María de Espinosa, and had been married to Águeda de Santiago for over 34 years, with no children.

Captain Don José de Quesada, who had been in "this province" for over three years and was indebted to the deceased Doña Gertrudis de Chavarría Navarro, donated all sums owed to him by various people as a merchant to Doña Antonia de Alvarado, the legitimate daughter of Doña Gertrudis.

Pedro Rasero de Rojas gave a receipt to his father-in-law, Alférez Tomás de Chaves, for 105 pesos, covering a debt related to Martín de Avellaneda's death and a personal debt to the Bishop. The receipt also included a 10-year-old mulata, 5 mules, 100 cattle, and land at Río Grande and Río Virilla, all belonging to Pedro's wife, Rosa Viterbo de Chaves.
The testament of María de Sibaja, legitimate daughter of [parents not mentioned], was recorded.

A woman, whose parents were Baltasar de Ortega and Jerónima Gómez, is identified as the widow of Francisco López. She has a daughter, Francisca Victoria López, who has been married twice. The widow also raised a 5-year-old girl, María de la Candelaria, and owns a cacao plantation in Matina.

Alférez Andrés de Siles issued a codicil to his will, revoking a previous clause about his burial. Having recovered his health and promised to join the Third Order of Saint Francis, he now requests to be buried in the habit of the Order in its holy church in the city, with a simple burial.

Tomasa de Quirós, daughter of García de Quirós and Josefa Machado and widow of Benito Várela, made her will. She bequeathed the remainder of her assets, after mandates and debts, to Fray José de Roca, guardian of the Convent, for distribution as previously communicated.

Gobernador don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones arranged for José de Ortega, a 12-year-old orphan, to be apprenticed to master carpenter Lucas de Jesús for six years. During this time, Lucas de Jesús is to teach José de Ortega the carpentry trade.

people_involved: Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
Doña Juana Damiana de Mora Salado
Alférez Juan José Vásquez de Aguilar
summary: Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón, a prominent ecclesiastical official, sold his 52-year-old zambo slave named Baltasar to Alférez Bernabé de Segura for 200 pesos. Baltasar had previously been purchased by Gascón from Sarjento Mayor Francisco López Conejo. Bernabé de Segura and his wife, Doña Juana Damiana de Mora Salado, committed to the payment, with Alférez Juan José Vásquez de Aguilar acting as guarantor.

people_involved: Doña Juana Damiana de Mora Salado
Alférez Juan José Vásquez de Aguilar
summary: Alférez Bernabé de Segura and his wife, Doña Juana Damiana de Mora Salado, sold a 23-year-old mulata slave named Josefa to Alférez Juan José Vásquez de Aguilar for 450 pesos. Josefa had been part of Doña Juana Damiana de Mora Salado's dowry from her parents.

Alférez Teodomiro Arias and his wife, Doña Francisca de Escalante Paniagua, incurred a debt of 120 pesos to the Cofradía de la Concepción, received from its Mayordomo Capellán José Antonio Bermúdez. They mortgaged their house on the royal street as security for this obligation.

Capitán Diego Santiago de Cárdenas made his will, detailing his marriage to Doña Manuela Valerín and their five children. He also listed several slaves by name, color, and age, noting one, Gil de Salazar, had been a fugitive for over nine years. Additionally, he donated a plot of land to María del Carmen Sánchez, a girl he had raised.

Doña Juana de Aguiar, widow of Alférez Felipe Beimúdez, sold a house in the city to her son, Capitán José Antonio Bermúdez, for 1100 pesos. The buyer and his wife, Doña Baltasara de Escalante Paniagua, assumed responsibility for several chaplaincies associated with the property, benefiting Doña Gertrudis de Alvarado, Doña Sebastiana de Alvarailo, and Francisco de Enciso Hita.

people_involved: Capitán don Diego de Barros y Carvajal
summary: Capitán don Diego de Barros y Carvajal, his wife Doña Josefa Pérez de Muro, and Doña Águeda Pérez de Muro, acting as heirs of their father Don José Pérez de Muro, granted power of attorney to Don Gabriel de Uriola Echavarría, a resident of Panamá.

people_involved: Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina
summary: Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina granted general power of attorney to Don Antonio Parladorio, Capitán don Lucas Fernández Pardo, and Capitán Isidro Antonio Prandina, the latter residing in Santiago de Guatemala.

people_involved: Doña Jerónima de la Riva y Agüero
summary: Capitán Diego de Zamora, son of Sebastián de Zamora and Lucía de Ocampo Golfín, made his will. He was married to Doña Jerónima de la Riva y Agüero and had five children. He mentioned owning a house and enclosures built by his father, located about a league away, on land purchased from the Cofradía de la Concepción. His brother, Sarjento Mayor Antonio Aurelio Zamora, was named his executor.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Lacayo de Briones
Licenciado don Pedro Lacayo de Briones
summary: Sarjento Mayor José Antonio Lacayo de Briones, Justice Mayor and Captain General of the province, revoked a previous power of attorney sent from Granada to Madrid. He then re-granted it to his father, Licenciado don José Lacayo de Briones, and his brothers, Licenciado don Pedro Lacayo de Briones and Don Marcos Lacayo de Briones, authorizing them to seek a 2000-peso loan in Madrid, Viana, or elsewhere, payable in various cities.

Doña Francisca Jiménez, widow of Capitán Francisco Alvarez de Oviedo, and her guarantor Eusebio Jiménez, committed to pay 1033 pesos 5 reales to her minor legitimate daughters, Doña Gertrudis and Doña Manuela Alvarez de Oviedo, as their paternal inheritance.

Juan Fernández Martínez, originally from Sedaño, Burgos, and son of Agustín Fernández and María Martínez, made his will. He was married to Doña Cayetana de Acosta Arévalo, with whom he had five minor children. His assets included a cacao plantation in Matina with 900 trees and a city plot that was part of his wife's dowry.

people_involved: Presbítero Licenciado Juan Antonio de Moya
Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Moya
summary: Don Jerónimo Manuel Ramos and his wife, Doña María Polonia de Moya, received 256 pesos 4 reales 9 maravedís from Presbítero Licenciado Juan Antonio de Moya. This sum represented Doña María Polonia de Moya's share from the estate of her father, Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Moya, derived from the value of a cacao hacienda and a slave.

Capitán Alonso de Porras committed to an obligation in favor of José, Marcelo, Aurelia, and Cecilio de Alvarado, who are minor legitimate children of the deceased Domingo de Alvarado and Juana Cordero.
Capitán Juan Francisco de Ibarra granted power to Capitán Blas de Ancheta to sell a 13-year-old 'popo' slave named Juan. Ibarra had previously purchased this slave from Bernardo Pacheco.

Capitán Blas de Ancheta, using the power granted to him, sold the slave Juan to Don Diego de Barros y Carvajal. The purchase was made on behalf of Licenciado Don José Velazco Jiménez de Luna, who was the Sacristán Mayor of the Santa Iglesia parroquial of Granada, Nicaragua, for 200 pesos.

Manuela Ramírez, widow of Sárjente Andrés Palomino, made her will. She declared holding 200 pesos belonging to an orphan girl named Antonia, whom she raised, and used this money to purchase a 6-year-old Creole slave named Leocadia in Antonia's name. Manuela also mentioned her children, Salvador and the deceased Josefa.

Alférez José Calderón made his will, detailing his family and bequests. He left a house near the ermita de la Soledad and an estate in Agua Caliente to his daughter María, and mandated the creation of a chaplaincy with 900 pesos from a cacao plantation, naming Nicolás de Astúa as the first chaplain. He also noted that his mulatto slave, Antonio Morales, had run away about 10 years prior.

people_involved: Diego Fernández Vivas Bravo de Laguna
María de la Serna y Reyes
summary: Capitán Don Juan Fernández Vivas, a native of Tegucigalpa, Honduras, made his will. He detailed his extensive properties in Esparza, including livestock and a hacienda, and mentioned debts owed to him by Licenciado Don Juan de Chaverri and Licenciado Don José de Guevara. He also instructed his executors to send land-related papers to Guatemala and left 100 pesos to Doña Josefa de Bonilla for her dowry.

Don Jerónimo Manuel Ramos, a native of Cádiz, provided a dowry letter for his wife, Doña María Polonia. The dowry, totaling 2152 pesos, included a 23-year-old mulatto slave named Rafaela and cacao plantation rights, and was delivered to Licenciado Don Juan Antonio de Moya.

Hermano Francisco de Aguirre, acting as executor for the deceased Sárjento Juan Masís, sold a house to José Masís, Juan's son, for 550 pesos. José Masís stated he bought the house for Ayudante Nicolás de Estrada, and as patron of the chaplaincy founded on the house, he would ensure Estrada secured the capital and income.

people_involved: Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín
summary: Capitán Don Alvaro de Guevara provided a bond in a lawsuit where Sarjento Mayor Blas González Coronel was suing the estate of the deceased Gobernador Don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín. Capitán Don Miguel Calvo was ordered to pay González Coronel 327 pesos and 6.75 reales from the sale of four slaves, contingent on a bond for better right, which Guevara provided.

Francisca Barboza, widow of Sárjento Juan Masís, made her will. She noted that the partition of her estate was contested by her son José Masís, who claimed a slave named Juan Ventura and a cacao plantation as his separate property. She also ordered the freedom of her slaves Antonio and Juana, and mentioned her deceased daughter Francisca Masís, who had three children with Alférez Tomás de Chaves.

Capitán Don Diego de Barros y Carvajal, his wife Doña Josefa Pérez de Muro, and Doña Águeda Pérez de Muro obligated themselves for three thousand pesos to Presbítero Licenciado Don José Velazco Jiménez de Luna, residing in Granada, Nicaragua. This sum represented the value of a 3360-tree cacao plantation in Matina, which Don José Pérez de Muro had planted for Velazco. The obligation was cancelled in 1719 by Velazco's attorney, Sebastián Vicente Alvarez.

Francisco Gamboa and his wife Lorenza de Quesada declared that a 700-tree cacao plantation in Matina, inherited from Lorenza's deceased father Don Alonso de Quesada, was to be divided between Lorenza and her brother Domingo de Quesada.

Francisco de Chaves sold an enslaved person named Juan de Chaves, 34 years old, to Capitán Gerardo de Azofaifo for 200 pesos. Juan de Chaves was inherited by Francisco from his father, Capitán don Gregorio de Chaves.
José de Baeza and his wife María Magdalena Maroto sold 100 heads of cattle to Capitán Gabriel Maroto for 200 pesos. These cattle were part of María Magdalena Maroto's dowry.

Ayudante Nicolás de Estrada and his wife doña Lorenza Muñoz Hidalgo obligated themselves for 550 pesos to the Chaplaincy founded by Sarjento Juan Masís. This sum was for the purchase of the founder's house by José Masís on behalf of Estrada and his wife.

Hermano Francisco de Aguirre, as executor of Sarjento Juan Masís, founded a chaplaincy for recited masses with a capital of 550 pesos. This capital was owed by Nicolás de Estrada and his wife from a previous deed. José Masís, son of Juan Masís, was named patron.
Alférez Manuel Antonio de Arleguí leased a cacao plantation with 300 trees in the Valle de la Reventazón to Francisco de Echavarría for three years, at an annual rent of 40 pesos.

Doña María Antonia de Ballesteros and Capitán Pedro de Torres obligated themselves to hold an enslaved mulata named Antonia, or pay her value of 300 pesos, at the order of Capitán Alonso de Porras. This was related to an inheritance from María Antonia's deceased parents, Capitán Juan de Ballesteros Saavedra and doña Juana de Torres, and required a bond until María Antonia married.

Ayudante Nicolás de Estrada leased a cacao plantation and a plantain grove in the Valle de la Reventazón to José de Trejos for three years. The lease also included four mule beasts, seven hides, four hens, and a rooster, for an annual price of 225 pesos, with Sarjento Nicolás de Quirós as guarantor.

people_involved: Alférez don Antonio de la Riva Agüero
summary: Alférez Luis Peláez sold a house of adobe and tile to Alférez don Antonio de la Riva Agüero for 400 pesos. 200 pesos were held as a perpetual annuity for the chaplaincy founded by Francisco Enciso Hita, with Licenciado Félix Esteban Hoces Navarro as chaplain, and the other 200 pesos were paid in cash.

José de Acosta Arévalo and his wife doña María de Ballesteros Saavedra sold an enslaved black woman named Josefa, 13 years old, to Francisco Cartín for 200 pesos. Josefa had been a donation to doña María from her uncle Laureano de Ballesteros.

Nicolás González, a resident of the Valle de Barba, granted freedom to an enslaved black man named Diego de Zúñiga, who was born and raised in the house of María de Zúñiga (Nicolás's mother), in exchange for 300 pesos.

people_involved: Capitán don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos
Juez Comisario General don Diego de Herrera Carapuzano
Gobernador don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín
summary: Capitán don Antonio de la Vega Cabral received his embargoed goods from Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos. These goods had been seized by Juez Comisario General don Diego de Herrera Carapuzano during the residency trial of Gobernador don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín.

Teniente Pedro Rodríguez Palacio received a similar receipt from Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribaren for goods that had been embargoed for the same reason, likely related to the residency trial of Gobernador don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín.

people_involved: Sárjenlo Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Sárjenlo Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín performed a similar action for Sárjenlo Mayor Antonio Aurelio Zamora, for the same reason, likely related to the residency trial of Gobernador don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín.

people_involved: Sárjenlo Mayor don Blas González Coronel
summary: Sárjenlo Mayor don Blas González Coronel received a similar receipt from don José de Mier Cevallos for the same reason, likely related to the residency trial of Gobernador don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín.
Alférez don José de Morales received a similar receipt from Mier Cevallos for the same reasons, likely related to the residency trial of Gobernador don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín.

Doña Isabel de Ocampo Golfín, widow of Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes, received her husband's embargoed goods from Capitán Mier Cevallos for the same reason, likely related to the residency trial of Gobernador don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín.

people_involved: Maese de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba
Capitán don Diego de Barros y Carvajal
summary: Doña Águeda Pérez de Muro, widow of Maese de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba, gave a receipt to Capitán don Diego de Barros y Carvajal for goods that had been embargoed from her husband.

Sárjenlo Mayor Domingo Guerrero, a resident of Esparza, made his will in Barba before Capitán Juan Rodríguez. He was the legitimate son of Capitán Matías Guerrero and doña María González de Saavedra, both deceased residents of Utrera. He was a widower of doña Gertrudis de la Mata, with whom he had children doña Francisca, Domingo (deceased), and doña Lucía (married), and also a widower of María Jiménez, with whom he had no children.

Capitán Francisco Pérez de Cote made his will in Barba. He was the legitimate son of Bmé. Pérez de Cote and Luisa Guerrero, deceased residents of Medina (Castilla). He was a widower of doña Manuela Hidalgo, with whom he had children Manuel (deceased), doña María, and doña Francisca. He was married a second time to doña María de Zamora, daughter of Sebastián de Zamora and doña Luisa Quintana, and they had children Antonio, Juana Manuela, and Petronila.
Clara de las Salas, legitimate daughter of Pedro Alonso de las Salas and María de Brenes, made her will. She donated a house to Juana de las Salas, whom she had raised as a daughter.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Blas González Coronel
doña Juana Josefa de Arburola y Ribaren
Capitán Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribaren
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Blas González Coronel made a dowry letter in favor of his future wife, doña Juana Josefa de Arburola y Ribaren. She was the legitimate daughter of Capitán Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribaren and doña Josefa de Hoces.

Capitán don Miguel Calvo, general syndic for the San Francisco religious order, sells a cacaotal in Matina to Bernardo Pacheco. This property was previously delivered to Pacheco by the convent in 1708, with a condition of no censo for four years. Pacheco and his wife, María Valerino, now obligate themselves to a 5% censo on 250 pesos for the property, which was originally left to the convent by the late Capitán Benito Valerino.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Francisco de la Madriz Linares
don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín
summary: Sargento Mayor Francisco de la Madriz Linares and Capitán Juan Sancho de Castañeda, as executors of don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín, declare and donate a 12-year-old Mina-caste slave named José to don Diego Rodríguez Menéndez. The deceased had sent José to Menéndez as remuneration and due to their close kinship, but without a formal deed. The slave was purchased by Granda y Balvín using funds from his Matina properties from the Royal Company for the introduction of blacks in America.

Francisco de la Madriz Linares and his wife, doña Manuela de Quirós, obligate themselves for 500 pesos to Dominga and Lucía. These two are the legitimate daughters of Santiago de Moya and Pascuala de los Reyes, who were residents of Ujarrás, concerning their hereditary assets.

Gabriel de Montenegro, his wife Manuela de Chinchilla, and Gertrudis Ricardo obligate themselves for 166 pesos 5 1/2 reales to Juan and Francisco de Villalobos, the legitimate sons of the deceased Juan de Villalobos and Gertrudis Ricardo. These funds were previously under the guardianship of don Juan de Vivas and his wife doña Josefa de Moya, and are now received by the obligors from don Antonio de Lutrera, doña Josefa de Moya's second husband.

people_involved: Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos
Maese de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Capitán Manuel García de Argueta acts as a guarantor, obligating himself to pay the heirs of Capitán Alonso Gil Moreno if ordered by justice. This action is requested by Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos, attorney for doña Águeda Pérez de Muro, widow of Maese de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba, concerning 165 pesos 5 reales from excess jewels left by the deceased in Guatemala as collateral.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz
Capitán don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: Sargento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz, a resident of Cartago and neighbor of Guatemala, along with Capitán don Antonio de la Vega Cabral as guarantor, obligate themselves to pay 1210 pesos to the Royal Treasury in Cartago. This sum is for the tithes of the city, which Sáenz leased for two years, with payments due in halves in January 1715 and 1716.

This entry records the will of José de Trejo, who was single and the legitimate son of the late Juan de Trejo and Ana de Aguilar. His uncle was Capitán Diego de Aguilar, and his brother Matías Trejo, along with his mother Ana de Aguilar, were named as executors.
This entry records the will of Margarita Venegas, a single woman native to Cartago. She had three minor natural children: Josefa, Francisco, and José Antonio.

people_involved: Presbítero Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Capitán Juan Cayetano Jiménez, owner of a house and plot in Cartago, acknowledges a 5% censo on 300 pesos. This property, acquired from doña Micaela Duran de Chaves, is subject to the censo in favor of a chaplaincy founded by doña Micaela, with Presbítero Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas serving as the chaplain.

people_involved: don José de Casasola y Córdoba
doña Josefa de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Doña Águeda Pérez de Muro, widow of don José de Casasola y Córdoba, obligates herself to her minor legitimate daughter, doña Josefa de Casasola y Córdoba, for 3516 pesos 6 reales. This sum represents the daughter's share from the third part of the estate of don José Pérez de Muro, who was doña Águeda's father.

people_involved: Capitán don Diego de Barros y Carvajal
summary: Capitán don Diego de Barros y Carvajal owes Capitán José Velando, a resident of Panamá and executor/heir of Capitán Sebastián de Chavarría, 1243 pesos 6 reales. This is the remaining balance of a larger sum owed to the deceased. Barros y Carvajal commits to paying this debt in Panamá in 1715, by remitting 50 or more mule beasts.

people_involved: Francisco de los Santos y Carpió
summary: Francisco de los Santos y Carpió, a member of the order of penitence and resident of Panamá, grants general power of attorney to Alférez Juan José Vázquez, who resides in Cartago and is a neighbor of Granada, Nicaragua.

people_involved: doña Josefa de los Santos y Torres
summary: This entry records the will of Capitán Pedro de Torres Cordero, a resident of the Curriravá valley. He was married to doña María Meléndez and had a daughter, doña Josefa de los Santos y Torres, who married the late Antonio Chapuí. He inherited land from his parents, Alférez Esteban de Torres and doña Catalina de Monterroso, including shares for his two absent brothers, Bernardo and Francisco. His will details his assets, including livestock and two slaves, José and Mónica, the latter of whom was to be freed upon his death as per his deceased sister doña Francisca de Torres's wishes. He also instructed his executors, his wife and Capitán Antonio Ulate, to establish a chaplaincy with 200 pesos left by his sister and to give 100 pesos and other items to his niece, doña Francisca Ballesteros.
Francisco Cartín and his wife, Isabel de Quirós, sell a cacaotal with 270 trees in Barbilla, inherited by Isabel, to Pedro de las Salas for 200 pesos.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan de Echavarría Navarro
summary: This entry records the will of doña Ambrosia de Echavarría Navarro, the legitimate daughter of the late Capitán don Juan de Echavarría Navarro and doña Ana de Retes.

people_involved: Doña Antonia María de Acosta Arévalo
summary: Doña Antonia María de Acosta Arévalo, widow of don Agustín de Alvarado, obligated herself to her minor legitimate children, Antonia and Pedro, for 637 pesos 7.5 reales of their paternal inheritance. She mortgaged a cacao plantation in Matina with 2000 trees as security for this obligation.

people_involved: Doña Jerónima de la Riva y Agüero
Antonia Josefa (daughter of Riva y Agüero)
María Josefa (daughter of Riva y Agüero)
José Manuel (son of Riva y Agüero)
summary: Doña Jerónima de la Riva y Agüero, widow of Capitán Diego de Zamora, obligated herself to her four minor children: Micaela, Jerónima, Antonia Josefa, María Josefa, and José Manuel. This obligation was for 449 pesos 1.5 reales from their paternal inheritance, amounting to 162 pesos 2 reales and 13 maravedíes for each child.

people_involved: Doña Antonia María de Acosta Arévalo
summary: Doña Antonia María de Acosta Arévalo leased a cacao plantation in Matina, comprising 2000 trees, to her brother José de Acosta Arévalo. This plantation had been adjudicated to her in the succession of her deceased husband, don Agustín de Alvarado. The lease was for 2 years, priced at 125 pesos for the first year and 150 pesos for the second.

Doña Agustina Campos de Quirós granted freedom to her 34-year-old pardo slave, Manuel de Campos. Manuel is the son of Isabel, another slave belonging to Doña Agustina, who inherited Isabel from her mother, Doña Bárbula Altamirano.

people_involved: Capitán don Diego de Barros y Carvajal
summary: Capitán don Diego de Barros y Carvajal and his wife Doña Josefa Pérez de Muro, owners of a house on the royal street, obligated themselves to pay an annual 5% census. This census was imposed by Doña Josefa's father, don José Pérez de Muro, as a capellanía of 1500 pesos in favor of Licenciado don José de Velasco, a presbyter.

Capitán Francisco Gutiérrez emancipated his 20-year-old son, Francisco, and granted him 931 pesos in assets. Among these assets were 500 cacao trees located in Barbilla, which were valued at 750 pesos.

Capitán Francisco Gutiérrez and his wife Gertrudis Ruiz leased a cacao plantation in Matina, containing 1450 trees, to Francisco Gutiérrez, the son of the Captain and his first wife. Gertrudis had inherited this plantation from her first husband, Juan Ginés de Hinojosa. The lease was for 3 years at an annual price of 150 pesos.

A dowry letter was issued for Gaspar Arias, a resident of the Barba valley and legitimate son of Andrés Arias and Doña Isabel Hidalgo, in favor of his wife Doña Francisca de Quesada. Doña Francisca is the legitimate daughter of Alférez José de Quesada and the deceased Doña Francisca Sánchez, with a dowry of 500 pesos.

Capitán Blas de Ancheta and his wife Manuela de Conejo obligated themselves to the Royal Treasury of Cartago for 300 pesos. This amount was for the tithes of Esparza and its jurisdiction, which Capitán Ancheta had successfully bid for a period of 2 years.
Antonio Solano and Manuela Ricardo, a married couple, made a joint will before witnesses in the ejidos of Cartago. They had no children.

Antonio Solano appeared and ratified a written memory on common paper as his will, delivering it to the escribano. This memory was made jointly with his wife, Manuela Ricardo, and mentions that Capitán Antonio Solano of Esparza possesses some mules. The private memory itself was not attached to the record.

Doña Gertrudis Guerrero leased a cacao plantation in the Matina valley, containing 700 trees, to Alférez Gregorio de Mesa. She inherited this plantation from her deceased husband, Andrés Chacón. The lease was for 3 years at 200 pesos annually, with Capitán Felipe de Mesa acting as guarantor for the payment.

Doña María de Aguiar, a widow, leased a cacao plantation in the Reventazón valley, with 500 trees, to Ayudante José de Chavarría. She inherited this plantation from her husband, Luis Guzmán. The lease was for 3 years, with prices of 50 pesos for the first year, 62.5 for the second, and 75 for the third.

people_involved: Doña Angela de la Paz y Flores
Sarjento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Ocampo Golfín
Alférez Juan José Vázquez de Aguilar
summary: Doña Angela de la Paz y Flores, widow of Sarjento Mayor don Sebastián de Sandoval Ocampo Golfín (who died around 1697), sold an 18-year-old dark mulatto slave named Nicolás to Alférez Juan José Vázquez de Aguilar, a resident of Granada, Nicaragua. She inherited Nicolás from her deceased husband, and the sale price was 300 pesos.
José Antonio, a mestizo orphan who had been raised by Doña Sebastiana de Alvarado, was handed over to master shoemaker José Lobo. The document recording this transfer was not signed.

people_involved: Doña Magdalena López de Luque y Leal
Doña Juana Josefa de Arburola y Ribaren
Juana (daughter of Isabel, slave of Blas)
Maese de Campo don José Agustín de Estrada
summary: Sarjento Mayor Blas González Coronel, a native of Sevilla, made his will. He is the legitimate son of the deceased Manuel González Coronel and Doña Magdalena López de Luque y Leal, and was previously widowed from Doña Bernarda de Fonseca, with whom he had a son, Manuel, now a Subdeacon in León, Nicaragua. He is currently married to Doña Juana Josefa de Arburola y Ribaren. His assets include a cacao plantation in Tuis and lands in Aserrí, and he lists several creditors and debtors, including the estate of Gobernador Granda y Balvín for the apprehension of 105 enslaved people.

A dowry letter was issued for Juan de Trejo, legitimate son of the deceased Juan de Trejo and Ana de Aguilar, in favor of his wife Leonor de Mora. Leonor is the legitimate daughter of the deceased Basilio de Mora and Lorenza Milanés. The assets, totaling 500 pesos, were delivered by The. Severino de Aguilar, Leonor's stepfather and Lorenza Milanés's husband.

people_involved: José Ramón (son of Margarita López de la Flor)
Capitán don Francisco de Noguera y Moncada
Capitán don Diego de Barros y Carvajal
summary: Don Pedro Florencio del Águila and his wife Margarita López de la Flor obligated themselves to the minor José Ramón, son of Margarita and her first husband Capitán don Francisco de Noguera y Moncada, for 739 pesos from his paternal inheritance. They mortgaged a caballeria of land in Santa Ana, adjacent to lands of Capitán don Diego de Barros y Carvajal, which included a house, sugar mill, sugarcane, and cattle, with Capitán Juan de Astúa serving as guarantor.
On August 10th, Hermano Francisco de Aguirre, the Cabildo, Justicia y Regimiento of Cartago made a disposition. (The text provided is incomplete for this event).

A public school was mandated by a Royal Cédula to teach reading, writing, and arithmetic, providing good education and doctrine to children. The grantor was assigned 25 pesos in cacao annually, derived from the canoe rental at the Reventazón river crossing on the Matina road, to fund the school. The grantor was obligated to teach up to twelve poor children of noble families for free, while the Cabildo would set fees for others, and no other public or secret schools for children were permitted.

Lieutenant Pedro Rodríguez Palacio, Alguacil Mayor and regidor of Cartago, and his wife Teresa de Hoces Navarro, obligated themselves for 350 pesos to the beneficiary priests, funds belonging to the chaplaincies of the Santa Iglesia parroquial. They mortgaged an adobe and tile house on the royal street, which they had built on a plot purchased from Alférez Manuel Antonio de Arleguí.

Ayudante Juan de Torres leased a cacao plantation with a thousand trees in Matina to Cristóbal de Chavarría for two years. The plantation belonged to Doña Ana de Escalante Paniagua, Juan de Torres's wife, with an annual price of 6 tercios of cacao. Captain Miguel Calvo served as the guarantor for the agreement.

Sargento Mayor Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, a perpetual regidor, obligated himself for 400 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Doña Eugenia de Abarca Alatras. This sum was provided by Captain Miguel Calvo, the patron of the chaplaincy. Francisco de Ocampo Golfín mortgaged his house and lands in the Barba valley, and the obligation was cancelled in December 1714.

María de Chaves, widow of Pedro de Aguilar, and Alférez Tomás de Chaves, acting as her guarantor, obligated themselves for 254 pesos. This obligation was made in favor of María's minor children: Juan José, María, Juan, Rafael, Catalina, and Agustín, who were also the children of her deceased husband.

Doña Antonia, Doña Josefa Ventura, and Doña Gertrudis de Alvarado, heirs of Don Jorge de Alvarado and Doña Gertrudis de Chavarría Navarro, granted power of attorney to Captain Don José de Quesada. This authorization was for him to collect what was due to them in Panamá, where their father, Don Jorge, had died, and to handle general legal matters related to these claims.

Doña Micaela Duran de Chaves made a codicil to her 1711 testament. Instead of giving 14 cattle to her slave María, who had since died, the cattle were to be given to Don Sebastián de Garita, majordomo of the Cofradía de las Animas, to benefit the confraternity.

Captain Don Alonso de Porras made his testament, stating he was married to Doña Ana de Castro and had no children. He owned a house, corrals, and two 'caballerías' of land in the Curriravá valley, specifically in La Mata Redonda, which he had purchased from Alférez Tomás de Chaves. He listed debts to his nephew José Arias, the heir of Juan Albo, and the heirs of Domingo de Alvarado and Juana Coto.

Diego Chacón made his testament, identifying himself as the widower of Leonor Gómez and the legitimate son of Francisco Chacón and Juana de Guevara, both deceased. He listed his children: Francisco, Baltasara, Diego, Clara (deceased), and Francisca, noting that his three daughters were married and Francisca was already a widow. He also mentioned his granddaughter Manuela, daughter of his son Francisco.
Nicolás Méndez, a 14-year-old orphan, was formally apprenticed for five years to Ayudante Matías Masís, who was a master blacksmith.

Alberto de Iraola, legitimate son of Lucas de Iraola and Juana de Bonilla, issued a dowry letter for 531 pesos in favor of his wife, Josefa Nicolasa Solano. Josefa Nicolasa Solano was identified as the legitimate daughter of Nicolás Solano and Juana Ricardo.

Captains Juan Francisco de Ibarra and José Antonio Bermúdez posted bail for Alférez Nicolás de Quirós, who was imprisoned by order of the Gobernador. Quirós was released under strict conditions, including living maritally with his wife Francisca Martínez in his mother-in-law María Machado's house, not leaving for a year, and not crossing the Taras river, under penalty of 200 pesos and two years of imprisonment in Nicaragua. The guarantors clarified he could visit his haciendas in Matina and Ujarrás as long as he respected the river boundary.

Sargento Juan Fernández Bulagai posted bail for his brother, Antonio Fernández, who was imprisoned. Antonio Fernández's case was pending in the Juzgado de la Santa Hermandad before Don José Nicolás Sarmiento de Sotomayor.

Don José Nicolás Sarmiento de Sotomayor and his wife Doña María Catarina Ortiz de Rosas sold an enslaved person named Juan, described as pardo, small in stature, and about 15 years old, to Captain José Antonio Bermúdez for 250 pesos. María Catarina Ortiz de Rosas had received Juan as a donation from her deceased grandparents, Captain Don Pedro de Alvarado and Doña Catalina de Vida Martel.
Juan Alejandro Leitona owed 200 pesos to María de Salazar, a widow. The debt was specified to be paid in cacao, delivered to María de Salazar's residence in the Aserrí valley.

people_involved: Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín
summary: Captain Juan Cayetano Jiménez, owner of an enslaved person named Juan (Mina caste, about 20 years old), who he bought from the estate of Don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín for 210 pesos, was ordered to grant Juan his freedom. This manumission was executed by order of Sargento Mayor Don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones, Justicia Mayor and Capitán General of the province, upon the Royal Treasury returning the 210 pesos, with the involvement of albaceas Francisco de la Madriz Linares and Juan.

Alférez Jacinto de Rivera sells a cacao plantation with 2000 trees in Matina to Doña Antonia María de Acosta Arévalo. The payment of 1250 pesos was made in 1704 by her deceased husband, Don Agustín de Alvarado, but the deed was never formally executed until this date.

Alférez Antonio de Ángulo and his wife Josefa Fernández sell an enslaved Black man named Gaspar Rodríguez, who is over 50 years old, to Captain Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribarén for 100 pesos. Josefa Fernández had received Gaspar Rodríguez as part of her dowry from her father, Alférez Francisco Fernández.

Don Gregorio de Alvarado issues a codicil to his 1712 testament, declaring various active and passive debts. He also states that his assets have increased with the addition of an enslaved Conga woman named María, who is a little over 20 years old.

Eight indigenous men, including Bernardo de Aguilar and Jerónimo Zamora, who work at the city's brickyard, accept the Cabildo's decree from October 17th. This decree grants them administration of the brickyard for two years, requiring them to repair it and pay annual rents, with Sargento Mayor Francisco de la Madriz Linares acting as their guarantor.

Captain José Felipe Bermúdez, son of the late Lieutenant Felipe Bermúdez and Doña Juana de Aguiar, provides a dowry letter for his wife, Doña María Teresa de Sandoval. The marriage is set for November 4th, and the dowry includes 1011.5 pesos, among which is an enslaved 'mulata azambada' named María Paula, aged 20, valued at 400 pesos.

Manuela de Segura, widow of Alférez Baltasar Ramírez, obligates herself to her minor legitimate children, Juan, Josefa, Antonia, Gertrudis, and Gregoria Ramírez, for 735 pesos 3.5 reales from their paternal inheritance. Alférez Don Antonio de la Riva Agüero acts as her guarantor.

Doña Isabel de Guevara, daughter of the late Captain Don José de Guevara and Doña Inés de Sandoval Ocampo Golfín, makes her testament. She is married to Don Agustín González, who is absent, and her son, Francisco González, is in Nicaragua. She mandates 700 pesos, entrusted to her by an unnamed person, be given to Licenciado Don Juan Antonio de Moya, a presbyter, to fulfill communicated instructions.
Alférez Don Antonio de la Riva y Agüero acknowledges a debt of 113 pesos to Manuela de Segura, a widow. This amount is the same for which he acted as guarantor for the deceased José de Trejos.

Doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar, widow of Antonio de Acosta Arévalo, founds a chaplaincy of masses. The capital is secured on a cacao plantation in Matina, on which she charges a census of 840 pesos from her deceased husband's assets. Her son, Captain Gaspar de Acosta Arévalo, is named the patron, and Licenciado Don Manuel de Guzmán is the first chaplain.

Doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar acknowledges a debt of 200 pesos, received from Captain Antonio Alvarez de Ulate, executor of Captain Pedro de Torres, for a chaplaincy founded by Torres. She mortgages her cacao plantation in Matina, which is already burdened with 840 pesos for her deceased husband's chaplaincy. Captain Juan de Chaves is the patron and Licenciado Don Manuel de Guzmán is the chaplain for Torres's chaplaincy.

Doña Petronila, Doña Nicolasa, Doña María, and Doña Manuela Martínez, all over 25 years old and daughters of Doña Micaela de Luna and Alférez Eugenio Martínez, give receipt for their inheritance from their deceased parents.

Captain Antonio Alvarez de Ulate, as executor of Captain Pedro de Torres, founds a chaplaincy of masses for the souls of Francisca de Torres (sister of the founder), the founder, and others. The capital of 200 pesos was left by Francisca de Torres and is the same amount given as a census to Doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar. Manuel Antonio Chapuí, grandson of the founder, is named perpetual chaplain once ordained, with Licenciado Don Manuel de Guzmán serving in the interim.

In Matina, before Lieutenant Governor Luis Gutiérrez, Alférez Manuel Antonio de Arleguí grants power of attorney to his wife, Doña Gracia Gertrudis de Hoces Navarro. This power allows her to grant her own power of attorney to Don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro, who is in Guatemala, to sell an enslaved mulatto named José, who escaped from Nicaragua eight years prior.

Doña Gracia Gertrudis de Hoces Navarro, wife of Alférez Manuel Antonio de Arleguí, grants the power of attorney mentioned in the previous document. She adds that she inherited the mulatto slave from her mother, Doña Juana de Echavarría Navarro.

people_involved: María de la O y Céspedes
summary: Alférez Don José de Morales, Ordinary Mayor and Lieutenant Governor, and his wife Doña María de la O y Céspedes, obligate themselves for 100 pesos to Sargento Mayor Antonio Aurelio de Zamora, to be paid within four months. They provide an enslaved 'pardo' man named José Ventura, aged 14, as collateral.

Captain José de Saborío and his wife Juana Josefa de Ballesteros obligated themselves to Francisca de Ballesteros, daughter of Captain Juan de Ballesteros, for 90 pesos. The funds were received from Captain Pedro de Torres, who was acting as the executor.

Captain Pedro de Torres and his wife María Morales Meléndez obligated themselves to Francisca de Ballesteros, legitimate daughter of Captain Juan de Ballesteros and Juana de Torres, for 125 pesos. This sum was a donation from Francisca de Torres's will, and Juan Hidalgo, Francisca's tutor, delivered the money.
Francisco Ramírez and his wife María de Tapia obligated themselves to Francisca de Ballesteros for 100 pesos. Captain Pedro de Torres, acting as executor, delivered these funds.

people_involved: Josefa (daughter of Micaela Pérez de Luna)
summary: The will of Micaela Pérez de Luna was recorded. She was the legitimate daughter of Captain José de Luna, originally from Perera, Spain, and Josefa de Echavarría Navarro, and the widow of Captain Eugenio Martínez. Her will mentions her children Petrona, Josefa (married to Captain Juan Cayetano Jiménez), Nicolasa, and María Manuela, along with several slaves and their children.

Bernardo Cortés, a resident of the Barba valley, sold a 23-year-old black slave named José Felipe to José de Quirós for 350 pesos. Cortés had previously acquired José Felipe from Lieutenant José de Escalante Paniagua.

The will of Antonia María Ballesteros, legitimate daughter of Captain Juan de Ballesteros and Juana de Torres, was recorded. She made bequests to her aunt Ana de Torres, her niece María Antonia Ramírez, her sister Francisca de Ballesteros, and another niece named Francisca.

A dowry letter was issued by Francisco Rodríguez de Castro, son of Alférez Juan Rodríguez de Castro (from Castilla la Vieja) and María Monterroso, in favor of his wife Juana Josefa de Tenorio. Juana Josefa is the daughter of Alférez Cristóbal Tenorio and Laureana de Chaves, and the dowry amounted to 597 pesos.
Captain Alonso de Porras obligated himself for 98 pesos in favor of the minor José Albo, who is the legitimate son of Alférez Juan Albo and María Ramírez.

locations: Nueva población de la ayuda de parroquia de Nuestra Señora de la Concepción
summary: María Morales Meléndez, widow of Captain Pedro de Torres, and her guarantor Alférez Tomás de Chaves, both from Curridavá, obligated themselves for 490 pesos. This sum represents an inheritance from Catalina de Monterroso, María's mother, and is owed to Francisco and Bernardo de Torres, who are María's brothers-in-law.

The will of Sergeant Major Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, a perpetual councilman of Cartago, was recorded. He was the son of the deceased Diego de Ocampo Golfín and María de Mora, and was married to Magdalena Pérez de Luna. His will details his children, extensive properties including land, livestock, and a sugar mill, and lists numerous slaves. It also mentions debts owed to him and shared interests in land with relatives and colleagues.

people_involved: Josefa de los Santos y Torres
summary: Captain Francisco Alejandro de Bonilla and his wife Josefa de los Santos y Torres, residents of Curridavá, obligated themselves to Manuel Antonio Chapuí for 556 pesos 2.5 reales. Manuel Antonio is the son of Josefa de los Santos y Torres and her first husband Antonio Chapuí, and the obligation relates to a debt previously held by Captain Pedro de Torres and María Morales Meléndez.

Francisca de Acosta Arévalo, widow of Gregorio de Alvarado, and her guarantor José de Acosta Arévalo, obligated themselves for 953 pesos 4 reales. This sum is for the paternal inheritance of her legitimate minor son, Cayetano de Alvarado.

Francisca de Acosta Arévalo obligated herself for 500 pesos to a chaplaincy founded by her deceased husband, Gregorio de Alvarado. The chaplaincy is secured by a cacao plantation in Malina, which was previously owned by Agustín de Alvarado and has since been adjudicated to Francisca.

Alférez Tomás de Chaves and Felipe de Mesa posted bail for Salvador Ramírez. Ramírez was being prosecuted for concealing assets that belonged to the heirs of the deceased Baltasar Ramírez, a crime he had confessed to and was convicted of.

people_involved: Juan Gómez de Ocón y Trillo
summary: Captain Juan Cayetano Jiménez and Alférez Pablo Antonio Lizondo posted bail for Captain Juan Gómez de Ocón y Trillo. Trillo was imprisoned due to charges arising from a residency review of his tenure as Alcalde de la Hermandad and Juez de Campo during the years 1712 and 1713.

Several prominent citizens of Cartago agreed to fund and establish a School of Cristo in the city, which would be dependent on the one in Guatemala. Various individuals pledged different amounts of money, cacao trees, or cattle for its maintenance and for the priests accompanying Bachiller Pedro Morales de Meléndez. Sarjento Mayor José Sáenz later requested certification of this deed to send to the School of Cristo's fathers in Guatemala.

people_involved: Padre Prepósito de la Escuela de Cristo
summary: Captain Manuel García de Argueta founded a capellanía (chaplaincy) of masses, endowing it with 500 pesos on his house in Cartago. He appointed the Padre Prepósito of the soon-to-be-founded School of Cristo as the chaplain, tasking him or any cleric from the congregation to say a sung mass for Saint Joseph on his feast day, including a procession.

people_involved: Juan López de la Rea y Soto
summary: Juan López de la Rea y Soto, a public scribe who purchased his offices in Santiago de Guatemala in 1712 for 450 pesos, provided Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribaren as guarantor for the remaining 150 pesos of his debt. The debt was later cancelled in 1720 by Doña Josefa de Hoces Navarro, Arburola's widow, upon payment.

people_involved: Juan López de la Rea y Soto
summary: Juan López de la Rea y Soto received 100 pesos from Doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco, a widow. This sum was charged on her houses, which she had purchased from the estate of Licenciado Agustín de Torres, and belonged to a capellanía founded by Vasco Solano, of which López de la Rea y Soto was the patron.

Alférez José de Quirós received 325 pesos from Feliciano de Fuentes, a 58-year-old slave of Captain José de Laya y Bolívar, to secure Fuentes' freedom. Quirós then gave Laya y Bolívar a 23-year-old slave named José Felipe, whom he had purchased from Alférez Bernardino Cortés. Feliciano de Fuentes, originally bought by Bolívar from the estate of Doña Francisca de Acuña y Sibaja, was thus granted his liberty.

Captain Manuel de Navas, Doña Gertrudis de Laya y Bolívar, and Doña Rosa de Laya y Bolívar (with her husband Captain Juan de Guevara's permission) settled a dispute over inherited plantain groves. These groves, known as 'la troja,' 'Sicasquiós,' and 'el trapiche,' were inherited from Doña Mariana de Sibaja, mother of Navas and mother-in-law to the other two women, and they agreed to share them equally. Another plot, 'el Turis,' which Navas and Gertrudis had purchased from Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral, was to belong solely to them, with titles for the women pending confirmation from Guatemala.

Alférez Gabriel de Laya y Bolívar assumed a 560-peso debt to the Cofradía de las Benditas Animas, managed by Licenciado Don Juan de Rivas Chaverri. This debt originated from Captain Don Juan Fernández Vivas, who had received the sum from María Noriega for the Cofradía but failed to acknowledge it after delivering livestock. As part of the agreement, Vivas gave Gabriel de Laya y Bolívar a major livestock site called San Judas in the Landecho valley, which Vivas had previously bought from Juan Calvo, to cover any missing livestock.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
Padre Predicador Fray Francisco de San José
Capitán Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribaren
summary: In 1703, the indigenous man Diego López, who owned 200 cacao trees in El Riachuelo, Matina, died without heirs. He requested Padre Fray Francisco de San José to take the trees in exchange for masses. The Padre accepted the donation for mission funds and sold the trees to Capitán Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribaren. Years later, Sarjento Mayor Antonio de la Vega Cabral, as syndic, sought security for Arburola's heirs, which Gobernador Lacayo de Briones authorized after a satisfactory report from Fray Antonio de Andrade.

Alférez Francisco Calvo sold an enslaved woman named Juana, described as 'pardo blanca' and about 40 years old, to Ayudante Sebastián Vicente Alvarez, a resident of Granada, for 175 pesos. Juana was part of an inheritance from Francisco Calvo's father, Capitán Miguel Calvo.

people_involved: Maese de Campo don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina
don José Mauricio Serrano de Reina
summary: Maese de Campo don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina, a lieutenant official of the Royal Treasury, granted a general power of attorney to his brother, don José Mauricio Serrano de Reina, who resided in Guatemala.

people_involved: Licenciado Presbítero don José de Velasco Jiménez de Luna
summary: Capitán José Antonio de Espinosa, on behalf of Licenciado Presbítero don José de Velasco Jiménez de Luna, purchased two enslaved individuals, Agustín (10, mina) and María (18, mandinga), from the Real Asiento in Panamá for 400 pesos. These slaves were sent from Esparza to Cartago in August of the previous year (1715) to Ayudante Sebastián Vicente Alvarez, who was instructed to forward them to Granada. Agustín died in Cartago in December of 1715.

people_involved: Teniente General don José de Mier Ceballos
summary: Francisco Bustamante accused Nicolás Muñoz, Lorenza Muñoz, Micaela, and María Josefa of theft, but Lorenza counter-complained against Bustamante for sexual misconduct. The Governor acquitted the accused of theft due to insufficient proof and condemned Bustamante to pay Lorenza Muñoz for her 'estado' and clothing. Bustamante appealed, and the accused were released on bail.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: Sarjento Mayor Francisco de la Madriz Linares and Capitán Manuel García de Argueta acted as guarantors for Francisco Bustamante, who was condemned to pay 411 pesos 4 reales. This sum included funds for Lorenza Muñoz's 'estado' and clothing, a payment to the Royal Chamber, and legal costs. The guarantors eventually paid the sum on March 2, 1717, as the appeal's revocation did not arrive.

people_involved: The. General don Diego de Barros Carvajal
summary: Teniente General don Diego de Barros Carvajal provided jail bail for Francisco Bustamante in connection with the ongoing legal case.

people_involved: Capitán don Diego de Barros y Carvajal
Licenciado don José de Velasco Jiménez de Luna
summary: Capitán don Diego de Barros y Carvajal and his wife, doña Josefa Pérez de Muro, were obligated to pay 3000 pesos in cacao to Licenciado don José de Velasco Jiménez de Luna for a cacao plantation in Matina. They were jointly committed with doña Águeda Pérez de Muro, Josefa's sister. Since doña Águeda made the payment alone, Diego and Josefa ceded the cacao plantation to her.

people_involved: Alférez Lucas Ruiz de la Guardia
summary: Diligences for the nuncupative will of Alférez Juan Picado were conducted by Capitán Germán Rodríguez in San José de Abangares. Picado mandated a chaplaincy, naming Licenciado don Manuel Ordóñez as patron and chaplain, with Claudio Picado and Sarjento Pascual Solano as substitutes due to Ordóñez's absence in Panamá. The Governor approved the will's legalization on August 18, 1716. Juan Picado stated he was married to Agustina Arcia.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco de Noguera y Moncada
doña Margarita López de la Flor
summary: Capitanes Juan de Astúa and Gabriel Maroto became guarantors for the minor José Ramón de Moncada for 739 pesos, related to an inheritance. This was a new deed ordered by the Governor, replacing an earlier guarantee by Astúa for Pedro Florencio del Águila and the deceased Margarita López de la Flor (José Ramón's mother). By 1724, Astúa was embargoed and gave the Santana hacienda to Moncada as payment for his inheritance.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
Capitán don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
Capitán don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
Capitán don José Antonio Bermúdez de Aguiar
Sarjento Mayor don José Mauricio Serrano de Reina
summary: Several prominent individuals acted as guarantors for Sarjento Mayor don José Mauricio Serrano de Reina, who was named the official Accountant of the Royal Treasury, replacing Capitán don Juan Martínez Vaquero. The guarantee was for 2100 pesos. This guarantee was cancelled in 1717 when Serrano provided other securities upon the deed's arrival in León.

José de Echavarría and his wife María Calvo grant freedom to their mulata slave, Manuela Calvo, who is about 50 years old. Manuela pays 50 pesos for her freedom. María Calvo inherited Manuela from her father, Capitán don Miguel Calvo.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Sargento Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín and his wife doña Magdalena Pérez de Luna establish a chaplaincy for recited masses with a capital of 2000 pesos. The chaplaincy is designated for any of their sons (don Francisco, don Nicolás, or don Juan) who becomes ordained, or one of their grandsons, son of their legitimate daughter doña Josefa de Ocampo. The capital is secured by their residence and other assets in Barba.

Capitán José de Miranda, with Capitán José de Echavarría as his guarantor, agrees to pay 260 pesos to Manuela Vásquez to settle a lawsuit. The payment includes 60 pesos in Castilian goods after ships return from Panama, 100 pesos in 100 arrobas of tallow by August 1718, and 100 pesos in gentle mules by August 1718. Manuela Vásquez is the legitimate daughter of Aparicio Vásquez and Ana de Alvarado, former residents of Cartago now in Esparza.

Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra, don José de Quesada, and don José Felipe Bermúdez post bail for don Antonio Salmón Pacheco, who was imprisoned for illicit commerce in the Valle de Malina. Pacheco, who was the Lieutenant General of the Governor in that valley, had appealed his sentence.

Ayudante Miguel de Céspedes, defender of don Antonio Salmón Pacheco, requests that Pacheco be relieved from house arrest and allowed to move freely within the city and valleys of the jurisdiction. The Governor (don Pedro Ruiz de Bustamante) agrees, and the bail from March 12 is ratified by Quesada and Bermúdez, with don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco replacing the absent Ibarra. Pacheco's lawyer in Guatemala had died.

Doña Ana de Torres, widow of Miguel Gamboa and daughter of the deceased Ayudante Esteban de Torres and doña Catalina de Monterroso, makes her will. She owns two slaves, Juana (20, mulata) and her daughter María (3), and a house and land in Curridavá. She leaves her house and land to Antonia María Ballesteros and her two slaves to her sister Mariana de Torres.

Gaspar Fernández Solano makes his will, detailing his family and assets. He was widowed from Juana González, with whom he had a daughter, María Fernández, married to Nicolás de Prado. He is currently married to Margarita Chacón, with whom he has four children: Ana (married to Juan José de Chaves), Josefa, Juan José, and Petronila. He owns a mulata slave, a ranch in Río de Itiquís near Poás, and mentions a grandson, José Antonio.
José de Arrieta, an orphan boy about 12 years old, son of the deceased Miguel de Arrieta and María de la Estrella, is apprenticed to José Valeriano de las Salas, a master tailor, for 5 years.
Juan Francisco de Villarreal, an orphan boy about 12 years old, is apprenticed to Sargento Carlos de Umaña, a master shoemaker, for 5 years.

Ayudante Nicolás de Estrada, a native of Cartagena de Indias and legitimate son of don Francisco de Estrada and doña María Mejía, makes his will. He is married to doña Lorenza Muñoz Hidalgo and they have six children: Antonio, Sebastiana, Hilario, Luisa, Pedro José, and María Josefa. He owns cacao plantations in the Valle de la Reventazón, a house and lot, and livestock.

Capitán Francisco Gutiérrez makes his will, detailing his family, assets, and debts. He was widowed from Nicolasa de Flores, with whom he had five sons, and is now married to Gertrudis Ruiz, with whom he has a 7-year-old son and is expecting another child. He owns slaves, cacao plantations in Matina, and houses in Cartago, and mentions a debt owed by Cayetano Muñoz related to peace talks with the Mosquito people. He also declares three foster children.

Juan Fernández Martínez and his wife doña Cayetana de Acosta sell a city lot in Cartago to Capitán don Alvaro de Guevara for 50 pesos. They had acquired the lot as a dowry from doña Josefa de Aguilar.

Sarjento Carlos de Umaña and his wife Ce... de Quirós pledged 100 pesos to a chaplaincy founded by doña Eugenia de Abarca Alatras. They mortgaged their house and lot, which were adjacent to the property of their son, Sarjento Gregorio de Umaña. Captain Miguel Calvo was the patron and Licenciado don Juan de Guevara was the chaplain of this foundation.

Margarita Chacón, widow of Gaspar Fernández Solano, along with her guarantor Ayudante Matías Masís, committed to pay 255 pesos to Josefa Fernández Solano. This sum represented Josefa's legitimate inheritance as the daughter of Margarita Chacón.

Don Alonso Bernabé Cabeza de Vaca, with Sarjento Mayor Francisco de la Maririz as his guarantor, obligated himself to his minor son, José Manuel, for 702 pesos and 27 maravedís. This amount was José Manuel's share from the estate of his deceased mother, doña Juana de Moya, who was the late wife of Don Alonso.

Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, a presbyter and consultant of the Holy Office, made his will, detailing his properties including a house in Cartago, a cattle ranch in Valle de Aserrí, and several slaves. He appointed new patrons and chaplains for various chaplaincies he oversaw, such as those founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela, María Yáñez, and Francisca del Castillo.
