The will also included specific bequests to family members, instructions for the sale of certain slaves, and named his executors and heirs.

Inés de Olivares, widow of Mateo Jiménez, made her will in Valle de Barba, listing her deceased parents Juan de Olivares and María de Brenes, and her five children. She detailed her slaves, including María, who was over 50 and to be freed, along with her mulato children. Inés also noted her son Pablo had been absent for eleven years, believed to be in the jurisdiction of Comayagua, and appointed her nephew Juan Jiménez as her executor.

Licenciado Presbítero don Juan Antonio de Moya, with permission from Cura Rector Diego de Ángulo Gascón, granted general power of attorney to The. Pedro Rodríguez Palacio. Moya, preparing for a trip to Matina valley by order of the Bishop, authorized Rodríguez to execute a deed of cession for a house formerly owned by Bachiller don Francisco de Rivas y Velasco, accepting the transfer with the burden of chaplaincy censos. However, the transaction was noted as incomplete.

people_involved: Pedro José Antonio Sáenz de Quintanilla
summary: Sarjento Mayor Blas González Coronel sold a house and fenced lot in Cartago to Sarjento Mayor don Pedro José Antonio Sáenz de Quintanilla, who was also Alcalde Ordinario and Teniente de Gobernador. The property, which bordered the public plaza and Captain Domingo García de Estrada's house, carried an 850-peso burden from chaplaincy censos, which the buyer and his wife, doña María de la Rosa, agreed to assume. The seller had acquired parts of the property from Captain José de Quirós and doña Jerónima de Retes.
María de Jesús y Chaves, a widow, sold a house located on the royal street to The. don Antonio de Utrera for 100 pesos.

A dowry letter was prepared for the marriage of Don Pedro de Alvarado, son of the late Captain Pedro de Alvarado and doña Catalina de Vida Martel, to doña Angela de Guevara, daughter of Captain don Alvaro de Guevara and the late doña María Sáenz. The marriage was scheduled for the following day, January 27th, with a dowry totaling 2577 pesos, including houses and furniture valued at 1300 pesos.

Captain Miguel Calvo, son of Depositario General Tomás Calvo and doña Eugenia de Abarca Alatras, made his will. He was the Síndico of the San Francisco Convent and noted his house in Cartago was mortgaged for 100 pesos to a chaplaincy served by his nephew, Licenciado don Juan de Guevara, a resident of Nicaragua. The will also detailed various assets, including a loan of 200 pesos secured by silver items from the deceased Captain don Cristóbal Martín Cubero, and a gold ring held as collateral for 8 pesos belonging to the heirs of don Jorge de Alvarado.

people_involved: Manuela (mulata, mother of Manuela, José, Francisco)
summary: An inventory of an unnamed testator's estate includes various slaves and their children, properties in Quercua, Las Cóncavas, and Reventazón, and credits. The testator's will details natural children with former slave Ana Cardoso, their freedom status, and instructions to free María de Ochoa and found a capellanía.

people_involved: Capitán Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribarén
summary: Sárjento Mayor Blas González Coronel, a perpetual Regidor of Cartago, obliges himself to the Royal Treasury for 337 pesos 4 reales, representing the balance of his accounts. Capitán Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribarén acts as his guarantor for this payment, which can be made in money or cacao.

people_involved: Don José de Casasola y Córdoba
Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: Doña Águeda Pérez de Muro, widow of Don José de Casasola y Córdoba, is involved in a lawsuit against Capitán Nicolás de Valenzuela concerning her deceased husband's assets, which were part of her dowry. After being awarded the assets, she provides Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral and Doña Ambrosia González Camino as guarantors to ensure she does not dispose of them before the Audiencia resolves Valenzuela's appeal.

Capitán Blas de Ancheta and his wife Manuela Conejo sell a house with adjacent enclosures in the ejidos of Cartago to Capitán Nicolás de Guevara for 450 pesos. The property was originally purchased from Alférez Antonio Rodríguez, and the new owners, Nicolás de Guevara and his wife Doña Francisca de Acosta Arévalo, assume responsibility for two associated capellanías.

Capitán Nicolás de Guevara and his wife Doña Francisca de Acosta Arévalo obligate themselves to Capitán Blas de Ancheta for 200 pesos, which they agree to pay in cacao. This obligation was later cancelled in 1717.

people_involved: Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: José del Bustillo, a trader preparing to depart for Nicaragua, grants power of attorney to Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral to execute his will. He designates his soul as his heir and mandates the establishment of a capellanía.

Domingo de Ayesta issues a codicil to his closed will, revoking a previous clause that had allocated 200 pesos to his brother, Don Miguel de Ayesta, who is currently located in the Corpus mineral in Honduras.

The closed will of Domingo de Ayesta, who died in the home of Don Bernardo Marín, is opened. The will identifies him as a bachelor, native of Villafranca (Vizcaya), and the legitimate son of Juan de Ayesta and Antonia de Garmendía.

Miguel Lizondo's will details his family, identifying his deceased parents as Alférez Juan Matías Lizondo and Doña Francisca Benavente, his wife as Gertrudis Falcón (daughter of deceased José Falcón and Ana Romero), and listing his nine children and an unborn child, along with his brothers Pablo and Francisco Lizondo.

people_involved: Capitán Don Francisco Duque de Estrada
summary: José Francisco Cartín sells Victorino, a 40-year-old pardo slave, to Capitán Don Francisco Duque de Estrada, the Lieutenant Governor in Esparza, for 250 pesos. Cartín had received Victorino from the justice system as payment for a 300-peso debt owed by Sárjento Mayor Blas González Coronel, but the sale document was not signed.

Feliciana Chinchilla, widow of Alférez Francisco Fernández, leases a cacaotal containing 1500 fruit trees in the Matina valley to Capitán José de Bonilla for a period of three years, at an annual rent of 175 pesos.

María Calderón, a widow, sells a cacaotal with over two thousand trees in Matina to Don Jerónimo Muñoz Ramos for 850 pesos. She and her deceased husband, Martín de Civitola, had originally purchased this property from Capitán Don András de Salazar in 1701, and the current sale price is tied to several capellanías; the document was not signed.

people_involved: Doña Juana de Vera y Sotomayor
summary: The. Don Jerónimo Muñoz Ramos and his wife Doña María Polonia de Moya obligate themselves to two capellanías: one founded by Doña Juana de Vera y Sotomayor for 250 pesos, and another founded by Doña Inés Pereira for 100 pesos. Neither of these obligation documents was signed.

Alférez Juan Francisco Marín Laguna sells his half of a house in Cartago to Capitán Don Bernardo Marín for 240 pesos. The other half of the house belongs to his sister, Doña María Marín Laguna, who is married to Don Bernardo. Both siblings inherited the house from their mother, Doña Catalina de Moya, and the sale price is subject to a capellanía founded by Comisario Baltasar de Grado.

people_involved: Don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones
Licenciado Don Faustino Raimundo Lacayo de Briones
Bachiller Don Miguel Antonio Lacayo de Briones
summary: Don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones, Justice Mayor and Captain General, grants additional power of attorney to his brothers, Licenciado Don Faustino Raimundo Lacayo de Briones and Bachiller Don Miguel Antonio Lacayo de Briones, both residing in Madrid, without revoking a previous power granted in 1713.

Doña Margarita de Morales sells Juana Josefa, a 20-year-old pardo slave, to Capitán Juan de Luque, a resident of Cartago and neighbor of Granada, Nicaragua. The slave is described as having a good appearance, round face, and not being mortgaged or subject to any of the grantor's debts.

Don Bernardo Marín and Doña María Marín Laguna obligate themselves for 240 pesos to a chaplaincy founded by Comisario Baltasar de Grado. The obligation is secured by a house they purchased from Don Juan Francisco Marín Laguna.

people_involved: Licenciado Don Manuel de Escalante y Panlagua
summary: Capitán Juan Cayetano Jiménez, an Ordinary Mayor, sells a house and its lot in Cartago to Licenciado Don Manuel de Escalante y Panlagua for 300 pesos. The property was originally acquired from Doña Micaela Duran de Chaves and is encumbered by a 300-peso chaplaincy founded by Doña Micaela, which the buyer assumes.

people_involved: Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Peina
summary: Feliciana de Chinchilla and Capitán Don José de Bonilla, as a tenant of her cacao plantation, obligate themselves to Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Peina for 282 pesos. This sum represents the remainder of a larger debt owed by Capitán Basilio Picado Maircna, a resident of León, Nicaragua, with Bonilla agreeing to pay in cacao from his lease.

people_involved: Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Peina
summary: The debt obligation made by Feliciana de Chinchilla and Capitán Don José de Bonilla to Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Peina, related to Capitán Basilio Picado Maircna's debt, was cancelled in 1719.

people_involved: Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Alférez Ensebio Jiménez sells a 12-year-old black slave named Juan Esteban to Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona for 200 pesos. Jiménez had previously purchased Juan Esteban from Bartolomé Giraldo, a resident of Panama.

people_involved: Licenciado Presbítero Don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Capitanes Sebastián de Garita and Don Andrés de Salazar, acting as executors for the deceased Licenciado Presbítero Don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, sell a house and lot in Cartago to Ayudante Miguel de Céspedes for 100 pesos.
Ayudante Miguel de Céspedes obligates himself for 100 pesos to the executors of Padre Cascante de Rojas. He promises to pay this sum in cacao.
The obligation made by Ayudante Miguel de Céspedes to the executors of Padre Cascante de Rojas for 100 pesos, to be paid in cacao, was cancelled in 1719.

people_involved: Sárjente Mayor Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: Sárjente Mayor Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral and his wife Doña Ambrosia González Camino obligate themselves for 300 pesos to Doña Francisca de Ballesteros. Doña Francisca is identified as a minor and the daughter of Capitán Juan de Ballesteros.

Ayudante Nicolás de Estrada leases a cacao plantation in the Reventazón valley to Andrés Calvo for three years. The plantation includes a thousand cacao trees and an annexed plantain grove with 300 heads, with an annual rent of 150 pesos.

María de Sibaja, a widow, leases a cacao plantation in Matina with a thousand trees to Alférez Francisco Calvo for three years. The annual rent is 10 zurrones of first-quality cacao, to be delivered in Cartago.

people_involved: Licenciado Don Juan Antonio de Moya
summary: The. Don Antonio de Utrera and his wife Doña Josefa de Moya sell a large cattle ranch in San José de Tenorio to Don José Fernando de Moya for 500 pesos. The property, including livestock, was originally acquired by Doña Josefa and her first husband, Capitán Don José de Vivas, from Doña Josefa's brother, Don Pablo de Alvarado. The 500 pesos are tied to a chaplaincy founded by Doña Josefa, with Licenciado Don Juan Antonio de Moya as patron and chaplain, and the buyer assumes this responsibility.

people_involved: Licenciado Don Juan Antonio de Moya
summary: The obligation related to the 500 pesos from the cattle ranch sale, tied to Doña Josefa de Moya's chaplaincy, was cancelled in 1718 by Licenciado Don Juan Antonio de Moya.

Alférez Francisco Calvo, Ayudante José de Chavarría, and his wife María Calvo obligate themselves for 500 pesos to a chaplaincy founded by Capitán Don Miguel Calvo, located in the Convento de San Francisco. They mortgage a house and lot facing the San Juan hermitage, with these funds designated for a sung mass.

Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra, patron of Capitán Don Miguel Calvo's chaplaincy, cancelled 250 pesos of the 500-peso obligation, which Alférez Francisco Calvo had paid. The remaining 250 pesos were taken by Don Luis de Sotomayor and his wife Doña Isabel Ramona de Utrera, who mortgaged an estate in Ujarráz in 1734.

people_involved: Alférez Don Antonio de la Riva y Agüero
Licenciado Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro
summary: Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribaréri's will details his family, including his parents, wife, and ten children, with some daughters' marriages noted. He inventories his assets, which include properties in Cartago, a mill, slaves, livestock, and a cacao plantation in Matina. The will also mandates the founding of a chaplaincy and appoints patrons for existing ones.
Ayudante José de Chavarría and his wife María Calvo grant freedom to their approximately 50-year-old slave, María Sanabria. María Calvo had inherited María Sanabria from her father, Don Miguel Calvo.
Capitán José Carranza and his wife Ana Micaela Calvo grant freedom to their pardo slave, Juan, who is over 40 years old. Ana Micaela Calvo had inherited Juan from her father, Don Miguel Calvo.
Pedro José de la Vega, a minor and legitimate son of the deceased Juan de la Vega and Juana Rodríguez, is apprenticed for 10 years to Capitán Blas de Ancheta, a master silversmith.
José Antonio, a zambo minor of about 7 years, son of the deceased Nicolás llama and Luisa Calvo, is apprenticed to Capitán José Carranza, a master silversmith.

Capitán José Carranza, married to Ana Micaela Calvo, acknowledges receipt of 1884 pesos. This sum includes a "negra bozal" slave named Josefa, which Ana Micaela inherited from her father, Capitán Don Miguel Calvo, through his will.
Feliciana Calvo, natural daughter of the late Don Miguel Calvo, received 1884 pesos as an inheritance left to her by her father's will.

Sarjento Mayor Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral, acting as executor for Captain Don Miguel Calvo, established a chaplaincy. This foundation ensures an annual mass is sung to Nuestra Señora del Trono in the Convent of San Francisco, with Captain Juan Francisco Ibarra as patron and the Convent's Guardian as chaplain, funded by a capital of 500 pesos.
Don José Nicolás Sarmiento de Sotomayor leased a cacao plantation in Matina, containing 460 trees, to Captain Juan Francisco de Ibarra. The lease is for three years at an annual rent of 100 pesos.

Captain Nicolás de Guevara and his wife Doña Francisca de Acosta Arévalo committed to a chaplaincy founded by Don Gregorio de Alvarado, Doña Francisca's first husband. This obligation is for 500 pesos, secured by a mortgage on a cacao plantation in Matina, though the deed was not completed.

Francisco de Morales and his wife Juana Cordero obligated themselves for 140 pesos to a chaplaincy founded by Don Francisco Enciso Hita. Captain Juan Francisco de Ibarra is the patron and Licenciado Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro is the chaplain, with the obligation secured by a mortgage on a 500-tree cacao plantation that Morales had purchased from Ibarra.

Francisco de Aguirre, as executor of Don Gregorio de Alvarado, established a chaplaincy for recited masses. Don Cayetano de Alvarado, the legitimate son of the deceased and Doña Francisca de Acosta Arévalo, is designated as the perpetual chaplain, with Presbítero Don José Nicolás de Guzmán (currently in Guatemala) serving until Cayetano is old enough to be ordained. Meanwhile, Licenciado Don Manuel de Guzmán, José Nicolás's brother, will recite the masses, all based on a 500-peso capital.
Captain Nicolás de Estrada granted his wife, Doña Francisca de Acosta Arévalo, a general power of administration.

Captain Antonio de Soto Barahona and Jacinto de Ocampo obligated themselves to Captain José Carranza for 200 pesos. They acted as guarantors for Juan Calvo, an enslaved mulatto belonging to Carranza, to secure Calvo's freedom upon payment of this sum. The obligation was cancelled in 1716.
Ana Cardoso sold an enslaved person named José de Alvarado, a 5-year-old mulatto blanco inherited from Captain Don Miguel Calvo, to Sarjento Mayor Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral for 100 pesos.

Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral, as Syndic General of the Missionary Fathers of the Talamanca Reduction, transferred a cacao plantation in El Riachuelo to the heirs of Captain Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribaren. This plantation was originally obtained by Fray Francisco de San José from the indigenous man Diegí» López, and Manuel Antonio de Arburola Ribaren, son of the Captain, accepted the transfer.
Juan de Benavides, a minor mestizo and son of the deceased Nicolasa de Benavides from Barba, was apprenticed to Nicolás de Sanabria, a master tailor, for a period of six years.

Nicolás Hernández, married to Felipa de Santiago, made his will. He declared his house in El Salitral on royal lands, some livestock, and various credits from his trading activities. He left a portion of his assets to a girl named María whom he had raised, named Juan Salvador and Antonio de Aguilar as executors, and designated his wife as his sole heir.

Margarita Hernández Barquero sold an enslaved pardo girl named Ana Teresa Barquero, 7 years old, to Captain Don José de Alvarado for 100 pesos. Ana Teresa was born in the household and is the daughter of Baltasara, an enslaved woman inherited by Margarita from her father, Ayudante Francisco Hernández Barquero.

María Calderón, widow of Martín de Civitola, sold a cacao plantation of 2000 trees in Matina to Don Miguel de Alvarado for 850 pesos. She and her husband had acquired this plantation from Captain Don Andrés de Salazar, and the buyer, along with his wife, will assume responsibility for several chaplaincies associated with the property.

Don Alonso Bernabé Cabeza de Vaca obligated himself for 500 pesos to a chaplaincy founded by Don Francisco Enciso Hita, with Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra as patron and Licenciado Don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro as chaplain. Captain Don José Vivas, Alguacil Mayor, delivered the funds when Alonso married Doña Juana de Moya, now deceased. The obligation was secured by a mortgage on the house that belonged to Don Antonio de Moya and a sugar mill with a cane field, with Don Antonio de Utrera and Doña Josefa de Moya acting as guarantors. The debt was cancelled in 1724 when the debtor sold the mill and cane fields to Captain Don Cristóbal Muñoz de la Trinidad.

Lieutenant Domingo de Inza owes Sarjento Francisco de Chavarría 100 pesos, which is the remaining balance for the enslaved mulatto Antonio de Alvarado. Upon payment, Chavarría will grant a letter of freedom.

Captain Don José de Alvarado y Jirón owes Captain Francisco Martínez 160 pesos, which he will pay in cacao delivered to the city. In Martínez's absence, the payment will be made to his wife, Doña Lorenza Venegas. This debt was cancelled in 1716.

Doña Manuela Valerino, widow of Captain Diego Santiago de Cárdenas, obligated herself to her minor legitimate children—José, Manuel, Diego Antonio, Petronila, and María de Cárdenas—for 1119 pesos and 4 reales, representing their paternal inheritance, with each child receiving 269 pesos and 7 reales.
Sebastiana de Arrieta leased a cacao plantation in Matina, containing 400 trees, to Ayudante Manuel Venegas. The lease is for three years at an annual rent of 50 pesos.

José de Gamboa sold a property with a house and corrals in Mata Redonda, Curridava valley, to Gonzalo Martínez for 610 pesos, including livestock. Gamboa had purchased this property from Doña Antonia Solano, and the buyer, along with his wife Josefa de Chaves, will assume responsibility for several chaplaincies associated with the property.
Licenciado Don Diego de Ángulo Gascón sold a cattle ranch in the Curridava valley, specifically in the Mata Redonda area, to Gonzalo Martínez for 200 pesos.

Doña Beatriz de Morales sold an enslaved mulatto boy named Juan Benito, 9 years old, to Ayudante Cristóbal González Vallejo, a resident of León, Nicaragua. Juan Benito is the son of Cecilia, an enslaved woman inherited by Beatriz from her parents, Juan de Morales and Doña [unnamed mother].
Beatriz de Miranda was involved in a transaction for 175 pesos. Juan José Camacho served as a witness for this transaction.
Feliciana Chinchilla, widow of Alférez Francisco Fernández, obligated herself to the Cofradía de la Concepción for 380 pesos. She mortgaged her houses in Cartago as security for this obligation.

Sarjento Antonio de Miranda and his wife Doña Ana María Maroto sold a 19-year-old black criolla slave named Leonor to Capitán Pedro Pantoja for 350 pesos. Leonor, daughter of Lucía, had been given as a dowry to Ana María by her mother, Doña Luisa Calvo.
Don Miguel de Alvarado Jirón owed 375 pesos to María Calderón, a widow. This debt was later cancelled in the year 1735 by the creditors.

Don Miguel de Alvarado Jirón and his wife Doña María de Torres obligated themselves for 500 pesos to a chaplaincy founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela, mortgaging a cacao plantation in Matina. This obligation was cancelled in 1735 by Presbítero Juan José Camacho, as the debtors had transferred the cacao plantation to Don Gil de Alvarado.

Capitán Juan Francisco de Ibarra obligated himself for 140 pesos to a chaplaincy founded by his grandfather, Tomás Calvo. He mortgaged a house that was adjudicated to him after the death of his mother, Doña Francisca Calvo, in 1706. This document was not completed.

Doña Luisa Calvo, daughter of Depositario general Tomás Calvo and Doña Eugenia de Abarca Alatras, and widow of Alférez José Maroto, made her will. She listed her children, including deceased sons José and Miguel, and daughters Gertrudis (married to Manuel de Herrera), Ana María (married to Sarjento Antonio de Miranda), and María Magdalena (married to Don José Baeza). The will detailed dowries given to her daughters, properties in Cartago and Matina, livestock, and several slaves, also making provisions for two orphan girls she raised.

Capitán Juan Francisco de Ibarra sold a 25-year-old black bozal slave named Sebastiana to Sarjento José Damián de Molina for 300 pesos. Ibarra had previously acquired Sebastiana from Alférez Bernardo Pacheco.

Doña Catalina González Camino granted power to her husband, Don José de Mier Cevallos, to make her will. She named her legitimate son, Manuel Martín Cubero, from her first marriage to Capitán Cristóbal Martín Cubero, as an heir, along with Nicolás, José Miguel, and Gabriel, her legitimate sons with her current husband, Mier Cevallos.

Sarjento José Damián de Molina and his wife Josefa Fernández sold a house in Cartago, along with four surrounding plots, to Licenciado Don Manuel López Conejo, a presbítero. The sale price was 600 pesos, with 390 pesos of that amount owed to various chaplaincies.

Juana Calderón, a widow, leased a 500-tree cacao plantation in Matina to Sarjento Antonio de Ocampo for two years at an annual rent of 125 pesos. This cacao plantation had been given to Juana as a dowry by her father, Alférez José Calderón.

Capitán Francisco Gutiérrez posted bail for José de Acuña, who was imprisoned for bringing Juan Agustín from the Matina valley. José de Acuña claimed Juan Agustín fell ill on the journey and did not arrive in the city.

Alférez Don Sebastián de Garita and Hermano Francisco de Aguirre, acting as executors for the deceased Presbítero Licenciado Don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, sold three individuals—Cayetana (23 years old), José (4 years old), and Carlos (8 years old)—to Capitán Don Andrés de Salazar for 550 pesos.

José Nicolás Masís sold a 20-year-old black bozal slave named Ventura to Capitán Antonio de Soto Barahona for 400 pesos. Ventura had been inherited by José Nicolás from his father, Sarjento Juan Masís.
Matías Barahona, a minor orphan who had lost both his parents, was handed over to José de Masís, a master tailor, for a period of 10 years.
José Manuel de Barros, a 10-year-old zambo, son of Petrona de Ocampo, was handed over to Matías Masís, a master blacksmith, for a period of 10 years. This document was incomplete.

Doña Tomasina de Ocampo Golfín made a codicil to her 1713 will, disposing of her slaves. She stipulated that her mulata slave María serve her nephew Francisco Montero de Espinoza for 12 years before gaining freedom, with any of María's children born free. Another mulata slave, Micaela, was to be given to her niece Josefa de Ocampo Golfín, who was to pay 100 pesos to Tomasina's brother, Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, who in turn was to give 50 pesos to Doña María Polo, daughter of Capitán Vicente Andrés Polo.
Capitán Juan Rodríguez, son of the deceased Andrés Rodríguez and María de Espinosa, and widower of Doña María de Sibaja, made his will. He listed his children as Micaela, Juan, María, and Gaspar.

Sarjento Mayor Antonio Aurelio Zamora made his testament in Barba, detailing his extensive properties including land, livestock, and eight enslaved people. He also noted cacao held by Capitán Diego Miguel de Algarín and his brother Alférez Gregorio Gordiano de Zamora in León, and mandated the establishment of a chaplaincy with his brother-in-law Capitán José de Saborío as patron. The testament also mentioned an enslaved person, José Ventura, belonging to Alférez José de Morales, held as collateral.

Alférez José de Quesada, a native of Málaga, made his testament in Barba. He was a widower of Doña Francisca Sánchez, who brought several enslaved people and other goods as dowry, though the receipt was lost in a pirate attack on Esparza. He had four children with Francisca and later married Doña Ana Jiménez, with whom he had six more children. He was involved in a lawsuit in 1684 with his sister-in-law Doña Juana Sánchez over dowry goods, and another with Antonia Pereira regarding the freedom of her enslaved son, Francisco.

Antonio Jiménez Maldonado made his testament in Barba, detailing his marriage to Doña Mariana Hidalgo and their twelve children. He specified the marriages of four of his daughters, including Ana Jiménez to Alférez José de Quesada. He owned a house, a sugar mill, land inherited from his mother, an estancia in Bagaces with livestock, and three enslaved people: María and her two children, Ana María and Francisco Antonio. He appointed his wife and son Juan Jiménez as executors.
Doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco, a widow, leased a cacao plantation in Matina to Capitán Luis Gutiérrez for an additional two years at an annual rent of 200 pesos.

Capitán José Carranza, a master silversmith, made his testament. He was the son of Capitán Juan de Carranza and Inés de Villavicencio, and was married to Ana Micaela Calvo, daughter of Capitán don Miguel Calvo. They had three daughters: Petronila, Inés, and Rosa María.

Doña Josefa de Bonilla, daughter of Sarjento Mayor Alonso de Bonilla and Juana Benita, made her testament. She was the widow of Alférez don Antonio de Porras, with whom she had no children. She named her sister Doña Sebastiana as a legatee and her nephew Juan de Bonilla, a minor cleric, as another beneficiary, and bequeathed a cacao plantation in Matina to the Cofradía del Rosario.

Clara Calvo, a free mulatta and former enslaved person of Capitán don Miguel Calvo, made her testament. She bequeathed part of her estate to María de la Candelaria, a child she raised since birth and referred to as her daughter.
Capitán Luis Gutiérrez was indebted to Francisco Martínez for 200 pesos, to be paid in cacao.

people_involved: Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: Doña Ambrosia González Camino granted power to her husband, Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral, to make a will. Their daughter, María Josefa Vega Cabral, was named as the heir.
Juan Fernández Martínez leased a cacao plantation with 800 trees in Matina to Alférez Marcos Daniel. The lease was for two years at an annual rent of 125 pesos.
Capitán Luis Gutiérrez owed Capitán Manuel García de Argueta 250 pesos, to be paid in cacao. Capitán Antonio de Soto Barahona served as the guarantor for this debt, which was cancelled in 1717.

people_involved: Presbítero Licenciado Don Juan de Guevara de la Cerda
Capitán Juan de Guevara de la Cerda
Licenciado Don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
Licenciado Don Manuel Jiménez de León
summary: Presbítero Licenciado Don Juan de Guevara de la Cerda, a resident of Granada, made his will. He bequeathed extensive livestock holdings in Bagaces and El Salto, as well as slaves María and her children Baltasara and Ventura. His parents were named as heirs, and Licenciado Don Diego de Ángulo Gascón and Licenciado Don Manuel Jiménez de León were appointed as executors.

people_involved: Sárjente Mayor Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: Doña Manuela de Quirós granted power to her husband, Sárjente Mayor Francisco de la Madriz Linares, to make a will. Their son, Dionisio, was named as the heir.

Don Gil de Alvarado sold a farm (estancia) located by the Lajuela River to his brother, Don Juan Manuel de Alvarado, for 100 pesos on credit. The property included a house, sugarcane field, plantain grove, and other crops, and the transaction was cancelled in 1735.

people_involved: Capitán Don Diego de Barros Carvajal
summary: Capitán Don Diego de Barros Carvajal sold an enslaved man named Juan Román, 28 years old, to Capitán Francisco Gutiérrez for 500 pesos. Juan Román had previously been purchased from José Márquez de Cabrera, a resident of Villa de los Santos.

people_involved: Presbítero Licenciado Don Manuel de Guzmán
summary: Capitán Francisco Gutiérrez pledged 525 pesos to the Chaplaincy founded by Doña Juana de Echavarría Navarro, for which Presbítero Licenciado Don Manuel de Guzmán served as patron and chaplain. As security, he mortgaged a house near Cartago on the road to Ujarraz, and a cacao plantation with 2000 trees in Barbilla.

people_involved: Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: Doña Francisca Jiménez, a widow, sold an enslaved man named Felipe, approximately 20 years old, to Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral for 250 pesos. Felipe had been acquired from the estate of her deceased husband, Capitán Francisco de Oviedo, following proceedings in 1712.

people_involved: Doña Mariana López de la Flor
Doña Baltasara López de la Flor
summary: Doña Mariana and Doña Baltasara López de la Flor leased a cacao plantation with 1400 trees in Matina to Alférez Manuel Antonio de Arleguí for three years at an annual rent of 175 pesos. They had inherited the estate from their mother, Doña Ambrosia de Echavarría Navarro, and the lease was cancelled in 1719.

people_involved: Presbítero Licenciado Don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
Licenciado Don Juan de Guevara de la Cerda
Licenciado Don Manuel Jiménez de León
Doña Bárbara Rosa Pomar y Villegas
Don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones
Licenciado Don Pedro Pomar de Villegas
Licenciado Don Andrés Gallo de Pinedas
summary: Hermano Francisco de Aguirre, as executor for Presbítero Licenciado Don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, established a chaplaincy for the souls of Juan Fernández de la Fuente, his wife Doña María Duran de Chaves, and their daughter Doña Ana de la Fuente. The assets were invested in a ranch in Bagaces, previously owned by the recently deceased Licenciado Don Juan de Guevara de la Cerda. Licenciado Don Manuel Jiménez de León and Gobernador Lacayo de Briones arranged for the foundations to be transferred to the Governor's family, with Don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones named as perpetual chaplain.

people_involved: Doña Josefa de Aguilar y Santiago
summary: Francisco Martínez sold a house and plot of land in Cartago to Doña Josefa de Aguilar y Santiago for 850 pesos. The property had been acquired from the estate of his deceased wife, Doña Lorenza Venegas, with 375 pesos of the sale price owed to various chaplaincies.

Marcelo Sánchez Mundaca, a resident of Esparza, along with Alférez Gregorio Picado and Ayudante José de Chavarría as guarantors, pledged 330 pesos to the Royal Treasury. This obligation was for the tithes that Sánchez Mundaca had auctioned for the current year and for 1717.

locations: Ermita de Nuestra Señora de la Soledad
people_involved: Presbítero Licenciado Don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
summary: Capitanes Juan de Aslúa and Blas de Ancheta, stewards of the Confraternity of Nuestra Señora de los Angeles, with permission from Presbítero Licenciado Don Diego de Ángulo Gascón, leased a productive cacao plantation in Matina to Alférez Marcos Daniel for three years. The annual rent was 161 pesos, which Marcos Daniel and his wife, Clara de Quirós, were obligated to pay.

Alférez Don Francisco de Moya made his will, identifying his parents as Sarjento Mayor José de Moya and Doña Mayor de Benavides. He was married to Doña Manuela de Alvarado, daughter of Capitán Don José de Alvarado and Doña Petronila de Retes, and they had two children, Doña Nicolasa Cayetana and Don José Francisco. His assets included a house in Ujarráz and a sugar mill.

people_involved: Alférez Don Antonio de la Riva Agüero
summary: Alférez Don Antonio de la Riva Agüero sold an enslaved man named Antonio, approximately 25 years old, for 300 pesos to Capitán Juan Francis-. Antonio was among those apprehended in Matina in 1710 and subsequently brought to and auctioned in Cartago.

Ayudante José de Chavarría and his wife María Calvo sold an 8-year-old mulata slave named Manuela to Governor José Antonio Lacayo de Briones for 150 pesos. Manuela was inherited by María Calvo from her father, Miguel Calvo.

The testament of the deceased doña Manuela de Quirós was granted by her husband and attorney, Sarjento Mayor Francisco de la Madriz Linares. She owned several slaves, a cattle ranch in La Candelaria, and another ranch near Ujarraz, and had a debt to a chaplaincy founded by her first husband, Captain Pedro de Ibáñez, and guardianship over the minor children of Santiago Moya. Her heir was her son, Dionisio Vicencio.

Captain Juan Francisco de Ibarra and his wife doña Petronila de Moya obligated themselves to the Royal Treasury for 4000 pesos, allowing Ibarra to administer the Treasury. They mortgaged properties in Cartago, 3000 cacao trees in Matina, and 8 slaves. Antonio de la Vega Cabral, Francisco de la Madriz Linares, Gabriel Maroto, Domingo de Inza, and José de Chavarría served as guarantors.

Alférez Pedro de Moya and doña Angela Sáenz, who had no children, made their testament, detailing properties in Cartago, near the Toyogres river, and a cacao plantation in Matina. They left legacies to several nieces and nephews, including José Antonio Bonilla, José Segundo de Moya, Josefa Francisca, Lorenza, and Juana María. They also mandated the founding of a chaplaincy with 1000 pesos, naming Licenciado Juan Antonio de Moya as patron and José Antonio Bonilla as perpetual chaplain, or alternatively Manuel Sáenz or another family member, until Licenciado Gregorio de Moya could be ordained.

Sarjento Francisco Hernández Barquero, as executor for Francisco Granados, sold a black slave named Manuel, over 30 years old, to Captain Diego de Aguilar for 400 pesos. This sum was tied to a chaplaincy founded by Captain Pedro de Alvarado, for which Licenciado Presbítero don Hermenegildo de Alvarado was the chaplain. The buyer took responsibility for this sum, with payments noted in 1719 and 1722.
María González, a widow, sold a 12-year-old mulata slave named Juana, born and raised in her house and daughter of Isabel, to Alférez Juan Masís for 200 pesos.

Captain José de Quesada, a native of Cádiz, made an agreement in favor of his fiancée, doña Antonia de Alvarado, for 1539 pesos. José is the legitimate son of Francisco de Quesada and Angela María de Castro, and Antonia is the legitimate daughter of the deceased Captain Jorge de Alvarado and doña Gertrudis de Echavarría Navarro.

Doña Josefa de Aguilar y Santiago, a widow, sold a house in the ejidos of Cartago to Captain Gabriel Maroto for 900 pesos. The house was previously owned by her daughter Francisca de Acosta Arévalo and her deceased husband Antonio de Acosta Arévalo, who had bought it from the deceased Licenciado don Francisco de Salazar. The sale proceeds were allocated to several chaplaincies.

Manuela Ricardo, legitimate daughter of Antonio Ricardo and Antonia Ma ar, and widow of Antonio Solano, made her testament. She had no children and named Juan de Fonseca, who was the executor of her husband, as her heir.

An incomplete testament of doña Lorenza Venegas, legitimate daughter of the deceased Sarjento Mayor Pedro Lorenzo Venegas and doña Jerónima de Retes. She was married to Captain Francisco Martínez and had seven children. She also raised and left legacies to two individuals named Pedro and Manuela.

The testament of Tomasina de Ocampo Golfín, made on December 12, 1713, was opened on January 7, 1716, the day she died. She was the legitimate daughter of the deceased The. Diego de Ocampo Golfín and María de Mora Salado, and widow of Felipe Gómez Macotela and Lázaro de Hortas Morcilla. She owned several slaves, and mandated that María be given her freedom.

people_involved: María de la O y Guevara
summary: Francisco Cartín, legitimate son of the deceased José Daniel Cartín and María de la O y Guevara, made his testament. He was married to Isabel de Quilos, daughter of the deceased Captain José de Quirós and Mariana González, and had three minor sons: José, Bernardo, and Cayetano.

Nicolás Masís, natural son of Francisca Barbosa, made his testament. He was married to Josefa de Alvarado and had three children: Domingo, Francisco, and Juana Josefa. His wife and brother, Juan Masís, were named as executors.
Doña Lorenza Venegas issued a codicil to clarify some accounts.
Miguel Masís, legitimate son, made his testament. (Entry is incomplete).
Francisca Barbosa, a bachelor, died today at 11 AM. She mandated the founding of a chaplaincy, with her brother, Alférez Juan Masís, as patron and don Manuel Sáenz, currently studying, as chaplain.
José Hidalgo sold a 13-year-old Creole Black enslaved woman named Teresa to Capitán don Gregorio Sáenz for 150 pesos. Hidalgo had previously purchased Teresa from José Gamboa.

people_involved: Reverendo Padre Fray Juan de Santiago
summary: Gregoria de Flores y Barbosa, daughter of the deceased Catarina de Flores y Barbosa and wife of Capitán don Andrés de Salazar, made her will in Valle de Aserrí. She had no children but bequeathed 200 pesos to Andrea, an orphan she raised, and mentioned her sister Lorenza de Flores. The will was witnessed by one person due to an epidemic, with Reverendo Padre Fray Juan de Santiago present.
Hermano José Hidalgo obligated himself to pay 165 pesos 6 reales to each of his children, Santiago and Gregoria Hidalgo, as their maternal inheritance from his deceased wife, doña Juana Arias.

Hermano José Hidalgo, legitimate son of the deceased Juan Hidalgo and doña María de Alfaro, and widower of doña Juana de Arias, made his will. He listed his children as María, Santiago, and Gregoria, noting that María was married to Capitán Andrés Antonio Pestico.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Antonio Aurelio de Zamora
summary: Doña Francisca de Saborío, widow of Sargento Mayor Antonio Aurelio de Zamora, obligated herself to pay 420 pesos to each of her legitimate children (Juan José, Eugenio, Antonio, Miguel, Lucía Efigenia, Francisco, and Cayetano de Zamora) as their paternal inheritance. Capitán José de Saborío acted as guarantor.

In 1726, after Doña Francisca de Saborío's death, her obligation for her children's inheritance passed to her second husband, Capitán Francisco de Flores. Capitán José de Saborío withdrew his guarantee, and the obligation then transferred to Capitán Juan José de Zamora, who obligated himself for four of his siblings, following the death of Eugenio.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Antonio Aurelio de Zamora
summary: Doña Francisca de Saborío obligated herself for 700 pesos to a chaplaincy founded by her deceased husband, mortgaging her house and three caballerías of land.
In 1726, Capitán Francisco de Flores took over the obligation for the chaplaincy founded by Doña Francisca de Saborío's deceased husband.

Capitán don Andrés de Salazar and his wife doña Gregoria de Flores obligated themselves for 250 pesos to a chaplaincy founded by doña María Yáñez, mortgaging a property with a sugar mill, livestock, and a house in Valle de Aserrí.
Capitán don Andrés de Salazar and doña Gregoria de Flores obligated themselves for 100 pesos to a chaplaincy founded by Luis Cascante de Rojas, using the same mortgaged property.
Capitán don Andrés de Salazar and doña Gregoria de Flores obligated themselves for 100 pesos to a chaplaincy founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela, using the same mortgaged property.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Antonio Aurelio de Zamora
Padre Guardián del Convento de San Francisco de Barba
summary: Capitán José de Saborío, acting as executor for the deceased Sargento Mayor Antonio Aurelio de Zamora, founded a chaplaincy for masses. The capital of 700 pesos was owed by Doña Francisca de Saborío, the founder's widow, secured by her house and three caballerías of land.

Juana de Chaves, widow of Alférez Juan de Torres, along with Alférez Francisco de Loria as guarantor, obligated themselves to pay 384 pesos 5 reales to her grandchildren Marcelo, Lorenza, and Antonio. Marcelo and Lorenza were legitimate grandchildren, while Antonio was a natural grandchild.

people_involved: Antonia Josefa (daughter of Antonio de Chaves)
summary: José Sendín de Sotomayor obligated himself to pay 168 pesos 6 reales to Antonio, Mateo, and Antonia Josefa, minor children of Antonio de Chaves, an indigenous person from Pacaca. Gonzalo Martín and Marcos Zamora acted as guarantors.

people_involved: Antonia Josefa (daughter of Antonio de Chaves)
summary: In 1726, Juan Ramos and Juana Solano, as heirs of the deceased minor children of Antonio de Chaves (Antonio, Mateo, and Antonia Josefa), provided a receipt for the inheritance.

The commencement of a will by Capitán Francisco Alejandro de Bonilla, legitimate son of Capitán Francisco de Bonilla and doña Leonor de Vargas. He is married to doña Josefa de Torres, who is the widow of Antonio Chapul and the legitimate daughter of the deceased Capitán Pedro de Torres and doña María Meléndez. They have a 7-month-old daughter, María Antonia, and Manuel Antonio Chapuí is mentioned as the son of doña Josefa's first husband.

Marcos Zamora obligated himself to pay 65 pesos 3 reales 1 cuartillo and 1 maravedí to each of his minor children (Cristóbal, María, Manuel, Francisco, Juana, Bárbara, and Efigenia Zamora) as their maternal inheritance from his deceased wife, Sebastiana Delgado.

Blas Suárez obligated himself to pay 91 pesos 7 reales to each of his legitimate children (María del Carmen, Sebastiana, Petronila, Juan, Pascual, Alfonsa, Gregoria, Margarita, Antonia, Manuela, Cosme, José Nicolás, and Nicolás Suárez) as their maternal inheritance from his deceased wife, María de Chaves.

Doña Elena de Umaña, widow of Capitán Juan Rodríguez, obligated herself to pay 63 pesos 4 reales to each of her minor legitimate children (Juana, Bernardo, José, Miguel, and Gabriel) as their paternal inheritance. Gaspar Rodríguez and Juan de Ugalde acted as guarantors.

people_involved: Francisco (raised by Juana de Benavente, brother 1)
Francisco (raised by Juana de Benavente, brother 2)
summary: Juana de Benavente, legitimate daughter of Bartolomé de Benavente and Antonia de Vargas, and widow of Diego de Chaves (with whom she had no children), made her will. She bequeathed her house and some furniture to Casilda de Esquivel, whom she raised and helped marry, and left some items to Rodolfa, whom she also raised. She also raised two brothers named Francisco.

A dowry letter was issued for the upcoming marriage on September 13th between Capitán don Nicolás de Guevara and doña Francisca de Inza. Capitán don Nicolás de Guevara is the widower of doña Francisca de Acosta Arévalo and the legitimate son of Capitán Juan Antonio de Guevara and doña Clara de Echavarría Navarro. Doña Francisca de Inza is the legitimate daughter of Capitán Domingo de Inza and doña Alfonsa Muñoz Hidalgo. The dowry was 1215 pesos 4 reales.

Isabel de Quirós, widow of Francisco Cartín, obligated herself to pay 189 pesos 6 reales and 11 maravedíes to each of her minor children (José, Bernardo, and Cayetano) as their paternal inheritance. Alférez Marcos Daniel acted as guarantor.
An incomplete record from September 15 in Barba mentions Capitán Gerardo de Azofeifa.
Juana de Chaves, widow of Alférez Juan de Torres, purchased a mulato slave named Juan de Chaves, approximately 40 years old. The slave was acquired from Francisco de Chaves for 350 pesos.

Alférez Gregorio de Segura, legitimate son of the deceased Captain Bernabé de Segura and Juana Solano, made his will. He was married to Josefa de Sandoval and listed his seven children: Francisco, Catalina, Angela, Rosa, Olaya, Josefa, and Elena, noting that Catalina was married to José de Acuña.
Juan Pérez de Solera committed to his granddaughter, Juana Machuca, for 150 pesos from her inheritance. Juana Machuca was the daughter of his deceased daughter Isabel Salado and Lorenzo Salado.

Francisco Martínez, widower of Doña Lorenza Venegas, committed to his minor children Teresa, María, Bernarda, Francisca, José Miguel, and Manuel Antonio. The total obligation amounted to 1945 pesos, 3 reales, and 10 maravedíes.

Captain Francisco Alejandro de Bonilla and his wife Doña Josefa de Torres committed to Manuel Antonio Chapuí for 1205 pesos from his inheritance. Manuel Antonio Chapuí was the son of Doña Josefa de Torres and her first husband, Antonio Chapuí, with Marcos de Zamora acting as guarantor. This obligation was later cancelled in 1735.

Doña Francisca Garita, widow of Captain Francisco Javier de Segura, committed to the chaplaincy founded by Juan Bautista Ricardo for 167 pesos. This obligation was inherited from her deceased husband and secured by a mortgage on her house in Barba.

Doña Francisca Garita committed to Alférez Salvador Murillo for 220 pesos, which belonged to Salvador's siblings, Jerónimo and Lucía Murillo. This was an obligation of her deceased husband, Francisco Javier de Segura, and was secured by a mortgage on a mill in the valley of Barba.

Doña Francisca Jiménez, legitimate daughter of the deceased Mateo Jiménez and Inés de Olivares, and widow of Francisco Alvarez de Oviedo, made her will. She had two daughters, Gertrudis and Manuela, and owned property including a house in Cubujuquí (also called La Concepción), 5 slaves, and livestock. She mandated the founding of a chaplaincy, designating Alférez Francisco de Flores as its patron.

Nicolás Arias and his wife Doña Gertrudis de Oviedo committed to Manuela de Oviedo, legitimate daughter of the deceased Captain Francisco Alvarez de Oviedo and Doña Francisca Jiménez, for 1343.5 pesos from her inheritance. Andrés Arias and his wife Doña Isabel Hidalgo served as guarantors. A portion of this obligation, 1100 pesos, was transferred to Captain Don José de Baeza in 1718.

Alférez Diego Hurtado de Coque, acting as executor for Doña Francisca Jiménez, formally founded the chaplaincy she had established in her will of December 3rd. The chaplaincy was endowed with a capital of 368 pesos and 3.5 reales, secured by the founder's house in the valley.

Nicolás Arias and his wife Doña Gertrudis de Oviedo committed to the chaplaincy founded by Doña Francisca Jiménez, for which Alférez Francisco de Flores was the patron, for 368 pesos. They mortgaged a ranch in the valley with 300 cattle, houses in the villa, and 5 slaves, with Andrés Arias and Doña Isabel Hidalgo as guarantors.

Alférez Antonio Valerino, who leased a cacao plantation from his sister Doña Petronila, subleased it for one year to Gregorio de Ureña for 250 pesos in cacao. Ureña was specifically exempted from paying for canoes or road maintenance, only the 'repartimiento del Padre' (10 pesos).

Juan Bautista Noguera, a native of Palma in the kingdom of Mallorca, made his will, naming his soul as his heir. Alférez Teodomiro Arias was appointed as executor and accepted the role on August 27th.
Gregorio de Ureña committed to Francisco de Espinoza for 125 pesos, which were payable in cacao.
Don Antonio de la Riva Agüero issued a receipt to Francisco Martínez for 6 sacks of cacao.
Francisco González guaranteed Gregorio de Ureña for the 250 pesos that Ureña owed to Antonio Valerino for a lease agreement.
Gonzalo Martínez leased a hacienda from Captain Nicolás de Guevara for a period of one year, agreeing to pay 200 pesos.
Domingo de Quesada leased a hacienda to Gregorio de Ureña for one year, with the agreed payment being 300 pesos.

people_involved: María de la Paz y Quirós
summary: Domingo de Quesada subleased a cacao hacienda, owned by María de la Paz y Quirós, to Nicolás de Quirós for 4 sacks of cacao. This transaction, like others in this section, was executed in Matina.
Captains Don Pedro and Don Gil de Alvarado provided bail for Captain Tomás de Chaves, securing his release from prison.

Ana de Aguilar, legitimate daughter of the deceased Pedro de Aguilar and Ana Velázquez, and widow of Juan de Trejos, made her will. She listed her eight children, her grandsons Francisco and Cayetano Barboza, and mentioned raising two orphans, Juana and José de Trejos.
Pedro de Salas, legitimate son of the deceased Francisco de Salas and Leonor Chacón, made his will.

Captain Esteban de Zúñiga, widower of Bárbara Corzo, made his testament in Puebla de los Angeles. He bequeathed a gilded wooden baldachin to Nuestra Señora de los Angeles and left his house in the 'población de los pardos' to Bernardo de Zúñiga.

Sarjento Mayor Juan de Zabaleta, a native of Fuenterrabía, Navarra, made his testament. He was married to Antonia de Hoces Navarro and had five children. He noted a debt of 350 pesos owed to him by General José de Zozaya, residing in Quito.
Doña María de Chaves, widow of Tomás Andrés Polo (Sr.), granted permission to her son, Captain Tomás Andrés Polo, to make his testament.

Captain Tomás Andrés Polo, son of Tomás Andrés Polo (Sr.) and María de Chaves, made his testament. He was married to Josefa López de la Flor and had no children. His wife's uncle, Captain Francisco López de la Flor, a resident of Panamá, was mentioned.

Salvador Ramírez, widower of Magdalena Milanés, made his testament. He had six children, but only Manuela was still alive. His nephew Francisco Navarro and grandson Salvador Palominos were also mentioned.

Francisco Granados, a native of the Kingdom of Genova, made his testament. He was a widower of Francisca Brígida, with whom he had six children. He was remarried to Josefa Agüero, with whom he had three more children.

Alférez Carlos Granados obligated himself to pay 150 pesos to his siblings Diego and Gertrudis, and 77 pesos to his half-siblings (children of Francisco Granados and Josefa Agüero: Francisco Diego, María, Juan, and Catalina). Nicolás Granados and Francisco Granados (son) acted as guarantors.

Captain José de Mier Cevallos and his wife, Catalina González del Camino, obligated themselves for 200 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Captain José de Vargas Machuca, mortgaging their house in the city.
Ayudante José de Chavarría owed 100 pesos to Ayudante Nicolás de Estrada, with José Felipe Calvo as guarantor. This debt was cancelled in 1720.
Alférez Juan de Masís, acting as executor for his deceased mother Francisca Barboza, granted freedom to a slave named Antonio.

Francisco Martínez sold a 36-year-old slave named Eugenia, who had belonged to his deceased wife Lorenza Venegas, to Pedro de Alvarado Jirón for 400 pesos. The payment involved mules and the assumption of a 100-peso debt to the Cofradía de la Concepción by Pedro de Alvarado Jirón and his wife Angela de Guevara.

Doña Isabel de Ocampo Golfín, widow of Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes, obligated herself for 100 pesos to the Cofradía de la Concepción. She mortgaged her house and plot in the city, which had belonged to her deceased parents, Diego de Ocampo Golfín and María de Mora.

Sarjento Mayor Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, as executor for his deceased sister Tomasa de Ocampo Golfín, sold a house in the city to Captain José Felipe Bermúdez and his wife Teresa de Sandoval for 700 pesos. Part of the sum was for a debt to the Convento de San Francisco de Cartago, and the remainder was for founding a chaplaincy as ordered by Tomasa. Captain José Antonio Bermúdez and his wife Baltasara Escalante Paniagua also guaranteed the sum.

Alférez Juan de Masís, son of Sarjento Juan Masís and Francisca Barboza, received a dowry letter for his marriage to María Fernández Martínez, daughter of Juan Fernández Martínez and Cayetana de Acosta Arévalo. María's grandmother, Josefa de Aguilar, contributed to the dowry, which included a 12-year-old pardo slave named Juana.

Hermano Francisco de Aguirre, as patron of the chaplaincy founded by Alférez Pedro Martínez de Colina, sold houses, two cauldrons, and a steelyard to Alférez Tomás de Chaves for 525 pesos. These items had belonged to Andrea Calderón, the founder's widow, and were subject to a 500-peso annuity.

Alférez Tomás de Chaves and his wife Tomasa de Quirós obligated themselves for 525 pesos to the previously mentioned chaplaincy, mortgaging the purchased property. This obligation was later cancelled in 1734 by Licenciado Lorenzo de Quesada.

José Nicolás Sarmiento de Sotomayor and his wife María Catalina Ortiz de Rosas obligated themselves for 100 pesos to the Cofradía del Rosario, a sum returned by Francisca Calvo, widow of Captain Juan Francisco de Ibarra. They mortgaged half a house located three leagues west of the city at 'los tres ríos,' which José Nicolás had inherited from his mother María Antonia Venegas.

people_involved: María de la O y Céspedes
summary: Captain José de Morales, perpetual councilman, and his wife María de la O y Céspedes obligated themselves for 150 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela. This sum originated from the value of a 35-year-old slave named Isabel, received from the estate of the deceased Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes. Presbítero Juan José Camacho accepted the obligation.

Doña Isabel de Ocampo Golfín, widow of Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes, obligated herself for 200 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Juana de la Portilla, a debt from her deceased husband. She mortgaged a house in Cartago as collateral.

Doña Isabel de Ocampo Golfín made another obligation for 100 pesos to a chaplaincy founded by Doña Juana Moscoso, a debt from her deceased husband. Licenciado don Manuel de Guzmán was the current chaplain, and Isabel provided the same guarantee.

people_involved: Doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar
summary: Doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar, a widow, sold a 20-year-old female slave named Antonia, of Popo caste, to Capitán Manuel García de Argueta for 300 pesos. Antonia had been purchased from Capitán Francisco Palo, agent for the Royal Asiento of Panama in 1710, and was apprehended on the Matina coast.

people_involved: Doña Catalina Carrasco de la Peña
Doña Ana de Salazar y Peralta
summary: Don Fernando Marín Poveda, originally from Santo Cristo de Mudela, made his will. He was a widower of Doña Juana Cedeño and had returned her dowry to Doña Sebastiana de Gracia. He was engaged to Doña Catalina González Camino, whom he named his universal heir.

Capitán Tomás de Chaves, married to Tomasa de Quirós, declared the assets he received from his father and his father-in-law (Sárjente Juan Masís) through his first wife, Francisca Masís. These assets included property at Río Grande, livestock, and three slaves: Francisco (23), Bernarda (20), and Juana (2).
Capitán Tomás de Chaves declared 440 pesos in assets received upon his second marriage to Tomasa de Quirós.

Capitán Tomás de Chaves made his will, declaring 2983 pesos as maternal inheritance for his children Tomasa and José Felipe, from his first wife Francisca Masís. His second wife, Tomasa de Quirós, was pregnant, and his brother, Licenciado don José de Chaves, was named executor.

Doña Gertrudis Guerrero made her will. She was a widow of Andrés Chacón and José Hermenegildo Romero, and mother to Josefa Liberata, Manuel, Antonio, and Antonia. She owned four slaves and a cacao plantation in the Matina valley at San Juan.

people_involved: Don Alonso Bersabé Cabeza de Vaca
summary: Don Alonso Bersabé Cabeza de Vaca, widower of Doña Juana de Moya, obligated himself to his son Manuel José for 700 pesos, which was Manuel José's maternal inheritance received by Alonso in 1714.

Bernarda Vázquez, a widow, leased a cacao plantation in Matina to Capitán Gaspar de Acosta Arévalo for three years at 100 pesos annually. This plantation was inherited from her mother, Gregoria Calderón, and originally belonged to her grandfather, Alférez José Calderón.

people_involved: Juan López de la Rea y Soto
summary: Juan López de la Rea y Soto, a scribe, leased a cacao plantation with 800 trees in the Reventazón valley to Aparicio Carrillo for three years. The rent was 50 pesos for the first year and 100 pesos for the subsequent two years.

María de Quirós, widow of Pedro de Salas, leased a cacao plantation in Barbilla to Domingo de Quesada for three years, with an annual rent of 5 zurrones of cacao. The plantation consisted of parts from her dowry, and purchases from her brother-in-law Francisco Cartín and her brother Nicolás de Quirós.
Capitán Nicolás de Guevara and his wife Doña Francisca de Inza obligated themselves to Capitán Manuel García de Argueta for 218 pesos and 6 reales.

Marcelo Gutiérrez made his will. He was the legitimate son of Capitán Francisco Gutiérrez and the late Nicolosa de Flores, and was married to Antonia Orozco. They had seven children: Juan José, María de la Rosa, Antonio, Isabel María, Gaspar de los Reyes, Teodora, and Manuela Gertrudis.

Sarjento Juan González made a codicil to his 1712 will. With his son Miguel's death, his daughter Antonia became the sole heir. He also bequeathed a cacao plantation in Barbilla, formerly belonging to his son Felipe Romero, to two boys he raised, Juan and Nicolás.

Doña Manuela de Salazar, a widow, donated a slave named Petronila, just over a year old and daughter of her other slave María, to her granddaughter Juana Manuela. Juana Manuela was the legitimate daughter of Don Gil de Alvarado and Doña Josefa González del Camino.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: Capitán don José de Morales, Perpetual Regidor and custodian of the estate of the late Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes, sold an 18-year-old mulato slave named José, son of Isabel (another slave of the deceased), to Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral for 200 pesos.

Ayudante José de Chavarría and his wife María Calvo granted freedom to Juliana Nicolasa, a mulata blanca slave about 6 years old. Juliana Nicolasa was the daughter of Juana Calvo, a mulata slave who had belonged to Capitán don Miguel Calvo, María Calvo's father.

Antonia Orozco, widow of Marcelo Gutiérrez, obligated herself for 852 pesos and 1/2 real of paternal inheritance in favor of her seven minor children. Pedro Molina, his wife Juana de Oviedo, and José de Orozco served as guarantors.
Alférez Juan Masís was named as the executor for Miguel.

A Masís brother founded a chaplaincy for masses with 880 pesos, which his brother José Masís had situated in two cocoa plantations in Barbilla. The chaplaincy provided 4 pesos per mass, with the remaining 4 pesos for wine, bread, and wax. Don Manuel Sáenz was designated as the first chaplain.

people_involved: Doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar
summary: Doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar obligated herself for 375 pesos to her grandson, Cayetano de Alvarado, for the value of two slaves. This obligation was later cancelled in 1721 by order of the Governor and Captain General because the slaves were confiscated, and a new obligation for 337 pesos 4 reales was made by doña Francisca de Inza in favor of the minor.

people_involved: Beneficiado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
summary: Alejo Ramírez, husband of Josefa Fernández (widow of Alférez Antonio de Ángulo), sold a cocoa plantation named Las Viejas in the Barbilla valley to Beneficiado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón, the oldest priest in the city, for 740 pesos.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Francisco de la Madriz Linares
Beneficiado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
Licenciado don José Francisco de Alvarado
doña Rita Josefa García de Argueta
summary: Sarjento Mayor Francisco de la Madriz Linares obligated himself for 1550 pesos to a chaplaincy founded by Capitán Pedro Ibáñez, with the assets of his deceased wife, doña Manuela de Quirós, and his uncle, Cura don Diego de Ángulo Gascón, as collateral. This obligation was later cancelled in 1751 by Licenciado don José Francisco de Alvarado, who had received the chaplaincy credits from Licenciado don Manuel López Conejo, and the credit had been transferred in parts to several individuals.

The will of Sarjento Mayor Francisco López Conejo was opened at the request of his son-in-law, don José de Alvarado. Francisco López Conejo, a native of Málaga, was married to doña María de Quirós and had six children: Josefa (married to don José de Alvarado), Manuel (a priest), Luis (a Franciscan religious), Pablo, Diego, and Eulalia. The will was made on December 13, 1716.

people_involved: Alférez don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad
Capitán don Diego Muñoz de la Trinidad
doña Antonia Josefa de Arburola Rivarén
summary: Alférez don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad, a native of Panamá, provided a dowry of 1753 pesos to doña Antonia Josefa de Arburola Rivarén. He was the legitimate son of Capitán don Diego Muñoz de la Trinidad and doña Maria de Pesquera, and she was the legitimate daughter of the deceased Capitán Lorenzo de Arburola Ribarén and doña Josefa de Hoces Navarro.

Alférez don Pedro de Moya and his wife, doña Angela Sáenz, exchanged slaves with Capitán Francisco Martínez. Moya and Sáenz gave a black slave named José (Mina caste), while Martínez gave a mulatto slave named Eugenia with a three-month-old child.

Alférez don Pedro de Moya leased a cocoa hacienda in the Matina valley, belonging to him and his wife doña Angela Sáenz, to Capitán Francisco Martínez. The hacienda had about 2000 trees and was leased for two and a half years for 188 pesos and 4 reales.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: Sarjento Mayor Francisco de la Madriz Linares obligated himself to his son, Dionisio Vicencio, for 1678 pesos and 2 reales, representing the inheritance Dionisio received from his mother, doña Manuela de Quirós.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Francisco de la Madriz Linares
doña Rita Josefa García de Argueta
summary: Sarjento Mayor Francisco de la Madriz Linares, a native of Rivadesella, Asturias, provided a dowry to doña Rita Josefa García de Argueta. He was the son of Antonio de la Madriz and doña María Borrero, and she was the daughter of Capitán Manuel García de Argueta and the deceased doña Antonia Láinez de Istueta. The document is incomplete.

people_involved: Capitán don Pedro Enríquez de Castro
summary: Don Diego de Arvizeta, a resident of Panamá, owed Capitán don Pedro Enríquez de Castro 220 pesos. This money was lent to Arvizeta to pay the Royal Treasury in Cartago for the transit rights of one hundred mules he was taking to Panamá.

Ayudante Matías Masís posted bail for Nicolás Méndez, who was imprisoned due to a verbal complaint from Juana Bonilla, a free parda, alleging he took her virginity. Méndez was released because he offered to marry Bonilla, and he was an apprentice who grew up in Masís's house.
Capitán Francisco Martínez granted general power of attorney to Francisco de Aguirre.

people_involved: Capitán don Antonio de la Riva Agüero
summary: Capitán don Antonio de la Riva Agüero and his wife, doña Catarina de Arburola, sold a cocoa plantation with 560 trees on the banks of the Matina river to Capitán Francisco Martínez for 400 pesos.
Alférez Marcos Daniel owed Sárjente Agustín Guerrero 150 pesos. This debt originated from Gonzalo Martín, who had ceded the debt to Guerrero, for six mules Daniel had purchased from Martín.

The will of Lucía Picado, legitimate daughter of the deceased Melchor Picado and Ana María de la Concepción, and widow of Cristóbal Mejía, was opened. She had thirteen children, with six still alive. Her deceased son Antonio, who was married to María de Villalobos, died in the Matina valley without children. Her daughter María was married to José de Rojas (deceased), Gertrudis to José de Ortega, and Ana to Marcelo de Flores.

Don Pedro Jirón de Alvarado and his wife, doña Angela de Guevara, obligated themselves for 100 pesos to the Cofradía de la Concepción, receiving the money from the Mayordomo, Capitán don José Antonio Bermúdez. They mortgaged their adobe and tile house in the city.

people_involved: Doña Angela de la Paz y Flores
Teniente don Antonio de Utrera y Medina
summary: Doña Angela de la Paz y Flores, widow of don Sebastián de Ocampo Golfín, sold a 16-year-old mulatto slave named Sebastiana, daughter of her slave Josefa, to Teniente don Antonio de Utrera y Medina, a resident of the Ujarraz valley.

Doña Angela, to whom Sebastiana was adjudicated in 1697 after her husband's death, sought to sell Sebastiana. Sebastiana initially resisted being bought by Utrera, but after Doña Angela requested the Teniente Gobernador to find a buyer for 312 pesos (200 for Sebastiana and 112 to cover Doña Angela's debt to Utrera), Utrera ultimately purchased her for that amount.
Don Antonio de Escalante Paniagua sold a cacao plantation in Barbilla, comprising 320 trees, to Capitán Manuel García de Argueta for 250 pesos.

Doña Ana de Escalante Paniagua, whose husband Ayudante Don Juan de Torres was absent in Nicaragua, leased a cacao plantation of about a thousand trees in the Valle de Barbilla to Don José Antonio Bermúdez. The lease was for three years, with Bermúdez obligated to provide 6 zurrones of cacao annually.
Mateo de los Santos, a 12-year-old mestizo and son of the free mulata María del Carmen, was handed over to José de las Salas, a master tailor, for a period of six years.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
Capitán Don Juan Sancho de Castañeda
Maese de Campo Don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín
Don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones
summary: Sarjento Mayor Don Francisco de la Madriz Linares and Capitán Don Juan Sancho de Castañeda, as executors of the deceased Maese de Campo Don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín, committed to pay Don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones 1647 pesos 4 reales 16 maravedís from Granda y Balvín's accrued salaries in the Royal Treasury of León. This sum covered debts including those from a 1607 residency and a condemnation by Governor Lacayo de Briones. They also issued a draft for 842 pesos 3 reales 15 maravedís for funds related to the Royal Audiencia of Guatemala and the Court of Deceased Estates from Juan Ángel Malatesta's intestate death, all of which were Granda y Balvín's responsibility, as certified by José de Guzmán.
Teniente Domingo de Inza and his wife Doña Alfonsa Muñoz Hidalgo sold a country house of tile and adobe, located in the common lands of this city by the Molino River, to José Masís for 400 pesos.

José Masís, legitimate son of the deceased Sárjento Juan Masís and Francisca Barboza, and married since 1711 to Teodora Molina, legitimate daughter of Juan Molina and Juana Galindo, acknowledged receipt of 1380 pesos in assets that were delivered to him upon his marriage.

José Masís and his wife Teodora Molina pledged 880 pesos to the Chaplaincy founded by Miguel Masís, José's brother. They mortgaged a cacao plantation with 1200 trees in the Valle de Barbilla as collateral for this obligation.

Juan Taimes de Segura committed to pay Capitán Don José de Quesada 90 pesos, with 38 pesos in cacao and the remaining 52 pesos with a saddle mule, a pack mule, and two tobacco cases. Doña Juana Damiana de Mora acted as guarantor, offering her mulata slave named María as security.

Capitán Don Nicolás de Guevara sold a 25-year-old Conga slave named María, who had previously belonged to his deceased first wife Doña Francisca de Acosta Arévalo, to Sarjento José Damián de Molina for 250 pesos.

Sarjento Mayor Esteban Nieto, a native of Sevilla and son of Licenciado Diego Nieto and Juana de Soto y Hermosilla, made his will on April 4, 1717, and died the following day. He instructed that a 'lignum crucis' and an image of Nuestra Señora de los Reyes be given to Antonio Nozariquez (or his heirs) in payment of a 400-peso debt from their service in Chile. He also bequeathed various items to Isabel Morales, María Solano, Isabel's brothers, and the child Agustín, requesting to be buried in old clothes.
Antonia González, legitimate daughter of Sarjento Juan González and the deceased María de Espinoza, granted freedom to her mulata slave named María Nicolasa, who was over 35 years old.

people_involved: Licenciado Don Juan Méndez de Sotomayor
summary: Capitán Don Bernardo Marín owed Licenciado Don Juan Méndez de Sotomayor 324 pesos, payable in cacao or mules. This amount represented the final balance of a 405-peso debt Marín owed to Capitán Juan de Porras, a resident of Panamá, for whom Méndez de Sotomayor held power of attorney to collect.

people_involved: Presbítero Licenciado Don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
General Don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones
Doña Bárbara Rosa Pomar y Villegas
summary: Doña María de Quirós, widow of Sarjento Mayor Francisco López Conejo, pledged 100 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Luis Cascante de Rojas. Following the death of the chaplain and patron, Presbítero Licenciado Don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, on January 18, 1715, the patronage transferred to General Don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones, as husband of Doña Bárbara Rosa Pomar y Villegas, with their children serving as chaplains. Doña María mortgaged her cattle ranch in La Catuielaria, including livestock, houses, and sugarcane fields, as security.

locations: ribera del río de La Lajuela
people_involved: Alférez Don Juan Manuel de Alvarado
summary: Alférez Don Juan Manuel de Alvarado owed Juan Hidalgo, a resident of Valle de Barba and guardian of Doña Francisca de Ballesteros, 100 pesos at 5% interest. This debt was originally owed by Francisco Ramírez, a resident of Valle de Currirava. Alvarado mortgaged a house with land and fences on the bank of the La Lajuela River as collateral, and the debt was cancelled in 1721.
Capitán Don José de Bonilla and his wife Doña Manuela Sáenz made an obligation in favor of a chaplaincy (the text is cut off).

Juan Fernández de la Fuente and María Duran de Chaves founded a chaplaincy, which was initially patroned and served by Presbítero Licenciado Gaspar Cascante de Rojas. Currently, General José Antonio Lacayo de Briones is the patron through his wife, Bárbara Rosa Pomar y Villegas, a cousin of the founders. A house in the city's common lands is mortgaged for 100 pesos.

people_involved: Manuel Antonio de Arburola y Ribarén
summary: Nicolás Arias from Barba valley sold an enslaved mulato named Antonio, approximately 38 years old, to Manuel Antonio de Arburola y Ribarén for 310 pesos payable in cacao. Antonio had been previously purchased from the estate of Alférez Francisco de Oviedo. This transaction was cancelled in 1718.
Pedro, a 14-year-old pardo and legitimate son of the deceased Francisco Calvo and María de Céspedes, was delivered to Alférez Francisco de Espinoza, a master tailor, for a five-year apprenticeship.
Manuel, a 12-year-old orphan, was delivered to Juan Calixto de Segura, a master shoemaker, for a five-year apprenticeship.

Juan Guzmán provided a dowry of 499 pesos for his future wife, Josefa Fernández Solano, the legitimate daughter of the deceased Hermano Gaspar Fernández Solano and Margarita Chacón. Their marriage was scheduled for the following day, but the document was not signed.
Jorge de Mora leased a cacao plantation in Matina, containing 400 trees, to Captain Juan Francisco de Ibarra for three years at an annual rent of 50 pesos.

Captain Pedro Rodríguez Palacio, a Regidor and Alguacil Mayor, and Sergeant Major Blas González Coronel, an Alcalde Mayor provincial and perpetual Regidor, granted general power of attorney to Captain Nicolás de Valenzuela. Nicolás de Valenzuela was a resident of Santiago de Guatemala, serving as Notary Mayor of the Santa Cruzada and Escribano Mayor of Cabildo.

Doña Josefa de Aguilar, widow of Antonio de Acosta Arévalo, leased a cacao plantation in the Matina valley, comprising 1200 trees, to Captain Jerónimo Manuel Ramos for three years at an annual rent of 325 pesos.

Ayudante Miguel de Céspedes and his wife Juana de Bonilla formally recognized a census related to a chaplaincy. Licenciado Juan José Camacho was identified as the chaplain for this particular chaplaincy.

María Hernández Barquero, a widow, sold an enslaved parda named Juana, aged 7, to Captain Francisco de Flores for 150 pesos. Juana was born in María's house and was the daughter of Clemencia, a mulata inherited by María from her deceased father, Ayudante Francisco Hernández Barquero.

Doña Baltasara de Escalante Paniagua granted power to Governor José Antonio Lacayo de Briones to draft her will. She designated her husband, Captain José Antonio Bermúdez, as her heir, as she had no forced heirs.

Don José Nicolás Sarmiento de Sotomayor, son of the deceased Bernardo Sarmiento de Sotomayor and Antonia María Venegas, provided a dowry for his wife, Doña María Catarina Ortiz de Rosas. The dowry included 1800 pesos, an enslaved mulato named Juan (10 years old, son of María Micaela), 750 cacao trees in Matina, and 475 pesos in cacao, with assets received from his wife's grandparents and stepfather.

people_involved: Francisco de Guevara de la Cerda
summary: Licenciado Manuel López Conejo, chaplain of a chaplaincy founded by Captain Pedro Ibáñez and the deceased Manuela de Quirós, sold an enslaved "mulata blanca" named Juana for 300 pesos to Captain Francisco de Guevara de la Cerda, a resident of Granada, Nicaragua, currently in this city. Juana had been given to Manuel as payment for overdue debts by Sergeant Major Francisco de la Madriz Linares, Manuela's second husband.

Doña Águeda Pérez de Muro, widow of Maese de Campo José de Casasola y Córdoba, sold an enslaved person named Manuela Josefa, 26 years old and of a somewhat white complexion, to Governor José Antonio Lacayo de Briones for 400 pesos. Manuela Josefa had been a donation from Águeda's father, Captain José Pérez de Muro, and part of the estate of her mother, Mariana de Echavarría Navarro.

Doña Antonia María Venegas, a widow, sold a "caballería de tierra" in Los tres ríos, located about three leagues west of the city, to Captain José de Alvarado y Jirón for 50 pesos. The land's boundaries were precisely described by rivers and hills.

Bernardo de Aguilar, Gaspar de los Reyes, Francisco Calvo, Andrés de la Cruz, and Juan de Ortega, indigenous concessionaires of the city's brickyard, who pay 25 pesos annually, provided Captain Domingo de Inza as their guarantor. Their lease for the brickyard was set to expire on May 31, 1719.

Lucrecia Martínez Enríquez, widow of Baltasar de Mora, transferred 150 pesos of paternal inheritance to her son-in-law Juan Francisco de Morales, intended for his wife María Manuela de Mora. Additionally, she provided 20 heads of cattle, two sacks of cacao, and various clothing and household items.

Isidro de Acosta, natural son of the deceased Diego López, made his will. He was married to María Núñez and had two sons, Manuel and Silvestre. His possessions included a house on Diego Núñez's plot and a cacao plantation in Matina.

María Calderón, a widow, and her son Antonio de Segura leased a cacao plantation in Matina, consisting of 400 trees, to Captain Gaspar de Acosta Arévalo. The lease was for three years at an annual rent of 100 pesos.

Juan González de Ochoa, through a codicil, established a chaplaincy for recited masses, funded by the value of a cacao plantation in Barbilla with approximately 500 trees, which he inherited from his deceased son José. He appointed Licenciado Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro as the patron and José Miguel de Arburola as the chaplain.

Captain Manuel García de Argueta, who purchased enslaved Diego (from Cabo Verde) from the estate of José de Casasola y Córdoba for 400 pesos, granted a 200-peso discount on the price. Don Diego de Lamas, a resident, agreed to pay the remaining 200 pesos to García Argueta, thereby securing Diego's freedom, on the condition that Diego would accompany Lamas to explore the hills.

Don Diego de Lamas presented written traditions and notes to a judge, requesting legal protection to explore and prospect for mines in an area spanning from Quebrada del Limón near Pacacua to the junction of Río de Turrubales and Río Grande, including the Cerro del Gallo. The judge granted his request, and Lamas offered incentives to 'el negro' and Capitán García if veins or mines were discovered.

Alférez Don Sebastián de Garita, a Public Notary and Notary of the Holy Office of the Inquisition in Cartago, leased a cacao plantation with 2000 trees in Matina to Gabriel Lobo for three years at an annual rent of 100 pesos. The cancellation of this lease occurred in 1720.

Alférez Jerónimo de Morales, as patron of a chaplaincy founded by Don Antonio Machado with a capital of 2630 pesos, granted power of attorney to Licenciado Juan José Camacho. The chaplaincy was intended for the founder's children, close relatives, the convent's guardian, and Camacho, who was Machado's nephew.

Doña Petronila de Moya, legitimate daughter of Capitán Don Esteban de Moya and Doña Rafaela de Alvarado, and wife of Capitán Juan Francisco de Ibarra, granted her husband power to make a will. Her heirs were her children Francisca, Miguel, María Catalina, and Manuela de Ibarra, with her husband and her brother, Licenciado Don Gregorio de Moya, named as executors.
Sargento José Damián de Molina posted bail for his slave, Sebastiana, who was facing a criminal charge alongside Alférez Carlos Granados.

people_involved: Don Alonso Bersabé Cabeza de Vaca
Maese de Campo Don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín
summary: Doña Nicolasa Guerrero made her will, requesting burial in the church and convent of Ujarrás where she resided. She declared her slaves, named her adopted orphans, and detailed her relationship with Maese de Campo Don Lorenzo Antonio de Granda y Balvín, stating he promised marriage and had a daughter with her, Antonia. She also mandated the founding of two chaplaincies and named her executors and heirs.

Alférez Luis Peláez and his wife, María de los Santos, owed Capitán Tomás de Chaves 524 pesos for 150 cattle and 4 mules, mortgaging their adobe and tile house in Cartago. A marginal note indicates that Chaves received payment from Peláez's widow in 1723.
Antonio de Bonilla sold a 28-year-old 'arara' slave named Antonia to Jacinto de Campos for 400 pesos.

Antonio de Umaña owed Capitán Tomás de Chaves (the younger) 150 pesos, which he had received from Alférez Francisco de Espinoza. This credit originally belonged to Alférez Carlos Granados, who had transferred it to Chaves.

people_involved: Licenciado Don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
summary: Licenciado Don Diego de Ángulo Gascón, the most senior priest in Cartago, sold a cattle ranch in La Mata Redonda to Gonzalo Martin for 300 pesos. He had acquired the ranch from Licenciado Don Gregorio de Moya, who was currently pursuing studies in Santiago de Guatemala.
