Francisco Martínez made his will, identifying his parents, wife Doña Lorenza Venegas, and six children. He listed his slaves, granting freedom to one named Mateo after his death, and mentioned a silver-hilted iron sword pawned at Capitán Manuel García's house. He died on the same day, October 2nd.

Capitán Juan Francisco de Ibarra, widower of Doña Petronila de Moya, executed a will on her behalf, as authorized by a power of attorney granted on September 15th. Doña Petronila de Moya was buried within the main chapel of the Convent.

Don Gil de Alvarado and his wife, Doña Josefa González Camino, obligated themselves for 100 pesos to a chaplaincy founded by Comisario Baltasar de Grado, currently served by Licenciado don Manuel de Guzmán. This debt was later redeemed by Capitán Domingo de Inza and his wife, Doña Alfonsa Muñoz Hidalgo. The couple mortgaged their house, which bordered the Cabildo houses and the house of Doña Catalina de Vida Martel.

Capitán José Antonio Bermúdez and his wife, Doña Baltasara Escalante Panlagua, obligated themselves to the Royal Treasury for 500 pesos. This sum was for the office of Regidor and Depositario general, which Bermúdez had won in auction. Don Antonio de Soto Barahona and Don Felipe Bermúdez served as guarantors for the obligation.

Juan Patricio de Sandoval, natural son of Don José de Sandoval and Ana López de Santiago, made his testament in Valle de Barba. He detailed his two marriages, first to Inés de Rojas (with whom he had Agustín, Bernarda, and Josefa) and then to Teodora de Quirós (with whom he had Isabel, María Lorenza, Juan Francisco Isabel, Cayetano, and Sebastián). He also mentioned his son-in-law Esteban de Vargas and his niece Catalina de Avila.

The married couple Alberto Cascante and María Guerrero made their testament in Valle de Aserrí, stating they had no children together. María Guerrero had previously been married to Miguel de Prendas, with whom she had five children: Josefa, Juan José, Micaela, Miguel, and María del Carmen Prendas. Her sister was Ana de Quesada, and Miguel Coronado was her son from a previous relationship.

Don Gregorio Sáenz, a resident of Cartago, sold an enslaved Creole woman named Teresa, approximately 13 years old, for 300 pesos. The buyer was Ayudante Sebastián Alvarez, a resident of Granada, Nicaragua, who was currently residing in the province.

Capitán Bernardo Cortés sold a piece of land in the plain of the Ciruelas River to Sarjento Pedro Loria for 100 pesos. The property was bordered by the river to the East and the royal road to the West.
Capitán Bernardo Cortés sold another piece of land in the same location, the plain of the Ciruelas River, to Alférez Mateo de las Alas for 25 pesos.
Capitán Bernardo Cortés sold a third piece of land in the plain of the Ciruelas River to Marcos Morera for 40 pesos.

Lucrecia Murillo, widow of Matías de Madrigal, made her testament, mentioning her deceased married children Nicolás and María de Madrigal. She identified Doña Micaela Rodríguez as her daughter-in-law and Francisco de las Alas as her son-in-law. Her brother Salvador Murillo and sister-in-law Clara de Esquivel were also noted, and her numerous grandchildren from both families were named as heirs.

locations: Valle de San Luis de Aserrí
summary: Laureano Guerrero and Ana de Vargas Machuca, a married couple, made their testament in Valle de San Luis de Aserrí. They listed their children, including Sebastiana (married to Juan Valverde) and Antonia (married to Alférez Cayetano de Herrera), and a deceased son Juan (married to Doña Nicolasa Valverde). Their granddaughter Francisca Guerrero and niece Isabel de Vargas were also mentioned, along with details of their land purchases from natives of Pacacua and Luis Cascante.

Capitán Luis Morera and his wife Gregona de Segura owed 300 pesos to Lucrecia de Murillo, a widow, and mortgaged a sugar mill and 200 cattle as security. This debt was cancelled in 1720 by Francisco de las Alas, acting as the executor.
José Rosales, a minor and son of Josefa Rosales, was delivered to Marcos de Segura, a master blacksmith, for a period of 7 years.
José García, an orphan, was delivered to Pedro Méndez, a master blacksmith, for a period of 6 years.
Cayetano de Alvarado, described as a free 'pardo' individual, was delivered to Pedro Salvador Juárez, a master hatmaker, for a period of 10 years.

Salvador Murillo made a codicil to his testament, which he had granted in 1712 jointly with his wife, Clara de Esquivel. He noted 420 pesos belonging to his brother Jerónimo Murillo and mentioned his nephew Bernardo Pacheco. His wife and 'Hermano' Francisco Montero de Espinoza were named as executors, with the codicil granted before Pablo de Sibaja, Lieutenant Governor and Judge of the Countryside.
Capitán Bernardo Cortés sold a piece of land in the plain of the Ciruelas River to Alférez Francisco Loria for 40 pesos. The land was bordered by the river to the East and the royal road to the West.

people_involved: María de la Rosa de Chaves
summary: Alférez Tomás de Chaves and Juana de Solís made their testament in San Antonio Curriravá, listing their seven children and their spouses. They also detailed their enslaved people, including Feliciana and her daughters, with Feliciana to be granted freedom. The testament described their extensive land holdings, noting a portion belonging to their son-in-law José de Quirós, near the 'potrerillo' of Capitán Juan de Chaves.

Chaves (head of household) holds 700 pesos belonging to his god-daughters, Petronila and her sister, who reside in León, Nicaragua. He also allocates 1200 pesos to his son, José de Chaves, who is studying for the priesthood, to ensure he receives an equal inheritance with his other siblings. The family owns a piece of land located between the Virilla river and Tibás.

locations: Convento de San Bartolomé de Barba
summary: Chaves (head of household) and his wife clarified the foundation of a capellanía, originally established by an escritura in 1710. They stipulated that if their son, José de Chaves, does not become ordained, the capellanía will revert to the Convento de San Bartolomé de Barba.

Chaves (head of household) and his wife donated a two-year-old mulata slave named María to their son, José de Chaves. This donation, valued at 100 pesos, was intended to be counted towards his legitimate inheritance.

Gonzalo Martín and his wife, Josefa de Chaves, obligated themselves to the Convento de San Francisco de Cartago for 190 pesos. This debt was originally owed by José de Gamboa and was secured by a house and land bordering properties of Capitán Francisco Alejandro de Bonilla and the Torres and Tiribí rivers.
Gonzalo Martín and Josefa de Chaves, for the same reason as a previous obligation, committed themselves to the Cofradía de la Concepción for 180 pesos.
Juan Duran, widower of María Calderón, obligated himself to his legitimate daughters, Ana and Francisca Duran. He committed to paying each daughter 91 pesos as their maternal legitimate inheritance.
A codicil by Lucrecia Murillo states that José Núñez now owes 50 pesos, a debt previously held by Nicolás de Alfaro. The codicil also notes the deaths of Lucrecia's brothers, Salvador and Jerónimo.

Isabel de Carvajal, widow of Marcos de Torres, obligated herself to her daughter Lorenza for 160 pesos. This sum was awarded to Lorenza from the estate of her grandfather, Alférez Juan de Torres, with Alférez Francisco Loria and his wife Angela de Chavarría acting as fiadores.

Gertrudis Rosales, widow of Lorenzo de Torres, obligated herself to her son Marcelo for 160 pesos. This amount was awarded to Marcelo from the estate of his grandfather, Alférez Juan de Torres, with Ramón de la Cruz and his wife Gregoria Rodríguez serving as fiadores.

Juana de Chaves, widow of Alférez Juan de Torres, obligated herself to her natural grandson, Antonio de Torres, for 64 pesos and 4 reales. This sum was awarded to Antonio from the estate of his grandfather, Alférez Juan de Torres, with Alférez Francisco Loria acting as fiador.
Sarjento José Damián de Molina sold a 25-year-old black Arara slave named Sebastiana to José de Quirós for 300 pesos. Molina had previously purchased Sebastiana from Capitán Juan Francisco de Ibarra.

people_involved: Maese de Campo don Pedro Ruiz de Bustamante
summary: Maese de Campo don Pedro Ruiz de Bustamante, who holds the titles of Gobernador and Capitán General, granted general power of attorney. The primary recipient was Capitán don Miguel de Montúfar, Treasurer General of the Real Haber de la Santa Cruzada and a resident of Santiago de Guatemala, with Capitán Juan Gregorio Vázquez as the secondary recipient.

Alférez Agustín Guerrero obligated himself to Rodulfa de Chaves, an orphan girl, for four mule beasts valued at 100 pesos. These animals were bequeathed to Rodulfa in the will of Diego de Chaves and were delivered by Diego's brother, Capitán Juan de Chaves, with Sarjento Laureano Guerrero acting as fiador.

Tomás de Salvatierra obligated himself to doña Catalina de Hurtado, mother of his deceased nephew Alférez Diego de Hurtado, for 54 pesos and 2 reales. This sum was awarded to doña Catalina from Diego's estate, and the funds were delivered to Salvatierra, with Capitán Alonso de Porras and Marcos de Zamora serving as fiadores.

Don Juan José Camacho obligated himself for 150 pesos to a capellanía. His mother, doña Beatriz Morales, a widow, acted as fiadora, mortgaging her house in the city and two mulata slaves, Manuela Josefa (9 years old) and Josefa Nicolasa (5 years old).

people_involved: Don José Nicolás Sarmiento de Sotomayor
Presbítero Licenciado don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro
Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Don José Nicolás Sarmiento de Sotomayor and his wife, doña Catalina de Rosas, obligated themselves for 150 pesos to a capellanía founded by doña Luisa Calvo, whose chaplain is Presbítero Licenciado don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro. They received the funds from the capellanía's patron, Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona, and mortgaged a cacao plantation on the Matina river. Doña Catalina de Rosas's grandparents, Don Pedro de Alvarado and doña Catalina de Vida Martel, also served as fiadores.

Alférez Nicolás de Guevara and his wife, doña Francisca de Inza, obligated themselves for 100 pesos to the capellanía founded by doña Luisa Calvo. They mortgaged a house and adjacent land, located in the city's ejidos near the Reventado river, which they had purchased from Capitán Blas de Ancheta.

people_involved: Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona and his wife, doña Petronila de Hoces, obligated themselves to the heirs of Francisco Martínez and doña Lorenza de Venegas for 675 pesos from their inheritance. Subsequent receipts show payments made to Capitán Vicente Polo (husband of doña Teresa Martínez) on July 11, 1721, Sárjente Mayor don Pedrojosé Sáenz on December 15, 1721, and Don Juan Antonio Villar Hevia on March 23, 1725.
Capitán Juan Francisco de Ibarra obligated himself to the same heirs of Francisco Martínez and doña Lorenza de Venegas.

Sarjento Mayor Blas González Coronel and Licenciado Presbítero Manuel José González Coronel exchanged slaves. Blas gave Lorenza, a 25-year-old Conga black woman, and Manuel gave Agustín, a 26-year-old Creole black man, son of Eugenia, who was donated by Lorenza Venegas.
Licenciado Manuel José González Coronel sold the black woman Lorenza to Captain José Antonio Bermúdez for 400 pesos.

Doña Nicolasa de Morales granted power of attorney to Captain Pedro Enríquez, a trader bound for Panama, to sell a mulato named Ignacio, who is currently in the possession of Licenciado José de Uriola Chavarría in Cartago.

people_involved: Juan López de la Rea y Soto
summary: Doña Antonia María Acosta Arévalo, a widow, acknowledged a 260-peso censo debt to the chaplaincy founded by Comisario Baltasar de Grado, currently served by chaplains Manuel de Guzmán and Juan Antonio de Moya. She mortgaged her house in Cartago, which previously belonged to Juan López de la Rea y Soto. A marginal note from 1735 indicates she returned the house to chaplain José Miguel de Guzmán.

José Macis and his wife Teodora Molina obligated themselves for 550 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Juan Macis, José's father. They mortgaged their house in Cartago, acquired from Captain Domingo de Inza, and a cacaotal with 1000 trees in Barbilla.
Captain Bernardo Marin, with José Macis as guarantor, obligated himself to Captain José de Bonilla for 200 pesos, payable in cacao.

Sarjento Francisco de Piedra, acting as attorney for his aunt Doña Maria Jiménez, sold an 18-year-old mulato slave named José Jiménez to Captain Eusebio Jiménez for 300 pesos. José Jiménez had been a donation to Maria from her father, Mateo Jiménez, upon her marriage to the deceased Miguel Reinóse.

Doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco, a widow, leased a cacaotal with over 1200 trees in the Matina valley to Captain Gaspar de Acosta for 3 years at 225 pesos annually. She had acquired the cacaotal from the estate of her first husband, Captain Rodrigo de Gadea y Marrufo.

Captain José de Quesada and his wife Doña Antonia de Alvarado obligated themselves for 330 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Alférez Antonio Machado, whose patron is Alférez Jerónimo Morales and chaplain is Licenciado Manuel Guzmán. They mortgaged their house in Cartago, with Doña Josefa Ventura de Alvarado acting as guarantor.

Don José de Baeza and his wife Doña María Magdalena Maroto obligated themselves for 1100 pesos to Doña Manuela de Oviedo, the minor daughter of the deceased Captain Francisco de Oviedo and Doña Francisca Jiménez. They mortgaged a property in the Barba valley, including slaves Ana and Antonio, and also mortgaged their slaves Gertrudis, María, Juan, Pedro, and José. Captain Antonio Solórzano acted as guarantor. Payments were made in 1718, 1719, and 1720 to Juan Manuel de Alvarado and Nicolás Arias.
Ayudante Miguel de Céspedes obligated himself for 50 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Alférez Antonio Machado, mortgaging a house in Cartago.

Captain Juan Cayetano Jiménez and his wife Doña Josefa Martínez obligated themselves for 500 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Comisario Baltasar de Grado. They mortgaged a house and lot in Cartago, bordering the Santa Iglesia Parroquial.
Juan Cayetano Jiménez and Josefa Martínez obligated themselves for 100 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Alférez Vasco Solano, mortgaging the same property as in the previous entry.
Juan Cayetano Jiménez and Josefa Martínez owed Doña Luisa Calvo, a widow, 206 pesos, which they agreed to pay upon Jiménez's return from a trip to Panama.

Captain Manuel de Arburola acted as guarantor for Alférez Luis Peláez for a 299-peso debt owed to Juana López. Peláez requested an extension until April, when Alférez Antonio de la Riva Agüero, who owes Peláez the amount, would return from Matina. A marginal note from 1718 states Riva Agüero paid 150 pesos and obligated himself for the rest.

Sarjento Mayor José de Baeza and his wife Doña María Magdalena Maroto granted power of attorney to Captain Antonio de Solórzano, who was traveling to Nicaragua, to sell a 36-year-old mulata slave named Ana. Ana had been purchased from Nicolás Arias, from the assets of Doña Manuela de Oviedo.

Captain José de Quesada, with Sarjento Juan Francisco de Ibarra as guarantor, obligated himself to the Royal Treasury for 350 pesos. This amount was for the tithes of Esparza for the years 1718 and 1719, which José de Quesada had won at auction in León de Nicaragua.

Doña Angela María de Arleguí, a widow, sold a 24-year-old white mulata named Manuela Josefa to Don Francisco de Bustamante, a resident of Cartago, for 300 pesos. Manuela Josefa was the daughter of Victoria, another mulata, whom Angela María inherited from her parents, Captain Francisco de Arleguí and Doña Juana de Echavarría.

Licenciado Presbítero Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro leased a cacaotal with 600 trees on the Reventazón riverbank to Andrés Calvo, a free mulato. Félix inherited the cacaotal from his parents. The lease was for 3 years, with payments of 50 pesos the first year and 100 pesos for the next two, and Calvo committed to planting an additional 1000 trees. Captain Manuel de Arburola y Ribarén acted as guarantor.

Alférez Nicolás de Quirós and his mother Mariana González, a widow, obligated themselves for 300 pesos to Ana de Trejo, a widow. This debt arose from a settlement with Ana, who had sued Quirós for failing to fulfill a marriage promise. Captain Marcos Daniel acted as guarantor.

Lieutenant Antonio Miranda and his wife Ana María Maroto sold a house in Cartago to Lieutenant General Domingo de Inza and his wife Alfonsa Muñoz Hidalgo for 300 pesos. The house, located on the royal street, had been previously donated to Miranda and Maroto by their aunt Magdalena Calvo.

Doña Eugenia Urbana Lainez, a widow of Captain Gaspar de Basterrica y Narvaiza and a resident of Esparza, granted general power of attorney to Sergeant Major Juan Francisco de Ibarra. A marginal note indicates that this deed was revoked in 1719.

Alférez Antonio de la Riva Agüero owed Governor Pedro Ruiz de Bustamante 200 pesos, which were to be paid in cacao at a rate of 25 pesos per twenty-thousand-count zurrón, delivered in Cartago. This debt was cancelled in May 1718.

Alférez Juan Miguel Cervantes, the legitimate son of Juan Miguel Cervantes and María de León, both from San Miguel, acknowledged receipt of goods given to him upon his marriage to Doña Gregoria Hidalgo. Gregoria is the legitimate daughter of Brother José Hidalgo and the late Juana Arias, and the goods included 579 pesos from her maternal inheritance.

The will of Sergeant Major Antonio Cabral, which was originally made on November 15, 1717, was opened on March 20, 1718, at the request of his cousin, José de Mier Ceballos. On this same day, Antonio Cabral's corpse was officially recognized.

Antonio Cabral's will stipulated that a sung mass be said on the day of his burial or the following day, followed by sung masses for a novena. He also requested 50 recited masses for his soul, 50 for souls in purgatory, and 100 for his parents and relatives, with an alms of 6 reales per recited mass, all to be said in the Convent.

Antonio Cabral's will ordered the establishment of a chaplaincy with 500 pesos, in accordance with his wife's wishes. His daughter, María Josefa, was designated as the patroness, and the chaplain would be one of her future sons, or failing that, one of the sons of Antonio Lacayo de Briones.

people_involved: Francisco Antonio de Rivas y Contreras
summary: Antonio Cabral's will detailed his extensive estate, including a cacao plantation in Matina, other properties, livestock, and inheritances in Portugal. It also listed numerous debts owed to individuals like Juan Sáenz Cascante in Lima, orphans cared for by Magdalena Romero, Angela Golfín, and José Antonio Lacayo de Briones, and funds he held for Domingo de Ayesta's estate. The will also referenced his father-in-law Matías González Camino's estate and his role as a trustee for the Missionary Fathers of the Talamanca Reduction.

Antonio Cabral's will stipulated that after his funeral and honors, his daughter, María Josefa, should move to León de Nicaragua to live under the care and patronage of her uncle and godfather, Dean Nicolás de Salazar y Carrión. The Dean and General José Antonio Lacayo de Briones were named as the executors of his will.

Legal proceedings were initiated by Ayudante Miguel de Céspedes, the general defender of the poor, on behalf of José Vásquez. José, the legitimate son of Domingo Vásquez and Ambrosia de Brenes from Domingo's second marriage, sought to claim inheritance from his deceased father, whose first son, Pedro Antonio Vásquez, had been absent in Peru for over 20 years.

Following Domingo Vásquez's death, 1300 cacao trees in Matina were sold for 600 pesos. After 203 pesos were spent on burial and other necessary expenses, 397 pesos remained for his younger siblings as part of their maternal share, which José Vásquez sought to claim.

After an investigation confirmed José Vásquez's claim, he received 397 pesos from depositary Captain José de Guzmán, funds belonging to his absent half-brother Pedro Antonio Vásquez. Captain Luis Gutiérrez and his wife Inés de Quesada, along with Captain José de Chavarría and his wife María Calvo, acted as guarantors for Vásquez, ensuring the return of the money if the absent brother reappeared.

The will of Captain Marcos Daniel was recorded. He was a native of Callao, Peru, and the legitimate son of Juan Daniel and Catalina Cardoso. Married to Clara de Quirós, the widow of Captain Juan de Vida Martel, they had two children who died young. His wife was named as his sole heir.

The will of Sergeant Major Blas González Coronel was recorded. He was a native of Seville, the legitimate son of Manuel González Coronel and Magdalena Luque. He was married to Bernarda de Fonseca, the legitimate daughter of Captain Luis de Fonseca and Jerónima de Retes, and their son, Licenciado Presbítero Manuel González Coronel, was currently in Panama.

An unnamed individual, later identified as José Miguel de Arburola, renounces his purchased office of Alcalde Mayor Provincial and Regidor in Cartago. He transfers it to his two-year-old son, José Francisco. Capitán Antonio de Soto Barahona is appointed to exercise the office until José Francisco comes of age, or it will be held by the Cabildo.
Francisco de Guevara, a 12-year-old natural son of Úrsula de Garita, a mestiza, is delivered to Ayudante José de las Alas, a master tailor. This arrangement is for a period of four years.

Efigenio Gómez, a 10-year-old mulato and son of Ayudante Nicolás Gómez and Magdalena de Hoces (a mestiza), is delivered to Francisco de Aguirre, a master shoemaker. This agreement is set for a duration of four years.

Juan Camaño, a 12-year-old mulato and legitimate son of Francisco Camaño (a negro) and Juana Valerino, is delivered to Miguel Pereira, a master shoemaker. The terms of this delivery are for five years.
Jacobo de Brenes, a 14-year-old legitimate son of Aparicio de Brenes and María Chacón, is delivered to Miguel Pereira. This arrangement is for a period of three years.

people_involved: Capitán Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribarén
Sargento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: Ana Cardoso, a free mulata, cedes a 100-peso credit against the assets of the deceased Sargento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral to Doña Josefa de Hoces Navarro. This credit, originating from the sale of a mulato named Francisco, is used to establish a capellanía for two masses and to provide income to José Miguel de Arburola, who is chosen as the chaplain.

people_involved: El Licenciado Presbítero don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
summary: Ana Chacón, legitimate daughter of the deceased Diego Chacón and Jerónima de Peñaranda, makes her will. She declares her assets, including a plot of land donated to Manuel de Salas by her sister Francisca Chacón, and names her sister Margarita Chacón, Beneficiado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón, and Capitán Gaspar de Acosta as her executors, with her soul as the heir.

Pablo de Alvarado, son of José de Alvarado and Francisca de Astorga, provides a dowry of 482 pesos for his future wife, María Cayetana Solano. María Cayetana is the legitimate daughter of Nicolás Solano and Juana Ricardo, and their marriage is scheduled for two days later.

people_involved: Doña Isabel de Guevara y Sandoval
summary: Ayudante Nicolás de Estrada leases a cacao hacienda with approximately one thousand trees on the Reventazón riverbank. The hacienda is leased to Alférez Francisco González and his mother, Doña Isabel de Guevara y Sandoval, for three years at an annual rent of 350 pesos.

Nicolás Arias and his wife Doña Gertrudis de Oviedo, residents of Barba valley, along with guarantor Alférez Andrés Arias, obligate themselves to Doña Manuela de Oviedo, a minor. They owe 375 pesos, delivered by her tutor Hermano José Núñez, and mortgage their mulato slaves Teodoro and Cayetana, 300 cattle, and other horses as collateral.

Capitán Gaspar de Acosta Arévalo, son of Antonio de Acosta Arévalo and Doña Josefa Santiago de Aguilar, makes his will. He is married to Doña Gertrudis Valerino and has no children, owning and leasing several cacao haciendas in Marina. He names his wife as his heir, with the consent of his mother, Doña Josefa.

Juan Alejandro Leitona, son of the deceased Sargento Baltasar Leitona and María Valverde, provides a dowry for his future wife, María Antonia de Maroto, natural daughter of the deceased José Maroto. Doña Luisa Calvo, a widow, delivers the assets totaling 454 pesos 2 reales, with the marriage scheduled for the upcoming Sunday, the 12th of the month.

Doña Luisa Calvo, a widow, donates a 10-year-old mulata slave named Ramona, daughter of her deceased slave Lucía, to María Maroto. María, also 10 years old, is the natural daughter of Doña Luisa Calvo's deceased legitimate son, Capitán Gabriel Maroto, and had been raised by Doña Luisa.

people_involved: El Licenciado Presbítero don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
summary: El Licenciado Presbítero don Diego de Ángulo Gascón, the oldest Cura Rector, donates a 17-year-old mulata slave named María, daughter of his slave Juliana, to Doña Juana Josefa de Ángulo. This donation is in gratitude for Doña Juana Josefa's loving assistance after being raised by his niece, Doña Manuela de Quirós, and remaining in his household.

people_involved: Don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones
Doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
Capitán José Antonio Bermúdez y Aguiar
Don José Mauricio Serrano de Reina
summary: Don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones, executor, and Doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral, sole heir of the deceased Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral, cede the rights to the tithes of the city and Matina valley for 1718 and 1719 to Capitán José Antonio Bermúdez y Aguiar. The tithes, originally auctioned in León, are sold for 1876 pesos 7 reales, payable in two annual installments, with a portion due to S.M., all to the satisfaction of Don José Mauricio Serrano de Reina.

people_involved: Capitán José Antonio Bermúdez y Aguiar
Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina
summary: Capitán José Antonio Bermúdez y Aguiar and his wife, Doña Baltasara Escalante Panlagua, obligate themselves to the Real Caja de León for 1876 pesos 7 reales. This sum represents the value of the tithe auction, and the obligation is accepted by Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina, lieutenant judge of the royal treasury officials.

people_involved: Don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones
Doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
Sargento Mayor Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones and Doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral, executor and sole heir of Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral, transfer a cacao hacienda in Matina valley to Sargento Mayor Juan Francisco de Ibarra and his wife Doña Catalina González González Camino. The hacienda, previously encumbered by debts of Don Matías González Camino, includes two mulato slaves; the ill Sebastián is replaced by José Tomás. The sale price is 3340 pesos, with the buyers responsible for settling pending credits, and a marginal note indicates a 1723 cancellation by Capitán don Francisco de Betancourt, husband of Doña María Josefa.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Sargento Mayor Ibarra and his wife obligate themselves to pay one thousand pesos to Doña Manuela de Salazar, a widow. They also acknowledge a separate debt of 500 pesos at 5% interest to Don Manuel Martín Cu...

An obligation of 500 pesos in cacao, possibly related to Manuel Martínez Cubero, was cancelled by Doña Manuela. Manuel is identified as the legitimate son of the late Captain Cristóbal Cubero and Doña Catalina González Camino, and grandson of Doña Manuela.

Alférez José de Morales, a native of León, Nicaragua, issued a dowry letter in favor of his future wife, Juana Josefa de Ángulo, whom he was to marry the following Sunday, January 26th. He delivered goods worth 1951 pesos and 4 reales to Cura Don Diego de Ángulo Gascón, with the document granted at Doña Isabel de Guevara's house.

Catalina Rosales, legitimate daughter of the late Tomás Rosales and María de Nieves, made her will. She was married to Hermano Andrés Peláez, and their daughter, Gertrudis Peláez, was married to Gregorio Picado. They resided in the city's common lands.

locations: puebla de los pardos de esta ciudad
summary: Clara de Quirós, widow of Captain Marcos Daniel and debtor to the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora de los Angeles for 172 pesos, provided her mother, Mariana González, as guarantor. Mariana González, also a widow, mortgaged her cacao haciendas in Matina to secure the debt.
María Calderón, a widow, leased a cacao plantation with 600 trees in Matina to Jerónima Pacheco. The lease was for one year at a cost of 125 pesos.

Doña Petronila Valerín, a widow, leased her cacao hacienda named San Antonio in the Matina valley, which had over 1500 trees, to Alférez Domingo de Quesada. The hacienda, bordering Nuestra Señora de los Angeles, was inherited from her father, Captain Jerónimo Valerín, and leased for three years in exchange for cacao.

Licenciado Presbítero Don Juan Antonio de Moya, patron and chaplain of a 500-peso capellanía founded by Doña Josefa de Moya, declared himself a debtor after Don José Fernando de Moya redeemed the principal. Juan Antonio guaranteed the sum by mortgaging a cacao plantation in Matina, which he had inherited from his father, Don Antonio de Moya.

people_involved: Antonio de la Riva y Agüero
summary: Alférez Antonio de la Riva y Agüero and his wife, Doña Catalina de Arburola y Ribarén, obligated themselves for 118 pesos to the minor children of the late Alférez Bartolomé de Meneses and Juana López. They mortgaged their residential house located in the city's common lands.

Feliciana de Chinchilla, widow of Alférez Francisco Fernández, leased a cacao plantation in Matina with 1500 trees to Sargento Antonio de Umaña for three years, at an annual rent of 200 pesos in cacao. Alférez Domingo de Quesada served as the guarantor for this agreement.

Captain Juan Sancho de Castañeda and his wife, Doña Juana de Alvarado, obligated themselves for 300 pesos to the heirs of Francisco de Chaves, a former resident and merchant in the province. This sum was originally owed by Sargento Mayor Don Antonio de Utrera y Medina, and a marginal note indicates the obligation was cancelled in 1736 by Doña Juana, then a widow.

Captain Francisco Gutiérrez sold a 27-year-old Creole black woman named María Candelaria to Captain Andrés Ignacio del Corral, a resident of Panama, for 300 pesos. Francisco Gutiérrez had originally acquired María Candelaria by purchase from Alférez Don Nicolás de Guevara.

Sargento Mayor Don José de Baeza and his wife, Doña María Magdalena Maroto, sold a 13-year-old mulatto boy named Antonio, son of the slave Ana, to Doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco, a widow. They had purchased Antonio from Nicolás Arias, from the assets of Doña Manuela de Oviedo, for 200 pesos.

Sargento Mayor Don Pedro José Sáenz sold a house, which bordered the public plaza to the west and was originally purchased from Don Blas González Coronel, to Licenciado Presbítero Don Manuel José González Coronel for 850 pesos. The buyer, Manuel José, assumed responsibility for several capellanías associated with the property.

Doña Manuela de Salazar, widow of Don Juan González Camino, founded a capellanía of masses with 500 pesos owed by Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra and Doña Catalina González Camino, her daughter. The funds were originally owed by Don Matías González Camino and later by his son-in-law, Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral. Her grandson, Don Manuel Martínez Cubero, was named chaplain, with provisions for other family members to serve if he was unavailable, and her sons-in-law, Don José de Mier Ceballos and Don Gil de Alvarado, were named patrons.
Pedro Méndez, the minor son of Simeón Méndez, was delivered to Francisco de Aguirre, a master shoemaker, for a period of one year. This arrangement likely served as an apprenticeship for the minor.

Domingo de Inza, husband of Alfonsa Muñoz Hidalgo, requested the delivery of two sacks of cacao belonging to his brother-in-law, Andrés Muñoz Hidalgo, who had been absent from the province for many years, and which were held by Doña Josefa de Hoces Navarro. The judge granted the request, and Domingo and Alfonsa obligated themselves for 50 pesos, the value of the cacao.

Don Juan Manuel de Alvarado, with Captain Don José de Alvarado as guarantor, obligated himself for 400 pesos in favor of Doña Manuela de Oviedo, a minor and daughter of the late Don Francisco de Oviedo and Doña Francisca Jiménez. They mortgaged a country estate, including a house, sugar mill, livestock, and sugarcane, located in the area called Santa Rosa.

Alférez Gregorio de Brenes and his wife, Petronila de Quirós, obligated themselves for 81 pesos to María Antonia and Gregoria, minor daughters of Antonio Ricardo and Luisa de Brenes. An attached note from Fray José de Naranjo, doctrinero of Ujarrás, confirmed the burial of María Antonia Ricardo and that Gregorio de Brenes had paid both the burial and previous betrothal fees for her.

Alférez Francisco Javier de Siles, legitimate son of Alférez Andrés de Siles and Doña María de Chaves, issued a dowry letter in favor of his wife, Doña Eugenia Basterrica y Narvaiza. Eugenia is identified as the legitimate daughter of Captain Gaspar de Basterrica y Narvaiza and Doña Urbana Gertrudis Lainez Ystueta, with the dowry valued at 2098 pesos, including 500 head of cattle.
Juan de la Mata, a 10-year-old white boy and natural son of Prudenciana de la Rosa, was delivered to Francisco de Aguirre, a master shoemaker, for a period of 5 years.

Pedro Ortiz, who was about to marry, was sued by Miguel and Manuel de Mora to fulfill his promise of marriage to their sister, Juana de Mora. He was imprisoned but, due to illness, was allowed to recover at the house of Capitán José Felipe Bermúdez after a bond was granted.
Alférez Luis Peláez and his wife, María de los Santos Solano, made an obligation for 50 pesos in favor of the minor children of Alférez Bartolomé de Meneses and Juana López.
Capitán Antonio de Soto Barahona owed 509 pesos, payable in cacao, to Capitán don Francisco de Bustamante, a native of Spain and a trader in the province. This debt was later canceled.
Capitán Felipe de Mesa made an obligation for 200 pesos in favor of Capitán don Francisco de Bustamante. This obligation was canceled in 1721.

Pedro de Ortiz made an obligation for 125 pesos in favor of Juana de Mora, as an agreement for her to withdraw her lawsuit regarding his promise of marriage. Capitán don Antonio Salmón Pacheco and Capitán don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco acted as guarantors.

people_involved: Don José Nicolás Sarmiento de Sotomayor
summary: Don José Nicolás Sarmiento de Sotomayor, as the dative executor of the intestate Lucrecia Martínez, founded a chaplaincy with a principal of 150 pesos. The funds were charged against an estate owned by Miguel de Zamora in the Currifravá valley. Don Antonio de Guevara was named chaplain, with Don José Antonio de Bonilla and others from the Sáenz lineage as successors, and Miguel de Mora as patron.

Miguel de Mora, from the Curriravá valley, made an obligation for 150 pesos in favor of the chaplaincy founded in the name of his mother, Lucrecia Martínez. In 1724, Juan Miguel Cervantes took over this principal with another mortgage.
Capitán Juan Sancho de Castañeda made an obligation for 300 pesos, payable in cacao, in favor of don Francisco de Bustamante. This obligation was canceled in 1721.

people_involved: Licenciado Presbítero don Manuel de Guzman
summary: Licenciado Presbítero don Manuel de Guzman, sacristán mayor of the parish, sold an adobe and tile house for 460 pesos to Capitán Luis Gutiérrez. A portion of the funds belonged to the chaplaincy of Comisario Baltasar de Grado and two confraternities.

Alférez Tomás de Chaves and his wife, Juana de Solís, founded a chaplaincy with a capital of 2000 pesos, situated on lands bordering the Sabana and Virilla river. Capitán Tomás de Chaves was named patron, and José de Chaves, their son, was named chaplain.

Inés de Olivares, a widow from Villa de Barba, sold an 18-year-old mulatto pardo enslaved man named Juan, born and raised in her house, for 300 pesos to Pedro de Ángulo y Sierra, a resident of Granada, Nicaragua.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Pedro Martínez de Ugarrio
summary: Doña Gertrudis Guerrero, a widow, sold a 9-year-old enslaved black boy named Gabriel, born and raised in her house, for 250 pesos to Sargento Mayor don Pedro Martínez de Ugarrio, a resident of Realejo.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Juan Francisco de Ibarra
Doña Ana de Peralta y Salazar
summary: Sargento Mayor Juan Francisco de Ibarra, married since April 19th, acknowledged receipt of his wife Doña Catalina González Camino's dowry, valued at 3003 pesos and 3/4 reales. The dowry included silver, jewelry, furniture, and four enslaved people: Manuela, María, José Cayetano, and Manuela Josefa.

Juan Francisco de Ibarra made an inventory of his own assets brought to his marriage with Doña Catalina, totaling 10162 pesos, including houses, land, livestock, a cacao plantation, and eight enslaved people. From this, 6619 pesos were deducted for debts, including those to his brother Andrés Lainez de Istueta and the dowry of his first wife Doña Petronila de Moya, with the remaining 3543 pesos to be distributed among his children from the first marriage.

Don Pablo López Conejo, married to Doña Teresa Jiménez Maldonado, received her dowry of 1270 pesos. Doña Teresa is the legitimate daughter of Antonio Jiménez Maldonado and Doña Mariana de Avila Hidalgo, who were married on July 3rd of the same month.

people_involved: R. P. Predicador exdefinidor Fray Diego Caballero
summary: Capitán José Felipe Bermúdez, Syndic of the Convent, sold a 7-year-old enslaved black boy to Ayudante Nicolás de Estrada. Doña Nicolasa Guerrero had delivered the boy to Bermúdez, as his value of 200 pesos belonged to R. P. Predicador exdefinidor Fray Diego Caballero, satisfying a 200-peso alms.
Estradi transferred an enslaved person named Cristóbal, son of Catalina (also an enslaved person belonging to Señora Guerrero), to Fray Diego in exchange for food and clothing provided to Fray Diego.

Pascual Salguero, a native of Granada, Nicaragua, issued a dowry letter for 1129 pesos in favor of his future wife, María Josefa de Vargas, who is the legitimate daughter of Capitán Diego de Vargas and Juana de Chavarría.
Alférez Domingo de Quesada owed Ayudante Nicolás de Estrada 200 pesos, payable in cacao. This debt was cancelled in 1719.

people_involved: General Don Diego de la Haya
summary: Several officials, including Mayores, Capitanes, and an Alférez, provided surety for the residency review of General Don Diego de la Haya, the Governor and Captain General of the province. A testimony for this review was later taken on May 22, 1834, at the request of Don José de Fuentes, the judge.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Sargento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra and Capitán Don Antonio Salmón Pacheco provided surety for the release of Capitán Luis Gutiérrez from prison. Gutiérrez was imprisoned for a criminal cause but was granted excarceration due to severe injuries from two wounds, requiring him to return home for treatment.

people_involved: Doña Baltasara López de la Flor
summary: Margarita Birquero sold an enslaved person named Petronila, 6 years old and daughter of another enslaved person named Baltasara de los Reyes (also owned by Margarita Birquero), to Doña Baltasara López de la Flor for 150 pesos.

people_involved: Licenciado Don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
summary: Doña María de Quirós, a widow, sold a ranch with livestock, houses, and corrals in La Candelaria, 8 leagues from the city, to Capitán Juan Gómez for 320 pesos. This sum was to cover an obligation to the chaplaincy founded by Capitán Pedro Ibáñez, whose patron was Licenciado Don Diego de Ángulo Gascón and chaplain was Licenciado Don Manuel Conejo.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Antonio Aurelio de Zamora
summary: Capitán Francisco de Flores, with several sureties, obligated himself to the seven legitimate children of the deceased Sargento Mayor Antonio Aurelio de Zamora and Doña Francisca de Saborío for 722 pesos, 2 reales, and 14 maravedíes each. A marginal note from 1720 indicates that Capitán José de Saborío received the total sum and executed a deed.

Capitán Francisco de Flores obligated himself for 700 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Antonio Aurelio Zamora in the convent of Barba, following the death of his wife, Doña Francisca de Saborío. This obligation was cancelled in 1720 by Capitán José de Saborío, the patron.

Sargento Tomás Meléndez, a native of Nicaragua, made his will, detailing his parents (Alonso Meléndez and María de Quiñones, both deceased) and his three marriages to Francisca de la Cruz (no children), Catalina de los Santos Chacón (seven children), and Isabel Peláez (six children), including the spouses of two of his daughters.

Capitán Juan Gómez obligated himself for 320 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Capitán Pedro Ibáñez, an obligation he assumed when purchasing a property in Candelaria from Doña María de Quirós. Alférez Jacinto de Campos, Doña Francisca de Benavente, and Bernarda Vásquez served as sureties.

people_involved: Capitán Don Diego de Barros y Carbajal
Sarjento Mayor Don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: A deed was cancelled in 1719, involving Sargento Mayor Don Francisco de la Madriz Linares as principal and Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona as surety, because two enslaved persons from the deed were delivered to Don Francisco G...., husband of Doña ....

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones
summary: Doña Águeda Pérez de Muro granted general power of attorney to Sargento Mayor Don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones, who was traveling to Granada.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Francisco de la Madriz Linares
Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
Maestre de Campo Don Pedro Ruiz de Bustamante
summary: Sargento Mayor Francisco de la Madriz Linares and Capitanes Juan de Astúa, Antonio de Soto y Barahona, and Manuel Antonio de Arburola Iribaren granted general power of attorney to Maestre de Campo Don Pedro Ruiz de Bustamante, who was traveling to Santiago de Guatemala.

people_involved: General Don Diego de la Haya Fernández
Maestre de Campo Don Pedro Ruiz de Bustamante
summary: Capitán Luis Gutiérrez, facing a criminal cause before General Don Diego de la Haya Fernández, requested the return of his cacao haciendas in Matina and Barbilla, which had been embargoed by Maestre de Campo Don Pedro Ruiz de Bustamante. Don José Felipe Bermúdez provided surety for Gutiérrez to manage the properties, as they were deteriorating.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo Don Pedro Ruiz de Bustamante
summary: Capitán Don Antonio Salmón Pacheco, against whom Maestre de Campo Don Pedro Ruiz de Bustamante pursued a cause (remitted to Santiago de Guatemala over a year ago), requested the return of his embargoed haciendas in Matina, which were being lost due to delay. Don Dionisio Pacheco provided surety, and the request was granted.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
Don Pedro Florencio de la Águila
summary: Sargento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra provided surety for the release of Sargento Mayor Don José Baeza from prison. Baeza was imprisoned for having wounded Don Pedro Florencio de la Águila.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo Don Pedro Ruiz de Bustamante
summary: Capitán Manuel García de Argueta granted general power of attorney to Maestre de Campo Don Pedro Ruiz de Bustamante, a resident of San Miguel and Santiago de Guatemala.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Don Pedro Martínez de Ugarrió
summary: Alférez José de Morales provided surety for Capitán Manuel García de Argueta, who was facing execution by Sargento Mayor Don Pedro Martínez de Ugarrió for two bundles of local clothing that García de Argueta admitted receiving via his pack train from León for delivery to Martínez.
Sebastián Vicente Alvarez, acting as attorney for General José Antonio Lacayo de Briones, sold an enslaved man named Antonio, a 20-year-old Mandinga, to Doña Águeda Pérez de Muro for 300 pesos.

Don Diego de la Haya Fernández, the Governor and Captain General, granted general power of attorney to Captains Don Manuel de Porras and Don Salvador Cano, who are Procurators of the Royal Audiencia of Santiago de Guatemala.

Don Diego de la Haya Fernández granted power to Captains Juan Gallarti y Urriticochea and Andrés Cabezas de Urizar, residents of León, Nicaragua, to collect his salary from the Royal Treasury officials in this province and Nicaragua, specifically from Treasurer Ambrosio de Betancourt and Accountant José Mauricio Serrano de Reina.
María Calderón, a widow, leased a cacao plantation with 500 trees in the Matina valley to Juan Alejandro Leitona for three years at 75 pesos per year, payable in first-grade cacao.

Captain Nicolás de Guevara granted freedom to his 36-year-old Pardo slave, Nicolás Barrantes, for 350 pesos. Nicolás Barrantes was inherited from Clara, Captain Guevara's deceased daughter with Francisca de Acosta, who died at a young age.

Captain Manuel García de Argueta made a provision in favor of his wife, Doña Dionisia Fallas, legitimate daughter of Captain Francisco Fallas de la Vega and Doña Mariana Solano. Their marriage took place on June 28, 1711, and the provision included 640 pesos and a dowry of 1000 pesos, which included a 7-year-old mulatto named Petronila at the time of their marriage.

Captain Francisco Bustamante was ordered to deliver or secure 425 pesos to Captain José de Mier Ceballos, who claimed the amount was taken by Maestre de Campo Pedro Ruiz de Bustamante. Bustamante presented Captain Pedro de Moya as his guarantor, promising to produce relevant documents within 90 days.

Lieutenant General Diego de Barros Carbajal certified that Captain Francisco Bustamante delivered 413 pesos to Captain José de Mier Ceballos by order of the Governor and Captain General, and subsequently cancelled the obligation.

Sergeant Francisco de Chavarría and his wife Feliciana Calvo sold a 12-year-old Creole mulatto named Blas to Doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco for 300 pesos. Blas had been given to them by Captain Miguel Calvo when he was one year old.

Licenciado Don Diego de Ángulo Gascón sold a cattle ranch near Santa Ana to Alejo Ramírez and his wife Josefa Fernández for 379 pesos and four reales. The payment was accounted for as part of Josefa Fernández's dowry from her first marriage to Alférez Antonio de Ángulo and for a cacao plantation he bought from Antonio de Ángulo in Matina.

Alférez Juan Cascante de Rojas sold a piece of land, inherited from Licenciado Don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas, to Juan Delgado for 50 pesos. The land is described by its boundaries, including Antonia Jiménez's old corrals.

This entry records the will of Gertrudis Peláez, legitimate daughter of Andrés Peláez and Catalina Rosales, and wife of Gregorio Picado. She mentions her son José, a girl she raised named María de la Rosa, her husband's nephew José Miguel, and her granddaughter Isabel, daughter of José Picado.

Sergeant Pascual Salguero and his wife María Josefa de Vargas obligated themselves for 200 pesos at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by the deceased Magdalena de la Portilla, whose patron and chaplain is Licenciado Don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín. The obligation was secured by houses and a plot in this city, received as a dowry from María Josefa's parents, Captain Diego de Vargas and Juana de Chavarría.
Licenciado Don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín cancelled the obligation in favor of Sergeant Major Don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí, who had purchased the mortgaged houses.

Manuel Nicolás de Echavarría sold a 9-year-old Creole mulatto named Juan Antonio to Captain Don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí, Lieutenant Governor and Captain General of the Matina valleys, for 225 pesos. Juan Antonio was entrusted to Echavarría by the Governor and Captain General, who received him in fideicomiso from his deceased father-in-law, Captain Don José Pérez de Muro.

Sergeant Gregorio de Umaña and his brother Antonio de Umaña obligated themselves to Captain Don Juan de Irogoyen, Alcalde Mayor of Nicoya, for 170 pesos. Antonio pledged a string of 12 mules used for transport on the Matina road as collateral.

people_involved: Manuel Antonio de Arburola y Rivaren
summary: This entry records the will of Captain Manuel Antonio de Arburola y Rivaren, legitimate son of Captain Lorenzo de Arburola y Rivaren and Doña Josefa de Oses Navarro. His executors are Licenciado Don Félix Esteban de Oses Navarro and Captain Don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí, and his mother is named as his heir.

people_involved: Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas
summary: Gregoria de Chaves, a widow, sells a straw house and wooden fences on land formerly owned by Licenciado don Gaspar Cascante de Rojas to her son-in-law, Juan de Salazar, for 5,000 pesos.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad
Alférez Antonio de la Riva Agüero
summary: Capitán don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad grants general power to Alférez Antonio de la Riva Agüero.

people_involved: Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos
summary: Alférez Jacinto de Rivera sells a plot of land in the city, which he acquired with his late wife Ana del Camino, to Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos for 150 pesos. The land is adjacent to the Parroquial Church and Cabildo houses, and the payment benefits the Capellanía of Alonso Gómez Macotela, managed by don Juan José Camacho.

Juan de Quesada, son of the late Alonso de Quesada and María López, records his will. He details his three marriages: first to the late Juana de Proa? (mother of Manuel), second to Margarita Solano (no children), and third to Francisca de Chinchilla (mother of Juan José). Alférez Gregorio Picado is named as the executor.

people_involved: Doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
Sargento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
Sargento Mayor don Antonio de Utrera y Medina
summary: Doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral, the sole heir of her late father Sargento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral, sells an 18-year-old enslaved mulato named José to Sargento Mayor don Antonio de Utrera y Medina for 300 pesos.

Licenciado don Manuel González Coronel sells a quarter caballería of land in the Valle de Aserrí to Nicolás de Estrada for 900 pesos. The property, which his late father don Blas González Coronel bought from the Cofradía de las Animas, includes a house, a sugar mill, livestock, and a 25-year-old enslaved mulato named Agustín.
Ayudante don Nicolás de Estrada married Lorenza Muñoz on November 30, 1704.

Ayudante don Nicolás de Estrada, son of don Francisco de Estrada and doña María Mejía, formalizes a dowry letter for his wife Lorenza Muñoz, whose assets were received from her uncle, Capitán don Miguel Calvo. The dowry totals 2398 pesos, including 600 cacao trees in the Reventazón river area and 150 cattle.

people_involved: Doña Angela de la Paz y Flores
Sargento Mayor don Antonio de Utrera y Medina
summary: Doña Angela de la Paz y Flores, a widow, sells a 50-year-old enslaved negra named Josefa, who was born and raised in her house, to Sargento Mayor don Antonio de Utrera y Medina for 75 pesos of cacao.
Capitán don Francisco de Bustamante grants general power to Capitán don Pedro de Moya.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
Sargento Mayor Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: Sargento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra had previously made an obligation on December 20, 1717, before Sargento Mayor Francisco de la Madriz Linares, concerning the value of the enslaved mulata Eugenia and her son Mateo, who were auctioned to Ibarra.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Sargento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra and his wife, doña Catalina González Camino, undertake a new obligation for 305 pesos at 5% interest, representing the value of the enslaved mulata Eugenia and her son Mateo. This new obligation was ordered by the Gobernador to be made jointly with his wife.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Gobernador Diego de la Haya cancels the obligation made by Sargento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra on March 2, 1725, after confirming from the death records that Ibarra had paid the 305 pesos.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
Doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
Sargento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: Sargento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra and doña Catalina González Camino purchased a productive cacao hacienda in the Valle de Matina for 3340 pesos on June 21, 1718, from Doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral, daughter and heir of the late Sargento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
Doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
Sargento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: Sargento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra and doña Catalina González Camino obligate themselves for 540 pesos at 5% interest to the Capellanía of the late Capitán Juan Francisco Valenzuela, a former resident of Granada, Nicaragua. This census is recognized on a cacao hacienda in the Valle de Matina, which they had purchased with this and other encumbrances.

people_involved: María de la Paz y Quirós
summary: Alférez Domingo de Quesada obligates himself to María de la Paz y Quirós for 400 pesos, payable in sixteen sacks of cacao (3 of second quality, 13 of first quality) delivered in the city, and three tame mules with the first cacao shipment.

Doña Francisca de Benavente, a widow, leases a cacao hacienda with 1800 trees in the Valle de Matina to Alférez Domingo de Quesada for three years. The rent is 6 sacks of good cacao for the first year and 8 sacks for each of the subsequent two years, delivered in the city.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
Capitán de Caballos don Francisco de Betancourt
Sargento Mayor don José de Baeza
summary: Several individuals, including Sargento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra and Capitán de Caballos don Francisco de Betancourt, guarantee Sargento Mayor don José de Baeza's entry into the office of Teniente de Jueces Oficiales de la Real Hacienda y Reales Cajas. The total guarantee is 2750 pesos, secured by various assets including enslaved people and haciendas.
Capitán Felipe de Meza obligates himself to Manuela Antonia, daughter of doña Josefa Lizondo, for 200 pesos, using a cacao hacienda in Matina as security.

Doña Francisca de Benavente, daughter of Bartolomé de Benavente and doña Agustina de Quesada, records her will. She was married to the late Alférez Juan Matías Lizondo, with whom she had seven children, including the deceased Francisco and Francisca, who is married to Antonio Nicolás de los Ríos.

people_involved: Doña Juana Damiana de Mora Salado
summary: Doña Juana Damiana de Mora Salado, a widow, sold a 10-year-old 'mulatillo blanco' named José Miguel, who was born and raised in her house and was the son of her mulata slave Josefa, to Capitán don José Antonio Bermúdez and his wife Doña Baltasara de Escalante Paniagua. The sale price was 150 pesos.

The will of María Calderón was recorded. She was first married to the deceased Sargento Baltasar de Segura, with whom she had three children: Antonio, Manuela, and Bartola. Her second marriage was to the deceased Bernabé Vásquez, with no children. She also raised her grandson, José de Segura, who was the legitimate son of José de Segura and Antonio Estrella, after his parents' deaths. Capitán Manuel de Arburola was named as her executor.

people_involved: Licenciado don Félix de Oses Navarro
summary: Capitán Teodomiro Arias sold his houses in Cartago to José Masís for 625 pesos. The property was encumbered with several charges, including 85 pesos to the Chaplaincy of the deceased Depositario Tomás Calvo, 300 pesos to the Chaplaincy of don Pedro de Alvarado, 120 pesos to the Chaplaincy of the deceased Alférez Vasco Solano, and 120 pesos to the Cofradía de la Concepción, all of which the buyer was obligated to recognize.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Sargento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra granted general power of attorney to Capitán don Manuel de Porras, a resident of Santiago de Guatemala and a Procurador of the Royal Audiencia.

Capitán don Pedro de Moya, Blas de Ancheta, and Ayudante José de las Alas, who were Mayordomos and deputies of the Cofradía de los Angeles in the Puebla de los pardos, leased a 1000-cacao-tree hacienda in the Matina valley to Baltasar de Moya, a free mulatto, for two years. The rent was 312 pesos in cacao, delivered to Cartago, with half due each year.

people_involved: Capitán Manuel de García de Argueta
summary: Ayudante Nicolás de Estrada and his wife Doña Lovenza Muñoz obligated themselves for 200 pesos at 5% interest to a Chaplaincy to be founded by Capitán Manuel de García de Argueta. This obligation was placed on their houses in Cartago, which bordered properties of Feliciana Chinchilla, the Convento de San Francisco, the Ermita de Nuestra Señora de la Soledad, and the houses of Alférez don Sebastián de Garita. The Chaplaincy was intended for the souls in purgatory and to enable Argueta's son, Licenciado don Rafael García Argueta, who was studying in Santiago de Guatemala, to be ordained. This obligation was cancelled by Capitán Manuel García de Argueta on November 29, 1721.

Doña Alfonsa Muñoz Hidalgo, wife of the absent Teniente Domingo Inza, and Juan Alejandro Leitona as guarantor, obligated themselves to Juan de la Oliva or don Francisco de Bustamante for 300 pesos. The payment was to be made in cacao delivered to Matina, and the debt belonged to Inza, who was currently in Matina.

people_involved: Licenciado don Juan Antonio de Moya
summary: Doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco, a widow, leased a 1200-cacao-tree hacienda in the Matina valley to Capitán Luis Gutiérrez for three years. The hacienda bordered properties of Licenciado don Juan Antonio de Moya and Doña Antonia de Acosta, and the river and mountain. The annual rent was 200 pesos in good cacao, delivered to Cartago.

people_involved: Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Silvestre de Meza leased a 500-cacao-tree hacienda in the Matina valley to Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona for three years. The hacienda bordered properties of Capitán Nicolás de Guevara and Francisco de Proa, and the mountain and river. The annual rent was 100 pesos in good cacao, delivered to Cartago. Silvestre de Meza cancelled this agreement on October 14, 1722, after receiving the full 300 pesos for the three years.

Antonio Nicolás de los Ríos and his wife Doña Francisca Lizondo, as principals, along with Capitanes Juan Gómez and Juan Guerrero as guarantors, obligated themselves to Francisco Antonio, Manuel, Nicolasa, and María Lizondo for 171 pesos and 1 real. This amount represented the legitimate paternal and maternal inheritance due to the four Lizondo children from their deceased parents, Francisco Lizondo and Juana Pineda.

Capitán don Nicolás de Guevara leased a 1000-cacao-tree hacienda in the Matina valley to Juan Alejandro Leitona for three years. The hacienda bordered properties of Doña Josefa de Aguilar, Silvestre de Meza, and Cayetana de Acosta, and the mountain. The annual rent was 175 pesos in cacao, consisting of 7 zurrones (6 of 1st quality and 1 of 2nd quality), delivered to Cartago.

Capitán don José de Quesada, a native of Cádiz and son of the deceased don Francisco de Quesada and Doña Angela María de Castro, being ill in bed, granted power to Licenciado don Manuel González Coronel to make his will. His heirs were his legitimate daughters, María Josefa and Manuela Josefa, with his wife Doña Antonia de Alvarado, whom he appointed as their tutor and curator. Licenciado don Manuel González Coronel was also named as his executor.

locations: Haciendas del Arado del río Grande de la Magdalena, jurisdicción de Honda, Reino de Santa Fe
summary: The will of the deceased Capitán don José de Quesada was executed by Licenciado don Manuel González Coronel, based on previously granted power. Quesada was first married to Petronila de la Rosa, who was raised by Antonia González de Sosa in the Haciendas del Arado del río Grande de la Magdalena, and they had a daughter named Rafaela. He was then married to Doña Antonia de Alvarado, legitimate daughter of Capitán don Jorge de Alvarado and Doña Gertrudis de Echavarría, with whom he had two daughters, María Josefa and Manuela Josefa.

Capitán Francisco Gutiérrez dictated his will, detailing his deceased parents, two marriages, and children from both unions. He also mentioned Josefa de Hinojosa, his second wife's daughter from a prior marriage, and three foster children. His wife, Gertrudis Ruiz, and his son, Alférez Francisco Gutiérrez, were named as albaceas.

Capitán Manuel Antonio de Arleguí entered into a contract with Isidro de Acosta for the cultivation of a cleared plot of land (roza) in the Matina valley. Acosta agreed to tend the land for two years and plant 2000 trees according to Arleguí's instructions, in exchange for 300 pesos in cacao.

people_involved: Licenciado don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro
summary: Ana Cardoso Calvo sold a 6-year-old mulatto slave named José to Licenciado don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro for 125 pesos. The slave had been born and raised in the household of Capitán Miguel Calvo, who had bequeathed him to Ana Cardoso Calvo in his will.

Doña Isabel de Ocampo Golfín, the widow of Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes, donated a cleared piece of mountain land in the Matina valley to her son, Ayudante Miguel de Céspedes. The property was bordered by haciendas belonging to Doña Águeda Pérez de Muro and Doña Gertrudis Guerrero, the mountain, and a pasture known as Chacón and the valley's river.

Alférez Pablo Lizondo formalized the sale of a hacienda containing 115 fruit trees in the Barbilla valley to Gertrudis Falcón, the widow of his deceased brother Miguel Lizondo. The transaction, valued at 115 pesos, was a previously agreed-upon deal that had not yet been legally documented.

Capitán Juan Guerrero and his wife, Doña Juana Manuela Lizondo, incurred a 100-peso obligation at 5% interest to the Cofradía de la Concepción of Ujarraz. This debt, which was redeemed by Capitán Francisco Gutiérrez, was secured by a sugar cane plot, their straw dwelling, and a straw house with a sugar mill in the Ujarrás valley, located approximately four leagues from the city.

Alférez don Sebastián de Garita, acting as Mayordomo of the Cofradía de las Animas, sold a criollo slave named José to Capitán Blas de Ancheta for 400 pesos. The slave had been bequeathed to the Cofradía by the deceased Bernardo Cortés.

people_involved: Capitán don José de Morales Tremiño
Sargento Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Capitán José Felipe Bermúdez and his wife, Doña Teresa de Sandoval, attempted to sell houses in Cartago to Capitán don José de Morales Tremiño and his wife, Doña Juana Josefa de Quirós, for 700 pesos. The houses, previously acquired from Sargento Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín (acting as albacea for his deceased sister Doña Tomasa de Ocampo), were bordered by properties of Alférez Sebastián de Garita, the Convent of San Francisco, María Chacón, and Pedro Ortiz, but the transaction was not completed.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Juan Francisco de Ibarra
Doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
Sargento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: Sargento Mayor Juan Francisco de Ibarra granted freedom to his negro ladino slave, Francisco Plaza, who was over 60 years old. Ibarra had acquired Francisco Plaza as part of a hacienda in Matina from Doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral, the daughter and sole heir of the deceased Sargento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral.

Sargento Esteban de Bonilla, as principal, along with Silvestre de Meza and his wife Josefa Elena de Soto as fiadores, incurred a 100-peso obligation at 5% interest to the Capellanía founded by the deceased Alonso Gómez Macotela. The obligation, secured by the fiadores' hacienda in Matina, was redeemed by Capitán Juan de Astúa as albacea for the deceased Alférez José Calderón and later cancelled on June 30, 1733, by Licenciado don Juan José Camacho.

Capitán Francisco Gutiérrez's will was restated, confirming his deceased parents, two marriages, and children. His heirs were named as Jerónimo, Luis, Francisco (from his first marriage), the children of Juan Marcelo (his grandsons), and Francisco (minor, from his second marriage). His wife, Gertrudis Ruiz, and his son, Alférez Francisco Gutiérrez, were designated as albaceas.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: Sargento Mayor Francisco de la Madriz Linares granted general power of attorney to his father-in-law, Capitán Manuel García de Argueta.

José Masís dictated his will, naming his deceased parents, his wife Teodora de Molina, and their five children. He also mentioned his brother Miguel Masís. Capitán Luis Gutiérrez and Juan Masís (his brother) were appointed as albaceas.

people_involved: Capitán don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí
summary: Several individuals, including Sargento Mayor José de Morales and Capitán José de Morales Tremiño and his wife Doña Juana Josefa de Quirós, provided a 2300-peso guaranty for Capitán José de Morales Tremiño. This was to secure his entry into the position of Teniente de Jueces Oficiales of the Royal Treasury, which required a 4000-peso bond. The guaranty for Manuel Antonio de Arleguí was later cancelled in April 1721, as he was not admitted by Tesorero don Ambrosio de Betancourt.

people_involved: Don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones
Don Lorenzo de Granda y Balvín
Coronel don Diego de la Haya Fernández
summary: Don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones, a former Justicia Mayor and Capitán General, was accused of illicit trade through the port of Matina. After clearing his name, he requested a residency dispatch, which was given to Don Pedro Martínez de Ugarrio. Martínez de Ugarrio was later illegally apprehended by Don Pedro Ruiz de Bustamante, who disobeyed a royal mandate, leading to Bustamante being fined and the commissions transferred to Coronel Don Diego de la Haya Fernández. Lacayo de Briones was ordered to reside in Granada, Nicaragua, and appointed Sebastián Alvarez as his general power of attorney.

Capitán Domingo García de Estrada, originally from the Principado de Asturias, executed his will. He was the legitimate son of Pedro Pantiella García de Estrada and Dominga García, and was married to Doña Catalina González Correa, daughter of Capitán Isidro González Correa and Doña Juana Ramír Corajo. He named his daughter Ana Efigenia, his servant Juan Rodríguez, and Don José de Guzmán as his executor.

Doña Jerónima de Retes, daughter of the deceased Capitán Jerónimo de Retes and Doña María Vásquez Coronado, made her will. She had been married three times: first to Alférez Luis de Fonseca (with whom she had a deceased daughter, Doña Bernarda María), second to Sargento Mayor Pedro Lorenzo Venegas (with whom she had a deceased daughter, Doña Lorenza Venegas), and third to Escribano Real Francisco Rodado. She also established a trust for Manuela Josefa, an orphan girl living with Capitán Lorenzo de Arburola and Doña Juana Josefa de Arburola, and named Licenciado don Manuel González Coronel as her executor.

people_involved: Teniente General don Diego de Barros
summary: Doña Josefa de Guevara, daughter of Juan Antonio de Guevara (missing for over 20 years) and the deceased Doña Clara de Echavarría, made her will. She mentioned her niece Juana Antonia, her brother Capitán don Nicolás de Guevara, and her cousin Licenciado don Manuel de Guzmán. She named José Antonio and Manuel Cayetano, two orphans she raised, as her heirs, and appointed Teniente General don Diego de Barros and Capitán don Nicolás de Guevara as her executors.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina
General don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones
summary: Maestre de Campo don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina granted power of attorney to General don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones. This was to represent him before the Real Audiencia of Santiago de Guatemala in a case concerning illicit trade and confiscations, which Serrano de Reina claimed was based on false witnesses. Lacayo de Briones was authorized to accept a favorable sentence or appeal an unfavorable one.

people_involved: Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos
Coronel don Diego de la Haya Fernández
Depositario General don Cristóbal Martín Cubero
summary: Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos and his wife Doña Catalina González del Camino were involved in a legal case before Governor Don Diego de la Haya Fernández regarding illicitly introduced enslaved people. Three enslaved individuals, Felipe, José, and María Victoria, were identified as having been adjudicated to Doña Catalina from her first marriage. Felipe had been sold in 1711 to Blas González Coronel and then to Capitán Manuel García de Argueta, while José and María Victoria remained with the couple. The couple obligated themselves for the enslaved people or their value pending resolution by the Real Audiencia.

people_involved: Coronel don Diego de la Haya Fernández
summary: Coronel don Diego de la Haya Fernández, the Gobernador y Capitán General, issued an authorization to Alférez Sebastián Guillen, Juez del Campo. This authorization allowed Guillen to receive the will of Don Carlos González de Tapia, who was gravely ill.

Don Carlos González de Tapia, a native of Vera Cruz in New Spain and the legitimate son of Pedro González de Tapia and Doña Teresa Ortiz de Sosa, executed his will. This event occurred on the same day that the Governor authorized Alférez Sebastián Guillen to receive his testament due to his grave illness.
Lieutenant General Manuel Antonio de Arleguí was designated as an executor (Albacea).

Sergeant Pascual Salguero and his wife María Josefa de Vargas obligated themselves for 100 pesos to the Chaplaincy founded by the late Magdalena de la Portilla, with Licenciado Francisco de Ocampo Golfín as patron. Lieutenant General Manuel Antonio de Arleguí redeemed this debt, charging it to land in the Valle de Barba that Salguero and Vargas had purchased from Victoria Carbonero, widow of Alférez Bernardo Cortés.

Captain Juan Sánchez de Camaño, a native of Cerezo and resident of Guayaquil, made his will. He declared three natural children with Florencia de Nao and detailed a debt owed by Diego de Lamas. He appointed several executors and beneficiaries, including Florencia de Nao and José de Escalada, for the remainder of his estate.

Captain Juan de Luque, a resident of Nicaragua, received 400 pesos in cacao from Captain Francisco de Betancourt. This payment was on account of a larger debt (721 pesos 6 reales) owed by General José Lacayo, as authorized by a letter from Granada dated July 9 of the same year.

Alférez Pedro Manuel de Moya, son of the late Sergeant Major Antonio de Moya and Isabel de Alvarado, is married to Micaela de Arburola and has three children: Juan Matías, José Manuel, and José Francisco. His brother Fernando de Moya and his wife Micaela were named as executors.

Sergeant Major Diego de Arviceita, a native of Navarra and resident of Panamá, made his will. He was married to Juana de Lara and had four children: Ángel, María, Matea, and Ignacio. Captain Antonio de Soto y Barahona was named as his executor.

José de Guzmán granted power of attorney to Captain Francisco López de la Flor, Factor of the Royal Treasury in Panamá, and Captain José Lebrón. The purpose was to sell an enslaved woman named Josefa, a criolla born in Guzmán's house.
Captain Domingo de Quesada granted general power of attorney to Captain Bernardo Marín.

Captain Vicente Andrés Polo and his wife Alfonsa de Bonilla, with Captain Juan García Adán as guarantor, obligated themselves for 100 pesos to José Antonio de Bonilla, their nephew. They received the money from Gregorio de Vargas and imposed the debt on a property in the Valle de Barba.

Francisco Ramiro Corajo granted power of attorney to Alférez Mateo de las Alas to collect 140 pesos. This debt was owed by Captain Domingo García de Estrada, a resident of Cartago who was absent from the city. The power was granted in the Valle de Barba.

Sergeant Major Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, a resident of Valle de Barba, made his will. He was married to Magdalena Pérez de Luna and had four children. He detailed extensive properties including a house, a hermitage, religious items, numerous enslaved people, livestock, and lands in various locations. His wife and two sons were named executors.

Alfonsa de Bonilla, daughter of the late Antonio de Bonilla and María de Grados, made her will. She was married to Captain Vicente Andrés Polo and had two children, José and María Polo. Her husband was named executor, and her children were her heirs.
Sergeant Major Francisco de Ocampo is mentioned in the registry.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
Licenciado don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Sargento Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, acting as executor for his deceased sister doña Tomasa de Ocampo Golfín, founded a chaplaincy as per her wishes. The chaplaincy was endowed with 872 pesos 4 reales, part of which was used to purchase houses in Cartago. The Licenciado don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, son of the founder, was named patron and chaplain, with his sons Nicolás and Juan, and later his grandchildren (children of doña Josefa de Ocampo Golfín), as successors.

Antonio González, son of Nicolás and Magdalena González, made his will in Barba. He was married to doña Águeda Murillo and had five children. His wife Águeda inherited from her deceased sister doña Catalina Murillo, and he also held funds for the children of Diego de Zúñiga, a mulatto slave of his father. His son-in-law, Francisco Alvarez de Ulate, was named an executor, and his sons Claudio and Gaspar were named heirs.

Juan Jiménez, son of Antonio Jiménez Maldonado and doña Mariana Hidalgo, issued a dowry letter in Barba in favor of his wife, doña María Polo. Doña María Polo was the legitimate daughter of Capitán Vicente Andrés Polo and doña Alfonsa de Bonilla. The dowry amounted to 501 pesos, with arras of 500 pesos.

Alejo Calderón and his wife Josefa Fernández, residents of Pacacua, sold houses and a plot of land in Cartago to Francisca de Hinojosa for 500 pesos. The property bordered lands previously owned by doña Clara de Chavarría and María Guerrero, and currently owned by doña Manuela de Quirós and doña Manuela de Salazar. The transaction took place at the sellers' residence in Pacacua.

Alférez José Hidalgo, a resident of San Luis de Aserrí, sold an enslaved mulata named Petronila, aged 29, and her infant mulatto son Pedro, to Alférez José de Quirós. José Hidalgo had previously acquired Petronila from the deceased doña María Duran. The sale took place at the buyer's home in San Antonio de Currirabá for 300 pesos.

Alférez Tomás de Chaves and his wife Juana de Solís, residents of San Antonio de Currirabá, sold a three-year-old mulata girl named Ana, daughter of their enslaved woman Feliciana, to their son-in-law Alférez José de Quirós for 100 pesos. The transaction occurred in Currirabá.

people_involved: Licenciado don Félix de Oses Navarro
summary: Mateo Sánchez Castañeda and his wife Ana de Olivares Gascón made their will in Barba, detailing their six living children and their marital statuses. The will also listed their enslaved people, Isabel (50, mulata) and her three children, and Manuel (24, negro mina), with Isabel designated for freedom upon the testators' deaths. Licenciado don Félix de Oses Navarro and Capitán Antonio Alvarez de Ulate were named executors.

Francisco Meléndez, a master carpenter, took on Juan José, a Spanish orphan from Barba, as an apprentice for six years. This arrangement was facilitated by Teniente de Caballos Corazas Francisco Montero de Espinosa, who also served as the Political Lieutenant Governor. The document notes that this agreement was not finalized.

Bernardo Salas, natural son of Francisco de las Alas and the deceased Andrea de Esquivel, made his will in Barba. He was married to María de Madrigal and had four children: José, Lorenza, Juana, and Jorge de las Alas. His wife María and Manuel González were named as executors.

Mateo Sánchez de Castañeda issued a codicil to his will (originally made on May 10th), declaring the dowry goods he provided to his daughter María, for which her husband, Leandro Sayas, had not given a receipt. The codicil was made in Barba.

José Lobo, a master shoemaker, received Juan Cervantes, a mestizo orphan from San Bartolomé de Barba, as an apprentice for seven years. Juan Cervantes' mother was named Juana. The apprenticeship was arranged by the Political Lieutenant Governor Francisco Montero de Espinosa and took place in the valley of Barba.

Capitán Antonio Alvarez de Ulate, acting as executor for the deceased Bernardo Cortés, founded a chaplaincy for the souls of Bernardo Cortés and Clara Morera. The endowment of 438 pesos was managed by Juan Cortés and his wife Sebastiana de Aguilar. Fray Francisco Guerrero, the parish priest of Barba, was named patron and chaplain, and the ten annual masses were to be held in the Chapel of Soledad in the Barba church.

locations: vega del río de las Ciruelas
summary: Juan Cortés and his wife Sebastiana de Aguilar, residents of Barba valley, obligated themselves for 438 pesos at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by Bernardo Cortés. This obligation was secured by a property they owned in the Ciruelas river plain, which included a house and a sugar mill.

Juan Cortés and Sebastiana de Aguilar sold a 10-year-old mulata slave named Alfonsa to Manuel González for 200 pesos. Alfonsa was inherited from Juan Cortés's deceased grandfather, Bernardo Cortés, and was adjudicated to Juan Cortés as the son of María Rodríguez, Bernardo's stepdaughter.

people_involved: Gobernador y Capitán General don Diego de la Haya Fernández
General don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones
summary: Juan Jiménez Maldonado, a resident of Barba valley and former Alcalde de la Santa Hermandad, granted power of attorney to Capitán Vicente Andrés Polo. Polo was to represent Maldonado before Gobernador don Diego de la Haya Fernández in the residency trial of ex-Gobernador don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones, as Maldonado expected to be implicated for his past administration of justice.

Magdalena González, widow of Nicolás González, made her will, naming her son Manuel González as her heir and executor. She disinherited her other children, Antonio, Andrea, and Leonor González, and also mentioned her mulata slave, Manuela.

José Rodríguez provided a dowry of 287 pesos and 50 pesos in arras to his wife, María Rodríguez de Sosa. The goods were received from María's grandmother, Magdalena González, and her uncle, Manuel González, having been previously held by her deceased grandfather, Nicolás González.
