Magdalena Rodríguez de Sosa received 370 pesos, including a slave and a wooden chest, from her grandmother Magdalena González and her uncle Manuel González. These assets constituted her legitimate paternal and maternal inheritance.

María de Madrigal, widow of Bernardo Salas, obligated herself for 194 pesos 3 reales and 6 maravedíes to her minor legitimate children, José, Lorenza, Juana, and Jorge, for their paternal inheritance. Capitán Tomás de Chaves and his wife Tomasa de Quirós served as guarantors.

people_involved: Capitán Tomás de Chaves, el mozo
summary: María de Madrigal declared that she had found a new guarantor and released Capitán Tomás de Chaves, el mozo, from his obligation. This was due to vexations he had experienced concerning his role as guarantor in the previous obligation.

Capitán José de Saborido and his wife doña Juana de Ballesteros obligated themselves for 243 pesos at 5% interest to the minor children of Juan de Saborido, a free mulato and their former slave, and María de Arguedas, both deceased. This obligation represented the children's paternal and maternal inheritance.

Sebastián Cayetano de Zamora, son of Capitán Sebastián de Zamora and Luisa de Quintana, provided a dowry of 624 pesos 4 reales and 200 pesos in arras to his wife doña Cecilia de Saborido. Doña Cecilia is the legitimate daughter of Capitán José de Saborido and doña Juana de Ballesteros.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
Licenciado don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín granted general power of attorney to his son, Licenciado don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín.

people_involved: Licenciado don Félix de Hoses Navarro
Sárjente Mayor don Francisco López Conejo
summary: Doña María de Quirós, widow of Sárjente Mayor don Francisco López Conejo, sold a 20-year-old Mina-caste black slave named Juan José to Licenciado don Félix de Hoses Navarro for 400 pesos. She had acquired the slave upon her husband's death.

Francisco de Chaves provided a dowry of 852 pesos and 500 pesos in arras to his wife, doña María Magdalena de Azofeifa, with whom he had been married for over five years. Doña María Magdalena is the legitimate daughter of don Pedro de Azofeifa and doña María Guijarro.
Alférez Tomás de Chaves sold a 45-year-old criollo black slave named Francisco to Capitán Blas de Ancheta for 400 pesos.

people_involved: Capitán don José de Morales Tremiño
summary: Capitán Antonio Solórzano and his wife doña Casilda de Morera, Alférez Tomás de Chaves and his wife Juana de Solís, Alférez Francisco de Loria, and Juan Cortés acted as guarantors for Capitán don José de Morales Tremiño. Tremiño was about to assume the role of Lieutenant of Royal Treasury Officials, and the group guaranteed 1700 pesos of his required 4000 pesos bond.

people_involved: Licenciado don Félix de Hoses Navarro
Sárjenlo Mayor don Francisco López Conejo
summary: Licenciado don Félix de Hoses Navarro declared that the slave Juan José, whom he purchased on November 6th from doña María de Quirós, actually belonged to his brother-in-law, Capitán Antonio de Barahona. Navarro had bought the slave on commission for Barahona and now formally transferred ownership.

Alférez Juan Jiménez Maldonado and his wife doña María Polo, along with Capitán Eusebio Jiménez Maldonado, obligated themselves for 200 pesos at 5% interest to the chaplaincy founded by doña Francisca Jiménez, of which Capitán Francisco de Flores is the patron. This obligation was secured by livestock they owned in the Bagaces valley.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don José de Morales
summary: Sarjento Mayor don José de Morales was serving as Teniente de Gobernador in 1720.

people_involved: Capitán don Miguel de Ayesta y Aguirre
doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: Capitán don Miguel de Ayesta y Aguirre obligates himself to the heirs of don Domingo de Cueto for 800 pesos. This sum was received from Capitán don Francisco de Betancourt, husband of doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral, who is an heir of Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral. The obligation settles a debt declared in the will of don Domingo de Ayesta, Miguel's deceased brother, and frees the assets of Antonio de la Vega Cabral from this debt by a decree from the Governor and Captain General.
Capitán Luis Gutiérrez and his wife Inés de Quesada obligate themselves to the minor children of the deceased Francisco Martínez and doña Lorenza Venegas for 100 pesos at 5% interest.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Bartolomé de Alvarado
Sarjento Mayor don Pedro de Alvarado
Capitán don José de Morales Tremiño
summary: Doña Sebastiana de Alvarado, widow of Sarjento Mayor don Bartolomé de Alvarado, makes her will. She names her 21-year-old adopted daughter, Francisca de Alvarado, as her heir. Her nephews don Francisco de Otárola, Capitán don José de Alvarado, Sarjento Mayor don Pedro de Alvarado, and Capitán don Gil de Alvarado are mentioned, with the latter and Capitán don José de Morales Tremiño appointed as executors.

people_involved: doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar
summary: Doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar obligates herself to the minor children of the deceased Francisco Martínez and doña Lorenza Venegas for 325 pesos at 5% interest. This obligation is secured by her dwelling houses in Cartago.

people_involved: doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar
Licenciado don Félix Esteban de Hoses Navarro
summary: Doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar acknowledges a 100-peso, 5% annuity (censo) on her dwelling houses in Cartago, which she purchased from the deceased Francisco Martínez. This censo benefits a chaplaincy founded by doña Eugenia de Abarca, with Licenciado don Félix Esteban de Hoses Navarro serving as chaplain.

people_involved: Teniente de Caballos Severino de Aguilar
summary: A dowry letter is issued for the upcoming marriage of Alférez don Francisco Manuel García, a native of Cádiz, and Manuela Victoria de Aguilar. The dowry amounts to 1013 pesos 4 reales and 200 pesos in arras. Miguel de Aguilar, Manuela Victoria's brother, donates his paternal and maternal inheritance to her.

people_involved: doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar
Juan López de la Rea y Soto
summary: Doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar, widow of Capitán don Antonio Acosta Arévalo, acknowledges an 840-peso, 5% annuity on her cacao plantations in the Matina valley. This censo is the principal for a chaplaincy founded on November 14, 1714, by her deceased husband for his soul, with their son Alférez José de Acosta as patron and Licenciado don Manuel de Guzmán as interim chaplain.

people_involved: doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar
summary: Doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar acknowledges a 200-peso, 5% annuity on her cacao haciendas. This censo belongs to a chaplaincy founded by the deceased Alférez Pedro de Torres for the soul of his sister, doña Francisca de Torres, with Capitán Juan de Chaves as patron and Licenciado don Manuel de Guzmán as interim chaplain.

people_involved: doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar
Licenciado don Juan Antonio de Moya
summary: Doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar acknowledges a 200-peso, 5% annuity on her dwelling houses in Cartago, which she bought from the deceased Francisco Martínez for 800 pesos. This censo is for the chaplaincy of Alférez Vasco Solano, with Licenciado don Juan Antonio de Moya serving as chaplain.

people_involved: doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar
summary: Doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar acknowledges a 75-peso, 5% annuity on her dwelling houses. This censo belongs to a chaplaincy founded by Depositario Pedro Solano, with Licenciado don Manuel de Guzmán serving as both patron and chaplain.

people_involved: doña Jerónima de Riva y Agüero
summary: Antonia González sells 500 cacao trees in the Barbilla valley to doña Jerónima de Riva y Agüero, bordering her sister Mariana González's hacienda and María de la Paz's property. She also sells an additional 225 contiguous trees, including a house site, for a total of 453 pesos 1 real.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan de Betancourt
doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: A dowry letter is issued for Capitán don Francisco de Betancourt and his wife doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral, who married on September 10, 1719. The dowry, after deducting debts from inventoried goods, amounts to 6701 pesos 1 real and 20 maravedíes.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: Capitán don Francisco de Betancourt sells a 10-year-old 'mulato blanco' named José de Alvarado to don Bernardo Vermes y Mogrovejo for 200 pesos. José de Alvarado was part of the estate of Betancourt's deceased father-in-law, Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral.

people_involved: doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: Capitán don Francisco de Betancourt and his wife doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral obligate themselves for 300 pesos at 5% to doña Francisca Ballesteros, a minor under the care of her uncle Juan Hidalgo. This debt was originally an obligation of the estate of Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral. The obligation was cancelled by Capitán don José de Saborido on February 22, 1738.

people_involved: doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: Capitán don Francisco de Betancourt and doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral obligate themselves for 450 pesos at 5% to two minor orphans under the care of Magdalena Romero. This debt was originally an obligation of the estate of Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral.

locations: Ciudad de los Reyes de Lima, Peru
people_involved: doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
Veinticuatro y Regidor don Juan Sáenz Cascante
Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: Capitán don Francisco de Betancourt and doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral obligate themselves for 1400 pesos to Veinticuatro y Regidor don Juan Sáenz Cascante, a resident of Lima, Peru. This debt was originally owed by the estate of Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral.

Sarjento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra granted freedom to his slave, José Cayetano, who is the grandson of his slave Manuela del Camino. The freedom was granted in exchange for 100 pesos received from Manuela del Camino.

Capitán Don Nicolás de Guevara recognized a 500-peso lien on a cacao plantation in Matina. This lien belongs to a Chaplaincy founded by the late Doña Francisca de Acosta Arévalo, who was his first wife and the widow of Don Gregorio de Azofeifa. The plantation was inherited by Don Nicolás from his daughter Clara Manuela, and José Cayetano de Azofeifa is the first patron and chaplain, with Licenciado Don Manuel de Guzmán serving as interim chaplain.

Capitán Don Nicolás de Guevara and his wife Doña Francisca de Inza obligated themselves to pay 150 pesos and 6 reales at 5% interest to José Cayetano de Azofeifa. This sum represents an inheritance José Cayetano received from his mother, Doña Francisca de Acosta Arévalo, who was also Don Nicolás's first wife.

María de Sibaja, a widow, leased a cacao plantation with 1000 trees in the Matina valley to José Meneses for two years. The annual rent was set at 225 pesos in cacao, equivalent to 9 zurrones. The property bordered land belonging to Capitán Lorenzo de Arburola, a river, and the mountain.

Mariana González sold a 427-tree cacao plantation named El Pigiba in the Barbilla valley to Alférez Domingo de Quesada for 427 pesos. This amount was used to pay a debt owed by her son, Alférez Nicolás de Quirós, to the buyer. The plantation bordered land of the deceased Miguel González, a stream, and another part of Mariana's hacienda, which she inherited from her late husband, José de Quirós.

A dowry letter was issued for the upcoming marriage of Capitán Don Bernardo Vermes Mogronejo and Doña Josefa Gadea Marrufo, scheduled for April 7. Don Bernardo, a native of Benavente, Castilla, is the legitimate son of Antonio Vermes Barquero and Doña Manuela Martínez Mogromejo. Doña Josefa is the legitimate daughter of the late Don Rodrigo Gadea Marrufo and Doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco. The dowry amounted to 3254 pesos, with arras of 500 pesos, and included a 12-13 year old black creole slave named Pablo José.

Doña Antonia de Acosta Arévalo, a widow, leased a 1500-tree cacao plantation in the Matina valley to Alférez Domingo Guerrero for three years. The rent for the first two years was 150 pesos of cacao annually, delivered to the city, and 200 pesos for the final year.
Capitán Blas de Ancheta and Alférez Francisco Calvo exchanged slaves. Ancheta traded Francisco Hidalgo for a mulatto boy, who was the son of Manuela Calvo, from Alférez Calvo.

Capitán José Felipe Bermúdez and his wife Doña Teresa de Sandoval sold a 23-24 year old zamba slave named Paula, daughter of Isidora, to Licenciado Don Hermenegildo de Alvarado for 300 pesos. They had received Paula as part of a dowry from Doña Petronila de Quirós, who was Doña Teresa's mother and Don José Felipe's mother-in-law.

people_involved: Capitán Don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí
B" Don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
summary: Pascual Salguero and his wife María Josefa de Vargas sold their adobe and timber house in Cartago to Capitán Don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí, Teniente General of Matina valley, for 500 pesos. The house was part of a dowry from María Josefa's parents, Capitán Diego de Vargas and Juana de Chavarría. The sale involved settling 100 pesos owed to Don Diego de Ángulo Gascón and 200 pesos to Licenciado Francisco de Ocampo Golfín.

people_involved: Don Diego de la Haya Fernández
Capitán Don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí
summary: Don Diego de la Haya Fernández, Gobernador y Capitán General, certified that Pascual Salguero and his wife obligated themselves for 100 pesos at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy of Magdalena de la Portilla. This obligation reduced Capitán Don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí's prior debt by 100 pesos.

people_involved: Capitán Don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí
summary: Licenciado Francisco de Ocampo Golfín received 100 pesos from Capitán Don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí, settling part of the debt mentioned in the earlier sale of the house.

people_involved: B" Don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
Capitán Don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí
summary: Beneficiados Don Diego de Ángulo Gascón and Don Manuel de Escalante Panlagua, curates of the parochial church in Cartago, received the remaining 100 pesos from Capitán Don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí, which were owed to the church.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Don Antonio de Moya
Sarjento Mayor Don Antonio de Utrera
summary: Doña Josefa de Moya, daughter of the late Sarjento Mayor Don Antonio de Moya and Doña Isabel de Alvarado, made her testament in Ujarraz. She is married to Sarjento Mayor Don Antonio de Utrera, a native of Motril, Spain. She named her living children, José Cayetano and Isabel Ramona, and mentioned her deceased children, Antonia and Pablo José. Doña Josefa established a chaplaincy, designating her son José Cayetano as the chaplain, or her brother Beneficiado Don Antonio de Moya if her son is not ordained. If neither, the role would pass to a nephew, either a son of her sister Doña Polonia de Moya and Capitán Don Jerónimo Manuel Ramos, or a son of her brother Don Pedro Manuel de Moya and Doña Micaela de Arburola. Her husband was named executor.

people_involved: Licenciado Don Juan Antonio de Moya
summary: Licenciado Don Juan Antonio de Moya donated the usufruct of a 3000-tree cacao plantation in Matina to his brother-in-law, Capitán Don Jerónimo Manuel Ramos, for a period of two years.

A dowry letter was issued for Capitán Don Eusebio Jiménez and his wife Doña María Francisca Alvarez, who married on February 6 of the current year. Don Eusebio is the legitimate son of Capitán Don Antonio Jiménez and Doña Mariana de Avila Hidalgo. Doña María Francisca is the legitimate daughter of Capitán Don Francisco Alvarez and the late Doña María de Vargas. The dowry totaled 890 pesos and 5 reales, with arras of 500 pesos, and included a 20-year-old mulatta slave named Josefa valued at 400 pesos.

people_involved: Ayudante Don José de Hoyo y Echavarría
summary: Licenciado Don Hermenegildo de Alvarado obligated himself to Ayudante Don José de Hoyo y Echavarría for 1001 pesos, representing the value of various goods. He committed to paying 200 arrobas of tallow in the ports of Alvarado and Avangares during November and December of the current year, and 20 mules in Cartago the following January.
Don José de Mier Cevallos, acting as the attorney for Hoyo, cancelled a debt of 1001 pesos. This transaction took place on August 14, 1722.

This entry records the testament of Diego de Quesada, son of the deceased Alonso de Quesada and María López Rubio. He was married to Doña Sebastiana de Quirós and listed eight children, with three daughters married to Jacinto Vicente Sotelo, José Jiménez, and Pedro Jiménez respectively. His wife and son Miguel de Quesada were named as executors.

people_involved: Margarita de la Haya y Bolívar
summary: This entry details the testament of Captain Francisco de Bonilla, son of the deceased Sarjento Mayor Alonso de Bonilla and Juana Benita Calvo. He was first married to Doña Leonor de Vargas, with whom he had four children, and is currently married to Doña Margarita de la Haya y Bolívar, with whom he has six children. His son, Captain Francisco Alejandro de Bonilla, and Don Alvaro de Guevara were named as executors.

José de Quirós, a resident of the Barba valley, sold a 27-year-old mulata named Petrona to Sergeant José Damián de Molina for 150 pesos. José de Quirós had previously acquired Petrona from Alférez José Hidalgo.

Alférez Francisco Manzano y Boyaín, a native of Utrera, Spain, entered into a dowry agreement for his marriage to Doña Francisca Hernández Barquero. The marriage took place on August 11, with a dowry of 1500 pesos and arras of 500 pesos, which included a 3-year-old mulata named Lorenza de la Trinidad and eight mules.
Doña Baltasara de Escalante Panlagua, the widow of Captain José Antonio Bermúdez, formally committed to paying the creditors of her deceased husband's estate.

Manuel de Salazar, with Captain Antonio Salmón Pacheco and Juan Calderón acting as guarantors, incurred an obligation of 275 pesos to Captain Juan Marín. Juan Marín was a resident of Realejo, Nicaragua, and was currently residing locally.

locations: paraje que llaman de los tres ríos
summary: Doña Antonia María Venegas, a widow, sold an adobe house with a wheat mill located near 'los tres ríos' to Captain José de Alvarado for 300 pesos. José de Alvarado and his wife, Doña Josefa López Conejo, were obligated to pay this amount to a chaplaincy founded by Captain Pedro de Alvarado, whose patron was Captain Gil de Alvarado and chaplain was Licenciado Hermenegildo de Alvarado.

Captain José de Alvarado and his wife, Doña Josefa López Conejo, formally recognized a censo (annuity/lien) of 300 pesos at 5% interest on the property they had purchased, as detailed in the previous document.

This entry records the joint testament of Alférez Francisco Solano and his wife Doña Juana de las Alas. They listed their parents, four children (one of whom, María, was married to Antonio de Bonilla), and several individuals they had raised or who were part of their household, including an orphan, a mulata servant, and other children. Captain Pedro de Moya was named as an executor.

Alférez Juan Masís sold a cacao plantation in the Barbilla valley, comprising 1076 trees and an adjacent cleared plot, to Alférez Jacinto de Rivera for 1430 pesos. The payment was allocated to two chaplaincies: one founded by Miguel Masís (with Juan Masís as patron and Manuel Sáenz as chaplain), and another founded by Sergeant Juan Masís (originally patroned by José Masís, now by Juan Masís). The buyer recognized these obligations.

Licenciado Don Juan Antonio de Moya, tenant of houses formerly belonging to Licenciado Don Francisco de Rivas y Velazco, incurred an obligation for 1130 pesos tied to these properties. This debt was distributed among several chaplaincies, each with specified patrons and chaplains, including those of Captain Pedro Ibáñez, Doña Gertrudis de Alvarado, Depositario Pedro Solano, Doña Juana Moscoso, and Captain Alonso Gómez Macotela.

people_involved: María de la Candelaria de Prendas
summary: This entry begins to record the testament of Segundo de Trejos, son of Juan de Trejos and Ana de Aguilar. He was married to María de la Candelaria de Prendas, daughter of Sergeant Jacinto Fernández, but the record is incomplete.
Captain Manuel García de Argueta sold a 40-year-old 'cabo verde' slave named Antonio to Juan Delgado, a resident of Aserrí, for 300 pesos.
Lieutenant Governor and Captain General, Sergeant Major Don José de Morales, apprenticed Francisco, a 12-year-old orphaned 'pardo' boy, to Assistant José de las Alas, a master tailor, for 6 years.
An incomplete will of Sergeant Blas Várela was recorded. He was the legitimate son of the deceased Antonio Várela and María de Santiago.
Gregorio Ureña obligated himself to Ensign Antonio Valerino for 125 pesos of cacao, to be paid by January 1719. This agreement was granted in Matina before Ensign Francisco Espinóla.
Captain Don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad leased a cacao plantation of 500 trees in the Matina valley to Sergeant Nicolás Ruiz for one year, for 75 pesos of cacao.

people_involved: Juana Josefa de Arburola y Ribarén
summary: Doña Juana Josefa de Arburola y Ribarén leased a cacao plantation of 500 trees, adjacent to another, to Sergeant Nicolás Ruiz for one year, for 50 pesos in cacao.

people_involved: María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
José Miguel de Arburola y Ribarén
summary: Captain Francisco Betancourt and his wife, Doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral, obligated themselves to Doña Josefa de Hoces Navarro for 100 pesos. This sum was a donation from Ana Cardoso for her son, Don José Miguel de Arburola y Ribarén, previously charged to the deceased Sergeant Major Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral, father of Doña María Josefa.

Doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar, a widow, donated a cacao plantation of 790 trees in the Matina valley to her son, José de Acosta Arévalo. The property bordered the haciendas of the minor Don Cayetano Azofeifa Alvarado and Captain Don Nicolás de Guevara.

The will of Feliciana de Chinchilla, widow of Ensign Francisco Fernández, was recorded. She named her daughter María Francisca Fernández as heir and appointed Sergeant Major Don José de Morales and José Bernardo as executors.

Following a court ruling against Nicolás de Arroyo for theft, and involving accomplices Juana Sáenz and her son Manuel Rivera, Lieutenant General Captain Manuel Antonio de Arleguí ordered Manuel Rivera to be apprenticed to master blacksmith Francisco Carrillo for 5 years.

An incomplete will of Captain Nicolás de Guevara was recorded. He was the legitimate son of the deceased Captain Don Antonio de Guevara and Doña Clara de Echavarría, married in second nuptials to Doña Francisca de Inza, and had a daughter, Juana Antonia de Guevara. His former wife was Doña Francisca de Acosta.

José de Acosta Arévalo petitioned to secure a 1000-tree cacao plantation in Matina belonging to the minor Don Cayetano Azofeifa Alvarado, which was unsecured. He offered to mortgage the property and provide a bond from his mother, Doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar, who was also the minor's grandmother, and the petition was approved.

Ensign José de Acosta Arévalo and his wife, Doña María Ballesteros, with the bond of Doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar, formalized an obligation for 1500 pesos related to a hacienda. This obligation was later cancelled on October 14, 1728, by Sergeant Major Don Francisco de la Madriz Linares, curator ad litem for the minor Cayetano Azofeifa Alvarado.

Assistant Nicolás de Estrada sold adobe houses in Cartago to Captain Don José de Morales for 600 pesos. These houses, inherited from the deceased Doña Isabel de Guevara, had 200 pesos of their value allocated to a chaplaincy belonging to Licenciado Don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, with the remaining 400 pesos payable in cacao.

The will of Assistant José de las Alas and his wife Sebastiana Barbosa was recorded. They had no children but raised an orphaned girl, Josefa de las Alas, whom they named as their heir. They established two chaplaincies and appointed the surviving spouse and Captain Don Pedro de Moya as executors.

Sergeant Major Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra and Doña Catalina González Camino obligated themselves for 420 pesos to the Royal Treasury of León, Nicaragua, for the value of tithes from Esparza and its valleys of Bagaces, which they had successfully bid for.

Sergeant Major Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra and his wife, Doña Catalina González Camino, granted power of attorney to Captain Don Francisco López de la Flor, a resident of Panama, to collect debts declared by the deceased Captain Don Fernando Marín, a former resident of Nata de los Caballeros.
An incomplete will of Ensign Sebastián Guillen and his wife María Magdalena de Orozco was recorded. Sebastián was the legitimate son of the deceased Juan Ruiz Guillen and María de Santiago.

people_involved: Ayudante José Valeriano de las Alas
summary: The legitimate children of the deceased Sargento Alberto de Orozco and Catalina Barquero are listed, including María Cayetana (married to Sargento Miguel Campos) and Josefa (married to Francisco Tames). Ayudante José Valeriano de las Alas is named as an albacea for the estate.

people_involved: Licenciado don Juan Moreno de Orejuela
summary: María Calvo, widow of Capitán José de Chavarría, grants power to Licenciado don Juan Moreno de Orejuela, an attorney in Ciudad de los Reyes, to apprehend Ramón Duran (also known as Raimundo), a Creole black man over 50 years old. Ramón Duran was dispersed in Chiriquí, where María Calvo's husband had drowned.

Alférez Juan Marín Laguna, son of the deceased Ayudante General José Marín Laguna and doña Catalina de Moya, establishes a dowry of 604 pesos and arras of 400 pesos for his wife, doña María de Bonilla. Doña María is the legitimate daughter of the deceased Capitán Juan de Bonilla and doña Francisca de Astúa. Their marriage took place on the 11th of the current month.

people_involved: doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
don José Miguel de Arburola y Ribarén
Sargento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: Capitán don Francisco de Betancourt and his wife, doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral, obligate themselves to doña Josefa de Hoces Navarro, mother of don José Miguel de Arburola y Ribarén, for 100 pesos at 5% interest. This money was donated by Ana Cardoso and was originally charged to the deceased Sargento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral, father of doña María Josefa.
Teniente General don José de Mier Ceballos certifies that Capitán don José de Alvarado and his wife, doña Úrsula López, have obligated themselves for the 100 pesos mentioned in a previous deed.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Capitán don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad grants power of attorney to General don Salvador Cano, a Procurador in the Audiencia de Guatemala. The document notes that it was not fully executed or registered.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad
Capitán don Manuel Antonio de Arburola y Ribarén
Sargento Mayor don Pedro Martínez de Ugarrio
summary: Capitán don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad and Capitán don Manuel Antonio de Arburola y Ribarén grant power of attorney to Capitán don Salvador Cano, a Procurador in the Audiencia de Guatemala. This power is specifically to pursue a case regarding the imprisonment of Sargento Mayor don Pedro Martínez de Ugarrio, who was a Juez pesquisidor y de residencia for the province.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
Capitán don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Sargento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra grants general power of attorney to his wife, doña Catalina González Camino, and to Capitán don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad.

The will of doña Petronila Valerín is recorded. She was the legitimate daughter of the deceased Capitán Jerónimo Valerín and doña Francisca de Esquivel, and the widow of Juan Antonio de Castro, with no children. Her sister doña Juana Valerín, nieces doña María Josefa Pacheco and Antonia Valerín, and servant José Valerín are mentioned. Licenciado don Manuel de Guzmán and Alférez Bernardo Pacheco are named as albaceas.

The will of Andrés Peláez is recorded. He was the natural son of the deceased Nicolás Peláez and Magdalena Rodríguez, and the widower of Catalina Rosales. He had two daughters, Gertrudis (married to Alférez Gregorio Picado) and the deceased Juana. He also raised an orphan girl named Petrona. His son-in-law Alférez Gregorio Picado and Bernardo Pacheco are named as albaceas.

people_involved: Capitán don Alonso Bersabé Cabeza de Vaca
Maestre de Campo don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina
summary: Capitán don Alonso Bersabé Cabeza de Vaca, Ayudante Matías Masís, Teniente Jacinto de Campos, and Sargento Matías Trejos provide surety for Maestre de Campo don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina for 1250 pesos. Serrano de Reina is traveling to Nicaragua to render final accounts for his position as Teniente de Oficiales Reales de la Real Hacienda. The deed was not completed due to a discrepancy with two of the guarantors.

The will of Sargento Miguel de Aguilar and his wife Manuela Solano is recorded. Miguel was the legitimate son of the deceased Matías de Aguilar and María del Cubillo, and Manuela was the legitimate daughter of the deceased Nicolás Solano and Antonia Sánchez. They had two daughters, Micaela (married to Tomás Camacho) and Josefa. The surviving spouse and Tomás Camacho are named as albaceas.

people_involved: Alférez don Juan Sanjurjo de Aguiar
summary: The will of doña Juana de Aguiar is recorded. She was the legitimate daughter of the deceased Alférez don Juan Sanjurjo de Aguiar and doña Isabel de Flores, and the widow of Teniente Felipe Bermúdez. Her children included Reverendo Padre Fray Miguel, the deceased Capitán José Antonio, and Capitán José Felipe, who is named as her heir and albacea.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina
summary: Ayudante Matías Masís, Teniente Jacinto de Campos, Juana Calderón, María Calderón, and Bernarda Calderón provide surety for Maestre de Campo don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina for 1250 pesos. Serrano de Reina is traveling to Nicaragua to render accounts for his position as Teniente de Oficiales Reales de la Real Hacienda.

Manuel de Salazar, legitimate son of Juan de Salazar and doña Ana de los Ríos (natives of Tacunga, Quito), establishes a dowry of 1706 pesos and arras of 300 pesos for his wife, María de Meza. María is the legitimate daughter of Capitán Felipe de Meza and Felipa de Artavia.

Capitán Francisco Jiménez, legitimate son of the deceased Alférez Antonio Jiménez and doña Mariana Avila Hidalgo, establishes a dowry for his future wife, doña Josefa de Bonilla. Doña Josefa is the legitimate daughter of the deceased Sarjento Mayor Juan de Bonilla and doña Francisca de Astúa. Their marriage is scheduled for January 1st of the upcoming year, but the document is incomplete.

Manuel de Chaves, natural son of Matías Madrigal and Ana de Chaves, and widower of Josefa de Benavente, made his will. He named his legitimate children Juan José and Gertrudis de Chaves, and his natural son Francisco (14 years old) whom he raised. Juan Lucas Solano (his son-in-law) and Francisco de las Mas were named as executors.

people_involved: Licenciado don Félix de Hoces Navarro
summary: Licenciado don Félix de Hoces Navarro granted power of attorney to Capitanes Antonio de Baiahona and don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí. They were tasked to compel doña Luisa Calvo, his aunt, to secure a house in his favor through a transfer deed, related to a chaplaincy founded by Licenciado don Marcos Machado, with Licenciado José Camacho as patron and chaplain.
Licenciado José de Chaves granted freedom to María de Chaves, a mulata slave. María was the daughter of Feliciana, a slave of Alférez Tomás de Chaves, and Juana de Solís.

Alférez Sebastián de Mores, as principal, and Juan Matías de Mores, his father, as guarantor, obligated themselves for 170 pesos at 5% interest. This obligation was in favor of the Cofradía de la Concepción del Convento de San Francisco del Espíritusanto de Esparza, secured by houses in the valley of Barba.

Juana de Chaves, a widow, sold a mulato named Juan de Chaves, over 40 years old, to Licenciado José de Chaves for 100 pesos. Juana had previously purchased Juan de Chaves from Capitán Gerardo de Azofeifa.

José de Hererra, a native of León, Nicaragua, granted general power of attorney to Capitán Antonio Alvarez de Ulate. The purpose was to collect 515 pesos in León from Capitán don Julián José Larios, which had been awarded to Hererra by the Royal Justice as the legitimate son of Juana de Inguanzo.

Sargento Cristóbal de las Alas and his wife, doña María Manuela de Saborido, obligated themselves for 100 pesos of cacao in favor of Lucrecia Murillo, Cristóbal's grandmother. This obligation was later cancelled on June 20, 1720, by Francisco de las Alas, Lucrecia Murillo's executor, in favor of Cristóbal de las Alas, his son.

people_involved: María de la Candelaria de la Cruz
summary: Gregoria Rodríguez de Sosa, legitimate daughter of Juan Rodríguez de Sosa and Clara Morera, made her will. She was married to Ramón de la Cruz and named their children: Vicente, Agustín, Basilio, Sebastián, and María de la Candelaria. Her husband, Ramón de la Cruz, was named as her executor.

Juana Victoria de Herrera, a widow, sold a fenced property to Pascual Salguero for 100 pesos. The property was located in the plain of the Ciruelas river and included a large house, a piece of sugarcane, and a plantain patch.

Juan Cortés obligated himself for 450 pesos in favor of his legitimate children with his deceased wife, Sebastiana de Aguilar, as their legitimate inheritance. He hypothecated a sugarcane plantation and a sugar mill as security for this obligation.

Cristóbal Ramírez and Gertrudis de Zúñiga obligated themselves for 50 pesos at 5% interest in favor of María Rosalía Cordero. This sum represented María Rosalía's paternal inheritance, which Bernardo Cordero, her uncle, delivered to them. They hypothecated a ranch in the Barba valley, near the Lajuela river.

Magdalena de Sosa, a resident of Barba valley, sold a 7-month-old mulatilla named María Manuela to Manuel González for 84 pesos. María Manuela was the daughter of Ambrosia González, Magdalena's slave, whom Magdalena inherited from her deceased parents, Juan de Sosa and Leonor González.

Pascual Salguero, a master tailor, took José Jorge, a 14-year-old Spanish boy and son of Juana Vásquez, as an apprentice for 7 years. José Jorge was delivered to Salguero by Capitán Francisco Montero de Espinosa, the Lieutenant General.

Inés de Olivares made a codicil to her will, modifying a previous disposition to her son, Pablo Jiménez, reducing his inheritance from two slaves to one due to his 17-year absence and lack of assistance. She also ordered the freedom of her mulata slave, María.

Capitán Luis Morera and his wife, Gregoria de Segura, obligated themselves for 172 pesos in favor of doña Juana Teodora and José de Madrigal, legitimate children of the deceased Capitán Nicolás de Madrigal and Micaela Rodríguez. This sum included inheritance and funds from their grandmother, Lucrecia Murillo, secured by a hacienda in the Ciruelas river valley.

Alférez Tomás de Chaves and his wife, Juana de Solís, sold five caballerías of land to their son-in-law, Alférez José de Quirós, for 50 pesos. The land was located in the valley of San Antonio de Curridavá, with boundaries described by quebradas, the Virilla and Torres rivers, and adjacent to lands of doña María Meléndez, with measurements previously done by Capitán Juan de Chaves.
Alférez Tomás de Chaves and his wife, Juana de Solís, sold one caballería of land in the same valley to their son-in-law, Blas Suárez, for 10 pesos.

An executor, fulfilling the codicil of Inés de Olivares, grants freedom to María de Brenes, who is over 60 years old. This María de Brenes was inherited by Inés de Olivares from her own mother, also named María de Brenes.

Petronila Alvarez, legitimate daughter of the deceased Sergeant Andrés Alvarez and Francisca Carbonero, makes her will. Her nephew is Martín Alvarez, and her uncle Andrés Carbonero is named as executor.

Pedro de Arroyo, natural son of the deceased Diego de Arroyo and María García, makes his will. He is married to Manuela Gallegos and lists his eight children. His married daughters include Tomasa, Francisca, and María (who is married to José de los Santos). His son-in-law is José Bolaños, and he has a 5-year-old granddaughter, Gregoria Venegas, whom he has raised. Alférez José de Quesada is named executor.

Alférez Don Pablo López Conejo and his wife Doña Teresa Jiménez Maldonado sell half a caballería of land in the 'río Segundo' valley to Andrés Arias for 40 pesos. The land borders the river, a fence that belonged to Atanasio Vásquez, Andrés Arias's house, and the royal road.

Sergeant Major Don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín and his wife Doña Magdalena Pérez de Luna, along with Captain Juan García de Adán and his wife Doña Josefa de Ocampo Golfín, obligate themselves to Doña Regina de Artunduaga of Panamá for 650 arrobas of tallow. This is to cover a debt owed by Captain Don Francisco de Bustamante, who requested they pay on his behalf. The tallow is to be delivered in Bagaces by November, from the cattle ranches 'El Higuerón' and 'Las Piedras' owned by Francisco de Ocampo Golfín. A portion (192 arrobas) is for Captain Don José de Olio as payment for 200 arrobas supplied by Captain Pedro Castellanos on behalf of Francisco de Bustamante, mediated by Governor Diego de la Haya Fernández.

In Cartago, Sergeant Major Don José de Olio y Echevarría, with power of attorney from Doña Rufina de Artunduaga (wife of Captain Don Antonio de Cheves y Subiza), cancels the debt for 650 arrobas. He receives payment from the heirs of Sergeant Major Don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín.

Cristóbal de Chaves receives 800 pesos as his paternal and maternal inheritance from his father, Tomás de Chaves. This inheritance includes 13 mule beasts, 150 cattle, 6 tame horses, 30 pesos paid to Ignacio Chacón on his behalf, and 22 pesos in cacao.

Juan García Adán, a native of Alcocer de las Ollas in Spain, makes his will. He is the legitimate son of the deceased Juan García Cordente and María Adán García, and is married to Doña Josefa de Ocampo Golfín. He names his three children, his uncle Andrés García (a cleric in Alcocer), and his wife and Captain Don Juan de Ocampo as executors.

locations: Valle de San Luis de Aserrí
summary: Atanasio de la Cruz Perera, legitimate son of Antonio Perera and María Mallén, issues a dowry letter for his wife Doña Andrea de Salazar. Andrea was raised by Captain Don Andrés de Salazar and Doña Gregoria de Rojas, who are considered her putative parents. The dowry is 460 pesos, and the arras (earnest money) is 200 pesos.

Nicolás de Alfaro makes his will, detailing his three marriages. He was first married to Catalina de Oviedo, then to the deceased María Morera, and finally to Doña Juana de Sibaja. He lists children from each marriage, and names his current wife and Captain Francisco de Flores as executors.
Sergeant Major Don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín and Doña Josefa de Ocampo Golfín (widow) grant general power of attorney to Licenciado Don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín.
Pedro Murillo, natural son of the deceased Jorge González and Andrea de Esquivel, makes his will. José Núñez is named as executor, and his natural son, Manuel Alfonso Murillo, is his heir.
Marcos de Segura, a master blacksmith, takes in Gregorio Romero, an orphaned mestizo boy native to this valley, as an apprentice for 10 years. The boy is delivered by the Lieutenant General.

Captain José de Saborido and his wife Doña Juana de Ballestirros, as principals, along with several captains and individuals as guarantors, obligate themselves to the seven legitimate children and heirs of the deceased Sergeant Major Antonio Aurelio de Zamora and Francisca de Saborido. The obligation is for 647 pesos 4 reales to each child, totaling 3896 pesos, representing their inheritance.

Esteban de Vargas established a dowry (carta dote) for his wife, Isabel de Sandoval. The dowry amounted to 614 pesos and 2 reales, with arras of 100 pesos. Isabel was the legitimate daughter of the deceased Alférez Juan Patricio de Sandoval and Teodora de Quirós, and the couple had married 10 years prior.

people_involved: María de la Candelaria de la Cruz
summary: Ramón de la Cruz obligated himself to his minor children, Basilio, Sebastián, and María de la Candelaria de la Cruz, and to his deceased wife, Gregoria Rodríguez de Sosa. This obligation was for 498 pesos, representing their maternal inheritance.

locations: Convento de San Francisco de Barba
summary: Capitán José de Saborido and his wife, Juana de Ballesteros, obligated themselves to the Chaplaincy founded by the deceased Sargento Mayor Antonio Aurelio de Zamora. This obligation was for 700 pesos at 5% interest, secured by the houses, sugarcane fields, and sugar kettles that previously belonged to Zamora, located at the Convento de San Francisco de Barba.

Pascual Salguero, a master tailor, accepted Juan Miguel Carbonero, a Spanish orphan native to 'este valle', as an apprentice for six years. Juan Miguel was delivered to Salguero by Teniente General Capitán Francisco Montero de Espinosa.

Pablo Barbosa, legitimate son of Juan Barbosa and Juana Chinchilla, established a dowry (carta dote) for his wife, Antonia de Andrade. Antonia, who was raised by Juan de Salazar and Margarita Rosa Delgado, received 200 pesos as dowry and 50 pesos as arras.

Teniente Nicolás de Estrada and his wife, Lorenza Muñoz, sold a plot of land in Cartago to Capitán don Diego de Barros y Carbajal for 30 pesos. The plot, previously purchased from Manuel Sandí, was bordered by the chapel of San Nicolás de Tolentino, a royal street, a plot owned by doña Ambrosia de Echavarría, their own dwelling, and the house of Capitán Pedro Palacio. The transaction was granted in San Luis de Aserrí, at the dwelling of Capitán don Andrés de Salazar.

Doña Josefa de Ocampo Golfín, widow of Capitán Juan García Adán, granted power to Francisco de Quirós. This power allowed Quirós to collect 600 pesos from Alférez José Suárez, a resident of Panamá, which Suárez owed to her deceased husband.

Juan de Ocampo Golfín, legitimate son of Sargento Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín and doña Margarita Pérez de Luna, made his testament. His parents were named as both executors and heirs of his estate.

Capitán Manuel García de Argueta granted general power to three individuals: first to Castellano don Francisco Montejo de Chavarría, second to Capitán don Domingo de Retana, and third to Capitán don José de Espinosa, all residents of Guatemala.

Capitán Juan Guerrero made his testament, detailing his family. He was the son of Cristóbal Guerrero and Gertrudis Enciso, and was widowed from his first wife, Leonor de Sojo (daughter of Alonso de Sojo and Antonia de Guevara), with whom he had a deceased minor daughter, Micaela. He married a second time to Juana Manuela Lizondo (daughter of Juan Matías Lizondo and Francisca de Benavente), and they had six children: Juan Francisco, Juana Josefa, the deceased Cristóbal, the deceased Gertrudis, María, and Gabriel. His executors were Alférez José Ramos and his second wife, Juana Manuela.

Gertrudis Falcon, legitimate daughter of the deceased José Falcón and Ana María Romero, and widow of Miguel Lizondo, made her testament. She listed her nine children: Basilio, Casilda, José Miguel, Félix, Luis, Cayetano, Leonor, Juan Ángel, and Josefa Nicolasa. Her son-in-law, Sargento Miguel López (husband of Casilda), was named as her executor.

Capitán Juan Gómez, acting as executor for the deceased Francisca de Benavente, leased a cacaotal of 1800 trees in the valley of Barbilla to Capitán Luis Gutiérrez for two years. This cacaotal had previously been leased by Francisca to Alférez Domingo de Quesada for three years, but Quesada had failed to pay or fulfill the conditions for the 1.75 years he possessed it. The annual rent was set at 9 zurrones of cacao.

Capitán don Bernardo Marín, as the principal, along with Capitanes don Antonio Salmón Pacheco and don Domingo Salmón Pacheco as guarantors, obligated themselves for 653 pesos and two reales of cacao. This amount pertained to a fideicomiso (trust) of 700 pesos established in the testament of the deceased doña Isabel de Guevara.

Capitán Manuel García de Argueta, as principal, and Sargento Mayor Francisco de la Madriz Linares with his wife Rita Josefa García de Argueta, and Capitán don Miguel de Alvarado with his wife María de Torres, as guarantors, obligated themselves for 1012 pesos. This obligation was made to secure the release of 16 zurrones of cacao, 108 cattle, and 28 old and thin mules, which had been granted by the Gobernador y Capitán General.

Doña Petronila de Hoces Navarro, wife of the absent Capitán Antonio de Soto y Karahona, as principal, and doña Luisa Calvo, as guarantor, obligated themselves for 125 pesos of silver or 190 pesos of cacao. This amount was for the enslaved man Jacobo, who was included among confiscated goods.

locations: Hacienda de Nuestra Señora de los Angeles
summary: Doña Petronila Valerin leased a cacaotal in the valley of Matina, consisting of 1000 trees in two sections (one called San Antonio), to Alférez Domingo de Quesada for three years. The cacaotal bordered the Hacienda de Nuestra Señora de los Angeles, Quesada's own hacienda, a river, and the mountain. The annual rent was 7 zurrones of first-quality cacao and 2 zurrones of second-quality cacao.

Licenciado don Manuel González Coronel, a Presbítero, sold a 12-year-old enslaved mulata named María Josefa to doña Baltasara de Escalante Paniagua for 200 pesos of silver. María Josefa was born in the seller's parents' house and inherited from them, being the daughter of the deceased Juana.

people_involved: María de la O y Céspedes
summary: Sargento Mayor don José de Morales and his wife, doña María de la O y Céspedes, sold a 35-year-old enslaved mulata named Isabel to Alférez Domingo de Quesada. They had acquired Isabel previously.

A capellanía (chaplaincy) founded by Alférez Juan Gómez Macotela, with Licenciado Juan José Camacho as its patron, holds a charge of 150 pesos. This charge is related to the death of Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes, who was a father-in-law and father.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Doña Josefa Santiago de Aguilar, a widow, leased a 1200-tree cacao plantation in the Matina valley to her son, Manuel Andrés de Acosta Arévalo. The three-year lease was for 225 pesos annually, and the plantation bordered properties of Sargento Mayor Juan Francisco de Ibarra and Capitán don Bernardo Marín, as well as the forest and a river.

people_involved: Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Manuel Andrés de Acosta Arévalo committed to Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona for eleven loads of first-quality cacao to be delivered in Matina, and four loads of the same to be delivered in Cartago. These four loads were in payment for a debt owed by his mother, Doña Josefa Santiago de Aguilar.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí
summary: Sargento Mayor don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí, a Lieutenant General, apprenticed Pedro Narciso Calvo, a 14-year-old free Zambo and legitimate son of the deceased Francisco Calvo and María de Céspedes. Pedro, who was previously under the charge of Alférez Francisco de Espinosa (a master tailor who absconded), was placed with Capitán Diego de Vargas, also a master tailor, for three years to complete his apprenticeship.

Capitán Juan de Torres leased an 800-tree cacao plantation in Barbilla to Doña Baltasara de Escalante Panlagua, a widow. This plantation was contiguous to another owned by Doña Baltasara, which had been given as a dowry to Capitán Juan de Torres's spouse, Doña Ana de Escalante Paniagua. The lease was for three years, with an annual payment of four loads of first-quality and one load of second-quality cacao delivered in Cartago.

Doña Francisca de Inza, a widow, acknowledged a 500-peso, 5% annuity (censo) in favor of a capellanía founded by Don Gregorio de Alvarado, with Licenciado don Manuel de Guzmán as its chaplain. This annuity, previously charged to her deceased husband Capitán don Nicolás de Guevara, was secured on the Santa Gertrudis estate in Matina, which bordered properties of Silvestre de Meza, a minor of Don Gregorio de Alvarado, the river, and the mountain, and had been awarded to Doña Francisca.

Capitán Juan Manuel de Alvarado committed to Juan Hidalgo, acting as tutor for Doña Francisca Ballesteros (legitimate daughter of the deceased Capitán Juan de Ballesteros and Doña Juana de Torres), for 100 pesos at 5%. This obligation, previously held by Francisco Ramírez, was secured by houses on the bank of the La Lajuela river, enclosed within a fence with a sugar cane plot, a copper pot, and 100 cattle.
Capitán José de Saborío, acting under power of attorney, cancelled an unspecified obligation.

Sargento Francisco de Echavarría and his wife Feliciana Calvo acknowledged a 300-peso, 5% annuity (censo) in favor of a capellanía founded by the deceased Francisco Solano, with Licenciado don Manuel de Guzmán as its chaplain. This annuity was charged on a house in the common lands (ejidos) of Cartago that they had purchased after the death of Capitán Nicolás de Guevara, subject to this encumbrance.

people_involved: Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Capitán don Antonio de Soto y Barahona granted general power of attorney to his wife, Doña Petronila de Hoces Navarro.

Doña Francisca de Inza, a widow, leased a 1007-tree cacao plantation in the Matina valley to Antonio de Umaña. This plantation, inherited from her deceased husband Capitán Nicolas de Guevara, bordered properties of Doña Josefa Santiago de Aguilar, Silvestre de Meza, Doña Cayetana de Acosta Arévalo (by the river), and the mountain. The lease was for three years, with payments of 125 pesos in cacao for the first year and 200 pesos in cacao for each subsequent year.

people_involved: Licenciado don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro
Sargento Mayor Juan Francisco de Ibarra
Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Doña Luisa Calvo, a widow, sold her dwelling houses in Cartago to Licenciado don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro, a Presbyter. The property bordered houses of Sargento Mayor Juan Francisco de Ibarra, a lot of Doña Micaela de Arburola, the house of Capitán Diego de Vargas, and a street and house of Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona. The 950-peso price was to be recognized by the buyer as 400 pesos to a capellanía founded by Don Francisco de Enciso Hita, 450 pesos to a capellanía founded by Antonio de Machado, and 100 pesos paid to the seller. Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona, acting as the buyer's attorney, accepted the deed.

people_involved: Licenciado don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro
summary: Sargento Francisco de Echavarría and his wife Feliciana Calvo acknowledged a 100-peso, 5% annuity (señorío) in favor of a capellanía founded by Don Francisco de Enciso Hita, with Licenciado don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro as its patron and chaplain. This annuity was charged on houses in the common lands (ejidos) of Cartago that they had purchased, subject to this encumbrance, from the estate of the deceased Capitán don Nicolás de Guevara.

Alférez Gregorio Picado, legitimate son of the deceased Antonio Picado and Margarita Gómez, made his will. He was married to Gertrudis Peláez, and they had three children: José and Margarita (both deceased), and Alférez José Picado (who was alive and named as his heir). His father-in-law Andrés Peláez and his son Alférez José Picado were named as executors.

locations: Convento de San Francisco de San Bartolomé de Barba
people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Antonio Aurelio de Zamora
summary: Juan Fernández Martínez and Doña Cayetana de Acosta Arévalo committed to Capitán José de Saborío for a 200-peso, 5% annuity (capellanía) founded upon the death of Sarjento Mayor Antonio Aurelio de Zamora, located in the Convent of San Francisco de San Bartolomé de Barba. This annuity was charged on a cacao plantation in Matina, bordering properties of 'la madre de Dios', Doña Francisca de Inza, the mountain, and the river.

people_involved: Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Capitán Manuel García de Argueta leased a 1500-tree cacao estate named 'las sesenta calles' in the Matina valley to Capitán Luis Gurierrez. The estate bordered properties of Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona (East), Capitán Pedro de Moya (West), the mountain, and the river. The lease was for three years, with an annual payment of 350 pesos in cacao.

people_involved: Licenciado don Rafael Antonio García de Argueta
Castellano don Francisco Montojo de Chavarría
summary: Capitán Manuel García de Argueta granted general power of attorney, first to his son Licenciado don Rafael Antonio García de Argueta, second to Castellano don Francisco Montojo de Chavarría, and third to Capitán don Luis Muñoz, all residents of Santiago de Guatemala.

people_involved: Doña Dionisia Fallas de la Vega
Licenciado don Rafael Antonio García de Argueta
summary: Doña Dionisia Fallas de la Vega, wife of Capitán Manuel García de Argueta, granted power to Licenciado don Rafael Antonio García de Argueta.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco Marcelino Falla de la Cueva
Maestre de Campo don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina
summary: An unnamed plaintiff engaged Capitán don Francisco Marcelino Falla de la Cueva and possibly Capitán Manuel García de Argueta to represent them in a civil lawsuit against Maestre de Campo don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina and Doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco. The plaintiff accused Doña Antonia Pacheco of an 'ultraje' committed against them in the sacred space of the San Francisco church. The case was in appeal before the Real Audiencia.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Capitán don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad leased a cacao plantation of 500 trees in the Matina Valley to Isidro de Acosta for three years. The rent was set at 75 pesos of cacao for the first year and 100 pesos of cacao for each of the subsequent two years.

people_involved: Licenciado don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Ayudante José de las Alas and his wife Sebastiana Barbosa acknowledged a 100-peso, 5% annuity (censo) for a chaplaincy founded by Magdalena de la Portilla, whose patron and chaplain is Licenciado don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín. This censo was previously charged to Josefa López de la Flor on properties that José de las Alas acquired from her in exchange for other houses.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Doña Juana Josefa de Arburola, a widow, leased a 500-tree cacao plantation in the Matina Valley to Isidro de Acosta for three years. The rent was 50 pesos for the first year and 65 pesos for each of the following two years, payable in cacao. The property bordered land belonging to Capitán don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad and Doña Josefa de Hoces.

people_involved: Doña Josefa López de la Flor
Licenciado don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Doña Josefa López de la Flor and Ayudante José de las Alas exchanged properties within the city and its common lands. José de las Alas agreed to take on a 100-peso censo on the acquired property, favoring Magdalena de la Portilla's chaplaincy, and also paid Doña Josefa an additional 300 pesos.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Pedro de Alvarado
summary: Severino de Arrieta and his wife María Falcón obligated themselves for 103 pesos 2 reales in favor of María's minor sons, José and Nicolás Ramírez, from her first marriage to Ventura Ramírez. Sargento Mayor don Pedro de Alvarado acted as guarantor. A marginal note indicates that on August 17, 1727, José Ramírez received 51 pesos 1 real from Arrieta in Barba Valley and canceled his portion.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz
summary: Juan Delgado and his wife Ana Cascante de Rojas sold a country estate and dwelling in the Escasú Valley to Capitán Juan de Astúa for 550 pesos. The property, which included houses and a sugar mill, was inherited by Ana from her deceased master, Luis Cascante de Rojas.

people_involved: Doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar
summary: Doña Francisca de Inza, a widow, obligated herself for 337 pesos at 5% interest to Don Cayetano de Alvarado, a minor son of don Gregorio de Alvarado and doña Francisca de Acosta. This obligation was previously held by her deceased husband, Capitán don Nicolás de Guevara. The rent was to be paid to Doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar, the minor's grandmother. A marginal note from July 19, 1731, indicates that Don Cayetano de Alvarado later canceled this obligation in favor of Don Pedro Jiménez Mondragón and Doña Francisca de Inza.

people_involved: Doña Baltasara López de la Flor
summary: Margarita Barquero sold a 3-4 year old 'mulatilla blanca' named Ana Gertrudis to Doña Baltasara López de la Flor for 250 pesos of silver. Ana Gertrudis was the daughter of Baltasara, Margarita's slave, whom Margarita had inherited from her deceased parents, Alférez Francisco Hernández Barquero and Ana de Espinosa.

An incomplete dowry letter was recorded for José Román, son of deceased Francisco Román and Ana Godines, in favor of his wife Josefa de Aguilar, daughter of Sarjento Miguel de Aguilar and Juana Manuela Solano.

people_involved: Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos
Maestre de Campo don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina
President and Oidores of the Real Audiencia of Santiago de Guatemala
summary: On January 29, 1721, Capitán Manuel García de Argueta wounded Don Bernardo Vermes Mogrovejo, who died shortly after. A criminal case was brought by Doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco and her daughter Doña Josefa Marrufü against García de Argueta, with Capitán Juan Díaz de Herrera also implicated. Maestre de Campo don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina was prosecuted and condemned to fines and costs by the Governor and Captain General on January 16, 1721. Capitán don Francisco de Betancourt acted as guarantor for Serrano de Reina. Both Serrano de Reina and García de Argueta appealed. On January 21, 1721, Serrano de Reina's fines were suspended, requiring him only to pay costs and provide a guarantee for further determinations by the Real Audiencia in Santiago de Guatemala. A royal provision related to this case was dispatched on July 30, 1722, by the Real Audiencia.

people_involved: Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina
summary: In March 1735, Maestre de Campo Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina was cleared of illicit trade charges and absolved of costs by a review sentence. His attorney, Doña Antonia Pacheco, presented this sentence, leading the Governor to cancel the relevant part of the document.

people_involved: Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina
summary: On July 23, 1735, Maestre de Campo Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina granted general power of attorney. The primary recipient was Doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco, and the secondary recipient was Doña Josefa Gadea Marrufo, both identified as widows.

people_involved: Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina
summary: On July 24, 1735, Captain Antonio de Soto y Barahona provided bail for Captain Juan Díaz de Herrera. Díaz de Herrera was implicated in a criminal case, initiated by Doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco and Doña Josefa Marrufo, against Captain Manuel García de Argueta for the fatal wounding of Don Bernardo Vermes Mogrovejo, a death also linked to a fight involving Maestre de Campo Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina and Díaz de Herrera.

people_involved: Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina
summary: Following his implication in the criminal case, Maestre de Campo Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina was sentenced to fines and a one-year suspension from his roles as Judge of the Fields and Captain of Cavalry. An appeal by García de Argueta, however, led to the suspension of the fines and a reduction of Serrano de Reina's suspension to four months, contingent on a bond.

people_involved: Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina
summary: On July 30, 1735, Captain Luis Gutiérrez and his wife Inés Margarita de Quesada, with Captain Antonio Salmón Pacheco as guarantor, committed to pay Maestre de Campo Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina 366 pesos of cacao in Cartago. They mortgaged a cacao plantation in Matina as security for this obligation.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina
Sarjento Mayor Don Pedro José Sáenz
Doña Dionisia Fallas de la Vega
summary: On August 1, 1735, Captain Manuel García de Argueta, with guarantors Sarjento Mayor Don Francisco de la Madriz Linares and Captain Don Miguel de Alvarado, committed to fulfill a definitive sentence. This sentence, stemming from the death of Don Bernardo Vermes Mogrovejo, condemned García de Argueta to two years of exile, fines, and forfeiture of weapons, and he subsequently appealed to the Real Audiencia.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí
summary: On August 2, 1735, Sarjento Mayor Don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí, acting as Lieutenant General, posted a 1500-peso bail for Captain Manuel García de Argueta, who was imprisoned for the criminal case. García de Argueta was permitted to serve his imprisonment in Arleguí's house without guards.

people_involved: Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina
summary: On August 9, 1735, Doña Josefa Gadea Marrufo, widow and heir of Don Bernardo Vermes Mogrovejo, and Maestre de Campo Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina mutually guaranteed each other as preferred creditors to Don Bernardo Vermes's estate. Doña Josefa received the goods as heir, while Serrano de Reina received 39 pounds of purple thread as payment for a larger debt owed to him by the deceased.

people_involved: Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina
Doña Dionisia Fallas de la Vega
summary: On August 12, 1735, Maestre de Campo Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina and Doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco acknowledged a lawsuit initiated by Doña Dionisia Fallas de la Vega, wife of Captain Manuel García de Argueta, before the Governor. This suit concerned injurious words against Serrano de Reina and Pacheco, but as Doña Dionisia failed to prove her claims, her husband was sentenced to fines and condemnations, from which he appealed to the Real Audiencia.

people_involved: Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina
summary: On August 12, 1735, Maestre de Campo Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina sought to retain Miguel Largo, a 'negro bozal' whose ownership had been declared property of His Majesty. Serrano de Reina, who had purchased Miguel Largo from Captain Luis Gutiérrez, requested his accompaniment on an upcoming trip to Nicaragua and Guatemala, guaranteeing his value with a deed from Gutiérrez and his wife, and a bond from Captain Don Antonio Pacheco.

people_involved: Capitán Don Juan de Vida Martel
Doña Juana de Vera y Soto Mayor
summary: On August 13, 1735, Captain Don Miguel de Alvarado sold a 2000-tree cacao plantation in the Matina valley to his brother, Don Gil de Alvarado, for 850 pesos. The property, previously acquired from María Calderón, widow of Martín de Civitola, carried obligations to three chaplaincies founded by Doña Juana de Vera y Soto Mayor, Doña Inés Pereira, and Alonso Gómez Macotela.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Don Pedro José Sáenz
Capitán Don Gil de Alvarado y Girón
summary: A marginal note by Sarjento Mayor Don Pedro José Sáenz, dated July 9, 1735, certifies that in his protocol from the previous year (1734), Captain Don Gil de Alvarado y Girón transferred the same cacao plantation, with its 850 pesos of encumbrances, to Licenciado Don Juan José Camacho.

people_involved: Doña Dionisia Fallas de la Vega
Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina
summary: On August 13, 1735, Captain Manuel García de Argueta initiated a criminal case against Doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco for public insults and threats, and against her and Maestre de Campo Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina for accusing him of treason. On June 29, 1735, the Governor and Captain General sentenced García de Argueta to pay fines to the Royal Chamber, funds for soldiers in Matina, money for public building repairs, and various legal costs.
Ayudante José Barquero appealed a sentence, which was granted with a 90-day term within the province, obligating him to abide by the definitive sentence.

Maestre de Campo Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina obligated himself for 1033 pesos 4 reales, as ordered by the Gobernador y Capitán General. This sum was from deposits made to him as Treasurer of the Royal Treasury, derived from goods embargoed from former Justicia Mayor and Capitán General Pedro Ruiz de Bustamante and fines from various neighbors. Serrano de Reina had previously represented that he took most of these goods as a loan for the Royal Treasury's urgencies and reported this to the Superior Government, from which he was to bring a clarifying dispatch.
José de Mier Cevallos cancelled an obligation, in conformity with a royal provision from the Audiencia de Santiago de Guatemala dated May 30, 1722.

Captain Sebastián de Garita, a native of Madrid, made his testament. He was married to Margarita de Aguiar and had no children. His wife was named his sole heiress and, along with Sarjento Mayor Pedro José Sáenz de Quintanilla and Captain Francisco Flores, an executor. The will also mentions his deceased parents, Sebastián de Garita and Catalina López Machuela del Amo, his sister-in-law Bernarda de Aguiar, and his deceased compadre Felipe Bermúdez, who was married to Juana de Aguiar, and their children Miguel, José Antonio, and José Felipe.
Sarjento Mayor José de Morales provided jail bail for Alférez Domingo de Quesada.

people_involved: José Nicolás de Sarmiento y Soto Mayor
summary: Sarjento Mayor Pedro de Alvarado y Girón and José Nicolás de Sarmiento y Soto Mayor provided jail bail for Ayudante Manuel Vanegas.

Captain Antonio Salmón Pacheco and Dionisio Pacheco, being prosecuted before the Gobernador y Capitán General for introducing iron from the Matina valley, obligated themselves for the outcome of their case. Gil de Alvarado acted as their guarantor.

Ayudante Miguel de Céspedes, Alférez José Picado, and Alférez Manuel Antonio de Alvarado provided jail bail for Alférez Matías de Avtrndañu, Francisco Calderón, and Nicolás González, who were imprisoned for introducing iron through Matina.
Sarjento Mayor José de Morales provided jail bail for Cristóbal Quesada.
Captain Felipe de Mesa provided jail bail for Alférez José Ramos and Sarjento José Meneses, who were imprisoned for introducing iron through Matina.
Captain Francisco Manzano provided jail bail for Sarjento Jerónimo Gutiérrez, who was imprisoned for the same reason as the previous case (introduction of iron through Matina).
Sarjento Mayor Pedro de Alvarado y Girón provided jail bail for Antonio Muñoz, who was imprisoned for introducing iron through Matina.
José Lebrón provided jail bail for Teniente Cayetano Muñoz, who was imprisoned for the same reason as the previous case (introduction of iron through Matina).
Captain Juan Sancho de Castañeda provided jail bail for Captain Manuel de Arburola y Ribarén, who was imprisoned for introducing iron through Matina.
Captain Dionisio Salmón Pacheco provided jail bail for Marcelo de Villavicencio, who was imprisoned for introducing iron through Matina.

people_involved: Juan Gómez de Ocón y Trillo
summary: Juan Gómez de Ocón y Trillo, Juan de Matamoros, Juana Lizondo, Gertrudis Falcón, and Margarita de Mora, as heirs and possessors of the assets of the deceased Francisca de Benavente, obligated themselves for various inheritances and debts. These assets included a cacao plantation of 1800 trees in Barbilla, currently leased by Alférez Domingo de Quesada. Debts included 50 pesos to Francisca (sister of Francisca de Benavente), cacao to María de Ortega and heirs of Juana Martel, 7 pesos to heirs of Nicolás Camacho, cacao to José de Acuña for house work in El Guayabo, two cows to Luisa Peraza for servitude, 50 pesos to the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora de Ujarraz, 40 pesos and 3 cows to the children of Pablo Lizondo, and 177 pesos 7 reales each to Juan Matías and Josefa Lizondo.

people_involved: Juan Gómez de Ocón y Trillo
Gracia Gómez de Ocón y Lizondo
José Francisco Gómez de Ocón y Lizondo
Cayetano Gómez de Ocón y Lizondo
summary: Captain Juan Gómez de Ocón y Trillo and the other heirs of Francisca de Benavente obligated themselves for 355 pesos and 6 reales. This sum included 177 pesos 7 reales for Francisco Antonio, Manuel, Nicolás, and María, children of the deceased Francisco Lizondo, and another 177 pesos 7 reales for Gracia, José Francisco, and Cayetano, children of Juan Gómez de Ocón y Trillo and his deceased wife Eugenia Lizondo, all as part of their inheritance from Francisca de Benavente.

people_involved: Juan Gómez de Ocón y Trillo
Licenciado don Juan Miguel de Bonilla
summary: Captain Juan Gómez de Ocón y Trillo, as executor of the deceased Francisca de Benavente, established the Chaplaincy of masses she had ordered. The principal of 336 pesos 1.5 reales was charged to the cacao plantation in Barbilla, which was her sole asset and under the care of her possessors. Licenciado don Juan Miguel de Bonilla, currently in Guatemala, was named the Patron and Chaplain until a descendant of Francisca de Benavente could be ordained.
Doña Luisa Calvo, a widow, posted bail for Alejandro Leitona, who was imprisoned for smuggling iron through Matina.

Sergeant Francisco Hernández Barquero posted bail for Petronila de Segura, a widow, who was involved in a criminal case with her son, José de Araya. José de Araya was accused of assaulting Ensign Juan de Chaves.
Captain Luis Morera posted bail for Pedro Sánchez, a resident of the Barba valley, who was imprisoned for smuggling iron through Matina.
Lieutenant Field Judge Salvador Palomino posted bail for Lorenzo de Mena, who was imprisoned for smuggling iron through Matina.
Captain Dionisio Salmón Pacheco posted bail for José Vázquez, who was imprisoned for smuggling iron through Matina.
Captain Juan Marín Laguna posted bail for Ensign Nicolás de Quirós, who was imprisoned for smuggling iron through Matina.
Ensign Antonio de Ángulo posted bail for Sergeant Aparicio Carrillo, who was imprisoned for smuggling iron through Matina.

Magdalena de Piedra pledged 100 pesos at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by Doña Tomasina de Lerma. This obligation is secured by a 400-tree cacao plantation on the Matina riverbanks, currently leased by Ensign Lucas Blasco, and belongs to Magdalena as the granddaughter of the late residents Juan de Piedra and María de Madrigal.
Captain Manuel García de Argueta posted bail for his slave, Antonio, who is identified as a "negro."

Sergeant Major Pedro José Sáenz pledged 249 pesos and one and a half reales in silver to José Miguel Martínez, representing his maternal inheritance. Sáenz mortgaged a cattle ranch in the Aserrí valley as security.

Lieutenant General Captain José de Mier Cevallos certified that José Miguel Martínez, before becoming a friar in the Order of San Francisco, named Sergeant Major Pedro José Sáenz as his heir for the amount specified in the previous document and other sums, in case Martínez professed. Since Martínez had already professed years ago, the obligation was cancelled.

Sergeant Major Juan Francisco de Ibarra and his wife, Doña Catalina González del Camino, pledged their 8000-tree haciendas in Matina as collateral. This was to allow Ibarra to assume his newly appointed position as Lieutenant Accountant.

A dowry letter was issued by Bartolomé Trujillo, a native of Cádiz and son of Captain Gonzalo Trujillo and María Galindo Delgado, in favor of his future wife, Angela Sebastiana Sáenz Vázquez. Angela is the legitimate daughter of the late Captain Juan Sáenz Vázquez and Ana Escalante Paniagua. The dowry amounted to 1802 pesos and 4 reales, with a separate arras of 1000 pesos.

locations: Convento de San Bartolomé de Barba
summary: On January 8, 1722, Juan Fernández Martínez and his wife, Doña Cayetana de Acosta Arévalo, pledged 200 pesos at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by Sergeant Major Antonio Aurelio de Zamora at the Convent of San Bartolomé de Barba.

Juan Fernández Martínez and Cayetana de Acosta Arévalo stated they had made a similar obligation on September 5, 1721, before Sergeant Major Manuel Antonio de Arleguí, but that document was not processed. The 200 pesos for the chaplaincy were delivered by Diego de la Haya Fernández, who had purchased adobe and tile houses for 600 pesos on November 1, 1720, which suffered a 400-peso depreciation. Captain José de Saborido is the patron of the Chaplaincy, with Licenciados Manuel de Guzmán and Juan José Camacho serving as chaplains.

On November 2, 1721, Joseph de Saborido and Francisco Montero de Espinosa wrote to Sergeant Major Manuel Antonio de Arleguí, requesting the cancellation of a joint obligation made by Juan Fernández (and his wife) to the Barba Convent. This was because their matter with Sergeant Major José de Morales had been resolved, making the joint document unnecessary, and Saborido's individual obligation to the convent remained valid.

On January 13, 1722, Captain Domingo de Inza posted bail for Sergeant Francisco de Echavarría. Echavarría was facing charges before the Governor and Captain General for smuggling iron through the Matina valley.
On January 15, 1722, Sergeant Major Juan Francisco de Ibarra executed the will of Bachelor Gregorio de Moya, acting under a power of attorney.

Juan Francisco de Ibarra testified that in the previous year (1721), he met Bachelor Gregorio de Moya in Santiago de Guatemala. Moya decided to travel with Ibarra, and by the end of 1721, they reached Pastepeque, where Moya fell ill and died. This was confirmed by certificates from Fray José Francisco de Chaves, Fray José de Osorio, and Bachelor Felipe Nery Cornejo. Moya, son of the late Esteban de Moya and Rafaela de Alvarado, established a chaplaincy of 1000 pesos and named Ibarra as his executor, with Francisca, Josefa Francisca, Miguel, María Catalina, and Manuela as universal heirs.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz de Quintanilla
summary: Capitán don Bernardo Marín and Doña María Marín Laguna acknowledge debts (censos) totaling 925 pesos to a Capellanía (represented by Licenciado Juan José Camacho), Cofradía de las Animas, and Cofradía del Rosario. This obligation stems from their purchase of a 2000-cacao-tree hacienda in Matina and other properties in Cartago from the executors of Capitán don Sebastián de Garita. The remaining value of the hacienda is to be recognized to Doña Margarita de Aguiar, widow of Don Sebastián de Garita.

people_involved: don Diego de la Haya Fernández
summary: Capitán don Pedro de Moya acts as a guarantor for Capitán don Alvaro de Guevara in a legal case. The case concerns the introduction of iron through the Matina valley and is heard before the Gobernador y Capitán General, don Diego de la Haya Fernández.

Alférez Luis Peláez executes his will. He is identified as the legitimate son of Francisco Peláez and the late Ana de Flores, married to María de los Santos, and father to Antonia, Pedro, Gregoria, Josefa, and Gabriel. His brother Gregorio Peláez and his wife María de los Santos are named as his executors.
Doña María de Sibaja, a widow, leases a cacao plantation located in Matina to José Meneses. The lease agreement is for a period of three years, with a total price of 225 pesos to be paid in cacao.

people_involved: Sárjente Mayor don José de Baeza
summary: Sárjente Mayor don José de Baeza and Doña María Magdalena Maroto Ruiz obligate themselves for 100 pesos to Doña Manuela de Oviedo, whose guardian is Capitán Nicolás Arias. This obligation was later cancelled by Capitán Nicolás Arias on March 6, 1723.

Juan Fernández Martínez and Doña Cayetana de Acosta Arévalo lease a cacao plantation in Matina to Francisco Manuel García. The three-year lease is for 275 pesos, with payments structured over the years, and the property borders the hacienda 'La Madre de Dios', Francisca de Inza's property, a mountain, and a river.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz de Quintanilla
Sarjento Mayor don Pedro de Alvarado y Girón
summary: Doña Margarita de Aguiar, along with Sarjento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz de Quintanilla and Capitán Francisco de Flores (as executors of the late Capitán don Sebastián de Garita), sells a 2000-tree cacao plantation in Matina to Sarjento Mayor don Pedro de Alvarado y Girón for 825 pesos. The payment includes amounts designated for Licenciado Juan José Camacho and the Cofradía de las Animas, with the remainder to the grantors. The sale was later cancelled on December 11, 1728, by Capitanes Francisco de Flores and Cayetano Muñoz, and the Cofradía's mayordomo.

Capitán Antonio Francisco de Espínola, a resident, is preparing to depart for Panamá with 238 mules. He obligates himself for the 476 pesos in export duties and commits to sending the mules on the first available ship from Perico, Panamá, to La Caldera.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Licenciado don Manuel González Coronel obligates himself to Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra for 400 pesos. This sum is for ornaments Ibarra purchased as Mayordomo for the Parish Church. Ibarra later cancelled this obligation on November 12, 1723.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don José de Hoyo y Echavarría
don Diego de la Haya Fernández
summary: Sarjento Mayor don José de Hoyo y Echavarría, a resident of Panamá, obligates himself to Francisco Camejo, a native of Laguna in the Canary Islands residing in Cartago, for 416 pesos. The payment is due 20 days after Hoyo y Echavarría's arrival in Panamá. A marginal note from September 5, 1722, confirms the delivery of the deed and receipt by don Diego de la Haya Fernández, acting as attorney for Hoyo y Echavarría.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra, Lieutenant Accountant of the Royal Treasury, grants general power of attorney to don Pedro de Llanos. This power allows Llanos to collect debts owed to the Royal Treasury, administer royal assets, and manage Ibarra's personal affairs during his absence in Matina.

people_involved: Licenciado don Juan Antonio de Moya
summary: Doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco, a widow, leases a 1200-tree cacao plantation in Matina to Pedro Ortiz for three years. The lease is for 600 pesos, payable in cacao annually, and the property borders haciendas belonging to Licenciado don Juan Antonio de Moya and Doña Antonia de Acosta, as well as a river and a mountain.
Capitán Manuel García de Argueta and Doña Nicolasa Guerrero exchange slaves. Diego, a 'negro bozal' of Cabo Verde origin belonging to García de Argueta, is exchanged for another 'negro' named Felipe.

people_involved: Josefa Micaela de la Vega Cabral
Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
