summary: Capitán don Francisco de Betancourt and Doña María Josefa Cabral grant freedom to their 24-year-old white slave, Josefa Micaela de la Vega Cabral, who is married to Alférez Diego de la Cruz, for 300 pesos received from him. Josefa Micaela was inherited by Doña María Josefa Cabral from her late parents, Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral and Doña Ambrosia González Camino. They also free Victoria, a 10-month-old mulatto girl and daughter of Alférez Diego de la Cruz and Josefa Micaela, for 150 pesos received from him.

people_involved: Josefa Micaela de la Vega Cabral
don Diego de la Haya Fernández
summary: Alférez Diego de la Cruz and his wife Josefa Micaela de la Vega Cabral obligate themselves to don Diego de la Haya Fernández, the Gobernador y Capitán General. This obligation is for 300 pesos that Fernández lent them to secure Josefa Micaela's freedom.

An unnamed 'otorgante' was obligated to pay a debt. The Gobernador agreed to credit the 'otorgante' 152 pesos for a trip to Guatemala as a courier for confiscated enslaved people, reducing the remaining debt to 148 pesos.
Don Diego cancelled an obligation on July 2, 1726, as noted in the margin of the protocol.

Licenciado don Juan Antonio de Moya sold an enslaved 'negro bozal' of Congo origin named Juan Miguel for 300 pesos. The buyer was Captain don Pedro de Moya, acting as the representative for Captain don Juan de Luque Mariscal, a resident of Granada and Justicia Mayor of Nicoya.

people_involved: don José de Hoyo y Echavarría
summary: Doña Antonia de Hoces Navarro, a widow, granted power of attorney to Sarjento Mayor don José de Hoyo y Echavarría, who was residing in Cartago and preparing for a trip to Panama. The purpose was to collect debts, specifically 350 pesos owed by General don Juan de Sosaya, as declared in the will of Doña Antonia's late husband, Sarjento Mayor Juan de Zavaleta.

people_involved: don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares granted power of attorney to Sarjento Mayor don José de Hoyo Echavarría, who was departing for Panama, and secondarily to Castno. don Félix Gabriel de Moya, a resident of San Felipe de Puerto Belo. The purpose was to collect debts owed to Madriz Linares in those locations.

Captain don Francisco Garrido Berlanga, a widower, issued a dowry receipt in Panama for his future wife, doña Águeda Pérez de Muro, a widow. The dowry included 4393 pesos in silver, 14,417 pesos in cacao, various properties, goods, and several enslaved individuals. Doña Águeda declared her children with her late husband, don José de Casasola y Córdoba, were doña Josefa, José Francisco, and Juan Manuel.

people_involved: don José de Hoyo y Echevarría
don Diego de la Haya Fernández
summary: Sarjento Mayor don José de Hoyo y Echevarría, who was departing for Panama, granted general power of attorney to don Diego de la Haya Fernández.

Captain don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco acted as surety for 171 pesos in cacao, representing the assets left by the deceased Antonio Muñoz. This allowed Juan José Muñoz, Antonio's brother, to receive the inheritance.

Doña Gertrudis Guerrero, a widow, pledged two enslaved mulatas, Gertrudis and Gregoria, to Doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco, a widow, for two years. Doña Antonia lent Doña Gertrudis 250 pesos to pay for these enslaved women, who had been auctioned by the Gobernador y Capitán General due to illicit trade.
Doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco cancelled the pledge on September 5, 1722.

Doña Luisa Calvo, a widow, obligated herself to the Royal Treasury for 112 pesos in cacao for an enslaved man named Miguel, who was auctioned to her on the 12th of the current month. The transaction took place at her residence in the city's ejidos.

Alférez Francisco Solano, 'the elder,' as principal, and his son, Francisco Solano, as guarantor, obligated themselves to the Royal Treasury for 302 pesos 4 reales in cacao for a 'zambito' named Mateo, who was auctioned on the 15th of the current month.

On September 10, 1722, Alférez Francisco Solano returned the enslaved 'zambito' Mateo to the Gobernador because he could not pay the price. Teniente General don José de Mier Ceballos certified this event.

Doña Baltasara de Escalante Paniagua, a widow, obligated herself to the Royal Treasury for 310 pesos in cacao for an enslaved woman named Lorenza and her son, who were auctioned to her on the 11th of the current month.
Sarjento Mayor don Manuel José de Alvarado, Teniente de Oficiales reales, cancelled the obligation on September 15, 1724.

Licenciado don Manuel González Coronel, a Presbyter, as principal, and Doña Baltasara de Escalante Paniagua, a widow, as guarantor, obligated themselves to the Royal Treasury for 915 pesos. This sum covered the auction price of five enslaved individuals: Juan Manuel, Petronila, Bárbara, Juana María, and Isabel. A cacao hacienda in Barbilla was mortgaged as security.
Captain don Tomás López del Corral, Teniente de Oficiales de la Real Hacienda, cancelled the obligation on September 20, 1730.

Captain Juan de Astúa and his wife, Gertrudis Calderón, obligated themselves to the Royal Treasury for 658 pesos in cacao for an enslaved 'zambito' named José and an enslaved 'negrito' named Antonio, who were auctioned to Astúa.
Sarjento Mayor don Manuel de Alvarado, Teniente de Oficiales reales, cancelled the obligation on August 3, 1725.

Doña Luisa Calvo, a widow, acted as surety for Captain Luis Gutiérrez before the Royal Treasury for 150 pesos. This amount was for an enslaved 'negra' of Mina origin named Manuela, who was auctioned to Sarjento Mayor don José de Baeza, Doña Luisa's son-in-law, on behalf of the absent Gutiérrez in Malina.

people_involved: Don Diego de la Haya Fernández
summary: Don Diego de la Haya Fernández purchased some houses for 600 pesos, following ecclesiastical court proceedings. These houses were later involved in an obligation related to chaplaincies.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Juan de Vida Martel
Doña Juana de Ortega y Chaves
Capitán Don Pedro de Alvarado y Girón
Licenciado Don Manuel de Escalante Paniagua
summary: Doña Catalina de Vida Martel granted her will, in which she named her children as heirs (except Doña Juana), freed her slave Bartola, and ordered the establishment of a chaplaincy. Her executors included her son Licenciado Don Hermenegildo de Alvarado, Licenciado Don Manuel de Escalante Paniagua, and her son-in-law Capitán Juan Sancho de Castañeda.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Manuel de Alvarado
summary: Sargento Mayor Don Manuel de Alvarado, Lieutenant of Officials, cancelled an obligation related to tithes. This cancellation was based on a letter from Capitán Don Ambrosio de Betancourt, Treasurer of the Royal Treasury in Granada, confirming that Capitán Juan Sancho de Castañeda had paid his debt.

people_involved: Gobernador Don Diego de la Haya Fernández
summary: Gobernador Don Diego de la Haya Fernández ordered an inventory of cacao trees and slaves on haciendas in Matina and Barbilla belonging to Doña Águeda Pérez de Muro. Capitán de Caballos Bernardo Pacheco, Lieutenant Governor, appointed Alférez Francisco Gutiérrez and Sargento Jerónimo Gutiérrez as accountants, later replacing Jerónimo Gutiérrez with Sargento José Meneses due to illness. The inventory included haciendas formerly owned by Capitán Francisco Bonilla.

people_involved: Capitán Don Juan Manuel de Alvarado
summary: Capitán Juan Sancho de Castañeda and his wife, Doña Juana de Alvarado, along with Capitanes Don José and Don Juan Manuel de Alvarado as guarantors, obligated themselves to the Royal Treasury for 2205 pesos and 6 reales. This sum was the price for the tithes of Espiritusanto de Esparza and Cartago, auctioned on April 15th for a period of two years.

people_involved: Capitán Manuel Antonio de Arburola y Ribarén
José Miguel de Arburola y Ribarén
Licenciado Don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro
summary: Doña Josefa de Hoces Navarro, acting as the executrix for her deceased husband Capitán Lorenzo de Arburola, founded a chaplaincy for 10 recited masses with a principal of 400 pesos. Her son, Capitán Manuel Antonio de Arburola y Ribarén, was named patron, and her other son, José Miguel de Arburola y Ribarén, was named chaplain, with Licenciado Don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro serving as interim chaplain.

people_involved: Capitán Manuel Antonio de Arburola y Ribarén
Licenciado Don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro
summary: Capitán Manuel Antonio de Arburola y Ribarén and his wife, Doña Lorenza Fajardo, obligated themselves for 400 pesos at 5% interest to the chaplaincy founded by Capitán Lorenzo de Arburola and established yesterday by Doña Josefa de Hoces Navarro. They imposed this sum on a cacao hacienda in Matina, with Manuel Antonio as patron and Licenciado Don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro as interim chaplain.

people_involved: Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona and his wife, Doña Petronila de Hoces Navarro, obligated themselves to the Royal Treasury for 235 pesos of cacao. This was for the purchase of a Black woman named Juana Manuela and her son Ventura, who were auctioned to Antonio de Soto y Barahona on April 13th.

people_involved: Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
Don Diego de la Haya Fernández
summary: Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona and his wife, Doña Petronila de Hoces Navarro, obligated themselves for 400 pesos at 5% interest to Licenciado Don Manuel de Guzmán and Licenciado Don Juan José Camacho. This money was received from Don Diego de la Haya Fernández, who had purchased houses on November 1, 1720, which were subject to chaplaincies for which the Licenciados were patrons and chaplains. The couple mortgaged houses in Cartago.

people_involved: José Miguel de Arburola y Ribarén
summary: Capitán Don José de Alvarado and his wife, Doña Úrsula López Conejo, obligated themselves to Doña Josefa de Hoces Navarro for 100 pesos. This sum was a donation from Ana Cardoso to José Miguel de Arburola y Ribarén, which was previously the responsibility of Capitán Don Francisco Betancourt and his wife.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don José de Hoyo y Echevarría
summary: Sargento Mayor Don José de Hoyo y Echevarría, departing for Panama, declared that the Black slave Francisco, purchased by him for 290 pesos on April 14th, actually belonged to Capitán Luis Gutiérrez. Doña Luisa Calvo then guaranteed the stated amount to the Royal Treasury on behalf of Capitán Luis Gutiérrez, who was absent in Matina.
Proceedings were initiated for the opening of the will of Doña Catalina de Vida Martel, which was presented by Capitán Juan Sancho de Castañeda.

people_involved: Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
Sargento Mayor Don José de Hoyo y Echevarría
summary: Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona granted power to Sargento Mayor Don José de Hoyo y Echevarría, who was departing for Panama, to apprehend a 20-year-old Mina slave named Juan José. Antonio de Soto y Barahona had purchased this slave from Doña María de Quirós.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Manuel de Alvarado
summary: The obligation made by Capitán Juan Sancho de Castañeda and others for the tithes was cancelled on August 9, 1725, by Sargento Mayor Don Manuel de Alvarado, Lieutenant of Royal Officials.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Manuel José de Alvarado
Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: The obligation made by Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona and Doña Petronila de Hoces Navarro for the purchase of slaves was cancelled on November 24, 1728, by Sargento Mayor Don Manuel José de Alvarado, Lieutenant Accountant of the Royal Treasury.

people_involved: Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: An obligation made by Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona and Doña Petronila de Hoces Navarro was cancelled on December 18, 1728. This cancellation was performed by Licenciado Don Juan José Camacho, acting as patron and chaplain of the chaplaincy founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela.

Capitán José de Saborido and Alférez Juan José de Zamora obligated themselves to the Royal Treasury for 400 pesos. This sum was the cost of purchasing a Black woman named Manuela and her mulatto daughter, María, at an auction held on April 15th.
An obligation made by Capitán José de Saborido and Alférez Juan José de Zamora to the Royal Treasury was cancelled on December 14, 1737.

people_involved: Luis Fernando de Liendo y Goicoechea
summary: On December 20, 1740, Doña Úrsula López Conejo, now a widow, formally recognized an obligation she shared with her deceased husband, Capitán Don José de Alvarado. This recognition was attested by Luis Fernando de Liendo y Goicoechea.

people_involved: Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
summary: An inventory and initial valuation of the deceased Captain don José Pérez de Muro's haciendas and enslaved people (José, Cristóbal, Mateo, Domingo, Lorenzo) was conducted. On May 2nd, the Governor transferred the inventory to doña Águeda Pérez de Muro, whose husband, Captain don Francisco Garrido, contested the valuation. This led to the appointment of new appraisers, Captain don Jerónimo Manuel Ramos and Captain don José Felipe Bermúdez, with Nicolás Cásasela providing additional information.

Sargento Francisco de Chavarría and his wife Feliciana Calvo sold a cacao plantation of 807 trees in the Reventazón area, near the royal road to Matina valley, to Sargento Antonio de Umaña for 300 pesos of cacao. The property bordered land that formerly belonged to the deceased Jerónimo Guzmán.

María Calderón and Bernarda Vázquez leased cacao plantations to Sargento Gregorio de Umaña for three years, at 225 pesos of cacao per year. María leased 1000 trees inherited from her deceased father, Alférez José Calderón, and Bernarda leased an adjacent 500 trees also from the Alférez.
Bernarda Vázquez and Sargento Gregorio de Umaña declared that the lease agreement previously made between them was not valid for their part.
María Calderón and Sargento Gregorio de Umaña cancelled their part of the lease agreement because Gregorio de Umaña was unable to fulfill his obligations.

people_involved: Capitán don Diego de Barros y Carbajal
Maestre de Campo don Lorenzo de Granda
summary: Captain don Diego de Barros y Carbajal and his wife doña Josefa Pérez de Muro recognized a censo (annuity) of 720 pesos at 5% in favor of a chaplaincy founded by Comisario Baltasar de Grado, with Licenciado don Manuel de Guzmán as chaplain. This censo was charged on houses in the city that were auctioned to them in 1714 for 1245 pesos, and previously belonged to the deceased Maestre de Campo don Lorenzo de Granda.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Antonio Masís, a black man, was auctioned on April 26th due to illicit introduction, and Captain Juan Sancho de Castañeda intended to enslave him perpetually. To regain his freedom, Antonio Masís sought assistance from Sargento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra, who paid his auction price of 300 pesos. In return, Masís committed to working on Ibarra's haciendas in Matina during harvest seasons for four years, thereby restoring the freedom granted by his first master, Alférez Juan Masís.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Sargento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra cancelled Antonio Masís's obligation after receiving the 300 pesos from Masís, thereby fully securing Masís's freedom.

Doña Antonia Acosta Arévalo, a widow, became obligated to the Royal Treasury for 290 pesos of cacao. This amount represented the value of the auction of an enslaved black woman named Magdalena and her disabled daughter, Benita, to her.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
Teniente don Pedro de Alvarado Acosta
summary: Captain don Tomás López del Corral, Lieutenant of Royal Officials, cancelled the remaining 112 pesos of Doña Antonia Acosta Arévalo's debt. This cancellation occurred after Teniente don Pedro de Alvarado Acosta presented two previous receipts towards the debt.

Captain José Felipe Bermúdez and his wife doña Teresa de Sandoval became obligated to the Royal Treasury for 260 pesos of cacao. This sum was the value of the auction of an enslaved black woman named Antonia to them.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
summary: Captain don Tomás López del Corral, Lieutenant of Royal Officials, cancelled the debt owed by Captain José Felipe Bermúdez and doña Teresa de Sandoval to the Royal Treasury.
María Calderón, a widow, became obligated to the Royal Treasury for 251 pesos of cacao. This amount represented the value of the auction of an enslaved black man named Antonio to her.
María Calvo, a widow, became obligated to the Royal Treasury for 312 pesos and 4 reales in cacao. This sum was the value of the auction of an enslaved black woman named María to her.

María Calvo incurred an additional obligation for 220 pesos of cacao for the auction of a mulatto girl named María Josefa. This obligation was recorded separately as it had been omitted from the previous record.

people_involved: Alférez José Nicolás de la Haya
summary: Don Manuel de Alvarado, Teniente de Oficiales reales, received 532 pesos from Alférez José Nicolás de la Haya, who was acting as the agent for María Calderón, and subsequently cancelled the debt.
Doña Catalina de Arburola, a widow, obligated herself to the Royal Treasury for 225 pesos of cacao, which was the value from the auction of an enslaved black woman named Lorenza.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Manuel de Alvarado
summary: Sargento Mayor don Manuel de Alvarado, Teniente de Oficiales reales, cancelled the obligation made by Doña Catalina de Arburola to the Royal Treasury.
Doña Petronila Valerín obligated herself to the Royal Treasury for 520 pesos, representing the value from the auction of an enslaved black girl named Catalina and an enslaved black man named Ventura.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
summary: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral, Teniente de oficiales reales, cancelled the obligation made by Doña Petronila Valerín to the Royal Treasury.

Doña Josefa de Hoces Navarro, a widow, obligated herself to the Royal Treasury for 370 pesos of cacao, which was the value from the auction of an enslaved black woman named Magdalena and another enslaved black girl named María.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Manuel José de Alvarado
summary: Sargento Mayor don Manuel José de Alvarado, Teniente de Oficiales reales, cancelled the obligation made by Doña Josefa de Hoces Navarro to the Royal Treasury.

Capitán Diego de Aguilar obligated himself to the Royal Treasury for 465 pesos in cacao, for the auction of an enslaved man and woman who were his property and had been declared decomisos. He mortgaged a chácara he owned in the countryside as collateral.
Capitán Manuel García de Argueta obligated himself to the Royal Treasury for 290 pesos in cacao, which was the value from the auction of an enslaved black woman named Angola, María, held on April 11.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Sargento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra, Teniente de Contador de Real Hacienda, cancelled the obligation made by Capitán Manuel García de Argueta to the Royal Treasury.
Licenciado don Manuel González Coronel, a Presbítero, sold an enslaved Creole black man named Pablo José, 14 years old, to Licenciado don Hermenegildo de Alvarado, also a Presbítero, for 400 pesos.

Sargento Gregorio de Umaña bailed out his brother, Sargento Antonio de Umaña, who was imprisoned for a 150-peso cacao debt owed to Capitán don Jerónimo Manuel Ramos. Of this debt, Ramos had already received 36 pesos from José Campos, a free pardo, in the Matina valley, and Gregorio pledged four tame mules and four horses as collateral.

Licenciado don Hermenegildo de Alvarado, a Presbítero, sold an enslaved Creole black girl named Antonia, 12 years old, to Capitán Juan Sancho de Castañeda for 300 pesos. Antonia was inherited by Hermenegildo from his deceased mother, Doña Catalina de Vida Martel.

people_involved: Licenciado don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: Capitán Pedro Enríquez de Castro, a resident, sold a 44-year-old mulatto woman named Manuela to Licenciado don Francisco de la Madriz Linares, a Presbítero, for 100 pesos. Manuela had been previously purchased by Castro from Manuel González, a resident of the Barba valley.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón
Capitán don Gil de Alvarado y Jirón
Capitán don José de Alvarado y Jirón
Capitán don Miguel de Alvarado y Jirón
don Diego de la Haya Fernández
Sargento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: Sargento Mayor don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón and Capitanes don Gil, don José, and don Miguel de Alvarado y Jirón sold adobe houses with a tiled roof and a walled plot to don Diego de la Haya Fernández, the Governor and Captain General, for 1000 pesos of Matina cacao. The property was bordered by houses formerly belonging to Sargento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral (now his heirs), the house of arms, the living quarters of don Gil, and houses of Doña Antonia de Alvarado.

people_involved: Capitán don Miguel de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Capitán don Miguel de Alvarado y Jirón received the remaining payment of 115 pesos, 1 real, and 1 cuartillo for the house sale.

people_involved: Capitán don José de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Capitán don José de Alvarado y Jirón received 275 pesos and 6 reales and cancelled his part of the house sale transaction.

Beneficiado don Hermegildo de Alvarado obligated himself to pay 150 pesos to the Royal Treasury on behalf of Capitán Pedro Castellanos, owner and master of the ship "El Santo Cristo," because Castellanos owed him an equal sum and lacked the money.
Doña Águeda Pérez de Muro granted general power of attorney to her husband, Capitán don Francisco Garrido.

people_involved: Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Marín Cubero
Depositario General don Cristóbal Marín Cubero
summary: Capitán Juan de Astúa founded a chaplaincy for his soul, that of his wife Gertrudis Calderón, and his parents, with a principal of 1000 pesos for 11 annual masses and remaining funds for wax and wine. The chaplaincy was imposed on his straw-roofed houses, sugar mill, and large fenced plots with various types of sugarcane in the Aserrí valley, which he had purchased from Juan Delgado.

people_involved: don Diego de la Haya Fernández
Sargento Mayor don Antonio de Utrera y Medina
Sargento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Don Diego de la Haya Fernández, the Governor, sold houses in the city to Sargento Mayor don Antonio de Utrera y Medina for 800 pesos. These houses, previously auctioned in 1719 for 600 pesos of cacao, had been dismantled by de la Haya to build the Sala de Armas in the public plaza, leaving only the walls and plot which he then rebuilt. The original 600 pesos were charged to cacao haciendas owned by Juan Fernández Martínez and Doña Cayetana de Acosta in Matina (200 pesos) and the dwelling houses of Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona (400 pesos).

Licenciado don Hermenegildo de Alvarado, a Presbítero, obligated himself to the chaplaincy founded by the deceased Alférez Antonio Machado for 200 pesos at 5% interest, which he received from don Juan José Camacho.

Licenciado don Manuel de Guzmán, acting as chaplain, imposes an obligation on a cattle ranch located in the area named Miravalles. This action is taken while the designated patron and chaplain is being ordained.

people_involved: Capitán don Pedro de Alvarado y Girón
summary: Licenciado don Hermenegildo de Alvarado, a presbyter, obligates himself for 700 pesos to a chaplaincy founded by his deceased father, Capitán don Pedro de Alvarado y Girón. His brother, don José de Alvarado, redeemed 300 pesos, and Capitán Diego de Aguilar redeemed 400 pesos, with the sum imposed on a cattle ranch in Miravalles. Don Gil de Alvarado is the patron of this chaplaincy.

Licenciado don Hermenegildo de Alvarado, acting as executor for his deceased mother doña Catalina de Vida Martel, establishes a chaplaincy for one mass to be celebrated annually on May 3rd, the Day of the Holy Cross. The principal for this chaplaincy is 80 pesos, charged to the grantor, and don Gil de Alvarado is named as the patron.

Licenciado don Hermenegildo de Alvarado, as executor for his deceased mother doña Catalina de Vida Martel, grants freedom to Bartola de Alvarado, a black slave who belonged to his mother. This act fulfills one of his mother's final dispositions.

people_involved: Padre Guardián del Convento de San Francisco
summary: Andrés Peláez establishes a chaplaincy for his soul, that of his deceased wife Catalina de Rosales, and other obligations. He imposes 100 pesos on his dwelling houses located in the city's common lands, which include banana plantations and farmlands along the Taras river, on the road to Tejar. Two masses per year are to be said by the Guardian of the San Francisco Convent.

people_involved: Beneficiado don Juan de Rivas y Chaverri
summary: Doña Gertrudis Guerrero, a widow, sells a 16-year-old Creole black woman named María Gertrudis to Beneficiado don Juan de Rivas y Chaverri for 250 pesos.

Licenciado don Hermenegildo de Alvarado, a presbyter, sells Paula de Sandoval, a 28-year-old dark mulatto woman, and her 10-month-old dark mulatto son, to Capitán José Blanco for 500 pesos. Capitán José Blanco is a resident and neighbor of the town and port of Realejo in the province of Nicaragua. Alvarado had previously acquired Paula through purchase from Capitán José Felipe Bermúdez.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan de Ocampo Golfín
Licenciado don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
Sargento Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Capitán don Juan de Ocampo Golfín and Licenciado don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, acting as guarantor, obligate themselves for 300 pesos to a chaplaincy founded by the deceased doña Eugenia de Abarca Alatras. This sum was previously charged to Sargento Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, the father of Juan and Francisco.

Capitán Juan de Astúa, María Calderón, Juana Calderón, and Bernarda Vázquez agree to settle the estate of Alférez José Calderón, who died in 1715, which has been unresolved through various lawsuits. Astúa will manage the deceased's haciendas in Matina for four years, including one managed by Francisco Calderón, and collect rent from Gabriel Lobo. In return, Astúa will pay 187 pesos 6 reales to the Royal Treasury for two slaves confiscated from him (which the deceased had donated), two sacks owed to Monaster, another owed to Antonio Muñoz's heirs, and the 60-peso rent for the Cofradía de la Concepción. After four years, Astúa will return the haciendas in good repair, build a house where most convenient, and account to the Justice for the distribution of assets, setting aside 5% for a chaplaincy.

Juana Calderón, a widow, leases a hacienda in the Matina valley to Gabriel Lobo for three years, with an annual payment of 75 pesos of cacao. This hacienda borders lands of her deceased father, Alférez José Calderón, and was given to her as a dowry when she married the deceased Capitán Juan de la Madriz.

This entry records the will of Cecilia de Quirós, the legitimate daughter of the deceased Francisco de Quirós and Juana Hernández, and widow of Carlos de Umaña. She names her living children Gregorio, Juana, Antonio, María Gertrudis, Felipe, and Francisca, and her deceased children Carlos and Ambrosio. Her son Felipe de Umaña is appointed as executor, and Felipe and Gregoria are named as heirs.

Doña Petronila de Quirós, a widow, sells Isidora, a 58-year-old mulatto woman she inherited from her deceased parents, to Capitán José Blanco for 100 pesos. Capitán José Blanco is a resident and neighbor of the town and port of Realejo in Nicaragua.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Manuel de Alvarado
summary: Capitán Juan Sancho de Castañeda and his wife doña Juana de Alvarado obligate themselves to the Royal Treasury for 450 pesos, representing the value of two slaves, Pedro and Antonio, who were confiscated and subsequently auctioned to them. This obligation was later cancelled on February 1, 1725, by Sargento Mayor don Manuel de Alvarado, Lieutenant of the Judges of the Royal Treasury.

people_involved: Capitán don Antonio López del Corral
summary: Capitanes don Antonio and don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco obligate themselves to the Royal Treasury for 250 pesos of cacao, the value from the auction of a black woman named Luisa and her daughter Petronila. They declare that these slaves belong to their mother, doña Luisa de Abarca, a widow, and as possessors of her haciendas in Matina, they commit to the payment. This obligation was cancelled on February 23, 1729, by Capitán don Antonio López del Corral, Lieutenant Treasurer of the Royal Treasury.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz
summary: Don Gil de Alvarado and his wife doña Josefa González del Camino acknowledge a 500-peso annuity, at 5%, in favor of a chaplaincy founded by Alonso Gómez Mácetela. This annuity is charged to a 2000-tree cacao plantation in Matina, which borders a hacienda of don José de Guzmán and was purchased by them from Gil's brother, Capitán don Miguel Alvarado, for 850 pesos, including this encumbrance. The obligation was cancelled on July 13, 1735, by Sarjento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz, due to the hacienda being transferred to Licenciado don Juan José Camacho.

Don Gil de Alvarado Girón and doña Josefa González del Camino acknowledge a 100-peso annuity, at 5%, in favor of a chaplaincy founded by doña Inés Pereira. This annuity is charged to the cacao plantation in Matina that they purchased from Gil's brother, Capitán don Miguel de Alvarado.

This entry records the will of María de Arroyo, the legitimate daughter of the deceased Francisco de Arroyo and María Cardoso, and widow of Juan de Astorga. She had a daughter, Mariana de Astorga, who is married to Sebastián de Cárdenas, a native of the kingdoms of Castilla, who has been absent for over 20 years. Other children mentioned had died.

The text mentions an unnamed elderly woman whose daughter's fate is unknown. Her grandson, Clemente de Astorga, has been assisting and caring for her. Her granddaughter is married to Alférez Matías Trejos, who is also an executor, and her daughter Mariana is an heiress.

people_involved: Capitán don Antonio de la Riva y Agüero
summary: Doña Catalina de Arburola, widow of Capitán don Antonio de la Riva y Agüero, acknowledged a 200-peso census (lien) at 5% interest on her houses in the outskirts of Cartago. This obligation was in favor of the Chaplaincy of don Francisco Enciso Hita and stemmed from the purchase of the houses by her late husband from Alférez Luis Peláez and his wife María de los Santos.

people_involved: Don Gil de Alvarado y Girón
summary: Don Gil de Alvarado y Girón and his wife, Doña Josefa González del Camino, acknowledged a 250-peso census at 5% interest on a cacao plantation in Matina. This census was in favor of the Chaplaincy founded by Doña Juana de Vera and burdened the plantation they had purchased from Don Gil's brother, Capitán don Miguel de Alvarado.

people_involved: Don Diego de la Haya Fernández
Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
Don Gil de Alvarado y Girón
summary: Don Diego de la Haya Fernández, Governor and Captain General, sold a house with a kitchen and an enclosed plot of land in Cartago to don José Lebrón for 800 pesos of silver or 1500 pesos of cacao. The property, previously acquired from the heirs of Doña Catalina de Vida Martel, was bordered by properties belonging to the heirs of Capitán don Matías González Camino, don Antonio de la Vega Cabral, Doña Antonia de Alvarado, and don Gil de Alvarado. The sale was later cancelled by Don Diego de la Haya Fernández on October 22, 1723.

Doña Petronila de Quirós, a widow, sold an 8-year-old 'negrita criolla' named Ana Josefa to Capitán José Blanco, a resident of Cartago and neighbor of Realejo, Nicaragua. Ana Josefa is the daughter of a mulata named Paula, whom Doña Petronila had previously sold to Capitán Blanco on September 19. The price for Ana Josefa was 150 pesos of silver.

Sarjento José Damián de Molina sold a 30-year-old mulata named Petronila to Capitán José Blanco, a neighbor of Realejo, Nicaragua. Molina had acquired Petronila from Capitán José de Quirós, a resident of Barba, for 200 pesos of silver.

people_involved: Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Silvestre de Meza leased a cacao plantation of 500 trees in Matina to Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona for three years, at an annual rent of 100 pesos of cacao. The lease was later cancelled on November 24, 1728, by Josefa Elena.

Don José de Mier Cevallos, Lieutenant General, arranged for two indigenous boys, Jacinto and Pedro Manuel, aged 10-12, to be apprenticed to their uncle, Manuel de Ángulo, an indigenous shoemaker master, for four years. The boys are sons of Dionisia de Ángulo from Nicoya.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí
Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: Sarjento Diego de Morales, a free pardo from León, Nicaragua, acting on behalf of Juliana de Chavarría, a free mulata and widow of Francisco de León, received 259 pesos 7 reales of cacao from the estate of Francisco de León, who died intestate in the province. The payment was secured by Sarjento Mayor don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí. The transaction was cancelled on June 14, 1723, after Sarjento Diego de Morales provided a security paper for 66 pesos to Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares.

people_involved: El Licenciado don Manuel González Coronel
summary: El Licenciado don Manuel González Coronel, a Cleric Presbyter, sold a cacao plantation in the Atirro valley to Sárjento Francisco de Echavarría for 300 pesos of cacao. The plantation was inherited from his deceased father, Sárjente Mayor Blas González Coronel, who had purchased it from Juan López, an indigenous chief. In payment, Echavarría transferred a debt from Sárjento Antonio de Umaña, which originated from the sale of a cacao plantation in Reventazón by Francisco de Echavarría and his wife Feliciana Calvo on May 18, 1723. This latter property belonged to Feliciana, inherited from her natural father, Capitán don Miguel Calvo.

people_involved: El Licenciado don Manuel González Coronel
Licenciado don Félix de Oses Navarro
Don Gil de Alvarado y Girón
summary: El Licenciado don Manuel González Coronel, a Cleric Presbyter, sold a house and an enclosed plot of land in Cartago to don Pedro José Sáenz for 850 pesos. The property, which González Coronel had previously bought from Sáenz on September 15, 1718, was bordered by the public plaza and properties of other individuals. The buyer acknowledged the price as debts to three Chaplaincies: Doña Juana de Vera's, one founded by Don Domingo de Echavarría and Capitán don Miguel de Alvarado, and Capitán Pedro Ibánez's.

people_involved: Capitán don Gil de Alvarado y Girón
summary: José Vázquez, as the legitimate son of the deceased Domingo Vázquez, requested that Capitán don José de Guzmán pay him 407 pesos 4 reales of cacao. This payment was ordered and secured by a bond from better-right creditors, with Capitanes don Gil de Alvarado, Francisco de Manzano, and Sarjento José Meneses acting as guarantors.

José Vázquez received 407 pesos 4 reales of cacao from Capitán don José de Guzmán, as per the previous entry. Further investigations revealed that don José de Guzmán had purchased a Matina estate from Capitán don Juan Martel, who acquired it from Sarjento Mayor Blas González Coronel. This estate originally belonged to José Vázquez's father, Domingo Vázquez, and was sold at public auction after his death. The proceeds were intended for two sons from Domingo Vázquez's first marriage; one died in childhood, and the other, having gone to Peru over 32 years ago, is presumed dead, leaving José Vázquez as the sole rightful heir.

Juana Calderón, widow of Captain Juan de la Madriz, recognized a lien of 150 pesos 7 reales on her dwelling houses in Cartago. These houses bordered properties belonging to the heirs of Captain Jerónimo Valerino, Salvador Murillo, Doña Micaela Pérez de Luna, the parish church, and Doña Luisa de Abarca. The lien was in favor of a chaplaincy founded by Doña Juana de Vida Martel.

people_involved: Licenciado Don Félix de Oses Navarro
summary: Doña Baltasara de Escalante Paniagua, a widow, recognized a lien of 200 pesos at 5% interest on her dwelling houses. This lien benefited a chaplaincy founded by Don Francisco Enciso Hita, with Captain Manuel de Arburola as patron and Licenciado Don Félix de Oses Navarro as chaplain. The houses had been transferred to her deceased husband, Captain Don José Antonio Bermúdez, by his mother, Doña Juana de Aguiar.

Alférez Domingo de Quesada arranged to purchase cattle in the Matina valley from the Lieutenant General of Matina for 14 pesos cacao each. These cattle were originally intended to feed armed forces for peace negotiations with the Zambo and Mosquito Indians, who had promised peace to King Philip V. However, the peace talks were thwarted by Jamaican sloops.

Doña Baltasara de Escalante Paniagua, widow of Captain Don José Antonio Bermúdez, obligated herself to the Cofradía de la Concepción for 220 pesos at 5% interest, secured by houses in Cartago. This obligation stemmed from a lawsuit by the Cofradía regarding funds allegedly received by her deceased husband when he was their steward. She appealed the original payment order but recognized the 220 pesos.

people_involved: Licenciado Don Félix Esteban de Oses Navarro
summary: Juana Calderón, a widow, sold dwelling houses in Cartago to Licenciado Don Manuel González Coronel, a Presbyter Cleric, for 600 pesos. The houses bordered properties of Captain Jerónimo Valerino's heirs, Salvador Murillo, Doña Micaela Pérez de Luna, the parish church, and Doña Luisa de Abarca. The buyer agreed to recognize existing liens, including 150 pesos for the chaplaincy founded by Doña Juana de Vida Martel, whose patron was Captain Manuel de Arburola and chaplain was Licenciado Don Félix Esteban de Oses Navarro.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Pedro José Sáenz
Sargento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Sargento Mayor Don Pedro José Sáenz obligated himself for 100 pesos of silver to the minor children of the deceased Francisco Martínez and Doña Lorenza Venegas. This debt was originally charged to Sargento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra. Sáenz mortgaged a country estate in the Aserrí valley, which he had purchased from the heirs of Isabel Cascante.

Don Juan Francisco Sáenz, as the husband of Doña Francisca Martínez, cancelled an obligation. Doña Francisca was the legitimate daughter of Captain Francisco Martínez and Doña Lorenza Venegas, and an heir of her brother, Fray José Miguel Martínez.

Alférez Nicolás de Quirós and his widowed mother, Mariana González, who were sued by Ana de Trejos for 300 pesos, agreed to a settlement. They would give Ana de Trejos a cacao plantation of 400 trees in the Barbilla valley for six years to repay the debt. After this period, the plantation would be returned to Mariana González, its owner.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
Doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
Don Juan José Miguel de Bonilla
summary: Sargento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra and his wife, Doña Catalina González del Camino, founded a chaplaincy for 12 masses as ordered by the deceased Bachiller Don Gregorio de Moya. The principal of 1000 pesos was imposed on stone and lime houses in Cartago, where Doña Catalina held a 1200-peso right from her deceased brother, Bachiller Don Juan del Camino. The chaplain was designated as their son, Miguel Cayetano, or, in the interim, Don Juan José Miguel de Bonilla, who was studying in Santiago de Guatemala.
Teniente General Don José de Mier Cevalios arranged for José Antonio Murillo, a 14-year-old mestizo orphan, to be apprenticed to Teodomiro Arias, a silversmith master, for a period of five years.

people_involved: Don Diego de la Haya Fernández
Doña Josefa López de la Flor
summary: Don Diego de la Haya Fernández, the Governor and Captain General, and Doña Josefa López de la Flor, a widow, exchanged enslaved individuals. Don Diego traded a Zambo named Mateo, acquired the previous year, for a 28-year-old mulatto criollo named Juan Manuel, who was the son of Petronila, a former slave of Doña Josefa's deceased mother, Doña Ambrosia de Echavarría Navarro. Don Diego also paid an additional 75 pesos of cacao.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Manuel de Soto, a resident of Ujarraz, obligated himself for 100 pesos at 5% interest. This obligation was made in favor of the chaplaincy founded by the deceased Bachiller Don Gregorio de Moya, whose patron was Sargento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra.

An unnamed grantor was obligated to an unnamed Bachiller for 300 pesos, representing the paternal and maternal inheritance of his deceased wife, Doña Nicolasa Cayetana de Moya. The debt originated from her deceased parents, Capitán Don Esteban de Moya and Doña Rafaela de Alvarado. The grantor has paid 200 pesos but still owes 100 pesos in interest.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Don Pedro José Sáenz
Sarjento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: On February 8, Sarjento Mayor Don Pedro José Sáenz obligated himself to pay 50 pesos to the minor children of the deceased Francisco Martínez and Doña Lorenza Venegas. This sum was originally owed by Sarjento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra. Sáenz secured the obligation by mortgaging a country estate in the valley of Aserrí.

people_involved: Teniente General Don José de Mier Cevallos
summary: On February 11, Doña Gertrudis Guerrero, a widow, leased a cacaotal with over 1000 trees in Matina to Sarjento Francisco de Chavarría and Alférez Diego Sánchez for two years. The two-year lease was for 275 pesos, payable in cacao, and the property bordered land belonging to Teniente General Don José de Mier Cevallos.

On February 15, Doña Josefa de Aguilar, a widow, leased a 1300-tree cacaotal in Matina to Capitán Don José Felipe Bermúdez and his wife Doña Teresa de Sandoval for three years. The lease, priced at 275 pesos of cacao annually, was set to begin on September 1st, coinciding with the expiration of the usufruct previously sold by her deceased son, Manuel Andrés de Acosta.
On June 22, 1726, Doña Josefa de Aguilar cancelled the lease agreement for the cacaotal in Matina.

On February 23, Doña Luisa Calvo, a widow, leased a cacaotal in Matina to Alférez Diego Sánchez, described as "pardo," for two years. The terms included a payment of 175 pesos and the obligation for Sánchez to construct a house on the hacienda.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
Sarjento Mayor Don Bartolomé Bueno de Basorí
Sarjento Mayor Don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí
Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: On February 26, Marcos del Sáenz was involved in a lawsuit with Sarjento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra, who represented Don Manuel de Caminos regarding various merchandise. The case stemmed from a power of attorney granted to Ibarra in León, Nicaragua, on June 8, 1722, which was later ceded to Sarjento Mayor Don Bartolomé Bueno de Basorí on June 20, 1722. Sáenz provided Sarjento Mayor Don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí and Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona as guarantors for the judgment.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: On June 8, 1722, in León, Nicaragua, Don Manuel de Caminos granted power of attorney to Sarjento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra to perceive and collect sales of merchandise.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Don Bartolomé Bueno de Basorí
summary: On June 20, 1722, Don Manuel de Caminos ceded his rights to Sarjento Mayor Don Bartolomé Bueno de Basorí, who was to account for the effects under his charge to Caminos, or to Basorí in Caminos' absence.

On February 27, Alférez Diego Morera, a resident of Barba, made his will. He was the legitimate son of the deceased Diego Morera and María de las Salas, and was married to María de Segura, with whom he had four children: Matías, Leonarda, José, and Juana María. José Núñez, also a resident of Barba, was named as his executor.
On February 28, Capitán Don Pedro de Moya leased a 1500-tree cacaotal in Matina to Alférez Alejandro Leitona for three years, with a payment of 525 pesos in cacao.

On March 3, Sarjento Francisco de Chavarría obligated himself to Doña Josefa de Aguilar, who was acting as tutor for José Cayetano, for 150 pesos. This amount represented José Cayetano's inheritance from his deceased mother, Doña Francisca de Acosta Arévalo, who was the wife of the also deceased Don Gregorio de Alvarado.

On March 9, a dowry letter was issued for Capitán Don Pedro de Llanos, a native of Gijón, Asturias, in favor of Doña Josefa Gadea Marrufo, whom he married on August 24, 1722. Doña Josefa, the legitimate daughter of Don Rodrigo Gadea Marrufo and Doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco, was also the widow of Don Bernardo Vermes y Mogrovejo. The dowry amounted to 3660 pesos 5 reales, with arras of 500 pesos.
Capitán Don Pedro de Llanos married Doña Josefa Gadea Marrufo on August 24, 1722.

people_involved: Capitán Don Juan González del Camino
Doña Manuela de Salazar y Peralta
Sarjento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: On March 15, Don Gil de Alvarado made his will. He was the legitimate son of the deceased Capitán Don Pedro de Alvarado and Doña Catalina de Vida Martel, and was married to Doña Josefa González del Camino, with whom he had eight children. His will also listed three slaves and named his brothers, Licenciado Don Hermenegildo de Alvarado and Don Miguel de Alvarado, along with Sarjento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra and his brother Capitán Don José de Alvarado, as executors.
On March 20, Capitán Don Bernardo Marín leased a 450-tree cacaotal in Matina to Sarjento Baltasar de Moya for one year, at a price of 100 pesos in cacao.

people_involved: Don Diego de la Haya Fernández
Sarjento Mayor Don José de Hoyo y Echavarría
summary: On March 20, Don Diego de la Haya Fernández, serving as Governor and Captain General, granted general power of attorney to Sarjento Mayor Don José de Hoyo y Echavarría, Don Andrés Omboni, and Doña Josefa de Hoyo, all residents of Panama City.

people_involved: Doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
Sarjento Mayor Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: On April 14, Capitán Don Francisco de Betancourt and his wife Doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral owed Francisco and Diego Romero 450 pesos, a debt inherited from Sarjento Mayor Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral, the wife's father. To settle the debt, they transferred a 30-year-old mulato slave named Sebastián, valued at 350 pesos, and paid the remaining 100 pesos in cash.

people_involved: Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona, a native of Málaga, Spain, attempted to make his will while ill in bed. The Teniente General was called on the 18th and 20th to assist, but due to Barahona's fever and his wife Doña Petronila de Hoses's statement that he was unable to continue, the testament remained suspended.

On April 21, Doña Baltasara de Escalante Paniagua, a widow, obligated herself to pay 100 pesos to the Cofradía de la Concepción. This payment was the result of a condemnation in a claim by the Cofradía against the assets of her deceased husband, Capitán Don José Antonio Bermúdez, for funds he had received.

Capitán José Felipe Bermúdez and his wife, Teresa de Sandoval, obligated themselves for 100 pesos at 5% interest to the Cofradía de la Concepción. This debt was secured by houses they owned in the city.

Doña Juana Manuela Lizondo, a widow residing in Ujarraz, requested the Teniente General to come to her to execute her will. Unable to travel, the Teniente General commissioned Capitán Francisco de Betancourt, Teniente Juez of the city's fields, to handle the matter.

Doña Juana Manuela Lizondo, legitimate daughter of the deceased Alférez Juan Matías Lizondo and Francisca de Benavente, and widow of Capitán Juan Guerrero, executed her will in Ujarraz. Her children, Juan Francisco, Juana Josefa, María, and Gabriel Guerrero, were named, and Alférez Antonio Valerino and her son Juan Francisco Guerrero were appointed as executors.
Capitán Juan Cortés sold a 50-year-old mulata named Antonia to Don Diego de la Haya Fernández, who was the Gobernador y Capitán General. The sale was completed for a price of 115 pesos.

Doña Alfonsa Muñoz Hidalgo, whose husband Capitán Domingo de Inza was absent in Panamá, obligated herself to the Cofradía de la Concepción for 104 pesos and 3 reales. This sum was for building materials from destroyed houses that had belonged to the deceased Beneficiado Don Diego de Ángulo Gascón, and she mortgaged her own city residence. The obligation was later cancelled on October 4, 1736, having been transferred to Teniente Don Pedro Jiménez Mondragón and Doña Francisca de Inza.

The Teniente General arranged for Miguel Siles, a 14-year-old white mestizo orphan, to be apprenticed to Francisco Carrillo, a blacksmith official. The apprenticeship was set for a period of six years.

Don Juan Manuel de Alvarado sold his brother, Capitán Don Miguel de Alvarado, a 40-year-old mulata named María Micaela. This mulata had been inherited from their deceased mother, Doña Catalina de Vida Martel, and the transaction was for 300 pesos.

Doña Luisa Calvo, a widow, established a Capellanía for masses for her soul and that of her deceased legitimate son, Gabriel Maroto, with a principal of 1000 pesos. The funds were secured by various properties and debts owed by Nicolás Sarmiento de Soto Mayor, Catalina de Rojas, Sarjento Francisco de Chavarría, and Capitán José de Morales Tremiño and Juana de Ángulo. Don José Antonio Díaz de Herrera, currently studying in León, Nicaragua, was named Capellán, and Capitán Juan Díaz de Herrera, his brother, was designated as the future patron.
Capitán Don Gil de Alvarado provided bail for Gregorio Calvo, a free mulato, who had been imprisoned for cohabitation.

Capitán Don José de Morales Tremiño and his wife, Doña Juana de Ángulo, obligated themselves for 100 pesos of cacao to the Capellanía founded by Doña Luisa Calvo. Luisa Calvo is the patron, and her grandson, Don José Antonio Díaz de Herrera, is the Capellán, with the obligation secured by adobe and tile houses in the city.
Ayudante Matías Masís, Mayordomo of the Cofradía de la Concepción, obligated himself regarding a judgment in a lawsuit against him in the Curia. He had appealed the decision to the Bishop.

Gertrudis Peláez, widow of Alférez Gregorio Picado, who was obligated to pay 52 pesos 4 reales and 10 maravedíes to the Cofradía de la Concepción, appealed her case to the Bishop. She committed to abide by the final judgment.

Licenciado Don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, a cleric deacon, donated a country estate and dwelling in the Barba valley, approximately ten leagues from the city, to his first cousin, Doña Josefa Martínez de Herrera. Doña Josefa is the wife of Capitán Juan Cayetano Jiménez, and the property had been previously purchased by Golfín from Capitán Gregorio Siles.

Sarjento Mayor Don Pedro José Sáenz obligated himself to the Cofradía de la Concepción for 50 pesos at 5% interest, secured by a country estate in Aserrí. This sum included 30 pesos for a quarter solar of destroyed houses formerly belonging to Don Francisco Ramiro Corajo, which were sold to Sáenz by Capitán Don José Antonio Bermúdez, the Cofradía's Mayordomo, and 20 pesos redeemed by Mateo de Quirós.

Sarjento Francisco de Echavarría (Chavarría) owed Don Juan Sánchez Camaño, a trader in the province, 200 pesos of cacao. This debt was for local goods and was scheduled to be paid in the upcoming July.

The Teniente General arranged for Manuel, a 14-year-old free mulato orphan, to be apprenticed to Sarjento José Damián de Molina, a master shoemaker. The apprenticeship agreement was for a duration of six years.

Bernarda Vásquez, a widow, and Sarjento Gregorio de Umaña mutually agreed to terminate a cacao plantation lease contract for 500 trees in Matina, which they had originally signed on May 18, 1722. Gregorio de Umaña returned 38 pesos for the period the contract had been in effect.
Capitán Don Miguel de Alvarado posted bail for Nicolás Palacios, who was imprisoned for vagrancy. Palacios, in turn, committed to working as a muleteer on the convoys traveling to Matina.

Capitán Don Miguel de Alvarado and his wife, Doña María de Torres, exchanged a mulata named María Josefa, 18 years old, for a 40-year-old negro named Diego García, owned by Doña Nicolasa Guerrero of Ujarraz. María Josefa, who suffered from evacuations, was valued at 350 pesos, a sum that would be owed if she died from her condition. María Josefa was part of María de Torres's dowry from her father, Capitán Don Juan de Torres, while Diego García had been previously exchanged by Nicolasa Guerrero for another negro named Felipe with Capitán Manuel García de Argueta.

Alférez Jacinto de Rivera, legitimate son of the deceased Bernardo de Rivera and Estéfana Román, both natives of San Miguel de San Salvador, made his will. He was previously married to Ana del Camino, who was also deceased.

A list of children is recorded, including Pablo, Juana (deceased), Josefa Luisa, María Josefa, Cayetano, Ana, and Antonia Rivera. Josefa Petronila and Luisa are noted as married. A debt to Alonso de Parra, the indigenous mayor of Aserrí, is mentioned, and Ayudante General Miguel de Céspedes is named as an executor.

Capitán don Juan de Torres, still owing 350 pesos from his daughter doña María de Torres's dowry to Capitán don Miguel de Alvarado, pays the debt with a 22-year-old mulato named Manuel. Manuel came into Juan de Torres's possession after the death of his wife, doña María de Tamariz, who was also María de Torres's mother.

people_involved: Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Licenciado José de Chaves recognizes a censo (lien) of 190 pesos for the Convento de San Francisco, 180 pesos for the Cofradía de la Concepción, and 50 pesos for the Cofradía del Rosario, all at 5% interest, on houses he received from his sister Josefa de Chaves. The property borders lands of Capitán Francisco de Bonilla and the Torres and Tiribí rivers.

people_involved: Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Capitán don Pedro de Moya, Mayordomo of the Cofradía del Rosario, Ayudante Matías Masís, Mayordomo of the Cofradía de la Concepción, and Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona, Síndico of the Convento de San Francisco, cancel the censo obligations recognized by Licenciado José de Chaves.

people_involved: doña Juana María de Soto y Barahona
Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Teniente Cayetano Muñoz provides a dowry of 3343 pesos and arras of 500 pesos for his future wife, doña Juana María de Soto y Barahona. The dowry includes a 10-year-old mulatilla named Manuela Josefa (300 pesos), a 4-5 year old negrito named Dionisio (200 pesos), 500 cacao trees in Matina (1000 pesos), and 50 head of cattle (100 pesos).

people_involved: Capitán don José de Morales Tremiño
Licenciado don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro
summary: Capitán don José de Morales Tremiño and his wife doña Juana de Ángulo obligate themselves for 100 pesos at 5% interest to the Capellanía founded by doña Eugenia de Abarca. Licenciado don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro is the Capellán, and the obligation is secured by houses in the city.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan de Bonilla
Padre Guardián del Convento de San Francisco
Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Juan Bautista Bruno, a bachelor from Ruasca de la Ribera, Genova, makes his will. He leaves various sums to religious institutions and establishes a Capellanía, naming don Juan Miguel de Bonilla as the first Capellán, with the Padre Guardián of San Francisco acting as interim. His executors are Juan Francisco de Ibarra and Juan Francisco Marín Laguna, tasked with remitting his assets to his mother, Angela Bocafigo, or fulfilling his bequests if she is deceased.
Juan Bautista Bruno issues a codicil to his will, revoking previous donations and naming his mother, Angela Bocafigo, as his universal heir. This codicil was not finalized.

people_involved: doña María Elena de la Flor
don Diego de la Haya Fernández
summary: Doña María Elena de la Flor exchanges a 25-year-old mulato named Antonio, inherited from her deceased mother doña Ambrosia de Echavarría, with don Diego de la Haya Fernández for a 10-12 year old 'negrita criolla bozal' to be brought from Panamá. Until the negrita is delivered, don Diego will pay María Elena four pesos of cacao monthly.

people_involved: doña María Elena de la Flor
don Diego de la Haya Fernández
summary: Doña María Elena de la Flor receives a mulata named Manuela from don Diego de la Haya Fernández, fulfilling his obligation from a previous exchange.

Doña Agustina de Campos Quirós and doña María de Campos Quirós, daughters of the deceased Teniente Pedro de Campos Quirós and doña Bárbara Rodríguez Altamirano, grant freedom to their slaves. Agustina frees Miguel de Campos (mulato), and María frees Juana de Campos, both inherited from their mother.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
Sarjento Mayor don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí
summary: Capitán Francisco Alejandro de Bonilla and his wife doña Josefa de Torres, along with their guarantors Francisco de la Madriz Linares and Manuel Antonio de Arleguí, obligate themselves for 436 pesos 6 reales to Francisco and Bernardo de Torres. This debt was originally charged to doña María Meléndez, Josefa's deceased mother, who had declared in her will that a portion of her husband's parents' assets was delivered to her for her two absent brothers.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz
Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: In Aserrí, Sarjento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz certifies the cancellation of the obligation made by Capitán Francisco Alejandro de Bonilla. This occurs after his widow, doña Josefa de Torres, with new guarantors Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares and doña Gracia de Hoces Navarro, arranges for payments to Sebastiana de Torres and the heirs of the other Torres.

Juan Bautista Bruno issues a second codicil to his will, confirming his mother Angela Bocafigo's death based on a letter from his countryman Agustín Bruno in San Felipe de Portobelo. He leaves 200 pesos of cacao and 100 pesos in household items to doña Francisca de Astúa in gratitude for her care during his illness, and names his soul as heir.

Capitán José de Lumbre, a native of Lila, Flandes, makes his will. He states he left France over 30 years ago, learned of his wife's death and lack of children 5 years ago while in Vera Cruz. He served as a pilot on a balandra from San Felipe de Portobelo, captained by don Juan de Cuesta, which stopped in Matina and was later captured. Goods registered under his name belong to Miguel Perulia.

people_involved: Governor and Royal Officials of Portobelo
summary: An unnamed Captain of the balandra 'El Águila,' operating under a patent, captured two Jamaican sloops engaged in illicit trade off the coast of Portobelo. He requested his and his crew's share of the prize, but the Governor and Royal Officials of Portobelo refused, stating they needed a decision from His Majesty. The Captain estimated his share to be over 2500 pesos and noted that Captain Miguel de Enríquez of Portobelo owed him over 6000 pesos.

people_involved: Don Diego de la Haya Fernández
summary: Doña Angela María de Arleguí, a widow, sold a 9-year-old mulatto cuarterón named José Cayetano, son of her slave María, to Don Diego de la Haya Fernández, the Governor and Captain General, for 100 silver pesos.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
Doña Magdalena Pérez de Luna y Rivera
Licenciado Don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Sargento Mayor Don Francisco de la Madriz Linares, acting as attorney for Don Nicolás de Ocampo Golfín, established a chaplaincy of 8 masses for 1600 pesos on behalf of the deceased Doña Magdalena Pérez de Luna y Rivera. Don Juan de Ocampo Golfín was named the first chaplain, with his brother Licenciado Don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín serving as interim. The power of attorney for this action was granted in Bagaces on July 26, 1723.

people_involved: Beneficiado Don Juan Antonio de Moya
Doña María (sister of Juan Antonio de Moya)
María de Moya (slave of Juan Antonio de Moya)
José Manuel (son of María de Moya, slave)
summary: Beneficiado Don Juan Antonio de Moya, a Presbyter cleric, granted power to his brother Don José Fernando de Moya to make his will, requesting burial in the main church of Cartago in his sister Doña María's seat. He also declared that his slave María de Moya and her son José Manuel would be freed upon his death, with José Manuel going to his brother.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: Francisco Carrillo incurred a debt of 135 pesos of cacao to Sargento Mayor Don Francisco de la Madriz Linares for an iron anvil weighing 135 pounds. This debt was later cancelled on February 7, 1732.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí
Captain Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: José Felipe Calvo, a resident of Santiago de Alange in Tierra Firme, sold a two-caballería plot of land in Quercua, inherited from Captain Don Miguel Calvo, to Sargento Mayor Don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí and Captain Antonio de Soto y Barahona. The sale price was 200 pesos, paid in 8 cacao tercios.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
Sargento Mayor Don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
Sargento Mayor Don José de Baeza
Captain Don Manuel José de Alvarado
summary: Several prominent individuals, including Sargento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra and Sargento Mayor Don Francisco de la Madriz Linares, provided a 2000 peso bond for Captain Don Manuel José de Alvarado. Alvarado was entering the position of Lieutenant of Royal Officials, taking over from Ibarra.
The Lieutenant General arranged for Nicolás Alejos, a 12-year-old free pardo and son of María del Carmen, to be apprenticed to José Valeriano de las Alas, a master tailor, for a period of six years.

people_involved: Captain Don Matías González del Camino
summary: María Antonia González, the sole heir of the deceased Juan González, sold a plot of land in El Agua Caliente, which bordered María Calderón's property, to Captain Luis Gutiérrez for 75 pesos cacao. The land had been originally purchased by her father from Captain Don Matías González del Camino.

people_involved: Captain Don Alonso Bersabé Cabeza de Vaca
Captain Don Cristóbal Muñoz de la Trinidad
Licenciado Don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro
José Manuel (son of Alonso Bersabé Cabeza de Vaca)
Captain Don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Captain Don Alonso Bersabé Cabeza de Vaca sold his residence, including a sugar mill and plantations in the Ujarraz valley, to Captain Don Cristóbal Muñoz de la Trinidad for 1200 pesos. The property was inherited from his deceased wife, Doña Juana de Moya, and part of the payment was designated for his son José Manuel's guardianship. The transaction was partially cancelled on March 18, 1724, and on March 24, 1724, Don Cristóbal declared that the estate was co-owned with his brother, Captain Don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad.

people_involved: Captain Don Alonso Bersabé Cabeza de Vaca
summary: Captain Don Alonso Bersabé Cabeza de Vaca sold a 40-year-old black woman named Laureana de Moya and her 8-9 year old pardo son, Urbano, to Captain Don Pedro Pantoja, a merchant. These slaves had come into his possession after the death of his wife, Doña Juana de Moya, and were sold for 475 pesos cacao.

people_involved: Beneficiado Don Juan Antonio de Moya
Governor Don Diego de la Haya Fernández
summary: Beneficiado Don Juan Antonio de Moya, a parish priest, sold a 30-year-old mulata named María to Governor Don Diego de la Haya Fernández for 300 silver pesos. Don Juan Antonio had originally purchased María from General Don Juan Mariscal, the Lieutenant of Captain General of the Nicoya Party.

people_involved: Licenciado Don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Doña María Martínez de Herrera donated a 31-year-old mulatto named Cayetano to her first cousin, Licenciado Don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, a Deacon Cleric. Cayetano had been serving Don Francisco for five years prior to this formal donation.

people_involved: Captain Don Diego de Barros y Carvajal
Sargento Mayor Don Antonio de Utrera y Medina
summary: Captain Don Diego de Barros y Carvajal and his wife Doña Josefa Pérez de Muro obligated themselves to Sargento Mayor Don Antonio de Utrera y Medina for 43 sacks of prime cacao, valued at 1075 pesos, to be delivered in Cartago.

people_involved: Licenciado Don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Licenciado Don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín sold a 31-year-old mulatto criollo named Cayetano, previously donated by his cousin Doña María Martínez de Herrera, to Pedro Ortiz for 300 pesos cacao. Ortiz stated he was buying Cayetano on behalf of Captain Francisco Flores. By agreement with Flores, the mulatto was returned to the seller on January 28, 1724.

people_involved: Captain Don Alonso Bersabé Cabeza de Vaca
José Manuel (son of Alonso Bersabé Cabeza de Vaca)
summary: Captain Nicolás de Estrada and his wife Doña Lorenza Muñoz obligated themselves to Captain Don Alonso de Bersabé Cabeza de Vaca for 100 pesos, representing part of the maternal inheritance due to José Manuel, the minor son of Don Alonso and the deceased Doña Juana de Moya. This obligation was cancelled on March 28, 1731.

Capitán don Alonso Bersabé Cabeza de Vaca obligated himself for 322 pesos 7 reales cacao in favor of his minor son, José Manuel, as part of his maternal inheritance from his deceased wife, doña Juana de Moya. This obligation was later cancelled on April 21, 1732, with 52 pesos provided by justice for his son's cure and clothing.

Sargento Manuel de Rojas took possession of houses following the deaths of Capitán don Gregorio de Chaves and his sons Juan and Mateo de Chaves. These houses had encumbrances, including debts of 100 pesos from Juan de Chaves and 50 pesos from Mateo, owed to doña Sebastiana de Alvarado. Due to a lack of minted currency, Rojas agreed to pay Alvarado 100 pesos in cacao, obligating himself for 250 pesos of cacao.

Capitán José Fernández Castellanos and his wife doña Felipa Sendín recognized a census of 100 pesos at 5% interest for the chaplaincy founded by Comisario Baltasar de Grado, with Licenciado don Manuel de Guzmán as Chaplain. This census burdened half a house they acquired from don Francisco de Otárola and his wife doña Agustina. The census was cancelled on December 17, 1726, by Capitán don José de Guzmán, acting as attorney for Licenciado don Manuel de Guzmán.

Capitán José Fernández Castellanos and his wife doña Felipa Sendín recognized another census of 100 pesos at 5% interest on the same half-house, this time in favor of the Cofradía de la Soledad. This census was cancelled on April 28, 1726, by Teniente General don José Felipe Bermúdez, who received the 100 pesos.

Testament of Sargento Francisco de Orozco, legitimate son of the deceased Alberto de Orozco and Catalina Barquero. He was married to Gertrudis de Hinojosa, daughter of Juan Ginés de Hinojosa, and had two children who died young. He was previously married to Margarita de Piedra, daughter of Juan de Piedra and María Madrigal, with whom he had four children: Francisco Cayetano, Gregorio, Miguel (absent), and Manuela. His son-in-law was Pedro de Chinchilla, and his granddaughter was Catalina. Alférez Francisco Gutiérrez was named as albacea.

Gertrudis Falcón, a widow, gave a cacao plantation in Barbilla with 255 trees to Sargento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares as payment for 182 pesos she owed him, along with her sons Félix and José Miguel.

people_involved: Juan Gómez de Ocón y Trillo
Francisco Gómez de Ocón y Trillo
summary: Testament of Capitán Juan Gómez de Ocón y Trillo, legitimate son of the deceased Francisco Gómez de Ocón y Trillo and doña María Vázquez. He was married to Eugenia Lizondo, with whom he had two children: José Francisco (10 years old) and Cayetana (6 years old). The declaration of assets was suspended because the testator was not in his right mind.

Don Pedro de Moya sold a 28-year-old Mina-caste black slave named José to Sargento Mayor don Diego de Arviceta for 150 pesos of silver. Moya had acquired José through an auction of confiscated slaves.

Testament of doña Clara de Esquivel, a resident of the Barba valley, legitimate daughter of the deceased Andrés de Esquivel and Antonia de Madrigal. She was the widow of Alférez Salvador Murillo and had no children. She mentions her niece Juana Valerino, an orphan named Juana Marcela whom she raised, her brother Pedro Murillo whom she also raised, and her niece María de Esquivel whom she raised. She ordered the founding of a chaplaincy. Capitanes Bernardo Pacheco and Antonio de Ulate were named as albaceas.
Sargento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra granted general power of attorney to Sargento Mayor don Manuel de Alvarado and Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos.

Capitán Luis Gutiérrez obligated himself for 400 pesos cacao in favor of the chaplaincy ordered by the deceased Juan Bautista Bruno, which was to be founded by his albacea, Sargento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra. Gutiérrez received this amount from Ibarra and mortgaged a cacao plantation and a cleared field in Barbilla.

Sargentos Mayores don Francisco de la Madriz Linares and don Diego de Arviceta granted power to Sargento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra, who was about to travel to San Felipe de Portobelo, to purchase a balandra (sloop), the cost of which would be borne by all three.

Codicil of doña Josefa Nicolasa de Guevara, referencing her testament from September 15, 1719, made before Gobernador don Diego de la Haya Fernández. She mentions her mother doña Clara de Echavarría, her son José Antonio, three slaves (Isabel Ramona, Dionisia, José Cayetano Nicolás), and her niece Juana Antonia de Guevara. Sargento Mayor don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí and Licenciado don Manuel de Guzmán were named albaceas, and her son Manuel Cayetano was named heir.

Capitán Manuel García de Argueta obligated himself for 100 pesos at 5% silver interest to the Cofradía de la Concepción. He received this amount from Mayordomo Matías Masís, which was previously owed by doña Baltasara López de la Flor. He mortgaged some dwelling houses in this city (Cartago).

Capitán don Alvaro de Guevara sold three cacao plantations in the Barbilla valley to Alférez Domingo Guerrero for 500 pesos. One plantation was named 'el Pejibaye,' another was bought from the widow of José de Aguilar, and the third from the heirs of Josefa González. The payment was in favor of a chaplaincy founded by Alvaro de Guevara, of which he was the patron and Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara was the Chaplain.

Testament of José Meneses, legitimate son of Alférez Bartolomé Meneses and Juana López. His mother was named as his heir. Capitanes don José de Mier Cevallos and don Gregorio Sáenz were named as albaceas.
Capitán Manuel García de Argueta is mentioned in an incomplete entry.

Doña Dionisia Fallas de la Vega and her husband obligate themselves for 550 pesos of cacao to José Manuel, the legitimate minor son of Captain Alonso Bersabé Cabeza de Vaca and the deceased Doña Juana de Moya. This debt was originally owed by Captain Cristóbal Muñoz de la Trinidad, and houses in 'this city' are mortgaged to secure it.

Captain Manuel García de Argueta obligates himself to the Cofradía del Rosario for 50 pesos, which he received from Mayordomo Captain Pedro de Moya. This debt was previously owed by Doña Baltasara López de la Flor, and houses in 'this city' are mortgaged as security.

Captain José de Mier Cevallos and his wife, Doña Catalina González del Camino, grant freedom to their 35-year-old Pardo slave, Tomás Cubero. Catalina had acquired Tomás from her first husband, Don Cristóbal Martín Cubero.

Captain Juan Alejandro Leitona and his wife, María Antonia Maroto, obligate themselves for 100 pesos at 5% interest to the Capellanía founded by Diego Quintero. This debt was previously owed by Sargento Mayor Manuel Antonio de Arleguí, and houses in the common lands of 'this city' are charged.

Sargento Mayor Manuel de Alvarado grants power of attorney to Captain Juan de Alarcón, a resident of Santiago de Guatemala, to marry Doña Francisca Vázquez de Molina on his behalf. Francisca is the legitimate daughter of Alarcón and Doña Juana Ventura Vázquez de Molina.

people_involved: Angela de la Paz y Flores
summary: Doña Inés de Sandoval Golfín, a native of Comayagua, Honduras, and legitimate daughter of the deceased Alférez Real Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín and Angela de la Paz y Flores, makes her will. She was married to Captain Gil de Alvarado, had no children, but raised a girl named Josefa Nicolasa. Ayudante Nicolás de Estrada and Captain José Felipe Bermúdez are named as her executors.

Doña Josefa Nicolasa de Guevara sells a 14-year-old 'negrito' named Nicolás Policarpo, son of the black slave Dionisia, to Governor and Captain General Diego de la Haya Fernández for 150 pesos of silver. Josefa Nicolasa inherited Nicolás Policarpo from her mother.

Doña Josefa Nicolasa de Guevara makes a donation of 300 pesos of cacao to the Convento de San Francisco. This money is held by Governor Diego de la Haya Fernández, who, being present, obligates himself to 5% interest.

Alférez Juan Miguel Cervantes and his wife, Doña Gregoria Hidalgo, obligate themselves for 150 pesos of cacao at 5% interest to the Capellanía of the deceased Lucrecia Martínez. Alférez Miguel de Mora is the patron and Don Antonio de Guevara, a Presbyter, is the chaplain. They mortgage their dwelling houses in the valley of Aserrí.
Sargento Mayor Pedro José Sáenz obligates himself to the Cofradía de la Soledad, but the transaction was not completed.

Licenciado Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, a deacon, as principal, and José de Ocampo, a resident of Barba, as guarantor, obligate themselves to Don Diego de la Haya Fernández for 647 pesos of cacao, to be paid within 6 months. This obligation was cancelled on May 7, 1725.
Doña Josefa Martínez, wife of Juan Cayetano Jiménez (who has been absent for over 8 years), provides bail for her son, Cristóbal Jiménez.

Sargento Mayor Don Diego de Arviceta, a resident of Panama currently residing in 'this city', adds a codicil to his wills previously made in Panama and 'here'. This specific codicil was made in January of the current year before Sargento Mayor José de Bonilla, Lieutenant Governor.

A dowry letter is issued by Don José Lebrón, legitimate son of the late Diego Lebrón and Isabel Cortés of Marchena, in favor of his wife, Doña Manuela de Venegas, natural daughter of Doña Lorenza de Venegas. The dowry is 1588 pesos, with 200 pesos as arras, and includes a 19-year-old mulatta named Manuela Josefa valued at 350 pesos.

Beneficiado Don Juan Antonio de Moya obligates himself for 1000 pesos at 5% interest, which Sargento Mayor Don Antonio de Utrera redeems. This money belongs to the Capellanía founded by Captain Don José de Alvarado, for which Juan Antonio de Moya is the chaplain. The obligation is secured by a 3000-tree cacao plantation in Matina.

people_involved: María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
summary: Sargento Mayor Juan Francisco de Ibarra and his wife, Catalina González Camino, sell a 3000-tree cacao plantation in Matina to Captain Francisco de Betancourt and his wife, María Josefa de la Vega Cabral, who is the niece of the sellers. The buyers assume several debts to various Capellanías and the Royal Treasury. The sellers also transfer half of their stone and lime house in 'this city' to Catalina González Camino to balance the value of the cacaotal.

Captain Francisco de Betancourt leases a cacao plantation named 'El Hermoso' in Matina to Captain Francisco Alejandro de Bonilla for three years, at an annual price of 250 pesos of cacao. This plantation is contiguous to the one Betancourt bought on the 23rd of this month from Sargento Mayor Juan Francisco de Ibarra.

Beneficiado Don Juan Antonio de Moya obligates himself for 500 pesos of silver to the Capellanía founded by his aunt, Doña Josefa de Moya. Juan Antonio de Moya is the chaplain and patron of this Capellanía, and the debt is secured by a 3000-tree cacao plantation in Matina.
The will of Captain Juan Rodríguez de (name incomplete) is recorded.

Captain Gregorio Sáenz, son of Sargento Mayor Pedro José Sáenz and María de la Rosa, established a dowry of 362 pesos and arras of 50 pesos for his wife, Francisca de Castro, who is the legitimate daughter of Captain Juan Rodríguez de Castro and the deceased Petronila Arias.

Francisco de Bonilla founded a Capellanía for 4 recited masses, with Licenciado Manuel Martín Cubero serving as the Chaplain. The principal of 100 pesos, at 5% interest, was charged to Alférez Manuel Soto, who secured it with a thatched house, sugarcane field, and plantain grove in Ujarraz, which he had purchased from Bonilla for 150 pesos.

Sargento Mayor Juan Francisco de Ibarra, as patron of the Capellanía founded by his grandfather Tomás Calvo, and Captain Antonio de Soto y Barahona, as representative for Chaplain Licenciado Esteban de Hoces Navarro, received 50 silver pesos from Teniente General José Fernández Castellanos. This payment was an obligation of Captain Miguel Ortiz de Aldana and Agustina de Córdoba, charged against half a house incorporated into Fernández's property.

Don Bartolomé Trujillo and his wife Doña Angela Sáenz exchanged a cacaotal of 400 trees in the Matina valley (Barbilla), which was incorporated into another 274-tree cacaotal belonging to Doña Ana (Angela's mother), for a house in the ejidos of Cartago. Half of this house was given as a dowry by Doña Ana to Doña Angela and is located on the Camino de Co.

The widow Doña Antonia de Acosta Arévalo leased a cacao hacienda of 2000 trees in the Matina valley to Alférez Tomás del Camino for three years. The hacienda bordered the mountain and properties of Doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco and María Sibaja. The rent was 6 first-grade and 1 second-grade zurrones for the first year, and 200 pesos (in 7 first-grade and 1 second-grade zurrones) for each of the subsequent two years.

Captain Manuel García de Argueta obligated himself to the Capellanía founded by the deceased Depositario Tomás Calvo, whose patron is Sargento Mayor Juan Francisco de Ibarra and Chaplain is Licenciado Esteban de Hoces Navarro. The obligation was for 50 pesos at 5% interest, secured by a cacaotal in Matina.

Captain Manuel García de Argueta and his wife Doña Dionisia de Fallas obligated themselves to the Capellanía to be founded by Sargento Mayor Antonio de Utrera, for which Beneficiado Juan Antonio de Moya is the interim Chaplain and his son José Cayetano is the proprietor. The obligation was for 600 pesos at 5% interest (in cacao), secured by a cacaotal of over 6000 trees in the Barbilla valley.

Captain Pedro de Moya and his wife Doña Angela Sáenz exchanged a quarter of a house in Cartago, which they inherited from Doña Bárbara Lanini (Pedro's mother), for building materials (black wood posts, tiles, nails, and cedar wood) provided by Alférez Francisco Barquero.
