The house quarter was located near houses of Captain Juan López, Licenciado Diego de Campos, Sargento Mayor Pedro Sáenz, and Captain Bernardo Marín.

Captain Alvaro de Guevara leased three plots of cacaotal in the Barbilla valley to Alférez Juan de Bejarano for three years. Guevara claimed ownership after Alférez Domingo Guerrero, who had purchased them, was taken by the "zambo mosquito" (likely a disease or an event that removed him). The lease was conditional on Guerrero's return, at which point it would cease. The plots included one belonging to the minors of Josefa González, "el pejiballe," and one from José de Aguilar's widow. The rent was 100 pesos for the first two years and 150 pesos for the third.
Sargento Mayor Diego de Arviceta, a resident of Panama and soon to travel to San Felipe de Portobelo, granted general power of attorney to Captain Diego de Soto y Barahona.

Feliciana Chinchilla, widow of Alférez Francisco Fernández (a native of Spain), made her will. She ordered a Capellanía of masses, for which Don Manuel Sáenz would be patron and chaplain (to be ordained under its title), with Don Antonio de Guevara as interim. Her executors were Sargento Mayor Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón and her son José Bernardo. Her natural children, José Bernardo and María Francisca, were named as heirs.
Sargento Mayor Diego de Arviceta obligated himself to Sargento Mayor Manuel José de Alvarado for 914 pesos and 6 reales, to be paid within six months in Panama.

The widow Doña Luisa Calvo donated a young black slave named Juan de Dios, aged 8-9 years and son of her slave, to her grandson Licenciado José Antonio Díaz de Herrera, a Presbítero whom she had raised. The donation was effective from the day he sang his first mass.
Sargento Mayor Diego de Arviceta owed Captain Antonio de Soto y Barahona 753 silver pesos, to be paid within six months.
María Calderón, a widow, granted power of attorney to the Sargento.

Mayor Diego de Arviceta was granted authority over María Viviana, a mulata criolla fugitive. María Viviana had been part of a dowry from her father, Alférez José Calderón, to her deceased husband, Captain Juan de la Madriz.

Captain Manuel de Arburola y Ribarén committed 300 pesos of cacao to a chaplaincy founded by Pedro Solano, receiving materials from houses near the Reventado River. The chaplaincy's patron is Captain Alvaro de Guevara and its chaplain is Licenciado Antonio de Guevara. Arburola y Ribarén is also obligated for an additional 75 pesos of cacao, following an earlier offering by Sargento Francisco Echavarría for the same property.

Captain Manuel de Arburola y Ribarén acknowledged a 100-peso annuity for a chaplaincy established by Doña Luisa Calvo, which burdens the same property mentioned previously. Doña Luisa Calvo is the patroness, and Licenciado José Antonio Díaz de Herrera is the chaplain. Arburola y Ribarén will redeem the 100 pesos in cacao at a rate of 20 pesos per zurrón.

people_involved: Juan López de la Rea y Soto
summary: Manuela Ramírez, a widow and daughter of Lieutenant Salvador Ramírez and Magdalena Milanés, made a codicil to her will before public notary Juan López de la Rea y Soto. She was married to the deceased Alférez Andrés Palomino, and her only surviving child, Captain Salvador Palomino, was named her heir and executor.
Sargento Mayor Francisco de la Madriz Linares, who is preparing for a trip to San Felipe de Portobelo, granted general power of attorney to his wife, Doña Rita García de Argueta.

Felipe de Umaña, son of Sargento Carlos de Umaña and Cecilia de Quirós, established a dowry for his wife, María Francisca, daughter of the widow Feliciana Chinchilla. The dowry consisted of 742 pesos of cacao, with an additional 50 pesos of cacao as arras.

Doña María de Chaves, daughter of the deceased Alférez Mayor Francisco de Chaves and Doña Francisca de Zúñiga, made her will. She was widowed three times, having children with each husband, and granted freedom to her 60-year-old enslaved woman, Petrona, after her death. Her son, Captain Vicente Andrés Polo, was named executor.
José Bernardo Fernández incurred a debt of 400 pesos of cacao to Felipe de Umaña, to be delivered in Matina.
Licenciado Manuel José González Coronel, a Presbyter Cleric, sold a cacao plantation he inherited from his father in Tuis to Sargento Mayor Juan Francisco de Ibarra for 100 pesos of cacao.
María Calvo, a widow, granted general power of attorney to Alférez José Nicolás de la Haya.

Doña Luisa de Abarca, a widow, sold an enslaved criollo man named Jerónimo, approximately 16 years old and born in her house, to Maestre de Campo Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina, a Lieutenant General, for 250 pesos.

Doña Luisa Calvo, a widow, gifted a 4-year-old enslaved girl named Micaela, daughter of her enslaved woman María, to her granddaughter Juana Josefa Miranda. Juana Josefa is the daughter of Captain Antonio Miranda and Doña Ana María Maroto, who is Luisa Calvo's daughter.

Captain Juan Manuel de Alvarado sold an enslaved man named Pablo José, 16 years old and son of the mulata Micaela, to Sargento Mayor Antonio de Utrera for 200 silver pesos. Pablo José had been a donation from Alvarado's mother, Doña Catalina de Vida Martel.
Licenciado Manuel González Coronel, a Presbyter Cleric, sold a 10-year-old enslaved boy named Juan Manuel, son of his enslaved woman Isabel, to Sargento Mayor Antonio de Utrera for 170 pesos.

Doña Luisa Calvo, a widow, established a chaplaincy for masses for her soul and that of her deceased son, Captain Gabriel Maroto, with a principal of 1000 pesos. This new foundation replaces a previous one from May 8, 1723, which was annulled due to the property being lost. The funds are secured by various properties, including houses in Cartago and cacao trees in Matina, with Licenciado José Antonio Díaz de Herrera as chaplain and Luisa Calvo as patroness, followed by Juan Díaz de Herrera.

Captain Francisco Javier de Oreamuno granted power of attorney to Doña Josefa de Hoyo y Carrazco, a widow residing in Panama, to sell his enslaved man named Antonio. Antonio had deserted from the Mosquito Indians and was acquired by Oreamuno at a public auction of confiscated enslaved people.

On January 3, 1725, Licenciado Manuel José González Coronel, a Presbyter Cleric, publicly acknowledged having gambled at the house of Maestre de Campo Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina. This event is noted under the authority of Sargento Mayor Pedro José Sáenz, a Lieutenant General.

Serrano de Reina lost over a thousand pesos to a Maestre de Campo in a dice game, but the Maestre de Campo refused to honor the agreement after winning for five months. Fearing repercussions and an impediment to his trip to Tierra Firme, Serrano de Reina was asked to issue a legal note declaring the debt a loan. He also declared that 6 slaves belonged to S.M. as their value had not yet been paid.

José Carbonero, a resident of Valle de Barba, obligated himself to Eusebia de la Concepción, a resident of Pacaca, for a mule aged two to three years, to be paid within two months. He also declared that Juan Calvo owed Eusebia another mule.

José de Campos, as the principal, along with José de Aguilar and Miguel de Quesada as guarantors, obligated themselves to Manuela de Rojas, daughter of Dorotea de Trejos, for 100 pesos cacao, payable within two years.

Captain Miguel del Aya Bolívar sold a 40-year-old black slave named José Felipe to Captain Marcos Zamora for 250 pesos cacao. José Felipe had been inherited from Miguel's father, Captain José del Aya Bolívar.

Captain Manuel de Traña, a resident of Granada, Nicaragua, obligated himself to Governor and Captain General Diego de la Haya Fernández for 465 pesos of silver. He pledged 100 mules as collateral and promised to pay within three months of his arrival in Panama.
Don Diego de la Haya Fernández cancelled the obligation made by Manuel de Traña.

Captain Domingo de Quesada, son of Alférez Alonso de Quesada and Magdalena de Aguilar, issued a dowry letter for 608 pesos, with arras of 344 pesos, to his wife Doña Antonia Bermúdez. Antonia is the adopted daughter of Captain José Antonio Bermúdez and Doña Baltasara de Escalante Panlagua.

Sergeant Major Pedro de Alvarado leased a cacao plantation of 1358 trees in Matina to Captain Luis Gutiérrez for three years at a price of 225 pesos cacao. The plantation bordered properties belonging to Captain Pedro de Moya and Feliciana Chinchilla.

Beneficiado Don Juan Antonio de Moya, Cura of this parish, leased two cacao haciendas in Matina to Lieutenant General Don Francisco Alejandro de Bonilla for three years at 250 pesos cacao. One hacienda bordered properties of Don Francisco Betancourt and Doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco.

Captain Don José Morales Tremiño and his wife Doña Juana de Ángulo obligated themselves for 200 pesos cacao, imposed on their houses in Cartago, to a Chaplaincy to be founded by Don Antonio de Utrera. Beneficiado Don Juan Antonio de Moya was the interim Chaplain, and José Cayetano, son of Utrera, was the owner.

Manuel Venegas, married to Juana Sánchez and without children, declared his wife as his sole heir. Sergeant Major Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra and Captain Juan Marín Laguna were named as his executors.

Doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco, a widow, leased a cacao plantation of 1300 trees in Matina to Captain Luis Gutiérrez for three years at 200 pesos cacao. The plantation bordered her own property and that of Beneficiado Don Juan Antonio de Moya.

people_involved: José Nicolás Sarmiento de Soto Mayor
summary: Don José Nicolás Sarmiento de Soto Mayor and his wife Doña María Catalina Ortiz de Rosas sold a cacao plantation of 700 trees in Matina to Sergeant Major Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra for 700 pesos cacao. The buyer was also obligated to pay 150 pesos to the Chaplaincy of Licenciado Don José Antonio Díaz de Herrera.
María Calvo, a free parda, granted freedom to her 55-year-old black slave of Cabo Verde caste, Ramón Duran (a) Calvo, for 200 pesos cacao.
Captain Domingo de Quesada owed Doña Petronila Valerino, a widow, 300 pesos cacao, representing the remaining value of a cacao plantation lease set to expire in October.

Captain Don José de Guzmán and his wife Doña Antonia de Echavarría Navarro obligated themselves to the Cofradía de la Concepción for 100 pesos at 5%. This debt was originally owed by Alférez Francisco de Arleguí to the Cofradía de la Concepción de Esparza and transferred through an exchange with Juan Antonio Bogarín. They mortgaged their house in Cartago.
Ayudante Matías Masís, Mayordomo of the Cofradía de la Concepción, cancelled the obligation made by José de Guzmán and Antonia de Echavarría Navarro.

Captain Don José de Mier Cevallos and his wife Doña Catalina González Camino obligated themselves to the Real Caja for 1235 pesos cacao, the value of 8 confiscated slaves. These slaves, including Felipe Cubero, María Victoria, José, and their five children (Miguel, Juana, Pablo, and two unnamed), were Catalina's property, received as a dowry after the death of her first husband, Depositario General Don Cristóbal Martín Cubero.
Lieutenant of Royal Officials, Diego Morras, certified that Licenciado Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero paid the final remainder of a deed for which his parents were obligated.
Maestre de Campo Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina, preparing for a trip to León, Nicaragua, granted general power of attorney to Captain Dionisio Salmón Pacheco.
Licenciado Manuel González Coronel, a Presbyter Cleric traveling to Panamá, left general power of attorney to Lieutenant Cayetano Muñoz.
Licenciado Antonio de Guevara y Sáenz, a Presbyter Cleric traveling to Panamá, left power of attorney to Captain Antonio de Soto y Barahona.
Captain Juan de Astúa leased a cacao plantation in Matina to Sergeant Gabriel Lobo for 16 months, for 300 pesos of cacao payable in two installments, with the second payment due by San Juan of 1726.
Licenciado Manuel González Coronel, a Presbyter Cleric preparing for a trip to Panamá on Pedro Castellanos's ship at Caldera port, left his general power of attorney to Captain José Morales Tremiño.

Juan Fernández and José Damián de Molina (as husband of Josefa Fernández Bulagay) granted power of attorney to Licenciado Antonio de Guevara Sáenz, who was traveling to Panamá and the Kingdom of Perú. The purpose was to collect 1000 pesos left to Manuel Fernández by Captain Juan de Ibáñez de Orosi, and also to collect goods left by their brother's death in Perú.

Sargento Mayor Juan Francisco de Ibarra took on an obligation of 150 pesos cacao at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by Luisa Calvo, for which José Antonio Díaz de Herrera was Chaplain. This obligation was originally on José Nicolás Sarmiento, who had it imposed on a 700-tree cacao plantation on the Matina riverbank, which Ibarra had purchased with this recognized obligation.

Captain Francisco Gutiérrez made a codicil to his 1719 will. He clarified that Marcelo, Jerónimo, Luis, and Cristóbal, previously declared legitimate sons from his first marriage to Nicolasa de Flores, were not legitimate and he disinherited them. He also mentioned his son Lieutenant Francisco Gutiérrez, who supports him, and another son named Francisco from his second marriage to Gertrudis Ruiz.

Captain Cristóbal Muñoz de la Trinidad declared that the hacienda of sugarcane fields, dwelling house, and sugar mill in the Ujarraz valley, which he purchased in 1723 from Captain Alonso Bersabé Cabeza de Vaca, actually belongs to Captain Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad, for whom he bought it with money provided for that purpose.

Cristóbal García recognized a 190-peso census at 5% interest in favor of the San Francisco Convent, encumbering sugarcane haciendas, dwelling houses, and a sugar mill in the Aserrí valley, which he bought with this lien from Licenciado José de Chaves.
Lieutenant Cayetano Muñoz, Sota Síndico of the San Francisco Convent, cancelled the 190-peso census on Cristóbal García's haciendas, in the absence of Captain Antonio de Soto y Barahona.

Captain Dionisio Salmón Pacheco, preparing for a trip to Matina, substituted the power of attorney he held from Maestre de Campo Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina to Francisca Serrano de Reina, his wife.
Cristóbal García recognized a 180-peso census at 5% interest in favor of the Cofradía de la Concepción, encumbering the same haciendas mentioned in folio 43.
Ayudante Matías Masís, Mayordomo of the Cofradía de la Concepción, cancelled the 180-peso census on Cristóbal García's haciendas.
Cristóbal García recognized a 50-peso census at 5% interest in favor of the Cofradía del Rosario, encumbering the same haciendas.
Captain Pedro de Moya, Mayordomo of the Cofradía del Rosario, cancelled the 50-peso census on Cristóbal García's haciendas.

Sargento Mayor Francisco de la Madriz Linares and Licenciado Manuel López Conejo exchanged enslaved people: Francisco received Ventura, a 26-year-old Arara man, in exchange for María, a 25-year-old Congo woman.

Gertrudis Ruiz, widow of Alférez Juan Ginés de Hinojosa, made her will. She was the legitimate daughter of Juan Ruiz and María de Santiago. With Juan Ginés de Hinojosa, she had four daughters: Francisca (married to Miguel Matamoros), Gertrudis (married to Francisco de Orozco), Josefa (married to José de Chaves), and Catarina.

people_involved: Juan López de la Rea y Soto
summary: Captain Francisco Gutiérrez, who was married for a second time, had a minor son also named Francisco Gutiérrez. His executors were Captain Pedro de Moya and Juan López de la Rea y Soto, and all his children were named as heirs.

Gertrudis Peláez, a widow, made an obligation for 50 pesos, 1.5 reales at 5% interest, in favor of the Confraternity of the Conception. This obligation was imposed on her dwelling house located in the common lands of the city.
Don Antonio de Escalante Paniagua made an obligation for 50 pesos, 1.75 reales at 5% interest, in favor of the Confraternity of the Conception.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Francisco López Conejo
summary: A dowry letter was issued for the marriage between Don Lucas José Blasco and Doña Eulalia López Conejo. Don Lucas, son of the late Alférez Marcelo Blasco and Doña Clara de Vida Martel, received goods worth 1753 pesos from Doña Eulalia's brother, Licenciado Don Manuel López Conejo, with an additional 100 pesos for arras.

Juan Fernández and his wife Doña Cayetana de Acosta leased a cacao plantation in Matina to Juan Calvo for two years. The rent was set at 100 pesos for the first year and 125 pesos for the second year, payable in cacao delivered to the city.

Captain José Felipe Bermúdez and his wife Doña Teresa de Sandoval obligated themselves to the minor son of Simón Machado and María Venegas for 150 pesos of cacao. This amount was received from the justice in the form of five mules, at the request of María Venegas, whose husband Simón Machado was lost on the coasts of Matina, to secure the inheritance for her young son.

Sargento Nicolás de Quirós, a widower, obligated himself to hold 955 pesos of cacao adjudicated to his five legitimate daughters: Antonia, Nicolasa, María, Juana, and Rosa. Each daughter received 191 pesos as inheritance from their deceased mother and his wife, María López.

people_involved: Don Diego de la Haya Fernández
summary: Don Diego de la Haya Fernández, having purchased a 'negrito' named Nicolás Policarpo for 150 silver pesos or 300 cacao pesos from Doña Josefa Nicolasa de Guevara, made an obligation in favor of the Convent of San Francisco at 5% interest. This obligation was imposed on his dwelling houses, as part of a foundation Doña Josefa had established for the Convent.

locations: plaza principal de la Iglesia parroquial
people_involved: Don Diego de la Haya Fernández
Doña Petronila de Hoyo y Carrasco
summary: Don Diego de la Haya Fernández, Governor and Captain General, and his wife Doña Petronila de Hoyo y Carrasco, founded a Chaplaincy of sung masses, to be held every Friday at the Convent of San Francisco. They endowed it with 85 pesos of cacao annually, imposing this on their large dwelling house, which cost over 6000 pesos of cacao to build and was located facing the main square of the parish church.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: The will of Sargento José de Molina, a native of Guatemala, was recorded. He was married to Josefa Fernández Bulagay and had eight children: José Antonio, María Josefa, Rafael, Nicolasa, Juan, Francisco, Águeda, and María Antonia. His executors were Sargento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra and Captain Don Pedro de Moya.

people_involved: Don Diego de la Haya Fernández
Doña Petronila de Hoyo y Carrasco
Capitán Don Miguel de Hoyo y Echavarría
Doña Agustina Blanca de la Haya
Don José de Quirós y Toledo
Licenciado Don Juan Moreno de Orejuela
Doña Josefa de Hoyo y Carrasco
Teniente General Don José de Mier Cevallos
Sargento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: The will of Don Diego de la Haya Fernández, Governor and Captain General, and his wife Doña Petronila de Hoyo y Carrasco, was recorded. Don Diego, a native of Santa María, declared José Nicolás Próspero, a 26-year-old 'pardo' man, as his natural son, leaving him a sixth of his estate. Doña Petronila, a native of Panama, left significant sums to her niece Doña Francisca Ignacia Moreno and nephew Don José Moreno. The couple named each other as reciprocal heirs and appointed several executors, including Teniente General Don José de Mier Cevallos and Sargento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra.

people_involved: Don Diego de la Haya Fernández
Doña Petronila de Hoyo y Carrasco
summary: Don Diego de la Haya Fernández, Governor and Captain General, granted general power of attorney to his wife Doña Petronila de Hoyo y Carrasco, who was preparing for an upcoming trip to Panama.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Manuel de Alvarado
Doña Petronila de Hoyo y Carrasco
summary: Sargento Mayor Don Manuel de Alvarado, Lieutenant of Royal Officials, granted general power of attorney to Doña Petronila de Hoyo y Carrasco, who was preparing for an upcoming trip to Panama.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Captain Don Francisco de Betancourt and his wife Doña María Josefa Cabral obligated themselves to the Chaplaincy founded by Sargento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra for Licenciado Don Gregorio de Moya. Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra was the patron of this Chaplaincy, and the obligation was for 900 pesos of cacao at 5% interest, previously charged to Ibarra and his wife.

people_involved: Licenciado don Juan Antonio de Moya
summary: Catalina González Camino and her husband, Capitán don Cristóbal Martín Cubero, had an imposition placed on a 5000-foot cacao plantation they had purchased. This plantation bordered land owned by Licenciado don Juan Antonio de Moya, the Cura of the city, to the west, and a stream to the east.

Teniente General don Pedro José Sáenz apprenticed Antonio, the 10-11 year old son of Francisca de Salazar, to master tailor José Cayetano Fernández. The apprenticeship was set for a duration of six years.

Doña Angela Sáenz, with judicial permission due to her husband Don Bartolomé Trujillo's absence in Portobelo, leased a cacao plantation in the Barbilla valley to Doña Baltasara de Escalante Paniagua. The two-year lease required payment of four sacks of first-quality cacao and one sack of second-quality cacao, to be delivered in the city.

people_involved: Capitán don José de Escalante Paniagua
Licenciado don Manuel de Escalante Paniagua
Capitán don Juan Sancho de Castañeda
summary: This entry records the will of Doña Ana de Escalante Paniagua, who was the legitimate daughter of Capitán don José de Escalante Paniagua and Doña Manuela de Vida Martel. She was married twice, first to Capitán don Juan Marín Sáenz and later to Capitán don Juan de Torres, and had several children and a grandson, Pedro José Sáenz, whom she raised. Her brother, Licenciado don Manuel de Escalante Paniagua, and Capitán don Juan Sancho de Castañeda were named as executors.

people_involved: Teniente General don José de Mier Cevallos
summary: This entry details the will of Doña Manuela de Salazar, daughter of Capitán don Fernando de Salazar and Doña Ambrosia de Echavarría Navarro, and widow of Capitán don Juan González Camino. She mentions her daughters, deceased siblings, and two slaves, María and Petronila. She also established a chaplaincy for masses, naming her grandson Licenciado don Manuel Cubero as chaplain, and appointed several executors including Licenciado don Manuel Martín Cubero, Teniente General don José de Mier Cevallos, and Don Gil de Alvarado.

Capitán don José Antonio Sáenz and his wife Rosa Gutiérrez sold a 5-year-old 'negrita' named Agustina, daughter of Manuela, to Doña María Francisca Alvarez for 100 pesos plata. Agustina had been given to them by Capitán Luis Gutiérrez, fulfilling the wishes of Inés Bernal, who was Rosa Gutiérrez's mother.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Licenciado don José de Chaves, a Clerigo Presbítero, sold a 48-year-old mulato named Juan to Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra for 275 pesos cacao. Licenciado de Chaves had previously acquired Juan through a purchase from Juana de Torres.

people_involved: Doña Petronila de Hoyo y Carrasco
summary: Doña Antonia de Alvarado, acting for herself and her disabled sister Doña Gertrudis de Alvarado, granted power of attorney to Doña Petronila de Hoyo y Carrasco. Doña Petronila was traveling to Panamá to collect assets remaining after the death of their father, Capitán don Jorge de Alvarado, which occurred in that city.

people_involved: Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
Doña Juana María de Soto y Barahona
Sarjento Mayor don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí
summary: This entry records the will of Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona, a native of Málaga, Castilla, and son of Pedro Alonso de Soto and Doña María de Torres Barahona. He was married to Doña Petronila de Hoces Navarro and had several children, including Doña Juana María, Antonio, Tomás, Pedro, Teresa, and Nicolás. His will also lists eleven slaves and names his wife, Sarjento Mayor don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí, and Teniente Cayetano Muñoz as executors.

people_involved: Doña Petronila de Hoyo y Carrasco
summary: Doña Catalina González Correa, a widow, granted power of attorney to Doña Petronila de Hoyo y Carrasco. This authorization allowed Doña Petronila to collect a sum of pesos owed to Doña Catalina by Alférez Juan de Leguisamo in Panamá.

people_involved: Doña Ana Teresa Masiu y Velez
Capitán don Pedro Ortiz de Rosas
Capitán don Juan Sancho de Castañeda
summary: This entry describes a dowry letter for the marriage of Don Lucas del Fierro, a native of Isla de la Palma, to Doña Josefa Ortiz de Rosas. The dowry amounted to 1389 pesos, including 400 pesos as arras, and an 8-year-old mulatilla named Bernarda valued at 300 pesos cacao. Doña Josefa is the legitimate daughter of the deceased Capitán don Pedro Ortiz de Rosas and Doña Juana de Alvarado, who is now married to Capitán don Juan Sancho de Castañeda.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: Juana Calderón, a widow, sold a 12-year-old 'negrito' named Benito to Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares for 125 pesos de plata. Benito was born and raised in Juana Calderón's house and was the son of her mulata slave, María Egipciaca.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan Antonio de Villar Hevia
summary: Capitán don Juan Antonio de Villar Hevia and his wife Doña Bernarda Martínez incurred obligations totaling 460 pesos to two Cofradías and a chaplaincy, all at 5% interest. These obligations were secured by houses in the city that bordered Josefa Estrella's lot to the north and houses formerly owned by Don Diego de Campos to the south. The Mayordomos of the Cofradías, Capitán don Pedro de Moya and Ayudante Matías Masís, delivered the houses with these charges.

This entry records the will of Antonia González, the legitimate daughter of the deceased Alférez Juan González and María de Espinosa. She mentions a child she raised named José Nicolás and appointed Licenciado don Antonio de Gue as an executor.

people_involved: Alférez Real don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín
Doña Angela de la Paz y Flores
Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara Sáenz
summary: Doña Inés de Sandoval Golfín, a widow and legitimate daughter of the deceased Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín and Angela de la Paz y Flores, made her will. Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara Sáenz was named as her executor.

Doña Petronila Valerino, a widow, leased two cacao plantations, "San Antonio el mozo" and "San Antonio el viejo," in the Matina valley to Capitán Manuel de Arburola for three years at 200 pesos of cacao annually. She refused to lease them to Capitán Domingo de Quesada, who previously administered them, due to an unpaid debt of 300 pesos of cacao. The agreement was later rescinded on October 1, 1726.

people_involved: Don Diego de Barros y Carbajal
summary: Juan Rafael Ramírez and his wife Micaela Chinchilla sold lands inherited by Micaela from her father, Gaspar Chinchilla, to don Diego de Barros y Carbajal for 110 pesos of cacao. The property was located near the paraje de los chiqueros, bordered Victoria Chacón's land, and had the Río de Paz running through it.
José Damián de Molina, a native of Santiago de Guatemala, made a codicil to his will. His main will had been executed earlier in the same year.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Jaramillo de Andrade
Capitán don Francisco Alejandro de Bonilla
summary: The will of Capitán don Jacinto Jaramillo, who died on this day, was opened at the request of Capitán Francisco González. Jacinto Jaramillo, originally from Nata, had made his will on September 3, 1725, naming his children, don Andrés Jaramillo and doña Francisca Jaramillo, as heirs, and Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo and Capitán don Francisco Alejandro de Bonilla as executors.

Capitán Juan Francisco Marín Laguna and his wife, doña María de Bonilla, committed 100 pesos of cacao at 5% interest to a chaplaincy ordered by the deceased Juan Bautista Bruno. This obligation was secured by a small farm in the city's common lands, located by the Toyogres river and bordering Capitán don Pedro de Moya's property.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan Sancho de Castañeda
Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Don Lucas del Fierro and his wife, doña Josefa Ortiz de Rosas, sold a cacao plantation of 450 trees in the Matina valley to Capitán don Juan Sancho de Castañeda for 450 pesos of cacao. Doña Josefa had inherited this property from her grandparents, don Pedro de Alvarado and doña Catalina de Vida Martel, and it bordered properties belonging to Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra and the buyer.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don José de Bonilla
summary: Capitán don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco leased a cacao plantation of 2500 trees in the Matina valley to Alférez Domingo Guerrero for two years at 300 pesos of cacao annually. Dionisio managed the entire hacienda due to the absence of his brother, Capitán don Antonio Pacheco, who owned half. The plantation bordered properties of don José de Guzmán and Sarjento Mayor don José de Bonilla.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Pedro de Alvarado
summary: Don Pedro de Moya leased a cacao plantation of 1600 trees in the Matina valley to Sarjento Aparicio Carrillo and his son Antonio Carrillo for three years at 525 pesos of cacao annually. The plantation bordered properties of Sarjento Mayor don Pedro de Alvarado and Capitán Manuel García.
Doña María de Chaves granted permission to her gravely ill son, Capitán Juan de Astúa, to make his will in her residence.

people_involved: Capitán Juan López de la Rea y Soto
summary: Capitán Juan de Astúa, son of the deceased Capitán Juan de Astúa and doña María de Chaves, made his will. He was married to doña Gertrudis Calderón but had no children with her. He acknowledged a natural daughter, Josefa Nicolasa, with María Bonilla, and left her one-sixth of his assets. Nicolás de Astúa and Capitán Juan López de la Rea y Soto were named executors, with Nicolás de Astúa also being the heir.

people_involved: El Beneficiado don Juan Antonio de Moya
Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Utrera
summary: El Beneficiado don Juan Antonio de Moya granted general power of attorney, first to Capitán don Bernardo Marín, second to Capitán don Pedro de Moya, and third to Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Utrera.

people_involved: Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
Capitán de Granaderos don José Diez de Vivar
Don Diego de la Haya Fernández
summary: Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona, acting as agent for Capitán de Granaderos don José Diez de Vivar, sold an unbaptized enslaved man named Nicolás, of Mina origin and over 25 years old, to don Diego de la Haya Fernández (Governor and Captain General) for 200 pesos. Nicolás, a fugitive from Portobelo, bore brands from the Royal Accounting Office of Portobelo and the Royal English Company in Tierra Firme. The transaction was later cancelled on February 14, 1727.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Alférez José de Acosta Arévalo committed 68 pesos of cacao, which he owed to the deceased Juan Bautista Bruno, to a chaplaincy ordered by Bruno. He mortgaged 700 cacao trees in Matina as security. The obligation was cancelled on October 14, 1728, by Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra, Bruno's executor.

people_involved: Don Diego de la Haya Fernández
summary: Don Diego de la Haya Fernández, Governor and Captain General, sold two enslaved men to Capitán José de Quirós for 500 pesos of silver. One, named Nicolás, was an unbaptized Mina man over 25 years old, whom he had purchased the previous day. The other, named Pedro, also of Mina origin, had been acquired at a public auction.

people_involved: Teniente General don José de Mier Caballos
summary: Teniente General don José de Mier Caballos and his wife, doña Catalina González Camii o, granted power of attorney to Licenciado don Ma... (name incomplete).
A power of attorney was granted to Manuel Francisco Martín Cubero, the legitimate son of the grantor, to sell an enslaved Creole man named Miguel, who is 22 years old.

Sarjento Mayor Manuel de Alvarado, acting as attorney for Sarjento Mayor Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón and his wife Angela de Guevara, committed 100 pesos of cacao to a chaplaincy to be founded as ordered by the deceased Juan Bautista Bruno. This obligation was secured on a cacao plantation in Matina, bordering properties of Captain Pedro de Moya and Feliciana de Chinchilla.

Sarjento Mayor Juan Francisco de Ibarra and his wife Catalina González Camino granted power of attorney to Petronila de Hoyo y Carrasco (wife of Governor Diego de la Haya Fernández) and Captain Juan de Viveros. They did this as legitimate heirs of Captain Matías González Camino, to collect debts from María Moreno (widow of Alonso González de Nájera) and Antonio de Aguilar, as recorded by notary Juan Rubio de Muti in Panamá.

people_involved: María Josefa de la Vega Cabra
summary: Sarjento Mayor Juan Francisco de Ibarra and his wife Catalina González Camino, along with Captain Juan Francisco de Betancourt and his wife María Josefa de la Vega Cabra, granted power of attorney to Captain Plácido Osorio Galos, a resident of Panamá. They did this as heirs of Captain Matías González Camino (father and grandfather, respectively) to collect various debts in Panamá from multiple individuals.

Francisca López, a widow, leased a cacao plantation in the Matina valley to Pedro Ortiz for two years, at a price of 200 pesos of cacao per year. The plantation bordered properties of Josefa de Hoces and Antonia de Acosta Arévalo. The lease was later rescinded on March 18, 1726.
The lease agreement between Francisca López and Pedro Ortiz for a cacao plantation in Matina, originally made on November 27, was rescinded on March 18, 1726.

Margarita Barquero sold a 7-year-old mulatto girl named Juana Josefa to Mariana López de la Flor for 150 pesos of cacao. Juana Josefa was inherited by Margarita from her parents, Ayudante Francisco Barquero and Ana de Espinosa.

María Francisca Alvarez, widow of Captain Eusebio Jiménez, and Captain José de Alvarado y Jirón as guarantor, committed 130 pesos at 5% interest to a chaplaincy established by Eusebio Jiménez as executor for Captain Juan Gregorio Ramírez. The chaplaincy's patron and chaplain was Beneficiado Juan de Rivas y Chaverri, and the obligation was secured on the 'Zapotal' hacienda.

On March 24, 1730, before Governor Baltasar Francisco de Valderrama, Captain José de Alvarado y Jirón requested cancellation of an obligation because María Francisca Alvarez and her new husband Miguel de Mata had made a new obligation. The Governor granted the cancellation based on a letter from Chaplain Juan de Rivas y Chaverri.

Margarita Barquero, single daughter of Ayudante Francisco Barquero and Ana de Espinosa, made her will. She had a daughter named Juana María and owned two enslaved mulattoes, Manuel Tomás and his mother Baltasara de los Reyes, whom she granted freedom along with Baltasara's other daughter, María Josefa. Diego de Barros y Carbajal was named as her executor.

Sarjento Mayor Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón, preparing for a trip to León (Nicaragua), granted power of attorney to Sarjento Mayor Manuel de Alvarado and his wife Angela de Guevara. This power allowed them to commit 100 pesos at 5% interest to the chaplaincy of Juan Bautista Bruno on his behalf.

Josefa Fernández, widow of Sarjento José Damián de Molina, committed 530 pesos of cacao to her children José Antonio, Manuel, Juan, Nicolasa, and Francisco de Molina, representing their paternal inheritance. She mortgaged her house in the city as security.

Gertrudis Guerrero, a widow, leased a cacao hacienda in the Matina valley to Alférez Domingo Guerrero for two years, at 150 pesos of cacao per year. The hacienda bordered properties of José de Miar Ceballos and Ayudante Miguel de Céspedes.

Alonso de Bonilla provided a dowry of 2631 pesos for his future wife, Juana Beraita de Cardóse, the legitimate daughter of Alférez Miguel Calvo and María Pereira Cardóse. The dowry included a house, an estancia named 'Nuestra Señora de la Antigua' at 'Agua Caliente' with associated structures and a plantain grove (titles given by Diego de Artieda Chirinos), livestock, and various tools and implements.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan de Sanabria Maldonado
summary: An extensive inventory and appraisal of various goods, including clothing, jewelry, household items, silver, and livestock, was conducted, totaling 269 pesos for "arras". The appraisal was performed by Captain don Juan de Sanabria Maldonado and Captain Jerónimo de Retes, and recorded by Escribano Luis Machado.

A testimony was issued in 1671 by Francisco Frz. de Miranda, based on a document originally granted before the escribano Luis Machado. This likely refers to the official record of the appraisal of goods.

people_involved: Capitán y Sarjento Mayor Alonso de Bonilla
Capitán y Sarjento Mayor Juan de Vida Martel
summary: Captain and Sergeant Major Alonso de Bonilla, the oldest ordinary mayor of Cartago, dictated his last will and testament on August 13, 1671. He requested burial in the parish church with the habit of San Francisco, detailed various financial accounts, debts, and assets, including cacao plantations in the Valle de la Reventazón for each of his nine children. He also mentioned his deceased parents, his wife Juana Benita Pereira (married over 32 years), and her deceased parents.

An unnamed individual declared their assets, including a farm, livestock, an enslaved person named Pedro, and houses in Cartago. They designated their children as heirs, with Sebastiana, the youngest daughter, receiving an improvement. Their wife was named as tutor and property holder. The declarant also mentioned leasing cacao plantations from Nuestra Señora de los Angeles and the minor children of Francisco de Solís. This declaration was granted before Captain Juan de Echavarría Navarro, and a testimony was issued in 1672 by Francisco Frz. de Miranda.

Captain Bernardo Luis Guerrero, a resident of Granada, being ill and needing to travel to Panama by sea, granted power to Captain Silvestre de Guzmán to make his will on his behalf. Guerrero also intended to dispatch 150 mules, some belonging to Bachelor Diego de Larga Espada, to Panama by land with Guzmán. He named Guzmán, Bachelor Diego de Larga Espada (Cura of Managua), and Licenciado Felipe de Lara as executors, and his legitimate children Francisco and Ana María Antonia, and his wife Francisca de Larga Espada, as heirs.

Captain Gil de Alvarado leased a cacao plantation in the Matina valley to his brother, Captain Juan Manuel de Alvarado, for one year. The plantation bordered the haciendas of Lieutenant General Bernardo Pacheco and Captain José de Guzmán, and the river and mountain. The lease was for 275 pesos of cacao, to be delivered in Matina.
The cacao plantation lease between Captain Gil de Alvarado and Captain Juan Manuel de Alvarado, established on January 21, 1726, was cancelled on July 4, 1727.

Doña Margarita de Aguiar, a widow, sold her adobe and tile houses and their lot to her nephew, Captain José Felipe Bermúdez. The property bordered the houses and lots of Doña Lorenza Muñoz to the East.

A property buyer is obligated to pay various sums: 100 pesos to the Chaplaincy of Captain Pedro Ibáñez, 100 pesos to Licenciado don Manuel de Guzmán, 100 pesos to the Cofradía del Rosario, 50 pesos to the Convento de San Francisco, 100 pesos of cacao to doña Antonia María de Otárola, and 150 pesos to Tomasina de Rojas. The property is described as being near houses owned by Tronila Valerino, Capitán Cayetano Jiménez, and Licenciado don Francisco de Ocampo.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo, acting as the Syndic General for the Convento de San Francisco, officially cancels a 50-peso debt. This debt has been transferred and is now the responsibility of Teniente don Cayetano de Alvarado and his wife, doña Juana de Guevara.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Miguel de Guzmán
summary: Licenciado don José Miguel de Guzmán, representing Licenciado don Manuel de Guzmán (patron and chaplain of the chaplaincy founded by Comisario Baltasar de Grado), and Sarjento Mayor José Felipe Bermúdez declare a debt. With accrued interest, the sum owed by Bermúdez now totals 130 pesos, for which he formally obligates himself.

people_involved: Don José Ramón de Noguera y Moncada
Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de Noguera y Moncada
doña Margarita López de la Flor
Teniente General don Diego de Barros
summary: Don José Ramón de Noguera y Moncada sells a sugarcane hacienda, including sugar mills, livestock, and houses, located in Santana, to Capitán José Antonio de Arleguí. The property, inherited from his parents Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de Noguera y Moncada and doña Margarita López de la Flor, is valued at 550 pesos in goods, equivalent to 275 silver pesos, and borders lands of Teniente General don Diego de Barros.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno
Sarjento Mayor don Manuel de Alvarado y Barros
summary: Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno, a resident of Panama who is preparing for a trip there, grants power of attorney to Sarjento Mayor don Manuel de Alvarado y Barros. This authorization allows Alvarado to collect a debt of 180 silver pesos owed to Oriamuno by Capitán Teodomiro Arias.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Manuel José de Alvarado
summary: Don Diego de Icavalceta, a resident of Granada, Nicaragua, obligates himself to Sarjento Mayor don Manuel José de Alvarado for 1875 pesos and two reales of silver. This loan was provided to outfit Icavalceta's mule train for a journey to Panama, with the mules pledged as collateral for the payment.

people_involved: don Diego de la Haya Fernández
summary: Ayudante Sebastián Trujillo de Mena, a resident of Granada, Nicaragua, obligates himself to don Diego de la Haya Fernández for 370 silver pesos. This sum was lent to Mena for the outfitting of 31 mules, which are pledged as security for the debt.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Ayudante Sebastián Trujillo de Mena acknowledges a debt of 470 pesos to Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra. Mena commits to repaying this amount within a period of six months.

Margarita Barquero grants freedom to her mulatto slave, Baltasara de los Reyes, whom she inherited from her parents Ayudante Francisco Barquero and Ana de Espinosa. Additionally, Margarita also frees Baltasara's one-year-old daughter, María Josefa.

people_involved: Teniente de Capitán Manuel López Marroquín
summary: Teniente de Capitán Manuel López Marroquín obligates himself to Ayudante Manuel de Alvarado for a total of 200 pesos. This sum comprises 100 silver pesos and an additional 100 pesos in cacao, with the payment due in the upcoming October.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Josefa Fernández, legitimate daughter of Sarjento Juan Fernández and María de Brenes, and widow of Sargento José Damián de Molina, makes her will. She names her children José Antonio, María, Manuel, Nicolasa, Juan, Francisco, Águeda, and her deceased daughter María Antonia, whose daughter is Juana, and appoints Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra as her executor.

Sarjento Miguel López, a resident of Aserrí, acknowledges a debt of 150 pesos of cacao to Teniente don Pedro Jiménez Mondragón. This amount represents the remaining balance for the lease of a cacao plantation, and López commits to paying it in July.

people_involved: Doña Margarita de Flores y Aguiar
Capitán don Juan de San Jurge de Aguiar
doña Isabel de Flores y Quiñones
Teniente General don Sebastián de Garita
summary: Doña Margarita de Flores y Aguiar, legitimate daughter of the deceased Capitán don Juan de San Jurge de Aguiar and doña Isabel de Flores y Quiñones, and widow of Teniente General don Sebastián de Garita, makes her will. Having no children, she orders the immediate freedom of Ana Margarita and her four children: Manuela, María, Sebastián, and Esteban, and names Capitanes Francisco de Flores and Cayetano Muñoz as her executors.

people_involved: Doña Margarita de Flores y Aguiar
Teniente General don Sebastián de Garita
summary: Doña Margarita de Aguiar formally grants freedom to Ana Margarita, a mulatto born in her household, and to Ana Margarita's four children: Manuela, María, Sebastián, and Esteban. This act is performed out of gratitude for having raised them as her own and in fulfillment of a directive from her late husband, Teniente General don Sebastián de Garita, as stated in his will.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra obligates himself for 100 pesos, at 5% interest in cacao, to be imposed on a cacao plantation of 700 trees located in Matina. This obligation is made in favor of a chaplaincy that is to be founded according to the instructions of Juan Bautista Bruno.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
Sarjento Mayor don José Fernández Castellanos
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra grants a general power of attorney to Sarjento Mayor don José Fernández Castellanos. Castellanos is noted to be departing for Panama.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
Sarjento Mayor don Pedro de Alvarado
Padre Guardián del Convento de San Francisco
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra, acting as the executor for Juan Bautista Bruno (a native of Riasca de la Ribera, Republic of Genoa, son of Juan María Bruno and Angela Bocafigo), establishes a chaplaincy as per Bruno's will. The chaplaincy is endowed with a principal of 768 pesos cacao, distributed among several individuals, and names Capitán Juan Francisco Marín Laguna as patron, with don Juan de Bonilla and José Manuel Marín as potential chaplains, or failing them, the Padre Guardián of the Convento de San Francisco.

Capitán don Lucas José Velazco and don Diego López Conejo obligate themselves to the Royal Treasury for 720 pesos of cacao. This sum represents the value of two piraguas that were auctioned in the name of their attorney, Capitán don José Morales Tremiño, and are to be delivered in Matina to Licenciado don Manuel López Conejo.

María Barquero, widow of Pedro Solano and Lorenzo de Mora, made her will. She named her children from both marriages, including María (married to Jerónimo García), Manuela (married to José de Abarca), and her enslaved woman Vicenta and Vicenta's five children. She appointed Captain Pedro de Moya as her executor and improved her children Francisca and Lieutenant Miguel Solano in one-third of her assets.

Doña Josefa González Camino, wife of Captain Gil de Alvarado, granted him power of attorney to sell a 25-year-old mulatto named Baltasar de Alvarado, whom she inherited from her mother, Doña Manuela de Salazar.

Captain Alonso Bersabé Cabeza de Vaca, a native of Osuna, Spain, made his will. He was married first to Juana de Moya, with whom he had children who died young, leaving only José Manuel Cabeza de Vaca. His second marriage was to Jerónima Guerrero, with whom he had sons Esteban and Andrés, and other deceased children. He appointed Ayudante General Cosme Miguel de Céspedes as his executor.

María de la Rosa Falcon, along with Captains Felipe de Meza and Blas de la Candelaria, obligated themselves to José, Félix, Efigenia, Ana María, and Pedro de Segura for 17 pesos and 6 reales, which was their paternal inheritance from Antonio de Segura.

Francisca López, a widow, leased a cacao plantation in the Matina Valley to Captains Juan Antonio de Villar Hevia and Pedro González León for two years, at 200 pesos of cacao per year. The plantation bordered the hacienda of Doña Josefa de Hoces Navarro to the west and the monte and hacienda of Doña Antonia de Acosta to the east. A margin note from May 20, 1726, indicates Pedro González León withdrew from the lease, leaving Villar Hevia as the sole lessee.

Captain Miguel de Alvarado and his wife, María de Torres, sold a 50-year-old enslaved black man named Diego Casasola to Captain Juan Antonio de Villar Hevia and Pedro González León for 275 pesos of cacao. They had previously purchased Diego from Doña Nicolasa Guerrero. A margin note from May 13, 1726, states that González León renounced his share of the purchase to Villar Hevia.
Captain Antonio de Soto y Barahona granted general power of attorney to Licenciado Don Antonio de Guevara, a Presbyter cleric who was departing for Panama.

Doña María Francisca Alvarez, a widow residing in Aserrí, obligated herself to her children, José Antonio Jiménez (5 years old), María Jerónima Jiménez (3 years old), and Ignacio Antonio Jiménez (1.5 years old), for 610 pesos from their paternal inheritance from her deceased husband, Captain Eusebio Jiménez. She mortgaged the hacienda of El Zapotal.

Feliciana Chinchilla, a widow, obligated herself to the Chaplaincy founded by the deceased Alférez Antonio Machado for 50 pesos at 5% interest, which she received from Ayudante General Cosme Miguel de Céspedes. Juan José Camacho, a cleric, was the Chaplain of this Chaplaincy. She mortgaged a cacao plantation of 2,000 trees in the Matina River plain.

Sergeant Major José de Baeza and his wife, María Magdalena Maroto, recognized two censos (liens/annuities) totaling 700 pesos on houses they took over, which previously belonged to Captain José Felipe Bermúdez and his wife Teresa de Sandoval Golfín. A margin note from November 24, 1731, states that José de Baeza presented documents freeing him from these obligations, including one from Licenciado Manuel López Conejo (Vicar Judge) and another from Father Guardian Fray Diego Ruiz.

Doña María Francisca Alvarez, a widow, sold a 6-year-old enslaved black girl named Tomasa to Captain Gil de Alvarado for 100 silver pesos. María Francisca Alvarez had previously bought Tomasa from Don José Antonio Sáenz and Doña María de la Rosa Gutiérrez.

Captain Gil de Alvarado and his wife, Doña Josefa González Camino, obligated themselves to José Antonio de Castro, a minor, for 200 pesos of cacao at 5% interest, which was part of his maternal inheritance from his deceased mother, Doña Sebastiana de Aguirre. Doña María Francisca Alvarez was to be obligated for the remaining amount. A margin note from January 15, 1735, states that José Antonio de Castro canceled the obligation.

people_involved: María Ana López de la Flor
summary: Doña María Francisca Alvarez, as principal, and Captain Antonio de Soto y Barahona and Doña María Ana López de la Flor, as guarantors, obligated themselves for 207 pesos and 3 reales of cacao to José Antonio de Castro, referring to the same person from the previous document.

Alférez Antonio Rodríguez, son of Miguel Rodríguez (native of Nicaragua) and Isabel Gómez, made his will. He was a widower of Andrea del Castillo, with whom he had four living children. He was married a second time to Isabel Godínez, with whom he had eight children. His wife and son Francisco Rodríguez were appointed as executors.

Sergeant Major Juan Francisco de Ibarra granted power of attorney, first to Doña Petronila de Hoyo Chavarría, second to Sergeant Major José Fernández Castellanos, and third to Captain Nicolás Viveros, all residing in Panama, to obligate themselves on his behalf for 4,000 pesos. He immediately mortgaged a cattle ranch in Bagaces, containing 1,000 head of cattle and 400 mares.

The Ayudante Manuel de Alvarado granted power of attorney to Captain Pedro Enríquez de Castro, a resident of Panamá, to collect a sum of money from Licenciado Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero, a Presbítero.

Captain Bernardo Marín leased a cacao plantation in Matina to Sarjento Isidro de Acosta for a period of three years. The rent for the first year was 3 zurrones of cacao, and 100 pesos of cacao for the subsequent two years.

Francisca López, a widow, leased a cacao plantation in Matina to Pedro Ortiz for three years, at a rate of 200 pesos of cacao per year. The property bordered the haciendas of Doña Antonia de Acosta and Doña Josefa de Arburola.

people_involved: Juana Josefa de Arburola y Ribaren
summary: Doña Juana Josefa de Arburola y Ribaren and Doña Antonia Josefa de Arburola, wife of the absent Sarjento Mayor Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad, leased a 1,000-tree cacao plantation in Matina to José Meneses for three years, at a rent of 6 zurrones of cacao annually.

people_involved: Juana María de Soto y Barahona
summary: The testament of Teniente Cayetano Muñoz, son of the late Jerónimo Muñoz and María de la Rosa, was recorded. He was married to Doña Juana María de Soto y Barahona, daughter of Captain Antonio de Soto y Barahona and Doña Petronila de Hoces, and had two children, José Gabriel and María Manuela, and two slaves, Leoncio and Manuela. His executors were Sarjento Mayor Manuel Antonio de Arleguí and his father-in-law, Captain Antonio de Soto y Barahona.

Captain Pedro de Moya and his wife Doña Angela Sáenz obligated themselves to José, Bernardo, and Cayetano Cartín for 150 pesos plata, the value of a 16-year-old mulatto boy named Nicolás, sold by Isabel de Quirós's executor, Captain Juan Marín Laguna. They mortgaged their house and sugar mill near the Toyogres river.

Teniente General Pedro José Sáenz canceled the obligation made by Pedro de Moya and Angela Sáenz because the original deed was not executed. The mulatto boy Nicolás was instead purchased by Sarjento Mayor Juan Francisco de Ibarra.
Licenciado Francisco de Ocarapo Golfín, a cleric, donated a five-year-old mulatto boy named Jacinto, born in his house to one of his slaves, to his brother Don Nicolás de Ocampo Golfín.
Don Juan de Ocampo Golfín, a cleric, donated a black man named Miguel Cubero, aged 22 to 23 years, to his brother Don Nicolás de Ocampo Golfín.

Don Diego de la Haya Fernández, Governor and Captain General and Mayordomo of the Cofradía de los Angeles, along with other deputies, leased a cacao plantation named "La Madre de Dios" in Matina to Sarjento Mayor Don José de Bonilla for two years. The plantation bordered properties of Doña Cayetana de Acosta, Doña Petronila Valerino, and the minor of Don Gregorio de Azofeifa.

Doña Juana Manuela Lizondo, widow of Captain Juan Guerrero, and Captain Juan Díaz de Herrera as guarantor, obligated themselves to the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora de Ujarraz for 100 pesos of cacao, an obligation she shared with her late husband. She mortgaged a house and sugar mill in Ujarraz.
The obligation made by Juana Manuela Lizondo and Juan Díaz de Herrera to the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora de Ujarraz was transferred to Teniente de Capitán Nicolás Barrantes and his wife Luisa Proa.

Alférez Manuel Soto owed Don José Francisco de Moya 300 pesos of cacao, which was part of his maternal inheritance previously managed by Doña Cayetana de Moya, the deceased wife of Manuel Soto and sister of José Francisco de Moya. Manuel Soto mortgaged pigs, houses, sugarcane fields, and a sugar mill in Ujarraz.

Doña Josefa de Aguilar, a widow, leased a cacao plantation in Matina to Captain José Felipe Bermúdez for three years at 225 pesos of cacao annually. The property bordered the haciendas of Sarjento Mayor Juan Francisco de Ibarra and Ayudante General Bernardo Marín.
Doña Josefa de Aguilar canceled the lease agreement for a cacao plantation in Matina.

Captain Juan Francisco Marín Laguna and his wife Doña María de Bonilla obligated themselves to José, Bernardo, and Cayetano Cartín, children of Francisco Cartín and Isabel de Quirós, for 37 pesos and 7 reales from their maternal inheritance. They mortgaged their dwelling house, located next to Don Pedro de Moya's house, along with its fences and livestock.

Teniente de Capitán Miguel del Castillo obligated himself to María Martina, a mestiza and minor daughter of José Bautista, an indigenous person from Ujarraz, for 50 pesos of cacao from her paternal inheritance. This sum was the price of a plantain field that was ordered to be sold and purchased by Miguel del Castillo.
Sarjento Mayor Pedro Sáenz received 50 pesos from Miguel del Castillo and canceled the obligation related to María Martina's paternal inheritance.

Doña Ana de Escalante Paniagua made a codicil to her testament from the previous year. She retracted her earlier declaration of Pedro José Sáenz as her natural grandson but, due to having raised him and her affection, left him 100 pesos for his livelihood.

Alférez Nicolás de Quirós and his wife Antonia Peláez, along with Captain Francisco Gamboa and his wife Francisca Lorenza de Quesada as guarantors, obligated themselves for 88 pesos plata to the minor children of Francisco Cartín. The guarantors mortgaged an 800-tree cacao plantation in Matina.
José Cartín canceled the obligation made by Nicolás de Quirós and Antonia Peláez, with Francisco Gamboa and Francisca Lorenza de Quesada as guarantors.

Margarita Barquero sold an eleven-year-old mulatto boy named Manuel Tomás, born in her house to a now-free mulatta, to Captain José de Alvarado y Jirón. The mulatta was inherited by Margarita from her parents, the Ayudante Francisco Barquero.

people_involved: Doña Baltasara López de la Flor
Doña Mariana López de la Flor
Sárjenlo Mayor don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí
summary: Doña Baltasara López de la Flor and Doña Mariana López de la Flor leased a cacao plantation in Matina to Teniente de Capitán Nicolás Barrantes and Francisco Guerrero for three years. The lease required ten zurrones of cacao annually, to be delivered to Cartago. This plantation was previously leased by Sárjenlo Mayor don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí and bordered the hacienda of Capitán Francisco Gamboa and 'La Ibarrita'.

people_involved: Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos
summary: Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos and his wife, Doña Catalina González Camino, incurred a debt of 100 pesos at 5% interest to the Cofradía del Rosario, whose mayordomo was Capitán José Felipe Bermúdez. They mortgaged 700 cacao trees they owned on the Matina riverbank as security for this obligation.

people_involved: Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Capitán Cristóbal Fernández and his wife, Francisca Núñez, pledged 500 pesos of cacao to a Chaplaincy to be founded by Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona. This debt was secured by three thatched houses, two plots of sugarcane, a sugar mill, and a cornfield. The property bordered the land of Alférez Manuel de Rojas (formerly Capitán don Gregorio de Chaves) and the royal road from Cartago to Paso de Montano.

people_involved: Licenciado don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
Sárjente Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
Licenciado don Hermenegildo de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: On December 15, 1734, Licenciado don Antonio de Soto y Barahona, son of Sárjente Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona and chaplain of the Chaplaincy, declared that due to Cristóbal Fernández's death, the mortgage obligation passed to Francisca Núñez and Baltasar Fernández. They subsequently sold the mortgaged hacienda to Licenciado don Hermenegildo de Alvarado y Jirón, who then assumed the debt.

people_involved: Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
Licenciado don Félix de Hoces Navarro
summary: Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona and his wife, Doña Petronila de Hoces Navarro, founded a Chaplaincy for 10 recited masses with a principal of 500 pesos, charged to Capitán Cristóbal Fernández and Francisca Núñez. Their son, Antonio de Soto y Barahona, was named the first Chaplain, with Licenciado don Félix de Hoces Navarro, Doña Petronila's brother, serving as interim Chaplain until the son's ordination.

people_involved: Don Diego de la Haya Fernández
Teniente General don José de Bonilla
summary: Don Diego de la Haya Fernández, Governor and Captain General and Mayordomo of the Cofradía de los Angeles, leased the 'La Madre de Dios' cacao hacienda (500 trees) in the Matina valley to Juan Calvo, a free mulatto. This hacienda was previously leased by Teniente General don José de Bonilla, who drowned in the Reventazón river. The hacienda bordered properties of Doña Cayetana de Acosta and Doña Petronila Velerino, and another 1,000-tree plot bordered the hacienda of the minor son of don Gregorio de Azofeifa. The lease was for three years at 100 pesos of cacao annually.

Capitán don Francisco de Bustamante became obligated for 300 pesos of silver to the minor children of the deceased Francisco Cartín and Isabel de Quirós. This amount represented the value of the auction of Cartín's former house, which Bustamante left encumbered.

Alférez Juan Masís became obligated for 880 pesos of cacao to the Chaplaincy founded by his brother, Miguel Masís, and for 550 pesos of cacao to the Chaplaincy founded by his father, Sárjente Juan Masís. The latter obligation, previously redeemed by Ayudante Nicolás de Estrada from Juan's brother José Masís, reverted to Juan upon José's death. Juan Masís charged this debt to a cacao hacienda in the Barbilla valley, comprising 1076 trees and an adjacent cleared plot.

Capitán Manuel García de Argueta founded a Chaplaincy for 5 recited masses, imposing a principal of 500 pesos on a cacao plantation of over 6,000 trees in Barbilla and another cacao hacienda named 'las 60 calles' in Matina. His son, José Manuel García de Argueta, who was studying in Guatemala, was named the first Chaplain. Manuel García de Argueta was the patron, and upon his death, his son would assume the role.

people_involved: Sárjente Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Sárjente Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra became obligated for 150 pesos of silver to the minor children of Isabel de Quirós and her first husband, Francisco Cartín. This amount was the price of a 16-year-old mulatto boy named Nicolás, who was ordered to be sold by Isabel's executor, Capitán Juan Marín Laguna.

people_involved: Sárjente Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: On February 7, 1731, José Cartín and his tutor, Don Pedro de Moya, received 75 pesos from Sárjente Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra. Separately, Cayetano Cartín, enabled by justice and with the guarantee of his stepfather Alférez Francisco Granados, also received 75 pesos from Ibarra, completing the payment for the mulatto boy Nicolás.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
Capitán don Antonio Mohedas y Alvarado
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra granted general power of attorney to Capitán don Antonio Mohedas y Alvarado, a resident of Panama City. Mohedas y Alvarado held the titles of 'veinticuatro' and 'Alcalde Ord°' in Panama.

Capitán don José de Guzmán leased a cacao plantation, divided into two parts and comprising 2,000 trees, in the Matina valley to Jerónimo Pacheco for two years. One part bordered the 'Santo Cristo' hacienda, the river, and the mountain, while the other part, named 'la Ibarrita,' bordered haciendas of Doña Luisa de Abarca and Doña María Ana Flor. The lease was for 200 pesos of cacao annually.

Juana Calderón leased a 1,000-tree cacao plantation in the Matina valley to Sarjento Francisco de Chavarría for three years, pending the presentation of her deceased father Alférez José Calderón's death records. The plantation bordered a cleared plot of the same hacienda, and the lease required 150 pesos of cacao annually, delivered to Cartago.

people_involved: Capitán José de la Cruz y Morales
summary: María de Salazar Camino, widow of Capitán Mauricio Moreno (originally from Santiago de Veragua), granted power of attorney to Capitán Cipriano Moreno, or failing him, Capitán José de la Cruz y Morales. This power was to collect debts owed to her deceased husband, which belonged to her and her 9-year-old legitimate daughter, María Josefa Moreno.

people_involved: Sárjenlo Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Don Juan de Ocampo Golfín, acting as attorney for Francisca Rodríguez, sold an enslaved black man named Antonio to Sárjenlo Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra for 200 pesos of silver. Antonio had been awarded to Francisca in the estate proceedings of her deceased husband, Cristóbal García. The power of attorney for this transaction was granted in Bagaces on May 31, 1726, before Sarjento Mayor José de Morales.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra granted general power for his business affairs.
Doña Josefa de Aguiar sold a 13-year-old 'negrito' to Lieutenant Juan Masís for 200 pesos. She had previously purchased the 'negrito' and his mother at a public auction.

Doña Nicolasa Guerrero executed her will, naming her children José Miguel, Antonia, and Jerónima as heirs, with her absent son Tomás having 100 pesos held by Doña Francisca de Astúa from a benefactor. The will also stipulated that a 'negra' named María Gertrudis belonged to her daughter Jerónima. José Miguel Guerrero and Teniente Miguel del Castillo were appointed as executors.

Captain Manuel García Argueta established a Chaplaincy for 15 annual masses, endowing it with 1,500 pesos cacao from his plantations in Barbilla and Matina. His son, José Manuel García de Argueta, who was studying in Guatemala for ordination, was named the first Chaplain.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí
Sargento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Doña Antonia Josefa de Arburola, Doña Josefa de Hoces Navarro, Doña Micaela de Arburola, Doña Catalina de Arburola, and Sargento Mayor don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí provided a 2,000 ducados bond for Sargento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad. Don Tomás, husband of Doña Antonia Josefa de Arburola, was appointed Lieutenant Accountant of the Royal Officials of the Royal Treasury.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad
Sargento Mayor don Manuel José de Alvarado y Barros
Luis Fernamio de Liendo y Goicoechea
summary: Juana Calderón, a widow, became obligated to Sargento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad for 250 pesos plata, supplied by Sargento Mayor don Manuel José de Alvarado y Barros. Don Tomás was preparing to assume the role of Lieutenant of Royal Officials. The obligation was later cancelled on June 7, 1738, by the scribe Luis Fernamio de Liendo y Goicoechea.

people_involved: Don José Nicolás Sarmiento de Soto Mayor
Sargento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Several individuals, including Alférez Francisco de Chaves and Doña Juana Calderón, provided a 2,000 ducados bond for Sargento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad. Don Tomás was preparing to assume the position of Treasurer of the Royal Treasury for the province.

people_involved: Doña Josefa de Casasola y Córdoba
Mtre. de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Don Bernardo García de Miranda established a dowry of 12,657 pesos and arras of 1,000 pesos for his fiancée, Doña Josefa de Casasola y Córdoba. The dowry included various properties, cattle, a 12-year-old 'negra criolla' named Antonia, and two 30-year-old 'negros de Guinea' named Gregorio and Damián.

Doña Antonia and Doña Gertrudis de Alvarado, daughters of the deceased Don Jorge de Alvarado and Doña Gertrudis de Echavarría, granted general power of attorney to Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara, a cleric in Panamá, for their affairs in that city. Doña Antonia was noted as the widow of Captain don José de Quesada.

people_involved: Licenciado don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
Sargento Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Licenciado don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, a cleric, became obligated to the Confraternity of the Conception, whose Mayordomo was Ayudante Matías Masís. He secured a 100 pesos obligation at 5% interest on houses in the city inherited from his father, Sargento Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín.

people_involved: Capitán de Caballos José de Quirós
Sargento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Captain of Horses José de Quirós became obligated to Sargento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad for 140 pesos plata. As collateral, Quirós pledged Nicolás, a 30-year-old 'negro'. The obligation was cancelled on June 10, 1727.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Manuel José de Alvarado y Barros
Doña Petronila del Hoyo y Carrasco
Sargento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
M. R. P. fray Manuel de Santiago
summary: Sargento Mayor don Manuel José de Alvarado y Barros declared his continued obligation to deliver 494 pesos to Sargento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra in Panamá, for M. R. P. fray Manuel de Santiago, Minister Provincial of the Order of San Jorge. The obligation was cancelled by Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra on November 3, 1727.

Captain José Felipe Bermúdez became obligated to Captain Marcos de Zamora, Judge of the fields of Aserrí, for 265 pesos plata. The obligation was cancelled by Captain Marcos de Zamora on August 8, 1730.

Miguel de Mora received 425 pesos cacao from his deceased mother Catalina Delgado's estate. After deductions for funeral and legal costs, 364 pesos remained to be divided among him and his siblings Manuel and Juan de Mora. Miguel became obligated to his brothers for their shares, with Juan Julián de los Reyes as guarantor.

Alférez Francisco Granados, son of Francisco Granados and Francisca Brígida Chacón, provided a dowry of 501 pesos and 100 pesos arras to his future wife, Isabel de Jesús, daughter of Sargento Lucas de Jesús and Gregoria Várela.
Teniente Francisco Granados and Sargento Lucas de Jesús cancelled the previous dowry escritura, as another one with a different appreciation and valuation of goods had been granted.
Capitán José Felipe Bermúdez obligated himself for 200 pesos of cacao to B. don Manuel González Coronel.
The obligation made by Capitán José Felipe Bermúdez to B. don Manuel González Coronel was cancelled.

people_involved: D. José Antonio López del Corral
doña Francisca de Arburola y Ribarén
Sargento Mayor don Antonio López del Corral
Capiátn Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribarén
summary: D. José Antonio López del Corral, son of Sargento Mayor don Antonio López del Corral and doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco, provided a dowry letter of 1,783 pesos and 1,000 pesos arras to his future wife, doña Francisca de Arburola y Ribarén, daughter of Capiátn Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribarén and doña Josefa de Hoces Navarro.

people_involved: don Alonso Bersabé Cabeza de Vaca
summary: Capitán Luis Gutiérrez and his wife doña Francisca de Aguiar obligated themselves for 550 pesos of cacao at 5% to José Manuel, son of don Alonso Bersabé Cabeza de Vaca and doña Juana de Moya. This debt was previously held by Capitán Manuel García de Argueta, and they mortgaged houses and a mill in Barba, located by the Río Segundo.

Capitán Juan Sancho de Castañeda and his wife doña Juana de Alvarado obligated themselves for 300 pesos of silver to the minor doña María Josefa Tazón, or in her default, to Capitán don Pedro de Molina, from whom they received the money.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí
summary: Capitán Manuel García de Argueta leased a cacao hacienda named 'las sesenta calles' in the Matina valley, and another adjacent piece of hacienda, to Sarjento Mayor don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí for three years. The rent for the main hacienda was 9 zurrones of cacao annually, and for the smaller piece, the first year was free, followed by 100 pesos of cacao in each of the subsequent two years.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad leased a sugarcane hacienda with a sugar mill and a thatched house in Ujarraz to José Manuel de Segura for three years. They agreed to split the profits equally after deducting expenses.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Don José Antonio del Corral obligated himself for 543 pesos to Sarjento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad, who was acting as Lieutenant of royal officials for the Royal Treasury and Box.

people_involved: Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
B. don Félix de Hoces Navarro
summary: Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona granted general power of attorney for his affairs in Nicaragua to B. don Félix de Hoces Navarro, a qualifier of the Holy Office.

people_involved: Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero
Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero, a priest, obligated himself to the Convento de San Francisco for 300 pesos of silver at 5% for the value of houses and a plot of land. He had purchased these properties from the Convento's Syndic, Capitán Antonio de Soto y Barahona, and they had previously belonged to Licenciado don Manuel de Panlagua, carrying this obligation.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra, General Syndic of the Convento de San Francisco, cancelled the obligation related to the houses and land bought by Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero.

Juana Calderón, a widow, leased a cacao plantation with 900 trees to Capitán Francisco de Chavarría for 3 years at a price of 4 zurrones of cacao annually. This hacienda was left by her father, Alférez José Calderón, to establish a chaplaincy, and was given to her while the probate of her father and his executor, Capitán Juan de Astúa, was pending.

Capitán Francisco de Chavarría and his wife Feliciana Calvo obligated themselves to Teniente don Francisco de Alvarado for 300 pesos, the value of a house with fences and a plantain grove in Ujarraz. Alvarado had inherited this property upon the death of his mother, doña Juana de Aguirre, and the house was mortgaged.

Doña Francisca de Astúa, daughter of Capitán Juan de Astúa and doña María de Chaves, and widow of Capitán Juan de Bonilla, made her testament. She named her seven children (doña María, doña Francisca, doña Josefa, don Juan, doña Juana Benita, don José, and doña Antonia) and her granddaughter doña María Manuela Jiménez. Her sons-in-law, Capitanes Francisco Jiménez and Juan Francisco Marín Laguna, were appointed as executors.

people_involved: Sárjente Mayor don Antonio de Utrera
summary: Sárjente Mayor don Antonio de Utrera, a native of Almería in the Kingdom of Granada, made his testament. He was the legitimate son of don Sebastián de Utrera and doña María Medina, married to doña Josefa de Moya, and had two surviving children, José Cayetano and Isabel Ramona. His wife, who was the widow of Capitán don José Rivas, was named as his executor, and his children as heirs.

people_involved: Sárjente Mayor don Antonio de Utrera
Sarjento Mayor Manuel José de Alvarado
summary: Sárjente Mayor don Antonio de Utrera cancelled a debt of 250 pesos to Sarjento Mayor Manuel José de Alvarado, as related in his testament.

people_involved: Capitán don Diego de Barros y Carvajal
José de la Cruz y Morales
don Miguel de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Capitanes don Francisco Garrido, don Diego de Barros y Carvajal, José de la Cruz y Morales, Mateo de las Alas, don José Lebrón, don Miguel de Alvarado y Jirón, Sebastián Amores, and Teniente Juan Masís provided a bond of 4,000 pesos (500 pesos each) for don Baltasar Francisco de Valderrama to serve as Governor and Captain General.

people_involved: Sárjente Mayor don Antonio de Utrera
Sarjento Mayor don Juan de Castro
summary: Sárjente Mayor don Antonio de Utrera and his wife doña Josefa Moya sold a 19-year-old mulata slave named Paula to Sarjento Mayor don Juan de Castro, a resident of Guatemala, for 270 pesos of silver.

people_involved: Licenciado don Juan Antonio de Moya
Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Moya
summary: Licenciado don Juan Antonio de Moya, a priest of half-benefice in this city, made his testament. He was the legitimate son of Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Moya and doña Isabel de Alvarado. B. don Manuel González Coronel was named as his executor.

people_involved: Capitán José Nico'ás de la Haya
Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Following the death of Alférez Manuel de Soto, his assets were auctioned. Capitán José Nicolás de la Haya acquired Soto's thatched house, fences, two sugarcane fields, and a sugar mill in Ujarraz for 300 pesos. Of this, 100 pesos were for a chaplaincy founded by Br. don Gregorio de Moya, whose patron was Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra, and the remaining 200 pesos were to be paid within two years, with a slave as collateral.

A house, a sugarcane field, and fences in Matamoros were sold for 200 pesos. 100 pesos were designated for the Chaplaincy founded by Francisco Bonilla, whose patron and chaplain is Licenciado Manuel Cubero, with the remaining 100 pesos to be paid within two years.
On July 20, 1746, Captain Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra received 100 pesos from José Nicolás del Haya. This payment was for the Chaplaincy of Don Gregorio de Moya, of which Ibarra is the patron.

General Diego de la Haya Fernández became obligated to Captain Diego Guerrero, a resident of Granada, Nicaragua, for 1,689 pesos and 4 reales. This debt arose from accounts with the deceased Maestre de Campo Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina, father of Diego Guerrero's wife Francisca Serrano de Reina and her sister María Josefa Serrano de Reina. Diego de la Haya Fernández was to pay 1,000 pesos within three months and the remainder four months later.

On January 11, 1729, Doña Francisca Serrano de Reina, identified as the wife of Captain Dionisio Salmón Pacheco and substitute attorney for Don Diego Guerrero, received 100 pounds of purple thread from the debtor. This payment, combined with a previous abono of 289 pesos and 4 reales, left only 100 pounds of thread remaining on the debt.
On February 25, 1729, in the city of Espiritusanto de Esparza, Don Diego Guerrero fully canceled the obligation owed by General Diego de la Haya Fernández.

General Diego de la Haya Fernández donated houses he built on half a plot of land in 'this city' to Ana Efigenia, a poor and noble maiden. Ana Efigenia is the legitimate daughter of the deceased Captain Domingo García de Estrada and Doña Catalina González Correa. The property was bordered by the royal street, houses of Sergeant Major Pedro José Sáenz, houses of José de Guzmán, another half plot and house belonging to the Church and Chaplaincy of Juan José Camacho, and a plot of Angela María de Arleguí.

Manuela de Rojas, wife of Captain Marcos Zamora, granted power to her husband to jointly execute a deed of obligation. This deed was for the establishment of a Chaplaincy for the soul of Juana Sagaste, and it was granted in their home in Aserrí, before her husband, who served as the Lieutenant Judge of the fields.

Captain Marcos de Zamora, acting for himself and his wife Manuela de Rojas, obligated himself for 400 pesos at 4% interest. This obligation was in favor of the Chaplaincy founded by Juana Sagaste, and they imposed it upon their dwelling houses in Aserrí.

Lieutenant Antonio de Ángulo and Doña Francisca de Alvarado, along with Captain José de Morales Tremiño and his wife Doña Juana de Ángulo as guarantors, obligated themselves to Captain Marcos de Zamora for 400 pesos. They pledged a mulatta named Eugenia and a black man named Diego as collateral for this obligation.

Pedro López, a native of Atirro, assisted by his defender Captain José de Mier Cevallos, sold cacao haciendas in the area named 'Tuís' to Licenciado José Díaz de Herrera, a Presbyter cleric.
