These haciendas, inherited from his deceased father Juan López (former Governor of Atirro), comprised 965 cacao trees, valued at 2 reales each, totaling 241 pesos and 2 reales.

Lieutenant José Javier de Quesada and his wife Doña María Josefa Pacheco sold the house of Captain Bernardo Pacheco, who was María Josefa's father and José Javier's father-in-law, to Lieutenant Manuel de Alvarado for 250 pesos in cacao. Of this amount, 150 pesos belonged to Doña Francisca Pacheco due to a donation from Doña Clara de Esquivel for her share in the house, which was located in 'this city' behind the former house of Diego de Cárdenas.
Captain Bernardo Pacheco provided a letter authorizing the sale of his house by José Javier de Quesada and María Josefa Pacheco.
On August 19, 1729, the buyer, Manuel de Alvarado, presented proof of having paid the 150 pesos belonging to Doña Francisca Pacheco, and the obligation for that portion of the sale was canceled.

people_involved: María de la O y Céspedes
summary: Doña Isabel de Ocampo Golfín, widow of Alférez Nicolás de Céspedes, ceded houses and a 50-vara plot to Sergeant Major José de Morales and his wife Doña María de la O y Céspedes, who was Isabel's daughter. The property was bordered by houses of Francisco de la Madriz, José de Guzmán, Angela María de Arleguí, and José de Alvarado. The property carried a 400-peso encumbrance, with 200 pesos for Licenciado Francisco de Ocampo Golfín (her nephew and chaplain of Juana de la Portilla's Chaplaincy), 100 pesos for Licenciado Manuel de Guzmán (absent in Guatemala), and 100 pesos for the Confraternity of the Conception.

people_involved: María de la O y Céspedes
summary: Sergeant Major José de Morales and his wife Doña María de la O y Céspedes obligated themselves to Doña Isabel de Ocampo Golfín, who was María's mother and José's mother-in-law, for 437 pesos in cacao. This amount represented the remaining price for the previous cession of houses and land.
On May 23, 1729, Doña Isabel de Ocampo Golfín canceled the obligation related to the remaining price of the cession of houses and land.

people_involved: Micaela de Zamora Riva y Agüero
Jerónima de la Riva y Agüero
summary: A dowry letter was issued for Sergeant Francisco Monestel, legitimate son of the deceased Matías Monestel and Nicolasa de Benavides, in favor of his future wife Doña Micaela de Zamora Riva y Agüero, legitimate daughter of the deceased Captain Diego de Zamora and Doña Jerónima de la Riva y Agüero. The dowry was 870 pesos in silver, with 600 pesos as arras.

Captain Juan Sánchez de Camaño, a native of Galicia, made his testament. He declared his debtors and instructed his executors to collect the debts and send the funds to Panamá, then to Guayaquil to Lorenza de Mao, the mother of his children, or to his sons Isidro Sánchez de Camaño and the younger Juan Sánchez de Camaño. His executors were Licenciado Manuel González Coronel and Sergeant Major Juan Francisco de Ibarra, and the testament was written by Captain Bernardo Marín.
Captain Juan Sánchez de Camaño revoked a legacy of 50 pesos that he had ordered in his previous testament to Ana Josefa Murillo.
Doña Luisa Calvo, a widow, made a donation to an unnamed Licenciado.

Licenciado don José Díaz de Herrera sold the 25-year-old black slave Miguel to Alférez Francisco Gutiérrez for 400 pesos cacao. Miguel had been previously donated to Díaz de Herrera by his unnamed grandmother, and before that, Miguel had inherited from Capitán Gabriel Maroto, who was deceased.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
don Francisco de Paula y Salazar
summary: Doña Catalina González Camino, wife of Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra, donated 200 pesos of cacao to her niece, doña María Josefa Cabral, wife of Capitán don Francisco de Betancourt. This cacao was part of her inheritance as the legitimate daughter of the deceased Capitán don Matías González Camino and doña Ana de Peralta, and it came from a settlement against her uncle, don Francisco de Paula y Salazar, related to his father don Francisco de Salazar's administration of the Royal Treasury.

people_involved: Capitán don José Antonio de Arleguí
Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
summary: Doña Angela María de Arleguí, a widow, and her son, Capitán don José Antonio de Arleguí, sold a mulato named Diego, aged 18 to 20 years, to Capitán don Tomás López del Corral for 300 pesos cacao.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Don Miguel Sarmiento de Valladares, a resident of León, Nicaragua, obligated himself to Capitán don Juan de Ocampo Golfín for 332.5 pesos cacao, to be paid within the month. This obligation was cancelled on November 6, 1727.

Doña Gregoria Hidalgo, widow of Alférez Juan Miguel Cervantes, was involved in a criminal case concerning her husband's death, which involved a wound to the neck. She was condemned to personal and procedural costs, and to be banished from her home and all valleys for a year, living in the city under judicial supervision. This obligation was made because the cause of her husband's death could not be fully ascertained due to the escape of Andrés Miguel de los Reyes from jail.
Don Juan José Ramírez Corajo obligated himself to doña Josefa de Hoces Navarro for 423 pesos 4 reales plata, payable within three months.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
Licenciado don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
B° don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
summary: Teniente Antonio de Ángulo, as principal, and several guarantors, obligated themselves for 1,600 pesos plata, the value of a cacao hacienda with 1,304 fruit trees in the Matina valley. This hacienda, along with a slave named Diego, was previously owned by the deceased B° don Diego de Ángulo Gascón and was auctioned to Ángulo on August 24 of the same year.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí
Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí, legitimate son of the deceased Capitán Francisco de Arleguí and doña Juana de Echavarría, made his will. He was married to doña Gracia Gertrudis Navarro and had eleven children, and also listed five slaves. His wife and Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona were named as executors.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra and his wife doña Catalina González Camino obligated themselves for 750 pesos cacao, the price for which the office of regidor and Alce. Mayor provincial de la Santa Hermandad was auctioned to Ibarra. This obligation was cancelled on October 1, 1732, by Capitán don Tomás López del Corral.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra sold a piece of land to Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona for 75 pesos cacao. The land was described as an "embolsada" going up towards the volcano's mountain range, bordering a river to the East and the seller's own pasture ("las huacas") to the West.

people_involved: Capitán don Diego de Barros y Carvajal
summary: Capitán don Diego de Barros y Carvajal obligated himself to the Cofradía del Sacramento for 150 pesos at 5%, secured by a cacao plantation of 1,000 trees in Matina.

people_involved: El Licenciado don José Díaz de Herrera
summary: Licenciado don José Díaz de Herrera, a cleric, sold a stone enclosure in the Ujarraz valley, towards Pedregal, to doña Juana Manuela Lizondo, widow of Capitán Juan Guerrero, for 100 pesos cacao. This enclosure was built by doña María de Retes, who lived there for many years, and Díaz de Herrera had inherited it from his parents, who bought it from Sarjento Mayor Pedro José Sáenz.

Agustín Leitón, as principal, and doña Luisa Calvo, a widow, as guarantor, obligated themselves to Capitán don Pedro de Moya for 113 pesos cacao, payable in the following January. This debt originated from a lawsuit by Moya against Agustín Leitón and his brother, Capitán Alejandro Leitón, concerning a memory of clothes that Alejandro Leitón had brought to the city and which Agustín Leitón possessed.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón
doña Angela de la Paz y Flores
Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto
Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Licenciado Antonio de Guevara, a cleric, as principal, and two guarantors, obligated themselves for 500 pesos at 5% to a Capellanía founded by doña Angela de la Paz y Flores, and for 100 pesos at 5% to the Convento de San Bartolomé de Barba. These obligations were secured by lands in San Juan, previously owned by the deceased Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto, to which Licenciado Guevara had made an opposition. The 100 pesos obligation was cancelled on November 3, 1733, by Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo.

people_involved: El Licenciado don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Licenciado don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, a cleric, sold a building plot in the city to doña Baltasara de Escalante Paniagua, a widow, for 50 pesos. The plot was inherited from his parents and was encumbered with a 50-peso obligation to the Convento de San Francisco, which the buyer agreed to recognize. The plot bordered houses of doña Baltasara, doña Águeda Pérez de Muro, the seller's own plot, and a house of doña Nicolasa Martínez.

people_involved: Capitán don Pedro Enríquez de Castro
summary: María de Salazar, widow of Capitán Mauricio Moreno and resident of the Aserrí valley, granted power of attorney to Capitán don Pedro Enríquez de Castro.

Santiesteban, residents of Panamá, are authorized to collect 400 or more pesos from Cipriano Moreno. This debt is related to mules left in Panamá after the death of Santiesteban's husband, and José de Ascuraín is a guarantor for Cipriano Moreno.
Licenciado Don Manuel Conejo, a Presbyter cleric, grants general power of attorney to Captain Don José de Morales Tremiño.

Don Miguel Sarmiento Valladares, a resident of León, Nicaragua, makes his will. He names his wife, Doña Juana Vidaurre, as his heir and appoints Don Bernardo García de Miranda and Don Santiago Vidaurre as executors. He is the son of Don Antonio Sarmiento de Valladares and Doña María Paz y Estrada, and married to Doña Juana Vidaurre, daughter of Captain Don Bartolomé Vidaurre and Doña Juana de Salazar y Carrión.

Juana Calderón, a widow, obligates herself to the Cofradía de las Animas for 500 pesos at 5% interest to fund masses for her deceased father, Alférez José Calderón. This obligation is secured by a cacao plantation in Matina, which her father had left to establish a Chaplaincy.
Sarjento Mayor Don Baltasar Francisco de Valderrama, Governor and Captain General, grants general power of attorney to Captain Don Francisco de Dios, a resident of Guatemala.

General Don Diego de la Haya Fernández grants general power of attorney to Captain Don José de Mier Cevallos and, secondarily, to Captain Don Felipe Jiménez, Chancellor of the Royal Audiencia of Guatemala.

people_involved: Lorenzo Antonio de la Granda y Balvín
José Agustín de Estrada Azpeitia y Sierra
summary: Sarjento Mayor Don Francisco de la Madriz Linares grants general power of attorney to Licenciado Don Rafael García de Argueta and Captain Don José de Mier Cevallos to collect debts. Specifically, they are to collect 10,937 tostones, 3 reales, and 1 maravedí from Don Francisco Montojo y Echavjrría, owed to the estate of the former Governor Don Lorenzo Antonio de la Granda y Balvín, and 230 pesos from Don José Agustín de Estrada Azpeitia y Sierra, also owed to Don Lorenzo Antonio.
Sarjento Mayor Don José Fernández Castellanos grants general power of attorney to Doña Felipa Sendin de Soto Mayor, his wife.

José Gamboa and his wife Doña Petronila Vélez obligate themselves to the Chaplaincy founded by Captain Pedro Ibáñez, for which Licenciado Don Manuel López Conejo is patron and chaplain. They receive 150 pesos at 5% interest from Sarjento Mayor Don Francisco de la Madriz Linares, securing the obligation with their property in Aserrí.

Licenciado Don José de Chaves, a Presbyter cleric, sells an enslaved man named Diego, 30 years old, to Sarjento Mayor Don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón for 210 pesos of cacao. José de Chaves had previously purchased Diego from Captain Don Juan de Villar Hevia.

Captain de caballos corazas Don Tomás del Corral grants a dowry letter to his wife Doña Francisca de Ibarra, daughter of Sarjento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra and the deceased Doña Petronila de Moya. They married on January 12, 1727. The dowry includes money, cacao, cattle, and two enslaved women, Manuela Cayetana and Eugenia.

locations: Real y Supremo Consejo de Indias
summary: Sarjento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra, Regidor and Provincial Alcalde Mayor of the Santa Hermandad, grants power of attorney to Don Atanasio González Ramírez de Zarate, Don José de Leticia, and Don Marcos Antonio de Verastigui, all residents of Madrid, to obtain confirmation of his title before the Royal and Supreme Council of the Indies.

Captains Gregorio Yañez Farias and Francisco Farias, traders, grant power of attorney to Sarjento Mayor Don Francisco de la Madriz Linares to obtain licenses from the Governor and Captain General for their ships, 'Nuestra Señora de Regla' and 'Nuestra Señora del Rosario, San José y las Animas,' to travel between the port of La Caldera, Panamá, and other South Sea ports.

María Manuela Zeledón, widow of Sarjento Jerónimo Gutiérrez, leases a cacao plantation of 500 trees in the Matina valley, specifically in Barbilla, to Sarjento Juan Tablera, a free pardo. The plantation borders the property of Captain Francisco Gutiérrez, her father-in-law, and the lease is for 3 years at 100 pesos per year.

Mateo de Altamirano, traveling to León, Nicaragua, grants power of attorney to Captain Cayetano Muñoz y Bermúdez to collect a sum of goods from the estate of the deceased Don Miguel Sarmiento de Valladares. Mateo acts on behalf of his master, Licenciado Don Salvador de Altamirano, who had already made a claim against the estate.

Captain Sebastián Guillen and his wife María Magdalena de Orozco obligate themselves to the Chaplaincy founded by Captain Pedro Ibáñez, for which Licenciado Don Manuel López Conejo is patron and chaplain. They receive 200 pesos at 5% interest from Sarjento Mayor Don Francisco de la Madriz Linares, securing the obligation with their dwelling house in the ejidos of this city.

Captain Juan Jiménez, a resident of Barba, grants power of attorney to Captain Don Pedro Monge to represent him in this Gobernación in a lawsuit against Captain Francisco Farias, a trader in the port of La Caldera.

An incomplete entry lists several individuals, including Sarjentos Mayores Don Francisco de la Madriz Linares and Don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón, and Captains Don Cayetano Muñoz y Bermúdez, Don Alvaro de Guevara, Don José Felipe Bermúdez, and Don Miguel de Alvarado Ji...

Juan José de Arguello, Mateo de las Alas, don Andrés de Salazar, Gerardo Azofeifa, and Ayudante Nicolás de Estrada provided a guarantee of 2,000 ducados for Sargento Mayor don Manuel de Alvarado to serve as Lieutenant Accountant of the Royal Treasury and Royal Coffers.

Doña Angela Sáenz leased a cacao plantation in Barbilla, bordering the estate of her aunt Doña Baltasara Escalante Paniagua, to Capitán Cayetano Muñoz for three years at 100 pesos cacao per year. The lease was later cancelled.

Feliciana Chinchilla, a widow, leased a 1,200-tree cacao plantation in the Matina valley to her son José Bernardo and son-in-law Felipe de Umaña for three years. The plantation bordered don Pedro de Alvarado's estate to the East and Ruiz's estate to the West, with an annual rent of 200 pesos cacao in the city or 250 pesos in Matina.
The Teniente General arranged for José Cortés, a 14-year-old free mulatto and son of the deceased Juan Cortés, to be apprenticed to Master Armorer Francisco del Campo for a period of five years.
The Teniente General arranged for 8-year-old Juan de Campos, son of Antonio Campos and Estéfana Picado, to be apprenticed to Francisco Carrillo, a master blacksmith, for six years.

Capitán don Miguel de Alvarado and his wife doña María de Torres pledged 286 pesos to a Chaplaincy established by doña Sebastiana de Alvarado, with Licenciado don Hermenegildo de Alvarado as Chaplain and Capitán don Gil de Alvarado as patron. They mortgaged houses in the city's common lands. The obligation was cancelled by Capitán don Gil on November 15, 1734.

people_involved: don Miguel de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Doña Gertrudis Guerrero leased a cacao plantation in the Matina valley to Capitán don Miguel de Alvarado y Jirón for two years, at 106 pesos cacao per year, to be delivered in the city.

people_involved: don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: Capitán don José de Alvarado and his wife doña Josefa López Conejo pledged 100 pesos at 5% interest to a Chaplaincy founded by Capitán Pedro Ibáñez, with Licenciado don Manuel López Conejo as patron and Chaplain. Sargento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares redeemed this obligation, and houses in the city were mortgaged.

people_involved: don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
doña María de León y Garavito
don Pedro de León y Garavito
summary: Don Pedro Sánchez Monge, a bachelor from Lebrija, Spain, made his will, stating his assets and debts belonged to Sargento Mayor don Baltasar Francisco de Valderrama. He named his father and brothers as heirs and Sargento Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona as executor. On August 6, he secretly confessed to Licenciado don Manuel González Coronel that he was married in Cádiz to doña María de León y Garavito, contradicting his will, and authorized the confessor to reveal this secret after his death, declaring his wife as his true heir.

Capitán don Juan de Ocampo Golfín granted power of attorney to Licenciado don Rafael García de Argueta, a cleric residing in Guatemala, to secure for him one of the vacant offices of Regidor and Alférez Mayor or Regidor and Alguacil Mayor in this province before the Royal Audiencia.

people_involved: don José Francisco de Cásasela y Córdoba
don José de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Capitán don Francisco Garrido and his wife doña Águeda Pérez de Muro founded a Chaplaincy for 25 recited masses, endowing it with 2,000 pesos secured by two cacao plantations in Matina. Their son, don José Francisco de Cásasela y Córdoba, who was studying in Guatemala to be ordained, was named the first Chaplain, with the succession passing to his brother don Juan Manuel de Casasola, and then to the Convent of San Francisco.

people_involved: don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Capitán Pedro Enríquez de Castro, a resident of Cádiz, made his will. He was married to doña Ana Cantero de Luna and had four children: doña María, José, Andrés, and doña Juana Sebastiana de Castro. He named Licenciado don Manuel González Coronel and Sargento Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona as executors, and his wife and children in Spain as heirs.

people_involved: Doña Gracia Gertrudis de Hoces Navarro
don José Manuel García de Argueta
summary: Doña Gracia Gertrudis de Hoces Navarro, widow of Sargento Mayor don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí, obligated herself to Capitán Manuel García de Argueta for 175 pesos cacao. This obligation was cancelled on February 17, 1736, by Licenciado don José Manuel García de Argueta, acting as his father's executor.

María Machado, natural daughter of Capitán Antonio Machado and Magdalena Milanés, made her will. She was married to Gregorio Martínez, with whom she had five children, only one of whom, Magdalena Martínez, was still alive and married. Her granddaughter, Manuela Quirós, was the daughter of her deceased daughter Francisca Martínez. She named her son-in-law Francisco de Mora and her nephew Miguel de Aguilar as executors.
Capitanes don Gil de Alvarado and don José de Alvarado owed Capitán don Antonio Salmón Pacheco 200 pesos in silver, to be paid within one year.

people_involved: Alcaldes y naturales del pueblo de Aserri
summary: The Mayors and natives of the Aserri pueblo sold a plot of land called 'Santiago de la Granadilla', which they had purchased from Sargento Mayor Alonso de Bonilla, to Licenciado don José de Chaves, a Presbyter, for 100 pesos.
Capitán Mateo de las Alas and his wife Francisca Loria, residents of Barba, obligated themselves for 386 pesos cacao to the Cofradía de la Vera Cruz.
Manuel de Arburola y Ribarén cancelled an obligation related to houses that previously belonged to Captain Gregorio de Chaves.
Captain Dionisio Salmón Pacheco owed his brother, Captain Antonio Salmón Pacheco, 416 pesos in cacao. This debt was cancelled on March 9, 1729.

José Cascante and his wife Josefa de Mata, residents of Barba, established a Chaplaincy for 5 recited masses. The principal of 100 pesos was charged to Rafael Delgado and his wife Beatriz Salomona de Morales, with Juan José Solís, son of Beatriz and stepson of Delgado, named as the Chaplain while studying in Guatemala.

Doña Antonia López de la Flor sold a 23-year-old mulato named Bartolomé de la Flor to Captain Juan de Ocampo Golfín for 400 pesos plata, with the buyer obligated to pay 5% interest. The contract was later rescinded on July 21, 1733.

Alférez José de Acosta Arévalo transferred a 400-tree cacao plantation in Matina, received as a donation from his mother Josefa de Aguilar, to the minor Cayetano Azofeifa Alvarado. The transaction, assisted by Cayetano's curator Sergeant Major Francisco de la Madriz Linares, involved a price of 516 pesos, with portions allocated to a debt owed to Cayetano, a Chaplaincy founded by Juan Bautista Bruno, and cash received by Acosta Arévalo.

people_involved: Juana María de Soto y Barahona
summary: Captain Cayetano Muñoz Bermúdez and his wife Juana María de Soto y Barahona, purchasers of the former residence of Baltasara Paniagua, acknowledged existing censos on the property. These included obligations to the Holy Church's Chaplaincy, a Chaplaincy patroned by Sergeant Major Juan Francisco de Ibarra, and another patroned by Captain Gil de Alvarado; the 300 pesos censo was cancelled by Licenciados Manuel González Coronel and José Antonio Díaz de Herrera on December 20, 1730.

The minor Cayetano Azofeifa Alvarado, assisted by his curator Sergeant Major Francisco de la Madriz Linares, acknowledged a 68-peso censo at 5% interest. This censo, favoring the Convent of San Francisco and belonging to the Chaplaincy of Juan Bautista Bruno, was imposed on the cacao plantation he acquired on October 14th.

The minor Cayetano Azofeifa Alvarado, through his curator Sergeant Major Francisco de la Madriz Linares, leased the cacao plantation in Matina (acquired on October 14th) to Juan de Carmona and Salvador de Aguilar. The lease was for 3 years at 200 pesos of cacao per year, bordering the hacienda of Pedro Jiménez Mondragón to the North and the 'Madre de Dios' de los Angeles hacienda to the West.

Captain Diego de Aguilar established a Chaplaincy for 12 recited masses, with a principal of 500 pesos secured by cattle in 'this valley.' Juan José Solís, legitimate son of Eugenio Solís and Beatriz Salomona, currently studying in Guatemala, was named the first Chaplain, and Diego de Aguilar was the patron.

Captain Diego de Aguilar founded another Chaplaincy for recited masses, with a principal of 500 pesos. This was also secured by cattle in 'these valleys,' and Licenciado Antonio de Guevara was named the Chaplain, with Diego de Aguilar as the patron.

Sergeant Major Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad granted general power of attorney to his brother, Captain Jerónimo Muñoz de la Trinidad, a resident of Santiago de Guatemala. In second place, he granted power to his other brother, Captain Cristóbal Muñoz de la Trinidad, also a resident of Santiago de Guatemala.

Captain Juan de Ocampo Golfín incurred obligations totaling 420 pesos, secured by a 6-caballería land plot named 'Santiago de la Granadilla' in the valleys of Aserrí, which he acquired from Licenciado José de Chaves. These obligations included amounts for the Convent of San Francisco, the Confraternity of La Concepción, and the Confraternity of El Rosario, all at 5% interest.

Sergeant Major Pedro Sáenz obligated himself for 200 pesos of cacao at 5% interest, in favor of a Chaplaincy to be founded by Doña Josefa de Moya, widow of Sergeant Major Antonio de Utrera. He mortgaged a hacienda in the valleys of Escasú and Aserrí, which included a house, sugar mill, and cane fields on lands formerly belonging to Luis Cascante.

Sergeant Major Manuel José de Alvarado, Lieutenant Accountant, sold a plantain plantation with its enclosures in Ujarraz to José Manuel Segura, a resident of Ujarraz. Alvarado had acquired the plantation from Domingo López, an indigenous person, due to outstanding tributes owed to His Majesty, with the 57 pesos price going to the Royal Treasury.

Captain Manuel Sáenz and his wife Antonia de Bonilla sold a tiled room, two additional varas from Doña Benita de Bonilla's room, and half a plot of land to Francisco del Canto (master armorer) and his wife Josefa de Ibarra. This property, bequeathed by Francisca de Astúa, bordered rooms of Francisca, Benita, and Josefa de Bonilla, and the San Juan plot; the 200 pesos cacao price was payable within a year, and Captain Manuel Sáenz cancelled the obligation on June 9, 1731.

Doña Josefa de Moya, widow of Sergeant Major Antonio de Utrera, obligated herself to her minor children, José Cayetano and Isabel Ramona de Utrera, for 3,457 pesos and 2 reales of silver, representing their paternal inheritance.

people_involved: wife of José de Morales Tremiño
summary: Doña Josefa de Moya founded a Chaplaincy for masses with a principal of 1,000 pesos in cacao. This amount was distributed as 600 pesos charged to Captain Manuel García de Argueta, an additional 200 pesos also charged to him (previously held by Captain José de Morales Tremiño and his wife), and the remaining 200 pesos charged to Sergeant Major Pedro Sáenz.

people_involved: Doña Gracia Gertrudis de Hoces Navarro
Sárjenlo Mayor don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí
summary: Doña Gracia Gertrudis de Hoces Navarro, widow of Sárjenlo Mayor don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí, committed 1,330 pesos and 7 reales from her paternal inheritance to her minor children and her deceased husband.

Lorenza Milanés, daughter of Salvador Ramírez and María Milanés, and widow of both Basilio de Mora and Severino de Aguilar, made her will. Her children Leonor de Mora, Miguel de Aguilar, José Antonio de Aguilar, and Manuela Victoria de Aguilar are mentioned, with Miguel and José Antonio named as executors.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Capitán don Luis Gutiérrez committed 400 pesos cacao at 5% interest to the Capellanía founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela, of which Licenciado don Juan José Camacho is patron and chaplain. This obligation was imposed on a cacaotal in Barbilla with 2,300 trees, replacing a previous redemption by Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona and his wife.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Licenciado don Juan José Camacho, as the principal, and his mother doña Beatriz de Morales, as guarantor, committed 200 pesos cacao to Sarjento Mayor don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón, to be paid within 4 years at 5% interest. Doña Beatriz de Morales pledged an enslaved mulata named Manuela as collateral.
Doña Margarita Morales donated an enslaved woman named Incompleta to doña Ana de Morales. The record is incomplete.

Juan Lucas Solano, son of Salvador Ramírez and Ana Solano, made his will. He was married to Gertrudis de Chaves and had a daughter, Ana Josefa, who died at age 3. His wife Gertrudis and Capitán Juan José de Chaves were named executors, with his wife as the sole heir.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
Sarjento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad
Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos
Capitán don José Antonio López del Corral
Ex-Gobernador y Capitán General don Diego de la Haya Fernández
Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Utrera
Alférez don Antonio de la Riva
summary: Sarjentos Mayores don Juan Francisco de Ibarra and don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad, and Capitanes don José de Mier Cevallos and don José Antonio López del Corral, became new guarantors for ex-Gobernador don Diego de la Haya Fernández, who was preparing to travel to Panamá. They replaced four deceased original guarantors: Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Utrera, Capitanes Juan de Astúa and don Nicolás de Guevara, and Alférez don Antonio de la Riva.

A dowry letter was issued for Francisco Gutiérrez, son of Capitán Luis Gutiérrez and the late Inés de Quesada, in favor of his future wife doña Juana Blanco, daughter of the late don Juan Blanco and doña Inés de Herrera. The dowry amounted to 694.5 pesos, with 100 pesos as arras.

people_involved: Don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: Capitán don Bernardo Marín, who acquired a house in Cartago from Alférez Juan Marín Laguna and doña María Bonilla, recognized a lordship of 240 pesos at 5% interest. This obligation is in favor of the Capellanía founded by Baltasar de Grados, of which Licenciado don Manuel de Guzmán is patron and chaplain.

Manuela Conejo, widow of Capitán Blas de Ancheta, sold a 35-year-old enslaved 'negro criollo' named Juan José to Licenciado don Manuel González Coronel for 330 pesos. She had acquired Juan José after her husband's death.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don José Fernández Castellanos
summary: The Teniente General, Sarjento Mayor don José Fernández Castellanos, ordered an investigation into the sudden death of Teniente José Picado. On the same day, his widow María Jiménez (30 years old) and mother Gertrudis Peláez (59 years old) declared that Picado left no assets, as the house belonged to Gertrudis, and he left five children.

people_involved: Doña María Josefa Serrano de Reina
Capitán don José Antonio López del Corral
Mtre. de Campo don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina
summary: Capitán don Diego Guerrero, a resident of Granada, Nicaragua, acting with power from his wife doña Francisca Serrano de Reina and his sister-in-law doña María Josefa Serrano de Reina, leased a cacaotal in Matina with 3,250 trees to Capitán don José Antonio López del Corral for 250 pesos cacao annually. The cacaotal was inherited by the sisters from their deceased father, Mtre. de Campo don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina.
Doña Gertrudis Guerrero, a widow, sold a 15-year-old enslaved girl named Gregoria to Capitán don Matías de Besalduque, a resident of Cartago, for 270 pesos plata.

people_involved: Doña Antonia de la Granda y Balvín
Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
General don Lorenzo Antonio de la Granda
summary: Doña Nicolasa Guerrero, a widow, sold a 15-year-old enslaved boy named Juan to Capitán don Matías de Besalduque for 250 pesos plata, which she received in clothing from her daughter doña Antonia de la Granda y Balvín. The sale was consented to by Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares and Capitán Juan Sancho de Castañeda, as executors of the late General don Lorenzo Antonio de la Granda.
María Calvo, a widow, sold a 6-year-old enslaved mulata named Felipa Calvo to don Antonio Oriamuno, a resident of Panamá, for 165 pesos plata.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
Sarjento Mayor don José Fernández Castellanos
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares, acting as attorney for Capitán Francisco Farias and Capitán Gregorio Yañez Farias, committed to pay 3,759 pesos and 6 reales for the auction of a ship named 'Nuestra Señora de la Concepción' and tallow in Esparxa, which belonged to the deceased don José de Bustamante. Capitán Francisco Farias, the buyer, was guaranteed by Gregorio Yañez Farias. On August 10 of the same year, Capitán Francisco Farias delivered the money to the Gobernador y Capitán General, Sarjento Mayor don José Fernández Castellanos, who received it as judge of the mortuary cause.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
B" don Juan Antonio de Moya
summary: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral, acting as attorney for his mother doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco, leased a cacaotal in Matina with 1,300 trees to Nicolás de León for two years, at 200 pesos per year. The cacaotal bordered properties of doña Antonia de Acosta Arévalo and B" don Juan Antonio de Moya.

people_involved: Sárjenlo Mayor don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Sárjenlo Mayor don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón leased a 1,300-tree cacao plantation in Matina to Teniente Nicolás Barrantes for three years, with a rent of 21 zurrones of cacao. The plantation bordered properties belonging to don Pedro de Moya and Feliciana Chinchilla. However, the agreement was rescinded by both parties on September 1, 1731.

Capitán Juan Sancho de Castañeda owed Doña Juana Vidaurre, widow of Don Miguel Sarmiento de Valladares and a resident of León, 451 pesos, 3 reales, and 3 cuartillos, which was the remaining balance of a larger sum he received as her agent. On July 9, 1732, Licenciado don Manuel Martínez Cubero, acting as Doña Juana Vidaurre's agent, received this payment from Doña Juana de Alvarado, the widow of the now-deceased Sancho de Castañeda.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Capitán Cristóbal Fernández, a resident of Barba, owed Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona 394 pesos and 4 reales in cacao, based on their accounts. The debt was initially set to be paid within two months. On May 17, 1733, Doña Petronila de Hoces Navarro, the widow of the creditor, cancelled the debt.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz
summary: Miguel de Quesada and his mother, Doña Sebastiana de Quirós, obligated themselves for 170 pesos 3.5 reales to Miguel's legitimate children: Francisca, Juana Josefa, and José Bernardo, from his late wife Bernarda de Campos. They mortgaged an 800-tree cacao plantation in Matina as security. On September 10, 1735, Doña Sebastiana de Quirós, as the mother and guarantor of the now-deceased Miguel, requested cancellation from Sarjento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz, acting as the judge for her son's estate, as the guardianship funds were covered.

people_involved: Doña Catalina González Camino (wife of Ibarra)
Doña Ana de Salazar y Carrión
Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Doña Catalina González Camino, the legitimate daughter of the late Capitán Matías González Camino (a native of Villa Nueva de Extremadura, Spain) and the late Doña Ana de Salazar y Carrión (a native of Cartago), granted power to her husband, Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra, to make her will. Her husband was named as the sole heir, and both he and Miguel de Ibarra were appointed as executors.

people_involved: Capitán Francisco Fallas de la Vega
Capitán José de la Cruz y Morales
Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: Capitán Francisco Fallas de la Vega, a native of Cádiz and son of the late Jacinto Fallas and Doña Antonia de la Vega, made his will. He was married to Doña Mariana Solano, daughter of the late Capitán Pedro Solano and Doña María Vásquez, and they had eight children. The will also listed nine enslaved individuals with their ages and descriptions. His daughters María Marcelina and Dionisia were married to Capitán José de la Cruz y Morales and Capitán Manuel García de Argueta, respectively, and Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares and Mariana Solano were named as executors.

people_involved: Doña Josefa de Aguilar y Santiago
Sarjento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz
summary: José Miguel Martínez, son of the late Capitán Francisco Martínez and Doña Lorenza Venegas, made his will in preparation for entering the San Francisco order. He received 68 pesos 2 reales from the Gobernador y Capitán General for his guardianship, intended for his habit and other religious expenses. He also had 106 pesos with Doña Josefa de Aguilar y Santiago, from which he bequeathed 50 pesos to San Francisco and the remainder to Sarjento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz, who had cared for and educated him. If he died without professing, Don Pedro or his wife, Doña María de la Rosa, who raised him, would be his heirs and executors.

Gertrudis Ruiz, widow of Francisco Gutiérrez, sold an enslaved man named Ramón, inherited from her late husband, to her son Francisco Gutiérrez for 300 pesos. She received 200 pesos directly, and the remaining 100 pesos, at 5% interest, were designated for the chaplaincy founded by the late Doña Ana de Echavarría, for which Licenciado Manuel de Guzmán was the patron. Francisco Gutiérrez was obligated to pay this portion.

Teniente Francisco Gutiérrez formally obligated himself to the chaplaincy founded by the late Doña Ana de Echavarría for the 100 pesos at 5% interest mentioned in the previous document. To secure this obligation, he mortgaged a 500-tree cacao plantation located in the valley of Barbilla.

people_involved: P. Guardián del Convento de San Francisco
summary: Teniente Francisco Gutiérrez, legitimate son of the late Capitán Francisco Gutiérrez and his first wife Nicolasa de Flores, fulfilled his father's wishes by founding a chaplaincy for his father's soul. This chaplaincy involved 12 recited masses and was endowed with 500 pesos, secured by a 500-tree cacao plantation in Barbilla, with the P. Guardián of the San Francisco Convent as its patron.

people_involved: Capitán don José de Morales Tremiño
summary: Don Lucas Domingo del Fierro and his wife, Doña Josefa de Rosas, obligated themselves for 300 pesos at 5% interest to the San Francisco Convent. This payment was for the cession of houses in Cartago that were previously owned by Licenciado don Manuel Martínez Cubero, who had moved to Nicaragua. The property bordered the former house of Capitán Cayetano Jiménez to the South and the house of Capitán don José de Morales Tremiño to the North, with the church square to the West.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
summary: Capitán Luis Gutiérrez obligated himself for 641 pesos to Capitán don Tomás López del Corral. This amount represented a debt that Capitán Luis Gutiérrez owed to Doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco, who was the mother of Capitán don Tomás López del Corral. The payment was due within six months.

people_involved: Capitán de caballos corazas Bernardo Pacheco
Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
Teniente de Capitán Manuel de Alvarado
summary: Capitán de caballos corazas Bernardo Pacheco, as principal, and Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra, as guarantor, obligated themselves for 150 pesos at 5% interest to Doña Francisca Pacheco, the legitimate daughter of Bernardo Pacheco. This sum was redeemed by Teniente de Capitán Manuel de Alvarado and had been received by Doña Francisca as a donation from Doña Clara de Esquivel.

people_involved: Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos
Doña Catalina González Camino (wife of Cevallos)
summary: Capitán don Lucas Blasco and his wife, Doña Eulalia López Conejo, as assignees of a 1,100-tree cacao plantation in Matina from Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos and his wife Doña Catalina González Camino for 1,100 pesos, acknowledged a lordship of 400 pesos over the property in favor of various chaplaincies. However, this transaction ultimately did not go through.

Sarjento Aparicio Carrillo and his wife María del Rosario obligated themselves to Capitán don Pedro de Moya for 625 pesos in cacao, payable within two years. Of this amount, 350 pesos was for the lease of a 1,375-tree cacao plantation in Matina, which they were taking for the same period, and the remaining 275 pesos was a prior debt owed by Carrillo for a lease.

people_involved: Doña Mariana López de la Flor
Doña Baltasara López de la Flor
Capitán don Gil de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Doña Mariana López de la Flor and Doña Baltasara López de la Flor leased a 1,500-tree cacao plantation in Matina to Capitán don Gil de Alvarado y Jirón. The lease was for two years at 275 pesos of cacao annually, to be delivered to Cartago. This plantation had previously been leased by Nicolás Barrantes and Francisco Guerrero.

Manuel de Salazar and his wife, María de Meza, obligated themselves for 100 pesos of cacao to the Chaplaincy founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela, of which Juan José Camacho is the patron and chaplain. Josefa Elena de Soto, a widow, acted as guarantor, mortgaging a 700-tree cacao plantation in Matina.

Capitán José de Quirós, a resident of Aserrí, obligated himself to the Cofradía de la Concepción for 100 pesos at 5% interest. This debt was previously held by Doña Isabel de Ocampo Golfín and was secured by houses in Aserrí, including a sugar mill and 5 caballerías of land.

Capitán José Felipe Bermúdez and his wife, Doña Teresa de Sandoval, obligated themselves to Doña Josefa de Aguilar. This obligation was for the annual delivery of 6 zurrones of cacao, as part of the terms for the lease of a cacao plantation in Matina that Doña Josefa de Aguilar had granted to Capitán José Felipe Bermúdez.

people_involved: Capitán Francisco Fallas de la Vega
Sárjente Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: Doña Mariana Solano, legitimate daughter of the deceased Capitán don Pedro Solano and Doña María Vásquez, granted power to make a will to her husband, Capitán Francisco Fallas de la Vega, and to Sárjente Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares. She named them as her executors, with her children designated as her heirs.

people_involved: El B? don Manuel González Coronel
Licenciado don Juan Antonio de Moya
summary: El B? don Manuel González Coronel, acting as attorney for Licenciado don Juan Antonio de Moya, leased a cacao plantation in Matina to Capitán Luis Gutiérrez, a resident of Barba, for three years. The lease terms included no payment for the first year, followed by 200 pesos in cacao for each of the subsequent two years. The plantation bordered lands owned by Doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco and Capitán don Francisco de Betancourt.

people_involved: Capitán Francisco Fallas de la Vega
Sárjente Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
Capitán José de la Cruz y Morales
summary: The testament of Doña Mariana Solano, who died on November 19th, was granted by her attorneys, Capitán Francisco Fallas de la Vega (her widower) and Sárjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares. Her children, María Marcelina, Dionisia, Luisa, Antonia María, Josefa, Efigenia, Francisco, and Jacinto, were named as heirs. The will also listed several slaves and noted that Dominga and her daughter Feliciana had been declared free.

people_involved: Alférez Mor. don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín
Doña Angela María de la Paz y Flores
Capitán don Gil de Alvarado (the elder)
Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: The testament of Doña Inés de Sandoval Golfín, a native of Comayagua, was recorded. She was the legitimate daughter of the deceased Alférez Mor. don Sebastián de Sandoval Golfín and Doña Angela María de la Paz y Flores, and was married to Capitán don Gil de Alvarado. She had one daughter, Angela María, who died at two months old. She also freed her slave, Antonia Golfín, and named Licenciado don Manuel Martínez Cubero and Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra as her executors.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Díaz de Herrera
summary: The testament of Feliciana de Chinchilla, widow of Alférez Francisco Fernández, was recorded. A native of Avila in Castilla la Vieja and daughter of Francisco Fernández, she had no children with her husband but named her natural children, José Bernardo and María Francisca, as heirs. María Francisca was married to Felipe Umaña, and Licenciado don José Díaz de Herrera, Cura of Cartago, was appointed as executor.

Francisca de Sibaja, a widow, leased a 1,300-tree cacao plantation in Matina to Alférez Pedro Ortiz for three years at 200 pesos per year. This was the same plantation that Pedro Ortiz had previously leased until the preceding June.

people_involved: Capitán José Nicolás de la Haya
Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Capitán José Nicolás de la Haya and his wife, María Josefa de Echavarría, sold a 20-year-old mulata criolla slave named María Josefa, daughter of María (a black woman), to Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra for 300 pesos. Ibarra declared that he was purchasing the slave for his brother, don Andrés Láinez, a resident of Ica in the kingdom of Peru.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don José Fernández Castellanos
Mtre. de Campo don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Doña Luisa Calvo, a widow, obligated herself for 100 pesos at 5% interest to the Cofradía de la Concepción, whose Mayordomo was Ayudante Matías Masís. This debt, previously held by Sarjento Mayor don José Fernández Castellanos, was charged on a 1,000-tree cacao plantation in Matina and a mill in the ejidos of Cartago. The obligation was later cancelled on October 16, 1745, by Mtre. de Campo don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora, then Mayordomo of the Cofradía.

people_involved: El B? don Juan de Rivas y Chaverri
summary: Don Miguel de la Mata and his wife, Doña María Francisca Alvarez, residents of Aserrí, obligated themselves for 1,120 pesos at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by Capitán Juan Gregorio Ramírez. This obligation originated from Capitán Eusebio Jiménez, Doña María Francisca Alvarez's first husband. Capitán don José de Alvarado, who had previously acted as guarantor, requested exemption due to Doña María Francisca's remarriage, leading to this new obligation.

people_involved: Gobernador don Baltasar Francisco de Valderrama
summary: Gobernador don Baltasar Francisco de Valderrama opened his protocol, stating that the few documents processed before him during his first year of governorship in 1729 were recorded in his General Registers.

people_involved: Gobernador don Baltasar Francisco de Valderrama
Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
summary: Gobernador don Baltasar Francisco de Valderrama, acting as judge in the probate case of Licenciado don Diego de Ángulo Gascón (who died intestate on January 14, 1727), granted freedom to the slave Diego Ángulo. Diego Ángulo had been sold with the Matina cacao plantation to Teniente Antonio de Ángulo but secured his freedom by paying 375 pesos of cacao, his appraised value.

people_involved: Capitán don Alonso Bersabé Cabeza de Vaca
Antonia de la Granda y Balvin
Gobernador don Lorenzo Antonio de la Granda y Balvín
summary: Doña Nicolasa Guerrero, a single woman, made her will, naming her natural children María Jerónima, Antonia de la Granda y Balvin, and Capitán José Miguel Guerrero. She bequeathed slaves Catalina, María Elemberta, and Francisco to Antonia. Her will faced opposition regarding her house and slaves from the sureties of the deceased Gobernador de la Granda, who claimed these assets should cover his debts, but Nicolasa asserted they were her own property.

people_involved: Sárjente Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: Capitán don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco and his wife Doña Francisca Serrano de Reina obligated themselves for 300 pesos to the Chaplaincy founded by Capitán Pedro Ibáñez. The payment was received in the value of a slave named José, who was part of Ibáñez's estate and held by his widow, Doña Manuela de Quirós, who later married Sárjente Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares. The Chaplaincy's patron and chaplain was Licenciado Manuel López Conejo, who later cancelled this obligation on October 3, 1733, as Cura of Esparza.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan de Ocampo Golfín
B° don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
summary: Capitán don Juan de Ocampo Golfín guaranteed a bond for Teniente Antonio de Ángulo, who was the auction buyer of a cacao plantation in Matina from the estate of the deceased B° don Diego de Ángulo Gascón. The guarantee was secured with an 18-year-old slave named Nicolás, born and raised in Ocampo Golfín's house.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
summary: Eight individuals provided a 2,500 pesos bond for Capitán don Tomás López del Corral to assume the role of Lieutenant Accountant of the Royal Treasury (Rs. Cajas). He was transitioning into this position after serving as Lieutenant Treasurer.

locations: Santiago de Alanje de la provincia de Veragua
people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don José Fernández Castellanos
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco Manzano, acting on behalf of José Felipe Calvo from Veragua, sold a 22-year-old mulatto slave named Francisco to Sarjento Mayor don José Fernández Castellanos for 200 silver pesos. Francisco was one of two slaves inherited by José Felipe Calvo from his deceased father, Capitán don Miguel Calvo, a former resident of Cartago.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón
Sarjento Mayor don Manuel José de Alvarado y Baños
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón and his wife Doña Angela de Guevara provided bail for Sarjento Mayor don Manuel José de Alvarado y Baños, who was imprisoned in the city's chapter house due to shortfalls in his role as Lieutenant Accountant of the Royal Treasury. However, the bail was not processed.

Capitán Francisco de Morales and his wife Juana Cordero obligated themselves to the Royal Treasury for 335 pesos in cacao. This amount was due from Morales for two canoes that were auctioned in 1725 to Capitán don José Morales Tremiño, acting as agent for Licenciado don Manuel López Conejo. They mortgaged their dwelling houses in Aserrí as security.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
Doña Josefa de la Vega Cabral
Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Utrera y Medina
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra and Doña Josefa de Moya (a widow) exchanged slaves. Ibarra traded a 'ladino' slave named Tomás, of Congo origin, whom he had purchased from Doña Josefa de la Vega Cabral. Doña Josefa de Moya traded a 'mina' slave named Manuel, whom she had inherited after the death of her husband, Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Utrera y Medina.

Doña Francisca de Bonilla, widow of Alférez José Hidalgo and current wife of Alférez don José de Alvarado, obligated herself to Manuel Hidalgo, a minor, for 463 pesos from his paternal and maternal legacies. Manuel was the son of her first husband, José Hidalgo, and his second wife, Doña Ana de Quesada. She also confirmed having satisfied a 388 pesos debt to Santiago Hidalgo, son of her first husband and his first wife, Doña Ana Arias, mortgaging her houses in Aserrí.

Doña Francisca de Bonilla obligated herself to Pedro del Puerto for 75 pesos in cacao at 5% interest, representing his maternal inheritance and a share from his deceased brother Juan. Pedro del Puerto was the legitimate son of Domingo del Puerto and Doña Ana de Quesada, who was the second wife of Alférez José Hidalgo, whose widow was Francisca de Bonilla. She mortgaged her dwelling houses in Aserrí.

people_involved: Capitán don Esteban de Hoces Navarro
Capitán don Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribaren
Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Doña Josefa de Hoces Navarro, widow of Capitán don Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribaren, made her will. She was the legitimate daughter of the deceased Capitán don Esteban de Hoces Navarro and Doña Juana Calvo. She had ten adult children with Arburola, including José Miguel, who was studying for the priesthood and would become the patron and chaplain of a chaplaincy she established. Her executors were Licenciado don Manuel López Conejo and Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
Doña María de Torres y Barahona
Capitán don Esteban de Hoces Navarro
Licenciado don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona, a native of Málaga, made his will. He was married to Doña Petronila de Hoces Navarro and had six surviving children. He listed 14 enslaved people and named his wife, his sons Licenciado don Antonio de Soto y Barahona and Capitán don Tomás de Barahona, and Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara as his executors.
Capitán Juan Sancho de Castañeda, a native of Castilla in Asturias, made his will. He was the legitimate son of Juan Sancho de Castañeda and Dominga de (surname incomplete).

people_involved: don José Nicolás Sarmiento de Soto Mayor
summary: A description of Yoglar's family, including his wife, children from his current and her previous marriage, and his slaves. His wife, doña Juana de Alvarado, and his brother-in-law, Capitán don Gil de Alvarado, are named as executors.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: María de Arroyo, legitimate daughter of deceased Francisco de Arroyo and Mariana Cardoso, and widow of Juan de Astorga and Juan Madrigal, makes her will. Her granddaughter, Isabel de Cárdenas, who married Alférez Matías Trejos, died three years prior, leaving 10 children as heirs. Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares and Teniente de Capitán Juan Masís are named as albaceas.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don José de Baeza
Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
Capitán don Cayetano Muñoz y Bermúdez
Sarjento Mayor don Manuel de Alvarado y Baños
summary: Sarjento Mayor don José de Baeza obliges himself to pay 200 pesos of silver within a year to several captains and an ayudante. These individuals are guarantors for Sarjento Mayor don Manuel de Alvarado y Baños, the Accountant of the Royal Treasury, and had embargoed Baeza for the sum he holds belonging to Alvarado y Baños.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Antonio Díaz de Herrera
summary: Doña Josefa Nicolasa de Guevara obliges herself to the Cofradía de la Concepción for 200 pesos at 5% interest on cacao, secured by a straw house she owns. The house is bordered by properties of Licenciado don José Antonio Díaz de Herrera, Capitán don Francisco Garrido, Capitán don Dionisio Pacheco, and the heirs of Capitán Eugenio Martínez.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
Sarjento Mayor de los reales ejércitos don Baltasar Francisco de Valderrama
Muy Ilustre y Noble Cabildo de León
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares and his wife doña Rita García de Argueta obligate themselves for three years to pay 300 pesos annually for alcabalas and barlovento rights for Cartago. This agreement follows a resolution from a Junta held in León, Nicaragua, on March 13, 1731, which was communicated to Madriz Linares as Procurador Síndico, and his proposal was accepted by the Governor.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor de los reales ejércitos don Baltasar Francisco de Valderrama
Sarjente Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz
Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
Muy Ilustre y Noble Cabildo de León
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Baltasar Francisco de Valderrama (Governor and Captain General), Sarjente Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz (Teniente General), Capitán don Francisco Garrido (Teniente General), and Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares (Procurador Síndico), acting for the province due to lack of a Cabildo, grant general power of attorney to the Cabildo of León, Nicaragua, to represent Cartago before the Royal Audiencia of Guatemala regarding alcabalas and barlovento rights.

people_involved: Capitán don José Lebrón Cortés y Monroy
summary: Capitán don José Lebrón Cortés y Monroy and his wife doña Manuela Vanegas obligate themselves to don Francisco Grandellana, a native of the kingdoms of Castile, for 350 pesos of tallow for the upcoming February harvest in one of the ports of Bagaces. Grandellana later cancelled this obligation on March 28, 1733.

people_involved: Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara Sáenz
Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Capitán Gregorio Siles, residing in Barba, sells a 50-year-old mulatto slave named Juan de Chaves to Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara Sáenz, a Presbítero, for 200 pesos of cacao. Siles had previously purchased Juan de Chaves from Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra. Siles cancelled the sale on January 26, 1733.

people_involved: Capitán de caballos don Tomás López del Corral
doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Capitán de caballos don Tomás López del Corral and his wife doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo obligate themselves for any liabilities that might arise against him as Lieutenant of Royal Officials of the province. They mortgage their dwelling houses as security.

people_involved: Capitán don José Fernando de Moya
Sarjento Mayor don Salvador Suárez de Lugo
summary: Capitán don José Fernando de Moya, acting as executor for the deceased doña María Cecilia Vásquez Coronado, establishes a Capellanía for 7 masses to be held in the Barba parish aid. The Capellanía is funded by 828 pesos of cacao secured by a cattle ranch in Barba, with Capitanes Cayetano and Sebastián de Sandoval as patrons.

people_involved: Capitán don Diego de Barros y Carvajal
don Andrés de Barros y Carvajal
Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
José Manuel de Barros y Carvajal
Pedro Manuel de Barros y Carvajal
Diego Antonio de Barros y Carvajal
Juana María de Barros y Carvajal
summary: The will of Capitán don Diego de Barros y Carvajal, son of deceased don Andrés de Barros y Carvajal and doña María de los Ríos from La Coruña, Galicia, is recorded. He was married to doña Josefa Pérez de Muro, daughter of deceased Capitán don José Pérez de Muro and doña Mariana de Echavarría Navarro, and their children are listed. An unnamed Governor certifies the assets brought by his wife.

people_involved: José Miguel de Arburola y Ribaren
summary: Licenciado José Miguel de Arburola y Ribaren, a cleric, made his will. He named his sisters as heirs and Sarjento Mayor Juan Francisco de Ibarra as an executor. His parents, Captain Lorenzo de Arburola and Josefa de Hoces Navarro, were deceased.

Don Diego de Fuentes, a resident, received three notebooks of legal documents from Don José de Fuentes, the judge of the 'residencia' (judicial review) taken against the former Governor and Captain General, Don Diego de la Haya Fernández. Don Diego de Fuentes was obligated to deliver these documents to the Audiencia de Guatemala.

Teniente Francisco Granados established a dowry ('carta dote') for his wife, Isabel de Jesús, totaling 425 pesos and 1 real, plus 100 pesos in cacao as 'arras'. Both Francisco Granados's parents, Francisco Granados and Francisca Brígida Chacón, and Isabel de Jesús's parents, Sarjento Lucas de Jesús and Gregoria Várela, were deceased.

María de la Rosa Solís, widow of Captain José de Ocampo and resident of Barba, along with Captains Cayetano and Sebastián de Sandoval as guarantors, obligated themselves for 500 pesos at 5% interest to a Capellanía. This Capellanía was founded by the deceased Cecilia Vásquez Coronado in the Convent of San Francisco in Esparza, with the debt originally belonging to José de Ocampo, who left his assets to his wife. The obligation was cancelled on May 17, 1740, by Sarjento Mayor Juan Rodríguez de Robledo.

María de la Rosa Solís obligated herself for 952 pesos and 1.5 reales in cacao to her children, José, Blas, Francisco Javier, Pedro Vital, María del Rosario, Antonia Teresa, and José Ramón de Ocampo, representing their paternal inheritance. Captain Francisco Barrantes acted as guarantor for this obligation.

Captain José Saborío and his wife Juana de Ballesteros, residents of Barba, obligated themselves to Captain Juan Sancho de Castañeda, steward of the Cofradía de la Veracruz, for 400 pesos in cacao at 10% interest. This was for materials from houses previously owned by the deceased Captain Gregorio Chaves and sold by the Cofradía. They mortgaged houses, a sugar mill, and three plots of sugarcane in Barba, near Cubijuqui. The obligation was cancelled on February 22, 1738, having passed to Licenciado Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero.

Don Julián García de Argueta made a dowry agreement for his future wife, Doña Ana Sánchez de Castañeda, daughter of Captain Juan Sánchez de Castañeda and Doña Juana Petronila de Alvarado. The dowry, totaling 1,800 pesos and 4 reales, included two enslaved people (Antonia, 18, and Manuel, 8) and 500 cacao trees in Matina. Their marriage was scheduled for January 22nd.

Captain Tomás López del Corral leased a cacao plantation in Matina, owned by his mother Antonia Salmón Pacheco, to Don Julián García de Argueta. The lease was for three years at 200 pesos of cacao annually, for a plantation with 2,000 trees bordering properties of Pe. Juan Antonio de Moya and Antonia de Acosta. López del Corral acknowledged receipt of the lease value on July 15, 1733.

Manuel de Salazar, as principal, and Captain Felipe de Meza, his father-in-law and guarantor, obligated themselves for 100 pesos in cacao at 5% interest to a Capellanía. Juan José Camacho, a cleric, was the patron and chaplain of this Capellanía. Felipe de Meza mortgaged a cacao plantation of 2,000 trees in Matina as security.

Captain Francisco de Bustamante, a bachelor merchant from Rivadeo, Spain, died while making his will, without formally naming executors. He had two natural children in Spain. The Teniente General, the interim priest Manuel José González Coronel, and Fray Miguel Hernández certified that Bustamante intended to name Sarjento Mayor Baltasar Francisco de Valderrama and Captain Pedro de Moya as executors. The Teniente General declared the will valid and appointed Valderrama as the first executor and Captain José Antonio del Corral in place of Moya, who was excused.

Sarjento Mayor Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón and his wife Angela de Guevara obligated themselves for 150 pesos at 5% interest to a Capellanía. This Capellanía was founded by the deceased Alférez Antonio Machado, and Juan José Camacho, a cleric, served as its patron and chaplain. They mortgaged a cacao plantation of 1,300 trees in Matina as security.

Captain Juan Jiménez, a resident of Barba, sold a cattle ranch named 'San Pedro' in Bagaces to Licenciado Francisco de Ocampo Golfín for 1,400 pesos. Jiménez received 600 pesos in the form of two enslaved people, Nicolás de Ocampo (7 years old) and María Antonia. Ocampo Golfín obligated himself for the remaining 800 pesos at 5% interest for the benefit of Jiménez's daughter, María Teresa Jiménez.
Josefa de la Mata, identified as the widow of José Cascante, is mentioned in an entry that abruptly ends, indicating an incomplete record of an event.

An unnamed principal and Ayudante José Núñez, acting as guarantor, obligated themselves for 324 pesos in favor of the minor children, Francisco and Casilda. These minors are the children of the grantor and her deceased husband.

Doña Margarita de Bonilla, as the principal, and Capitán don José Lebrón, as guarantor, obligated themselves for 60 pesos in cacao. This obligation was made in favor of doña Josefa de Moya, who is the widow of Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Utrera.

Licenciado don José Antonio Díaz de Herrera, a half-benefice priest, donated a tile and wood house on its plot in the city's outskirts to Josefa del Carmen Alvarado. Upon her death, the house is to revert to her children, José Antonio, María del Carmen, and one yet to be born.

Don Nicolás de Ocampo Golfín and his wife doña Manuela Bricia Bazterrica acquired houses that were auctioned off due to the death of Capitán don Francisco Bustamante for 460 pesos plata. They acknowledged a 300-peso censo (pupilar usury) on these properties, benefiting the minor children of Francisco Cartín, whose curator is Capitán don Pedro de Moya.
José Cartín canceled a debt of 150 pesos that was due to him, as noted in the margin of a previous record.

B° don José Antonio Díaz de Herrera, acting as the executor for Cayetano Cartín, canceled a debt of 150 pesos. This amount was received from Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra, who was the executor for don Nicolás de Ocampo.

Sarjento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz obligated himself for 100 pesos at 5% interest to a Capellanía founded by Juana Sagaste, whose chaplains are the city's priests. Capitán Marcos Zamora redeemed this obligation, and Sáenz hypothecated houses in Aserrí as security.

The Teniente General placed Francisco, a 13-year-old free pardo and son of Juana (a conga woman), into an apprenticeship. Francisco is to serve as an apprentice to the master blacksmith Tomas Calvo for a period of five years.

Capitán Francisco Gutiérrez, with authorization from his brother Teniente Francisco Gutiérrez, sold Miguel Maroto, an enslaved man of Mina caste, aged 28, to Capitán don Bernardo García de Miranda for 400 pesos cacao. The Teniente had acquired Miguel from Licenciado don José Díaz de Herrera, a half-benefice priest of this city.

A dowry contract was established by Cristóbal Jiménez in favor of doña Josefa Sáenz Vásquez. Josefa is the legitimate daughter of Sarjento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz and doña María de la Rosa Vásquez, with the dowry amounting to 705 pesos 4 reales and arras of 94 pesos 4 reales.
Rosa Leitón, the widow of Mata, sold a cacaotal located in Matina to Alférez Sebastián de Quesada. The sale was concluded for a price of 100 pesos in cacao.

people_involved: Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: A dowry contract was initiated by Juan José de Cuende, a native of Estella, Navarra, and resident of this city, for his future wife doña María Catalina de Ibarra. María Catalina is the legitimate daughter of Sárjente Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo and the late doña Petronila de Moya. Doña Catalina González del Camino, Ibarra's wife, donated 136 pesos in jewels to her stepdaughter, but the contract ultimately did not proceed.

Capitán don Pedro de Moya sold a cacaotal with 300 trees in the Barbilla valley to Capitán don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco for 200 pesos cacao, an amount Moya owed to Pacheco. Moya had originally acquired the cacaotal as payment for a 276-peso debt from the deceased Nicolás González.

Doña María Josefa Cabral, wife of Capitán don Francisco de Betancourt (absent in Matina), took charge of the houses in this city belonging to Sarjento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz. Sáenz had offered the houses due to several encumbrances, including obligations to Capellanías founded by Juan de Echavarría, Miguel de Alvarado, Juana de Vera, and Pedro Ibáñez, with various patrons and chaplains involved.

A dowry contract was established by José Antonio de Oriamuno, a native of Panamá, for his wife doña María Catalina de Ibarra, the legitimate daughter of Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra and the late doña Petronila de Moya. The dowry amounted to 2,055 pesos, and doña Catalina González Camino, wife of Sarjento Mayor Ibarra, donated half of her house and other jewels worth 636 pesos to her stepdaughter, with arras of 1,000 pesos.

A dowry contract was established by don Juan José de Cuende, a native of Estella, Navarra, Spain, for doña Manuela Josefa de Ibarra, the legitimate daughter of Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra and the late doña Petronila de Moya. The dowry totaled 2,658 pesos 4 reales, and doña Catalina González Camino, Manuela Josefa's stepmother, enhanced the dowry with half a house and other valuables amounting to 1,496 pesos 3 reales, with arras of 2,000 pesos.

Capitán don Tomás López del Corral and his wife doña Francisca de Ibarra sold Eugenia de Retes, a 45-year-old mulata parda, to Capitán don Juan Manuel de Alvarado for 200 pesos cacao. Francisca had received Eugenia as part of her dowry from her father, don Juan Francisco de Ibarra.

Sárjenlo Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra, acting as Mayordomo of the Cofradía de los Angeles, leased a cacaotal in Matina to Juan Calvo and his son Santiago Calvo. The lease was for one year at a cost of 100 pesos.

Don Nicolás de Ocampo Golfín sold a cattle ranch named 'las maderas negras' in the jurisdiction of Bagaces, bordering don Martín Garayar's property, to Diego José de Alvísua, a resident of Nicaragua. The sale included 30 tame horses and was priced at 1,300 arrobas of tallow, valued at 488 pesos plata.
Capitán Luis Morera and his wife Gregoria de Segura, residents of Barba, began the process of founding something, though the details of what they founded are incomplete in the record.

people_involved: Cura doctrinero del Convento de San Francisco de San Bartolomé de Barba
summary: A Capellanía (chaplaincy) was established with a principal of 300 pesos from a sugar mill and a cane field in the valley of Barba. The Cura doctrinero of the San Francisco de San Bartolomé de Barba Convent was named chaplain, with Luis Morera's sons, Alférez Salvador and Jorge Morera, designated as patrons after their parents' deaths.

Capitán Luis Morera and his wife Gregoria de Segura, children of deceased parents, granted their will in Barba. They named their children Alférez Salvador, Jorge, and Rosa María Morera (married to Capitán don Isidro Hidalgo) as heirs, and their sons Salvador and Jorge, along with Ayudante José Núñez, as executors. They also mentioned several slaves, granting freedom to Tomás.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco Baltasar Valderrama
Capitán don Nicolás de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Doña Josefa Martínez de Herrera, daughter of deceased Capitán Eugenio Martínez de Herrera and doña Micaela de Luna, and widow of Capitán Juan Cayetano Jiménez, made her will. She named her children Cristóbal, José Manuel, Cayetana Efigenia, and Ana Jiménez, and her sister doña Manuela Martínez. Sarjento Mayor don Francisco Baltasar Valderrama and Capitán don Nicolás de Ocampo Golfín were appointed as executors.

María Oviedo, daughter of José de Arroyo and Francisca de Oviedo, and widow of Cristóbal Cascante, made her will in the valley of Barba. Her children were María de la Rosa (married to Antonio Espino), Petronila, Andrés, and Francisco Cascante. Capitán Juan de Ugalde, Andrés Cascante, and Francisco Cascante were named as executors.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo, acting as majordomo of the Cofradía de los Angeles, leased a hacienda in the Matina valley to Sarjento Gregorio Calvo for one year for 100 pesos cacao.

people_involved: Licenciado don Manuel López del Corral
summary: B° don Manuel González Coronel leased a cacao plantation in Matina to Licenciado don Manuel López del Corral, a Presbyter cleric, for one year. The price was 7 zurrones of cacao to be delivered in Cartago.
Capitán José de Amores sold an enslaved woman named Ambrosia, 30 years old, to Capitán Sebastián de Sandoval for 200 pesos cacao.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares became obligated to the Real Caja for 216 pesos, a debt previously owed by Capitán Francisco Ugarte, a free mulatto from Granada, Nicaragua, related to a mule herd belonging to don Diego del Castillo. Capitán don Tomás López del Corral cancelled the obligation on March 27, 1731.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Capitán don José de Lebrón became obligated for 137 pesos 4 reales cacao to Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona, acting as agent for Capitán Cayetano Muñoz. This obligation stemmed from a previous vale issued by Lebrón to doña Cecilia Vásquez Coronado on June 22, 1729, in Esparza. On November 9, 1731, Capitán don Fernando de Moya noted that Lebrón had made a new obligation for the same amount to the Capellanía founded by doña Cecilia Vásquez Coronado.

people_involved: Capitán de caballos don Tomás López del Corral
summary: Capitán Nicolás de Astúa sold an enslaved black man named Antonio Cayetano, 16 years old, to Capitán de caballos don Tomás López del Corral for 300 pesos plata. Astúa had inherited Antonio Cayetano from his mother, Gertrudis Calderón.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Baltasar Francisco de Valderrama
Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Baltasar Francisco de Valderrama, Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo, and Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares granted general power of attorney to don Antonio Hipólito Ordóñez, Procurator of the Audiencia of Guatemala, and failing him, to Capitán don Felipe Jiménez, Chancellor of the Real Audiencia. This was to request instructions regarding an exhorto from the Cabildo of León, Nicaragua, concerning Capitán don Juan Manuel Muñoz's request for passage of a dispatch for the administration and collection of royal duties in both provinces.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Baltasar Francisco de Valderrama
Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: The same officials (Sarjento Mayor don Baltasar Francisco de Valderrama, Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo, and Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares) granted power to a procurator to be named by the Cabildo of León, Nicaragua, for the same purpose as the previous power of attorney regarding royal duties.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Díaz de Herrera
Comisario del Santo Oficio don Manuel González Coronel
summary: Licenciado don José Díaz de Herrera, a Presbyter cleric, recognized a censo of 500 pesos at 5% imposed on his houses in the public square of Cartago. This censo was in favor of the Capellanía founded by Alférez Antonio Machado, whose patron Juan José Camacho (cleric) had ceded it to Juan José Solís. The houses also had a 200 pesos censo for the Capellanía of doña Eugenia Abarca Alatras, the grantor's grandmother.

people_involved: Capitán Gaspar de Basterrica y Narvaiza
doña Eugenia Urbana Láinez de Istueta
Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: Doña Lucía Antonia de Basterrica, daughter of deceased Capitán Gaspar de Basterrica y Narvaiza and doña Eugenia Urbana Láinez de Istueta, made her will. She named her sisters doña Eugenia and doña Manuela as heirs, and her uncle Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo was mentioned. Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares and Capitán Francisco Javier de Siles were appointed as executors.

Capitán Sebastián de Sandoval, a resident of the Barba valley, obligated himself to don Baltasar Francisco de Valderrama for 245 pesos 6 reales plata. He agreed to pay within 6 months of his return from Panamá, where he was traveling, and mortgaged a sugar mill and a cane field in Barba.

Capitán Pedro Nolasco de Rebollo, a resident of Nicaragua, who was traveling to Panamá with a mule shipment, obligated himself to Capitán Sebastián de Sandoval for 245 pesos 6 reales. Sandoval had lent him this money for the mule expedition, and Rebollo agreed to repay it 40 days after his arrival in Panamá.

Capitán Sebastián de Sandoval took charge of a cattle site located across the Río Segundo in the Barba valley, six leagues from Cartago. The site belonged to the Cofradía del Sacramento, whose steward was Sarjento don Francisco de la Madriz Linares, and Sandoval acknowledged a lien of 60 pesos plata at 5% in favor of the Cofradía.

Capitán Jacinto de Fallas and his wife doña María Manuela de Echavarría granted power of attorney to Capitán José de la Cruz Morales, who was traveling to Panamá. The purpose was to collect assets due to them from the estate of Capitán José Miguel de Echavarría, who died in Panamá in 1726, having declared María Manuela his natural daughter and partial heir in his will, with Capitán don Francisco López de la Flor as executor.

people_involved: José Miguel de Arburola y Ribaren
summary: Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero, a Presbyter, made a donation to don José Miguel de Arburola y Ribaren. The donation consisted of 100 pesos from a chaplaincy that Francisco de Bonilla had founded on a sugarcane plantation in the Ujarraz valley, enabling Arburola y Ribaren to be ordained under its title.

A codicil was added to Capitán Sebastián Guillen's will, originally granted in 1720 before Teniente General don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí. The codicil noted that after 1720, Guillen had married his daughters Juana de la Candelaria to José Solís and Juana de la Paz to José de Alvarado, and that his son Diego Guillen was married. He named his wife María Magdalena de Orozco as tutor for their minor children, Josefa Efigenia and Manuel Guillen, and revoked a clause regarding a chaplaincy from a fifth of his assets.

Doña Gertrudis Guerrero leased a cacao plantation in Matina to don Julián García de Argueta, Teniente Juez de los campos, for three years at 150 pesos cacao per year. The boundaries of the plantation were described, and the lease was later cancelled on November 8, 1733.

Doña Josefa de Fallas, a resident of Aserrí, granted freedom to Polonia de Fallas, an 8-year-old 'mulata blanca'. Josefa had inherited Polonia from her deceased parents, Capitán Francisco de Fallas and doña Mariana Solano.

people_involved: José Miguel de Arburola y Ribaren
summary: Victoria Chacón founded a chaplaincy for 11 recited masses, imposing a principal of 500 pesos on a cacao plantation in Matina, valued at 600 pesos. She also allocated 100 pesos for her funeral, stating her advanced age and lack of forced heirs. Bachiller don José Díaz de Herrera was named the patron, to recite masses until don José Miguel de Arburola y Ribaren could be ordained.

Don Manuel de Salazar committed to maintaining a public school for boys in Cartago, teaching doctrine, reading, writing, and arithmetic, for payment according to local custom. He also agreed to teach four noble children of poor parents for an initial 50 pesos and 25 pesos in subsequent years, an offer made by Gobernador Valderrama, Teniente General don Juan Francisco de Ibarra, and Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares, who was also the Procurador General.

Doña Josefa de Moya, a widow, attempted to sell a 40-year-old enslaved man named Manuel to don Bernardo García de Miranda and his wife doña Josefa de Casasola y Córdoba for 350 pesos cacao. Josefa de Moya had inherited Manuel upon the death of her husband, Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Utrera, but the transaction was cancelled.

people_involved: José Miguel de Arburola y Ribaren
summary: Doña Josefa de Hoces Navarro, a widow, founded a chaplaincy for two recited masses for the soul of Ana Cardoso, who had donated 100 pesos for this purpose over 14 years prior. Josefa used these funds to purchase houses in Cartago, formerly owned by don José de Alvarado. Her son, José Miguel de Arburola y Ribaren, was named patron and chaplain, with her brother, Licenciado don Félix de Hoces, serving as interim chaplain.

Capitán Diego de Meza leased a cacao plantation of 710 trees in the Matina valley to Agustín de la Riva for three years at 75 pesos cacao annually. This plantation represented half of the property possessed by his brother Gregorio de Meza, which they had inherited from their mother.

Juana Calderón, a widow and heir of Alférez José Calderón, fulfilled her father's will by founding a chaplaincy for 8 recited masses and one sung mass, with a principal of 600 pesos. The chaplaincy was imposed on 700 cacao trees along the Matina river. Don Dionisio de la Madriz, legitimate son of Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares, was named the first chaplain. Her son, José de la Madriz, was designated as the patron, and interim chaplains would be the parish priests.
