Her father, who died 15 years prior, had originally ordered this chaplaincy, naming Capitán Juan Astúa as patron and Nicolás de [last name incomplete] as the first chaplain.

Juana Calderón, a widow, established a Capellanía of 1,000 pesos in accordance with the will of her deceased father, Alférez José Calderón. This endowment was created to benefit the Cofradía del Santísimo, the third order of San Francisco, and the Cofradía de Verc Cruz. The funds were secured by a 1,000-tree cacao plantation located in Matina.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Francisco Guerrero leased a 400-tree cacao plantation in Matina for three years, paying 50 pesos cacao annually. The lease was granted by Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo, acting as tutor for doña Francisca Valentina de Pacheco, the minor daughter of Capitán Bernardo Pacheco. The property was to be received from don Pedro Jiménez Mondragón, who was the guarantor for the previous lessee, Juan Venegas, and included 6 hides and a grinding stone.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Alférez Antonio de Ángulo granted power of attorney to Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona. This authorization allowed Soto y Barahona to obligate Ángulo in favor of several Capellanías, including those founded by Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas, Comisario Baltasar de Grados, and Capitán Pedro Ibáñez. It also covered a Capellanía yet to be founded by Juana Sagaste, and the Cofradía del Rosario.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
Comisario don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona, acting as attorney for Alférez Antonio de Ángulo, acknowledged a 320-peso censo at 5% interest on the 'Las Viejas' cacao plantation. This plantation, comprising 1404 trees in the Barbilla river area, previously belonged to Comisario don Diego de Ángulo Gascón, Cura Beneficiado of Cartago. The censo was for the Capellanía instituted by Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas, with the Beneficiado Priests of the parish serving as its patrons and chaplains.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: On the same day, Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona, still representing Alférez Antonio de Ángulo, acknowledged another censo of 170 pesos at 5% interest on the 'Las Viejas' plantation. This censo was designated for the Capellanía established by Comisario Baltasar de Grados. The Beneficiado Priests of Cartago were named as the patrons and chaplains for this Capellanía.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Continuing his actions on May 23rd, Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona, on behalf of Alférez Antonio de Ángulo, acknowledged a 200-peso censo at 5% interest on the 'Las Viejas' plantation. This censo was established for the Capellanía founded by Capitán Pedro Ibáñez. B° don Manuel López Conejo was designated as the patron and chaplain for this particular Capellanía.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: On May 25th, Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona, acting in his capacity as attorney for Alférez Antonio de Ángulo, acknowledged a 50-peso censo at 5% interest. This censo was imposed upon the 'Las Viejas' plantation and was designated in favor of the Cofradía del Rosario.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Also on May 25th, Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona, representing Alférez Antonio de Ángulo, acknowledged a 200-peso censo at 5% interest on the 'Las Viejas' plantation. This censo was intended for the Capellanía that was to be founded by Juana Sagaste, with the Beneficiado Priests of the parish serving as its chaplains.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
José Manuel Bersabé Cabeza de Vaca
summary: On May 28th, Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo obligated himself for 100 pesos cacao to José Manuel Bersabé Cabeza de Vaca and the deceased doña Josefa de Moya. These funds had been held by Capitán don Nicolás de Estrada as pupillary usury. This obligation was subsequently cancelled by José Manuel Bersabé Cabeza de Vaca on May 15, 1734.

Doña Angela Sáenz, a widow, leased a 300-tree cacao plantation in the Barbilla valley to Capitán Cayetano Muñoz for three years, at an annual rent of 100 pesos cacao. The plantation bordered properties belonging to doña Baltasara de Escalante Paniagua. Doña Angela Sáenz later cancelled this lease on June 8, 1734.

people_involved: Comisario don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: Capitán Benito Barrantes, as heir to his mother María Sagaste, founded a Capellanía of 8 recited masses with a 400-peso principal, fulfilling a commitment made 41 years prior. This commitment involved his nephew, Capitán Juan Alvarez de Ulate, and the deceased Comisario don Diego de Ángulo Gascón, concerning assets from Juana Barrantes and María Sagaste. The 400 pesos were secured, with half on the 'Las Viejas' plantation (via Alférez Antonio de Ángulo's escritura on May 25th) and the other half on Capitán Marcos de Zamora's house in Escasú (from a 1727 escritura). Don Dionisio de la Madriz was named the first chaplain, with Benito Barrantes as patron.

people_involved: Doña Josefa de Aguilar y Santiago
summary: Doña Josefa de Aguilar y Santiago, widow of Alférez Antonio de Acosta Arévalo, executed her will, detailing her family and bequests. She named her seven children and their spouses, including her deceased daughter Francisca and deceased son Gaspar. She freed her mulatto slave, Juan de Acosta, and bequeathed her 40-year-old Arara slave, Juana Manuela, to her grandson Cayetano Alvarado for funeral expenses. Her executors were her grandson don Cayetano de Alvarado and Ayudante Manuel de Alvarado.

Gertrudis Peláez, legitimate daughter of Andrés Peláez and Catalina Rosales, made her will. She was married to Alférez Gregorio Picado and had three children: Angela Josefa, José Ricardo, and María Margarita. Her son José Ricardo was married to doña María Jiménez, with whom he had four children. She also mentioned her godson Manuel Antonio and an orphan girl she raised, Antonia Josefa. Her will established a Capellanía, naming Enrique Molina as chaplain and Alférez Miguel Molina as patron.

Don Cayetano de Alvarado provided a dowry of 448 pesos and 4 reales, and 500 pesos in arras, to his wife Doña Juana Antonia de Guevara. Doña Juana Antonia is the legitimate daughter of the late Capitán don Nicolás de Guevara and Doña Francisca de Inza.

people_involved: Doña Ana Teresa Masui y Vélez
Capitán don Pedro Ortiz de Rosas
Ana Teresa (daughter of Lucas del Fierro)
summary: Don Lucas del Fierro, a native of Isla de la Palma, made his will. He was the legitimate son of the late Don José del Fierro and Doña Ana Teresa Masui y Vélez, and was married to Doña Josefa Ortiz de Rosas. He named his daughters Ana Teresa and Antonia de la Trinidad, and an unborn child, as heirs, with Capitán don Gil de Alvarado and Don Juan Sancho de Catañeda as executors.

Ayudante Matías Masís, son of the late Feliciano Masís and María de Madrigal, made his will. He was a widower of Antonia de Rojas and married to María del Carmen Salazar, with whom he had six children. He also acknowledged three natural children from previous relationships, Micaela and Ana Efigenia with Juana Brenes, and Juan José with Rosa Camilo. Ayudante Manuel Antonio de Alvarado and his wife were named executors.

people_involved: Doña Margarita del Haya y Bolívar
Sarjento Mayor don José del Haya y Bolívar
María Efigenia (daughter of Margarita del Haya y Bolívar)
summary: Doña Margarita del Haya y Bolívar, daughter of the late Sarjento Mayor don José del Haya y Bolívar and Doña María de Ortega of Esparza, made her will. She was a widow of Claudio de la Mata Linares, with whom she had a son, Miguel de la Rosa, and a second time a widow of Capitán Francisco de Bonilla, with whom she had four surviving children. Don José Díaz de Herrera and Miguel de la Mata Linares were named executors.

people_involved: Doña Josefa de Casasola y Córdoba
Capitán don José de Morales Tremiño
summary: Don Bernardo García de Miranda and his wife Doña Josefa de Casasola y Córdoba obligated themselves to the Convento de San Francisco for 300 pesos at 5% interest. This was for the purchase of a house adjacent to their own, which was previously possessed by the late Don Lucas Domingo del Fierro under similar obligations.

locations: Vega del río de las Cañas
people_involved: Doña Josefa Fallas de la Vega
Doña Efigenia Fallas de la Vega
Capitán Francisco Fallas de la Vega
summary: Doña Josefa and Doña Efigenia Fallas de la Vega, residents of Aserrí, recognized obligations of 200 pesos to a Capellanía founded by Capitán Pedro Ibáñez and 200 pesos to their absent brother Francisco Nicolas. These obligations were tied to a house and land inherited from their late parents, Capitán Francisco Fallas de la Vega and Doña Mariana Solano, which their brother Capitán Jacinto de Fallas had previously received but lost his share due to neglect.

people_involved: Capitán don José Antonio López del Corral
Doña Francisca de Arburola y Ribaren
summary: Capitán don José Antonio López del Corral and his wife Doña Francisca de Arburola y Ribaren obligated themselves for 150 pesos to the Convento de San Francisco and 350 pesos to a Capellanía. These obligations were secured by a house and lot, previously held by the late Capitán Pedro Rodríguez Palacio and his wife Doña Teresa de Oses Navarro, and now transferred to the current obligors.

people_involved: Capitán don Gil de Alvarado Jirón
summary: Doña Baltasara de la Flor and Doña Mariana de la Flor leased a cacao plantation in Matina, containing 1,800 fruit-bearing trees, to Capitán don Gil de Alvarado Jirón for one year. The payment was to be ten zurrones of first-quality cacao delivered in Cartago.
Doña Inés de Sandoval Golfín, a widow, sold a two-year-old mulatto slave named José Santiago, son of her slave Antonia, to Capitán don Dionisio Pacheco for 150 silver pesos.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
General don Diego de la Haya Fernández
Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares, acting as attorney for General don Diego de la Haya Fernández of Panamá, sold a 14-15 year old cuarterón slave named José to Capitán don Tomás López del Corral for 200 silver pesos. The slave had been previously purchased by General de la Haya Fernández from Doña Angela de Arleguí.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: Capitán Luis Gutiérrez provided Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares as a guarantor to enable the sale of his slave Manuela, who was mortgaged to the Royal Treasury for 125 pesos in cacao.

people_involved: Teniente General Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Teniente General Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo arranged for José Chinchilla, the eleven-year-old legitimate son of the late Francisco Chinchilla and Juana de Villalobos, to be apprenticed to Sarjento Juan Francisco de Aguirre, a master shoemaker, for five years.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: Doña Luisa Calvo, a widow, sold a 12-year-old black slave named Nicolasa, daughter of her former slave Francisca, to Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares for 200 pesos in cacao.

people_involved: Doña María Catarína Ortiz de Rosas
Capitán don José Nicolás Sarmiento de Soto Mayor
Antonia (daughter of María Catarína Ortiz de Rosas)
Josefa (daughter of María Catarína Ortiz de Rosas)
summary: Doña María Catarína Ortiz de Rosas, daughter of the late Don Pedro Ortiz de Rosas and Doña Juana de Alvarado, being ill, granted power to her husband, Capitán don José Nicolás Sarmiento de Soto Mayor, to make her will. She named their eight children as heirs and her husband as executor.

people_involved: Teniente de Capitán Pedro Jiménez Mondragón
Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Teniente de Capitán Pedro Jiménez Mondragón obligated himself to the Cofradía de los Angeles, whose Mayordomo was Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo, for 50 pesos annually for three years. This was for the lease of a cacao plantation in Matina belonging to the Cofradía.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
summary: Capitán Miguel López y Gamboa obligated himself for 286 pesos cacao, which Capitán don Tomás López del Corral had paid on his behalf. Of this, 225 pesos were for a debt to Comisario don Manuel González Coronel related to hacienda rentals in Matina, and the remainder to Capitán don Alvaro de Guevara. López y Gamboa hypothecated a cacao plantation in Río de Barbilla as security.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
summary: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral and his wife doña Francisca Josefa de Ibarra took charge of houses that previously belonged to doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco, Francisca Josefa's mother. They recognized several obligations, including 300 pesos to the Capellanía founded by Agustín Guerrero, 50 pesos to the Cofradía del Sacramento, 800 pesos to the Capellanía patroned by José Camacho, 100 pesos to the Convento de San Francisco, and 50 pesos to the Cofradía del Rosario, all at 5% interest.
Licenciado don Manuel López Conejo and don José Díaz de Herrera, Curas of the parish and patrons/chaplains of the Capellanía founded by Agustín Guerrero, cancelled a debt of 300 pesos.
Capitán José Lebrón, Mayordomo of the Cofradía del Rosario, cancelled a debt of 50 pesos.
Licenciado don Manuel del Corral and Juan José Camacho, Capellán and patron respectively of the Capellanía founded by Marcos Machado, cancelled a debt of 200 pesos.

people_involved: Sárjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Sárjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo, Síndico General of the Convento de San Francisco, cancelled a debt of 100 pesos.
Licenciado don Juan José Camacho, patron and Capellán of the Capellanía founded by Licenciado Marcos Machado, cancelled a debt of 100 pesos.
Licenciado don Juan José Camacho, as patron of the Capellanía founded by Licenciado Marcos Machado, cancelled a debt of 400 pesos.
Licenciado don Juan José Camacho, as patron and Capellán of the Capellanía founded by Marcos Machado, cancelled a debt of 100 pesos.

people_involved: Capitán José Nicolás de la Haya
summary: Capitán José Nicolás de la Haya and his wife María Josefa de Echavarría, with Miguel del Castillo as guarantor, obligated themselves for 100 pesos at 5% interest to the Convento de San Francisco. This amount belonged to the Capellanía founded by Lucas Hernández.

people_involved: Don José Ramón de Noguera y Moncada
Sárjente Mayor don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí
summary: Don José Ramón de Noguera y Moncada made a provision of 484 pesos 4 reales, including 200 pesos as 'arras', in favor of his wife doña Ana de Arleguí. Their marriage had been celebrated on October 2nd of the same month.

Capitán don Antonio Salmón Pacheco obligated himself for 150 pesos at 5% interest to the Capellanía founded by Luis Guerrero, whose patrons and chaplains were Curas don Manuel López Conejo and don José Díaz de Herrera. These pesos had been redeemed by Capitán Tomás López del Corral, and a cacao plantation in Matina was hypothecated.
A debt of 150 pesos from Capitán don Antonio Salmón Pacheco to the Capellanía founded by Luis Guerrero was cancelled.

Capitán don Antonio Salmón Pacheco obligated himself for 50 pesos at 5% interest to the Cofradía del Rosario, which had been redeemed by Capitán Tomás López del Corral. He charged this debt against a cacao plantation of 800 trees in Matina.

Capitán don José Lebrón, Mayordomo of the Cofradía del Rosario, received 50 pesos from Capitán don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco, executor for his brother don Antonio Salmón Pacheco, thereby cancelling the debt.

Capitán don Juan González obligated himself to his five younger siblings (Eugenia, Ana María, Angela, Luisa, and Antonia González) for 47 pesos each, representing their inheritance from their deceased father, Manuel González. He hypothecated a house, a sugar cane plot, a sugar mill, and 10 tame mules in the valley of Barba, at a place called El Zanjón.

people_involved: Guardián del Convento de San Francisco
summary: José de las Salas obligated himself for 150 pesos at 5% interest, which the deceased Ayudante Matías Masís had given him to establish a Capellanía. He charged this debt against a house with a plantain grove in the common lands of the city. The Guardián of the Convento de San Francisco was named interim Capellán until José Manuel de Cárdenas was ordained.

Ayudante Manuel Antonio de Alvarado, acting as executor for the deceased Ayudante Matías Masís, founded a Capellanía for 7 masses for the souls of Matías Masís and his first wife, Antonia de Rojas. The principal of 150 pesos, held by José de las Salas, was designated for this Capellanía. José Manuel de Cárdenas was named Capellán, with masses to be said at the Convento de San Francisco until his ordination, and José de las Salas as the patron.

people_involved: Doña María de la O de Céspedes
Sarjento Mayor don José de Morales
summary: Doña Isabel de Ocampo Golfín, daughter of the deceased Diego Ocampo Golfín (from Spain) and María de Mora, made her will. She was married to Regidor Nicolás de Céspedes, and they had three living children: doña Josefa, doña María de la O, and don Miguel de Céspedes. Her daughter María de la O was married to Sarjento Mayor don José de Morales. She also mentioned Ambrosio de Céspedes, a young man she had raised, and named her son-in-law and son as executors.

María del Carmen de Salazar, a widow, obligated herself for 708 pesos. Of this amount, 608 pesos were adjudicated in favor of her five children: Antonia, Francisco Manuel, Martín Amores, Cayetano, and Juan Antonio.

The wife of the deceased Ayudante Matías Masís and the sons of Francisco Masís inherited property. This inheritance included a half-forge, which was burdened with an obligation for the Pe. Guardián de San Francisco to say two masses annually during Francisco Masís's lifetime. After Francisco's death, this obligation ceases, and the forge's value will be distributed among his sons.

people_involved: Son of Capitán don Miguel de Bolívar
Son of Capitán don José de Miranda
B" don Juan de Rivas Chaverri
summary: Doña Josefa de Moya, a widow, obligated herself for 425 pesos at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by Doña Cecilia Vásquez Coronado. She received these funds from Capitán don Fernando de Moya, Doña Cecilia's executor. The Chaplaincy's chaplains include sons of Capitán don Miguel de Bolívar and Capitán don José de Miranda, with B" don Juan de Rivas Chaverri serving as interim chaplain.

Capitán don José Lebrón and his wife, Doña Manuela Vanegas, obligated themselves for 137 pesos and 4 reales of cacao at 5% interest to the same Chaplaincy mentioned in event 151. They mortgaged houses in the city, which were bordered by properties belonging to Doña María Catalina, Doña Manuela de Ibarra, General don Diego del Haya, Doña Antonia de Alvarado, and Capitán don Gil de Alvarado.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan Sancho de Castañeda
Doña Juana Eufrasia Sancho de Castañeda
Capitán don Esteban Ruiz de Mendoza
summary: Doña Juana de Alvarado, widow of Capitán don Juan Sancho de Castañeda, obligated herself to her three minor children (Doña Juana Eufrasia, José Manuel, and Doña Gertrudis Sancho de Castañeda) for 904 pesos, 6 reales, and 10 maravedíes, representing their paternal inheritance. A marginal note from October 25, 1740, indicates that Capitán don Esteban Ruiz de Mendoza (widower of Doña Juana Eufrasia), don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda, and don Rafael de Mier Cevallos (husband of Doña Manuela Gertrudis) canceled this obligation in favor of Doña Juana.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan Sancho de Castañeda
summary: Doña Juana de Alvarado recognized a 300-peso obligation she and her late husband, Capitán don Juan Sancho de Castañeda, had to the heirs of Francisco de Chaves, who died 42 years prior without known heirs. A marginal note from October 30, 1736, states that Doña Juana delivered the 300 pesos to Capitán don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco, who was the Alcalde Ordo and Teniente de Gobernador, and he canceled the obligation.

Capitán don Fernando de Moya, executor for Doña Cecilia Vásquez Coronado, sold a 9-year-old Creole slave boy named José Francisco and a 10-year-old Creole slave girl named Mónica to his sister, Doña Josefa de Moya, for 425 pesos.

people_involved: Sárjente Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz
summary: Sárjente Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz obligated himself to María Martina Bautista for 50 pesos, representing her paternal inheritance. This inheritance, consisting of a plantain field and an enclosure in Ujarraz (her father's hometown), was redeemed by Miguel Castillo. A marginal note from May 8, 1737, indicates the obligation was canceled.

people_involved: Sarjento mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: Sarjento mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares and his wife, Doña Rita García de Hergueta, obligated themselves for 600 pesos at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by Capitán Pedro Ibáñez. B? don Manuel López Conejo is the patron and chaplain. This obligation relates to 1550 pesos belonging to the Chaplaincy after the death of Doña Manuela Quirós (Francisco's former wife and Ibáñez's widow), of which 950 pesos had already been redeemed, leaving the 600 pesos.

people_involved: Doña Micaela de Arburola y Ribaren
Capitán Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribaren
Guardián del Convento de San Francisco
Sarjento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Doña Micaela de Arburola y Ribaren, legitimate daughter of the late Capitán Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribaren and Doña Josefa de Hoces Navarro, and widow of don Pedro Manuel de Moya, made her will. She had three sons with Pedro Manuel: Juan Matías, José Manuel, and José Francisco. She ordered a Chaplaincy, naming her son Juan Matías as patron. If her sons are not ordained, her nephews José Joaquín de la Trinidad and José Tiburcio González Coronel will be chaplains, with her brother don José Miguel de Arburola and don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí as interim chaplains, and the Guardián del Convento de San Francisco saying masses until ordination. She appointed her brother-in-law, Sarjento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad, to value her assets.

people_involved: Sárjente Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz
summary: On November 22, Sárjente Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz, acting as Teniente General of the city by baton deposit, took charge of this protocol.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
Sarjento mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral and his wife, Doña Francisca de Ibarra, obligated themselves to Sárjenlo Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares for 600 pesos plata, to be paid in two installments of 300 pesos each in October 1732 and one year later. A marginal note from October 6, 1736, indicates the obligation was canceled.

people_involved: Doña Francisca de Arburola y Ribaren
Don José Antonio López del Corral
Capitán Manuel de Arburola y Ribaren
summary: Doña Francisca de Arburola y Ribaren, acting with power from her absent husband don José Antonio López del Corral, obligated herself for 312 pesos 3 reales. This sum was adjudicated to the minor children of her deceased brother, Capitán Manuel de Arburola y Ribaren, from the estate of their mother, Doña Josefa de Hoces Navarro. She received this deposit because her brother's estate was not yet finalized. A marginal note from October 17, 1738, states that Doña María Lorenza Fajardo and Capitán Juan Francisco Guerrero received this sum from Doña Francisca, belonging to the minor children Manuel Valentín, Nicolás Felipe, and Francisca Liberata de Arburola. It also declares that upon the death of José Martín, his share reverted to his mother, Doña María Lorenza.

A Chaplaincy was founded by Licenciado don Manuel López Conejo, interim Cura of the city, acting as executor for Doña Josefa de Hoces Navarro. Doña Josefa, the legitimate daughter of the late Alférez Esteban de Hoces Navarro and Doña Juana Calvo, mandated three recited masses. The principal of 373 pesos was secured on a portion of Doña Josefa's former residence, while Doña Rosa de Arburola owned the shop, kitchen, and other parts of the lot. José Miguel de Arburola, son of Doña Josefa, was named patron and chaplain, with the closest relative serving until his ordination.

Doña Catalina González del Camino declared that she was first married to Capitán don Cristóbal Martín Cubero, receiving a dowry of 6093 pesos. Her husband died in 1707, leaving an 8-year-old son named Manuel, and his assets only covered her dowry.

people_involved: Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos
summary: Doña Catalina González del Camino married Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos in early January 1709. He brought no assets other than his honesty and services to His Majesty.

people_involved: Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos
Gobernador y Capitán General Mtre. de Campo don Lorenzo Antonio de la Granda y Valbín
summary: In 1710, Gobernador y Capitán General Mtre. de Campo don Lorenzo Antonio de la Granda y Valbín appointed Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos as his Teniente General. This occurred when the Gobernador went to conquer the rebellious indigenous people in the mountains of Talamanca, leaving Cevallos in charge of political and military government.

people_involved: Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara y Sáenz
summary: On September 17, 1731, Don Cristóbal Jiménez sold a mulatillo named Juan José, who was one year and four months old, to Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara y Sáenz for 150 pesos of cacao. Juan José was the son of Josefa, Don Cristóbal's mulata slave.
On October 5, 1731, José Nicolás de la Haya sold a piece of land to Sarjento José de Sojo, a resident of Ujarraz, for 50 pesos of cacao.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco Ibarra
Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
summary: On October 20, 1731, Capitán don Antonio Salmón Pacheco obligated himself to the Convento de San Francisco for 100 pesos at 5% interest, received from Síndico Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco Ibarra. This debt, redeemed by Capitán don Tomás López del Corral, was charged against a cacao hacienda in Malina, bordering the hacienda of his brother, Capitán don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco.

people_involved: Doña Francisca de la Madriz Linares
summary: On March 23, 1737, Sarjento Mayor don Pedro Carazo, Síndico of the Convento de San Francisco, declared that after don Antonio Salmón Pacheco's death, he received the 100 pesos from his executor, Capitán don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco. Carazo then passed these funds to Capitán don Juan Nicolás Viveros and Doña Francisca de la Madriz Linares.

people_involved: Doña María de la O Céspedes
Sarjento Mayor don José de Morales
summary: On January 14, 1732, Don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno and his wife Doña Ana Efigenia García sold a 7-year-old mulatilla named Mónica de la Cruz to Doña María de la O Céspedes, wife of Sarjento Mayor don José de Morales, for 130 pesos. The mulatilla had been purchased from the estate of Doña Cecilia Vásquez, and a judge authorized the sale as Sarjento Mayor Morales was a refugee.

On January 15, 1732, Teniente don Pedro Jiménez Mondragón and his wife Doña Francisca de Inza obligated themselves to Doña Alfonsa Muñoz Hidalgo for 104 pesos of silver at 5% interest, payable within one year. They mortgaged a wooden, tile-roofed house they were building on a lot bordering the Sabana.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don José de Baeza
summary: On January 16, 1732, Sarjento Mayor don José de Baeza and his wife Doña Magdalena Maroto sold a 14-year-old mulatillo slave named José Enrique, son of their slave Ana Gertrudis, to Don Tomás López del Corral for 250 pesos.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz
Licenciado don Manuel López del Corral
Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de Utrera
summary: On March 6, 1732, Sarjento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz obligated himself for 200 pesos at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by Alférez Antonio Machado, whose patron was Licenciado Juan José Camacho and interim chaplain was Licenciado don Manuel López del Corral. This debt, redeemed by Capitán don Tomás López del Corral, was secured by his houses and hacienda in the valley of Iscasú, which also had other existing debts to various confraternities and a chaplaincy founded by Doña Josefa de Moya.

people_involved: Licenciado don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
Capitán don Tomás de Soto y Barahona
Doña Juana María de Soto y Barahona
Sarjente Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: On March 6, 1732, Doña Petronila de Hoces Navarro, Licenciado don Antonio de Soto y Barahona, and Capitán don Tomás de Soto y Barahona obligated themselves to pay Capitán Cayetano Muñoz 1000 pesos in cacao over five years. This was because 500 cacao trees, promised to Muñoz upon his marriage to Doña Juana María de Soto y Barahona, were not delivered during the lifetime of her father, Sarjente Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona.

people_involved: Doña Juana María de Soto y Barahona
summary: On April 8, 1741, Doña Juana María de Soto y Barahona, widow of don Cayetano Muñoz and second wife of don Manuel José Gómez, cancelled the obligation related to the cacao trees.
On March 17, 1732, Capitán don Lucas de Velazco granted power of attorney to Licenciado don Manuel López Conejo, interim priest of the city, for his lawsuits and business, and to make his will.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don José de Baeza
summary: On April 29, 1732, Licenciado don Manuel López Conejo substituted his power of attorney to Sarjento Mayor don José de Baeza, as he had to serve the curacy of Esparza.

people_involved: Sarjente Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
Licenciado don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
Capitán don Tomás de Soto y Barahona
summary: On April 5, 1732, Doña Petronila de Hoces Navarro, widow of Sarjente Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona, obligated herself to her minor children, Doña Ana Teresa and Don Nicolás, for 498 pesos 2 reales of silver each, or 750 pesos of cacao if no money was available. This sum was their paternal inheritance, and she mortgaged her house and cacao plantations, with her elder sons, Licenciado don Antonio and Capitán don Tomás de Soto y Barahona, acting as guarantors.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Antonio Díaz de Herrera
summary: On May 20, 1732, Don Alfonso Ulloa, son of Don José de Ulloa and Doña Isabel de Siles, provided a dowry letter for his future wife, Doña María Josefa Maroto, totaling 1201 pesos 4 reales. The dowry, delivered by Licenciado don José Antonio Díaz de Herrera and Doña Luisa Calvo, included a 24-year-old black woman named Ramona and her three mulatilla daughters: Juana (8 years), Brígida (5 years), and Lorenza (3 years).
On May 24, 1732, Don Gil de Alvarado posted bail for Antonio de Aguilar, who was imprisoned by judicial order in a criminal case against Francisco de la Cerda.

On June 4, 1732, Capitán don Manuel Sáenz and his wife Doña Antonia de Bonilla received a straw house, lot, and cultivated lands outside the city's common lands, which Capitán Nicolás de Astúa had transferred to them. This property had previous charges against Capitán Juan de Astúa, Nicolás's father.
An escritura (deed) involving Gertrudis Calderón and a Capellanía founded by Pedro Ibáñez did not pass. The Capellán, Licenciado don Manuel López Conejo, did not consent to the agreement.

people_involved: Don José Miguel de Mier Cevallos
Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos
Doña Dionisia Falla de la Vega
summary: A dowry letter was issued for the marriage of Don José Miguel de Mier Cevallos and Doña Ana García de Argueta. The dowry amounted to 728 pesos 2 reales, including cacao and an additional 117 pesos from a benefactor. Their marriage had taken place on June 29th previously.
Alférez Matías de Trejos, a widower, obligated himself to his nine children for 858 pesos and 4 reales from their inheritance. Each child was to receive 95 pesos and 2 reales.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don José de Moya
Doña María Mayor de Benavides Moreno
Maestre de Campo don Juan Francisco Sáenz Vásquez
summary: Don Pedro de Moya and Doña Angela Sáenz made their wills, both being ill and without succession. They named their nephews and nieces, Don José Antonio de Bonilla and Doña María Ambrosia de Bonilla, as heirs and ordered the foundation of capellanías.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Doña Francisca de Ibarra granted power to her husband, Don Tomás López del Corral, to make a will. Their daughters, Josefa Joaquina and María Josefa, were designated as heirs.

people_involved: Teniente don Pedro Jiménez de Mondragón
Doña Felipa Santiago Rodríguez de Palacios
Capitán Domingo de Inza y Sasueta
summary: Teniente don Pedro Jiménez de Mondragón, a native of Panamá, made his will. He was married to Doña Francisca de Inza, who had previously been married to Capitán Nicolás de Guevara. Pedro and Francisca had five children, and Francisca had one daughter from her previous marriage who was married to Don Cayetano Alvarado. Pedro was also a proprietor and tenant of cacao plantations in Matina.

Cayetano Cartín, a single man and native of Cartago, made his will. He named his siblings, Manuel, Tomás, María, Gabriela, and José, as his heirs. He also imposed an obligation on José to make a visit to N. Señora del Viejo with four candles.

people_involved: Doña Manuela de Bazterrica y Narvaiza
Capitán Gaspar de Bazterrica y Narvaiza
summary: Doña Manuela de Bazterrica y Narvaiza granted power to her husband, Don Nicolás de Ocampo Golfín, to make a will. She named their children, Manuel Antonio and María Leonida de Ocampo Golfín, as her heirs.

people_involved: Licenciado Pro. don Manuel González Coronel
Licenciado Pr° don Juan Antonio de Moya
Pro. Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara y Sáenz
summary: Licenciado Pro. don Manuel González Coronel, acting as attorney for Licenciado Pr° don Juan Antonio de Moya, leased a cacao hacienda in the Matina valley. The hacienda was leased to Pro. Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara y Sáenz for 100 pesos annually over three years.

people_involved: Licenciado Pr° don Juan Antonio de Moya
summary: Don Juan Matías de Moya obligated himself to his younger brothers, Don José Manuel and Don José Francisco de Moya, for 914 pesos of cacao. This amount was adjudicated to them from their deceased mother, Doña Nicolasa de Arburola's estate, and included a debt owed by the cura Licenciado don Juan Antonio de Moya.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra sold a fruiting cacao hacienda named Jara in Matina to Baltasar de Vargas, a resident of the Barba valley. The sale price was 14 zurrones of cacao.

people_involved: Alférez don Luis de Soto Mayor
summary: Doña Clara de Vida Martel, a widow, sold a fenced plot of land in the common lands of Cartago to Alférez don Luis de Soto Mayor. The property was located behind her house, past the Toyogres river, and sold for 125 pesos of cacao.

people_involved: Capitan don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno
Doña Ana Efigenia García de Estrada
summary: Capitan don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno and Doña Ana Efigenia García de Estrada transferred a house to Don Juan García de Argueta and Doña Ana Sánchez de Castañeda. The house was tied to a Capellanía founded by Doña Cecilia Vásquez de Coronado, with Don Fernando de Moya as administrator. The buyers accepted the associated obligation, which was later taken over in 1739 by Capitan José Miguel de Céspedes and Doña Ignacia Miranda, with approval from Capellán Licenciado don Manuel López Conejo.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
Doña Manuela de Bazterrica y Narvaiza
summary: Don Nicolás de Ocampo Golfín granted power to Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra to make his will. He named his children, Manuel Antonio and María Leonida de Ocampo, as heirs. This power was a substitution for a previous power granted by his recently deceased wife, Doña Manuela de Bazterrica y Narvaiza.

people_involved: Capitan don Tomás de Soto Barahona
summary: Doña Francisca de Sibaja, a widow, leased a cacao hacienda in the Matina valley to Capitan don Tomás de Soto Barahona for two years. The lease was for 250 pesos of cacao and was cancelled in October 1733.

people_involved: Capitán Domingo de Inza y Sasueta
summary: A dowry letter was issued for Don Pedro de Zavaleta, a native of Hernani, Spain, in favor of his future wife, Doña Sebastiana de Inza, a native of Cartago. The dowry amounted to 1580 pesos.

Doña Agustina de Campos, legitimate daughter of Teniente Pedro de Campos Quirós and Doña Bárbara Rodríguez Altamirano, granted freedom to her slave Cayetano de Campos. This act was carried out in accordance with the provisions of her mother's will.
Doña Agustina de Campos, for the same reason as the previous event (her mother's will), granted freedom to her slave José Manuel de Campos. This was a separate act of manumission.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: The will of spouses Don Nicolás de Ocampo and Doña Manuela de Bazterrica was executed by their attorney, Sarjento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra. The will mentioned selling haciendas in Bagaces to move to Cartago for religious reasons and to raise their children, Manuel Antonio and María Leonida, away from the countryside. It also included bequests to Capitán Francisco Javier de Siles and his wife Doña Eugenia de Bazterrica, who is the children's aunt.

Teniente Juan Masís obligated himself to Gertrudis and Gregoria Ramírez for 200 pesos of cacao, representing funds Salvador Ramírez had given to José Masís. This obligation was later cancelled in 1736 by the husbands of Gertrudis and Gregoria, Capitán Don Miguel de Bolívar and Santiago de la Candelaria, respectively.

people_involved: Capitán Don Tomás López del Corral
Pro. Licenciado Don Gregorio López del Corral
summary: Capitán Don Tomás López del Corral, acting as attorney for his brother Pro. Licenciado Don Gregorio López del Corral, leased a cacao hacienda in the Matina valley to Don Pedro de Zavaleta. The hacienda, which belonged to their mother Doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco, was leased for three years at a price of 375 pesos, already paid.

people_involved: Doña Juana Josefa de Arburola y Ribaren
summary: Doña Juana Josefa de Arburola y Ribaren, a widow, leased a cacao hacienda in the Matina valley to Teniente Francisco García. The hacienda, previously managed by the deceased Isidro de Acosta, was leased for three years at an annual price of 62 pesos.

people_involved: Don José de Baeza y Espinosa de los Monteros
Pro. Licenciado Don Manuel López Conejo
summary: Don José de Baeza y Espinosa de los Monteros executed the will of Capitán Don Lucas Velasco, acting as his attorney. The power of attorney was originally granted to Pro. Licenciado Don Manuel López Conejo in March 1732 and later substituted to Baeza. Lucas Velasco was married to Doña Eulalia López Conejo, and they had two daughters, Petronila and Gertrudis.

Nicolás Palacios obligated himself to his minor nieces, María and Antonia, who are the daughters of his brother Lucas Palacios. Each niece was to receive 62 pesos and 6 reales from their paternal inheritance.

Antonio de Aguilar, widower of Petronila Hernández, obligated himself to his three minor children, María Josefa, Antonia, and Pedro de Aguilar. Each child was to receive 95 pesos and 3.5 reales from their maternal inheritance.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Don Antonio de Utrera
summary: Don Luis de Sotomayor, a native of Lima, Peru, established a dowry for his wife, Doña Isabel Ramona de Utrera, daughter of Sarjento Mayor Don Antonio de Utrera and Doña Josefa de Moya. The dowry included 3714 pesos 4 reales, a house in Cartago, three slaves (Dionisia, Mónica, José Francisco), worked silver, and 1000 pesos invested in a sugar cane hacienda in Ujarraz belonging to his mother-in-law.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Don Baltasar Francisco de Valderrama
Capitán Don Tomás López del Corral
Doña María Ventura de la Cueva y Valladares
summary: Sarjento Mayor Don Baltasar Francisco de Valderrama, Governor and Captain General of the province, sold his 19-year-old mulatto slave, Juan Miguel, to Capitán Don Tomás López del Corral for 300 pesos of silver. Juan Miguel, a native of León, Nicaragua, had been purchased by Valderrama from Capitán Don Domingo de Figueroa and his wife Doña María Ventura de la Cueva y Valladares.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Sarjento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra, as steward of the Confraternity of Nuestra Señora de los Angeles, leased two plots of cacao land in the Matina valley to Capitán Francisco de Chavarría. The three-year lease required Chavarría to care for a 600-tree clearing and cost 50 pesos annually.

people_involved: Sárjenlo Mayor Don Alonso de Bonilla
summary: Doña Sebastiana de Bonilla, daughter of the deceased Alonso de Bonilla and Juana Benite, executed her will. She revoked a previous donation of adobe rooms to Capitán Francisco Alejandro de Bonilla, citing his failure to uphold the contract for her care. Instead, she bequeathed the rooms to Licenciado Don Juan de Bonilla, who had contracted to provide for her necessities and bury her in the San Francisco church in Cartago, and named him her executor.

people_involved: Doña Baltasara López de la Flor
Capitán Don José López de la Flor
Doña Margarita López de la Flor
Don Ramón de Noguera y Moncada
Doña Josefa López de la Flor
General Don Juan López de la Flor
summary: Doña Baltasara López de la Flor, daughter of the deceased Capitán Don José López de la Flor and Doña Ambrosia de Echavarría Navarro, established a Chaplaincy of recited masses with 1,500 pesos of cacao, using a cacao hacienda in Matina as assets. Don Vicente de Morales was named the chaplain, with provisions for Don Alfonso del Águila and the sons of Don Ramón de Noguera y Moncada as successors. The masses were to be applied for the souls of her parents, herself, Doña Josefa López de la Flor, and General Don Juan López de la Flor.

people_involved: Doña Baltasara López de la Flor
Doña Mariana López de la Flor
summary: Doña Baltasara and Doña Mariana López de la Flor leased a cacao hacienda in the Matina valley, consisting of 1,400 trees and bordering the 'Ibartita' property, to Capitán Don Gil de Alvarado. The lease was for two years at a price of 275 pesos of cacao.
Doña Antonia de Echavarría Navarro was noted as the legitimate mother of Licenciado Don Manuel de Guzmán, a Presbyter who was absent.

people_involved: José Francisco de Baeza Espinosa de los Monteros
summary: José Francisco de Baeza Espinosa de los Monteros, acting as attorney for Licenciado Manuel López Conejo, the interim priest of Esparza, ceded a tile and adobe house to Captain Francisco Javier de Oriamuno and his wife, Ana Efigenia García de Estrada. The house was burdened with debts from chaplaincies belonging to Padre Guzmán and Pe. Conejo, and others involving Licenciado José Camacho. Oriamuno and his wife took responsibility for these obligations as holders and depositaries.

Captain Francisco Javier de Siles and his wife, Eugenia de Bazterrica, committed to pay 691 pesos and deliver some furniture to the minor children of Nicolás de Ocampo, named Manuel Antonio and María Leonida. These assets were handed over by Sergeant Major Juan Francisco de Ibarra, who was the executor of Nicolás de Ocampo's estate.

Captain Francisco Javier de Siles made his will, identifying himself as the legitimate son of Alférez Andrés de Siles and María de Chaves, and his wife, Eugenia de Bazterrica, as the legitimate daughter of Captain Gaspar de Bazterrica and Eugenia Urbana Láinez Instueta, all deceased. He noted that his wife's dowry of cattle was lost and that his current assets were received from his sister-in-law, Lucía de Bazterrica. The couple had no children.

people_involved: Miguel de la Haya y Bolívar
summary: Luis de Sotomayor and his wife, Isabel Ramona de Utrera, committed to a chaplaincy founded by Cecilia Vá'íquez de Coronado for 227 pesos, which they received from her executor, Captain Fernando de Moya. The chaplains for this endowment were the sons of Captain Miguel de la Haya y Bolívar and José de Miranda, residents of Esparza. They mortgaged adobe and tile houses in Cartago as security.

Juan Matías de Moya, legitimate son of the deceased Captain Pedro Manuel de Moya and Micaela de Arburola, and executor of his mother's will, founded a chaplaincy for recited masses with 366 pesos of cacao. The first chaplains were designated as his legitimate brothers, José Francisco and José Manuel de Moya, if ordained, or failing them, nephews José Joaquín de la Trinidad and José Tiburcio González Coronel. José Miguel de Arburola, brother of the testatrix, was appointed interim chaplain, followed by José Hermenegildo de Arleguí. Juan Matías de Moya was named the patron, followed by his brothers.
Doña Clara de Vida Martel, a widow, committed to pay 200 pesos of cacao to Doña Eulalia López Conejo, also a widow. The document for this obligation is incomplete.

Doña Josefa de Aguilar, a widow, made a codicil to her will, previously made before Lieutenant General Juan Francisco de Ibarra. She revoked the donation of her 40-year-old enslaved woman, Juana Manuela, to her grandson Cayetano de Alvarado, instead stipulating that Juana Manuela would pass to her daughter, Cayetana de Acosta, wife of Juan Fernández, upon Josefa's death.

Doña Josefa de Aguilar clarified a previous statement in her codicil, declaring that Pedro Ortiz's debt to her for a lease was 125 pesos, not 200 pesos, and that Ortiz would pay it after the year of the agreement expired.
José Manuel Sotelo committed to pay Miguel González 100 pesos of cacao within one year.
Alférez Antonio Carballo, who leased the Río Grande canoe for one year, committed to pay Captain Ramón Noguera Moneada, the Mayordomo de propios, 30 pesos for the lease.

José Manuel Sotelo, as the principal, and his grandmother, Doña Sebastiana de Quirós, as guarantor, renewed their obligation to Miguel González for 100 pesos. This was a re-establishment of a previous obligation due to a lack of guarantee.
Captain José Barquero sold an enslaved mulatto boy named Benito Vital, approximately 5 years old, to Captain of Caballos Corazas Cayetano Muñoz y Bermúdez for 100 pesos.

Captain Julián García de Ergueta and his wife, Ana Josefa Sancho de Castañeda, committed to the Royal Treasury for 600 pesos of cacao, which they received from Lieutenant of Royal Officials Tomás López del Corral. They mortgaged a cacao plantation of 500 fruit trees in the Matina valley, bordering properties of Sergeant Major Juan Francisco de Ibarra and Doña Juana de Alvarado.
Lieutenant of Royal Officials Diego Morras received 600 pesos from Sergeant Major Julián García de Ergueta, settling a previous obligation to the Royal Treasury.

Captain Nicolás Estrada and his wife, Lorenza Muñoz Hidalgo, committed to a chaplaincy established by the deceased Alférez Diego Quintero del Castillo and Francisca Hernández, former residents of Esparza, for 100 pesos at 5%. They mortgaged their residence in Cartago, which bordered properties including that of Sergeant Major José Felipe Bermúdez. The patron of the chaplaincy was José Díaz de Herrera, and Alférez Pedro Ortiz redeemed the 100 pesos.

Captain Francisco Javier de Oriamuno and his wife, Ana Efigenia García de Estrada, received a herd of cattle and horses, along with a house and corral, from Sergeant Major Juan Francisco de Ibarra, who was also the Provincial Mayor of the Santa Hermandad. This estate, located at Las Piedras, belonged to the deceased Nicolás de Ocampo and was valued at 637 pesos of cacao. Oriamuno and his wife received it from Ibarra, as Ocampo's executor, with the obligation to acknowledge a 100-peso chaplaincy for Captain Germán Rodríguez's soul and 150 pesos for Rodríguez's minor daughter, who was in Nicaragua.

An obligation of 387 pesos is recognized in favor of the minor children, José Manuel and María Leónidas, legitimate children of the deceased Nicolás de Ocampo Golfín and Manuela de Bazterrica. Capitán don Dionisio Pacheco is provided as a guarantor for this and other obligations.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Franco de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Don Juan José Alvarado leased two plots of fruiting cacao trees (approximately 1,000 trees) on the Matina river from Sarjento Mayor don Juan Franco de Ibarra y Calvo, who is the Mayordomo of the Cofradía de N. Señora de los Angeles. The three-year lease included an obligation to cultivate and reseed a 2,000-tree clearing belonging to the Cofradía.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo, as albacea of the deceased Pedro Jiménez Mondragón, and his widow, Doña Francisca de Inza, leased a cacao hacienda (approximately 1,000 trees) and 10 tame mule beasts to Don Cayetano de Alvarado in the Matina valley. The three-year lease was for 250 pesos of cacao annually, to be delivered in the city.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco Javier de Siles
Doña Eugenia de Bazterrica y Narvaiza
Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Capitán don Francisco Javier de Siles and his wife, Doña Eugenia de Bazterrica y Narvaiza, obligated themselves for 120 pesos of cacao to the minors José Manuel and María Leónidas, children of the deceased don Nicolás de Ocampo and doña Manuela de Bazterrica. They received this sum from Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo, albacea of don Nicolás, and hypothecated two mule beasts as collateral.

people_involved: Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero
summary: Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero leased a fruiting cacao hacienda on the Matina river to Alférez Baltasar de Moya for four years. Moya was obligated to create a clearing of 1,800 trees in Barbilla and deliver it planted at the end of the lease, receiving a load of meat and a machete in Matina for initial work.

people_involved: Don Luis Fernando de Liendo y Goicoechea
Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero
summary: Escribano don Luis Fernando de Liendo y Goicoechea canceled a previous obligation, as Alférez Baltasar de Moya had granted a new deed of obligation for 187 pesos in favor of Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero before him.

Juan Fernández Martínez and his wife, Doña Cayetana Acosta Arévalo, leased a fruiting cacao hacienda in the Matina valley to Francisco Manuel García for three years at a price of 250 pesos. The hacienda bordered Madre Dios, Doña Francisca Inza's hacienda, the mountain, and the river.

people_involved: Doña Angela de la Paz Flores
summary: Doña Josefa de Moya, widow of don Antonio Utrera, granted freedom to her 25-year-old slave, Sebastiano Golfín. She had acquired Sebastiano with her deceased husband through purchase from the deceased Doña Angela de la Paz Flores.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Díaz de Herrera
summary: Capitán Felipe de Meza, legitimate son of the deceased Ayudante Juan de Meza and Andrea de Ortega, made his will. He was the widower of Felipa López de Artavia, with whom he had children Juan Gregorio, Diego, and María Josefa de Meza. He left the site of Ujarraz to his daughter María Josefa de Meza and named Licenciado don José Díaz de Herrera as his albacea.

Doña Sebastiana de Bonilla, legitimate daughter of Sarjento Mayor Alonso de Bonilla and Doña Ana Benita Calvo, made her will. She was married to Sarjento Mayor Francisco de Espinosa and had two deceased children, José and Nicolasa de Espinosa. She named her nephew, Juan Antonio de Moya, and his wife, Doña Antonia María de Guzmán, as her albacea and heirs.
The Teniente General placed Gabriel Hernández, a 10-11 year old free mestizo and son of María Roque and Sarjento Cayetano Lobo (a shoemaker), into an apprenticeship for five years.

people_involved: Capitán de Caballos Corazas don Tomás López del Corral
summary: Cristóbal de Umaña and his wife, Doña Francisca de Alfaro, residents of the Barba valleys, sold a 20-year-old mulato criollo slave named Juan de Alfaro to Capitán de Caballos Corazas don Tomás López del Corral for 300 pesos plata. Doña Francisca had received Juan de Alfaro as part of her dowry.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Capitán don Juan de Ocampo Golfín sold a 20-year-old mulatillo slave named Nicolás to Capitán Luis Morera, a resident of the Barba valleys, for 300 pesos plata. Juan de Ocampo Golfín had previously purchased Nicolás from Licenciado don Hermenegildo de Alvarado.

people_involved: Teniente de Capitán don Cayetano de Alvarado
Capitán de Caballos Corazas don Tomás López del Corral
summary: Teniente de Capitán don Cayetano de Alvarado obligated himself for 300 pesos to the Capellanía instituted by the deceased Alférez Antonio Machado. He received this sum from Licenciado don Juan José Camacho, the patron of the Capellanía, which had been redeemed by Capitán don Tomás López del Corral. Alvarado imposed this obligation on a cacao hacienda of 1,500 trees in the Matina valley, bordering Nuestra Señora's hacienda, Doña Francisca de Inza's hacienda, and the mountain.

people_involved: Capitán de Caballos Corazas don Tomás López del Corral
summary: Licenciado don Juan José Camacho, as principal and Capellán, and Josefa Elena de Soto, as guarantor, obligated themselves for 200 pesos at 5% interest to the Capellanía founded by the deceased Alférez Antonio Machado. This sum was also redeemed by Capitán don Tomás López del Corral.

Francisco Arias, as principal, and Francisco Gamboa, as guarantor, obligated themselves for 100 pesos at 5% interest to Licenciado don Juan José Camacho, Presbítero, who is the patron and Capellán of the Capellanía founded by the deceased Alonso Górafz Macoteloa. This sum was redeemed by Capitán Juan de Astúa, albacea of the deceased Alférez José Calderón. The obligation was secured by a thatched house and a plantain orchard owned by Juana de Vergara, who consented to the encumbrance.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don José Fernández Cast...
summary: Licenciado don Juan José Camacho, a Clérigo Presbítero, obligated himself to the Cofradía de la Concepción, located in the Convento de San Francisco, of which Sarjento Mayor don José Fernández Cast... is the Mayordomo.

locations: solar del Capitán Juan de Astúa
casa y solar del Ayudante Nicolás de Estrada
casa pajiza de don Luis de Soto Mayor
summary: A Mayordomo sold a solar (plot of land) in 'this city' to Don José Fernández Castellanos for 50 pesos. The solar's boundaries are described, including properties belonging to Captain Juan de Astúa, Ayudante Nicolás de Estrada, and don Luis de Soto Mayor. The solar, along with a house to be built there, serves as collateral for the debt.

Doña Francisca de Inza, widow of Lieutenant Captain don Pedro Jiménez Mondragón, obligated herself to her five minor children for 241 pesos 2 reales of cacao, which they inherited from their deceased father.

people_involved: Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Francisca de Hinojosa, legitimate daughter of the deceased Alférez Juan Ginés de Hinojosa and Gertrudis Ruiz, made her will. She was the widow of Miguel de Matamoros and had two married sons, Miguel and Juan, and a foster daughter named Manuela. Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba was named her executor.

people_involved: Capitán don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón
Capitán don Juan de Ocampo Golfín
Sarjento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz
summary: The will of doña Josefa de Moya was opened, presented by her brother, Capitán don Fernando de Moya. Doña Josefa had died on July 17 of the same year around 4 AM. Several individuals, including Capitán don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón and Capitán don Juan de Ocampo Golfín, served as witnesses.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan de Ocampo Golfín
Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Capitán don Juan de Ocampo Golfín, a resident of Valle de Barba, obligated himself to Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo, who was the tutor of the minors José Manuel and María Leónidas, children of the deceased don Nicolás de Ocampo. This obligation was for 200 pesos of cacao, stemming from a two-year-old purchase of a wild mare herd from his brother, don Nicolás de Ocampo, and was guaranteed with the Higuerón site.

Alfonso González, legitimate son of the deceased Salvador González and Mariana Barquero, made his will. He was married to María Teresa de la Flor and had children Juan, José, and Manuela González, in addition to others who died. He also raised three women and one boy as his children, to whom he bequeathed two stubborn cows each. His wife and his brother, Sarjento Miguel González, were named executors.

people_involved: don Juan Pérez de las Cuevas
don Manuel Pérez de las Cuevas
summary: Don Juan Pérez de las Cuevas, a native of Fraguas in Burgos, Spain, and a resident of Villa de los Santos in Tierra Firme, made his will. He was married to doña Lorenza Garrido de Posada and had two daughters, Bárbara del Carmen (deceased) and another unnamed daughter born in 'this city'. His wife was named universal heir, and Capitán don Antonio de Oriamuno was named executor.

Pedro Ortiz, natural son of Eugenia Ortiz, made his will. He was married to María Calvo and had four children: Rafael, Nicolás, Antonio Leónidas, and Antonia Josefa, who were named his heirs. His mother-in-law, Juana Garita, and Capitán Cayetano Muñoz were named as executors.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
doña Felipa Sendín de Soto Mayor
summary: Don José Fernández Castellanos, a native of Toledo, Spain, granted power to testate to his compadre, Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo, whom he also named as his executor. His legitimate daughters, Antonia Josefa and Francisca Javiera Fernández Castellanos (children of his deceased wife doña Felipa Sendín de Soto Mayor), were named his heirs.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Díaz de Herrera
summary: Licenciado don José Díaz de Herrera, Cura and Lieutenant Vicar, obligated himself to a chaplaincy instituted by the deceased doña Gertrudis de Alvarado for 300 pesos. The funds, which Capitán Cayetano Muñoz had redeemed, were imposed on a cacao plantation of 750 trees in the Valle de Matina.
María Calvo, widow of Pedro Ortiz, obligated herself to her four minor children for 647 pesos 6 reales from their paternal inheritance. Capitán Cayetano Muñoz served as guarantor for this obligation.
Don José de Alvarado and his wife doña Francisca de Bonilla, residents of Valle de Curridabat, obligated themselves for 50 pesos.

people_involved: Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Doña Baltasara Escalante Panlagua redeemed three slaves, María Efigenia (23, black), and her two zambo children, Rita (1) and Francisco Javier (2). She had received these slaves from Licenciado don Francisco de Ocampo. The slaves are then mortgaged in favor of Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo, acting as Síndico for the Convento de San Francisco.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
Doña Josefa de Aguiar y Santiago
Sarjento Mayor don José Felipe Bermúdez
Capitán don Antonio Elias de Arleguí
summary: Licenciado don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría, acting as an agent for Licenciado don Manuel de Guzmán, leased a cacao plantation in Matina for three years to Capitán don Antonio Elias de Arleguí. This plantation belonged to Doña Josefa de Aguiar y Santiago, who owed a significant debt, and was under embargo by Visitador don Manuel López Conejo. The lease was for 125 pesos of cacao annually, totaling 375 pesos, and Arleguí accepted the terms.

people_involved: Capitán de Caballos Corazas don Tomás López del Corral
summary: Doña Francisca de Inza obligated herself to the Real Caja for 350 pesos of cacao, which she received from Capitán de Caballos Corazas don Tomás López del Corral. She mortgaged a cacao plantation of 1,000 trees in Matina and some houses in Cartago as security for this obligation.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Díaz de Herrera
Vicario don Manuel José González Coronel
summary: Licenciado don José Díaz de Herrera obligated himself for 200 pesos of silver at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by the deceased Doña Eugenia Abarca. Licenciado don Hermenegildo de Arleguí is the patron and chaplain of this endowment. The obligation was secured by Díaz de Herrera's dwelling houses, which bordered the public square and properties of Vicario don Manuel José González Coronel and Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Díaz de Herrera
summary: Licenciado don José Díaz de Herrera made a second obligation for 100 pesos of silver at 5% interest to the same chaplaincy, which Antonio Umaña had redeemed. This obligation was secured by a cacao plantation of 750 trees in the Matina valley. The plantation bordered a clearing owned by Capitán don Tomás Barahona, a river, and a mountain.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don José de Baeza
Capitán don José de Morales Tremiño
Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
Mtre. de Campo don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Sarjento Mayor don José de Baeza and his wife Doña Magdalena Maroto obligated themselves to the Convento de San Francisco for 300 pesos of silver at 5% interest, secured by an adobe and tile house. This house bordered properties of Don Bernardo García de Miranda, Capitán don José de Morales Tremiño, and the Parish Church, and was previously managed by Doña Josefa de Moya. Subsequently, on March 20, 1734, José de Baeza paid 200 pesos to Síndico don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo, and on September 5, 1746, Doña Magdalena Maroto paid the remaining 100 pesos to Síndico don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora.

María Barquero, a widow and daughter of Francisco Hernández Barquero and Ana de Espinosa, made her testament. She had no children from her first marriage but had six children with her second husband, Pedro Solano, and also mentioned grandchildren through her daughter Juana Solano. She listed several slaves, including Vicenta Josefa, whom she granted freedom upon her death, and appointed her brother Capitán Francisco Barquero and son Pedro Solano as executors, with her children and grandchildren as heirs.

Capitán Tomás de Chaves obligated himself for 100 pesos at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by Laureano Ballestero, which is administered by the Guardian of the Convento de Barba. These pesos had been redeemed by Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara. The obligation was secured by a herd of cattle and horses owned by Chaves in Río Grande.

Juana Calderón obligated herself for 100 pesos at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by Magdalena de la Portilla, with Licenciado don Francisco Ocampo as its patron. These pesos were redeemed by José de las Salas. She mortgaged a cacao plantation of 700 trees in Matina, bordering a stream, the Hacienda de la Puerta, and a river, but the transaction was not completed.

Capitán Marcos de Chinchilla sold a piece of land to Capitán Francisco Javier de Siles, Teniente Juez de los Campos, for 50 pesos in cacao currency. The land, located about a league from Cartago, was defined by borders including the 'riachuelo del albañil', Juan Gómez's ditch, an avocado tree and houses of Juan de Aguilar, and the royal road to Chicagres.

Juana Calderón, widow of Capitán Juan de la Madriz, obligated herself for 150 pesos of cacao at 5% interest to the Chaplaincy founded by Ayudante Matías Masís. The interim chaplain was the Guardian of the Convento de San Francisco, or Hermano José de las Salas if José Manuel de Cárdenas, the designated chaplain and patron, was not ordained. This obligation was secured by a 700-tree cacao plantation in Matina, bordering a stream, the Hacienda de la Puerta, and a river, with the pesos having been redeemed by Hermano José de las Salas.

people_involved: Licenciado don Manuel José González Coronel
summary: Gertrudis Ruiz, a widow, sold a productive cacao plantation of 250 trees in the Matina valley to Sarjento Pascual Salguero for 250 pesos of cacao. The plantation's boundaries included the hacienda of the deceased Francisco Fernández, the hacienda of Licenciado don Manuel José González Coronel, a river, and a mountain.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don José de Baeza
Capitán de Caballos Corazas don Tomás López del Corral
summary: Sarjento Mayor don José de Baeza and his wife Doña Magdalena Maroto initiated a sale transaction with Capitán de Caballos Corazas don Tomás López del Corral. The details of what was sold are not provided as the entry is incomplete.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
summary: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral, a Lieutenant of Royal Officials of the Royal Treasury, sold an enslaved mulatilla named Isabel, aged 12-13, for 300 silver pesos. Isabel was the daughter of another enslaved woman belonging to del Corral.

people_involved: Síndico general del Convento de San Francisco de Cartago
summary: Doña Josefa de Moya, a widow, purchased an adobe and tile house in Cartago, situated west of the church's high ground, from the General Syndic of the San Francisco Convent for 300 pesos. The property is subject to a 5% annual charge, and don Bernardo García de Miranda will possess it with the same obligation.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don José Fernández Castellanos
summary: Don Alfonso de Ulloa and his wife Doña María Maroto sold a 7-year-old Creole mulatilla slave named Juana Josefa to Sergeant Major don José Fernández Castellanos for 155 pesos. Juana Josefa and her mother, Ramona Maroto (also their slave), were originally given as a dowry to Doña María. The deed for this transaction was not signed.

locations: Ciudad del Espíritu Santo de Esparza
people_involved: Sárjente Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: Captain Luis Gutiérrez and his wife Doña Francisca de Aguiar pledged a cacao plantation of 3,000 trees in the Barbilla valley as security for 200 pesos. This obligation was made in favor of a Chaplaincy founded by Captain Pedro Ibáñez, whose current patron and chaplain is Don Manuel López Conejo, the priest of Esparza, after Sergeant Major don Francisco de la Madriz Linares repaid and redeemed the sum.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
summary: Captain don Tomás López del Corral, Lieutenant of Royal Treasury Officials, granted conditional freedom to his 45-year-old enslaved man, Gregorio Camaño, whom he had purchased from don Pedro Mondragón's estate. Gregorio's freedom was contingent upon him cultivating and caring for a new 5,000-tree cacao plantation in the Barbilla valley until it became fruit-bearing and well-maintained.

locations: houses of heirs of Capitán Sebastián Meléndez
houses of Capitán don José Antonio López del Corral
people_involved: Capitán don José Antonio López del Corral
summary: Doña Manuela Valerino, widow of Captain Diego de Cárdenas, founded a Chaplaincy for masses with 1,000 pesos in cacao, the local currency. The foundation included houses and three undeveloped plots in the city, bordering the hermitage of San Nicolás, María Golfín's house, the heirs of Captain Sebastián Meléndez, and Captain don José Antonio López del Corral. Her legitimate son, Manuel José de Cárdenas, was named the first perpetual chaplain, with consent from her other three children.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
summary: Sergeant Major don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo declared that he had given his daughter, Doña Francisca de Ibarra, various goods and jewels upon her marriage to Captain don Tomás López del Corral. He further delivered 200 pesos as an advance on her inheritance, in the form of one hundred mares requested by Captain del Corral to stock his ranch in the Landecho valley, which del Corral accepted.

people_involved: Doña Baltasara López de la Flor
Capitán don José López de la Flor
Unnamed son of Josefa and don Vicente de Morales
don Mariano López de la Flor
summary: Doña Baltasara López de la Flor made her will, detailing her enslaved women Petronila (20), Gertrudis (16-18), and María del Carmen (1.5). She recounted her natural daughter Josefa's marriage to don Vicente de Morales, their deaths from smallpox, and the subsequent death of their son. To support don Vicente's priesthood, she founded a Chaplaincy of 1,500 pesos on a Matina cacao hacienda, naming him patron, and bequeathed half of another Matina cacao plantation shared with her brother don Mariano López de la Flor to the foundation. María del Carmen was to serve the Cofradía de los Angeles as a slave, with the condition that her future children would be free. She also listed debts to Micaela de Lara and named Licenciado don José de Guzmán and Presbítero Br. don Pedro Meléndez as executors, with don Vicente de Morales as her heir.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan López de la Rea
Sárjente Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: Doña Antonia de Sandoval, widow of Captain don Juan López de la Rea, made her will, listing her deceased children Juana Antonia, Juan José, and Manuel, and her living daughters Ana Nicolasa, Manuela Francisca, and María Antonia. She mentioned Ana Nicolasa's marriage to Juan Chacón and María Antonia's marriage to Pedro José Luardo. She also noted an orphan child, Juan José, whom she raised, who inherited cows from her son Manuel. Sergeant Major don Francisco de la Madriz Linares was named as her executor.

people_involved: Cofradía de Nuestra Señora de la Concepción
summary: Gertrudis Peláez, a widow, donated a ranch (estancia) valued at 600-700 pesos, located in the ejidos south of Cartago near the Taras river, to her nephew Enrique Molina. Enrique was studying in Santiago de Guatemala to become a priest, and the donation would take effect upon his ordination. The ranch was subject to an annual payment of 13 reales to the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora de la Concepción. Enrique's father, Miguel Molina, had died recently, leaving his mother, Juana Meléndez, in poverty.

Capitán Diego de Aguilar appoints Enrique Molina as patron and chaplain of a chaplaincy he intends to establish. The chaplaincy will be founded on an estate near Cartago, close to Quircot, which includes various assets like plantings, houses, furniture, oxen, cattle, and horses, valued at over a thousand pesos. The foundation will become effective once Molina is ordained as a priest.

Doña Luisa Calvo, a widow, sells her 40-year-old Popo slave named Francisco Zaroto to Capitán don Francisco de Betancourt for 300 pesos. She had previously acquired Francisco Zaroto by purchase from Sarjento Mayor Blas González Coronel.

people_involved: doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
summary: Capitán don Francisco de Betancourt and his wife, doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral, obligate themselves to the Royal Treasury of Cartago for 300 pesos in cacao.

people_involved: Teniente General don Diego de Barros y Carvajal
summary: Francisco de Arroyo y Oviedo, who began serving as a canoeist on the Reventazón river on August 15, 1732, obligates himself to serve for one more year. He commits to maintaining continuous service at the river crossing with a canoe at his own expense and delivering a sack of prime cacao to the Royal Justices or Steward in Cartago.

people_involved: Teniente General don Diego de Barros y Carvajal
summary: The Teniente General places Bonifacio de Campos, a free "pardo" boy aged 12-13 and son of Juana de Campos, with Felipe de Umaña, a tailor's official, for a period of 5 years.
Doña Antonia de Chavarría Navarro, a widow, leases two cacao plots in Matina to Capitán Tomás Cubero, a "pardo," for three years at 200 pesos of cacao annually.

people_involved: Pro. Licenciado don José Miguel de Guzmán
summary: The lease agreement between Doña Antonia de Chavarría Navarro and Capitán Tomás Cubero for cacao plots in Matina was cancelled in 1736 by Pro. Licenciado don José Miguel de Guzmán, acting on behalf of his mother, Doña Antonia.

Don Gil de Alvarado states he bought a cacao plantation in Matina from his brother, Capitán don Miguel de Alvarado, for 1,700 pesos. This property is burdened with 850 pesos from three chaplaincies. Due to ill health, Don Gil de Alvarado transfers the finca with its burdens to Presbítero Camacho.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan Sánchez de Castañeda
Br. don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones
summary: Doña Manuela Sáenz, a widow, sells a tiled house in the ejidos of Cartago to Capitán Julián García de Ergueta and his wife doña Ana Sánchez de Castañeda for 100 pesos. The property is encumbered by a chaplaincy founded by Luis Cardoso, and the buyers are obligated to pay this amount to Bdo. don Manuel González Coronel, attorney for Br. don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones.
The sale of the house by Doña Manuela Sáenz to Capitán Julián García de Ergueta and doña Ana Sánchez de Castañeda was cancelled on May 16, 1735, by Pro. González Coronel.

people_involved: doña Dionisia Fallas de la Vega
Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: Capitán Manuel García de Ergueta's codicil declares Pedro Félix José as his legitimate son with his second wife, doña Dionisia Fallas de la Vega. He details a chaplaincy for his son José Manuel García de Ergueta, mentions an inheritance advance to Capitán Julián García de Ergueta, a payment to Capitán don José Lebrón on behalf of don Rafael García de Ergueta, and a debt owed by his son-in-law Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares.

people_involved: doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: Capitán don Francisco de Betancourt and his wife, doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral, sell an old estate in the ejidos of Cartago to Capitán Cayetano Muñoz for 200 pesos. This estate was inherited by doña María Josefa from her deceased parents, Sarjento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral and doña Ambrosia González Camino, and borders the Agua Caliente river.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo, as Steward of the Confraternity of Nuestra Señora de los Angeles, leases two cacao plots on the Matina river banks to Capitán Francisco de Echavarría for 2.5 years. In return, Echavarría is obligated to cultivate a 2,100-tree cacao clearing belonging to the Confraternity.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo sells a cattle and horse ranch in San Miguel de Paso Hondo, Sagaces valley, to his son-in-law, Capitán don Antonio de Oriamuno, for 2,646 pesos. The property is burdened by a chaplaincy of Capitán Juan Calvo. Ibarra y Calvo donates 500 pesos of the price to his daughter, doña María Catarina de Ibarra, with the remainder to be paid in installments over 1735-1737.

people_involved: Alférez don Luis de Soto Mayor
doña Isabel Ramona de Utrera y Medina
Sarjento Mayor don José Fernando de Moya
summary: Alférez don Luis de Soto Mayor and his wife, doña Isabel Ramona de Utrera y Medina, acknowledge receiving 200 pesos from Sarjento Mayor don José Fernando de Moya, executor of the deceased doña Cecilia Vásquez de Coronado. This sum is part of the capital for a chaplaincy doña Cecilia ordered founded, and the couple obligates themselves to pay a 5% interest, mortgaging their house in Cartago.

people_involved: Don Ramón de Noguera y Moncada
Sarjento Mayor Don Jerónimo del Cubillo
Licenciado Don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero
Sarjento Mayor Don Francisco del Cubillo
summary: Don Ramón de Noguera y Moncada and his wife Doña Ana de Arleguí sold an enslaved Creole boy named Marcos Nicolás, aged 10-12, to Sarjento Mayor Don Jerónimo del Cubillo for 250 pesos. Licenciado Don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero acted as the buyer's attorney, based on a power of attorney issued in Esparza by Sarjento Mayor Don Francisco del Cubillo, acting on behalf of his father, Don Jerónimo del Cubillo.

locations: Ciudad de los Reyes del Perú
people_involved: Doña Juana Eufrasia Sánchez de Castañeda
Capitán Don Juan Sánchez de Castañeda
summary: Don Esteban Ruiz de Mendoza, legitimate son of the late Don Alonso Ruiz de Mendoza and Doña Lorenza Josefa de Tapia, established a dowry of 1607 pesos and 4 reales for his wife, Doña Juana Eufrasia Sánchez de Castañeda. Doña Juana is the legitimate daughter of the late Capitán Don Juan Sánchez de Castañeda and Doña Juana de Alvarado.

people_involved: Doña Isabel Ramona de Utrera y Medina
summary: Alférez Don Luis de Sotomayor and his wife Doña Isabel Ramona de Utrera y Medina sold an enslaved Creole woman named María Guerrero, about 21 years old, to Doña Catalma Siles for 200 pesos. Doña Isabel Ramona de Utrera y Medina had inherited María Guerrero from her deceased mother, Doña Josefa de Moya.

people_involved: Capitán Don Diego de Barros y Carvajal
Maese de Campo Don José de Casasola
Señor Arcediano de la ciudad de León de Nicaragua Don José de Velasco
Licenciado Don José Francisco de Casasola
summary: Capitán Don Diego de Barros y Carvajal and his wife Doña Josefa Pérez del Muro committed to a Chaplaincy founded by Don José Pérez del Muro for 1,500 pesos, charged on houses in Cartago. Licenciado Don José Francisco de Casasola, nephew of the grantors and now ordained as a Presbítero, requested recognition as the first Chaplain, with the Señor Arcediano Don José de Velasco serving in the interim.

people_involved: Doña Josefa Fallas de la Vega
Capitán Francisco Fallas de la Vega
summary: Doña Josefa Fallas de la Vega, a single woman and legitimate daughter of the late Capitán Francisco Fallas de la Vega and Doña Mariana Solano, granted freedom to her 6-year-old enslaved mulatilla named Antonia, to take effect upon Doña Josefa's death. Antonia is the daughter of Feliciana, another enslaved woman born and raised in Doña Josefa's parents' house.

locations: Vega del río de las Cañas
people_involved: Doña Efigenia Fallas de la Vega
Capitán Francisco Fallas de la Vega
summary: Pedro Mesena and his wife Doña Efigenia Fallas de la Vega, residents of Curridaba, recognized a 200-peso lien on a house and land they inherited from Doña Efigenia's deceased parents, Capitán Francisco Fallas de la Vega and Doña Mariana Solano. This lien belonged to a Chaplaincy founded by Capitán Pedro Ibáñez, and Bdo. Don Manuel López Conejo, Cura propio of Esparza and Visitador General, accepted it as the patron and chaplain.

people_involved: Capitán Don Diego de Barros y Carvajal
Bdo. Don Diego de Ángulo Gascón
summary: Capitán Don Diego de Barros y Carvajal and his wife Doña Josefa Pérez del Muro committed to a Chaplaincy founded by Capitán Pedro Ibáñez for 150 pesos, hypothecating a cacao plantation in Matina. This sum was the remaining balance of 450 pesos they had previously recognized when Bdo.
