Don Diego de Ángulo Gascón was the patron and chaplain, and Presbítero Don Manuel López Conejo accepted the current obligation.

people_involved: Doña Isabel Ramona de Utrera y Medina
summary: Alférez Don Luis de Sotomayor and his wife Doña Isabel Ramona de Utrera y Medina recognized a debt of 425 pesos owed by Doña Josefa de Moya, Doña Isabel's deceased mother, to a Chaplaincy founded by Doña Cecilia Vásquez de Coronado. As Doña Isabel was the sole heir, she and her husband jointly committed to an obligation of 850 pesos, hypothecating a hacienda in Ujarraz and a house and solar in Cartago, with Presbítero Don Manuel López Conejo serving as interim chaplain.

Teniente Francisco Gutiérrez granted freedom to Juan Román, an enslaved Black man he had purchased from his father's estate, Capitán Francisco Gutiérrez. This act was in compliance with a court sentence resulting from a lawsuit filed by Juan Román, which ordered his freedom in exchange for 500 cacao trees he had cultivated and additional cacao sacks provided by his free son, José Nicolás.

Teniente Francisco Gutiérrez sold a 500-tree cacao plantation in the Barbilla valley to Capitán Manuel García de Ergueta. This plantation was received by Gutiérrez as part of the payment for the freedom of the enslaved man Juan Román. The buyer agreed to pay 9 sacks of cacao, each valued at 25 pesos.

people_involved: Capitán Don José de Maroto Tremiño
Licenciado Don José Miguel de Arburola
Licenciado Don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí
Bdo. Don José Antonio Díaz de Herrera
Licenciado Don Manuel José González Coronel
summary: Doña María Josefa Cabral, wife of Capitán Don Francisco de Betancourt, obligated herself for 600 pesos previously owed by Doña Juana de Ángulo, widow of Capitán Don José de Maroto Tremiño. These 600 pesos were distributed among four Chaplaincies served by Licenciado Don José Miguel de Arburola, Licenciado Don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí, Bdo. Don José Antonio Díaz de Herrera, and Licenciado Don Manuel José González Coronel. She hypothecated her house and solar in Cartago.

people_involved: Capitán Don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno
Doña Ana Efigenia García de Estrada
Licenciado Don José Miguel de Arburola
Licenciado Don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí
summary: Capitán Don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno and his wife Doña Ana Efigenia García de Estrada obligated themselves for 850 pesos, taking over a previous obligation on a house from Doña María Josefa Cabral (wife of Capitán Don Francisco de Betancourt), which was originally from Doña Juana de Ángulo. The 850 pesos were distributed among several Chaplaincies and the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora del Rosario, and they hypothecated the house and solar in Cartago.

people_involved: Licenciado Don Manuel José González Coronel
Sarjento Mayor Don Blas González Coronel
summary: Licenciado Don Manuel José González Coronel, interim priest, synodal examiner, and Commissary of the Holy Office of the Inquisition, leased a thousand-tree cacao plantation in the Matina valley to Nicolás Vanegas, a free Black man from Granada, Nicaragua. The plantation, inherited from his father Sarjento Mayor Don Blas González Coronel, was leased for five years, with the condition that the tenant would clear new land.

Capitán Juan José de Cuende and his wife Manuela de Ibarra y Calvo obligated themselves for 146 pesos to Manuel Antonio and María Leonida de Ocampo Golfín. The Ocampo Golfín children are minors and legitimate heirs of the deceased Nicolás de Ocampo and Manuela Bazterrica.

people_involved: Licenciado Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Petronila de Hoces Navarro, widow of Sarjento Mayor Antonio de Soto y Barahona, founded a Chaplaincy with a principal of 1000 pesos, fulfilling her husband's testamentary wishes. Her son, Licenciado Antonio de Soto y Barahona, was named the first Chaplain, followed by her minor son Nicolás, and then her grandson José Gabriel. The capital included a cacao hacienda on the Matina river.

Bernarda de Villarreal, a widow, obligated herself to Clara Campos, a minor daughter of Miguel de Campos, for 271 pesos 6 reales and a half. This sum represented Clara's paternal inheritance from the estate of her grandfather, Capitán Jacinto de Campos. José de Campos, son of Capitán Jacinto, acted as guarantor for Bernarda, who is Clara's grandmother.

Sarjento Mayor Pedro José Sáenz and his wife María de la Rosa obligated themselves for 100 pesos to the Chaplaincy founded by Ana de Echavarría Navarro. The funds were previously located in Capitán Francisco Gutiérrez's house. Licenciado Manuel de Guzmán, the patron and Chaplain in Guatemala, was represented locally by his brother, Licenciado José Miguel de Guzmán, who served as Predicador general and Sacristán Mayor in Cartago.

people_involved: Licenciado Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Doña Catarina de Arburola, a widow, obligated herself for 200 pesos to the Chaplaincy founded by Francisco Enciso. Licenciado Antonio de Soto y Barahona served as Chaplain, having received the position from Licenciado Félix de Hoces Navarro, cura of Cuisalguaque. Catarina mortgaged her house, located across the Reventado river by the Taras river, which was valued at 600 pesos.

Angela Sáenz, widow and executor of Capitán Pedro de Moya, founded a Chaplaincy with two capitals of 150 pesos each. One capital was for an annual mass on December 8th, and the other was to support the ordination of a suitable relative. José Francisco de Moya, a cleric deacon and relative, was named the first Chaplain, with her nephew José Antonio de Bonilla as patron.

Capitán Luis de Sotomayor and his wife Isabel Ramona de Utrera obligated themselves to the Convento de San Francisco in Cartago for 200 pesos. This sum was a debt on a house formerly owned by Sarjento Mayor José de Baeza, which he had redeemed. The money was provided to Sotomayor and Utrera by Sarjento Mayor Juan Francisco de Ibarra, the Síndico General of the Convento, and they mortgaged their own house, which also carried a debt to the Chaplaincy of Cecilia Vásquez de Coronado.

Sarjento Mayor Pedro José Sáenz and his wife María de la Rosa sold a hacienda in the Aserrí valley to their son, Capitán Manuel Sáenz, for 750 pesos. The hacienda was encumbered with several mortgages to various religious entities, which Manuel Sáenz agreed to assume. The transaction, valued by the sellers at over 2,500 pesos, was executed before Juan José de Cuende, acting as Teniente General due to the absence of Capitán del Corral.

Ana Josefa Ángulo, widow of José de Morales Tremiño, made her testament, naming her six children: Josefa Gabriela, Juan José, María Manuela, Antonio, Diego, and Mariana de Morales. She appointed Vicario Manuel José González Coronel and Capitán Dionisio Salmón Pacheco as her executors.

A dowry letter was issued for the marriage of Capitán Juan Nicolás Viveros, Teniente of Esparza and native of Puerto Santa María, Spain, to Francisca de la Madriz Linares. Juan Nicolás was the son of Francisco Viveros and Antonia de Rojas, while Francisca was the daughter of Sarjento Mayor Francisco de la Madriz Linares and Josefa Rita García de Argueta. The dowry totaled 1,816 pesos, including the value of a 5-year-old zambita named Sebastiana and 500 cacao trees in the Barbilla valley.

Juan Matías de Moya sold a tiled cedar wood house and its plot located in the ejidos of Cartago, specifically within the pasture and hills belonging to Gracia de Oses Navarro. Gracia de Oses Navarro had previously founded something on this property while acting as the executor for her deceased mother, Micaela de Arburola.

A Chaplaincy valued at 366 pesos, for which Licenciado don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí serves as interim Chaplain, was sold to Capitán don Antonio Elias de Arleguí. The buyer committed to an annual tax of 5 Ojo on this sum.

people_involved: María Josefa de Barros y Carvajal
summary: Capitán don Domingo Antonio Rápela del Villar, originally from Santa María de Armea, Galicia, established a dowry of 2,468 pesos (including 1,000 pesos in cacao) for his future wife, doña María Josefa de Barros y Carvajal.

Doña Angela Sáenz, a widow, leased a cacao plantation with approximately 300 trees in the Barbilla valley to Capitán Cayetano Muñoz y Bermúdez for three years. The annual rent was 100 pesos, payable in cacao.

Don Antonio María Marín, a resident of Cartago, incurred a debt of 549 pesos 7 reales for clothing he sold. He is obligated to pay 474 pesos 2 reales to Domingo Ribera of Comayagua, and 65 pesos 5 reales to Gregorio de Silva. The debt was legally declared in Cartago after Domingo Ribera came to collect.

Sarjento Mayor don Jerónimo Muñoz de la Trinidad, a resident of Santiago de Guatemala, became indebted to Gobernador don Baltasar Francisco de Valderrama for 760 pesos. He agreed to pay 250 pesos to don Pedro Francisco Navarro upon reaching Guatemala and 510 pesos to Valderrama in Cartago. A marginal note indicates a cancellation on March 28, 1735, for 354 pesos of this debt.

Several prominent citizens granted power of attorney to Sarjento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad (in Guatemala) and Licenciado don Rafael García de Argueta. This power was specifically for representing them in the 'juicio de residencia' of former Governor don Diego de la Haya Fernández, a process overseen by Juez comisario don José de Fuentes, commissioned by President Pedro de Villalón and requested by Fiscal Pedro López de Ezeiza.

Sarjento Mayor don Pedro Carazo established a dowry of 2,690 pesos 2 reales for his future wife, doña Ana Teresa de Soto Barahona. The dowry included an enslaved boy named José (3 years old, valued at 300 pesos), an enslaved girl named Antonia Josefa (7 years old, valued at 225 pesos), and 500 cacao trees in Matina (valued at 500 pesos).

Don Esteban Ruiz de Mendoza and his wife, doña Juana Eufrasia Sancho de Castañeda, took on a 900-peso obligation tied to a house and plot formerly belonging to Licenciado don Diego de Campos Quirós. The sum was distributed among several chaplaincies and confraternities. Due to the property's damage and 24 years of unpaid interest, the couple received 6 years free of payments to repair the damages.

On September 7, the testament of Teniente Francisco Gutiérrez was opened, revealing he had died on September 5 on the road to Matina. The testament, granted on December 14, 1733, named his wife, Gertrudis de Hinojosa, as his heir and co-executor with Capitán don Miguel de Alvarado. He bequeathed properties including cacao haciendas in Barbilla and a house in Cartago, and left specific legacies to his foster daughter Nicolasa, Manuel Chinchilla, and his sister-in-law Catarina de Hinojosa.
On September 9, the testament of Sarjento Mayor don José Felipe Bermúdez was recorded. He was married to doña Teresa de Sandoval and had two children, don José Antonio and doña Juana Gertrudis.

people_involved: José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Licenciado Pro. don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría, who jointly leased a cacao hacienda from doña Josefa de Santiago Aguiar with Capitán don Antonio Elias de Arleguí for three years, transferred his lease to Capitán Juan José de Cuende for 125 pesos annually.

On September 24, the testament of doña Jerónima de la Riba was recorded. She was the widow of Diego de Zamora and had four children: Micaela, Antonia, María, and José Manuel. Her nephew, Félix de la Riba, was also mentioned.
Gertrudis de Hinojosa, widow of Teniente Francisco Gutiérrez, formally committed to paying any legitimate debts incurred by her late husband.

Gertrudis de Hinojosa obligated herself to the Convento de San Francisco for 500 pesos related to a Chaplaincy. Her late husband, Francisco Gutiérrez, was the patron and responsible party for this Chaplaincy, which his father had ordered to be founded and was situated on a cacao hacienda in Barbilla.

people_involved: Doña Ana Efigenia García de Estrada
summary: Don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno and his wife, Doña Ana Efigenia García de Estrada, took charge of a census. This information was recorded as a marginal note in the document.
An unnamed woman committed to an obligation in favor of the minor Nicolasa. This obligation was for 100 pesos, which Nicolasa's husband had left her.
The same unnamed woman undertook an obligation for 100 pesos. This sum represented a legacy from the deceased Manuel de Chinchilla, intended for his minor children.

Doña Josefa de Bonilla, the legitimate daughter of the deceased Don Alonso Bonilla and Doña Juana Benita Calvo, and widow of Don Antonio de Porras, made her will. She declared that she had no children.

people_involved: Capitán Don Pedro de Rosas J
summary: Don José Sarmiento de Sotomayor, son of the deceased Depositario General Don Bernardo Sarmiento de Sotomayor and Doña Antonia María Venegas, made his will. He was the widower of Doña María Catarina de Rosas and listed his children. Doña Catarina de Vida Martel, his wife's grandmother, had previously delivered the dowry goods to him.

people_involved: Doña Ana de Molina y Portilla
summary: Capitán Manuel García de Argueta, son of Capitán Marcos García de Argueta and Doña Ana de Molina y Portilla, executed a codicil to his will. He stipulated that his house should be inherited by his three daughters, Manuela, Alfonsa, and Juana, and also made provisions for his unnamed wife.

people_involved: José Manuel García de Argueta (1st marriage)
Sargento Mayor Francisco de la Madriz Linares
Doña Dionisia Falla de la Vega
Capitán Francisco Falla de la Vega
María Alfonsa García de Argueta (2nd marriage)
summary: The will of Capitán Manuel García de Argueta, who died at dawn on this day, was opened. It detailed his two marriages, first to Doña Antonia Lainez de Iztueta and then to Doña Dionisia Falla de la Vega, and listed his numerous children from both unions. The will also mentioned several slaves and a mandate to establish a chaplaincy with a thousand pesos.

people_involved: Don Diego de Barros y Carvajal
summary: In 1734, Don Diego de Barros y Carvajal initially held the position of Teniente General, and was subsequently succeeded by Don Pedro José Sáenz.

people_involved: Licenciado Don Antonio de Guevara y Sáenz
Licenciado Don Manuel José González Coronel
Pro. Licenciado Don José Miguel de Guzmán
summary: Licenciado Don Antonio de Guevara y Sáenz, with permission from his superior, stated that the deceased Doña Josefa de Aguilar had sold him houses in Cartago, which were burdened with a 375-peso cacao census. He then agreed with Don José Antonio de Oriamuno and his wife, Doña María Catarina de Ibarra, that they would receive a section of the house and solar, obligating themselves for the 375 pesos.

Juan Fernández Martínez and his wife, Doña Cayetana de Acosta Arévalo, leased a cacao plantation in the Matina valley to Capitán Juan de Bonilla for three years. The annual rent was 2.5 zurrones of cacao, and the plantation had previously been leased by Teniente Don Francisco García.

people_involved: Pro. Licenciado Don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Pro. Licenciado Don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín sold a 10-12 year old mulato criollo slave named Nicolás de Fallas to Don Martín Freyle for 300 pesos. Ocampo Golfín had acquired Nicolás through a previous purchase from Jacinto Fallas.

people_involved: Doña Josefa de Aguiar y Santiago
summary: Ayudante Manuel de Alvarado, acting as the executor for the deceased Doña Josefa de Aguiar y Santiago, granted freedom to her mulato slave, Juan de Acosta. This manumission was conditional on Juan de Acosta paying for 25 recited masses.

María Manuela de Ortega, a widow, sold a thatched house and an annexed pasture in the ejidos of Cartago to Capitán Don José Lebrón for 100 pesos. The property bordered the Toyogres, Barquero, and Agua Caliente rivers, and included a water ditch previously purchased by her deceased husband, Jerónimo Gutiérrez.

Teniente Diego Meza leased a cacao plantation with 700 fruit trees in Matina to José Miguel and Don José Matías de Chavarría for three years. The rent was 3.5 zurrones of cacao for the first year and 4 zurrones for subsequent years, and the property bordered that of Diego Meza's brother, Gregorio Meza.

Josefa Elena de Soto, a widow, leased a cacao plantation named 'El Riachuelo' in Matina to Capitán Don Diego López Conejo for three years at an annual rent of 100 pesos. Don Pedro de Alvarado was currently leasing the property.

people_involved: Maestro de Campo Don Juan Francisco Sáenz
Bdo. Don José Antonio Díaz de Herrera
summary: Don José Nicolás Sarmiento de Sotomayor, residing in Curridabat, agreed to an obligation for 120 pesos, which had been charged on stone houses built by former Gobernador Maestro de Campo Don Juan Francisco Sáenz but were later demolished. The money, belonging to the Confraternity of Nuestra Señora de los Angeles, was delivered to him by Bdo. Don José Antonio Díaz de Herrera. Don José Nicolás offered houses, a sugar mill, and land as a mortgage, though the deed was not finalized.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: Sargento Mayor Don Francisco de la Madriz Linares and his wife, Doña Rita García, undertook an obligation for 90 pesos in favor of a chaplaincy founded by Doña Inés de Benavides. This debt was secured by their adobe and tile houses, and Doña Manuela de Quirós had previously been obligated for it. Don José Francisco de Moya served as the chaplain.

people_involved: Diácono don José Francisco de Moya
summary: Doña Angela Sáenz, widow of Captain Pedro de Moya, obligated herself for 100 pesos to a Chaplaincy founded by Doña Rafaela de Alvarado, with Diácono Don José Francisco de Moya as its Chaplain. She mortgaged a country house, sugar mill, and crops located in the common lands of the city, bordering the Toyogres river.
Doña Inés de Sandoval Golfín executed a codicil, witnessed by Captain Don Cayetano Muñoz, to grant freedom to her mulata slave named Antonia.
The Justice arranged for José de Herrera, a boy, to be placed with Mateo de los Santos, a master tailor in Cartago, for a period of six years.

people_involved: Doña Jerónima de la Riba Agüero
summary: Captain Don Antonio Salmón Pacheco obligated himself to Doña Jerónima de la Riba Agüero for 300 pesos, to be paid in cacao. A later note from 1735 confirms that this debt was paid.

people_involved: Doña Jerónima de la Riba Agüero
summary: Doña Jerónima de la Riba Agüero, with the consent of her children José and Doña Antonia Zamora, sold a house and land to Captain Don Antonio Salmón Pacheco for 600 pesos, paid in cacao, mules, and clothing. Her current husband, Captain Don Alvaro de Guevara, was in Santiago de Guatemala attempting to recover the lost titles for the property.

people_involved: Doña María de Jesús Riba Agüero
Don José Nicolás Sarmiento de Sotomayor
Capitán don Gil de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Captain Don Diego López Conejo, his wife Doña María de Jesús Riba Agüero, Doña Antonia María Vanegas, and Don José Nicolás Sarmiento de Sotomayor obligated themselves for 286 pesos to a Chaplaincy founded by Doña Sebastiana de Alvarado, mortgaging their house "El Molino" near Curridabat. However, this obligation was later cancelled on November 27, 1734, because the Chaplain did not consent and Don José Nicolás Sarmiento de Sotomayor, the principal obligor, had died.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan de Ocampo Golfín
Licenciado don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Captain Don Juan de Ocampo Golfín, acting for his brother Licenciado Don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín and with the consent of Sarjento Mayor Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra, mortgaged the San Pedro ranch in Bagaces valley for 110 pesos. This temporary mortgage, replacing a dilapidated house in Cartago, secures a censo inherited from their father, Sarjento Mayor Don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, until a new house is built on the brother's sugarcane hacienda in Barba valley.

locations: Convento de San Francisco de Cartago
people_involved: Capitán don Juan de Ocampo Golfín
Licenciado don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
Sarjente Mayor don José Fernández Castellanos
summary: Captain Don Juan de Ocampo Golfín, again acting for his brother Licenciado Don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, mortgaged the San Pedro ranch for 100 pesos to the Confraternity of Nuestra Señora de la Pura y Limpia Concepción in Cartago. Sarjente Mayor Don José Fernández Castellanos consented to this, and 16 slaves from the Licenciado's Barba valley hacienda were also included in the mortgage, which would eventually transfer to the new house being built there.

people_involved: Pro. Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara y Sáenz
Sarjento Mayor don José Felipe Bermúdez
summary: Doña Angela María de Arleguí, with her children's consent, granted freedom to her mulata slave María de Arleguí, whose mother Victoria was an inherited slave. Pro. Licenciado Don Antonio de Guevara y Sáenz charitably paid 200 pesos for this freedom, with Don Luis de Sotomayor acting as his attorney.

people_involved: Licenciado don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
Licenciado Pro. don Manuel José González Coronel
summary: Don Juan de Ocampo Golfín, acting as attorney for his brother Licenciado Don Francisco, exchanged the plot and materials of the previously mentioned Cartago house with Licenciado Pro. Don Manuel José González Coronel. In return, Pe. González provided cedar wood, tiles, nails, posts, and sugarcane for a new house on Licenciado Francisco's sugarcane hacienda.

locations: Ermita de San Nicolás de Tolentino
people_involved: Licenciado don Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí
Presbítero don José Miguel de Guzmán Echavarría
summary: Doña Antonia de Echavarría Navarro, a widow, obligated herself for 100 pesos to the Chaplaincy of Comisario Baltasar de Grado, mortgaging her house in Cartago, which already carried a 69-peso encumbrance from another Chaplaincy founded by Doña Juana de Echavarría Navarro. Both Chaplaincies had Licenciado Don Manuel de Guzmán as their Chaplain. This debt was later paid on December 14, 1751, by Presbítero Don José Miguel de Guzmán Echavarría on behalf of his deceased mother.
A debt of 100 pesos is recorded against the houses of Captain Don José Nicolás de Bonilla, for which he and his wife, Doña Lucía de Alvarado, are responsible.

people_involved: Don Juan Manuel de Valderrama y Haro
Don Alonso José Rico y Villaroel
summary: Don Baltasar Francisco de Valderrama, Governor and Captain General of the province, granted power of attorney to his brother Don Juan Manuel de Valderrama y Haro, Don Alonso José Rico y Villaroel, and Don Cayetano de Valderrama. All three attorneys reside in Madrid and are tasked with representing Valderrama's services before the King and Royal Council, as well as managing his general affairs.

people_involved: Captain José de la Cruz Morales
summary: On July 17, it was noted that Captain José de la Cruz Morales had been dispatched earlier in the year to Tierra Firme with 208 mules for sale. Due to concerns about Morales's potential death, Alférez Don Carlos Custodio Galarza was granted power to claim the proceeds from the sale in Panama.

people_involved: Pro. Licenciado Don Manuel de Guzmán
summary: On July 19, Captain Don Gil de Alvarado and his wife Doña Josefa González Camino obligated themselves for 420 pesos to Capellanías founded by Vasco Solaño and Juan Alonso Solano. They mortgaged their house in Cartago, which they had recently rebuilt after a fire, with payments on the obligation set to begin on April 15, 1739. Pro. Licenciado Don Manuel de Guzmán serves as the Capellán for these foundations.

people_involved: Pro. Licenciado Don Manuel de Guzmán
summary: On July 20, Don Antonio de Oriamuno and his wife Doña María Antonia de Ibarra obligated themselves for 375 pesos to various Capellanías, including those founded by Pedro and Vasco Solano, as previously agreed on January 25 of this year. Pro. Licenciado Don Manuel de Guzmán is the Capellán for these foundations, and José Antonio de Oriamuno signed the document.

people_involved: Captain Don Tomás López del Corral
summary: On July 30, Captain Miguel López Gamboa and his wife Casilda Falcón sold 500 two-year-old cacao trees located in the Barbilla valley, adjacent to the Barbilla river, to Captain Don Tomás López del Corral at a price of two reales per tree.

people_involved: Pro. Licenciado Don Juan José Camacho
summary: On August 3, Pro. Licenciado Don Juan José Camacho, the priest of Matina valley and patron/Capellán of the Capellanía founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela, obligated himself for 500 pesos. This sum was offered by Don Gil de Alvarado, who ceded a cacao plantation in Matina as collateral for the principal and annuity.

people_involved: Pro. Licenciado Don Juan José Camacho
summary: On August 3, Pro. Licenciado Don Juan José Camacho obligated himself for 250 pesos to the Capellanía founded by Doña Juana de Vera, for which Licenciado Don Hermenegildo de Alvarado is Capellán and Don Gil de Alvarado is patron. Camacho mortgaged the same cacao plantation in Matina, consisting of 1,090 fruit-bearing trees, which Don Gil de Alvarado had returned.

people_involved: Pro. Licenciado Don Juan José Camacho
Canónigo Don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro
summary: On August 3, Pro. Licenciado Don Juan José Camacho, using the same cacao plantation as collateral, obligated himself for 100 pesos to the Capellanía served by Canónigo Don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro, who is a Canon of the Holy Cathedral Church of León.

people_involved: Captain Don Juan de Ocampo Golfín
Sarjento Mayor Don José de Morales
Licenciado Don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
summary: On August 9, Captain Don Juan de Ocampo Golfín obligated himself for 100 pesos to the Capellanía founded by Magdalena de la Portilla, whose patron is Sarjento Mayor Don José de Morales and Capellán is Licenciado Don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín. He mortgaged 13 'caballerías' of land in the Bagaces valley, which included a cattle ranch. This sum had previously been returned by Don Tomás López del Corral.

people_involved: Captain Don Luis Fernando de Liendo y Goico Echea
Don Diego de Liendo y Goico Echea
Doña Micaela de Ibarrola y Eguiguren
Muy Rev. P. fray Diego de Inza
summary: On August 10, a dowry letter was issued for Captain Don Luis Fernando de Liendo y Goico Echea and his wife Doña Baltasara de Inza. The dowry, totaling 1,485 pesos, included goods delivered by Fray Diego de Inza, Doña Baltasara's brother and Guardian of the San Francisco Convent, along with 200 pesos in silver reals from a benefactor.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Don José de Morales
summary: On August 11, José de Arce and his wife Gregoria Fonseca obligated themselves for 100 pesos to the Capellanía founded by Magdalena de la Portilla, whose patron is Sarjento Mayor Don José de Morales. They mortgaged a 'caballería' of land in the Santana valley, which contained a house, sugar mill, and cane field. This obligation was later cancelled by Morales in 1738.

people_involved: Captain Don Julián García de Argueta
summary: On August 12, Doña Antonia de la Granda, whose husband Don Tomás de la Madriz was in Panama, pledged her 50-day-old mulata infant slave, Juana Manuela (daughter of her slave María Josefa), to Captain Don Julián García de Argueta for 100 pesos to cover her and her family's living expenses.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor Don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: On August 16, Don Antonio González, a bachelor residing in Cartago and native of Olula in the Kingdom of Granada, made his will. He mandated the founding of a Capellanía, with his executor as patron and Don Dionisio de la Madriz as Capellán upon ordination. Failing him, other sons of Sarjento Mayor Don Francisco de la Madriz Linares and Doña Rita García de Argueta would serve, or masses would be said at the San Francisco Convent.

On August 16, Doña Cayetana Jiménez, a single woman and legitimate daughter of Captain Juan Cayetano Jiménez and Doña Josefa Martínez de Fuentes, made a statement, the details of which are not concluded in the provided text.
An enslaved woman named María Josefa, who is currently pregnant, has her unborn child granted freedom. A benefactor paid 25 pesos for the liberty of the child she will bear.

Captain Tomás López del Corral and Doña Francisca de Ibarra granted freedom to their enslaved mulatto, José Cayetano. His mother, María de Arleguí, paid 225 pesos for his liberty. José Cayetano was originally purchased from General Diego de la Haya Fernández, who had bought him from Doña Angela María de Arleguí.

Doña Jerónima de la Riba Agüero made her will, requesting burial in the Convento de San Francisco. She detailed her two marriages to Captain Diego Zamora and Captain Alvaro de Guevara, listing her children from the first marriage: Micaela, Antonia, María, and José. She also noted debts owed to her and appointed Licenciado José Antonio Díaz de Herrera as her executor.

Alférez Francisco Calvo sold his 16-year-old enslaved mulatta, Juana, to Licenciado Antonio de Guevara y Sáenz for 250 pesos. Juana was part of the estate inherited from Francisco's father, Captain Miguel Calvo.

Captain Luis de Sotomayor and Doña Isabel Ramona de Utrera committed to a 250-peso obligation for a chaplaincy founded by Captain Miguel Calvo, whose patron is Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra. They mortgaged a tiled house with a sugar mill in the valley of Ujarraz, which already had a 450-peso lien for a chaplaincy founded by Doña Cecilia de Vásquez Coronado, patroned by Don Fernando de Moya.

Licenciado Manuel José González Coronel, interim priest of Cartago, sold a deteriorated house and lot in Cartago to Captain Dionisio Pacheco for 200 pesos. González Coronel had acquired the property from Licenciado Francisco de Ocampo Golfín on July 5th of the same year in exchange for materials.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Antonio de Soto Barahona
summary: Baltasar Fernández committed to deliver a sugarcane plantation in Boca del Monte de Curridabá to Licenciado Hermenegildo de Alvarado. This property is subject to a 500-peso obligation to a chaplaincy founded by Sargento Mayor Antonio de Soto Barahona, an obligation established by Baltasar's father, Cristóbal Fernández.

Licenciado Hermenegildo de Alvarado Jirón obligated himself for 286 pesos to a chaplaincy founded by his aunt, Doña Sebastiana de Alvarado, of which Don Gil de Alvarado is the patron and Hermenegildo is the chaplain. The sum was offered by his brother, Captain Miguel de Alvarado, and his wife, Doña María de Torres. He mortgaged his mule ranch, Nuestra Señora de las Mercedes, in the valley of Bagaces.

Juan Carmena and Salvador de Aguilar, from the valley of Curridabá, sold a cleared plot for a cacao plantation in the valley of Malina to Captain José de Lebrón. The plot is intended for planting 2,000 cacao trees, and the 100-peso price was paid by the buyer with 8 tame mules.

Hermano José de las Alas and Sebastiana Barbosa made their will, leaving 100 pesos for wax for Holy Thursday. They stipulated that if their house is not sold, its value should fund a chaplaincy, with preference for sons of Juan Masís or Manuel de Alvarado, who are relatives. Captain Alfonso de Ulloa was named executor.

Licenciado Manuel José González Coronel obligated himself for 100 pesos to a chaplaincy founded by Comisario Baltasar de Grado, a sum redeemed by Doña Antonia de Alvarado. He mortgaged his house in Cartago, which faces the city plaza. Licenciado Manuel de Guzmán, residing in Santiago de Guatemala, is the patron and chaplain of this chaplaincy.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Antonio de Soto y Barahona
Licenciado Pro. Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Baltasar Fernández, with his mother Francisca Núñez's consent, sold a sugarcane plantation in Curridabat to Licenciado Hermenegildo de Alvarado. The sale included houses, a sugar mill, and a milpa plot, bordering Alférez Manuel de Rojas's property and the royal road to Río del Virilla. The buyer must assume a 500-peso cacao obligation to a chaplaincy founded by Sargento Mayor Antonio de Soto y Barahona, whose current patron and chaplain is Licenciado Pro. Antonio de Soto y Barahona.
Captain José de Quirós, residing in the valley of Curridabat, sold an enslaved black man named Pedro, of Mina caste and approximately 50 years old, to Captain Luis de Sotomayor for 80 pesos.

Don José Antonio Díaz de Herrera, priest of this parish, sold a cacao plantation on the Matina riverbank to Doña Baltasara de Escalante Panlagua, a widow. The plantation contained 1,400 fruit-bearing trees and was sold for 400 pesos.
A buyer is obligated to pay 300 pesos to a Capellanía founded by Eugenia de Abarca Alatras, of which Licenciado don Hermenegildo de Arleguí is the capellán.
Doña Manuela Martínez grants freedom to José Miguel de Luna, a mulatto slave born and raised in her house, who was inherited from her mother, Doña Micaela de Luna.

Doña Juana Manuela Lisondo, a widow, transfers a stone enclosure, an old sugar mill, a holed cauldron, two mule beasts, and 14 stubborn cattle in the Ujarraz valley to her son-in-law Luis Gutiérrez and her daughter Doña María Guerrero. They are obligated to the Cofradía de N. Señora de Ujarraz for 100 pesos.

people_involved: Doña Baltasara López de la Flor
Doña Mariana López de la Flor
Capitán don Gil de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Doña Baltasara and Doña Mariana López de la Flor lease a cacaotal in the Matina valley to Capitán don Gil de Alvarado y Jirón for two years, for 275 pesos of cacao. The notary for this transaction was don Pedro José Sáenz.
Doña Manuela Sáenz, a widow, leases a cacaotal in Matina to Cristóbal Jiménez for one year, for 100 pesos of cacao. Her son, don José Antonio de Bonilla, signs on her behalf.

people_involved: Wife of Capitán Juan Díaz de Herrera
summary: Doña Juana Manuela Lizondo, a widow, and Capitán Nicolás Barrantes, as her guarantor, obligate themselves to the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora de Ujarraz for 100 pesos at 5%. Doña Juana Manuela mortgages a stone enclosure, a sugar mill, and a cauldron in the Ujarraz valley. This obligation was previously shared with Capitán Juan Díaz de Herrera and his wife, but the guarantor is now changed at their request.

Capitán Juan Francisco Marín Laguna sells three-quarters of an adobe and tile house with half a lot in Cartago to Doña Antonia de Bonilla, a widow, for 240 pesos. The property is adjacent to Doña María Marín Laguna's house (sister of the seller) and other properties. The buyer is obligated to a Capellanía founded by Comisario Baltasar de Grado, whose capellán is Licenciado don Manuel de Guzmán, residing in Guatemala.

people_involved: Bdo. don Juan Antonio de Moya
Licenciado Pro. don Antonio de Guevara y Sáenz
summary: Capitán don Fernando de Moya, administrator of his brother Bdo. don Juan Antonio de Moya's assets, leases a cacaotal hacienda in the Matina valley to Licenciado Pro. don Antonio de Guevara y Sáenz, Calificador del Santo Oficio, for three years at 150 pesos of cacao per year.

Francisco Trejos obligates himself to his legitimate daughter, Juana Javiera, for 124 pesos 4 reales, which she inherited. Hermano Rafael Delgado acts as guarantor. This obligation was cancelled on August 6, 1735, because Juana Javiera died and her father became the heir.

people_involved: Doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar
summary: Juan Fernández Martínez and his wife, Doña Cayetana de Acosta, sell a 50-year-old Mina-caste black slave named Juana Manuela to Doña Baltahara de Escalante Panlagua for 150 pesos of cacao. The sale was permitted despite a prior codicil prohibiting it, as the slave had been seized by Juez Comisario don José de Fuentes to satisfy a debt Doña Josefa de Santiago y Aguilar owed to don Juan de la Cuesta.

people_involved: Pro. don José Miguel de Guzmán
Capitán don José López del Corral
summary: Doña Josefa de Bonilla, a widow, issues an unsigned codicil to her previous year's will. She revokes a clause that left part of a house to her executor, Pro. don José Miguel de Guzmán, because she had already sold it, along with a lot bought from Doña Benita de Bonilla, to Capitán don José López del Corral for 50 pesos, which he had provided for her illnesses and sustenance.

Francisca Serrano, a widow, makes her will, declaring a house and certain goods, including two fillies belonging to Pedro Juan Ramírez Prado, her natural son. She lists her children from her marriage: Alfonso, José, Antonio, Agustín, Juan, and Catarina, with only Agustín and Catarina (married to Bartolomé de Aguilar) still living. Her executors are Capitán don Miguel de Alvarado, Capitán Diego de Meza (her grandson), and the three sons of her son Juan Ramírez.

people_involved: Alférez Real don Manuel Bernardo de Quirós
summary: Capitán Juan Francisco Pérez, a resident of Cartago from Villa de los Santos, obligates himself to don Silvestre Suárez Gómez, a resident of Cartago from Mérida, Yucatán, for 1,240 pesos 2 reales. This money was lent to buy 100 mules and transport them to Los Santos. Alférez Real don Manuel Bernardo de Quirós (from Nata) and don José de Villacevallos (from Panamá) act as guarantors. The obligation was cancelled on March 11, 1737, by Suárez Gómez.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Miguel de Arburola
summary: Capitán don Luis de Sotomayor and his wife, Doña Isabel Ramona de Utrera, obligate themselves for 373 pesos to a capellanía founded by Doña Josefa de Hoces Navarro, which was previously administered by the deceased Licenciado don José Miguel de Arburola, son of the founder. They mortgage a hacienda in the Ujarrás valley with a house, sugar mill, cane fields, and cauldrons, which is already subject to other capellanías.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares, acting as the testamentary executor for don Antonio González, establishes a capellanía as ordered in don Antonio González's will of August 16, 1734. The capital is one thousand pesos of cacao.

An unnamed individual and his wife, Doña Rita García de Argueta, obligated themselves for a sum of money. This obligation was related to a new hacienda with 2,000 cacao trees located in the Barbilla valley.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Teniente Nicolás Barrantes and his wife, Luisa de Proa, obligated themselves for 100 pesos to the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora de Ujarrás. They mortgaged a straw chacara in the city's common lands, along with 14 tame mules, 30 horses, 4 yokes of oxen, 12 steers, and 8 stubborn cows. The debt was cancelled in 1753 by the mayordomo Maestre de Campo don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora.

Doña Josefa Lizondo, daughter of the deceased Damián Lizondo and Doña Antonia de Morales, made her will in this city. She was pregnant and had two natural daughters, Manuela Antonia de Mesa and Juana María, and had been married to José Antonio Molina for four years. Her 24-year-old slave, María Efigenia, was also pregnant, and Padre don Juan José Camacho, cura of Matina, was named as her albacea.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don José Fernández Castellanos
Doña Rosa de Arburola y Ribaren
Capitán Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribaren
summary: Sarjento Mayor don José Fernández Castellanos, son of don Francisco Fernández Castellanos and Doña María de León from Toledo, Spain, provided a dowry for his future wife, Doña Rosa de Arburola y Ribaren. Doña Rosa was the legitimate daughter of Capitán Lorenzo de Arburola y Ribaren and Doña Josefa de Hoces (Ozes) Navarro. The dowry, totaling 2,068 pesos, included a 20-year-old 'negra criolla' slave named Quiteria, a portion of a house, and 500 cacao trees in Matina.

Sarjento Pascual Salguero and his wife, María de Vargas, obligated themselves to don Luis de Soto Mayor for 100 pesos of good quality cacao, to be paid in two installments during the upcoming San Juan and Christmas harvests. This debt was incurred to cancel a credit that Doña Manuela Sáenz, a widow, held against Salguero, which she had executed for payment. The debt was cancelled in 1737.

Licenciado don Juan José Camacho, cura of Matina, sold two deserted city lots to don Tomás López del Corral, Teniente of the Royal Treasury officials. These lots, located north of the parish church and east of the town council houses, were burdened with 200 pesos from the chaplaincy founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela, of which Camacho was patron and chaplain.

Padre Camacho obligated himself to María Francisca, the legitimate daughter of José Antonio Molina and the deceased Doña Josefa Lizondo, for 121 pesos from her inheritance. He agreed to pay 5% annual interest to her father, José Antonio Molina, to help raise and support the minor, mortgaging a new cacao hacienda in Matina.

Camacho obligated himself to Juan José Morales for 160 pesos of cacao. This sum represented part of the inheritance adjudicated to Manuela Antonia de Mesa, Morales' wife, from the estate of her mother, Doña Josefa Lizondo.

people_involved: Sárjente Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Sárjente Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra, acting as mayordomo for the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora de los Angeles in Puebla, leased two plots of cacao hacienda in Matina to brothers Francisco and Agustín de la Riba for three years. The lessees were required to pay a zurrón of cacao in June and maintain the plots, including a thousand-tree clearing, and build a dwelling house.

people_involved: Br. don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones
Pro. don Manuel José González Coronel
summary: Teniente Pascual Salguero and his wife, María de Vargas, obligated themselves for 100 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Luis Carrioso, whose patron and chaplain was Br. don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones of Granada. The sum was delivered by Pro. don Manuel José González Coronel, and they mortgaged 340 fruit-bearing cacao trees in Matina.

people_involved: Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero
Capn. don Julián García de Hergueta
summary: Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero, a presbyter, sold half a city lot to Capn. don Julián García de Hergueta, Teniente General of the Matina valley, for 40 pesos cash. The lot was located on a corner of the Plaza, west of the Governor's houses, with a street in between.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Representatives of the chaplaincy of Vasco Solano and the Cofradías of La Concepción and El Rosario, along with Francisco del Campo, a master armorer, agreed to exchange houses. The Cofradías provided a house burdened with 460 pesos, while del Campo offered a house with a sala, two rooms, a kitchen, and half a lot, burdened with 75 pesos from the chaplaincy recited by Padre Camacho. All existing mortgages were transferred to del Campo's former property, which he received free of encumbrance.

people_involved: Licenciado Pro. don Juan José Camacho
Doña Josefa de Aguilar y Santiago
Pro. Bdo. don José Antonio Díaz de Herrera
summary: Licenciado Pro. don Juan José Camacho recognized a debt of 250 pesos plus 5% annual interest to the chaplaincy founded by Doña Luisa Calvo, whose capellán was Pro. Bdo. don José Antonio Díaz de Herrera. This obligation arose from Doña Luisa ceding a house named 'El Molino' in Matina to Camacho, which was previously owned by Capn. don Fernando de Salazar and Doña Josefa de Aguilar y Santiago, with the condition of assuming this debt.

Doña Manuela Valerín, a widow, and her daughters, Doña Petronila and Doña María de Cárdenas, donated a house in the city to José Manuel de Cárdenas. José Manuel was the son of Doña Manuela and her deceased husband, Capitán Diego Santiago de Cárdenas.

A house, valued at 1,500 pesos by two master carpenters and masons, was donated to Cárdenas. This donation was made to support his studies for the priesthood in Guatemala, with the condition that it would be nullified if he did not get ordained.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don José Felipe Bermúdez
summary: Doña Baltasara Escalante Paniagua, a widow, donated a 50-year-old slave named Juana Manuela, of 'casta mina,' to Doña Juana Gertrudis Bermúdez. Juana Manuela had been previously purchased from Juan Fernández Martínez and his wife Doña Cayetana de Acosta. The donation was made because Doña Juana Gertrudis is the daughter of Sarjento Mayor don José Felipe Bermúdez, who was the donor's deceased husband's brother and compadre.

people_involved: Doña Juana María de Soto y Barahona
summary: Doña Juana María de Soto y Barahona, widow of Capitán Cayetano Muñoz, obligated herself to her children for 1,262 pesos from her inheritance. The beneficiaries include José Gabriel, María Manuela, Clemencia, Juan Antonio Muñoz, and an unborn child, all legitimate children of her and her deceased husband.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Baltasar Francisco de Valderrama
Capitán don Miguel de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Baltasar Francisco de Valderrama, Governor and Captain General, was excommunicated by Bishop Mro. fr. Dionisio de Villavicencío, with the excommunication posted on church doors. Valderrama, unable to obtain absolution from the Provisor, granted power of attorney to Capitán don Miguel de Alvarado y Jirón to travel to Granada to request temporary absolution from the Bishop, allowing him to appeal to the Audiencia of Santiago de Guatemala.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Baltasar Francisco de Valderrama
Capitán don Miguel de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Sarjento Mayor don Baltasar Francisco de Valderrama further empowered Capitán don Miguel de Alvarado y Jirón to appeal before the Bishop, request testimony of his excommunication, and appeal to the Real Audiencia. He also sought relief from a 4,000 pesos fine, arguing it was unjust as he was complying with Royal decrees regarding the Inquisition and lacked funds, being owed five years of salary and heavily indebted.

Sarjento Mayor don Pedro Carazo obligated himself to pay 50 pesos to the Cofradía del Smo. Sacramento and another 50 pesos to the Cofradía de las Animas (both in the parish church) each time he played cards or dice. This commitment was made for the benefit of his health and family, though his signature was not present.

people_involved: Lic. don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Doña Juana de Ángulo, a widow, sold her 38-year-old mulata slave named María, who was born and raised in her house, to Lic. don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba for 400 pesos. The payment was due in January, but the transaction was later canceled.

people_involved: Sárjenlo Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: Manuel Fernández, a native of Jerez de la Frontera, committed to teaching Christian Doctrine, reading, writing, and counting to four noble, poor children for free, and to other paying students. In return, he requested a 'zurrón de cacao' from the city, which was granted by the Notary (Teniente General), Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares (Procurador Síndico), and Capn. Francisco Javier de Siles (Mayordomo de propios), recognizing the school's benefit to the community.

people_involved: Doña Juana María de Soto y Barahona
summary: Doña Baltasara Escalante Paniagua and Doña Juana María de Soto y Barahona resolved a dispute over a cacao plantation. Doña Juana María, widow of Capitán Cayetano Muñoz, had received a 'rozita' of 310 trees in her husband's estate, which Doña Baltasara claimed. They agreed that Doña Baltasara would receive 200 trees in the Barbilla valley.

Alférez Francisco de la Riba and his wife María de Acuña obligated themselves for 250 pesos to Francisca and Juana, the minor daughters of the deceased Miguel de Quesada, mortgaging a new hacienda with 1,000 trees in the Barbilla valley. The amount was later reduced to 225 pesos after don Francisco de Betancour denied owing 25 pesos to the deceased.

people_involved: Cabo de escuadra Baltasar de Moya
Pro. Lic. don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero
summary: Cabo de escuadra Baltasar de Moya, a free pardo, and his legitimate son Manuel Antonio de Moya sold a cacao plantation with 1,000 trees to Pro. Lic. don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero for 312 pesos and four reales. Baltasar had planted this alongside another plantation he was contracted to make for Cubero.

people_involved: Doña Juana María de Soto y Barahona
summary: Doña Cayetana Jiménez sold a 'mulata blanca' slave, who was born and raised in her house, to Doña Juana María de Soto y Barahona.
A mulata criolla named María Josefa, approximately 34 years old, who was adjudicated to an unnamed seller from the estate of her mother Josefa Martínez, is sold for 400 pesos of cacao.

Capitán don Tomás López Corral, acting as attorney for his brother Licenciado don Gregorio Corrales, leases a cacao plantation in Matina to doña Cayetana Jiménez for two years at 200 pesos annually. Doña Cayetana's brother, Cristóbal Jiménez, signs on her behalf.

people_involved: Capitán don Luis de Soto Mayor
summary: Capitán don Luis de Soto Mayor and his wife doña Isabel Ramona de Utrera sell Dionisia Hidalgo, a mulata criolla aged 18-20, to doña Águeda Pérez del Muro for 400 pesos of cacao or 320 silver reales. They had previously acquired Dionisia from doña Gregoria Hidalgo.

people_involved: Sárjente Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
summary: Teniente Miguel Matamoros, acting for himself and his brother Juan Matamoros (a resident of León de Nicaragua), sells an adobe house with its plot to Capitán don Juan Nicolás Viveros, Teniente General of Esparza, for 700 pesos of cacao. The Matamoros brothers inherited the house from their mother, Francisca de Hinojosa, and Viveros' father-in-law, Sárjente Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares, accepts the deed on his behalf.

people_involved: Capitán don Julián García de Hergueta
Licenciado don Juan Manuel García de Hergueta
Doña Dionisia Fallas de la Vega
summary: Capitán don Julián García de Hergueta obligates himself to doña Manuela García de Hergueta for 496 pesos 4 reales at 5% interest. This obligation is part of an arrangement where his brother, Licenciado don Juan Manuel García de Hergueta, gave Julián an estate as payment for his inheritance, with the condition that Julián would make this obligation to their sister and to the minor children of their deceased father, Capitán Manuel García de Hergueta, and doña Dionisia Fallas de la Vega.

Doña Manuela Sáenz, a widow, leases a cacao plantation in the Matina valley to don Cristóbal Jiménez for two years at 100 pesos annually. The first 100 pesos are to be given to her son, don Andrés de Bonilla, for clothing and to help him seek a living, with 25 pesos already received in fine cloth.

Juana Bernarda Vásquez, a widow, leases a 500-tree cacao plantation in the Matina valley to Sárjento Gregorio Calvo. Calvo is responsible for paying her debts, providing her with clothing and maintenance, and managing the estate until her sons, Benito and Fernando, are old enough to administer it.

people_involved: Presbítero Licenciado don José de Chaves
summary: Capitán don Francisco Garrido agrees to exchange an enslaved person, Cristóbal Manzano (50 years old), for Francisco Canela (negro, 60 years old), who is enslaved by Juana Solís. Francisco Canela, formerly enslaved by Garrido's wife doña Águeda Pérez del Muro, requested Garrido to buy him. Juana Solís' son, Presbítero Licenciado don José de Chaves, grants the exchange on her behalf.
The minor Juan José de Aguilar is handed over to his uncle, Sarjento Juan de Aguilar, a master shoemaker, for six years to learn the trade.

Alférez Francisco Solano and his wife doña Josefa de Soto obligate themselves and mortgage their property in Ujarrás to guarantee payment for 185 pesos received from José Francisco de Moya. This sum is part of 264 pesos that José Francisco and José Manuel de Moya, sons of don Pedro Manuel de Moya, received from the estate of doña Micaela de Arburola.

Don Pedro González de León, acting on behalf of José Francisco de Moya (residing in Esparza), acknowledges receiving 85 pesos from doña Josefa de Soto, now widow of Francisco Solano, as a partial payment towards an existing credit.

Capitán Juan José de Zamora sells a piece of land (250 varas front, 1000 varas deep) bordering Barranca and the Tibás river to Alférez Lorenzo Bustos for 50 pesos. Bustos states he has ceded a house plot from this land to his nephew Bartolomé, who helped with the payment.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno
General don Diego de la Haya Fernández
Pro. Licenciado don Francisco Javier Victoria
summary: Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno revokes the general power of attorney previously granted to his deceased uncle, General don Diego de la Haya Fernández, regarding chaplaincies in Panamá, as his uncle provided no account. He grants new power to Pro. Licenciado don Francisco Javier Victoria to request an interim collation of these chaplaincies for Licenciado don Manuel Sáenz (his wife's maternal uncle, a newly ordained priest in Panamá with limited income), until Oriamuno's son, don José Antonio de Oriamuno (1 year 8 months old), reaches the age for ordination. This transaction was not completed as the grantor changed his mind.
Francisco Carrillo, a master blacksmith, takes his nephew Esteban Sánchez, son of Francisco Sánchez and Manuela Carrillo, for three years to teach him the trade.

Domingo Guerrero and his wife Laureana Cayetana Solano obligate themselves to the minor children of José Norberto Guerrero (María de la Ascención, Laureana Cayetana, Antonia Josefa, and an unborn child) for 56 pesos, their paternal inheritance. They mortgage their house in Puebla and a plantain grove in Ujarrás.

people_involved: Pro. Beneficiado don Juan José Camacho
summary: Pro. Beneficiado don Juan José Camacho, the priest of Matina, donates María Antonia, a 4-month-old enslaved girl, to his goddaughter and relative, doña Manuela Antonia de Mesa. Camacho had acquired María Antonia's mother, María Efigeria, from the estate of doña Josefa Lizondo.

people_involved: Licenciado don Juan Manuel García de Hergueta
summary: Licenciado Pro. don Juan Manuel García de Hergueta received cacao plantations in the Barbilla valley upon the death of his father, Capitán Manuel García de Hergueta.

An unnamed grantor committed to a capellanía (chaplaincy) founded by Tomás Calvo for 50 pesos. Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra was the patron, and Don Félix Esteban de Hoces (Oses) Navarro, a Canon of the Cathedral of León, was the chaplain.

On December 5, an unnamed grantor obligated himself for 50 pesos to the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora del Rosario. This obligation was later cancelled on September 19, 1737, by the mayordomo José de las Alas.

On December 6, an unnamed grantor obligated himself for 600 pesos to a capellanía founded by Antonio de Utrera y Medina, with a mortgage on his haciendas. Juan Antonio de Moya was the interim chaplain, and due to his 'demencia,' Manuel González Coronel recited for him, later cancelling the obligation on November 17, 1737.

On December 16, an unnamed grantor obligated himself for 2,462 pesos to the minor children of his father and Dionisia Fallas de la Vega, mortgaging his Barbilla haciendas. His brother Julián had previously obligated himself to their sister Manuela García. Later, Dionisia received portions for Manuela (deceased), José Joaquín cancelled his part, and Dionisia received portions for Juana and Félix.

On December 17, Dionisia Meléndez, widow of Captain Salvador de Alarcón, obligated herself to her children Joaquín, Josefa, and María Catarina de Alarcón for 276 pesos and 2 reales from their paternal inheritance.

On December 18, Antonio de Guevara y Sáenz, Calificador del Santo Oficio, gave José Guerrero three plots of cacao haciendas in the Valle de Barbilla. This was in exchange for Guerrero's work in clearing and maintaining the cacao fields for five years, including regular cleaning and replanting, plus 26 pesos annually in local goods.

On December 19, Manuel Antonio Guzmán provided a dowry of 1,550 pesos to his future wife, María Teresa Garlinda. The dowry included a cacao hacienda with 700 trees, valued at 1,050 pesos, with the condition to provide Angela Martínez two sacks of cacao annually for life and cover her funeral expenses.

On December 22, Juan José Camacho, the priest of Matina, sold a 22-year-old mulata named María Efigenia to Captain José Antonio López del Corral for 300 pesos. Camacho had acquired María Efigenia from the estate of Josefa Lizondo.

On December 23, José de Villalba, a resident of Cartago, sold a 14-16 year old criollo boy named Juan Antonio to Captain Tomás López de Corral for 375 silver pesos. Villalba had purchased Juan Antonio from Gregorio Yangües, a resident of Santiago de Veragua.

On December 25, Captain José Antonio López del Corral and his wife Francisca de Arburola y Ribaren obligated themselves to the Royal Treasury for 500 pesos of cacao. This was for the auction of the office of Alguacil Mayor and perpetual Regidor of Cartago to López del Corral, payable over five years with their house as collateral. On May 19, 1740, Francisca de Arburola, now a widow, paid 400 pesos to Juan José de Cuende.

On March 16, 1735, Captain Luis de Sotomayor and his wife Isabel Ramona de Utrera obligated themselves to Licenciado Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero, a presbyter, for 246 pesos received in goods, to be paid in cash within one year. The obligation was cancelled on June 1, 1736.

On February 11, 1735, Captain Alfonso de Ulloa, Alcalde de la Santa Hermandad, ordered the banishment of Gregorio de Quirós from Cartago to Bagaces for public and scandalous cohabitation with his first cousin, Angela de Arrieta. Quirós was to be escorted beyond the Río Grande and forbidden to return without a dispensation to marry Arrieta, under penalty of lifelong exile to Puertobelo. Angela de Arrieta was to be placed in servitude, and their children were to be given trades.

On February 25, 1735, an auto was issued regarding a dispute where Antonia Bermúdez refused to receive water from María Marín Laguna's property. The ruling mandated Antonia Bermúdez to allow the water flow, as there was only one drain serving the main ditch that supplied the parish church and the San Francisco Convent, and María Marín Laguna's ancestors had enjoyed these water rights without dispute. Failure to comply would result in a 25-peso fine.
On February 20, 1735, an order was issued for the public good of Cartago to bring water from the Río Reventado, with the costs to be covered by public funds.

An order was issued to prevent people from diverting water from neighbors and to ensure acequias (irrigation ditches) are cleaned and maintained by Domingo de Ramos. Non-compliance carried a penalty of 10 pesos of cacao. The order was publicly announced in the plaza by Baltasar Calvo, the jail minister.

Alférez Lucas de Jesús requested a partition of goods for his children from his first marriage, as he had remarried. The assets included a house valued at 300 pesos by Capitán Feo. Barquero. An attached receipt showed Padre Antonio Raimundo de Estrada received 126 pesos from Pablo de Jesús for masses.

locations: Puebla de Nuestra Señora de los Angeles
summary: Juan de Fonseca's testament detailed his assets, including a tiled house in Puebla de Nuestra Señora de los Angeles and carpentry tools. He declared a debt of 82 pesos to R. P. fr. Antonio Sáenz for a construction project. José de las Alas was named as the executor.

people_involved: Don Luis Fernando de Lienda y Goico Echea
Sargento Mayor don Jerónimo Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Don Baltasar Francisco de Valderrama, Governor and Captain General, granted power of attorney to Licenciado don Roque de Ibarroeta, an attorney and relator in the Royal Audiencia of Guatemala, to collect a debt of 406 pesos from Sargento Mayor don Jerónimo Muñoz de la Trinidad.

people_involved: Doña Teresa de Soto y Barahona
Minor daughter of Capitán Germán Rodríguez
summary: Sargento Mayor don Pedro Carazo and doña Teresa de Soto y Barahona obligated themselves for 100 pesos for a Capellanía founded by Capitán Germán Rodríguez, 150 pesos for his minor daughter (with Inés Vásquez de Castro), and 387 pesos for doña María Leonida. They mortgaged a cattle hacienda in Las Piedras.

people_involved: Licenciado don Gregorio López del Corral
Capitán don Nicolás de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Doña Inés Vásquez, widow of Capitán Germán Rodríguez, granted power of attorney in Masaya to Licenciado don Gregorio López del Corral to reclaim a cattle hacienda in Bagaces. This hacienda, previously cared for by Sargento Pascual de Segura, was violently taken by Capitán don Nicolás de Ocampo nine years prior.

María Antonia Rodríguez, legitimate daughter of Germán Rodríguez and Inés Vásquez Coronado, was buried on October 10, 1732. Her death certificate was issued in 1737 by the cura of Masaya, don Clemente Rey Alvarez.

people_involved: Licenciado don Gregorio López del Corral
summary: The power of attorney previously granted to Licenciado don Gregorio López del Corral was substituted to don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco.
Don Dionisio Pacheco provided a receipt for 150 pesos.

Capitán Francisco Javier de Siles, tutor of doña María Leonida, received 200 pesos from doña Teresa de Soto Barahona, widow of don Pedro Carazo. Siles then distributed 100 pesos to don Bartolomé de León and his wife doña Juana Benita, and another 100 pesos to don Dionisio Pacheco.

Teniente Miguel Matamoros and his wife María Solís obligated themselves for 150 pesos of cacao in favor of the five minor children of the deceased José Solís and Juana Candelaria Guillen, who were under the care of their grandfather, Capitán Sebastián Guillen.

people_involved: Doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
Pro. Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara
summary: Capitán don Francisco de Betancourt and his wife doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral attempted to sell an enslaved mulata named Marta, about 20 years old, to Pro. Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara for 400 pesos of cacao. The transaction was not finalized.

people_involved: Doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
summary: Capitán don Francisco de Betancourt and doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral leased their cacao hacienda in Valle de Matina to Pro. don Juan José Camacho, cura of Matina, for one year for 300 pesos of cacao.

people_involved: Señor cura don José Antonio Díaz de Herrera
summary: María Zelidona, widow of Jerónimo Gutiérrez, obligated herself for 150 pesos to the Capellanía founded by doña Gertrudis de Alvarado. The funds were delivered by don José Antonio Díaz de Herrera. She mortgaged a cacao plantation in Valle de Barbilla.

people_involved: Licdo. don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero
summary: Capitán don Luis de Sotomayor and doña Isabel Ramona de Utrera sold an enslaved criollo named Juan Manuel, 22 years old, to Capitán don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco for 300 pesos. The sale was made to pay a debt to Licdo. don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero and other debts from their deceased parents.

Capitán don Silvestre Suárez Gómez, a resident merchant, sold an enslaved mulatillo named Nicolás de Falla, about 12 years old, to don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco for 200 pesos. Suárez Gómez had acquired Nicolás from doña María Teresa Jiménez Maldonado in Esparza.

people_involved: Capitán don Julián García de Argueta
Capitán don José Antonio de Oreamuno
Capitán don Tomás de Soto Barohona
Capitán don José Fernando de Moya
Coronel don Antonio Vásquez de la Cuadra
summary: Eight Captains provided a residency bond of 500 pesos each for Coronel don Antonio Vásquez de la Cuadra, the newly appointed Governor and Captain General of the province.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
Licenciado Pro. don Gregorio López del Corral
don José Antonio López del Corral
summary: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral granted power to his brothers, Licenciado Pro. don Gregorio López del Corral and don José Antonio López del Corral, to make his will. He named his children, Joaquina, María Josefa, Manuela Petronila, and Josefa Mónica, as his heirs.

people_involved: Pro. Licenciado don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Pro. Licenciado don Antonio de Soto y Barahona granted power to Capitán don Pedro de Llanos, Alguacil Mayor and Regidor in Granada, to collect 235 pesos owed to him by the estate of the late Bishop Fray Dionisio de Villavicencio. This debt was justified in the mortuary proceedings with certifications from Licenciados don José Santillán and don Baltasar de los Reyes, and declarations from don Andrés Martínez de Fleitas and Fernando Jerez.

Doña Luisa Calvo, a widow, donated her enslaved girl named María Micaela, approximately 12 years old and daughter of her other enslaved woman María Capitana, to her granddaughter doña Juana Josefa de Miranda. Juana Josefa is the legitimate daughter of Capitán don Antonio de Miranda and doña Ana Maroto.

people_involved: Capitán don José Antonio López del Corral
Sarjento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Capitán don José Antonio López del Corral, who is a Regidor and Alguacil Mayor, granted general power to Sarjento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad. The document was not signed.

people_involved: Don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad and his wife doña Antonia Josefa de Arburola obligated themselves to the confraternities of Vera Cruz de Barba, Concepción de Nuestra Señora in Cartago, and the Cartago Convent for a total of 203 pesos 4 reales. They received 150 pesos in wood and tiles from a stone house in 1729, with the rest being interest, and mortgaged their house and trapiche in the valley of Ujarraz.

people_involved: Capitán don Diego de Barros y Carvajal
summary: Doña Josefa Pérez del Muro, widow of Capitán don Diego de Barros y Carvajal, obligated herself to the Archicofradía del Santísimo Sacramento in the parish church for 150 pesos at 5% interest. She mortgaged a cacao plantation with 4,000 trees located in the valley of Matina.

people_involved: Bachiller don Rafael García de Argueta
summary: Capitán don José de Cuende, Procurador Síndico General of Cartago, granted general power to Bachiller don Rafael García de Argueta, a minor cleric residing in Santiago de Guatemala, to manage affairs on behalf of the city's Cabildo.

people_involved: Pro. Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero
summary: Capitán don Silvestre Suárez Gómez, a merchant residing in Mérida, Yucatán, granted general power to Pro. Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
Pro. Licenciado don Juan José Camacho
summary: Teniente don Cayetano de Alvarado and his wife doña Juana de Guevara obligated themselves for 535 pesos to the Cofradía de la Concepción, the Capellanía de Vasco Solano (served by Licenciado don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría), the Cofradía del Rosario, and a Capellanía served by Pro. Licenciado don Juan José Camacho. They mortgaged their adobe and tile house in Cartago, which previously belonged to Francisco de Ocampo.

Doña Ana Rodríguez de Castro, a widow residing in Aserrí, granted freedom to her enslaved mulatta Efigenia de Mora and Efigenia's daughter, María de la Rosa (about 6 years old), fulfilling the testament of her deceased husband, Capitán Alonso de Porras. The condition was that Efigenia would continue to serve Doña Ana during her lifetime, but this freedom was later revoked on January 17, 1739.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo
Doña Gabriela Josefa de Arleguí y Hoces Navarro
Sarjento Mayor don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí
Doña Engracia Gertrudis de Hoces (Oses) Navarro
Licenciado don José Hermengildo de Arleguí
Licdo. don Antonio de Soto Barahona
Doña Ana Teresa de Soto y Barahona
Jefe de Escuadra don Manuel López Pintado
Bachiller don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: A dowry letter was issued for the upcoming marriage of Sarjento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo and doña Gabriela Josefa de Arleguí y Hoces Navarro, totaling 3,418 pesos. The dowry included an 8-year-old enslaved mulatto named José Manuel, jewelry gifted by various relatives, and 2,000 pesos from an unnamed person for marriage expenses. Don Juan also provided 2,000 pesos as arras, including a 20-year-old enslaved man named Antonio, purchased from the Real Asiento de Panamá. Bachiller don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría signed on behalf of doña Engracia.

people_involved: Pro. Licenciado don José Manuel González Coronel
summary: Teniente don Cayetano de Alvarado and his wife doña Juana de Guevara re-obligated themselves to the Cofradía de la Concepción in the San Francisco convent of Cartago for 210 pesos, a debt previously mentioned on May 28. This obligation was canceled on August 29, 1749, by Pro. Licenciado don José Manuel González Coronel, the confraternity's mayordomo, after doña Juana made an oblation of the mortgaged house.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Miguel de Guzmán
summary: Teniente don Cayetano de Alvarado and doña Juana de Guevara acknowledged a debt of 200 pesos for a chaplaincy served by Licenciado don José Miguel de Guzmán, with their house as collateral. This debt was canceled in 1749 by Pro. Guzmán y Echavarría after doña Juana made an oblation of the house.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan José de Cuende
summary: Teniente don Cayetano de Alvarado and doña Juana de Guevara acknowledged a debt of 50 pesos to the Cofradía del Rosario in the parish church of Cartago, mortgaging their house. This debt was canceled in 1749 by Capitán don Juan José de Cuende, the confraternity's Mayordomo, after doña Juana made an oblation of the house.
Unspecified individuals recognized a debt of 75 pesos to the Chaplaincy served by Licenciado don Juan José Camacho, the priest of Matina. The debt was secured with a mortgage on their house.

Capitán Juan José de Zamora and his wife, doña Manuela de Bonilla, obligated themselves for 411 pesos to a Chaplaincy. This Chaplaincy was founded by Antonio Aurelio de Zamora, father of Juan José, and the debt was secured by a house in Rincón de Tibás, Barba valley, benefiting the Convento de Barba.

Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero sold a house to Capitán don Julián García de Argueta and his wife, doña Ana Josefa Sánchez de Castañeda, for 1250 pesos. The house was previously acquired from doña Antonia de Alvarado, and 350 pesos of the sale price were designated for chaplaincies founded by don Domingo de Echavarría and don Miguel de Alvarado, with Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos as patron and Martínez Cubero as chaplain.

people_involved: Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Juan Fernández Martínez offered to establish a school to teach Christian Doctrine, reading, writing, and arithmetic, committing to accept children whose parents couldn't pay if the Cabildo contributed 25 pesos. Alcalde don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo approved the request, requiring Martínez to provide free education to four children of noble families.

José de Hoyo, natural son of don Pablo de Hoyo and Simona de Atrieta, and a native of León de Nicaragua, granted power to Capitán don Antonio José de Oriamuno to make his will. He mentioned 300 pesos inherited from his father, which were held by his brother, also named José de Hoyo, a resident of Portobelo.

Doña María Isabel de Alarcón, residing in the Ujarrás valley, obligated herself to Rita and Josefa Guerrero, the legitimate daughters of the deceased Juan Guerrero, for 44 pesos from their inheritance.

Doña Antonia Acosta y Arévalo, widow of Capitán don Agustín de Alvarado and mother of doña Antonia Josefa de Alvarado, transferred assets to her son-in-law, Ayudante Manuel de Alvarado. These assets included an 18-year-old enslaved black woman named Juana Benita and 500 cacao trees in the Matina valley, totaling 2,068 pesos and 4 reales.

Sarjente Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo, acting on behalf of don Félix Ignacio Morillo of Panamá, sold an enslaved man named Antonio, of Cancán caste and about 25 years old, to doña Petronila de Hoces Navarro for 200 pesos of silver. However, the transaction was not finalized or signed.

people_involved: Padre Guardián del Convento de Cartago
Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Sarjento Cristóbal Solano, a resident of the Currirabá valley, obligated himself for 250 pesos to the Chaplaincy of Benito Valerín, whose chaplain is the Padre Guardián of the Convento de Cartago. This obligation was secured by a cacao plantation in Matina, with the consent of don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo, the Síndico of the Convento.

people_involved: Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: The will of Teniente Coronel don Antonio Vásquez de la Cuadra was opened on July 24, following his death earlier that morning. The will, dated July 22, 1736, identified him as a resident of Vélez Málaga, Spain, son of the deceased don José Vásquez de la Cuadra and doña María Sequida, and husband of the deceased doña María Peregrí, with whom he had two children, doña María and don José Vásquez de la Cuadra. The document detailed numerous debts and named don Baltasar Francisco de Valderrama and don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo as executors, with his children as heirs.

The will of Capitán don Antonio Salmón Pacheco was opened on July 26, following his death from a long illness. The will, dated July 1, 1735, declared him to be the legitimate, single son of the deceased Capitán don Antonio Salmón Pacheco and doña Luisa de Abarca. He owned four enslaved individuals (Ramón, Luisa, Petrona, and Manuela) and bequeathed 200 pesos and 600 cacao trees to Manuela Pacheco, a girl he had raised.

people_involved: Don Francisco Gil de Berríos el mozo
Señora de la ciudad de León
summary: An unnamed testador makes a will, ordering a chaplaincy for his brother Don Dionisio Pacheco's children, freeing his enslaved woman María Luisa, and donating his enslaved woman Manuela to his niece Juana María. He also mentions an item belonging to a lady from León, wife of Don Francisco Gil de Berríos el mozo, whose son is a priest in Nindirí.

people_involved: don José Antonio Díaz de Herrera
summary: Don José Antonio Díaz de Herrera, the oldest priest, donates a cacao plantation in Matina with 700 fruit-bearing trees to Francisco Antonio Javier de Herrera, a child of about 2 years old. He also commits to supporting the child until he is old enough to manage the hacienda, which is currently being raised by Antonia de Quirós.

people_involved: Doña Baltasara López de la Flor
Doña Mariana López de la Flor
Sarjento Mayor don José Felipe Bermúdez
summary: Doña Baltasara and Doña Mariana López de la Flor lease a cacao plantation in Matina to Sergeant Major don José Felipe Bermúdez for three years, at a price of 275 pesos of cacao annually. The lease, which is currently held by don Gil de Alvarado, is set to begin on September 11.

people_involved: Sárjenlo Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Doña Margarita de Morales, a widow, sells her enslaved mulata woman named Josefa Nicolasa, approximately 20 years old, to Sergeant Major don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo, a perpetual councilman and Provincial Mayor of the Santa Hermandad. The sale price for Josefa Nicolasa was 250 pesos.

Sergeant Juan de Montalbán and his wife María de Ángulo, residents of the Aserrí valley, sell a cattle-raising land site in San Cecilio de las Coranas to Ensign Manuel de Castro. María de Ángulo inherited this land from her father, Ensign Antonio de Ángulo, and her mother had previously sold two caballerías of land from this site to the deceased Juan Ramos.

Captain Francisco Morales, a resident of the Aserrí valley, undertakes an obligation for 100 pesos to the Confraternity of the Conception. This sum was previously held against the houses and hacienda of Captain José de Quirós, and Morales mortgages his own property in the Aserrí valley as security.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don José Felipe Bermúdez
summary: Lieutenant don Cayetano de Alvarado and his wife doña Juana de Guevara commit to paying 50 pesos to the Franciscan Convent. This amount was previously held against don José Felipe Bermúdez's house and passed to them upon the death of doña Margarita de Aguiar, widow of don Sebastián de Garita. They mortgage a cacao plantation in Matina with about 1,500 fruit trees.

people_involved: don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
summary: The Syndic of the Convent, don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora, cancels the obligation because doña Juana de Guevara made an offering of the mortgaged hacienda.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan Manuel de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Captain don Juan Manuel de Alvarado y Jirón, legitimate son of the deceased Captain don Pedro de Alvarado and doña Catalina de Villa Martel, provides a dowry of 1,039 pesos to his wife doña María Manuela de Casares. Doña María Manuela is the legitimate daughter of Captain don Domingo de Casares and doña Catalina de Siles, and the dowry includes various clothing items, a hat, a bedspread, and 50 pesos in coined silver.
Francisco Carrillo, a master blacksmith, takes Salvador Bautista, son of Petrona Bautista and about 14 years old, as an apprentice for five years to teach him the trade.

people_involved: Licenciado Pro. don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarna
summary: Licenciado Pro. don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría, Sacristan Mayor and General Preacher of the Holy Crusade, leases the cacao hacienda of the deceased doña Josefa Santiago de Aguiar to Matías and José de la Trinidad Jiménez for two years for 250 pesos. He acts as the representative for Licenciado don Manuel de Guzmán, to whom this amount belongs as interim chaplain.

people_involved: Licenciado Pro. don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarna
summary: Licenciado Pro. don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría, as the oldest priest-rector and ecclesiastical judge, confirms having received the payment for the leases.

Ensign Francisco de Oviedo, a resident of the Ujarrás highlands, sells a cacao roza, approximately two years old with about 1,600 trees, in the Reventazón valley to Brother José Antonio Carranza for 125 pesos.
The parties, Alférez Francisco de Oviedo and Hermano José Antonio Carranza, agree to adjust the price of the cacao roza to 500 pesos of cacao.

people_involved: Sárjenlo Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
Capitán don Juan José de Cuende
Don José Nicolás Sarmiento de Sotumayor
Doña María Catarina Ortiz de Rosas
don José Antonio Díaz de Herrera
summary: Sergeant Major don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo donates a cacao hacienda with 750 trees and 200 new trees on the Matina riverbank to his daughter doña Manuela de Ibarra, wife of Captain don Juan José de Cuende. This hacienda, acquired from the deceased don José Nicolás Sarmiento de Sotumayor and doña María Catarina Ortiz de Rosas, is subject to a 150-peso encumbrance for a chaplaincy served by priest don José Antonio Díaz de Herrera. He also donates a newly planted cacao roza as an advance on her legitimate inheritance.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la
summary: Captain don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco, First Vote Ordinary Mayor and Lieutenant Governor, and his wife doña Francisca Serrano de Reina, undertake an obligation for 300 pesos to the heirs of Francisco de Chaves, who died in Spain approximately 47 years ago. This sum has been in deposit, passing from possessor to possessor, without an heir appearing, and was previously held by doña Juana de Alvarado, a widow.

people_involved: Sarjento Mayor don Francisco de la
