summary: Sergeant Major don Francisco de la (incomplete name) takes the money that was held in deposit for the heirs of Francisco de Chaves.

Alférez José Miguel de Echavarría made his will, naming his parents, wife Águeda Molina, and five children. He requested a mule held by Alférez Lucas de Segura be given to R. P. Guardián Fray Diego de Inza, and noted that Sarjento José Morera owed him 20 guachipelí horcones to be delivered in Boca del Monte de Currirabá.

Teniente Francisco García and his wife Manuela Victoria de Aguilar transferred a straw house and its plot to Juan Antonio Camaño and his wife María de León. The property was burdened with a 100-peso capellanía founded by Hermano Andrés Peláez, which the buyers assumed.

Gertrudis Ruiz de Hinojosa, widow of Francisco Gutiérrez, sold a plot of land in Cartago to Micaela Gómez de Lara for 25 pesos. Gertrudis Ruiz de Hinojosa had inherited the land from her mother, Gertrudis Ruiz.

Don Fernando de Moya, administrator for his brother Pro. don Juan Antonio de Moya, leased a cacao hacienda in Matina to Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno for 3 years at 300 pesos annually. The hacienda was currently leased by Pro. don Antonio de Guevara Sáenz, with a marginal note indicating a cancellation and new deed on November 7, 1737, due to litigation.

people_involved: Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Sarjento Baltasar de Vargas, a resident of the Barba valley, declared a debt of 325 pesos to Sarjento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo. Vargas committed to completing a 2,000-tree cacao plantation and delivering the trees in four years, which would cancel the debt, and Ibarra would additionally provide him with 300 pesos worth of cacao.

Hermano José de las Alas took on an obligation for 175 pesos 4 reales from the inheritance of the minor children of the deceased Mateo de los Santos and María Magdalena Delgado. The minor children were Juan José and José Antonio, while their sister Josefa Tomasa was under the care of her grandmother, Micaela Cartín.

Don Juan de Dios Gómez, originally from Villa de los Santos, provided a dowry of 1,309 pesos for his future wife, doña María Alfonsa García de Argueta. The dowry included 400 pesos from her paternal inheritance, to be delivered by Capitán don Julián García de Argueta, and a two-month-old white mulatilla, daughter of Petronila, valued at 100 pesos.
Capitán don José de Lebrón granted general power of attorney to Licenciado Pro. don Manuel González Coronel, who was a Comisario del Santo Oficio and was preparing to depart for Nicaragua.

Licenciado Pro. don Antonio de Soto Barahona, Sarjento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo, and don Fernando Lozano formed a company to discover and exploit an ancient gold mine on Cerro Santa Ana, located about 8 leagues south of the city towards Pacaca. The first two partners agreed to provide all necessary provisions, labor, and tools, while Lozano contributed his mining expertise, with profits to be split into three equal parts. A marginal note indicates this agreement was nullified on November 5, 1737.

Licenciado Pro. don Antonio de Guevara Sáenz, owner of a 4,000-tree cacao plantation in Matina, compensated Sarjento Francisco Guerrero for his cultivation work and remaining 8 months of lease by granting him 1,000 trees. Guerrero was also obligated to care for the remaining 3,000 trees for six years, with their fruits also belonging to him. A marginal note from 1753 indicates Capitán don Manuel Cayetano de Guevara, as Guevara Sáenz's representative, declared the agreement concluded.

Alférez Francisco Solano made his will in Ujarrás, stating he had been married to doña María Josefa de Soto for 31 years and listing their four children: Juana, Juan Antonio, María del Carmen, and Francisco (6 years old). He detailed his assets, including three caballerías of land with a house, 2,000 plantain trees, and a sugar mill, and named don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad, don Tomás de la Madriz, and his wife as executors.

Don Lorenzo de Almádana, a resident of Santiago de Veragua, sold an enslaved man named Juan Romero, 22 years old, to Capitán don Antonio José de Oriamuno for 300 pesos. Almádana had purchased Juan Romero from Capitán don Juan Solís Cachero, also from Santiago de Veragua.

Capitán don Gregorio Sáenz and his wife doña Francisca de Castro obligated themselves for 750 pesos, secured by a tile-roofed house, a sugar mill, and a large fenced property in the Aserrí valley, which previously belonged to his brother, Licenciado don Manuel Sáenz. The property, being deserted, was given to Sáenz by the mayordomos and capellanes with a three-year grace period for reconstruction and replanting of sugarcane, with rent to begin on January 26, 1740, covering various capellanías and cofradías.
Capitán don Tomás López del Corral, Teniente de Oficiales de la Real Hacienda, sold something. The entry is incomplete.
Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno sells all the wood he possesses at the mouth of the Río Grande, intended for an 18-vara keel boat, for 550 pesos.

people_involved: don Juan Fco. de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Don Francisco Guerrero, acting on behalf of don Juan García Romero, sells a Mina-caste slave named José, approximately 18 years old, to S. Mor. don Juan Fco. de Ibarra y Calvo for 260 pesos. The slave is currently ill with a right leg injury from a mule kick.
Luisa González Romero, widow of Lorenzo de Villarreal, donates 300 cacao trees in the Barbilla valley to her daughter, Gertrudis Villarreal, who is married to Sarjento Gregorio Calvo.

Juana López, legitimate daughter of Alfonso López and Catalina Milanés, and widow of Bartolomé Meneses, makes her testament. She names her four children: Mª Candelaria, Bartolomé, José Gabriel, and Manuela.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
Licenciado Pro. don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Alférez Francisco Barquero and his wife, doña Manuela Valverde, make their testament, mentioning their parents, deceased son, and living daughter Francisca. They leave carpentry tools to their adoptive son Andrés Barquero, with the condition that he teach José Miguel Martínez. The testament details debts owed to Francisco Barquero by Capitán don Tomás López del Corral and Capitán don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco for construction work. They leave their house to their granddaughter Josefa Benita Manzano, whom they raised, and name their daughter Francisca Barquero and grandchildren as heirs, with Licenciado Pro. don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba and Pro. don José de Chaves as executors.

people_involved: S. Mor. don Carlos Custodio Galarza
summary: Capitán Juan José Zamora, a resident of the Barba valley, grants general power of attorney for lawsuits to S. Mor. don Carlos Custodio Galarza.
Capitán don Martín de Garayar, residing in the Bagaces valley, grants general power of attorney to S. Mor. don Pedro Carazo.
Doña Dionisia Meléndez, widow of Salvador Alarcón, grants power to her brother, Teniente don Manuel Meléndez, to make her will.

people_involved: Beneficiado don José Antonio Díaz de Herrera
summary: In the Valle de Curriravá, doña Ana Castro Rodríguez, legitimate daughter of Capitán Juan Rodríguez de Castro and doña Petronila Arias, and widow of Capitán Alonso de Porras, makes her testament. She had no children and names her slaves Efigenia and her children. She also requests an image of Nuestra Señora del Viejo be placed in the settlement of Boca del Monte, leaving the decision to Beneficiado don José Antonio Díaz de Herrera. S. Mayor Manuel Saborío is named as executor.

people_involved: Licenciado don Juan Pérez de Cote
Padre don Juan Antonio de Moya
summary: In the Valle de Barba, Sarjento Mayor Luis Gutiérrez adds a codicil to his 1736 testament, clarifying details about his Barbilla cacao plantation and establishing a chaplaincy for his and his two wives' souls. He addresses the debt for his slave Diego, granting him freedom upon his wife's death, and mentions a debt owed to him by Padre don Manuel Coronel. He also allocates 200 pesos to Reverendo Padre Fray Miguel Bermúdez.

locations: paso que llaman Toribio y de las Carretas
summary: In the Valle de Barba, María Morera, a widow, sells a house site and enclosed pineapple fields to Blas de Vargas for 70 pesos, payable within a year. This property, located in the Valle de las Ciruelas, was originally acquired by her deceased husband Antonio de Ocampo from don Nicolás Arias, husband of doña Gertrudis de Oviedo.

Capitán Juan José Zamora exchanges his old pineapple enclosure, thatched houses, and sugar mill on the Porrosatí river for a 7-year-old mulatto slave named Diego, given by don Juan Antonio Paniagua. Both items are valued at 150 pesos.

In the Valle de Barba, Capitán Gregorio de Siles and doña María de Quesada, both natives of Spain, make their joint testament. They had no children and name each other as reciprocal heirs, also mentioning their respective parents.
Alférez José Amador is mentioned in the Valle de Barba on this date, but the specific details of the event are incomplete in the provided text.

A widower from Valle de Aserrí, whose name is not provided, obligated himself to his six minor legitimate children: Josefa, Manuela, María, Domingo, Juana, and Nicolás Amador. Each child was entitled to 50 pesos and 3.5 reales from their maternal inheritance, following the death of their mother, Rosa Viterbo de Avendaño.

Ana Fernández, a widow and legitimate daughter of Gaspar Fernández and Margarita Chacón, made her will in Valle de Barba. She named her children Antonia Josefa, Juan Antonio, Elias de la Cruz, María del Carmen, Juana María, Manuela, Francisco, and Ana Margarita. Half of her 'quinto' (fifth part of inheritance) was to be given to Licenciado don Lorenzo de Quesada for a communicated purpose.

Teniente Pedro Sánchez, a widower of Lorenza de Fonseca, obligated himself to his six minor children: Efigenia, Ana María, María Cayetana, Joaquín, María Manuela, and Angela Petronila Sánchez. Each child was to receive 20 pesos.

people_involved: María de la Concepción de Chaves
summary: A dowry letter was issued by Jacinto Núñez de Alfaro in favor of María de la Concepción de Chaves, his future wife. María de la Concepción is the legitimate daughter of the late José de Chaves and Manuela González, and the dowry amounted to 382 pesos.

Doña Bárbara de Arias, widow of Capitán don Fernando de Moya, granted power to make her will to her father, Capitán Gaspar Arias, and her uncle, Capitán Gregorio de Siles, whom she also appointed as executors. Her legitimate daughter, Juana Micaela, was named as her heir.

A dowry letter was issued by José Francisco Valverde, legitimate son of Sarjento Sebastián de Valverde and the late doña Feliciana de Villalobos, in favor of his wife, doña María Susana de Umaña. María Susana is the legitimate daughter of Hermano Mauricio de Umaña and doña María Guzmán, and they had married three months prior, with the dowry amounting to 627 pesos.
Capitán Miguel Rodríguez, married to Juana de Sanabria, made his will in Valle de Barba, naming his children Francisco and Marcelo. The will was interrupted due to the testador's death.

people_involved: Francisco de la Trinidad de Arias
summary: Capitán Felipe de Arias, widower of doña Victoria Jiménez, obligated himself to his ten children: José Timoteo, María Efigenia, Francisco de la Trinidad, José Manuel, Eugenio, María Rosa, Antonia, Manuel Elias, Mateo Cornelio, and Ventura de Arias. Each child was to receive 78 pesos and 2.5 reales.

Cabo de escuadra Blas Solís and Pedro Solís, following the death of their mother doña Clara de Morera, obligated themselves to their minor brothers, Manuel and José Felipe Solís. Each minor brother was to receive 64 pesos and 2 reales from their maternal inheritance.

Capitán Cosme Ramírez, widower of Juana de Córdova (daughter of José de Córdova), obligated himself to his two daughters, Beatriz Olaya and Angelina María. Each daughter was to receive 68 pesos and 5 reales.

Ana Fernández issued a codicil to her will of March 25 of the same year, revoking her previous disposition regarding the 'quinto.' She now directed that the remaining inheritance be given to her sister, Josefa Fernández, for the upbringing, sustenance, teaching, and education of her daughters.

Margarita Solano and José Miguel Solano, following the death of José Antonio Valerio (Margarita's late husband), obligated themselves to the minor children Claudio Ramón and María de la Trinidad Valerio. These children, born to Valerio and Margarita, were each to receive 44 pesos and 1 real.

Capitán Isidro de Castro, widower of doña Antonia de Quirós, obligated himself to his four children: Josefa, José, Manuel, and Nicolás, for 1167 pesos and 3 reales of their inheritance. Capitán Marcelo de Morales served as guarantor. Marginal notes from 1742 indicate that Teniente José Nicolás de Zamora, upon marrying Antonia Josefa de Castro, received 291 pesos and 6.5 reales from Capitán Isidro. Another 1742 note shows don Juan Fernández, don Bruno de Arenal, don Gil de Alvarado Jirón, and his wife taking responsibility for the tutelage of the minor children don José, don Manuel, and don Nicolás de Castro, for 875 pesos and 4.5 reales.

María de Pachón received 100 pesos from Capitán Sebastián de Sandoval, belonging to a chaplaincy founded by Alférez Antonio de Ocampo, whose principal was 200 pesos. The other 100 pesos were with Licenciado don Lorenzo de Quesada, the chaplain, to whom María had previously delivered them. María then obligated herself for the newly received 100 pesos to Padre Quesada, hypothecating a house, enclosures, and a mulata slave named Alfonsa.

Francisco Félix García, a resident of Chiriquí, made his will in Valle de Curriravá. He was married to Teresa del Castillo and named Licenciado don Hermenegildo de Alvarado as his executor and co-heir along with his wife. If his wife were deceased, her share would go to Severiano Mesina to be divided between him and his niece, Clara de Vargas.

Capitán don Andrés de Salazar, widower of doña Gregoria de Flores and without succession, made his will in Valle de Escasú. He left a 22-year-old mulato named Carlos and a 40-year-old mulata named Cayetana in fideicomiso to Reverendo Padre Fray José Suaza, a Reductor in the province. Capitán Francisco de Flores and Hermano José Núñez were appointed as executors, and he requested burial in the church of Pacacua.

Juana de Sanabria and her legitimate son, Francisco Rodríguez, obligated themselves to Marcelo Rodríguez, who is also her son and the son of her late husband, Capitán Miguel Rodríguez, for 150 pesos and 1.5 reales. Francisco, being emancipated, acted as guarantor.

Doña María de Flores, a single woman, made her will in Valle de Escasú, requesting burial in the church of Pacaca. Her assets included an hermitage dedicated to Nuestra Señora de las Mercedes, containing various religious items. She owned three slaves: Juan (30), Baltasara (20), and Micaela (16). She owed Padre Reductor Fray José Suaza an unspecified amount, and stipulated that the hermitage be maintained as long as Padre Suaza remained in the area, after which its value would be converted into masses for the souls of herself, her parents, siblings, and servants.
A 'perol' (large pot or cauldron) was distributed among Josefa Barboza and her daughters. Other items were distributed among Juana Manuela, Ambrosia, Juana, Josefa Barboza, and Josefa Cascante.

Pascual Ramírez, married to María de las Salas and father of Josefa Ramírez, made his will. He was previously married to Margarita de Mora, with whom he had no children. His executors were his brother José Núñez and his step-son Domingo de Quesada.
Captain Sebastián Cayetano Zamora, acting as executor for Captain José Fernando de Moya, sold an enslaved person named Julián, 21 years old, to Captain Gregorio Siles for 200 pesos.

Juana de Segura, widow of Miguel Ramos, made her will. She had children: Juan (deceased, married to Margarita de las Salas), Francisco (married), Martina, Lucía, Bernarda, and María. She owned a house and a sugar mill in the town of Barba.

Manuel and Francisco Zamora, legitimate sons of Sergeant Major Antonio Zamora and Francisca Saborío, gave a receipt to their brother, Captain Juan José Zamora, for their inheritance, amounting to 647 pesos and 4 reales each.

Ventura Calvo and Alférez Francisco Calvo, acting as guarantor, committed to Narcisa Calvo for 127 pesos. This sum was her inheritance from her deceased parents, Pedro de Alcántara and Juana Cortés, of whom Narcisa was the legitimate daughter and heiress.

Antonio del Castillo and Antonia de Hoces, a married couple with no children, made their joint will. They declared Tomás de la Cruz, Nicolás Victorio, and Brígida de la Cruz as their heirs, having raised them as their own children.
Captains Gil de Alvarado Jirón and Gregorio Sáenz, acting as executors for María de Flores, sold an enslaved mulato named Juan, about 30 years old, to Captain Juan de Bonilla for 125 pesos.

Captain Sebastián Cayetano Zamora and his wife Cecilia Saborío committed to a chaplaincy founded by Cecilia Vásquez de Coronado, located in the parish church of Barba. The chaplaincy, with Juan de la Cruz Zumbado as chaplain and Sebastián de Sandoval as patron, was owed 828 pesos from an estate in Tenorio. They mortgaged a house, 20 caballerías of land, and livestock as collateral. Captain José de Saborío and his wife Juana Ballesteros acted as guarantors.

Juliana Monje, widow of Captain Ventura Barrantes, committed to her two minor children, Luisa de los Angeles and Pedro Benito Barrantes, for 71 pesos and 4 reales each. Brother José de las Salas served as guarantor. This obligation was later cancelled and replaced by another deed.

Antonio Hidalgo and his wife Josefa de Arleguí committed to their nephew Antonio de Ugalde, legitimate son of Captain Juan de Ugalde and Juana de Dios Hidalgo, for 322 pesos and 4 reales of his inheritance. In September 1737, Captain Isidro Hidalgo, Antonio's brother, took over this debt.

Manuela de Bonilla, widow of Captain Juan José Zamora, committed to her children Micaela, Juan Lucas, Salvador, José Antonio, José Miguel, José Joaquín, and Ana de la Asunción for 322 pesos they inherited from their deceased uncle Cayetano Zamora. José Antonio de Soto and his wife Josefa Cabezas acted as guarantors.

Captain Francisco de Alfaro and his wife Juana Manuela Pérez de Cote, owners of an estate in Valle de Barba, founded a chaplaincy of 100 pesos on their property. They named Juana Manuela's brother, Licenciado Juan Bautista de Cote, as the first patron and chaplain, with their children or the parish priest of S. Bmé. de Barba as successors.

María Candelaria de la Cruz, a widow, committed to Gabriel and Efigenia Sánchez (children from Gregorio Sánchez's first marriage) for 158 pesos and 3 reales from their mother's inheritance, and to Francisco, Antonio, and Petronila (her children with Gregorio Sánchez) for 231 pesos and a half real from Gregorio Sánchez's inheritance. Captain José de Alfaro was the guarantor. In 1738, Captain Isidro de Castro took over the share of the minors Gabriel and Efigenia.

Sergeant Toribio Jiménez sold a plot of land with a thatched house, a sugar cane field, and a banana plantation in Valle de Barba to Andrés de Villalobos for 200 pesos. The land, which bordered the royal road to Guayabo and the Quebrada de las Cañas, was part of his mother Ana Valverde's property, originally purchased from José de Ballesteros, husband of Toribio's sister Juana Jiménez. 100 pesos of the sale price were to be obligated to the Convent of San Francisco in Esparza.
Miguel de Escalante Paniagua and his wife Bárbara Ruiz committed to Juan, Isidro, and Pedro Alvarez, legitimate sons and heirs of Isabel de Aguilar, for 87 pesos.

Captain Tomás de Chaves and Tomasa de Quirós made their joint will, stating their children were deceased. They named their granddaughter María Lizondo as heir to over 1100 pesos. Tomás de Chaves also declared a 100-peso debt to the Convent of Barba, which was actually owed by Beneficiado Juan de la Cruz Zumbado, for whom Chaves had signed as a favor.

Lieutenant Miguel de Alfaro and his wife Angela de Arias committed to José Eugenio, Juan Esteban, María, and Clara Rodríguez, legitimate children of the deceased Alférez Gregorio Rodríguez and Juana de Jesús Martínez, for 319 pesos and 4 reales of their inheritance.
Captain Isidro Hidalgo was involved in an unspecified transaction in Valle de Barba. The record is incomplete.

Doña Rosa Morera and her unnamed husband obligated themselves to their nephew, Antonio de Ugalde, for 322 pesos 4 reales from an inheritance. This inheritance was previously an obligation of Teniente Antonio Hidalgo.
Don Gil de Alvarado and Don Gregorio Sáenz, as executors for Doña María de Flores, sold a 30-year-old mulata named Baltasara to Hermano Mauricio de Umaña for 100 pesos.

Capitán Sebastián Cayetano Zamora and Doña Cecilia Saborío obligated themselves to pay for a capellanía founded by Capitán Don Andrés de Salazar. The capellanía was funded by 550 pesos from the auction of Salazar's estate, which Zamora acquired for 710 pesos. Sarjento Mayor Diego de Soto, Sarjento Mayor Miguel Jiménez, and Capitán José de Quirós acted as guarantors.
Pedro de Solís, son of José Solís and Clara Morera, established a dowry of 240 pesos 6 reales for his wife, Doña Casilda de Alfaro, daughter of Hermano Nicolás de Alfaro and Doña Juana Sibaja.

María Jiménez, widow of Miguel Reinoso, made her will. She had a legitimate daughter, María Josefa, married to Andrés de Villalobos, and a natural son, José Nicolás, who was in Nicaragua. Her brother is Capitán Felipe Arias.

Doña Juana de Sibaja, widow of Capitán Juan de Porras and later of Hermano Nicolás de Alfaro, made her will, detailing her children from both marriages: Juan Antonio (deceased), José Ángel, and Alonso with Porras; and Esteban, José, and Casilda with Alfaro.

Doña Juana de Sibaja, a widow, requested an inventory and partition of her assets, totaling 441 pesos, which were then distributed between her sons Esteban and José de Alfaro, children of Hermano Nicolás.

Capitán José Tomás de Hoces, with Capitán Tomás Morera as guarantor, obligated himself to pay 260 pesos 7.5 reales to Petronila, Marcos, Francisco, Basilio, and Marcelo de Hoces, the legitimate children of the deceased Josefa Morera.
Capitán Sebastián Cayetano Zamora, acting as executor for Don Fernando de Moya, sold a tile and wood house located behind the Cubujuquí parish to Capitán Sebastián de Sandoval for 320 pesos.

Esteban de Alfaro, with Capitanes Gaspar González and Alonso de Porras as guarantors, obligated himself for 150 pesos to a capellanía founded by Doña Cecilia Vásquez Coronado. This obligation was previously held by his mother, Doña Juana de Sibaja, who ceded a cauldron as collateral. Licenciado Don Manuel López Conejo is the chaplain.

José de Zúñiga, son of José de Zúñiga (father) and Ana de Chaves, established an obligation of 267 pesos 4 reales in favor of his wife, Andrea Josefa de Ocampo, who is the legitimate daughter of Capitán José de Ocampo and María Rosa Solís.

people_involved: Don Juan Francisco de Escalante y Paniagua
summary: Don Juan Francisco de Escalante y Paniagua and his wife Doña Juana Teresa de Viera sold a 13-year-old mulata named Gertrudis, inherited by Don Juan Francisco from his parents, to Doña Catalina de Siles for 250 pesos.
Capitán Felipe Arias sold a 20-year-old enslaved woman named Isabel to Capitán Gaspar de Arias for 200 pesos. Isabel had been inherited by Felipe's deceased wife, Victoria Jiménez, from her parents.

Juan de Rojas and his wife María Josefa de Aguilar obligated themselves for 223 pesos 2 reales to Juana, Gabriela, María Candelaria, Gregorio, and María Rita, the legitimate children of Sárjento Toribio de Rojas and his deceased wife María de Mora. Francisca de Rojas was paid, and Sárjento Toribio de Rojas acted as guarantor.
Blas de Salazar, widower of María Núñez, obligated himself to pay 38 pesos 3 reales to each of his minor legitimate children: Juana Petronila, María Martina, Felipe Santiago, and Juliana.
Pedro de Solís, widower of Doña Casilda de Alfaro, obligated himself to pay 220 pesos from his son's maternal inheritance to his minor legitimate son, Juan Manuel Solís.
Doña Gertrudis de Oviedo, a widow, sold a 35-year-old mulato named Teodoro de Oviedo, whom she inherited from her parents, to Teniente Miguel de Alfaro for 200 pesos.

Andrés de Acosta, with Teniente José de Madrigal as guarantor, obligated himself to pay 80 pesos to each of his minor sisters, Antonia and María Manuela, who are the daughters of the deceased Lázaro de Acosta and Doña Felipa Gómez.

people_involved: Doña Felipa Gómez de Ocon y Trillo
summary: Sarjento Mayor Diego de Soto and his wife Doña Sebastiana Jiménez obligated themselves for 220 pesos to a capellanía served by Licenciado Don Manuel López Conejo, Cura of Esparza. This obligation was previously held by Lázaro de Acosta and Doña Felipa Gómez de Ocon y Trillo. They mortgaged a honey-boiling cauldron, 12 mules, and 80 cattle. The capellanía was founded by Juan Gómez.

Hermano José de las Salas and his wife Juliana Monje obligated themselves for 125 pesos to Lucía de los Angeles and Pedro Benito, the legitimate children of Capitán Ventura Barrantes, Juliana's first husband, for their paternal inheritance. A marginal note indicates a 1738 deed for this amount by Capitanes Nicolás and Benito Barrantes and Juliana Monge, freeing José de las Salas.

Cayetana Matamoros, widow of Teniente José Chacón, obligated herself to pay 13 pesos 5 reales to each of her minor sons, José, Silvestre, Gregorio, Andrés, and Francisco Chacón, from their paternal inheritance.

Sarjento Agustín Zamora obligated himself to the five orphaned children of José Picado and Juana Santos (Micaela, María Josefa, Pablo José, María Antonia, and Luisa Picado) for 71 pesos and 5 reales from their inheritance. This document was executed in Valle de Barba before Teniente General José Fernando de Moya, with José de Alvarado Jirón serving as Alcalde ordinario of Cartago.

Gregorio Ortiz, a resident of Valle de Aserrí, obligated himself to his siblings Josefa, Antonio, and María de Mora for 87 pesos and 4 reales. This sum represented their inheritance from their deceased mother, Simona de Mora.

Hermano Juan Pérez, a widower residing in Valle de Curriravá, obligated himself to his minor son, Francisco Pérez, for 54 pesos and 6 reales from his maternal inheritance. This transaction secured the son's share of the estate.

Juan Pérez also obligated himself to his grandchildren, José, Juan, Nicolás, and Aurelia Murillo, who are the children of Felipe Murillo and Micaela Pérez. This obligation was for 87 pesos, representing their inheritance.

Teniente Bartolomé de Araya, widower of Paula Montero, obligated himself to his four minor children (José, Manuel, Pablo José, and José Matías) for 26 pesos and 1/2 real. This amount constituted their maternal inheritance and was granted in Curriravá.

Leonor de los Reyes, a widow from Valle de Iscasú, obligated herself to her three children (Luis Antonio, María Josefa, and Cayetano Raimundo de Bustamante) for 120 pesos from their inheritance, with her brother Gaspar de los Reyes as guarantor. This escritura was renewed on December 22, 1738, involving Leonor de los Reyes, her second husband Juan de Dios Arias, and the guarantor.

Bernardo de Esquivel, from Valle de Iscasú, obligated himself to his siblings Pedro, Margarita, Isidora, Catalina, and María de Esquivel for 77 pesos and 2.5 reales, representing their inheritance from their deceased mother, María Hidalgo. His emancipated brother, Nicolás de Esquivel, was also mentioned, and Juan de Salazar and Alférez José de Arce served as guarantors.

Juan Ramón and José de los Santos Ramos, sons of the deceased Juan Ramos and Juana Solano from Valle de Iscasú, obligated themselves to their siblings Angela María, José Antonio, and María Antonia Ramos for 126 pesos from their inheritance. Juan Montalbán acted as the guarantor for this transaction.

Sarjento José Morera, widower of Juana González, obligated himself to his three minor children (Isidora, Juana Josefa, and José Joaquín Morera) for 15 pesos and 1 real from their inheritance. His other daughter, Ana Margarita, was mentioned, and Isidora was noted as being married to Tomás Bermúdez.

Alférez Antonio Sáenz, widower of Angela María Cortés, obligated himself to Quiteria, Catarina, and Antonio Horacio de Campos for 48 pesos of inheritance. These individuals were the legitimate children and heirs of Esteban Campos and Angela María Cortés, who had been married to Campos in her first nuptials.

Juan and Vicente Hernández, legitimate sons of the deceased Félix Hernández and Juana de Acuña, obligated themselves to their siblings Bárbara, María de la Rosa, Teodoro, José Manuel, and Juana Hernández for 115 pesos and 1 real from their inheritances.

locations: Ermita de Nuestra Señora de la Soledad
summary: Doña Luisa de Miranda, widow of Capitán José de la Rosa Barquero and mother/tutor of Juan Ramón, Leonida, and José Lorenzo Barquero, obligated herself to her children for 339 pesos and 4 reales. This sum was adjudicated to them from the estate of Alférez Francisco Barquero and Doña Manuela Valverde, and she hypothecated her house near the Ermita de Nuestra Señora de la Soledad.

Sarjento Mayor Francisco Manzano Boyayn and his wife Francisca Barquero, along with José Manuel Castillo and his wife Manuela Josefa Manzano, sold a house and a plantain grove in the ejidos of Cartago to Sarjento Mayor José Felipe Bermúdez for 525 pesos. The property originated from the estate of Alférez Francisco Barquero and Doña Manuela Valverde, with Francisca receiving her inheritance share and Manuela Josefa receiving her portion as a third and fifth by way of improvement from her grandparents' assets.

people_involved: Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
Juana Gertrudis de Bermúdez y Aguiar
José Felipe de Bermúdez y Aguiar
María Teresa de Sandoval y Golfín
summary: A dowry letter was issued for 2181 pesos from Don Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra, legitimate son of the deceased Sarjento Mayor Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo and Doña Petronila de Moya, to his wife Doña Juana Gertrudis de Bermúdez y Aguiar. Juana Gertrudis is the legitimate daughter of Sarjento Mayor José Felipe de Bermúdez y Aguiar and Doña María Teresa de Sandoval y Golfín.
The justice system placed José Felipe Quirós, an orphaned boy aged 12-13 and son of Angela Quirós, with Alférez José Antonio de Jesús, a master carpenter, for a period of 6 years as an apprentice.

Presbítero Licenciado Hermengildo de Alvarado y Jirón obligated himself to the Cofradía del Rosario, located in the parish church, for 100 pesos at 5% interest. He hypothecated his hacienda in Miravalles as security for this obligation.

people_involved: Pedro Antonio de Carrandi y Menán
Silvestre de Villa Alta y Guzmán
summary: Don Pedro Sendín y Rivero, preparing to depart for Panama with 160 mules, obligated himself to the Royal Caja for 180 pesos of unpaid export duties, promising to pay Teniente de Oficiales Reales Pedro Antonio de Carrandi y Menán in Panama 20 days after arrival. Sarjento Mayor Juan Rodríguez de Robredo of Cartago and Capitán Silvestre de Villa Alta y Guzmán of Villa de Nicaragua served as guarantors, though this escritura was ultimately not processed.

people_involved: Silvestre de Villa Alta y Guzmán
summary: Sarjento Mayores Francisco de la Madriz Linares and Juan Rodríguez de Robredo, both residents of Cartago, along with Capitán Silvestre de Villa Alta y Guzmán, guaranteed the 180 pesos debt for Pedro Sendín y Rivero, as referenced in the previous entry. This document was subsequently cancelled at the margin.

Doña Petronila Valerín, a widow, leased a cacao plantation in Matina to Cristóbal Solano from Valle de Aserrí for three years. The plantation bordered Hacienda de la Madre de Dios and a river, with annual rents set at 100 pesos for the first year, 125 for the second, and 150 for the third.
Sarjento Mayor Francisco Garrido and his wife Doña Águeda Pérez del Muro are mentioned at the beginning of an entry, but the details of the transaction are incomplete in the provided text.

Licenciados don Juan Manuel and don José Francisco de Casasola, sons of doña Aguoda, donated 300 fruit-bearing cacao trees in Matina (La Gamalotal hacienda) to Matías Jiménez. Jiménez was obligated to plant an additional 2000 trees over five years, which were then to be donated to Nuestra Señora de los Dolores.
Matías Jiménez formally committed to fulfilling the agreement made in the previous deed, which involved the donation and planting of cacao trees in Matina.

Presbítero Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero pledged 300 pesos at 5% interest to the Cofradía de la Santa Vera Cruz in the Franciscan convent of Cartago. He mortgaged a cacao plantation in Matina, managed by Alférez Baltasar de Moya, with the Cofradía's representatives accepting the obligation.

Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno and don Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra pledged 220 pesos to the Real Caja for export duties on 110 mules transported to Tierra Firme by don Francisco de Ayerdi, a resident of León (Nicaragua). This obligation was later cancelled on January 10, 1739, by Treasurer Pedro Antonio Carrandi y Menán.

Presbítero Licenciado don Gregorio López del Corral leased a fruit-bearing cacao hacienda in the Matina valley, inherited from his parents, to Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno for one year at a price of 150 pesos.

Don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora, sued by doña Águeda Pérez del Muro to marry her daughter doña María Manuela de Barros, provided Capitán don Tomás López del Corral as guarantor to be released from jail. The case was referred to the Provisor and Vicar General, but the marriage did not proceed.
Doña Luisa Calvo, a widow, leased a fruit-bearing cacao hacienda with 440 trees in Matina to Sárjenlo Juan Miguel Trejos for two years at an annual price of 125 pesos.
Doña Francisca de Arburola y Ribarén, a widow, granted general power of attorney to Presbítero Licenciado don Gregorio López del Corral.

Don Pedro Cortina, a resident of Granada (Nicaragua), pledged 100 pesos to the Real Caja for export duties on 50 mules he transported to Tierra Firme. Don José Antonio de Oriamuno and don Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra served as his guarantors, and the obligation was later cancelled.

Official proceedings were conducted for the opening of the will of the deceased Sárjenlo Mayor don José Felipe Bermúdez. The will, dated October 31, 1737, detailed his family, property including a hacienda in Matina called 'La Punta', enslaved people, debts, and instructions for a capellanía. The proceedings were overseen by Teniente General don José de Mier Cevallos with several witnesses.

The will of the deceased Sárjenlo Antonio de Umaña was recorded, detailing his parentage, two marriages, and three daughters from his first marriage. His brother, Felipe Umaña, was named as his executor.

people_involved: José Cayetano de la Madriz Linares
summary: José Cayetano de la Madriz Linares pledged 500 pesos at the request of his mother, Juana Calderón, distributing the sum among three religious entities. He mortgaged an old hacienda he owned in Matina as security for this obligation.

people_involved: María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
summary: Capitán don Francisco de Betancourt and his wife, doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral, sold an 8-day-old enslaved boy named Juan Elias, son of their enslaved woman Ambrosia Cabral, to Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno and his wife, doña Ana Efigenia de Estrada, for 50 pesos.
Presbítero Licenciado don Manuel José González Coronel sold an enslaved woman named Petronila, approximately 22 years old, to Capitán don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco for 325 pesos in cacao.

Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno, Mayordomo of the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora de los Angeles, leased two parcels of cacao hacienda belonging to the Cofradía on the Matina riverbank to his brother, Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno, for three years at an annual price of 50 pesos.

Don José Antonio de Oriamuno and his wife, doña María Catarina de Ibarra, pledged 300 pesos to the capellanía founded by Capitán Juan Calvo, mortgaging their hato in Valle de Bagaces called 'El Paso Hondo.' The capellanía was established in 1724 by don Juan Francisco de Ibarra as executor. The obligation was cancelled in 1750 by Bachiller Presbítero don José Manuel García de Argueta upon payment by don Juan José de Cuende.

Antonio Várela, acting for himself and his brother Gregorio, agreed to undertake repairs on a tiled house in Cartago, located on the road to Ujarraz. This house, valued at 200 pesos, was part of their deceased father Blas Várela's estate and was to be shared among five siblings, with Gertrudis Ruiz de Hinojosa receiving a portion contingent on these repairs.

Juliana Monge, widow of Benito Barrantes, committed to securing 125 pesos from the inheritance of her children, Lucía de los Angeles and Pedro Benito Barrantes. Captain Nicolás Barrantes of Cartago and Benito Barrantes from Barba valley served as guarantors for this obligation, replacing Brother José de las Alas.

Don Juan Marín de Laguna, acting as curator for Beneficiado don Juan Antonio de Moya, leased a 1500-tree cacao plantation in Matina to Captain don Francisco Meoño and his wife, doña Josefa María de Laguna, who is the daughter of the grantor. The lease is for three years at 200 pesos annually, replacing a previous lease to don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno and his wife for 300 pesos, which was rescinded after an ecclesiastical dispute.

María Calderón, a widow, leased a 460-tree cacao plantation in Matina, adjacent to her sister Juana's property, to Manuel Calderón. Manuel, described as a young man she raised, will lease the plantation for three years at an annual cost of 100 pesos.

Captain José de Alfaro, representing María Candelaria de la Cruz, sold a five-year-old mulatto girl named Juana María to don Francisco de Arburola for 180 pesos of cacao. Juana María is the daughter of Francisca de la Cruz, an enslaved woman owned by María Candelaria de la Cruz, and was originally a donation from Clara Morera, her grandmother.

Captain Isidro de Castro of Curriravá valley committed to paying 150 pesos to Gabriel and Efigenia Sánchez, the legitimate children of the late Gregorio Sánchez and María de la Candelaria Cruz. This sum was previously held by Sánchez's widow, guaranteed by Captain José de Alfaro, and Castro mortgaged his property in Curriravá as security.

people_involved: José Cayetano de la Madriz Linares
summary: Captain Antonio de Zamora transferred 479 pesos, owed to Ramona de Sandoval, to Juana Calderón and her son José Cayetano de la Madriz Linares. This debt, previously shared by Zamora and his wife Felipa de Sandoval, included 400 pesos for an enslaved man named Lorenzo, inherited by Ramona and her siblings, plus 79 pesos in cacao. The new debtors mortgaged a cacao plantation in Matina, while Ramona Sandoval was residing in Cartago with doña Josefa de Bonilla.

Doña Angela Sáenz, a widow, leased a cacao plantation in Matina, comprising approximately 1700 trees, to Captain don Julián García de Argueta. The plantation, previously managed by don José Manuel Jiménez, was leased for three years at an annual price of 112.5 pesos.

Doña María Teresa de Sandoval, widow of Sergeant Major don José Felipe de Bermúdez, committed to paying 260 pesos and one real to the Royal Treasury, a debt left by her deceased husband. She mortgaged a house and country fences, which her husband had purchased from Alférez Francisco Barquero, as security for this obligation.

people_involved: minor child of Simón Machado and María Venegas
summary: Doña María Teresa de Sandoval acknowledged her deceased husband's 100-peso debt to the Cofradía de la Concepción and mortgaged an adobe house. This house was already encumbered by several other debts, including chaplaincies for Beneficiado don Manuel López Conejo and Beneficiado don José de Guzmán y Echavarría, a debt to the Cofradía del Rosario, and a guardianship fund for a minor child of Simón Machado and María Venegas.

Doña María Teresa de Sandoval committed to paying 130 pesos to the chaplaincy established by Comisario Baltasar de Grado, whose current chaplain, Presbítero Licenciado don Manuel de Guzmán, is in Santiago de Guatemala. She used the same house as collateral that was mentioned in the previous legal document.
Doña María Teresa de Sandoval reaffirmed her obligation to the Cofradía del Rosario for the previously mentioned 100 pesos, securing the debt with the same property as before.
Doña María Teresa de Sandoval committed to a 100-peso obligation for the chaplaincy served by Presbítero Licenciado don Manuel López Conejo, using the same mortgaged property as collateral.

people_involved: minor child of Simón Machado and María Venegas
summary: Doña María Teresa de Sandoval obligated herself for 120 pesos to a minor child of the deceased Simón Machado and María Venegas, using the same mortgaged property. This obligation originated from a deed signed by her husband in 1725.
Doña María Teresa de Sandoval committed to her son, José Antonio Bermúdez, for 1506 pesos and 3 reales, representing his paternal inheritance.

The justice system placed Francisco Paula, a 10-11 year old orphan and legitimate son of María Josefa Padilla, as an apprentice with master tailor Sergeant José Cayetano Fernández. However, Fernández later renounced his charge in October 1738 after Francisco ran away and was subsequently taken in by his relative, assistant Salvador Muñoz.

people_involved: Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdova
summary: Doña Águeda Pérez del Muro and her son, Presbítero Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdova, reached an agreement with Alférez don Luis de Sotamayor and his wife, doña Isabel Ramona de Utrera. They exchanged an enslaved mulatto woman, Dionisia Hidalgo (21-22 years old) and her 2-year-3-month-old daughter, Antonia Catarina, for two other enslaved individuals, Mónica (17) and José Francisco (16), plus an additional 125 pesos of cacao. The original sale of Dionisia to doña Águeda occurred in 1735, and the new enslaved individuals were acquired in 1731.

people_involved: Juana de Oviedo de la Vega
summary: Alférez Alberto de Irola made his will, detailing his two marriages and children from each. He was first married to Josefa Nicolasa de Segura, and then to María Gertrudis de Molina. He owed money to Padre Fray Juan de Paniagua, and Teniente Miguel Cabtill was named his executor.

people_involved: María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
summary: Capitán Francisco de Betancourt and his wife María Josefa de la Vega Cabral, who inherited a mulata slave named Marta from her parents, granted freedom to Marta's daughter, Benita Rosalía. Benita Rosalía, described as white and 4 years old, was freed in exchange for 100 pesos and 25 pesos in cacao, paid by a benefactor.

people_involved: José Nicolás López de la Flor
María Rita López de la Flor
José Antonio López de la Flor
summary: Mariana López de la Flor obligated herself to José Nicolás, María Rita, and José Antonio López de la Flor, who were minors raised by her deceased sister Antonia López de la Flor. This obligation was for 372 pesos they received as inheritance.

María, Ana, and Josefa Fernández, all widows, sold their mulatillo slave, Juan Francisco Chacón, who was about 10 years old, to Presbítero Licenciado don José Manuel García de Argueta for 130 pesos. They had inherited Juan Francisco Chacón from their mother, Margarita Chacón.

Luis de Sojo and his wife Juana Solano, residents of Ujarraz, acknowledged a 100-peso debt owed to the Convento de S. Francisco de Cartago by Juana's deceased father, Alférez Francisco Solano. This debt was secured by a tiled house in Ujarraz that Francisco Solano had dismantled, and they obligated themselves to rebuild and mortgage it.

Sarjento Mayor Francisco Garrido and his wife Águeda Pérez del Muro donated 2000 cacao trees, being cultivated by Matías Jiménez in Matina, to the brotherhood of Nuestra Señora de los Dolores at the ermita de la Soledad. The fruits are to perpetually cover the brotherhood's expenses, with the donors reserving the right to direct their use during their lifetime. Presbíteros Juan Manuel and José Francisco de Casasola, and later the sons of their sister Josefa de Casasola, are to say the masses.

people_involved: José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Baltasara López de la Flor sold a white mulatilla slave named Josefa Nicolasa, who was 1 year and 4 months old, to Presbítero Licenciado don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría for 100 pesos. Josefa Nicolasa was the daughter of Petronila, a mulata slave Baltasara had purchased from Margarita Barquero.

Capitán Juan José de Cuende posted bail for Sarjento Juan Francisco de Aguirre, who was imprisoned by order of Capitán Francisco Javier de Siles, Alcalde de la Santa Hermandad. Aguirre was involved in a lawsuit with Ayudante José de las Alas concerning an alleged assault.

Antonia de Hoces Navarro, a widow, donated a 14-year-old mulata slave named Juana to her granddaughter, Antonia Zavaleta. Juana was the daughter of another slave, Josefa, and was born and raised in Antonia de Hoces Navarro's house. Manuela de Zavaleta, Antonia Zavaleta's mother, accepted the donation on her behalf.

Presbítero Licenciado Manuel González Coronel sold a 44-year-old criollo black slave named Juan José to Teniente don José de Jinesla for 300 pesos. Manuel González Coronel had acquired Juan José from Manuela Conejo, a widow.

Francisco Carrillo, a master blacksmith, obligated himself to the minor children of the deceased Manuel Chinchilla and Teresa Ruiz (Teresa, Luisa, Manuela, Francisca, and Catalina de Chinchilla) for 100 pesos. This money was given to him by Gertrudis Ruiz de Hinojosa, who stated it was left by her husband, Francisco Gutiérrez, for the Chinchilla children.

Capitán Juan de Ocampo Golfín, acting as executor for the deceased Capitán Tomás de Chaves, ratified the sale of a property across the Río Grande. This property had been sold by Chaves to his nephew, Juan Suárez, for 100 pesos.

people_involved: Luis Fernando de Liendo y Goicoechea
summary: Notario Luis Fernando de Liendo y Goicoechea granted general power of attorney to Capitán José de Luna y Estrada and Cristóbal de Perdomo, who were procurators in the Audiencia de Guatemala.

Capitán Juan Francisco Guerrero and his wife Lorenza Fajardo obligated themselves for 234 pesos to Lorenza's minor children from her first marriage to Capitán Manuel de Arburola. This sum was delivered by Francisca de Arburola, and the children were named Manuel Valentín, Nicolás Felipe, and Francisca Liberata de Arburola.

Capitán Juan José de Cuende and his wife Manuela Josefa de Ibarra obligated themselves for 200 pesos to a chaplaincy founded by Luisa Calvo, mortgaging their hacienda Sarmiento in Matina. This obligation was partly inherited from Manuela's father, Juan Francisco de Ibarra, and partly from funds provided by Licenciado José Manuel García de Argueta. The chaplaincy, after the death of Beneficiado José Antonio Díaz de Herrera, passed to Bachiller Rafael García de Argueta in Guatemala, and this formal obligation was made at the request of his brother, Presbítero Manuel García de Argueta, who serves as interim chaplain.

Capitán Juan José de Cuende and Manuela Josefa de Ibarra obligated themselves for 285 pesos and 6 reales to Gobernador y Capitán General Francisco Antonio de Carrandi Menán. This sum belonged to the estate of Bartolomé Bueno de Bastorí, a former Contador Juez Oficial Real of León. Capitán Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra served as their guarantor.

people_involved: José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Beneficiado José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría, the oldest priest in the parish, acted as attorney for his brother, Presbítero Licenciado Manuel de Guzmán y Echavarría, who was in Santiago.
An unnamed chaplain and patron of a hacienda, formerly owned by Doña Josefa Santiago de Aguilar, leased the hacienda to Alférez Matías Jiménez for two years at an annual rent of 125 pesos.

people_involved: Gobernador y Capitán General don Francisco Antonio de Carrandi y Menán
Don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad
Capitán don Juan de Ocampo Golfín
Capitán don Juan Antonio de Villar Hevia
Capitán don Manuel Francisco de Porcio
summary: Governor and Captain General Francisco Antonio de Carrandi y Menán presented several individuals, including Don José de Mier Cevallos and Don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad, as his guarantors for his residency and the administration of royal tribute rights. Each guarantor pledged 250 pesos.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan de Ocampo Golfín
Capitán don Luis Fernando de Goicoechea
summary: Capitán don Juan de Ocampo Golfín, acting as the executor for the deceased Capitán don Tomás de Chaves, sold a 3-year-old mulatto slave named Antonia to Capitán don Luis Fernando de Goicoechea for 150 pesos. The transaction was granted before Teniente General Mier Cevallos.

Don José Manuel Jiménez sold a plot of land, adjacent to one belonging to Nuestra Señora de Concepción, to Alférez don Luis de Sotomayor for 25 pesos. José Manuel Jiménez had previously acquired this plot from his brother, don Cristóbal Jiménez.

Doña Francisca de Inza, a widow, leased a cacao hacienda in the Malina valley, consisting of 1000 trees and bordering her son-in-law don Cayetano de Alvarado's property, to Agustín de la Riba for three years at 50 pesos per year. Agustín de la Riba's brother, Francisco de la Riba, appeared as his representative.

people_involved: Capitán don Antonio Elias de Arleguí
Licenciado Presbítero don José Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Capitán don Antonio Elias de Arleguí pledged 100 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Magdalena de la Portilla, for which Licenciado Presbítero don José Francisco de Ocampo Golfín served as chaplain. He mortgaged a 'caballería de tierra' with 50 cattle in the Santa Ana valley as security.

Gregorio Várela sold the materials of a house to Sárjenlo Francisco Guerrero for 250 pesos. This house was referenced in a previous deed signed on May 5 of the same year by Gregorio Várela and his brother Antonio Várela.
The justice system placed José Nicolás de Rojas, a 12-year-old orphan, with Alférez Antonio de Jesús, a master carpenter, for six years.
A partially missing protocol entry indicates that a mulatto slave named Manuel de Utrera y Guevara, belonging to Padre Guevara, was delivered to master silversmith Bruno de Luna for five years.
A missing page from the protocol, which was the last of this protocol according to the index, contained the will of Gertrudis Ruiz de Hinojosa.

Juana de las Salas, widow of Alférez Francisco Solano, made her will, naming her deceased parents Tomás de las Salas and Mauricia Muñoz, her deceased children José, Francisco, and Nicolasa, and her living children María, Manuel, and Sebastián Solano. Her son-in-law, Alférez Antonio de Bonilla, was named executor, and her children and grandsons were heirs.

people_involved: Juan José de Salas alias Zúñiga
summary: Juan José de Salas, also known as Zúñiga, pledged 200 pesos at 5% cacao to the five minor children of the deceased Francisco del Campo and Josefa de Ibarra. This pledge was for the value of a forge he purchased from Francisco del Campo's estate.

people_involved: Padre predicador fray José Gregorio de Morales
summary: Lucas Brenes, son of Alférez Gregorio de Brenes and Petrona de Quirós, made his will. He was married to Doña María Nicolasa Ramos, who was pregnant. Padre predicador fray José Gregorio de Morales acted as his executor and signed on his behalf as Lucas could not write.

people_involved: Doña Mariana López de la Flor
José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Doña Antonia de Echavarría, a widow, leased two cacao haciendas in the Matina valley to Ramón de la Rosa for three years. The total rent was 575 pesos, with 75 pesos for the first harvest and 100 pesos for subsequent ones. Her son, José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría, signed on her behalf.

people_involved: Teniente de Capitán reformado Miguel Romero
Juan Bautista de la Guerra y Solórzano
Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno
summary: Teniente de Capitán reformado Miguel Romero, son of the deceased Capitán Diego Romero and Doña María Ana de Morales, made his will. He was married to Doña Mariana de Flores and had children including Manuel Antonio, Doña Micaela, and Juan José Romero. His wife and children were heirs, and Licenciado don Juan José Camacho and Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno were named executors.

people_involved: Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno
summary: Sargento Mayor Juan Manuel Saborío sold land in the Poas area to Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno for 100 pesos in silver. Saborío had purchased these lands on March 26, 1732, from Doña Ana Rodríguez de Castro, widow of Capitán Alonso de Porras, excluding a portion Doña Ana had sold to Capitán don Francisco de Flores on March 18, 1732.
The text indicates that a will was being made by Bachiller don Eusebio Me..., but the entry is incomplete.

people_involved: Bachiller don José Manuel García de Hergueta
Teniente de Capitán don Manuel Meléndez
Reverendo Padre Leandro del Santísimo Sacramento
summary: An inventory of the possessions of Meléndez, a priest, is detailed, including numerous religious books. It is noted that he donated his house to his cousin, Viviana Meléndez. Bachiller don José Manuel García de Hergueta and Teniente de Capitán don Manuel Meléndez are named as his executors.

people_involved: Capitán don Luis Fernando de Liendo y Goicoechea
summary: Capitán don Luis Fernando de Liendo y Goicoechea grants power of attorney to don Juan Bautista Miralles, an agent in Madrid, to handle his affairs and obtain confirmation of his Public Notary office.
Tomasa de Quirós, widow of Capitán Tomás de Chaves and resident of Valle de Barba, grants general power of attorney to Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara, a priest.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Francisco de Moya
summary: Licenciado don José Francisco de Moya, a priest, grants general power of attorney to Capitán don Gil de Alvarado.

Alférez Francisco de Oviedo, residing in Ujarraz, obligates himself to Hermano José Antonio de Carranza for 502 pesos of cacao, representing the remaining price of a cacao plantation in Valle de Reventazón that Carranza sold to him. The plantation serves as collateral for the debt.

people_involved: Doña Teresa de Claver y Valderrama
Sargento Mayor don Baltasar Francisco de Valderraraa
Licenciado don Gregorio López del Corral
summary: Doña Teresa de Claver, widow of Sargento Mayor don Baltasar Francisco de Valderraraa (former Governor and Captain General of the province), grants power of attorney to Licenciado don Gregorio López del Corral, a priest, to collect her late husband's salary from the Royal Treasury in León, Nicaragua. The claim is supported by a dispatch issued on April 19, 1738, and a liquidation signed by don José de Uterrarte.

people_involved: Capitán de Caballos Corazas don Miguel Cayetano de Iuarra
Alférez don José Antonio de Bermúdez
Sargento Mayor don José Felipe Bermúdez
Guardián del Convento de San Francisco
summary: A chaplaincy is founded by Capitán don Miguel Cayetano de Iuarra and Alférez don José Antonio de Bermúdez, acting as executors for their late father, Sargento Mayor don José Felipe Bermúdez. The principal of 168 pesos is secured by a cacao hacienda in Matina, and Doña María Teresa de Sandoval, mother of the founders and widow of José Felipe, will be responsible for the principal. The Guardián del Convento de San Francisco is the interim chaplain.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don José Felipe Bermúdez
summary: Doña María Teresa de Sandoval, widow of Sargento Mayor don José Felipe Bermúdez, obligates herself to the chaplaincy her late husband founded for 168 pesos at 5% interest, secured by a cacao hacienda in Matina.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
Licenciado don José Manuel García de Hergueta
Doña Francisca de la Madriz Linares
summary: Capitán don Juan Nicolás Viveros, gravely ill, grants power to Sargento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares and Licenciado don José Manuel García de Hergueta (a priest) to make his will. His legitimate daughters, Manuela and Tomasa de Viveros, born to Doña Francisca de la Madriz Linares, are named as his heirs.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Vicente de Morales
Doña Mariana López de la Flor
Licenciado don Gregorio López del Corral
Sargento Mayor don José Felipe Bermúdez
summary: Licenciado don José Vicente de Morales and Doña Mariana López de la Flor lease a cacao hacienda in Matina with 1400 trees to Licenciado don Gregorio López del Corral, represented by his agent Capitán don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco, for two years at 275 pesos of cacao. The hacienda, currently held by the heirs of Sargento Mayor don José Felipe Bermúdez, will be delivered on September 11 of the current year.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás de Soto y Barahona
summary: Capitán Antonio de Zamora, resident of Valle de Barba, transfers the guardianship of 400 pesos belonging to the minor doña María de Sandoval to Capitán don Tomás de Soto y Barahona. Zamora declares he and his wife, doña Felipa Sandoval, took charge of this and other minors' funds on December 3, 1735, with guarantors. Soto y Barahona accepts the transfer and mortgages a cacao plantation. On December 7, 1747, José Nicolás de Villalobos, doña María de Sandoval's husband, received the 400 pesos.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor reformado Diego de Soto
Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto
summary: Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara, a priest, sells a 50-year-old mulatto slave named Antonio to Sargento Mayor reformado Diego de Soto, a resident of Valle de Barba, for 160 pesos of silver. Guevara had acquired the slave from the estate of the deceased Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Vicente de Morales
Doña Mariana López de la Flor
Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno
doña Baltasara López de la Flor
summary: Licenciado don José Vicente de Morales, a priest, sells adobe rooms, a corridor, and a kitchen to doña Mariana López de la Flor for 400 pesos of cacao. The property, inherited by Morales from his mother-in-law doña Baltasara López de la Flor, is bordered by properties of doña Josefa Pérez de Muro and Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno. The buyer must obligate herself for 100 pesos belonging to the minor Domingo de Noguera y Moncada, and pay the remaining 300 pesos to the seller in annual installments of 25 pesos.
Capitán don Cayetano de Alvarado and his wife doña Juana de Guevara obligate themselves to the chaplaincy founded by don Francisco de Enciso Hita.

people_involved: Licenciado don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
Canónigo don Félix de Hoces Navarro
summary: Canónigo don Félix de Hoces Navarro ceded a Capellanía to Licenciado don Antonio de Soto y Barahona for $200 at 5% interest, secured on houses located on the other side of the Reventado River, near the Taras River.
The principal of the Capellanía mentioned in the previous deed was transferred to don Félix Sáenz on October 20, 1757.

people_involved: doña Josefa de la Vega Cabral
Síndicos del Convento de San Francisco
Religiosos del Convento de San Francisco
Beneficiado don Juan Antonio de Moya
summary: Capitán don Francisco de Betancourt and his wife doña Josefa de la Vega Cabral obligated themselves for $900 at 5% interest to a Capellanía founded by Bachiller don Gregorio de Moya. This sum was charged against 5000 cacao trees in the Matina Valley, bordering land formerly owned by Beneficiado don Juan Antonio de Moya.

people_involved: Licenciado don Manuel García de Hergueta
summary: Doña Francisca de Inza, widow of Capitán don Pedro de Mondragón, obligated herself for $104 and 3 reales at 5% interest to the Cofradía de la Concepción. This amount represented the value of materials from a demolished stone house, previously charged to her mother's house, and was imposed on her own house.

people_involved: Mayordomo de propios de esta Ciudad
Sargento Mayor don José de Morales
summary: Antonio de Azofeifa and his wife doña Juana Manuela de Hidalgo obligated themselves for $100 at 5% interest to the Mayordomo de propios of the City. This sum, originally charged to Sargento Mayor don José de Morales' houses since December 30, 1716, was now imposed on their lands and cedar house located across the Virilla River.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don José Fernández de Castellanos
doña Felipa Sendín de Soto Mayor
doña Francisca Javiera Fernández de Castellanos
Doctor don Francisco Javier de Iglesias y Contreras
Licenciado don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Sargento Mayor don José Fernández de Castellanos, son of deceased don Francisco Fernández de Castellanos and doña María de León from Toledo, made his testament on January 2, 1738. He was married to doña Felipa Sendín de Soto Mayor and had two daughters, doña Josefa and doña Francisca Javiera, the latter married to Doctor don Francisco Javier de Iglesias y Contreras. He granted his slave Francisco Calvo a $50 reduction on his $250 price for freedom, and named Sargento Mayor don Francisco Garrido and Licenciado don Antonio de Soto y Barahona as albaceas.

people_involved: Isabel (mulata esclava of Diego de Aguilar)
Capitán don Juan José de Cuende
summary: This is a continuation of the testament of Diego de Aguilar, a single man, declaring assets including four slaves (José, Manuel, Antonia, Isabel) and two Capellanías. He recognized Nicolasa de Aguilar (alias la Morales), married to José Carranza, as his natural daughter. He also established a Capellanía for lay masses, naming his nephew Alférez Matías Trejos as patron, and Capitán don Juan José de Cuende and Alférez Matías Trejos as albaceas. The testament was granted in Cartago, and Clemente de Astorga signed for the testator.

María de Vergara, single daughter of deceased Manuel de Vergara and María de Aguilar, made her testament. Among her assets were livestock bequeathed by her uncle Diego de Aguilar. She named Diego de Romero as albacea and her niece and goddaughter Manuela Camacho as heir. The testament was granted in Diego de Romero's house in the ejidos.

people_involved: doña Lorenza de Arburola y Rivarén
Capitán Lorenzo de Arburola y Rivarén
summary: Capitán don Antonio de Ángulo, married to doña Lorenza de Arburola y Rivarén (daughter of deceased Capitán Lorenzo de Arburola y Rivarén and doña Josefa de Hoces Navarro), made his testament. He had no children and named his wife, his sisters doña Francisca and doña Juana de Ángulo, and his niece Francisca Joaquina (?) de Bonilla as heirs. Don José Miguel de Guzmán, the local parish priest, was named as an albacea.

Gertrudis Ruiz de Hinojosa, a widow, made her will. She was the legitimate daughter of Captain Juan Ruiz and María Santiago, and had been married twice, first to Alférez Juan Ginés de Hinojosa and then to Captain Francisco Gutiérrez. Her heirs included her daughters Gertrudis, Josefa, Catalina, and the children of her deceased daughter Francisca, with her son-in-law Alférez José Manuel de Segura and nephew Alférez José Antonio de Jesús named as executors.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno
doña Ana Efigenia García de Estrada
Beneficiado don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
Licenciado don Gregorio López del Corral
Alférez don Luis de Soto Mayor
summary: Captain Cosme Damián Gutiérrez, acting as executor for his deceased father Sergeant Major Luis Gutiérrez, along with his brothers José, Matías, and Luis, and on behalf of his absent brother Francisco Gutiérrez, sold cacao haciendas in the Barbilla valley to Captain don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno. The sale price was $3192, with the buyer and his wife, doña Ana Efigenia García de Estrada, assuming various financial obligations to the Royal Treasury, convents, and several beneficed priests.

people_involved: Licenciado don Juan Pérez de Cote
Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno
summary: Captain Cosme Damián Gutiérrez, as executor for his deceased father Sergeant Major Luis Gutiérrez, founded a chaplaincy for 6 recited masses. Licenciado don Juan Pérez de Cote was appointed as the interim chaplain, with the provision for a relative to take over if ordained, or the parish priest of San Bartolomé de Barba otherwise. Captain don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno was obligated for the principal sum of $318, to be imposed on the haciendas he had previously purchased.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno
doña Ana Efigenia García de Estrada
summary: Captain don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno and his wife, doña Ana Efigenia García de Estrada, assumed an obligation of $512 and 4 reales to the Royal Treasury. This debt originated from the confiscation of a black slave named Diego, previously charged to the deceased Sergeant Major Luis Gutiérrez, and was imposed on the haciendas they purchased. A marginal note indicates that don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno made a final payment of $287 and 2 reales of cacao on June 21, 1755, to satisfy this obligation.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno
doña Ana Efigenia García de Estrada
summary: Captain don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno and his wife obligated themselves for $400 at 5% interest to the Convento de San Francisco. This obligation was a direct result of the purchase of haciendas mentioned in folio 34.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno
doña Ana Efigenia García de Estrada
Licenciado don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Captain don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno and his wife recognized a debt of $160 at 5% interest for the chaplaincy served by Licenciado don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría. This recognition was made in virtue of the same obligation stemming from the hacienda purchase.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno
doña Ana Efigenia García de Estrada
summary: Captain don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno and his wife recognized a perpetual annuity (censo) of $240 at 5% interest on the Barbilla haciendas. This obligation was for the chaplaincy served by Beneficiado don Juan José Camacho, who was the parish priest of the Malina valley.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno
doña Ana Efigenia García de Estrada
summary: Captain don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno and his wife recognized a debt of $200 at 5% interest, imposed on the same haciendas, for the chaplaincy served by Beneficiado don Manuel López Conejo. Manuel López Conejo was identified as the parish priest of Esparza.

people_involved: Capitán don Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra
Capitán don Juan José de Cuende
summary: Captains don Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra and don Juan José de Cuende provided judicial bail for Captain don Juan de Salvatierra. This action was taken in a legal case against Salvatierra concerning the death of don José Manuel de Barros.

people_involved: Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara Sáenz
doña Lucía Nicoiasa Jirón de Alvarado
doña María Josefa Jirón de Alvarado
doña Angela Josefa Jirón de Alvarado
doña Antonia Josefa Jirón de Alvarado
doña María Ana Jirón de Alvarado
Sargento Mayor don Pedro Jirón de Alvarado
summary: Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara Sáenz, a Presbyter Cleric, donated 4025 cacao trees in the Barbilla valley to his nieces, the six legitimate daughters of Sergeant Major don Pedro Jirón de Alvarado and doña Angela de Guevara. Sergeant Major don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón accepted the donation on behalf of himself and his daughters. José Guerrero was cultivating the land until May 9, 1740.

Captain Cayetano de Herrera requested the aggregation of documents to formalize his purchase of land from Sergeant Felipe Monge, which included a simple sale from February 17, 1739, and a declaration of boundaries by Monge on February 15, 1740, due to his illness. The aggregated documents also included a 1633 testimony of a land sale in Cartago by Juan Sánchez Crespo, executor of Beatriz Osorio, to Juan Alonso, for a site previously owned by Luis Cascante de Rojas, Lucas Cardoso, and given as dowry by Andrés Benito. Felipe Monge stated he inherited the site from his father, Sergeant Juan Alonso Camacho.

people_involved: Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara Sáenz
summary: Cayetano Prado (also known as Campos), a free mulatto, ceded and transferred a cacao roza of 950 trees in the Matina valley to doña Antonia de Echavarría Navarro. The transaction, valued at $237 and 4 reales, was applied towards a larger debt that Cayetano Prado owed doña Antonia for the lease of her haciendas. The property bordered lands owned by Sergeant Salguero, Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara, and Sergeant Francisco Guerrero.

Alférez Miguel Castillo, acting as Mayordomo of the Cofradía de la Concepción of Ujarraz, leased the Hacienda de Nuestra Señora in Valle de Barbilla for three years. The annual rent was $50 of cacao, and the property was leased to Sargento Mayor Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón.

Capitán Francisco Javier de Oriamuno and his wife Doña Ana Efigenia García de Estrada obligated themselves for $318 pesos at 5% interest. This obligation was in favor of the chaplaincy founded by Capitán Cosme Damián Gutiérrez, who was the executor of his father, Sargento Mayor Luis Gutiérrez. The chaplaincy's chaplain is Licenciado Juan Pérez de Cote, and the obligation is secured on haciendas in Barbilla, which they purchased from Gutiérrez's heirs.

Capitán Francisco Javier de Oriamuno and his wife Doña Ana Efigenia García de Estrada obligated themselves to the heirs of Sargento Mayor Luis Gutiérrez, based on the same purchase mentioned previously. They owed specific amounts to Francisco Gutiérrez ($292.5), José Gutiérrez ($167), Luis Gutiérrez ($192), and Matías Gutiérrez ($247), with the latter three having already received the balance of their $292.5 share. The obligation was secured on the Barbilla hacienda.

The will of the deceased Capitán Juan Nicolás Viveros was granted by his father-in-law, Sargento Mayor Francisco de la Madriz Linares, acting under a power of attorney dated April 16. Juan Nicolás Viveros was married to Francisca de la Madriz Linares and had three children: Manuela, Tomasa, and one unborn. The executors were Francisco de la Madriz Linares and Licenciado Manuel García de Hergueta, with the daughters named as heirs.

people_involved: Manuel Esteban de Alvarado y Jirón
Lucía Nicolasa de Alvarado y Jirón
María Josefa de Alvarado y Jirón
Pedro José de Alvarado y Jirón
Angela Josefa de Alvarado y Jirón
José Joaquín de Alvarado y Jirón
Antonia Josefa de Alvarado y Jirón
José Gabriel de Alvarado y Jirón
María Ana de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: The will of Sargento Mayor Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón was recorded. He was the legitimate son of the deceased Capitán Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón and Doña Catalina de Vida Martel, and was married to Doña Angela de Guevara, with whom he had eleven children. His executors were his brother Miguel de Alvarado and his brother-in-law Licenciado Antonio de Guevara, a Clerigo Presbítero, with his children designated as heirs.

Licenciado José Manuel García de Hergueta, a Clerigo Presbítero, leased a cacao hacienda belonging to the Cofradía de la Concepción de Ujarraz. The hacienda, located in the Valle de Barbilla, was leased to Don José Manuel Jiménez for a period of 6 years at an annual rent of $50 in cacao.

Capitán Juan de Ocampo Golfín sold a site named 'Aserríes' to Sargento Mayor Miguel Jiménez for $100 in silver. Juan de Ocampo Golfín provided the titles for the property, which he had previously acquired from Licenciado José de Chaves.

people_involved: Francisco Javier de Iglesias y Contreras
summary: Capitán Isidro de Castro, acting as the attorney for Doña Ana de Castro, the widow of Capitán Alonso de Porras and a resident of Valle de Barba, sold an enslaved 'mulatilla blanca' named María de la Rosa. María de la Rosa, who was born in Doña Ana's house, was sold to Doctor Francisco Javier de Iglesias y Contreras for $100 in silver.

people_involved: Francisco Antonio de Carrandi y Menán
summary: The Escribano announced the opening of a 'residencia' (judicial review) for Maestre de Campo Francisco Antonio de Carrandi y Menán, covering his tenure as governor of this province, and for other Justice Ministers of his time. The judge presiding over this residencia was Governor and Capitán General Francisco de la Olaechea.

Alférez Baltasar de Moya, a free mulatto, sold a cacao plantation consisting of 2000 non-fruiting, 3-year-old trees. The plantation was located in the Valle de Barbilla, specifically in the area named El Bejuco, and was sold to Capitán José Nicolás de Bonilla for 2 reales per tree, totaling $500 pesos of cacao.

A dowry letter was issued for Juan Sáenz (who signed as 'don Juan Francisco Sáenz'), the legitimate son of Capitán Juan Sáenz and Ana Escalante Paniagua, and his wife Josefa Efigenia de Guillen, the legitimate daughter of Capitán Sebastián Guillen and María Magdalena de Orozco. The wife's assets were valued at $510 and 2 reales of cacao. Juan Sáenz, a widower of Francisca Martínez, contributed $653 and declared he held $200 belonging to his children from Francisca (María Josefa, Tomás José, Candelaria Josefa, and José Antonio de Sáenz) as their maternal inheritance. Capitán Patricio de Orozco of Nicoya and Capitán Francisco Javier de Siles served as appraisers.

Licenciado Manuel José González Coronel, a Clerigo Presbítero, obligated himself for $150 in silver at 5% interest to the chaplaincy founded by Doña Juana de Vida Martel. Licenciado José Hermenegildo de Arleguí is the patron and chaplain of this endowment. The obligation was secured on Manuel José González Coronel's residence, which was described by its neighboring properties.

people_involved: Juan José de la Madriz Linares
summary: Sargento Mayor Francisco de la Madriz Linares obligated himself for $216 in cacao currency at 5% interest to the chaplaincy founded by the deceased Doña Francisca de Benavente, securing it on a hacienda in Valle de Barbilla with 1380 cacao trees that he purchased from her estate. Licenciado José Manuel García de Hergueta was appointed interim chaplain. This was mandated by Doctor Miguel de Ziliera y Velazco, who, after no heirs of Francisca de Benavente came forward, appointed Juan José de la Madriz Linares (son of Francisco de la Madriz Linares and Rita García de Hergueta) as the proper chaplain, with Francisco de la Madriz Linares to pay interest from 1730 until Juan José is ordained Presbítero.

A payment of 150 pesos made by the Sargento Mayor to don Juan de Bonilla was declared illegitimate due to lack of proper mandate. Doña Benita de Bonilla was ordered to return items from the deceased don José, and don Raimundo de Larga Espada, as executor for his deceased brother don Diego, was to deliver four mules or their value to the Sargento Mayor.

people_involved: Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno
Licenciado don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí
summary: Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno and doña María Catalina de Ibarra acknowledged a $100 debt to a chaplaincy, stemming from their purchase of a house from Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara. The house had been previously bought by Guevara from the deceased doña Josefa de Aguilar in 1734.

people_involved: Teniente Coronel don José Joaquín de Nava
summary: Miguel Fuentes and Paula Paniagua cancelled the $100 debt related to the chaplaincy before Teniente Coronel don José Joaquín de Nava, who was the Gobernador y Capitán General of the province.

Don Francisco de Olaechea, Gobernador y Capitán General, pledged 200 pesos of silver to the Cofradía del Santísimo Sacramento for two years if he gambled with cards or dice. He also pledged another 200 pesos if he provided money for others to play these games, with an exception for the game of 'pachanga' with trusted individuals.

people_involved: Doña María Ana López de la Flor
doña Baltasara López de la Flor
Licenciado don José Vicente de Morales
summary: Doña María Ana López de la Flor pledged $2000 to a chaplaincy founded by her deceased sister, doña Baltasara López de la Flor, with Licenciado don José Vicente de Morales as chaplain. This obligation was secured by a cacao hacienda in Matina valley, which doña María Ana had inherited and acquired at auction after her sister's death.

people_involved: Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla
summary: Juana Calderón and her son José de la Madriz Linares transferred $400, representing the value of a 31-year-old Congo slave named Lorenzo, to Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla. This sum was part of the guardianship funds for the minor Ramona de Sandoval, whose deceased parents, Capitán Cayetano de Sandoval and doña Teresa Paniagua, had resided in Barba valley.
Martín de Chavarría, husband of doña Ramona de Sandoval, cancelled the obligation related to the guardianship funds.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan José de Cuende
Capitán don Antonio Elias de Arleguí
Licenciado don José Francisco de Moya
Cura don Juan Antonio de Moya
summary: Doña Polonia de Moya, with Capitanes don Juan José de Cuende and don Antonio Elias de Arleguí as guarantors, pledged $1500 for chaplaincies established by the deceased don José de Alvarado and doña Josefa de Moya. The obligation, secured by a cacao hacienda in Matina valley, is managed by Licenciado don José Francisco de Moya, who succeeded the late Cura don Juan Antonio de Moya as chaplain.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo
Teniente de Capitán Agustín de la Riva
summary: Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo, representing the Franciscans, sold a fruiting cacao hacienda in Matina valley to Agustín de la Riva, a free mulatto. The hacienda, previously owned by Benito Velerín who founded a 150-peso chaplaincy on it, was sold for $150.

people_involved: Capitán don Antonio Elias de Arleguí
summary: Doña Polonia de Moya, a widow, leased a 1500-tree fruiting cacao hacienda in Matina valley to Capitán don Antonio Elias de Arleguí for four years at $150 per year. This hacienda had been adjudicated to her upon the death of her brother, Beneficiado don Antonio de Moya.
The lease agreement between Doña Polonia de Moya and Capitán don Antonio Elias de Arleguí for the cacao hacienda was cancelled.

people_involved: Teniente de Capitán José de Jinesta
summary: Doña Francisca de Arburola, a widow, leased a cacao hacienda in Matina valley, inherited from her deceased parents, to Teniente de Capitán José de Jinesta for three years. The lessee was obligated to plant a new clearing next to the hacienda and clean it four times.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Baltasar Francisco de Balderrama
Capitán don José de Luna y Estrada
summary: Doña Teresa de Claver, widow of Sargento Mayor don Baltasar Francisco de Balderrama, granted general power of attorney to Capitán don José de Luna y Estrada, a procurator in the Real Audiencia of Santiago de Guatemala.

people_involved: Capitán de Caballos Corazas don Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra
Sargento Mayor don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
Licenciado don José Manuel García de Hergueta
Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
