summary: Capitán don Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra, patron of a chaplaincy founded by his deceased father, transferred $1400 to his nephew don José Antonio de Oriamuno and his wife doña María Catalina de Ibarra. This sum was for a rural hacienda inherited from their parents, with the recipients obligating themselves to the chaplaincy, which has Licenciado don José Manuel García de Hergueta as interim chaplain.

people_involved: Doña María Ana López de la Flor
Licenciado don Gregorio López del Corral
doña Baltasara López de la Flor
Licenciado don José Vicente de Morales
summary: Doña María Ana López de la Flor, through her agent Capitán don Dionsio Salmón Pacheco, leased a 1600-tree fruiting cacao hacienda in Matina valley to Licenciado don Gregorio López del Corral for two years. Although half of the hacienda was designated for a chaplaincy for Licenciado don José Vicente de Morales from her deceased sister doña Baltasara López de la Flor, doña María Ana had claimed it as her own earlier in the year.

locations: Ciudad de los Reyes de Lima
summary: José Barrantes, a native of Ciudad de los Reyes de Lima, made his testament.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan José de Cuende
summary: An unmarried man, whose deceased parents were residents of Lima, made a will. He declared no forced heirs but recognized Captain Benito Barrantes as his grandfather, though he was not acknowledged as such due to being a foreigner. He named Captain don Juan José de Cuende and Lieutenant Diego Ortiz as executors, with Diego Ortiz designated as the heir.
On December 4th of the same year, the unnamed testador annulled his will, stating his intention to travel to Tierra Firme and other reasons.

Doña Ana Rodríguez de Castro, widow of Captain Alonso de Porras, granted freedom to her mulata slave Efigenia and Efigenia's daughters, María de la Rosa (11 years old) and María del Rosario (5 years old). Efigenia was obligated to perform 36 masses for Doña Ana.

people_involved: Capitán don José Manuel Sánchez de Castañeda
Capitán don Juan Sánchez de Castañeda
Doña Baltasara de la Madriz Linares
Sargento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
Sargento Mayor don José de Morales
Capitán don Luis de Soto Mayor
Bachiller don José Manuel García de Hergueta
summary: Captain don José Manuel Sánchez de Castañeda, son of Captain don Juan Sánchez de Castañeda and doña Juana de Alvarado Jirón, established a dowry for his fiancée, doña Baltasara de la Madriz Linares, daughter of Sargento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares and doña Rita García de Hergutta. The dowry included a 12-year-old mulata slave named Ana Josefa, valued at $300, with $200 contributed by her uncle, Bachiller don José Manuel García de Hergueta.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz
summary: Governor Olaechea declared receipt of 92 pesos of cacao from Sargento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz, the Alguacil Mayor de residencia. This cacao belonged to the absent Miguel de Orozco as inheritance from his deceased father, Francisco de Orozco, and was deposited because Miguel's stepmother, Gertrudis de Hinojosa, refused to accept it.

Francisca López, a widow, leased a cacao hacienda with 1500 fruit-bearing trees in the Matina valley to don José de la Jinesta, a Lieutenant Captain, for three years. The annual rent was 7 'zurrones' of cacao, each valued at $25, to be delivered in Cartago.

Doña Manuela Sáenz, a widow, leased a cacao hacienda with 700 fruit-bearing trees in Matina to Captain don Cristóbal Jiménez for three years. The property bordered lands of don Dionisio Pacheco and Sargento Mayor don Julián García, with the river to the South and mountains to the North. The annual rent was $112 in cacao, delivered in Cartago.

people_involved: Licenciado don Manuel José González Coronel
summary: Licenciado don Manuel José González Coronel, a Presbyter Cleric, leased a cacao hacienda with 900 fruit-bearing trees in the Matina valley to don José Manuel Jiménez for three years. The hacienda bordered properties of doña Luisa Maroto and Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara, with the river and mountain on other sides. The annual rent was 4 quintales of cacao.

people_involved: Capitán don Esteban Ruiz de Mendoza
Doña Baltasara López de la Flor
summary: Captain don Antonio de Oriamuno, acting as attorney for Licenciado don Vicente Morales, a Presbyter Cleric, sold a mulata slave named Gertrudis and her one-year-old mulatillo son, Manuel Antonio, to Captain don Esteban Ruiz de Mendoza. These slaves were acquired after the death of doña Baltasara López de la Flor, for a price of $400 in cacao.

people_involved: Doña Antonia de Granda y Balvín
Maestre de Campo don Lorenzo de la Granda y Balvín
summary: Don Tomás de la Madriz and his wife, doña Antonia de Granda y Balvín, sold a 50-year-old negra slave named Catalina to José Antonio de Jesús, a master carpenter. Doña Antonia had inherited Catalina from her natural father, the deceased Maestre de Campo don Lorenzo de la Granda y Balvín, for a price of $150 in cacao.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí
Father of Don Juan de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Don Juan de Ocampo Golfín obligated himself for $200 at 5% interest to the Capellanía founded by doña Eugenia Abarca. This debt, previously held by his father and situated on 13 caballerías of land in El Higuerón, was now imposed on the same land, 800 head of cattle, and two black slaves. Licenciado don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí was the proprietary chaplain.

people_involved: Capitán de Caballos Corazas don Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra
Sargento Mayor don José Felipe Bermúdez
Guardián del Convento de S. Francisco
summary: Captain de Caballos Corazas don Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra, acting as executor for his deceased father Sargento Mayor don José Felipe Bermúdez and in the absence of his brother Alférez don José Antonio Bermúdez, founded a Capellanía of recited masses. The principal of $250 in cacao was charged to a cacao hacienda of 1900 trees in Matina. Doña María Teresa de Sandoval, widow of José Felipe and mother of Miguel, who held the hacienda, was to be obligated for the principal, and the Guardian of the Convent of S. Francisco was named interim chaplain.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad
Don Cristóbal Muñoz de la Trinidad
Don Alonso Bersabé Cabeza de Vaca
Licenciado don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
Maestre escuela don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro
summary: Sargento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad and his wife doña Antonia Josefa de Arburola obligated themselves for $500 in silver to a Capellanía founded by don Francisco Enciso, of which Maestre escuela don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro was the patron. This obligation stemmed from a previous sale by don Cristóbal Muñoz de la Trinidad to them of a property in Ujarraz, which included a sugar mill and cane fields, and which had been previously sold to their brother don Alonso Bersabé Cabeza de Vaca. Licenciado don Antonio de Soto y Barahona, the proprietary chaplain, requested this recognition.
In October 1739, Doña Ana Rodríguez de Castro, residing in the Barba valleys, sold a 4-year-old mulatilla named Andrea Susana, daughter of her slave Efigenia, to doña Antonia de Echavarría Navarro.

Licenciado don Manuel Sáenz, a Presbyter Cleric, sold a house and kitchen built on posts with a straw roof and its solar to Josefa Fernández. The property was bordered by houses and solars belonging to Francisco Carrillo, Micaela Alegría, Doña Josefa Sáenz, and Doña Manuela Sáenz, with a royal road in between. The sale price was $175 in cacao.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad
Doctor don Miguel de Ziliera y Velazco
Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno
Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
Licenciado don José Francisco de Casasola
Señor Cura don José Miguel de Guzmán
summary: Sargento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad and his wife doña Antonia Josefa de Arburola acquired houses made of adobe, covered with cedar wood and tiles, through an auction. These houses, previously owned by Doctor don Miguel de Ziliera y Velazco, were bordered by properties of Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno, doña Josefa Pérez de Muro, Licenciados don Juan Manuel and don José Francisco de Casasola, and Señor Cura don José Miguel de Guzmán. The property recognized a censo of $1190 in cacao, distributed among several capellanías including those of Pedro Ibáñez, don Agustín Guerrero, doña Gertrudis de Alvarado, Pedro Solano, doña Juana Moscoso, and Alonso Gómez Macotela.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan González de Aranda
summary: Don Mateo Alvarez de Ayllon and Capitán don Juan González de Aranda, a merchant in Panamá, settled their reciprocal accounts. The agreement involved Don Mateo Alvarez de Ayllon providing 20 mules for saddle and cargo to Capitán don Juan González de Aranda, thereby concluding their financial dealings.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan González de Aranda
summary: Capitán don Juan González de Aranda, a native of Cádiz, Spain, executed his will. He was the legitimate son of the late don Francisco González and doña Manuela Bernarda de Aranda, and had been married in Cádiz to the late doña Teodora María de Obregón, with whom he had several children who also passed away after their mother. He entrusted the 20 mules from a previous transaction to don Bartolomé de León, naming him as his executor and heir.

people_involved: Capitán de Caballos Corazas don Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra
summary: Capitán Diego Isidro de Aguilar ceded and transferred 500 pesos of cacao from a capellanía he instituted and founded, for which Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara served as interim Capellán. The recipients were Capitán de Caballos Corazas don Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra and his wife doña Juana Gertrudis de Bermúdez. In return, the couple obligated themselves with a herd of 500 head of cattle and cacao haciendas located in Matina.

people_involved: Licenciado don Juan José de Solís y Miranda
summary: Capitán Diego de Aguilar transferred a $500 censo from a capellanía he founded, for which Licenciado don Juan José de Solís y Miranda was the Capellán, to Francisco Carrillo, a master blacksmith, and his wife Petronila Cascante. Carrillo and Cascante obligated themselves with an adobe house to be built on the outskirts of the city. The grantor stipulated that in the absence of the proprietary Capellán, the capellanía would pass to the legitimate grandchildren, the children of José Antonio de Carranza and Nicolasa de Aguilar y Morales, and subsequently to the children of Alférez Matías Trejos.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan Manuel de Alvarado
summary: On this date, Capitán don Juan Manuel de Alvarado and his wife doña Juana María de Galarza assumed the obligation for the $500 that was previously the responsibility of Francisco Carrillo and his wife.
Juan José de Morales and his wife Manuela de Mesa sold a five-year-old mulatilla named María Antonia to don Andrés Fernández. The transaction was completed for a price of $150 in cacao.

Doña Lorenza de Arburola, widow of Capitán don Antonio de Ángulo, acknowledged a debt of $940 at 5% interest, which had been charged to her late husband. This debt was allocated to various capellanías, including those founded by Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas, Comisario don Baltasar de Grados, Pedro Ibáñez, and Juana Sagssti, as well as to the Cofradía del Rosario. The obligation was secured by a hacienda named 'Las Viejas,' comprising 1288 trees in the Matina valley.

people_involved: Don Juan José de Chavarría y Mendizábal
summary: Don Juan José de Chavarría y Mendizábal, a native of Spain, committed to teaching four orphaned Spanish children from the city. He was to receive 25 pesos of cacao monthly from the Illustrious Cabildo, plus additional fees per student based on their academic progress. He pledged to treat and discipline the children with love, provide a good example, take them to religious services, promote good customs, and deter them from vice, provided the Governor and Captain General prohibited private schools.

people_involved: Capitán don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda
summary: The Mayordomo and Deputies of the Cofradía de San Nicolás Tolentino sold a solar, originally donated by doña Josefa Pérez de Muro, to Capitán don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda. The property was bordered by the house and solar of Capitán don José de Alvarado, the property of doña Manuela Valerín, a royal road to the north, and another solar belonging to San Nicolás to the south. The sale price was $25.00.

Capitán don Gregorio de Mesa, the legitimate son of the late Capitán Felipe de Mesa and Felipa López de Artavia, executed his will. He was married to Teodora de Molina and had a son named José Nicolás. He appointed his wife as the albacea (executor) and his son as the sole heir.

people_involved: Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Teniente de Capitán Francisco Guerrero, a free mulatto, obligated himself to Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba, a Presbyter Cleric, for $139 in cacao in the Matina valley. This amount represented a debt originally owed by Juan Andrés de Córdoba, which Casasola y Córdoba had paid to various individuals in the city.

people_involved: Capitán don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda
Don Luís Fernando de Liendo y Goicoechea
Sargento Mayor don Julián García de Hergueta
summary: Capitán don José de Lebrón, acting on his own behalf and for his minor children, sold an adobe house with a tiled roof to Capitán don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda for 1250 pesos of cacao. The house was bordered by the property of don Luis Fernando de Liendo y Goicoechea, the house and solar of Capitán don Gil de Alvarado, the house of Sargento Mayor don Julián García de Hergueta, and the residence of the Gobernadores.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Manuel García de Hergueta
summary: Doña Angela María de Arleguí, widow of don Juan Antonio Serrano, sold a plot of land in Cartago to Licenciado don José Manuel García de Hergueta for $75 cacao. The land's boundaries were described by properties belonging to don José de Morales, don Luis de Soto Mayor, don Pedro José Sáenz, and don José Miguel de Céspedes. Doña Angela María had previously acquired the land from Jacinto de Rivera.

people_involved: Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno
Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
summary: Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno leased a 700-tree hacienda in the Matina valley, adjacent to Capitán don Tomás López del Corral's property, to don Andrés Fernández for two years at $75 cacao annually. This agreement was later cancelled on May 27, 1741.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan de Ocampo Golfín
Cura de la Parroquial de Cubujuquí
summary: Capitán don Juan de Ocampo Golfín, acting as executor for Capitán Tomás de Chaves, established a chaplaincy for recited masses. The endowment included a cattle ranch valued at $100 and 100 head of cattle located beyond the Río Grande, totaling $244 and 5 reales. Ocampo Golfín was named the patron, and the parish priest of Cubujuquí was designated as the chaplain.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco
Capitán don Esteban Ruiz de Mendoza
Capitán don Juan de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco, serving as Teniente General, recorded that Capitán don Esteban Ruiz de Mendoza had made an obligation of $150. This obligation was subsequently redeemed by Capitán don Juan de Ocampo Golfín, leading to the cancellation of the related escritura.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo
Sargento Mayor don Julián García de Hergueta
Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos
Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno
Alférez don Luis de Soto Mayor
summary: Several Sergeants Major, Captains, and an Alférez provided a judicial bond of two thousand pesos for don Juan Gemmir y Lleonart, who was the Teniente Coronel of the royal armies of Europe and the Governor and Captain General of the province. This bond was related to his residency trial.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo
Sargento Mayor don Julián García de Hergueta
summary: Sargentos Mayores don Pedro Carazo, don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo, and don Julián García de Hergueta provided a bond for Governor and Captain General don Juan Gemmir y Lleonart concerning penalties of the chamber.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos
summary: Sargento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares and Captains don José de Mier Cevallos and don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco provided a bond for Governor and Captain General don Juan Gemmir y Lleonart regarding arms and war supplies.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo
Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos
summary: Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo and Captains don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco and don José de Mier Cevallos provided a bond for Governor and Captain General don Juan Gemmir y Lleonart concerning the monte de piedad (pawn shop/charitable fund).

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don José Antonio de Oriamuno
summary: Sargento Mayor don José Antonio de Oriamuno, acting as Mayordomo of Nuestra Señora de los Angeles, leased two plots of fruiting cacao hacienda named 'La Madre de Dios' in the Matina valley to Capitán don Juan de Salvatierra for two years. The lease included the condition of replanting a clearing belonging to the Confraternity.

people_involved: Beneficiado don José Antonio Díaz de Herrera
Bachiller don Rafael García de Hergueta
Licenciado don José Manuel García de Hergueta
Capitán don Juan Díaz de Herrera
summary: Beneficiado don Juan José Camacho obligated himself for $650 at 5% interest to a chaplaincy founded by the late doña Luisa Calvo, associated with a property called 'El Molino' near Cartago. The chaplaincy's succession was outlined, involving Beneficiado don José Antonio Díaz de Herrera, Bachiller don Rafael García de Hergueta (residing in Santiago de Guatemala), Licenciado don José Manuel García de Hergueta (current patron), and Capitán don Juan Díaz de Herrera.

Beneficiado don Juan José Camacho sold a 23-year-old mulatto slave named Carlos de Salazar to doña Lorenza de Arburola, a widow, for $388 cacao. Camacho had previously purchased Carlos from Capitán Cayetano de Zamora for $300.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don José Antonio de Oriamuno
summary: Sargento Mayor don José Antonio de Oriamuno, as the one-year lessee of Cartago's tile factory, committed to repairing the house, shed, and other structures. After one year, he was to pay $25 cacao to the Mayordomo de propios and sell tiles at 12 pesos and 4 reales of cacao per thousand.

people_involved: Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos
Alférez don Luis de Soto Mayor
Sargento Mayor don José Antonio de Oriamuno
summary: Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos, acting as Procurador General, cancelled the obligation related to the tile factory lease. Alférez don Luis de Soto Mayor, as Mayordomo de propios, confirmed receipt of the tile factory and the $25 payment from Sargento Mayor don José Antonio de Oriamuno.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
summary: This codicil to doña Luisa Calvo's testament (dated March 24, 1737) stipulated that her dwelling houses, built by Capitán don Tomás López del Corral for $180 cacao, be adjudicated to her granddaughter doña Juana de Miranda, wife of Capitán Francisco García, as part of her inheritance. Doña Luisa also noted having paid $100 to María Manuela Maroto and owing $100 to her grandson Gabriel Maroto.
Doña Luisa Calvo made her testament before the same Escribano.

people_involved: Padre Procurador que es ó fuere del Colegio de San Pedro y San Pablo de la Compañía de Jesús
summary: Doctor don Francisco Pacheco Portocarrero, Archdeacon of Cuzco Cathedral in Peru, granted power of attorney to the Procurator of the Colegio de San Pedro y San Pablo of the Society of Jesus in Mexico City. This power was to collect 2107 loads and 37 pounds of Guayaquil cacao from don Francisco Suárez (a resident of Cádiz) or don Juan de Galarza (master of the ship 'Nuestra Señora de Belén'), and an additional 5000+ pesos in doubloons from Suárez in Mexico City.

Don Juan de Dios Gómez sold half a 'caballería' of land to Alférez Juan Calderón for $50 pesos cacao. The land's boundaries were described by the 'lava tripas' stream, a stone marker, the Quiroses road, and lands belonging to doña Josefa Pérez de Muro, located on the road to the town of Ujarraz. The document was not signed.

people_involved: Capitán don Antonio Elias de Arleguí
Sargento Mayor don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí
doña Engracia Gertrudis de Hoces Navarro
doña Josefa Petronila de Alvarado y Jirón
Capitán don José de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: This dowry letter was issued by Capitán don Antonio Elias de Arleguí in favor of his wife, doña Josefa Petronila de Alvarado y Jirón. The document specified Antonio as the legitimate son of the late Sargento Mayor don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí and doña Engracia Gertrudis de Hoces Navarro, and Josefa as the legitimate daughter of the late Capitán don José de Alvarado y Jirón and doña Úrsula Josefa López Conejo.

locations: Valle de la Concepción de Ujarraz
people_involved: Capitán don Tomás de la Madriz
summary: Teniente de Capitán Sebastián de Quesada, a resident of Ujarraz, made his testament. He was the legitimate son of the deceased don Alonso de Quesada and Clara de Rojas. He had children from his first marriage to doña Francisca de Mesa, and was currently married to doña Nicolasa Valerín, who was pregnant. His children were named as heirs, and Capitán don Tomás de la Madriz and Manuel Felipe de Alarcón were appointed as executors.

Ayudante General don Nicolás de Estrada made his testament. He was the legitimate son of the deceased don Francisco de Estrada and doña María Megía, and was married to doña Lorenza de Muñoz Hidalgo, with whom he had several children including a priest, don Antonio Raimundo, and doña Luisa Silvestre, widow of don Francisco Velazco. Nicolás de Estrada also declared that he arrived in this province in 1704, bringing a sloop with over a thousand pesos in goods belonging to don Francisco Canzela. His wife and son, don Antonio Raimundo, were named executors.

people_involved: Teniente de Capitán Juan Manuel Camacho
doña Josefa Sendin de Soto Mayor
summary: Teniente de Capitán Juan Manuel Camacho and his wife, doña Josefa Fernández de Castellanos, sold a 30-year-old mulatto slave named Francisco Calvo to Capitán don José de Jinesta for 200 silver pesos. Doña Josefa had inherited the slave from her deceased parents, don José Fernández de Castellanos and doña Josefa Sendin de Soto Mayor.

people_involved: Capitán don Esteban Ruiz de Mendoza
Capitán don Ramón de Noguera y Moncada
Sargento Mayor don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí
doña Engracia Gertrudis de Hoces Navarro
Antonio Cayetano de Noguera y Moncada
Antonia Josefa de Noguera y Moncada
summary: A dote letter was issued for Capitán don Esteban Ruiz de Mendoza, widower of doña Eufrasia Sancho de Castañeda, and doña Ana de Arleguí, widow of Capitán don Ramón de Noguera y Moncada. Doña Ana had two children from her first marriage, Antonio Cayetano and Antonia Josefa de Noguera y Moncada. The dote amounted to $1961.

people_involved: Teniente de Capitán don Pedro de Alvarado
summary: Doña Clara de Vida Martel, a widow, sold an adobe and timber house in the city's common lands to Teniente de Capitán don Pedro de Alvarado for 382 pesos of cacao. The house was encumbered with two censos: $100 for a chaplaincy patroned by Licenciado don Juan José Camacho, Cura of Matina, and $132 for the tutelage of Petronila and Rita de Velazco, minor daughters of her deceased son, don Lucas Velazco.

people_involved: Teniente de Capitán don Pedro de Alvarado
summary: Teniente de Capitán don Pedro de Alvarado formally recognized the $100 censo on the house he purchased through the previous deed. This censo was in favor of the chaplaincy patroned by Licenciado don Juan José Camacho, Cura of the Matina valley.

people_involved: Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos
doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho de Castañeda
Capitán don Juan Sancho de Castañeda
doña Juana de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: A dote letter was issued for don Rafael de Mier Cevallos, son of Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos and doña Catalina González del Camino, in favor of his future spouse, doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho de Castañeda. The dote amounted to $2241, with arras of $1000, and included 500 cacao trees in Matina and a 36-year-old black woman named Isabel.

locations: pueblo de San Antonio de Curriravá
people_involved: doña Antonia López de la Flor
summary: Alférez Patricio de Orozco, a resident of Nicoya, and don Pedro González de León, as guarantor, obligated themselves to the Convent of San Antonio de Curriravá for $464 and 5 reales at 5% interest for a chaplaincy founded by doña Antonia López de la Flor. Don Francisco Morales, the convent's syndic, accepted the obligation. The guarantee was temporary until Patricio de Orozco brought his wife, Bernarda Martínez, from Nicoya to formalize the obligation, which was cancelled for don Pedro González de León on December 9, 1741, due to a new guarantor.

Don Juan Gemmir y Lleonart, Lieutenant Colonel of Spanish Infantry and Governor and Captain General of this province, granted general power of attorney. The power was conferred upon Licenciado don Gregorio de Retana, a resident priest of Guatemala City, and to don Francisco Elias and don Félix Elias de Saldívar, also residents of Guatemala City.

Don Francisco Díaz de Molleda and his wife, doña Bárbara Rita Jiménez, sold a 50-year-old mulatta named Baltasara de León to Beneficiado don Juan José Camacho for $175. Doña Bárbara had inherited Baltasara from her father.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Sargento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad acted as guarantor for Nicolás Palacios for $158. This money belonged to the minors José Antonio and María Nicolasa Palacios, who were the children of the deceased Lucas Palacios and Catalina González, and grandchildren of Isabel Montero.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan Díaz de Herrera
Capitán don Manuel Díaz de Herrera
Sargento Mayor don José Lorenzo de Viera
Capitán don Tomás de Soto y Barahona
summary: Capitán don Juan Díaz de Herrera made his testament. He was the legitimate son of the deceased Capitán don Manuel Díaz de Herrera and doña Gertrudis Maroto, and was married to doña María Leonor de Viera, daughter of the deceased Sargento Mayor don José Lorenzo de Viera and doña Leonor Jiménez. Their daughter, María Leonarda, was named his sole heir, and Capitán don Tomás de Soto y Barahona and don Manuel José Gómez were appointed as executors.

people_involved: Beneficiado don José Miguel de Guzmán
summary: Beneficiado don José Miguel de Guzmán, the parish priest, leased a 1000-tree cacao plantation in the Matina valley to Alejo Calvo, a free mulatto, for three years. This hacienda had been ceded to Guzmán on October 30, 1738, by doña Francisca de Inza, a widow, due to overdue interest on a $500 chaplaincy principal charged against it. The previous lessee was Teniente Agustín de la Riva, and the rent was $25 per harvest or $50 annually.

people_involved: Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero
Alférez don Luis de Soto Mayor
summary: Alférez Baltasar de Moya, a free mulatto, obligated himself to Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero for $187 of cacao. He mortgaged a plantain plantation in the Ujarraz valley, which bordered the river to the east and Alférez don Luis de Soto Mayor's sugarcane and plantain hacienda to the west.

people_involved: Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero
summary: Juan Antonio Sáenz entered into a 5-year agreement to cultivate and maintain a 2500-tree cacao plantation in Matina owned by Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero. In exchange, Martínez Cubero granted Sáenz the use of a 900-tree cacao plantation along the Matina river for the same duration, allowing him to enjoy its products.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí
summary: Josefa de Alvarado, a free mestiza, secured a $100 loan at 5% interest, which was the principal of a chaplaincy established by doña Eugenia de Abarca Alatras. The funds were previously managed by Antonio de Umaña, and the chaplaincy's patron and chaplain is Licenciado don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí. Josefa de Alvarado used her house as collateral for this obligation.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan José de Cuende
summary: Teresa Fernández, widow of Agustín de la Riva, and Francisco de la Riva, acting as guarantor, committed to pay $150 in cacao to the Royal Treasury. This sum originated from the lease of the Las Lomas cacao hacienda in Matina, which the late doña Cayetana de Acosta had rented to Agustín de la Riva. The obligation was a result of the Royal Treasury's claim against doña Cayetana's heirs for outstanding debts, and it was later cancelled on August 14, 1742, by Capitán don Juan José de Cuende.

people_involved: Cura don José Miguel de Guzmán
summary: Manuela Josefa de Arleguí, a free parda and daughter of the late Victoria de Arleguí, made her testament on November 17. Among her possessions was an enslaved black woman named María de los Dolores, and she named Cura don José Miguel de Guzmán as her executor. However, on November 28 of the same year, she revoked this testament, having previously granted power to testament.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan Manuel de Alvarado y Jirón
Licenciado don Juan José de Solís y Miranda
summary: Capitán don Juan Manuel de Alvarado y Jirón and his wife, doña Juana María Custodio Galarza, committed to a $500 obligation at 5% interest for a chaplaincy established by Capitán Diego de Aguilar, whose chaplain is Licenciado don Juan José de Solís y Miranda. They received this sum from Francisco Carrillo and Petronila Cascante, who were previously obligated, in the form of a house on the city's outskirts, which now secures the $500 debt.

Martín Alvarez, a resident of Barba valley, requested the protocolization of land titles for a parcel by the Ciruelas river. He inherited this land from his deceased aunt, Petronila Alvarez, who in turn inherited it from her late father, Andrés Alvarez, Martín's grandfather. The protocolization was sought because doña Mariana Hidalgo and her son Pedro Jiménez were disputing Alvarez's ownership of the property.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz
Sargento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad
Licenciado don José Manuel García de Hergueta
Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno
summary: Sargento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz committed to a $200 obligation at 5% interest for a chaplaincy established by doña Rosa de Arburola, whose patron is Sargento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad. This obligation is secured by Sáenz's houses and lot, which are bordered by prominent residents including the Governor and Captain General. The census for this chaplaincy was previously the responsibility of doña Francisca de Ibarra.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Manuela Josefa de Arleguí, a single free mulata, had her testament granted by her attorney, Capitán don Juan de Ocampo Golfín, on December 2. Her possessions included a 5-year-old mulata girl named Luisa, and she also raised two boys, Dionisio and Manuel. Licenciado don Francisco de Ocampo was named as the executor and keeper of her goods, with doña Petronila de Hoces as the alternate.

Teresa Fernández, the widow of Teniente de Capitán Agustín de la Riva, committed to pay 69 pesos and 2 reales to each of her minor children, María Josefa, José Nicolás, Francisco Javier, and Francisco Antonio de la Riva. This payment represents their legitimate paternal inheritance.

Petronila de Aguilar, the widow of Teniente de Capitán Diego Mesa, committed to pay $125 and 5 reales to each of her minor children: Manuela Josefa, María Francisca, María Catalina, and Juan Vicente de Mesa. This payment represents their paternal inheritance.

Doña Úrsula Josefa López Conejo, widow of Capitán don José de Alvarado, committed to a $100 obligation at 5% interest for a chaplaincy established by don Pedro Ibáñez, whose patron and chaplain is Beneficiado don Manuel López Conejo, the Priest of Esparza. This obligation is secured by her cattle hacienda in Rincón de las Pavas, along with her houses and a mill in Tres Ríos, which are already burdened with a $625 census.

people_involved: Capitán don José de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Doña Úrsula Josefa López Conejo, widow of Capitán don José de Alvarado y Jirón, acknowledged a $187 census at 5% interest for a chaplaincy served by Beneficiado don Lorenzo de Quesada, the Priest of Barba valley. This obligation, previously held by her late husband, was imposed on the same property mentioned in the preceding entry, which includes her hacienda, houses, and mill.

people_involved: Licenciado don Juan Salvador de la Haya y Bolívar
summary: Doña Úrsula Josefa López Conejo acknowledged a $400 obligation at 5% interest for a chaplaincy founded by doña Cecilia Vázquez Coronado, with Beneficiado don Manuel López Conejo, the Priest of Esparza, as chaplain. This debt, originally her deceased husband's, was charged on the Las Pavas property. The obligation was later cancelled on November 4, 1744, by Licenciado don Juan Salvador de la Haya y Bolívar, after it was transferred to don Francisco Javier de Iglesias.

people_involved: Capitán don José de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Doña Úrsula Josefa López Conejo acknowledged a $57 obligation at 5% interest related to the guardianship of Cristóbal Duran. This debt was originally the responsibility of her late husband, Capitán don José de Alvarado y Jirón, and his brother, Capitán don Gil de Alvarado.

people_involved: Capitán don José de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Doña Úrsula Josefa López Conejo committed to pay $17 and 7 reales to each of her nine minor children: don Fermín, don Joaquín, doña Teresa, doña María Manuela, doña Gertrudis, doña Antonia, don José Francisco, don Vicente, and don José Antonio de Alvarado. This payment represents their legitimate paternal inheritance from their deceased father, Capitán don José de Alvarado y Jirón.

people_involved: don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro
summary: Doña Úrsula Josefa López Conejo acknowledged a $100 census at 5% interest, owed to don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro, the Maestre-escuela of the Cathedral of León in Nicaragua. This obligation was likely secured by her properties, as mentioned in previous entries.

people_involved: Don José Miguel de Arburola y Rivaren
summary: Ana Cardoso made a donation to Doña Josefa de Hoces Navarro for her son, Don José Miguel de Arburola y Rivaren. The donation was related to properties owned by Doña Josefa in the city, bordering properties of Sargento Mayor don José Morales and Capitán José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda.

people_involved: Don Luis Fernando de Liendo y Goicoechea
Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo
summary: Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo conferred general power of attorney to don Manuel Antonio del Bal, a resident of the city of Panamá. Don Luis Fernando de Liendo y Goicoechea, the Public Scribe, recorded this event.

people_involved: Capitán don José Marín de Laguna
Licenciado don José Manuel García de Argueta
Capitán don Juan Francisco Marín de Laguna
summary: The will of Doña María Marín de Laguna was recorded. She was the legitimate daughter of the deceased Capitán don José Marín de Laguna and Doña Catalina de Moya, and widowed first from Miguel de Acosta and then from Sargento Mayor don Bernardo Marín. She appointed her brother, Capitán don Juan Francisco Marín de Laguna, and Licenciado don José Manuel García de Argueta as executors, and established a chaplaincy for masses.

people_involved: Don Francisco de Saravia y Rueda
summary: Don Francisco de Saravia y Rueda committed to teaching four orphaned Spanish children in the city. He would be paid $25 of cacao by the Cabildo, following an ancient custom and royal decree for public schools, and outlined his teaching methods and religious duties, requesting a ban on private schools from the Governor.

people_involved: Gobernador y Capitán General don Juan Gemmir y Lleonart
Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo
Señor don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro
summary: Gobernador y Capitán General don Juan Gemmir y Lleonart, a Lieutenant Colonel of Spanish Infantry, granted general power of attorney to Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo and Señor don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo
Señor don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro
summary: Licenciado don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría, the Parish Priest, granted general power of attorney to Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo and Señor don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro.

people_involved: Licenciado don Manuel Gabriel de Mier Cevallos
Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo
Señor don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro
summary: Licenciado don Manuel Gabriel de Mier Cevallos, the Sacristan Mayor of the Parish, granted general power of attorney to Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo and Señor don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro.

people_involved: Licenciado don Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí y Hoces
Don Luis Fernando de Liendo y Goicoechea
summary: Doña Micaela de Bonilla obligated herself for $240 at 5% interest in favor of the chaplaincy founded by don Baltasar de Grados, currently served by Licenciado don Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí y Hoces. The obligation was secured on her houses, which bordered properties of Doña Josefa de Bonilla, Doña María Marín de Laguna, Doña Bernarda Martínez, and Don Luis Fernando de Liendo y Goicoechea.

people_involved: Licenciado don Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí y Hoces
summary: Doña María Teresa de Sandoval, a widow, obligated herself for $130 at 5% interest in silver coin to the chaplaincy founded by don Baltasar de Grados and served by Licenciado don Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí y Hoces. This obligation was secured on her adobe and tile houses, bordering properties of the deceased don Nicolás de Estrada, Doña Lorenza Muñoz Hidalgo, the Valerinos, the deceased Cayetano Jiménez, and Doña Tomasa Golfín.

people_involved: Doña Dominga de Guzmán y Echavarría
Licenciado don Juan José de Solís y Miranda
Doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
Capitán don Miguel de Alvarado y Jirón
Doña Luisa de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Capitán don Juan de Salvatierra and his wife, Doña Dominga de Guzmán y Echavarría, obligated themselves for $760 at 5% interest. The funds were distributed among the Cofradía de la Concepción, Convento de San Francisco, a chaplaincy founded by Antonio Machado (served by Licenciado don Juan José de Solís y Miranda), and Doña María Jerónima Guerrero. The obligation was secured on their adobe and tile houses, bordering properties of Doña Antonia de Acosta Arévalo, Don Francisco de Beiancourt, Doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral, heirs of Don Juan Fernández and Doña Cayetana de Acosta, and Capitán don Miguel de Alvarado y Jirón and Doña Luisa de Guzmán y Echavarría.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez Robredo
Capitán don Luis de Soto Mayor
Licenciado don Juan José de Solís y Miranda
summary: The obligations made by Capitán don Juan de Salvatierra and Doña Dominga de Guzmán y Echavarría on February 3, 1741, were cancelled. Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez Robredo (Síndico de San Francisco), Capitán don Luis de Soto Mayor (Mayordomo de la Concepción), and Hermano Rafael Delgado (attorney for Licenciado don Juan José de Solís) performed the cancellation because Licenciado don Manuel Sáenz had taken charge of the obligations.

people_involved: El Beneficiado don Juan José Camacho
Licenciado don Manuel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: El Beneficiado don Juan José Camacho obligated himself for $150 of cacao at 5% interest in favor of the chaplaincy founded by Pedro Solano, currently served by Licenciado don Manuel de Guzmán y Echavarría. The obligation was secured on a cacao plantation in the Matina valley, bordering former haciendas of Capitán don Gil de Alvarado and haciendas of Doña Antonia de Echavarría.

people_involved: Doña Juana de Ángulo y Quirós
Licenciado don Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí y Hoces
summary: Doña Juana de Ángulo y Quirós, a widow, obligated herself for $100 of cacao at 5% interest in favor of the chaplaincy founded by don Baltasar de Grados and served by Licenciado don Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí y Hoces. This was secured on her adobe house, bordering properties of Gregorio Brenes, Josefa de Bonilla, Juana de Umaña, and Gertrudis Ruiz.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamu-
summary: An incomplete entry records an obligation made by Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamu-.

people_involved: Licenciado don Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí y Hoces
summary: Doña Ana Efigenia de Estrada and her husband obligated themselves for $160 in cacao currency at 5% interest to a capellanía founded by don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín. The capellanía is currently owned and served by Licenciado don Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí y Hoces. This obligation is secured by cacao plantations in Valle de Barbilla, purchased on June 16, 1739, and bordering Gertrudis Ruiz la moza's property.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don José de Morales
doña María de la O. de Céspedes
summary: Sargento Mayor don José de Morales, a native of Santiago de Chile, made his will. He was married to doña María de la O. de Céspedes and had eight children, including three religious sons (Fray José Gregorio, Fray Antonio, Fray Juan), two secular sons (Justo Ventura, Nicolás), and three daughters (Beatriz, María Catarina, Ana Victoria). His daughter María Catarina married don Manuel Porcio, to whom she gave a mulata named Mónica, and his assets included a 14-year-old mulatilla named Ana Antonia.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan José de los Ríos
Teniente General don Pedro Fernández de los Ríos
doña Ana Manuela de Alvarado y Jirón
Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero
summary: Capitán don Juan José de los Ríos provided a dowry letter for his wife, doña Ana Manuela de Alvarado y Jirón, for 800 pesos, including 500 pesos from her first cousin, Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero. Don Juan José explained the delay in acknowledgment was due to an untimely marriage, as he had to travel to Tierra Firme shortly after returning from Pacaca.

people_involved: Teniente don José Miguel de Echavarría
summary: Teniente don José Miguel de Echavarría obligated himself to supply 2400 stakes of laurel, zapotillo cimarrón, and guatuso at the mouth of the Matina River for the construction of a fortress. Don José Miguel de Céspedes and don José Antonio de Bonilla acted as guarantors. This obligation was later canceled on June 14, 1742, by don Juan José de Cuende.

people_involved: Doña Juana de Alvarado y Jirón
don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda
don Félix José García de Argueta
summary: Doña Juana de Alvarado y Jirón founded a capellanía of recited masses in the Santa Iglesia Parroquial with a capital of 500 pesos of cacao, secured by a hacienda in Matina. Her son, don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda, was named the first patron, followed by her son-in-law, don Julián García de Argueta. Her grandson, don Félix José García de Argueta, was designated the first chaplain, with Licenciado don Manuel Sáenz serving as interim chaplain.

Francisca Serrano, widow of Juan Ramírez, sold wooden houses in the ejidos of Cartago to Diego de Meza for 250 pesos of cacao. As Diego de Meza had died, his widow, Petronila de Aguilar, accepted the deed as guardian of their children. María Serrano, Agustín Ramírez, and Catalina Ramírez also accepted the escritura.

people_involved: Licenciado Presbítero don José Manuel García de Argueta
summary: Francisco Carrillo, son of the deceased Manuel Carrillo and Catalina Córdoba, made his will. He was married to Petronila Cascante and had children: José Cayetano, Agustina (married to Manuel Sanabria), and Antonia. He named his son José Cayetano and Alférez Matías Trtrjos as executors and mandated funds for a capellanía, with Licenciado Presbítero don José Manuel García de Argueta as the first chaplain.

María Barquero, widow of Pedro Solano and of advanced age, donated several Creole, white mulatto slaves to her family. She gave María Antonia to her son Pedro Solano, Ana Santiago to her daughter Manuela Solano, and Manuela Josefa (with her three children) to her daughter Francisca Solano. She also donated a mulatillo to the children of her deceased daughter Juana Solano, and another mulatillo named Manuel to the children of her deceased son José Solano. She ordered the freedom of Juan (mulato) and Josefa Vicenta (mother of all the slaves) upon her death, and retained Silvestre to cover funeral expenses. Experts José Manuel de Segura and Juan Calderón appraised Manuel and Francisco at 200 pesos of cacao each.
Miguel Víquez declared possession of a white mulatillo named Francisco, which belonged to his four children from his first marriage with the deceased Juana Solano, by donation.

María Barquero made a donation, and a mulato named Manuel was sold to Pedro Carazo. Carazo assumed the debt for the three minor Víquez children (Elías, Miguel, Antonia) and paid the portion for the emancipated Andrés Víquez, after deductions for alcabala and escritura.
Captain Francisco Meoño took over the debt that Pedro Carazo had assumed in favor of the three minor Víquez children.

Pedro Solano and Teresa Várela petitioned the Teniente General, referring to a donation by María Barquero. They requested the sale of the mulato Manuel to provide clothing for the minor Solano children, who were in extreme destitution and unable to attend mass. The Teniente General approved, ordering the value to be given to Pedro Solano for three children and Teresa Várela for the other two.

Pedro Solano, Teresa Várela, Francisco Garro, José Garro, Jacinto Martínez, and Miguel Solano received 200 pesos in goods from Captain Pedro Parada. This payment was for a 'mulatillo blanco' named Manuel, which their grandmother María Barquero had donated to them.
The same individuals who received payment for the mulatillo Manuel formally transferred its ownership to Captain Pedro Parada, a resident of Panamá, for 200 pesos.
Doña Juana de Ángulo, a widow, sold a 19-year-old 'mulata blanca' named Petronila, who was born in her house, to Teniente Francisco de Segura for 150 pesos.
Petronila Cascante, widow of Francisco Carrillo, obligated herself to her legitimate daughter Antonia for 192 pesos and 2 reales from her inheritance.
José Manuel Chinchilla, husband of Antonia Josefa Carrillo, cancelled an obligation after Petronila Cascante, Antonia's mother, had died.
José Cayetano Carrillo, as the executor of his deceased father Francisco Carrillo, established a chaplaincy of 100 pesos as mandated in his father's will, which was dated April 19 of the same year.

Petronila Cascante and her son José Cayetano Carrillo declared that Francisco Carrillo had sold an adobe house with its plot to Captain Juan Manuel de Alvarado for 750 pesos. Carrillo and Petronila had originally bought the house as just walls from Licenciado José de Chaves, and Carrillo completed its construction.

Captain José Castán, a bachelor and sick, made his will. He was the legitimate son of Salvador Castán and Francisca Díaz from Los Pasajes, Guipúzcoa. He listed his possessions, debts, and named Pedro Carazo and José Antonio de Oriamuno as executors, and his mother as his heir, or his siblings Ignacio and Bernarda if she was deceased.

Captain Pedro de León obligated himself to the minor children of Juan Francisco Sáenz and the deceased Francisca Martínez (María, Tomás, Candelaria, Antonio Sáenz) for 225 pesos, which Juan Francisco Sáenz had given him in various goods. Juan Francisco Sáenz signed as father and tutor.
Juan Francisco Sáenz received 56 pesos 2 reales from Pedro González de León, representing the share for his son Tomás, who was by then deceased.

people_involved: Luis Fernando de Liendo y Goicoechea
summary: Captain Francisco Javier de Oriamuno and his wife Ana Efigenia de Estrada obligated themselves to the minor Leonida de Ocampo for 361 pesos 5 reales, received from Captain Luis Fernando de Liendo y Goicoechea, with the consent of Leonida's uncle and tutor, Captain Francisco Javier de Siles. They mortgaged a cleared land in Barbilla.
Captain Benito de Alvarado y Jirón cancelled the obligation made by Francisco Javier de Oriamuno and Ana Efigenia de Estrada to Leonida de Ocampo.
Don Joaquín de Beregañea, an Alférez for the company garrisoning the fort at the Matina river mouth, was arrested by order of the Gobernador and held in the house of Dr. Francisco Lafons in Cartago.

Gobernador Juan Gemmir y Lleonart, currently imprisoned, was granted permission to take nine baths under bail. Captain José Miguel de Céspedes acted as his guarantor, obligating Gemmir y Lleonart to return to prison afterward.

On August 23, Doña Mariana López de la Flor leased a cacao plantation in Matina, consisting of 1900 fruit trees, to Don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno for one year at 275 pesos. The property was encumbered by a 2000-peso chaplaincy established by Mariana's sister, Doña Baltasara López de la Flor, with Licenciado Presbítero Don José Vicente de Morales serving as its Chaplain.
On August 29, Miguel Zamora, a widower, formally committed to paying his daughter, María del Carmen Zamora, 175 pesos. This sum represented her inheritance from her deceased mother, Juana de Quesada.

On September 1, Doña Angela Sáenz, a widow, attempted to lease a cacao plantation in Matina, with approximately 1900 fruit trees, to Capitán Don José Manuel Jiménez for three years at an annual rent of 125 pesos. However, this agreement was not finalized.

On September 2, Doña Antonia de Echavarría, a widow, leased two cacao plantations in Matina, including 'La Ibarrita,' to José de Arce for three years. The rent was 200 pesos, with a reduced payment of 100 pesos for the first year due to the plantations being overgrown. Her son, Beneficiado Don José de Guzmán y Echavarría, the Cura rector of Cartago, signed the agreement for her.

people_involved: María Elena López de la Flor
summary: On October 14, Doña María Elena López de la Flor sold a 9-year-old mulatto boy named José Nicolás to Presbítero Licenciado Don Gregorio López del Corral for 200 pesos. José Nicolás was the son of Manuela Josefa de la Flor, an enslaved woman belonging to María Elena, who had acquired Manuela Josefa through a trade with Don Diego de la Haya.

people_involved: José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Capitán Don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda and his wife, Doña Baltasara de la Madriz Linares, took on a 900-peso cacao obligation tied to their house, which had previously belonged to Presbítero Don Diego de Campos de Quirós. The debt included 600 pesos for chaplaincies founded by Vasco Solano and Pedro Solano, managed by Capitán Don José Cevallos, and eventually transferred to Presbítero Licenciado Don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero. The remaining 300 pesos were owed to various confraternities and a foundation by Don Manuel Gómez de Lara, with one 100-peso debt being cancelled in 1750.

people_involved: José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: On October 21, Sargento Mayor Don Francisco de la Madriz Linares, originally from Llanes, Asturias, and son of deceased parents, granted power to his current wife, Doña Rita García de Argueta, to execute his will. He also designated his brother-in-law, Licenciado Don José Manuel García de Argueta, and Cura Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría as alternate executors. He was previously married to Doña Manuela de Quirós, with whom he had a son, Don Dionisio de la Madriz Linares.

people_involved: Luis Fernando de Liendo y Goicoechea
summary: Don Luis Fernando de Liendo y Goicoechea, a public scribe, granted power of attorney to Don José de Luna y Estrada, a resident of Guatemala.

On October 29, Doña Petronila Valerino, a widow, leased a cacao plantation in Matina to Beneficiado Don Juan José Camacho, the Cura of Matina, for three years at 450 pesos. However, this deed was later rescinded on October 30, 1742.
On October 30, Beneficiado Don Juan José Camacho granted general power of attorney to Don Nicolás Alvarez.

On November 32, Alférez Juan Masís's will was recorded, detailing his family and assets. He was married to Doña María Fernández de Acosta, with whom he had eight children, and also had a natural son named Juan. His estate included livestock, a cacao hacienda in Barbilla, and three enslaved individuals: Juan Ventura, José, and María de la Cruz. His daughter Juana María was married to Ventura Cayetano Lumbides, and his executors were his wife and Sargento Mayor Don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo.

people_involved: Juan José de la Madriz Linares
Ana Rita de la Madriz Linares
María Águeda de la Madriz Linares
María Josefa de la Madriz Linares
summary: On November 15, the will of Sargento Mayor Don Francisco de la Madriz Linares was executed by his attorneys, following his death on October 22. The will detailed his two marriages: first to Doña Manuela de Quirós, with whom he had a son, Dionisio; and second to Doña Rita García de Argueta, with whom he had nine children. His estate included a ranch, a cacao plantation in Barbilla, and five enslaved individuals. His daughters Francisca and Baltasara were married to Capitán Don Juan Nicolás Viveros (deceased) and Capitán Don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda, respectively.

On December 9, Alférez Patricio de Orozco, a resident of Nicoya, declared that on October 15, 1740, he formally acknowledged a debt of 464 pesos 5 reales to the Convento de Curriravá. This debt was associated with a chaplaincy founded by Doña Antonia López de la Flor, and Don Pedro González de León served as his guarantor.

An unnamed person, unable to fulfill a solidary obligation, presented Capitán Francisco de Morales as a new guarantor to de León. Morales, a resident of the Aserrí valley, mortgaged a house, sugar mill, and cane fields in the valley for security.

people_involved: Don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad
Licenciado Presbítero Don Antonio Raimundo de Estrada
summary: Don Pedro José Sáenz obligated himself for 200 pesos to a chaplaincy founded by Doña Rosa de Arburola, with Don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad as patron and Licenciado Presbítero Don Antonio Raimundo de Estrada as interim chaplain. Due to illness and financial difficulties, Sáenz agreed with his sister Doña Manuela de Sáenz and her son Don Andrés de Bonilla to take over his mortgaged house in Cartago and assume the debt.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco
Padre guardián del Convento de San Francisco
summary: Sargento Mayor Don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco, acting as the testamentary executor for his brother Capitán Don Antonio Salmón Pacheco, founded a chaplaincy. The chaplaincy was endowed with 845 pesos in cacao, secured by a cattle ranch near Cartago, and Don Dionisio would serve as patron, with the Father Guardian of the San Francisco Convent as interim chaplain.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Pedro José Sáenz
Capitán Don Francisco Javier de Oriainuno
Licenciado Don José Manuel García de Hergueta
Sargento Mayor Don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad
Licenciado Don Antonio Raimundo de Estrada
summary: Sargento Mayor Don Pedro José Sáenz transferred his house in Cartago to his sister Doña Manuela Sáenz and her son Don Andrés de Bonilla for 330 pesos. The payment included 200 pesos for the chaplaincy founded by Doña Rosa de Arburola, 76 pesos for Comisario Don Manuel González Coronel, and 54 pesos in cacao or local produce for Sáenz.
Licenciado Manuel José González Coronel, Comisario de la Inquisición, canceled the obligation for 76 pesos.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Pedro José Sáenz
summary: Sargento Mayor Don Pedro José Sáenz canceled the obligation for 54 pesos.

Licenciado Don Antonio de Guevara, a Cleric Presbyter, sold a 12-13 year old 'mulatillo blanco' named Juan José to Capitán Don Gaspar Arias, a resident of the Barba valleys, for 175 pesos in silver. Guevara had acquired Juan José by purchase from Capitán Don Cristóbal Jiménez.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo
Doctor Don Diego Suárez de Figueroa
summary: Sargento Mayor Don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo granted general power of attorney to Doctor Don Diego Suárez de Figueroa and Don Juan de Escudero, who reside in Madrid.

Alférez José Antonio de Jesús, son of Sargento Lucas de Jesús and Gregoria Várela, made his will. He was married to María de Quirós, daughter of José de Quirós Abado and Teresa Mora, and named his four children as heirs, with his father and brother Pablo de Jesús as executors.

people_involved: Capitán Don Gil de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Don Juan Fernández and Don Bruno de Arenal, as principals, and Capitán Don Gil de Alvarado y Jirón and his wife Doña Josefa González del Camino, as guarantors, obligated themselves for 291 pesos, 6 reales, and 1/2 real to Don José, Don Manuel, and Don Nicolás de Castro, representing their maternal inheritance. Doña Antonia Josefa, another minor, had already received her share upon marrying Teniente José Nicolás de Zamora.

Don Bruno de Arenal, acting for himself and Don Juan Fernández, stated that Capitán Isidro de Castro as principal and Capitán Marcelo de Morales as guarantor had obligated themselves to the minors, thereby canceling the previous escritura.

people_involved: Alférez Don Luis de Soto Mayor
Beneficiado Don Juan Antonio de Moya
summary: Doña Polonia de Moya, a widow, leased a cacao plantation with 1500 trees in the Matina valley to Alférez Don Luis de Soto Mayor for three years, at a rate of 150 pesos in cacao per year. She had inherited the plantation upon the death of her brother, Beneficiado Don Juan Antonio de Moya.

María de Sibaja leased a productive cacao plantation to Capitán Don José Jinesta for three years, at a rate of 125 pesos in cacao per year. María had acquired the plantation upon the death of her mother, Francisca de Sibaja.

people_involved: Capitán Don José de Mier Cevallos
Maestro Don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro
Don Manuel Gabriel de Mier Cevallos
summary: Capitán Don José de Mier Cevallos granted power of attorney to Maestro Don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro, Archdeacon of the Cathedral of León (Nicaragua), to claim what was owed from the Royal Treasury. This claim was for the time his legitimate son, the deceased Don Manuel Gabriel de Mier Cevallos, served as Sacristán Mayor until September 15, 1741.

María de Quirós, widow of Alférez José Antonio de Jesús, obligated herself for 473 pesos in cacao to her four minor children (Luis, Magdalena, María Francisca, and Juana Josefa de Jesús) as their paternal inheritance. Pablo de Jesús acted as guarantor for this obligation.

Pablo de Jesús obligated himself for 50 pesos to Francisco Javier de Rojas, the legitimate son of Francisco de Rojas and Josefa de Astorga, as his inheritance from them, which had been under the care of the deceased José Antonio de Jesús. Pablo de Jesús also committed to keeping the minor for ten years, teaching him carpentry, and providing him with tools after this period.

Doña María Fernández, widow of Alférez Juan Masís, obligated herself for 880 pesos in cacao to the chaplaincy instituted by Miguel Masís, and for 550 pesos in cacao to the chaplaincy founded by Sargento Juan Masís, her deceased husband's father. Both obligations were charged to a cacao plantation in the Barbilla valley that she had inherited.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo
summary: Sargento Mayor Don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo, General Syndic of the San Francisco Convent, canceled the 550 pesos obligation, which Simón Cásasela had taken over.
Manuel Sáenz cancelled a debt of $880, which Simón Casasola, a free pardo, had taken responsibility for.

María Fernández, widow of Alférez Juan Masís, along with José Antonio Masís and Ventura Lumbides as guarantors, committed to pay $625 and 7 reales from the paternal inheritance to Gabriel, Miguel, María Catarina, Rita Josefa, Antonia Josefa, and María Francisca Masís, who are the six legitimate children and heirs of María Fernández and her deceased husband.
María de Quirós, a widow, sold an enslaved Black woman named Catarina, who appeared to be 50 years old, to Alférez Manuel Felipe de Alarcón for $150 in cacao.

Francisco de Oviedo and his wife Francisca Solano owed $100 in silver to the Convent of San Francisco in this city. This debt, originally held by the deceased Alférez Francisco Solano and his wife Juana de las Alas, was secured by three caballerías of land in the highlands of Ujarraz, now belonging to the current debtors. The $100 was part of a chaplaincy founded by Luisa Hernández.

Captain Miguel de Ibarra and María Teresa de Sandoval sold a house with a plantain grove and wooden fences, located in the common lands of this city, to Beneficiado Juan José Camacho, the priest of Matina valley, for $525. María Teresa de Sandoval had acquired the property from Sargento Mayor Francisco Manzano and Francisca Barquero, who were heirs of Alférez Francisco Barquero.

Captain Francisco Javier de Iglesias and his wife Francisca Javiera Fernández Castellanos committed to pay $400 in silver at 5% interest to Úrsula Josefa López Conejo. This money belonged to a chaplaincy founded by Cecilia Vázquez Coronado, for which Beneficiado Manuel López Conejo, the priest of Esparza, was the chaplain. The obligation was secured by their houses in this city, which were bordered by properties of Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina, María Sibaja, and Francisca de Arburola.

people_involved: Juan Salvador de la Haya y Bolívar
summary: On November 4, 1744, Joaquín de Alvarado stated that the previous obligation was cancelled because Francisco Javier de Iglesias had made a new commitment to the chaplaincy of Cecilia Vázquez Coronado. At this time, Licenciado Juan Salvador de la Haya y Bolívar was the patron and chaplain of the chaplaincy, a role previously held by his mother.

Captain Francisco Javier de Iglesias and his wife Francisca Javiera Fernández Castellanos committed to pay $187 in silver at 5% interest to a chaplaincy founded by Pedro Ibáñez. The chaplaincy's chaplain was Beneficiado Lorenzo de Quesada, the priest of Barba valley, and its patron was Captain Francisco de Flores. This sum was previously charged to the Las Pavas estate by Úrsula Josefa López Conejo, widow of Captain José de Alvarado, from whom Iglesias and Castellanos received the funds.

Lieutenant Cristóbal de Quesada and his wife María Josefa Ramírez, as principals, and Antonia Ramírez as guarantor, committed to pay $1037 and 4 reales in cacao at 5% interest to Nicolás, María Lorenza, Sebastián, Gregoria, and José Simón de Quesada. These minors were the children of the deceased Lieutenant Sebastián de Quesada and Francisca de Mesa, and the money was their inheritance. They mortgaged their house in the common lands of this city.

On July 9, 1744, Lieutenant Juan de Mesa, attorney for the minors, cancelled the obligation due to a new commitment made by Lieutenant Cristóbal de Quesada. Cristóbal de Quesada stated that the minors were his nephews and nieces.

Captain Miguel de Alvarado y Jirón donated one hundred head of cattle and twenty-five breeding mares, located in Miravalles, jurisdiction of Esparza, to his son, Miguel de Alvarado. Miguel de Alvarado, who was 24 years old at the time, was also the son of the deceased María de Torres.

Captain Isidro de Castro, as principal, and Captain Marcelo de Morales, as guarantor, both residents of Curriravá valley, committed to pay $875, 4 reales, and one cuartillo in cacao currency at 5% interest to José, Manuel, and Nicolás de Castro. These minors were the children of Isidro de Castro and the deceased Antonia de Quirós, and the money was their inheritance.

Cayetano Badilla and his wife María Isabel de Quesada, residents of Ujarraz, committed to pay $207 and 4 reales at 5% interest to José Simón de Quesada, the minor son of the deceased Lieutenant Sebastián de Quesada and Francisca de Mesa. This sum was previously owed by Lieutenant Cristóbal de Quesada, from whom Badilla and Quesada received it.
On September 1, 1750, Lieutenant Francisco de la Riva stated that he and his wife María de Acuña had taken over this obligation, thereby cancelling the debt for Badilla.

people_involved: María de la Rosa y Sojo
summary: María de la Rosa y Sojo, widow of Alférez Gregorio de Mesa, and Lieutenant Juan de Mesa, residents of Ujarraz valley, committed to pay 622 pesos and 4 reales in cacao at 5% interest to María Lorenza, Gregoria, and Sebastián de Quesada. These minors were the children of the deceased Lieutenant Sebastián de Quesada and Francisca de Mesa. The obligation was previously held by Lieutenant Cristóbal de Quesada, from whom they received it.

On September 20, 1751, Captain Tomás de la Madrid, executor of the deceased Lieutenant Juan de Mesa, along with Francisco Chaves and Agustín Pérez (husbands of María Lorenza and Gregoria de Quesada, respectively), and Sebastián de Quesada, cancelled the obligation.

Nicolás de Quesada, as principal, and Brother Manuel Felipe de Alarcón, as guarantor, received $207 and 4 reales in cacao currency from Cristóbal de Quesada. This money, held by Cristóbal de Quesada as pupillary usury, belonged to Nicolás de Quesada as inheritance from his deceased father, Lieutenant Sebastián de Quesada, and he could dispose of it upon marriage or legal emancipation.

Luisa Calvo, the legitimate daughter of the deceased Captain Tomás Calvo and Eugenia de Abarca, made her will. She was the widow of José Maroto, with whom she had several daughters, including María Magdalena Maroto, and she ensured all her daughters were married. She also raised her granddaughters Juana de Miranda (from 6 months old) and Manuela de Baeza (from a young age), and mentioned her great-grandson Pablo de García.

Felipe de Umaña and his wife María Francisca Fernández committed to pay $200 in cacao at 5% interest to Bernabé de Ugalde, the minor son of the deceased Captain Juan de Ugalde. They received this money from Captain Pedro de Ugalde, a resident of Barba. They mortgaged 600 fruit-bearing cacao trees in the Matina valley, bordering properties of the deceased Sargento Mayor Pedro de Alvarado and Sargento Pascual Salguero.
Josefa Nicolasa de Guevara sold an unspecified item to Captain Miguel de Alvarado y Jirón.
A 25-year-old mulatto slave named José Cayetano, son of Isabel Ramona (also a slave), was sold for $250 silver and $50 cacao.

Capitán Francisco Meoño obligated himself for $142 and 4 reales of cacao at 5% interest to Miguel, Luis, and Antonia Víquez, minor children of the deceased Miguel Víquez and Juana Solano. The debt was under the charge of Sargento Mayor don Pedro Carazo, and a house in the city's ejidos was mortgaged.

On November 12, 1753, Nicolás de Acuña, as husband of Antonia Víquez, and Luis Víquez, on his own behalf, cancelled the obligation. They declared that their father, Miguel Víquez, had received Miguel's share as his legitimate heir before his death.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz
summary: Ayudante José de las Alas, son of the deceased Diego Santiago de las Alas and María Madrigal, made a codicil. His will was granted on December 2, 1734, before Sargento Mayor don Pedro José Sáenz. He declared no descendant heirs and named Capitán don Alfonso de Ulloa and Manuel de Alvarado as executors.

Doña Juana de Ángulo, a widow, sold her mulatto slave named Juan Manuel, who was born and raised in her house and was the son of her slave María Morales, to Capitán don Martín de Garayar, a resident of the Barba valley. The price was $200, half silver and half cacao.

people_involved: Señor Maestro don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro
summary: Don Juan Gemmir y Lleonart, Lieutenant Colonel of Spanish Infantry and Governor and Captain General of the province, granted general power of attorney to Señor Maestro don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro, Archdeacon of León Cathedral, to collect his salary from the Royal Coffers of León.

people_involved: Alférez don Luis de Soto Mayor
summary: Alférez don Luis de Soto Mayor sold a plot of land next to the San Francisco Convent to doña Francisca Pacheco for $25 cacao. The plot bordered properties of doña Josefa Sáenz, Dionisia Calderón, Francisca de Mora, and the Romeros, and Luis de Soto Mayor had purchased it from Capitán José Manuel Jiménez.

Doña Sebastiana de Quirós, widow of Diego de Quesada, sold a cacao plantation in the Matina valley to don Francisco Lafon Bidor, a surgeon. The plantation bordered properties of doña Petronila Valerín and doña Micaela de Bonilla, the river, and the mountain. The price was $600 cacao, with $446 remaining to be received.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo
summary: On September 3, 1746, Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo, as executor for the deceased don Francisco Lafon Bidor and doña María Leonor de Miranda, and don José Antonio de Bonilla, as tutor for their minor son, cancelled the debt related to the cacao plantation sale.
Teresa Fernández, widow of Teniente Agustín de la Riva, obligated herself for $125 cacao to Teniente Francisco de la Riva.

people_involved: Doña María Ana López de la Flor
summary: Doña María Ana López de la Flor leased a cacao plantation with 1900 fruit-bearing trees in Matina to Alférez Miguel Quirós for two years at $275 cacao. The plantation bordered properties of Capitán Francisco Gamboa and doña Antonia de Echavarría, the mountain, and the river.

people_involved: Doña Antonia de la Granda y Balvín
Capitán don Tomás de la Madriz
summary: Doña Antonia de la Granda y Balvín, with her husband Capitán don Tomás de la Madriz's permission, made an inter vivos donation to him of two mulatto slaves: Francisco Justo (3 years old) and Isidro de la Paz (2 years old), both sons of her slave María Josefa de Alvarado.

people_involved: Licenciado don Manuel García de Ergueta
summary: Tomasa de Quirós, legitimate daughter of the deceased García de Quirós and Josefa Machado, and widow of Capitán Tomás de Chaves, made her will. She named her adopted daughter Ana María de Quirós as her heir and granted freedom to her mulatto slave Dionisia upon Ana María's marriage. Licenciado don Manuel García de Ergueta was named executor.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo
summary: Capitán don Cristóbal José Obando granted general power of attorney, first to Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo and second to don Diego Morras.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco
Beneficiado don José Miguel de Guzmán
summary: Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco sold a 30-year-old mulatto slave named Ramón Poveda to Beneficiado don José Miguel de Guzmán, the parish priest. Dionisio had acquired Ramón from the estate of his deceased brother, Capitán don Antonio Salmón Pacheco. The price was $300 silver.

Capitán don Cayetano de Alvarado and his wife doña Juana de Guevara obligated themselves for $250 cacao at 5% interest to doña Ángela Sáenz, a widow. They mortgaged a cacao plantation clearing in Matina, at a place called La Puentezuela.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo
Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco
summary: Capitán don Cristóbal José Obando granted general power of attorney, first to Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo and second to don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco.

people_involved: Don Manuel de Ayala y Escobar
summary: Don Juan Gemmir y Lleonart, Governor and Captain General and Lieutenant Colonel of the European armies, granted power of attorney, first to don Manuel de Ayala y Escobar, Secretary of the President of Panama, and second to don Martín de Achurra, a resident of Panama, for specific matters detailed in a letter sent with don Bartolomé de León.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco
Sargento Mayor don Julián García de Ergueta
summary: Doña Manuela Sáenz, a widow, leased a fruit-bearing cacao plantation in the Matina valley to Guillermo Serec for three years at $200 cacao. The plantation bordered properties of Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco and Sargento Mayor don Julián García de Ergueta, the river, and the mountain.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: José Matías de Chavarría obligated himself for $58 cacao at 5% interest to Tomasa de los Santos, minor daughter of the deceased Mateo de los Santos. The debt was previously under the charge of the deceased José de las Alas. Chavarría mortgaged 62 fruit-bearing cacao trees in Matina, which he had purchased from Sargento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don José Antonio de Oriamuno
summary: Sargento Mayor don José Antonio de Oriamuno and his wife doña María Catarina de Ibarra obligated themselves to the Royal Treasury for $500 cacao, which was the amount for which something was auctioned.
Captain Juan José de Cuende, Lieutenant of Royal Treasury Officials, cancelled the position of Provincial Mayor and City Councilman. This position was for 5 years at an annual salary of $100.

Rosa Falcon, legitimate daughter of the deceased José Falcon and Ana Romero, and widow of Alférez Antonio Segura, made her will. Her children included Félix, María Efigenia (married to Lieutenant Gregorio de Brenes), Ana María (married to the deceased Francisco Castillo), and Pedro Manuel. Captain Tomás Cubero was named her executor.

Domingo de Araya, a principal, and his son José de Araya, acting as guarantor, committed to pay $75 in cacao to Isabel Sánchez. Isabel was a minor daughter left orphaned by the death of Carlos Sánchez.

Pedro Solano, a resident of Ujarraz valley and executor for his deceased mother María Barquero, sold a 20-year-old mulato named Silvestre Solano to Licenciado Antonio de Soto y Barahona, a Presbyter Cleric, for $200 in cacao.

Doña Petronila de Hoces Navarro, widow, stated that upon the death of her son, Licenciado Antonio de Soto y Barahona, she inherited the mulato Silvestre Solano. Her son had instructed her to grant Silvestre his freedom after 5 years, which she was now executing.

Pedro Manuel Segura committed to pay $84 and 6 reales in cacao within one year. He was to pay $42 and 3 reales to Lieutenant Gregorio de Brenes and the remaining $42 and 3 reales to Miguel de la Cruz.
Captain José Lebrón granted general power of attorney. The primary recipient was Captain Diego Morras, and the secondary recipient was Licenciado Manuel José González Coronel.

Antonio de Torres committed to pay $58 in cacao for the guardianship of Juan José de los Santos, a guardianship previously held by the deceased José de las Salas. He mortgaged a cacao plantation of 400 trees in the Barbilla valley as security.
Doña Sebastiana de Quirós, a widow, granted power to José Felipe Jiménez to collect $446 in cacao from Don Francisco Lafon.

Captain José de Mier Cevallos, as Procurator General of the city, sold two 100-vara square plots of land at the city's edge, in an area called El Pedregal, to María de Quirós for $20. The plots bordered lands of Petronila de Aguilar, Damián Casasola, and Elvira Duran.

people_involved: Padre guardián del Convento de San Francisco
summary: Captain Alfonso de Ulloa and Lieutenant Manuel Antonio de Alvarado, as executors for the deceased spouses José de las Alas and Sebastiana Barbosa, founded a chaplaincy. It was endowed with $600 in cacao at 5% interest, secured by the deceased couple's former home. Manuel Antonio de Alvarado was named the primary patron, and Captain José Antonio de Acosta the secondary.

Lieutenant Manuel Antonio de Alvarado, patron of the chaplaincy founded by José de las Alas, sold a house and associated property to Captain Alfonso de Ulloa for $700 in cacao and $100 in silver. The property was burdened with various chaplaincy and confraternity debts, including one served by Licenciado Francisco José de Ocampo Golfín.

Captain Francisco Javier de Oriamuno and his wife, Doña Ana Efigenia García de Estrada, committed to pay $500 at 5% interest for a chaplaincy benefiting the Convent of San Francisco. This chaplaincy was founded by the deceased father of the also deceased Captain Lieutenant Francisco Gutiérrez. These funds were previously managed by Gertrudis de Hinojosa and secured by a cacao plantation in Barbilla valley.

Captain Alfonso Manuel de Ulloa, who acquired the house and property associated with José de las Alas's chaplaincy, committed to pay various debts. These included $100 in silver for the chaplaincy served by Licenciado Francisco José de Ocampo Golfín, $100 in cacao for the Confraternity of Vera Cruz, and $600 in cacao for the chaplaincy of the deceased José de las Alas.

Gertrudis Ruiz, a widow, sold an adobe house with a cedar roof and its plot to Licenciado José Francisco de Moya, a Presbyter Cleric, for $500 in cacao. The property bordered those of Micaela Alegría, Sergeant Major Juan Rodríguez de Robredo, Doña Juana de Ángulo, and Doña Angela de Guevara.
Licenciado José Francisco de Moya committed to pay $100 in cacao to Captain José Manuel Segura.

Doña Rita García de Ergueta, widow of Sergeant Major Francisco de la Madriz Linares, transferred a house and associated property, including a sugar mill, tools, oxen, and a mulato named Manuel García (over 60 years old), to General Francisco Javier de Siles. The property, valued at $600 in cacao, was tied to a chaplaincy founded by Antonio González. Francisco Javier de Siles and his wife, Doña Eugenia de Bastarrica, jointly committed to pay the $600 at 5% interest for the chaplaincy.
Licenciado Francisco de Moya, a Presbyter Cleric, committed to pay $250, with $100 designated for a chaplaincy he was instructed to found.

A financial obligation of $250, previously charged on Doña Angela Sáenz's rural property, was transferred to a house she purchased from Gertrudis Ruiz. This transaction is related to a capellanía founded by Captain Pedro de Moya, of which Doña Rafaela de Alvarado is a beneficiary and Ayudante General José Antonio de Bonilla is the patron.

people_involved: José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Licenciado Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero obligated himself for $561 and 4 reales of cacao (at 5% interest) for the materials and four plots of the hermitage of San Juan Evangelista, which were auctioned to him by Beneficiado José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría, the parish priest.

Captain José Manuel Segura obligated himself for $100 of cacao (at 5% interest) to the minor children of the deceased Salvador del Castillo and Josefa de Aguilar: Juan, Gertrudis, Joaquín, Francisco Javier, and Rodulfa del Castillo.
Manuel de Sanabria issued a dowry receipt for $252 of cacao to his wife, Agustina Carrillo, who is the legitimate daughter of the deceased Francisco Carrillo and Petronila Cascante.

locations: Fuerte de San Fernando de la boca del río de Matina
