summary: Captain and Warden José de Sierra, acting for himself and on behalf of Lieutenant Joaquín de Beregañea and Alférez José Velazco (all from the San Fernando fort company), granted general power of attorney to Captain Francisco de la Pfistora, specifically for collecting their salaries.
Licenciado José Francisco de Moya, a Presbyter Cleric, granted general power of attorney to Alférez Luis de Soto Moyor.

Captain Antonio Elias de Arleguí, Lieutenant General and Political Judge, apprenticed Nicolás de Villalobos, an 11-year-old boy and legitimate son of the deceased Francisco de Villalobos and Catalina Siciliana, to master carpenter Alférez Andrés Barquero for six years.

María Calderón, a widow, sold a plot of land in Agua Caliente to Sergeant Major Dionisio Salmón Pacheco for $100 of cacao. The land bordered properties formerly belonging to the deceased Juan González and Captain Antonio Salmón Pacheco.

Alférez Matías Jiménez obligated himself for $116 of cacao (at 5% interest) to Bernabé Antonio de Ugalde, a minor son of the deceased Juan de Ugalde and María de la Rosa Rodríguez. Jiménez received the sum from Captain Pedro de Ugalde, the minor's guardian, and mortgaged a cacao plantation in the Matina valley.

Sergeant Major José Antonio de Oriamuno, as Steward of the Confraternity of Nuestra Señora de los Angeles, granted power of attorney to Salvador de Zavala, a ship owner, to collect $4000 from Francisco Suárez, residing in Mexico City. This sum was a donation Suárez made to the image of Nuestra Señora de los Angeles.

Captain Esteban Ruiz de Mendoza and his wife, Doña Ana de Arleguí, obligated themselves for $150 of cacao (at 5% interest) to a capellanía founded by Captain Tomás de Chaves. They secured this with a cacao plantation in the Matina valley, having received the sum from Captain Juan de Ocampo Golfín.

people_involved: José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Doña Lorenza de Arburola Iribaren, widow of Captain Antonio de Ángulo, transferred a cacao plantation named 'Las Viejas' in the Matina valley to José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría. The plantation was burdened with $940 in annuities from various capellanías and the Cofradía del Rosario, which Guzmán y Echavarría accepted.

people_involved: Juan José Fernández de los Ríos
summary: Licenciado Hermenegildo de Arleguí, a Presbyter Cleric, sold a 30-year-old Creole mulatta slave named Josefa Nicolasa to Captain Juan José Fernández de los Ríos, a resident of Santiago de Alanje, Tierra Firme, for $300 in silver. Arleguí had previously purchased her from Captain Miguel de los Reyes.

Antonio de Torres, natural son of the deceased Gaspar de Torres and Margarita de Rojas, made his will. He was married to Manuela Josefa Cartín, legitimate daughter of Tomás Delgado and Micaela de Cerdas, with whom he had a two-year-old daughter, María Josefa Torres. His executors were Lieutenant Francisco de la Riva and Simón Cásasela.

locations: Iglesia de Nuestra Señora de la Soledad
people_involved: Juan Manuel de Cásasela y Córdoba
summary: María and Juana Calderón, sisters and widows, sold a plot of land to Licenciado Juan Manuel de Cásasela y Córdoba for $50 of cacao. The land bordered a street, the house of Doña Ana de Escalante Paniagua, and the Church of Nuestra Señora de la Soledad.

locations: Fuerte de San Fernando de la boca del río de Matina
summary: Licenciado José Francisco de Moya, Royal Chaplain of the San Fernando fort and legitimate son of Captain Francisco de..., made his will.

people_involved: José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Beneficiado José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría nullified the obligation made by Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero regarding the materials of the hermitage of San Juan Evangelista. This was due to an order from the Dean and Cabildo of the vacant See of the Bishopric, which mandated the materials be used for the parish church's construction.

people_involved: José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría (Cura), José Francisco de Alvarado (Teniente de Cura), and Captain José Nicolás de Bonilla (Steward of the Cofradía del Rosario) cancelled the obligation related to the 'Las Viejas' plantation. This cancellation occurred because Juan de Montalván and his wife, María Efigenia Ángulo, had taken over the obligation.

people_involved: Capitán don Luis de Soto Mayor
summary: An unnamed Royal Chaplain of the fort had an estate that included salary owed. His will ordered a capellanía, for which Capitán don Luis de Soto Mayor was named as the patron and executor. The deceased Moya and Manuela de Alvarado are mentioned in relation to the estate.

people_involved: Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos
Sargento Mayor don José de Morales
summary: Antonio de Azofeifa and doña Juana Manuela de Hidalgo sold a tiled house in Barba to Capitán Benito Barrantes. They then transferred a $100 cacao obligation (5% interest), previously redeemed by Sargento Mayor don José de Morales from Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos, to a new house they were building on a plot bought from José Calderón, next to doña Antonia de Alvarado's property.

Capitán don Alfonso de Ulloa and doña Francisca Díaz de Herrera sold a 12-13 year old mulatilla named Francisca Lorenza, born and raised in their house, to Andrés de Villalobos, who was acting on behalf of Capitán Francisco Fernández de Silva, for $275 plata.

people_involved: doña Jerónima de la Riva Agüero
summary: Doña Antonia de Zamora sold a tiled house and a 50-vara plot of land, which she inherited from her mother doña Jerónima de la Riva Agüero, to Capitán don Miguel Antonio Fajardo for $425 cacao.

people_involved: doña Jerónima de la Riva Agüero
don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Doña Antonia de Zamora, single and daughter of the deceased Capitán Diego Zamora and doña Jerónima de la Riva Agüero, made her will. She named don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría as her executor and María and Pablo Zamora, children she raised, as her heirs.

people_involved: Beneficiado don José Antonio Díaz de Herrera Garbanzo
summary: José Bernardo Fernández sold his inherited share of a cacao hacienda in Valle de Malina to his brother-in-law, Felipe de Umaña, for $60 cacao. The hacienda, inherited from his deceased mother Sebastiana Chinchilla, carried a $300 obligation for a capellanía founded by doña Gertrudis de Alvarado.

people_involved: doña Josefa López de la Flor
summary: Capitán don Miguel Antonio Fajardo sold a straw house and kitchen on a 50-vara plot to Capitán don José de Quesada for $175 cacao on credit. The transaction was later cancelled on June 30, 1744.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan Díaz de Herrera
summary: Capitán Juan Francisco Guerrero and his wife doña Lorenza Fajardo obligated themselves for $450 plata (5% interest) to the minor children of Ayudante Matías Masís and María del Carmen. This obligation was secured on a house they received from Capitán don Juan Díaz de Herrera and doña María Leonor de Viera, who previously held the debt.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan Manuel de Alvarado
summary: Juan Gómez Rico sold a 50-vara plot of land to Alférez Manuel Guillen for $50 cacao. The plot was bordered by properties of Juan de Aguilar and Capitán don Juan Manuel de Alvarado, and the royal road to the Church of Los Angeles.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan de Salvatierra y Seas
doña Dominga de Guzmán y Echavarría
Licenciado don Juan Solís de Miranda
summary: Licenciado don Manuel Sáenz obligated himself for $760 plata, charged on houses previously owned by the deceased Capitán don Juan de Salvatierra y Seas and doña Dominga de Guzmán y Echavarría. The funds were allocated to the Cofradía de la Concepción, Convento de San Francisco, a capellanía of Antonio Machado, and doña María Jerónima Guerrero.

locations: Fuerte de San Fernando de la boca del río de Matina
people_involved: Capitán y Alcaide don José de Sierra
Capitán don Francisco de la Pastora
summary: Capitán and Alcaide don José de Sierra, acting for himself and for Teniente don Joaquín de Beregañea and Alférez don José de Velazco, granted general power of attorney to Capitán don Francisco de la Pastora to collect their salaries.

people_involved: Teniente General Capitán don Elias de Arleguí
summary: Tomasa de Quirós made a codicil to her will, originally granted in 1742 before Teniente General Capitán don Elias de Arleguí. She revoked the clause leaving her slave Dionisia to her adoptive daughter Ana María, instead ordering Dionisia to be sold for masses for her soul.

Capitán don José Lebrón, a native of Ecija, Spain, being sick in bed, granted power to testate to Licenciado don Manuel González Coronel, whom he also named as his executor. Lebrón died during this act, leaving legitimate children with his deceased wife, doña Manuela Josefa Vanegas.

people_involved: Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla
summary: Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla sold a 4-year-old mulatilla named María de las Nieves, whom he had purchased from Pablo Solórzano, to Ana Morales for $150 plata.
Francisco Nicolás de Guevara, a master tailor, took Manuel Félix González as an apprentice for a period of 5 years to teach him the tailoring trade.

The will of the deceased Capitán don José Lebrón was formally granted by his attorney, Licenciado don Manuel González Coronel. The will confirmed his marriage to the deceased doña Manuela Josefa Vanegas.

An unnamed testador, son of the deceased Don Diego Lebrón and Doña Isabel Cortés from Marchena, Spain, makes a will. He names his children as heirs and appoints himself and Don Pedro de León as albaceas. He also bequeaths coral bracelets, held by Don Diego del Castillo in Granada, to his daughter María Josefa Salvadora.

Felipe de Umaña and his wife María Francisca Fernández obligate themselves for 300 pesos of cacao at 5% interest to a capellanía founded by Doña Gertrudis de Alvarado, which was previously managed by the deceased Capitán Cayetano Muñoz. The obligation is secured by a cacao hacienda in Matina, partly inherited by María Francisca from her mother Feliciana Chinchilla and partly bought by Felipe from his brother-in-law José Bernardo Fernández.

people_involved: Capitán don Salvador de Zavala y Barróla
Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco
summary: Capitán don Salvador de Zavala y Barróla, a trader and owner of the vessel "Nuestra Señora del Carmen y Señor San José," grants general power of attorney to Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco.

people_involved: Teniente Coronel don Juan Gemmir y Lleonart
summary: Sargento Mayor don Pedro Carazo owes 560 pesos of silver to Teniente Coronel don Juan Gemmir y Lleonart, who is the Governor and Captain General of the province. This debt was later cancelled on July 15, 1744.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez Robredo
summary: Capitán don Miguel de Ibarra and his wife Doña Juana Bermúdez obligate themselves for 200 pesos at 5% interest to a capellanía founded by Doña Cecilia Vázquez Coronado, receiving the money from Doña Rosa Solís, widow of Capitán José de Ocampo. The obligation is secured by a cacao hacienda in the Matina valley, and the Síndico General of San Francisco, Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez Robredo, accepts.
Doña Juana Calderón, a widow, owes 178 pesos of silver or cacao to Capitán don Salvador de Zavala. She offers a mulatto slave, valued at 300 pesos, as collateral.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco de la Pastora
summary: Capitán don Francisco de la Pastora grants general power of attorney to his wife, Doña Francisca de Arburola.

people_involved: Doña María de la Rosa González
summary: Capitán José de Alfaro, a resident of the Barba valley, makes his will. He is the legitimate son of the deceased Nicolás de Alfaro and María de Morera, and is married to Doña María de la Rosa González. He names his five children as equal heirs and appoints Capitán Rafael de Alfaro as albacea.

people_involved: Doña María de Jesús de la Riva
summary: Capitán don Diego López Conejo and his wife Doña María de Jesús de la Riva obligate themselves for 150 pesos at 5% interest to the capellanía founded by Doña Cecilia Vázquez Coronado, receiving the sum from Capitán Alonso de Porras. The obligation is secured by a house they own in the Aserrí valley, and Beneficiado don Manuel López Conejo, Cura of Esparza, is the Capellán.

people_involved: Teniente de Capitán don Alejo Pérez
summary: Sargento Juan José Jiménez and his wife Catarina de Ugalde, residents of the Barba valley, sell a plot of land and their dwelling house on it to Teniente de Capitán don Alejo Pérez for 150 pesos in goods. The land was originally acquired from Capitán Miguel de Alfaro.

Doña Casilda de Morales (Morera?), a resident of the Aserrí valley, sells a piece of land to Capitán don Camilo de Mora, Judge of the fields in the same valley, for 35 pesos in goods. The land was originally acquired from María de Fuentes.

Capitán don José de Alvarado and his wife Doña Francisca de Bonilla, residents of Aserrí, make their will. Doña Francisca was previously married to Capitán José Hidalgo, with whom she had no children, and they also have no children in their current marriage. They name each other as albaceas and universal heirs.

Juan de Loria, a native and Alcalde of Currira-vá, sells a tile and post house located on the Tiribí river plain, near the royal road to Currira-vá and the road from Aserrí, to Capitán don Pablo López Conejo for 60 pesos of cacao. The house was previously adjudicated to the minor children of Domingo Gutiérrez.
Don Rafael de Mier Cevallos, a resident of the Aserrí valley, sells a 12-year-old mulatto slave named Micaela, inherited from his parents, to Capitán Miguel de Mora for 200 pesos.

people_involved: Teniente de Capitán José Nicolás de Zamora
Capitán José de la Cruz Morales
summary: Teniente de Capitán José Nicolás de Zamora and Manuela de Rojas, widow of Capitán Marcos de Zamora and guardian of minor José de Zamora, residents of the Aserrí valley, sell a black slave named Francisca Javiera to Licenciado don Hermenegildo de Arleguí. The slave was acquired by José Nicolás and the minor José from the estate of Capitán José de la Cruz Morales as payment for tutelage.
Capitán José Mores makes his will. He is married to Magdalena de Sosa and names their five children as his heirs.
Manuela Josefa de Chavarría, being ill, granted power to make her will to Licenciado don Francisco de Ocampo. She named him as her executor and universal heir.

people_involved: Licenciado don Francisco José de Ocampo
summary: Licenciado don Francisco José de Ocampo, a Presbyter Cleric, executed the will of the deceased Manuela Josefa de Chavarría. She was single, had no forced heirs, and Ocampo was confirmed as her executor and heir.

Ambrosio Vanegas, a resident of Nicaragua, leased a cacao plantation in the Matina valley from doña Angela Sáenz. The lease was for three years at $100 cacao annually, with the first year being free. The plantation bordered the hacienda of Beneficiado don Juan José Camacho.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Diego de Soto
Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto
summary: Sargento Mayor don Diego de Soto made his will, naming his six children as heirs and Capitán don Martín de Garayar as executor. He also bequeathed 25 pesos to his brother Nicolás de Soto.

Lucía Rodríguez made her will, detailing her family and heirs, including her four daughters. She granted freedom to her mulata slave, Lorenza, in recognition of her good behavior and advanced age. The will was granted in the house of Tomás Calvo.

locations: vega del río de las Ciruelas
summary: Alférez Cristóbal Víquez and his wife doña Manuela de Oviedo sold a plot of land, previously acquired from doña Mariana de Hidalgo, to José Méndez for $22. The land was located in the vega of the Ciruelas river, bordering lands of Capitán Luis Morera and Antonio Rodríguez.
María del Carmen de Rojas, widow of Andrés de Araya, obligated herself for $285 and 4 reales to her six minor children. This sum represented their legitimate paternal inheritance.

people_involved: Capitán de Caballos Corazas Francisco de Sandoval
summary: Capitán de Caballos Corazas Francisco de Sandoval, a resident of Tierra Firme, sold a plot of land in the Barba valley to María Pachón de las Alas for $50 cacao. He had inherited the land from his father, Capitán Sebastián de Sandoval, and it bordered the house of Manuel Nicolás de Chavarría.

Magdalena Sosa, widow of Capitán José de Amores, sold a mulato slave named Francisco Antonio (25-30 years old) to Sargento Mayor Diego de Soto for $300 cacao. Soto paid $100 and obligated himself for the remaining $200 to a chaplaincy belonging to the Convento de San Bartolomé de Barba, which was previously managed by her deceased husband.

Sargento Mayor Diego de Soto and his wife doña Sebastiana Jiménez formally obligated themselves for $200 to the chaplaincy founded by the deceased Capitán José de Amores, which belonged to the Convento de San Bartolomé de Barba. This obligation was secured against their hacienda and houses in the Barba valley.

people_involved: Beneficiado don Juan de Rivas y Chaverri
summary: Cristóbal de Umaña and his wife doña Francisca de Alfaro, having been awarded a ranch, acknowledged obligations totaling $950 for three chaplaincies, including one founded by Beneficiado don Juan de Rivas y Chaverri. They mortgaged the ranch, livestock, their house, sugar mill, and three slaves to secure these debts.
Magdalena de Sosa, widow of Capitán José de Amores, obligated herself for $619 and 3 reales to her six minor children. This sum represented their legitimate paternal inheritance.

Ana Solano made her will, detailing her family, including her eight children and sister Josefa Solano. Her son-in-law, Rafael de Herrera, was named as the property manager, and Ayudante José Núñez and Capitán Gregorio Siles were named as executors.
Capitán Agustín de Quesada, widower of Petronila de Madrigal, acknowledged a debt of $293 to his five minor children. This amount represented their legitimate maternal inheritance.

Capitán Tomás Calvo owed $120 and a plot of land to Narcisa Calvo, which were part of her paternal and maternal inheritance from Alférez Francisco Calvo. A marginal note from December 16, 1750, indicates that Juan Antonio de Alvarado and Narcisa Calvo cancelled this debt to Victoria Lascares, widow of Capitán Tomás Calvo.

Capitán don Francisco de Flores, acting as executor for the deceased Alférez Francisco Calvo, established a perpetual chaplaincy for recited masses. He designated a forge valued at $150 cacao as its assets, with Capitán Tomás Calvo as the patron responsible for the $141 principal.

Captain don Miguel Calvo bequeathed a forge to his son, Alférez Francisco Calvo, with the condition that after his death, Francisco would establish a chaplaincy of masses for Miguel's soul using the forge's proceeds.

people_involved: Beneficiado don Juan Manuel del Corral
Licenciado don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
summary: On October 28, 1770, Beneficiado don Juan Manuel del Corral, the parish priest of Heredia, received the forge from Gregorio Calvo, heir of the deceased Tomás Calvo. This action fulfilled the obligation related to the chaplaincy established by Captain Miguel Calvo, with Licenciado don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín named as chaplain or the Cura of Cubujuquí in his absence, and Captain don Martín de Garayar acting as guarantor.

people_involved: Licenciado don Juan Pérez de Cote
summary: Captain Andrés de Ocampo and his wife Juliana Solera founded a chaplaincy of masses. The principal for this chaplaincy included a sugar mill, a pan, and two mules, valued at 200 pesos of cacao, with Licenciado don Juan Pérez de Cote named as the chaplain.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Juan Manuel de Saborío
summary: Captain Francisco de Sandoval granted power of attorney to Sergeant Major Juan Manuel de Saborío. This power allowed Saborío to sell an enslaved person that Sandoval had inherited from his deceased father's estate.

Captain Manuel de Zamora, acting as the executor for the deceased Captain Sebastián de Sandoval, established a chaplaincy of masses as directed in Sandoval's will. The assets for this chaplaincy included the deceased's residence, another house in Barba, and five enslaved individuals. Doña María Manuela de Quesada, Sandoval's widow, was obligated for the value of these assets, which were adjudicated to her, and their son Francisco was named as the first choice for chaplain.

Doña María Manuela de Quesada declared that she had paid 25 pesos in cash for the visit rights of her deceased husband's will. A judge then reduced her total obligation from 823 pesos of cacao to 779 pesos of cacao, reflecting the cash payment.

Doña Manuela de Flores, widow of Captain Manuel de Ulate, obligated herself for 722 pesos and 3 reales to her children, Juan Manuel and María Catalina de Ulate. This sum represented their paternal inheritance.
Doña Manuela de Flores cancelled her previous obligation, having entered into a new joint obligation with her husband.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco
Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo
summary: Captain don Salvador de Zavala deposited 416 pesos and 7 1/4 reales with Sergeant Major don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco. This deposit was to cover a claim made by Sergeant Major don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo, a tax collector, regarding cacao cargo on Zavala's ship during voyages in February and September 1741, and its current cargo.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo
Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco
summary: Sergeant Major don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo cancelled the obligation from the previous event. This was done after Sergeant Major don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco, acting as Zavala's general agent, presented a letter from don Pedro de Herrarte, Treasurer of royal taxes, ordering the cancellation due to a new obligation undertaken by Zavala in Guatemala.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco
summary: Sergeant Major don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco, acting as general agent for Captain don Salvador de Zavala, acknowledged a debt of 3000 silver pesos to the estate of the deceased Captain don Félix del Mar. This debt was for a ship belonging to Del Mar that Salmón Pacheco had purchased at auction in the port of Alvarado, with payment due within five months.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco
summary: Don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco delivered 500 pesos as a partial payment towards his obligation for the ship.

people_involved: Teniente Coronel don Juan Gemmir y Lleonart
Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco
summary: The Governor and Captain General, acting as judge for the estate of Captain don Félix del Mar, declared that the entire obligation for the ship was satisfied. Don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco remained responsible only for 159 pesos and 2 reales belonging to different individuals, leading to the cancellation of this specific obligation.

people_involved: Licenciado don Gregorio López del Corral
summary: Ana Morales sold an enslaved mulatta named Rosa, aged 10, to Licenciado don Gregorio López del Corral for 150 silver pesos. Rosa was born in Ana's house to Nicolasa, another enslaved mulatta, whom Ana had inherited from doña Margarita Morales.
Diligences were initiated for the opening of the testament of Diego García, requested by Manuela Gutiérrez.

people_involved: Capitán don José Antonio de Barros y Carvajal
summary: The testament of Diego García, a free black man, was opened. He was married twice, first to Ana Santiago with no children, and then to his current wife Manuela Gutiérrez. His daughter, Ana Efigenia García, was named his universal heir, and Captain don José Antonio de Barros y Carvajal and don José Antonio de Acosta were appointed as his executors.

locations: Castillo de San Fernando de la boca del río de Matina
summary: The testament of don Joaquín de Beregañea, Lieutenant of Infantry at the Castillo de San Fernando de la boca del río de Matina, was opened. He was identified as the legitimate son of don Bernardo de Beregañea.

people_involved: Margarita de la Cruz y Quesada
summary: An unnamed testador, native of Pamplona, married to Margarita de la Cruz y Quesada in La Habana, made a will. Having no children, his soul was named as heir. Captain Francisco Fernández de la Pastora and José Antonio de Bonilla were named as executors.

Sergeant Major Dionisio del Basto and Miguel Torrijos, residents of Santiago de Veragua, committed to pay Licenciado Francisco Vandín Salgado, a priest from the Diocese of Panamá, $2100 in silver. This payment is due within one year in León, Nicaragua.

people_involved: Pedro Antonio de Carrandi y Menan
summary: Dionisio del Basto and Miguel Torrijos, with Martín de Icaza as guarantor, committed to pay Sergeant Major Pedro Antonio de Carrandi y Menan $489 in silver within six months in Cartago. The payment is to be made to Pedro González de León, then Juan Rodríguez de Robredo, and finally delivered to Juan Antonio Flores y Cienfuegos (or Diego de Castillo in his absence) in Nicaragua.

Alférez Luis de Soto Mayor leased a cacao hacienda belonging to Polonia de Moya to José Antonio González for two years. The hacienda, which borders properties of Licenciado Gregorio Corral and María Josefa Cabral, was leased for $150 cacao per year.
Doña Josefa de Bonilla, a widow, sold a 28-30 year old Creole slave named Juan, born in her house to one of her parents' slaves, to Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara Sáenz for $300 in silver.

Beneficiado Juan José Camacho, the priest of Matina valley, sold a 25-year-old mulatto slave named Josefa Nicolasa de Morales to Sergeant Major Miguel Jiménez, a resident of Aserrí valley. Josefa Nicolasa had previously been purchased from Captain Tomás del Corral for $250 in silver.

The will of Licenciado Gregorio López del Corral, a priest and legitimate son of the deceased Antonio López del Corral and Antonia Salmón Pacheco, was recorded. His brother was Captain Tomás del Corral, but the will was not executed.

Licenciado Antonio de Guevara Sáenz, a priest, granted general power of attorney to Ventura de Beteta y Arrollave, a resident of Santiago de Guatemala. This power was for collecting assets owed to his deceased father, Captain Alvaro de Guevara, who had passed away in Santiago de Guatemala.

Beneficiado Juan José Camacho, the priest of Matina valley, sold a 20-year-old mulatto slave named Manuela Josefa, inherited from his mother Beatriz de Morales, and her two-year-old son José Gregorio, to Marcos José de Arana, a resident of Granada, Nicaragua. The price for both was $368 and 4 reales in silver.

Tomasa de Quirós, a widow, sold two plots of land located across the Río Grande de la Canoa to Captain Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra for $200 in cacao currency. These lands were part of the estate of her deceased husband, Tomás Chaves.

Captain Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra committed to pay $100 at 5% interest to the chaplaincy established by the deceased Juana Moscoso. This obligation, previously held by Captain José de Quirós, is secured by 400 head of cattle on Ibarra's lands across the Río Grande de la Canoa.

people_involved: José Andrés de Robles y Castro
summary: The will of Sergeant Major José Andrés de Robles y Castro, a native of Málaga, Spain, was recorded. He was the legitimate son of the deceased Andrés de Robles and María de Duran, and was married to Úrsula Medina de Rojas in Antequera, Spain, with whom he had three children: Fernando, María Antonia, and María Tomasa. The will detailed provisions for his children regarding inherited haciendas, and named Licenciado Manuel José González Coronel and Luis Diez Navarro as executors.
Sergeant Major Manuel Saborío, acting as attorney for Captain Francisco de Sandoval, sold a 15-year-old black slave named Francisco de Sandoval to Captain Miguel de Alvarado for $250 in silver.

Manuela Josefa Cartín, as principal, and Lieutenant Francisco de la Riva and Simón Cásasela, as guarantors, committed to pay $550 in cacao to María Josefa de Torres, the minor daughter of Manuela Josefa and the deceased Antonio de Torres. This sum represents María Josefa's legitimate inheritance, as Manuela Josefa received haciendas in Barbilla from her husband's estate in exchange for her marital assets and this obligation.

Manuela Josefa Cartín, as widow, and Francisco de la Riva and Simón Cásasela, as executors of Antonio de Torres' estate, sold a new hacienda with 587 trees in Matina to Captain José Nicolás de la Haya to pay debts. They also sold 314 trees from a fruit-bearing hacienda, with the total price being $837 and 7 reales.

Lieutenant Francisco de la Riva committed to pay $100 at 5% interest to the legitimate children of the deceased Manuel Chinchilla. This sum was originally bequeathed to Chinchilla by Captain Francisco Gutiérrez, and Gutiérrez's wife, Gertrudis Ruiz de Hinojosa, transferred this obligation to Francisco de la Riva.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí
Su Senoria el Juez privativo del derecho y composición de tierras
summary: The Arleguí brothers (José Hermenegildo, Antonio Elias, and Manuel Felipe) granted power to don Luis Diez Navarro to represent them before the land judge in Santiago de Guatemala. Their aim was to secure a title for two 'caballerías' of land in the Valle de Santa Ana, based on prior proceedings before don Jerónimo del Rosal.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Capitán don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora granted general power of attorney to don Luis Diez Navarro, who was preparing for a trip to Guatemala.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don José Antonio de Oriamuno
Capitán don Tomás Fernández de los Ríos
don Juan Bautista Alvarez de Lemus
summary: Sargento Mayor don José Antonio de Oriamuno, a perpetual councilman and provincial mayor, granted power to Capitán don Tomás Fernández de los Ríos to collect a debt of 492 pesos from don Juan Bautista Alvarez de Lemus, both residents of Santiago de Alanje.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco Javier de Siles
Sargento Mayor don José Antonio de Oriamuno
doña Eugenia Urbana Láinez de Iztueta
summary: Capitán don Francisco Javier de Siles and his wife, doña Eugenia de Bastarrica, sold a 'caballería' of land in Siü'o Viejo to Sargento Mayor don José Antonio de Oriamuno for 50 pesos of cacao. The land, adjacent to the city's common lands and the buyer's property, had previously belonged to doña Eugenia de Bastarrica's mother, doña Eugenia Urbana Láinez de Iztueta.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
Capitán don José Antonio de Acosta
summary: don José de Sierra, Castellano and Captain of San Fernando fort, granted power to testate to Capitán don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora and don Nicolás de Sierra. This was done in Valle de Matina before the interim Teniente General, with Capitán don José Antonio de Acosta witnessing and authorizing the power as Sierra was near death. Sierra declared his marriage to doña Rosa Maldonado in Guatemala City and named his three children as universal heirs.

locations: Fuerte de San Fernando de la boca de Matina
people_involved: Capitán don José Antonio de Acosta
summary: An inventory of the deceased don José de Sierra's papers and goods was conducted at the Fuerte de San Fernando de la boca de Matina. This was done before Capitán don José Antonio de Acosta, following Sierra's request to hand over his assets to his administrator, José Nicolás de la Haya, for delivery to his executors.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
Anselmo de Jesús Antonio de Sierra
summary: The executors, Capitán don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora and don Nicolás de Sierra, executed the will of don José de Sierra. The will confirmed his marriage to doña Rosa Maldonado in Santiago de Guatemala, named their three children as heirs, and identified his parents as don Juan de Sierra and doña Josefa de Pareja from Puerto de Santa María, Spain. It also ordered the redemption of a 1000 peso 'censo' on his wife's house.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás de la Madrid
summary: Capitán don Tomás de la Madrid and his wife doña Antonia de Granda, residents of Valle de Ujarraz, sold a 15-year-old Creole slave named José Filoteo to Teniente de Capitán Antonio Valverde for 150 pesos of silver.

people_involved: doña Laureana López de Ortega y Chaves
Licenciado don Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí y Hoces
summary: The heirs of the deceased doña Laureana López de Ortega y Chaves (Juan de Umaña, don Cristóbal Tenorio, Francisco de Castro, and Juan Antonio de Castro) acknowledged an 80 peso silver obligation to a chaplaincy. This chaplaincy, founded by Francisco de Paz, was established on lands inherited from doña Laureana, and Licenciado don Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí y Hoces served as its chaplain.

people_involved: Alférez don Luis de Soto Mayor
Licenciado don José Francisco de Moya
Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo
Sargento Mayor don Julián García de Ergueta
summary: Alférez don Luis de Soto Mayor, as executor of the deceased Licenciado don José Francisco de Moya, established a chaplaincy of 'misas rezadas' as per Moya's will. The chaplaincy was endowed with 375 pesos of cacao, secured on Moya's former house and the houses of Sargento Mayor don Julián García de Ergueta and his wife. Licenciado don Manuel Sáenz, the poorest cleric and closest relative of the deceased, was appointed as the chaplain.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Julián García de Ergueta
summary: Sargento Mayor don Julián García de Ergueta and his wife, doña Ana Sancho de Castañeda, formally obligated themselves for 125 pesos of cacao to the chaplaincy founded in the previous entry, securing this amount on their residential properties.

people_involved: Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla
summary: Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla granted Juan Antonio Valerín a cacao plantation clearing of 1500 trees in El Bejuco. Valerín was to cultivate and maintain the plantation for three years, receiving 60 pesos of cacao annually for his work.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco
Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez Robredo
summary: don Pedro León González Vimera, a native of Puerto de Cubillero in Asturias, granted power to testate to Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco and Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez Robredo.

people_involved: doña Magdalena Suárez de los Cabos
doña María Josefa de Barros y Muro
Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez Robredo
Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco
summary: don Pedro León González Vimera executed his own will, stating his origin from Consejo de Pravia, Asturias, and identifying his parents as don Domingo González Vimera and doña Magdalena Suárez de los Cabos. He detailed his two marriages: first to the deceased doña María Martínez, with whom he had two daughters (Juana María and Francisca Petronila González), and second to doña María Josefa de Barros y Muro, widow of don Domingo Rápela, with whom he had no children. He named Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez Robredo and Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco as his executors.

people_involved: José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Captain Antonio de Barros Carvajal, acting as executor for the late free black Diego García, established a chaplaincy of recited masses as per García's will. The endowment, totaling $200 cacao, was funded partly by García's assets and partly by his widow, Manuela Gutiérrez, and charged upon cacao trees and land in Pontezuela, Matina. Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría was designated as the Patron and Chaplain.

Manuela Gutiérrez, widow of Diego García, undertook an obligation for $645, 3 reales, and 1 cuartillo. This sum represented the paternal legitimate inheritance due to her daughter, Ana Efigenia García.

Captain Francisco Fernández de la Pastora and his wife, Francisca de Arburola, incurred an obligation for $841, 7 reales, to a creditor with superior rights. This amount was to be paid from the assets of the late Captain Félix del Mar, representing the remaining balance of a loan Francisco had extended to Félix for his ship's outfitting.

people_involved: José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Captain José Nicolás de Bonilla and his wife, Lucía de Alvarado y Jirón, obligated themselves for $900 cacao for a house in Cartago, currently inhabited by Juana Calderón and her children. The payment was allocated to three different chaplaincies: one founded by Micaela Duran de Chaves, another by Vasco Solano, and a third by Baltasar de Grados, with specific amounts designated for each.

people_involved: José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Beneficiado José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría and Licenciado Antonio de Guevara declared that the $600 census benefiting the chaplaincies they served had been transferred by the original obligor to José de Flores and Angela de Alvarado. Consequently, they cancelled the initial obligation.

people_involved: Antonio de Soto y Barahona (Sargento Mayor)
summary: The testament of Licenciado Antonio de Soto y Barahona, a Clerigo Presbítero, was recorded. He named Licenciado José Hermenegildo de Arleguí and his brother, Captain Tomás de Soto y Barahona, as his executors, and designated his mother, Petronila de Hoces Navarro, as his universal heir.
Captain José Jinesta formally granted general power of attorney to Sargento Mayor Juan Rodríguez de Robredo.

Sargento Mayor Dionisio Pacheco and his wife, Francisca Serrano de Reina, established a chaplaincy of recited masses with a principal of $1000 cacao, to be charged on their new 3000-tree cacao plantation in Valle de Barbilla. Their son, Nicolás Pacheco, who was studying for the priesthood in Santiago de Guatemala, was designated as the first Chaplain.

people_involved: Juan Salvador de la Haya y Bolívar
summary: Francisco Javier de Iglesias and his wife, Francisca Fernández Castellanos, incurred an obligation for $400 at 5% interest to Licenciado Juan Salvador de la Haya y Bolívar, for the chaplaincy founded by Cecilia Vázquez Coronado. This obligation was secured by their residence in Cartago, which was described with its specific boundaries.

people_involved: Juan Salvador de la Haya y Bolívar
summary: Luis de Soto Mayor and Isabel Ramona de Utrera obligated themselves to the chaplaincy founded by Cecilia Vázquez Coronado, served by Licenciado Juan Salvador de la Haya y Bolívar, for $652 silver and $200 cacao at 5%. This obligation was secured by a house in Cartago, with its boundaries detailed by neighboring properties.

people_involved: Antonio de Soto y Barahona (Sargento Mayor)
summary: Licenciado Hermenegildo de Alvarado y Jirón, a Clerigo Presbítero, sold a sugarcane hacienda, house, and equipment to Captain Tomás López del Corral for $1400 cacao. The payment was distributed among a chaplaincy founded by Sargento Mayor Antonio de Soto y Barahona, the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora del Rosario, and the seller himself. Hermenegildo had acquired the hacienda from Baltasar Fernández with his mother's consent.
On June 18, 1753, Captain José Nicolás de Bonilla, acting as the current Mayordomo of the Cofradía del Rosario, received $100 in cacao currency from Captain Tomás López del Corral.

people_involved: Juan Salvador de la Haya y Bolívar
summary: Licenciado Juan Salvador de la Haya y Bolívar, a Clerigo Presbítero, formally granted general power of attorney to Sargento Mayor Juan Rodríguez de Robredo.

people_involved: José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
Juan Salvador de la Haya y Bolívar
summary: Sargento Mayor Julián García de Ergueta sold a tiled house in Cartago to Juana Calderón, a widow, for $500. The payment included $300 silver for the chaplaincy founded by Cecilia Vázquez Coronado, with the remaining $200 to be paid in two installments from upcoming harvests.

Juana Calderón, a widow, sold a 19-20 year old mulatto slave named Juan, who was born in her household to her mulatto slave, to José de Guzmán, a trader in Cartago. The sale price for Juan was $260 in silver.

people_involved: Don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro
summary: Don Miguel Fermín and Don Félix Joaquín Alvarado recognized and assumed their deceased mother Doña Úrsula Josefa López Conejo's obligations. These included two $100 chaplaincies, one for Doña Josefa de Hoces Navarro and another founded by Don Pedro Ibáñez. They imposed these debts on their estate, which included cattle, houses, and a mill in Tres Ríos.

Don José Francisco de Alvarado, serving as the Lieutenant Priest of the Parish, received $100 from his brother, Don Joaquín de Alvarado. This payment was for the chaplaincy founded by Ibáñez, for which Don José Francisco was both patron and chaplain.

Don Miguel Fermín and Don Félix Joaquín Alvarado committed to pay their eight siblings a total of $3005 and 1.5 reales. This sum represented each sibling's share of their paternal and maternal inheritance, with each receiving $429 and 2.5 reales.
Capitán Don Elias de Arleguí acted on behalf of Doña Teresa and Doña Gertrudis de Alvarado to cancel an unspecified obligation. This action resolved a financial matter for the two sisters.
Don José Francisco de Alvarado, who was the guardian of Doña Antonia Manuela de Alvarado, canceled an obligation on her behalf. This action settled a financial matter for his ward.

people_involved: Capitán Don José Nicolás de Bonilla
Vicario Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
Capitán Don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno
summary: Capitán Don José Nicolás de Bonilla made his will, naming his mother Micaela de Bonilla as universal heir if his unborn child did not survive, otherwise the child would inherit. He was married to Doña Lucía de Alvarado and had a brother, Don Miguel Chavarría. The executors appointed were Vicario Don José Miguel de Guzmán and Capitán Don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno.

people_involved: Doña Ana Teresa de Soto y Barahona
summary: Doña Ana Teresa de Soto y Barahona, widow of Sargento Mayor Don Pedro Carazo, committed to pay $487 in obligations. This included $100 for a chaplaincy for the soul of Germán Rodríguez, benefiting the city of Esparza, and $387 owed to Doña María Leonida, the minor daughter of Don Nicolás de Ocampo Golfín and Doña Manuela de Bastarrica.

people_involved: Teniente de Capitán Don Benito Alvarado
summary: Teniente de Capitán Don Benito Alvarado and his wife Doña María Leonida de Ocampo canceled an obligation for $387. This action settled a debt related to Doña María Leonida's inheritance.

people_involved: Doña Ana Teresa de Soto y Barahona
summary: Doña Ana Teresa de Soto y Barahona presented a receipt for $100, indicating that Beneficiado Don Juan de Bolívar had taken charge of this specific obligation. This resolved a portion of her outstanding debts.

people_involved: Doña Ana Teresa de Soto y Barahona
summary: Doña Ana Teresa de Soto y Barahona committed to pay her five legitimate children with her deceased husband, Sargento Mayor Don Pedro Carazo, their paternal inheritance. Each child, including Doña Petronila, Don José Antonio, Doña Ana Gertrudis, Doña Micaela, and Don Francisco Carazo, was due $144 and 5 reales, totaling $723 and 4 reales.

people_involved: Capitán Don Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra
Doña Ana Teresa de Soto y Barahona
summary: Capitán Don Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra and his wife Doña Juana Gertrudis Bermúdez obligated themselves for $343 in silver, received from Doña Ana Teresa de Soto y Barahona. This money, originally deposited by Sargento Mayor Don Pedro Carazo, belonged to a chaplaincy founded by Capitán Juan Gregorio Ramírez, whose chaplain was the guardian of the San Francisco Convent in Esparza. They secured this obligation with a cattle ranch of over 400 heads.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
Doña Ana Teresa de Soto y Barahona
summary: Doña Petronila de Hoces Navarro, widow of Sargento Mayor Don Antonio de Soto y Barahona, declared that Don Pedro Carazo, her deceased son-in-law, had given her 100 pesos with instructions to give a specific room in her house to his wife, Doña Ana Teresa, if he died intestate. As Don Pedro died without a will, Doña Petronila transferred the room, located at a corner with the San Juan solar, to Doña Ana Teresa.

people_involved: Don Nicolás de Soto y Barahona
Doña Ana Teresa de Soto y Barahona
summary: Doña Petronila de Hoces Navarro declared she held the inheritance of her son, Capitán Don Tomás Barahona, who, though of age, had not claimed it, having only received a mulatto boy named Tomás. She stated that Don Tomás managed her assets legally and had independently acquired a cacao estate in Barbilla, a cattle ranch in El Pedregal (Ujarraz valley), and two slaves: Francisco (23, bought from Capitán Cayetano Sandoval) and Manuel (1.5, bought from María Calvo). Doña Petronila also gave Don Tomás a 10-11 year old mulatta named Rita, and her other children, Don José Manuel Gómez (husband of Doña Juana María Barahona), Don Nicolás de Soto y Barahona, and Doña Ana Teresa de Soto y Barahona, confirmed this declaration.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo
summary: Capitán Isidro de Castro obligated himself for $100 at 5% interest, received from Sargento Mayor Don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo, Syndic of the San Francisco Convent. This obligation was originally for $200 on Capitán Francisco Bonilla and his wife Doña María Leonor de Vargas, but their house collapsed, reducing the value. Castro imposed the new obligation on a house in the city, bordering properties of Doña Juana Ángulo, Doña Micaela Bonilla, the heirs of Juan López, and Sargento Mayor Don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco
summary: Pedro de Aguilar, a native of Panama, sold a 45-year-old Congo slave named Tomás to Sargento Mayor Don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco for $165 in silver. Aguilar had previously acquired Tomás through purchase from Antonia Santiago.

people_involved: Vicario Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
Don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro
summary: Beneficiado Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría granted general power of attorney to Maestro Don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro, who was the Archdeacon of the Cathedral of León, Nicaragua. This authorization allowed Don Félix Esteban to collect the full stipend assigned to Don José Miguel as the priest of this city, along with any other outstanding debts.

people_involved: Capitán Don José de Mier Cevallos
summary: Capitán Don José de Mier Cevallos obligated himself for $80 in cacao to José Antonio and María Nicolasa Palacios, who were minors. These minors were the legitimate children of the deceased Lucas Palacios and Catarina González.

people_involved: Fray José de San Antonio y Cevallos
summary: Legal proceedings were initiated against Nicolás Palacios and Sargento Mayor Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad concerning 125 pesos of cacao from Lucas Palacios's estate, half of which belonged to minors. Muñoz de la Trinidad became obligated for this sum on October 20 of that year. Later, the Governor learned Muñoz had died in Tierra Firme without assets, and Nicolás Palacios had left the province, leaving 80 pesos of cacao with Francisco Fernández de la Pastora. An unnamed grantor is now taking responsibility for this obligation, hypothecating his inherited goods from his deceased sons, Fray José de San Antonio y Cevallos and Gabriel de Mier Cevallos, shared with his wife Doña Catarina González Camino.

Juan José de Cuende and Clemente Astorga, acting as executors for Captain Diego Isidro de Aguilar, established a chaplaincy of recited masses. They allocated 500 pesos of cacao from the deceased's former houses, which were located near properties belonging to Doña Águeda Pérez de Muro, Teodora Molina, José Esquivel, and Don José Antonio Fajardo. The current guardian of the San Francisco Convent was appointed chaplain, and the convent's Mayordomo as patron.
Juan José de Cuende and Clemente Astorga, as executors of Captain Diego Isidro de Aguilar and fulfilling his will, granted freedom to the enslaved black man Manuel Granados.
Juan José de Cuende and Clemente Astorga, as executors of Captain Diego Isidro de Aguilar, granted freedom to the enslaved black man José Aguilar.
Juan José de Cuende and Clemente Astorga, as executors of Captain Diego Isidro de Aguilar, granted freedom to the enslaved black woman Antonia de Aguilar.
Juan José de Cuende and Clemente Astorga, as executors of Captain Diego Isidro de Aguilar, granted freedom to the enslaved woman Isabel Céspedes.

Juan José de Cuende and Clemente Astorga, as executors of Diego Isidro de Aguilar, founded a second chaplaincy of recited masses. This one was endowed with 500 pesos principal, charged against Diego's former country house, located in the city's common lands near the Taras river. Enrique de Molina was named the proprietary chaplain, with the condition that he could be ordained through it. If he failed, the chaplaincy would pass to Diego's grandchildren, sons of José Antonio Carnuza, who would also be the patrons.

José Antonio Carranza issued a receipt for 2943 pesos and 2 reales in cacao currency, representing the value of the assets his wife, Nicolasa de Aguilar, inherited from her deceased father, Captain Diego Isidro de Aguilar.

Doña Isabel María de Alarcón, a resident of Ujarraz valley, declared that she possessed a plantain field planted by Manuela Palma on her land in Ujarraz. After Manuela Palma's death, leaving a daughter Antonia López, the plantain field was valued at 25 pesos of cacao, and Doña Isabel María de Alarcón obligated herself for that sum.

Captains Don Antonio Elias de Arleguí, Don Esteban Ruiz de Mendoza, and Don José Nicolás de Bonilla received an unspecified deposit of goods. The inventory of these goods remained with the Governor, signed by him and several other individuals including Doña Gabriela de Arleguí and Don Juan José de Cuende.

people_involved: Don Matías Rodríguez de las Varillas
Don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Captain Don Juan José de Cuende, his wife Doña Manuela de Ibarra, Sargento Mayor Don José Antonio de Oriamuno, and Captain Don Miguel de Ibarra guaranteed two thousand ducats. This was after Cuende received the title of Lieutenant of the city and its jurisdiction from royal officials of Nicaragua and Costa Rica. Don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora previously held this position. Doña María Catarina de Ibarra and Doña Juana Bermúdez also obligated themselves.

Doña Gabriela de Arleguí, widow of Sargento Mayor Don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo, obligated herself to a creditor for 3418 pesos, representing the value of her dowry goods received from her deceased husband's estate.

Doña Angela de Guevara Sáenz, widow of Sargento Mayor Don Pedro de Alvarado, made her will on January 22, 1745. She was the legitimate daughter of the deceased Don Alvaro de Guevara and Doña María Sáenz. Her children were Don Esteban, Doña Lucía (married to Captain Don José Nicolás de Bonilla), Doña María, Doña Angela, Don Pedro, Doña Antonia, Doña Mariana, Don Gabriel, and Doña Petronila. Her brother was Padre Guevara.

On January 25, 1745, Don Salvador de Luque Mármol, a trader in the province, obligated himself to pay Captain Don José de Tagle, a resident of the city, 300 silver pesos one month after both arrived in Panama, where they were traveling. He hypothecated 80 mule beasts he was taking to that Kingdom.

people_involved: Doña Francisca de la Madriz Linares
Licenciado Don José Manuel García de Argueta
summary: On February 26, 1745, Captain Don José Antonio de Oriamuno and his wife Doña María Catarina de Ibarra acknowledged a 150-peso annual census payment at 5% interest to the Santa Iglesia Parroquial. This sum was delivered by Doña Francisca de la Madriz Linares, widow of Don Juan Nicolás de Viveros, represented by Licenciado Don José Manuel García de Argueta. They hypothecated an adobe house with a tiled roof.
On July 15, 1758, Juan José de Cuende, acting as Lieutenant of Royal Officials, cancelled a document, likely related to the census payment mentioned previously.
On February 26, 1745, Sargento Mayor Miguel Jiménez, a resident of the Aserrí valleys, obligated himself for 150 pesos.

Doña Rosa Solís redeemed a perpetual annuity (censo) of 5% annual interest, which benefited the Convent of San Francisco in Esparza. This annuity originated from a chaplaincy founded by Doña Cecilia Vázquez de Coronado. A house located between the Torres and Virilla rivers was mortgaged in connection with this transaction.

people_involved: Doña María Josefa de Barros y Carvajal
Capitán Don Pedro González de León
summary: Doña Josefa Pérez de Muro, a widow, paid a dowry debt of 1000 pesos of cacao that she had promised for her daughter, Doña María Josefa de Barros y Carvajal's first marriage to Don Domingo Rápela del Villar. After Villar's death and her daughter's second marriage to Capitán Don Pedro González de León, Doña Josefa paid the debt with 668 cacao trees from her large hacienda named San Juan in Matina.

people_involved: Capitán General Don Tomás de Rivera y Santacruz
summary: Alférez Don José de Velazco granted power of attorney to Capitán Don Salvador de Zavala, a resident of Guatemala. Zavala was tasked with requesting from the Captain General of the Kingdom, Don Tomás de Rivera y Santacruz, a reform of the Alférez position at the San Fernando fort, located at the mouth of the Matina River.

people_involved: Teniente Coronel Don Juan Gemmir y Lleonart
summary: Teniente Coronel Don Juan Gemmir y Lleonart, who served as Governor and Captain General of the province, granted general power of attorney. This power was given to Don Juan Patricio de Escudero and Don Manuel de Grandal, who were business agents residing in Madrid.

people_involved: Capitán Don José Nicolás de Bonilla
summary: Capitán Don José Nicolás de Bonilla became obligated for 100 pesos of cacao (or 50 year-old calves) and an annual rent of five pesos (or a small jar of lard). This sum was previously held by Capitán Pablo Solórzano, who resided in the Barba valleys, and Solórzano had acquired the underlying land through the death of his father-in-law, Capitán Tomás de Chaves. The document was not concluded or signed.

people_involved: Doña Mariana de Barros y Muro
Capitán Don Diego de Barros y Carvajal
summary: A dowry letter was issued for Alférez Don José de Velazco, a native of Elche, Valencia, in favor of his wife, Doña Mariana de Barros y Muro. The dowry amounted to 1671 pesos and 4 reales, including a 9-year-old mulatto girl named Josefa, a plot of land, and a cacao hacienda named Velazco. Doña Mariana was the legitimate daughter of the deceased Capitán Don Diego de Barros y Carvajal and Doña Josefa Pérez de Muro.

locations: Ermita de Nuestra Señora de la Soledad
people_involved: Presbítero Don Maximiliano Antonio de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Doña Antonia de Echavarría Navarro, a widow, sold a cacao hacienda in Matina with 730 trees to Manuel Carrillo for 912 pesos and 4 reales. Carrillo also assumed responsibility for 850 pesos of chaplaincy debts and mortgaged the hacienda and his house, the plot of which belonged to his wife, Juana Nicolasa de Vida Martel. Later, in 1799, Manuel's son, Benito Carrillo, presented a 1777 document from Presbítero Don Maximiliano Antonio de Alvarado y Jirón to cancel the original deed, revealing that after Manuel's death, his widow, Juana Nicolasa, had abandoned the hacienda, which was then auctioned.

people_involved: Licenciado Presbítero Don José Francisco de Alvarado
Presbítero Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Doña Antonia de Echavarría Navarro obligated herself for 380 pesos and an annual 5% rent to a chaplaincy founded by Pedro Ibáñez, whose chaplain was Beneficiado Don Manuel López Conejo. She mortgaged her adobe and tile house, which bordered the Ermita de San Nicolás. A marginal note from 1751 indicates that Licenciado Presbítero Don José Francisco de Alvarado, the chaplain, canceled the obligation after receiving payment from Presbítero Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría, the Vicar Priest of Cartago.

Doña Antonia de Echavarría Navarro further obligated herself for 669 pesos at 5% interest to a chaplaincy founded by her deceased sister, Doña Juana de Echavarría Navarro. Doña Juana was the late wife of Capitán Don Francisco de Arleguí, and the same house was mortgaged for this obligation.

people_involved: Capitán Don José Nicolás de Bonilla
summary: Capitán Don José Nicolás de Bonilla obligated himself for 100 pesos at 5% interest to the Convent of San Francisco. This debt was originally owed by Capitán Pablo Solórzano, residing in the Barba valleys, and was secured by land Solórzano inherited from his father-in-law, Capitán Tomás de Chaves. Solórzano transferred this encumbered land to Bonilla.

people_involved: Capitán Don José de Mier Cevallos
Sargento Mayor Don Julián García de Argueta
summary: Capitán Don José de Mier Cevallos leased a cacao hacienda he owned in the Matina valley to Sargento Mayor Don Julián García de Argueta. The lease was for a period of two years at an annual rent of 200 pesos.

people_involved: Padre Licenciado Don Juan Manuel de Casasola
Licenciado Don Manuel José González Coronel
summary: Gertrudis Ruiz de Hinojosa, daughter of the late Juan Ginés de Hinojosa and Gertrudis Ruiz, made her will with her mother's permission. She had been married twice, first to Francisco de Orozío, with whom she had a daughter who died young, and then to Francisco Gutiérrez, with no surviving children from that marriage. She ordered the founding of chaplaincies, naming her nephew José Silverio de Segura as the first chaplain, to be funded by her cacao haciendas in Barbilla. She also made specific bequests, including selling a velvet skirt to buy a mantle for Nuestra Señora de los Dolores, and named several legatees and executors.

people_involved: Doña Mariana López de la Flor
Don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Doña Mariana López de la Flor leased a cacao hacienda with approximately 1400 trees in Matina to Manuel Carrillo for two years, at an annual rent of five zurrones of cacao. A marginal note from 1749 indicates that Don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora, acting on behalf of a chaplaincy in the Convent, declared receipt of payment.

people_involved: Presbítero Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Capitán Nicolás Barrantes, a free mulatto, made his will. He was married to Luisa Proa, also a free mulatto, and they had five children: Juan, María, Benito, Pedro, and Manuel. His estate included a cacao hacienda in Matina called El Chiletw, which he had purchased from his sister-in-law, Juana Proa. Presbítero Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría and Don Manuel Fernández Acosta were named as his executors.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco
Maestre de Campo Don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Sargento Mayor Don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco delivered 116 pesos of silver to Maestre de Campo Don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora, who held the position of Lieutenant of Royal Officials.
A company that Capitán don Antonio Salmón Pacheco had with his brother was found to have an outstanding balance related to the administration of tithes for the year 1727.

people_involved: don José Manuel Jiménez de Luna
summary: María Sibaja leases a cacao plantation in Matina, consisting of about 2000 trees, to don José Manuel Jiménez de Luna for 3 years and 6 months. The annual rent is 50 pesos, reflecting the poor condition of the property.

Doña María Marín Laguna, a widow, executes her will. She establishes a chaplaincy, naming don Manuel Fernández as patron and don Cosme Fernández as chaplain, with Licenciado don Manuel Sáenz serving in the interim. Her executors are don José Nicolás de Ulloa and don José Antonio de Acosta, and her heirs are the daughters of her brother don Juan Francisco Marín and doña María Bonilla.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral pays don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora, Lieutenant of Royal Officials, 120 pesos and 3 reales. This payment comes from the assets of don Antonio Pacheco, who was the tithe farmer in 1729.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
Licenciado Presbítero don Gregorio del Corral
summary: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral grants general power of attorney to his brother, Licenciado Presbítero don Gregorio del Corral.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan Díaz de Herrera
summary: Doña Luisa Calvo, a widow, makes her will. She names her daughter doña María Magdalena Maroto and her grandchildren Capitán don Juan Díaz de Herrera, doña Juana Josefa de Miranda (whom she raised from 6 months old), and doña Manuela de Baeza as her heirs.

people_involved: don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco pays don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora, Lieutenant of Royal Officials, 17 pesos and 3 reales. This payment is to settle the outstanding balance owed by don Antonio Pacheco, who was the tithe administrator in 1729.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan José de Cuende
summary: Capitán don Juan José de Cuende and his wife doña Manuela Josefa Ibarra grant freedom to Antonio de la Riva, a 40-year-old black man. Doña Manuela Josefa Ibarra inherited Antonio from her parents, and the freedom is granted because he fulfilled a 1737 commitment to cultivate a 2000-tree cacao plantation.

people_involved: Padre guardián del Convento de Cartago
don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda
summary: Diego de Aguilar, a bachelor, makes his will in Taras, witnessed by don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda, Judge of the fields, as ordered by the Governor. He names his natural daughter Nicolasa de Aguilar and her husband José Carranza, and orders the freedom of his four enslaved people upon his death. He also establishes two chaplaincies, one with Enrique Molina as chaplain and another to be served by the Guardian Father of the Convent of Cartago, and names don Juan José de Cuende and Clemente Astorga as executors.

people_involved: Licenciado Presbítero don José Manuel García de Argueta
Sargento Mayor don Antonio de Oriamuno
summary: Licenciado Presbítero don José Manuel García de Argueta sells a piece of land in El Sitio Viejo, which belonged to his mother doña Antonia Láinez de Iztueía, to Sargento Mayor don Antonio de Oriamuno for 50 pesos.

Simón de Casasola, married to Enmenia Brenes, makes his will. He names their children José Benito, María Gertrudis, María del Rosario, and Juan de Dios, and appoints don Andrés Fernández and don Manuel Guzmán as his executors.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
Licenciado Presbítero don José Manuel González Coronel
summary: Maestre de Campo don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora, acting as Mayordomo of the Cofradía de Concepción and patron of a chaplaincy founded by Capitán Diego de Aguilar, sells the house associated with the chaplaincy to Licenciado Presbítero don José Manuel González Coronel. The sale includes an encumbrance of 500 pesos at 5% interest.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno
summary: Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno and his wife doña Ana Efigenia de Estrada acknowledge a debt of 300 pesos at 5% interest, which is charged against their house in the city.

Doña Josefa Pérez de Muro, a widow, leases two cacao plantations in Matina, named San Juan, to her son don José de Velazco for 3 years. The lease includes a payment of 700 pesos at term end, 36 pesos in cacao annually, a copper pot (half price donated), and two mules in exchange for two sacks of cacao.

people_involved: Capitán don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón
Capitán don Pedro Ortiz de Rosas
doña María Catarina Ortiz de Rosas
Capitán don Juan Sancho de Castañeda
doña Juana Eufrasia Sancho de Castañeda
don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda
doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho de Castañeda
Presbítero Licenciado don Hermenegildo de Alvarado
don José Nicolás Sarmiento de Sotomayor
Capitán don Lucas Domingo del Fierro
Capitán don Julián García de Argueta
summary: Doña Juana de Alvarado makes her will, detailing her family and bequests. She was married first to Capitán don Pedro Ortiz de Rosas, and then to Capitán don Juan Sancho de Castañeda, having children from both marriages. She names her brothers, her enslaved people (Antonio Granda, Pedro Rosa, Gertrudis), and specifies the inheritance of her house to two of her children. She also mentions the spouses of her daughters.

people_involved: Capitán don Esteban Ruiz de Mendoza
doña Baltasara de la Madriz Linares
summary: Several individuals entered into marriage: Juana Eufrasia married Capitán don Esteban Ruiz de Mendoza; don José Manuel married doña Baltasara de la Madriz Linares; and doña Manuela Gertrudis married don Rafael Cevallos.

people_involved: Licenciado Presbítero don Antonio de Guevara Sáenz
Capitán don Juan Manuel de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Licenciado Presbítero don Antonio de Guevara Sáenz sold the "San Juan" hacienda in the Barba valley to Capitán don Juan Manuel de Alvarado y Jirón and his wife, doña Juana María Custodio Galarza, for 3000 pesos. The payment involved cacao, recognition of two capellanías, funds for captive redemption, and annual silver payments, with the buyers reserving the right to redeem the debt with hacienda produce.

people_involved: Beneficiado don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
doña Luisa de Guzmán y Echavarría
don José Miguel de Alvarado y Torres
summary: Capitán don Pablo Conejo, a widower residing in Barba valleys, sold a mulata slave named María del Rosario, about 18 years old, to Capitán don Miguel de Alvarado for 210 pesos in cacao and 50 in silver. The payment was sourced from cattle previously donated by Beneficiado don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría to his sister, doña Luisa de Guzmán y Echavarría, who was the seller's wife. The transaction was also noted by don José Miguel de Alvarado y Torres, the seller's son from his first marriage.

people_involved: Doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
summary: Doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral, a widow, sold a 15-year-old mulatilla named Lorenza, daughter of her slave Ana Benita, to Ana Murales for 270 pesos in silver.

people_involved: Doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
Cura don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral obligated herself for 100 pesos at 5% interest to a capellanía founded by Diego Quintero del Castillo and Francisca Hernández, former residents of Esparza. She mortgaged her house, which had previously recognized this and other liens in 1733, at the request of Cura don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría.

people_involved: Presbítero Licenciado don Juan José Camacho
summary: Presbítero Licenciado don Juan José Camacho, Cura of Matina, who had remated a house belonging to the deceased Capitán Jerónimo Valerín, obligated himself for 400 pesos in capellanías weighing on the property. He mortgaged his cacao hacienda in the Matina valley, which contained 4000 fruit trees, as security.

people_involved: Presbítero Licenciado don Juan José Camacho
Presbítero Licenciado don Manuel José González Coronel
summary: Presbítero Licenciado don Juan José Camacho sold the house that previously belonged to Capitán Jerónimo Valerino to Presbítero Licenciado don Manuel José González Coronel, Comisario del Santo Oficio, for 400 pesos. The house was located near the Altozano of the parish.

people_involved: Presbítero Licenciado don Juan José Camacho
summary: Presbítero Licenciado don Juan José Camacho obligated himself for 100 pesos at 5% interest to the Cofradía de Concepción, a debt previously held by doña Juana de Miranda. He mortgaged his hacienda in Matina as security for this obligation.

people_involved: Presbítero Licenciado don Juan José Camacho
summary: Presbítero Licenciado don Juan José Camacho sold a mulata slave named Baltasara, approximately 50 years old, to Alférez Pedro de Aguilar for 125 pesos. Camacho had acquired Baltasara by purchase from doña Josefa de Bonilla in 1741.

people_involved: Cura don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Miguel de Ocampo and his wife Isabel de Rojas obligated themselves for 273 pesos and 6 reales to a capellanía founded by Angela María Chavarría, for which Cura don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría served as Capellán. They mortgaged their house, trapiche, perol, and other tools located on the bank of the Ciruelas river in the Barba valleys.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan González del Camino
Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martín Cubero
Capitán don José de Mier Cevallos
summary: Doña Catalina González del Camino executed her will, detailing her two marriages, her children, and her properties including a house in Cartago, haciendas in Matina, and an estancia. She also listed numerous slaves and established a capellanía, naming her husband and son as executors and her children and grandchildren as heirs. The will was notarized by don José Antonio de Oriamuno.

people_involved: Beneficiado don Juan Antonio de Moya
summary: Doña Polonia de Moya executed her will, identifying her parents, her absent husband, and her four children. She detailed the lineage of her deceased daughter, María Nicolasa, and her grandson, José Antonio Brenes, and named her son, don Juan Antonio Ramos, as her executor.

people_involved: Cura don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Doña Francisca de Ángulo, a widow, obligated herself for 100 pesos to a capellanía founded by María Sagaste, with Cura don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría serving as its patron and capellán. She mortgaged 756 cacao trees located in a valley, which she had inherited from her brother, Capitán don Antonio de Ángulo.

people_involved: Don Manuel Francisco de Orozco y Quesada
summary: Doña María Josefa de Quesada and her son Don Manuel Francisco de Orozco y Quesada cancelled a deed.

people_involved: Licenciado Presbítero don Juan José Solís
Presbítero Licenciado don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí
summary: Don Antonio and Don Juan Félix de Guzmán, merchants in Cartago, took on obligations for two chaplaincies: one for 500 pesos established by Alférez Antonio Machado, and another for 200 pesos founded by Doña Eugenia Abarca. The capital for these obligations was secured by houses south of Cartago's public square, previously occupied by Don Francisco Lafons Vidor.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás de Soto y Barahona
summary: Capitán Don Tomás de Soto y Barahona, having acquired a hacienda in the Ujarraz valley, committed to recognizing existing mortgages and paying rent to the relevant chaplaincies as determined by the ecclesiastical tribunal.
Don Pedro de Alvarado, acting as a patron, cancelled a debt of 275 pesos.

Simón de Casasola took on an obligation for 550 pesos related to a chaplaincy founded by Sargento Juan Masís, whose son Juan Masís is the patron. Doña María Fernández redeemed this sum, and Casasola mortgaged his cacao hacienda in the Barbilla valley.

people_involved: Bachiller Presbítero don José Manuel García de Argueta
summary: A deed from 1750 was cancelled by Simón de Casasola, as Bachiller Presbítero Don José Manuel García de Argueta had taken and secured the sum.

people_involved: Presbítero Licenciado don Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí
Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo
summary: Presbítero Licenciado Don Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí granted general power of attorney to Sargento Mayor Don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo, who is identified as his brother-in-law.

Simón de Casasola and his wife María Efigenia Brenes took on an obligation for 880 pesos for a chaplaincy founded by Miguel Masís, with Juan Masís as patron and Licenciado Don Manuel Sáenz as chaplain. They mortgaged their hacienda in Barbilla.

people_involved: Bachiller don José Manuel García de Argueta
summary: A deed from 1750 recorded that Bachiller Don José Manuel García de Argueta took a specific sum.

people_involved: Doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho de Castañeda
Doña Juana de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Don Rafael de Mier Cevallos and his wife Doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho de Castañeda transferred their rights to a house where Doña Juana de Alvarado y Jirón, their mother, died. In exchange, Don Esteban Ruiz de Mendoza and his wife Doña Ana de Arleguí transferred their current residence to Cevallos and his wife.

people_involved: Doña Josefa de Casasola y Córdova
summary: Doña Águeda Pérez de Muro, a widow, committed to her grandchildren Félix José, Águeda Mariana, Bernardo Félix, and Bartolomé Félix de Miranda, for 1786 pesos and 4 reales, representing their inheritance from their deceased mother, Doña Josefa de Casasola y Córdova, who was the daughter of Doña Águeda.
Miguel de Jesús Campos issued a receipt to his mother-in-law, Doña María Fernández, for 104 pesos that his wife received as an inheritance from Teniente Juan Masis.

people_involved: Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla
Sargento Mayor don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Capitán Don José Nicolás de Bonilla provided a dowry for his wife, Doña Lucía de Alvarado, the legitimate daughter of the deceased Sargento Mayor Don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón and Doña Angela de Guevara. The assets were delivered by Licenciado Don Antonio de Guevara, Doña Lucía's uncle, following the death of her mother, and included various items and cacao trees.

Juana Calderón, a widow, sold an enslaved person named Hilario, approximately 12 years old and the son of another enslaved mulata woman she owned, to Capitán Don Diego Morras for 160 pesos. The record is incomplete.

people_involved: Doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho de Castañeda
Capitán don Juan Sancho de Castañeda
Doña Juana de Alvarado y Jirón
Presbítero Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho de Castañeda, legitimate daughter of the deceased Capitán Don Juan Sancho de Castañeda and Doña Juana de Alvarado y Jirón, and legitimate wife of Don Rafael de Mier Cevallos, granted power to Presbítero Licenciado Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba to make her will.

people_involved: Presbítero Beneficiado don Manuel López Conejo
summary: Hilario Monge, a resident of Aserrí valley, declared receiving 250 pesos from Doña Rita García de Argueta, which was held as a census from a chaplaincy served by Presbítero Beneficiado Don Manuel López Conejo. Pending formal consent to transfer the sum to Monge, he obligated himself to Doña Rita and mortgaged his three adobe houses, sugar mill, and cane field in Aserrí valley.

people_involved: Don Pedro de Flores y Vargas
Sargento Mayor don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón
Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla
summary: Ayudante Don José de Flores, originally from Extremadura, received a dowry for his wife, Doña Angela Josefa de Alvarado, the legitimate daughter of the deceased Sargento Mayor Don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón and Doña Angela de Guevara. The assets were received from Capitán Don José Nicolás de Bonilla, Doña Angela's executor, and included 225 pesos inheritance, plus 600 cacao trees donated by Licenciado Don Antonio de Guevara, Doña Angela Josefa's uncle.

people_involved: Doña Angela Josefa de Alvarado y Jirón
Cura y Vicario Presbítero don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Don José de Flores and his wife Doña Angela Josefa de Alvarado y Jirón took on an obligation for 600 pesos in cacao, which Don José Nicolás de Bonilla had managed and provided them with a hacienda portion. They then obligated themselves to two chaplaincies: one founded by Vasco SoLno, served by Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría, and another founded by Comisario Baltasar de Grado, for which Don Antonio de Guevara is patron and chaplain. They mortgaged their haciendas.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Maestre de Campo Don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora, Lieutenant of Royal Officials of the Royal Treasury, granted general power of attorney to Don Santos García, a resident of the city traveling to Santiago de Veragua, and secondarily to Don Juan Martín de Icaza, also from Santiago de Veragua.

people_involved: Licenciado Presbítero don Hermenegildo de Alvarado
summary: Don Fermín de Alvarado, son of the deceased Captain don José de Alvarado and doña Úrsula López Conejo, made his will before an upcoming trip to Tierra Firme. He declared himself single, owned a cacao plantation in Matina managed by Tomás Maroto, and noted a debt owed to him by his uncle, Licenciado Presbítero don Hermenegildo de Alvarado. He and his brother don Joaquín de Alvarado were guardians of their seven siblings, and he named his brothers don Elías de Arleguí and don José Francisco de Alvarado as executors, with several other siblings as heirs.

people_involved: Licenciado Presbítero don Juan Salvador del Aya y Bolívar
summary: Capitán Vicente Andrés Polo and his wife doña Josefa Teresa Martínez Gamboa, residents of La Mata Redonda, obligated themselves for 300 pesos of silver to the chaplaincy founded by doña Cecilia Vázquez de Coronado. Licenciado Presbítero don Juan Salvador del Aya y Bolívar, interim priest of Esparza, was the patron and chaplain. They mortgaged a large cattle ranch in La Mata Redonda, previously owned by don Francisco Javier de Iglesias, and their current country estate with its fences, sugar mill, tiled house, and cane fields.

people_involved: Presbítero Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero
Capitán don Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra
summary: Capitán José Miguel de Céspedes and his wife doña Ignacia de Miranda purchased a cacao hacienda named El Hermoso in the Matina valley from doña María Josefa Cabral, a widow. The purchase included the obligation to recognize existing debts on the property. With ecclesiastical approval, they committed to 240 pesos for a chaplaincy founded by don Francisco Valenzuela, 500 pesos for a chaplaincy founded by doña Manuela de Salazar, and 900 pesos for a chaplaincy founded by Bachiller don Gregorio de Moya, leaving the hacienda mortgaged.

Juan Manuel and Gaspar de Ángulo, free mulattoes and sons of the late Alférez Diego de Ángulo, obligated themselves to their mother Felipa de Chavarría and their two sisters, Micaela Jerónima (a widow) and Josefa (a minor), who lived with their mother. They received a cacao hacienda in Matina with 1265 trees and acknowledged the shared ownership of the hacienda, which they were to administer until a division could be made.

locations: Fuerte de San Fernando de Matina
summary: An attempt was made to record the will of Capitán don Francisco Antonio de Echaves, the current Alcaide of Fuerte de San Fernando de Matina, a native and resident of Guatemala. However, the process was interrupted because the testator suffered an accident, becoming incoherent and speaking out of his mind from midnight on February 19 until around 11:30 AM on February 21, preventing the will from being completed.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco Javier de Sites
summary: Capitán Bartolomé de León and his wife doña Benita de Bonilla obligated themselves for 100 pesos of cacao to doña María Leonida de Ocampo. Doña María Leonida, a minor, was the legitimate daughter of Capitán don Nicolás de Ocampo and doña Manuela Bastardea, and was under the guardianship of Capitán don Francisco Javier de Sites.

people_involved: Presbítero Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero
Sargento Mayor don Julián García de Argueta
