summary: Presbítero Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero, acting with power of attorney for don Diego Guerrero, a resident of Granada, Nicaragua, leased Guerrero's productive cacao haciendas in Matina to Sargento Mayor don Julián García de Argueta for one year and 200 pesos. The power of attorney mentioned Guerrero's cousin, Padre Gregorio Corrales, and his uncle, don Dionisio, and noted that Guerrero was married to doña Francisca.

José Matías Chavarría sold five caballerías of land in El Barbudal to Francisco Andrés Morera, a resident of Esparza. Chavarría had acquired these lands from his mother-in-law, Manuela Masís, noting that two of the five caballerías belonged to his two absent brothers-in-law. The price was 200 pesos in local goods.

people_involved: Presbítero Licenciado don Gregorio del Corral
Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
summary: Presbítero Licenciado don Gregorio del Corral and Capitán don Tomás López del Corral granted general power of attorney to Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Pacheco.

Doña Luisa de Miranda, a widow, sold a house in 'this city' to José Miguel Solís. In exchange, Solís gave her a thatched house in El Ojo de Agua and 200 pesos. Solís's wife, doña Francisca de Miranda, appeared on his behalf. A marginal note indicates a debt cancellation in 1748.

people_involved: doña Petronila de Quirós y Ángulo
summary: Doña Teresa de Sandoval, daughter of Capitán Manuel de Sandoval Golfín and doña Petronila de Quirós y Ángulo, and widow of don José Felipe Bermúdez, made her will. Her daughter, doña Juana Bermúdez, was married to don Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra, and she had several grandchildren named de Ibarra. Her son, don José Antonio Bermúdez, was deceased.

people_involved: Capitán don Pedro González de León
summary: Doña Josefa Pérez de Muro, a widow, granted power of attorney to her son, don Antonio de Bairos, to represent her in a lawsuit against Capitán don Pedro González de León concerning the ownership of a cattle ranch and lands in Santa Ana.

people_involved: Capitán don Pedro González de León
Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo
summary: Capitán don Pedro González de León granted general power of attorney to Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo.

people_involved: Capitán don Esteban Ruiz de Mendoza
Presbítero Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdova
summary: Capitán don Esteban Ruiz de Mendoza sold an enslaved woman named Gertrudis de la Flor, approximately 30 years old, whom he had purchased from the deceased Presbítero don Vicente Morales. The purchase was made by Presbítero Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdova, acting on behalf of doña Francisca Casco y Vilches, a widow and resident of León de Nicaragua, for 260 pesos in silver.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan José de Cuende
Capitán don Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra
summary: Capitán Tomás Calvo and his wife Victoria de Lascares obligated themselves for 100 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Bachiller don Gregorio de Moya. This sum was previously held by Capitán José Nicolás del Haya, who paid interest to Capitán don Juan José de Cuende for the studies of his son, Juan Fermín. The change of debtor was made with the consent of Capitán don Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra, the patron of the chaplaincy, and they mortgaged their house.
Don Romualdo Oriamuno canceled a debt, acknowledging receipt of the owed sum from Gregorio Calvo. Joaquín Ortiz subsequently took responsibility for the debt.

Doña María Manuela Palacios made her will. She was the widow of Juan González, with whom she had a son, José Antonio, whose inheritance was held by Juan Morera. She was currently married to Tomás Galarza, and named Manuel González Coronel and Juan Rodríguez de Robredo as her executors.

Doña Ana de Escalante Paniagua made her will, detailing her family and bequests. She was the daughter of deceased José Escalante Paniagua and Manuela Martel, and had been married twice, first to Juan Sáenz, with whom she had four children, and then to Juan de Torres. She arranged for her house to be given to Manuela Vázquez and left clothing and a box to Francisco Ramón, a child she raised.

Doña Antonia de Granda y Balvín made her will in Cartago, at the house of Manuel Meléndez. She was the natural daughter of the deceased Governor Lorenzo de Granda y Balvín and Nicolasa Guerrero, and was married to Tomás de la Madriz. She made provisions for her slaves, including granting freedom to Joaquín and ordering the sale of María Josefa de Alvarado for funeral expenses.

Presbítero Licenciado Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero and Capitán José de Mier Cevallos, acting as executors for doña Catarina González Camino, granted freedom to Antonia, a mulata slave. This act was carried out in accordance with the deceased's testamentary wishes.

Capitán José Manuel Jiménez de Luna and his wife, doña Ana García de Argueta, obligated themselves to their children, Ramón and Bárbara, for 575 pesos inherited from their grandmother, doña Catarina González Camino. They mortgaged 575 cacao trees from Hacienda San Juan, which Ana García de Argueta had received as part of her first husband's estate.

José Alejo Pérez, with Capitán Martín de Garayar as his guarantor, obligated himself for 100 pesos to the Convento de San Francisco de Esparza. The sum was offered by Capitán Francisco Pérez de Cote and delivered to Pérez with the consent of Francisco Fernández de la Pastora, the Síndico General of the Franciscan religious order.
Capitán Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra granted freedom to his slave, Micaela de Ibarra. He had inherited her from his parents and acknowledged her good service and her role in raising him.

Capitán Gaspar Arias, a resident of Valle de Barba, sold a 17-year-old mulato slave named Juan José Jiménez to Capitán Miguel de Alvarado for 200 silver pesos. Arias had previously purchased the slave from Licenciado Antonio de Guevara.

Doña María Marín de Laguna made a codicil to her will, originally dated May 14, 1745. She bequeathed her house, which had a 300-peso chaplaincy, to her nieces, daughters of her brother Juan Marín and María de Bonilla. She also made provisions for a chaplaincy on her hacienda and left specific items to her nieces.

Presbítero Bachiller Juan de Pomar y Burgos sold a 26-year-old Caravalí slave named José to Maestre de Campo Francisco Fernández de la Pastora for 300 silver pesos. The slave had been acquired from the Real Asiento before the fire in Panamá City, when José Davison was the Factor.

Francisco Fernández de la Pastora purchased a 24-year-old mulato slave named Francisco Cubero from Sargento Mayor José Antonio de Oriamuno, who was acting on behalf of the estate of doña Catarina González Camino. Francisco Cubero, born in Catarina's house, had been a runaway but had since reappeared.

Don Pedro José de Alvarado, son of the deceased Sargento Mayor Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón and Angela de Guevara, provided a dowry of 1075 pesos for his future wife, doña María Manuela de Baeza. The dowry included two mulata slaves, Águeda and her daughter María Manuela, along with various valuable items and clothing.

Don Eugenio de Cubillo, from the jurisdiction of Bagaces and acting as administrator of his mother's assets, sold a 25-year-old mulato slave named Marcos de Arleguí to Capitán José Nicolas de Bonilla for 250 silver pesos. The slave had originally been purchased from Ramón Noguera.

José Felipe Jiménez, acting as attorney for his grandmother Sebastiana de Quirós, committed to pay 50 pesos in cacao to Juan Francisco Lafons. This payment was a result of a lawsuit concerning the estate of the deceased Francisco Lafons Vidor, who was Juan Francisco Lafons' legitimate father.

Presbítero Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero granted freedom to his mulatto slave, José Cubero, who was approximately 27 years old. José Cubero had been inherited by Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero from his mother, Catalina González del Camino.

Capitán Tomás Calvo made his will, identifying himself as the legitimate son of the deceased Francisco Calvo and María Araujo. He was married to María Victoria Lascares and listed their children as Josefa, Gabriela, Gregorio, Francisco, and Tilmos. His assets included a house with a complete blacksmith forge.

Alférez Juan de Mesa and his wife María Jerónima committed to pay 100 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Luisa Hernández. This payment was for building materials from a house provided by Juana de las Salas, the widow of Francisco Solano. They mortgaged a house that had previously belonged to Alférez Francisco Fernández.

Maestre de Campo don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora, Lieutenant of Royal Officials of the Royal Treasury, revoked all previous powers of attorney. He then granted general power to don Francisco Pérez Mere, and in his absence or default, to don Miguel Díaz, both of whom were business agents in the Royal Councils of Madrid.

Doña Sebastiana de Quirós made her will, identifying herself as the legitimate daughter of the deceased Sebastián de Quirós and Isabel de Guevara, and the widow of Diego de Quesada. She had five living daughters: Juana, Manuela, Josefa Cayetana, Micaela, and Catarina, with the first two and the last already paid their inheritance. She bequeathed a cacao plantation in Matina to her remaining daughters and a 1500-tree plot to her grandson, José Felipe Jiménez, who, along with her daughter Josefa Cayetana, were named executors.

Gertrudis Ruiz made her will, stating she was the legitimate daughter of the deceased Juan Ruiz Guillen and María Rodríguez. She was first married to Juan Ginés de Hinojosa, with whom she had four daughters: Francisca (married to Miguel Matamoros), Gertrudis (married to Francisco Orozco), Josefa (married to Sargento Mayor José de Chaves), and Catalina (married to Capitán José Manuel Segura). Her second marriage was to Francisco Gutiérrez, with whom she had a son who died before marrying.

Sargento Mayor don Julián García de Argueta, acting on behalf of Diego Guerrero (who was in Matina and had purchased the 'El Hermoso' cacao plantation from the heirs of Capitán José Miguel de Céspedes), committed to several payments. These included 240 pesos to a chaplaincy founded by don Francisco Valenzuela, 500 pesos to one founded by doña Manuela de Salazar (with Presbítero Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero as chaplain), and 200 pesos to a chaplaincy ordered by Bachiller don Gregorio de Moya.

Doña María Manuela Palacios made her will, identifying herself as the natural daughter of doña Francisca de Bonilla. She was the widow of Juan González, with whom she had a son named José Antonio. She had married a second time to don Tomás Galarza, but had no children with him.
The minor Juan Antonio Rodríguez was formally handed over to José Carrillo, a master blacksmith, for a period of seven years, presumably as an apprentice.

Manuel Felipe Alarcón, a resident of Ujarraz, made his will. He was the legitimate son of the deceased Agustín Alarcón and Juliana Guerrero, and was married to María Abarca. His surviving children were Vicente (married) and Manuela (single). This document, along with the four preceding ones, was granted before Teniente General don Juan José de Cuende.

people_involved: José Cayetano de la Madriz Linares
Luis Fernando de Liendo y Goicoechea
José Antonio de Liendo y Goicoechea
summary: Proceedings for the opening of doña Baltasara de Inza's will took place on January 3, 1747, the day she died at sunrise, having made her will on December 30, 1746. She was the legitimate daughter of Domingo de Inza and Alfonsa Muñoz Hidalgo, first married to Luis Fernando de Liendo y Goicoechea (with whom she had four sons: José Antonio, Manuel, Lucas, and Diego), and second to Diego Morras y Maulcón (with no children). Her will specified bequests to her husband and mother, designated her mulatto slave Antonia to serve her children, and named Licenciado don Manuel García de Argueta, Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco, and her sister doña Sebastiana de Inza as executors.

Licenciado Presbítero don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero sold a mulatto slave named Rita Cubero, approximately 20 years old, to Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla for 250 pesos plata. Rita Cubero had been inherited by Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero from his mother, doña Catalina González del Camino.

people_involved: Licenciado Presbítero don Antonio de Guevara Sáenz
Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla
summary: Licenciado Presbítero don Antonio de Guevara Sáenz sells an enslaved man named José Guerrero to Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla for 300 silver pesos. Guevara Sáenz had previously purchased José Guerrero from don Francisco Guerrero, a resident of Santiago Alanje.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo
Capitán don Antonio Elias de Arleguí
summary: The will of Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo, Captain Alcaide of Fuerte de San Fernando, is granted by his wife, doña Gabriela Josefa de Arleguí, acting by power of attorney. The will details his parentage, his marriage to doña Gabriela Josefa, their seven legitimate children, and mentions accounts with don Juan Antonio de Arce in Granada. Licenciado don José Hermenegildo and Capitán don Antonio Elias de Arleguí, brothers of doña Gabriela Josefa, are named as executors.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
Sargento Mayor Antonio de Soto y Barahona
don Tomás de Soto y Barahona
Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero
Presbítero Licenciado don Hermenegildo de Alvarado
summary: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral and doña Francisca de Ibarra assume an obligation for 500 pesos related to a chaplaincy founded by Sargento Mayor Antonio de Soto y Barahona, whose patrons are doña Petronila de Hoces and don Tomás de Soto y Barahona. They also take on a 100-peso obligation for the Cofradía del Rosario, currently managed by Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero. These sums were previously the responsibility of Presbítero Licenciado don Hermenegildo de Alvarado, and a hacienda is mortgaged.

people_involved: Licenciado don Raimundo Antonio de Estrada
Teniente don Julián García de Argueta
don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro
summary: Catalina Simona de Torres, widow of Francisco Guerrero, establishes a chaplaincy for the suffrage of her late husband's soul, fulfilling his unfinished will. Francisco Guerrero's brother, Diego Guerrero, completed the will, naming himself as patron and Licenciado don Raimundo Antonio de Estrada as chaplain. The chaplaincy was visited on March 23, 1747, by don Félix Esteban de Hoces Navarro.

Catalina Simona de Torres obligates herself to her children, Blas de la Candelaria, Manuela Petronila, and Ana Manuela Guerrero, for their paternal inheritance from Francisco Guerrero's estate. She mortgages her cacao hacienda, which is already encumbered by the chaplaincy mentioned in the previous document.

people_involved: Teniente don Benito de Alvarado Jirón
doña María Leonida de Ocampo Golfín
Capitán don Gil de Alvarado Jirón
Capitán don Nicolás de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Teniente don Benito de Alvarado Jirón and his wife, doña María Leonida de Ocampo Golfín, attempt to sell two caballerías of land named "Las Maderas Negras" in the "Las Piedras" site to Capitán don Gil de Alvarado Jirón, their father and father-in-law. Doña María Leonida inherited this land from her father, Capitán don Nicolás de Ocampo Golfín, for 30 silver pesos, but the transaction did not go through.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
summary: Don José Zayas Bazán, a native of Havana residing in Cartago, grants power of attorney to Capitán don Tomás López del Corral to collect a debt of 993 pesos and 4 reales from don Juan José Escobedo. Escobedo is described as a native of Seville, between 35 and 40 years old, with specific facial features.

people_involved: Capitán don Pedro González de León
doña Magdalena Suárez de los Cabos
doña María Josefa Barros y Carvajal
summary: Capitán don Pedro González de León, a native of Puerto de Cubillero in Asturias, makes his will. He details his parentage, his two marriages (first to doña María Martínez, second to doña María Josefa Barros y Carvajal), and his children from the first marriage: Juana María, Joaquín (deceased), and Petronila González de León. He also mentions being responsible for 225 pesos belonging to the children of don Juan Francisco Sáenz and doña Francisca Martínez, and orders the foundation of a chaplaincy.

people_involved: Presbítero Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero
summary: Presbítero Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero grants freedom to Manuela Cubero, a "mulata blanca" about 25 years old, whom he acquired from her mother, doña Catalina González Camino. In exchange for her freedom, he receives 150 silver pesos from Manuela Cubero.

people_involved: Coronel don Juan Gemmir y Lleonart
Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
Capitán don Juan Martín de Icaza
summary: Coronel don Juan Gemmir y Lleonart, Governor and Captain General, grants power of attorney to Capitán don Tomás López del Corral and Capitán don Juan Martín de Icaza (a resident of Santiago Alanje) to sell two enslaved "negras criollas" from Havana. These are Josefa de los Angeles Aviles, about 35 years old, and Andrea Carmena, about 26 years old, both purchased in Havana years prior.

people_involved: Presbítero Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero
summary: Presbítero Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero, acting as heir and executor of his deceased mother, doña Catalina González Camino, and with the Visitador General's license, founds a chaplaincy. He serves as both patron and chaplain, funding it with 550 cacao pesos secured by a cacao hacienda in Matina with 1500 new trees.

people_involved: Presbítero Licenciado don Manuel José González Coronel
summary: Presbítero Licenciado don Manuel José González Coronel, Mayordomo of the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora de la Concepción in the Convento de Cartago, seeks to transfer a chaplaincy of 500 cacao pesos, originally founded by Capitán Diego de Aguilar on a house, to his own hacienda of 3,000 new cacao trees in the Valle de Matina. He obtained the Visitador General's license, and the Deputies agree to the change.

people_involved: don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda
summary: A Cofradía (Brotherhood) was mentioned with don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda, don Manuel Cayetano de Guevara, don José Antonio de Bonilla, and don Miguel Antonio Fajardo as members. The Cofradía was noted as 'No pasó', indicating it was not formalized or approved.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad
Presbítero Licenciado don José Miguel de Arburola y Ribarén
summary: Doña Antonia Josefa de Arburola, widow of Sargento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad, made her will. She listed her deceased parents, deceased husband, nine children (one deceased), and two deceased siblings. Her daughter Doña Josefa Lorenza is married to don Luis Arnesto de Troya.

people_involved: Presbítero Licenciado don Juan Bautista Pérez de Cote
Presbítero don Antonio de Guevara Sáenz
summary: Pablo Solórzano and his wife María Josefa Lizondo obligated themselves for 170 pesos cacao to Manuel Antonio de Alfaro, representing his inheritance from his deceased parents Francisco Alfaro and Manuela Pérez. They paid the sum to Manuel Antonio's tutor, Presbítero Licenciado don Juan Bautista Pérez de Cote, and then transferred the obligation to Presbítero don Antonio de Guevara Sáenz, offering a site inherited from Tomás de Chaves plus 20 pesos cacao.

The obligation made by Pablo Solórzano and María Josefa Lizondo was declared null and void in 1750. This was because Capitán don Juan de Ocampo opposed the transfer, claiming ownership of the site offered as collateral.

Gabriel Narciso Maroto, natural son of the deceased Capitán Gabriel Maroto and Manuela de Segura, made his will. He was single and without children, owned a hacienda in Matina and two racehorses, and owed a horse to his sister Antonia Ramírez. Teniente Cristóbal de Quesada was named his executor.

Doña Ana Antonia de Guevara, whose husband Teniente don Cayetano de Alvarado was absent in Peru, obligated herself for 250 pesos cacao to a capellanía founded by don Pedro Ibáñez. The sum, previously owed by Doña Manuela Sáenz and redeemed by Doña Angela Sáenz, was secured by a cacao plantation in Matina, specifically in La Potiteziiela. Don José Francisco de Alvarado acted as attorney for the capellanía's patron and chaplain, Beneficiado don Manuel López Conejo.

people_involved: Beneficiado don Juan Salvador del Aya y Bolívar
summary: Don Juan José de Cuende, Notary of the Holy Office, and his wife Doña Manuela de Ibarra obligated themselves for 550 pesos plata for a capellanía, 150 pesos for the parish of Esparza, and 200 pesos for the Convent of Esparza. These sums were delivered by Capitán Cristóbal de Umaña, and the obligation was secured by their hato 'La Laguna' in the valley of LanJecho, which they committed to maintain.

Fermín de Amador, widower of Antonia Masís, obligated himself to his sons José Tomás, José Francisco, and Manuel Vicente de Amador for 111 pesos 6.5 reales, representing their maternal inheritance. This sum was liquidated from the estate of his mother-in-law, María del Carmen Salazar. He also received the inheritance share of his deceased son, Isidro Cayetano, who died after Antonia Masís.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don José Antonio de Oriamuño
Capitán don Miguel Cayetaño de Ibarra
don Juan Francisco de Ibarra Calvo
summary: Sargento Mayor don José Antonio de Oriamuño transferred 1400 pesos plata from a capellanía, founded by don Juan Francisco de Ibarra Calvo, to Capitán don Miguel Cayetaño de Ibarra and his wife Doña Juana Gertrudis Bermúdez. The transfer was secured by a hacienda in Matina.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don José Antonio de Oriamuño
Sargento Mayor don Manuel de Saborío
summary: Sargento Mayor don José Antonio de Oriamuño sold a pasture named Sarchí, located within Poás, for 100 pesos to Capitanes don Martín de Garayar and Alonso de Porras. Oriamuño had acquired this site from Sargento Mayor don Manuel de Saborío in 1739, excluding a portion previously sold by Doña Ana Rodríguez de Castro to Capitán Francisco de Flores.

people_involved: Capitán don Esteban Ruiz de Mendoza
Ayudante General don José Antonio de Bonilla
summary: Capitán don Esteban Ruiz de Mendoza granted special power of attorney to Ayudante General don José Antonio de Bonilla to collect 103 pesos 6 reales from the estate of don Juan Rodríguez Robredo.
Don José de Sierra, who was Capitán Alcaide of the Fuerte de San Fernando, died in the valley of Matina at the end of 1743.

people_involved: Maestre de Campo don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Maestre de Campo don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora and his wife Doña Francisca de Arburola formalized an obligation. Don Francisco, as executor of the late don José de Sierra, had been entrusted with 5643 pesos 1 real from Sierra's estate by Visitador don Luis Diez Navarro. After various payments and his own claim, and at the Gobernador's request before his departure to Talamanca, they acknowledged holding 5322 pesos 6 reales in deposit from the estate.
Alférez Salvador de Mendoza, acting as attorney for Doña Rosa Maldonado, the widow of don José de Sierra, received 1000 pesos from the estate.
Doña Angela Sáenz, a widow, leased a cacao hacienda in Matina to Juan Pascual Bejarano, a free pardo, for three years at 40 pesos annually.

people_involved: Capitán José Nicolás de la Haya
General don Diego de la Haya
María Nicolasa Geralda de la Haya
summary: Capitán José Nicolás de la Haya, a native of Panamá and natural son of General don Diego de la Haya and Isabel María Márquez, made his will. He was married to María Josefa Chavarría, with whom he had a daughter, María Nicolasa Geralda de la Haya. He mentioned his wife's cacao hacienda in La Reventazón, his own cacao plantations in Barbilla, and a site in Ujarraz valley previously owned by Licenciado don Francisco de Moya. He also mentioned his brother-in-law José Matías Chavarría, Manuel Fonseca, and a debt owed by José Camacho.

Maestre de Campo Francisco Fernández de la Pastora, who is the principal leader of the conquest in Talamanca, and his wife Francisca de Arburola y Ribaren, grant each other reciprocal power to make a will. This action is taken before his upcoming trip to the Talamanca mountains.
Doña Clara de Vida Martel, a widow, sells a straw house constructed with posts and wattle-and-daub, along with half a plot of land located in this city, to José Manuel Campos for 92 pesos.

Captain Pedro de Alvarado sells a house made of posts and adobe, covered with tiles, located on the outskirts of this city, to Alférez José Alejo Calvo for 382 pesos cacao. The property is burdened with 132 pesos for the tutelage of minors Petronila and Rita de Velazco, and 100 pesos for a chaplaincy patroned by Beneficiado Juan José Camacho. The buyer assumes these debts, and the property previously belonged to Doña Clara de Vida Martel.

people_involved: María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
summary: Ana Morales sells her 16-year-old enslaved mulatta, Lorenza Cabral, to Don Diego José de Toledo, a resident of Granada, for 260 pesos plata. The payment was delivered by Captain Don Mateo Ayón (Ayllon), and Lorenza Cabral had previously been owned by Doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral.

Doña Alfonsa Muñoz Hidalgo, legitimate daughter of Bartolomé Muñoz Hidalgo and Sebastiana Calvo, makes her will. She was married to (name broken) Inza and had five married daughters, including Francisca, Sebastiana, Baltasara, and Isabel. Her deceased daughter Baltasara, who was married to Luis de Goicoechea, left a legacy for her children, and her sons-in-law Nicolás de Sierra and Diego Morraz are named as executors.

Juan Rafael Ramírez and his wife Micaela de Chinchilla sell the land where they currently reside to Ventura Lizondo. The property measures 112 varas from North to South and 200 varas from East to West, situated next to the Las Cañas (also known as Tatiscú) river.

people_involved: José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Doña Josefa Pérez del Muro, legitimate daughter of the deceased José Pérez del Muro and Mariana de Echavarría, and widow of Captain Diego de Barros y Carvajal, makes her will. She lists her children, including José Antonio, María Josefa, María Manuela, Mariana, and Juana (who is single), and details her possessions, which include three enslaved individuals: Antonio (criollo), Francisco (bozal), and Juan Antonio (mulatto). Her son-in-law is José de Velazco, and her executors are Licenciado José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría and her nephew Licenciado Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba.

Doña Juana Gertrudis de Bermúdez, legitimate daughter of the deceased Sargento Mayor José Felipe Bermúdez and María Teresa de Sandoval, grants power to make a will to her husband, Captain Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra. Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra is the Teniente General of the Matina valley, and they have five children: Juan Francisco, Ramona, Joaquina Manuela, Vicenta, and Eulalia de Ibarra.

Captain Francisco Gamboa, legitimate son of Ignacio de Aguilar and Inés de Gamboa from the Aserrí valley, makes his will. He was previously married to Francisca Lorenza de Quesada, with whom he had three sons who all died without succession, and is now married to María de la Paz Gómez without children. He orders the founding of a chaplaincy, naming Teniente Cristóbal de Quesada or his eldest son Francisco de Quesada as patron, and mentions his stepson Francisco Antonio Gamboa.

Juan Antonio Masís, legitimate son of Matías Masís and María del Car (name broken), makes his will. He names his brother Francisco Masís, his cousin Bartola Ancheta, and his aunt Manuela Ortiz. His uncle, Alférez Manuel de Alvarado, is appointed as his executor, and his brother Juan (?) Martín Masís is designated as his heir.

people_involved: Elias de la Cruz de Chaves
summary: Ana Solano, a resident of the Barba valley and legitimate daughter of the deceased Gaspar Solano and Margarita Chacón, makes her will. She is the widow of Captain Juan José de Chaves and lists her eight children, two of whom are married. Felipe de Ocampu is mentioned as her son-in-law.

people_involved: Fray Manuel de Liendo y Goicoechea
summary: Don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda and his wife Doña Baltasara Madriz obligate themselves for 100 pesos in favor of the four minor children of Doña Baltasara Muñoz Hidalgo and Don Luis de Goicoechea. A marginal note from 1753 indicates that Don Nicolás de Sierra, as the testamentary executor of Fray Manuel de Liendo y Goicoechea, confirmed receiving these 100 pesos.

Teniente José Antonio Masís and his wife Doña Juana Francisca Mondragón obligate themselves for 100 pesos at 5% interest to a chaplaincy ordered to be founded by Doña Baltasara Muñoz Hidalgo. A marginal note from 1753 states that Don José Nicolás de Bonilla later assumed this obligation.

Alférez Don José de Velazco and his wife Doña Mariana de Barros y Carvajal obligate themselves for 1000 pesos at 5% interest for several chaplaincies and confraternities. This includes funds for the chaplaincies of Vasco and Pedro Solano, the Cofradía de la Concepción, the Cofradía del Rosario, and a parish fund from Sargento Mayor Miguel Gómez de Lara, as well as advances made by Licenciado Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero on a house previously owned by Padre Diego de Campos.

Captain Don Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra, Teniente General of the Matina valley and executor of his mother-in-law Doña María Teresa de Sandoval, founds a chaplaincy of recited masses. This chaplaincy is for the repose of the souls of the founder, her husband José Felipe Bermúdez, her son Don José Antonio, and her mother Doña Petronila de Quirós. The capital of 190 pesos cacao is located on the cacao hacienda that Bermúdez owned in the Matina valley, at a place called La Pontezuela.

A capellanía (chaplaincy) is established, with Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra designated as the Capellán. The terms specify that if none of the grantor's sons are ordained, the capellanía will pass to the sons of the grantor's brothers.

Agustín Ramírez, a brother of the third order, makes his will. He details his parentage, his previous marriage to Lorenza Marín with whom he had sons Manuel and Alejo, and his current marriage to Manuela Josefa Rivera with whom he has a daughter Juana Antonia.

Doña Juana Gertrudis Bermúdez's will is processed through her widower and proxy, Don Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra. Her children, Juan Francisco, Ramona, Joaquina, Manuela, Vicenta, and Eulalia de Ibarra, are named as heirs.

people_involved: Don Juan Bautista Gemmir y Lleonart
Don Ignacio Antonio Gemmir y Lleonart
Doña María de Loreto Gemmir y Lleonart
Doña María de la Concepción Gemmir y Lleonart
summary: Don Juan Gemmir y Lleonart, the Gobernador y Capitán General, being ill, grants power to his wife, Doña Mariana Crespité de Mora, to make his will. This new will is to align with a joint will they made in Havana in 1733, and he requests burial in the Santa Iglesia Parroquial of "esta ciudad" (Cartago).

people_involved: Licenciado Don Manuel José González Coronel
summary: Juan Rafael Ramírez and his wife Micaela de Chinchilla add a codicil to their 1744 will. They confirm that four sons and three daughters have been married and provided for, and they order the founding of a capellanía from a fifth of their estate, with the first ordained descendant or Licenciado Don Manuel José González Coronel serving as Capellán.

people_involved: Don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
Licenciado Don Andrés Patricio de Oconor
summary: Following the death of Teniente Coronel Don Juan Gemmir y Lleonart, Maestre de Campo Don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora assumes the role of Gobernador de armas and grants general power to Presbítero Licenciado Don Andrés Patricio de Oconor and Don José Bazán, both residing in León de Nicaragua.

people_involved: Licenciado Don Andrés Patricio de Oconor
summary: Doña Mariana Crespité de Mora, widow of Don Juan Gemmir y Lleonart, grants power to Presbítero Licenciado Don Andrés Patricio de Oconor to collect her deceased husband's salaries from the Cajas de León, covering the period up to his death on November 5th of the same year.

people_involved: Presbítero Licenciado Don Juan José Camacho
Beneficiado Don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones
summary: Presbítero Licenciado Don Juan José Camacho obliges himself for 100 pesos to a capellanía founded by Luis Cascante de Rojas, currently served by Beneficiado Don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones. This sum was previously held by Capitán Don Andrés de Salazar and secured by a property in the valley of Iscasú, which Camacho acquired with this encumbrance.

people_involved: Coronel Don Gaspar Porcel y Bustamante
Don Juan Bautista Gemmir y Lleonart
Don Ignacio Antonio Gemmir y Lleonart
Doña María Loreto Gemmir y Lleonart
Doña María de la Concepción Gemmir y Lleonart
summary: Don Juan Gemmir y Lleonart's testament is processed by his widow and proxy, Doña Mariana Crespité de Mora. The document details her previous marriage to Coronel Don Gaspar Porcel y Bustamante, their two sons born in Havana, and the 7300 pesos she brought into her marriage with Gemmir y Lleonart. It also mentions 880 pesos in jewelry left in Havana with Don José Fernández Romero.

Doña Engracia de Hoces Navarro, a widow, obliges herself for 207 pesos 4 reales to Juan Francisco Lafons. This sum was received from her daughter, Gabriela de Arleguí, whose deceased husband, Capitán Don Juan Rodríguez Robredo, had been the depositary of goods belonging to the deceased Doña María Leonor de Miranda.

people_involved: Doña Antonia de la Granda y Balvín
summary: Don Tomás de la Madriz, widower of Doña Antonia de la Granda y Balvín, grants freedom to a mulatto named Joaquín, approximately 4 years old, in accordance with his deceased wife's will.

people_involved: Capitán Don Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra
summary: Capitán Don Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra obliges himself to his children for 4684 pesos 2 reales, representing their maternal inheritance from the estate of their grandmother, Doña Teresa de Sandoval.

locations: casa del Ayudante Manuel de Alvarado
people_involved: Don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
Don José Cayetano de la Madriz Linares
summary: Proceedings are held for the opening of Juan Rafael Ramírez's sealed will, originally made on January 25, 1744. He died on December 10, 1747, and his body was recognized the following day at Ayudante Manuel de Alvarado's house. The document details his family, including his parents, wife, and numerous children.

Doña Mariana Crespité de Mora, widow of Don Juan Gemmir y Lleonart, grants power to Don Juan Feliciano Ramírez and Don José Briceño, residents of León, to collect her deceased husband's outstanding salaries from the Real Caja.

people_involved: Capitán Don José Nicolás de Bonilla
summary: Capitán Don José Nicolás de Bonilla grants power to Don Pedro José de Alvarado, who is traveling to Nicaragua, to sell a 20-year-old slave named Rita Cubero.

people_involved: Teniente Coronel Don Luis Diez Navarro
Brigadier Don Alonso Fernández de Heredia
summary: Teniente Coronel Don Luis Diez Navarro, having been appointed to "this government" by Brigadier Don Alonso Fernández de Heredia, provides guarantors for his residency.

Capitán Francisco Esquivel obligates himself for 131 pesos to Juan Antonio de Arias, the minor son of the deceased Tomás Arias. Sargento Mayor Diego de Soto acts as guarantor for Esquivel in this transaction.
Don Diego Jurado, a trader from the Reino de Tierra Firme, sells an enslaved man named Antonio, approximately 30 years old, to Capitán don Juan de Aguilar, a resident of Nicaragua, for 250 pesos.

Doña María Manuela de Quesada, widow of Capitán Sebastián de Sandoval, sells a plot of land in Poás to Sargento Mayor Diego de Soto for 100 pesos. The land is described by its boundaries, including the Trancas and Vigía rivers, the royal road to Sarchí, and the mountain.
Doña María Manuela de Quesada sells an enslaved man named Manuel Antonio to Sargento Mayor Diego de Soto for 400 pesos cacao. This transaction follows a previous land sale between the same parties.

Sargento Mayor Diego de Soto and his wife, Doña Sebastiana Jiménez, obligate themselves for 400 pesos to a chaplaincy founded by Capitán Sebastián de Sandoval. They received the sum from Doña María Manuela de Quesada and hypothecate a dwelling house and a sugar mill house as security.

Luisa Martina de Oses makes her will, identifying herself as the natural daughter of Candelaria de los Santos and an unnamed father, and previously married to an unnamed person and then Gregorio Carbonero. Having no children, she names Tomasa de la Cruz, Nicolás Víctor, and Brígida de la Concepción, whom she raised, as her heirs.

A dowry letter is issued for José Miguel González, son of Francisco González, in favor of his wife Martina de Ugalde, legitimate daughter of Capitán Juan de Ugalde and María Rosa Rodríguez. Capitán Pedro Jiménez, Martina's brother-in-law and tutor, delivered goods worth 373 pesos and 6 reales.

people_involved: Pb° don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
Sargento Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo
Doña María Magdalena Pérez de Luna
summary: An unsigned and unfinished will belongs to Presbyter don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín. He is identified as the legitimate son of the deceased Sargento Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo and Doña María Magdalena Pérez de Luna.

Capitán Cayetano de Herrera obligates himself for 236 pesos to his grandchildren: Pedro Cayetano, Antonia Josefa, Bartola Josefa, Juana Josefa, and Juan Francisco. These grandchildren are the children of his daughter, María de Herrera.

people_involved: Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto
summary: Sargento Mayor Diego de Soto makes his will, identifying his parents as Capitán Diego de San Martín y Soto and Doña .... Zamora, and his wife as Doña Sebastiana Jiménez. He lists his children and details assets including building materials for a house, which Capitán Francisco de Segura is contracted to build.

people_involved: Señor Cura don Juan de Pomar y Burgos
summary: A dowry letter is issued for Capitán Matías de Sandoval, legitimate son of Capitán Cayetano de Sandoval and Doña Teresa Paniai^ua, in favor of his wife Doña Juana de León. The dowry goods, valued at 1209 pesos, were delivered by Señor Cura don Juan de Pomar y Burgos.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Capitán Andrés de Ocampo and his wife Juliana Solera make their wills. Andrés is the natural son of the deceased Sargento Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín and María Rodri..., while Juliana is the legitimate daughter of Juan Pérez de ... and Gregoria Guti.... Their children are Rosa María, married to Basilio Carbonero, and Santiago, who died without succession after marrying Casilda Cascante; Juliana was also previously married to Tomás de Córdova.

Capitán Francisco de Chaves and Hermano Cayetano Benavides, acting as testamentary executors for Manuela Barrantes, establish a chaplaincy with a capital of 215 pesos cacao. The chaplain will be the chaplain or priest of the parish church of Cubujuquí.

Capitán Juan Alejandro de Mora makes his will in Valle de Aserrí, identifying his deceased parents as Capitán Miguel de Mora and Eugenia de Chaves, and his wife as Doña Viviana Meléndez. He has no children and mentions his aunt Clara Sánchez. An annotation notes his death by April 15 and the will's remittance by the Judge of the Fields, Don Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco Fernández de Montenegro
summary: Eugenia de Ocampo, widow of Capitán don Francisco Fernández de Montenegro, makes her will, listing her children as Viviana, Tomás, Santiago, Lucía, and Antonia Josefa. The will was executed before Don Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla, Judge of the Fields.
Francisco de Esquivel and his wife Lucía de Zamora obligate themselves for 200 pesos to a chaplaincy. They hypothecate a tiled house located behind the parish church of Valle de Barba as security.

locations: Convento de San Antonio de Currirabá
summary: Don Manuel de Hidalgo, with Capitán don Miguel de Alvarado as guarantor, obligates himself for 464 pesos 5 reales to a chaplaincy founded by Antonia López de la Flor, associated with the convent of San Antonio de Currirabá. This debt was previously owed by the deceased Alférez Patricio de Orozco, whose assets were transferred to Hidalgo by justice to cover it.
Cabo de escuadra Cayetano Morales obligates himself for 100 pesos and 5% interest to the Confraternity of the Conception, which is located in the convent of Cartago.

Rafael de Aguilar has purchased two plots of land near the Tiribí river in San Antonio for 40 pesos, one from Doña María Hidalgo and another from Jacinto de Fallas. The document is incomplete, but Aguilar is seeking information regarding possession of these lands.

Alférez Juan Suárez, owner of a house and property that belonged to the deceased Manuela Barrantes, acknowledges a chaplaincy of 215 pesos imposed on it. This chaplaincy was established by Barrantes' testamentary executors, Capitanes Francisco de Chaves and Cayetano Benavides, in favor of the parish curacy of Cubujuquí.
An unnamed individual made an obligation of 102 pesos cacao, at a rate of 100 grains per real, in favor of their legitimate children: Antonio, Nicolás, Isidro, and Baltasara.
An obligation was made for 164 pesos and 4 reales cacao in favor of Alonso and Nicolasa, the minor children of the deceased Pablo de Sibaja and María González.

people_involved: José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría, the Beneficiado, Cura, Vicar, and Ecclesiastical Judge of Cartago, granted power of attorney to Bachiller Don Andrés Patricio de Oconor and Don José Manuel Bazán, residents of León, to collect the full synod for his curacy from the Royal Coffers.

Lieutenant Francisco de la Riba and his wife, María de Acuña, obligated themselves for 100 pesos to a chaplaincy served by Presbítero Lic. Juan José Camacho. This sum, previously redeemed by Alejo Calvo, was secured by a tiled house near the Toyogres river, and they mortgaged a cacao plantation in the Barbilla valley.

Captain Julián García de Argueta obligated himself to the minor María Nicolasa Palacios for 40 pesos from her maternal inheritance, which Don José de Mier Ceballos had held. He also obligated himself to her brother, José Antonio Palacios, for 40 pesos delivered by Santiago Valverde.

Doña Mariana Crespité de Mora, widow of Don Juan Gemmir y Lleonart, sold an enslaved mulatto girl named Juana and an enslaved mulatto boy named Luis to Presbítero Lic. Don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero for 275 silver pesos.

people_involved: Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdova
summary: Doña Mariana Crespité de Mora granted general power of attorney to Presbítero Lic. Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdova.

Pedro Chinchilla and his wife, María Manuela Bascos, obligated themselves for 50 pesos to Marcos and Antonia, minor children of Manuel Chinchilla and Baltasara Leitona, with a thatched house and enclosure serving as security.

Sergeant Major Don Julián García de Argueta and his wife, Doña Ana Sánchez de Castañeda, obligated themselves for 200 pesos to the minor children of Doña Baltasara de Inza, a sum delivered by Presbítero Don Manuel Martínez Cubero. A marginal note from 1753 indicates that Captain Don Nicolás Sierra, executor of Don Manuel de Liendo y Goicoechea, confirmed receipt of this sum.
Lieutenant Nicolás Castillo and his wife, Margarita Jiménez, made an obligation in favor of the minor Juan Antonio de Mesa.
Captain Pedro Padilla, a master blacksmith, took an unnamed minor as an apprentice for six years.

Don Pedro de Alvarado y Acosta and his wife, Doña Paula González, obligated themselves for 132 pesos to Doña Petronila and Doña Rita Blasquez, minor daughters of Don Lucas Blasquez and Doña Eulalia López Conejo. This obligation was tied to a house and plantain grove near the Toyogres river, which the Alvarado-González couple had purchased from Alejo Calvo's estate.

Josefa Elena Acosta sold a plot of land for 30 pesos cacao to Captain Don Gil de Alvarado Jirón. The incomplete deed mentions the plot's borders with 'las Estrellas' to the North and walls built by Don Juan Francisco Sáenz to the South.

Don Juan Antonio Ramos sold a plot of land for 25 pesos cacao to Captain Don Luis de Sotomayor. Ramos had inherited the land from his mother, Doña Polonia de Moya, who had bequeathed it to him and her grandson, José Antonio Brenes, who is also Ramos's nephew.
María Rita de la Flor sold a plot of land to Hermano José Carranza for 30 pesos.
The minor José Bernardo Villalobos was apprenticed to master José Manuel Chinchilla for a period of six years.
Nicolás del Castillo and his wife, Margarita Jiménez, made an obligation in favor of the minor Juan Antonio, son of Gregorio de Mesa and Rosa López.
Captain José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda sold an enslaved black man named Antonio Granda, approximately 50 years old, to Captain Manuel de Guzmán Portocarrero for 100 pesos.

people_involved: Antonia de la Granda y Balvín
María Josefa de Alvarado y Torres
summary: Captain Don Tomás de la Madriz, widower of Doña Antonia de la Granda y Balvín, granted a letter of freedom to his enslaved woman, María Josefa de Alvarado y Torres.

Micaela Chinchilla, widow of Hermano Juan Rafael Ramírez, founded a chaplaincy with a capital of 123 pesos, secured by a house and its associated properties. Lic. Presbítero Don Manuel José González Coronel was named as the patron and chaplain.
Margarita Piedra, widow of Pedro Solano, sold an 18-year-old enslaved mulatto woman named María Antonia to Captain Don Tomás de Barahona for 200 pesos.
Micaela Chinchilla, a widow, sold a quarter of a 'caballería' of land located near the Ujarrás road to Sergeant Francisco Martínez for 25 pesos.

Captain Luis Bernabé Centeno, a resident of Chiriquí, granted power of attorney to Alférez Don Félix de la Riba Agüero to represent him in the Audiencia de Guatemala and seek confirmation for the public notary office he had acquired.
Micaela Chinchilla, widow of Juan Rafael Ramírez, sold a quarter of a 'caballería' of land to Salvador Pasos.
Presbítero Juan José Camacho made an obligation of 50 pesos in favor of the Cofradía de la Concepción.
Micaela Chinchilla sold a plot of land to Tomás de Urnaña for 30 pesos.

Captain Don José de Mier Ceballos sold 'La Quinta' enclosures, located in the common lands of the city in Agua Caliente, to Alférez Don Luis Arnesto de Troya for 30 pesos. He had inherited this property from his deceased wife, Doña Catarina Gon...

people_involved: María Josefa de la Trinidad Chavarría
summary: Captain Tomás López del Corral and his wife Francisca de Ibarra granted freedom to their 5-month-old slave, María Josefa de la Trinidad Chavarría. Her father, Juan Antonio Chavarría, paid 50 pesos for her liberation. María Josefa's mother, Manuela Cayetana de Moya, was also a slave of the grantors.

Don Gil de Alvarado Jirón, son of deceased parents, granted power to his wife, doña Josefa González Camino, to make his will. The will named their ten legitimate children as heirs. This document outlines the family's inheritance plans.

María Josefa Chavarría, widow of Captain José Nicolás del Haya, obligated herself to her daughter, María Nicolasa Geralda, for 569 pesos 3 reales from her inheritance. Her brother, Juan Antonio Chavarría, served as the guarantor for this obligation.

Micaela Chinchilla, widow of Juan Rafael Ramírez, obligated herself to her four children, Mariana, Lucía, Manuel Gabriel, and Fernando Joaquín Ramírez, for 134 pesos. This act secured a financial commitment to her offspring.

Sargento Mayor don Antonio de Oriamuno and his wife doña María Catarina de Ibarra sold their 35-year-old slave, Antonia Josefa, and her 2-year-old son, Miguel Antonio, to Presbítero Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero for 300 pesos and 160 pesos cacao, respectively. They noted that Antonia Josefa's husband, Vicente, also their slave, was a fugitive and would be delivered to the buyer if found.
Micaela Chinchilla sold a piece of land to Mateo Quirós for 25 pesos. The land was located next to the road leading to Ujarraz and bordered a stream.

people_involved: José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Laureano Madriz y Obando committed to performing clearing and other work for Presbítero don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría. The agreed payment for these services was 400 pesos cacao.

Captain Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, a resident of Barba valley, sold a 15-year-old black slave named Rosa de Ocampo to Captain don Tomás López del Corral, who was acting on behalf of his sister, doña María Quiteria López del Corral. Rosa de Ocampo had been acquired from the estate of the deceased Licenciado don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, and the sale price was 280 pesos plata.

The will of don Gil de Alvarado Jirón was granted by his widow and representative, doña Josefa González Camino. The document is noted to be incomplete and in very poor condition, with missing sections.

Doña Mariana Crespité de Mora, widow of Teniente Coronel don Juan Gemmir y Lleonart, acknowledged that her deceased husband held 273 pesos 5 reales of silver, along with papers and belongings, belonging to the heirs of Teniente don José de Lete. She made this declaration as she was preparing to depart for La Habana.

Teniente de Oficiales Reales don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora received a deposit of two thousand pesos from doña Mariana Crespité de Mora for the residency trial of her deceased husband, D. Juan Gemmir y Lleonart. The deposit included various forms of wealth, such as doblones, gold, silver pieces, a diamond cross, jewelry, and clothing.

Captain don José Nicolás Bonilla granted freedom to his mulatto slave, Marcos de Arlegui, who was approximately 25 years old. Bonilla had previously purchased Marcos for 200 pesos from Captain Eugenio Cubillo, a resident of the Bagaces valleys.

Don Rafael de Mier Cevallos sold a 20-year-old black slave named Cristóbal to Captain don Miguel de Alvarado for 275 pesos. Cristóbal had been inherited by Rafael from his mother, doña Catarina González Camino.

Captain don Juan de Ocampo Golfín, a resident of Barba valley, sold a house in San Bartolomé de Barba to José Ventura Sanabria. The property's boundaries were detailed, and it was noted that Juan de Ocampo Golfín had originally purchased the lot from a native named Marcos Ramírez with the consent of the community and Fray José Miguel Martínez, the Reverend Father Guardian.

A dowry letter was issued for don Félix Joaquín de Alvarado, son of Captain don José de Alvarado and doña Úrsula López Conejo, in favor of his wife doña María Francisca del Corral. María Francisca is the daughter of Sargento Mayor don José Antonio del Corral and doña Francisca de Arburola y Ribaren, who is now married to Maestre de Campo don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora. The dowry totaled 2398 pesos, including a 16-year-old mulatta slave named Juana and 1000 cacao trees.

people_involved: José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
Fr. Gaspar, Cardinal de Molina y Oviedo
summary: Presbítero José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría granted power of attorney to Doctor don Miguel de Zilieza Velasco, a lawyer and Canon of the Metropolitan Holy Church of Guatemala. This power allowed Zilieza Velasco to appear before His Eminence don Fr. Gaspar, Cardinal de Molina y Oviedo, though the document is incomplete.

Maestre de Campo don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora, at the request of don Cristóbal Ignacio de Soria, the newly elected Governor of the province, obligated himself to the Royal Treasury of León for 1098 pesos. This payment covered the 'media anata' tax for the Governor, allowing him to assume his position.

A residency bond was established in favor of Governor don Cristóbal Ignacio de Soria. Eight individuals, including don José Antonio de Oriamuno and don Benito de Alvarado, acted as guarantors, each committing 250 pesos.
An entry from January 9, 1750, mentions don Tomás de Soto Barahona and don Miguel... The record is incomplete, and further details are missing.
Don Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra acted as a guarantor for Governor don Cristóbal Ignacio de Soria regarding the administration of deceased persons' assets.
On January 18, Don Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra again acted as a guarantor for Governor Soria, this time concerning the management of chamber penalties.
On January 19, Don Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra provided a guarantee for Governor Soria regarding the administration of weapons and other war supplies.
On January 20, Luis Arnesto de Troya and don José Zumbado acted as guarantors for Governor Soria concerning matters related to the Monte de Piedad (Pawnshop/Charitable fund).
On January 23, Don Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra and don José Zumbado provided a guarantee for Governor Soria regarding the administration of the stamped paper revenue.

On January 1, 1749, Juan Calderón, son of deceased Antonio Calderón and Isabel de Alvarez, made his will. He detailed his two marriages, first to Micaela de Brenes and second to Josefa de Coto. His son José Calderón and Capitán José Manuel de Segura were named as executors.

people_involved: don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
summary: On January 4, 1749, Don Francisco Javier de Salvatierra, with several guarantors including Don Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra, obligated himself for 1035 pesos and 5 reales received from don Manuel de la Cerda, tutor of Manuel José de Salvatierra. This obligation was later cancelled on April 13, 1750, by don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco acting as attorney for the tutor and minor.

people_involved: El Alférez don Luis de Sotomayor
doña María de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: On January 6, 1749, Ensign don Luis de Sotomayor sold a plot of land to doña María de Alvarado y Jirón for 55 pesos.
On January 7, 1749, Don Juan José de Cuende, Teniente General, and his wife, doña Manuela Josefa de Ibarra, made an obligation in favor of a chaplaincy. The document is heavily damaged.

people_involved: Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola
summary: On January 9, 1749, doña Águeda Pérez de Muro, daughter of Pérez de Muro and doña Mariana, made her will. She was married twice, first to an Alguacil Mayor with whom she had children including Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola. The rest of the document is illegible.

people_involved: Pb° don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero
summary: On January 13, 1749, don José Antonio de Oriamuno and his wife, doña María Catarina de Ibarra, attempted to sell an enslaved man named Santiago Llamazarez, approximately 25 years old, to Presbyter don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero for 300 silver pesos, but the transaction did not go through.

people_involved: Pb° don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero
Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno
summary: On January 16, 1749, Presbyter don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero leased a cacao plantation to Captain don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno for three years, with an annual rent of 200 pesos in cacao.
On January 17, 1749, a codicil (amendment to a will) was made by the unnamed mother of Francisca de Hinojosa.

locations: Valle de la Boca del Monte
people_involved: Beneficiado don Juan Salvador del Aya y Bolívar
summary: On April 18, 1749, don Hilario Polo and his guarantor don Tomás López del Corral, residents of the Boca del Monte valley, made an obligation in favor of a chaplaincy belonging to Beneficiado don Juan Salvador del Aya y Bolívar, the priest of Esparza.

people_involved: Lic. Pb° don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero
don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda
don José de la Madriz Linares
summary: On April 21, 1749, the will of Licenciado Presbyter don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero was opened, confirming his death. The will, dated December 6, 1748, detailed his roles as Consultor del Santo Oficio and Subdelegado de la Santa Cruzada, and listed his extensive properties including cacao plantations, livestock, and eleven enslaved individuals. He also listed his valuable library and ecclesiastical vestments.

people_involved: Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdova
summary: A 'mayordomo de fábrica' made a detailed will describing his possessions, including clothing, furniture, and religious items. The will mentions a previous order by Visitador Don Félix de Hoces for the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora del Carmen to donate 100 pesos cacao to the parish church for a bell. The testator also specified that his silver spurs and boot buckles should be melted down to create cruets and a tray for the church, with his soul as the heir and Presbyters Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría and Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdova as executors.

people_involved: Capitán don Pedro González de León
summary: Capitán don Pedro González de León made a codicil to his will, but its content is illegible in the record.
Don Diego de Soto, a resident of Valle de Barba, received various livestock and goods at the San Pedro ranch, to be held at the disposal of chaplaincies or creditors.

people_involved: Don Ignacio de Iglesias y Soto-mayor
Capitán don Bernardo García de Miranda
Doña Josefa de Casasola y Córdova
summary: Don Ignacio de Iglesias y Soto-mayor, a native of Badajoz and legitimate son of Capitán don Mariano (?) de Iglesias and Doña María Caldera y Guerrero, issued a dowry letter in favor of his wife, Doña Águeda García de Miranda, who is the legitimate daughter of Capitán don Bernardo García de Miranda and Doña Josefa de Casasola y Córdova.

people_involved: Presbítero Licenciado don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí
summary: Doña Teresa and Doña Gertrudis de Alvarado committed to pay 100 pesos for the chaplaincy founded by Ana Cardoso, for which Presbítero Licenciado don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí is the interim chaplain. They offered their house as collateral.
Juan José de Salas purchased a piece of land bordering the road to Los Potreros, north of the Toyogres River, for 50 pesos. The seller's name is illegible.

people_involved: Don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora, the Syndic of the Convent, sold a plot of land to Doña Antonia de Hoces Navarro for 25 pesos.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don José de Castellanos
Doctor don Francisco Javier de Iglesias
Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
Comisario don José Manuel González Coronel
summary: Doña Francisca Javiera Fernández Castellanos, legitimate daughter of Sargento Mayor don José de Castellanos and Doña Felipa Sendín de Sotomayor, made her will. She is married to Doctor don Francisco Javier de Iglesias (currently absent) and has two children, Felipa Margarita and José Ensebio. She mentions a debt to Don Carlos Galarza for teaching her son to write and appoints Vicario José Miguel de Guzmán and Comisario don José Manuel González Coronel as executors.
Governor don Luis Diez Navarro granted power of attorney to don Francisco Rodríguez, a resident of Guatemala.
Francisco de Saborío purchased a 'caballería' of land in Las Ciruelas, Valle de Barba, from an unnamed widow for 50 pesos.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás de la Madriz
summary: Capitán don Tomás de la Madriz, a widower residing in Ujarraz, granted freedom to a 4-year-old mulatto boy named Luis Fernando, the son of his slave María Josefa Alvarado. This act was carried out according to the will of his late wife, Doña Antonia de Granada.

Capitán don José de Flores and his wife, Doña Angela de Alvarado (also referred to as Doña Angela de Guevara), leased a cacao plantation in Matina to Licenciados don Hermenegildo de Alvarado and don Manuel Sáenz for four years.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
Presbítero Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara
Licenciado don Francisco de Luna Victoria
summary: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral gave a 28-year-old black man named Juan Antonio Gutiérrez to Presbítero Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara. This was in payment for another black man that López del Corral owed Guevara, which he had received from Licenciado don Francisco de Luna Victoria and subsequently sold in Guatemala.
Doña Antonia de Hoces Navarro sold a 19-year-old Creole slave named Josefa Isidora de Hoces (Oses), who was born in her house, to Juan Méndez for 300 pesos cacao.
Manuel Carrillo granted power of attorney to don Carlos Custodio Galarza to collect a debt from the estate of Pablo de Jesús.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don José Antonio de Oriamuno
summary: Sargento Mayor don José Antonio de Oriamuno sold a 13-year-old black slave named María Estéfana to Governor don Luis Diez Navarro for 250 pesos plata. María Estéfana was inherited by Oriamuno's wife, Doña María Catarina de Ibarra, from her father, don Juan Francisco de Ibarra.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don José Antonio de Oriamuno
summary: Sargento Mayor don José Antonio de Oriamuno granted power of attorney, but the details are incomplete due to a torn document.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Francisco de Casasola y Córdova
Bachiller don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdova
Doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho de Castañeda
summary: In 1750, Licenciado don José Francisco de Casasola y Córdova and Bachiller don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdova, both presbyters, donated a mulatto slave to Doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho de Castañeda, wife of don Rafael de Mier Cevallos. This donation was in gratitude for her care of their deceased mother, Doña Águeda Pérez de Muro, and for continuing to care for the two donors in their home.
Don Cayetano Guandica, a native of Masaya, began writing his testament, but it is incomplete.

José Manuel Chinchilla received a dowry for his wife, Antonia Josefa Carrillo. The dowry included assets from the deaths of her father, Francisco Carrillo (1741), and her mother, Petronila Cascante, as well as a donation from her brother, José Cayetano Carrillo. Manuel Sanabria and Agustina Carrillo were also involved in receiving assets from Francisco Carrillo's estate.

people_involved: Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdova
summary: Manuel Antonio Jiménez committed to delivering 3,000 cacao trees in the Matina valley to Bachiller Presbítero Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdova by March 1755. This obligation originated in 1738 with Manuel Antonio's deceased father, Matías Jiménez, who could not fulfill it.

Juan Cristóbal Alvarez and his wife Viviana Meléndez, residents of La Boca del Monte, sold a house in Valle de Aserrí to Manuela Victoria de Aguilar for 150 pesos. Viviana had received the house as a donation from her first cousin, Bachiller Eusebio Meléndez.

Dionisio Salmón Pacheco, acting as attorney for Manuel José de Salvatierra and Manuel de la Cerda (residents of Nicaragua), received 1171 pesos 1 real from Francisco Javier de Salvatierra, a trader in the province. An additional 47 pesos were paid to Manuel de la Cerda.

people_involved: Four minor children of José Francisco Valverde and María Josefa Sáenz
summary: Captain José Francisco Valverde received 56 pesos 2 reales from Pedro González de León, which belonged to his deceased wife, María Josefa Sáenz. Following María Josefa's death, 225 pesos belonging to their four minor children were placed with Pedro de León for pupillary interest.

people_involved: Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdova
summary: Bachiller Presbítero Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdova sold a 3-year-old criollo slave named Miguel Antonio to Captain Juan José de Cuende for 100 silver pesos. Casasola had acquired Miguel Antonio at an auction of the deceased Presbítero Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero's assets.

people_involved: José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Presbítero Licenciado Juan José Camacho obligated himself for 100 pesos of cacao at 5% interest to a chaplaincy founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela, for which Camacho is the patron and chaplain. This obligation was previously held by Teniente Francisco de la Riba and his wife María de Acuña. Camacho mortgaged a 4,000-cacao-tree hacienda in Matina, with the consent of Vicario José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría.

María Josefa de Vargas, widow of Pascual Salgüero, donated an old straw house to her only daughter, María Gertrudis. María Gertrudis's husband, Manuel Calderón, also appeared to accept the donation. María Josefa had purchased the property from Pedro Ortiz.

Manuela Gertrudis Sancho de Castañeda, with her husband Rafael de Mier Cevallos's permission, leased a 500-cacao-tree hacienda in Matina to Ramón de la Rosa. The lease was for three years at 75 pesos of cacao annually. She inherited the hacienda from her parents.

Simón de Casasola, a free pardo, transferred a 2,207-cacao-tree hacienda to Bachiller Presbítero José Manuel García de Argueta. The hacienda carried debts for a chaplaincy founded by Miguel Masís (previously owed by Teniente Juan Masís and María Fernández) and to the Convento de San Francisco (owed by María Fernández). Simón de Casasola, planning to leave for Nicaragua, transferred the obligation and hacienda to García de Argueta.

Captain Juan José de Cuende declared having received 550 pesos of cacao belonging to the Convento from Padre García (José Manuel García de Argueta). Cuende and his wife, Manuela de Ibarra, undertook the obligation for these funds.
Presbítero Manuel Sáenz declared that 550 pesos of the 880 pesos due to him as chaplain had been transferred to Efigenia Brenes.

José Valerín, as steward of San Benito, leased a cacao hacienda in Barbilla to Sergeant Gaspar Ángulo for three years. The annual rent was 25 pesos of cacao delivered in the city or 30 pesos of cacao in the valley.

Petronila Valerín, a widow, leased two cacao hacienda plots in the Matina valley to Captain José Miguel de Echavarría, Alcalde de la Santa Hermandad. The lease was for three years with profits to be shared. She inherited these properties from her parents.

Presbítero Bachiller José Manuel García de Argueta obligated himself for 200 pesos to a chaplaincy founded by Luisa Calvo, for which he is the patron and chaplain. This obligation was previously held by Juan José de Cuende and his wife Manuela de Ibarra. García de Argueta mortgaged a 6,000-cacao-tree hacienda in Barbilla, which already had existing obligations from chaplaincies founded by his father, Manuel García de Argueta, and Juan Calvo.

Captain Juan José de Cuende and his wife Manuela de Ibarra obligated themselves for 550 pesos to a chaplaincy founded by Juan Masís (the Sergeant), whose son Juan Masís is the patron. These funds were previously managed by Presbítero Bachiller José Manuel García de Argueta and now belong to the Convento de San Francisco. They mortgaged a cacao plantation in Matina.
Dionisia Fallas, widow of Captain Manuel García de Argueta, obligated herself for 989 pesos in favor of her children, Juana and Félix García.

Presbítero Bachiller José Manuel García de Argueta settled a debt by giving a cacao plantation in Barbilla, which he had purchased from Simón de Casasola. He also assumed a 550-peso debt owed to the deceased Manuela García and Francisco, whose heir is the grantor, and provided an additional 439 pesos.

people_involved: José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Beneficiado José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría granted conditional freedom to his enslaved mulatto, Ramón Poveda, aged about 34. Ramón, originally bought for 300 pesos from Sargento Mayor Dionisio Pacheco, would gain perpetual freedom if he repaid the 300 pesos within two years, with Simón de Casasola serving as his guarantor.

people_involved: María Elena López de la Flor
José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Doña María Elena López de la Flor sold a 5-year-old mulatto boy named José Francisco to Beneficiado José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría for 100 pesos. José Francisco is identified as the son of Manuela Josefa de la Flor, a black woman inherited by María Elena from her parents.

Presbítero Bachiller José Manuel García de Argueta committed to a 300-peso obligation for a chaplaincy established by Capitán Juan Calvo. Capitán Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra is the patron, and García de Argueta is the chaplain, with Sargento Mayor José Antonio de Oriamuno having been previously obligated for this sum, and a cacao plantation in Barbilla mortgaged.

Capitán Juan José de Cuende and his wife, Doña Manuela de Ibarra, committed to a 150-peso obligation to the Santa Iglesia parroquial. This debt was previously held by Don José Antonio de Oriamuno and his wife, Doña María Catarina de Ibarra, and they mortgaged a cacao plantation named La Sarmiento in the Matina valley.

Sargento Pedro Hernández and his wife Juana de Sandoval, residents of Ujarraz valley, committed to pay 25 pesos plus 5% interest to Sargento Lázaro Sojo. This sum belongs to Antonia López, a minor daughter of Manuela Palma, and originates from a plantain patch on land owned by the deceased Doña Isabel María de Alarcón, which was managed by her son-in-law Pedro Sáenz.

Presbítero Licenciado Juan José Camacho made his will, detailing various chaplaincies he managed and his role as patron and chaplain for others. He owned cacao plantations in Matina and Santa Ana, held tutelage over children of Luisa Miranda and María Francisca Meneses, and had three enslaved mulatto children, one of whom (José Antonio) was pledged to José Antonio Masís. He replaced José Antonio with another enslaved boy, Juan Manuel, and made several bequests, including cacao trees to Francisca Inza and her daughters, and named several executors.

Padre Camacho added a codicil to his will, acknowledging his natural son, Manuel Camacho, born before he took clerical vows, and bequeathing him a sixth of his remaining assets. He also instructed his executor, Dionisio Pacheco, to receive 450 pesos for a matter communicated to him for the discharge of his conscience.
María Sibaja sold a piece of cacao plantation in the Matina valley to José Antonio González for 75 pesos. She had received this land as a donation from her aunt, Magdalena Sibaja.
María Sibaja sold a piece of cacao plantation in Matina to Presbítero Licenciado Antonio de Guevara for 101 pesos.

Presbítero Licenciado Manuel José González Coronel and Ana de los Santos Guillen, as executors of Gertrudis de Hinojosa, established a chaplaincy with a capital of 400 pesos in cacao, secured by a country house. Capitán José Manuel de Segura is the patron, and González Coronel is the interim chaplain until José Silverio Segura is ordained; if José Silverio is not ordained, the chaplaincy will revert to the Convento for the Cofradía de Concepción.

Sargento Mayor Dionisio Pacheco granted power of attorney to Maestre de Campo José Antonio Lacayo de Briones, a resident of Granada, Nicaragua, to collect 400 pesos plus 41 years of interest from the estate of Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reyna. This debt was owed by Francisco Bruno and his deceased wife, María Leocadia Pacheco, to Francisca de Reyna, who is Dionisio Pacheco's wife.

Presbítero Licenciado Antonio de Guevara y Sáenz granted freedom to Juana Calvo, a mulata blanca about 36 years old, whom he had purchased for 300 pesos from Francisco Calvo. Her five children, Gertrudis, Joaquín, Ana Josefa, Manuela de Jesús, and Pablo José, were also granted freedom.

Teniente Francisco de la Riba and his wife María Acuña committed to pay 207 pesos and 4 reales to José Simón de Quesada, the minor son of the deceased Teniente Sebastián de Quesada and Doña Francisca de Moya. This sum was received in the form of a property in the Ujarraz valley, which included a house and a sugar mill, previously managed by Cayetano Badilla and María Isabel de Quesada.

Francisco José de Ocampo, with José Albino Morúa as his free mulatto guarantor, committed to an obligation in favor of the chaplaincies of Don Hermenegildo de Alvarado y Jirón, who is the Teniente Cura of the new settlement of La Boca del.

people_involved: Licenciado don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Don Francisco José de Ocampo opposed the estate of the deceased Licenciado don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín. He sought Sargento Mayor Miguel Jiménez and Capitanes José Antonio Porras and Nicolás Granados as guarantors for the mortuary cause. Ocampo offered to pay 70 pesos in costs to Licenciado don Hermenegildo de Alvarado, and a guarantor mortgaged a cacao plantation in Matina.

people_involved: Presbítero Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara y Sáenz
summary: Presbítero Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara y Sáenz, as Mayordomo of the Cofradía de los Angeles, leased a cacao plantation in Matina to José Albino Morúa, a free pardo. The lease was for three years at an annual rent of 100 pesos.

Capitán José Nicolás Castillo and his wife Margarita Villegas, residents of Ujarraz, committed to a chaplaincy founded by Gertrudis de Hinojosa, for which Capitán José Manuel de Segura is the patron, for 400 pesos. They mortgaged 800 cacao trees in Matina and a tiled house in Ujarraz, with the house also securing 100 pesos belonging to Juan Antonio Mesa, minor son of Sargento Gregorio de Mesa.

people_involved: Presbítero Bachiller don Juan de Pomar y Burgos
Señor Beneficiado don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones
summary: Presbítero Bachiller don Juan de Pomar y Burgos, interim priest of Barba, committed to several chaplaincies, including those instituted by Diego Quinteros and patroned by the Cura de Cartago, and those patroned by Beneficiado don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones (Cura de Granada), and those to be received by Licenciado don Juan José Solís (Presbítero in Guatemala), plus funds for the Convento de San Francisco in Cartago. He mortgaged a hacienda and lands in Santana, including a house, sugar mill, livestock, and land.

Ayudante Cayetano Lobo posted bail for Teniente Antonio Miguel Hernández, who was facing a lawsuit. The suit was brought by his stepsons Juan, José Manuel, and José Nicolás Carranza, alleging concealment of assets from the estate of Nicolasa de Aguilar. The case was later canceled by the Carranzas.

people_involved: Capitán don Pedro de Flores y Vargas
summary: Capitán don José de Flores, a native of Casares, Spain, made his will. He was the legitimate son of Capitán don Pedro de Flores y Vargas and doña María López y Cordenares, and was married to doña Angela de y Jirón. His living children were Antonia Francisca and Juan Manuel.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás de Soto y Barahona
summary: Alférez José Calderón and his wife Josefa de Ibarra (?) committed to Capitán don Tomás de Soto y Barahona for 67 pesos. This debt was originally owed by José Calderón's father, Juan Calderón.

people_involved: Presbítero Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara y Sáenz
summary: Don Francisco José de Ocampo and his guarantor José Albino Morúa committed to Presbítero Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara y Sáenz for 100 pesos. This transaction was ultimately not completed.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
Presbítero Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara y Sáenz
summary: Don Francisco José de Ocampo and José Albino Morúa committed for 100 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Sargento Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín. Presbítero Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara y Sáenz is the interim chaplain, having received all chaplaincies previously held by the deceased Licenciado don Hermenegildo de Alvarado. They mortgaged a cacao plantation in Barbilla.

Teniente Pedro de Segura sold a somewhat damaged thatched house with fences, ditches, and a plantain grove, located in the Tejar area within the common lands of Cartago. He had inherited this property from his mother, and the sale was for 125 pesos to Miguel Fajardo.
Manuel Gabriel Cervantes acknowledged owing 50 pesos to Micaela Solano for his promise to marry her. Tomás Maroto acted as guarantor for this debt.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan Antonio de Castro
R. P. Guardián fray José Pacheco
summary: Doña Petronila Valerino made her will, identifying herself as the daughter of the deceased Capitán Jerónimo Valerino (from Genova) and doña Francisca de Esquivel, and the widow of Capitán don Juan Antonio de Castro (from Sevilla), with no children. She bequeathed books and statues to her nephews R. P. Guardián fray José Pacheco and R. P. fray Antonio Valerino, and her servant Lorenza Valerino. Her sisters doña Manuela and doña Juana were legatees, and her niece doña María Antonia de Quesada was named heir.

people_involved: Presbítero don Juan Manuel de Cáseasela y Córdova
summary: Pedro Manuel Lacayo and Andrés Maroto committed to establish a cacao plantation of 4000 trees for Presbítero don Juan Manuel de Cáseasela y Córdova. The obligation was later canceled for Maroto, as Lacayo assumed the full responsibility.
José Manuel Carranza, with Juan Carranza and José Nicolás Carranza as guarantors, committed to the chaplaincy founded by Capitán Diego de Aguilar for 500 pesos in cacao.

people_involved: Teniente Coronel don Luis Diez Navarro
summary: Teniente Coronel don Luis Diez Navarro, an engineer and Inspector General, donated an enslaved 'negrita' named María Estéfana, whom he had acquired from don José Antonio de Oriamuno, to don Luis Antonio Diez Navarro, who was 14 months old.

people_involved: Teniente Coronel don Luis Diez Navarro
summary: Teniente Coronel don Luis Diez Navarro donated the small house he lived in to doña María Ambrosia de Bonilla, a widow. The house bordered the residences of the Governors to the South.
José Nicolás Carranza, with Miguel Masís as guarantor, committed to María Candelaria Carranza for 499 pesos and 3 reales in cacao.

José Manuel Carranza, with Martín González and his wife Benita Carranza as guarantors, committed to his sister Ramona Carranza for 499 pesos and 3 reales. This amount represented Ramona's share from their mother Nicolasa de Aguilar's estate.
Juan Carranza, with Teniente Antonio Miguel Hernández and his wife María Josefa Carranza as guarantors, committed to José Antonio Carranza. The record of this obligation is incomplete.

A correction was made on page 136 of the Cartago protocols, removing the statement 'hijo legítimo del Alférez Diego López de Ortega' from a record, indicating that the previously recorded father-son relationship is to be suppressed.
A name was corrected from 'Ausiria' to 'Asiúa' on page 142 of the Cartago protocols.
A name was corrected from 'Joaquín' to 'Juatt' on page 185 of the Cartago protocols.
A name was corrected from 'Félix de Coto' to 'Felipe Coto' on page 200 of the Cartago protocols.
A name was corrected from 'Lucia' to 'Luisa' on page 238 of the Cartago protocols.
A name was corrected from 'Villa?iés' to 'Milanés' on page 235 of the Cartago protocols.
A name was corrected from 'Alcoba' to 'Alcolea' on page 291 of the Cartago protocols.
A name was corrected from 'Nih'iez' to 'Yáñez' on page 310 of the Cartago protocols.
A name was corrected from 'Granados' to 'Grados' on page 323 of the Cartago protocols.
A name was corrected from 'Liogaíes' to 'Rosales' on page 325 of the Cartago protocols.
A name was corrected from 'Troyo' to 'Arroyo' on page 329 of the Cartago protocols.
A year was corrected from '1798' to '1698' on page 436 of the Cartago protocols.
A name was corrected from 'Raquel' to 'Miguel' on page 452 of the Cartago protocols.
A name was corrected from 'Criarle' to 'Oñate' on page 470 of the Cartago protocols.
A name was corrected from 'Sosa' to 'Coca' on page 154 of Tomo II of Cartago protocols.
