A name was corrected from 'Pedro' to 'Isidro' on page 323 of Tomo II of Cartago protocols.
A name was corrected from 'Baltodano' to 'Maldonado' on page 419 of Tomo II of Cartago protocols.
A name was corrected from 'Marín' to 'Martin' on page 492 of Tomo II of Cartago protocols.
A name was corrected from 'Nicolasa' to 'Micaela' on page 116 of Tomo III of Cartago protocols.
A name was corrected from 'Selva' to 'Celis' on page 4 of Tomo I of San José protocols.
A name was corrected from 'Unaníse' to 'Unanue' on page 58 of Tomo I of San José protocols.
A name was corrected from 'Paz' to 'Pao' on page 117 of Tomo I of San José protocols.
A name was corrected from 'Valverde' to 'Velarde' on page 201 of Tomo I of San José protocols.
A name and title were corrected from 'Don Dionisio' to 'Doña Dionisia' on page 207 of Tomo I of San José protocols, indicating a gender correction.
A name was corrected from 'Carmona' to 'Carranza' on page 29 of Tomo II of San José protocols.
A name was corrected from 'Lorenzo' to 'Leonzo' on page 229 of Tomo II of San José protocols.
A name was corrected from 'Agustín' to 'Martín' on page 238 of Tomo II of San José protocols.
A name was corrected from 'Córdova' to 'Cardoso' on page 67 of the Heredia protocols.

Nicolás Molina, as principal, and Pedro Manuel Abarca, as guarantor, made an obligation. This obligation was related to Josefa Valeriana Cortés, who was the only remaining minor out of three, until she was emancipated.

Juan Manuel de Silva, a resident of León, Nicaragua, as principal, and Captains Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón and Pedro González de León, as guarantors, made an obligation to the Royal Treasury. This obligation was cancelled in September 1754, noting that Pedro González de León was deceased.

Antonia de la Rosa Orozco, legitimate daughter of Alberto de Orozco and Juana Gutiérrez, made her will. She had eight children, with three remaining: Juan, María de la Rosa (married to Miguel Segura), and Isabel María (married to Juan Francisco). Her deceased daughter Manuela Gertrudis was married to José Antonio Brenes, and she mentioned her granddaughter María Josefa. Captains Francisco de los Reyes and Pedro de Alvarado were named as executors.
Francisco de los Reyes and his wife, María de Aguilar, made an obligation for 4 pesos.

Pablo Solórzano and his wife, María Josefa Orozco, sold an enslaved mulatta named Juana de Chaves to Captain Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón for 270 pesos plata. María Josefa Orozco had inherited Juana de Chaves from her mother, Tomasa de Chaves.
Francisco de los Reyes and his wife, María de Aguilar, residents of the Ujarraz valley, received 205 pesos from Captain Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón.

Manuel, José Nicolás, María Agueda, and Juana Manuela de Molina sold a tiled house and lot in Cartago to Domingo de Alvarado for 300 cacao coins. The property was bounded by houses of Bachelor Manuel López Conejo, a Castilian mulberry tree, Manuel Antonio Taulera's lot, and María de Molina's lot.

Alférez Luis Arnesto de Troya and his wife Josefa Muñoz de la Trinidad, as principals, and Catarina, Lorenza, and María de Arburola, as guarantors, made an obligation for 5550 pesos for the assets of Licenciado Juan José Camacho. Presbyter José Manuel García de Ergueta and Sergeant Major Dionisio Salmón Pacheco, as executors, accepted this. Later, in November 175x, Sergeant Major José Antonio de Oriamuno and María Catarina de Ibarra became new guarantors for Arnesto, cancelling the previous ones.

Francisca de Angulo, a widow, made an obligation for 100 pesos plata to a chaplaincy founded by Juana Sagaste and established by Benito Barrantes. This sum, part of 200 pesos redeemed by Captain Marcos Zamora, was received by Francisca as the value of an enslaved woman named Eugenia, whom she had possessed since 1737, but had not formalized the obligation until now. The obligation was charged against a cacao plantation in Del.

Manuel Carrillo and Domingo de Alvarado entered into an agreement where Domingo received a cacao plantation of 400 trees and 50 pesos of cacao from Manuel. In return, Domingo committed to planting and cultivating 2000 cacao trees, retaining the right to their fruit for 10 years, after which he would return the plantation to Manuel.
Petronila de Hoces Navarro, legitimate daughter of Captain Esteban de Hoces Navarro and Juana de Calvo (both deceased), made her will. She was married to 'el Ao don'.

Hilario Monje and Francisca Irene Cordero, residents of Aserrí, obligated themselves for 250 pesos plata to the Capellanía founded by don Pedro Ibáñez. This sum was redeemed by doña Rita García de Ergueta, who had made an obligation in 1746. Don José Francisco de Alvarado is now the patron and chaplain, replacing B" don Manuel López Conejo. They hypothecated land, a house, a sugar mill, a cane field, and fences in Aserrí.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí
summary: Doña María Magdalena Maroto, a widow, sold a young mulatto slave named Manuel, son of her slave Ana Gertrudis, to Licenciado don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí for 200 pesos.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
Mtre. de Campo don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral obligated himself for 100 pesos plata to the Convento de San Francisco, whose syndic was Mtre. de Campo don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora. Doña Bernarda Martínez had redeemed these funds. The transaction was not completed.

people_involved: Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Manuel Antonio Jiménez, as principal, and Sargento Benito Moscoso and Nicolás Salguero, as guarantors, obligated themselves to plant and care for 3000 cacao trees over 5 years on the hacienda belonging to Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco
summary: A dowry letter was issued for the marriage of Alférez don Lucas Pacheco and doña Ana Teresa del Fierro. The dowry amounted to 1008 pesos 6 reales in cacao, with arras of 500 pesos in cacao, and included two slaves: Tomasa (30 years old) and Francisco Javier (14 years old).

people_involved: Licenciado don José Francisco de Casasola y Córdoba
Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Licenciados don José Francisco and don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba attempted to obligate themselves for a Capellanía founded by their mother, doña Agueda Pérez de Muro, over cacao haciendas named "Foto y Bonilla" in Matina. This obligation was not completed.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Francisco de Casasola y Córdoba
Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Licenciados don José Francisco and don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba obligated themselves for 2000 pesos plata to the Capellanía founded by their deceased mother, doña Agueda Pérez de Muro, on the "Foto y Bonilla" cacao haciendas in Matina. This obligation was cancelled on February 28, 1753.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Francisco de Casasola y Córdoba
Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Licenciados don José Francisco and don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba obligated themselves for 1000 pesos plata to the Capellanía founded by their deceased mother, doña Agueda Pérez de Muro, on the "Velazco" cacao hacienda in Matina. This obligation was cancelled on March 1, 1753.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Francisco de Casasola y Córdoba
Capitán don José Pérez de Muro
doña María Ana López de la Flor
doña Teresa de Soto y Barahona
summary: Licenciado don José Francisco de Casasola y Córdoba obligated himself for 1500 pesos cacao to the Capellanía founded by his deceased grandfather, Capitán don José Pérez de Muro. This obligation was placed on the houses he currently owned in Cartago, which were previously owned by doña Joseta Pérez de Muro.

Doña Lorenza de Arburola, widow of Capitán don Antonio de Angulo, made her testament. She had no children and left 100 pesos, along with two haciendas in Barbilla and two slaves, Carlos and Ana Antonia (10-11 years old).

people_involved: Doña Antonia Muñoz de la Trinidad
Capitán Don Félix José de L Agúero
summary: This document details an inheritance from Doña Josefa de Hoces Navarro, who bequeaths a house and other assets to her niece, Doña Antonia Muñoz de la Trinidad, for having raised her. Another niece, Doña de la Encarnación, and an orphan raised by Francisco Esteban are also mentioned. Captains Don Antonio de Arleguí and Don Félix José de L Agúero are named as executors.

people_involved: Alférez Don Luis Arnesto de Troya
summary: Alférez Don Luis Arnesto de Troya and his wife Josefa Muñoz de la Trinidad, along with Sargento Mayor Don [name missing], are involved in an obligation for 5550 pesos in cacao to the heirs of Licenciado Don Juan José Camargo. This amount was the result of an auction of haciendas and their annexes in the Matina valley. The obligation was to be freed by a payment made on September 14, 1775.

people_involved: Bachiller Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Bachiller Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba, a cleric, sells a house of 22 varas, made of adobe and tile, located at the site named Río Reventado near the town of Quircot, to Capitán José Antonio Vázquez. The house was inherited maternally, and the price was 190 plata.

people_involved: Br. Don José Francisco de Casasola y Córdoba
Br. Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Pedro Manuel Lacayo, a free pardo, obligates himself to clear land and plant 4000 trees in a place designated by Br. Don José Francisco de Casasola y Córdoba when he descends to the Matina valley. Lacayo had previously made this obligation on December 14 with Andrés Maroto to fulfill it when they took possession of the "Foto y Bonilla" haciendas, which belonged to Don José Francisco and his brother, Br. Don Juan Manuel. Since the obligation was not yet fulfilled, Lacayo makes a new one to Don José Francisco, who now owns the haciendas after dividing assets with his brother.

people_involved: Br. Don José Francisco de Casasola y Córdoba
Doña Josefa de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Br. Don José Francisco de Casasola y Córdoba, a Presbyter cleric, obligates himself for 576 pesos 3 reales plata to his nephew, Don Bartolomé de Miranda. This amount corresponds to what Don Bartolomé was due from the estate of Doña Josefa de Casasola y Córdoba, and which Doña Agueda Pérez de Muro, the deceased mother of the grantor, was obligated to pay. In May 1763, Don Bartolomé García de Miranda, who was already married, received his inheritance.

people_involved: Capitán Don Cristóbal Ignacio de Soria
summary: Capitán Don Cristóbal Ignacio de Soria, Lieutenant Commander General and Governor of the province, grants general power of attorney to Capitanes Don Bartolomé de Eguizabal and Don Manuel de Gálvez, who are residents of Santiago de Guatemala.

people_involved: Bachiller Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
Doña Josefa de Casasola y Córdoba
Don Félix José García de Miranda
Don Bernardo José García y Miranda
summary: Bachiller Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba obligates himself for 1152 pesos 7 reales for the guardianship of his nephews, Don Félix and Don Bernardo Miranda. This amount was adjudicated to them from the estate of Doña Josefa de Casasola y Córdoba and was the responsibility of Doña Agueda Pérez de Muro, the deceased mother of the grantor. The value was received from the estate in the form of a mulata named Bárbara, valued at 250 pesos, another named Benita, and other effects. Don Félix José García de Miranda cancelled in January 1752, and Don Bernardo José García y Miranda cancelled in February 1761.

people_involved: Licenciado Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
Licenciado Don José Francisco de Alvarado
summary: Licenciado Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría sells a house in "this city" to Licenciado Don José Francisco de Alvarado for 400 pesos in cacao currency. The house is bordered by properties belonging to Doña Rita García de Ergueta, Doña Josefa de Rosas, Antonia López, and the buyer himself.

people_involved: Licenciado Don Antonio de Guevara y Sáenz
summary: Francisco José de Ocampo sells a 30-year-old black slave named Salvador to Licenciado Don Antonio de Guevara y Sáenz for 300 pesos plata. Salvador was among other slaves received by donation from the deceased Don Francisco de Ocampo. 200 pesos were paid in cash, and the buyer is obligated for 100 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Doña Magdalena Pérez de Luna, which was previously the seller's responsibility, with José Albino Morúa as guarantor.

people_involved: Licenciado Don José Francisco de Alvarado
B* Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
Teniente General Don José Antonio de Bonilla
summary: Licenciado Don José Francisco de Alvarado, as principal, and his sisters Doña Ana Teresa and Doña Gertrudis de Alvarado, as guarantors, obligate themselves for 380 pesos of cacao to the chaplaincy founded by Pedro Ibáñez. This obligation was previously held by B* Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría, who redeemed it, and it is situated on a house purchased by Don José Francisco from Don José Miguel. On March 16, 1753, Don José Francisco transferred this lien to the hacienda and mill of Los Tres Ríos, leading to the cancellation of this obligation.

Gu Ibarra sells a 16x6 vara adobe house on a 50 vara lot to don Manuel Hidalgo, a resident of Aserrí valley. The house, which Gu Ibarra inherited from her deceased first husband Francisco del Campo, is bordered by properties belonging to doña Josefa González del Camino, doña Antonia de Alvarado, Manuel Fernández, and doña María Cayetana de Alvarado. The price was 350 pesos cacao.

people_involved: Doña María Elena López de la Flor
Licenciado don José Francisco de Alvarado
summary: Doña María Elena López de la Flor sells a 14-year-old enslaved black woman named María to Licenciado don José Francisco de Alvarado, a Presbítero. María is the daughter of Manuela Josefa de la Flor, who was also an enslaved person inherited by Doña María Elena from her parents. The transaction price was 200 pesos plata.

Micaela Chinchilla, a widow, sells a piece of land to Simón Chacón. The land's boundaries are described by natural features including a poró tree, a higuito tree, Paso Blanco, a river, and Junquillal.
Don Pedro de Moya and doña Angela Sáenz establish a chaplaincy for masses through a will. Don Pedro de Moya is mentioned as a testamentary executor, though parts of the entry are illegible.

people_involved: Capitán José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda
summary: Capitán don José and his wife doña Juana Galarza incur an obligation for 250 pesos plata at 5% interest, mortgaging a cattle ranch in Miravalles, within the jurisdiction of Bagaces. Capitán José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda receives the sum and redeems them.
Gregorio Brenes sells a house to his son, whose first name is illegible but shares the surname Brenes, for 100 pesos in cacao currency.

people_involved: son of don Agustín de A
summary: An illegible entry mentions a son of the deceased don Agustín de A.
The signature of Cristóbal Ignacio de Soria is noted at the bottom of a document.

people_involved: Alférez don Luis de Soto Mayor
summary: José Cubero sells a 20-year-old mulato named Vicente Cubero to Alférez don Luis de Soto Mayor. The remainder of the entry is illegible.

people_involved: doña María Francisca López del Corral
summary: Don Joaquín de Alvarado and his wife doña María Francisca López del Corral incur an obligation for 550 pesos plata. 100 pesos are for the Cofradía de la Concepción in Cartago, and the remaining 450 pesos are to be paid in two installments in August and December of the current year.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Francisco de Alvarado
wife of don Gabriel Marco de Ocaña
summary: Licenciado don José Francisco de Alvarado, Teniente Cura and Capellán of a chaplaincy founded by the deceased Pedro Ibáñez, takes charge of an obligation secured by a country house (from Sebastián Guillén's heirs) and a mill in Tres Ríos. On September 14, 1752, Alvarado cancels the obligation as don Gabriel Marco de Ocaña and his wife assume responsibility.

people_involved: Bachiller don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
Licenciado don José Francisco de Alvarado
summary: Bachiller don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba, a Presbítero, and don Juan Sáenz exchange a piece of land. The land was acquired by Casasola from Licenciado don José Francisco de Alvarado, who obtained it from the assets of an individual named de Alvarado. The property is bordered by a house of de Alvarado, a house of fray José de Guzmán, a royal street, and a lot of don Francisco Javier de Siles.

people_involved: Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara Sáenz
summary: Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara Sáenz, a Presbítero and Capellán, incurs obligations for two chaplaincies founded by Vazco Solano and Juan Alonso Solano. He improves the security of these obligations by transferring them from a house bought from doña Josefa González del Camino to a hacienda with 3400 cacao trees in the Matina valley, valued at 3400 pesos plata.

people_involved: Pe. Guardián del Convento de San Francisco
summary: Manuel José González Coronel and Ana de los Santos Guillén, as executors of the deceased Gertrudis Ruiz de Hinojosa, established a Capellanía of masses. This Capellanía included funds for souls in purgatory, a payment to the Cofradía de la Veracruz, and 1394 pesos for 25 recited masses and wax. José Silverio de Segura, nephew of Gertrudis, was designated to be ordained through this Capellanía, with Capitán José Manuel Segura as the patron.

people_involved: Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara Sáenz
Licenciado don José Manuel García de Ergueta
Capitán don Antonio Elías de Arleguí
summary: On January 23, Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara Sáenz committed 600 pesos at 5% interest to the Capellanía founded by the late doña Luisa Calvo. Licenciado don José Manuel García de Ergueta served as the chaplain and Capitán don Antonio Elías de Arleguí as the patron. The 600 pesos were secured by a property called El Molino, which had previously belonged to Capitán don Fernando de Salazar and doña Josefa de Aguilar.

people_involved: Licenciado don Manuel José González Coronel
summary: Licenciado don Manuel José González Coronel and Ana de los Santos, acting as executors for Gertrudis Ruiz de Hinojosa, attempted to establish a Capellanía of masses. However, this specific founding did not proceed as noted, having been established in a previous deed.

people_involved: Teniente de Capitán Juan Manuel Camacho
summary: On January 29, Teniente de Capitán Juan Manuel Camacho committed 520 pesos in cacao currency to his legitimate sons, Juan José, Manuel José, and José Nicolás Ambrosio. This sum represented their maternal inheritance from their deceased mother, doña Josefa Fernández Castellanos.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Antonio de Oriamuno
summary: The testament of the deceased Alférez Matías Trejos, son of Juan de Trejos and Ana de Aguilar, was recorded. He had children with his first wife, Isabel Cárdenas, and was remarried to doña María Jiménez. His will established a Capellanía, naming his grandson Andrés Fernández as the proprietary chaplain, with Capitán Andrés Fernández as the patron. Sargento Mayor don Antonio de Oriamuno and Teniente de Capitán Clemente Astorga were named executors.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Francisco de Alvarado
Alférez don Luis Arnesto de Troyo
summary: Don Gabriel Marco y Ocaña and doña Joaquina López del Corral committed 200 pesos to the Capellanía founded by Pedro Ibáñez and 50 pesos to the Capellanía founded by don Miguel de Alvarado. Licenciado don José Francisco de Alvarado served as both patron and chaplain for both Capellanías. The obligations were secured by a house in the city's fields (formerly of Sebastián Guillén's heirs) and a city lot near the parish church.

people_involved: Licenciado don Manuel José González Coronel
Licenciado don José Manuel García de Ergueta
summary: On January 26, Licenciado don Manuel José González Coronel and Ana de los Santos Guillén, as executors of Gertrudis Ruiz de Hinojosa, formally established a Capellanía of masses. José Silverio de Segura, nephew of the deceased, was named the first proprietary chaplain. The Capellanía was founded for 1000 pesos, secured by two haciendas, after a third hacienda named San Jerónimo was lost. The parish priest was named interim chaplain for the sung masses, and Licenciado don José Manuel García de Ergueta for the recited masses, with Capitán José Manuel Segura as patron.
Doña Josefa Liberata Chacón sold a one-month-old mulatto slave girl named Manuela Chacón, who was the daughter of another of her slaves, to Francisco de Quirós for 50 silver pesos.

people_involved: Tesorero de las bulas de la Santa Cruzada
summary: Governor Don Cristóbal Ignacio de Soria, with Don José Nicolás de Bonilla as his guarantor, obligated themselves to the Treasurer of the Santa Cruzada for 1292 pesos plata. This sum covered the cost of the bulas for the current year, which had been delivered to Soria by the Lieutenant of Royal Officials.

Simón Casasola made his last will and testament. He named his wife, María Efigenia de Brenes, and their five children (Manuel José Benito, María Gertrudis, María del Rosario Tímotez, Juan de Dios Casasola, and Leonidas de la Trinidad Casasola) as his heirs. Captain Don Andrés Fernández and Don Manuel de Guzmán Portocarrero were appointed as his executors.

people_involved: Bachiller Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
Sargento Mayor Don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco
Capitán Don Esteban Ruiz de Mendoza
Licenciado Don José Francisco de Alvarado
summary: Bachiller Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría granted freedom to his mulatto slave, Ramón Poveda. Poveda had been purchased from Sargento Mayor Don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco for 300 pesos plata, and in May 1750, he was given a license to earn this sum for his manumission. Poveda delivered the required amount in cacao, with portions distributed to Captain Don Esteban Ruiz de Mendoza, Captain José Manuel Segura, Manuel Meléndez, and Licenciado Don José Francisco de Alvarado.

people_involved: Bachiller Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
Licenciado Don Antonio de Vargas Machuca
Licenciado Don José Francisco de Alvarado
summary: Bachiller Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría transferred the 'Las Viejas' cacao and fruit hacienda in the Matina valley to Juan de Montalván and his wife María Efigenia de Angulo, residents of Escasú. The hacienda, originally acquired from the late Doña Lorenza de Arburola, was sold for 940 pesos. The payment was allocated to various chaplaincies founded by Licenciado Don Antonio de Vargas Machuca, Comisario Don Baltasar de Grados, Juana Sagaste, and Capitán Pedro de Ibáñez (whose chaplaincy was patroned by Licenciado Don José Francisco de Alvarado), as well as to the Cofradía del Rosario.

people_involved: Licenciado Don José Francisco de Alvarado
summary: Licenciado Don José Francisco de Alvarado, Lieutenant Priest, obligated himself to the Convento de Curriravá for 464 pesos and 5 reales in cacao currency. He received this sum from his brother, Don Joaquín de Alvarado. To secure this obligation, he encumbered his properties in Los Tres Rios, which included a tiled house, a sugar mill with its house, a flour mill, and a plot of land with cane and plantains.

people_involved: Mtre. de Campo Don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
Sargento Mayor Don Carlos Custodio Galarza
Bachiller Don Juan de Pomar y Burgos
summary: Alférez Don José Velazco, who was imprisoned by order of the Governor Don Cristóbal Ignacio de Soria and was ill, was granted release to his home for treatment. Mtre. de Campo Don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora and Sargento Mayor Don Carlos Custodio Galarza served as his guarantors. Bachiller Don Juan de Pomar y Burgos, a physician approved by the Court of Mexico, visited him.

people_involved: Alférez Don Luis de Soto Mayor
summary: María Josefa de Chavarría, widow of José Nicolás del Haya, sold land in the pueblo of Ujarrás to Alférez Don Luis de Soto Mayor for 30 pesos plata. This land, which she and her husband had purchased in 1727 from Manuel de Soto, bordered the buyer's cane hacienda, house, and sugar mill, and the Río Caliente to the south.

Gregorio Orozco and his wife Juana de Salas made their will, naming each other as reciprocal executors and heirs, as they had no children together. Juana de Salas had previously been married twice; first to Francisco Rodríguez, with whom she had children Gregoria, Pablo, and Efigenia, and then to Pedro de [illegible], with whom she had no children.

people_involved: Mtre. de Campo Don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
Capitán José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda
Sargento Mayor Don Cristóbal de Gálvez
summary: Mtre. de Campo Don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora and Capitán José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda granted general power of attorney to Sargento Mayor Don Cristóbal de Gálvez, a resident of Guatemala City.

people_involved: Don Luis Fernando de Liendo Goicoechea
summary: Fray Manuel de Liendo Goicoechea, a Franciscan friar, made his will. He was identified as the legitimate son of Don Luis Fernando de Liendo Goicoechea and Doña Baltasara de Inza.

people_involved: Licenciado don Manuel José González Coronel
summary: Don Gabriel Marco de Ocaña sold a slave to Licenciado don Manuel José González Coronel for 200 pesos. This transaction is recorded in the Cartago protocols for 1753.

Capitán Nicolás de Amador, a resident of Aserrí, sold a house and land in Palo Grande, bordering the Jorco river, to Pedro Chinchilla and his wife María Vargas for 100 pesos plata. Amador had previously bought the property from José Caparrosa for 50 pesos, who in turn acquired it from Capitán Cayetano Morales.

Doña Rosa de Chaves, a widow, obligated herself to pay 82 pesos and 4 reales to each of her grandsons, Manuel Antonio and Juan de Morales, as their inheritance from their deceased father, Capitán Marcelo de Morales. She also obligated herself for 22 pesos and 4 reales to another grandson, José Hermenegildo. She mortgaged her house in Aserrí for these obligations.

Don Pedro Fernández and his wife Doña Catarina Tenorio, residents of Aserrí, obligated themselves for 100 pesos cacao to a chaplaincy founded by Manuela Barrantes. Alférez Juan Suárez had redeemed this amount, and B* don Lorenzo de Quesada, the parish priest of Barba, was the patron and chaplain. Capitán Jorge Morera acted as guarantor.

people_involved: Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara Sáenz
summary: Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara Sáenz, a cleric, sold a house with a fence and 125 plantain trees to Sargento José Antonio Salguero for 200 pesos cacao. The property bordered lands of Josefa Guerrero, Petronila Ramírez, 'tierras de la puebla', and María Quirós. Guevara Sáenz had acquired the property from Capitán Jorge Morera.

people_involved: Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara Sáenz
summary: Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara Sáenz granted general power of attorney to Capitán Manuel Cayetano de Guevara.
Doña Josefa del Camino, widow of Don Gil Alvarado, donated a 15-year-old 'mulato blanco' slave named Joaquín, who was born and raised in her house, to her son Don Domingo de Alvarado.

people_involved: Don Domingo de Alvarado y Jirón
Doña Josefa de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Don Domingo de Alvarado y Jirón donated a house of adobe and tile to his sister Doña Josefa de Alvarado y Jirón, as she had no place to live and their mother, Doña Josefa del Camino, did not own a house in the city. The house, which Domingo had bought from the heirs of José Molina for 300 pesos cacao, bordered properties of Sebastiana de Utrera, Manuel Antonio Taulera, Rosa Golfín, and a house built by Francisco Molina.

Sargento José Antonio Salguero obligated himself to clear land for 2000 cacao trees for Capitán don José Nicolás Bonillas. In return, Salguero received 200 pesos cacao, a third of meat, an axe, and a machete for the clearing and planting.

people_involved: Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara y Sáenz
Sargento Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara y Sáenz, a cleric, obligated himself for 270 pesos plata to a chaplaincy founded by Sargento Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín for the soul of Doña Tomasa de Ocampo. The chaplaincy was previously held by Licenciado don Francisco de Ocampo, and upon his death, it passed to Guevara y Sáenz. The obligation was secured by a cacao plantation of 3400 trees in Matina.

people_involved: Licenciado don Manuel de Casasola Córdoba
Licenciado don José Francisco de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Licenciado don Manuel de Casasola Córdoba, a cleric, assumed sole responsibility for a 1500 pesos plata chaplaincy obligation. This chaplaincy was founded by his deceased mother, Doña Agueda Pérez de Muro, on a cacao plantation named Velazco in Matina, which he inherited. He had previously obligated himself with his brother, Licenciado don José Francisco de Casasola y Córdoba, in 1751 before the Teniente General.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Francisco de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Licenciado don José Francisco de Casasola y Córdoba, a patrimonial priest, inherited a cacao plantation of 2910 trees in Matina from his deceased mother, Doña Agueda Pérez de Muro, on which she had founded a chaplaincy.

people_involved: Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: An unnamed grantor, who is the patron and chaplain of a 2000 pesos silver capellanía, takes full responsibility for an obligation previously shared with his brother, Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba. This transfer of obligation, originally established by a 1751 deed, occurred after the distribution of their deceased mother's assets.

Don Andrés Fernández and Doña Josefa Trejos grant their 24-year-old son, Andrés José, an inheritance valued at 1000 pesos to support his priestly studies in Nicaragua. The inheritance includes a tiled house and estancia near "this city" (Cartago), bordering the Taras River, and 900 cacao trees in Matina, specifically in the area called El Kiachuelo.

people_involved: Doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
Sargento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
Licenciado don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí
Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno
summary: On March 10, Doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral, legitimate daughter of the deceased Sargento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral and Doña Ambrosia del Camino, grants power to testate to Licenciado don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí and Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno. Her heirs are her five children: Don Manuel Antonio, Doña Nicolasa, Don Jerónimo, Don Juan, and Don Francisco Antonio de Betancur.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Francisco de Alvarado
B" don José Miguel de Chavarría
summary: On March 16, Licenciado don José Francisco de Alvarado purchased a tiled house in "this city" from B" don José Miguel de Chavarría for 400 pesos of cacao. The house was bordered by properties belonging to Doña Rita García de Ergueta, Doña Josefa de Rosas, Antonia López, and Doña Teresa and Doña Gertrudis de Alvarado.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Francisco de Alvarado
summary: On March 16, Licenciado don José Francisco de Alvarado, who is the patron and chaplain of a capellanía founded by Pedro Ibáñez, transferred a 380 pesos cacao obligation from the newly purchased house. He moved this obligation to a hacienda with a sugar mill, two cane fields, banana plantations, and a mill, located at "los tres ríos," to improve its security.

people_involved: Don Félix José García de Ergueta
Sargento Mayor don Julián García de Ergueta
Doña Juana María de Soto y Barahona
summary: On March 17, a dowry letter was issued for the upcoming marriage of Don Félix José García de Ergueta and Doña Clemencia Muñoz. The dowry, totaling 1375 pesos, included an 11-year-old enslaved mulatilla named Ramona valued at 200 pesos, and 500 cacao trees in Barbilla. The arras (earnest money) was 500 pesos silver.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Francisco de Alvarado
B" don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: On March 20, Licenciado don José Francisco de Alvarado, a Presbyter, sold a house with posts and a tiled roof in "this city" to Doña Bárbara Madriz Linares for 400 pesos of cacao. The property, previously acquired by Alvarado from B" don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría, was bordered by properties of Doña Rita García de Ergueta, Doña Josefa de Rosas, Doña Antonia López, and his sisters Doña Teresa and Doña Gertrudis de Alvarado.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás Lopez del Corral
Licenciado don Gregorio López del Corral
Licenciado don Juan Antonio de Moya
summary: On March 21, Capitán don Tomás Lopez del Corral, acting as heir to his deceased brother Licenciado don Gregorio López del Corral, founded a capellanía for the souls of his parents, Don Antonio López del Corral and Doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco, and his brother. The capellanía, with a principal of 800 pesos cacao and 5% interest, was secured by the "la Corrales" cacao hacienda in Matina. Don José Tiburcio Marenco was named the first chaplain, with Capitán Tomás Lopez del Corral as the patron, and succession plans outlined for both roles.

On April 4, the will of María Teresa Fernández, natural daughter of the deceased Sargento Mayor don José Morales and María Fernández, was recorded. She was married to Agustín de la Riva and had five children, with María and Francisco Antonio de la Riva still living and named as her heirs. Her daughter María was married to José Nicolás Caamaño, and her executors were her son Francisco de la Riva and her son-in-law José Nicolás Caamaño.

people_involved: Capitán de caballos corozas don Juan José de Cuende
Sargento Mayor don José Antonio Oriamuno
Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
summary: On April 14, Capitán de caballos corozas don Juan José de Cuende granted general power of attorney. His wife, Doña Manuela de Ibarra, was named first, followed by Sargento Mayor don José Antonio Oriamuno, and then Capitán don Tomás López del Corral.

people_involved: Capitán de caballos corozas don Juan José de Cuende
Sargento Mayor don José Antonio Oriamuno
Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
Mtre. de Campo don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
summary: On April 14, Don Juan José de Cuende, a native of Estella in the Kingdom of Navarra, granted power to testate to his wife Doña Manuela de Ibarra, Sargento Mayor don José Antonio Oriamuno, Capitán don Tomás López del Corral, and Mtre. de Campo don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora. His four legitimate children, Doña Manuela, Don Romualdo, Don Diego, and Don Salvador de Cuende, were named as his heirs.

people_involved: Capitán don Cristóbal Ignacio de Soria
Mtre. de Campo don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones
summary: On April 26, Capitán don Cristóbal Ignacio de Soria, Governor of "this province," granted special power to Mtre. de Campo don José Antonio Lacayo de Briones, who is the provincial mayor and perpetual councilman of Granada, Nicaragua, to sell an unspecified item on his behalf.

people_involved: Manuel de Jesús Galán de Torres
summary: Manuel de Jesús Galán de Torres, a 21-22 year old 'negro criollo' from La Habana, was purchased by Doña María Galán de Torres, wife of the seller, from Doña María Vía Monte for 250 silver pesos approximately ten years prior to this document. Both women were residents of La Habana.

people_involved: María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
Lic. don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí
Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno
Sargento Mayor don Antonio de la Vega Cabral
summary: On April 30, the testament of the deceased Doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral was granted by her attorneys, Lic. don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí and Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno. She was married to don Francisco de Betancour and had five living children. Her assets included several enslaved individuals, and she left improved portions of her estate to Nicolasa, Manuel Antonio, and Juan.

people_involved: Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla
Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno
summary: On May 17, 1753, the continuation of Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla's testament detailed his assets, including several enslaved individuals and a cacao plantation managed by Sargento don José Antonio Salguero. The testament also named his brother don Miguel de Echavarría, mother doña Micaela de Bonilla, and his wife doña Nicolasa Inés de Alvarado and Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno as executors.

people_involved: Capitán don Antonio Elías de Arleguí
Licenciado don José Francisco de Alvarado
summary: On May 18, Licenciado don Manuel Sáenz, Lieutenant Priest of Valle de Aserrí, and Capitán don Antonio Elías de Arleguí, acting as attorney for Licenciado don José Francisco de Alvarado, leased the 'Za Moya' cacao hacienda in Matina to José Antonio González for six years. However, on September 24, 1753, Lic. Manuel Sáenz cancelled the agreement because González refused to proceed due to the hacienda's deteriorated condition.

people_involved: Don Félix José de la Riva y Agiero
summary: On May 24, Don Félix José de la Riva y Agiero took on an obligation for 600 pesos cacao for houses built by don Pedro Rodríguez Palacios, which were auctioned to him. A significant portion of this debt was for a chaplaincy founded by don Lorenzo de Arburola as executor for Licenciado don Antonio Vargas Machuca. The house was mortgaged and its boundaries were described, mentioning several neighbors.

people_involved: Don Joaquín de Alvarado y Jirón
Capitán don Manuel Felipe de Arleguí
Lic. don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí
summary: On May 25, Don Joaquín de Alvarado y Jirón sold a solar (plot of land) to Capitán don Manuel Felipe de Arleguí for 25 pesos cacao. The solar's boundaries were described, bordering properties of Lic. don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí and doña Catarina de Arburola.

On May 26, Capitán don José Antonio Vic sold half of a solar, which included a tiled house, to Juan Pablo de Morales for 20 pesos. The document mentions a Licenciado don Manuel, but his full name is incomplete.

people_involved: Capitán don Cristóbal Ignacio de Soria
summary: On June 13, Capitán don Cristóbal Ignacio de Soria, Governor of the province, granted power of attorney to don Juan Feliciano Ramírez, a resident of León, to collect his Governor's salaries from the Royal Officials in León. This power of attorney superseded previous ones given to Capitán José Antonio de Arichaval, don Santiago de Vílchez Andavide, and don Antonio Sáenz, all residents of León.
Lieutenant José Antonio Masís and his wife, Juana Francisca de Mondragón, granted power of attorney to José Florencio de Soto, a resident of Panama. The transaction was not concluded.

people_involved: María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
summary: Licenciado José Hermenegildo de Arleguí, acting as the testamentary executor for the deceased María Josefa de la Vega Cabral, sold four enslaved individuals to his brother, Captain Antonio Elías de Arleguí. The sale included Josefa (55, black), Tomasa (35, mulatto), María (8, mulatto, daughter of Tomasa), and Elías (15, mulatto), for a total of 975 pesos in cacao currency.
Licenciado José Hermenegildo de Arleguí, in his capacity as executor, sold an enslaved mulatto woman named Francisca, 40 years old, to Captain Tomás de Soto y Barahona for 300 pesos of cacao.
Licenciado José Hermenegildo de Arleguí, acting as executor, sold an enslaved 'mulatillo blanco' named Isidro, 14 years old, to Félix José García de Ergueta for 250 pesos of cacao.
Teodora Molina, a widow, sold a cacao plantation located in Matina to Julián Trigo, a merchant in the province, for 100 pesos.

Félix Cayetano Masís sold half a 'caballería' of land in 'Las Cabullas' to Juan José de Zúñiga for 25 silver pesos. The land's title is held by Juan Fonseca, who had previously bought the majority of these lands from Félix Cayetano Masís's siblings, inherited from their deceased parents Matías Masís and María del Carmen Salazar.

people_involved: María Elena López de la Flor
summary: Captain José Nicolás de Bonilla and María Elena López de la Flor attempted to exchange enslaved individuals: Bonilla's 10-year-old enslaved boy, José Francisco, for López de la Flor's 12-year-old enslaved girl, María del Carmen. The exchange did not proceed.

Captain of Cavalry Chop Ignacio de Soria, Governor and Captain General of the province, granted power of attorney to his nephew, Lieutenant Colonel Antonio Pereira y Soria (Commander in Havana), Captain of Infantry Antonio Ramírez Estenos, and Captain of Grenadiers Luis Pacheco (resident of Havana). This power was for them to receive the assets left by his recently deceased wife, María Galán de Torres, who died in Havana and named him as her heir in her will.

Ayudante José Hilario Albino Morúa incurred a debt of 150 pesos of cacao at 5% interest, secured by a cacao plantation of 1000 fruit-bearing trees in the Barbilla valley. This debt is in favor of the Chaplaincy founded by Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, whose patron is now Licenciado Antonio de Guevara y Sáenz, following the death of Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, who was the previous proprietor.
Diego Jurado, a resident of Panama, stated that upon leaving Panama, he executed a deed of obligation before public notary Juan Torres, in favor of Pedro de (name incomplete).

people_involved: Capitán don Cristóbal Ignacio de Soria
summary: Arichaga owed 895 pesos plata and had already paid 182 pesos 41% reales to Captain Don Cristóbal Ignacio de Soria, the Governor and Captain General. The Governor, acting on Arichaga's instructions, required him to make a new obligation for the remaining 712 pesos 31% reales, which Arichaga agreed to, hypothecating 50 mules from Chiriquí.

Félix Cayetano Masís formally sold a piece of land called 'Las Cabullas' to Juan Fonseca for 40 pesos plata. This land was inherited by Félix from his deceased parents, Matías Masís and María del Carmen Salazar. The sale had actually occurred over two years prior without a formal deed.

Licenciado Don Manuel Sáenz, a Presbyter, leased 'La Moya' hacienda, a 1500-tree cacao and fruit plantation in the Matina valley, to José Antonio González for three years. The annual rent was 75 pesos of good cacao, valued at 25 pesos per zurrón. The hacienda bordered properties of the deceased Padre Corrales and Padre Cubero.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Manuel García de Ergueta
summary: José Masís committed to pay 25 pesos of cacao annually for two years to the capellanía founded by Gertrudis Ruiz de Hinojosa. This obligation is tied to a cacao hacienda in the Barbilla valley, which José Masís is leasing from the capellanía's patron, Captain José Manuel Segura. The hacienda carries a principal obligation of 200 pesos.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Julián García de Ergueta
Capitán don Manuel García de Ergueta
doña Ana Narcisa Sancho de Castañeda
doña Francisca de Paula García de Ergueta
doña Bárbara Agueda García de Ergueta
doña Ana María García de Ergueta
Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla
summary: This is the testament of Sargento Mayor don Julián García de Ergueta, who died before formally signing it, as certified by Bonilla. He declared his parents, wife, seven living children, and mother-in-law. Among his assets, he listed enslaved individuals Antonia and her children, and Manuel, who had escaped and was known to be in Granada at Don José Layo's house, with instructions for his recovery.

people_involved: Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla
Licenciado don Manuel José González Coronel
summary: Captain Don José Nicolás de Bonilla sold an enslaved boy named Juan Manuel, aged 13-14, to Licenciado Don Manuel José González Coronel for 160 pesos plata. Bonilla had purchased Juan Manuel three years prior from the estate of the deceased Licenciado Don Juan José Camacho, a Presbyter.

people_involved: doña Josefa de Aguilar y Santiago
B” don José Miguel Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: This is the testament of Doña Antonia de Acosta, daughter of Antonio de Acosta Arévalo and Doña Josefa de Aguilar y Santiago (both deceased), and former spouse of Don Agustín de Alvarado. She named her children Antonia Josefa and Pedro de Alvarado, their spouses, and her executor, B” Don José Miguel Guzmán y Echavarría. Her 14 grandchildren, children of her deceased children, were her heirs.

people_involved: Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla
summary: Captain Don José Nicolás de Bonilla took on an obligation of 100 pesos of silver for the capellanía founded by the deceased Doña Baltasara de Inza. This obligation was previously held by Lieutenant José Antonio Masis and his wife, Doña Juana Francisca Mondragón.

people_involved: Mtre. de Campo don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
Capitán don Cristóbal Ignacio de Soria
summary: On October 29, Mtre. de Campo Don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora declared that on April 19, 1747, while serving as executor for the deceased Don José de Sierra, Captain Alcaide of San Fernando fort, he and his wife, Doña Francisca de Arburola, jointly executed a bond and guarantee for 5322 pesos 6 reales plata. This action was taken at the request of the Governor and Captain General, Don Cristóbal Ignacio de Soria.

On October 6, the unnamed spouse of a deceased person paid 1052 pesos towards the estate settlement. Salvador Mendoza, agent for Rosa Maldonado, received 1000 pesos, and the Teniente Gral. received 52 pesos for costs. The remaining debt for the estate was 4270 pesos.

After the estate settlement concluded, various payments were due to individuals and heirs, totaling 1284 pesos 7 reales. These amounts were held in deposit because the named beneficiaries or their agents were not present in the city to receive them.

people_involved: Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: On October 30, Manuel Antonio Jiménez, with guarantors Benito Moscoso and Nicolás Salguero, acknowledged failing to fulfill an August 1, 1751, obligation to plant 3000 cacao trees on Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba's hacienda and cultivate them for 5 years until August 1, 1756. He agreed to pay for the 556 missing trees by providing three times that amount from his new fruit hacienda and to return 1231 fruit trees received earlier.

On October 31, José Miguel García, with Pedro de Alvarado as guarantor, undertook an obligation of 140 pesos 3 reales to Joaquín, Javier, and Rodulfa de Castillo. This stemmed from the estate of García's deceased mother, Victoria de Aguilar, who owed money to the five minor children of the deceased Salvador del Castillo. José Miguel García inherited his mother's cacao hacienda with this obligation. On August 19, 1757, Francisco Javier Castillo and Micaela Rodulfa Castillo received their shares, and noting their deceased brother Joaquín had received his, they cancelled their part.

On November 2, José Miguel García undertook an obligation to his four minor siblings, Gregorio, Manuel, Francisca, and Gertrudis García, for 261 pesos 2 reales related to their guardianship from their mother Victoria de Aguilar's estate. Victoria de Aguilar had left a cacao hacienda in the Valle de Barbilla, which José Miguel García inherited with these obligations. On March 29, 1756, Gregorio García and Juan Ignacio Rodríguez, husband of Gertrudis García, cancelled their part.

On November 5, Andrés Fernández and his wife María Trejos undertook an obligation of 182 pesos 1 real each to the minor children Juan Manuel and María del Rosario Carranza. This obligation arose from the estates of their deceased parents, Pablo Carranza and María Nicolasa de Trejos, and also from the estate of Alférez Matías Trejos. On March 3, 1756, Antonio López, husband of María del Rosario Carranza (also referred to as María Nicolasa Carranza), received his wife's share, leaving the obligation for Juan Manuel Carranza active.

On November 6, Juan Masís and his wife Josefa Fernández declared an obligation related to the estate of Alférez Matías Trejos. Manuel Trejos, son of Matías and Josefa's first husband, was adjudicated 265 pesos 2 reales. Upon Manuel's death, this amount passed to his five children with Josefa. Shares were received by Miguel Castro (husband of Josefa Micaela Trejos), Domingo Noguera (husband of Rita Josefa Trejos), and Josefa Fernández (for her deceased minor son José Antonio Trejos). Josefa also secured 106 pesos 1 real for her minor children, María Petronila and José Francisco Trejos. On October 8, 1774, Alfonso González, husband of María Petronila Trejos, cancelled her part.

On November 6, Gabriel de Quesada and his wife Antonia Trejos, with Sargento Mayor José Antonio de Oriamuno as guarantor, undertook an obligation of 265 pesos 2 reales to Benita Trejos, minor daughter of the deceased Alférez Matías Trejos, from his estate. This obligation was marked "No pasó," indicating it was not processed or finalized.
An event involving Sargento Mayor José Antonio de Oriamuno was initiated on November 19, but the details are incomplete in the provided text.

locations: Ciudad de los Reyes de Lima
people_involved: María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
Children of María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
summary: María Josefa de la Vega Cabral passed away, and her will declared a debt of 1400 pesos of cacao, inherited from her deceased father Antonio de la Vega Cabral, owed to Juan Sáenz Cascante in Lima. When 260 pesos remained unpaid, the judge ordered the sale of one of her slaves, but her children opposed and offered to guarantee the sum.

Capitán Manuel Felipe de Arleguí, as Procurador General of Cartago, ratified the sale of a 90-vara square plot of land in Cartago to Margarita Coto for 10 pesos. The plot was bordered by properties belonging to Manuela de Angulo and Rita Ramírez, the savanna, and the royal road from San Francisco.

In 1742, at the request of Procurador Síndico General José de Mier Cevallos, Governor Juan Gemmir y Leonard authorized the sale of city plots around Cartago to benefit population growth and fund necessary city repairs. The Procurador was empowered to sell these plots and deliver the proceeds to Alférez Luis de Soto Mayor, with Margarita Coto being one of the purchasers.

people_involved: Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Licenciado Manuel José González Coronel, Vicario Juez Ecco., granted general power of attorney to Br. Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba, a patrimonial Presbítero.

people_involved: Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Maestre de Campo Francisco Fernández de la Pastora granted general power of attorney to Br. Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba, a patrimonial Presbítero.

Gabriel de Quesada, his wife Antonia Trejos, and Sargento Mayor José Antonio de Oriamuno obligated themselves for 360 pesos and 2 reales. This sum included amounts adjudicated to Benita Trejos from the estates of her father, Alférez Matías Trejos, and her deceased mother, Isabel de Cárdenas, which Matías had been responsible for.

people_involved: Children of Francisco Gamboa and Lorenza de Quesada
Brothers of Francisco de Quesada (son of Cristóbal)
summary: Sargento Mayor Dionisio Salmón Pacheco and Capitán Antonio Elías de Arleguí, as executors of the late Capitán Francisco Gamboa, established a chaplaincy for masses for the souls of Francisco Gamboa, his first wife Lorenza de Quesada, and their two legitimate children. Ramón Poveda obligated himself for the principal of 645 pesos and 5.5 reales of cacao, with Francisco de la Riva providing a guarantee by mortgaging a cacao hacienda in Valle de Barbilla. Teniente Cristóbal de Quesada was named patron, succeeded by his eldest son Francisco de Quesada and then his other brothers.

people_involved: Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Br. Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba, who purchased the late Capitán Miguel de Ibarra's houses for 800 pesos of cacao, paid 155 pesos cash to Ibarra's executor, Sargento Mayor José Antonio de Oriamuno. For the remaining 645 pesos, he obligated himself to pay various chaplaincies and confraternities, including those served by Licenciado José Francisco de Alvarado and Sacristán Mayor Cayetano de Arleguí.

On January 10, 1755, Licenciado Cayetano de Arleguí, Sacristán Mayor, and Antonio Elías de Arleguí (as proxy for the absent Licenciado José Francisco de Alvarado), along with Félix Meneses (Mayordomo of Cofradía de la Concepción) and José Astúa (Mayordomo of Cofradía del Rosario), cancelled the obligations related to the sale of Miguel de Ibarra's houses.

Manuel de Guzmán Portocarrero and his wife Teresa Galindo obligated themselves for 300 pesos of cacao, representing the value of goods left by the deceased María Marín Laguna. They were to use 200 pesos to build a house for María's minor son, Juan Miguel Marín, and pay the remaining 100 pesos to José Calderón. María Marín Laguna had died under the authority of her father, Capitán Juan Francisco Marín Laguna, who sought the obligors.
By order of the Gobernador, the obligation undertaken by Manuel de Guzmán Portocarrero was cancelled on April 12, 1758, as he had satisfied the amount due.

people_involved: Closest cleric from the lineage of Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero
summary: Capitán Juan de Ocampo Golfín, as executor of Presbítero Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero, founded a chaplaincy for 8 recited masses for the soul of Capitán Domingo de Quesada. The principal of 500 pesos of cacao was charged to a cacao hacienda in Valle de Matina. The patrons and chaplains were to be the sons of Teniente Cristóbal de Quesada and other descendants of Domingo de Quesada, prioritizing the eldest, or the closest cleric from Martínez Cubero's lineage if none were ordained.

The will of Cristóbal de Quesada details his family. He was the legitimate son of Manuel de Quesada and María Gil de Quirós. He was first married to María de Bonilla, with whom he had Josefa Gregoria, Josefa Benita, Justa Rufina, and Antonia Manuela. He arranged marriages for Josefa Benita with Gregorio Acuña and Josefa Gregoria with Juan Carrillo. His second marriage was to Francisca Barboza, with whom he had Antonia María, Ana Josefa, and Félix José.

A will is being processed for Manuel de la Trinidad, naming his wife and Rafael Delgado as executors, and his nine children, including Francisca Ambrosia and José Felipe, as heirs. All mentioned children are alive.

Sargento Mayor José Antonio de Oriamuno and his wife, Catarina de Ibarra, grant each other reciprocal power to make a will. They name each other as executors and their two sons, Romualdo and José Francisco de Oriamuno, as heirs. José Antonio is from Panama, son of José de Oriamuno and Josefa Vázquez Meléndez, while Catarina is from 'here', daughter of Sargento Mayor Juan Francisco de Ibarra and Petronila de Moya.

Ayudante Mayor Juan Cristóbal Alvarez, residing in Aserrí, grants power to Captain José Manuel de Segura to collect 65 pesos of cacao from Doña Manuela de Zavaleta. This debt originated from the estate of her late husband, Captain José de Ginesta, and was owed to Alvarez's predecessor, Alejandro de Mora, in Cartago.

The will of the deceased Captain Juan José de Cuende is being processed by his attorneys: his widow Manuela Josefa de Ibarra, Sargento Mayor José Antonio de Oriamuno, and Maestre de Campo Francisco Fernández de la Pastora. He was married to Manuela Josefa and had four living children: Manuela, Romualdo, Diego, and Salvador, who are named as heirs, along with twelve enslaved people as part of his assets. The power of attorney for this will was granted on April 24, 1755.

José Nicolás de Bonilia and José Antonio de Bonilia (the latter acting as curator for the minor children of the deceased Sargento Mayor Pedro de Alvarado and Doña Chavarría) sold a house to Marcos de Alvarado. The house, previously the residence of the deceased parents, was encumbered with 500 pesos for a chaplaincy and 1000 pesos for the five minor children. Marcos de Alvarado agreed to pay 400 pesos to a chaplaincy of the San Francisco Convent, 100 pesos to the Cofradía de la Concepción, and 500 pesos for the guardianship.

people_involved: Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Presbítero Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba purchased the former residence of the deceased Captain Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra for 800 pesos of cacao. He paid 155 pesos cash to Sargento Mayor José Antonio de Oriamuno, the executor, and committed to pay the remaining 645 pesos to various chaplaincies and confraternities, including those associated with Licenciado José Francisco de Alvarado and Padre Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí.

people_involved: Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: To improve the security of the obligations from a previous house purchase, Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba transferred the debts from Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra's former house to another property he acquired, which was the former residence of his deceased brother, Licenciado José Francisco de Casasola, valued at 2000 pesos. On September 20, 1757, the obligations were cancelled by Padre José Francisco Alvarado, Félix Joaquín de Meneses (representing Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí and the Cofradía de la Concepción), and José Manuel González (representing the Cofradía del Rosario).

people_involved: Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba and Manuela Gertrudis Sancho de Castañeda exchanged properties. Juan Manuel traded the house he acquired from the estate of Captain Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra for a house that Manuela Gertrudis inherited from her parents.

Captain Benito de Alvarado y Jirón, Félix García de Ergueta, Rita García de Ergueta, and Bárbara de la Madriz Linares acted as guarantors for Captain José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda. They guaranteed 2000 pesos in silver, a sum required by the Cabildo for his appointment as alderman (regidor) and general depositary of the city.

Antonio Barros y Muro acquired the "San Juan" cacao plantation in Matina, previously owned by his deceased mother, for 1563 pesos. He paid 146 pesos and 3 reales upfront and committed the remaining balance to a chaplaincy.
Félix García de Sancho, who was preparing for a trip to Matina, granted power of attorney to his wife.

Alférez don José Velazco and doña María Ana de Barros obligate themselves for 136 pesos (cacao) to don Carlos Galarza, the executor of doña Josefa Pérez de Muro. This obligation is for a chaplaincy ordered by doña Josefa and is charged against a cacao plantation in Matina. Doña María Ana signs as "doña María Ana Varros y Muro".

people_involved: don Félix José de la Riva y Agüero
summary: Alférez don José Velazco and doña María Ana de Barros obligate themselves for 180 pesos (cacao) for a chaplaincy of the San Francisco Convent. This sum was previously charged on the houses of the deceased don Pedro Rodríguez Palacios and doña Teresa de Hoces Navarro, and was under the care of the deceased don Félix José de la Riva y Agüero, who delivered it on September 20, 1753. They mortgage their 1000-cacao-tree hacienda in Matina.

people_involved: Capitán don Antonio de Barros y Carvajal
summary: Capitán don Antonio de Barros y Carvajal states that on December 8, 1753, he acquired a hacienda with 1042 cacao trees in an auction for 1385 pesos. This hacienda was part of the assets left by his deceased mother, doña Josefa Pérez de Muro. He obligates himself for 1378 pesos in favor of the chaplaincy his mother ordered to be founded, mortgaging this hacienda, named "San Juan," and another 1400-tree hacienda adjacent to it, which he inherited from his mother.

people_involved: Capitán don Antonio de Barros y Carvajal
Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola
summary: Carlos Custodio Galarza, as executor of doña Josefa Pérez de Muro, establishes a chaplaincy of recited masses as ordered by doña Josefa. The principal sum is 1610 pesos, composed of 1378 pesos from Capitán don Antonio de Barros, 136 pesos from Alférez don José Velazco and doña María Ana de Barros, and 96 pesos from doña Josefa's house. The grandchildren of doña Josefa are named patrons and chaplains, with Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola as interim chaplain.

people_involved: Coronel don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Coronel don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora, newly appointed Governor and Lieutenant Captain General of the province, presents several individuals as guarantors for legal judgments. These individuals, including don Gregorio de Siles and don Pedro Jiménez, obligate themselves for 200 pesos plata.

people_involved: don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría Casasola y Córdoba
Capitán don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda
Sargento Mayor don José Antonio Oriamuno
summary: Several individuals, including clerics, captains, and widows, commit to paying 12 pesos (cacao) annually to Fray Jerónimo Soto Mayor while he is in "this city." In return, Fray Jerónimo obligates himself to care for and assist the sick in their families. Fray Jerónimo, originally sent to the province to ask for alms, has been practicing medicine due to a lack of doctors, benefiting the community.

people_involved: don Félix Joaquín de Alvarado Jirón
Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
summary: Don Félix Joaquín de Alvarado Jirón sells a tiled house in "this city" to Capitán don Tomás López del Corral. The house was originally acquired by don Diego Guerrero as the husband of doña Francisca Serrano. The price includes 325 pesos (cacao) for a chaplaincy founded by Bernardo Cortés, 100 pesos plata for the Confraternity of the Conception, and 175 pesos (cacao) received in cash.

people_involved: don Félix Joaquín de Alvarado Jirón
Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca
summary: Don Félix Joaquín de Alvarado y Jirón sells a cacao hacienda with 1448 trees in the Barbilla valley to Capitán don Tomás López del Corral. This hacienda was inherited from his father. The price is 600 pesos (cacao): 420 pesos for a chaplaincy founded by Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca, and 180 pesos received in cash.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
don Félix Joaquín de Alvarado Jirón
summary: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral obligates himself for 325 pesos (cacao) for the chaplaincy founded by Bernardo Cortés, which is prayed in the San Francisco Convent in Barba. This obligation is charged on the house he bought from don Félix Joaquín de Alvarado.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
summary: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral obligates himself for 100 pesos plata to the Confraternity of the Conception. This sum is charged on the same house mentioned previously.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca
don Félix Joaquín de Alvarado Jirón
summary: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral acknowledges a 420-peso cacao annuity (censo) at 5% interest, in favor of the chaplaincy founded by Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas Machuca. This annuity is charged on the 1448-tree hacienda he bought from don Félix Joaquín de Alvarado.

people_involved: don Tomás de Soto y Barahona
summary: Don Tomás de Soto y Barahona donates various stipulated goods, valued at 811 pesos (cacao), to his niece doña María Gertrudis Carazo, wife of don Félix José García Casasola.
Doña Teresa Barahona, widow of don Pedro Carazo, delivers the dowry goods of her daughter, doña María Gertrudis Carazo, wife of don Félix José García Casasola, valued at 818 pesos (cacao).

Don Félix José García Casasola and his wife doña María Gertrudis Carazo declare the assets they brought to their marriage. These assets include 576 pesos 3.5 reales plata (equivalent to 864 pesos 5 reales cacao) inherited by don Félix from his parents.

people_involved: don Tomás de Soto y Barahona
summary: An unnamed grantor's assets included 1779 pesos cacao, with 811 pesos donated by her uncle don Tomás de Soto y Barahona, and 818 pesos from her dowry. Presbítero don Juan de Casasola is mentioned in relation to 643.5 reales cacao.

Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla states that don José Antonio de Oriamuno is a court guarantor, along with others, for 250 pesos cacao owed by Capitán de Caballería don Cristóbal Ignacio de Soria, a former Governor of the province. Bonilla declares he will be responsible for this sum if it is demanded.
Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla grants general power of attorney to don José Lacayo de Briones.

Don Juan Manuel de Saborío, ill in bed, grants power to Bdo. don Lorenzo de Quesada, Cura of the villa of Cubujuquí, to make his will. He names his legitimate children, Lucía, Ramón, Lorenzo, and Vicente de Saborío, as his heirs.

people_involved: Br. don José Manuel García de Ergueta
Br. don Juan José de la Madriz Linares
Sargento Mayor don Julián García de Ergueta
Sargento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz
summary: Br. don José Manuel García de Ergueta, a Presbítero, establishes a chaplaincy for nine masses with a principal of 600 pesos cacao. His nephew, Br. don Juan José de la Madriz Linares, is named patron and chaplain, with the sons of his deceased brother, Sargento Mayor don Julián García de Ergueta, as alternates. The chaplaincy is based on a house on a lot owned by his sister, doña Rita García de Ergueta, widow of Sargento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz.

Doña Josefa González del Camino, daughter of don Juan González del Camino and doña Manuela Salazar, and widow of don Gil de Alvarado, makes her will. She names all her children as heirs but annuls a previous donation to her son don Domingo due to his ingratitude.

Doña Josefa González del Camino issues a codicil to her will, revoking the clause that annulled a donation of a mulato named Joaquín to her son don Domingo. She reinstates the donation, citing her son's improved conduct.

Residents of the valleys of Aserrí and Barba, including don Antonio Pérez de Cote and others, grant power to don Cristóbal de Gálvez Corral, a resident of Guatemala. Their aim is to petition the Supreme Government to convert the settlement of Cubujuquí in the Valle de Barba into a villa.

people_involved: B* don José Miguel Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: A partial deed is mentioned, involving Manuel de Alvarado, doña Paula González, and B* don José Miguel Guzmán y Echavarría.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
Capitán don José de la Aguila
summary: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral grants power to Capitán don José de la Aguila to compel don Manuel de Ortiz to declare if he transported López del Corral by ship from Realejo to Paita years ago, on orders from his brother Coronel don Antonio Ortiz, who was to pay for the passage. López del Corral also seeks information on whether Ortiz paid anything and if he knows about two carpets sent from Lima for his sister-in-law, doña Nicolasa Restan.

José Antonio Masís, don Agustín Marín, and Manuel de Jesús Campos, along with their brother Miguel Masís, grant freedom to José Antonio, a 27-year-old mulato blanco. José Antonio was the son of their slave Juana Masís and was inherited from their deceased parents, Juan Masís and doña María Fernández. Having paid his value of 300 pesos cacao, his freedom is granted.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
Sargento Mayor don José de Bonilla
summary: Alférez Manuel Carrillo sells stone and thorn fences to Capitán don Tomás López del Corral for 100 pesos cacao. The property, located in the city's ejidos, borders land of the heirs of the deceased Capitán don Juan Marín Laguna, the savanna, the Toyogres river, and former land of the deceased Sargento Mayor don José de Bonilla. Carrillo had purchased it from don Luis Arnesto de Troya for 165 pesos cacao.

people_involved: doña Manuela Petronila López del Corral
Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco
summary: Don Domingo de Alvarado, son of the deceased Capitán don Gil de Alvarado and doña Josefa González Camino, and widower of doña Manuela Petronila López del Corral, provides a dowry of 2178 pesos 4 reales and arras of 500 pesos for his future wife, doña Estéfana Salmón Pacheco. Doña Estéfana is the daughter of Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco and the deceased doña Francisca Serrano de Reina. The dowry includes two mulata slaves, Juliana and Manuela, and a house to be built by don Dionisio.

Capitán José Manuel Segura, a resident of the city's countryside, makes his will. He is the son of Francisca de Segura and an unknown father. He was widowed from his first wife, doña Antonia Chacón, with whom he had two children who died in infancy, and was married a second time to María de... (name incomplete).

people_involved: Doña Ana Teresa de Soto y Barahona
summary: Don Juan Teruel, Lieutenant General and Political Judge of the Barba and Aserrí valleys, established a dowry for his wife, Doña Petronila Carazo. The dowry included 1261 pesos and 6 reales, 500 pesos in 'arras,' a 10-year-old mulatto boy named Juan José valued at 200 pesos, and gold jewelry worth 249 pesos cacao, which was a gift from a relative of Doña Petronila.

people_involved: Licenciado Don Antonio Raimundo de Estrada
Capitán Don José Nicolás de Bonilla
summary: Doña Lorenza Muñoz Hidalgo, daughter of the late Doña Sebastiana Calvo, made her will. She was married to Don Nicolás de Estrada from Cartagena de las Indias, with whom she had 16 children, including several who survived and others who died in infancy or as priests. She also raised an orphan girl named Dominga and appointed Captain Don José Nicolás de Bonilla as her executor.

locations: paraje de la Pontezuela del valle de Matina
summary: Manuela Gutiérrez leased a cacao plantation with 975 fruit-bearing trees in the Pontezuela area of Matina Valley to Assistant Luis Ibarra for three years. The agreement stipulated a rent of 100 pesos cacao per year and the obligation for Ibarra to maintain the hacienda and an old clearing in good condition.

Cayetana Cubero, widow of Melchor de los Reyes, sold a cacao plantation in Barbilla Valley, adjacent to former haciendas of Simón Casasola, to Ensign Antonio Miguel Hernández. The plantation, consisting of 1340 trees, was sold for 1005 pesos, with 200 pesos paid upfront and the remainder in four annual installments. Cayetana noted that half of the sale price belonged to her minor son, Antonio Dionisio de los Reyes.

people_involved: Doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho de Castañeda
Licenciado Don José Francisco de Casasola
Licenciado Don Juan Manuel de Casasola
summary: Doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho de Castañeda, a widow, granted freedom to her mulatto enslaved woman, Micaela Barboza, who she received as a donation from Licentiates Don José Francisco and Don Juan Manuel de Casasola. She also freed Micaela's two daughters, Benita (4 years old) and Paula (7-8 months old), with the condition that each daughter would pay for one mass annually upon turning 16 for the grantor's soul.

people_involved: Licenciado Don Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí
Capitán Don José Nicolás de Bonilla
summary: Don Tomás López del Corral and his wife, Doña Francisca de Ibarra, pledged 100 pesos silver at 5% interest to the chaplaincy founded by Commissioner Don Baltasar de Grados, for which Licentiate Don Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí served as chaplain. Captain Don José Nicolás de Bonilla later redeemed this obligation and charged it to his cacao plantation in Matina, named San Miguel.

people_involved: Capitán Don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno
Teniente de Capitán Manuel Antonio de Cárdenas
Licenciado Don Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí
summary: Captain Don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno sold a cacao plantation with 1900 fruit-bearing trees in the Barbilla Valley, adjacent to Captain José Manuel Segura's hacienda, to Lieutenant Manuel Antonio de Cárdenas. The plantation, originally from the estate of Sergeant Major Luis Gutiérrez, was valued at 3192 pesos cacao, with portions of its value recognized as obligations to chaplaincies founded by Francisco Gutiérrez, Juan Bta. Bruno, and Commissioner Baltasar de Grados.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Francisco de Alvarado
Licenciado don Juan Bautista Pérezide Cote
summary: A total of 1818 pesos cacao in obligations from various chaplaincies, including one founded by Luis Gutiérrez, is recorded. The buyer of an unspecified property is responsible for these obligations, providing collateral in Valle de Barba and naming Francisco Ramos and Catarina de Torres as guarantors.
On March 18, 1768, the unnamed chaplains of the chaplaincies involved in the previously mentioned obligations cancelled them.

people_involved: Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola
summary: On September 3, doña Ramona de Sandoval, daughter of the late Capitán Cayetano Sandoval and doña Teresa Paniagua, executed her will. She named her husband, don Martín de Chavarría, and Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola as executors, with her husband as the sole heir, and mentioned her slave Lorenzo and sister doña Manuela de Sandoval.

On September 14, Micaela Chinchilla, widow of Juan Rafael Ramírez, sold a piece of land inherited from her father, Gaspar Chinchilla, to don Manuel de Guzmán Portocarrero for 25 pesos cacao. The land, located in the city's fields, bordered a ditch, the Tatiscú river/well, a site previously sold by her late husband to Pedro Chinchilla, and the property of Nicolás Villalobos.

On September 20, Doña Ana Madriz leased two cacao haciendas, 'Las Animas' and 'El Riachuelo,' in Calderón, Matina, to don Juan de Benavides for nine years. Don Juan was to maintain the 1300-tree haciendas, with usufruct in the first year and profit-sharing thereafter, after accounting for costs and a census payment on 'Las Animas' to the souls, for which Licenciado don Manuel González Coronel was chaplain.

people_involved: Capitán don Domingo Boniche y Luna (son)
Capitán don Domingo Boniche y Luna (father)
summary: On September 23, Capitán don Domingo Boniche y Luna, natural son of the late Capitán don Domingo Boniche y Luna of Panamá, granted power of attorney to don Juan de Urriola, a resident of Panamá and Regidor Alcaide de Cruces y Capitán a Guerra, to represent him in his deceased father's estate proceedings.

people_involved: doña María de Arburola y Rivaren
summary: On October 19, sisters Doña Antonia and Doña Rita Jiménez sold a 26-year-old mulatto slave named Félix Luna to Doña María de Arburola y Rivaren for 300 pesos cacao. Félix Luna was inherited from their mother, Doña Cayetana Jiménez, and was born to a mulata slave named María Josefa while in their mother's possession.

On October 20, don Gabriel Marcos de Ocaña and doña Joaquina López del Corral obligated themselves for 150 pesos cacao at 5% interest to the Convento de San Francisco in Cartago. They mortgaged their portion of a house that had belonged to doña Francisca de Arburola, doña Joaquina's mother.

Doña Bernarda Martínez redeemed a 150 pesos obligation. This sum originated from the value of materials from a destroyed house belonging to Capitán don Francisco de Bonilla and his wife doña Margarita Bolívar, which was also encumbered in favor of the Convento de San Francisco.

people_involved: Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno
summary: On January 11, 1773, Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno, Syndic of the Convento de San Francisco, received the 150 pesos from doña Joaquina López del Corral and formally cancelled the obligation.

people_involved: Teniente de Capitán Manuel Antonio Cárdenas
Licenciado don Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí
Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno
summary: On October 22, Teniente de Capitán Manuel Antonio Cárdenas, a resident of Valle de Barba, obligated himself for 160 pesos at 5% interest to the chaplaincy founded by Comisario don Baltasar de Grados, for which Licenciado don Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí is chaplain. This obligation is secured by the hacienda he acquired from Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno on September 1st of the same year.

people_involved: Teniente de Capitán Manuel Antonio Cárdenas
Guardián del Convento de San Francisco
summary: On October 23, Teniente de Capitán Manuel Antonio Cárdenas acknowledged censos totaling 900 pesos at 5% interest on the same hacienda mentioned previously. These censos were for chaplaincies founded by Francisco Gutiérrez (500 pesos) and Juan Bautista Bruno (400 pesos), both served by the Guardian of the Convento de San Francisco.

On October 25, Victoria Láscares, widow of Capitán Tomás Calvo, obligated herself for 141 pesos cacao, representing the value of a forge her late father-in-law, Alférez Francisco Calvo, had designated for a chaplaincy in his will. Her deceased husband, Tomás Calvo, had failed to formalize this obligation, which now burdens a house she owns in Cartago, and B* don Lorenzo de Quesada, the priest of Cubujuquí, is the chaplain.

people_involved: Capitán don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda
summary: On October 25, Capitán don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda, the General Depositary, received all goods from the inventory proceedings of Coronel don Francisco (name incomplete) for deposit.

people_involved: Capitán don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda
summary: Capitán Nicolás Barrantes, son of the deceased Juana Barrantes and an unknown father, made his will. He was married to Luisa Bartola de Proa and had five children: Juan (who was married), María, Pedro, Benito, and Manuel Barrantes. His wife and Capitán don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda were named as executors, and his five children were his heirs.

María Sibaja leased a 500-tree cacao plantation in the Matina valley to Esteban Rodríguez for four years. The property bordered Doña Manuela Zavaleta's hacienda to the north, Don Miguel de Alvarado's clearing to the south, and the river and mountain on other sides. The annual rent was 40 pesos of cacao.

people_involved: Doña Baltasara Marcela de Escalante Paniagua
summary: Doña Baltasara Marcela de Escalante Paniagua, a widow, made a codicil to her will, which was originally from 1705. She revoked a clause granting 100 pesos to Doña Gabriela Sarmiento, stating she had already given Sarmiento more than 200 pesos after Sarmiento married Don Miguel Antonio Fajardo. The codicil also mentioned her intention to free four slaves: María Josefa, María Bernarda, Rita Josefa, and José Joaquín, though the text is incomplete.

people_involved: Doña Antonia de la Granda y Balvin
summary: Don Tomás de la Madriz granted freedom to his mulatto criollo slaves, Francisco Justo (18 years old) and Isidro de la Paz (17 years old). These slaves were sons of María Josefa de Alvarado, a mulatto slave who had belonged to Doña Antonia de la Granda y Balvin, the deceased wife of Don Tomás, who had received them as a donation in 1742.

people_involved: Licenciado don Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí
summary: Licenciado don Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí, a Cleric Presbyter, granted a general power of attorney to Don Félix Joaquín de Meneses.

Capitán don Domingo Boniche, acting as the Syndic for the Convent of San Francisco, leased an 800-tree cacao plantation named "Las Flores" in Matina to Don Domingo de Alvarado. The lease was for five years at an annual rent of 40 pesos of cacao.

Doña Angela de Alvarado leased a 700-tree cacao plantation in the Matina valley to Don Alonso Pardo for three years. This hacienda, which she had received as a donation from Presbítero don Antonio de Guevara, bordered another hacienda belonging to Don José Nicolás de Bonilla. The annual rent was 89 pesos of cacao.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
Doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Doña María López del Corral, legitimate daughter of Capitán don Tomás López del Corral and Doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo, made her will.
