She was married to Don Marcos de Alvarado and had four minor children: Bruno, Isabel, Jerónimo, and José Manuel. Her husband and Don Hilario Polo were named as executors, and her four children were her heirs.

people_involved: Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral
summary: Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral granted a general power of attorney to her husband, Don Gabriel Marco de Ocaña, who was residing in Santiago de Guatemala.

Doña Juana Antonia de Guevara, whose husband Don Cayetano de Alvarado had been absent for over ten years, granted power of attorney to Don Clemente Rey Alvarez (Archdeacon of León Cathedral) and Capitán don Francisco de Hoces. They were to represent her in a pending lawsuit in the Bishopric of Nicaragua concerning a chaplaincy principal being claimed from her.

Margarita Villaga, wife of Capitán Nicolás Castillo, who resided in the Ujarraz valley, granted her husband power to execute a bond in favor of the Convent of San Francisco de Esparza. This obligation, for a sum to be received as a census, was to be made jointly with her.

people_involved: Doña Ana Teresa del Fierro y Rosas
Doña Antonia Eufracia del Fierro y Rosas
Doña Ana Teresa Masier y Vélez
Don Lucas Domingo del Fierro y Masier
Doña María Hermenegilda del Fierro y Masier
summary: Doña Ana Teresa del Fierro y Rosas (wife of Don Cayetano Pacheco) and her single sister Doña Antonia Eufracia del Fierro y Rosas (over 25) granted power of attorney to Don Cristóbal de Gálvez Corral of Guatemala. They sought division and partition of assets left by their paternal grandmother, Doña Ana Teresa Masier y Vélez, which they believed were deposited with their aunt, Doña María Hermenegilda del Fierro y Masier. Their father was the deceased Don Lucas Domingo del Fierro y Masier, and their mother was Doña Josefa de Rosas.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás de Soto y Barahona
summary: Capitán don Tomás de Soto y Barahona provided a bond for Don José Prudenciano de Peralta, allowing him to serve as Public Scribe of the Cabildo and Government. Peralta's title, issued by the Kingdom's Government, was for five years, with an obligation to pay 150 pesos of cacao annually. A later note from October 24, 1764, indicates Peralta's debt was cancelled after paying 100 pesos silver (or 200 pesos cacao).

Antonio Miguel Hernández and his wife María Carranza pledged 150 pesos of cacao to the Cofradía de la Concepción. They mortgaged their dwelling house, with a sugar mill and cane fields, located in the city's outskirts.

people_involved: Licenciado don Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí
summary: Antonio Miguel Hernández and María Carranza pledged 190 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Pedro Solano, for which Licenciado don Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí was the current chaplain. They mortgaged their house, cane fields, and sugar mill in the city's outskirts.
Antonio Miguel Hernández and María Carranza pledged 150 pesos to the Cofradía del Rosario.

Don José Manuel González Coronel, the Ecclesiastical Vicar, leased a cacao plantation in Matina to Francisco Ramos and his mother Catarina Simona de Torres for three years. The plantation was contiguous to another property they owned, and the rent was 200 pesos of cacao.

Captain Miguel Alvarado y Jirón sold a 39-40 year old mulatto slave named José Cayetano to José Martín de Echavarría. Alvarado y Jirón had previously purchased José Cayetano from Josefa Nicolasa de Guevara. The transaction was for 250 pesos plata and 50 pesos cacao.

people_involved: Manuela Josefa de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Doña Manuela Josefa de Ibarra y Calvo, a widow, sold a cacao plantation named 'La Gallega' in the Matina Valley to Juan de Dios Román and Manuel de Jesús Román, who are described as free pardos. She had inherited the plantation from her father and acquired the remaining shares from other heirs. The sale price was 8 reales per cacao tree.

José Hilario Morúa obligated himself for 550 pesos cacao at 5% interest to a chaplaincy founded by Miguel Masís, for which Licenciado Manuel Sáenz is the current Chaplain. These funds were previously redeemed by Efigenia Brenes and are secured by 2100 cacao trees located in the Matina Valley.

José Joaquín Guzmán received the assets of his wife, Ramona Carranza. These assets were inherited by Ramona from her deceased parents, José Ant° Carranza and Nicolasa Aguilar, and had been under lease by Antonio Miguel Hernández, Ramona's brother-in-law. The total value of the assets amounted to 595 pesos 2 reales.

Don Miguel de Neveras, a resident of Panama, obligated himself for 739 pesos 5 reales to Don José Antonio Arichavala, a resident of León, Nicaragua. Don José Nicolás de Bonilla acted as the attorney for Arichavala in this transaction.

Don José Velazco and his wife, Doña Mariana de Barros y Muro, sold a mulatta slave named Antonia Josefa to Miguel Alvarado. Doña Mariana had received Antonia Josefa as part of her dowry. The sale was for 275 pesos cacao.

people_involved: Félix Joaquín de Alvarado y Jirón
Fray Pedro de Soto y Barahona
summary: Don Félix Joaquín de Alvarado y Jirón, a resident of Granada, Nicaragua, and currently residing in Cartago, was commissioned by Fray Pedro de Soto y Barahona to sell indigo dye on credit. Captain Tomás de Soto y Barahona, representing Fray Pedro, claimed 445 pesos from Félix Joaquín in the Tribunal de Gobernación for the remaining debt. Félix Joaquín agreed to pay the Padre in Nicaragua.

people_involved: Félix Joaquín de Alvarado y Jirón
Coronel Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Félix Joaquín de Alvarado y Jirón and Gabriel Marco de Ocaña (husbands of María Francisca and Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral, respectively), along with Manuela Fernández de la Pastora, were in a lawsuit with Manuela Josefa de Ibarra before the Tribunal de Gobernación. Manuela Josefa claimed 545 pesos from the estate of Coronel Francisco Fernández de la Pastora (Manuela Fernández's father and Francisca de Arburola's second husband) for a loan, and the parties agreed to settle the dispute. Gabriel Marco de Ocaña represented Manuela Fernández de la Pastora as her curador ad litem, as she was between 18 and 25 years old.

Manuel Cayetano de Guevara, as the principal, along with Miguel Antonio Hernández and his wife María Carranza as guarantors, obligated themselves. Manuel Cayetano was the successful bidder for a cacao plantation in the Barbilla valley, which belonged to the deceased Gertrudis de Hinojosa, for 1794 pesos cacao. These funds were designated for a chaplaincy established by Gertrudis, with José Manuel de Segura serving as its patron.

Luis de Soto Mayor, acting as attorney for Beneficiado Antonio Guevara y Sáenz (who was in Masaya, Nicaragua), sold a cattle ranch named 'Rosales' in Puas to Miguel de Alvarado for 60 pesos plata. The land had been acquired by Antonio Guevara y Sáenz from Captain Francisco de Flores, a former resident of the Barba valley, on April 27, 1735, with the deed executed before Teniente Gobernador Sebastián Sandoval. The power of attorney for Antonio Guevara y Sáenz was granted in León on April 11, 1755.

Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral, daughter of the deceased José Antonio López del Corral and Francisca Arburola Iribaren, made her will. She was married to Gabriel Marco de Ocaña, with whom she had a son who died young, and declared her unborn child as her heir.

Don Manuel Cayetano de Guevara committed to release Antonio Miguel Hernández and María Carranza from a 1674 pesos obligation within two years. This obligation arose from their guarantee for him on February 20 of the same year, related to a chaplaincy to be founded by Gertrudis de Hinojosa.

Presbítero José Manuel González Coronel, as executor of Gertrudis de Hinojosa's will (granted in 1745), founded a chaplaincy for 23 masses. Her nephew, José Silverio de Segura, was named the first chaplain, with Captain José Manuel Segura as patron, and Manuel Cayetano de Guevara was responsible for the principal sum from a hacienda in Barbilla.

Don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda sold a 'negro bozal' (an unacculturated African slave) to Colonel Don José González Rancaño, the Governor of the province. The price for the slave, acquired in a public auction, was 225 pesos plata.

Josefa Cartín leased a cacao hacienda in the Barbilla valley for five years to Sargento Mayor Don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco. The property was noted to border the hacienda of Captain Don Francisco de la Riva to the East.

Don José Hilario Polo, Don Gabriel Marco de Ocaña, and Don Antonio Barros y Muro guaranteed Don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno for 500 pesos. Oriamuno was to pay this sum to the Royal Treasury in three annual installments, starting from the day he took possession of his employments.

people_involved: Juana María de Barros y Muro
summary: Don Francisco Lozano de Cárdenas and his wife, Doña Juana María de Barros y Muro, became obligated to Beneficiado Don Juan de Casasola for 350 pesos cacao. This amount represented the price of a hacienda they had leased.

Licenciado Don Manuel Sáenz, as the auction buyer of a sugar mill hacienda and other assets from the deceased Doña Francisca Bonilla in the Aserrí valley, acknowledged a debt of 484 pesos 2 reales cacao. This sum included a charge for a chaplaincy ordered by Bonilla, with Sáenz obligating the hacienda and agreeing to pay 5% interest.

Don Manuel González Coronel, acting as Ecclesiastical Judge due to the renunciation of the original executors, proceeded with the foundation of the chaplaincy ordered by the deceased Doña Francisca de Bonilla. The principal sum of 384 pesos 2 reales cacao was charged to Presbítero Don Manuel Sáenz, as detailed in the previous document.

people_involved: Ana Rita de la Madriz Linares
summary: Don Félix Sáenz and Doña Ana Rita de la Madriz Linares obligated themselves for 200 pesos plata at 5% interest to a chaplaincy, whose current chaplain was Licenciado Don Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí. This debt, originally charged to an illegible person and Doña Juana de Guevara, was secured by houses in the city now owned by Sáenz and Linares through auction. A marginal note from January 1787 indicates Francisco Ramos received payment from Pedro Puente in late June of the previous year.

people_involved: Doña Ana de la Madriz Linares
summary: Doña Ana de la Madriz Linares is responsible for 200 pesos plata, a debt also associated with her deceased husband. This debt is now cancelled.

Captain Don José Francisco de Arleguí acts as a guarantor for 200 pesos plata. This action releases Sergeant Major Don José Antonio de Oriamuno from his role as guarantor for Captain Don Domingo Boniche, who is a Lieutenant of Royal Officials in the province.
Captain Don Manuel Soler, Governor and Lieutenant Captain General of the province, grants general power of attorney to Sergeant Major Don Martín Díaz de Corcuera, a resident of León, Nicaragua.

people_involved: Doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo
Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Captain Don Tomás López del Coral, ill in bed in Masaya, grants power to his wife, Doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo, to make his will. His wife, Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría, and Captain José Antonio de Bonilla are named as executors, and his six legitimate children are named as heirs. The will was granted before Governor Don José González Rancaño.

people_involved: Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral
Unnamed husband of Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral
summary: Doña Tomasa Cavero lent 300 pesos plata to the husband of Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral in 1751, with an obligation to repay it the following year with interest. This transaction was recorded in a public deed before Don José Bermúdez, a Public Scribe in Panamá.

people_involved: Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral
Unnamed husband of Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral
summary: Doña Tomasa Cavero died intestate, and her sister Doña Rosa Cavero inherited the debt owed by Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral's husband. Doña Rosa conferred power to Don Lorenzo de la Peña to collect the debt, and on October 10, Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral became guarantor for her husband's debt.

people_involved: Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdova
Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral
summary: On August 8, 1766, Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdova, acting on behalf of Doña Rosa Cavero (who had substituted power from Don Lorenzo de la Peña), received the 300 pesos from Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral. The debt was then cancelled.

people_involved: Doña Juana María de Barros y Muro
summary: Don Francisco Lozano Cadenas and his wife, Doña Juana María de Barros y Muro, assume a 100-peso debt to the Cofradía del Rosario, which was previously owed by Don Tomás López del Coral. They secure this debt with a cacao plantation in Matina.

people_involved: Doña Juana María de Barros y Muro
summary: Don Francisco Lozano Cadenas and Doña Juana María de Barros y Muro assume a 100-peso cacao debt to the Cofradía de la Concepción, located in the Convent of Ujarráz. This debt had been redeemed by Captain Nicolás Barrantes, and they now secure it with a cacao plantation in Matina.

people_involved: Don Luis Fernando Sancho de Castañeda
summary: A group of residents from Cartago and the valleys of Aserrí and Barba act as guarantors for the residency of Governor and Lieutenant Captain General Don Manuel Soler. This guarantee was granted in the town of Cubujiquí.

people_involved: Doña María Elena de la Flor
Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Doña María Elena de la Flor grants power to her sister, Doña Josefa de la Flor, to make her will. Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría is named as executor, and having no heirs, she designates her soul as the beneficiary.
A legal document was signed by Don Félix Joaquín Meneses and Don Juan Segundo. Doña Gabriela, stating she could not write, had one of the witnesses sign on her behalf.

people_involved: Licenciado Don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí
summary: Doña Quiteria Delgado assumes a debt of 405 pesos 5 reales cacao to the chaplaincy founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela, whose patron is Rafael Delgado. This obligation stems from a legal dispute in the Ecclesiastical Court concerning two chaplaincies, one founded by Macotela and another by Doña Eugenia de Abarca, both located in a house formerly owned by Doña Luisa Salmón Pacheco. The judge prioritized Macotela's chaplaincy, and Doña Quiteria mortgages the house and a cacao plantation in Barbilla.

Doña Bernarda Martínez makes her will, identifying her deceased parents, Capitán Francisco Martínez and Doña Lorenza Venegas, and her deceased first husband, Don Antonio de Villarevia, from Asturias, with whom she had three children. She also declares three later children, Francisca Javiera, José Francisco, and Ana Josefa Martínez, and designates her house for these three youngest children. Don José Antonio de Oriamuno is named as executor.

Manuel Brenes makes his will, identifying his deceased parents, Marcos Brenes and Cayetano de Arce. He also mentions his first marriage to Olaria de Segura and their three children: Juana, Isidro, and Juan.

An unnamed individual's will or testament details his family, including his second wife María Manuela Salas and their children. He provides for his stepson Eduardo Badilla and arranges the marriage of his daughter María Antonia. He also leaves 25 pesos cacao to his brother José Antonio Brenes and names his wife and Manuel Meléndez as executors. The document was granted before José Manuel Fernández, Juez de los Campos.

people_involved: Antonia Josefa Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Don Martín de Chavarría, as principal, and his mother Doña Micaela de Bonilla, as guarantor, obligated themselves to Doña Antonia Josefa Muñoz de la Trinidad for 300 pesos cacao. This obligation was a result of a condemnation against Martín de Chavarría in the Ecclesiastical Court at the request of the creditor, with payments due at the San Juan harvest and Christmas.
Captains Nicolás Ulloa and Manuel José de Guzmán posted bail for Captain Ramón Poveda, who was imprisoned due to an ongoing legal case.

people_involved: Juana Francisca (slave of Catarina de Siles)
José Antonio (slave of Catarina de Siles)
Juan José (slave of Catarina de Siles)
Síndico del Convento de San Francisco
José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Doña Catarina de Siles, daughter of the late Captain Andrés de Siles and Doña María de Chaves, made her testament. She was married to Don Domingo de Cáceres, originally from Trujillo, Peru, who had left the city years ago. Her deceased children included María Manuela (married to Juan Manuel de Alvarado), Josefa Lucía, and José Martín (who became Fray Francisco de San José). She ordered a chaplaincy on her house and granted freedom to her slaves upon her death, provided each said a mass for her. Her executors were Bachelor Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría and Don Nicolás Ulloa.
Captain Don Esteban Ruiz de Mendoza posted bail for Captain Diego Guerrero, who was imprisoned due to an ongoing legal case before the Governor.
Don Domingo de Alvarado posted bail for Don Antonio José Graliano, who was imprisoned due to an ongoing legal case before the Governor.

people_involved: José Antonio de la Cruz Matus
Juana Francisca (slave of Manuel José González Coronel)
summary: Don Manuel José González Coronel sold a 15-year-old enslaved girl named Juana Francisca, daughter of an enslaved woman named Bárbara (inherited from his parents), to Don José Antonio de la Cruz Matus, a resident of Granada. The transaction was for 250 pesos plata.

Sergeant Major Don José Antonio de Oriamuno granted power of attorney to his son, Don José Francisco de Oriamuno, who was traveling to Nicaragua. The purpose was to sell an enslaved mulatto named Blas de la Candelaria, approximately 30 years old, whom José Antonio had received as a dowry from his father-in-law, Sergeant Major Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra, through his wife Doña María Catarina de Ibarra. The intended sale price was 300 pesos plata.

people_involved: Mateo José de Navia y Bolaño
summary: The Governor, Captain Don Manuel Soler, and Don José Nicolás de Bonilla, Lieutenant of Royal Offices, sold an enslaved Creole mulatto named Juan Nicolás Mompos, approximately 20 years old, to the Bishop Don Mateo José de Navia y Bolaño. Juan Nicolás Mompos was an enslaved person of His Majesty, apprehended in the Matina valley, and sold for an appraised price of 150 pesos plata, with the Bishop agreeing to pay any difference if the final auction price exceeded this amount.

Ensign Don José Velazco and his wife Doña Mariana Barros y Carvajal sold 3/4 of a caballeria of land in Santana to Captain Don Antonio Elías de Arleguí for 50 pesos cacao. The land's title was held by Mariana's sister, Doña Juana María de Barros, and bordered properties owned by Licenciado Don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí. The sellers had inherited this land from Mariana's sister, Doña María Manuela de Barros, who left it to their son, José Miguel Velazco.

Don Pedro de Ulloa sold a 14-year-old enslaved mulatto girl named María Eusebia Ulloa to Don Pedro José de Alvarado for 200 pesos plata. María Eusebia was the daughter of an enslaved mulatto woman named Juana Garvanzo, who belonged to Doña María Garvanzo, the mother of the seller.
Doña Catarina de Arburola Iribaren is mentioned in relation to her deceased son, Don Félix J..., though the full context of the mention is incomplete due to a torn document.
A mulatto slave named Francisco de la Flor, inherited from an unnamed grantor, was recognized as belonging to the grantor's grandson, Félix José de la Riva.

A dowry letter was issued for Don Juan Quintín Maestre, son of Benito Maestre and Encarnación Chaves, and Doña Antonia Micaela de Segura, daughter of Capitán José Manuel de Segura and Catarina Ruiz de Hinojosa. The dowry included 2234 pesos 4 reales in cacao and 500 pesos in cacao as arras.

people_involved: Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
José Antonio de la Cruz Matus
summary: Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba sold a negrito slave named Francisco, approximately 18 years old, to Don José Antonio de la Cruz Matus for 300 pesos plata. Casasola y Córdoba had acquired Francisco on May 26, 1758, through an exchange with Coronel Don José González Rancaño.

people_involved: Licenciado don Manuel José González Coronel
José Antonio de la Cruz Matus
summary: Licenciado don Manuel José González Coronel sold a 40-year-old female slave, inherited from his parents, along with her four children (María Josefa, 18; Jerónima, 12; Manuela Josefa, 9; José Antonio, 4) to Don José Antonio de la Cruz Matus for 1125 pesos.

people_involved: José Antonio de la Cruz Matus
Licenciado don Manuel José González Coronel
summary: Don José Antonio de la Cruz Matus, a resident of Granada, obligated himself to Licenciado don Manuel José González Coronel for 1305 pesos. He agreed to remit 705 pesos upon arrival in Nicaragua and bring 600 pesos from Guatemala, invested as indicated by the creditor, hypothecating the slaves he had previously purchased.

people_involved: Doña María Manuela de los Dolores y Miranda
summary: Doña Josefa Liberata Chacón, a widow residing in the Ujarrás valley, sold a 12-year-old mulatto slave named Nicolasa Cayetana, daughter of a black slave named Rosa, to Doña María Manuela de los Dolores y Miranda for 200 pesos plata. Nicolasa Cayetana was inherited by Josefa Liberata Chacón from her parents.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Andrés de Bonilla
Capitán don Félix García de Ergueta y Sancho
Capitán don José Martín de Chavarría
José Manuel de los Reyes y Guzmán
Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla
summary: Several individuals, including Sargento Mayor don Andrés de Bonilla and various Capitanes, provided a guarantee of 2600 pesos for Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla, who was appointed Teniente de Oficiales Reales.

people_involved: Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla
Doña Lucía de Alvarado y Jirón
Sargento Mayor don Andrés de Bonilla
Capitán don Félix García de Ergueta y Sancho
José Manuel de los Reyes y Guzmán
summary: Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla and his wife, Doña Lucía de Alvarado y Jirón, presented themselves and several other individuals as guarantors for his service as Teniente de Oficiales Reales, who then obligated themselves.

people_involved: Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
Licenciado don Manuel José González Coronel
summary: Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría requested the opening of the testament of the deceased Licenciado don Manuel José González Coronel, believing he was named as an executor.

people_involved: Licenciado don Manuel José González Coronel
Sargento Mayor don Blas González Coronel
B” don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
Licenciado don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí
summary: The testament of Licenciado don Manuel José González Coronel, Comisario del Santo Oficio, was recorded. He ordered a chaplaincy, with the first chaplain to be a child of Capitán don José de Lebrón and Doña Manuela Josefa Banegas, and named B” don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría and Licenciado don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí as executors.

people_involved: Capitán don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Capitán don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón leased a cacao hacienda in the Barbilla valley, containing over 1470 trees, to Juan Francisco Colina for four years at 87 pesos of cacao per year.

Doña Angela de Alvarado, a widow, leased a cacao hacienda in Barbilla to José Cubero, a free mulatto, for three years at 97 pesos of cacao per year. This rental was later cancelled on October 18, 1862.

Doña Baltasara Paniagua, a widow, leased a cacao hacienda in the Barbilla valley to Don Juan Benavides for three years. The rent was 125 pesos for the first year and 150 pesos for each of the subsequent two years.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín
Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara Sáenz
summary: Alférez Hermenegildo Maroto and his wife Luis Valeriano obligated themselves for 208 pesos 2 reales in cacao, derived from 138 pesos 6.5 reales segregated from the estate of Presbítero don Hermenegildo de Alvarado. This sum pertained to a chaplaincy founded by Sargento Mayor don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín and Doña Magdalena Pérez de Luna, which was vacant due to the death of Licenciado don Antonio de Guevara Sáenz. The obligation was secured by a new hacienda in the Barbilla valley.
A testament was recorded for Doña Baltasara Paniagua, daughter of Paniagua, stating she had been married three times.
Capitán José Antonio Bermúdez married an unnamed individual. He did not contribute any assets to the marriage.

people_involved: José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Marco de Ocaña, a resident of Colmenar, made a testament. The document mentions her husband, José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría, as an executor, and her son, José. The escritura is noted as being completely torn.

An unnamed woman, daughter of deceased Juan de Ginés de Hinojosa and Gertrudis Ruiz, and wife of Capitán José Manuel de Segura, made her testament. She had children José Silverio and Antonia Micaela de Segura, and inherited 300 pesos cacao from a deceased son of her husband and his first wife, Antonia Chacón. She arranged the marriage of Antonia Micaela to Juan Quintín Maestre and held 200 pesos in trust for Catarina Chinchilla and Manuela de Segura. Her two children were named as heirs.

locations: Ciudad de los Reyes de Lima
people_involved: Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdova
Jacinta María de Santa María y Torrejos
summary: Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba sold a 10-year-old enslaved girl named María Josefa, daughter of Antonia Francisca, to Doña Jacinta María de Santa María y Torrejos, a resident of Lima. Antonia Francisca was previously owned by Juan Manuel's sister, Josefa de Casasola y Córdoba, who had purchased her from María Feliciana de Iriondo of Santiago de Guatemala. The sale price was 200 pesos, and Luis de Soto Mayor accepted on behalf of the buyer.

people_involved: José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Doña Serafina de Guzmán y Echavarría, daughter of the deceased Capitán José de Guzmán and Antonia Margarita de Echavarría Navarro, granted freedom to her 5-year-old mulatilla slave, Josefa Benita. Josefa Benita, daughter of Antonia Josefa de la Flor, was freed due to the extensive service her mother provided to Serafina and her brother, Cura José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría.

Capitán Pascual Doria, a merchant from Panamá, owned the ship 'Nuestra Señora del Carmen' docked at Puerto de Caldera and preparing to depart for Tierra Firme. He committed to not carrying contraband goods, under penalty of 1000 pesos plata, guaranteed by the ship itself.

Doña Catarina de Arburola y Rivaren, a widow, donated a 3-year-old enslaved girl named Cayetana Fulgencia to her grandson, Don Félix Francisco de la Riva. Cayetana Fulgencia was the daughter of another enslaved woman named Juana Ventura, who was born in Catarina's house.

María Calvo, widow of José de Chavarría, sold a 15-year-old mulatilla slave named María Andrea to Don Félix Mondragón, a resident of Granada, Nicaragua. María Andrea was the daughter of a mulata slave inherited by María Calvo from her father, Miguel Calvo. The sale price was 200 pesos plata.

Doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho de Castañeda, daughter of deceased Juan Sancho de Castañeda and Juana de Alvarado, and widow of Rafael Cevallos, made her testament. She mentioned her deceased daughter Juana Loreta, numerous nieces and nephews, and ordered a capellanía of masses with Antonio Maximiliano de Alvarado as chaplain and her brother, Capitán José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda, as patron. Her assets included an enslaved mulata, Micaela Barboza, and her four children: María de los Dolores, Paula Josefa, Cecilia, and José Joaquín. Her brother, José Manuel, was named executor.

María de Acuña, being ill in bed, granted power to her husband, Capitán Francisco de la Riva, to make her testament. Her four legitimate children, Manuela Josefa, Manuela, Angela, and Rosa de la Riva, were named as heirs. Her husband and José Francisco Ca.... were appointed as executors.

Teniente de Capitán Diego Ortiz del Castillo, son of the deceased Juana de Madrigal, made his testament. He was a widower of Ana Montoya, with whom he had a daughter, Tomasa. He later married Ramona de Quesada, also deceased, who had a natural daughter named Ana Josefa Hernández.

people_involved: José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
María Josefa de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: An unnamed woman, married to Antonio Ortiz, leaves 5% of her assets. Her executors are her husband, José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría, and María Josefa de Guzmán y Echavarría. Her heirs include her daughter Tomasa de Ortiz and Félix Francisco de Ortiz, whom she raised as a son.

Sargento Mayor Juan Manuel Caballero of Chiriquí sells a 25-30 year old Carabadí slave named María Trinidad de los Ríos to Captain José Nicolás de Bonilla for 250 silver pesos. Caballero had previously purchased her on May 17 of the same year from José del Carmen Vestia, with Juan Rangel as the public scribe.

people_involved: Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Presbítero Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba offers his enslaved man, Juan, freedom if he can acquire 200 pesos of cacao in Matina within two years. Josefa Guerrero and her son Fernando Masís provide the requested guarantee for Juan to fulfill this condition.

This entry records the will of Manuela Benita Carranza, daughter of the deceased José Antonio Carranza and María Nicolasa Morales. She is married to José Martín González and names her four minor children, Eusebio Antonio, José Nicolás, María Josefa, and José Lorenzo González, as heirs. Bachiller José Manuel García de Ergueta, a Presbítero, is appointed as her executor.

people_involved: José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
Manuel José de los Reyes y Guzmán
summary: Vicario José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría donates a house he built on his own land to Manuel José de los Reyes y Guzmán, a free mulatto minor under 14. The land was originally purchased from Juan José Paniagua, the minor's father. The house borders properties owned by Captain Antonio de Barros, the late Licenciado Manuel López Conejo, Manuel Antonio Taulera, and Captain Manuel José de Guzmán.

Alférez Juan Salmón Pacheco sells an 18-year-old mulatta slave named Teresa de Reina and her 8-month-old mulatto son, José Antonio, to Andrés de la Cruz Matus for 360 pesos in total. Juan Salmón Pacheco had inherited Teresa from his mother, Francisca de Reina.

people_involved: María Teresa de Larga Espada Gavello
summary: Captain Romualdo Muñoz de la Trinidad, widower of María Teresa de Larga Espada Gavello, establishes a dowry of 562 pesos and arras of 500 pesos for his current wife, Tomasa Josefa Gómez. Romualdo is the son of the deceased Captain Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad and Antonia Josefa de Arburola, while Tomasa is the daughter of Juan de Dios Gómez and Alfonsa García de Ergueta.

This entry details the will of María Josefa Carranza, daughter of the deceased José Antonio Carranza and María Nicolasa Morales. She is married to Antonio Miguel Hernández and names her seven children as heirs, including Josefa Micaela who is married to Juan Franco Colina. Bachiller José Manuel García de Ergueta and Pedro José Corrales are appointed as executors.

people_involved: José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Captain Esteban Ruiz de Mendoza, as the principal, along with Marcos de Alvarado and Félix García Sancho as guarantors, obligate themselves for 909 pesos 2 reales of cacao. This amount is owed from Ruiz de Mendoza's role as tithe collector in Matina since 1757, and the guarantee was demanded by the city's priest, José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría.

Captain José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda and his wife Baltasara de la Madriz Linares obligate themselves for the accounts of Sancho de Castañeda's tithe collection since 1758. They also agree to cover 268 pesos in cacao if Antonio de Soto Mayor, a resident of León, fails to pay for a previous credit sale.

Sargento Mayor Dionisio Salmón Pacheco, acting as attorney for Pablo de Selva Mayor of Granada, sells a 20-year-old black enslaved man named José Fermín to Miguel de Alvarado Jirón for 300 pesos. Pablo de Selva Mayor had purchased José Fermín from José Francisco de Oriamuno, who was acting as attorney for his father, José Antonio de Oriamuno.
An incomplete entry from September 22 mentions Teniente de Caballería José Antonio.

García leased a cacao plantation of approximately 1500 trees in the Matina valley, near Chirripó, to Juan Francisco Colina. The lease was for three years, commencing on the upcoming October 12th, with an annual rent of 150 pesos cacao.

people_involved: Licenciado don Manuel José González Coronel
Comisario don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
Doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí, as executor for the deceased Licenciado don Manuel José González Coronel, sold the Licenciado's former house and lot in Cartago to don Domingo de Alvarado for 600 pesos cacao. The payment was divided, with 500 pesos allocated to the Cofradía de la Concepción and 100 pesos to a chaplain. On February 20, 1772, Arleguí and Teniente Francisco Molina, as Mayordomo of the Cofradía, received the payments from Alvarado, thereby canceling the obligation.

people_involved: Doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo
Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
summary: Doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo, a widow, sold a 1200-tree cacao plantation in the Barbilla valley to Juan Francisco Colina for 620 pesos cacao. This hacienda had been acquired by her late husband, Capitán don Tomás López del Corral, from Capitán don Joaquín de Alvarado. Colina was to pay 420 pesos to a chaplaincy founded by the late Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas, with the remaining 200 pesos paid in two installments.

people_involved: Doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo
Cura don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Juan Francisco Colina obligated himself for 420 pesos cacao to the chaplaincy founded by the late Licenciado don Antonio de Vargas, which was under the charge of doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo. The current patron and chaplain was Cura don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría. Colina mortgaged the cacao hacienda he had recently acquired as security for this obligation.

people_involved: Cabo de escuadra José Miguel de Arce
Licenciado don Manuel José González Coronel
summary: Cabo de escuadra José Miguel de Arce obligated himself for 400 pesos cacao to the chaplaincy founded by Gertrudis Ruiz, which was previously served by the late Licenciado don Manuel José González Coronel and is now patroned by Capitán José Manuel de Segura. This obligation was secured by a 1200-tree cacao plantation in La Fontezuela, Matina valley, which Capitán Nicolás Castillo had previously possessed with this encumbrance and then offered, with Arce taking it as an occupant.

Don Félix Joaquín de Alvarado, a resident of Masaya, Nicaragua, obligated himself for 300 pesos cacao to one of the chaplaincies managed by don José Francisco de Alvarado. These funds were previously charged to don Rafael de Céspedes' houses in Cartago. Alvarado mortgaged a cacao plantation in La Pontezuela, Matina valley, as security.

people_involved: Doña Tomasa Joaquina López del Corral
Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla
summary: Doña Tomasa Joaquina López del Corral, a widow, obligated herself for 150 pesos plata to the Convento de San Francisco, through its Síndico General, Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla. The obligation was later canceled, with the sum being invested in repairing the San Francisco church. The exact date of cancellation is not visible due to a damaged document.

Juan Manuel Carranza, a 22-year-old single man and legitimate son of the late Pablo Carranza and María Nicolasa Trejos, made his will. He named his sister, María del Rosario Carranza, and appointed don Andrés...des as his executor, with his soul designated as the heir. This document, like many others, is partially damaged.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno
summary: In the year 1762, Capitán don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno and don José Antonio de Oriamuno served as interim governors.
On February 25, 1762, doña Ana Jiménez sold an enslaved mulatta named María Francisca to don Juan José de Carrión. María Francisca was 30 years old and the daughter of María Josefa Jiménez.

people_involved: Capitán don Luis de Soto Mayor
Teniente de Capitán don José Antonio Jiménez
summary: Capitán don Luis de Soto Mayor sold a 33-year-old mulato slave named Juan Vicente to Teniente de Capitán don José Antonio Jiménez for 200 pesos plata. Soto Mayor had previously acquired Juan Vicente from José Cubero for the same price.

Don Juan José Carrión attempted to sell a 30-year-old slave named María Francisca to don Felipe de Paz, a resident of Panamá, for 300 pesos cacao. Carrión had purchased María Francisca from doña Ana Jiménez for the same amount, but this transaction was not signed or completed.

Don Juan José Carrión sold a 30-year-old mulata slave named María Francisca to don José de Uriza, a local trader. Carrión had acquired María Francisca from doña Ana Jiménez for 300 pesos cacao, and the current sale was for 200 pesos cacao and 50 pesos plata.

people_involved: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora
Br. don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora granted general power of attorney to Br. don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba.

people_involved: Capitán don Miguel Antonio de Unanue
summary: Capitán don Miguel Antonio de Unanue, a resident of Panamá, granted power of attorney to don Juan Ignacio Villalba and don Domingo Eguizalva, residents of Santiago de Guatemala. They were authorized to represent him in the auction of 12 caballerías of arable land in the jurisdiction of Esparza.

people_involved: Teniente de Capitán don José Antonio Jiménez
Capitán don Luis de Soto Mayor
summary: Teniente de Capitán don José Antonio Jiménez sold a 33-year-old mulato slave named Juan Vicente to don Pablo Campusano, a resident of Nicaragua residing in Cartago. Jiménez had previously purchased Juan Vicente from Capitán don Luis de Soto Mayor for 200 pesos plata, selling him for the same amount.

people_involved: Capitán don José Miguel de Céspedes
summary: Juan Miguel de Céspedes, preparing to become a Franciscan religious, made his will. He bequeathed a cleared land in Matina, made by his father, and his maternal inheritance (after his mother's death) to his uncles and aunts for raising him. He named his mother as the primary heir and his uncles as secondary heirs and executors, also stating he did not consent to the liberation of his mother's three slaves.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás de Soto y Barahona
summary: Capitán don Tomás de Soto y Barahona granted freedom to Ubalda, a 40-year-old mulata. He had purchased Ubalda from the heirs of doña Francisca de Arburola for 350 pesos plata.
Don Felipe de Paz Seldán, a resident of Panamá, granted general power of attorney to don Juan Esteban Castaño Aredondo, also from Panamá and currently residing in Cartago.

Doña María Masís, a widow, freed Juan Agustín, a 30-year-old slave she inherited from her deceased parents, Juan Masís and doña María Fernández. Juan Agustín was the son of Juana Masís, also a slave of her parents, and his freedom cost 300 pesos cacao.

people_involved: Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla
summary: Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla, owner of land in San Jerónimo, Nicoya, granted power of attorney to Capitán don Pedro José Zeledón. Zeledón was authorized to sell the lands for 501 pesos plata, with the buyer assuming a 175 pesos chaplaincy debt to the Convento de San Francisco de Granada, Nicaragua.

people_involved: Capitán don Antonio de la Riva
Don José Nicolás de la Riva y Agüero
Don Félix José de la Riva y Agüero
Don Esteban de la Riva y Agüero
Doña Ana Gertrudis de la Riva y Agüero
Don Félix Francisco de la Riva
summary: Doña Catarina Lucrecia de Arburola, widow of Capitán don Antonio de la Riva, made her will, confirming a 1761 donation of a 3-year-old slave, Cayetana Fulgencia, to her grandson don Félix Francisco de la Riva. She listed her children, surviving daughter Ana Gertrudis, and other slaves, and ordered a chaplaincy to be served by her grandson don José Joaquín de Quinteros, naming don Félix Joaquín Meneses as her executor.

people_involved: Licenciado don Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí
Sargento Mayor don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí
Licenciado don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí
summary: Licenciado don Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí, a Presbyter Cleric, made his will on July 29. He was the chaplain for several chaplaincies founded by individuals like Vasco Solano and Baltasar de Grados. His brother, Licenciado don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí, and his mother, doña Engracia de Hoces Navarro, were named as albaceas, with his mother also being the sole heir.

On August 3, Capitán don Pedro José Lebrón donated his 30-year-old mulata slave, Juana, to doña Lucila de Alvarado. Juana was born and raised in the house of Capitán don Martín de Garayar, who gave her as a dowry to his daughter, Dª María Hipólita de Garayar, Lebrón's first wife. Lebrón, feeling obligated to doña Lucila, who was the mother of his second wife, doña Agueda Ramona de Bonilla, made the donation.

people_involved: doña Catarina de Arburola y Ribaren
don Félix de la Riva y Agúero
Licenciado don Francisco de Paula Merino
summary: On August 4, don Félix Joaquín Meneses, as the executor of the late doña Catarina de Arburola y Ribaren, sold the 33-year-old black slave Francisco Custodio to don Joaquín Corona for 250 pesos plata. Doña Catarina had inherited Francisco Custodio from her son, don Félix de la Riva y Agúero, who had purchased him in Santiago de Veragua from Licenciado don Francisco de Paula Merino for 300 pesos plata.

people_involved: Gobernador y Teniente de Capitán Gral. Interino don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno
Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno
summary: On September 2, the interim Governor and Lieutenant Captain General, don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno, granted power of attorney to his son, Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno, for the purpose of making a will. Don José Antonio is also identified as the Lieutenant Governor of the Barba valleys. His mother, doña Ana García de Estrada, is mentioned as deceased.

people_involved: Ayudante Mayor don Félix Joaquín Meneses
summary: On September 6, María Calvo, natural daughter of the late Capitán don Miguel Calvo and Ana Cardoso, made her will. She was the widow of Capitán Jose de Chavarría and had several children, with only María Josefa and Antonia Josefa still living. She also named her slaves José Cayetano, Rosa, and Ana, granting José Cayetano 50 pesos towards his freedom and stipulating Rosa's freedom after serving her sick daughter Antonia Josefa. Ayudante Mayor don Félix Joaquín Meneses was named albacea, and her two living daughters and grandsons Juan Antonio and Manuel Nicolás de Chavarría were heirs.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás de Soto y Barahona
Sargento Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
doña Ana Teresa de Soto y Barahona
doña Joaquina de MATADO y Casasola
Capitán don Antonio Elías de Arleguí
summary: On September 22, Capitán don Tomás de Soto y Barahona, son of the late Sargento Mayor don Antonio de Soto y Barahona and doña Petronila de Hoces Navarro, made his will. He listed several slaves and made specific bequests, including a mulatillo Benito to his nephew don Francisco and a mulatillo Juan Antonio to Juanito Teruel. His sister, doña Ana Teresa de Soto y Barahona, received half a house, which would pass to his niece doña Gertrudis Carazo, and then to her daughter doña Joaquina de MATADO y Casasola. Doña Gertrudis Carazo was named universal heir and an albacea, along with Capitán don Antonio Elías de Arleguí.

On October 30, Benito Casasola, a free pardo, incurred an obligation of 300 pesos cacao to don Pablo José del Basto, a resident of Nicaragua. A marginal note indicates the obligation was cancelled by the creditor on September 27.

people_involved: Br. don José Elías de Arleguí
don José Antonio de la Cruz Matus
don Andrés de la Cruz Matus
summary: On November 2, Br. don José Elías de Arleguí, a Presbyter and executor of Don Manuel José González Coronel, granted power of attorney to Br. don Juan Cuaresma, a Presbyter residing in Managua. This power was for Cuaresma to represent Arleguí in the obligation deeds for a chaplaincy founded by González Coronel, which don José Antonio de la Cruz Matus (with his wife) and don Andrés de la Cruz Matus of Masaya were to grant for 800 pesos plata.

people_involved: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora
Capitán don Miguel Antonio de Unanue
Maestre de Campo don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
Dr. don José de León Tercero
summary: On November 3, Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora sold the 40-year-old mulato slave Ignacio de la Madrid to Capitán don Miguel Antonio de Unanue, a resident of Panamá. Doña Manuela had inherited Ignacio from her father, Maestre de Campo don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora, who had originally purchased him from Dr. don José de León Tercero, a Presbyter Cleric.

people_involved: Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno
summary: José Silverio de Segura, a native of Cartago and resident of Masaya, grants power of attorney to Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno to represent him in the estate proceedings of his maternal grandmother, Gertrudis Ruiz de Hinojosa.

people_involved: Br. don Juan Manuel López del Corral
doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo
Licenciado don Juan Salvador de Laya y Bolívar
summary: Br. don Juan Manuel López del Corral, as debtor, and his mother doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo, as guarantor, obligate themselves for 400 pesos plata to a chaplaincy founded by doña Josefa Gertrudis de Nava, secured by the Santa Cruz de las Juntas hacienda. The obligation was later declared to be under the charge of Don Marcos de Alvarado and his wife doña María López del Corral, who cancelled it on August 21, 1765.

Capitán José Manuel de Segura makes his will, detailing his three marriages and children. He disinherits his son José Silverio de Segura for marrying a mulata in Masaya and acting hostilely regarding his maternal inheritance. He names Capitán don Nicolás de Ulloa and Antonia Micaela de Segura as executors, with Antonia Micaela as the sole heir, and leaves bequests to his servants.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco
summary: Alférez don Domingo de Alvarado grants power to don Joaquín Montoya to sell Juliana, an 18-year-old mulata slave, for 300 pesos plata. Juliana was part of the dowry of Alvarado's wife, doña Juana Estéfana Salmón Pacheco, from her father, Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco.

people_involved: doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo
Sargento Mayor don Juan Francisco Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo sells Manuela Cayetana, a 40-year-old mulata slave, to don Pablo José del Basto for 156 pesos. Manuela Cayetana was inherited by doña Francisca as part of her dowry from her father, Sargento Mayor don Juan Francisco Ibarra y Calvo. Doña Francisca also leases her San Miguel fruit hacienda in the Barbilla valley to Teniente don José Hilario Polo for three years at 400 pesos cacao per year.

Manuela Josefa Calvo, natural daughter of Capitán don Francisco Calvo and the late María del Carmen Torres, grants power of attorney to don Francisco Méndez, a resident of Santiago de Veragua, to claim her maternal inheritance.

people_involved: Don Félix Francisco de la Riva
Capitán don José Francisco de Arleguí
Doña Catarina Lucrecia Arburola y Ribaren
summary: Don Félix Francisco de la Riva sells Cayetana Fulgencia, a 5-6 year old negrita slave, to Capitán don José Francisco de Arleguí for 200 pesos plata. Cayetana Fulgencia is the daughter of Juana Ventura, a negra slave who was formerly owned by Doña Catarina Lucrecia Arburola y Ribaren and donated to Don Félix Francisco de la Riva.

Don Félix Joaquín Meneses, as executor of the deceased María Calvo, sells Ana, a 30-year-old negra slave, to don Vicente Rodríguez for 144 pesos plata. Ana is the daughter of María Calvo, a slave born and raised in the house of Don Miguel Calvo, from whom María Calvo inherited her.

people_involved: Doña Ana Gertrudis de la Riva
Doña Catarina Lucrecia Arburola y Ribaren
summary: Doña Ana Gertrudis de la Riva, wife of Don Luis Quinteros, sells a house with its own walled plot to Don Joaquín Corona for 200 pesos plata. The house was inherited from her mother, Doña Catarina Lucrecia Arburola y Ribaren. The deal was rescinded on April 6 of the same year.

people_involved: Hermano novicio Fray Juan Miguel de Céspedes
Gobernador don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno
summary: Hermano novicio Fray Juan Miguel de Céspedes makes a codicil to his will, originally made on June 26, 1762. He revokes clauses that left his maternal inheritance to his uncles and aunts and a clause denying freedom to his mother's slaves, ceding all his rights and actions to his mother, Doña Ignacia de Miranda.

people_involved: Doña Ana Gertrudis de la Riva
Doña Catarina Lucrecia Arburola y Ribaren
summary: Don Luis Quinteros and his wife Doña Ana Gertrudis de la Riva sell a house of adobe and tile with its own walled plot to Teniente don José Hilario Polo and his wife Doña Joaquina Corral for 225 pesos plata. They had inherited the house from their mother, Doña Catarina Lucrecia Arburola y Ribaren.

people_involved: Catarina Lucrecia de Arburola y Rivaren
summary: The heirs of Doña Catarina Lucrecia de Arburola y Rivaren sold a cacao hacienda with 1800 fruit-bearing trees in the Matina valley to Captain Don Tomás de Soto y Barahona for 500 pesos plata. The hacienda bordered properties belonging to Doña María de Arburola and Doña Lorenza Fajardo.

Doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo, a widow, sold a house of adobe and tile and two walled plots in 'this city' to Don José Joaquín Corona for 600 pesos cacao and 50 pesos plata. The property was bordered by houses of Don Marcos de Alvarado, Teodora Molina (deceased), Padre Don Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba, and Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora. The sale included obligations to a capellanía founded by Sargento Mayor Don Antonio de Utrera and the Cofradía del Santísimo Sacramento, with a 5% interest rate on both.
On October 17, 1763, the contract for the sale of the house and plots between Doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo and Don José Joaquín Corona was rescinded.

people_involved: Juana María de Barros y Carvajal
summary: Don Juan Carrión and Doña Antonia Jiménez de Luna, his wife, became obligated for 150 pesos cacao at 5% interest to the Cofradía del Rosario. This obligation was previously held by the deceased Don Francisco Lozano Cadenas and his wife Doña Juana María de Barros y Carvajal, who had made an oblation of 1000 fruit-bearing cacao trees in the 'San Juan' hacienda in Matina valley. This hacienda also carried obligations for 125 pesos to the Curato de Cubujuquí and 200 pesos to a capellanía founded by Doña Rosa de Arburola.
Don Juan Carrión and Doña Antonia Jiménez de Luna recognized a 125 pesos censo at 5% interest on the hacienda under their charge, which belongs to the Curato de Cubujuquí in the Barba valley.

Don Juan Carrión and Doña Antonia Jiménez de Luna were responsible for a 200 pesos cacao obligation at 5% interest on the 'San Juan' hacienda. This obligation belonged to the capellanía founded by the deceased Doña Rosa de Arburola, of which Don Luis Arnesto de Troya was the patron.

Manuel Antonio Jiménez, legitimate son of the deceased Alférez Matías Jiménez and María Antonia Loaiza, made his testament. He was married to Doña Antonia María de Alvarado, legitimate daughter of Ayudante Manuel de Alvarado and the deceased Doña Antonia Josefa de Alvarado, and they had no children. His wife and Captain Don Manuel Guzmán Portocarrero were named albaceas, and his wife was the sole heiress. The testament was granted before Captain Don Pedro José Corrales, interim Alcalde de la Santa Hermandad.

Nicolás de Acuña made his testament. He was married to Juana Calderón, who was the widow of Juan Ríos, and they had no children, nor did Juana have children from her first marriage. Licenciado Don Manuel José García de Ergueta, a Presbítero, was named albacea. His wife was the heiress, and upon her death, the albacea would inherit. The testament was granted in the fields of 'this city' before Captain Don Félix Joaquín Meneses, Lieutenant Governor of Esparza.

people_involved: María Francisca de Alvarado y Jirón
María Manuela Baeza Espinosa de los Monteros
summary: A dowry letter (Carta dote) was issued by Don Antonio de la Fuente, a native of Astorga in the kingdoms of Castilla, son of Don Ignacio de la Fuente and Doña María Mendaña, in favor of his wife Doña María Francisca de Alvarado y Jirón. María Francisca was the legitimate daughter of Teniente de Infantería Don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón and Doña María Manuela Baeza Espinosa de los Monteros. The dowry amounted to 1842 pesos plata, with arras of 900 pesos plata.

Manuela Calvo, natural daughter of Captain Tomás Calvo and the deceased María del Carmen de Torres, granted power of attorney to Don Félix de Quintas, a resident of Santiago de Veragua, to claim her maternal inheritance on her behalf.

Doña María Lorenza Fajardo, legitimate daughter of the deceased Sargento Mayor Don Rafael Fajardo and Doña Josefa Sáenz, made her testament. She was the widow of Captain Don Manuel de Arburola, with whom she had four children (Valentín, José Martín, Felipe, and Liberata), though José Martín died young. She was also the widow of Captain Don Juan Francisco Guerrero, with whom she had two living sons (José Francisco and Juan Agustín) and five other children who died in infancy. Her son Don Felipe was named albacea, and all her children were her heirs.

Don José de Uriza, a resident, being executed for various debts, pledged his mulata slave named María Francisca Jiménez to the Royal Justice. He was traveling to Bagaces to acquire cattle to satisfy his debts and left the slave as collateral until his return, with a deadline of the entire month of July.

José Miguel Zamora leased a cacao hacienda with 600 fruit-bearing trees in the Barbilla valley to Pedro Valerín, a free black man, for five years. The hacienda was bordered by the mountain, Fernando Masís's hacienda, Don José Miguel García's hacienda, and Captain Don José Nicolás de Bonilla's hacienda. The annual rent was 50 pesos cacao payable in 'this city'.

people_involved: Don José Manuel García de Ergueta
Licenciado don Juan José de la Madríz Linares
Sargento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
Doña Francisca de la Madriz Linares
Doña Baltasara de la Madriz Linares
Doña Bárbara de la Madriz Linares
Doña Petronila de la Madriz Linares
Don Juan José de la Madriz Linares
Doña Ana Rita de la Madriz Linares
Doña Agueda de la Madriz Linares
Doña Rosa de la Madriz Linares
summary: Doña Rita García de Ergueta, being ill, granted power to her brother, Don José Manuel García de Ergueta, a priest, to make her will. Her executors were her brother and her son, Licenciado don Juan José de la Madríz Linares. Her heirs were her eight children with her deceased husband, Sargento Mayor don Francisco de la Madriz Linares.

people_involved: Br. don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Br. don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba, a priest, donated a house of tile and cedar wood on a plot he purchased from Tomás Molina to his godchildren, the orphans Don José Antº Pacheco and Don José Tomás Pacheco. These orphans were raised by Doña Francisca Pacheco, whose property bordered the donated plot, along with those of Doña Antonia Josefa Mondragón, Don Miguel Fajardo, and Francisco Palacios.

Manuela Josefa Cartín, a widow, leased her productive cacao hacienda named 'La Torres' in the Barbilla valley, comprising 2300 trees, to Benito Casasola. The lease was for four years, with an annual rent of 150 pesos cacao payable in Cartago or Matina.

people_involved: Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla
summary: Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla leased two productive cacao haciendas in the Barbilla valley to Sargento José Miguel García. One hacienda, 'El Bejuco,' had 1300 trees, and the other had 700 trees, for a total of 5 years. The rent was 125 pesos cacao for the first year and 150 pesos for each of the subsequent four years, payable in Cartago.

people_involved: Doña Engracia Gerd de Hoces Navarro
Capitán don Esteban de Hoces Navarro
Sargento Mayor don Manuel Antº de Arleguí
Licenciado don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí
Don José Ramón Noguera de Moncada
Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo
Doña Petronila de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Doña Engracia Gerd de Hoces Navarro, daughter of the deceased Capitán don Esteban de Hoces Navarro and Doña Juana Calvo, and widow of Sargento Mayor don Manuel Antº de Arleguí, made her will. She named her seven living children as heirs and appointed her sons, Licenciado don José Hermenegildo and Capitán don Antonio Elías, as executors. She also listed her slaves: Mateo (26, mulato), María Antª (mulata), and Juana (18, mulata).
Doña Angela de Alvarado, a widow, leased a cacao hacienda with 500-600 trees in the Barbilla valley to José Cubero, a free mulato. The lease was for three years, with an annual rent of 100 pesos.

people_involved: Teniente de Cabilleda don Félix Sáenz
summary: Teniente de Cabilleda don Félix Sáenz released Don Francisco Nogales, a resident of León and a trader, from house arrest in Cartago. Nogales had been imprisoned at the request of Don Juan Garau de Cors's representatives due to his alleged complicity in the abstraction of assets administered by Don Vicente Rodríguez.

people_involved: Doña Francisca de Ibarro y Calvo
Teniente de Guzmanes don José Francisco de Oriamuno
summary: Doña Francisca de Ibarro y Calvo, a widow, leased her productive cacao hacienda named 'San Miguel' in the Barbilla valley, with 5600 trees, to her son, Don Tomás López del Corral, for seven years. The annual rent was 400 pesos cacao, payable in Cartago, and the lease was accepted by Teniente de Guzmanes don José Francisco de Oriamuno on behalf of Don Tomás, using a power of attorney granted in Matina on November 13 before Capitán don José Hilario Polo.

people_involved: Doña Dionisia Fallas de la Vega
Capitán don Francº Fallas de la Vega
Capitán don Manuel García de Ergueta
Doña Juana Cayetana García de Ergueta
Don José Joaquín García de Ergueta
Don Miguel Francisco García de Ergueta
Don Juan Manl. García de Ergueta
Br. don José Manuel García de Ergueta
Presbítero don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí
summary: Doña Dionisia Fallas de la Vega, daughter of the deceased Capitán don Francº Fallas de la Vega and Doña María Ana Vázquez Solano, and widow of Capitán don Manuel García de Ergueta, made her will. She named her four living children and the legitimate children of her deceased son Joaquín as heirs, and appointed Br. don José Manuel García de Ergueta and Presbítero don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí as executors. She also listed her slaves: Rita Josefa (32, mulata), José Policarpo (28, mulato), and José Miguel (9, mulato).

Don José Joaquín de Nava, Captain of the Navarra Regiment and provisional Governor of the province, granted power of attorney to Don José Antº de Arichavala, a resident of León, Nicaragua. This power allowed Arichavala to collect Nava's salaries as Governor and any other outstanding debts from the Royal Treasury.

people_involved: Teniente de Capitán don Cayetano de Alvarado
summary: Doña Juana Antonia de Guevara, wife of Teniente de Capitán don Cayetano de Alvarado (absent for over 20 years), leased a hacienda with 780 productive cacao trees and an adjacent clearing in the 'la pontezuela' area of the Barbilla valley to Capitán Manuel José Guzmán. The lease was for three years at 100 pesos cacao per year, though a marginal note indicates the agreement was cancelled on April 12, 1765.
Simón de Quesada and his wife María Josefa Castillo, residents of the Ujarraz valley, are mentioned in the registry.

An obligation for 176 pesos and 33% cacao was made, which was adjudicated from the estate of Captain Antonio de Bustamante to his three legitimate children: Juana Antonia, Francisco Ant?, and Roque de los Angeles. Each child received 58 pesos and 63% reales, and the obligation was specified not to accrue interest.

people_involved: doña Ana Gertrudis de la Riva
summary: Lieutenant don José Hilario Polo and his wife doña Joaquina López del Corral obligated themselves for 225 pesos plata at 5% interest to the Cofradía de la Concepción. This amount was part of a larger sum redeemed by don Domingo de Alvarado, and the obligation was secured by a house in Cartago that they had purchased from don Luis Quinteros and doña Ana Gertrudis de la Riva.

people_involved: Licenciado don Manuel José González Coronel
summary: Don Domingo de Alvarado redeemed 300-odd pesos plata, which originated from a 500 pesos cacao debt burdening a house he owned. This house had previously belonged to the deceased Licenciado don Manuel José González Coronel, and the original debt was established by the deceased Diego Isidro de Aguilar.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don José Antonio de Oriamuno
doña Manuela de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Sergeant Major don José Antonio de Oriamuno, acting as attorney for doña Manuela de Ibarra y Calvo, a resident of Nicaragua, leased a cacao plantation named Sarmiento in the Matina valley to Pedro Salguero. The plantation, comprising 2600 trees, was leased for 3 years at 200 pesos cacao per year, bordered by haciendas of doña Ana Sancho and don Hilario Polo.

people_involved: Manuel José Nicolás de la Rosa
doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
summary: Doña Nicolasa de Betancur sold five enslaved individuals to don Antonio de la Fuente for 1400 pesos cacao. The enslaved people, including Manuel José Nicolás de la Rosa (25), Juan Elías (24), Isidro (23), José Felipe (9), and María Josefa de los Angeles (15), were inherited by Nicolasa from her deceased parents, don Francisco de Betancur and doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral.

people_involved: Capitán don Miguel Antonio de Unanue
summary: Doña Ana Jiménez incurred a debt of 100 pesos cacao to Captain don Miguel Antonio de Unanue, a merchant, to be paid by mid-November of that year, or 64 pesos in money if cacao was not provided. She pledged a 15-16 year old mulato named Pablo Jiménez, whom she had inherited from her parents, as collateral. The debt was cancelled on June 8, 1765.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás de Soto y Barahona
doña Ana Gertrudis de la Riva
summary: Captain don Tomás de Soto y Barahona, owner of an 1800-tree cacao plantation in the Matina valley, which he had purchased on April 21, 1763, from don Luis Quinteros and doña Ana Gertrudis de la Riva for 500 pesos plata, donated this hacienda to his relative don Francisco Esteban de Arburola, as he had no heir.

people_involved: Bachiller don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdova
Bachiller don Juan Salvador de Laya y Bolívar
Br. don José Francisco de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Bachiller don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdova sold two adobe houses to Bachiller don Juan Salvador de Laya y Bolívar, a Presbyter, for 2500 pesos plata. The payment was to be made in 1000 heads of cattle, delivered in Garayito in three installments in May of 1765, 1766, and 1767. The houses were inherited by Juan Manuel and his deceased brother José Francisco from their mother, doña Agueda Pérez de Muro, with Juan Manuel inheriting his brother's share upon his death. The sale was cancelled on September 7, 1767.

people_involved: Capitán José Miguel de los Reyes
don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdova
B* don Diego de Angulo Gascón
summary: Captain José Miguel de los Reyes, as principal, and Sergeant Major Miguel Jiménez, as guarantor, obligated themselves for 50 pesos cacao to don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdova. This amount was for materials delivered from the dismantled house of the deceased Bachiller don Diego de Angulo Gascón, which was associated with a chaplaincy. The obligation was secured by a house and plantain grove in Aserrí and was cancelled on September 23, 1764.

people_involved: Ayudante Mayor don Félix Joaquín Meneses
Br. don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí
summary: Assistant Major don Félix Joaquín Meneses, as executor of the deceased doña Catarina Lucrecia de Arburola, founded a chaplaincy for recited masses according to her will dated July 27, 1762. The principal was 130 pesos cacao at 5% interest, with don Luis Quinteros as patron and don Joaquín Quinteros, Catarina's grandson, designated as chaplain, with Br. don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí serving as interim chaplain until Joaquín's ordination.

people_involved: Capitán don Miguel Antonio de Unanue
Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco
summary: A testimony was given on September 10, 1764, regarding a power to testate granted by don Simón Negra, a native of Villa de Llanza, Gerona, to Captain don Miguel Antonio de Unanue. This power was granted on August 29, 1764, in Cartago, before Sergeant Major don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco.

Don Simón Negra's will was executed by his attorney, Don Miguel Antonio de Unanue. Being single and having lost his parents, he named his sister, Doña Ana María de Negra, as his heir. The will stipulated that she use the inheritance to settle family pensions, commission an altarpiece for the Heart of Jesus in the parish church of Llanza, and establish a chaplaincy of recited masses, with her most suitable son or closest relative serving as chaplain.

people_involved: Teniente de Capitán Fermín de León
Capitán don Juan de Ocampo Golfín
summary: Teniente de Capitán Fermín de León and his wife, Juana Manuela de Flores, residents of Escasú, obligated themselves for 180 pesos plata at 5% interest to the Cofradía de la Concepción. This debt, which had been under their charge for five years, was originally delivered by the deceased Capitán don Juan de Ocampo Golfín. The obligation was secured by land across the Río Grande, 65 heads of cattle, and a house in Escasú with a sugar mill and cane fields.

people_involved: Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla
Doña Lucía de Alvarado y Jirón
Cura don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
Don Pedro José León de Bonilla
Don Juan José Benito de Bonilla
summary: Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla, gravely ill in bed, granted power to his wife, Doña Lucía de Alvarado y Jirón, to make his will. She, along with Cura don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría, were named as executors. His four children, Don Pedro José León, Doña María Petronila, Don Gregorio Javier, and Don Juan José Benito de Bonilla, were designated as his heirs.

people_involved: Doña Josefa López de la Flor
Teniente de Capitán don Juan Antonio Muñoz
Sargento Mayor don Diego de Laya Fernández
summary: Doña Josefa López de la Flor, a widow, sold the 16-year-old slave Juana Antonia to Teniente de Capitán don Juan Antonio Muñoz, a resident of Nicaragua, for 200 pesos plata. Juana Antonia was the daughter of Clara and granddaughter of María, both 'negras,' with María having been purchased from the former Governor Sargento Mayor don Diego de Laya Fernández. Don Francisco Carazo accepted the sale on behalf of the buyer.

people_involved: Doña María Ana de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Don José de Cruz and his wife, Doña María Ana de Alvarado y Jirón, obligated themselves for 150 pesos cacao at 5% interest, related to a chaplaincy previously charged on the destroyed houses of B" don Diego Angulo Gascón. They imposed this obligation on their current house in the city plaza. A marginal note indicates that the Governor, by order of S" don Pedro José Chamorro, cancelled the obligation on February 28, 1767, after Cruz paid the 150 pesos.

José Francisco Chaves, a free mulatto, along with his guarantors Gregorio Calvo and Francisco Palacios, obligated themselves for 200 pesos cacao to Francisco Bruno de Chaves. This was to secure the freedom of José Francisco's sister, María Josefa, who was a slave of Francisco Bruno de Chaves, with 14 months granted to obtain the money. A marginal note indicates Francisco Bruno cancelled the obligation on May 7, 1766.

Francisco Bruno de Chaves and his wife, Lorenza de Quesada, residents of Ujarrás, granted freedom to their 32-year-old slave María Josefa. This act of manumission was granted in virtue of the obligation made on the same day, and María Josefa had been inherited by Francisco Bruno from his parents.

people_involved: Br. don Juan Salvador de Laya y Bolívar
summary: Don Tomás Benito Hidalgo, son of Don Juan Hidalgo and Doña María Ambrosia de Bonilla, presented a dowry for his wife, Doña María Benita de Nava, whom he married on the 26th of the current month. Doña Benita, an orphan from Granada, Nicaragua, was brought to this province by her uncle, Br. don Juan Salvador de Laya y Bolívar. The dowry included a house and lot in Cartago valued at 2500 pesos, and 300 pesos from the sale of two slaves (Basilio and Juan Félix) held in deposit in Granada, totaling 3570 pesos 6 reales plata, with arras of 500 pesos plata.

people_involved: Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno
Capitán don Miguel Antonio de Unanue
summary: Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno sold one hundred heads of cattle from 'tierra arriba' to Capitán don Miguel Antonio de Unanue for 200 pesos plata, or 2 pesos per head. The cattle were located in the area known as 'las sabanas de don Carlos' within the jurisdiction of Esparza.

Manuel Antonio Jiménez and his wife, Antonia Josefa de Alvarado, obligated themselves for 100 pesos cacao at 5% interest to the Cofradía de las Animas. They received this money from Doña Beatriz Salomona Morales, widow of the deceased Rafael Delgado, who previously held the debt. The obligation was secured by a house, sugar mill, and cane fields in the San Antonio area of the Aserrí valley.

people_involved: Teniente de Infantería don José Antonio Jiménez
Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo
summary: Teniente de Infantería don José Antonio Jiménez, son of Capitán don Francisco Jiménez and Doña Josefa de Bonilla, presented a dowry for his wife, Doña Petronila Rodríguez de Robredo, whom he married on the 9th of the current month. Doña Petronila was the legitimate daughter of the deceased Sargento Mayor don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo and Doña Gabriela Josefa de Arleguí. The dowry amounted to 1020 pesos cacao, with arras of 1000 pesos cacao.

people_involved: Capitán don Félix Joaquín de Alvarado
summary: Sargento Tomás Maroto, as principal, and Capitán don Félix Joaquín de Alvarado, as guarantor, obligated themselves for 2250 pesos of cacao. This sum was the principal of a chaplaincy founded by the deceased Capitán don Francisco Garrido and his wife, Doña Agueda Pérez de Muro, and was secured by a productive cacao hacienda in Matina with 2000 trees.

people_involved: Br. don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Details of two capellanías were discussed: one for 2250 pesos charged to the 'Velazco y Muro' hacienda, and another for 2500 pesos founded on the 'Foto y Bonilla' hacienda in Matina. Br. don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba was the proprietary chaplain for both.
Maroto, a free mulatto, canceled the bond of Alvarado. In its place, Maroto mortgaged 2500 cacao trees he owned in the Chirripó valley.

people_involved: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora
Coronel don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
doña Francisca de Arburola y Rivaren
summary: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora, the legitimate daughter of Coronel don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora and doña Francisca de Arburola y Rivaren, and wife of don Juan Sierra, granted general power of attorney to her husband.

people_involved: B* don Diego de Angulo Gascón
Sargento Mayor don Andrés de Bonilla
Licenciado don Francisco de Ocampo Galfín
summary: Don José Martínez obligated himself for 258 pesos in cacao for a capellanía, related to the destruction of houses belonging to B* don Diego de Angulo Gascón. He received materials and funds from Sargento Mayor don Andrés de Bonilla, which were part of a capellanía previously held by Licenciado don Francisco de Ocampo Galfín and now by Licenciado don Ramón de Azofeifa. Martínez mortgaged a house he had purchased from don Andrés de Bonilla.

María Josefa Cartín, a widow, sold half of a productive cacao hacienda named 'La Zorres' in the Barbilla valley, comprising 1300 trees, to José Cubero for 1300 pesos cacao, payable over four years. The other half had been adjudicated by Royal Justice to her legitimate daughter, María Josefa Torres, from her deceased husband Antonio de Torres.

people_involved: Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral
don José Antonio López del Corral
doña Francisca de Arburola y Rivaren
Coronel don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral donated a 7-year-old mulatto slave named Ana Tiburcia, daughter of Petronila, to Ana Gertrudis Morales, a resident of León. The slave was acquired from her mother's estate to settle a debt owed by Coronel don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora, her mother's last husband, to don Cayetano Pavón of Guatemala. Manuel Morales, Ana Gertrudis's brother, accepted the donation.

people_involved: Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla
summary: Micaela de Segura, a widow, leased a productive cacao hacienda with 1030 trees in the Barbilla valley to Juan Manuel Sáenz for three years at 90 pesos cacao annually. The hacienda bordered properties belonging to the deceased Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla, José Miguel García, and Francisco Soto.

people_involved: Teniente de Capitán don José Antonio Jiménez
summary: Don Pedro José Corrales and his wife doña María Josefa Fernández Martínez, both without children, made their will, naming the survivor as heir. Don Cosme Damián Fernández Martínez, brother of the testatrix, and Teniente de Capitán don José Antonio Jiménez were appointed as executors.

people_involved: Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
Br. don Miguel de Oconor y Andravide
summary: Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría, Cura of this city, granted general judicial power to Br. don Miguel de Oconor y Andravide, Vicario of León, Nicaragua.

people_involved: Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
Licenciado don Esteban Catalán de Roda
summary: Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría (Cura) and don Pedro José Corrales (Mayordomo of the Cofradía de los Angeles) authorized Teniente Manuel Antonio Jiménez to sell Tomás Moreno, a 10-12 year old zambo slave. Tomás Moreno had been donated to the Cofradía on July 8, 1764, by Licenciado don Esteban Catalán de Roda, who inherited him from his father don Juan Catalán Pérez.

people_involved: Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral
doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora
don José Miguel Francisco de Corona
summary: Following the death of don José Joaquín de Corona, 667 pesos plata were adjudicated from his estate to his legitimate son, don José Miguel Francisco de Corona. Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral (mother of José Miguel Francisco) and don Juan de Sierra and his wife doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora (as guarantors) obligated themselves to pay this sum.

people_involved: Don José Miguel Francisco de Corona
Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral
summary: Don José Miguel Francisco de Corona declared that, being married, his mother Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral delivered his guardianship to him.

people_involved: Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno
Capitán don Tomás de Soto y Barahona
summary: Teniente Manuel Antonio Cárdenas and his wife doña María de Quesada obligated themselves to pay 190 pesos in cacao within one year to Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno. This sum was the appraised value of a house inherited by the children of the deceased doña Bernarda Martínez (Francisco, Javiera, and Ana Josefa), whom Oriamuno represented as executor. Capitán don Tomás de Soto y Barahona acted as guarantor.

people_involved: Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno
summary: Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno canceled the obligation related to the house of doña Bernarda Martínez's children.
Don Pedro de España, a resident of Santiago de Veragua and a merchant, granted general power of attorney to don Vicente Rodríguez.

people_involved: Doña Juana Josefa de Arburola y Rivaren
Br. don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí
Capitán don José Joaquín de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Doña Juana Josefa de Arburola y Rivaren, widow of Capitán don Blas González Coronel, made her will. She was the legitimate daughter of Capitán don Lorenzo de Arburola and Doña Josefa de Hoces Navarro. Her two sons died at ages 4 and 14 in León, Nicaragua, and she named Br. don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí and Capitán don Joaquín de Alvarado y Jirón as her executors.

people_involved: Br. don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
Doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Br. don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba, steward of the Cofradía de Sacramento, recorded that Doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo owed 50 pesos plata plus 52 pesos 4 reales in interest to the Cofradía. Doña Francisca offered a 50-vara plot of land next to her house to cancel the debt. The document was not signed and did not pass.

people_involved: Don José Manuel García de Ergueta
Licenciado don Juan José de la Madriz Linares
Don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda
summary: Don José Manuel García de Ergueta, a priest and Sacristán Mayor, made his will. He stated that his sister, Doña Rita García de Ergueta, had died, and her will was not executed due to her son's absence in Nicaragua. He also declared ownership of a newborn slave, Isidora, daughter of his slave Antonia, who was formerly owned by Doña Baltasara de Inza's heirs. His heirs were don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda and Doña Baltasara Madriz, with Capitán don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda and Capitán don Francisco de Arleguí as executors.

people_involved: Doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo
Br. don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo, a widow, sold a 50-vara plot of land to Br. don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba, a Presbítero. The price of 102 pesos 4 reales covered her 50-peso principal debt and 21 years of interest owed to the Cofradía del Sacramento.

people_involved: Doña Josefa López de la Flor
summary: Doña Josefa López de la Flor, widow of Capitán don Tomás Andrés Polo, granted freedom to her slaves, effective upon her death. The slaves included María, her daughter Juana (40), Juana's daughters Antonia Josefa (17) and Tomasa (9), and Antonia Josefa's daughter Juana Antonia (2).

Juan de Dios and Manuel de Jesús Román acted as guarantors for the slave Juan Antonio Gutiérrez, valued at 300 pesos cacao, to obtain his freedom by next August. Juan Antonio belonged to Doña Antonia, Doña Mariana, and Doña Petronila Alvarado y Jirón, who inherited him from their deceased uncle, Presbítero don Antonio de Guevara.

people_involved: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Don Juan de Sierra and his wife Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora obligated themselves to Don Antonio de la Fuente, a Notario apostólico, for 450 pesos plata, equivalent to 28 sacks of cacao plus 3 pesos. They hypothecated their slaves, María del Rosario and Rosa, as collateral. The obligation was cancelled on October 16 of the same year.

people_involved: Capitán don José Joaquín de Alvarado y Jirón
Doña María Francisca López del Corral
Br. don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
