summary: Capitán don José Joaquín de Alvarado y Jirón and his wife Doña María Francisca López del Corral obligated themselves for 1100 pesos cacao, 600 to the Convento de San Francisco and 500 to a chaplaincy served by Dr. don José Antonio Carazo of Trujillo. They received this principal from Doña Francisca de Ibarra, widow of don Tomás Corrales, in the form of adobe and tile houses in the city, bordered by don Marcos de Alvarado and Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba.

people_involved: Juan Salvador de Laya y Bolívar
summary: Houses belonging to Don Juan de Sierra are located next to property associated with Juan Salvador de Laya y Bolívar, on the main street.
Haciendas with 2000 cacao trees in Matina, specifically in the Pontezuela area, were mortgaged.

people_involved: Ana Teresa de Soto y Barahona
summary: Doña Ana Teresa de Soto y Barahona, acting as attorney for her son Don José Antonio Carazo, cancelled a 900 pesos debt. This cancellation occurred because Don Juan de Sierra and his wife Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora took over the obligation.

Captain Don Tomás de Soto y Barahona leased a 4000-tree cacao hacienda in the Matina valley to Antonio Araya, a free pardo. The lease was for 3 years at a total price of 1275 pesos cacao, paid in installments over the years.

people_involved: Juan Salvador de Laya y Bolívar
summary: Marcos de Alvarado y Jirón and his wife María López del Corral obligated themselves for 400 pesos plata at 5% interest to a chaplaincy founded by Doña Josefa Gertrudis de Nava. The obligation was secured by a country hacienda in the Landecho valley, named Santa Cruz de las Juntas, and a tiled house in Cartago, along with 400 cattle and a donkey with mares in Landecho. The chaplaincy's current chaplain is Licenciado Don Juan Salvador de Laya y Bolívar.

On August 29, Alférez Miguel de Jesús Pérez, a resident of Managua, obligated himself for 900 pesos plata to Sargento Mayor Don José Antonio de Oriamuno. This obligation was later cancelled on January 20, 1766.

On September 10, Presbítero Don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí, executor of the deceased Licenciado Don Manuel José González Coronel, sold a cacao hacienda in the Matina valley with 1881 trees to José Antonio González Coronel for 2800 pesos cacao. Arleguí donated 300 pesos of the price to the buyer, with the remaining 2200 pesos obligated to a chaplaincy founded by Don Blas González Coronel, whose patronage had passed to the Convento de San Francisco after Manuel José's death.

people_involved: María Catarina de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: On September 13, Don Juan de Benavides and Doña Ignacia Miranda, along with Captain Juan Nicolás Castillo and Margarita Villagra, took over the obligation of 8550 pesos cacao. This debt was previously held by Sargento Mayor Don José Antonio de Oriamuno and his wife Doña María Catarina de Ibarra y Calvo, related to chaplaincies charged on cacao haciendas in Matina left by Licenciado Don Juan José Camacho. The couples mortgaged four enslaved people and two pole-built houses in the Ujarrás valley as security.

On September 19, Don Juan de Sierra and his wife Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora obligated themselves for 150 pesos cacao at 5% interest. This principal was part of a chaplaincy previously charged on destroyed houses belonging to Bachiller Don Diego de Angulo Gascón. The obligation is now charged on 4000 cacao trees in Matina.

On October 9, Teniente de Capitán Manuel Antonio de Cárdenas acknowledged an obligation of 1818 pesos cacao at 5% interest, related to various chaplaincies. He had acquired a cacao hacienda in Barbilla from Captain Francisco Javier de Oriamuno on September 1, 1756, with the condition of taking on this debt. One of these chaplaincies, for 318 pesos, was founded by Sargento Mayor Luis Gutiérrez, and its interim chaplain is Licenciado Don Juan Bautista Pérez de Cote.

On October 22, Doña Manuela de Zavaleta leased a cacao hacienda in the Matina valley, comprising 1270 trees, to Don Javier de la Riva. The lease was for 3 years at a price of 125 pesos per year, with the hacienda bordering property of Doña Juana Josefa de Arburola.

people_involved: María Josefa de la Vega Cabral
summary: On October 30, Lorenzo Marín (as debtor) and several other couples (as guarantors) obligated themselves for 100 pesos cacao at 5% interest to a chaplaincy founded by Diego Quinteros. They received the sum in materials from the destroyed house of the deceased Doña María Josefa de la Vega Cabral. This obligation was cancelled on November 16, 1784, by Juan Manuel Barrios, who took over the debt.

people_involved: Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdova
summary: On November 2, Doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho de Castañeda, a widow, granted freedom to her enslaved people José Joaquín Ramos and Cecilia, children of her enslaved woman Micaela Barboza. She had acquired Micaela from her husband, Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdova, with the condition of granting freedom after her death. She also affirmed the freedom of María Dolores and Paula, Micaela's daughters. José Joaquín's freedom is effective after Don Juan Manuel's death, and Cecilia's after Manuela Gertrudis's death.

On November 4, Captain Don José Antonio de Oriamuno obligated himself for 150 pesos cacao to Francisco, Javiera, and Ana Josefa, the minor children of the deceased Doña Bernarda Martínez, for whom Oriamuno is the executor. He received this sum from Teniente Manuel Antonio de Cárdenas and his wife Doña María de Quesada, to whom he had sold a house as executor.
Javiera and Ama Josefa cancelled a debt on behalf of Doña Bernarda, which had a one-year term. This cancellation was recorded on the margin of a document.

people_involved: Doña Angela de Alvarado y Jirón
Don José Francisco de Alvarado y Jirón
Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral
Licenciado don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí
summary: Doña Angela de Alvarado y Jirón, a widow, obligated herself for 250 pesos cacao for a chaplaincy associated with Don José Francisco de Alvarado y Jirón. This obligation was charged on a house in the city, previously held by the late Don Gabriel Marco de Ocaña and his wife Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral, and bordered properties of Doña Josefa Simona de Bonilla, Don Luis Arnesto de Troya, the public plaza, and chaplaincy houses of Licenciado don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí.

people_involved: Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla
Doña Lucía Nicolasa de Alvarado y Jirón
Don Juan José Benito de Bonilla
summary: The testament of the late Capitán don José Nicolás de Bonilla was granted by his widow, Doña Lucía Nicolasa de Alvarado y Jirón, based on a power of attorney from the previous year. The testament detailed his family, including his mother, children (some deceased), and sons-in-law, and named his slaves and executors.

people_involved: Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
Doña Angela de la Paz y Flores
Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
Capitán don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda
Licenciado don José Manuel García de Ergueta
summary: Don Gregorio de Aragón and his wife Doña Dominga Sancho de Castañeda obligated themselves for 1900 pesos cacao, covering several chaplaincies founded by Vasco Solano, Don Sebastián Golfín, Doña Angela de la Paz y Flores, Doña Luisa Calvo, and Doña Josefa de Aguilar. They received these sums from Capitán don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda, who was the executor for the late Licenciado don José Manuel García de Ergueta, and the obligation was tied to a cacao hacienda in Valle de Matina.

people_involved: Doña Josefa Francisca López de la Flor
Don José López de la Flor
Doña Mariana López de la Flor
Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco
summary: Doña Josefa Francisca López de la Flor, a widow, revalidated the freedom she had granted to several slaves earlier in the year and granted freedom to two more: a two-month-old mulatto girl named Benita Teresa de Jesús (daughter of Antonia Josefa) and a 50-year-old mulatto man named Mateo. Her testament also mentioned her parents, late husband, sister, niece, and named her executor.

Doña María Josefa García, a resident of Sello de Aserrí, sold a 13-year-old slave named Diego, son of her deceased slave Nicolasa, to Don Félix Joaquín Alvarado for 200 pesos cacao. Don Félix Joaquín Alvarado's wife and attorney, Doña María Francisca Corrales, accepted the purchase on his behalf.

Presbítero Don Andrés Joaquín Fernández obligated himself for 500 pesos cacao for a chaplaincy founded by Capitán Diego de Aguilar. This obligation was charged on a house in the city previously owned by Manuel Carranza.
Don Juan de Sierra acted with a power of attorney from his wife. The full details of the transaction are not provided as the text is cut off.

people_involved: don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Doña Manuela Pastora granted special power of attorney to don Cayetano Pavón, a resident of Santiago de Guatemala. This power was for obtaining copies of notes, additions, and warnings against don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora, which were represented by don Manuel Alejo de Errarte, the royal accounts auditor of Guatemala City, before the Royal Audiencia.

people_involved: doña Manuela Gertrudis Pda cho de Castañeda
Capitán don Juan Sancho de Castañeda
doña Juana de Alvarado y Jirón
Licenciado don Maximiliano Antonio de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: The will of doña Manuela Gertrudis Pda cho de Castañeda, legitimate daughter of the deceased Capitán don Juan Sancho de Castañeda and doña Juana de Alvarado y Jirón, and widow of Rafael Ceballos, was opened. She established two capellanías, one on her dwelling house and another on a 500-cacao tree hacienda in Matina, naming B* don Maximiliano Antonio Alvarado and her brother José Manuel Sancho as patrons/chaplains respectively. She also granted freedom to her enslaved people: Micaela, her daughters, and a son.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don José Antonio de Oriamuno
summary: Sargento Mayor don José Antonio de Oriamuno leased a 1500-tree cacao hacienda in Matina to Pedro Manuel Salguero. The lease was for 5 years at 125 pesos per year, and the hacienda bordered properties belonging to don Hilario Polo and one named Sarmiento.

people_involved: doña María Cayetana de Alvarado y Jirón
Capitán don Gil de Alvarado y Jirón
don Nicolás de Soto y Barahona
Capitán don Miguel de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: The will of doña María Cayetana de Alvarado y Jirón, who died on January 22, was opened. She was the legitimate daughter of the deceased Capitán don Gil de Alvarado y Jirón and doña Josefa González del Camino, and widow of don Nicolás de Soto y Barahona. She had a natural daughter, doña Ana Efigenia, with don Arde. de Araujo, who was named her heir. The will, granted in Cartago on December 30, 1765, also mentioned her enslaved mulata María Josefa, whom she bought from don Tomás Corrales and doña Francisca de Ibarra, and her enslaved Manuel Antonio.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don José Antonio de Oriamuno
summary: Don Juan de Benavides and his wife doña Ignacia Miranda, along with Capitán Juan Nicolás Castillo and his wife Margarita Villagra, formalized an obligation to the Cofradía de la Concepción for 225 pesos cacao. This obligation stemmed from a previous agreement on September 13, 1765, for 5550 pesos cacao, charged on haciendas left by the deceased B* don Juan José Camacho and managed by Sargento Mayor don José Antonio de Oriamuno and his wife doña Catarina de Ibarra, for various capellanías.

Don Juan de Benavides and his wife doña Ignacia Miranda, along with Capitán Juan Nicolás Castillo and his wife Margarita Villagra, formalized an obligation for 1200 pesos cacao (or 800 silver) at 5% interest. This obligation was for capellanías founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela, charged on the same haciendas previously mentioned in relation to B* don Juan José Camacho.

Don Juan de Benavides and his wife doña Ignacia Miranda, along with Capitán Juan Nicolás Castillo and his wife Margarita Villagra, obligated themselves for 1725 pesos cacao (1150 silver) at 5% interest. This obligation was for the capellanía founded by Alonso Machado, charged on the same haciendas.

people_involved: Licenciado don Manuel de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Don Juan de Benavides and his wife doña Ignacia Miranda, along with Capitán Juan Nicolás Castillo and his wife Margarita Villagra, obligated themselves for 375 pesos cacao. This obligation was for the capellanías founded by Licenciado don Manuel de Alvarado y Jirón, charged on the same haciendas.

people_involved: Doña Antonia de la Trinidad del Fierro
summary: Doña Josefa Ortiz de Rosas, widow of Lucas del Fierro, acting for herself and as representative for Doña Antonia de la Trinidad del Fierro (deceased) and Doña Eufracia del Fierro, along with Doña Ana Teresa del Fierro and her husband Don Cayetano Salmón Pacheco, granted power of attorney. The power was given to Don Santiago del Fierro, Sargento Mayor, Dr. Don Francisco Ignacio Fierro, Cura, and Don Santiago Rodríguez de León, all associated with the island of Palma de las Canarias.

José Hilario Morúa obligated himself for 300 pesos cacao to Doña Joaquina, Doña Buenaventura, and Doña Francisca Leonarda Sáenz, who are minors represented by their father, Teniente Don Félix Sáenz. This sum was originally owed to Licenciado Don Manuel Sáenz, who, before traveling to Nicaragua, donated it to the three minors, who are his granddaughters.

people_involved: Br. Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
Capitán Don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno
summary: Br. Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba, as executor for Doña Baltasara de Escalante Paniagua, established two chaplaincies as per her will dated January 4, 1761. One chaplaincy of 200 pesos was for the Cofradía de la Concepción, and another for 1274 pesos 31.5 reales was for Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría, Cura, or the Convento de San Francisco, funded by cacao haciendas in Matina.

people_involved: Don Pedro del Río Talca y Guevara
Antonia de la Trinidad de Alvarado
summary: Manuel Antonio de Alvarado made his testament, detailing his family, including his deceased parents, deceased wife, and nine living children. He also acknowledged a natural daughter with Ana Vanegas, an enslaved person inherited from his mother-in-law, and named his children's spouses and executors. He made improvements to his two single daughters.

Doña Manuela de Zavaleta, a widow, obligated herself for 150 pesos cacao to the Cofradía de la Concepción. This obligation, previously managed by Capitán Don José Manuel Sancho, is charged against her house in Cartago.

people_involved: Capitán Don José Antonio de Oriamuno
summary: Manuel José Benito Casasola made his testament, outlining his family including his deceased father, mother, wife, deceased infant daughter, and sister. He named Capitán Don José Antonio de Oriamuno and Don Tomás López del Corral as his executors, and his mother, María Efigenia Brenes, as his heir.

people_involved: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora
Don Joaquín de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Don Juan de Sierra and Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora obligated themselves for 500 pesos cacao for a chaplaincy, whose chaplain is Br. Dn. José Antº Carazo, Cura of Trujillo. This obligation, previously held by Don Joaquín de Alvarado y Jirón and Doña María Francisca del Corral, is secured by their house in Cartago and a cacao hacienda in Matina, with Doña Ana Teresa Barahona representing the chaplain.

On September 1, 1802, Subteniente Don Lorenzo Carazo, acting as heir and representative for the deceased Br. Don José Antonio Carazo, declared that the chaplaincy had transferred to his brother, Presbítero Don Manuel Carazo. This followed a new deed issued by Doña Manuela de la Pastora on November 28, 1800, for the same 500 pesos in favor of the new chaplain.

people_involved: Licenciado Don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí
summary: Don Tomás López del Corral and Doña Rosa de la Madriz obligated themselves for 820 pesos plata for two chaplaincies: 720 pesos for one founded by Baltasar de Grados, and 100 pesos for one instituted by Doña Eugenia de Abarca Alatrás. Licenciado Don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí is the patron and chaplain, and the obligation is secured by a house in Cartago and cacao trees in Matina.

On July 10, 1783, Don Antonio de la Fuente, acting as the general representative for Presbítero Don Fernando de Arleguí, cancelled an obligation. This cancellation occurred because the responsibility for the obligation had transferred to Doña Encarnación Sancho on May 19 of the same year.

people_involved: Doña María de Arburolas y Rivaren
summary: Doña María de Arburolas y Rivaren, who is single, made her testament. She stipulated that her enslaved person, Juan Cayetano Arburola, aged 46, would be freed after her death upon payment of 50 pesos cacao by Tomás de Arburola for the benefit of her soul.

people_involved: Capitán don José Antº de Oriamuno
summary: Tomás de Arburola inherited from Capitán don José Antº de Oriamuno and subsequently assigned the inheritance without any interest.

people_involved: Capitán don José Romualdo de Alvarado
summary: Capitán don José Romualdo de Alvarado was appointed Administrator and warehouse keeper for the provincial tobacco monopoly, obligating him to the Royal Treasury. It was stipulated that his salary would cancel this obligation after one year.

locations: Villa de la Trinidad de Sonsonate
summary: Antonio de Avendaño, acting as attorney for the arrested don Martín de Chavarría, sold a mulatto slave named María Manuela Chavarría to don Francº Serrano for 300 pesos cacao. This sale was to satisfy a debt don Martín owed to doña Antonia, which held priority due to don Martín's conviction in Matina, with the slave serving as a special mortgage for the credit.

people_involved: Doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo
Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
doña María Cayetana de Alvarado y Jirón
Sargento Mayor don Juan Francisco Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo, widow of Capitán don Tomás López del Corral, sold a 16-year-old mulatto slave named María Josefa to don Rafael de Salazar, executor for doña María Cayetana de Alvarado y Jirón, for 100 pesos silver and 25 cacao. Doña Francisca declared that she and her late husband had made this sale to Doña María Cayetana in 1756, but the formal deed was never executed.

people_involved: Don Andrés Antonio González de Araujo
Dª María Cayetana Alvarado y Jirón
doña Ana Efigenia González y Alvarado
doña Bernarda de Villalta y Guzmán
summary: Don Andrés Antonio González de Araujo obligated himself for 1452 pesos cacao, which were awarded from the estate of Dª María Cayetana Alvarado y Jirón to his minor natural daughter, doña Ana Efigenia González y Alvarado. He presented a bond from his wife, doña Bernarda de Villalta y Guzmán, and his mother-in-law, Dª María Sánchez Prieto, dated July 18, 1767, before Escribano don José de Peralta in Nicaragua, stating that Andrés would take doña Ana Efigenia, who is under 12, to Nicaragua.

José Nicolás Carranza and his wife Luisa Masís sold three tiled sheds on a half-lot in Cartago to don José Francisco Guerrero for 100 pesos cacao. The property, measuring 50 varas long and 25 varas wide with 33 varas of wall, was bordered by properties of don Domingo Alvarado, Angela Masís, and Manuela Meneses.

people_involved: Br. don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: José Joaquín Paniagua leased a hacienda with 1450 fruit trees in Barbilla to Fernando Lobo for three years. Paniagua had acquired the hacienda through an ecclesiastical court auction for 1464 pesos 3 1/2 reales, as it belonged to two chaplaincies founded by Br. don Juan Manuel de Casasola as executor for doña Baltasara Paniagua. The rent was set at 5 zurrones of cacao for the first year and 6 for each subsequent year, to be delivered in Cartago.

people_involved: Don Andrés Antonio González de Araujo
Capitán don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda
doña Ana Efigenia González y Alvarado
summary: Don Andrés Antonio González de Araujo, a resident of Nicaragua, sold a house in Cartago to Capitán don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda for 420 pesos cacao. Andrés owned the house as the father and guardian of his natural daughter, doña Ana Efigenia González y Alvarado, whom he was taking to Nicaragua. The house was bordered by properties of don José Lebrón, the Cabildo, and doña Josefa Alvarado.

people_involved: Capitán don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí
doña Engracia Gertrudis de Hoces Navarro
Capitán don Antonio Elías de Arleguí
summary: Doña Josefa Gabriela de Arleguí, daughter of the late Capitán don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí and doña Engracia Gertrudis de Hoces Navarro, and widow of don Juan Rodríguez de Robredo, made her will. She had ten children from two marriages, five with her first husband and five with her current husband, Félix Joaquín Meneses. Her brother, Capitán don Antonio Elías de Arleguí, and her husband were named executors, with her children from the first marriage receiving a larger share of the inheritance.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco
Licdo. don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
Lic. don Juan Félix de Villalobos
summary: Don Francisco Carazo obligated himself for 100 pesos silver to a chaplaincy founded by the late doña Baltasara de Alvarado, widow of don Luis Goicoechea, which was administered by doña Luisa de Alvarado. He mortgaged a donkey and 80 mares in Zapotal, Esparza, and was to pay 5% interest to Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco, doña Baltasara's executor. On August 17, 1771, Licdo. don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba received the 100 pesos from Carazo to remit to Lic. don Juan Félix de Villalobos, a judge of chaplaincies, at the request of don Lucas Goicoecha, doña Baltasara's son.

people_involved: Síndico del Convento de San Francisco
summary: Don Nicolás de Ulloa, acting as the executor of doña Catarina Siles' will from August 21, 1759, established a chaplaincy valued at 579 pesos cacao. The Padre Guardián was designated as the chaplain and the Síndico of the San Francisco Convent as the patron. This chaplaincy was imposed upon doña Catarina's former house.

people_involved: don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Benito Casasola and his wife Leonor Méndez committed to 400 pesos cacao, which were part of a chaplaincy at the San Francisco Convent, where Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba served as Síndico. These funds had previously been under the responsibility of Capitán Benito de Alvarado. As collateral, they mortgaged a cacao hacienda with 1000 trees in Matina.
Benito Casasola obligated himself to don Pedro Fernández for a sum of 1700 pesos cacao.

people_involved: don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Benito Casasola made a donation to the Virgin of Matina, consisting of a cacao hacienda with 1000 trees, three years old. Of these, 500 trees were his direct donation, and the other 500 were paid for by Br. don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba and don José Manuel Sancho, each contributing 25 pesos. Both don Juan Manuel and don José Manuel accepted the donation.

locations: Villa de San José del Valle de Aserrí
people_involved: don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
doña María de Guzmán y Echavarría
doña Juana Manuela de Guzmán y Echavarría
doña Antonia de Guzmán y Echavarría
Br. don Juan de Pomar y Burgos
summary: Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría, along with doña María, doña Juana Manuela, doña Antonia de Guzmán y Echavarría, and doña Dominga de Guzman, acted as guarantors for Br. don Juan de Pomar y Burgos. This guarantee was to secure the amount for which the tithes of the province would be auctioned, as don Juan de Pomar y Burgos was bidding for them.

Don Francisco Bruno de Chaves and his wife María de Quesada, residents of Valle de Ujarraz, sold an 8-year-old mulatto slave named Francisco to don José Antonio Jiménez for 200 pesos cacao. Don Francisco had inherited the slave from his mother, doña Josefa Chacón.

people_involved: don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Pedro Guzmán, while ill in bed, granted power of attorney to his wife, Antonia Justa Gonzalez, to execute his will. His wife and Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba were named as his executors. His heirs were designated as his wife, his son Mateo, and Pedro Manuel Salguero, who was the former husband of his daughter Antonia.

Doña Josefa Gabriela de Arleguí issued a codicil to her will from the previous December 20, revoking a clause that stipulated her second marriage children's inheritance would be pensioned by her first marriage children if assets were insufficient. She declared that the Matina hacienda belonged exclusively to the children of her first marriage and designated a plot of land for her daughter Dominga Robredo.

people_involved: don Felipe Joaquín de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Capitán de Caballería don Felipe Joaquín de Alvarado y Jirón posted bail for don Juan de Sierra, who was imprisoned for having wounded don Antonio de la Fuente.

people_involved: doña Lucía de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Doña Lucía de Alvarado y Jirón, widow of don José Nicolás de Bonilla, acting for herself and her minor children, along with don Carlos Ruiz Fernández, husband of doña María Petronila, obligated themselves to the Royal Treasury. This was to cover any liabilities arising from don José Nicolás's past role as Lieutenant of Royal Officials, with the obligation limited to the inherited assets of the children and the widow's dowry.

José Nicolás Rodríguez and Manuel Calvo, along with their minor siblings Juan Miguel, Joaquín, and María Francisca Rodríguez, granted power of attorney to don José del Aguila, the Mayor of Santiago de Veragua. This power was for claiming the inheritance due to them from María del Carmen de Torres, who died in the Villa de los Santos, having named her husband don Francisco (with whom she had no children) as her executor.

people_involved: don Felipe Joaquín de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Don José Joaquín de Nava sold a 26-year-old black slave named Toribio Gudiño to Capitán don Felipe Joaquín de Alvarado y Jirón for 450 pesos cacao. Don José Joaquín de Nava had previously acquired Toribio through purchase from don Antonio Pao.

Don Antonio de la Fuente and his wife doña María Francisca de Alvarado obligated themselves to Capitán don Romualdo de Oriamuno for 2640 pesos plata. This amount represented the value of 100 tercios of cacao (at 25 pesos each) and 80 pounds of purple snail thread that Oriamuno had sold to them. They offered the grantor's cash book as a guarantee for the debt, which was later cancelled on November 26, 1771.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí
Presbítero don Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí
Br. don Juan de Pomar y Burgos
summary: Licenciado don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí, acting as the executor for his deceased brother Presbítero don Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí, established a chaplaincy for four recited masses. The principal of 150 pesos plata had been invested for two years in the dwelling houses of Br. don Juan de Pomar y Burgos, the priest of Villa Nueva.

Two nephews, Don Francisco Robredo and Don Fernando de Arleguí, are aspiring to the priesthood. The patronage is currently held by their brother, Don Antonio Elías de Arleguí, and upon his death, it will pass to Don Manuel Felipe and Don Francisco Arleguí, always remaining with the closest and eldest relative.

Don Ramón de Céspedes issued a dowry letter in favor of his wife, Ana Catarina Carrillo, who is the legitimate daughter of José O Carrillo and Josefa de Aguirre. The dowry amounted to 460 pesos in cacao and 200 pesos.

Pedro Salguero donated a cacao plantation with 1746 trees in the Matina valley to the Virgin of Sorrows of the local parish. The plantation bordered an hacienda called La Laureana to the East and another hacienda belonging to the same image (Virgin of Sorrows) to the West.

people_involved: Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: The will of the deceased Pedro Guzmán was granted by his wife, Antonia González, acting with power of attorney. His children were Mateo and the deceased Antonia Josefa, and the executors were Antonia González and Padre don Juan Manuel de Casasola. The heirs were Mateo and Pedro Salguero, as the widower of Antonia Josefa.

people_involved: Doña María de la Luz Salmón Pacheco
summary: Doña María de la Luz Salmón Pacheco, widow of Don Joaquín Montoya, granted power of attorney to Don Isidro José del Río and Don Bernardino Carreño. This was because her husband died in Panama, where he had given power to testate to Don Agustín de Gana and Don Bernardo de Silva, leaving his two daughters and his wife as heirs.

Francisca Solano granted freedom to her two enslaved women, Manuela Josefa Barquero, a 55-year-old mulata, and Antonia Josefa Barquero, Manuela's 25-year-old daughter. Francisca had inherited them from her mother, and their freedom was to commence upon Francisca's death.
Don José de Uriza, a resident, granted freedom to his enslaved woman, María Francisca Luna, a 40-year-old criolla. He had acquired her by purchase from Don Juan Carrión.

people_involved: Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
Capitán don Miguel de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría, the local priest, being ill in bed, granted power to testate to Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba. The executors were Capitán don Miguel de Alvarado y Jirón and Don Bartolomé García y Casasola, and the sole heir was Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba.

Doña Francisca de Inza, a widow, incurred a debt of 350 pesos of cacao to the Royal Treasury, receiving funds from Don Tomás López del Corral. She granted a deed in favor of the Royal Treasury on October 8, 1733, but failed to fulfill the obligation, mortgaging a 4000-tree cacao hacienda in Matina.

people_involved: Doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo, who had assumed a debt of 350 pesos of cacao to the Royal Treasury, presented the amount on December 21. The Governor then cancelled the debt.

people_involved: Doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo
Licenciado don Juan Manuel López del Corral
summary: Doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo granted general power of attorney to her son, Licenciado don Juan Manuel López del Corral, who was the priest of the town of Heredia.

people_involved: Doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo
Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina
Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco
summary: A court sentence on September 9 confirmed Doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo's right to 225 pesos related to the 'Felipe Díaz' pasture. Her deceased husband, Don Tomás López del Corral, had bought the pasture for 350 pesos, with the obligation to pay 250 pesos to Don Francisco Bruno Serrano de Reina and Doña Antonia Salmón Pacheco, a sum that eventually fell to Don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco. Doña Francisca was condemned to pay 125 pesos in silver still owed to Don Dionisio's estate.

people_involved: Licenciado don Juan Manuel López del Corral
Doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo
Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco
summary: Licenciado don Juan Manuel López del Corral, acting as general attorney for his mother Doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo, sold the 'Felipe Díaz' pasture to Don José Nicolás Salmón Pacheco, a Presbyter Cleric, who represented the succession of his deceased father, Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco. The sale price was 350 pesos, with 125 pesos covering a previous debt, 100 pesos received in silver, and the remaining 125 pesos donated to the buyer due to uncertainty if Don Tomás had paid them.

people_involved: Capitán don Miguel de Alvarado y Jirón
Capitán don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón
Don José Hermenegildo de Alvarado y Jirón
Don José Miguel de Alvarado y Jirón
Don José Manuel de Alvarado y Jirón
Don Juan José Silvestre de Alvarado y Jirón
Don José Cayetano de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Capitán don Miguel de Alvarado y Jirón, son of the deceased Capitán don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón and Doña Catarina Vida Martel, made his will. He was married to Doña María Josefa de Torres, a native of Nicaragua and daughter of the deceased Capitán don Juan de Torres and Doña María Romero Tamaris. Their children included Don José Hermenegildo, Don José Miguel, Don José Manuel, Don Juan José Silvestre, and Don José Cayetano, with three having died in infancy.
Isabel Fernández married and died shortly after, leaving a son named Joaquín who subsequently died around 12 years old.

people_involved: Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría married Bárbara de la Madriz Linares, who later died, leaving their daughter Micaela de Alvarado.

people_involved: Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
Doña Luisa de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría entered into a second marriage with Doña Luisa de Guzmán y Echavarría, but they did not have any children together.

people_involved: Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Fourteen years prior to the current record (1765), Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría purchased a mulatto slave named Juan Manuel Zamora, who later escaped and has not been heard from since.

people_involved: Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría acquired the property known as Las Cóncavas through a purchase from María Calvo.

people_involved: Don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón
Doña Luisa de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: In October 1765, Capitán Don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón gifted a mulatto slave named Fermín Oriamuno to his wife, Doña Luisa de Guzmán y Echavarría.

people_involved: Doña Ana Efigenia García de Estrada
Doña Dominga Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: In November 1765, Don José Antonio de Oriamuno, as the legitimate son and universal heir of his deceased parents, ratified the sale of a 500-tree cacao plantation in Barbilla, Matina valley, to Doña Dominga Muñoz de la Trinidad, a transaction initiated by his father around 1762 but never formalized.

people_involved: Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
Doña Luisa de Guzmán y Echavarría
Don Miguel de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: In November 1765, the testament of the late Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría was executed by his attorney. The testament established a chaplaincy, granted freedom to the slave Antonia Josefa and her children, and included a donation of a mulatto slave to his wife, Doña Luisa de Guzmán y Echavarría.
In November 1765, Don Miguel Camino, a free Pardo, executed his testament, designating his wife, Gertrudis de Campos, as his universal executrix and heir, given that they had no children.

Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón, legitimate son of the deceased Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón and Angela de Guevara Sáenz, made his testament. He was married to María Manuela de Baeza and had several children, some living and some deceased in infancy. His mother-in-law was María Magdalena Maroto, and his daughter María Francisca de Alvarado was married to Antonio de la Fuente.

José Camino made his testament, identifying his wife as the legitimate daughter of Juan de Alvarado. He listed his slaves as Juana, Alejandro, José M...., and Juan José Masís. Captains Antonio Elías de Arleguí and José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda were named as his executors, and his heirs were his siblings and his wife.

María Catarina Chavarría, daughter of the deceased Joaquín Chavarría and Baltasara Trejos, made her testament. She was the widow of Bartolomé Picado, with whom she had four daughters, and was remarried to José Antonio Hernández, with whom she had a son. Her executors were her current husband and Lieutenant Clemente Astorga, and her heirs were her children.

Ana Sancho de Castañeda leased a cacao and fruit hacienda named 'Las Sesenta Calles' in the Matina valley to her son, Lieutenant of Cavalry Manuel José García. The lease was for 5 years at an annual rent of 107 pesos of cacao. The hacienda comprised 2070 trees.

José Nicolás Rodríguez and Manuela Calvo granted power of attorney to Captain José de la Aguila to claim goods left by the deceased María del Carmen Torres. José Nicolás Rodríguez also acted on behalf of his siblings Juan Miguel, Joaquín, and María Francisca Rodríguez. The Rodríguez siblings were legitimate children of the deceased José Manuel Rodríguez, who was the son of María del Carmen Torres from her first marriage to Jacinto Rodríguez.

Captain Juan Nicolás Castillo and Margarita Villagra, along with the deceased Juan de Benavides and his wife Ignacia Miranda, made an obligation for capellanías following a sentence in the mortuary cause of Licenciado Juan José Camacho. As tenants of the haciendas, Castillo and Villagra obligated themselves for various sums to different capellanías, including those founded by Alonso Gómez Macotela and Antonio Machado, and those belonging to Licenciado Hermenegildo de Alvarado y Jirón. They mortgaged two houses in Ujarrás and 2130 cacao trees in Matina.

Sargento José Solano, legitimate son of José Miguel Solano and Felipa Villalobos, made his testament. He was married to María Micaela Valverde, daughter of the deceased Francisco Valverde and Inés Granados, and they had four living children and three who died in infancy. His daughter Antonia de la Trinidad Solano was married to José Antonio Lumbides and had a daughter, while María Josefa Solano was married to Gregorio Calvo. Pedro José Corrales and Nicolás Ulloa were named as his executors, and his children were his heirs.

Angela de Alvarado leased a cacao plantation named 'La Angelita' in the Barbilla area of the Matina valley to Juan Francisco Lumbides. The lease was for three years for 300 pesos of cacao. The plantation consisted of 770 fruit-bearing trees.

Pedro Lebrón and Lucía Solórzano, widow of Gregorio Martínez and resident of Heredia, obligated themselves for 457 pesos 4 reales of cacao at 5% interest to a capellanía founded by Licenciado Manuel González Coronel. Pedro Lebrón mortgaged a ranch named 'Tenorio' in the Bagaces valley, while Lucía Solórzano mortgaged a house made of cedar wood and tile.

A fianza (surety) was provided to Don Antonio de Azofeifa, documented in an escritura before Don Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla, Teniente of Heredia. The collateral for this debt included 28 furrows of sugarcane, two mules, and an old sugar mill located in La Lajuela.

Don Eusebio Pérez and his wife, Doña Petronila León, residents of Heredia, provided a fianza to Don Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla, who had won the auction for the office of Provincial Mayor and Santa Hermandad. They mortgaged a house in Heredia to secure the payment of 00 pesos cacao to the royal treasury in three annual installments.

people_involved: Don Juan Sáenz de la Fuente
Don Antonio Pablo de Silva y Romero
summary: Sargento Mayor Don Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla, residing in Barba valley, granted power of attorney to Don Juan Sáenz de la Fuente and Don Antonio Pablo de Silva y Romero, both residents of Madrid. This power was for them to petition His Majesty for the confirmation of his titles as Provincial Mayor and Regidor of Cartago.

Don Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla, whose Provincial Mayor title was issued by the Real Audiencia on November 4, 1766, granted power of attorney to Don José Esteban Pérez of Guatemala City. This was to address the delay in receiving the title from Procurador Don Casimiro Esteban de Arrea and to ensure its confirmation within the required five-year period.

José Masís, a free mulatto who had purchased his freedom, created his will. He was the natural son of Juana Masís, a former slave of Captain Juan Masís and Doña María Fernández, and was married to María Francisca Calvo, with whom he had several children. His executors were José Espinosa and José Manuel de Guzmán, and his heirs were his wife and son.

Juan Francisco Ramos and Doña Francisca de Miranda sold three enslaved mulatas—Manuela Petronila (23 years old), Benita Ramona (8 years old), and María de Jesús (1.5 years old)—to Captain Don Joaquín de Alvarado, represented by his wife Doña María Francisca del Corral. The younger enslaved women were daughters of Manuela Petronila, who Doña Francisca de Miranda had acquired as the daughter of another enslaved woman inherited from her parents.

people_involved: Presbítero Don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí
summary: Presbítero Don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí, acting as executor for Presbítero Don Manuel González Coronel, established a capellanía for masses, fulfilling Coronel's closed will from August 2, 1760. The endowment, totaling 2027 pesos 4 reales, was secured by several individuals in Nicaragua and Barba valley, with its interest designated for papal bulls, church upkeep, aid to the local poor, and as a stipend for the chaplain, Don Pablo Lebrón, a relative of the founder.

people_involved: Capitán Don Esteban Ruiz de Mendoza
summary: On December 3, 1768, Capitán Don Esteban Ruiz de Mendoza posted bail for Don Antonio Cayetano de Noguera, who was facing criminal charges for tobacco smuggling. The prosecution was led by Sargento Mayor Don Domingo Cavello, the Governor and Commander General of Nicaragua province.
Esteban delivers his debtor, who is subsequently imprisoned in León.
Ana Morales sells a copper pot weighing 8 arrobas to her son-in-law, Juan Pablo Morales, and his wife, Manuela Silvestre Vázquez, for 100 pesos plata or 150 pesos cacao.

Francisco de Soto and his wife, Teresa Ruiz, sell two caballerías of land in Aranjuez to Antonio Miguel Hernández for 50 pesos cacao. Francisco de Soto had acquired this land from Captain José Manuel Segura, who, in his testament dated April 11, 1766, declared he had sold the land (originally bought from Captain Francisco Morera) to his stepson, Francisco Soto.

Captain José Manuel Segura's testament, executed before Gregorio Huesca, Lieutenant Governor of Esparza, declares that two caballerías of land, which he had purchased from Captain Francisco Morera, were sold to his stepson, Francisco Soto.

Doña Manuela de Zavaleta, a widow, leases her cacao plantation named La Catalana in the Matina valley, comprising 1414 trees, to Ramón Céspedes for two years. The rent is 100 pesos cacao for the first year and 130 pesos cacao for the second.

Doña Manuela de Zavaleta pledges 100 pesos plata at 5% interest to the chaplaincy founded by Licenciado Manuel José González Coronel. She receives the funds from Licenciado Hermenegildo de Arleguí, the executor of Manuel José González Coronel, and mortgages the La Catalana hacienda in Matina.

Teniente Manuel Antonio Cárdenas and his wife, María de Quesada, pledge various sums to several chaplaincies and the Cofradía del Rosario, all at 5% interest. These obligations are secured by the 'Zas Viejas' hacienda in Matina, a 2000-tree clearing in Barbilla, and a house in the city.

people_involved: Romualdo José Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Captain Romualdo José Muñoz de la Trinidad and his wife, Tomasa Gómez, pledge 210 pesos 3 reales plata at 5% interest to Juan Silverio Segura, who is absent, for his share of his deceased father José Manuel Segura's estate. They mortgage a house in the city near the Ermita de la Soledad.
Juan Silverio Segura, a resident of Masaya, cancels an obligation made in his favor by Romualdo José Muñoz de la Trinidad and Tomasa Gómez.

Antonia Micaela Segura, a widow, pledges 150 cacao trees in Barbilla (Matina) to her absent brother, Juan Silverio Segura, as part of their inheritance from their father, José Manuel Segura, agreeing to pay 10 pesos annually for them.
Juan Silverio Segura cancels the obligation made in his favor by Antonia Micaela Segura.

José Francisco Reyes and his wife, María Francisca Masís, residents of Aserrí, grant freedom to their slave, María de la Cruz Masís. This is done in exchange for 100 pesos plata and 100 pesos cacao paid by José Masís, a free mulatto and brother of María de la Cruz Masís.
Ana Eras, widow of Damián Castella, acknowledges receiving a hacienda with 500 cacao trees, valued at 250 pesos cacao, from Damián during his lifetime.
Cayetana Sandoval, widow of Jacinto Quirós, leases a cacao hacienda with over 1000 trees in the Barbilla valley to Félix García de Ergueta for two years, at a rent of 150 pesos cacao per year.

Captain Joaquín de Alvarado y Jirón grants power of attorney to Francisco de la Llana, a resident of León (Nicaragua), to bid before the Ecclesiastical Cabildo for the tithes of the Matina valley for three years, offering 600 pesos plata annually.

José Nicolás Camaño and his wife, María Josefa de la Riva, pledge 100 pesos cacao to the Cofradía de la Vera Cruz, an obligation previously held by Ventura Elizondo. They mortgage a hacienda with over 1000 trees in La Pontezuela, Matina.

Félix Joaquín de Alvarado y Jirón, as executor for Francisca de Arburola, establishes a chaplaincy of masses as per her will, with a principal of 300 pesos cacao secured by a hacienda in Matina. Due to the death of Nicolás de Alvarado, the original patron, an interim chaplain is appointed, and future patrons will be chosen from other family members.

locations: El Viejo de la villa del Realejo
summary: Francisca de Arburola executed her testament in El Viejo de la villa del Realejo before Corregidor Pedro Aparicio. In her will, she declared herself the widow of José Antonio López Corral, named her grandson Nicolás de Alvarado as the first chaplain, and appointed Licenciado José Hermenegildo de Arleguí, Joaquín de Alvarado, and Gabriel Marcos de Ocaña as her executors.
Captain Manuel Sancho de Castañeda and his wife, Baltasara de la Madriz, are mentioned in an incomplete record.

Félix García de Ergueta exchanged an enslaved mulato named Félix Luna, approximately 40 years old, for an enslaved negrito named José García, aged 18 to 20. José García was part of an inheritance from the deceased Presbítero don Manuel José García.

Don José Antonio de Oriamuno, acting as executor for doña María de Arburola, stated that doña María had informed him that the enslaved Félix Luna, for whom she held a bill of sale, actually belonged to don Félix García. Consequently, Oriamuno returned Félix Luna to don Félix García.

Francisca Petronila Valverde, legitimate daughter of Francisco Valverde and Inés Granados and widow of Francisco Tristán, made her will. She named her children Dominga Estéfana (11 years old), José (9 years old), and Rita Josefa (born after her widowhood) as heirs, and appointed her cousins Andrés Barquero and Tomás Granados as executors.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan Lucas de Zamora
summary: Captains don Juan Lucas de Zamora and don Manuel de Bonilla settled a lawsuit with don Pedro Lebrón concerning 650 pesos unjustly collected from the estate of doña Bárbara de Arias, their mother-in-law. Lebrón agreed to pay 350 pesos within eighteen months, partly in cattle valued at Bagaces prices and partly with a house in Heredia.
Teresa Palomino, a widow, leased her fruiting cacao hacienda named 'la Salas' in the Valle de Barbilla to José Manuel de Guzmán.

people_involved: Br. don Juan Salvador de Laya y Bolívar
summary: Don Carlos Ruiz Fernández and his wife, doña María Petronila de Bonilla, committed to pay 137 pesos 4 reales in cacao currency to a chaplaincy. This chaplaincy was founded by doña Cecilia Vázquez Coronado and is served by Br. don Juan Salvador de Laya y Bolívar, with the obligation tied to their house in the city, formerly owned by don José Lebrón.

people_involved: Capitán don Miguel Es Alvarado y Jirón
Doña Luisa de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Capitán don Miguel Es Alvarado y Jirón and his wife, doña Luisa de Guzmán y Echavarría, sold a pasture near Río Seco, above La Puebla, to José Masis. The property, bordered by Río Toyogres and neighbors like don Luis de Soto, Sandí, and Pablo Fonseca, was sold for 275 pesos cacao, with 139 pesos designated for masses.

Don José García, a resident of Villa de San José, posted bail for his sick brother-in-law, don Nicolás de Basto, who was implicated in a criminal case. The case involved Pedro Fuentes, who was accused of stealing goods from Manuel Díaz and was also imprisoned.

people_involved: Doña Ana Teresa de Soto y Barahona
summary: The widow doña Ana Teresa de Soto y Barahona gifted 200 pesos in silver to her son, don Francisco Carazo. This money had been sent to her two years prior by her other son, Doctor don José Antonio Carazo, who was residing in the Kingdom of Peru.

people_involved: Br. don Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: Br. don Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo, the interim priest, leased his cacao hacienda 'La Ibarra,' comprising 2400 trees in the Valle de Matina, to don Nicolás Robredo for five years. The rent was 225 pesos cacao for the first year and 250 pesos for each of the subsequent four years.

people_involved: Capitán don Romualdo José Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: An incomplete record mentions Capitán don Romualdo José Muñoz de la Trinidad, Gregoria Mena (widow of don Antonio Barros y Muro), and José Eusebio de O... on April 20, 1769.
Barros y Muro exchanged a pasture named "Cerrado," inherited from don Antonio, for a 14-vara adobe and tile house located on Gregoria's solar.

Don Andrés Fernández and his wife doña María Trejos donated a quarter part of seven caballerías and one cuerda of land to Pedro Manuel Salguero. This land, located in Angelina or Cuercuá, was originally granted to don Andrés and his partners by His Majesty, as documented in a royal title issued in Guatemala on September 22 of the previous year.

people_involved: don Benito de Alvarado y Jirón
Presbítero Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Doña Leonida de Ocampo Golfín, legitimate daughter of don Nicolás de Ocampo Golfín and doña Manuela Bastarrica, being ill, granted power to her husband, don Benito de Alvarado y Jirón, to make her will. Her husband and Presbítero Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba were named as executors, and her six children were designated as heirs.

people_involved: Don Felix Joaquín de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Don Felix Joaquín de Alvarado y Jirón sold his 12-13 year old mulatto slave, Diego, to don Tomás López del Corral for 250 pesos cacao. Diego had run away from don Felix and was with don Tomás, refusing to return; don Felix had originally purchased Diego from don Ramón Saborido of Villa Nueva.

people_involved: Don Felix Joaquín de Alvarado y Jirón
don José de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Don Felix Joaquín de Alvarado y Jirón, son of the deceased don José de Alvarado y Jirón and doña Josefa Urdina, made his will. He named his wife doña María Francisca Corrales and his two living children, Ana Josefa (5) and Santiago de Alvarado (2), as heirs, and left 100 pesos cacao to his sister doña María Manuela de Alvarado for her children's upbringing. He also established a chaplaincy, with his son or nephew don Fernando de Arleguí as patron/chaplain, and appointed don José Romualdo de Oriamuno and his wife as executors.

people_involved: Capitán don Francisco Fallas de la Vega
Sargento Mayor don José Fernández Castellanos
summary: Don Manuel Trinidad Fallas, a resident of San José, sold his 28-year-old mulatto slave, Fernando Fallas, to Capitán don Francisco Carazo for 200 pesos plata. Fernando was inherited from Don Manuel's mother, doña Antonia María de Fallas (whose will was dated Oct 19, 1746), and his biological mother, Gertrudis, was a slave donated to doña Antonia by her father, Capitán don Francisco Fallas de la Vega (whose will was dated Apr 30, 1729). Gertrudis's mother, Dominga, was acquired by Capitán don Francisco Fallas de la Vega through a dotal letter to doña Mariana Solano on Feb 18, 1729.

people_involved: Doña Francisca de la Madriz Linares
summary: Doña Francisca de la Madriz Linares, a widow, committed to pay 300 pesos cacao at 5% interest to the Cofradía de la Vera Cruz. This debt was secured against her hacienda in Matina, which contained 600 fruit-bearing cacao trees.

people_involved: Capitán don Romualdo José Muñoz de la Trinidad
don Juan de Laya y Bolívar
summary: Doña Nicolasa Martínez de Luna sold half a solar in Cartago to Capitán don Romualdo José Muñoz de la Trinidad for 25 pesos cacao. She had received the property as a donation from her mother, doña Magdalena Pérez de Luna. The property bordered don Félix García, doña Ramona Bonilla, Juana Calderón's former property, Licenciado Cecilia Paniagua, and don Juan de Laya y Bolívar.

Diego de Goicoechea, represented by his brother, sold an enslaved woman named Antonia and her daughter to Manuel Sancho de Castañeda. The price for Antonia was 250 pesos cacao, and for her daughter, 50 pesos plata. The seller stated that he received Antonia as payment for his rent and that she had her daughter while in his possession, which prevented him from traveling.

people_involved: B. don José Francisco de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Juan Pablo Morales and his wife, Manuela Silvestre Vázquez, committed 150 pesos to fund a capellanía established by doña Juana de Vida Martel, with B. don José Francisco de Alvarado y Jirón serving as chaplain. This obligation was secured by their house in Cartago and two sweet cane farms in the Ujarraz valley. Don Juan Francisco Bonilla later took over and canceled this obligation on June 21, 1781.
Don Juan Francisco Bonilla took charge of and canceled an obligation related to the capellanía of doña Juana de Vida Martel on June 21, 1781.

people_involved: Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno
doña María de la Encarnación Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Don Juan Francisco Jiménez, legitimate son of don José Manuel Jiménez and doña Ana García, provided 418 pesos 2 reales and 200 pesos plata as arras to his wife, doña Ana María de Oriamuno. Doña Ana María is the legitimate daughter of Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno and doña María de la Encarnación Muñoz de la Trinidad.

The residents of the new settlement of San José, Aserrí valley, including several named individuals, obligated themselves to maintain the church's lamp and material structure. This commitment followed a dispatch from the Bishop on August 5th of that year, which granted them their request. The capellanía was founded by don Bernardo Valverde.

people_involved: Doña Juana de Soto y Barahona
doña María de los Dolores Gómez
summary: Doña Juana de Soto y Barahona, learning of her son don José Gabriel Muñoz's death in Nicaragua, and being named his universal heir (as he had no children but was married to doña María de los Dolores Gómez), granted power of attorney. She authorized don Mauricio de Orozco and her daughter-in-law, doña María, to represent her and collect the inheritance.

Buenaventura Lizondro and his wife, Margarita de Aguirre, obligated themselves for 100 pesos at 5% interest to the Archicofradía del Sacramento. They mortgaged their house, described as 19 varas, made of posts and tile, located in the fields of Cartago.

people_involved: doña María de la Luz Pacheco
Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco
Lic. don José Nicolás Salmón Pacheco
summary: Heirs of Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco, including his children and their spouses, were involved in a legal dispute. A court sentence from the previous month ordered Lic. don José Nicolás Salmón Pacheco to return 1100 pesos cacao to the estate, comprising funds taken from the maternal and paternal inheritance, inventoried cacao, and money received by Pedro Salguero from don Cayetano Pacheco related to a debt from don Tomás López del Corral. The Licenciado appealed, and the grantors obligated themselves for the results as ordered by the Gobernador.

people_involved: Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno
doña María de la Encarnación Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno and his wife, doña María de la Encarnación Muñoz de la Trinidad, sold a pasture outside Cartago to Juan José Arias for 30 pesos cacao. The property, measuring 160 by 142 varas, was acquired by Oriamuno from the heirs of doña María, doña Lorenza, and doña Antonia Josefa de Arburola. It bordered lands of don Tomás Corrales, don Manuel Felipe de Arleguí, the sellers, and Antonio Valverde.

people_involved: doña María de la Luz Pacheco
Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco
summary: Don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco, doña Antonia Pacheco, doña María de la Luz Pacheco, don Francisco Pacheco, and don José Nicolás de Echavarría (husband of doña Eufemia Pacheco) leased a cacao hacienda to don Juan Jiménez. The hacienda, inherited from their father Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco, included 2064 cacao trees, a house, an axe, a canoe, and two machetes, for an annual rent of 210 pesos and 2 reales, with the lease term at don Juan's discretion.

people_involved: doña Dominga Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Doña Josefa de Fallas, a resident of Aserrí Valley, sold a young mulatto named Juan Marcos Fallas, son of Antonia (mulata), to doña Dominga Muñoz de la Trinidad for 200 pesos cacao. Doña Josefa had inherited Juan Marcos from her parents, and her son José Manuel Fallas signed the document on her behalf.

people_involved: doña Luisa de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Don Antonio de Azofeifa, acting as attorney for don Juan Francisco de Aguilar and Francisco de Sandoval (who purchased the Miravalles ranch from the estate of the deceased don Miguel de Alvarado for 1500 pesos plata), obligated his principals to pay 200 pesos 3 reales plata to don Miguel's widow, doña Luisa de Guzmán y Echavarría, and 514 pesos plata to doña Isabel de Fernández, as adjudicated in the estate. The ranch and 1500 pesos from each debtor's cacao haciendas in Nicaragua were mortgaged.

An obligation for 785 pesos 5 reales plata was made in favor of Doña Micaela de Alvarado, a minor and granddaughter of Don Miguel de Alvarado. Don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda, her tutor, was involved in this transaction, which also included a mortgage.

people_involved: Juan de la Haya y Bolívar
summary: Presbítero Don José Hermenérnidó de Arleguí sold a 16-year-old mulato slave named Juan Francisco Arleguí to Licenciado Don Juan de la Haya y Bolívar for 200 pesos plata. José Hermenérnidó inherited the slave from his deceased brother, Presbítero Don Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí, who had purchased him from Doña Rosa María de Chaves on January 31 of an unspecified year before Teniente General Don Antonio de Azofeifa.

locations: Provincia de la Trinidad de Sonsonate
summary: Don Antonio de la Fuente, tobacco supplier for Nicaragua and subdelegate judge of land measures, and his wife Doña María Francisca de Alvarado, along with four guarantors, obligated themselves for 6000 pesos plata to Br. Don Manuel Lorenzo García, owner and chaplain of the ship 'La Fama'. This was for the freight of 2000 'dere' of tobacco and cacao from La Caldera to Acajutla. Additionally, Don Antonio de la Fuente granted general power to Don Juan Feliciano Ramírez, majordomo of León Cathedral, Nicaragua.

Doña María Francisca Corrales, widow of Don Joaquín de Alvarado, unconditionally donated a 'roza' (clearing) with 1411 cacao trees in El Tocino, Matina Valley, to Francisco Castillo. Don Joaquín had originally declared this 'roza' in his will of May 28 of this year for Castillo, his estate manager, but with a condition that María Francisca removed due to gratitude for Castillo's services.

Don Antonio de la Fuente and his wife Doña María Francisca de Alvarado sold a 27-year-old mulato slave named Isidro Cabrales to Doña Isabel Fernández for 200 pesos plata. They had previously acquired Isidro Cabrales by purchase from Doña Nicolasa de Betancourt.

people_involved: Juan José de la Madriz Linares
summary: Don Alfonso Manuel de Ulloa, as a debtor, and his son Don Francisco Fermín de Ulloa, as guarantor, obligated themselves for 850 pesos cacao for various chaplaincies and cofradías. These obligations were initially Alfonso's as a tenant of a farm near Cartago, and due to a decrease in his assets' value, his son guaranteed the debt by mortgaging his maternal guardianship funds. The escritura was later cancelled on January 18, 1772, following a dispatch from visitador Don Juan José de la Madriz Linares dated January 33, 1771.

locations: Posa azul (?) del valle de Matina
summary: José Francisco Riva, as principal, and Capitán Francisco de la Riva, as guarantor, obligated themselves to Don Ventura D...os for 686 pesos cacao plus mule freight, committing to plant and deliver a 'roza' with 1000 cacao trees in Matina Valley. Additionally, Capitán Francisco de la Riva guaranteed a 133 pesos cacao loan from Don Ventura to Santiago and Gerardo Riva, mortgaging a cacao hacienda in Barbilla.

Doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo leased her hacienda 'San Miguel' in Barbilla Valley, containing 5600 fruit-bearing cacao trees, to her son Don Tomás López del Corral for 5 years at 400 pesos per year. Don Tomás had previously leased the same hacienda for 7 years, with that agreement from November 20, 1763, set to expire on the same day and month of the current year.

Don Antonio de la Fuente and Doña María Francisca de Alvarado sold a 38-year-old mulato slave named Manuel Nicolás Cabrales to Don Juan Garau de Cors for 200 pesos plata. Manuel Nicolás Cabrales had been previously purchased by them from Doña Nicolasa Cabrales on May 29, 1764.

Doña Benita de Bonilla sold a black slave named Facúnda to Don Manl. Guillén, a resident of Tierra Firme, for 90 pesos cacao. Facúnda was acquired from the estate of the deceased Dª Francisca de Bonilla, and her intrinsic value was also 90 pesos.

people_involved: Doña Rosa de la Madriz Linares
Don Antcnio rat de Sd SA
summary: Don Tomás López del Corral and Doña Rosa de la Madriz Linares obligated themselves for 200 pesos plata at 5% interest, redeemed by Don José Gómez Toscano, agent for Don Manuel Antonio de Unanue. The funds were split between the Convento de San Francisco and a chaplaincy held by Presbítero Don José de Alvarado. Doña Francisca de Ibarra acted as guarantor, mortgaging her hacienda "San Miguel" in the Barbilla valley, while the debtors mortgaged a 6000-tree plantation in the same valley. On March 21, 1776, Don Pedro Tiburcio Machado cancelled the obligation, taking responsibility for the 200 pesos, which were then allocated to the Cofradía de la Concepción and a chaplaincy held by Don Antcnio rat de Sd SA.

Don Tomás López del Corral sold a 13-year-old mulato named Diego to Don José Gómez Toscano, a native of Perú, for 200 pesos plata. Don Tomás had purchased Diego from Don Joaquín de Alvarado on May 2, 1769.

people_involved: Capitán Don José Romualdo de Oriamuno
summary: Pedro Manuel Salguero made his will, identifying himself as the legitimate son of José Pascual Salguero and María Josefa Vargas. He was first married to Antonia Josefa Guzmán, with whom he had a daughter, María Josefa Benita, who died at three months, preceded by her mother. He inherited goods from Pedro Guzmán, Antonia's father. He is currently married to Isabel Ramona de Quesada, with whom he has a one-month-old daughter, Juana Josefa. His brother-in-law is Mateo Guzmán. His executors are Capitán Don José Romualdo de Oriamuno and his current wife, and his daughter Juana Josefa is his heir. The will was granted before Don José Antonio de Oriamuno, by commission of the Governor.

José Miguel Arce, legitimate son of José Nicolás Arce and Gregoria Fonseca, made his will. He was married twice, first to Francisca Torres and then to María Magdalena Gómez, both deceased. With Francisca Torres, he had six children, one of whom died, and five are living: María Antonia (married to Pedro Méndez), Manuela Cayetana (single), Micaela del Carmen, Juana Catarina, and Juana Josefa. With María Magdalena Gómez, he had four children, only one of whom, José Martín (about two years old), is living. Simón Valerín was the first husband of his second wife. His father-in-law is Efigenio Gómez. His executor is Ayudante Pedro Vicente Chavarría, and his six living children are his heirs. The will was granted before José Nicolás de Echavarría, Alcalde de la Santa Hermandad.

people_involved: Dª Teresa de Soto y Barahona
Doña Ana Jacoba de Alvarado y Jirón
Don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Don Francisco Carazo provided a dowry for his wife, Doña Ana Jacoba de Alvarado y Jirón. The dowry included a 12-year-old mulata named Juana Antonia, valued at 200 pesos, and 1809 pesos 6 reales plata, with arras of 500 pesos plata. Don Francisco is the legitimate son of Don Pedro Carazo and Dª Teresa de Soto y Barahona, and Doña Ana Jacoba is the legitimate daughter of Don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón and Doña María Manuela de Baeza.

Don Juan Dionisio Salmón Pacheco, Don Cayetano Salmón Pacheco, and his wife Doña Teresa del Fierro obligated themselves to a chaplaincy founded by Doña Catarina de Siles for 579 pesos, located in her house behind the Convento de San Francisco. Don Cayetano and his wife took the house for themselves, now responsible for 54 pesos. Don Juan Dionisio took responsibility for the remaining 525 pesos, charging it to the "Felipe Díaz" pasture, which his brother Don Cayetano transferred to him, having inherited it from their deceased parents, Don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco and Doña Francisca Serrano de Reina.

Don Miguel Antonio Fajardo and his wife Doña Gabriela Sarmiento obligated themselves to Don Juan Dionisio Salmón Pacheco for 300 pesos plata, to be repaid upon their son Don Benito Fajardo's return from Panamá, where he was sent for business. They mortgaged their house in this city. Don Antonio Pao, their son-in-law, signed for Doña Gabriela. On May 15, 1772, Don Juan Dionisio cancelled the obligation.

Don Mateo Erdocia, a native of Spain, and Agustín de Gana, a resident of Panamá, were involved in the transfer of the ship "Santísima Trinidad." Don Juan Mateo del Castillo, the ship's owner, owed Agustín de Gana 10235 pesos 7.5 reales plata. To settle the debt, Don Juan Mateo offered the ship for 9000 pesos plata, which Agustín accepted. The ship was delivered in Puntarenas on March 18 by Don Tomás Benito Hidalgo, Lieutenant Governor of Esparza.

Don Antonio de la Fuente obligated himself to Capitán Don Mateo Erdocia for 25 reales de plata for the freight of each tobacco trunk transported on Erdocia's ships to the Port of Acajutla in the villa of La Trinidad. Payment is due 20 days after disembarkation.

Don Mateo Erdocia, owner and master of the "San Agustín y San Antonio" chata, and Pedro Manuel Salguero as guarantor, obligated themselves to the royal coffers of Guatemala for 200 pesos plata, a new tax on 80 jars of aguardiente from Perú. Don Mateo brought the aguardiente from Panamá and, unable to sell it in this province, is transporting it to Sonsonate. The tax is 10 reales per jar, payable within 4 months.
Licenciado Presbítero don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí grants power of attorney to his brothers, don Antonio Elías and don Manuel Felipe Arleguí, naming them as executors.
After the valuation of the Santa Ana hacienda, including houses, oratory, and cane fields, José Hermenegildo de Arleguí donates one-third of it to don Antonio Elías.
On June 8, 1775, Governor Bobadilla recorded that Presbítero don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí had given a new power of attorney before him.

Don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco, doña María de la Luz, don Francisco Pacheco, and doña Eufemia Pacheco (represented by her husband José Nicolás de Chavarría) lease a hacienda in Matina with 2064 cacao trees, a house, and tools to don Esteban López and José Miguel Badilla, residents of Valle de Ujarraz. The property, inherited from their father Dionisio Salmón Pacheco, is leased for 210 pesos and reales of cacao annually, for a term at the lessees' will.
Presbítero don Juan Francisco de Ibarra grants a general power of attorney to don José Antonio de Oriamuno.

Don Esteban Ruiz de Mendoza and his wife doña Joaquina López del Corral sell a mulata named Teresa, who was born and raised in their house, to Presbítero don Juan Francisco de Ibarra for 150 pesos in silver.

Sargento Mayor don José Antonio de Oriamuno and his wife doña María Catarina de Ibarra grant freedom to a two-year-old mulatilla named Manuela de la Trinidad, daughter of their enslaved woman Juana María, having secretly received payment for her freedom.

Pedro Manuel Salguero makes a codicil to his testament, previously made before don José Antonio de Oriamuno on February 28 of the same year. He revokes a clause concerning a communication with Presbítero Avendaño and declares he has paid debts to Capitán don Romualdo de Oriamuno, José Miguel García, and don Mateo Erdocia, also noting sums owed to him.

people_involved: María de la Encarnación Muñoz de la Trinidad
María Josefa Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Don José Antonio de Oriamuno and his wife doña María de la Encarnación Muñoz de la Trinidad undertake an obligation in favor of doña María Josefa Muñoz de la Trinidad, a minor and daughter of the deceased doña Dominga Muñoz de la Trinidad, concerning all the gold, pearl, silver jewelry, and used clothing listed in the inventory left by the deceased.

people_involved: Doña María Josefa Muñoz de la Trinidad
Doña Dominga Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Don Félix García de Ergueta obligates himself to Doña María Josefa Muñoz de la Trinidad for various properties she inherited from her deceased mother, Doña Dominga Muñoz de la Trinidad. The inherited assets include a house in Cartago, religious items, furniture, tools, a mulatto slave named Juan Marcos Fallas, and cacao trees in Valle de Matina.

locations: La Pontezuela del Valle de Matina
summary: Tomás de Arburola and his wife, Dorotea Molina, commit to paying 400 pesos in cacao to the Convento de San Francisco. They secure this obligation by mortgaging their house in Cartago and a chaplaincy on the Santa Teresa hacienda, located in La Pontezuela del Valle de Matina, which includes 900 cacao trees and was previously managed by José Miguel Arce.

José Nicolás Rodríguez and José Antonio Venegas, acting for themselves and their minor siblings, grant power of attorney to Don Isidro de Icas of Santiago de Veragua. Their purpose is to collect inherited goods from the deceased María del Carmen de Torres, who died in Villa de los Santos, which are currently held by her widower and executor, Don Francisco Méndez.

people_involved: Doña Juana María de Soto y Barahona
summary: Doña Juana María de Soto y Barahona, a widow, donates a cacao plantation with 2000 two-year-old cacao trees in Valle de Barbilla to her son, Don José Manuel Gómez, who is over 25 years old. She makes this donation to ensure his undisturbed possession, acknowledging his industry and his contribution of 12 mules from Nicaragua to her hacienda.

people_involved: Capitán Don Miguel Antonio de Unanue
Capitán Don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Captain Don Miguel Antonio de Unanue, a resident of Panama, sells his large cattle hacienda named 'el Carmen' in Valle de Bagaces to Captain Don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón for 1423 pesos plata. The sale encompasses land, livestock, tools, and structures, with the caveat that two caballerías of land had been previously sold to Francisco Antonio Pérez.

Francisco Fonseca grants power of attorney to Don Francisco Ortíz, a procurator, to seek an injunction from the Real Audiencia against a lawsuit initiated by Don José Florencio de Soto. Fonseca expresses concern about potential bias, as the assessor to the Governor in León is Don José Florencio's nephew.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don José Antonio de Oriamuno
summary: Doña Isabel Fernández, a widow, sells Juan José, a 45-year-old mulatto slave, to Sargento Mayor Don José Antonio de Oriamuno for 100 pesos plata. She had inherited Juan José from her deceased father-in-law, Capitán Don Miguel de Alvarado, and was awarded him at a value of 150 pesos, effectively granting a 50-peso discount to the buyer.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don José Antonio de Oriamuno
summary: María Portugués's last will and testament is executed, with Don José Antonio de Oriamuno, the Ayudante de Gobierno, serving as the official before whom it was granted.

A sick woman, known as 'la Portugués,' made a verbal declaration of her assets to a representative of the Governor, stating she would not make a will due to limited means. She bequeathed her house, land, and 20 cattle to Don José Antonio de Ibarra to fulfill a private agreement, explicitly excluding her three children who had already received their inheritance.

Gregorio and Gabriela Calvo sold a dilapidated house, inherited from their deceased parents Tomás Calvo and Vittoria Láscares, to Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla for 400 pesos cacao. Their brothers, Tomás, Miguel, and Francisco Calvo, residing in Masaya, had not responded to requests to participate in the sale, so Gregorio took responsibility for their share.

On the same date as the initial sale, Gregorio and Gabriela Calvo agreed to sell the same house to the Gobernador for 400 pesos cacao, as it was adjacent to his property. The sellers received the payment for this transaction.

Don Antonio de la Fuente and his wife, Doña María Francisca de Alvarado, sold the 18-year-old mulata Petronila Alvarado to Don Tomás López del Corral for 200 pesos plata. Doña María Francisca had originally received Petronila as part of her dowry from her parents.

people_involved: Capitán don José Romualdo de Oriamuno
summary: Don Manuel de Galisteo, a resident of Santiago de Guatemala, obligated himself to Captain Don José Romualdo de Oriamuno for 4800 pesos plata, a loan to fund his journey to Acapulco, Mexico. He pledged repayment upon the return of the ship 'San Francisco Javier,' owned and captained by Don Miguel Antonio de Unanue, and also mortgaged a 4000 pesos deed from Don Andrés Muñoz of Nicaragua. This obligation was later cancelled in March 1774.

Don Félix Joaquín Meneses, appointed Colector General for the parish, along with guarantors Gregorio Calvo and his wife María Josefa Solano, obligated themselves to the Curato and the church's factory. Meneses was to collect 6% of the Curato's benefits and nothing for the factory, securing the obligation with a brickyard, land, livestock, two city lots, and horses.

people_involved: Capitán don José Romualdo de Oriamuno
Son of Don Joaquín de Alvarado
Benef* don José Francisco de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Captain Don José Romualdo de Oriamuno, as the executor of Don Joaquín de Alvarado's will (dated May 28, 1769), established a chaplaincy for 8 masses. The principal of 489 pesos one real cacao was situated on Don Joaquín's 1800-cacao-tree hacienda in Matina, bordering Doña Manuela Pastora's property. Don Fernando de Arleguí, Don Joaquín's nephew, was named patron and chaplain, replacing Don Joaquín's deceased son, with Don José Francisco de Alvarado y Jirón serving as interim chaplain.

people_involved: Doña María Francisca López del Corral
summary: Doña María Francisca López del Corral, widow of Don Joaquín de Alvarado, obligated herself for the 489 pesos 1 real at 5% cacao, which constituted the principal of the chaplaincy established in the preceding deed. She confirmed the hacienda's location bordering Doña Manuela Pastora's property.

Licenciado José Nicolás Salmón Pacheco, Antonia Sarmiento, Francisco Pacheco, and José Miguel García undertake obligations. José Nicolás is responsible for 617 pesos 3 reales cacao for 505 cacao trees belonging to his minor nieces, Marta and Feliciana Pacheco, daughters of his deceased brother Félix and Antonia. Antonia Sarmiento is obligated for 609 pesos 6 reales in movable and semi-movable goods, which were adjudicated from the estate of Dionisio Salmón Pacheco, the minors' grandfather. Francisco Pacheco and José Miguel García act as guarantors.

Licenciado Presbítero José Nicolás Salmón Pacheco obligates himself for 1845 pesos cacao at 5% interest. This sum includes 1000 pesos for a chaplaincy founded by his parents, Dionisio Salmón Pacheco and Francisca Serrano de Reina, and 845 pesos for a chaplaincy founded by his uncle, Antonio Salmón Pacheco. The principal is charged against a hacienda with 1725 cacao trees in the Barbilla valley, with an additional 220 pesos cacao charged to another hacienda of 505 trees in the same valley to compensate for a shortage.

Don Tomás López del Corral grants power of attorney to Joaquín de Oconor, a resident of León (Nicaragua), and to Licenciado Juan Félix Villalobos, a cleric. This power allows them to obtain a dispatch on his behalf for the administration and collection of tithes in the Matina valley.

Cayetana Sandobal, a free mulatta and widow of Jacinto Quirós, leases a cacao hacienda with 1000 fruit-bearing trees in the Barbilla valley to Captain Tomás López del Corral. The lease is for a period of three years at a rate of 100 pesos cacao per year.

people_involved: Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Doña María Josefa Barros y Muro makes her testament, detailing her family and bequests. She leaves a pearl necklace and gold earrings to her nieces, Ana María and María Susana Lozano Cadenas. She also bequeaths a small hacienda of 300 cacao trees in Barbilla to her slaves, Manuel Valentín and José Mateo, and grants freedom to her slaves María Josefa Barros, José Mateo, and Manuel Valentín after her death. Her sisters, Juana and Mariana de Barros y Muro, are named as heirs, and Licenciados Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba and José Antº de Alvarado are her executors.

The Governor, Teniente Coronel José Joaquín de Nava, records the death of Don Benito de Alvarado y Jirón, son of deceased Gil de Alvarado y Jirón and Josefa González Camino. This event leads to the suspension of a power to make a will that Benito had initiated.

Doña Ignacia Miranda, a widow, grants freedom to her mulatta slaves: María Mauricia, Benita Josefa, Francisca Benita, and Francisca Baltasara. She does this because her only heir, her son Fray Miguel de San Pedro, has renounced his inheritance as a religious person.
Don Lucas de Liendo y Goicoechea is noted as a resident of the town of 'Ps' and also 'here', implying Cartago. This record likely pertains to his legal declaration of residence.

people_involved: don Lucas de Liendo y Goicoechea
don Luis Fernando de Liendo y Goicoechea
summary: Don Lucas de Liendo y Goicoechea, acting as attorney for his brother don Diego de Goicoechea, sold a tiled house in Cartago to Captains don Tomás López del Corral and don Manuel Sancho de Castañeda. The house was inherited from their deceased parents, don Luis Fernando de Liendo y Goicoechea and doña Baltasara Inza. The sale price was 412 pesos cacao, with a portion allocated to a capellanía founded by Baltasar de Grados.

Don Antonio Javier de Roa, a native of Tepaca in the Obispado de la Puebla de los Angeles and residing in Cartago, granted general power of attorney to don Pedro Pablo de Ibarra. Don Pedro Pablo de Ibarra serves as the Secretary of the Holy Office of the Inquisition in Mexico City.

On January 21, don Ramón de Gambarte, a native of Spain residing in Cartago, granted power of attorney to don Felipe Rubio y Morales. This power was for representation before the Audiencia in a civil and criminal complaint against don Bernardo Antonio Malvido, concerning an outstanding balance and loss from an account settlement in Cartago.

people_involved: doña María Leonida de Ocampo Golfín
don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
Presbítero don José Antonio de Alvarado
