summary: On January 21, doña María Leonida de Ocampo Golfín, widow of Captain don Benito de Alvarado, granted power to make a will to don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba, the Ecclesiastical Vicar. She named Presbyter don José Antonio de Alvarado and don Bartolomé García as her executors.

people_involved: doña María Leonida de Ocampo Golfín
summary: On January 21, doña María Leonida de Ocampo Golfín amplified her will, leaving one-fourth of her assets to her two daughters, not exceeding 1000 pesos. She also designated one-fifth of her estate for the benefit of her soul, with 300 pesos from this portion specifically for her son, Fray José Antonio de Alvarado, to cover habits and other expenses related to his ordination.

On January 22, doña Ana Jiménez, a widow, ratified the sale of a mulato named Pablo Jiménez to don Tomás López del Corral. This sale had originally occurred approximately four years prior, and the price for Pablo Jiménez was 200 pesos plata.

people_involved: don Lucas de Liendo y Goicoechea
don Luis Fernando de Liendo y Goicoechea
don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: On January 24, don Lucas de Liendo y Goicoechea, acting for himself and his brother don Diego de Goicoechea, sold a 7-year-old mulata named Isidora to Captain don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón. Isidora is the daughter of Antonia Inza, who was formerly a slave of their mother, doña Baltasara de Inza, and is now owned by don Manuel Sancho de Castañeda. The sale price was 200 pesos plata.

On January 24, don Juan de Goytia, residing in Señorío de Vina, acknowledged a debt of 2081 pesos and 3 reales of silver to don Manuel de Galisteo, a resident of Guatemala and a merchant in Nicaragua. This debt was the remaining balance for clothing items sold on credit, with the payment deadline having expired two years prior, and don Juan de Goytia committed to pay within one year.

people_involved: don Lucas de Liendo y Goicoechea
summary: Don Manuel Sancho de Castañeda and don Tomás López del Corral sold a re-roofed house and lot to don Juan Caballero for 700 pesos cacao. They had acquired this property from don Lucas de Liendo y Goicoechea on January 15, as recorded in folio 3 of the registry.
On January 25, Francisco Carazo and his wife doña Jacoba de were involved in an unspecified transaction or event.

An obligation of 400 pesos cacao and 105 pesos plata was made to the Convento de San Francisco and Cofradía de la Concepción, respectively, by the purchasers of the former home of Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón and Angela de Guevara. The house was acquired for 650 pesos cacao and 50 pesos plata, and additional properties including another house, corral, livestock, and horses were mortgaged. Don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón (father of Jacoba) acted as guarantor.

Alférez Real Don Antonio de la Fuente, Syndic of the Convento de San Francisco, cancelled the 400 pesos portion of an obligation related to the former home of Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón and Angela de Guevara.

Don Juan Caballero and Doña Isabel de Alvarado, with Don Tomás López del Corral and Doña Rosa de la Madriz Linares as guarantors, obligated themselves for 850 pesos cacao. This sum included payments for the Convento de San Francisco, Cofradía de la Veracruz (founded by José de las Salas), and a chaplaincy (founded by Francisco de Ocampo, served by Ramón Azofeifa), with their house in the city, formerly belonging to Doña Baltasara de Inza, mortgaged. The obligation was previously held by Alfonso Manuel de Ulloa, who redeemed it with three enslaved people.

Doña Dominga Sancho de Castañeda, widow of Don Gregorio Aragón, attempted to lease a cacao plantation with 1900 fruit trees to Don Gregorio de Lacalle for five years at 95 pesos per year. This hacienda was under her charge according to a deed she signed with her husband on November 24, 1765, but the transaction did not go through.

people_involved: Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: The will of the deceased Doña María Leonida de Ocampo Golfín was granted by her attorney, Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba. She was the widow of Don Benito de Alvarado y Jirón, with whom she had several children: José Antonio (a religious man), Rita Josefa, José Rafael, José Antonio, Juan José, José Isidro, and María Jena Sn de Alvarado.

Félix and Juana de Dios Garvanzo, siblings of the deceased José Antonio Coronel, and María Sabina González, his widow, amicably divided his assets. The widow received the house, which was José Antonio's residence before their marriage, while the siblings took the movable goods. The Garvanzo siblings were Coronel's half-siblings through their mother, María Golfín.

people_involved: Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho de Castañeda, daughter of Juan Sancho and Juana de Alvarado, and widow of Rafael Cevallos, made her will. She ordered two chaplaincies, one for her nephew José Miguel Sancho de Castañeda and another for her cousin Maximiliano Antonio de Alvarado, with her brother Manuel Sancho as patron. She revoked freedom letters for her enslaved people (María Dolores, Paula, José Joaquín, Cecilia) due to ingratitude, and left a document with her confessor, José Nicolás Salmón Pacheco, detailing the investment of her assets. Her enslaved woman Micaela Barboza was received as a donation in 1750 from Licenciados Francisco and Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba.

Félix and Juana de Dios Garvanzo sold a cacao hacienda named "La Coronela" in the Matina valley to Don José Nicolás de Chavarría for 2800 pesos cacao. This hacienda was previously owned by their deceased brother, José Antonio Coronel, who acquired it from Presbítero Don Hermenegildo de Arleguí, executor of Licenciado Don José Manuel González Coronel. The payment included funds for a chaplaincy founded by Don Blas González Coronel, cash, and a discount for the buyer, José Nicolás de Chavarría, who accepted the terms with his wife, Doña Eufemia Salmón Pacheco.

Don Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón (son of the deceased Pedro de Alvarado y Jirón and Angela de Guevara Sáenz) made his will. He was married to Doña María Manuela de Baeza, and they had several living children. He also mentioned Doña María Magdalena Maroto, his mother-in-law, and arranged the marriages of his daughters: María Francisca with Don Antonio de la Fuente, and Ana Jacoba with Don Francisco Carazo.

people_involved: Don Juan Manuel de Casasúla y Córdoba
summary: A document lists seven enslaved individuals: Juana Chaves, Eusebia Ulloa and her sons Alejandro and José María, José Manuel Pérez, Juan José Masís, and Isidora Inza. Doña Lucía de Alvarado is mentioned as a sister, and her husband Don Juan Manuel de Casasúla y Córdoba and son-in-law Don Francisco Carazo are named as executors, with her children as heirs.

people_involved: Don José Francisco Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Don José Francisco Alvarado y Jirón, a Beneficiado and local priest, obligated himself for 600 pesos plata at 5% interest. This sum covered 208 cattle, 21 beasts, a small plantain field, and a dilapidated house and corral in Abangares, valued at 500 pesos, plus 100 pesos he voluntarily donated to the Cofradía de los Angeles. The obligation was later cancelled on December 23, 1776, by Don Pedro Aymerich, Mayordomo of the Cofradía.

people_involved: Don José Francisco Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Don Ventura Barraganes and Doña Narcisa de Bonilla obligated themselves for 200 pesos cacao at 5% interest to the Convento de San Francisco in Curriravá, intending to use the sum to build their house. Don José Francisco Alvarado y Jirón later redeemed this obligation. On June 21, 1831, Presbítero Aniceto Chacón, priest of Curridabat, cancelled the capellanía after its transfer to Cura Salvador Matamoros, with Cura Francisco M. Oreamuno, Dolores Suárez, and José Santiago Ramírez signing as witnesses.
Don Alfonso Manuel de Ulloa granted freedom to his 50-year-old enslaved woman, Antonia Brígida Ulloa.

people_involved: Licenciado don Juan José Madriz Linares
summary: Don Gregorio de la Calle and his wife Doña Micaela de Alvarado granted general power of attorney to Licenciado don Juan José Madriz Linares, the priest of Posoltega, specifically to represent them in the estate proceedings of Don Miguel de Alvarado, Doña Micaela's grandfather.

Don José Antonio García and his wife Doña Anta Romualda Ramírez obligated themselves for 400 pesos cacao at 5% interest, secured by a house formerly owned by Presbítero don Gabriel de Cevallos. The sum was allocated to the Cofradía de la Concepción, Nuestra Señora del Rosario, and a Capellanía founded by brothers Pedro and Vasco Solano. On December 7 of the same year, José Durán and Matías Bonilla, free mulatos, cancelled the obligation as it became their responsibility.

Don Antonio de la Fuente, acting as attorney for Don Juan Garau de Cort, sold the 27-year-old enslaved woman María Ramona Guerrero to Don José Joaquín de Nava for 325 pesos plata. The power of attorney was granted in León on February 8 of the same year before notary Benito José Abaunza, stating Don Juan had purchased María Ramona from Don Manuel de Molina.

people_involved: Don Diego de Lava y Fernández
Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno
summary: Don Antonio de la Fuente and his wife Doña María Francisca de Alvarado obligated themselves for 1500 pesos cacao, the price of a house they acquired at auction. This sum was designated for two capellanías: 1200 pesos for one founded by Don Diego de Lava y Fernández and Doña Petronila de Hoyo, and 300 pesos for another founded by Doña Josefa Nicolasa de Guevara, both associated with the Convento de San Francisco. On January 13, 1774, Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno, Síndico of the Convento, cancelled the obligation as Pedro Manuel Salguero assumed responsibility for it.
Doña Manuela de Zavaleta, a widow, granted freedom to her enslaved man Matías Zavaleta, who was born and raised in her household, in exchange for 200 pesos cacao.

people_involved: Doña María Josefa Muñoz de la Trinidad
Doña Dominga Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Don Félix García de Ergueta granted freedom to his enslaved mulato, Juan Marcos Fallas, for 133 pesos 3 reales plata. Don Félix had inherited Juan Marcos as part of his mother's estate, which belonged to Doña María Josefa Muñoz de la Trinidad, the natural daughter of Doña Dominga Muñoz de la Trinidad.

Don Mateo Erdocia, with Don Pedro del Valle and Don José de Torres as guarantors, obligated himself to deliver 400 petacas of tobacco (comprising 400 conservillas and 4 net arrobas) from the upcoming harvest to Don José Antonio Guerrero, the Factor of the Royal Tobacco Monopoly in Granada.
Don Andrés José Fernández and his wife Doña María Trejos obligated themselves for 400 pesos cacao at 5% interest, serving as the principal for a capellanía founded by the deceased Diego de Aguilar.

A house, previously a dwelling, was ordered to be delivered for its demolition, associated with a 100-peso debt. Don Andrés, a Presbyter, and José Fernández, a Chaplain, mortgaged their house, described as twenty varas long, made of adobe and tile, with a walled plot.

people_involved: Guardián del Convento de San Francisco
Don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad
Licenciado don José Francisco de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Don Miguel Antonio Fajardo and Doña Gabriela Sarmiento obligated themselves for a 100-peso silver debt at 5% interest, funding a chaplaincy. This chaplaincy is currently served by the Guardian of the San Francisco Convent until a grandson of Don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad, the appointed chaplain, is ordained. The 100 pesos were redeemed by Licenciado don José Francisco de Alvarado y Jirón, and they mortgaged their house.
Pedro Manuel Ro, husband of Isabel Ramona de Quesada, received a house with its plot, located within the city, from Gabriel de Quesada. This house was given as part of his wife's inheritance.

Joaquín Ortiz and María Francisca Utrera obligated themselves for 100 pesos of cacao at 5% interest, for a chaplaincy founded by Br. don Gregorio de Moya. The same amount was redeemed by Gregorio Calvo, and the heirs of the late Don Justo Francisco de Ibarra are patrons and chaplains of this foundation. They mortgaged a cacao plantation in Barbilla Valley and their house in the city's Puebla.

people_involved: El Alférez José Manuel Guzmán de Ada
B* don José Francisco de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: El Alférez José Manuel Guzmán de Ada and his wife Cecilia de Zúñiga, residents of the city's Puebla, obligated themselves for 266 pesos of cacao at 5% interest. This amount was part of a larger sum redeemed by B* don José Francisco de Alvarado y Jirón, belonging to the Convento de Curriravá. They mortgaged a 3-year-old cacao plantation in Barbilla Valley.

people_involved: Don José Benito Gómez de Altamirano
summary: Don José Benito Gómez de Altamirano, a resident of León, granted power of attorney to Don Joaquín de Alvarado. This power allows Don Joaquín to obligate Don José Benito as a guarantor for amounts received in guardianships belonging to the minor children of the deceased Don Benito de Alvarado and Doña Leonida de Ocampo, who were Don Joaquín's in-laws. Don Joaquín can mortgage a large cattle ranch named San Cristóbal de Tolapa in León, Nicaragua, along with another house and plot in León.

Antonia Micaela Segura, a widow, leased a hacienda with 900 fruit-bearing cacao trees in the Barbilla Valley to Don Gabriel Conejo for three years. The lease agreement stipulated a payment of 100 pesos cacao per year.

Don Gabriel Masís and his wife Doña Margarita Felipa de Iglesias sold a 14-year-old "negrito" named Francisco Masís to Don Francisco Leal, a Knight of the Order of Santiago and Colonel of Militias, for 250 pesos silver. Don Gabriel Masís had inherited Francisco Masís from his parents.
Gregorio Orozco's will states he was married to Juana Salas and had no children. He named Bruno Orozco as his executor and bequeathed two colts to him.

Antonia Trejos's will details that her mother brought a 700-tree hacienda in Matina and 12 mules into her marriage. These assets were subsequently divided equally among her children. Antonia is identified as the legitimate daughter of Matías Trejos and Isabel de Cárdenas.

Juan and José Cosme Portuguez, along with Juan Francisco de Vega (husband of María Leonida Portuguez), who are natural children of María Portuguez, agreed to give Juan Portuguez fifteen heads of cattle. This agreement, stemming from their mother's estate, was made to prevent future disputes, with Juan accepting it as his full maternal inheritance.

people_involved: Presbítero don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí
summary: Miguel Fuentes and Paula Paniagua obligated themselves for 100 pesos of cacao to a chaplaincy founded by doña Eugenia de Abarca, with Presbítero don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí serving as Chaplain. This obligation was previously held by don José Antonio de Oriamuno and doña María Catarina de Ibarra, and they hypothecated a 1500-cacao tree plot in the Valle de Matina.

people_involved: don Manuel Francisco de Orozco y Quesada
summary: Doña María Josefa de Quesada and her legitimate son, don Manuel Francisco de Orozco y Quesada, obligated themselves for 150 pesos of cacao to a chaplaincy founded by the late doña Juana Sagaste. This obligation was originally held by doña Francisca de Angulo, who inherited a 700-cacao tree plot in Barbilla from her uncle, don Antonio de Angulo. The current obligors received 124 existing trees and an additional 12 trees 'defended by doña Mariana Morales' to complete the value, and hypothecated a new plot of over 2000 trees in the same valley.

people_involved: Don Manuel Francisco de Orozco y Quesada
summary: On November 9, don Manuel Francisco de Orozco y Quesada obligated himself for 300 pesos of cacao to a chaplaincy founded by doña Micaela Durán, with Presbítero don Manuel Antonio Sandoval as Chaplain. He received this sum from don José Antonio de Oriamuno, representing the value of a house that belonged to his father, don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno, who was originally responsible for the obligation.
On November 25, don Antonio de la Fuente granted general power of attorney to his wife, doña María Francisca de Alvarado.

On December 7, Matías Bonilla and Manuela Valerino obligated themselves for 100 pesos of cacao to the Cofradía del Rosario and another 100 to the Cofradía de la Concepción. José Durán and María Antonia Marino obligated themselves for 200 pesos of cacao to a chaplaincy previously served by the late Presbítero don Gabriel de Cevallos. Don José Antonio García, who bought the Presbítero's house, paid 400 pesos to clear these obligations. The first couple hypothecated a 700-tree cacao plot in Poza Azul and a 500-tree plot, while the second couple hypothecated 500 fruit-bearing trees in the San Antonio hacienda in Barbilla.

people_involved: Doña Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: On December 14, doña Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo sold her son, don Tomás López del Corral, the San Miguel cacao hacienda, consisting of 4901 trees, which she inherited from her parents. The sale price was 2450 pesos and 4 reales, with two chaplaincy obligations (one founded by don Francisco de Ocampo and Ana Victoria Morera, and another of 100 pesos plata for the chaplaincy served by Presbítero don Cayetano de Arleguí) remaining with the buyer.

people_involved: Don Pedro Tiburcio Machado y Ugarte
summary: On March 21, 1776, don Pedro Tiburcio Machado y Ugarte cancelled a 100 pesos plata obligation related to a chaplaincy served by Presbítero don Cayetano de Arleguí, as this obligation was now his responsibility.

people_involved: Teniente Coronel don José Joaquín de Nava
doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: On December 20, Teniente Coronel don José Joaquín de Nava sold an enslaved woman named Ramona Guerrero and her 6-month-old daughter, Ana Gertrudis, to doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo for 370 pesos plata. Nava had purchased Ramona on April 30 of the same year from don Antonio de la Fuente, who was acting as the agent for don Juan Garau de Cort, and Ana Gertrudis was born in Nava's house.

people_involved: Bachiller don Juan Manuel López del Corral
summary: On December 21, don Tomás López del Corral sold an enslaved mulato man named Pablo Jiménez to Bachiller don Juan Manuel López del Corral, who is the Cura of the villa of Heredia. Tomás had acquired Pablo from doña Ana.
A purchase was made by Jiménez for 240 pesos plata.

Manuel Sancho de Castañeda, Baltasara de la Madriz Linares, Pedro Manuel Salguero, Isabel Ramona de Quesada, José Miguel García, and Antonia Masís granted power of attorney to Tomás López del Corral. This was for him to travel to León, Nicaragua, and bid on the tithes to be collected from Río Grande to the Matina valley.

people_involved: Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Licenciado Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba, acting as executor for the deceased Pedro de Alvarado, founded a chaplaincy for 25 masses. The principal was 1032 pesos plata, representing a fifth of Alvarado's assets, with the Guardian of the San Francisco Convent serving as interim Patron and Chaplain.

people_involved: Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Agustín Masís, a free mulatto from Puebla and natural son of Juana Masís (a former slave of María Masís), made his will. He was married to Josefa Joaquina Valerín, had no children, named Josefa's husband Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba as executor, and his wife Josefa as his heir.

Francisco Carazo and Jacoba de Alvarado, along with María Francisca de Alvarado (wife and attorney of Antonio de la Fuente) and Tomás de Soto y Barahona (as guarantors), obligated themselves for 1032 pesos dinero at 5% interest for the chaplaincy founded by the deceased Pablo de Alvarado. They mortgaged their house, land, and 500 cacao trees in the Matina valley at El Bejuco, among other properties.

people_involved: María de Jesús de la Riva
summary: Miguel López Conejo, legitimate son of Diego Conejo and María de Jesús de la Riva, provided a dowry letter for his wife Ana Micaela Carazo, legitimate daughter of Pedro Carazo and Teresa de Soto y Barahona. The dowry totaled 826 pesos 2 reales, including two enslaved mulatto children, José Joaquín and Francisca de la Encarnación, and 300 pesos plata in arras.

people_involved: Ana Teresa de Soto y Barahona
summary: Francisco Carazo, legitimate son of Pedro Carazo and Ana Teresa de Soto y Barahona, received part of his paternal and maternal inheritance from his mother. This inheritance included two enslaved men, Francisco Solano (approx. 40 years old) and Diego Barahona, along with livestock, silver items, and cash, totaling 654 pesos 1 real plata.

María Francisca de Alvarado, acting for herself and as attorney for her husband Antonio de la Fuente, obligated herself for 516 pesos plata to Francisco Carazo. She mortgaged 4000 cacao trees in the Matina valley at Poza Azul. A marginal note indicates that Francisco Carazo, then Captain of Granaderos, received the payment from Antonio de la Fuente on January 26, 1786.

people_involved: Juan Carlos de Vílchez y Cabrera
summary: Angela de Alvarado y Jirón, a widow, obligated herself for 600 pesos cacao at 5% interest, representing the principal of a long-standing chaplaincy under her charge belonging to the Diocese. This obligation was mandated in favor of Bishop Juan Carlos de Vílchez y Cabrera and was charged against a hacienda with cacao trees she owned in the Barbilla valley.

Francisco de la Riva obligated himself for 107 pesos cacao currency at 5% interest, which was the principal of a chaplaincy founded by the deceased Juan Rafael Ramírez and had been in his possession for a long time. The Guardian of the San Francisco Convent served as the Chaplain, and the chaplaincy was endowed with Francisco de la Riva's house in Puebla.

people_involved: María Josefa de las Mercedes Soto Mayor
Juan Salvador de la Haya y Bolívar
summary: Tiburcio Pedro Machado y Ugarte and his wife María Josefa de las Mercedes Soto Mayor obligated themselves for 1473 pesos plata and 200 pesos cacao, with portions designated for the chaplaincy of Presbyter Juan Salvador de la Haya y Bolívar and the San Francisco Convent. This obligation originated from María Josefa's parents, Isabel Ramona de Utrera and Luis de Soto Mayor, and involved assets including their house, enslaved people, and land in Ujarraz valley. Marginal notes record partial cancellations in 1784 and 1785 by Juan Zeledón de los Reyes and Antonio de la Fuente, involving Pedro Manuel Salguero.

Tiburcio Pedro Machado y Ugarte sold four enslaved individuals to Antonio Cervantes, a resident of Bagaces valley. The enslaved people were Dionisia Utrera (50-year-old mulatta), Juana Utrera (25-year-old mulatta), Rafael Utrera (6-year-old son of Juana), and Petronila Utrera (3 years old), for a total of 650 pesos cacao.

people_involved: Don José Miguel Sancho de Castañeda
B. don Juan José Madriz Linares
summary: Don José Miguel Sancho de Castañeda, a Cleric Presbyter, granted general power of attorney to his uncle, B. don Juan José Madriz Linares. Madriz Linares was the Cura of the town of Posoltega at the time of this legal action.

people_involved: B. don Juan José Madriz Linares
summary: Josefa Guerrero, a widow, and her legitimate son, José Fernando Masís, took on a debt of 500 pesos cacao at 5 ojo interest for the chaplaincy of Patriarch Señor San José. This chaplaincy was founded by Gabriela Ruiz and is currently served by B. don Juan José Madriz Linares. To secure the obligation, Josefa mortgaged her 800-tree cacao hacienda "el Santo Cristo," and José Fernando mortgaged a 1200-tree cacao plantation, both located in the Barbilla valley.

María Josefa de Aguilar, the widow of Juan de Dios Rojas, sold a house made of bahareque and tile, measuring 6 varas long, to her son-in-law, Juan Prado. The property was located in the ejidos of the city and was sold for 75 pesos cacao.

Gabriel de Quesada, as principal, and Pedro Manuel Salguero, as guarantor, obligated themselves to Josefa Jacoba de Rojas. This obligation covered 261 pesos 3 reales cacao from her maternal inheritance, derived from her grandmother Antonia Trejos, and 131 pesos 1 real cacao from her paternal inheritance. Josefa Jacoba is the legitimate daughter of the deceased Juan de Dios Rojas and Josefa de Quesada, and the granddaughter of Gabriel de Quesada.

Francisco Javier Quesada recorded that Pedro Manuel Salguero's guarantee was canceled. Josefa Guerrero provided a new guarantee in his place, with José Raimundo Zamora acting as the public notary for this transaction.

people_involved: B. don Juan Manuel López del Corral
summary: B. don Juan Manuel López del Corral, the Cura of Villa Vieja, sold a mulatto slave named Pablo Jiménez to his brother, don Tomás López del Corral, for 240 pesos plata. Don Juan Manuel had originally purchased Pablo Jiménez from don Tomás on December 21 of the previous year.

people_involved: Doña Luisa de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Doña Luisa de Guzmán y Echavarría, widow of don Miguel de Alvarado, granted freedom to her slave María del Rosario Conejo and all of María del Rosario's legitimate children. She explained that her husband had donated María del Rosario to her with the explicit instruction to free her, and that the children were born into her possession. Doña Luisa, having no forced heirs and being grateful for their good services, chose to emancipate them.

people_involved: doña Juana de Soto y Barahona
don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
R. P. Fray Francisco Cayetano Muñoz
don Félix García Ergueta y Sancho
María del Rosario (slave, mother of Benita)
don Tomás de Soto y Barahona
Capitán don José Romualdo Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Doña Juana de Soto y Barahona made her will, detailing her family and bequests. She was married twice, first to don Dionisio Muñoz, and then to don Manuel José Gómez, having children from both unions. Her will included the emancipation of one slave, María Josefa, and the donation of another, Benita, to her granddaughter doña Felipa Josefa García. She also established a chaplaincy, naming her grandson don Félix García Ergueta as the proprietary chaplain, and designated her children as heirs and Capitán don José Romualdo Muñoz de la Trinidad as executor.

people_involved: Pe. Guardián del Convento de San Francisco
summary: José Simón de Quesada and his wife, María Josefa Castillo, took on an obligation for 300 pesos cacao at 5 ojo interest. This sum represented the principal of a chaplaincy established by doña Rosa de Arburola, for which the Father Guardian of the Convento de San Francisco served as interim chaplain. They received 300 cacao trees in the Matina valley, which formed the basis of the chaplaincy, and additionally mortgaged a 1200-tree plantation in the Barbilla valley.

Don José Antonio de Oriamuno, the Síndico General of the Convento de San Francisco, reported that Simón de Quesada had died. His widow, María Josefa Castillo, subsequently delivered the hacienda, which is now under the management of a different party.

people_involved: doña Juana de Soto y Barahona
summary: Doña Juana de Soto y Barahona issued a codicil to her will, revoking a previous instruction to charge her son, don Manuel José Gómez, for hacienda harvests he administered. She also clarified the disposition of a pasture in Agua Caliente, directing it to don Juan Bonilla, who had already paid part of its value towards her illness expenses. Additionally, she corrected the description of her dwelling house, stating it was made of "horcones y bahareque" rather than "adobes."

Antonia García and her mother, Ana Gómez, sold cacao trees to Alférez José Nicolás Camaño in the Matina valley. Antonia sold 400 trees at 8 reales each, while Ana sold 100 trees at 6 reales each, all located in the area known as La Pontezuela.

people_involved: Don Tiburcio Pedro Machado y Ugarte
Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
summary: Don Tiburcio Pedro Machado y Ugarte sold a 30-year-old mulatto slave named Manuela de Utrera for 225 pesos plata to Capitán don Tomás López del Corral. He also sold Manuela's 6 to 7-year-old mulatto son, Félix Utrera, to the same buyer for 150 pesos plata.

people_involved: Br. don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
doña Mariana de Barros y Muro
summary: Tomás Maroto obligated himself for 136 pesos cacao to a chaplaincy associated with Br. don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba. This debt, previously held by doña Mariana de Barros y Muro, was secured by 136 cacao trees in the Matina valley, which Maroto now manages. These trees are adjacent to an additional 2500 cacao trees that Maroto already oversees for the same chaplain.

people_involved: Doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho de Castañeda
Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho de Castañeda, a widow, sold her slave, José Joaquín Ramos, to Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba for 100 pesos. José Joaquín Ramos was born in her house and is the son of her slave, Micaela Barboza.

people_involved: Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: On July 22nd of the same year, Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba granted freedom to the recently purchased slave, José Joaquín Ramos.

Don Manuel López Espinosa, a notary for the ship "Santa Ursula" (also known as "el Granadero"), acting as attorney for Captain Fabián de la Serna, obligated himself to Don Mateo Erdocia for 217 pesos and 1.5 reales of silver. This amount was owed to Erdocia after an account liquidation, and the ship was anchored in Puntarenas, preparing for a voyage to Acapulco.

people_involved: Presbítero don Juan Salvador de la Haya y Bolívar
summary: Pedro Manuel Salzuero and his wife, Isabel Ramona de Quesada, obligated themselves for 592 pesos of silver at 5% interest. This debt included funds for a chaplaincy founded by Doña Cecilia Vázquez de Coronado, and other sums belonging to the Convent of San Francisco, previously owed by Isidro Castro and from a chaplaincy founded by Pedro Ibáñez. They mortgaged 600 fruit-bearing cacao trees and a three-thousand-tree cacao plantation in the Matina valley.

people_involved: Captain Don Romualdo José Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Captain Don Romualdo José Muñoz de la Trinidad provided bail for Don Mateo Erdocia, who was imprisoned due to an ongoing criminal case.

people_involved: Doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho de Castañeda
summary: Doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho de Castañeda, a widow, granted freedom to her 18-year-old slave, Paula de los Dolores, upon Paula's marriage to José Antonio Sebastián Camaño. The freedom was granted in exchange for 200 pesos of silver, which was her value.

Doña Ana Sancho, a widow, leased a fruit-bearing cacao hacienda named "Las Sesenta Calles," containing 100 trees in the Matina valley, to Matías Umaña for five years. The annual rent was 225 pesos of cacao, and Doña Ana's son, José Antonio García, signed on her behalf.

people_involved: Don Benito de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Don Joaquín de Alvarado and his wife, Doña Rita de Alvarado, obligated themselves for 8945 pesos of cacao to the four minor children of the deceased Don Benito de Alvarado y Jirón and Doña Leonida de Ocampo Golfín, representing their inheritance. They would pay 5% interest only on Don José Antonio's share, as they were responsible for raising and educating the other three. They mortgaged the San Nicolás de las Piedras ranch and their house in Cartago.

people_involved: Don José Benito Gómez de Altamirano
summary: Don Joaquín de Alvarado, acting as special attorney for Don José Benito Gómez de Altamirano, a resident of León, Nicaragua, obligated Gómez de Altamirano as a guarantor. He mortgaged Gómez de Altamirano's San Cristóbal de Tolapa cattle ranch in León's jurisdiction, along with Gómez de Altamirano's house in León. The power of attorney for this was granted in Cartago on July 6th of the previous year.

people_involved: Captain Don José Miguel Ruiz de Molina
Don Pablo de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Additional guarantors, including Don Antonio Cervantes and his wife Doña Josefa Ramírez, Captain Don José Miguel Ruiz de Molina and his wife Simona Delgado, Bruno Chaves and his wife Doña Juana Recio, and Don Pablo de Alvarado y Jirón and his wife Doña María Filiberta Recio, were represented by their attorney Antonio de Avendaño. These individuals, all residents of the Bagaces valley, granted power of attorney for this purpose to Don Cayetano de Alvarado on April 29th and May 1st of the previous year, with testimonies of these powers attached.
Don Cayetano de Avendaño made a substitution related to Don Tomás Hidalgo, Captain of Esparza, as recorded in a protocol on August 14.
On October 20, 1779, Don José Antonio de Alvarado cancelled his part of an obligation, having received payment the previous year.

people_involved: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Don Mateo Erdocia, with Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora and Doña María Francisca Corrales as guarantors, obligated themselves to Captain Don José Romualdo de Oriamuno for 6895 pesos and 2 1/2 reales of silver, which he had lent, to be repaid within 6 months.

people_involved: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora
summary: The obligation involving Don Mateo Erdocia, Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora, Doña María Francisca Corrales, and Don José Romualdo de Oriamuno was cancelled on May 24, 1774.

Doña Efigenia Marina, a widow, sold a house and lot to Don José Miguel Velazco for 500 pesos cacao. The property was bordered by a royal street, a vacant lot of the Meoño family, Doña Mánuela de Alvarado's property, and Elías Valverde's property.

people_involved: Licenciado Don Juan Manuel de Camol y Córdoba
summary: Licenciado Don Juan Manuel de Camol y Córdoba founded a chaplaincy for masses for the souls of the deceased Don Benito de Alvarado and Doña Leonida de Ocampo Golfín. The chaplaincy was endowed with 675 pesos cacao, charged to a cacao plantation in the Matina valley, and Don Juan Manuel was the patron and chaplain, with Don Mariano Iglesias as a successor.

people_involved: Licenciado Don Juan Manuel de Camol y Córdoba
summary: On May 19, 1773, Don Juan Adan cancelled an obligation related to the chaplaincy, having taken charge of it on that date.

people_involved: Licenciado Don Juan Manuel de Camol y Córdoba
Doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo
Don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda
summary: Licenciado Don Juan Manuel de Camol y Córdoba, as Mayordomo, obligated himself for 75 pesos cacao to the Archicofradía del Sacramento and for 150 pesos cacao to the Cofradía del Rosario. These obligations were charged to his hacienda in El Guaitil, with the latter having been redeemed by Don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda and Doña Francisca de la Madriz.

people_involved: Licenciado Don Juan Manuel de Camol y Córdoba
summary: On May 19, 1773, Don Juan Adan declared that both censos (obligations) related to the Archicofradía del Sacramento and Cofradía del Rosario were now his responsibility.

Don Francisco Ramo has a pending lawsuit with Doña María Francisca de Alvarado, representative of Don Antonio de la Fuente, to collect a debt owed to Don José González Robez. Ramo hypothecates various assets to settle accounts with Don Antonio de la Fuente upon his return from Nicaragua.

people_involved: Don Romualdo José Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Don Romualdo José Muñoz de la Trinidad, as Syndic Procurator of the city, leased a pasture named Los Hornos, located in the vicinity of Villa Vieja and belonging to the city, to Don Lora Saborío and Don Pedro Jiménez for 10 years at a price of 2 pesos.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Blas González Coronel
Teniente Coronel Don José Joaquín de Nava
summary: On January 11, 1773, Félix Antonio Jiménez and Magdalena Casasasola obligated themselves for 2200 pesos of cacao for a chaplaincy founded by Sargento Mayor Don Blas González Coronel. They mortgaged a cacao plantation, with Antonio de Arizaga and the Angulo siblings as guarantors. The obligation was previously held by Don José Nicolás Chavarría, and Félix Antonio Jiménez intended to take over the hacienda with Matías Barrantes after his brother Felipe Jiménez's death.

Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla grants power to Captain Don Mauricio de Orozco, perpetual councilman of Nicaragua, and Don Manuel José Gómez, a resident of the same, to obtain his appointment as Regidor and Depositario General before the Royal Audiencia, for which he bid 500 pesos cacao payable over 5 years.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Antº Lacayo de Briones
Presbítero difunto don Juan José Camacho
Br. don Juan José de Pomar
summary: Don Juan Mejías and Doña María Micaela Sáenz, residents of Aserrí, obligate themselves for 250 pesos plata to the Convento de San Francisco, 100 pesos plata to the Curato of the city, 100 pesos plata to a capellanía of Licenciado don José Antº Lacayo de Briones (Cura of Granada), and 100 pesos plata to a capellanía of the deceased Presbítero don Juan José Camacho, currently managed by Presbítero don Bernardo Hidalgo (Cura interino of San José). These sums are received in a hacienda named Santa Ana, with 100 pesos previously redeemed by Don José de Cruz held in deposit by Mejías and his wife.

people_involved: Capitán don Antonio de la Fuente
summary: Antonio Miguel Hernández, son of Pedro Hernández and Agustina Navarro, and widower of María Manuela González, makes his will. He is married to María Josefa Carranza and has several children with her. He names his wife and Captain Don Antonio de la Fuente as albaceas and his children as heirs, also mentioning his responsibility for 500 pesos cacao for the tutelage of a child of Cayetana Cuba.

people_involved: Doña Teresa de Soto y Barahona
summary: Doña Teresa de Soto y Barahona, a widow, grants freedom to her slave, José Mª Barahona, to take effect after her death.

people_involved: Teniente Coronel don Juan Fernandes de Bobadilla
summary: Teniente Coronel don Juan Fernandes de Bobadilla, appointed Governor of the province, grants general power to Don Manuel de Molina, a resident of León, Nicaragua.

people_involved: Teniente Coronel don Juan Fernández de Bobadilla
Capitán don Juan Fermín de Ayzinena
summary: Teniente Coronel don Juan Fernández de Bobadilla grants power to Captain Don Juan Fermín de Ayzinena, a resident of Guatemala, to obtain the validation of his title as Governor of the province before the Royal Audiencia and to be placed in possession of the office, also granting him general judicial power.

people_involved: Teniente Coronel don Juan Fernández de Bobadilla
Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
Don Bartolomé de Miranda y Casasola
Don Pedro Tiburcio Machado y Ugarte
summary: Teniente Coronel don Juan Fernández de Bobadilla names several individuals, including Captain Don Tomás López del Corral and Don Pedro José Corrales, as fiadores (guarantors) for his residency, with each person responsible for 250 pesos plata.
José Francisco Flores obligates himself for 500 pesos cacao at 5% interest to a capellanía founded by Don Baltasar de Grados, secured by 300 cacao trees in the Barbilla valley.

people_involved: Doña Baltasara de Escalante y Paniagua
Licenciado don José Alejandro Escalante y Paniagua
summary: Francisco Antonio Meneses obligates himself for 1165 pesos cacao at 5% interest to a capellanía founded by the deceased Doña Baltasara de Escalante y Paniagua, whose chaplain is Licenciado don José Alejandro Escalante y Paniagua, and for 300 pesos cacao at 5% interest to the Cofradía de la Concepción, secured by a cacao hacienda and a 1600-tree cacao plantation in Barbilla.

Doña María Francisca Corrales, widow of Don Joaquín de Alvarado, obligates herself for 528.5 pesos cacao at 5% interest and 190 pesos plata principal for a capellanía belonging to the Convento de San Francisco, which José Espinosa delivered to her deceased husband as a redemption, with the principal originally under the charge of Juan Carmona, hypothecating her cacao haciendas in Matina.

people_involved: Doña Luisa de Guzmán y Echavarría
Doña Antonia de Guzmán y Echavarría
Doña Dominga de Guzmán y Echavarría
Br. don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
Capitán don Antonio de la Fuente
Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Ca
summary: Doña Luisa de Guzmán y Echavarría, daughter of deceased Don José de Guzmán and Doña Antonia de Echavarría Navarro, and widow of Don Miguel de Alvarado, makes her will. She frees her slave Fermín Oriamuno after her death and mentions having already freed Meal del Rosario and his children. She also details the inheritance of a house with her sisters, Antonia and Dominga, from their deceased brother José Miguel, which is to fund a capellanía, and names several families as potential chaplains.

people_involved: Doña María Josefa Marín y Laguna
Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
Doña Francisca de Ibarra y Calvo
Don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda
Doña Francisca de la Madriz Linares
summary: Don Juan de Piedra Adan and Doña María Josefa Marín y Laguna purchased Hacienda Guattil in the Barbilla valley from Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba for 3825 pesos of cacao. Payments were directed to the seller, various confraternities, and chaplaincies for Doña Leonida de Ocampo, Don Benito de Alvarado, and Doña Agueda Pérez de Muro. The buyers mortgaged two cacao plantations in Barbilla and El Agua Fría.

Doña Manuela de Zavaleta, a widow, leased her cacao plantation named Za Catalana in the Matina valley to Juan Laureano Duarte, a free mulatto. The lease was for six years at a price of 92 pesos cacao per year.

people_involved: Don Juan Fernández de Bobadilla y Grandi
summary: Don Tomás López del Corral and Pedro Manuel Salguero provided a bond for Don Juan Fernández de Bobadilla y Grandi, who was appointed Governor and Lieutenant Captain General of the province. This bond covered the branches of tributes, cruzada, and the court of intestates, supplementing a previous bond from February 25th of the same year.

people_involved: Tte. don Agustín López de Ortega
summary: The final part of a dowry letter was granted by Carlos Ambrosio del Arca to his wife, Doña Isabel López de Ortega, for 1834 pesos with 500 pesos arras. The goods were received from Tte. don Agustín López de Ortega, with a 100 peso debt remaining. Domingo de Otálora and Capitán Bartolomé Muñoz Hidalgo appraised the goods, while Capitán Francisco Ramírez, Agustin Guerrero, and Mateo Niño served as witnesses.

people_involved: Teniente don Agustín López de Ortega
summary: A dowry letter was granted by Alférez Ignacio de Artavia, son of the late Ignacio de Artavia and Doña Catalina de la Jara, to his future wife, Doña María López de Ortega, daughter of the late Ayudante Domingo López de Ortega and Doña Antonia de Córdoba. The dowry totaled 1317 pesos with 500 pesos arras, in anticipation of their marriage the following day. Capitán Francisco Ramírez and Ayudante Francisco Sáenz de Espinosa were appraisers, and Carlos Ambrosio del Arca, Teniente don Agustín López de Ortega, and Licenciado Judas de Rivera Morillo were witnesses.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan de Echavarría Navarro
summary: Doña María Vázquez de Coronado, widow of Capitán Jerónimo de Retes, made her will, naming her four daughters as heirs and detailing their marriages. She freed four indigenous servants (Lucas, Pascual, Domingo, Pedro) and left a legacy to María Vázquez. Her estate included assets in the Ujarrás valley, and her executors were Capitán don Juan de Echavarría Navarro, Domingo de Otálora, and Capitán don José de Alvarado.

Don Pedro José Corrales and Doña María Fernández Martínez, a childless couple, made their will. Their assets included a 15-year-old mulatto boy named Juan José, purchased from Don Juan Mejía y Alvarado and Doña Micaela Sáenz. They stipulated that their house, currently in sale negotiations with José Miguel García, should be sold to him if they died before the transaction. Their executors included the surviving spouse, Don José Antonio Jiménez, and Don Manuel Felipe de Arleguí.

Pedro Manuel Salguero and his wife Isabel Ramona de Quesada obligated themselves for 1900 pesos of cacao at 5% interest to the Convento de San Francisco. This sum included funds from chaplaincies founded by Don Diego de Laya Fernández and Doña Petronila de Hoyo, and Doña Josefa Nicolasa de Guevaia, which were previously secured by a house on the city plaza bought by Don Antonio de la Fuente. The remaining 400 pesos also passed to Don Antonio.

Obligations previously managed by the deceased Benito Casasola are now guaranteed by Don Antonio. Two cocoa plantations with 1400 trees and a 5-year-old clearing of 1300 trees in the Matina Valley are mortgaged as security for these obligations.

Escribano Lombardo issued a testimony of a deed, by order of the Governor. This testimony was to be added to a lawsuit between the Syndic of the Convent and Doña María Francisca de Alvarado, who is the widow of Don Antonio de la Fuente.

Don Antonio Pao obligated himself to Don Antonio de la Fuente for 2000 pesos, which he received in Castilian goods to sell. He is to return any unsold goods at the original price and pay for sold goods in tobacco bundles by the following May.

Fernando Masis and Josefa Guerrero, a widow, obligated themselves for 466 pesos, with portions owed to Don Juan Romero and Don Miguel de Echavarría. The debt to Echavarría covered expenses for collecting 1000 pesos Masis owed in Matina. They mortgaged property in Matina and José Miguel García acted as surety, while Juan Pablo Morales signed for Josefa Guerrero after José Antonio de Alvarado notified her of the order.

Don Tomás López del Corral and Don Julián de Azofeifa presented a document to the Governor, withdrawing a criminal complaint filed by López del Corral against Azofeifa. The complaint aimed to vindicate López del Corral's credit from denigrations made by Azofeifa before the Tithe Judge. The Governor ordered the proceedings to be annulled and the transaction recorded.
Luisa Chaves, a widow, sold an 11-year-old enslaved mulata named Luisa to Don Félix García for 200 silver pesos. The enslaved girl was part of Luisa Chaves' inheritance from her parents.

people_involved: Doña María Josefa de la Cruz
summary: Doña Manuela de Zavaleta, a widow, donated several enslaved mulatto children to her heirs. These included José Dolores (4), María Josefa, and José Calixto (6), all children of María Manuela, to her children Don Francisco, Doña Dominga, and Doña Antonia Josefa Jinesta. She also donated Juana Antonia (12), daughter of Magdalena, to Doña Gertrudis de Zavaleta, and José Benito (19 months), son of María Manuela, to her granddaughter Doña María Josefa de la Cruz. Her children agreed to the last donation as heirs.

people_involved: Presbítero Don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí
Doña Ana Engracia de Hoces Navarro
summary: The heirs of Doña Ana Engracia de Hoces Navarro, including several Arleguí siblings and their relatives, declared that they had extrajudicially distributed her assets. They committed to proportionally satisfy any legacies if her lost will were to reappear.
Doña Lucía de Alvarado, a widow, sold an enslaved mulata named María de los Dolores, approximately 22 years old, to Manuel Carranza for 250 silver pesos.

Don Nicolás de Ulloa, with Don Miguel de Echavarría and Don Juan José de Ulloa as sureties, obligated himself for 280 pesos and 5 reales in cacao currency. This debt stemmed from his accounts as Mayordomo de propios between 1771 and 1773, and also for any uncollected ejido funds.

Don José Antonio Jiménez, Mayordomo de propios, confirmed receiving 280 pesos and 5 reales from Don Nicolás de Ulloa at the slaughterhouse built by Ulloa for the city. Additionally, he received 75 pesos and 2 reales in cacao, which was an outstanding amount, thereby cancelling the debt.
Juan Miguel Rodríguez and his wife, Leonida de la Trinidad Casasola, sold a cocoa plantation with 275 fruit-bearing trees in the Barbilla Valley to Pedro Manuel Salguero for 275 pesos in cacao.

people_involved: Don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda
Presbítero Don José Miguel Sancho de Castañeda
Ex-Gobernador Don José Joaquín de Nava
summary: Don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda provided surety for his son, Presbítero Don José Miguel Sancho de Castañeda, who was the Sacristán Mayor. This surety was for a lawsuit established against the former Governor Don José Joaquín de Nava.

A dowry letter was issued by Don Juan Fernández, a native of Spain, in favor of his wife, María Antonia Carranza. The dowry amounted to 448 pesos and 6 reales in silver, with an additional 200 pesos as arras.

people_involved: Beneficiado Don Juan Francisco de Ibarra
summary: Doña Joaquina López del Corral, widow of Don Esteban Ruiz de Mendoza, obligated herself for a debt of 530 pesos and 4 reales owed to Don Antonio Cayetano de Noguera. She had received her deceased husband's assets with the responsibility to acknowledge his debts, and 450 pesos of the original 980 pesos and 4 reales debt had already been paid.
Don Gregorio Ramírez provided surety for Don Francisco Ramo, who was imprisoned for an unspecified cause.
José Miguel García posted bail for don Cecilio Romero, who was imprisoned due to a debt claimed by don Juan Adan. The case was being heard before the Government Court.

José Felipe González took responsibility for 400 pesos of cacao, which was the principal of a chaplaincy belonging to the Cofradía de las Animas. This debt was previously managed by his deceased mother, doña Quiteria Delgado, and was secured by a hacienda with 730 cacao trees in the Barbilla valley.

people_involved: doña Luisa de Guzmán y Echavarría
doña Dominga de Guzmán y Echavarría
doña Antonia de Guzmán y Echavarría
Capitán don Antonio de la Fuente
Licenciado don José Guzmán y Echavarría
Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Doña Luisa, doña Dominga, and doña Antonia de Guzmán y Echavarría, sisters, sold a house to Captain don Antonio de la Fuente for 712 pesos 4 reales cacao in cash. An additional 487 pesos 4 reales cacao was to be recognized as the principal of a chaplaincy for the soul of their deceased brother, Licenciado don José Guzmán y Echavarría, a former Cura of this city.

people_involved: don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
B* don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba acknowledged receiving 100 pesos silver from doña María Francisca de Alvarado, wife of don Antonio de la Fuente, to cover a debt owed by B* don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría to don Juan María Sáenz, a minor. This payment resulted in a reduction of 150 pesos of cacao from a previous obligation, along with additional deductions for ecclesiastical costs and certification from a 1762 protocol handled by don Romualdo Trinidad.

people_involved: doña María Francisca López del Corral
summary: Francisco del Castillo and his wife Rosa Rivas obligated themselves for 525 pesos in cacao currency at 5% interest, for various chaplaincies including those founded by don Pedro Ibáñez, and don José de Alvarado and doña Francisca Bonilla. These funds were previously managed by doña María Francisca López del Corral, and they mortgaged their cacao hacienda named 'Pocino' in the Matina valley.

people_involved: doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora, don Tomás López del Corral, and José Miguel García posted bail for don Mateo Erdocia, who was involved in a lawsuit initiated by don Bernardo la Cuadra for unpaid salaries from a clothing store. The case was being heard by don José Nicolás Zamora in Villa Nueva, and don Mateo Erdocia was preparing to depart for Panamá.

Don Benito Portela, a resident of Darién, sold a canoe named 'San José' to don Mateo Erdocia for 600 pesos silver in cash. The sale included the condition that Erdocia would pay the sailors' wages from the day the canoe anchored in Puntarenas until the current date.

people_involved: Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
B* don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Licenciado don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba, as the heir of the deceased B* don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría, a former Cura, founded a chaplaincy for recited masses as per the latter's will. The principal of 457 pesos 4 reales cacao was secured by the deceased's former residence, with the Licenciado designated as the Patron and Chaplain.

people_involved: doña Josefa Muñoz de la Trinidad
don José Franc? Santos de Troya
summary: Don Luis Arnesto de Troya and his wife doña Josefa Muñoz de la Trinidad obligated themselves for 500 pesos silver to don José Franc? Santos de Troya, a child aged 7-8 years in their care, as a form of guardianship. They committed to raising, sustaining, clothing, and educating the minor, mortgaging their dwelling house adjacent to the city plaza.

people_involved: doña Josefa Joaquina López del Corral
Sargt? Mayor don José Ant? de Oriamuno
summary: Doña Josefa Joaquina López del Corral, a widow, sold two cacao plantations on the banks of the Matina to Sergeant Major don José Ant? de Oriamuno for 256 pesos silver. These plantations, one with 871 fruit-bearing trees and another with 625, were inherited from her mother, doña Francisca de Ibarra.

people_involved: doña Antonia de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Doña Antonia de Guzmán y Echavarría, having inherited a mulata named Andrea Susana from her mother, acknowledged that Andrea Susana had five children in her possession: Juan Pablo del Rosario, Francisco Antonio, María Manuela, Ana Efigenia, and Manuela Josefa, whom she had raised. The text implies a declaration or transaction regarding their status, but the full details are cut off.

Don Juan Mejía, a resident of Villa Nao, provided a jail bond for his stepson, Don Gregorio Castro. Don Gregorio Castro was imprisoned along with Don Francisco Ramo for a cause related to tobacco smuggling.

people_involved: Don Pedro Antonio de la Puente
Capitán don Antonio de la Fuente
summary: Don Pedro Antonio de la Puente formally granted general power of attorney to Captain Don Antonio de la Fuente.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
Doña Franca de Ibarra y Calvo
Capitán don José Romualdo de Oriamuno
summary: Doña Josefa Joaquina del Corral executed her will, detailing her marital history, lack of children with her husbands, and provisions for her slaves Juana María (and her son Pedro Alcántara), Manuel Antonio, and José Domingo to be freed. She also mentioned properties, debts, and named her mother as initial heir and Capitán don José Romualdo de Oriamuno as executor.

people_involved: Doña Franca de Ibarra y Calvo
Capitán don José Romualdo de Oriamuno
summary: Doña Josefa Joaquina del Corral added a codicil to her will, clarifying that the freedom of her slaves would be funded from one-fifth of her assets. She revoked the clause leaving her house to her mother and, having remembered her natural son, Juan José (aged about 28), she instituted him as her universal heir, instructing her executor to diligently seek him out.

Don Joaquín de Alvarado, a resident of León, and his wife Doña Rita de Alvarado, obligated themselves to pay 120 pesos plata to the four minor children of the deceased Don Benito de Alvarado and Doña Leonida de Ocampo Golfín, who were also the parents of Don Joaquín and Doña Rita.

Don José Antonio de Alvarado cancelled his portion of the 120-peso obligation. This cancellation was recorded before Don Antonio de la Fuente, who was then Alférez Real, Regidor, and Alcalde ordinario de 1er. voto.
Don Juan de Alvarado, acting for himself and his brother Don Isidro, cancelled their portions of the obligation. This transaction took place before Gobernador Acosta.
Don Antonio de la Fuente provided a jail bond for Don Bernardo de la Cuadra, who was imprisoned for a criminal cause.
Don Bernardo de la Cuadra, a native of Spain, granted general power of attorney for lawsuits to Don Antonio de la Fuente.

José Miguel Portugués made his will, identifying himself as the natural son of the deceased María Dionisia Portugués, widower of Juana de Quesada (with whom he had a daughter, María del Carmen), and current husband of Isabel María Fuentes (with whom he had four children). He named his sister María Josefa Portugués and his son-in-law Gregorio Brenes, and appointed Miguel Fuentes as his executor.

people_involved: Doña María Francisca López del Corral
summary: Don Pedro Aymerich, originally from Burdiles, Cataluña, executed his will. He was married to Doña María Francisca López del Corral, who was the widow of a different Don Joaquín de Alvarado, and they had a 7-month-old daughter. His assets included the 'La Sancho' hacienda, and he had debts in Matina, which his slave Toribio Gudiño was instructed to pay. He also mentioned a purchase on credit from Don Benito Portela.

people_involved: Capitán Romualdo José Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: An enslaved person named Antonio was valued at 120 pesos. Don Benito, who is traveling to Panama, will write to Antonio regarding his financial interests. Antonio's parents died in Lurdzlz, where his inheritance is located, and he mandates its collection. His wife and Capitán Romualdo José Muñoz de la Trinidad are named as his executors, and his daughter is his heir.
Don Antonio de la Fuente sold a 34-year-old mulata named Rosa Pacheco to Manuel Carranza for 225 silver pesos. Rosa Pacheco had previously been acquired by Don Antonio from Don Cayetano Pacheco.

people_involved: El Bachiller Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo
summary: El Bachiller Juan Francisco de Ibarra y Calvo, a priest from Nicaragua residing locally, leased his hacienda 'la Ibarrita' in the Matina valley to Tomás Arburola and his wife Antonia Josefa Quirós for three years. The hacienda contained 2800 fruit-bearing cacao trees, and the lease required 100 pesos cacao annually, with Arburola also obligated to plant and cultivate an additional 2000 cacao trees.

Juan Miguel Gutiérrez obligated himself for 100 silver pesos at 5% interest to the Cofradía de la Concepción. This sum had been redeemed by Fermín León and was originally charged to Don Juan de Ocampo. Don José Antonio de Oriamuno, Mayordomo of the Cofradía, mortgaged a sugarcane plantation with its sugar mill and kettles as security.

people_involved: Doña Ana Rita Gómez de Lara
Guardián del Convento de San Francisco
summary: Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla and his wife Doña Ana Rita Gómez de Lara, who acquired the former house of Presbítero Manuel Francisco Cubero for 600 pesos cacao, recognized their debts. They owed 100 pesos to the Cofradía del Rosario, 200 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Don Domingo Chavarría (whose chaplain is Presbítero Francisco Antonio Robredo), and 300 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Pedro Ibáñez (recited by the Guardian of the Convent of San Francisco), pledging 5% interest and mortgaging the house.

On January 17, 1772, the Gobernador stated that ecclesiastical proceedings confirmed the chaplaincy founded by Don Domingo Chavarría was 300 pesos, and the one founded by Pedro Ibáñez was 200 pesos. Presbítero Francisco Antonio Robredo requested this rectification.

people_involved: Don Tomás de Soto Barahona's brother
summary: Don Tomás de Soto Barahona leased a cacao plantation in the Matina valley and another named Zeresifa, belonging to his brother, to Simón Barboza, a free mulato from Villa Nueva, for six years. The lease price was 150 pesos cacao for the first year and 200 pesos cacao for subsequent years.

Don José Antonio de Oriamuno granted power of attorney to Don Isidro Guerrero, a resident of León, to bid on the tithes of the province of Cartago according to instructions sent by letter. This power also included general authority for lawsuits.
Don José Romualdo de Oriamuno and Don Manuel Antonio Jiménez guaranteed Don José Antonio de Oriamuno for the value of the tithes of the province of Cartago that would be auctioned to him.

Don José Antonio de Oriamuno and Don Julián de Azofeifa declared their agreement to jointly acquire the tithes of the province of Cartago by bidding in León. They committed to forming a company for its administration, sharing profits and losses, and equally participating in any litigation for collection, with no payments made from products until the auction price is satisfied.

Don Antonio de la Fuente, Don Tomás López del Corral, and Gabriel de Quesada guaranteed Pedro Manuel Salguero for the value of the tithes he intended to bid on. These tithes covered the area from the mouth of Monte del Aguacate to the Matina valley.

people_involved: Doña Ana Rita Gómez de Lara
summary: Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla and his wife Doña Ana Rita Gómez de Lara guaranteed Don Julián de Azofeifa for the price at which the tithes of the province of Cartago, for which he intends to bid, would be auctioned to him.

people_involved: Doña María Francisca López del Corral
summary: Don Pedro Aymerich and his wife Doña María Francisca López del Corral attempted to sell a cacao plantation of 930 trees in the Matina valley to Don Tomás Corral for 456 pesos 2 reales cacao. The plantation bordered properties of Doña Manuela Pastora, Doña Joaquina Corral, and the former property of Don Nicolás Robredo, with the Chirripu river to the west. The sale did not go through.

Ramona Carranza, legitimate daughter of the deceased José Antonio Carranza and María Nicolasa Morales, made her testament. She was the widow of José Joaquín Guzmán, with whom she had one surviving daughter, Manuela Josefa (around 14 years old), and the second widow of Francisco Fonseca, who died intestate in Nicaragua, with whom she had two surviving sons, José Andrés and Juan Andrés. She named her brother Juan Carranza as guardian for her children and Antonio de Avendaño as executor.

people_involved: Doña María Francisca López del Corral
summary: Don Pedro Aymerich and his wife Doña María Francisca López del Corral began a sale to the Teniente Coronel.

Francisco Antonio Barrantes and José Miguel García (principal and guarantor) commit to pay 49 pesos 1.5 reales to José Gabriel and María de los Dolores, minor children of Francisco Fajardo, as their inheritance. José Miguel García mortgages a 700-tree cacao plantation in Matina. Additionally, they commit to pay 22 pesos 4 reales for a mule and 10 pesos paid by don José Antonio de Oriamuno for a cloak bought at auction.

Don Juan Dionisio, doña Estéfana, doña Antonia Pacheco, don Fermín Mondragón (husband of doña Luz Pacheco), and don Nicolás Cleto de Chavarría (husband of doña Eufemia Pacheco) lease a 2604-cacao tree hacienda in Matina to Miguel Badilla for 7 years. The annual rent is 270 pesos 3.5 reales in cacao. The ownership of the trees is specified among the lessors, and the value of a house, an axe, a canoe, and two machetes is included in the tree count.

people_involved: Don Romualdo José Muñoz de la Trinidad
doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora
don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdaba
summary: Don Romualdo José Muñoz de la Trinidad and his wife doña Tomasa Gómez de Lara commit to pay 100 pesos (at 5% interest) to the Cofradía del Rosario. This debt was previously held by doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora, from whom they received the funds. They mortgage their dwelling house, and don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdaba is the Mayordomo of the Cofradía.
Don Julián de Azofeifa grants general power of attorney to don José Antonio de Oriamuno.

Ramón Bautista, a resident of Villa Vieja de San José, commits to doña María Manuela Miranda for 600 pesos (in cacao and silver) and seven mules she lent him to exploit his work on a shared basis. He mortgages his house on the main street of the villa, a pasture with cattle and horses, and a silversmith's workshop with materials.
Don José Joaquín de Nava grants power of attorney, first to don José Esteban Pérez, a merchant from Guatemala, and second to don Francisco Ortiz, a Procurador of the Real Audiencia.

people_involved: don Romualdo José Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Don José Antonio de Oriamuno, don Romualdo de Oriamuno, don Romualdo José Muñoz de la Trinidad, don José Antonio Jiménez, and don Juan Miguel López Coneo grant power to don Juan Fermín de Alicinera, a resident of Guatemala, to petition the Superior Government of the Kingdom. The goal is to obtain for the grantors the positions of Alférez Real, Alcalde Provincia, Alguacil Mayor, Regidor Fiel Ejecutor, and Depositario General, respectively, which they have agreed to hold before the Governor of this province.

people_involved: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora acts as guarantor for Pedro Manuel Salguero for the amount at which he will be awarded the administration of the tithes of this province for three years. She mortgages her dwelling house in Cartago, 7000 cacao trees in the Matina valley, and 5 enslaved persons.

people_involved: Doña Rosa de la Madriz Linares
summary: Doña Rosa de la Madriz Linares, acting for herself and as attorney for her husband don Tomás López del Corral, guarantees Pedro Manuel Salguero for the price of the auction of the tithes of Cartago, Matina valley, Villa Nueva, and Villa Vieja. She mortgages 12000 fruit-bearing cacao trees in the Matina Valley. An attached power of attorney from don Tomás to his wife, dated Feb 17 in Matina before don José Miguel Velazco (Lieutenant Governor), states that a new obligation was required due to the previous one not specifying the mortgage.

Don Antonio de la Fuente and his wife doña María Francisca de Alvarado guarantee Pedro Manuel Salguero for the value of the auction of the tithes of Cartago, Matina valley, Villa Nueva, and Villa Vieja. They mortgage two houses in Cartago: one on the corner of the main plaza and another on the west side of the main street.

people_involved: don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda
summary: Don Antonio de la Fuente and his wife doña María Francisca de Alvarado (debtors), along with don José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda, don José Antonio García, and doña Lucía de Alvarado (guarantors), commit to don Félix Francisco Bejarano for 6873 pesos 6 reales. This is for the purchase of 1005 pounds of purple thread from don José Medina, representing Bejarano, to be paid in March, including 100 mules (half female, half male, no breeding stallions) valued at 18 pesos each.

Don Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla replaces doña Lucía de Alvarado as guarantor for don Antonio de la Fuente and his wife, in favor of don Félix Francisco Bejarano, for the amount stemming from the previous negotiation.

Bejarano granted a power of attorney to Juan Manuel Caballero to collect a debt from Antonio de la Fuente and his wife. On January 18, 1777, Juan Manuel Caballero fully canceled this obligation using the aforementioned power.

people_involved: José Juaquín de Nava y Cabezudo
summary: José Juaquín de Nava y Cabezudo, before returning to Spain, made a significant donation to Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral and her three daughters: Francisca Leonarda de Jesús, María Catarina, and Manuela Petronila. The donation included two houses, a wheat mill, a pasture, household items, two enslaved mulatto girls (Petronila Josefa and Manuela), and two cacao haciendas. Joaquina Tomasa retains lifetime usufruct of the properties, and the daughters can choose whether to collect education expenses from José Miguel de Ocaña, Joaquina's son, incurred in Guatemala.

Angela de Alvarado leased a cacao hacienda in the Barbilla valley to Francisco de Jesús Chavarría for five years. The first year's payment is ten zurrones of cacao, each worth 25 pesos, to be delivered in Cartago or Matina, with subsequent payments following custom.

Pedro Manuel Salguero granted power of attorney to Luis Bravo, from León, to pursue an adultery accusation against Presbyter José Manuel Sancho de Castañeda. The case file is currently in Guatemala due to an appeal filed by Castañeda.

Brunou Chaves, a resident of Bagaces, granted power of attorney to José Joaquín Paniagua of Cartago. Paniagua is tasked with requesting the cancellation of a bond given to Joaquín de Alvarado for the lease of assets inherited by the minor children of the deceased Benito de Alvarado and Leonida de Ocampo.

Fray Hermenegildo Rodríguez, a Franciscan and the priest of Tucurrique, granted power of attorney to José Mansarraga, the Syndic of the Franciscan Order. Mansarraga is authorized to collect the synod due to Fray Hermenegildo for his administration of the curacy.

Antonio de la Fuente, acting with power from Manuela Josefa de Ibarra (substituted by Diego José de Cuende), sold two cacao haciendas in the Matina valley to Luis Demetrio Coronado, a Minorite Cleric from Heredia. The haciendas, one named Sarmiento and another contiguous one, were sold for 1400 pesos, which the original owner received.
Luis Demetrio Coronado leased the aforementioned cacao haciendas to Pablo José Cubero for a term of seven years. The annual rent is 189 pesos in cacao, to be delivered in Cartago.
Cayetana Sandoval leased a cacao hacienda in the Barbilla valley to Manuel José Guzmán for three years, at an annual rent of 100 pesos.
On April 4, 1787, Cayetana Sandoval canceled the previous lease obligation, paying 300 pesos.
Don Nicolás de Ulloa sold a small farm (chácara) located in the common lands of Cartago to José Miguel García for 150 pesos in cacao.
Fray Mariano Benítez granted power of attorney to Don José Mansarraga to collect the stipend (Sínodo) due to him as the parish priest (Cura doctrinero) of the town of San Bartolomé de Barba.

Don Pedro Nicolás Fernández sold various assets, including 15 mules, 2 houses, a sugar mill, land with sugarcane and plantains, and 2 yokes of oxen, to Don Francisco Aguilar y Santos for 35 sacks of cacao, each valued at 25 pesos, to be delivered in Cartago within one year.
Don Pedro Nicolás Fernández and Don Francisco Aguilar y Santos rescinded their previous sale agreement, rendering the deed invalid.

Pablo Cubero accepted the role of guardian for his four minor siblings (María, Ana, Vicente, and Dionisio) and the administration of their inheritance from their mother, Juana Cubero, totaling 760 pesos 5 1/2 reales. He mortgaged a cacao plantation in Matina Valley and his mother's former house in Cartago, with Don Francisco Aguilar y Santos acting as guarantor.

Don Miguel Fuentes and his wife, Paula Paniagua, committed to pay 247 pesos 5 reales in cacao to the minor heirs María de las Nieves, José de la Concepción, and José Miguel Dionisio, children of the deceased José Miguel Zamora (also known as Portugués). This payment is to complete the purchase of a cacao plantation from Zamora, to be given to the heirs upon reaching adulthood, with specific interest terms after the first five years.

people_involved: Presbítero Don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí
summary: Presbítero Don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí granted power to his brothers Antonio Elías and Manuel Felipe to make his will. He declared his five siblings (Antonio Elías, Manuel Felipe, Francisco, Micaela, and Juan) as heirs, immediately donating one-third of his estate to Antonio Elías, with the remaining two-thirds to be distributed among his other siblings after his death. Manuel Felipe and Antonio Elías were named executors.

Don Gregorio de la Calle and his wife, Doña Micaela de Alvarado, guaranteed a 500-peso debt to the Royal Treasury for Don Juan Mejía, who had been awarded the positions of Regidor and Fiel Ejecutor. They mortgaged a house in Cartago and a cacao farm in Matina Valley as collateral.
Blas José de Jesús, a master carpenter, took Matías Méndez, a 15-year-old boy, under his care with the obligation to teach him the carpentry trade for five years.

A codicil to the will of Don José Antonio de Oriamuno and Doña María Catarina de Ibarra made several provisions, including exempting their son Don José Francisco from responsibility for asset administration, appointing Don José Romualdo as guardian for Don José Francisco's minor children due to his mental state, and annulling the clause leaving the enslaved mulatto boy José Manuel to their grandson Juan José.

Don Antonio de la Fuente sold a cacao plantation in Matina Valley to José Miguel García for 473 pesos 2 1/2 reales. This plantation was originally purchased by Don Antonio at a public auction of Doña Joaquina López del Corral's assets. Don Antonio also transferred the 275-peso encumbrance from two chaplaincies on the plantation to his own residence.

people_involved: Don Romualdo Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: José Miguel García sold a mulatto boy named Francisco Ocaña to Don Romualdo Muñoz de la Trinidad for 200 pesos in silver. José Miguel García had previously purchased this enslaved person on August 5th.

Don José Antonio de Oriamuno and Doña María Catarina de Ibarra established a chaplaincy for recited masses with 1600 pesos, representing a fifth of their assets, secured by a cacao hacienda in the Matina valley at La Pontezuela. Their grandson, Don Juan José, was named the proprietary chaplain, with provisions for his brothers or descendants if he didn't take orders, and Don José Romualdo de Oriamuno as the patron.

people_involved: Don Juan Manuel López del Corral
Don Antonio de Avendaño y Aguilar
summary: Don Juan Manuel López del Corral, the priest of Villa Vieja, granted power of attorney to Don Antonio de Avendaño y Aguilar.

Don Francisco de Arleguí's will details his family, including his deceased wife Doña Bárbara Madriz Linares and their five children. It mentions his wife's cattle in Miravalles, a cacao plantation in Barbilla valley leased by Don Gregorio Lacalle, and a house in the city donated by his brother Don Manuel Felipe de Arleguí to his children. He named his five children as heirs and appointed Don Antonio Elías and Don Manuel Felipe de Arleguí as executors and guardians.

On August 19, Fray José de Villa Nueva granted power of attorney to Don José Manzarraga to collect the Synod due to him as the former doctrinal priest of Ujarraz, covering the period from January 1st to June 7th of the current year.

On August 22, Don Antonio de la Fuente committed to pay 150 pesos to the Confraternity of the Sacrament of Villa Vieja and 125 pesos in cacao to the Chaplaincy founded by Doña Catarina de Arburola, mortgaging his house in the city as security.

people_involved: Doña Isabel Ramona de Utrera y Medina
summary: Doña Isabel Ramona de Utrera y Medina's will identifies her as the widow of Don Luis de Soto Mayor, originally from Lima, with whom she had four children. The first two daughters died young, and María Mercedes is married to Don Pedro Tiburcio Machado. She also mentions two elderly, uninventoried slaves, Pablo and Antonio, and names her son José Antonio Soto Mayor and son-in-law Don Pedro Tiburcio Machado as executors.

people_involved: Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral
summary: On August 23, Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral granted power of attorney to Don Tomás López del Corral to make her will. She declared her two sons, Don José Miguel de Ocaña and Don José Francisco Corona, as heirs, and appointed Don Pedro Aymerich and Don José Antonio Jiménez as executors.
On August 20, Don Pablo Mora, from the city of Granada, granted power of attorney to Don Gabriel Espinoza.
On August 27, Don Gregorio Lacalle granted general power of attorney to his wife, Doña Micaela de Alvarado.

On August 29, Fray Francisco Muñoz, Fray Antonio del Valle, Fray Juan Guerrero, Fray Pablo Chacón, and Fray Eugenio del Valle jointly granted power of attorney to Don Antonio de la Fuente to collect the Synod due to them from the places where they had served as priests.

people_involved: Don Antonio de Avendaño y Aguilar
Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral
summary: On August 29, Don Antonio de Avendaño y Aguilar and his wife Doña Lucía Josefa de Badilla obligated themselves to the Chaplaincy of the Franciscan Convent in the city for 220 pesos plata, a debt previously held by Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral.
On September 4, Antonio Cayetano García and his wife Catarina Castillo sold a cacao plantation located in Pontezuela, Matina valley, to Sebastián Camaño for 440 pesos cacao.

people_involved: Capitán Don Romualdo José Muñoz de la Trinidad
Presbítero Don José Nicolás Salmón Pacheco
summary: On September 25, Manuel Carranza sold a mulatto slave named José Pacheco to Capitán Don Romualdo José Muñoz de la Trinidad for 280 pesos plata. Carranza had previously acquired the slave by purchasing him from Presbítero Don José Nicolás Salmón Pacheco.
On September 27, Pedro Manuel Salguero granted general power of attorney to Don Antonio de la Fuente.

people_involved: Doña Ana Rita Gómez de Lara
Doña Rosa de la Madriz Linares
summary: On September 25, Don Francisco de Bonilla, his wife Doña Ana Rita Gómez de Lara, and Don Manuel Antonio Jiménez replaced Don Tomás López del Corral and his wife Doña Rosa de la Madriz Linares in a surety given to Pedro Manuel Salguero for a certain value.

A document was granted concerning tithes that were auctioned from this province. The specific details of the auction and the parties involved are not provided, only the date of the document's issuance.
Pedro Manuel Salguero granted a general power of attorney to José Joaquín Paniagua. This legal action transferred broad authority from Salguero to Paniagua.

Félix Joaquín Meneses, acting as the executor for Joaquina López del Corral, sold an enslaved mulatto woman named Juana María and her son Pedro Alcántara to José Antonio de Oriamuno. The sale price for Juana María was 74 pesos and 2.5 reales, and for Pedro Alcántara, 100 pesos.
Doña Teresa de Soto y Barahona granted her son, Francisco Carazo, the power to make a will on her behalf. This indicates her intention to formalize her last wishes through her son.

people_involved: Maximiliano Antonio de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Tomás López del Corral obligated himself to Maximiliano Antonio de Alvarado y Jirón, the parish priest, for 260 pesos of silver. This obligation was later cancelled by Cura Alvarado y Jirón on August 6, 1776.

people_involved: Maximiliano Antonio de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: The obligation made by Tomás López del Corral to Maximiliano Antonio de Alvarado y Jirón on October 24, 1776, was cancelled. This cancellation was recorded by Cura Alvarado y Jirón.

Francisco Carazo executed a will on behalf of his mother, Teresa de Soto y Barahona, detailing her marriage to Pedro Carazo and naming her children as heirs. The will also listed enslaved individuals, María Josefa, Antonia Barahona, and Manuela, as well as properties in San Francisco del Zapotal and Santa Eulalia. It specified that María Josefa and her daughter Manuela were to be given to José Antonio Carazo, and an enslaved girl named Gertrudis was property of Petronila Carazo.

Magdalena Angulo, a free mulatto widow, withdrew her legal action against Sebastián Villarreal, who was imprisoned in the Royal Jail due to her complaints. Félix Joaquín Meneses, acting as Villarreal's defender, agreed to pay a 100-peso fine to settle the matter.

Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla, the Lieutenant Governor and a resident of Heredia, granted a general power of attorney to Lieutenant Colonel José Joaquín de Nava. This transfer of authority empowered Nava to act on Bonilla's behalf.
Tomás López del Corral granted general power of attorney to his wife, Rosa de la A Linares. This legal action empowered his wife to act on his behalf.

Fray Mariano Benítez, the parish priest of San Bartolomé de Barba, granted power to José Manzarraga, a resident of León and general syndic of the Convent of San Francisco. This power allowed Manzarraga to collect a year's stipend owed to Fray Benítez from the Royal Treasury.
