people_involved: Fray Juan Agustín Guerrero de Arcos
summary: Several priests from various parishes, including Ujurraz, San Antonio, Curridavá, Aserrí, Pacaca, Cot, Quircot, Tobosi, Tucurrique, and Atirro, granted power to José Manzarraga, a resident of León. This power enabled Manzarraga to collect their earned stipends from the Royal Treasury, supported by their certifications.

people_involved: Antonio de la Trinidad de Soto
María de la Rosa de Soto
Juan de Jesús Cayetana de la Rosa de Soto
summary: Francisco Javier de Soto, while ill, made his will, detailing his parentage, marriage to María Teresa Chinchilla, and their twelve children as heirs. The will also mentioned their house, purchased from the heirs of Juan Rafael Ramírez, two enclosures in Chircagres, and a debt owed to his nephew Juan Cayetano Soto. Manuel José de Soto was named as an executor.

people_involved: Pedro Tiburcio de Machado y Ugarte
summary: Pedro Tiburcio de Machado y Ugarte and his wife, María Mercedes de Soto Mayor, obligated themselves for 100 pesos to the Convent of San Francisco. They also committed to equal sums for two chaplaincies, one founded by Francisco de Ocampo Golfín and María Magdalena Pérez de Luna (with Antonio Ramón de Azofeifa as chaplain), and another with Francisco Antonio Robredo as chaplain. These sums were previously owed by Tomás López del Corral.
Individuals received funds and mortgaged their house in Cartago and a sugar cane plantation with a mill and plantain grove in the Ujarraz valley from 'del Corral'.
On June 13, 1786, Miguel Fuentes and his wife took responsibility for 100 pesos from the chaplaincy of Presbítero Robredo. This entry was noted as unsigned.

people_involved: Doña María Francisca López del Corral
Don José Antonio de Oriamuno (Sargento Mayor)
Presbítero Don Juan Salvador de Laya y Bolívar
summary: On January 20, Don Pedro Aymerich and Doña María Francisca López del Corral obligated themselves for 450 pesos plata for a chaplaincy. This sum was previously charged to Don José Antonio de Oriamuno and is now prayed for by Bachiller Don Gregorio José Gutiérrez, interim priest of Esparza.

locations: La Pontezuela del Valle de Matina
people_involved: Doña Manuela de Ibarra y Calvo
Don José Antonio de Oriamuno (Sargento Mayor)
summary: On January 20, Francisco de Aguilar y Santos and his wife, Doña Manuela de Ibarra y Calvo, obligated themselves for 600 pesos plata for a chaplaincy of the Convent of San Francisco in Esparza, previously held by Don José Antonio de Oriamuno. They mortgaged 3000 cacao trees in El Bejuco and La Pontezuela del Valle de Matina.
On July 5, 1786, Don José Romualdo Zamora, Síndico of the Convent of Esparza and a resident of Villa Vieja, formally accepted the mortgage of cacao trees as valid.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don José Antonio de Oriamuno
summary: On January 22, Sargento Mayor Don José Antonio de Oriamuno stated he received power from Doctor Don José Cistue to present a royal provision for a new census of indigenous people and tributaries in the province and Nicoya. His nephew, also named Don José Antonio de Oriamuno, was to assist in Nicoya, based on a dispatch from November 14, 1775.

people_involved: Capitán Don José Romualdo de Oriamuno
Sargento Mayor Don José Antonio de Oriamuno
summary: Capitán Don José Romualdo de Oriamuno acted as guarantor for Sargento Mayor Don José Antonio de Oriamuno and his nephew, who were tasked with the census commission.

On February 6, Don José Francisco de Rojas and Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla agreed to exchange properties: Rojas's sugar cane plantation in Ujarraz for Bonilla's 2000-tree clearing in Barbilla, Matina valley.

An amendment to the property exchange stated Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla would deliver 1700 trees and donate 600 more to Don José Francisco de Rojas, with Miguel Maroto planting an additional 300. In compensation, Don José Francisco would give Don Juan 100 pesos of cacao in Matina.
On November 8, 1786, the property exchange agreement between Don José Francisco de Rojas and Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla was rescinded.

people_involved: Don José Antonio de Oriamuno (Sargento Mayor)
summary: On February 27, Don José Antonio de Oriamuno, Síndico General of the Convent of San Francisco, granted power to Don José Manzarraga, Síndico General of the Convent of León, to collect Fray Francisco Jirón de Alvarado's accrued stipend from the Royal Treasury.

people_involved: Don Tomás de Soto y Barahona
Doña Teresa de Soto y Barahona
summary: On March 28, Don Tomás de Soto y Barahona and Don Juan Miguel López Conejo, as executor for Doña Teresa de Soto y Barahona's heirs, leased two cacao plantations in Matina valley to Felipe Solano for three years.
Don Félix García Ergueta sold a farm, including a dwelling, a house with a sugar mill, a cane plot, and a pasture, to Tiburcio Sáenz. He had previously acquired it from Miguel Arce's executor.

people_involved: Teniente Coronel Don Juan Fernández de Bobadilla
summary: On March 8, Don Manuel Antonio de Jiménez, Francisco Delgado, Miguel Piedra, and Ramona Carranza granted power to Don Manuel de Molina to request land titles. Molina was to confirm lands measured by Teniente Coronel Don Juan Fernández de Bobadilla for the first three, and for Ramona Carranza, to secure title for the Retes pasture after her previous purchase was nullified by the Gobernador.

On March 26, Doña Clemencia Muñoz made her testament, identifying her deceased parents, her husband Don Félix García y Ergueta, and her children. She detailed specific items bequeathed to her daughter, Doña Felipa, who is married to Don Benito Fajardo.

An inventory of goods is mentioned, including a 'mulata blanca' named Ramona and her four children: Francisco (12), Rafael (>11), María Manuela (9), and Hipólito (4). The deceased's son, Don Félix, who studied in Nicaragua and is now in Tres Ríos, did not incur any study expenses. Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla is the executor, and the sole heirs are Doña Felipa, Don Félix, and Don Benito.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don José Antonio de Oriamuno
Don Félix Antonio de la Campa
summary: Sargento Mayor don José Antonio de Oriamuno grants power of attorney to Don Félix Antonio de la Campa, a Procurador of the Royal Audiencia. This power allows him to claim payment for services rendered in the new census of tributary indigenous people in the province, acting as the representative for Doctor don José Cistue, and also for his nephew Don José Antonio de Oriamuno's work in the Nicoya district census.

Doña Josefa Valverde, a widow, sells a house made of bahareque and cedar wood, covered with tiles, to Antonio de Arizaga, a resident of Puebla. The price is 250 pesos of cacao (equivalent to 150 pesos silver), which she receives from Don Esteban Venegas. An attached letter from Arizaga, dated March 30 from Barbilla, confirms his acceptance of the deed.

people_involved: Teniente Coronel don José Joaquín de Nava
summary: Doña María Francisca de Alvarado, acting as the wife and general attorney for Don Antonio de la Fuente, obligates herself to Teniente Coronel don José Joaquín de Nava for 3000 pesos silver. She agrees to pay a 5% premium due to the inherent risk and lack of a special mortgage, with payment due by the following July. The obligation was cancelled by Nava on January 22, 1777.

people_involved: Beneficiado don Maximiliano Antonio de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: The Beneficiado Don Maximiliano Antonio de Alvarado y Jirón, who serves as the Cura of this parish, grants general power of attorney to Presbítero Don Félix José Galarza, a resident of León.

Doña María Fernández, widow of Don Pedro José Corrales, states that her husband left no forced heirs. Extrajudicial proceedings for the distribution of his assets, according to his will, were presented to the Gobernador by her and the executor Don José Antonio Jiménez, and the Gobernador approved them, ordering her to accept an obligation to the creditors with the best right, which she does.

Don José Antonio de Oriamuno, the Síndico General for the San Francisco religious order, leases three cacao plantations named Las Flores, La Gamboa Chiquita, and La Arburola, totaling 900 trees in the Matina valley and belonging to the Convento, to José Francisco Castillo, a resident of Ujarraz. The lease is for 20 pesos cacao per year, with no specified duration.

people_involved: Presbítero don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí
Presbítero don Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí
summary: Presbítero don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí, fulfilling his deceased brother Presbítero don Francisco Cayetano de Arleguí's wishes, founds a chaplaincy for 9 recited masses, with an alms of 2 pesos silver. The principal of 200 pesos silver, obtained from selling a slave left for this purpose by his brother, is charged to his residence. His nephew, Don Fernando de Arleguí, is the proprietary chaplain, with the Convento de San Francisco as an alternative, and the patronage passes from the grantor to his brother Don Antonio Elías, and then by lineage.

Félix Joaquín Meneses grants power of attorney to Don José Sánchez, a Royal Scribe in Guatemala City, to request confirmation of the title for two 'caballerías' of land he owns in Agua Caliente, near the city, before the Private Judge of Lands.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don José Antonio de Oriamuno
Capitán don José Romualdo de Oreamuno
summary: Sargento Mayor don José Antonio de Oriamuno and Capitán don José Romualdo de Oreamuno grant general power of attorney to Don José Sánchez for all their lawsuits.

people_involved: Doña María Francisca López del Corral
summary: Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla and his wife Doña Ana Rita Gómez obligate themselves for 485 pesos cacao at 5%, belonging to a chaplaincy founded by Pedro Ibáñez. Don Pedro Aymerich and his wife Doña María Francisca López del Corral are now redeeming these amounts, which were previously charged to José Espinosa and a 'Fulano Mesa.' They mortgage a hacienda and two 'rozas' in Matina. (This entry is incomplete and was not passed).

Doña Manuela de Zavaleta, a widow, confesses that she received 200 cacao trees in the Matina valley as a donation for her daughter, Doña Gertrudis de Zavaleta. Having previously obligated herself to give Doña Gertrudis 100 pesos upon her majority, they have now agreed that Doña Manuela will transfer a house, located in the patio of her own residence, as payment for the obligation, which Doña Gertrudis accepts.

Fray Juan Guerrero de Arcis, Cura of Cot, Quircot, and Tobosi, and Fray José Joaquín Hidalgo, Cura Doctrinero of San Luis, Aserrí, and Curridabat, grant power of attorney to Don José Manzarraga, a resident of León and Síndico of the Convento, to collect 6 months of synod payments they have earned as Curas.

Fray Francisco Eugenio del Valle, Cura Doctrinero of Asunción de Pacaca, and Fray Francisco Muñoz, Cura of Ujarraz, grant power of attorney to Don José Manzarraga to collect 6 months of synod payments they have earned as Curas.
Don Antonio Elías de Arleguí, Síndico procurador of this city, is mentioned along with other neighbors in an incomplete entry.

Several hacendados in the Matina Valley collectively committed to paying 760 pesos of cacao annually to a Chaplain. This payment was for providing mass and sacraments, with services to be held on festive days in both Barbilla and Matina, each having a straw-roofed hermitage. The agreement stipulated that the obligation would cease if Matina became a populated town requiring standard church fees.

Captain José Nicolás Camaño and his wife, María Josefa Rivas, committed to paying 100 pesos of cacao to a chaplaincy established by the late Diego Quintero del Castillo. This obligation was previously held by Francisca Velazco y Estrada, who redeemed it on May 3rd of the same year. To secure this, they mortgaged their 3000-tree cacao hacienda, San José de la Pontezuela, in the Matina Valley, which was also burdened with another 100 pesos of cacao for the Cofradía de la Concepción.
Don Agustín de Ulloa sold a 12-vara long, tile-roofed house built on posts, with a walled and fenced lot, to María Antonia Carrillo. The sale price for the property was 150 pesos of cacao.

Don Tomás López del Corral and his wife, Doña Rosa de la Madriz Linares, committed to sums of 119 pesos 4.5 reales silver and 55 pesos 2 reales cacao, which originated from the estate of the late Doña Joaquina López del Corral. They received these funds from the Gobernador, who had them deposited with Don José Antonio Jiménez. The new depositaries agreed to return the sums if needed for the ongoing probate of Don Tomás López del Corral, or to hold them until Joaquina's heir appeared; a copy of this deed was made on June 22, 1786, for the deceased grantor's cause.

Don Felipe de Arburola, acting as executor and heir of his deceased mother, Doña María Lorenza Fajardo, sold 240 productive cacao trees to Miguel Arburola, a free mulatto. The transaction was for 280 pesos of cacao.

This entry details the testament of the late Presbítero Don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí, which was granted by his attorneys and brothers, Don Antonio Elías and Don Manuel Felipe de Arleguí. The power of attorney was originally granted on June 8, 1775, before the Gobernador. The testament lists various religious books among his possessions.

Simón Uriza, a resident of the Bagaces Valley, granted power of attorney to Don Pedro Antonio de la Puente. This power was for Pedro Antonio to represent Uriza's wife, Doña Mónica del Corral, in the probate proceedings of her deceased father, Don Tomás López del Corral.

This entry records the testament of Doña Micaela de Arleguí, who was ill in bed and unmarried. She was the legitimate daughter of the late Don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí and Doña Engracia de Hoces Navarro. Her brothers, Don Francisco and Don Manuel Felipe de Arleguí, were named as executors, and her sister, Doña Juana de Arleguí, was designated as her sole heir.

This entry details the testament of Don José de la Cruz, a native of Sevilla, who was ill in bed and unable to sign due to an impediment in his right hand. He was married to Doña Mariima Alvarado, and they had three children: Rafaela, Manuel Silvestre, and Pedro José. The house they lived in was inherited by his wife from her late uncle, Don Antonio de Guevara. His executors were Don José León de Bonilla and his wife, with his children named as heirs. The testament was granted before Captain Don Juan Miguel López Conejo, Alcalde of the Santa Hermandad, commissioned by the Gobernador.
Don Nicolás Reyes, a resident of Villa Vieja, sold a donkey for 100 pesos silver and 20 breeding mares at 3 pesos 4 reales silver each to Don Francisco Aguilar y Santos.

Don Francisco Aguilar y Santos and his wife, Doña Manuela de Ibarra, committed to paying 244 pesos 7 reales silver to the minor Don Juan María Sáenz. They received these funds from the Gobernador in the form of a slave named Juan José, 8 cows, and 20 pesos in cash and reales, and mortgaged a cleared plot of land with 4000 trees in La Pontezuela, Matina Valley. A marginal note from the Gobernador indicates that Doña Micaela Sáenz did not deliver the 8 cows, claiming she had spent them for the minor's benefit.

Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla leased a hacienda in the Matina valley for three years. The hacienda included 4000 fruit-bearing cacao trees and 600 cleared trees, with an annual rent of 400 pesos cacao.

Juan de Dios Brenes and his wife, María Francisca Pacheco, incurred an obligation of 379 pesos 4 reales in cacao currency. This amount was due to Manuel José Coto, José Pascual Coto, and María Josefa Coto, representing their inheritance from their deceased father, José Miguel Coto, who was María Francisca Pacheco's first husband. José Nicolás Segura, María Josefa Coto's husband, later canceled his portion of the debt on November 28, 1777.

Don Francisco Aguilar y Santos and don Simón de Uriza exchanged goods. Aguilar traded a donkey, which he had acquired from don Nicolás Reyes for 100 pesos, for 25 cows from Uriza's herd in Curubicí, and also exchanged 20 mares for 28 steers. Aguilar confirmed receipt of the livestock on August 23, 1777.

José Domingo Coto received 125 pesos 4 reales in cacao as inheritance from his deceased father, José Miguel Coto. His uncle, Pablo José Coto, assumed guardianship of José Domingo Coto, which he will relinquish when José Domingo turns 25 years old.

Doña María Francisca López del Corral, with her husband don Pedro Aymerich's permission and at the request of her first deceased husband don Joaquín de Alvarado, donated a 1400-tree, 8-year-old cacao plantation in the Matina valley to the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora de Matina. Juan Carranza, the Cofradía's mayordomo, accepted the donation.

María Teresa Chinchilla, widow of Francisco de Soto, obligated herself for 1648 pesos 4 reales and 48 grains of cacao to her twelve minor children as their paternal inheritance, mortgaging a cacao plantation in Barbilla. Her son, Manuel José de Soto, acted as guarantor. A new deed involving María Teresa Chinchilla, don Gabriel García, and his wife was issued on July 8, 1777, canceling the original obligation.

Don Carlos Ruiz Fernández and his wife doña Petronila de Bonilla, along with don José León de Bonilla, received their paternal inheritance from the estate of don José Nicolás de Bonilla through their mother doña Lucía de Alvarado. Fernández and his wife received 737 pesos, 1 1/4 reales, and 16 maravedíes, with José León de Bonilla receiving an equal sum.

José Martín González, son of Miguel Jerónimo González and Efigenia Rodríguez, made his will. He was a widower of Benita Carranza, with whom he had three living children, and was currently married to Juana Antonia Masís, with whom he had five living children. His son-in-law, José Manuel Molina, was the guardian for his first two sons, and his wife and Capitán José Antonio Jiménez were named executors, with his children as heirs.

Don Antonio de la Fuente purchased the office of Alférez Real and Regidor for 500 pesos cacao, initially to be paid in three installments over five years. However, the Gobernador noted that don Antonio paid the full 500 pesos immediately, thus nullifying the need for the payment schedule and the associated deed.
Alejandro Alfaro provided a dowry letter for his wife, María Agustina Carranza. He received goods valued at 506 pesos plata from her father, Manuel Carranza, as part of the dowry.

Capitán don Pedro Aymerich and his wife doña María Francisca Corrales incurred an obligation of 600 pesos plata at 5% interest to the Cofradía de los Angeles, of which Pedro Aymerich was mayordomo. This debt had previously been the responsibility of Bachiller don José Francisco de Alvarado, the Cura of Nicoya.

Four Franciscan friars, Fray Francisco Muñoz (Ujarraz), Fray Juan Guerrero (Concepción de Quircot and annexes), Fray Joaquín Hidalgo (San Luis de Aserrí and annex), and Fray Francisco Eugenio del Valle (Asunción de Pacaca), granted power of attorney to don José Manzarraga, Síndico general of the Franciscan convents in Nicaragua and a resident of León, to collect their assigned synod from the Royal Coffers.

José de la Trinidad Chavarría requested the Alcalde to visit his home so his wife could make a will. The Alcalde, stating he was gravely ill, commissioned don José Nicolás de Chavarría, Alcalde de la Santa Hermandad, to attend to the matter.

María Manuela Acuña, daughter of Félix José Acuña and Francisca Méndez, made her will in her home in the fields of the city. She was married to José de la Trinidad Chavarría, who was named her executor and heir, and had a deceased daughter named María Josefa. She also bequeathed a cow and a filly to each of Josefa Matea, María Eufracia, and María Josefa de los Angeles, whom she had raised, with the last also receiving a loom.
Manuel Carranza sold a small farm (chácara) located in the common lands (ejidos) of the city to José Antonio Sáenz.

people_involved: Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Cristóbal de Moya and Tomasa Román, along with their sons Manuel Antonio and Francisco Joaquín Moya, committed to pay 2625 pesos in cacao currency. This debt was distributed among several capellanías and cofradías, including those founded by Francisco Garrido and Agueda Pérez de Muro, and one for Leonida de Ocampo. The debt was secured by a hacienda in Barbilla del valle de Matina, which they were receiving, consisting of 2600 cacao trees.

Don Francisco Carazo obligated himself to Lieutenant Colonel Juan Fernández de Bobadilla for 500 pesos plata. This sum was given to Carazo via a draft against Manuel de Molina, a resident of León, which Carazo then endorsed to Julián de Azofeifa. The payment was due in June, and the obligation was cancelled on October 8th of the same year.

This entry details the joint will of Presbyter Andrés Fernández and his mother, María Josefa de Trejos. They named two enslaved women, Andrea and María Antonia Fernández, and mentioned José Joaquín Fernández, a boy they raised. They established a capellanía for the Convento de San Francisco using the proceeds from their house, and appointed Manuel Felipe Arleguí and José Antonio Jiménez as executors.

José Miguel García and his wife Antonia Masís obligated themselves for 525 pesos at 5% interest to the Convento de San Francisco. This debt was secured by a pasture known as Felipe Díaz's, located in Cartago, and was previously the responsibility of Juan Dionisio Pacheco.

Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla and his wife Doña Ana Rita Gómez sold a fenced pasture in the common lands of Cartago, specifically in the area called "el Agua Caliente," to Lieutenant Colonel Don José Joaquín de Nava for 500 pesos cacao. Bonilla acquired half of the property as a donation from his late mother-in-law, Juana María Barahona, and the other half through a fulfilled communication.

people_involved: José Romualdo Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Captain José Romualdo Muñoz de la Trinidad, Lieutenant Governor of San José, leased the tithes of San José and its district, including those from indigenous people and all uncollected arrears from the previous year, from Pedro Salguero, the tithe farmer for the jurisdiction. The two-year lease began on January 1st, 1777, for 340 pesos plata annually, and Salguero cancelled it on August 14, 1778.

Don Julián de Azofeifa owed Don Francisco Carazo 900 pesos in cash, to be paid in July. Azofeifa received this sum via a draft against Manuel de Molina, a resident of León. He agreed to pay the sum in cattle from the "hato de doña Ana" at a rate of twenty reales per head, without interest.

Lieutenant Colonel José Joaquín de Nava granted power of attorney to Tomasa Joaquina López del Corral, a widow, to sell, donate, or exchange three pastures on his behalf. Two of these pastures were in the common lands of Cartago (one in Agua Caliente and one in Taras), and the third was outside the common lands, next to Doña Joaquina's mill.

Doña Joaquina López del Corral, a widow, granted power of attorney to Lieutenant Colonel Joaquín de Nava, who was about to depart for Guatemala, to sell an enslaved mulatto man named Francisco Ocaña, aged 25, for whatever price he could obtain.

Don Francisco Carazo obligated himself for 256 pesos plata at 5% interest to a capellanía founded by Doña Francisca Bonilla, a debt previously held by Santiago Cruz of Aserrí. Carazo received the funds from Captain José Antonio Jiménez, acting as attorney for his brother-in-law, Presbyter Manuel Antonio Sandoval, who resided in Somotillo, León, and was the chaplain of the said capellanía.

Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla, acting as executor for Doña Clemencia Muñoz, granted freedom to María Manuela García, a ten-year-old mulatto girl who was enslaved by Doña Clemencia. This act was performed because Bonilla received 125 pesos plata, the appraised value of the girl, from José Miguel García.

Don José Romualdo Zamora granted power of attorney to Don Francisco Ortiz, a procurator of the Royal Audiencia in the new city of Asunción de Guatemala. Ortiz was tasked with requesting a title for Zamora as a public and Cabildo scribe for Cartago, a position Zamora won by auction for 325 pesos cacao, payable in three installments over five years.

This entry details the will of Don José Cayetano Carrillo, the illegitimate son of the late Francisco Carrillo and Petronila Cascante. He was married to María Josefa Aguirre and they had six children, including José Francisco del Rosario and José Antonio.
Ana Catalina Carrillo was put in a relationship with Don Ramón Céspedes.
Don Lucas Antonio de Arleguí left a calf to each of his servants, Isabel María and Efigenia, and another calf to each of his grandchildren, Esteban Antonio and Ana Josefa.
Don Lucas Antonio de Arleguí owed his stepson, José Antonio Solano, a 'macho de lazo y reata'.

people_involved: Presbítero don Fernando Antonio de Arleguí
summary: Don Lucas Antonio de Arleguí died on January 16, as reported by his brother, Presbítero don Fernando Antonio de Arleguí.

people_involved: Presbítero don Fernando Antonio de Arleguí
summary: On January 17, the sealed will of Don Lucas Antonio de Arleguí was opened, following a petition by his brother, Presbítero don Fernando Antonio de Arleguí.

people_involved: Doña Rafaela de la Peña Medrano
summary: Upon the death of his wife, Doña Rafaela de la Peña Medrano, Don Lucas Antonio de Arleguí inherited a fifth of her assets. He requested the Governor to summon an heiress in Granada for the inventory of her father, Don Juan Antonio Medrano's, estate, which was pending.

people_involved: Don Juan Antonio de la Peña Medrano
summary: Don Lucas Antonio de Arleguí was responsible for 71 pesos 3 reales and 155 pesos 5 reales worth of goods from the estate of Don Juan Antonio de la Peña Medrano, a former Corregidor of Nicoya. These goods included various items of clothing, textiles, pistols, and household items, as recorded by executor Juan Pablo Quirós before he left for Nicaragua.

people_involved: Capitán don José Romualdo de Oriamuno
Doña Josefa Petronila de Alvarado Jirón
summary: Don Lucas Antonio de Arleguí named Capitán don José Romualdo de Oriamuno and don Félix Joaquín Meneses as executors. He left a fifth of his assets to his brother, Presbítero don Fernando de Arleguí, for masses for his soul and his ancestors, and named his mother, Doña Josefa Petronila de Alvarado Jirón, as his heiress.

The will of Juana Josefa Calderón, legitimate daughter of the deceased Esteban Calderón and Jacinta de la Roque, was recorded. She was married twice, first to Juan Ríos (with whom she had a son who died in infancy) and then to Nicolás de Acuña (no children). She raised María Petronila.

Juana Josefa Calderón left legacies of livestock to her sister Antonia Calderón (who is 'impedida') and her nephews Blas Calderón, Felipe Hermenegildo Calderón, Juan Andrés Acuña, Nicolás de la Encarneción Acuña, and Gregorio García. Juan Andrés Acuña was named executor.

people_involved: Doña Josefa Petronila de Alvarado y Jirón
Don Juan Antonio de la Peña Medrano
summary: Don Félix Joaquín Meneses and Doña Josefa Petronila de Alvarado y Jirón, as executor and mother of the deceased Don Lucas de Arleguí, granted power of attorney to Don Juan Antonio Muñoz, Don Salvador Cuende, and Don Luis de Aguilar, all residents of Nicaragua. Their task was to collect the deceased's assets, settle outstanding matters with Juan Pablo Quirós regarding 100 pounds of purple thread for sale in Guatemala, and collect debts from the estates of deceased Corregidores Don Manuel Mella and Don Juan Antonio de la Peña Medrano, where Don Lucas had served as interim Corregidor.

people_involved: Capitán don Tomás López del Corral
summary: The will of Doña María López del Corral, legitimate daughter of Capitán don Tomás López del Corral and Doña Francisca de Ibarra, was recorded. She was married to Don Marcos Alvarado y Jirón and had ten living children and four deceased children.
Among Doña María López del Corral's assets were a mulata named Antonia Basilia and her two children, Manuela Serapia and Lucía de Alvarado.
Doña María López del Corral stipulated that a fifth of her assets, after deducting funeral expenses, should be distributed among her four daughters.

Francisca Javiera Castillo, widow of José Miguel Badilla, obligated herself for 1635 pesos and 4.5 reales in cacao currency to her two minor children, Manuela Josefa and Félix Badilla. This sum was adjudicated to them as their paternal inheritance.

Doña Paula González, a widow, leased a hacienda comprising 573 cacao trees, a house, and banana plantations in the Matina valley to José Nicolás Molina for a period of 5 years. The annual rent was set at 57 pesos and 4 reales, payable in cacao.

people_involved: Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: María Cayetana Rodríguez, widow of Tomás Maroto, and her son Manuel Jerónimo Maroto, obligated themselves for 2386 pesos in cacao at 5% interest for two chaplaincies. They received a hacienda with 2567 cacao trees in Velazco del Valle de Matina, previously managed by Tomás Maroto, and mortgaged an adjacent 1962-tree plot from Maroto's estate.

people_involved: Doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho de Castañeda
Doña Juana de Alvarado y Jirón
Don José Miguel Sancho de Castañeda
summary: Doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho de Castañeda made her will, detailing the distribution of her estate, including her house and the freeing of five enslaved women upon her death. She established a chaplaincy on her Matina cacao hacienda, naming her nephew Don José Miguel Sancho de Castañeda as patron and chaplain, and appointed Don Antonio de la Fuente and Don José Antonio de Oriamuno as executors.

Don José Nicolás de Chavarría, Alcalde de la Santa Hermandad, obligated himself for 115 pesos and 4 reales of silver at 5% interest to Doña Marta and Doña Feliciana Pacheco, minor daughters of the late Doña Antonia Sarmiento, as their inheritance. He also agreed to lease a 600-tree cacao hacienda in Matina, left by Doña Antonia Sarmiento and managed by Antonio Basilio, for 50 pesos cacao annually to the minors.
Don Antonio Pao, the defender of the minors, cancelled an obligation because it was transferred to Félix Camacho via a new deed on the same day.

Antonia Maroto, widow of Blas Guerrero, leased a 630-tree cacao plantation in the Matina valley to Juan Ramón Ortega for 5 years. The annual rent, consisting of three 'tercios' of cacao, was to be paid first to Doña Manuela Baeza to whom Antonia Maroto owed money, and the remainder to Antonia Maroto.

José Francisco González took charge of two chaplaincy funds previously managed by his deceased brother Felipe González. These funds, totaling 600 pesos in cacao, were secured by two cacao haciendas in Matina, 'La Hermenegilda' and 'La Quiteria', and were designated for the Convento de San Francisco and the Cofradía de las Animas, respectively, with a 5% interest payment.

locations: El Bejuco del Valle de Barbilla
summary: Doña Manuela Baeza and her son-in-law Don Francisco Carazo leased their combined cacao haciendas in El Bejuco del Valle de Barbilla to José Miguel Cárdenas for 5 years. Doña Manuela's three haciendas totaled 4460 trees, and Don Francisco's adjacent hacienda had 500 trees, with rents paid in cacao 'tercios'.

people_involved: Don Bartolomé García Miranda y Casasola
Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Don Bartolomé García Miranda y Casasola made his will, naming his natural son Don Manuel García Miranda as heir and his uncle Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba as executor. He arranged for the freeing of an enslaved woman, María Francisca, and her three sons after his death, and noted a debt to Francisco Moscoso for work in Matina.
Manuel Carranza sold a 40-year-old mulata named Rosa Pacheco to Doña Josefa Petronila de Alvarado, a widow, for 200 pesos plata. Carranza had previously acquired Rosa Pacheco through purchase.

Francisca Morera, widow of Luis Quirós, obligated herself to her seven minor children (Paula, Manuel, Francisco, Javier, Ildefonso, Manuel José, and Lorenzo Quirós) for 572 pesos and 3 reales plata, representing their paternal inheritance. This amounted to 81 pesos, 6 reales plata, and 20 grains of cacao for each child.

Doña Petronila Cárdenas sold a quarter of a house in Cartago to José Miguel Cárdenas, whom she raised, for 100 pesos plata. She also transferred another quarter of the house to her natural son José Francisco Cárdenas and a stone-fenced pasture in Cartago's common lands to her natural son Domingo Noguera, both without price, as they were her natural heirs. The house bordered her sister Doña María Cárdenas's property.

people_involved: Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
Br. don José Francisco de Casasola
summary: Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba donated a criolla negra named María Francisca and her three children (José Francisco, Juan José, and Serapio Casasola) to his nephew, Don Bartolomé García de Miranda. The negra had been acquired by Juan Manuel in a public auction along with other assets left by his deceased brother, Br. don José Francisco de Casasola. The condition of the donation was that the recipients could not be sold and would gain their freedom upon the death of the donee.

María Nicolasa Fonseca, widow of Juan Manuel Valerín, made her testament. She had three living children with Juan Manuel: María Loreta, María Antonia, and Cayetano Valerín. María Loreta was married to Nicolás Maroto, and María Antonia was married to Miguel Jerónimo Maroto. Her children were named as her heirs, and Don Manuel José García was appointed as her executor.

Siblings Juan Dionisio, Estéfana, Antonia, Luz, and Eufemia Pacheco leased a fruiting cacao plantation in the Matina valley, containing 2644 trees, to Don Gregorio de la Calle and his wife Doña Micaela de Alvarado for 5 years. The annual rent was 264 pesos and 12 reales cacao. The lessees mortgaged another fruiting cacao plantation of 200 trees and a 1600-tree clearing, also in the Matina valley, as security.

people_involved: Maximiliano Antonio de Alvarado y Jirón
Juana María de Galarza y Pinillos
summary: Don Maximiliano Antonio de Alvarado y Jirón, a prominent cleric, made his testament in 1777. He was the legitimate son of Captain Don Juan Manuel de Alvarado and Doña Juana María de Galarza y Pinillos. He left an annual income to his sister Doña María del Carmen Alvarado and a house in Cartago to his sister Doña Ana Rita de Alvarado, with provisions for these assets to eventually become capellanías. The Governor certified that Mariano Umaña received jewels belonging to the deceased Pedro Araya, which the testador had held for Araya's two daughters.
The Presbyter Don Francisco Antonio Robredo granted general power of attorney for lawsuits to Don Francisco Aguilar y Santos in 1777.

Don Gregorio de la Calle and his wife Doña Micaela de Alvarado obligated themselves for 150 pesos at 5% interest to a capellanía founded by Don Pedro de Moya and Doña Angela Sáenz, for which Presbyter Don Manuel Sáenz was the chaplain. They mortgaged a house in Cartago, which bordered the property of Beneficiado Don José Francisco de Alvarado.
Doña Lucía de Alvarado was responsible for an unspecified obligation.

Doña Micaela de Alvarado, wife of don Gregorio de la Calle, granted power of attorney to don Tomás López del Corral. This power allowed him to collect debts owed to her from tutelas in Nicaragua and over 800 pesos owed to her grandfather, don Miguel de Alvarado, by a resident of León, as she is his heir.

Pedro Manuel Salguero borrowed 2864 pesos 4 reales from Teniente Coronel don José Joaquín de Nava to pay his tithes, with don Antonio de la Fuente and doña María Francisca de Alvarado as guarantors. The debt was paid on June 15 of the same year by don Antonio de la Fuente to don Francisco Javier Lombardo, Nava's special attorney, in Granada, Nicaragua.

people_involved: Don Maximiliano Antonio de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Mariano Umaña, a resident of Villa Vieja, received jewels and money from don Maximiliano Antonio de Alvarado y Jirón, the city's Cura. These items were left by Pedro Araya upon his death for his two minor daughters, and Umaña received them because he married one of the daughters, María Rafaela Araya.

people_involved: Doña Antonia Engracia de Hoces Navarro
summary: Don Antonio Elías de Arleguí made his testament, detailing his family, property, and heirs. He was married to doña Josefa Petronila de Alvarado and had six children. He designated his brother don Manuel Felipe and his son don Lucas as executors, and left a fifth of his assets to his son don Fernando if he became a priest, with all six children as heirs.

Pedro José Lizondro committed to pay 76 pesos 4 reales to the three minor legitimate daughters of the deceased Cayetano Masís and Juana Francisca Astorga, as their paternal inheritance. On November 7, 1781, Juana Francisca Astorga received this sum from Lizondro because all three of her minor daughters had died in a smallpox epidemic.

people_involved: Don Tomás de Soto y Barahona
summary: Don Julián de Azofeifa committed to pay 510 pesos in cacao currency to the Royal Treasury for the office of Provincial Mayor, which he won at auction. He received the title for this office on May 25, 1776, from President don Martín de Mayorga, with don Tomás de Soto y Barahona as his guarantor.

people_involved: Doña María Rafaela de la Peña
Don Juan Antonio de la Peña Medrano
summary: Doña María Rafaela de la Peña, a native of Granada and daughter of don Juan Antonio de la Peña Medrano and doña Jacoba Vargas, made her testament. She is married to don Lucas Antonio de Arleguí, is seven months pregnant, and designated her husband as executor and heir to a fifth of her estate. If the child is not born, her grandmother, doña Valentina Zurita, will inherit.

people_involved: Ayudante don José Antonio de Oriamuno
summary: Don Manuel Antonio Jiménez, Francisco Delgado, and Miguel Piedra declared their acquisition of 21 caballerías and 51 square cuerdas of land in Purires. They obtained the title on September 16, 1776, confirmed by the Real Audiencia on October 7, 1776, and took possession on February 22, 1777. Numerous individuals contributed financially to cover the costs associated with this land acquisition.

A group of individuals contributed a total of 450 pesos and 4 reales to receive corresponding plots of land, establishing them as legitimate owners. Additionally, it was declared that the cattle and small herds of San Nicolás, San Francisco de Paula, and La Concepción de Matina, along with their houses and corrals, were situated on these lands with the consent of the new proprietors, though their right of occupation was temporary and did not confer positive property rights.

people_involved: Doña Teresa de Soto y Barahona
summary: The legitimate heirs of the deceased Doña Teresa de Soto y Barahona, including Doña Ana Micaela Carazo (represented by her husband Don Juan Miguel López Conejo), Doña Petronila Carazo (acting for herself and her brother Don José Antonio Carazo), and Don Francisco Carazo, declared receipt of their inheritance. They agreed to pay any justified debts against the estate proportionally, with Don Julián de Azofeifa also acting as curator for Doña Gertrudis Carazo.

people_involved: Capitán Don Antonio Elías de Arleguí
Presbítero Don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí
summary: Don Manuel Felipe, Don Francisco, and Don Lucas Antonio de Arleguí, along with their sisters Doña Micaela and Doña Juana, declared an extrajudicial division of the assets of the deceased Presbítero Don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí, with the Governor's approval. They also addressed three capellanías: one was redeemed with a slave named Manuel Baeza given to Don Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla, another is managed by Don Manuel Felipe, and the third, founded by the deceased Presbítero Don Cayetano de Arleguí, is to be secured by Don Fernando Antº de Arleguí.

Francisco Antonio Pérez de Cote, a resident of Villa Vieja, granted power of attorney to Don Manuel de Molina, a resident of León. This power enables Don Manuel de Molina to request a title and confirmation for lands known as 'del Río Segundo' from the private court of royal land rights, following a survey conducted at Pérez de Cote's request.

people_involved: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora
Don Juan Antonio de la Peña
summary: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora granted power of attorney to Don Francisco Ortiz, Procurator of the Royal Audiencia, to represent her in a lawsuit. The suit, initiated by Don Juan Antonio de la Peña, concerns items claimed as assets of Don Mateo Herdocia, including a San Antonio image, furniture, and silver, which Doña Manuela asserts are her proven property.

people_involved: Doña Ana Rita Gómez de Lara
summary: Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla granted power of attorney to his wife, Doña Ana Rita Gómez de Lara, to represent him in a contentious lawsuit. The suit was against Don Julián de Azofeifa concerning a debt of 250 pesos, to be paid in cacao, which Bonilla owed.

people_involved: Don Félix José García y Sancho
summary: Don Félix José García y Sancho committed to pay 1214 pesos, 3 reales, and 5 octavos of silver to his minor sons, Don Benito and Don Félix García. This payment constituted their inheritance from their late mother and his wife, Doña Clemencia Muñoz.

people_involved: Presbítero Don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí
summary: Don Manuel Felipe de Arleguí, as heir to his deceased brother Presbítero Don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí, established a chaplaincy with a principal of 200 pesos plata. His nephew, Don Fernando de Arleguí, was appointed as the chaplain and patron. The chaplaincy was founded on the deceased's house, which was valued at 400 pesos and already had a 200-peso encumbrance.

María Teresa Chinchilla, widow of Francisco de Soto, committed to pay 1648 pesos, 4 reales, and 48 grains of cacao to her twelve minor children as their paternal inheritance. Don Gabriel García and María de la Candelaria Jiménez guaranteed the obligation, mortgaging a cacao plantation in Matina, mules, and cattle.
José Miguel de Jesús González received from his mother-in-law, María Teresa Chinchilla, the inheritance corresponding to his wife, Ana Gertrudis Soto.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Manuel Antonio de Sandoval
Doña María Francisca López del Corral
summary: Capitán Don José Antonio Jiménez, representing his brother Presbítero Don Manuel Antonio de Sandoval, reported that Capitán Santiago Bermúdez had redeemed properties securing a 256-peso chaplaincy founded by Doña Francisca de Bonilla. The debt is now transferred to Don Francisco Carazo. Jiménez also handled 50 pesos belonging to the Convento de San Francisco, located on the same lands, receiving them from Bermúdez and delivering them to Fray Francisco García, noting Doña María Francisca López del Corral's obligation as a tenant.

people_involved: Juan José de Zúñiga y Salas
Teniente General Don Miguel de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Josefa de Guevara, a widow, sold a piece of land to Martín González for 50 pesos cacao and 25 pesos plata. The land, previously owned by Matías Masís, included an irrigation ditch and bordered the Toyogres river and a royal road. Her deceased husband, Juan José de Zúñiga y Salas, had acquired this land in two separate purchases in 1749 and 1753.

people_involved: Juan José de Zúñiga y Salas
Teniente General Don Miguel de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Juan José de Zúñiga y Salas purchased half of a 'caballería de tierra' from Cosme de Salazar. The transaction was recorded before Teniente General Don Miguel de Alvarado y Jirón.

people_involved: Juan José de Zúñiga y Salas
summary: Juan José de Zúñiga y Salas purchased the other half of a 'caballería de tierra' from Félix Cayetano Masís. The transaction was recorded before Capitán Don José Antonio Bonilla, who was also a Teniente General.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don José Antonio de Oriamuno
summary: Don Simón de Uriza and Doña Mónica López del Corral, residents of Bagaces, borrowed 191 pesos 4 1/2 reales plata from Sargento Mayor Don José Antonio de Oriamuno. The loan was to pay a debt for a donkey and mares owed to Don Francisco Aguilar y Santos and cover deed costs, with repayment due next January. They mortgaged the animals and livestock from their Curubicí ranch in Bagaces as security.

people_involved: Don Pedro Nicolás Rodríguez de Robredo
summary: Don Francisco Aguilar y Santos and Doña Manuela de Ibarra committed to pay 1033 pesos 6 reales in cacao currency to Doña Manuela's minor children, Doña Gertrudis, Don Miguel, and Don Pedro Nicolás Rodríguez de Robredo, as their paternal inheritance from the deceased Don Cayetano Robredo. They mortgaged a cacao plantation and the deceased's house to secure this obligation.
Manuel Carranza, a resident of Villa Nueva, is mentioned, but the details of the event are incomplete as the text chunk ends here.

people_involved: Cap. don Romualdo José Muñoz de la Trinidad
Capitán don Anto de la Fuente
summary: A 'negro criollo' named Juan Pío, 25 years old, was sold for 300 pesos plata to Captain Romualdo José Muñoz de la Trinidad. Juan Pío had previously been acquired by purchase from Captain Anto de la Fuente.

Benito Gómez and his wife María Gertrudis Casasola, residents of Puebla, obligated themselves for 275 pesos 3 reales of cacao, representing 218 cacao trees and 6 reales in beans. This amount was inherited by Juan Casasola, minor son of the deceased Benito Casasola and grandson of the deceased Efigenia Brenes. They mortgaged a hacienda in the Barbilla valley.

Don Francisco Aguilar y Santos and his wife Doña Manuela de Ibarra, along with Doña Joaquina and Doña Vicenta de Ibarra (the latter with the Governor's license due to her husband's absence), and on behalf of their absent sister Doña Ramona de Ibarra, acknowledged a debt of 342 pesos 4 reales of cacao at 5% interest. This debt was originally owed by their deceased father, Don Miguel Cayetano de Ibarra, to the Convent of San Francisco in Esparza. They mortgaged 1000 fruit-bearing cacao trees on the hacienda 'la Pontezuela' in the Matina valley, belonging to Doña Joaquina.

Don Francisco Aguilar y Santos granted power to his wife, Doña Manuela de Ibarra, to represent him in a lawsuit before the Ecclesiastical Vicar Judge. The lawsuit concerned a chaplaincy branch under his responsibility, as well as all his other legal disputes and actions.
Doña Manuela de Ibarra substituted the power she held from Don Francisco Aguilar y Santos to Don Antonio de la Fuente.

Don Pedro Antonio de Iribarren, a native of Orán in the Kingdoms of Spain and a resident, granted power to Don Manuel de Molina, a resident of León (Nicaragua). This power allowed Molina to request the examination of witnesses before the Lay or Ecclesiastical Court in León, concerning Iribarren's knowledge and freedom of status, with the original information to be returned to him.

people_involved: Doña Ana Rita Gómez de Lara
summary: Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla and his wife Doña Ana Rita Gómez de Lara obligated themselves for 300 pesos of cacao to the Royal Treasury. This amount was for the office of Regidor and Depositario General, which Bonilla had acquired at auction on March 16, 1774, and whose title was confirmed on June 30 of the same year. Doña Joaquina López del Corral acted as guarantor.
Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla exhibited 176 pesos 5 1/2 reales of silver. The Governor subsequently cancelled 213 pesos of the obligation.

people_involved: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora
Don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
Teniente Coronel don José Joaquín de Nava
summary: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora, legitimate daughter of the deceased Don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora and Doña Francisca de Arburola, revoked the general power she had granted to Don Juan de Sierra, with whom she had married. Sierra had been absent for about ten years due to a rumor in the city that he was married in the Kingdom of Lima. Manuela then granted general power to Teniente Coronel Don José Joaquín de Nava to handle all her lawsuits and to collect an inheritance she was due in Málaga, Spain, as the only daughter of Don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora, who was interim Governor of the province.

people_involved: Teniente Coronel don José Joaquín de Nava
summary: Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla granted special power to Teniente Coronel Don José Joaquín de Nava to vindicate him from any charges resulting from secret or public investigations in the Royal Audiencia of Guatemala. Once vindicated, Nava was to obtain for Bonilla the title of Regidor Depositario General of the city. Nava was also empowered to collect 300 pesos from Don Francisco Ortiz, Bonilla's former attorney, which Don Manuel Molina, a resident of León, had issued in Bonilla's favor.

Don José Francisco de Arleguí, widower of Doña Bárbara Madriz, and Don Gregorio de la Calle, husband of Doña Micaela Alvarado (daughter of the deceased Doña Bárbara and Don Miguel de Alvarado), settled a dispute extrajudicially. Arleguí had administered Micaela's assets, and friendly accounts showed some grievances against him. Gregorio, on behalf of his wife, donated 50 cattle, 3 mules, 9 mares, 14 horses, and other unspecified goods to Francisco.
Don Francisco Aguilar y Santos and José Mi- (details incomplete in text).

A cacao hacienda in the Valle de Barbilla, with approximately 1300 trees, was sold for 3 reales per tree. This sale represented the legitimate inheritance for doña Bárbara's son. A penalty of 800 pesos was stipulated for any party failing to uphold the agreement.

people_involved: Teniente Coronel don José Joaquín de Nava
summary: Cristóbal de Ocampo filed a lawsuit against Miguel García on February 19, claiming he had paid 225 pesos to Teniente Coronel don José Joaquín de Nava and 70 pesos to himself on García's behalf. García denied the debt, stating it was already satisfied, and they agreed to settle and withdraw the action.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco
summary: Don Cayetano Salmón Pacheco, son of Sargento Mayor don Dionisio Salmón Pacheco and doña Francisca Serrano de Reina, executed his will. He was married to doña Ana Teresa del Fierro and named his four living daughters—María Mercedes, María de los Dolores, María Ramona, and Cruz Juana de Dios—as his heirs, with his brother-in-law don Fermín Mondragón as albacea.

Don Manuel Benito Fajardo and his wife doña Felipa García sold a mulata slave named Ramona García, approximately 30 years old, to don José Antonio Jiménez for 200 pesos plata. Doña Felipa García had inherited Ramona from her deceased mother, doña Clemencia Muñoz.

people_involved: don Félix José García y Sancho
summary: Don Félix José García y Sancho sold a mulatillo slave named Francisco García, approximately 14 years old, to don Manuel Benito Fajardo for 172 pesos plata. Francisco was part of the estate of his deceased wife, doña Clemencia Muñoz, and after an adjudication, Félix José returned an excess amount to the albacea.

On January 7, 1773, Don Benito Fajardo, his wife doña Felipa García, and don Pedro Fernández acted as guarantors for don Juan Francisco de Bonilla, the Depositario General and Regidor of Cartago, for 1000 pesos. Fajardo and García were responsible for 500 pesos, and Fernández for the remaining 500 pesos.

On January 7, 1773, don José Antonio García, don José Manuel García, and doña Cecilia Escalante y Paniagua also acted as guarantors for don Juan Francisco de Bonilla for 1000 pesos. Don José Antonio García was responsible for 500 pesos, and the other two for 250 pesos each, though doña Cecilia later withdrew her guarantee.

On January 13, 1773, don Juan Francisco de Bonilla and his wife doña Ana Rita Gómez became debtors for 2000 pesos to the city's deposit fund, which Bonilla administered as Depositario General. Don José Antonio García and don José Manuel García acted as their guarantors.

On January 24, 1773, don Julián Azofeifa, Alcalde Provincial and Regidor, committed to pay 152 pesos and 1.5 reales plata to the four minor children of the deceased Juan Paulino Alvarado. This action canceled a previous deed from May 22, 1773, made in favor of José Miguel Ruiz and his wife Simona Delgado.

On January 24, 1773, don Manuel Felipe de Arleguí committed to pay 100 pesos to the chaplaincy managed by Beneficiado don Ramón de Azofeifa, the Cura of Chinandega. This chaplaincy was previously under the care of Manuel Felipe's deceased brother, don Hermenegildo de Arleguí.

On January 31, Pedro Jesús Hernández donated 100 pesos and a jacón horse as arras to his fiancée, María de las Nieves Chavarría. María de las Nieves, an orphan, later declared on October 14, 1778, that she received these items from her husband's albacea, as Pedro Jesús died 24 hours after their marriage.
On February 5, doña María Cecilia Castillo, widow of don Juan Francisco Lafons Vidor, donated a cacao hacienda named La Chacona in the Matina valley to her son, Rafael Ceferino Castillo.

On February 11, doña Antonia Guzmán sold a 12-year-old mulata slave named Ana Efigenia Guzmán to doña Manuela de Ibarra, wife of the absent don Francisco Santos, for 200 pesos de plata. Ana Efigenia was born in Antonia's house and was the daughter of another slave owned by Antonia.

On March 15, Antonio Meneses Araya leased a canoe on the Río Reventazón for 5 years, agreeing to pay 3 tercios of cacao annually. He also committed to transport hacienda owners and their cargo for 300 pesos annually, and other individuals for two tercios of cacao per load or person.

people_involved: Teniente Coronel y Gobernador don Juan Fernández de Bobadilla
summary: On March 18, Teniente Coronel and Gobernador don Juan Fernández de Bobadilla granted special power of attorney to don Francisco Navera, Treasurer Judge of the Royal Coffers of Nueva Guatemala. This power allowed Navera to present attestations of Bobadilla's services to His Majesty the King and request a promotion.

On April 29, doña María Francisca Velazco, who had married don Marcos de Alvarado three days prior, requested that her own capital contribution to the marriage be specified. This was to prevent future disputes, as her husband was a widower of doña María López del Corral.

Experts Don José Miguel Porras and Don Felipe de Arburola were appointed to appraise goods for Don Marcos. The appraisal totaled $2049, 3 reales, which was increased by 500 pesos from a husband's personal funds.
Don Marintiliad Antosos de Alvarado, Cura and Vicario of Cartago, granted general power of attorney to Don Domingo Nicolás Galarza, a Notary and resident of León, Nicaragua.

Don Marintiliad Antosos de Alvarado granted special power of attorney to Don Félix de la Campa, a Procurador numerario of the Real Audiencia of Guatemala. This power was for collecting 'novenos de los diezmos' and 183 annual pesos assigned to Alvarado for his administration of the Curato in Cartago.

Pedro Jesús Hernández, gravely ill, made his will. He declared that he had illicit relations with María de las Nieves Chavarría, his future wife, after a promise of marriage, resulting in her pregnancy. He named their unborn child as his sole heir, with provisions for masses for his soul if the child did not survive or was not baptized. Don Antonio de la Fuente was named executor.

Brothers Cristóbal, Gabriel, Nicolás, and Juan Ramírez formalized the sale of a piece of land near Cartago to María Gertrudis Molina. The land had previously been sold verbally by their deceased parents to Juana Oviedo, who then sold it verbally to Molina.

Don José Miguel García made his will, detailing his family, including his wife Doña Antonia Masís and eight surviving children. He listed his enslaved people and made provisions for his orphaned nieces, Teresa and Micaela García, and for masses for his soul. He also mentioned freeing the enslaved person María Manuela the previous year and named his wife and Don Manuel Felipe de Arleguí as executors.

Don Francisco Aguilar y Santos and Doña Manuela de Ibarra sold the cacao harvests from their properties in 'La Puente' in Matina to Don Pedro Alcántara Zamora. The negotiation was effective from March 17th to July 22nd, with the tenant paying 800 pesos in two installments: 400 pesos in April and the remainder in August.

Manuel Molina and María del Carmen González became obligated for 500 pesos to the capellanía founded by Diego Isidro de Aguilar, whose chaplain is Presbítero don Andrés Fernández and patron is don Manuel Carranza. After Jacinto Cascante withdrew his guarantee, Molina and González mortgaged two houses in Cartago and a cacao hacienda in Matina, in addition to previously offered properties.

A codicil was added to the will of José Cayetano Castillo on July 15. The original will had been granted on June 4, 1777, before Don José Miguel Porras, who was a Regidor and Alcalde ordinario of second vote in Cartago.

Doña Antonia Guzmán granted freedom to her 13-year-old enslaved woman, Maria Manuela de la Trinidad, after receiving 200 pesos. Maria Manuela was born in Doña Antonia's house to another enslaved woman owned by Doña Antonia, named Andrea.
Juan Matías Carmona became obligated to Doña Cecilia Castillo for the three-year lease of a cacao hacienda named 'La Chacona' in Matina.

Don Bartolomé García Miranda, Notary of the Holy Office, and Pedro Manuel Salguero made an agreement not to claim any value from each other in the future. They stipulated that anyone violating this pact would pay a 50 peso fine, to be used for the wax of the Blessed Sacrament of the local parish and delivered to the Mayordomo of the Confraternity.

Doña María de Quesada, a widow, made her will. She declared her son, Manuel Quesada, as her heir and appointed Don Joaquín de Orizmuno as her testamentary executor. She had been married to Don Manuel Antonio Cárdenas, and they had no children together.

locations: El Bejuco del valle de Matina
summary: Doña Lucía de Alvarado, a widow, leased a cacao hacienda she owned in El Bejuco del valle de Matina to José Fermín Calvo for five years. The annual rent was 100 pesos of cacao, to be delivered in Cartago.

people_involved: Don José Antonio de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Doña Manuela Baeza, widow of Don Pedro Alvarado, provided a dowry letter for her daughter, Antª de Alvarado, wife of Don José Antonio de Alvarado y Jirón. Don José Antonio received 793 pesos 6 reales as his wife's paternal inheritance, 300 pesos as a donation from her uncle Fray José Francisco Baeza, and 520 pesos 2 reales as a dowry from Doña Manuela. He also added 500 pesos of his own as arras, which included a 15-year-old enslaved 'negrita' named Isidora, valued at 200 pesos.

Doña Baltasara Madriz, a widow, leased a cacao hacienda named 'La García' in Matina to Pablo Francisco Cubero for five years, with an annual rent of 150 pesos of cacao to be delivered in Cartago. A margin note indicates Baltasara canceled this obligation on October 20, 1883.

José Antonio García, needing to travel to Matina, granted a special and transferable power of attorney to his wife, Doña Romualda Ramírez. This power allowed her to receive and grant the corresponding deed to the Franciscan Convent of Esparza for 250 pesos and its interest, a sum they had offered to lend.

Don José Antonio de Oriamuno, Lieutenant Governor of Heredia, recognized a 500 peso cacao obligation from three capellanía branches, previously held by the deceased Antonio Miguel Hernández and his wife María Carranza, on their house and chacara. These obligations included funds for Nuestra Señora del Rosario of Cartago's Parish, the Confraternity of Nuestra Sra. de Concepción, and a capellanía recited by Presbítero don Francisco Robredo. To secure the principal and 5% interest, four caballerías of land in Oricuajo and the livestock there were mortgaged.

José Felipe and Francisco Hernández, sons of the deceased Antonio Miguel Hernández and María Carranza, took charge of the guardianship of their three younger siblings: Rita Quiteria, María Josefa del Rosario, and Diego Nicolás. They also assumed administration of each minor's inheritance, valued at 683 pesos 6 reales per child.
Tomás Alvarado sold a cacao plot in Barbilla del valle de Matina to Alonso Porras for 180 pesos of cacao.

Don Gregorio Castro, a resident of Villa Nueva and husband of Doña Feliciana Pacheco, claimed the inheritances for his wife and his sister-in-law, Marta Pacheco. These inheritances, from their deceased parents Don Félix Pacheco and Doña Antonia Sarmiento, had been under the care of their tutor, Don José Nicolás Chavarría, due to their minority at their mother's death.

people_involved: Don José de los Santos Bolaños
summary: Don Antonio Rodríguez, Don Félix Zamora, and Don José de los Santos Bolaños, residents of Heredia, became guarantors for Eduardo, Julián, and Pedro Arcia, also from Heredia. The Arcia brothers were imprisoned in Cartago for contraband, accused by Don Tomás López del Corral, the tobacco supplier for the province, Nicoya, and Nicaragua.

Don Alonso Porras (son) requested to be released from responsibility for 600 pesos of cacao, which belonged to a chaplaincy he was obligated to for the soul of his deceased father, Don Alonso Porras. This chaplaincy corresponded to Beneficiado Don Ramón de Azofeifa, the priest of Chinandega. The 600 pesos were charged to his pasture in El Burro, which he sold to Don Fernando Ant? de Arleguí, who took over the encumbrance.

José Santos Bolaños and Juan Manuel Solís, residents of Heredia, guaranteed Eduardo Arcia, also from Heredia, for the value of an embargo. The Provider of the Royal Monopolies of Granada, Nicoya, and Bagaces had seized 10 mules, a horse, and various tools from Arcia. These items were returned to him by the General Depositary and Alderman of Cartago, Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla, pending the resolution of the contraband case against him.

people_involved: Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral
Presbítero Don José Antonio de Bonilla
summary: Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral committed to pay 420 pesos of silver plus 5% interest for a chaplaincy that Don Tomás Benito Hidalgo was previously obligated to, and which belonged to Presbítero Don José Antonio de Bonilla. She mortgaged a mill in the outskirts of Cartago and her dwelling house.
Don José Martínez sold a cacao plantation in Matina, specifically in a place called Pontezuela, to Don Gregorio de la Calle for 90 pesos. The plantation bordered land belonging to the Ibarra family.

Doña Manuela Baeza handed over 793 pesos and 6 1/2 reales to her son, Rafael de Alvarado. This money was his inheritance from his father, Don Pedro de Alvarado, and Doña Manuela had been holding it as his guardian.

Don Rafael and Don José Antonio de Alvarado, who are brothers, granted general power of attorney to Don Juan Dionisio Pacheco. This was to pursue a lawsuit they had initiated against Don Joaquín de Alvarado concerning the full satisfaction of their inheritances from their deceased parents.

Sebastiana Zúñiga, a widow and resident of the Bagaces valley, gave power of attorney to her brother-in-law, Manuel Morera, a resident of Nicaragua and currently residing in Cartago. This was for him to handle a pending appeal in the government court to declare null and void the sale of iron and cattle made by Don José León de Bonilla, the Lieutenant of Esparza, which the Provincial Mayor Don Julián de Azofeifa had bought as an asset.

Don José Perie, a Captain of Infantry and Major Adjutant of the Madrid plaza, and newly appointed Governor of this province, granted general power of attorney to Don Manuel de Molina, a resident of León (Nicaragua).

Don José Perie granted general power of attorney to Don Mariano Ezeta Duda Goitia, Senior Official of the Court of Accounts, and to Don Juan Manuel de Zelaya, lawyer of the Royal Audience and general advisor of the royal tobacco monopoly, both residents of Guatemala. This was specifically to obtain the approval of his title as Governor before the Royal Audience and to be given possession of the position.

people_involved: Capitán don José Romualdo de Oriamuno
Capitán don Romualdo José Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Don José Perie presented his guarantors for residency: Captain Don José Romualdo de Oriamuno, Captain Don Pedro Aymerich, Don Tomás, Captain Don José Antonio Jiménez, Captain Don Romualdo José Muñoz de la Trinidad, Don Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla, Captain Don Francisco Antonio Pérez, Don Juan Agustín Porras, Don Isidro Jiménez, and Don Antonio Rodríguez. The first five were residents of Cartago and the others from Villa Vieja, with each responding for 250 pesos of silver.
Don José Antonio Jiménez and Don Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla, in addition to their previous guarantee, also guaranteed Governor Perie concerning the court of intestates.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don José Antonio de Oriamuno
B” Don José Francisco Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Sargento Mayor Don José Antonio de Oriamuno and his wife Doña María Catarina de Ibarra made a codicil to their closed will and a previous codicil granted before the Governor in 1775. They modified the chaplaincy for their grandson Don Juan José Oriamuno, reducing the number of masses and noting 500 pesos spent on his studies to be deducted from his father's inheritance. They also changed the executor from B” Don José Francisco Alvarado y Jirón to Capitán Don José Antonio.
Don José Uriza and his wife, Doña Mónica López del Corral, owe 200 pesos plata.

people_involved: Teniente Coronel Don José Joaquín de Nava
Presidente Gobernador y Capitán General de este Reino
summary: Don José Antonio Jiménez and his wife, Doña Petronila Rodríguez Robredo, received 14346 pesos, 6 reales, and 3 cuartillos in goods from Teniente Coronel Don José Joaquín de Nava for safekeeping and sale. Nava had been notified to appear before the President Governor within 90 days. José Miguel García and Doña Antonia Masís served as guarantors for this arrangement.

people_involved: Teniente Coronel Don José Joaquín de Nava
summary: Don Antonio de la Fuente, acting on a power of attorney from Don José Joaquín de Nava (dated June 11, 1781, from Granada to Governor Don Juan de Flores), canceled the deposit agreement with Don José Antonio Jiménez. The letter also authorized Don José Antonio Jiménez to cancel a deed granted by Jerónimo Flores.

people_involved: Jerónimo de las Mercedes y Flores
Teniente Coronel Don José Joaquín de Nava
Presidente Gobernador y Capitán General de este Reino
summary: Jerónimo de las Mercedes y Flores, a resident of Villa Vieja, declared he held 1199 pesos and a cuartillo in goods belonging to Teniente Coronel Don José Joaquín de Nava. After an accounting, he paid Nava 70 pesos and discounted 10 pesos, leaving 1119 pesos and a cuartillo under his care, which included a debt from Juan Silverio Villalta. He was to hold these funds until the President Governor decided on Nava's case.

people_involved: Jerónimo de las Mercedes y Flores
summary: Don José Antonio Jiménez, using the power of attorney mentioned in a previous deed, canceled the agreement with Jerónimo de las Mercedes y Flores regarding the goods held for Don José Joaquín de Nava.

people_involved: Teniente Coronel Don José Joaquín de Nava
Presidente Gobernador y Capitán General Don Martín de Mayorga
summary: Teniente Coronel Don José Joaquín de Nava declared that he was notified on May 6 to leave the city within 15 days and appear before President Governor Don Martín de Mayorga within 90 days, as per a Royal Order. He committed to presenting himself, unless prevented by a hernia and inflammation or other accidents, and Don Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla acted as his guarantor.

José Manuel de Aguilar sold a piece of land in 'Ciénega del Junquillal' to Pedro Lizondro for 9 pesos cacao. The land was given to Aguilar by the heirs of Juan Rafael Ramírez, who had appropriated land previously sold by their deceased uncle, Marcos Chinchilla, to Francisco Javier de Siles, Aguilar's father. The deed included a detailed description of the land's boundaries.

Pedro Lizondro sold the piece of land he acquired in the previous deed, along with three poró wood fences and a round wooden shed, to Hipólito Cristiano Morales for 150 pesos cacao. The property included a ditched pasture that was not part of the sale.
On December 18 of the same year, Hipólito Cristiano Morales returned the purchased property to Pedro Lizondro because he was unable to pay for it.

Cristóbal, Nicolás, Juan, and Manuel Gabriel Ramírez, along with their other siblings, sold a piece of land to Teresa Ruiz, widow of Juan Francisco Soto, for 30 pesos cacao. The land, where Teresa Ruiz already had possession, was originally granted to their ancestors by former Governor Chirino and inherited from their parents. The payment was intended to complete the guardianship of their sister, María Cayetana.

people_involved: Doña María Josefa Muñoz de la Trinidad
Doña Dominga Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Don José Manuel Hidalgo granted a dowry to his future spouse, Doña María Josefa Muñoz de la Trinidad, an orphan and daughter of the deceased Doña Dominga Muñoz de la Trinidad. The dowry included assets received from Doña María Josefa's tutor, Don José Antonio de Oriamuno, such as her deceased mother's house (valued at 1000 pesos plata) and a 13-year-old mulatilla named Luisa.

An enslaved man named Marcos Fallas was valued at 200 pesos, and an enslaved mulata named Juana María and her son Pedro Corrales were valued at 175 pesos. These valuations contributed to a total inventory value of 4392 pesos 3 reales.

people_involved: Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno
don Francisco Esteban Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno, as Síndico general of the Convento de San Francisco, founded a chaplaincy with a principal of 1800 pesos in cacao currency. This foundation was based on an inter vivos donation of 1800 cacao trees to don Francisco Esteban Muñoz de la Trinidad, located on the La Arburola and La Jiménez haciendas in the Matina valley, with the condition of funding the chaplaincy upon his death.

people_involved: Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno
summary: On August 31, 1779, Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno, Síndico, noted that the finca supporting the chaplaincy had deteriorated by 400 pesos. Consequently, the principal and the obligation of the tenant, don José Miguel Velazco, needed to be reduced, requiring a new deed.

people_involved: doña Juana de Soto y Barahona
summary: Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla granted power of attorney to don Tomás López del Corral to collect 300 pesos plata from don Manuel de Córdoba, Procurador of the Audiencia of Guatemala, for Cabildo office expenses. López del Corral was also authorized to collect a sum from Presbítero don Francisco Javier Quijada in Nicaragua, which was owed to don Gabriel Muñoz and passed to Bonilla as part of his wife's inheritance from her mother, doña Juana de Soto y Barahona.

Don José Miguel Velazco and his wife doña Antonia Josefa Marín obligated themselves for 1800 pesos cacao at 5% interest to the Convento de San Francisco, related to the previously founded chaplaincy. They mortgaged 4000 cacao trees located in the Matina valley as security.

people_involved: Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno
summary: On August 31, 1779, Capitán don José Antonio de Oriamuno, Síndico, stated that the principal of this chaplaincy was reduced to 1400 pesos due to the deterioration of the mortgaged finca. The tenant, don José Miguel Velazco, was required to issue a new obligation for the reduced sum, and the original obligation was cancelled.

people_involved: Capitán don José Romualdo de Oriamuno
summary: Don José Rafael de Alvarado received a dowry letter for his wife, doña Josefa Bartola de Oriamuno, from her parents, Capitán don José Romualdo de Oriamuno and doña Antonia Manuela de Alvarado. The dowry included a house, an enslaved mulata named Josefa Petronila, and one hundred heads of cattle, totaling 1309 pesos plata.

people_involved: Licenciado don José Nicolás Salmón Pacheco
doña María Josefa Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: On January 11, 1779, don Manuel Hidalgo sold an enslaved mulatillo named Pedro Corrales, son of his enslaved woman Juana María, to Licenciado don José Nicolás Salmón Pacheco for 100 pesos plata. The sale was granted before Gobernador don José Perie, noting that the mulatillo had been previously purchased by the tutor of doña María Josefa Muñoz de la Trinidad with a resale price restriction.

people_involved: doña Engracia Gertrudis de Hoces Navarro
don Tomás de Soto y Barahona
summary: On January 2, 1779, don Manuel Felipe de Arleguí, son of don Manuel Antonio de Arleguí and doña Engracia Gertrudis de Hoces Navarro, made his testament in Cartago. Married to doña Isabel Fernández and childless, he bequeathed his house to his wife and named his siblings, don Francisco, doña Micaela, and doña Juana de Arleguí, along with his wife, as heirs. Capitán don José Antonio Jiménez and his wife were appointed as executors.

people_involved: Fray Francisco Antonio de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Several Curas doctrineros and a Síndico General, representing Fray Francisco Antonio de Alvarado y Jirón, granted power of attorney to don Francisco Díaz de Mayorga, a resident of León, Nicaragua. This power was given to allow Mayorga to collect the synod assigned to them, based on accompanying certifications. The act was granted before Capitán don José Antonio Jiménez, Alcalde Ordinario.

Doña Manuela de Zavaleta, a widow, declared and ratified the sale of the fetus of her enslaved mulata, Manuela, to her daughter Doña Dominga for 25 pesos plata a year prior. The intention was for the child, now a 7-month-old mulatilla named María Catarina, to belong to Doña Dominga's daughter, Juana Nazaria, who received the pesos as a gift. Doña Dominga de Zavaleta accepted the sale on behalf of her daughter.

people_involved: Teniente Coronel don Juan Fern de Bobadilla
summary: Teniente Coronel don Juan Fern de Bobadilla, an ex-Gobernador, granted power of attorney to don Manuel de Molina, a resident of León, Nicaragua. This power allowed Molina to petition the Real Audiencia de Guatemala, stating that the legal term for his residency review had passed without a judge being appointed, and to request a commission to conclude his charge.

Don Joaquín de Alvarado granted power to Antonio de Avendaño to represent him in a lawsuit. The suit was filed by don Rafael and don José Antonio de Alvarado, identified as sons of don Joaquín's father-in-law, don Benlito de Alvarado, and doña Leonida de Ocampo. The Alcalde then passed the protocol to the Escribano who had been given possession.

people_involved: don Francisco (brother of Manuel Felipe de Ada)
summary: Don Manuel Felipe de Ada added a codicil to his will, which was originally dated February 2nd of the same month. In this codicil, he declared additional assets, including a petaca de tabaco owed to don Pedro Fernández. He also revoked a clause concerning his brother don Francisco, redirecting his brother's share to be distributed among don Francisco's four daughters.

Don Luis Demetrio Coronado, a Clérigo, granted power of attorney to don José Miguel Porras, a Regidor of the Ayuntamiento. This power authorized Porras to dispose of Coronado's hacienda named 'la Sarmiento' located in the valley of Matina, allowing him to sell, donate, or alienate it as he deemed fit.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Andrés de Bonilla
don Rafael de Alvarado y Baeza
summary: Several residents from Cartago and Heredia, including Sargento Mayor don Andrés de Bonilla and don Juan Dionisio Pacheco (representing don Rafael de Alvarado and don José Antonio de Alvarado), acted as guarantors for don Antonio de la Fuente, who was appointed Teniente de la Real Caja. The Escribano noted that Pacheco's power of attorney did not explicitly authorize this guarantee, but Pacheco stated he received extrajudicial authorization and would make it valid, also personally guaranteeing de la Fuente.

people_involved: Doña Teresa de Soto y Baraho
summary: Don Julián de Azofeifa obligated himself for 791 pesos plata, a sum corresponding to his mother-in-law, Doña Gertrudis Carazo, from the estate of Doña Teresa de Soto y Barahona, Doña Gertrudis's mother. As Doña Gertrudis is demented, the assets were delivered to Don Julián as the husband of Doña Joaquina García y Miranda, who is the legitimate and sole heir. The assets, received from co-heir don Miguel López Conejo, included 350 cattle, 20 mares, 8 horses, and a colt.

José Lorenzo Meneses, natural son of María Ambrosia Flores, made his will. He declared he was first married to Cayetana Chavarría, with whom he had two living children, José and Angela Meneses. He is currently married in second nuptials to Gertrudis García, with whom he has no children, and noted that Gertrudis was an enslaved woman of Doña Tomasa Gómez.

An unspecified individual is recommended to Francisco Delgado, who holds the title of AS. This recommendation is related to a payment of 300 pesos for the individual's freedom, for which the deed has not yet been granted.
José Cayetano, a natural son, is declared legitimate as part of an inheritance. He is listed among the heirs, alongside two other unnamed children.

people_involved: Doña Tomasa Joaquina López del Corral
summary: Doña Tomasa Joaquina López del Corral, widow of Don Gabriel Marco de Ocaña, grants power of attorney to her son, Don José Miguel de Ocaña. This power allows him to obligate her in loans or guardianships and to act in land measurement proceedings for the Tenorio site in the jurisdiction of Bagaces.

people_involved: Doña Engracia Gertrudis de Hoces Navarro
Presbítero Don José Hermenegildo de Arleguí
Don Tomás de Soto y Barahona
summary: The will of Don Manuel Felipe de Arleguí is recorded. He names his parents, wife Doña Isabel Fernández, and details his property, including enslaved mulatas Antonia and her daughter Ana. His executors are Capitán Don José Antonio Jiménez and his wife, and his heirs include his sisters Doña Micaela and Doña Juana, his wife Doña Isabel, and four nieces, daughters of his brother Don José Francisco.

José Joaquín Coronel Paniaona, acting as attorney for Don Julián Azofeifa and Beneficiado Don Ramón de Azofeifa, leases the Las Camachas cacao hacienda in Matina Valley. The hacienda, containing 3000 cacao trees, is leased to José Vargas y Rivas and José Miguel Calvo for five years, with specific payment terms and an obligation to construct a house.

José Vargas y Rivas owes Don Tomás Barahona 280 pesos of cacao, to be paid in three installments. Don Tomás declares that the payment will be made in Matina, without freight charges, and delivered to Don Francisco Carazo, as it belongs to his uncle Padre Carazo for interest.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Antonio Ramón de Azofeifa
Capitán Don Tomás de Soto y Barahona
summary: Don Ramón Esquivel and his wife Doña Andrea de Azofeifa, residents of Villa Vieja, assume a debt of 100 silver pesos previously owed by the deceased Don Manuel Felipe de Arleguí. This debt is for a chaplaincy served by Presbítero Don Antonio Ramón de Azofeifa, Cura of Chinandega, with Capitán Don Tomás de Soto y Barahona acting as guarantor and mortgaging his house in Cartago.

people_involved: Don Juan Antonio de la Peña
summary: Don Manuel Torre y Romero, a resident of Spain, substitutes Antonio Avendaño with the power of attorney he holds from Don Juan Antonio de la Peña. This substitution is made because Don Manuel needs to depart for another province.
