people_involved: Gobernador Don Juan Fernández de Bobadilla
summary: Doña Manuela Zavaleta's will is recorded, detailing her parents, deceased husband Don José Ginesta, and deceased children José Gabriel and María Josefa. She lists her property, including several enslaved individuals, and mentions that the mulata Isidora was freed after her husband Juan Méndez paid 200 pesos of cacao, with the remaining debt forgiven by the heirs except for Doña Ramona Bermúdez. Manuela also specifies debts to her children and the distribution of enslaved children to her heirs and granddaughter.

Don Antonio de la Fuente granted power to Don Francisco Ortiz, Procurator of the Royal Audiencia of Guatemala, to request permission to appear before the Tribunal. This was to contest executive proceedings initiated by Governor Don José Perie on behalf of Don Antonio's creditors in Guatemala City, concerning debts for which Don Antonio had already made an assignment of assets.

people_involved: Don José de los Santos Lombardo
summary: Doña Guadalupe de Alvarado, widow of Don Pedro José Lombardo, granted power to her father-in-law, Don Francisco Javier Lombardo. This power allowed him to collect the inheritance due to her minor son, Don José de los Santos Lombardo, from the estate of Doña Manuela Josefa Ramos in Panama City, as Doña Manuela Josefa had died there leaving known assets.

José Joaquín Coronel y Paniagua, acting as executor for Don Bartolomé García, leased a hacienda with 1000 fruit-bearing cacao trees to Tomás Alvarado. The hacienda is located in Bonilla del Valle de Matina, and the lease was for 5 years at 100 pesos per year.

Ramona Quesada sold a house in Cartago, measuring 12x6 varas, to José Francisco Valerín for 125 pesos cacao. The property was bordered by houses belonging to Pablo Cubero, José Antonio Rodríguez, María Josefa Gómez, and Felipe Fuentes.

Don Francisco de los Santos and his wife, Doña Manuela de Ibarra, re-assumed a previously litigated censo (annuity/mortgage) of 600 silver pesos at 5% interest, owed to the Convent of San Francisco in Esparza. They mortgaged 3000 fruit-bearing cacao trees and 3000 newly planted cacao trees in the Matina Valley as collateral, with José Gregorio Calvo, Blas Rodríguez, and Doña Joaquina de Ibarra acting as guarantors.

Don José Alonso Porras granted power to Don Juan Manuel Caballero, a resident of Santiago de Veragua, to reclaim a stolen mule. The mule, described as piebald, with a piece missing from one ear, and prone to kicking, was stolen from Cartago and believed to have been sold in Chiriquí along with other stolen items.
Pedro Avila sold a plantation of 1200 cacao trees, 5 years old, located in the Matina Valley next to the hacienda named 'la Arburola,' to Joaquín Romero for 200 pesos cacao.

people_involved: Don Maximiliano Antonio de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Don Pedro José Ulloa sold a house of adobe and tile, with a walled solar, in Cartago to the Beneficiado Don Maximiliano Antonio de Alvarado y Jirón, the city's priest. The property was bordered by houses and solars of Petronila Mesa, Santos Rivera, Doña Teresa Trujillo, and Joaquín Cartín, and included a table and a bed/cot for 150 silver pesos and 100 pesos cacao.

people_involved: Doña Rita López de la Flor
summary: Doña Isabel Fernández, over 25 years old, out of great affection for Andrea Fernández whom she raised as a daughter, donated a house and several pieces of furniture in Cartago to Andrea. The house was bordered by properties of Micaela Hernández, Pedro Manuel Salguero, Doña Rita López de la Flor, and Juan Casimiro Zúñiga.

people_involved: Don Maximiliano Antonio de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: The Beneficiado Don Maximiliano Antonio de Alvarado y Jirón, priest of Cartago, granted general power to Don Bernardo Echaitia Cerezo, or in his absence, to Don Francisco Gómez de Cos or Don Félix Gil, who were Business Agents in the Court and Villa of Madrid.

Don José Antonio de Oriamuno obligated himself for 400 silver pesos at 5% interest to a chaplaincy, for which Presbyter Don José Antonio de Bonilla was the chaplain. This obligation was previously held by Don Marcos de Alvarado, who transferred it to Don José Antonio de Oriamuno in the form of land, cattle, and a plantain plantation in Las Juntas de Landecho.

people_involved: Doña María de Laya y Bolívar
summary: Escribano Don José Romualdo Zamora recorded on February 8, 1786, that Doña María de Laya y Bolívar took over the option related to the obligation previously held by Don José Antonio de Oriamuno. This action resulted in the cancellation of the original obligation.

Antonio de Avendaño and his wife, Lucía Josefa de Badilla, obligated themselves for 50 pesos in cacao currency at 5% interest to Ramón Quesada. This amount represented Ramón's inheritance from his grandmother, which he could not manage due to being mentally incapacitated.
Proceedings were initiated for the opening of the sealed will of Sargento Mayor Don José Antonio de Oriamuno and his wife Doña María Catarina de Ibarra.

people_involved: Doña María Catarina de Ibarra y Calvo
Doña Antonia de Alvarado y Jirón
Doña María de la Encarnación Sancho de Castañeda
summary: Don José Antonio de Oriamuno requested and granted his testament on April 27, 1775, before Governor Don Juan Fernández de Bobadilla, due to the death of his wife, Doña María Catarina de Ibarra y Calvo, on the same day. The testament detailed inheritances for their legitimate sons, Don José Romualdo and Don José Francisco, including enslaved individuals, and made provisions for the freedom of some slaves after their death, established a capellanía, and bequeathed a mulatillo to their grandson, Don Juan José Oreamuno.

On July 21, the executor of Doña Manuela de [tea y] and her heirs, Doña Dominga, Doña Antonia, and Doña Gertrudis Zavaleta, sold a mulata named María Manuela to Presbítero Don José Miguel Sancho, acting as the representative for Don Pedro Puente, for 200 pesos plata. Don José León de Bonilla signed the transaction as the grantor.

people_involved: Capitán Don Juan Miguel López Conejo
summary: On July 19, Don José Antonio Jiménez, acting as the attorney for Doña Ramona de Ibarra, who resided in Nicaragua, sold a house in Cartago to Don José Romualdo Zamora for 450 pesos cacao. The house, previously owned by Don Andrés Bonilla, was described by its boundaries and included a gravamen of 108 pesos cacao for a capellanía belonging to Don Antonio Ramón de Azofeifa. The power of attorney for this sale was granted in Rivas, Nicaragua, on April 10 of the same year.

people_involved: Capitán de granaderos Don Francisco Carazo
summary: On January 19, 1781, Don José Antonio Jiménez, acting as an attorney, cancelled a debt of 342 pesos cacao, receiving the equivalent amount in silver. This transaction, overseen by Captain Don Francisco Carazo, left an outstanding obligation of 108 pesos related to a capellanía.

people_involved: María Antonia (slave of Andrés José Fernández)
summary: Presbítero Don Andrés José Fernández, who had previously granted a joint testament with his mother in 1777, outlines his current will and assets. He orders a capellanía of masses for the Convento de San Francisco, grants freedom to his slave Ana Josefa after his death, and directs that his other slave, María Antonia, be given to his aunt Doña Isabel Fernández for 150 pesos.

people_involved: Capitán Coronel don Romualdo José de Oriamuno
summary: A will or set of bequests is detailed, establishing chaplaincies for the souls of the deceased and his grandfather Matías Trejos. Various goods and animals are distributed to individuals including family members and servants. Don José Antonio Jiménez and Capitán Coronel don Romualdo José de Oriamuno are named as executors.

Don José Miguel Velazco and his wife Doña Antonia Josefa Marín obligate themselves for 1400 pesos at 5% interest to the Convento de San Francisco. This new obligation references a previous one from a 1778 protocol, recorded before Gobernador don José Perie.

By order of Vicario Ramón de Azofeifa, an Escribano cancels an obligation. Doña Antonia Josefa Marín, now widowed from Don José Miguel Velazco, withdraws from the tenancy of haciendas 'la Arburola' and 'la Jiménez'. The principal was replaced and improved by 262 cacao trees, now totaling 1662 trees across 'la Jiménez' and the new 'la Velazco' hacienda.

Doña María Fernández, a widow from Villa Nueva, obligates herself to her minor son, Miguel de Jesús Carranza, for his inheritance from his deceased father, Manuel Carranza. She also takes on an obligation for two other sons she had with Don Vicente Saborío, committing to use the interest for the upbringing and education of all three children.

people_involved: Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral
summary: Don José Sebastián Fernández is appointed Administrator of the Bagaces tobacco tercena by Don Tomás López del Corral. Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral acts as his guarantor, mortgaging her haciendas in Matina valley and a mill in Cartago.
Doña Rosa Madriz, acting as the wife and executor of the deceased Don Tomás López del Corral, cancels the guarantee for Don José Sebastián Fernández after he has satisfactorily rendered his accounts.

Doña Dominga Zavaleta sells Ana Catarina, a 3-year and 3-month-old mulatilla and daughter of her slave María Manuela, to Don Pedro Puente for 132 pesos. Don Gregorio Ignacio Castro acts as the buyer's representative.

Doña Antonia Masís, widow of José Miguel García, obligates herself for 6719 pesos and one real of cacao, representing the inheritance from her deceased husband, to their seven minor children. Each child is to receive 959 pesos and reales.

Don José Miguel Porras, a simple Regidor of the Ayuntamiento, resigns his office before completing his three-year term. He cites personal financial difficulties, the distance of his residence from the city, and the negative impact on his properties and family as reasons for his inability to continue serving.
Don José Antonio de Oriamuno and Don Marcos de Alvarado exchange 106 heads of cattle, moving them between the locations of Las Juntas and Oricuajo, both within the jurisdiction of Landecho.

José Fermín Calvo, a free mulatto, takes on an obligation of 250 pesos of cacao at 5% interest for a chaplaincy of the local parish. This obligation is secured by the cacao hacienda 'la Curita' in Matina valley, previously held by Francisco Flores. Fernando Masís provides a guarantee, mortgaging his own hacienda in Matina.

people_involved: Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral
summary: Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral obligates herself for 200 pesos of silver at 5% interest for a chaplaincy of Presbítero don Fernando de Arleguí, secured by land near the Río Grande. This obligation was previously held by Don Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla, and Doña Joaquina mortgages her Matina Valley properties.

people_involved: Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral
summary: Don Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla, a Colonel of Infantry, declares that the transfer of the chaplaincy obligation to Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral did not proceed due to issues with the land provided to her. As a result, the obligation remains his responsibility.

Doña Micaela Segura leased a cacao hacienda with 1000 fruit-bearing trees in the Matina Valley to Ventura Prado for three years. The lease was for 100 pesos of cacao annually, and the hacienda bordered properties of Félix Cerdas and Soto.

people_involved: Presbítero don Elías Antonio de Arleguí
summary: Presbítero don Elías Antonio de Arleguí obligated himself for 600 pesos at 5% interest in cacao currency for a chaplaincy founded by his late father. The chaplaincy's assets, including a breeding donkey and 30 mares, were received from don José Martín Porras in Poás, with his brother, don Elías Antonio de Arleguí, serving as guarantor.

Don José León de Bonilla sold an enslaved person named José Manuel, described as white with black eyes and straight black hair, for 200 pesos to don Juan Francisco de Bonilla. José Manuel was noted to be free of various ailments and vices, and the price was the same as when he was adjudicated to the seller as the executor of doña Manuela Zavaleta.

Doña Antonia Zavaleta sold an enslaved person named José Antonio, approximately 9 years old, white with reddish hair and black eyes, to don José Nicolás Chavarría for 115 pesos in money. José Antonio was described as free of illness, vice, or defect that would hinder his service.

people_involved: Don Romualdo José Muñoz de la Trinidad
Beneficiado Cura Juan de Jesús Urrutia
summary: Don José Antonio de Alvarado and doña Ana de Alvarado obligated themselves for 100 pesos silver at 5% interest, funds that belonged to the parish church and were previously held by doña Manuela Zavaleta, then passed to don Romualdo José Muñoz de la Trinidad as the church's Mayordomo. They hypothecated 4 caballerías of land with 400 heads of cattle in Las Piedras, Bagaces. A marginal note from June 26, 1827, indicates that C. Rita Alvarado, daughter of the deceased C. José Antonio Alvarado, satisfied the principal and interest, leading to the cancellation of the obligation.

people_involved: Doña Juana Rosalía Muñoz de la Trinidad
Teniente Coronel don Romualdo José Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Don José Gregorio de Oriamuno provided a dowry for his wife, doña Juana Rosalía Muñoz de la Trinidad, which included various goods received from her parents, Teniente Coronel don Romualdo José Muñoz de la Trinidad and doña Tomasa Josefa Gómez. The dowry totaled 937 pesos 2 reales silver, plus 100 pesos in arras, and included a house, furniture, and clothing.

Nicolasa Cabrales granted freedom to her eight enslaved people, whom she had inherited. The freed individuals were Tomasa (60), Antonia (40), Juana Antonia (22), José Antonio (20), Juan José (19), Manuel de la Concepción (18), José de Jesús (16), and Dionisio de Jesús (4).

people_involved: Teniente Coronel don Romualdo José Muñoz de la Trinidad
Sargento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad
Doña María Teresa de La Espada
Doña María Micaela Muñoz de la Trinidad
Doña María Teresa Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Teniente Coronel don Romualdo José Muñoz de la Trinidad, son of Sargento Mayor don Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad and doña Ana Josefa de Arburola, made his testament. He was first married to doña María Teresa de La Espada, with whom he had two daughters, doña María Micaela and doña María Teresa. After his first wife's death, he left his and his daughters' assets with his mother-in-law, doña Inés de Castro, due to financial difficulties from his wife's long illness and losses from a small ranch. He incurred debts to don Mateo Cardoso, Domingo Zapata, and Manuel Díaz for his relocation. He later married doña Tomasa Josefa Gómez.

Gómez de Lara redeemed 200 pesos plus 200 pesos in interest, which he paid to Matías Díaz de Corcuera, the Syndic of the Convent of León. The remaining 325 pesos were redeemed using assets from Gómez de Lara and his first wife, which were entrusted to his brother-in-law, Presbítero Manuel de Larga Espada, for the redemption.

Around 1760 or 1761, Gómez de Lara had 700 pesos worth of goods sent to the Matina valley for sale by José Miguel García. During this period, a Zambo Mosquito invasion occurred in the valley, resulting in the complete loss of all the goods.
Gómez de Lara arranged the marriage of his daughter, Juana Rosalía, to Captain Gregorio de Oriamuno.
Gómez de Lara's second wife inherited 14 pesos upon the death of her relative, Manuel Trinidad Fallas.

Gómez de Lara instructed Juan Tomás González to sell various goods, including eight arrobas of garlic and three of cilantro, transported on five mules, in Chiriquí. Juan Tomás González has not returned since this mission.

On November 10, Julián Azofeifa and Félix Sáenz, imprisoned in Cartago for flogging Sergeant Juan Cabrera in Bagaces, were ordered to be transferred to the Castillo de San Juan de la Laguna in Nicaragua. Due to difficult terrain, Tomás de Soto y Barahona and José Fermín de Mondragón acted as guarantors, allowing them to travel without shackles and ensuring their delivery to Lieutenant General Ignacio Mestre in Granada.
On November 11, Julián de Azofeifa granted general power of attorney to José Antonio Porras.

On November 13, the widow Tomasa Joaquina López del Corral donated an 8-month-old mulatilla named Josefa Rudecinda, daughter of her slave Petronila, to her daughter Manuela Petronila. This donation was a gift Manuela Petronila had received from a benefactor, and Tomasa's sons, José Miguel de Ocaña and José Francisco Corona, consented to it.

On November 16, Bernardino de los Angeles Alvarado and his wife Francisca Javiera Castillo, residents of Ujarraz, became obligated for 1635 pesos and 4.5 reales of cacao. This sum belonged to Félix and Manuela Badilla, inherited from their deceased father, José Miguel Badilla, who was Francisca's first husband.

On November 24, Captain Francisco Carazo obligated himself for 200 pesos plata at 5% interest for a chaplaincy, with Presbítero Fernando Antonio de Arleguí as the chaplain. This debt was previously held by Colonel Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla, who had offered land in El Salvaje as security. Carazo then mortgaged eleven caballerías he owned in Santa Eulalia, along with livestock and other assets, which he had purchased from Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla.
On November 25, 1780, Presbítero Fernando Antonio de Arleguí cancelled the obligation related to the chaplaincy.

On November 26, Francisco de Arleguí obligated himself to his three daughters, Benita, Antonia, and María Josefa de Arleguí, for 214 pesos and one real of silver each, inherited from the deceased Manuel de Arleguí. He also committed to delivering the share of his other daughter, Andrea, who was married to Fernando Chavarría.

On December 6, Manuela Fernández de la Pastora stated that after public edicts were posted for bids on communal pastures in Poás, she made an offer for the Tambor pasture. The Cabildo granted her the right to lease it for an annual rent of 25 pesos plata, based on a value of 500 pesos, obligating her to the public funds.

On December 7, Manuela Fernández de la Pastora granted power of attorney to José Insaurrandiaga, a Sublieutenant of militias from Panamá. This power was to inquire before the Tribunal of the Inquisition of the Kingdom of Peru about the status of the case against José Garino, a native and resident of Cuenca, for having entered into marriage with her.

A legal case was brought against Garino, who used the alias Juan Sierra, for bigamy. He was already married in Cuenca and had children with an unnamed woman in 'esta ciudad' before fleeing the province when his previous marriage was revealed.

Mariano Fonseca, representing the residents of Quebrada Seca and Río Segundo, granted power of attorney to Don Francisco Ortiz. The purpose was to enforce a court sentence against Don Francisco Antonio Pérez, compelling him to surrender land titles he held, which were acquired at the expense of the aforementioned residents.

Doña Dominga and Doña Antonia Zavaleta formally acknowledged a debt (censo) of 150 pesos at 5% interest to the Cofradía de la Concepción. This debt was inherited from their deceased mother, Doña Manuela Zavaleta, and was charged against their residence located south of the Convento de San Francisco.
Don José Antonio de Oriamuno, as the Mayordomo of the Cofradía de la Concepción, officially cancelled the debt (censo) that Doña Dominga and Doña Antonia Zavaleta had recognized on December 10.

Antonio Arizaga, a free mulatto, settled his accounts with Don Esteban Venegas, agreeing to owe 528 pesos 6 reales in cacao. A larger debt was partially paid by transferring ownership of a house in Puebla, valued at 150 pesos plata, to Don Esteban Venegas.

Doña Lucía de Alvarado made her testament, detailing her family, including her deceased parents and husband, and her living and deceased children. She listed her assets, including a mulatta slave named Josefa and her two children, and established a chaplaincy for her son Don Gregorio Javier, naming Don José León Bonilla and Don Carlos Ruiz as executors.

people_involved: Doña Lucía de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Doña Lucía de Alvarado y Jirón formally established a chaplaincy of 10 recited masses, endowing it with her cacao hacienda 'el Bejuco' in the Matina valley, valued at 1000 pesos. She designated her son, Don Gregorio Javier, who was studying for the priesthood, as the chaplain, with the patronato passing to him upon her death and then to other family members or the Convento de San Francisco.

people_involved: Don José Antonio Soto Mayor y Utrera
summary: Don José Antonio Soto Mayor y Utrera, who was single, made his testament. He named his deceased parents, acknowledged his natural son José Vicente as his heir, and appointed Miguel Cárdenas as his executor. He also mentioned his sister, Doña María Mercedes Soto Mayor.

Doña Antonia Romero, widow of Don Francisco Zavaleta, committed to her four minor children (Antonia, José Francisco, Juana Rita, and José Zavaleta) for 707 pesos from their paternal inheritance. This sum included 507 pesos her husband inherited from his mother, Doña Manuela Zavaleta, and an additional 200 pesos Doña Manuela had acknowledged owing Don Francisco in her testament.
Don José Romualdo Zamora was recorded as the Public Scribe of the Cabildo and Government in the year 1750.

Several Curas doctrineros and a prosíndico, representing various pueblos, granted power of attorney to don Mateo Mantilla, a resident of León, Nicaragua. Mantilla is authorized to collect their annual stipends from the Royal Treasury in León and to demand an accounting from don Francisco Mayorga, the General Syndic of the Franciscan order, for stipends from the previous year (1779) that have not yet been paid.

people_involved: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora
Bachiller don Rafael Severino Ramírez de Arellano
Alférez Real don Antonio de la Fuente
summary: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora granted power of attorney to Bachiller don Rafael Severino Ramírez de Arellano, a native of León and resident of Guatemala, and secondarily to don Antonio Talavera, a Procurator of the Royal Audiencia. This power was for general litigation, specifically for a contentious case in appeal, initiated by Alférez Real don Antonio de la Fuente.

people_involved: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora again granted power of attorney, this time primarily to don Francisco Ambrona, secondarily to Bachiller don Severino Ramírez, and thirdly to don Antonio Talavera, all residents of Guatemala. This power was for general litigation, specifically for the contentious case against don Antonio de la Fuente, which had been decided in her favor but was now under appeal by him.

people_involved: María Josefa de las Mercedes Garvanzo y Guerrero
summary: Manuel Jerónimo Maroto and his wife, María Josefa de las Mercedes Garvanzo y Guerrero, committed to pay don Pedro Fernández 6 tercios of cacao. One tercio was for money lent for their wedding, due in March of the current year, and the remaining five tercios were for a debt owed by Maroto's deceased father from a 1773 deed. They assumed this debt in exchange for a plantain plantation in Ujarraz that belonged to the deceased father.

Doña Gertrudis Zavaleta, to settle a debt of 100 pesos principal and 50 pesos interest (in cacao currency) owed by her deceased mother, Doña Manuela Zavaleta, to a chaplaincy of Beneficiado don Manuel Antonio Sandoval, sold an enslaved person named Leonardo, 7 years old and white-skinned. Don José Antonio Jiménez, acting as Sandoval's attorney, purchased Leonardo for 100 pesos silver (or 150 pesos cacao), agreeing to pay the principal and interest to Sandoval.
Capitán don Joaquín de Alvarado granted general power of attorney for all his lawsuits to Antonio de Avendaño, who was the Commander of mulatto militias.

people_involved: doña María de la Luz Salmón Pacheco
summary: Doña Antonia Josefa Mondragón, legitimate daughter of deceased don Pedro Jiménez de Mondragón and doña Francisca de Inza, made her will. She named her natural son, don José Fermín de Mondragón (married to doña María de la Luz Salmón Pacheco), as her heir, and Capitán José Joaquín Coronel as her executor. She also mentioned raising her granddaughter, doña María del Carmen.

people_involved: Cura don Maximiliano Antonio de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Doña Gabriela Morales, a widow, exchanged property with don Faustino de Ugalde and his wife doña Rita de Alvarado, and don Juan Gutiérrez and his wife doña María de Alvarado. Doña Gabriela gave a lot with a house (formerly belonging to Cura don Maximiliano Antonio de Alvarado y Jirón), a small house she lived in on the same lot, and 50 pesos in cacao currency. In return, she received a house on half a lot in Cartago, settling an earlier agreement from about four years prior with the deceased Cura Maximiliano.

people_involved: Doña Antonia de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Doña Antonia de Guzmán y Echavarría sold an enslaved girl named Manuela Josefa, approximately 10 years old, with light eyes and 'loro' color, to don José Antonio Jiménez for 150 pesos in cash. Manuela Josefa was the daughter of Andrea, who was also an enslaved person belonging to Doña Antonia.

people_involved: Doña Antonia de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Doña Antonia de Guzmán y Echavarría, legitimate daughter of don José de Guzmán and doña Antonia Echavarría, made her will. She was single and mentioned that her mother had donated an enslaved woman named Andrea Susana to her. Andrea Susana had three children while in her possession: Juan Pablo, Francisco Antonio, and Manuela Josefa.

Approximately six years prior to the current registry date, an unnamed slave owner, facing indigence, revoked a previous grant of freedom to her slaves, which had been issued before Gobernador Bobadilla. She had sold Manuela Josefa and Ara Efigenia (to Doña Manuela Ibarra), and another slave had been freed by her father.

Don José Antonio Jiménez was appointed as the executor for an unnamed individual. This individual's will stipulated that her slaves, being her only assets, would gain their freedom after they attended to her during her illness, arranged her burial, and covered the costs of their freedom documentation.

people_involved: Doña María Josefa de Barros y Muro
Parents of Doña María Josefa de Barros y Muro
summary: On March 8th, Doña María Josefa de Barros y Muro granted freedom to her slaves: María Josefa, 40, and her sons Manuel Valentín, 27, and José Antonio Mateo, 22. María Josefa had been inherited from her parents, and her children were born while in Doña María Josefa's possession.

people_involved: Mother of Presbítero don Andrés Fernández
summary: On March 9th, Don José Antonio Jiménez, acting as executor for the deceased Presbítero don Andrés Fernández, sold the slave María Antonia to don Antonio de la Fuente for 150 pesos. Although the Presbítero's will intended María Antonia for his aunt, doña Isabel Fernández, for funeral costs, María Antonia refused to serve doña Isabel and chose don Antonio as her master.

On March 14th, Don José Romualdo de Oreamuno, a Colonel, sold the slave Josefa Petronila, aged 19-20 and daughter of Casimira Ibarra, to Ramón Antonio de Azofeifa, the interim Cura of Cartago, for 250 pesos. Josefa Petronila had previously been offered as a dowry to his daughter, doña Bartolamé Oreamuno, upon her marriage to the absent don Rafael de Alvarado, obligating Don José Romualdo to compensate his daughter for the sale.

people_involved: Beneficiado don Maximiliano Antonio de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: On April 1st, Don Juan Gutiérrez and don Faustino de Ugalde, husbands to co-heirs doña María del Carmen and doña Ana Rita de Alvarado, granted power to Licenciado don Félix José Galarza of León. This power allows him to collect the unpaid annual synod from the Royal Coffers of León, which was owed to the deceased Beneficiado don Maximiliano Antonio de Alvarado y Jirón, who passed away on October 25, 1776, for towns he administered in Cartago.

On April 1st, Don José Antonio Jiménez sold the 34-year-old slave Ramona to Ramón Antonio de Azofeifa, the interim Cura of Cartago, who was acting as an agent for doña Rita Tejedor of Pueblo del Viejo, Nicaragua. The sale was for 219 pesos, and Ramona had originally been purchased from doña Clemencia Muñoz.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan Francisco de Bonilla
summary: On April 1st, Capitán don Juan Francisco de Bonilla sold the 10-year-old slave Hipólito to Ramón Antonio de Azofeifa, the interim Cura of Cartago. Azofeifa was acting as an agent for Presbítero don José Antonio Posadas, a resident of León, and the sale was for 200 pesos.

On April 5th, Antonia Josefa Chavarría granted freedom to her 38-year-old slave, Juana Dominga Chavarría. Juana Dominga had been donated to Antonia Josefa by her mother, María Calvo, when Juana Dominga was a child.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan Francisco de Bonilla
summary: On April 7th, Capitán don Juan Francisco de Bonilla, serving as Regidor and Depositario General, delegated his general power of attorney to Capitán José Joaquín Coronel Paniagua. This was due to Bonilla's necessary absence from Cartago to Matina for services to the Royal Crown.

people_involved: Capitán don Juan Francisco de Bonilla
summary: On April 13th, Capitán don Juan Francisco de Bonilla sold the 32-year-old slave Toribio Gudiño to don José Romualdo Zamora, who was acting as an agent for Presbítero don Demetrio Coronado, for 312 pesos. Toribio Gudiño had been previously acquired from don Pedro Aymerich, and the sale was notarized by Alcalde Ordinario Luis Arnesto de Troya due to the Escribano's involvement.

Doña Antonia Flores, sole heir of her deceased mother Doña Angela de Alvarado, leased a cacao plantation with 1500 trees in the Valle de Matina, Barbilla, to José Fernando Masís for six months. Masís also acted as a guarantor for Don Fernando Chavarría, who owed Doña Antonia 7.5 tercios of cacao for the months of June and July.

people_involved: Don Pedro Antonio de la Fuente
summary: Doña Ana Rita Madriz, as principal, and Don José Antonio Jiménez, as guarantor, obligated themselves for 382 silver pesos to Don Antonio de la Fuente. This debt originated from Don Pedro Antonio de la Fuente for three slaves, and Doña Ana Rita, as his mother-in-law, took responsibility for it, hypothecating her house in Cartago and 1000 cacao trees in Matina.

Don Antonio de la Fuente, the creditor, canceled the debt mentioned previously, having received the sum from the guarantor Don José Antonio Jiménez, following an execution established against the debtor.
Don José Antonio de Alvarado granted general power of attorney for lawsuits to Don Antonio de la Fuente, as Don José Antonio was preparing to travel to Bagaces and Nicaragua.

people_involved: Presbítero Don José Nicolás Salmón Pacheco
summary: Doña Teresa Fierro, widow of Don Cayetano Pacheco and guardian of their four minor children, obligated herself for 223 pesos and 4 reales in cacao currency. This sum represented the inheritance due to her children from the deceased Presbítero Don José Nicolás Salmón Pacheco, with her daughters Mercedes, Ramona, and Cruz Pacheco being named.

people_involved: Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba, a cleric, granted general power of attorney to Coronel Don Gabriel Lacayo, a resident of Granada. This power was specifically to collect ten pesos in interest from Don Gabriel Espinosa, due on June 1st, for a principal of 200 pesos that had been transferred to Espinosa and was previously held by Don Juan Manuel's deceased father-in-law, Don José Fernández Montezuma.

people_involved: Presbítero Don José Nicolás Salmón Pacheco
summary: Doña Estéfana Pacheco, widow of Don Domingo Alvarado, obligated herself for 1845 pesos at 5% interest for two chaplaincy branches. These chaplaincies were previously managed by her deceased uncle, Presbítero Don José Nicolás Salmón Pacheco, and were founded for him and his father, Don Juan Dionisio Pacheco, with their patronato belonging to her lineage and interest now paid to the Convento de San Francisco. The branches were secured by a cacao plantation in Matina and other assets.

Presbítero Don Félix Alvarado, at the instance of his mother Doña Estéfana Pacheco, was admitted by the Ecclesiastical Court to take charge of 1383 pesos 6 reales of cacao from the obligation. He received these funds as capellán of the chaplaincies to find new tenants, and consequently, he canceled the obligation.

José Joaquín, Antonia, and Juan Romero received the assets left by their deceased brother Cayetano Romero, which were in the possession of Pedro Lizondro. They obligated themselves for any debts that might arise against these inherited assets.

people_involved: B. Don Maximiliano Antonio de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Pedro Lizondro, as principal, and Ventura Lizondro, as guarantor, obligated themselves for 200 pesos at 5% interest. This debt was originally owed by Don Faustino Ugalde to the deceased Beneficiado Don Maximiliano Antonio de Alvarado y Jirón, with interest to be paid to Doña María del Carmen Alvarado, his sister, or her eldest son. Pedro Lizondro hypothecated his house in Cartago, 100 cows, 20 mares, and a chacra in Ujarraz.

people_involved: Presbítero Don José Nicolás Salmón Pacheco
summary: The numerous heirs of the deceased Presbítero Don José Nicolás Salmón Pacheco, who died intestate, sold a mulatto boy named Pedro Corrales for 100 pesos to Don Tomás López del Corral, as they could not afford to keep him. The deceased had acquired Pedro Corrales from Don Matías Hidalgo. The sale was signed by several heirs and the buyer.

people_involved: Doctor Don Pedro José Chamorro Soto Mayor
summary: Doña María Fernández sold a mulatto slave named Juan José Chavarría, approximately 22 years old, to Don José Francisco de Alvarado, who was acting as attorney for Doctor Don Pedro José Chamorro Soto Mayor, Dean and Canon of the Cathedral of León. Doña María Fernández had previously purchased the slave from Don Juan Mejías and his wife Doña Micaela Sáenz, residents of Villa Nueva.

Doña Francisca Javiera Castillo, a native of Ujarraz, made her will. She was married three times and had children from her first two marriages. Her will detailed her slave Juan José, properties in Agua Fría (Matina) and Cartago, and named Antonio de la Fuente as executor, with her two living children as heirs.

Don Felipe Gallegos, a Sergeant from Guatemala residing in Cartago, granted power of attorney to Don Manuel Molina of León. The purpose was to obtain the Bishop's permission for Gallegos to marry Doña Lucía Guadalupe de Alvarado, a widow from Cartago who was previously married to Don Pedro Lombardo.

Lieutenant Colonel Don Juan Fernández de Bobadilla, serving as interim Governor due to the proprietary Governor Don José Perie's absence, presented his residency guarantors. A list of prominent individuals, including Captain Don Francisco Carazo and Don José Antonio Jiménez, served as his sureties.

Miguel Fuentes and his wife Paula Castillo mortgaged their house and lot in the suburbs of Cartago for 100 pesos of cacao currency. This obligation was in favor of the chaplaincy founded by Don Juan Bautista de Bruno, with Bachelor Don Manuel Antonio Sandoval as chaplain, and the funds were received from Sandoval's brother and attorney, Don José Antonio Jiménez.

Captain Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla granted power of attorney to Don Manuel José Gómez, a resident of Nicaragua. The purpose of this power was to liquidate outstanding accounts that Bonilla had with Don Manuel José Molina, a merchant from León.

Don Tomás López del Corral sold an enslaved man named Diego to Don Juan Flores, a Captain in the fixed battalion of Guatemala. Diego, described as 'loro' colored, was acquired by López del Corral at a public auction on August 26th, having been captured from the English on the North coast of Matina. The slave was to be sent to the buyer in Granada.

Don Tomás López del Corral sold an enslaved man named José Antonio, approximately 24 years old, to Captain Don Francisco Carazo, acting as attorney for Presbyter Don José Antonio Posadas. José Antonio was acquired by López del Corral at a public auction after being captured from the English on the North coast of Matina.

Magdalena Casasola, widow of Gaspar Angulo, leased a cacao plantation named San Benito in Matina, containing 1743 fruit-bearing trees, to Sebastián Camaño. The lease was for three years at 175 pesos of cacao annually, without affecting the ongoing probate case of Gaspar Angulo.

Don Juan Miguel López Conejo and his wife Doña Ana Micaela Carazo undertook an obligation for 228 pesos 4 reales of silver to the San Francisco Convent. This debt was transferred from Commander Antonio de Avendaño via a house and lot, which was previously occupied by Joaquina López del Corral. The obligation was later cancelled on July 15, 1793, by José Prieto, the Convent's Syndic.

people_involved: José Gordiano Fernández de la Pastora
Manuela Josefa Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Joaquín Romero, a single man over 25, donated a cacao plantation of 1200 trees in the Matina Valley to Don José Gordiano Fernández de la Pastora. Romero had purchased this land from Pedro Avila in May 1795, and made the donation out of affection and a sense of justice.

people_involved: José Gordiano Fernández de la Pastora
Manuela Josefa Fernández de la Pastora
summary: José Joaquín Romero made a further donation to Don José Gordiano Fernández de la Pastora, in addition to the previous one. This donation included 6 cows and 4 pregnant mares, which Doña Manuela Josefa accepted on behalf of her son.

Doña Francisca Miranda, with permission from the Mayor due to her husband's absence, sold an 18-year-old 'mestiza blanca' enslaved woman named Antonia Apolinaria to Don Luis de Cueto, the Chief Constable of León. Antonia Apolinaria was born and raised in Miranda's house.

Don Marcos de Alvarado, widower of Doña María López del Corral, was ordered to return 471 pesos 1 real in the probate case of his father-in-law, Don Tomás López del Corral. This amount represented an overpayment Marcos de Alvarado had received in his wife's dowry, and he delivered it to the Chief Constable.

Don Marcos sold his house in Cartago to his brother-in-law, don Tomás López del Corral, for five hundred pesos. Don Tomás returned twenty-eight pesos seven reales to don Marcos and committed to distributing the remaining funds to the other heirs. The house was bordered by properties belonging to doña Mariana Alvarado, Capitán don Pedro Aymerich, doña Ramona Bonilla, and doña Manuela Angulo.

Gregorio Brenes, son of Gregorio Brenes and Petronila de Quirós, made his last will and testament. He was married to Efigenia Falcon, with whom he had five children: Juan de Dios and Domingo Antonio (living and married), and José Cayetano, Manuel José, and Juan José (deceased and unmarried). He owned houses in Tejar and on doña Francisca Pacheco's plot in Cartago, and named don José Antonio Jiménez as an executor.

people_involved: Presbítero don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
Alférez Real perpétuo y Maestre de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba
don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
Presbítero don Fernando Antonio de Arleguí
R. P. Presidente actual de dicha conquista
summary: Presbítero don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba, son of don José de Casasola y Córdoba and doña Agueda Pérez del Muro, made his will, detailing several capellanías under his charge. He declared his three slaves, Gabriel, Mónica, and Enrique, free, and made provisions for his servant María Francisca's children and a boy named José Antonio Rivera. He also mentioned his role as tutor to his nephews don Félix and don Bernardo Miranda, and a debt from the Talamanca conquest from the year '73.

people_involved: Presbítero don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
R. P. Presidente actual de dicha conquista
summary: Presbítero don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba's accounts from the 1673 Talamanca conquest showed a deficit of 422 pesos plata. He ordered 600 pesos of this amount to be delivered in livestock, as agreed with the current President of the conquest.

people_involved: doña Rosa de la Madriz Linares
summary: Gravely ill, don Tomás López del Corral granted power to testate to Presbítero don José Antonio Bonilla and his wife, doña Rosa de la Madriz Linares, also naming them as executors.

people_involved: doña Rosa de la Madriz Linares
summary: The testament of the now deceased don Tomás López del Corral was executed by his appointed representatives, Presbítero don José Antonio de Bonilla and his widow, doña Rosa de la Madriz Linares. His assets included eight slaves and he had been assigned 1000 pesos annually for three years for his work collecting tobacco for His Majesty. His eight children were named as heirs.

Don Juan de Alvarado paid his mother-in-law, doña María Francisca del Corral, 140 pesos plata. This payment was equivalent to one-tenth of the dowry doña Ana Josefa de Alvarado (Juan's deceased wife and María Francisca's daughter) brought into their marriage, settling the arras.

Don Juan de Alvarado and doña Ana Josefa de Alvarado donated an 11-year-old enslaved girl named Tomasa to Capitán don Pedro Aymerich, who was the stepfather of doña Ana Josefa. Tomasa had been received as part of a dowry, as recorded in a previous deed.

people_involved: doña María Josefa de Barros y Muro
don Domingo Antonio Rapela del Villar
summary: Doña María Josefa de Barros y Muro, a widow, made her will, declaring her enslaved person, Manuel Valentín Barros, as her heir due to his care for her. She also granted freedom to her enslaved woman María Josefa and her son Manuel Valentín Barros, and bequeathed her room to her niece Susana.

Doña Francisca del Corral, with the consent of her daughter doña Ana Josefa de Alvarado and son-in-law don Juan de Alvarado, donated a 13-year-old enslaved girl named María de Jesús to her second husband, don Pedro Aymerich. María de Jesús had been purchased from doña Francisca Miranda.

Don Antonio de la Fuente, acting on behalf of Presbítero don Luis Demetrio Coronado, sold a cacaotal hacienda named 'la Sarmiento' and an adjacent plot in Valle de Matina to don Rafael Ceferino del Castillo and his brother don Florencio del Castillo. The payment was received from their mother, doña María Cecilia del Castillo, as the buyers were minors. The power of attorney for Coronado was originally granted to José Miguel Porras in 1779 and then substituted to Antonio de la Fuente in Villa Vieja in 1787.

Gertrudis Casasola, widow of Benito Gómez, obligated herself to pay 430 pesos, 2 reales, and 4 cacao grains to her five minor children. This sum represented their paternal inheritance, with each child receiving 86 pesos, 8 manos, and 4 cacao grains.

people_involved: Alférez Real don Antonio de la Fuente
summary: Several Franciscan priests and curas doctrineros from various towns, along with Alférez Real don Antonio de la Fuente (representing Fray Francisco Antonio de Alvarado), granted power of attorney to don Benito José de Abaunza, Administrator of Alcabalas in León, Nicaragua. This power was for collecting their annual stipends from the Royal Coffers.

Benito Valerino, a free mulatto from Puebla, obligated himself for 670 pesos, 1 real, and 6 cacao manos to Antonia Polonia and José Tomás Garvanzo, minor children of the deceased Juana de Dios Garvanzo. This sum was their inheritance from two pieces of land in Valle de Matina, and Valerino mortgaged 1200 fruit trees.

José de los Santos Chavarría made his will, declaring his future children with his wife, doña Ana Josefa Frutos, as his heirs. He appointed his brother Diego Martín Chavarría as albacea, with Presbítero don Fernando Arleguí as a substitute.

Presbítero don José Antonio Bonilla, acting as albacea for don Tomás López del Corral, called upon don Sebastián Fernández de Urrutia to pay 473 pesos plata. This amount was owed from the sale of Castilian clothes by López del Corral to Urrutia.

people_involved: Presbítero don Juan José de Oreamuno
doña Juana Muñoz de la Trinidad
don Romualdo Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Don Gregorio José de Oreamuno granted special power of attorney to his brother, Presbítero don Juan José de Oreamuno. This power allowed Juan José to represent Gregorio's wife, doña Juana Muñoz de la Trinidad, in asserting her rights as an heir in the estate of her father, don Romualdo Muñoz de la Trinidad.
Doña Manuela de Ibarra leased land.
Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla deposited a cacao hacienda named La Robredo (also known as La Ibarra) in the Matina valley for five years, at an annual rate of 200 pesos, to Joaquín Catalán.

people_involved: Doña Florentina de Aragón y Bobadilla
summary: Don Juan Fernández de Bobadilla granted power of attorney to his wife, Doña Florentina de Aragón y Bobadilla, to make his will, declaring her his sole heir. He also appointed her and Lieutenant Rafael Gutiérrez de Cárdenas as executors. He requested freedom for his slave, Antolino, due to his good behavior and loyalty.

Doña Florentina de Aragón, as the principal, along with Don Antonio Sáenz de Bonilla and Don José Antonio Jiménez as guarantors, secured the financial responsibility incurred by her deceased husband, Don Juan Fernández de Bobadilla, during his tenure as Interim Governor. They requested the lifting of the embargo placed on his assets by Ordinary Mayor Don Francisco Carazo.

people_involved: Doña Florentina de Aragón y Bobadilla
summary: This entry records the will of Don Juan Fernández de Bobadilla, which was granted by his wife, Doña Florentina de Aragón y Bobadilla, based on the power of attorney documented on folio 6 of this protocol.

Don Manuel José Hidalgo committed not to harm anyone or gamble any value. He agreed to pay 200 pesos to the Confraternity of the Most Holy Sacrament for breaking the first commitment and 100 pesos to the Confraternity of the Souls in Purgatory for the second.
On December 3, 1781, Don Manuel José Hidalgo cancelled the previous obligation he had undertaken.
Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla, a General of Cartago, sold a slave named José Manuel for 230 pesos to Don José Antonio Posadas, with Don Ramón Antonio de Azofeifa acting as Posadas's attorney.
Don Ramón Antonio de Azofeifa, acting on behalf of Don José Antonio Posadas, purchased a 22-year-old slave named Francisco Guzmán from Doña Antonia Guzmán for 120 pesos.

Blas de Jesús, son of Lucas de Jesús and Lorenza de Artavia, and married to Dominga Jiménez, made his will. He declared his children (Pedro José Segundo, José Rafael, José Hipólito, José Alejandro, Eusebia Casimira, and an unborn child) as heirs. He also bequeathed 50 pesos of cacao to María Antonia, a girl he raised, and 6 pesos each to his sister Francisca Josefa and his mother-in-law. His wife and Commander Don Antonio de Avendaño were named executors.
Doña Juana García sold an 11-year-old slave named Pedro Pablo García for 159 pesos to Royal Ensign Don Antonio de la Fuente, who was acting on behalf of Don Fernando Chamorro.
Doña Juana García sold two slaves, María Rufina (28 years old) and her 7-year-old daughter Manuela de los Angeles, for 400 pesos to Don Manuel Gómez, a resident of Managua.

Don Miguel Gómez, as debtor, and Don Andrés Bonilla, as guarantor, committed to Doña Juana García for 400 pesos, which Gómez would pay within four months upon his return from the Kingdom of Tierra Firme. This debt stemmed from the sale of slaves to Gómez, and the slaves were deposited with Bonilla to be returned to García if Gómez failed to pay.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Juan José de Oriamuno
summary: Don Félix Joaquín Meneses, a native of Havana and widower of Doña Gabriela Arleguí, made his will. He declared his children Antonia, Engracia, Paulino, Antonia Manuela, and Juana as heirs, granting a larger share (one-third of his assets plus his 52% share) to the first three and the last child. Presbyter Don Juan José de Oriamuno was named executor, with his daughter Antonia as a substitute.

An unnamed woman obligates herself to Nicolás and Lorenzo González, minor sons of an unnamed father, for 234 pesos 2 reales of cacao. This debt originates from the maternal inheritance due to the minors in equal parts.
On September 19, 1786, Lorenzo González declares having received 117 pesos 1 real from his father, representing his share of the maternal inheritance that his father was administering.

Don Tomás de Soto Barahona, son of Don Antonio Barahona and Doña Petronila de Hoces, grants power to testate to his nephew, Captain of Grenadiers Don Francisco Carazo. Don Francisco Carazo and Doña Petronila Carazo are named as executors, with included documents addressing the validity of this power.

Don José Antonio Bonilla, executor of the late Don Tomás López del Corral (who was a Tobacco Supplier for the Royal Tobacco Monopoly in this province and Granada), grants power to Don Roberto Sacasa or, failing him, Don Dionisio Guerrero, residents of Granada, to liquidate and settle outstanding accounts related to the tobacco business.

people_involved: Teniente Coronel don Juan Agustín Porras
Capitán de Infantería don Juan Flores
Teniente Coronel don Juan Fernández de Bobadilla
summary: Several residents of Villa Vieja, including Teniente Coronel don Juan Agustín Porras, act as guarantors for Captain of Infantry don Juan Flores. This guarantee is for his responsibility as Interim Governor of the province, a position conferred upon him following the death of Teniente Coronel don Juan Fernández de Bobadilla.

people_involved: El Presbítero don José Antonio de Bonilla
summary: Presbyter Don José Antonio de Bonilla, acting as executor for Don Tomás López del Corral, grants general power of attorney to Don Manuel Antonio Arana, a resident of the city of Granada.

Don Francisco Carazo, acting as attorney for Don Tomás de Soto Barahona, executes a will. He names Doña Gertrudis, Micaela, Petronila (nieces of Don Tomás), Doña Joaquina Miranda and her husband Don Julián Azofeifa, and himself as heirs, specifying inheritances including slaves and a farm in Ujarraz. The will also grants freedom to four slaves: José Antonio, Francisca Cabral, Rita, and her daughter María Manuela.

people_involved: El Presbítero don Luis Demetrio Coronado
summary: Presbyter Don Luis Demetrio Coronado grants general power of attorney to his brother-in-law, Don Romualdo Zamora.

Gregorio Brenes, son of Gregorio Brenes and Petronila de Quirós, and married to Epifania Segura y Falcón, executes his will. He names his living and deceased sons as heirs and makes a donation of animals to María Leonor and her children, whom he raised. Don José Antonio Jiménez is appointed as executor.
Juan de Dios and Domingo Antonio Brenes petition for the distribution of assets in accordance with the previously granted will, seeking to take possession of their respective inheritances.

Josefa Cartín, natural daughter of Micaela Cartín and widow of Antonio de Torres, executes her will. She names her son Manuel Francisco and the children of her deceased sons José Antonio and Joaquín as heirs, and allocates a portion of her estate to Antonia Josefa and José de Jesús, whom she raised. Don Felipe Arburola is named as executor.

Doña Gertrudis Sarmiento, legitimate daughter of Don José Nicolás Sarmiento and Doña María Catarina de Rosa, and widow of José Miguel Chavarría, executes her will. She declares her eight children as heirs, and her son Nicolás Anacleto is appointed as executor.

people_involved: El Presbítero don José Antonio Robredo
Señor Alférez Real don Antonio de la Fuente
summary: Presbyter Don José Antonio Robredo grants general power of attorney to Royal Ensign Don Antonio de la Fuente, as Robredo is preparing to depart for the province of Nicaragua.

people_involved: Don Manuel de la Torre y Romero
summary: Don Manuel de la Torre y Romero, a native of Spain, grants general power of attorney, prioritizing Don Juan Gil del Barrio, then Licenciado Don Mariano Ezeta, and finally Don José Angel de Navas, all residents of Nueva Guatemala.

people_involved: El Depositario General don Juan Francisco de Bonilla
Doña Ana Rita Gómez de Lara
El Presbítero don Francisco Antonio Robredo
summary: General Depositary Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla and his wife Doña Ana Rita Gómez de Lara obligate themselves to Presbyter Don Francisco Antonio Robredo for two chaplaincies. One, founded by Don Domingo Chavarría and managed by Don Francisco Cubero, was secured by a house auctioned to the Bonillas; the other, managed by Doña Clemencia Muñoz, passed to them upon her death.
Don José Antonio de Oriamuno grants special power of attorney for lawsuits to Don Pedro de Irivarren, who resides in Guatemala.

people_involved: El señor Beneficiado don José Miguel Sancho
summary: Beneficiary Don José Miguel Sancho grants power of attorney to Don Pedro de Irivarren, in a manner similar to the previous entry.

Pascual Bejarano, legitimate son of Antonio Casasola and María Nicolasa Bejarano, and married to María Marín, executes his will. He declares his wife, his living son Félix, and any future legitimate children born during their marriage as heirs. Don Manuel Quesada is named as executor.

people_involved: Don Manuel de la Torre y Romero
summary: Don Manuel de la Torre y Romero, a native of Spain, grants general power of attorney to Don Manuel de Molina, a resident of León.

people_involved: Don Manuel de la Torre y Romero
summary: Don Manuel de la Torre y Romero grants general power of attorney, on one hand to Don Manuel José de Zea, a resident of Masaya, and on the other hand to Don Manuel Antonio de Triana.

people_involved: Presbítero Don José Antonio de Bonilla
Beneficiado Don José Antonio de Alvarado
summary: Don Fernando Madrigal, acting as guarantor, requested the cancellation of a 100-peso debt obligation. The principal of this debt, originally owed to a chaplaincy under Presbítero Don José Antonio de Bonilla, had been transferred to the new Chaplain, Beneficiado Don José Antonio de Alvarado, Royal Priest of Esparza.

Don Benito Rodríguez, a resident of Pueblo Viejo de Nicaragua, committed to repay 144 pesos to the General Depositary, Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla, within one year. This sum was a loan provided by Bonilla.

Juan Miguel Gutiérrez, son of Juan José Gutiérrez and Ana Gertrudis Granados, made his will. He was married to Juana Micaela Írola, with whom he had six children. He named his wife and children as heirs, and José Nicolás Villalobos as his executor.

Due to financial difficulties caused by her husband's long absence, Doña Manuela Ibarra sold a cacao plantation owned by her husband, Don Francisco de los Santos, in the Matina valley for 700 pesos to Don Manuel José García.

Don Juan Flores, interim Governor, granted power of attorney to his future father-in-law, Don José Alcalá, and Don Pedro Saelves y Salas, to formalize his marriage to Rosalía de Alcalá y Guerra in Spain. This was due to the difficulties he faced in traveling to Spain himself.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Juan José de Oriamuno
summary: Doña Ana Josefa de Alvarado, wife of Don Juan de Alvarado, granted power to her cousin, Presbítero Don Juan José de Oriamuno, to make her will. She named her legitimate daughter, María Feliciana, as her heir, and appointed her attorney and Don José León de Bonilla as executors.

people_involved: Presbítero Don José Antonio de Bonilla
summary: Don Juan Manuel Paniagua, as debtor, and Don Fernando Madrigal, as guarantor, committed to pay 100 pesos to a chaplaincy founded by Doña Cecilia Vázquez Coronado, which was under the care of Presbítero Don José Antonio de Bonilla. The debt was secured by Paniagua's house and cane fields near Río Segundo.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Fernando Antonio de Arleguí
summary: Doña Dominga Guzmán y Chavarría made her will, having no forced heirs. She bequeathed part of her assets to her servants and the remainder for alms and masses for her soul. Presbítero Don Fernando Antonio de Arleguí was named executor.

people_involved: Beneficiado Don Antonio Ramón de Azofeifa
summary: Don Julián de Azofeifa, Provincial Mayor and Alderman, granted power to his brother, Beneficiado Don Antonio Ramón de Azofeifa, to make his will. He declared his wife, Doña Joaquina Miranda, and his siblings as heirs, and appointed his attorney and Don Fermín Mondragón as executors.

Don José Mateo García sold an enslaved person named José Miguel García, 25 years old, for 240 silver pesos to Don Rafael Gutiérrez de Cárdenas, Lieutenant of Infantry of the fixed Battalion of Guatemala. José Miguel García was inherited by Don José Mateo García from his mother, Doña Juana García.

Manuel Cayetano and Pedro Valerín, brothers, committed to pay 66 pesos and 1.5 reales to the General Depositary Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla. This sum originated from their father's debt for clothes, and they pledged their services in the Matina valley's troop to amortize it.

Don José Antonio Arnesto and his wife, Doña Antonia Masís, declared their enslaved person, Juan de Ocampo, free. This manumission was granted in exchange for Juan de Ocampo returning 30 pesos, part of his original purchase cost from the public auction of Don Miguel Unanue's assets.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Juan José de Oriamuno
summary: Doña Josefa de Alvarado's will was formally granted by Presbítero Don Juan José de Oriamuno, acting under the power of attorney he had received on September 18th.
María Francisca Calvo is mentioned as the widow of José Masís.

Don Antonio de Oriamuno sells a pasture, measuring 370 by 238 varas and located next to Río Seco and bordered by the Toyogres river, to Don Manuel Torre y Romero for 140 pesos. This pasture was originally acquired through a purchase from Don Miguel Alvarado and Doña Luisa Guzmán, his wife.

people_involved: Don Pedro Antonio de la Puente
summary: The Royal Ensign, Don Anton de la Fuente, grants special power of attorney to Don Francisco Ramo, a resident of Villa de Nicaragua. This power is for Ramo to collect a sum of pesos from the estate of the deceased Don Pedro Antonio de la Puente, which Don Anton de la Fuente paid as guarantor for de la Puente for clothing he was lent.

Don José Antonio Chavarría and his wife, Doña Vicenta Ibarra, take on two chaplaincy obligations transferred to them by Don Francisco Ramo, tied to a farm in El Tejar near Aserrí de Villa Nueva. One obligation benefits the Franciscan Convent of Cartago for 250 pesos, and the other benefits Presbyter Don Francisco Antonio Robredo for 200 pesos. They mortgage their house and a cacao plantation in Matina as security.

Don José Mateo García sells Agustina, an enslaved woman around 15 years old and daughter of Manuela, to Doña Cecilia Durán, a resident of Villa de Nicaragua, for 235 pesos. García also grants power of attorney to Don Pedro de Iribarren, residing in Guatemala, to collect 670 pesos from the General Court of Deceased Estates in Guatemala for food supplied to the deceased Governor Don Manuel Soler.
Don Julián de Azofeifa's will is granted through his attorney. Further details are referenced in folio 97, entry of September 27.

people_involved: Presbítero Don José Antonio de Bonilla
summary: Presbyter Don José Antonio de Bonilla grants his general power of attorney to the Royal Ensign and Alderman of Cartago, Don Antonio de la Fuente.

people_involved: Don Rafael de Alvarado y Ocampo
summary: Don Rafael de Alvarado y Ocampo obligates himself to pay 60 pesos in cash to Presbyter Don José Antonio Bonilla. This debt originates from a guarantee Bonilla provided for Don Pedro Moreira, a resident of Bagaces, and is due by the end of next April.

people_involved: Don Cristóbal de Ocampo y Golfín
summary: Doña Josefa Alfaro, a resident of Villa Vieja, grants special power of attorney to Don Cristóbal de Ocampo y Golfín. This power is for him to request that her inherited assets, brought into her marriage with her deceased husband Don Manuel Fernández, be excluded from the estate in the ongoing probate case.

Don José Antonio Bonilla, as a debtor, along with his guarantors Don Andrés de Bonilla and his wife Doña María Bolívar, and Don Tomás de Alvarado and his wife Doña María del Rosario, obligate themselves for 1000 pesos to Don Manuel Galisteo, the Administrator of Revenues. This serves as a guarantee for Bonilla to administer a 'tercena' in Bagaces, offered by Don Francisco Argiello, the Tobacco Administrator of Granada.

The Royal Ensign Don Antonio de la Fuente and his wife Doña María Francisca de Alvarado obligate themselves for 100 pesos to the Confraternity of Nuestra Señora de Concepción of the Franciscan Convent in Cartago. This debt was originally owed by Juan Miguel Gutiérrez, who transferred a cacao plantation in the Matina valley to them to cancel his debt, and they mortgage the same property.

people_involved: Don Rafael de Alvarado y Ocampo
summary: Don Antonio de Oriamuno, widower of Doña María Catarina de Ibarra, is constituted as the depositary of 7779 pesos and 1 real, representing the assets of his deceased wife's estate, as per an inventory. This action is taken at the request of his son, Romualdo, who is the heir and executor of his mother. Doña Baltasara Madriz, Doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho, Don Nicolás Ulloa, and Don Rafael de Alvarado y Ocampo serve as guarantors.
José Segura grants power of attorney to his son-in-law, José de los Dolores Sandoval, to collect and receive the assets belonging to his son, Lucas Segura, who died intestate, in Villa de Nicaragua.

José Antonio Sáenz sold a chácara (farm/estate) in the outskirts of Cartago to José Nicolás Camaño for 380 pesos plata (or 570 pesos in cacao), payable within three years. The property included a tiled house, a straw house with a sugar mill, sugarcane plots, oxen, and other items, bordered by the Taras river, José Ramírez's fences, and Sabana Grande. On November 22, 1784, Sáenz acknowledged receiving 138 pesos from Camaño and granted an obligation with a bond for the remaining amount.

Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla, the General Depositary, received 87 pesos 2.5 reales of silver in deposit. These funds represented three horses and various small items belonging to Felipe Jiménez, which were involved in a legal case concerning Jiménez.

Don Gregorio de la Calle, preparing for an expedition to the North Sea, granted power of attorney to Don Felipe Sancho de Castañeda. Castañeda was tasked with representing Calle in legal matters concerning the estate of the deceased Doña Luisa Guzmán, specifically regarding a claim by Calle's wife, Doña Micaela de Alvarado.

people_involved: Don Isidro Jerónimo Pérez de Arellán
Alférez Real Don Antonio de la Fuente
summary: Don Isidro Jerónimo Pérez de Arellán, a resident of Panama departing for there, granted power of attorney to Alférez Real Don Antonio de la Fuente for his local business affairs. De la Fuente was specifically authorized to represent Arellán in the Corregidor's Court of Suitiaba, Nicaragua, for a claim against Don Feliciano Agedrone, Corregidor of Nicoya, concerning unjustly embargoed and appropriated goods.

Don Manuel Hidalgo granted power of attorney to Don José Fermín Mondragón. Mondragón was authorized to formalize and present Hidalgo's accounts as the Mayordomo de propios for the previous year to the City Council of Cartago.

Don José Miguel Chacón, a resident of Villa Nueva, was apprehended by tobacco guard Don Esteban Zamora at Monte del Aguacate while transporting contraband tobacco to Nicaragua. His goods were embargoed, and he was remitted to Administrator Don Manuel Galisteo's court. Galisteo allowed Chacón to post bail, obligating him to pay double the contraband value, court costs, and guard expenses. Chacón mortgaged three mules, twelve cattle, and six mares, with his father-in-law, Don Pedro Nicolás Fernández, as guarantor. On January 28, Galisteo canceled the obligation after Fernández paid 95 pesos 5 reales.

people_involved: Capitán de Infantería Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla
summary: Captain of Infantry Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla granted general power of attorney to Don Juan Gil del Barrio, a resident of Nueva Guatemala.

Don Francisco Pacheco sold an enslaved man named Lucas, approximately 25 years old, to Doña Antonia Mondragón for 100 pesos plata. Lucas had been inherited by Francisco from his father, Dionisio Pacheco. The sale was partly a gesture of goodwill and in reciprocation for benefits received from Doña Antonia's son, Don José Fermín Mondragón.

people_involved: Alférez Real Don Antonio de la Fuente
summary: Doña Juana García, represented by her attorney Alférez Real Don Antonio de la Fuente, sold an enslaved mulatto woman named María Rosalía, 27 years old, and her 5-year-old daughter, María Francisca, to Doña María Cayetana Donaire, a resident of León, for 415 pesos de plata.

people_involved: Alférez Real Don Antonio de la Fuente
summary: Doña Juana García, through her attorney Alférez Real Don Antonio de la Fuente, sold an 11-year-old enslaved mulatto boy named Francisco, born in her house to her enslaved woman Rosalía, to Don Francisco Ignacio de Argúello, a tobacco factor in Granada, for 175 pesos plata.

Don José Fermín Mondragón, acting as the testamentary executor for the deceased Don Julián de Azofeifa, received the assets of Azofeifa's estate in deposit. The inventory of these assets amounted to 4074 pesos 3 reales de plata.

Doña Manuela Josefa Reyes, a resident of Villa Vieja, through her attorney Don Ramón Azofeifa (the city's priest), sold an enslaved mulatto boy named Juan Antonio, 20 years old, born and raised in her house, to Bachiller Don José Antonio Posadas, a resident of León, for 225 pesos plata. An attached authorization allowed Juan Antonio to seek a new master by presenting his value of 225 pesos plata.

people_involved: Alférez Real Don Antonio de la Fuente
summary: Doña Juana García, through her attorney Alférez Real Don Antonio de la Fuente, sold an enslaved mulatto girl named María Rufina, 22 years old, and her 8-year-old daughter, Manuela de los Angeles, to Don Fernando Chamorro Soto Mayor, Administrator of the Royal Mail Revenue in Granada, Nicaragua, for 400 pesos plata.

people_involved: Coronel Don José Romualdo de Oreamuno
summary: Colonel Don José Romualdo de Oreamuno obligated himself for 400 pesos of cacao. This obligation was secured by a house, which was bordered by the properties of Doña Antonia Arleguí to the East and Doña Isabel Fernández to the West.

A house previously owned by Tomás de Soto y Barahona, located next to doña Manuela Ibarra's property and formerly the residence of Presbítero don Cayetano de Arleguí, was valued at 400 pesos due to its poor condition. The property had a chaplaincy imposed on it, requiring a 5% payment to an unknown chaplain.

On February 19, Alférez Real don Antonio de la Fuente and his wife doña María Francisca de Alvarado obligated themselves to doña Juana García for 700 pesos, the price of several slaves they purchased from her. Doña Juana García later cancelled this obligation on August 16, 1785.

On February 21, doña Antonia Romero sold a 13-14 year old mulatto slave named José de los Dolores Zavaleta to Teniente Coronel don Juan de Ayza for 180 pesos. Don Juan de Ayza, the interim Governor of Granada and Commander of San Juan Castle, was represented by his agent don Antonio de la Fuente. An earlier advertisement from December 27, 1781, for the sale of the same slave was included, signed by Joaquín Coronel on behalf of the seller.

On February 21, José Fermín Calvo, a free mulatto from Puebla, committed to maintaining a canoe service at the Reventazón river crossing for five years. He agreed to pay 75 pesos cacao annually to the Fondos de Propios and would receive 300 pesos cacao annually from hacienda owners in the Matina Valley for this transport service, with additional charges for non-hacienda users.

On February 27, Joaquín Romero, also known as Catalán, declared that his sister Antonia had sold a slave named José de los Dolores for 180 pesos. This slave was part of the paternal inheritance for Antonia's minor children, coming from the estate of doña Manuela Zavaleta through her deceased son, Francisco Agapito, who was the minors' father. Joaquín Romero initially took responsibility for this sum for his nephews, mortgaging livestock, but on February 12, 1788, the obligation was transferred to Antonia Romero, who received the sum from Joaquín Romero's widow.

On February 28, Manuel Antonio Jiménez reported the division of assets following the death of his wife, Ignacia Nicolasa Gutiérrez. His stepson, Francisco González, received 272 pesos 3 1/2 reales of cacao as inheritance. Jiménez took responsibility for the remaining 207 pesos 7 1/2 reales to provide for Juana Moscoso, González's wife, and their daughter, as Francisco González had been absent for about 16 years. The obligation was cancelled on October 9, 1795, by Juana Moscoso, identified as Francisco González's wife.

On February 28, José Aguilar, as principal, and Juan de Dios Brenes, as guarantor, obligated themselves for 272 pesos 3 1/2 reales to Juan José de Jesús. This sum represented the minor's inheritance from his maternal grandmother, Ignacia Nicolasa Gutiérrez, and was received from Manuel Antonio Jiménez, Ignacia's widower. Juan José de Jesús is the son of José Aguilar and the deceased Brígida González.

On March 1, Manuel Antonio Jiménez obligated himself to his minor children, Nicolasa, Ventura, and Juan Francisco Jiménez, for 538 pesos 1 1/2 reales of cacao. This sum represented their inheritance from their mother, Ignacia Nicolasa Gutiérrez, who was Jiménez's wife in her second marriage.
On March 7, don Francisco Javier Lombardo, originally from the Kingdom of Tierra Firme, granted general power of attorney to José Joaquín Coronel for his business affairs in the area.

people_involved: Don Juan Domiago de Albisú y Loinaz
summary: Don Francisco Juan de Pasos, a priest in Nicoya, sought a transfer from his current post due to health issues caused by the climate. He aimed for a vacant Deanato in León or another Canonicato within the Obispado of Nicaragua and Costa Rica. To facilitate this, he granted power of attorney to Don Vicente Aguado, Don Simón de Zavala, and Don Juan Domiago de Albisú y Loinaz, all residents of Madrid.

people_involved: Doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho de Castañeda
summary: Lucía Francisca Coto sold a house and lot in Cartago to Doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho de Castañeda for 100 pesos plata. Doña Manuela then donated this property to her enslaved women, Dolores, Cecilia, Ana de Jesús, María Josefa, and Antonia Camaño, who were promised freedom upon her death. However, on December 23, 1786, Doña Manuela revoked the donation due to perceived ingratitude.

people_involved: Don Juan Domingo de Albizú y Loinaz
summary: On March 23, Don Francisco de Paula Soto, Deacon and Secretary to Bishop Don Esteban Lorenzo de Tristán, sought a vacant Deanato or Canonicato in León. As a Spaniard from Jaen, he desired to serve God and the King in America. He granted power of attorney to Don Vicente Aguado, Don Simón de Zavala, and Don Juan Domingo de Albizú y Loinaz in Madrid to manage his application for one of these positions.

On April 1, Captain Don Francisco Carazo, acting as curator for his demented sister Doña Gertrudis Carazo, authorized Don Miguel Candaneo of Chiriquí to sell an enslaved man named Clemente. Clemente, approximately 25 years old, was born in the Carazo household, is married to María de Jesús Moya, and had previously fled from Cartago to Tierra Firme with merchant Don Miguel Gómez.

On April 2, Don Domingo de Endara, a Spaniard residing in Cartago and general attorney for Don Agustín de Gana of Panamá, prepared to depart from Cartago. He transferred his power of attorney to Don Antonio de la Fuente, entrusting him with the management of both his own and Don Agustín's business affairs in the city.

Don Antonio de Bonilla, acting as the depositary for the assets of the "semi fatuo" Don Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla, sold an enslaved mulatto man named Apolinario to Governor Don Juan Flores. Apolinario, about 22 years old and previously purchased by Don Ventura from María Manuela Razero, was sold for 158 pesos and 2 reales plata to cover Don Ventura's debts and maintenance.

On April 12, several friars from various towns and reductions, along with Don Antonio de la Fuente (acting as prosíndico for Fray Francisco de Alvarado), granted power of attorney to Don Luis Cueto, Alguacil Mayor and Regidor of León. This authorization allowed Cueto to collect their synod from the Royal Coffers for the year 1781.

On April 12, Captain Don Juan Flores, the interim Governor and General Commander of arms for the province, granted power of attorney to Don Santiago de Prado, Captain of the militias of León. This authorization allowed Don Santiago to settle Don Juan's government accounts with the Royal Coffers.

Doña Tomasa Gómez de Lara, represented by her attorney Francisco de Paula Soto, sold an enslaved mulato named José Pacheco, approximately 32 years old, to Lieutenant Colonel Manuel Díaz de Gallo. The sale was for 200 silver pesos.

people_involved: Doña Rosa de la Madriz Linares
summary: Doña Rosa de la Madriz Linares sold an enslaved black man named Francisco Corrales, approximately 30 years old, to José Brea, a resident originally from Tierra Firme. The transaction was for 200 silver pesos.

Captain Rafael Gutiérrez de Cárdenas sold an enslaved mulato named José Miguel García, approximately 26 years old, to José Brea for 230 silver pesos. Gutiérrez de Cárdenas had previously purchased José Miguel García from José Mateo García.

An extrajudicial partition of the estate of the deceased María de la Candelaria Cruz was conducted, with appraisers Tomás Solera and Tomás Ruiz. The total estate was valued at 476 pesos 4 reales, including an enslaved mulato named Manuel de Jesús. After deductions, the remaining funds were distributed among her legitimate children and the 'quinto' was divided between her natural son Juan and the enslaved Manuel de Jesús.

María de la Candelaria Cruz granted her will in Quebrada del Tigre, jurisdiction of Villa Vieja, before Judge Juan Miguel Porras. She named her four legitimate children as heirs and bequeathed half of the 'quinto' to her natural son Juan and the other half to her enslaved mulato, Manuel de Jesús. The will also detailed her family history, including her parents and three marriages.
Juan Manuel del Corral signed a receipt for 18 pesos for the funeral and burial services of María de la Candelaria Cruz in Villa Vieja.
Pedro José Guevara signed a receipt for 4 reales of silver in Cartago for 'mandas forzosas' (obligatory bequests).
Antonio Mateo Molina, the Síndico de mercedes y redención de cautivos, signed a receipt for 4 reales of silver in Cartago for 'mandas forzosas'.
José Antº Jiménez provided a receipt for 4 reales of silver for a 'manda forzosa' to Nuestra Señora de Guadalupe.
An 'acta de visita' (visitation record) was signed by Esteban Lorenzo, Bishop of Nicaragua, and his Secretary, Francisco de Paula Soto, incurring 10 pesos in fees.

Father Francisco de Paula Soto, Secretary of Chamber to the Bishop Esteban Lorenzo, who was visiting the province, granted power of attorney to Francisco Padilla, a resident of the town of Nicaragua. This power allowed Padilla to collect overdue rents from the tenants of Soto's chaplaincies.

Antonio Ramón de Azofeifa, the city's priest, granted power of attorney to Licenciado Rafael Ceferino Ramírez, an attorney of the Royal Audiencia of Guatemala. This was to pursue the collection of 'novenos' (ninths) that had not been paid to the Parish by the Royal Board of Tithes of León for many years.

Nicolás and Manuel Gabriel Ramírez, acting for themselves and their siblings, ratified the sale of a quarter caballería of land by their deceased father, Juan Rafael Ramírez, to José Calderón. The land, originally granted by Governor Chirino, bordered lands of Ventura Lizondro and the Taquis ravine, and was sold for 16 silver pesos.

Mariana, daughter of José Calderón, confirmed that her father had sold the same land (previously acquired from Juan Rafael Ramírez) to José Salvador Mora for the same price. José Salvador Mora's sons and heirs, Pedro José and Manuel Silverio Mora, accepted this transfer.

Juana Irola, widow of Juan Miguel Gutiérrez and guardian of their six minor children, obligated herself to them for 55 pesos and 7 reales of cacao. This amount represented each child's paternal inheritance.

people_involved: Don Rafael de Alvarado y Ocampo
summary: Don Rafael de Alvarado y Ocampo and Doña Ana Josefa de Ulloa obligated themselves for 160 pesos plata at 5% interest to the Convento de San Francisco in Esparza. The debt was managed by Don Tomás Benito Hidalgo. They mortgaged their house in Cartago, located near Don Nicolás Ulloa's house.

Doña Florentina de Aragón, a native of Spain, made a codicil to her closed will. She reduced a 3000 pesos chaplaincy by 1000 pesos, to be given to the Bishop for distribution among poor girls, beggars, and others in Cartago, to clear her conscience and that of her deceased husband, Don Juan Fernández de Bobadilla. She also bequeathed 30 pesos to the wife of the deceased José Montoya.

people_involved: Capitán Don Rafael Gutiérrez de Cárdenas
summary: Capitán Don Rafael Gutiérrez de Cárdenas, a native of Spain, sold a 26-year-old mulatto slave named José Miguel García to Don Andrés González de Araujo, a perpetual Regidor of Villa de Nicaragua, for 250 pesos. The sale was conducted through Don Antonio de la Fuente, and Don Rafael had originally purchased the slave from Don José Mateo García.

people_involved: Señor Obispo Don Esteban Lorenzo de Tristán
summary: Don José Romualdo Zamora and Doña Juana Rita Coronado obligated themselves for 100 pesos cacao at 5% interest to the Convento de San Francisco. This related to a chaplaincy founded by the deceased Presbítero Don Antonio de Guevara on a mill near Cartago. The couple took possession of the mill, valued at 100 pesos due to its poor condition, with the approval of Bishop Don Esteban Lorenzo de Tristán, who was visiting.

people_involved: Don Romualdo Muñoz de la Trinidad
Señor Gobernador Don José Joaquín de Nava
summary: Doña Tomasa Gómez, widow of Don Romualdo Muñoz de la Trinidad, sold a pasture called 'Cerrado' to Tiburcio Sáenz for 150 pesos. Her deceased husband had acquired this pasture from the widow and son of Don Antonio Barros y Muro on April 20, 1769, before Governor Don José Joaquín de Nava. On June 16, 1783, Doña Tomasa delivered a certification and royal deed for the pasture to Tiburcio Sáenz.

This entry details the will of Antonio Miguel Piedra, legitimate son of deceased Francisco Piedra and Ana Monestel. He was married to Teresa de Jesús Quesada and had nine children. His wife and son José Antonio were named as executors, and the will was granted in Purires.

people_involved: Teniente Gobernador Don José Miguel Porras
Don Gregorio Sáenz Vázquez de Quintanilla
summary: Diligences were initiated for the opening of Don Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla's will, requested by Don Francisco Taguada, one of the executors. Don Ventura, a Colonel of militias and resident of Villa Vieja, died at 2 AM on the day of the request, having suffered from dementia since February or March of the previous year.
