His assets included five slaves and lands across the Río Grande, known as 'del P. Ibarra'.

Don Bernardo Gómez granted his will in Villa Vieja on March 3, 1780. He bequeathed properties and goods to various individuals, including a house to José Segundo, his dwelling to Juliana de Bonilla, and livestock to his nieces and nephews. He also ordered the freedom of his slaves José Ovares and Miguel Ignacio after his death and established a chaplaincy for the San Francisco Convent.

On September 7, 1778, in León, Don Bernardo Gómez, former tithe collector for Bagaces and Nicaragua, signed a document before Escribano Real Don José Peralta. This document obliged him to deliver the tithes to Baltasar José de Silva, the principal lessee.

Don Bernardo Gómez, a tithe collector in 1779 and 1780, agreed with Don Diego Medrano, agent for Baltasar José de Silva, to liquidate pending tithe accounts. Bishop Don Esteban Lorenzo de Tristán mediated the process, resolving all disputes. Don Bernardo was found to owe 1684 pesos 4 reales to Silva, payable in installments through August 1783.

During the tithe account liquidation in 1780, it was declared that 173 cattle, belonging to the tithes and charged to Don Bernardo Gómez, were lost. This occurred due to a strong storm while the second batch of livestock was being sent to the Hacienda de San Jerónimo. It was agreed that Don Bernardo could collect any found cattle as his own, provided he notified Medrano for verification.

Doña Florentina de Aragón, a native of Spain, made additions to her closed will, granted on June 5. She requested a solemn mass at the San Francisco Convent after her death and clarified that a lost account of sums deposited with Don Rafael de Cárdenas should not be used against him. She bequeathed cacao to her nephew Don Pedro de Iribaren, money to her servants Polonia Bejarano and Juana, and jewelry to Doña Petronila Sancho, also clarifying ownership of a slave.
Doña Manuela Pastora, who leases a pasture in the area named Tambor, bordering the Río de Peras in the common lands of Cartago, granted a sublease for this pasture to Rafael Pacheco.

Don Francisco Carazo, acting as executor for Don Tomás López del Corral, sold an enslaved woman named Petronila, approximately 30 years old, and her two sons, Ciriaco (12) and Manuel José (11), to Don Manuel Torre y Romero. The sale, for 550 pesos plata, was intended to satisfy López del Corral's debt in the tobacco sector.

Don Manuel Alfonso de Ulloa granted freedom to his 40-year-old mestizo slave, Lorenzo Ulloa, in exchange for 100 pesos cacao. Lorenzo was acquired from a slave named Juana, who was brought into Ulloa's marriage by his deceased wife. Ulloa's legitimate heirs, Don Pedro, Don Francisco, Doña Petronila de Ulloa, and Doña Juana (wife of Don Pedro Ramírez), all consented to the manumission.

people_involved: Don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
summary: Doña Petronila Carazo, a widow, established a 1000-peso patrimony for her son, Don Juan Diego Teruel, who is studying for the priesthood in Peru. This endowment, combined with 1500 pesos from capellanías founded by his maternal great-grandparents, Don Antonio de Soto y Barahona and Doña Petronila de Hoces Navarro, ensures he has the required funds for his ecclesiastical status. The patrimony includes her city house, two slaves, and half of a large cattle ranch in El Zapotal (Bagaces), shared with her brother, Captain Don Francisco Carazo, along with other properties in Matina and the city.

Lieutenant Colonel Don Juan Flares, the interim Governor and a native of Spain, granted general power of attorney to Don Esteban Melgar. Melgar holds the positions of Cavalry Captain and Senior Officer of the Presidency and Captaincy General in Nueva Guatemala.

Don Francisco Carazo, Don Santiago de Bonilla, and Don José Tomás de Alvarado granted power of attorney to Don Juan Gil del Barrio, a merchant residing in Nueva Guatemala. This power was given to allow Gil del Barrio to bid on their behalf for the titles of Provincial Mayor, Chief Constable, and Simple Alderman, respectively.

Teresa de Jesús Quesada, acting as guardian for her nine minor children, obligated herself to them for 81 pesos and 3 reales of cacao each. This sum represented their inheritance from her deceased husband and their father, Miguel Piedra.

Don José María de Peralta, a native of Spain, and Doña Ana Benita Corrales, who had already engaged and were honor-bound to marry, granted power of attorney to Don Manuel Torre y Romero. This power allowed him to handle all necessary arrangements for their marriage before the ecclesiastical court or other relevant authorities.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Antonio Fernando de Arleguí
Presbítero Don José Francisco de Alvarado
summary: Presbyter Don Antonio Fernando de Arleguí, who was preparing to depart for Nicaragua, granted general power of attorney to his uncle, Presbyter Don José Francisco de Alvarado. This power was specifically for collecting the income from Arleguí's capellanías.

On October 1st, Hipólito Recinos, a resident of Esparza, recognized a census of 200 pesos plata at 5% interest, which he held in favor of the Curacy of Esparza. This action followed a dispatch from the Bishop dated June 26th of the same year, mandating recognition of such censos under penalty of excommunication. Recinos had acquired this census upon the death of Felipe Paredes, who had it situated on a property called 'Cuajasal' near Esparza, which Recinos received in April 1778. Don José Antonio de Oriamuno served as guarantor.

people_involved: Alcalde Ordinario Don José Nicolás Chavarría
summary: On October 18th, María Bartola Ancheta appeared before Mayor Don José Nicolás Chavarría, requesting to sell her deceased son Pedro Vicente's house to support his six minor children (her grandchildren), as she was too poor to educate them. Pedro Vicente and his wife Simona Cubero had died in 1780. Don Juan Fargo was proposed as the buyer, and Don José Antonio Sáenz was appointed as an expert to value the house, which he assessed at 50 pesos plata or 75 cacao. Fargo agreed to the price, paid 10 pesos upfront, and was given 8 months to pay the remainder in installments.
Astúa, Fargo's father-in-law, signed a document regarding a payment of 13 pesos plata to a grandmother. The exact month is abbreviated as 'bre'.

people_involved: Manuel Franc? de Orozco y Quesada
summary: Don Manuel de Quesada, acting as tutor for the minor children of the late Blas de Jesús, sold a chácara (farm) with houses and oxen in Cartago to Don Fermín Mondragón for 550 pesos and one real of silver. The property was bordered by land belonging to Pedro Aymerich and Ramón Román, and the river Molino. The price was held in deposit until taken at interest, with shares for the minors and Doña Dominga Jiménez, who inherited from her deceased daughter Eusebia.

Doña Dominga Jiménez received 118 pesos 6 1/2 reales plata, equivalent to 178 pesos 2 reales of cacao, and cancelled her part. This transaction is noted in the margin and relates to her inheritance from her daughter Eusebia.

Don Fermín Mondragón formally obligated himself to the minor children of the late Blas de Jesús (Pedro José, José Rafael, José Hipólito, and José Alejandro) for their inheritance shares, totaling 153 pesos, 3 reales, and 93 granos each. He also committed to delivering the widow Dominga Jiménez's share and the minors' total share when it is taken at interest. Doña Tomasa Joaquina del Coral acted as guarantor.

people_involved: Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba, Comisario of the Inquisition and administrator of two Cofradías, presented his accounts to Bishop Esteban Lorenzo de Tristán. He was found to owe 1659 pesos in cacao, but due to his diligence and his family's historical contributions to the Cofradía del Rosario, the Bishop reduced his debt by 159 pesos, leaving a balance of 1500 pesos. Casasola y Córdoba then obligated and mortgaged two new cacao haciendas in the Matina valley to cover this debt.

people_involved: Paula Manuela Muñoz de la Trinidad
María de la Encarnación Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Doña Tomasa Gómez de Lara, as principal, and Captain Don José Gregorio de Oreamuno, as guarantor, obligated themselves for 680 pesos 2 reales and 6 octavos of silver. This sum was for the benefit of Tomasa's minor daughters, Paula Manuela and María de la Encarnación Muñoz de la Trinidad, who inherited it from their late father, Don Romualdo Muñoz de la Trinidad.

Don Pedro Nicolás Fernández, a native and resident of Villa Nueva, made his will. He was the legitimate son of the late Juan Fernández and Cayetana Acosta, and was married to Doña María Catalina Tenorio, with whom he had eight children, including María Josefa, Félix, Miguel, José de la Cruz, José Encarnación, and Juan José.

Details emerge regarding the estate of the deceased Vicente Saborío, whose widow, María Josefa, resides in Murciélago and rents out another house to José del Campo. The estate's executors are Alférez Real Antonio de la Fuente and José Honofre Ra. Half of the remaining assets are designated for María Josefa, a quarter for masses, and the rest for their eight children, including María Atanasia and José Cipriano.

Lorenzo Martínez, a resident of Villa Vieja, grants power of attorney to Alférez Real Antonio de la Fuente. This power enables de la Fuente to represent Martínez in a lawsuit against Father Ramón Antonio de Azofeifa. The suit seeks 228 pesos and 4 reales in cacao, plus eleven years of accrued interest, based on a deed Azofeifa granted to Martínez's deceased mother, Lucía Solórzano.

Doña Petronila Carazo, a widow, establishes a 2000-peso patrimony for her son, Juan Diego Teruel, who is studying for the priesthood in Peru. This new foundation replaces a previous one involving chaplaincies managed by Mtro. José Antonio Carazo, which were originally founded by her grandparents, Antonio de Soto y Barahona and Petronila de Hoces Navarro. As she is elderly and has no other heirs, the foundation is made over all her assets.

Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora establishes a 2000-peso patrimony for her son, Juan José de Sierra, who is studying Grammar with the firm intention of becoming a priest. The assets funding this patrimony include 4000 cacao trees in Matina, a farm in the city's common lands, her residence, an adjacent house, 50 heads of cattle, and five enslaved people.

Doña Petronila de Ulloa grants freedom to her 23-year-old enslaved woman, Encarnación, whom she inherited from her mother. Encarnación is being freed because she is preparing for marriage and for other reasons. However, she is required to accompany Petronila de Ulloa for the remainder of Petronila's life.

Pedro Ramírez, along with his wife Juana Ulloa, and her siblings Pedro Ulloa, Francisco Ulloa, and Petronila Ulloa, sell three enslaved women to Luis de Cueto, a resident of León. Pedro Ramírez sells Francisca (26) and her daughter María (7), inherited by his wife. All siblings jointly sell Cayetana (27), whose sale was mandated to cover debts from their deceased mother's estate.

Pedro Ulloa and Francisco Ulloa sell two enslaved men, Cayeteno Leonardo (19) and José Antonio (21), to Luis de Cueto, Alguacil Mayor and Regidor of León. Both enslaved men were inherited from their deceased mother and are sons of Juana, an enslaved woman their mother brought into her marriage with Alfonso Manuel de Ulloa.

Francisca Mariana Calderón and Cecilia Calderón reciprocally donate their shares of a jointly built house to each other, located next to María Manuela Alvarado's house. They also establish provisions for their burial in the San Francisco Convent and the creation of a chaplaincy from their remaining assets, to be managed by the Convent's Guardian. This arrangement is contingent on neither sister selling the house nor having children, as they currently have no forced heirs.

Magdalena Casasola, a free mulata from Puebla, leases her San Benito cacao plantation in the Matina valley, which contains 1743 trees, to her son-in-law Antonio Arizaga for five years. The rent is set at one-third of cacao every two months and two-thirds at the end of the year, to be delivered to the city.

Doña María del Carmen Alvarado grants power of attorney to Gregorio Castro to collect a debt of 200 pesos. This amount was lent at interest by her deceased brother, Beneficiado Maximiliano de Alvarado, to Juan Agustín Alvenda, also deceased, who was originally from Nicoya.

Fuentes and his mother-in-law, Lego Moscoso, received 207 pesos and 1.5 reales of cacao from Manuel Antonio Jiménez. These goods were held in deposit by Jiménez and belonged to Francisco González, who had been absent for many years. Legal proceedings were initiated before Alcalde Ordinario José Nicolás Anacleto Chavarría by Fuentes, as husband of Antonia Josefa González, to obtain the delivery of these goods.

On December 20, Manuel Torre y Romero, Alcalde Ordinario of Cartago, presented a power of attorney granted by his brother Juan de Torre y Romero in Madrid on January 30, 1781. This power authorized Manuel to collect debts from Governor José Perie and other debtors. The testimony was issued by Escribano Rodrigo Antonio Benites de Rivera in Madrid on February 20, 1782, and authenticated the next day by three other Escribanos del Rey. Manuel later substituted this power to Mariano Ezeta and, in his absence, to Juan Gil del Barrio, who resided in Nueva Guatemala.

On December 24, Antonio de la Fuente, Alférez Real, and Juan Francisco de Bonilla, Depositario General and regidores of the city council, granted power of attorney to Juan José de Medina (and Manuel Córdoba in his absence). This action was taken in response to a Royal provision received the previous day from the Supreme Tribunal of the Real Audiencia, requiring them to appoint a procurator to represent them in a pending case against Governor José Perie.

On December 24, Dionisia Guerrero obligated herself to her minor nephew, Juan Rafael, for 147 pesos 6 reales, representing his maternal inheritance from his deceased mother, Joaquina Guerrero. Andrea Guerrero, who was in charge of Juan Rafael and his assets, was also obligated to maintain him. A margin note from May 31, 1787, states that Dionisia had sold half a house to Andrea in 1783, and upon Juan Rafael's death, his inheritance passed to his aunts Dionisia, Andrea, Micaela, Pedro, Rafaela, and Juana de la Rosa Guerrero, with Juana's share going to her children after her death. All parties confirmed receipt of their shares and cancelled the obligation.

Josefa Chavarría obligated herself to her minor son, José Nicolás, for 108 pesos and 5 reales of cacao, which she received from her mother-in-law, María Portuguez, with Trinidad Chavarría and Manuela Acuña as guarantors. Legal proceedings were initiated by María Portuguez to compel Josefa to provide a receipt for the goods, as Governor Perie had forced María to give Josefa the paternal inheritance of Nicolás Cerdas, Josefa's deceased husband, despite María's claim that the goods were hers. A margin note from December 12, 1785, indicates the Escribano cancelled the obligation due to a new one being made.

Manuela Fernández de la Parra obligated herself for 108 pesos of cacao at 5% interest for a chaplaincy fund managed by Cura Ramón de Azofeifa, mortgaging her house. The license from Bishop Gaitán stated that the fund was previously managed by Ramona Ibarra, residing in Nicaragua, and was secured by a house in Cartago's Convento square, which Ramona sold to Romualdo de Zamora, who then redeemed it from this census.

Juana García donated a cacao plantation with 700 fruit trees in the Valle de Mata to her daughter Manuela. This donation was made when Manuela married José Rodríguez, who has since died, leaving a legitimate heir. Juana's son, José García, signed on her behalf.

José Miguel Rodríguez, a resident of Villa Nueva, sold a piece of land to the Cofradía de las Animas of this city, represented by its Mayordomo, Pedro José Lizondro. The land's boundaries are described in detail, extending from the Cofradía's ranch house towards the south, west, and north, near settlements and the Bermúdez stream.

people_involved: Beneficiado don Ramón Antonio de Azofeifa
summary: Don José Antonio de Oreamuno sold a 30-year-old mulato slave named José Francisco Oreamuno to Presbítero don José Antonio Posadas, a resident of León, for 200 pesos. The transaction was facilitated by Beneficiado don Ramón Antonio de Azofeifa, the Cura of the city, acting as Posadas's attorney, and recorded by Escribano José Romualdo Zamora.

people_involved: Coronel don José Joaquín de Nava
summary: Doña Tomasa Joaquina del Corral granted power to Coronel don José Joaquín de Nava, who resided in Granada, Nicaragua, to sell her runaway slave named Juan Gregorio. The slave was known to be located in Granada.

people_involved: Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
Presbítero don Francisco de Paula Soto
summary: Don Manuel José García sought to be awarded capellanías previously renounced by Comisario del Santo Oficio don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba, which were originally founded by doña Agueda Pérez del Muro. He empowered Presbítero don Francisco de Paula Soto and don Fermín Mondo to solicit these capellanías, as he intended to pursue a sacerdotal state and was studying grammar, following the Bishop's directive to post edicts.

people_involved: Alférez Real don Antonio de la Fuente
summary: Alférez Real don Antonio de la Fuente, acting as Síndico General for the San Francisco Convents in the province and on behalf of the Padres Curas of several towns, granted power to don Luis Cueto and don Mateo Mantilla. Their task was to collect the synod for the past year from the Royal Coffers in León.

Don José Tomás de Alvarado and his wife, doña María del Rosario Bonilla, obligated themselves for 300 pesos plata at 5% interest to the Beneficio of Esparza. They mortgaged their house in Cartago and 55.5 caballerías of land with a house, corrals, and cattle in Santana, within the Bagaces jurisdiction, contiguous to Mateo.

Doña Antonia Masís empowered Diego Chavarría to sell her runaway mulato slave, José Domingo, for 150 pesos plata. José Domingo was known to be in Granada at the house of don Fernando Chamorro, having gone there to find his wife, whom don Fernando had purchased, as indicated by a letter sent to don Antonio de la Fuente.

people_involved: Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
Alférez Real perpétuo y Maestre de Campo don José de Casasola y Córdoba
Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
Esclavo of Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba, a cleric, made his will. He was responsible for capellanías founded by his parents, don José de Casasola y Córdoba and doña Agueda Pérez del Muro, and another co-founded by his mother and don Francisco Garrido. He had renounced a capellanía for himself and his brother, don José Francisco Casasola, and was chaplain for others founded by don Baltasar de Grados and one he founded for the soul of don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría, leaving some clothes to his slave.

Doña Isabel Fernández dictates her will, detailing her properties including haciendas in Bonilla and Barbilla, and establishing a chaplaincy for Nuestra Señora de Dolores with her nephew, don Mariano José Iglesias, as patron and his son, don Tomás, as chaplain. She also grants freedom to her slaves Gabriel, Mónica, and Enrique, and names her executors and heirs.

Doña Isabel Fernández, a widow twice, dictates her will, specifying the distribution of her house for masses and to don Francisco Arleguí. She also grants freedom to her mulata slaves Antonia and Ana upon her death and lists numerous legatees, including family members and servants, and names her executors.

Alférez Real don Antonio de la Fuente and his wife doña María Francisca de Alvarado obligate themselves for 613 pesos and cacao, representing the paternal inheritance of the minor sons of the deceased Blas de Jesús. The minors are with their mother, doña Dominga Jiménez, and the inheritance was received from don Fermín Mondragón, with their house in the main plaza serving as collateral.

Doña Dominga Jiménez receives the tutelage for her minor sons, Pedro José, José Rafael, José Hipólito, and José Alejandro de Jesús, and cancels the obligation related to their inheritance. This event is noted in the margin of the Feb 22 obligation.

Francisco Javier Quesada obligates himself for 393 pesos cacao to his minor granddaughter, Josefa Jacoba de Rojas, whose inheritance he has held since 1782. He replaces the original surety, his son-in-law Pedro Salguero, with Josefa Guerrero after Salguero requested release from the Gobernador.

people_involved: don Miguel del Aya y Bolívar
summary: An unnamed testator, sick in bed, is dictating a will, mentioning the parents of two legitimate sons (don José de Bonilla and doña Manuela Sáenz; don Miguel del Aya y Bolívar and doña Isabel Miranda) and listing several of their own children.
Josefa Marcelina, a slave, was sold by Doña María del Rosario Bonilla for 200 pesos. The payment for this transaction was made to Don Tomás de Alvarado, Doña María del Rosario's husband.

Juan José, the two-year-old son of Josefa Marcelina and also a slave, was sold by Doña María del Rosario Bonilla for 80 pesos. The payment for this sale was made to Don Tomás de Alvarado, Doña María del Rosario's husband.

people_involved: Presbítero don Juan Salvador del os y Bolívar
summary: Presbítero don Juan Salvador del os y Bolívar made donations to his nieces Doña Juana Josefa, Doña María Cruz, Doña Justa, and Josefa de la Cruz. Josefa de la Cruz passed away before her uncle, the donor.

people_involved: Doña María Gertrudis del Aya y Bolívar
summary: Don Andrés de Bonilla and his wife, Doña María Gertrudis del Aya y Bolívar, executed their testament. Their sons, Presbítero don José Antonio Bonilla and Don Santiago Bonilla, were named as executors, and their children were designated as heirs.

people_involved: Doña María Gertrudis del Aya y Bolívar
summary: Don Andrés de Bonilla and Doña María Gertrudis del Aya y Bolívar provided goods to their daughter, Doña María del Rosario Bonilla, upon her third marriage to Don Tomás de Alvarado.

Capitán don Luis de Aguilar, a resident of Rivas, granted power of attorney to Silvestre Carbajal y Grimaldo, who resides in Cartago. This power allowed Carbajal y Grimaldo to collect a debt from the estate of the deceased Don Alonso Porras, related to clothes for Aguilar's shop.

On October 31, 1782, Don Fermín Mondragón purchased a farm and annexes, formerly belonging to Blas de Jesús, for 825 pesos, 2 reales, and cacao. The sale price was initially held in deposit by Mondragón, then taken by Don Antonio de la Fuente and his wife at interest.

As Don Fermín Mondragón did not have the complete sum for the farm, he agreed with the interim Governor, Don Juan Flores, that Flores would provide the sum and keep the farm. Mondragón subsequently granted security of possession for the farm to Flores.

people_involved: Coronel don José Romualdo de Oreamuno
Presbítero don Juan José de Oreamuno
summary: Coronel don José Romualdo de Oreamuno and his wife, Doña Antonia Manuela Alvarado, granted power of attorney to their son, Presbítero don Juan José de Oreamuno. This power allowed him to represent them in the estate of Doña María Catarina de Ibarra, who was the mother of Don José Romualdo.

Doctor don Pedro Jimena, the Provider and Vicar General of the Bishopric, residing in Cartago for convalescence, gave power of attorney to Don Martín de Serna, a merchant from Guatemala. This power enabled Serna to represent Jimena in the Real Audiencia, following specific instructions.

Don Felipe Arburola and Doña Manuela Josefa de Estrada, who had no children, made their testament. The surviving spouse was named as the primary executor and heir, with Presbítero don José Antonio Bonilla as the ultimate executor and their soul as the final heir.

On October 27 of the previous year, José María de Poma acquired the farm, sugar mill, and other assets of the deceased Antonio de Avendaño through auction for 300 pesos. Poma was unable to pay the price by the deadline and sought assistance from Dr. don Pedro Jimena, the Vicar General.

Don Pedro Jimena, Provider and Vicar General of the Bishopric, founded a chaplaincy for the Reina de los Angeles, whose image is in her sanctuary in Puebla. The chaplaincy was endowed with properties, including a farm, a sugar mill, and sugarcane fields near the Agua Caliente and Toyogres rivers, valued at 300 pesos. These assets were acquired by Jimena from the estate of Antonio Avendaño, which had previously been remated to José María de Peralta.

Lucía Josefa Badilla attempted to obligate herself for 300 pesos to the chaplaincy founded by Doctor don Pedro Jimena in favor of Nuestra Señora de los Angeles. However, this transaction was not completed.

people_involved: Doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho de Castañeda
summary: Doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho de Castañeda sold a house in Cartago to Don Ramón Azofeifa, the parish priest, for 700 pesos plata. The property was bordered by houses and lots belonging to Doña Lucía de Alvarado, Doña Joaquina Corrales, and Doña María Francisca Estrada. Marginal notes indicate payments were received on September 14, 1785 (400 pesos) and January 1788 (100 pesos), with the transaction fully cancelled on September 23, 1788.
Lucía Josefa Badilla obligated herself for 300 pesos to the Chaplaincy of los Angeles, which was founded by Doctor don Pedro Jimena. Antonia Masís served as the guarantor for this obligation.

people_involved: Don Juan José Calderón y Bonilla
summary: Don Luis de Cueto, a resident of Cartago and Regidor and Alguacil Mayor of León (Nicaragua), granted power of attorney to Don Agustín de Gana, a merchant from Panamá. This power was to collect 3000 pesos for 100 tercios of cacao from Nicaragua, and an additional 725 pesos plata, from Don Juan José Calderón y Bonilla, a resident and merchant of León.

Don Luis de Cueto granted power of attorney to Don Miguel Cuido, a resident of Chiriquí, and in a secondary capacity, to Don Mateo López of Santiago de Veragua. This power was for the same purpose of collection as the previous grant to Don Agustín de Gana.

Manuela Josefa de Estrada, legitimate daughter of the deceased Don Nicolás de Estrada and Doña Lorenza Muñoz Hidalgo, and married to Don Felipe Arburola, made her will. She declared no children and named her soul as heir, revoking a previous will (folio 36) where she had named her husband as heir. Presbítero Don José Antonio Bonilla, or Presbítero Don Juan José Oreamuno in his absence, were named as executors.
Don Luis de Cueto, a resident, granted power of attorney to Don Manuel de Oreamuno, a resident of Cartago. This power was for the same purpose as the grants mentioned in folios 49 and 50.

Don Mariano José Iglesias, a native of Cartago and resident of León, leased the cacao haciendas named Dolores in Matina to Matías Barrantes (a) Carmona for three years at 100 pesos of cacao per year. These haciendas, comprising 4100 fruit trees, were left by his uncle Don Juan Manuel de Casasola for a chaplaincy. The contract was rescinded on May 27, 1783.

Presbítero Don Juan José Oreamuno, acting as attorney for Don José Romualdo de Oreamuno, and Don Antonio Oreamuno, and Don José Antonio Oreamuno (defending Don José Francisco Oreamuno, who is demented), all Oreamunos, settled a lawsuit concerning the estate of Doña María Catarina de Ibarra. Doña María Catarina was the wife of Don Antonio and mother of Don José Romualdo and Don José Francisco. They agreed to reduce the valuation of Don Antonio's house by 200 pesos, count sums received by Don José Romualdo and Don José Francisco as maternal inheritance, and impose the chaplaincy ordered by Doña María Catarina only on the Matina haciendas. The 500 pesos spent on Presbítero Don Juan José's studies would be counted against his father, Don José Romualdo, from the maternal share.

José Francisco Taguada, as husband of Doña Francisca Sierra, along with Doña Antonia, Doña Nicolasa, and Doña Felipa Sierra, all natives of Cartago, sold a house in the city for 200 pesos. They inherited the house from their deceased parents. The property was bordered by houses of Don Antonio Oreamuno, the former house of Don Tomás Barahona, Doña Manuela Ibarra, and Don Rafael de Alvarado.

José Francisco Taguada, acting as executor for Don Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla, founded a chaplaincy as ordered in Bonilla's sealed will. This chaplaincy was established for the benefit of Bonilla's soul and that of his deceased wife, Doña Micaela de Ugalde.

Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Cora took on an obligation for 2066 pesos 5 reales for a chaplaincy at the San Francisco Convent and 371 pesos cacao for the Esparza Convent, both at 5% interest. These obligations were previously managed by Don Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla and were secured by his cattle hacienda on the Río Grande.

Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Cora declared that her obligation had passed to Don Ruperto Pérez and his wife. This transfer was formalized by an escritura (deed) before the Gobernador of Villa Vieja, leading to the cancellation of her original obligation.
Don Salvador Oreamuno stated that the obligation for the Esparza Convent, amounting to 372 pesos, was still active and under his charge.

Doña Encarnación Sancho, whose husband Don José Francisco de Oreamuno was mentally ill and without a home, sought and received permission from the Gobernador to take on an 820 pesos silver censo obligation. This was for a house located in front of the San Nicolás hermitage, arranged with the general attorney of Presbítero Don Fernando Antonio de Arleguí, to secure a place to live.

Doña Encarnación Sancho formalized her obligation for 820 pesos at 5% interest. Of this sum, 720 pesos were for a chaplaincy founded by Baltasar de Grados, and 100 pesos for one founded by Doña Eugenia de Abarca Alatras, with Presbítero Don Fernando Antonio de Arleguí serving as patron and chaplain for both.

The undated testament of sisters Doña Micaela and Doña Juana María Arleguí, legitimate daughters of the deceased Don Manuel Antonio de Arléguí and Doña Eugenia de Hoces, outlines their bequests. They owned slaves Ventura and Juana Josefa, who were to be freed after their deaths, and named their niece María Josefa Arleguí, Antonia Manuela Meneses, Cecilia Jiménez, and Francisca Josefa as beneficiaries, with Don José Antonio Jiménez as executor.

Andrea Guerrero owed 125 pesos of cacao to her sister Dionisia Guerrero, who was acting as guardian for a nephew left in her care by their deceased sister Joaquina Guerrero. On May 30, 1787, Dionisia Guerrero cancelled this debt.

Don Miguel Jerónimo Alvarado and Don José Mariano Iglesias, natives of Cartago and residents of León, dissolved their partnership, which had been formed in 1781 before Escribano Silvestre Prado in León. The partnership was for the administration of tithes in Cartago and its valleys, with Alvarado as the rematario, and Iglesias received 100 pesos upon his withdrawal.

Don José Francisco Taguada, acting as executor for the deceased Don Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla, sold an enslaved woman named María Cayetana, 30, and her 8-year-old daughter Pascuala Bailón. The sale was made to Don Manuel Antonio Arana of Granada, through his attorney Teniente Coronel Don Juan Flores, for 275 pesos plata.
Presbítero Don Juan José de los Reyes, who was departing for Esparza to serve as interim priest, granted power of attorney to Don Antonio de la Fuente for the purpose of collections.

Juan de la Rosa Maitín and his wife Felipa Neri took on an obligation for 37 pesos 1.5 reales of silver at 5% interest to Ramón Quesada, for a semifáto (item/asset) they held. This obligation was previously held by the deceased Antonio de Avendaño.

Don José Antonio Jiménez granted power of attorney to Presbítero Don Francisco de Paula Soto, the Bishop's Secretary, to sell an enslaved man named José Francisco Chaves. Chaves, a 25-year-old shoemaker who had fled to Nicaragua, was believed to be with Presbítero Don Manuel Antonio Sandoval, the grantor's half-brother, and was to be sold for a minimum of 250 pesos.
Doña Antonia Masís sold an enslaved 'bozal' man named OpUnEo to Don Fernando Chamorro, a resident of Granada, for 125 pesos in cash.

Don Manuel González and his wife Rosa González donated a wheat and corn mill, located in Villa Vieja at a place called 'la piedra grande', to Don Rafael del Castillo. This donation was made in gratitude for various benefits received through Rafael's mother, Doña Cecilia del Castillo.

people_involved: Coronel Don José Romualdo de Oreamuno
summary: Don Ramón Aquel, acting as the general attorney for Presbítero Don José Antonio Posadas of León, sold an enslaved mulatto named José Francisco Oreamuno to Coronel Don José Romualdo de Oreamuno for 212 pesos 4 reales of silver. Posadas had previously purchased José Francisco from Don Antonio Oreamuno, who is the father of Don José Romualdo.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Don Antonio de la Fuente, as the executor of the late Presbítero Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba, established a chaplaincy in favor of Nuestra Señora de los Dolores. This act fulfilled the will of the deceased, dated February 16 of the same year, and named Don Tomás, son of Don Mariano José de Iglesias, as the chaplain, with his father as the patron.

Don José María Peralta and his wife Doña Ana Benita Corrales committed 200 silver pesos at 5% interest to the chaplaincy for Nuestra Señora de los Dolores. This obligation was later transferred on July 29, 1788, to Don Jose Antonio Oreamuno and Don Tomás Hidalgo.

Don José María Peralta and Doña Ana Benita Corrales committed 143 pesos 3 reales of cacao to the minor children of Miguel Arce, Martín and Juana Josefa. This cacao was previously owed by Antonio de Avendaño.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Don Mariano José de Iglesias, a resident of León, leased the cacao haciendas named Dolores in the Matina valley to Don Manuel Sánchez Cabal, a native of Spain, for five years at 150 pesos annually. These haciendas were part of the chaplaincy for Nuestra Señora de Dolores, established by Iglesias's uncle, Presbítero Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba.

people_involved: Doña Juana Gómez de Pineda y Meléndez
summary: Don Gregorio García, a native of Villa Catón de la Cepeda, Spain, made his will while ill in bed. He is a widower of Doña Juana Gómez de Pineda y Meléndez, with whom he had a son, Manuel Juan García, who was left in the care of his godfather and general attorney, Don Juan Fernández Velazco, about 19 years prior. Don Antonio de la Fuente was named as the executor, and Manuel Juan García as the heir.

El Beneficiado Don Ramón Azofeifa sold a house and its plot in Villa Vieja to Don Francisco Taguada for 90 silver pesos. The property was bordered by the seller's house, Doña María Josefa de Soto's house, and the properties of Don Simón Paniagua and Doña Ana Zamora.

Don Antonio de la Fuente granted power of attorney to Don Juan Manríquez and Don Basilio Roma, merchants from Nueva Guatemala, to collect a debt from the estate of the deceased Don Domingo Endana. The Governor had referred this case to the General Court of Deceased Estates in Nueva Guatemala.

people_involved: Teniente Coronel Don Juan Fernández de Bobadilla
Teniente Don Rafael Gutiérrez de Cárdenas
summary: Doña Florentina de Aragón, a widow from Spain, declared her intention to marry Teniente Don Rafael Gutiérrez de Cárdenas of Guatemala. For the required royal license, a deposit of twenty thousand reales de vellón is needed for the Monte Pío Militar, and Doña Florentina stated she had already deposited one thousand (reales) with Don Felipe Gallegos.
Don Felipe acknowledges receipt of a deposit.

Benita Núñez, a widow, assumes a debt of 200 pesos cacao to the Convento de San Francisco, previously owed by Don Dionisio Mora. She secures this obligation by mortgaging a house and a cacao plantation in El Bejuco, Matina Valley.

Doña Manuela Josefa Aguirre and her two sons, José Antonio and José del Rosario Carrillo, obligate themselves to her minor children, María Josefa, José Miguel, and José Nicolás Carrillo, for 564 pesos and 6 reales 3 cuartillos and 18 granos of cacao, which they inherited from the deceased José Cayetano Carrillo.

people_involved: Don Francisco de la Rosa Zamora
Presbítero don Joaquín Isidro de Quesada
summary: Don José Antonio Zamora, tutor and administrator for the minor Don Francisco de la Rosa Zamora, grants power of attorney to Manuel José de Astúa. This is for a lawsuit initiated by Presbítero don Joaquín Isidro de Quesada against Francisco's assets, stemming from Don Juan Lucas Zamora (Francisco's father) having been a guarantor for Don Manuel Fernández regarding a chaplaincy.
Juliana Bonilla, an orphan, grants power to her husband, Cristóbal de Ocampo, to make her will. She names him as her sole heir, and Captain José Joaquín Coronel is appointed as the executor.

Don Lorenzo, Don Antonio, and Don Diego Bonilla, along with Don Bautista Paniagua (husband of Doña María de Jesús Bonilla) and Don José Francisco Taguada (executor of Don Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla), all residents of Villa Vieja, reach a settlement in a lawsuit concerning their share of Don Ventura's estate.

The will of José Cayetano de Castro, a native of Villa Nueva, son of Don Manuel de Castro and Doña María Magdalena de Porras, and married to Juliana Josefa Jiménez, is detailed. He had no children, named his wife and Don Antonio de la Fuente as executors, and designated his soul as the heir, with legacies to his wife.

people_involved: Don José Sebastián Fernández de Urrutia
summary: Don José Sebastián Fernández de Urrutia and his wife Doña Antonia Josefa de Arleguí obligate themselves for 200 pesos cacao, secured by a house. This obligation is tied to a chaplaincy founded by Doña Catarina Correa for the Beneficio de la ciudad de Esparza.
Don Ramón de Azofeifa, the local priest, grants power of attorney to Teniente Coronel Don Santiago Prado, a resident of León, to collect the synod assigned to his curacy from the Royal Coffers.

Beneficiado Don Juan José Zeledón, responsible for 200 pesos plata for chaplaincies of Cura Don Ramón de Azofeifa, presents Don José Rodríguez and his wife Nicolasa Zeledón as new guarantors, mortgaging their house in Villa Nueva and an enslaved mulatto named Bernardo Mora. By January 20, 1789, the obligation was transferred to Don Juan José Castro in León.

Juliana Bonilla's will, granted by her widower and attorney Cristóbal de Ocampo Golfín, details that they had several children who died in infancy and one in utero. Captain José Joaquín Coronel is the executor, and Cristóbal de Ocampo Golfín is the sole heir.
Don José Fermín Mondragón, as executor of Don Julián de Azofeifa, grants power of attorney to Don José León de Bonilla to represent him in the estate proceedings.

people_involved: Doña Manuela de la Luz Aguilar
summary: Don Jerónimo Alvarado, husband of Doña Manuela de la Luz Aguilar and resident of León, is informed about an order to inventory the assets of his deceased father-in-law, Don José Miguel Aguilar. He grants power of attorney to Don José de Castro and Don Melchor Toruño, residents of León, to represent him in these inventories. The document was granted in Villa Vieja.
In Villa de Heredia, Don José Lorenzo Saborido sells a piece of land to Tomás Luna.

Lorenzo, Antonio, and Diego Bonilla sold five caballerías of land located in Río Grande, within the jurisdiction of Villa Vieja, to Juan Luis Lizamo, a resident of León. This land was a legacy from their uncle, Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla, and was sold for 180 pesos plata.

José Francisco Taguada, acting as the executor for Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla, sold two caballerías of land across the Río Grande to Pedro Espinoza, a fellow resident of Villa Vieja. The property's boundaries were detailed, including a reference to where María del Carmen Guevara collects water, and the sale price was 50 pesos plata.

José Francisco Taguada, in his capacity as executor for Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla, sold nine caballerías of land located across the Río Grande to Cayetano Gutiérrez. The extensive boundaries of the property were described, mentioning features like Cerro Grande and Quebrada del Cajón, with a sale price of 225 pesos plata.

Mariano José Iglesias, patron of a chaplaincy established by his uncle Presbítero Juan Manuel de Casasola, and Andrea Delgado, Casasola's heir, granted power of attorney to Captain José Joaquín Coronel. This power was for Coronel to represent them in the estate proceedings, as Iglesias and Delgado were traveling to León.

José Francisco Taguada, as executor for Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla, sold thirteen and a half caballerías of land in Río Grande to Presbítero José Antonio Bonilla, who was acting as executor for his deceased father, Andrés Bonilla. The land's boundaries were specified, noting its adjacency to lands owned by Cayetano Gutiérrez, and the transaction was for 237 pesos, 4 reales.

A chaplaincy was founded as per the will of Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla, with a principal of 1500 pesos plata, naming the Padre Guardián as chaplain and the Síndico of the Convento de San Francisco as patron. This foundation occurred because Eliaos Bonilla, Ventura's ward and wife of Cristóbal Ocampo, died without forced heirs, as stipulated in the will. Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral obligated herself for the 1500 pesos, hypothecating her assets, an obligation later cancelled on July 29, 1788, with Joaquín de Oreamuno assuming responsibility.

José Antonio del Campo, a native of Spain, received the dowry assets of 1495 pesos 4 reales from his mother-in-law, María Manuela Miranda, for his wife, María Mercedes Guerrero. They had married on December 14 of the previous year (1788), and the arras amounted to 150 pesos.

José Antonio de Oreamuno granted power of attorney to Juan José de Medina, a Procurator of the Real Audiencia, to collect the remaining debt from the estate of Manuel Soler, a former Governor of the province. The debt was deposited in the general court for deceased persons' assets, and Oreamuno was guaranteed 200 pesos by Santiago Botaro's bond.

Alférez Real de de la Fuente, acting as the general syndic for the San Francisco Convents in the province and on behalf of the parish priests of several pueblos, granted power of attorney to Luis Cueto (absent) and Tomás Quintana. This power was for them to collect the annual synod assigned to these priests.

José Manuel Guzmán Portocarrero sold a fifteen-year-old slave named Pablo Guzmán to Florentina de Aragón. Pablo was the son of Antonio Guzmán and Francisca Siles, who were slaves of Portocarrero's deceased parents, and the sale price was 250 pesos.

Fernando Chavarría and his wife Andrea Arleguí obligated themselves for 400 pesos at 5% interest, in favor of a chaplaincy for Nuestra Señora de los Dolores. This chaplaincy was founded by Presbíteros Cayetano and Hermenegildo Arleguí, and is currently served by Presbítero Francisco Robredo, following the death of Presbítero Fernando Arleguí. (Note: This obligation was recorded but not signed or passed).
José Antonio de Oreamuno began a sale transaction, but the details of what was sold and to whom are incomplete in the record.

Diego Chavarría was adjudicated a piece of land near Cartago, which was part of the estate of his deceased wife, Doña María Catalina de Ibarra. The land's boundaries were described as extending from the cerro de la Cruz to Caracol, an ojo de agua, and a ciénaga. The price for the land was 50 pesos plata.

locations: Quebrada Honda del Morte del Aguacate
people_involved: Alférez Real don Antonio de la Fuente
summary: Don José Romualdo Zamora granted power of attorney to Beneficiado don Luis Demetrio Coronado, a resident of León, to bid on his behalf for the tithes of the Villa Vieja party of the Gobernación. This area is described as extending from the Virilla river to Quebrada Honda del Morte del Aguacate. The document was granted before Alférez Real don Antonio de la Fuente, as the Escribano was a party.
Mateo Molina granted power of attorney to Martín Tagu, a resident of León, to bid on his behalf for the tithes.

people_involved: Don Juan de la Cruz de Alvarado
Capitán José Silvestre de Carvajal y Grimaldo
Legitimate children of Don Juan de la Cruz de Alvarado
Natural children of Don Juan de la Cruz de Alvarado
summary: The will of Don Juan de la Cruz de Alvarado was recorded. He was the son of Don Juan de Alvarado and Doña María de la Cruz, originally from Tierra Firme, and was married to Doña Josefa de la Cruz, with whom he had two legitimate children who were his heirs. He also had two natural children before his marriage. Capitán José Silvestre de Carvajal y Grimaldo was named as an albacea.

The will of José Chavarría was recorded, stating he was the legitimate son of the deceased Joagúía Chavarría and Tasara Trejos. He was married to Manuela Chavarría but had no children. His brother was Diego Chavarría, and his albaceas were his brother-in-law Juan Antonio Matamoros, or Manuel José de Astúa in Matamoros's absence. His soul was named as his heir.

people_involved: Deceased mother of Doña Antonia Zavaleta
summary: Doña Antonia Zavaleta sold a house in Paclada, which she inherited from her deceased mother, to José de Rodríguez, a resident of Nicaragua. The sale price was 200 pesos.

Doña Engracia de Aguilar, a resident of Nicaragua currently residing locally, granted power of attorney to Don Manuel Torre y Romero to represent her in a claim. The claim, made by the heir of Don Miguel Alvarado and the albacea of Doña Luisa Guzmán Echavarría, concerned the auction of the Miravalles hato, previously held by Doña Engracia's deceased father, Don Juan Francisco Aguilar, and Francisco Sandoval. Doña Engracia needed to return to her homeland.

people_involved: Capitán José Silvestre de Carvajal y Grimaldo
summary: Capitán José Silvestre de Carvajal y Grimaldo, natural son of Don José Liberato de Carvajal and Juana de las Mercedes Delgado (both from Panamá), granted power to testate to Cristóbal de Ocampo. His spouse, Dolores Castillo, was named as his heir and albacea.

Manuel Morúa acknowledged a debt of 75 pesos of cacao to Don José Ramón Cevallos, to be paid in two installments: 25 pesos on August 25 and 50 pesos in October. The document was signed by Gregorio Morúa.

people_involved: Capitán José Silvestre de Carvajal y Grimaldo
summary: The will of the deceased Capitán José Silvestre de Carvajal y Grimaldo was granted by his attorney, Cristóbal de Ocampo. It stated that he was married to Dolores Castillo for a short time and they had no children. His widow, Dolores Castillo, was named as his albacea and heir.

people_involved: Alférez Real don Antonio de la Fuente
Unnamed sobrinos carnales of Don Félix García Argueta
summary: Alférez Real don Antonio de la Fuente, holding assets from the intestate estate of the deceased Don Félix García Argueta, adjudicated a slave named José García to the heirs (nephews/nieces) residing in Villa de Nicaragua. José García, an elderly, dark-skinned slave valued at 50 pesos of cacao, was part of their inheritance. Don Antonio de la Fuente then granted José García a letter of freedom after 33 pesos 3 reales plata were exhibited as equivalent.

Doña Joaquina Tomasa del Corral granted power of attorney to her son, Don José Miguel Ocaña, residing in Granada, to sell a slave named Petronila, along with any children she has or may have, in that city.

María de Jesús Quirós leased a hacienda with 1000 fruit-bearing cacao trees, located in El Bejuco of the Barbilla valley, to Felipe Neri Tristán. The lease was for 3 years at a rate of 50 pesos cacao per year.

Teniente Coronel don Juan Flores, the interim Governor, granted power of attorney to Don Joaquín Inocencio de Ibarra, Senior Officer of the Postal Revenue in Guatemala City. This power allowed Ibarra to sell any properties belonging to Don Juan Flores that might be found in Guatemala City.

people_involved: Beneficiado don Juan José Zeledón y Reyes
summary: Beneficiado don Juan José Zeledón y Reyes, Cura of Somoto, obligated himself for 200 pesos plata and 200 cacao (at 5 ojo) for capellanías founded by Doña Cecilia Vázquez Coronado. These capellanías were previously charged to Don Pedro Machado, who had them secured on a house that belonged to his deceased mother-in-law, Doña Ramona Utrera.

people_involved: Juan José de los Reyes Zeledón
Padre don Juan Salvador del Aya y Bolívar
señor Obispo don Esteban Lorenzo de Tristán
summary: Juan José de los Reyes Zeledón acquired a house from doña Francisca Madriz y Linares, which is tied to a capellanía obligation. The chaplaincy was previously held by Padre don Juan Salvador del Aya y Bolívar and Br. don José Antonio Bonilla. However, during a visit by Bishop don Esteban Lorenzo de Tristán, it was clarified that the capellanías belonged to the Curato de Esparza.

Don José Francisco Taguada, acting as executor for don Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla, sold two caballerías of land on the other side of the Río Grande to doña María del Carmen Guevara. The land borders Jerónimo Flores's property and is described by natural landmarks. The sale was for 50 pesos.

people_involved: Unnamed wife of Juan Pablo Morales
summary: Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla and his wife, doña Ana Rita Gómez, took on an obligation for 150 pesos plata at 5% interest. This debt was previously held by Juan Pablo Morales and his wife, and it pertains to a capellanía founded by doña Juana de Vida Martel. Padre don Fernando Arleguí was the former chaplain, succeeded by Padre don Nicolás Hidalgo upon his death.

Don Antonio de la Fuente, as executor for doña Luisa de Guzmán, and doña Micaela de Alvarado, as heir of don Miguel de Alvarado, attempted to sell two mulatas to doña Florentina de Aragón. The mulatas were Antonia Josefa and her daughter Ana de los Dolores. This transaction did not go through.

Don Antonio de la Fuente, acting as executor for doña Luisa de Guzmán, sold an enslaved woman named Antonia Josefa, 38 years old, to doña Florentina de Aragón. Antonia Josefa had been adjudicated to doña Lucía, the widow of don Miguel de Alvarado, in his estate. The price was 100 pesos plata.

Doña Joaquina Tomasa del Corral sold a 19-year-old mulato pardo enslaved man named Juan Gregorio to don Lorenzo Guillén, a native of Panamá. Juan Gregorio is the son of Petronila, an enslaved woman belonging to del Corral, and was born in her house. The price was 206 pesos.

people_involved: Teniente de Ejército don Felipe Gallegos
summary: Miguel Arburola and Juan de la Rosa Maitín posted bail for Captain of Pardos Joaquín Coronel. The Governor is prosecuting Coronel for treating Army Lieutenant don Felipe Gallegos disrespectfully. This incident involved Coronel breaking Gallegos's head with a cane in the cloisters of San Francisco on the last Holy Thursday, following a complaint Gallegos filed against Coronel.

Don Joaquín de Oreamuno granted freedom to Leonardo, an enslaved man about 12 years old, who was given to him as a dowry by his father-in-law, don José Antonio Jiménez. Leonardo was acquired from the estate of doña Manuela Zavaleta and is the son of Magdalena, an enslaved woman who belonged to Zavaleta. Doña Dominga Zavaleta paid 200 pesos plata for Leonardo's freedom.

María Antonia Marín and her son Manuel Durán took on an obligation for 200 pesos of cacao at 5% interest. This capellanía belongs to Presbítero don Gregorio Bonilla, having been adjudicated to him by the Bishopric's Mitra because its original foundation could not be found.

people_involved: Presbítero don Joaquín Isidro de Quesada
summary: Don Francisco Ulloa, a resident of Villa Vieja, took on an obligation for 370 pesos cacao at 5% interest. This debt was previously held by don Manuel Fernández Bonilla and pertains to a capellanía founded by doña Manuela de Oviedo, whose chaplain was Presbítero don Joaquín Isidro de Quesada. Ulloa had to obtain a license from Vicario don Ramón de Azofeifa due to the deaths of Bonilla and Quesada.

Doña Nicolasa Meléndez, daughter of doña Manuela Valerín, made her will while ill in bed. She is single and has no children. She named her first cousin doña Catarina Meléndez and her servants María de los Dolores and Joaquina Meléndez as beneficiaries, with Presbítero don Pablo Molina as her executor.

people_involved: Unnamed widow of Juan Manuel Ramírez
summary: Don Simón Paniagua and his wife doña Bárbara Zamora, residents of Villa Vieja, took on an obligation for 185 pesos plata at 5% interest. This sum included 100 pesos previously owed by the deceased Juan Manuel Ramírez (now paid by his widow) and 85 pesos owed by the deceased don Antonio Marín. These funds belong to a capellanía founded by don Francisco de Ocampo.

people_involved: Simón de Jesús Escalante y Paniagual
summary: Simón de Jesús Escalante y Paniagual mortgaged his house and other properties located in Villa Vieja.

Don José Francisco de Oriamuno sold an enslaved person named Antolino, approximately 13 years old and described as 'color loro,' to Don Lorenzo Guillén, a resident of Panamá, for 300 pesos. Antolino was the son of Petronila, an enslaved person belonging to Don Antonio Oriamuno.

Don Luis Cueto, Alguacil Mayor and Regidor of León, and Pedro José Elizondo formed a three-year company to collect tithes in the local jurisdiction. Don Luis Cueto was the successful bidder for the tithe collection rights, valued at 2400 pesos annually.

José Manuel Barrios and his wife, Juana Gertrudis Salguero, assumed a debt of 100 pesos in cacao, at 5% interest, previously held by Lorenzo Marín. This debt was for chaplaincies established by Diego Quinteros for the benefit of the city, and was secured by a house near Doña Lucía de Alvarado's mill, which was sold to Barrios and Salguero with this obligation.

Don Marcos de Alvarado and his wife, Doña María Francisca de Velazco, assumed a 600-peso cacao debt at 5% interest. This lien was previously held by Presbítero don Fernando Arleguí and was secured by a pasture in Poás, 21 mule mares, two old houses, and other small items, which were transferred to Alvarado and Velazco on January 18 of the previous year. The debt belonged to a chaplaincy founded by Don Alonso Porras, with Cura don Ramón de Azofeifa as its Chaplain.

José Nicolás Camaño, as the principal debtor, along with José Miguel Cárdenas and José Manuel Barrios as guarantors, became obligated to José Antonio Sáenz, a master carpenter, for a debt of 432 pesos in cacao owed by Camaño.

Mariano Fonseca, representing the residents of Quebrada Seca in Villa Vieja, granted power of attorney to Don Juan José Medina, a Procurador of the Real Audiencia. Medina is tasked with handling an appeal against a sentence from the Lieutenant Governor of Villa Vieja, concerning a land dispute with Don Francisco Antonio Pérez, who claims ownership of lands paid for by the residents.

Benita Bonilla granted power of attorney to Don Sebastián Guevara, a resident of Nicaragua, to represent her before the Bishop's Tribunal in León. This representation is for a lawsuit against Juan Matamoros, a resident of 'this city,' demanding that he fulfill his promise to marry her.

Don José Antonio de Oreamuno sold a piece of land located near the hills west of 'this city' to Pedro Lizondro for 60 pesos. The land is bordered on the west by the Coris stream, and its other boundaries are described in relation to Don Romualdo Oreamuno's pasture.
Francisco Umaña's will was granted in Villa Vieja. Joaquín and Jacoba de Alcarado were named as executors, and an unnamed heiress was designated.

Francisco Carázo and his wife, Doña Ocampo, are responsible for the tutelage of minors Bernadé and Antonia Josefa Ramírez. They have also paid the share of a married heiress from the inheritance of the minors' brother. Joaquín is mentioned as an executor, possibly related to this or the previous will.

A request was added for Don Fran (likely Francisco Carázo) to take charge of the tutelage of the minors of Don Tomás, who died in military service. On July 27, 1785, Don Felipe Chavarría, tutor of the minor Don José Francisco, received his share from Carazo.

people_involved: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora
Doña Rosa de la Madriz Linares
summary: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora committed to pay Don Vicente del Corral, minor son of the deceased Don Tomás López del Corral and Doña Rosa de la Madriz Linares, 166 pesos and 5 reales. This money is part of 1000 pesos given by Don Matías de Gálvez to the heirs of Don Tomás and his wife for military service in the North Coast and Matina Valley during a past war.

people_involved: Doña María de la Luz Aguilar
summary: Doña María de la Luz Aguilar, residing in Villa Vieja and originally from León, granted general power of attorney to her husband, Don Jerónimo de Alvarado, who is currently in León.

Jos Antonio Cárdenas and his wife Benita Masís committed to pay 64 pesos and 2 reales in cacao, representing an inheritance for the minor Claudio de Jesús. This inheritance is through Claudio's deceased father, Juan José López, who was the son and heir of Francisco Nicolás López. Capitán Miguel Cárdenas acted as guarantor.

Pedro Regalado de Rojas, a resident of Cartago, granted power to his uncle, Manuel Antonio Jiménez, to create his will. He named his legitimate daughters, Antonia Magdalena and María Josefa de Rojas, born from his marriage to Juana Josefa de Quesada, as his heirs, along with any future descendants. His uncle and sister, Micaela Rojas, were appointed as executors.

Doña Francisca Miranda, daughter of the deceased Pedro Fernández Miranda and Ana María Maroto, made her will. She was married twice, first to José Miguel Solís and second to Francisco Ramo, and ordered her slave, Ana Miranda, to be freed upon her death. She designated her nephew-in-law, Alcalde Ordinario José Antonio del Campo, as the preferred buyer for her house in Cartago and also named him as an executor, while also detailing financial matters involving her husband in Guatemala and funds in Tegucigalpa.

Alférez Real Antonio de la Fuente, acting as Síndico General of the Seraphic Order in Costa Rica province, granted power to Francisco de Icaza, Administrator of Posts in León, and Luis Cueto, Regidor and Alcalde General Mayor in León, to collect the annual stipends assigned to the regular priests of the province's towns from the Royal Coffers.

Manuel Galisteo, a resident of Nueva Guatemala, who was about to depart for that city but had various matters to attend to locally, granted general power of attorney to Antonio Pao, Lieutenant Governor of Villa Nueva.

Francisco Miguel Delgado, son of the deceased Bernardo Delgado and Juana Picado, all residents of Cartago, made his will in Purires. He was married to Jerónima Garro and named his three minor children, Rita Josefa, Félix de la Rosa, and Marcos Antonio Delgado, as his heirs. His wife and Francisco Carazo were appointed as executors.

The will of the deceased Pedro Regalado de Rojas, who died on January 10th, 1785, was granted by his attorney, Manuel Antonio Jiménez. Rojas was married to Juana Josefa de Quesada, with whom he had two minor daughters, Antonia Magdalena and María Josefa, both under 14 years old, who were named as his heirs. Manuel Antonio Jiménez and Micaela de Rojas, the testator's sister, were named as executors.

Escribano José Romualdo Zamora, following a superior dispatch, received $250 that he had overpaid for the auction price of his office, as per a Royal order. To provide the required guarantee, he named Manuel José García as his guarantor and mortgaged a sugar mill near Cartago and his residence. The transaction was granted before Juan Flores, interim Governor.

José Romualdo Zamora granted power of attorney, first to José Manuel de Laparte, Secretary of the Chamber of the Royal Audiencia of this Kingdom, and second to Juan José Medina, Procurator of the same Audiencia, to represent him before the Audiencia. This was done before Alcalde Ordinario José Antonio del Campo.

Micaela Josefa Hernández, daughter of the deceased Antonio Miguel Hernández and María Carranza, made her will. She was married first to Juan Francisco Colina, with whom she had three living children, and second to Francisco Lozano, with whom she also had three living children. Her six living children were named as heirs, and Alférez Real Antonio de la Fuente was named as an executor.

Alférez Real Antonio de la Fuente and his wife, María Francisca de Alvarado, obligated themselves for $800 in silver at 5% interest, on behalf of María de Jesús Salazar, a minor under twelve. This money was received from a benefactor, partly in cash and partly as a slave named Miguel Francisco Baeza, purchased from Manuela Baeza for $100 with the minor's money. The slave was held by R. P. Fray Francisco Baeza, with the only obligation being to educate and clothe him.

In a marginal note, María Francisca de Alvarado and her son-in-law Ignacio Llórente, acting as attorneys for Antonio de la Fuente, manifested that they had delivered $700 of the obligation to Ignacio Céspedes, husband of María de Jesús Salazar. The remaining $100 was the value of the slave, Miguel Francisco Baeza, who Fray Francisco Baeza had disposed of.

Baltasara Solano and her guarantor, Juan de Dios Brenes, obligated themselves for $91 and 4 reales, representing the paternal inheritance share of Baltasara's six minor children: Juan Ramón, Francisco Rudesindo, Francisca Micaela, Juana del Espíritu Santo, José Policarpo, and Julián Santana Brenes, from their deceased father Cayetano Brenes.

Don Esteban Venegas granted general power of attorney, first to Martín Venegas, second to Dionisio Venegas, third to Gregorio Venegas (all Venegas), and fourth to Pedro Santana, Alférez of the Extremadura Regiment, all residents of Panama City.

José Miguel Venegas, as the husband of the deceased Manuela Josefa Calvo y Torres, who was the daughter of Manuela del Carmen Torres (a native of Cartago who died in Santiago de Veragua after marrying Francisco Méndez without leaving children or forced heirs), granted power of attorney on his own behalf and on behalf of his children with Manuela Josefa Calvo to Mateo José López, Alférez Real of Santiago de Veragua.
Baltasar Nieto, a resident of La Mesa, was appointed to collect the assets left by the deceased Manuela del Carmen. These assets were intended for her children, who were designated as her sole heirs.
On April 18, María de la Luz Aguilar, a native of León, granted general power of attorney to her husband, Miguel Jerónimo de Alvarado, who was currently in León.

On April 20, Doña Gertrudis Zabaleta granted freedom to her slave, Juana Antonia Zabaleta, who was approximately 23 years old. Juana Antonia had been inherited by Gertrudis from her deceased mother, Doña Manuela Zabaleta.

On April 20, Don Francisco Carazo and his wife Doña Jacoba de Alvarado committed to pay 1000 pesos to Doña Ignacia de la Rosa, a native of Tierra Firme and a local resident, with an annual interest of 5%.

On January 18, 1796, the debt was cancelled. Don Francisco Carazo, who was deceased, paid $200, and the remaining $800 was paid by his executors: Presbítero Don Pablo José Molina, Doña Jacoba Alvarado, and Don Lorenzo Carazo, to Doña Ignacia de la Rosa.
On May 11, Juan de la Rosa Maitín, a bidder for a gallera auction, granted power of attorney to Don Francisco Ambrona, a Procurator of the Audiencia of Guatemala, to secure the auction in his favor.

On April 30, Don José Miguel Flores and his wife Doña Juana Antonia Gutiérrez, residents of Villa Vieja, became obligated for 1066 pesos and 4.5 reales in silver, representing the tutelage of Juan Antonio, a minor. Juan Antonio is the son of Doña Juana Antonia and her first, deceased husband, Don Alejandro Alfaro.

locations: Hospital de San Juan de Dios
people_involved: José Severino de Castilla y Guzmán
summary: On May 3, Beneficiado Don José Severino de Castilla y Guzmán, a native of León (Nicaragua) and current priest of Villa Nueva, made his will. He made various bequests to relatives and associates, and appointed Don Ramón Azofeifa and Don Juan José de Oreamuno as his executors.

On May 6, Lieutenant Colonel Don Juan Flores, Sergeant Major in Granada, sold a chácara (farm) to Don José María Peralta for $500 in silver. The property, acquired from Don Fermín Mondragón, included various structures and land, with $200 of the price designated as a donation to María de los Dolores Lobo.

On May 6, Don Juan Flores donated $200 to María Dolores Lobo, whom he had raised after her mother, Manuela Lobo, abandoned her. This sum was to be managed by José María Peralta, with annual interest paid to Doña Joaquina López del Corral for María Dolores's upbringing and education.

On November 21, 1794, the donation to María Dolores Lobo was cancelled. This action was based on an order issued the previous day by Governor Don José Vázquez y Téllez, and a royal provision from October 7, 1790, which mandated the cancellation.

On May 17, Lieutenant Colonel Don Juan Flores, having ceased his interim governorship, granted general power of attorney to Don Antonio Pao and, secondarily, to Don José Antonio de Oreamuno. This was in preparation for his travel to Granada for his battalion and then to Spain for personal business.

On May 21, Captain Don Francisco Carazo, acting as executor for Don Tomás de Soto y Barahoaa, sold a walled solar to Colonel Don José Romualdo de Oreamuno for $150. The property had been previously acquired from Presbítero Don Manuel Cubero.

On May 24, Doña Estefanía Pacheco sold a slave named Miguel Jerónimo Pacheco, approximately 29 years old, to Don Juan de Zabala, the tobacco administrator. Estefanía had acquired Miguel Jerónimo from her brother, Don Juan Dionisio Pacheco, as payment for a debt.

On May 25, Don José Francisco Rojas, legitimate son of the deceased Don Miguel de Rojas and Doña Micaela Guzmán, made his will. He was married to Doña Antonia Nicolasa Mario and had no children, naming his mother as his heir and Don Pedro Lizondro as his executor.

Bartola Ramos and José Tomás Ramos, residents of Valle de Ujarraz, committed to pay $107 in silver. This sum represents the inheritance due to María Josefa, María Magdalena, and Manuel Atanasio Villarreal, who are the minor children of Bartola Ramos and the late Ramón Villarreal.

Don José Antonio Jiménez appointed Don Toribio Ramírez, a resident of Nicaragua, to retrieve an enslaved person named José Francisco Chaves. Chaves, described as about 27 years old, had escaped from Jiménez and taken refuge with Jiménez's deceased half-brother, Presbítero Don Manuel Antonio Sandoval.

Don Manuel Torre y Romero, a Spaniard, sold an enslaved woman named Petronila, aged about 32, and her two sons, Ciríaco (15) and Manuel José (13), to Doña María Cayetana Donaire, a resident of León. The sale, conducted through his attorney Don Alejandro Lampar, was for $650, and the enslaved individuals had originally been purchased from the estate of Don Tomás Corral.

people_involved: Canónigo Don José Albino de la Plata
summary: Don Antonio Ramón de Azofeifa, the local parish priest, authorized Canon Don José Albino de la Plata, residing in León, to collect the synod for his curacy.

Don Felipe Gallegos and his wife, Doña Guadalupe Alvarado, committed to pay $75 in cacao to Beneficiado Don Ramón de Azofeifa, the local Cura. This obligation, carrying a 5% interest rate, pertained to a chaplaincy originally established by Padre Don Manuel Camacho and previously overseen by Doña Benita Bonilla.

people_involved: Alférez Real Don Antonio de la Fuente
summary: Don Sebastián Fernández and his wife Doña Antonia Arleguí committed to pay $100 in cacao with 5% interest, an obligation previously held by Doña Sebna. de Bonilla and belonging to the Convento de San Francisco. This debt was secured by a property on the main plaza. The obligation was cancelled on December 5, 1786, by Don Antonio de la Fuente, the Syndic of the Convento de San Francisco.

people_involved: Alférez Real Don Antonio de la Fuente
summary: Alférez Real Don Antonio de la Fuente authorized Don Eusebio Alvarado to make a bid or lease the Cofradía del Santísimo de Esparza. This action was prompted by news that all confraternities in that region were to be put up for lease.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Antonio de Oreamuno
summary: On July 25, Don Juan José de Oreamuno, a Cleric Presbyter acting as his father's attorney, requested the opening of his grandfather Don José Antonio de Oreamuno's will, who had passed away that day. The will itself was dated July 5, 1781.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Antonio de Oreamuno
Doña María de la Encarnación Sancho de Castañeda
Doña Bárbara Josefa Sancho de Castañeda
Beneficiado Don José Miguel Sancho de Castañeda
Don José Felipe Sancho de Castañeda
summary: The closed will of Sargento Mayor Don Antonio de Oreamuno, dated July 5, 1781, was opened. He was a native of Panama, son of deceased Don José de Oreamuno and Doña Josefa Vázquez Meléndez. He had two marriages: first to the late Doña María Catarina de Ibarra, producing sons Don Romualdo and Don José Francisco, and second to Doña Bárbara Josefa Sancho de Castañeda, with no issue. The will detailed his heirs, including a one-third improvement for his son Don José Francisco and his grandchildren Don José Nicolás and Doña María Josefa, and appointed his wife Doña Bárbara, Beneficiado Don José Miguel Sancho de Castañeda, and Don José Felipe Sancho de Castañeda as executors. Due to Don José Francisco's incapacitation, his wife, Doña María de la Encarnación, was named his and their children's tutor.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Antonio de Oreamuno
summary: This entry refers to the continuation of a property transfer deed. The deed was originally granted by Don José Antonio de Oriamuno to Don Gregorio Oreamuño, concerning the transfer of a possession.

people_involved: Alférez Real Don Antonio de la Fuente
summary: Alférez Real Don Antonio de la Fuente, acting as tutor for the minor Juan José Ergea of Villa Nueva, granted power of attorney to Don Francisco Icaza, the Post Administrator in León, and secondarily to Don Manuel Galisteo, also of León. Their task was to collect $1000 in León, an inheritance left to Juan José Ergea by his deceased natural father, Don Manuel Ergea.

Don Mateo José García and Don Miguel Guzmán reported that Pedro García wounded Fermín Enrique in self-defense during a minor altercation. As Enrique has completely recovered, García, who was imprisoned, was released on bail.
Don Joaquín de Alvarado, a local resident, and Don Francisco Ulloa, from Villa Vieja, resolved a legal dispute involving mutual debts through a settlement.
Doña Teresa Trujillo sold Manuela Guzmán, an enslaved woman born and raised in her household, described as black with light eyes, to Capitán Don José María Peralta for $300.

people_involved: Doña Juana Muñoz de la Trinidad
Doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho de Castañeda
summary: Capitán Don Gregorio Oreamuno and his wife Doña Juana Muñoz de la Trinidad committed to pay $200 with 5% interest to Doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho de Castañeda. This obligation was later cancelled on October 22, 1787, after being transferred to Pedro José Lizondro.

Juana Josefa de Quesada, as principal, and Josefa Micaela de Rojas, as guarantor, committed to pay $332.5 reales for the paternal inheritance of Antonia Magdalena and María Josefa Rojas, minor daughters of Quesada and the late Pedro Regalado de Rojas. Additionally, they obligated themselves for $42 belonging to Juana Sotela, a demented person under Quesada's care, which Pedro Regalado de Rojas had previously managed.

Juana Josefa de Quesada and Josefa Micaela de Rojas committed to pay $200 with 5% interest for a chaplaincy of the Convento de San Francisco de Esparza. This debt, previously held by Juana Josefa de Quesada's deceased husband, Pedro Regalado de Rojas, was secured by 99 head of cattle. The obligation was cancelled on January 3, 1786, by Don Joaquín de Oreamuno, who assumed responsibility for it.
Doña Florentina de Aragón, a widow, committed to pay $525 in cacao with 5% interest, related to a chaplaincy.

A capellanía (chaplaincy) was under the charge of José Miguel García and his widow Antonia Masís. The associated property included a pasture and a 'caballería de tierra' located in the Felipe Díaz area, immediately adjacent to the volcano of this city towards the West.

Coronel José Romualdo Oreamuno, acting as albacea for his mother María Catarina de Ibarra, founded a capellanía with $1173. This was done in fulfillment of his mother's closed will, which she had granted with her husband Sargento Mayor José Antonio de Oreamuno on April 27, 1775. Presbítero Juan José de Oreamuno, son of José Romualdo Oreamuno, was named the chaplain, and the assets were situated in three contiguous cocoa and 'rt.zas' haciendas in the Matina valley, named La Lacayo, La Pola, and La Ibarra.

people_involved: Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: José Nicolás Anacleto Chavarría and his wife Eufemia Salmón Pacheco sold an adobe and tile house with its walled plot to José Antonio del Campo for $466-5 reales. The house was inherited by Eufemia from her deceased father Dionisio Salmón Pacheco, and its boundaries were defined by properties belonging to various individuals including Francisco Pacheco, Estéfana Pacheco, Cecilia Escalante, Juana Miranda, Gabriela Sarmiento, and the deceased Padre Juan Manuel Casasola.

The sale of the house by José Nicolás Anacleto Chavarría and Eufemia Salmón Pacheco to José Antonio del Campo was rescinded on November 10, 1786. This rescission was due to a lawsuit initiated by Estéfana Pacheco concerning the sale of the property.

people_involved: Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Antonio de la Fuente, acting as albacea for Presbítero Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba, sold a house in this city to José Nicolás Anacleto Chavarría for $625. The house, made of adobe, posts, and tile with a walled plot, bordered properties of María del Aya y Bolívar, Estéfana Pacheco, and José Antonio del Campo.

Tomás Hidalgo sold an enslaved man named José Hidalgo, 27 years old, with light eyes and a regular build, to Juan Blas de Amillatigui, a resident of Panamá, for $270. José Hidalgo was born and raised in Tomás Hidalgo's house.

Pedro José Elizondo, acting as an agent for Luis Cueto y Landa, a resident of León, and on his own behalf, sold the tithes corresponding to the Villa Nueva district to Gregorio Ramírez, a resident of Tres Ríos, for $400 annually. This district extended from the Virilla river to the towns of Curridabat and Aserrí, inclusively, with the exception of tobacco tithes. Cueto y Landa was the lessee of the city's tithes for a three-year period, and Elizondo was his partner.

Bernardino Alvarado and his wife Tomasa Solano, residents of Újarraz, sold an enslaved woman named Dominga de los Angeles Solano and her 6-month-old son, José, to Ramón de Azofeifa for $300. Dominga, described as 19 years old, dark-skinned, and short with light eyes, was the daughter of Carmen Flor, an enslaved woman belonging to Tomasa Solano's mother.

Juan de Dios Brenes and his wife María Francisca Pacheco obligated themselves to Manuela Sancho de Castañeda for $100 at 5% interest. They mortgaged their dwelling house located in this city as collateral.
The obligation made by Juan de Dios Brenes and María Francisca Pacheco to Manuela Sancho de Castañeda for $100, secured by their house, was canceled on October 10, 1789.
José Santana Jiménez and his wife María Antonia Carranza, residents of Villa Nueva de Aserrí, declared and appraised the assets that each contributed to their marriage.

Capitán Gregorio de Oreamuno received in deposit the inventoried assets belonging to the deceased Sargento Mayor José Antonio Oreamuno, totaling $3098-2 reales. This deposit was requested by Tomás Alvarado, the defender of the minor children of the deceased José Francisco Oreamuno.

people_involved: Juan Salvador del Aya y Bolívar
summary: María del Aya y Bolívar, widow of Andrés Bonilla, obligated herself to her three minor children, Miguel, Justa, and María Cruz Bonilla, for their paternal inheritance share of $15-2 reales and 134 maravedíes each. Additionally, she obligated herself for 100 cattle that the two daughters received as a donation from their uncle, Presbítero Juan Salvador del Aya y Bolívar. Santiago Bonilla served as guarantor.

Rosa Madriz sold an enslaved 'mestizo blanco' named Pedro, about 20 years old, to Pedro José Elizondo for $100. Pedro had previously belonged to Rosa's deceased husband, Tomás Corrales, who acquired him from the heirs of Presbítero Nicolás Salmón Pacheco. The sale included a condition from Pedro's original owner, Joaquina Corrales, that he could not be resold for a higher price. Felipe Chavarría received the $100, as he had lent the sum to Rosa with the slave's value as collateral.

Tomás de Alvarado and his wife María del Rosario Bonilla sold an enslaved mulata named Marcelina, 30 years old, and her 9-year-old son, Juan José, to María del Aya y Bolívar for $200 and $80 respectively.

María del Aya y Bolívar took charge of $440 from two censos (annuities/mortgages) belonging to the Beneficio de Esparza, located on lands across the Río Grande. These censos were annexed to capellanías founded by Cecilia Vázquez Coronado, for which José Ant° Alvarado, the priest of Esparza, was currently the chaplain. The censos were previously held by Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla, who transferred them to María del Aya y Bolívar and her deceased husband Andrés de Bonilla.

The obligation taken on by María del Aya y Bolívar regarding the censos was canceled on December 22, 1815. This cancellation occurred after her son, José Antonio Bonilla, presented testimony indicating that the obligation had been transferred to Víctor Rojas.

Josefa Chavarría, as the principal, along with Trinidad Chavarría and his wife Manuela Acuña as guarantors, obligated themselves for $194-7 reales. This sum represented the inheritance share of José Nicolás, the minor son of the deceased Nicolás Cerdas and Josefa Chavarría, from the estate of María Portugués, who was Josefa Chavarría's mother.

people_involved: María Josefa de la O. Ulloa
summary: Don Pedro, Doña Petronila, and Don Francisco Ulloa granted freedom to María Josefa de la O. Ulloa, an enslaved person. This act was related to Don José de Dios Ulloa's impending marriage to María Josefa, who was formerly enslaved by Don Alfonso Ulloa. The heirs of Don Alfonso Ulloa either declared payment for their share or donated it to María Josefa.

Don Manuel Torre y Romero, a native of Spain, conferred a general power of attorney. He appointed Licenciado Don Mariano Ezeta in the first place, Don José Agustín Navas in the second, and Don Juan José Medma, a procurador of the Royal Audience, in the third.

people_involved: Capitán Comandante de pardos Joaquín Corl.
summary: Don Santiago de Bonilla, needing to be absent, granted power to Captain Comandante de pardos Joaquín Corl. to represent him.
