This representation was for a pending legal case concerning costs, damages, and prejudices, in which the captains of the current Governor had been condemned, and which was now before an assessor.

Don Antonio de la Fuente, acting as attorney for Don Antonio Pérez by substitution from Don Jorge Francisco de Lamas, sold an enslaved Zambo named Francisco Graciano to Don José Antonio Oreamuno for $200. The original power of attorney from Pérez to Lamas, granted on March 18, 1785, in Villa de los Santos, authorized Lamas to apprehend the runaway enslaved person in Nicaragua and sell him.

Tomás Solera, a resident of Villa Vieja, had satisfied the defender of the minor Don José Francisco Ibarra for $172 and $25 in costs. However, Solera still owed $53, for which he obligated himself, having been charged as a guarantor for Don Julián Azofeifa since 1777.
Don Gregorio Oreamuno received the $53 owed by Tomás Solera and canceled the debt.

Alejandro Lampar granted power to Don Pedro Ayerdi, a resident of León, to obligate him in favor of Doña María Cayetana Donaire, also of León. This obligation was for the sum corresponding to a clothing order placed at her shop.

Jerónima Garro obligated herself for $1048-7 reales, which represented the paternal inheritance of her minor children, Rita Josefa, Félix, and Marcos Antonio Delgado. This sum was from the estate of her deceased husband, Francisco Miguel Delgado.

Don Joaquín de Oriamuno obligated himself for $200.00 plata at 5% interest to the Convento de la ciudad de Esparza. This debt was previously held by Pedro Rojas and, after his death, passed to his wife Juana de Quesada and sister-in-law Micaela Rojas. Don Joaquín hypothecated 70 mares, a donkey, and his house in the city as collateral.

people_involved: Don Tomás Cortés de la Quintana
summary: Don Antonio de la Fuente, acting as Síndico General of the San Francisco Convents, granted power of attorney. He appointed Don Francisco Icaza in the first place and Don Tomás Cortés de la Quintana in the second, both residents of León, to collect the synod assigned to the Curas doctrineros and reductores of the province for the previous year from the Royal Coffers.

Pedro Valerín, a free mulatto from the Puebla of this city, leased the canoe for the Reventazón crossing for three years. He obligated himself to pay three portions of cacao, transport hacendados for free, and maintain the canoe. In return, he would receive $300 annually from hacendados and collect two reales of cacao per load or person from non-hacendados.

people_involved: Doña María Josefa Barros y Muro
summary: Valentín Barrios, a free mulatto from the Puebla of this city, sold three-quarters of a caballería of land to Don José Francisco de Arleguí for $25.00. This land, located in Santaña, had been donated to Valentín by his deceased wife, Doña María Josefa Barros y Muro, and its exact boundaries were unknown to the grantor.

people_involved: Doña María Josefa Rosa Aymerich y Llenas
summary: The will of Captain Don Pedro Aymerich was opened, requested by his widow Doña María Francisca Corrales. The joint will was executed on October 22, 1785, before Escribano Don José Romualdo Zamora, and Don Pedro died on January 17, 1786. The will detailed their parentage, lack of children together, Doña María Francisca's previous marriage and children, and their assets including haciendas and eight enslaved people. Provisions were made for a capellanía with Doña María Francisca's nephew, Don Juan de Sierra, as chaplain.

An unnamed testator makes a will, stipulating that any inheritance from his parents in Cataluña, Spain, should go to his wife, and upon her death, to his natural son, Francisco Javier. This ensures the natural son receives a share of the family's potential assets.

Don Isidro Zamora, a resident of Villa Nueva, obligates himself to the Cofradía de la Concepción for $75.00 silver at 5% interest, taking over a debt previously held by Basilio Quesada. He hypothecates his house in Villa Nueva as collateral. The obligation was later cancelled on June 11, 1792, having been transferred to Don Claudio Castro and his wife.

people_involved: Doña María del Aya y Bolívar
Presbítero don José Antonio de Bonilla
summary: Doña María del Aya y Bolívar obligates herself to the Capellanías, for which her son, Presbítero don José Antonio de Bonilla, is patron and chaplain, for $400.00 at 5% interest. This debt was previously held by Don José Antonio Orearauno, and she hypothecates her house in Cartago. The obligation was cancelled on October 22, 1815, when Don José Antonio de Bonilla, Cura of Villa Vieja, received the $400.00 and interest from his mother.

people_involved: Don Blas del Aya y Bolívar
Don José Miguel del Aya y Bolívar
summary: Don Blas del Aya y Bolívar, son of the deceased Don José Miguel del Aya y Bolívar and Doña Gertrudis Ramírez, and a former resident of Esparza, makes his will. He is married to Clara Josefa Mercedes Osejo, with whom he has no children, and donates 20 heads of cattle and two horses to his brother, Don Francisco Taguada, naming him and his wife as executors.

María Leonida Portugués, daughter of María Portugués and widow of Juan Francisco Vega, makes her will in her house in Taras, near Cartago. She leaves a fence to her 'muchacha' María Josefa Portugués, improves her natural son Francisco Javier in one-third of her assets, and names Don Antonio de la Fuente as executor, with her natural sons Manuel José and Francisco Javier as heirs.

Residents of Ujarraz, including officials and citizens, are involved in a lawsuit against Don Ramón de Azofeifa and Fray Antonio de la Concepción concerning the dispossession of the image of Nuestra Señora de Ujarraz. The image's face and hands are now in the Convento de San Francisco in Cartago with a new body. The Ujarraz residents grant power of attorney to Don Antonio de la Fuente to represent them in this dispute.

Pedro Manuel Salguero sells a 'caballería y tres cuartos de tierra' (land) located in Angelina de Cuetcua to Diego Martín Chavarría for $80.00. This land had previously been donated to Salguero by Don Andrés Fernández and Doña María Trejos.

people_involved: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora grants power to testate to B" don Ramón de Azofeifa, whom she also names as her executor. Her heirs are her natural children, Doña Rafaela, Don Nicolás, and Don Esteban, and her legitimate son, Don Juan Sierra, whose father, also named Don Juan Sierra, was discovered to be married to another woman after the son's birth, a fact unknown to Doña Manuela.

María Manuela, Pedro José, Felipe Atanasio, and José Manuel Mesa, residents of Valle de Ujarraz, agree to an extrajudicial division of the modest assets left by their deceased parents, José Antonio Mesa and María Francisca Calderón. All heirs are present, except María Micaela Mesa, who renounces her share, having already received something. The total capital distributed is $128.6 reales.

Don José Rodríguez, a resident of Villa Nueva, states that Don Juan José Zeledón Reyes, also from Villa Nueva, has died, leaving a capellanía of $200.00 for Don Ramón de Azofeifa, secured by a house, a slave named Bernardo Mora, and the guarantee of Rodríguez and his wife. To recover and sell the slave, who is in León, Nicaragua, to cancel the obligation, Rodríguez grants power of attorney to Don Francisco Icaza and Don Manuel Galisteo.

Don Francisco Arleguí leases a productive cacao plantation in the Valle de Matina, consisting of 3749 trees, to Miguel Fuentes, a free mulatto from the Puebla of Cartago. The lease term is 3 years, with an annual rent of $370.00 in cacao.

Don Mateo Mora and Don Dionisio Mora, residents of Villa Nueva de San José, acting on behalf of their community for the measurement and composition of lands known as El Rincón de las Pavas, grant power of attorney to Don Juan Zabala, an accounting official in the tobacco branch of the Guatemala Directorate, to handle the remaining procedures for confirming the land title, as the measurement diligences are complete.

Pedro de Herrera, a resident of Villa Vieja in the Zanjón district, leases a pasture (potrero) named 'el Maestre de Campo don José Sandoval' from the common lands (ejidos) of his neighborhood. The pasture is bounded by the Porrosatí river to the East and the Quebrada de la Cruz to the West.
An agreement was made regarding land boundaries, with an annual payment of $19 to the Mayordomo de propios, Don José León de Bonilla. This agreement was later cancelled.
An earlier land agreement from November 10 of the previous year (1786) was cancelled. The Zanjón neighborhood took over the pasture, improving the price by $2.

Don Antonio de la Fuente took on the lease for the tobacco and sugarcane aguardiente factory in the city and its annexes, including several towns. He agreed to pay $530 annually, with Doña Manuela Baeza acting as his guarantor.

Tomás Ruiz, a resident of Villa Vieja in Alajuela, leased the largest part of the Tambor pasture, which belonged to the city. The annual price was $15, and the lease was cancelled on January 11, 1795.
Rafael Pacheco leased a portion of the same pasture mentioned in the previous escritura. He agreed to pay $10 annually for his part of the land.

locations: El Bejuco del Valle de Matina
summary: José Manuel González, in gratitude to Doña Cecilia del Castillo, donated various assets to her three children: Rafael Ceferino, José Florencio, and Luis Teodoro Castillo. These donations included copper kettles, a new hacienda with cacao trees in Matina acquired from Ramona Quesada (widow of Ventura Prado), and a small ranch with livestock, to be shared equally among the children.

Captain Francisco Carazo granted power of attorney to Don Juan José Medina, a Procurator of the Royal Audiencia. This power allowed Medina to bid before the Private Land Judge on land measurements in Tenorio, Bagaces, that had not been confirmed by Don Antonio Cervantes.

Josefa Nicolasa Padilla and her children, Paula and José Santiago Paniagua, appointed experts to appraise the assets received by the children as part of their inheritance. Paula's husband, Miguel Fuentes, signed the receipt for her. Josefa Nicolasa also declared that her son José Eugenio Paniagua, who had supported her for nine years, would inherit her house upon her death, a decision agreed upon by the other children.

Miguel Fuentes and his wife Paula Paniagua y Cantillo, residents of Ujarraz, took on a $100 debt (census) owed to Presbyter Don Francisco Robredo, which was previously the responsibility of Captain Don Pedro Machado. They offered 1500 cacao trees in Matina as collateral for the 5% annual payment.

people_involved: El Beneficiado Don Ramón Antonio de Azofeifa
summary: Lieutenant Don Rafael Alvarado took on a $480 silver debt related to a chaplaincy fund. This fund was previously managed by Beneficiado Don Ramón Antonio de Azofeifa and belonged to the Esparza Benefice.
Don José Moscoso y Atencio married Juana Josefa Arguedas in Villa Vieja.

Don José Moscoso y Atencio, a native of Spain, granted power of attorney to Don Juan Sánchez of León, Nicaragua, to collect his inheritance in Puerto Real, Spain. From the collected funds, $110 would be paid to Sánchez for Moscoso's transport from Europe.

people_involved: El Sarg. Mayor Don José Antonio Oreamuno
summary: Captain Don Gregorio Oreamuno received $2023 worth of assets from the estate of the deceased Sergeant Major Don José Antonio Oreamuno in deposit. These assets were located in Sagaces (likely Bagaces) at the Paso Hondo ranch.

people_involved: Marqués Don Juan Fermín de Aycinena
summary: Don Antonio de la Fuente made a $500 donation to Doña María Josefa González Madriz, to be given upon her marriage, with a condition for poor girls if she misbehaved. This was on behalf of Don Andrés Antonio González of Nicaragua, who also wrote about finding a large pearl, attempting to sell it to Marqués Don Juan Fermín de Aycinena, and ultimately gifting it to the Princess.
Don Mateo Hernández, husband of Doña María Josefa González Madriz, received the $500 donation previously arranged for his wife.

A power of attorney was granted in Villa Nueva before Antonio Pao, Lieutenant Governor and Political Judge. This power, signed by several residents, was for the measurement and composition of royal lands in Rincón de Pavas.

Don Mateo and Don Dionisio Mora, residents of Villa Nueva de San José, transferred the power of attorney they held from their community to Don Antonio de Talayera Vascón, a Procurator of the Royal Audiencia. This power was for the measurement and composition of royal lands in Rincón de Pavas.

An unnamed heir of José Manuel Mora, from Nueva de San José, sold a property in Patarra to Pedro UUoa for $190 silver. The property included a house, a sugar cane plot, and 20 heads of cattle, which José Manuel Mora had previously agreed to sell.

Juan Carranza, acting as Mayordomo for the Confraternity of Nuestra Señora de Matina, leased a cacao plantation with 1300 trees in Matina to Pedro Manuel Salguero. The lease was for 5 years at a rate of $50 cacao per year.

Captain José Peralta sold an enslaved woman named Manuela Guzmán to Pedro José Elizondo for $300 silver. Manuela Guzmán, described as 16 years old, black, and light-eyed, was born and raised under the ownership of Teresa Trujillo.

Jerónimo Alvarado and María Alvarado, acting as principal and guarantor respectively, received the assets left by their deceased father, Marcos Alvarado. These assets were located in Poás and had been under the care of José Manuel Carvajal.

José de León Bonilla, as executor for the deceased Tomás López del Corral, granted power of attorney to Manuel Galisteo and Franco. Icaza in León. Their task was to sell an enslaved man named Pablo Luna, who had escaped about a year prior and was reportedly imprisoned in León.

Captain Juan Francisco de Bonilla and his wife Rita Gómez, as principal and guarantor, became obligated to Alférez Real Antonio de la Fuente and Captain Francisco Carazo. This obligation was for amounts they had supplied during an execution process initiated by Governor Ferie against Bonilla and other Captains, where they were condemned to pay fines, costs, damages, and losses by order of the Supreme Tribunal.

Tomás Alvarado, a resident of Villa Nueva, granted power of attorney to José Ignacio Alvarado, or failing him, Agustín Castro. Their purpose was to collect the assets left by his deceased son, José León de Alvarado, in Chinandega, following notification of his death to the provincial Governor by the Corregidor of Subtiaba.

Martín González and his wife Juana Masís became obligated to Nicolás González, son of Martín and his first wife Benita Carranza, for $117 and one real. This amount represented half the price of a house in the city's outskirts that Nicolás inherited from his mother. The other half was already given to Martín's other son, Lorenzo González, upon his marriage.

Antonio de la Fuente leased the Hacienda del Sacramento in Esparza for 10 years at a cost of $41 and 1/6 reales. Manuela Baeza, his mother-in-law and a widow, served as his guarantor. The lease had initially been awarded to Julián Daniel, who died on April 1st.

Teresa Chinchilla, widow of Francisco Soto, was responsible for the guardianship of her children's inherited paternal assets. Initially guaranteed by Gabriel Gra. and Candelaria Jiménez, she released them and appointed Andrés Brenes and his wife Catalina Soto as new guarantors.

Lieutenant Santiago de Bonilla became obligated to the Convent of San Francisco for $600 in cacao. This debt was originally Juan Caballero's, then fell to Tomás López del Corral as his guarantor upon Caballero's absence, and finally passed to Bonilla after Corral's death, secured by a house. Bonilla's mother, María del Aya y Bolívar, served as his guarantor.

Ramón Puche, a bachelor from Cartagena de Indias, made his will, naming his mother Clara Manuela Pupo as his heir and co-executor with his brother-in-law Sebastián de Hoce for Cartagena, and Antonio de la Fuente for Cartago. He declared no children and mentioned a box of merchandise belonging to Captain Pedro Ayarín, which was consigned for sale to his deceased companion Ramón María Blasco.

Antonio de la Fuente, acting as curator for Micaela de Alvarado due to her 'ineptitude,' granted freedom to José Ángel, the son of Micaela's enslaved woman, Ana Barrios. Juan Bobadilla, who claimed to be José Ángel's father and intended to marry Ana, provided $50 silver for the manumission with the consent of his mistress, Florentina de Aragón. José Ángel was born and baptized on October 4th.

Blas Zúñiga y Mena, son of the deceased Salvador de Mena and Bernarda Zúñiga, made his will. He was married to Juana Valverde and had three children: María Antonia Cecilia, Pedro José, and Sebastián Zúñiga (who died young without children). María Antonia Cecilia married José Manuel Guzmán, and Pedro José married Cayetana Villalobos. Blas also raised his granddaughter Antonia Josefa and mentioned his grandchildren José Bruno and Rafaela. His two surviving children were named as heirs, and Pedro José Zúñiga and Manuel José de Astúa were appointed as executors.

Residents of Villa Nueva living in Escasú, including a long list of named individuals, granted power of attorney to José Miguel González. Their objective was to pursue a legal case against Micaela Sáenz, demanding she produce the title to the lands they inhabit. If she failed to prove ownership, they sought to have the land auctioned and obtain title in the name of the community, challenging her annual charges.
Tomás Arrióla, a free mulatto from Puebla, is mentioned at the beginning of an entry that is cut off, with no further details available in this chunk.
Francisco Cubero incurred a debt of $500 to Doña Baltasara Madriz. This amount represented the outstanding balance for the lease of a cacao plantation located in Matina.

Micaela Irola received news from her son Tomás Calderón about the death of her other son, José Bernabé, which occurred in San Miguel on June 19th of the current year. Consequently, Micaela granted power to Tomás to collect the assets left by the deceased José Bernabé.

Doña María de Alvarado sold a portion of her solar, where her house was built, to her son-in-law Don Felipe Gallegos for $50 silver. The property's boundaries were described, noting its adjacency to the properties of Micaela Ruiz and Don José Antonio Oreamuno.

Captain Miguel Cárdenas and his wife Ana Catalina Carrillo obligated themselves for $678.5 reales in cacao. This sum originated from the estate of Doña Juana Céspedes and was adjudicated to Esteban and Ana Josefa Céspedes, who are minor children of Ana Catalina Carrillo from a previous marriage. Further diligences were requested to specify the cacao trees on the 'la Céspedes' hacienda in Matina.

Francisco Javier Godínez, Francisco Morales, Rafael Trejos, and Felipe Córdoba, along with other residents of Villa Vieja, leased the 'el del Mtre. de Campo don José de Sandoval' pasture, located in Birrí, for $21 annually. This arrangement followed their request for the lease, offering an improved price, after Pedro Herrera, the previous lessee, renounced his lease for $19, having charged the residents double.

Captain Don Francisco Carazo and his wife Doña Jacoba de Alvarado obligated themselves for $1000, which they received from Doña Cecilia del Castillo and belonged to her minor son, Rafael Ceferino del Castillo. They agreed to pay 6% interest on this sum, and the obligation was later cancelled on September 19, 1798.

Prudencio Picado obligated himself for $528.6 reales in silver to his minor children: Manuel Joaquín, José Tomás, José de los Angeles, and María de las Mercedes Picado. This sum represented their inheritance from their deceased mother, Mónica Trejos, with Prudencio's brother-in-law, Joaquín Trejos, serving as guarantor. The document, however, was not signed.

Colonel Don José Romualdo Oreamuno sold a piece of land intended for pasture, located in the city's countryside, to Don José Antonio del Campo for $65. The land's boundaries were specified, noting its adjacency to a pasture owned by Pedro Elizondo and another belonging to the seller.

people_involved: Doña María de la Encarnación Sancho de Castañeda
summary: Doña María de la Encarnación Sancho de Castañeda, acting as guardian for her minor children Don José Nicolás and Doña María Josefa Oreamuno, obligated herself for 6840 pesos. This amount represented their inheritance from their deceased father, Don José Francisco Oreamuño, which originated from the estate of their paternal grandparents, Don José Antonio Oreamuno and Doña María Catalina de Ibarra.

Don Antonio de la Fuente, in his capacity as general syndic of the San Francisco Convent, granted power to Don Francisco Icaza and, secondarily, to Don Manuel Galisteo, both from León. Their mandate was to collect the previous year's stipend for the doctrinal and reductive priests of the province from the Royal Coffers in León.

Following the death of her son, José de la Cruz Navaro, in the pueblo of Tuistepe, Dionisia Guerrero, as the sole heir to his various assets, granted power to Domingo Brenes to collect these properties on her behalf.

The testament of Juan Fonseca was recorded, detailing his family history. He was the son of the late Juan Fonseca and Petronila Masís, married first to Francisca Zamora and then to Josefa Cayetana Guillen, and had several children and grandchildren. The testament named his heirs and appointed Juan Matamoros as his executor.

Trinidad Portugués sold a 'caballería de tierra' located in 'Angelina' of Quercua to Diego Chavarría for $50 silver. This land was part of his paternal inheritance and had been under the guardianship of his deceased mother.

María Nieves, Miguel, and Concepción Portugués, siblings of Trinidad Portugués, sold their rights in the same 'caballería de tierra' in 'Angelina' of Quercua to Diego Chavarría for $20. This transaction occurred shortly after their brother Trinidad had sold his portion of the inherited land to the same buyer.

people_involved: Doña Rosa de la Madriz Linares
Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Doña Rosa de la Madriz Linares, widow of Don Tomás López del Corral, received $166.6 reales in silver from Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora. This sum was designated for the guardianship of Doña Rosa's minor son, Don Vicente Corrales.

A request was made to the Governor concerning the guardianship of four minor children, with one guardianship designated for Don Atanasio Corrales. An existing obligation previously in favor of Don Atanasio was transferred to Don Vicente, and an obligation from Don Francisco Carazo was also transferred to Don Vicente.
Don Manuel José de Zea granted general power of attorney to Don Andrés Enríquez, who was a resident in Nueva Guatemala.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don José Antonio Oreamuno
summary: Don Felipe Sancho, who was preparing to depart for other provinces and had a pending judicial demand before the Governor, granted power of attorney to Don Manuel José García. The demand concerned the estate of the deceased Sargento Mayor Don José Antonio Oreamuno, with Sancho claiming his fees as executor.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Joaquín Isidro de Quesada
summary: In Villa Vieja, Don Juan Ventura Reyes and his wife Doña Juana Pérez, as principals, along with Don Nicolás Reyes and his wife Doña Gertrudis Porras, as guarantors, undertook an obligation for $428 and one real. This obligation was for a chaplaincy founded by Presbítero Don Joaquín Isidro de Quesada for the coadjutors of Villa Vieja, secured by a house and a slave.

Doña Micaela de Arleguí made her will, detailing her inheritance from her deceased parents and sister, including a house and half the value of a slave named Ventura. She bequeathed livestock to Francisca Josefa, arranged for Ventura's freedom after masses, donated land and goods to Presbítero Don Francisco Antonio Robredo, and left furniture to her four nieces and other goods to her servant Jacoba and Jacoba's daughter, Francisca Josefa. Don José Antonio Jiménez and Don Manuel Torre y Romero were named executors.

Doña Dominga and Doña Antonia Zabaleta sold their 25-vara long house to Doña María Josefa de Soto, who intended to settle in the city. The property bordered Doña Ignacia de la Rosa, Doña María Antonia Pacheco, Presbítero Don Pablo Molina, and the Convento de San Francisco, with two small houses belonging to their sister Doña Gertrudis excluded from the sale. The sale price was $350, and the sellers had inherited the property from their mother.
Doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho sold a tiled house and a walled plot in the city to Doña Dominga Zabaleta for $125. The property was bordered by Don Manuel Hidalgo and Doña Ignacia de la Rosa.
Teniente Coronel Don José Perié, who was the Governor and Captain General, granted general power of attorney to Don Antonio Talavera Vasconcelos, a Procurator of the Royal Audiencia.

Juan José Acosta, a resident of Villa Vieja, sold a piece of land to Don José Miguel Flores, also from Villa Vieja, for $24 silver. The land, located in Los Íarguaces, included Flores's house and a pasture, bordering properties of Javier Ramos and Don Cayetano Gutiérrez.

Rosario Casasola, widow of Simón Bogarín, sold a small cacao plantation in the Matina Valley to José Antonio Cárdenas for $28 silver. The property, inherited from her parents Simón Casasola and Efigenia Brenes, was located in Poza Azul and bordered the buyer's hacienda, La Corofiela, a lost hacienda (formerly her parents'), and Manuel Salguero's property.
Doña Micaela de Arleguí granted judicial power to Presbítero Don Francisco Antonio Robredo.

people_involved: Señor Dean Don José Antonio de la Huerta
Presbítero Don Joaquín Isidro de Quesada
summary: Don Juan Ventura Reyes, a resident of Villa Vieja, sold a 12-year-old slave named Ambrosio Salguero to Beneficiado Don Ramón de Azofeifa, who was the Cura and Vicar of the city and attorney for Dean Don José Antonio de la Huerta of León Cathedral. The slave was acquired from a chaplaincy founded by Presbítero Don Joaquín Isidro de Quesada in Villa Vieja, and the price was $200 silver.

Josefa Brígida Valverde made her will, identifying herself as the daughter of Francisco Valverde and Inés Granados, and widow of Francisco Quirós. She listed her ten children (seven deceased sons, three living daughters). She declared Manuela de Jesús and her five children as her slaves, noting that the three female slave children were already given to her daughters, and instructing her daughters to free the male slave children after their deaths. She also bequeathed items to Nicolás, a boy she raised, and named Manuel Miguel de Aguilar and her daughter María de Jesús Quirós as executors, with her three daughters as heirs.

Don José Miguel Ocaña apprenticed his 12-year-old slave boy, José Joaquín Ocaña, to Agustín Núñez, a master tailor, for four years. For the first two years, $2 silver per month would be paid for the boy's upkeep and training, and for the subsequent two years, Agustín Núñez would retain the value of the boy's labor.
Doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho granted power, though the specific details of the power are not provided in the text.
A general power of attorney was granted to José Antonio Oreamuno.

Martín González, son of deceased Miguel González and Efigenia Alvarado, made his will. He was married twice, first to Manuela Benita Carranza and then to Juana Antonia Masís, having children with both. His son José Isidro received a calf from his grandfather Juan Masís, and his son-in-law was José de la Trinidad Rivera.
Francisco Javier Quesada sold one 'caballería' and three-quarters of land in the area named Angelina to Diego Chavarría. The transaction was completed for a price of $80.

Manuel de Jesús Jiménez and his wife María Josefa Abarca sold a house of 8 varas long with a three-panel fence to Francisco Javier Quesada for $100. The property was bordered by Elias Quesada, Miguel Arburola, and María Nicolasa Abarca.
Presbyter Juan José de Oreamuno granted general power of attorney to Presbyter Rafael Agustín de Allestas. Rafael Agustín de Allestas served as the master of ceremonies at the Cathedral of León.

Fermín Mondragón, as majordomo of the parish church's factory in 'this city,' granted power to Mateo Mantilla and Manuel Galisteo of León. This power was for collecting the 'novenos' assigned by His Majesty from the Royal Coffers for the church's factory.

Nicolás Cleto Chavarría sold a house with half a lot in 'this city' to Presbyter Félix García for $450 in silver. The property, acquired from the estate of Comisario Juan Manuel de Casasola, was bordered by properties of María del Aya y Bolívar, Pedro Salguero, and Estefanía Pacheco.

María Ignacia de la Rosa, natural daughter of deceased Luis de la Rosa and Margarita Rodríguez from Panama, made her will. She had two living sons, Lino José and Gregorio de la Rosa, and gifted a trunk of clothes to her companion Gertrudis Zabaleta. Presbyters Juan José de Oreamuno and Pablo Molina were named executors.

Manuela Baeza, daughter of deceased José Francisco de Baeza and Magdalena Maroto, made her will. She was married to Pedro de Alvarado and had many children, some living and some deceased. She owned several enslaved people, one of whom, Eusebia, was to be freed, and appointed her son-in-law Antonio de la Fuente as tutor for her minor children and María Dolores.

Juana Miranda, legitimate daughter of deceased Antonio Miranda and Ana María Maroto, being ill, granted power to her daughter María Manuela Miranda to make her will. Presbyter Pablo Molina and María Manuela Miranda were named executors, and her children Pablo García and María Manuela Miranda were heirs.

José Francisco Hernández, son of deceased Antonio Miguel Hernández and María Carranza, made his will. He was married to María del Rosario Chavarría and had six minor children. Diego Chavarría and his wife were named executors, and his wife was appointed tutor for their minor children.

Magdalena Casasola leased her San Benito cacao plantation in Matina to Esteban Venegas for one year. Josefa Benita Ángulo also delivered a new cacao plantation from her deceased husband Antonio Arizaga to Venegas to settle a debt. Magdalena Casasola later extended her contract until August 1789 on February 14, 1788.

Manuela Fernández de la Pastora took on a debt of 50 silver pesos related to the Sacrament of 'this parish.' This debt was originally the responsibility of Comisario del Santo Oficio Juan Manuel de Casasola, and she committed to paying 5% interest.

people_involved: Juan Manuel de la Encarnación López
summary: María Petronila Núñez, daughter of deceased Calixto Núñez and Petronila Cerdas, made her will. She was the widow of Francisco Nicolás López, with whom she had six children. One of her sons, Juan José López, was deceased and left a son named Claudio.

Santiago González, Vicente Moya, Ramón Rodríguez, and José Gregorio Rodríguez, residents of Villa Vieja, purchased 7 caballerías of land belonging to the late José Alonso Porras in Potrerillo, near the Virilla River. They declared that 3.5 caballerías of this land belong to Santiago Flores, who had already paid for his share, separated by a ditch and fence from Quebrada Bermuda to the Virilla River. The total price was $217.

Doña Manuela Josefa Reyes, a poor widow from Villa Vieja, was ordered by a Royal Provision from the Audiencia de Guatemala to grant power of attorney for a lawsuit left pending by her late husband, Francisco Antonio Pérez. The lawsuit concerned land titles with the residents of Quebrada Seca. She conferred this power to the Procurador de pobres at the Royal Audiencia, or failing that, to the Marqués de Aycinena in Nueva Guatemala.
Don Francisco Ulloa, a resident of Villa Vieja, owes Pedro José Lizondro, a local resident, $345 in silver. The debt is to be paid in the upcoming April.

people_involved: Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora obligated herself to the Cofradía del Sacramento for $50 in silver, received for half a fenced lot that previously belonged to Comisario Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba. Casasola y Córdoba had ceded it to Pedro Salguero after his death, and Salguero then transferred it to Manuela. She hypothecated her house, a small farm (chácara), and livestock as security, as this was a new obligation mandated by the Registrar of Mortgages because the previous one lacked hypothecation.

Don Miguel Guzmán granted power of attorney to don Manuel Torre y Romero to represent him in a case against don Felipe Chavarría before the Ecclesiastical Court. The case concerned his marriage, which was described as 'lacerated in a certain way'.

This is the testament of Antonia Josefa González, legitimate daughter of the late José Miguel González and Gertrudis Meléndez. She was the widow of Pedro Guzmán. Her children were Mateo and Josefa Guzmán. Josefa Guzmán was married to Pedro Salguero and died, leaving a daughter who also passed away. Her son Mateo was named heir and executor.

Don Francisco Antonio de Echavarría, a merchant from Guatemala, native of Spain, and residing locally, sold the tithe party of Valle de Matina for three years to don José Miguel Velazco, a resident of this city, for $550 per year. Echavarría was the auction winner through his agent Simón Pérez in León. A marginal note indicates that Baltasar Echavarría cancelled this on December 11, '93.

Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora obligated herself again for $50 in silver to the Cofradía del Sacramento, concerning half a lot located in the block where María Francisca Corrales, María del Aya y Bolívar, and Presbítero Félix García have their houses. This obligation was previously held by Pedro Manuel Salguero. María Francisca Corrales, Fermín Mondragón, and Joaquín Romero acted as guarantors, as this was a new obligation at the instance of the Registrar of Mortgages.

Don Antonio de la Fuente, as agent for don José Antonio de Alvarado, provided don Juan de Alvarado as a guarantor for $800, enabling José Antonio de Alvarado to begin administering the tobacco tercena (store/monopoly) in the Villa de Sagaces.
José Antonio Sáenz and his wife Gertrudis Alvarado granted freedom to their enslaved person, Francisco Javier Alvarado, for $125 in silver, which he had paid them.

José Manuel González transferred a house he bought from José Antonio Jiménez to María Manuela Guzmán. The house, which belonged to Jiménez's brother, Presbítero Manuel Antonio Sandoval, is located in the same block as the late Meléndez's house, towards the west. González made the transfer on behalf of a benefactor of María Manuela, who had paid the house's value. Jiménez ratified the sale he made to González.

Alférez Real Antonio de la Fuente, Alcalde Provincial Francisco Carazo (both Regidores), and Captain Juan Francisco de Bonilla (former Depositario General) granted general power of attorney to Juan Zabala (Contador de la renta de tabaco) and, secondarily, to José García Granados, both residing in Nueva Guatemala. This was to represent them in a lawsuit initiated by the current Governor of the province before the Supreme Tribunal of this Kingdom, concerning half-salaries he demanded, as they were all included in the 'causa de capitulantes' against him.

José de la Cruz Muñoz (principal) and Martín Muñoz (guarantor), residents of Villa Vieja, obligated themselves for $34.5 reales. This money was received from Alférez Real Antonio de la Fuente, who collected it from the estate of the late Juan Manuel Panlagua. The funds belonged to Teresa Guzmán and, through her, to her grandchildren María Manuela and Felipe González, children of Manuel González and Petronila Soto (who is now married to José de la Cruz Muñoz). After deductions, $28.5 reales remained, with half going to Petronila (who inherited from her son Felipe, who died after his father) and the other half to María Manuela.

Juan Antonio Porras, a resident of Villa Vieja, received $34.5 reales from Alférez Real Antonio de la Fuente. These funds were collected from the estate of the late Juan Manuel Panlagua and belonged to Teresa Guzmán, and through her, to her grandson Ceferino González, a minor son of Juan Antonio González and Ana Benavides, who is currently with his mother. After deducting costs, $28.5 reales remained, for which Porras obligated himself to the minor.
An obligation of $15 1/2 rs. was ratified before José Miguel Porras, who was the Teniente of Villa Vieja at the time. The specific parties involved in the obligation are not named in this record.

Pedro José Elizondo and Joaquín Trejos received goods in deposit. These goods belonged to Prudencio Picado and Encarnación Trejos, respectively, and had been embargoed by José Peralta, the Alcalde de la Santa Hermandad, due to a criminal case of incest.

Don José Antonio Bonilla and his wife, doña Antonia Manuela Meneses, obligated themselves for $570 cacao to a capellanía, whose chaplain was Presbítero don Francisco Antonio Robredo. Later, on January 24, 1824, this obligation was canceled when Beneficiado Nicolás Bonilla, cura of Alajuela, made an obligation in the Capellanías Court, leaving the entrance hall and a piece of land to Bonilla.

Don Manuel Guzmán took charge of $200 from a capellanía branch located in the house of don José Antonio Bonilla, for which Presbítero don Francisco Antonio Robredo was the Capellán. This obligation was later canceled on July 28, 1792, as it had been transferred to don Manuel Torre y Romero.

Manuel de Jesús Román made his will, identifying his parents as Juan Salazar Román and Francisca Fonseca, and his wife as María de los Santos Fernández, with whom he had a son who died at age 4. He appointed Alférez Real don Antonio de la Fuente and his wife as albaceas, and ordered a Capellanía to be established on his cacao plantation in Matina, with the Cura of Cartago as patron and chaplain.

Beneficiado don Antonio Ramón de Azofeifa granted general power of attorney. The primary recipient was don Agustín Franco de Mera, Beneficiado of the Church of Buen Lucero in Madrid, and in second place, don Juan Torre y Romero, a resident and merchant of Madrid.

Don Ramón Puche, a merchant, acted as guarantor for Pedro José Elizondo, by order of the Governor, while doubts were resolved regarding the collection of royal rights on commission interests belonging to Francisco Diez Catalán and Sebastián de Hoze, merchants from Cartagena de Indias. The obligation was later canceled on March 2, 1789, after the rights were satisfied by Ignacio Rucavado and Ramón Puche.

Doña Josefa Alegría Marroquín, out of affection and for services rendered, donated her house, small furnishings, and her share in the solar to María de la Rosa Hernández and her daughter María Gertrudis Alegría. The property was bordered by the house of doña María Fernández to the South, the royal street and house of don Manuel Quesada to the North, the royal street to the East, and the solar and house of don José León Bonilla to the West.

Coronel don José Romualdo Oreamuno sold a large cattle ranch in the area of Los Guacimos del Río Grande to Beneficiado don Antonio Cayetano Chacón, Cura of Jinotepe, for $1787-4 rs. The sale included 156 cattle, 2 yokes of oxen, a breeding donkey, 9 tame horses, 2 colts, 47 mares, houses, corrals, and plantain groves, all situated on 11.5 caballerías of land, with don Félix José Fernández accepting on behalf of the buyer.

people_involved: Fray Juan Luis de Soto y San Martín
Lorenzo Fernández de Munilla y Foronda
summary: The Reverend Father Fray Juan Luis de Soto y San Martín granted general power of attorney. The primary recipient was don Lorenzo Fernández de Munilla y Foronda, an Agent in the Court of Madrid, followed by don Manuel Ayala and don Vicente Aguado.

Antonio de Segura and his wife, María Antonia Martel, obligated themselves for $150 cacao to the Cofradía de la Concepción, whose mayordomo was don José Antonio Oreamuno. They agreed to pay 5% interest and mortgaged their dwelling house near the Soledad.

Gregorio Calvo made his will, identifying his deceased parents as Tomás Calvo and María Victoria Lascares. He was first married to Rosaura Pacheco, with whom he had a son, Alejandro Calvo, both deceased, and is currently married to María Josefa Solano, with whom he has children Cecilia, Ramona, Vicenta, José Antonio, Pedro María, and Clara de la Trinidad Calvo. He appointed Presbítero don Juan José Oreamuno and Capitán don Gregorio Oreamuno as albaceas, naming his children as heirs.

José de la Trinidad Alvarado made his will, identifying himself as the natural son of the deceased Juana Efigenia Alvarado. He is married to María Antonia Barrios, with whom he has a living son, Rafael Mauricio Alvarado. He appointed Capitán de pardos don Miguel Cárdenas as his albacea and as the tutor for his son, who is also his heir.

Don José Perié granted power to don Antonio Talavera, Procurador of the Real Audiencia, to appoint one or two arbitrating judges. These judges were to decide a civil lawsuit he had pending with don Manuel Torre y Romero, a native of Madrid and resident there, concerning the liquidation of accounts from a company they had formed in Madrid.

Pedro José Elizondo sold an enslaved woman named Manuela Guzmán to Presbítero don Félix de Jesús García for $314-2 rs. Manuela Guzmán, described as black with light eyes and about 18 years old, was born and raised in the house of doña Teresa Trujillo, and Elizondo had purchased her from don José Peralta the previous year.

Juan Manuel Solís and Juan Manuel Fonseca, residents of Villa Vieja, granted power to don Antonio Talavera, Procurador of the Real Audiencia. This power was for him to obtain titles for lands, the necessary documents for which they had sent to him.

José Nicolás Camaño made his will, identifying himself as the natural son of the deceased Bernarda Alvarado, with his father unknown. He is married to María Josefa de la Riva, daughter of the deceased Agustín de la Riva, and they have children Sebastián (deceased, married to Paula Sancho and had children), Teodora (married to Cayetano Gutiérrez), Antonia Josefa, Teresa, Félix Antonio, and Ana María Camaño. He appointed his children Félix Antonio and Antonia Josefa as albaceas.

Don José Antonio García leased a cacao plantation in the Matina Valley to Marcelino Calvo and Manuel de Jesús Arrióla for three years. The annual rent was set at 7 tercios of cacao, to be delivered in Matina.

Candelaria Carranza, legitimate daughter of the deceased José Antonio Carranza and Nicolasa Aguilar, made her will. She was married to José Prudencio Rojas and named eight surviving children as heirs, with Juan and Ramona Carranza appointed as executors.

Bernardo Bermúdez donated his house to his grandson, Mateo de Jesús Ramírez. The donation was conditional on Mateo paying for Bernardo's burial and masses for his soul if Mateo were to die before him, and the document was not signed.

people_involved: Presbítero don Juan José de Oreamuno
summary: Andrea Guerrero, legitimate daughter of the deceased Miguel Guerrero and Doña María Josefa Masís, made her will. She was single and childless, naming her deceased sister Joaquina, living sisters Micaela and Dionisia, and nieces Ana María Pérez, Magdalena Tames, Eufrasia Sojo, and Dolores Pérez. Presbítero don Juan José de Oreamuno was named executor, and her soul was named heir.
Pedro José Elizondo became obligated to Doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho for $200 at 5% interest. This debt was previously the responsibility of Capitán don Gregorio Oreamuno.
Don Rafael de Alvarado posted bail for Gertrudis Alvarado, who was imprisoned for complicity in cattle theft. The theft was attributed to her and two unnamed slaves from 'this city'.

people_involved: Benef. don Manuel Antonio Chapuí y Torres
summary: Don Cleto Chavarría and Doña Eufemia Pacheco took on a debt of $150 at 5% interest for a chaplaincy, with Presbítero don Francisco Robledo as chaplain. The obligation was linked to the former residence of Benef. don Manuel Antonio Chapuí y Torres in Villa Nueva, and they mortgaged their house in 'this city'.
The obligation of $150 taken on by Don Cleto Chavarría and Doña Eufemia Pacheco in 1787 was cancelled by Don Francisco Ulloa. The responsibility for the debt had transferred to him and his wife.

people_involved: Doña Rosa de la Madriz Linares
summary: Doña Rosa de la Madriz Linares, a widow, took responsibility for $500 in guardianship funds belonging to her three minor children: Doña Venancia, Don Vicente, and Don Pedro Corrales. This obligation was secured by her residence in 'this ciudad', located opposite the house of Doña María Francisca Corral.

Don Pablo Coronado became obligated for $200 silver at 5% interest to the Confraternity of Nuestra Señora del Viejo in Nicoya. He guaranteed this debt with livestock located in the Lagartos site, within the jurisdiction of Bagaces.
José Maroto posted bail for Encarnación Trejos, who was facing charges for alleged illicit relations with her brother-in-law, Prudencio Picado.

Don José Francisco González, legitimate son of the deceased Don Nicolás González and Doña Juana Alfaro from Villa Vieja, made his will. Married to Doña María Josefa de Soto and childless, he bequeathed half his assets to a young girl named Juana, whom he recognized as his daughter from an illicit union, currently under the care of her aunt, Doña Ramona Ulloa, in Villa Vieja. Presbítero don Pablo Molina and Don Romualdo Zamora were named executors.

locations: Capilla Mayor de la iglesia de San Francisco
summary: Don Manuel Hidalgo and his wife Doña María Josefa Trinidad, with Capitán don Gregorio Oreamuno as guarantor, took on a $300 silver debt at 5% interest for the benefit of the town of Nicoya. This debt was previously held by the deceased Doña Mónica del Corral and her husband Don Simón de Uriza, and they mortgaged their house in 'esta ciudad'.

Luis Antonio Bustamante, José Vicente Alvarado, and Francisco Guerrero, all residents of Villa Nueva, posted bail for José Miguel Bustamante, José Montes, and Tiburcia León, also from Villa Nueva, who were facing charges for the illegal production of aguardiente.

María Micaela Valverde, legitimate daughter of the deceased Francisco Valverde and Inés Granados, and widow of José Solano, made her will. She named her three surviving children, María Josefa (widow of Gregorio Calvo), Félix José, and Gertrudis Cayetana, as heirs, with Ventura Elizondo appointed as executor.
Don José Antonio Oreamuno posted bail for Prudencio Picado, who was facing charges of incest with his two sisters-in-law, Rita and Encarnación Trejos.
Don José Antonio Oreamuno granted general power of attorney to Don Juan Zabala, the Tobacco Revenue Accountant, and secondarily to Don Agustín Zabala, both residents of Guatemala.

Don Bernardo Gómez, a resident of Bagaces, granted special power of attorney to Manuel José Astúa to represent him in a lawsuit before the Governor. The suit was brought by the attorney of Doña María del Carmen Lindo, a resident of León, concerning accounts with Don Bernardo's deceased brother, Don José Benito Gómez.
Don Alejandro Lampar granted general power of attorney, first to Don Juan Zabala, second to his brother Don Agustín Zabala, and third to Don José García Granados, all residents of Guatemala.

Don Antonio de la Fuente, as the General Syndic for the San Francisco Convents in 'this province', granted power of attorney to Don Mateo Mantilla and Don Manuel Galisteo, both residents of León. Their purpose was to collect the synod from the Royal Coffers in León, which was due to the doctrinal and reducing priests of 'these towns' for the previous year.

Doña Josefa Soniche sued Pérez in the Ecclesiastical Court for child support for their son, born when she was a widow. Pérez was condemned to pay $200 to doña Josefa and $3 monthly for the child's sustenance, starting October 13, 1786, after the lactation period ended. A letter from Father José Ant de Alvarado confirms the child's baptism on October 13.

people_involved: Obispo don Juan Félix de Villegas
summary: Fray Pablo Bancos, founder of the Hospital of San Juan de Dios in Cartago, granted power to Brother Antonio de la Fuente. This power allowed de la Fuente to solicit the 'noveno y medio' assigned to the hospital from the Royal Treasury of León, collecting arrears since 1784, and also $200 deposited by Bishop Juan Félix de Villegas.

people_involved: Presb don Juan de Pomar y Burgos
summary: Don Juan María Sáenz granted power to Pedro José Lizondro to handle the probate case of Presbyter Juan de Pomar y Burgos in León. Lizondro was to obtain testimony regarding a donation the Presbyter made to Sáenz when Sáenz was a minor.

José Ant Carrillo granted power to don Manuel Torre y Romero to represent him in a lawsuit. The lawsuit was filed by don Jerónimo Alvarado, acting as attorney for his brother don Joaquín Alvarado, concerning seven mule beasts that Carrillo bought from Juan Francisco Vega in Bagaces.

Don Tomás de Alvarado and his wife, doña María del Rosario Bonilla, took charge of a rural estate previously owned by doña Catalina Tenorio. The estate, located in Villa Nueva, Murciélago, by the Virilla river, was encumbered with a $915 cacao lien for the church of San Bartolomé de Barba and $150 silver for the parish church of Cartago.
Don José Corona posted bail for Nicolás Arizaga, an enslaved person belonging to Corona's wife, who was facing a criminal charge.

locations: paso del Guayabo del Río Segundo
people_involved: Beneficiado don Juan Manuel López del Corral
summary: Doña María Josefa de Soto sold a wheat mill, including its house and equipment, to Beneficiado don Juan Manuel López del Corral, the priest of Villa Vieja. The mill was located at the Guayabo del Río Segundo pass, near the royal road in Villa Vieja, and was sold for $100 in cash and $50 in goods.
Pedro José Lizondro granted general power of attorney to don Manuel Torre y Romero.

Doña Paula González granted power to Pedro José Lizondro to receive a legacy from don José Pascual Masís. This legacy was left by don Ramón Casimiro Alvarado, son of doña Paula, when he traveled to Lima, and Lizondro was also to collect other assets designated for her.

This entry records the will of Juan Romero, legitimate son of the deceased don José Romero and Juana de Dios Piedra. Juan Romero was a widower of Antonia Martina, with whom he had two living children, José Antonio and Rafaela. Don Esteban Venegas was named as the executor, and his two children were the heirs.
Doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho granted freedom to her enslaved woman, María Benita de los Dolores, for $200 in silver. Nicolás Gómez is mentioned as the husband of the enslaved woman.

people_involved: Don Jerónimo de Alvarado y Girón
doña María de la Luz Aguilar
summary: Don Jerónimo de Alvarado y Girón and his wife, doña María de la Luz Aguilar, took on a debt of $600 cacao or $400 silver at 5% interest. This debt was originally held by don Marcos de Alvarado, father of don Jerónimo, and belonged to a chaplaincy founded by don Alonso Porras, for which Beneficiado don Ramón de Azofeifa was the Chaplain, Cura, and Vicar of Cartago. They mortgaged an enslaved woman named Antonia Basilia Corrales and other assets.

Juana Catalina Sánchez leased a 700-tree cacao plantation in Valle de Matina, called Dolores, to Sebastián Vázquez for two years at $62 cacao per year. The lease was later extended on April 21, 1790, for two more years at $100 cacao per year.

Doña Antonia Romero, widow of don Francisco Agapito Jinesta, committed to her four minor children (Antonia, José, Andrea, and José Manuel) for $180 from their paternal inheritance. She received this money from doña Joaqivna Pastora, widow of don Joaquín Romero (Antonia's deceased brother), who was responsible for the obligation. Hermdo. Jiménez acted as guarantor, and Antonia also sought guardianship of her children.

Rafael Montoya, a resident of Bagaces, received livestock from Juan Navarro, which belonged to the minor Ramos Martínez, who was over 14 years old. Montoya, who is Ramos's first cousin and lives with him, took responsibility for the assets. The livestock was an inheritance from Ramos's deceased parents, Francisco Martínez and Josefa Abarca, and was previously held by Navarro, who also managed assets for Ramos's two younger siblings.

Juan Navarro committed to Josefa de la Cruz (13 years old) and José Rafael (11 years old), children of the deceased Francisco Martínez and Josefa Abarca, for various heads of livestock they inherited. Both minors were under Navarro's care.

locations: Convento de San Francisco de la ciudad de Esparza
people_involved: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora committed to the Convent of San Francisco in Esparza for $600 silver at 5% interest. This money was received from a cacao plantation in Matina, consisting of 1574 fruit-bearing trees, which was previously the responsibility of the deceased don Joaquín Romero.

Captain don Francisco Carazo granted power to don Manuel Galisteo, a resident of León, to represent him before the Intendancy. This was for the auction proceedings Carazo had requested for lands in Tenorio, Bagaces, which were surveyed by the deceased don Antonio Cervantes.

people_involved: Doña Engracia Gertrudis de Hoces Navarro
Doña Benita Arleguí de la Madriz
Doña Antonia Arleguí de la Madriz
Doña Andrea Arleguí de la Madriz
Doña María Arleguí de la Madriz
Don José Arleguí de la Madriz
summary: Don José Francisco de Arleguí made his testament, detailing his family, including his deceased parents, wife, and children. He named his daughters Antonia, Andrea, and María Arleguí, and his grandson Pedro Portocarrero (son of deceased Benita) as heirs. He also mentioned various debts and bequests to servants and specified executors for his will, which was granted before Don Tomás Benito Hidalgo.

Doña Ana Josefa Dionisia Alvarado granted power of attorney to Don Miguel Candaneo, a resident of Chiriquí, to collect overdue interest from Don Jaime Arauz, also of Chiriquí. This debt relates to the guardianship of Doña María del Carmen, daughter of Ana Josefa and her deceased husband, Don Valeriano Medina.

Don Alejandro Lampar owed Don Francisco Echeverría, a Spanish merchant, 2748.5 reales of silver for clothing goods purchased from his shop in Villa Nueva. To secure this debt, Lampar mortgaged his house in Cartago, located opposite Don Tomás Benito Hidalgo's house on the main street.

people_involved: Alférez Real Don Antonio de la Fuente
Presbítero Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Alférez Real Don Antonio de la Fuente and his wife, Doña María Francisca de Alvarado, obligated themselves for 827 reales in cacao to the Cofradía del Sacramento, a debt previously managed by the deceased Presbítero Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba. They mortgaged their living house and another house on the main plaza of Cartago.

people_involved: Beneficiado Don Rafael Baltasar de la Fuente
Alférez Real Don Antonio de la Fuente
summary: On January 11, 1816, Beneficiado Don Félix de Alvarado, mayordomo of the Cofradía del Sacramento, cancelled the obligation of Don Antonio de la Fuente and Doña María Francisca de Alvarado. This cancellation occurred because Beneficiado Don Rafael Baltasar de la Fuente had paid the sum, which was then allocated to the parish's fabric for rebuilding the temple.

Doña Petronila Carazo stated that Josefa Miranda, wife of her slave Juan José, had died in Bagaces, leaving a minor son, José Bernardo Bermúdez, from a previous relationship, who inherited cattle. Petronila Carazo committed to holding the minor and his assets. A marginal note from 1803 indicates José Antonio García presented a receipt from José Bernardo Bermúdez to his stepfather, Juan José Carazo, for the previous guardianship.

people_involved: Alférez Real Don Antonio de la Fuente
M. I. S. P. G. y Capitán General de este Reino
summary: Capitán Don Francisco Carazo accepted the deposit of all goods embargoed from Alférez Real Don Antonio de la Fuente, by order of the M. I. S. P. G. y Capitán General, due to fraud in the Alcabalas tax revenue under Antonio's charge. A marginal note from February 6, 1789, states that Antonio de la Fuente was freed and his goods returned, following a dispatch issued in León on January 14.

people_involved: Alférez Real Don Antonio de la Fuente
summary: On February 6, 1789, Alférez Real Don Antonio de la Fuente was released from prison and his embargoed goods were returned to him. This action was taken in virtue of a dispatch issued by the Intendente in León on January 14 of the same year.

people_involved: Alférez Real Don Antonio de la Fuente
summary: Don Manuel José García and Pedro José Lizondro provided bail for Alférez Real Don Antonio de la Fuente, both for his release from prison and for the outcomes of the ongoing case against him for fraud in the Alcabalas tax revenue.

Pedro José Lizondro granted power of attorney to Cristóbal de Ocampo Golfín to file a lawsuit against Romualdo Carvajal, a resident of Villa Vieja. The lawsuit aims to collect a sum owed by Carvajal due to the transfer of a simple obligation made in favor of Pedro José's father, Buenaventura Lizondro.

Capitán Don Francisco Carazo obligated himself to Don José Perié for 1000 pesos, which he received from Perié in a draft. This draft was to be covered by Don Mateo Mantilla, Perié's agent in León, and Carazo endorsed it to Don Manuel Galisteo in the same city.

On July 7, 1788, the obligation of Capitán Don Francisco Carazo to Don José Perié for 1000 pesos was cancelled. This cancellation occurred because the draft, which was to be covered by Don Mateo Mantilla in León, was returned unpaid due to a lack of funds in the Royal Coffers.

An extrajudicial partition of the estate of the deceased Josefa Brígida Valverde was carried out among her heirs, Lorenza de la Trinidad Quirós, María de Jesús Quirós, and Antonia Gertrudis Quirós, in accordance with her testament from May 15, 1787. The estate included houses in Chicagres and six slaves, with a total value of 1450.1 reales, which was distributed among the heirs after deductions.

people_involved: Don José de los Santos Lombardo
Don José Rudesindo de la Guardia
summary: Don Felipe Gallegos, tutor of the minor Don José de los Santos Lombardo, granted power of attorney to Don José Rudesindo de la Guardia and Don Clemente Pérez Granados, residents of Panamá. Their task is to collect assets from the estate of Doña Manuela Josefa Ramos, who died in Panamá, which were bequeathed to the deceased Don Pedro Lombardo (father of José de los Santos) or directly to the minor. Gallegos also represents José de los Santos in the intestate estate of Don Francisco Javier Lombardo, Pedro's father, who died in Villa Vieja.

people_involved: Alférez Real Don Antonio de la Fuente
summary: Don Manuel José García provided bail for Alférez Real Don Antonio de la Fuente, specifically in case the Superior Tribunal modifies the sentence in a lawsuit where de la Fuente acts as the agent for Don Manuel José Ortiz, a merchant.

A lawsuit was filed against Don Lorenzo Guillen for a debt of $1956 and 5 reales in silver with interest. His assets were ordered to be auctioned to cover the debt, and a bond was required by the law of Toledo.
On February 7, 1789, Don Lorenzo Guillen cancelled the bond related to his debt. The payment was verified as legitimate, resolving the legal obligation.

Doña Antonia Arleguí granted power of attorney to Presbítero don Sebastián Jiménez, a resident of Nicaragua. This power was for him to represent her children, Don Félix and Doña Ramona Cuende, in the estate proceedings of Doña Manuela Ibarra, who was the mother of Doña Antonia's deceased husband, Don Romualdo Cuende.

Doña Manuela, Doña Joaquina, and Doña Ana Ángulo sold part of an inherited solar to Doña Florentina de Aragón for $50 silver. The property, located in the main plaza of Cartago, measured 50 varas long by 25 varas wide and bordered Doña Mariana Alvarado's house and solar.

Don Manuel Arias and Doña Cayetana Mora, widow of Don Domingo Chinchilla, sold three caballerías and seventy-five and a half cuerdas of land in Bagaces, Abangares, to Doña María Cecilia del Castillo. This land had a history of ownership, including a sale in 1771 by Don Miguel Antonio de Unanue to Don Francisco Antonio Pérez, witnessed by Don Tomás Hidalgo as Lieutenant Governor of Esparza.

Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla, acting as representative for Don Miguel Ángel Núñez, sold a slave named Pedro Salguero to Don José Corona for $250 silver. Pedro Salguero, described as light-skinned and over 20 years old, was acquired by Núñez in an auction of Don Lorenzo Guillen's assets.

The Molina siblings, including Presbítero don Pablo José, Antonio Mateo, Antonio Ramón, María Antonia, and María Norberta, formalized an inheritance distribution agreement made during their deceased father Francisco Molina's lifetime. Male siblings received cattle and shared lands, pastures, a country house, and a plantain field in Ujarraz, with Mateo also receiving a house plot in Cartago. Female siblings received fewer cattle but were awarded the family house and its furnishings, where they live with their mother, who inherited the share of the deceased Antonia Josefa Molina.
Capitán de Granaderos don Francisco Carazo owed $1000 silver to Don José Acosta, a merchant. This debt was subsequently cancelled on December 3, 1788.
Margarita Coco sold a house and solar in Cartago to Leonardo Lobo for $72 silver. The property was bordered to the North by the house and solar of Concepción Salazar.

José Francisco Arleguí, a resident of Santana, received all the assets from the estate of Don José Francisco Arleguí in deposit. This transaction likely involved the transfer of estate management or inheritance.

Don José Miguel Ocaña, acting as Mayordomo of public revenues, leased a pasture called Rosales in Villa Vieja to Don Pedro Arias for $6 silver per year. The pasture's boundaries were clearly defined by natural features like the Ciruelas River and Rosales stream.

people_involved: Presbítero don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Don José Antonio Oreamuno and Don Tomás Hidalgo obligated themselves for $200 silver to a chaplaincy. This chaplaincy was founded by Presbítero don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba and dedicated to Nuestra Señora de los Dolores, with the funds previously managed by Don José Peralta.

Don Joaquín Oreamuno and his wife Doña Florencia Jiménez obligated themselves for $1500 to a chaplaincy founded by Doña Juliana Bonilla, receiving the funds from Doña Joaquina López del Corral in the form of a farm and cattle in Río Grande. This obligation was later cancelled on September 25, 1798, with various individuals, including Don Manuel Arburola and Capitán don Santiago de Bonilla, taking on portions of the principal.

Juan Manuel Solís, a resident of Villa Vieja in the Tibás neighborhood, granted power of attorney to Martín Taboada, a resident of León. Taboada was authorized to represent Solís before the Intendente in proceedings for the auction of lands in Tibás, in favor of Solís.

Don Manuel Antonio Acosta, a resident of Villa Vieja, leased the Rosales pasture for $7 per year, outbidding Don Pedro Arias who had previously leased it. Acosta represented himself and other neighbors who had claimed preference and offered an improved price. The petition was signed by several residents, including Juan Agustín Lara and Doña Antonia Ruiz.

Doña Antonia Ruiz, a resident of Villa Vieja, committed to an annual payment of 6 pesos and 6 reales for the lease of the Carrizal pasture. This obligation was previously held by her deceased husband, José Antonio Zamora, and Don Joaquín Zamora acted as her guarantor.
Don Lorenzo Guillen, a merchant, granted general power of attorney. The primary recipient was Don José María Lejarza, followed by Don Juan Manuel Zelaya, and then Don Pantaleón de Aguilar.

Don Lorenzo Guillen, a merchant from Panama, and Doña María Francisca Corral, acting as guarantor, committed to pay $2035 in silver. This payment was to Don Mateo Mora, a resident of Villa Nueva, who was representing Don José María Lejarza, a merchant from Guatemala.

Don José Antonio Jiménez, acting as the guardian for Doña Gertrudis Robledo, leased a cacao plantation in Matina, comprising 1300 trees, to Manuel Bogarín for a term of 5 years. The rent was set at 3 tercios of cacao for the first three years and 4 tercios for the subsequent two.

Don Alejandro Lagipar and his wife, Doña Ana María Oreamuno, committed to pay $820 in silver for a chaplaincy. This chaplaincy belonged to Presbítero Don Francisco Antonio Robledo and was previously the responsibility of Doña Encarnación Sancho de Castañeda.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba
summary: Don José María Peralta, an official of the tobacco administration, and his wife Doña Ana Benita Corrales, along with Don Tomás Hidalgo and his wife Doña Rita de Oreamuno (as guarantors), committed to pay $431.7 reales at 5% interest to the Cofradía del Rosario. This debt, previously held by Presbítero Don Juan Manuel de Casasola y Córdoba, was secured by mortgaging their houses and was later cancelled on October 16, 1792, with payments made to Don Joaquín de Arguedas and Don Sebastián Fernández.

people_involved: Doña Tomasa Joaquina López del Corral
summary: Doña Tomasa Joaquina López del Corral committed to pay $200 to the Convento de San Francisco de Esparza. This debt was previously held by the deceased Pedro Regalado de Rojas, and then by Don Joaquín Oreamuno, from whom she received 5 caballerías of land in Río Grande and $75 in cash. The obligation was later cancelled on August 18, 1809, having been transferred to Don Nicolás de Oreamuno and his spouse.

Doña María del Carmen Guevara, a resident of Villa Vieja, sold two caballerías of land located across the Río Grande to Gaspar González, also from Villa Vieja, for $75 in silver. She had acquired this land from Don Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla in 1784, and its boundaries were described in detail, including a large guácimo tree and various streams.

Don Sebastián Fernández de Urrutia, planning to travel to Nicoya where his wife resided, granted power of attorney to Don Santiago Bonilla. This power allowed Bonilla to represent him in the estate proceedings of his father-in-law, Don Francisco Arleguí.

Doña Joaquina Corrales sold two caballerías of land, located across the Río Grande in the area called 'la Sabana larga,' to Francisco de la Trinidad Suárez for $64 in silver. She had received this land from Don Joaquín Oreamuno via a cession deed dated September 16 of the previous month, with the land situated between the Cajón and Lajas streams.
Don José Antonio Jiménez granted general power of attorney to Don Joaquín de Oreamuno.
Presbítero Don Ramón de Azofeifa, the priest of this city, granted power of attorney to Licenciado Don Sebastián Jiménez, who resided in the town of Nicaragua.

Don José Perié, the Governor, appointed Licenciados Don Juan Manuel Zelaya and Don José Tomás Zelaya as his general attorneys. This appointment followed the death of his previous attorney in Guatemala.

people_involved: Teniente Coronel Don Rafael de Cárdenas
summary: Doña Florentina de Aragón granted power of attorney to Don Manuel Galisteo, a resident of León, to sell an enslaved person named Pablo Guzmán. Pablo Guzmán, who was acquired from Don Manuel Guzmán in 1784, was to be sent to León by Teniente Coronel Don Rafael de Cárdenas.

Don Miguel Guzmán and his wife Doña Antonia García received $100 in silver from Don Tomás Hidalgo, related to a chaplaincy of Nuestra Señora de los Dolores. They committed to this obligation and mortgaged their house in the city, which was described by its boundaries with neighboring properties.
Capitán Don Gregorio Oreamuno received...
A deposit was made for the estate of the deceased Don José Romualdo Oreamuno. The specific date and the person making the deposit are not mentioned in this fragment.

On October 21, 1788, Royal Ensign Don Antonio de la Fuente granted general power of attorney to Don José Asenjos, Don Carlos Portocarrero, and Don Manuel José Iglesias, who were attorneys in the Intendancy of León.

On October 23, 1788, Don José Perié, the current Governor of the province, made his will. He was the legitimate son of the deceased Don Maximiliano Perié and Doña María Barros, originally from Jerez de los Caballeros, Spain. He was married to Doña Isabel Rod y Perié, with whom he had a living daughter, Doña Josefa, named as his sole heir, and appointed Don Ramón de Azofeifa and Don Esteban Venegas as executors.

people_involved: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco
summary: On October 28, 1788, Royal Ensign Don Antonio de la Fuente and Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco (representing Don Agustín Gana of Panama) agreed to sell the boat "San José" for $1000 to Don Luis Demetrio Coronado, the priest of Nicoya, represented by notary Don José Romualdo Zamora. This sale occurred despite an ongoing dispute over the boat's ownership, which Don Antonio de la Fuente had initially bought from Don Joaquín Silva, believing it belonged to Don Agustín Gana, but later found it might belong to Don Alonso Velarde. A marginal note from November 26, 1789, confirms the sale to Don Antonio was finalized, and Núñez received the payment. The transaction was witnessed by Provincial Mayor Don Francisco Carazo.

On November 11, 1788, Captain Don Luis Blanco Desacido, a resident of Masaya currently in Cartago to conclude residency matters, granted general power of attorney to Don José Romualdo Zamora. This was done before the Provincial Mayor, as the notary was involved.

On November 14, 1788, Rafael Pacheco, who was about to marry, donated 30 heads of cattle, a mare, a horse, and his dwelling house to his elderly and poor mother, María Francisca Pacheco, to ensure her well-being. The house was bordered by properties belonging to Pedro Lobo, Juan Antonio Arias, and José Francisco Oreamuno.
On November 17, 1788, Manuel Antonio Jiménez emancipated his son, Juan Francisco, who was over 25 years old and single. The document was not signed.

On November 29, 1788, Pablo José Cubero, Captain of the "pardos" of the city's Puebla, made his will. He was the legitimate son of the deceased José Cubero and Juana Panlagua, and was single. He had a natural son, Manuel José, with Petronila Guerrero, whose whereabouts were unknown but believed to be alive, and named him as his heir. He owed money to his siblings Ana, Francisco, María, and the estate of his deceased brother Dionisio, and had paid a debt from the deceased Simona to Antonio Avendaño. Miguel Cárdenas and Antonio García were appointed as executors.

On December 3, 1788, Don José Antonio Bonilla (as husband of Doña Antonia Manuela Meneses) and Doña Antonia Manuela Meneses, Don Paulino Meneses, Doña Antonia Meneses, Doña Engracia Meneses, and Doña Juana Meneses granted general power of attorney. The primary recipient was Don José González de Navas, Colonel of the Santa Ana Grande militias, and secondarily, Don Juan José Medina, a procurator in Nueva Guatemala.
On December 6, 1788, Presbyter Don Alejandro Paniagua granted general power of attorney to Pedro José Lizondo, a resident of the local vicinity.

On December 30, 1788, Don Manuel José de Zea, the tobacco factor in the province, took charge of the stamped paper branch for the next two years. He provided Captain Don Mateo de Mora, a resident of Villa Nueva, as guarantor for $500.

locations: Hospital de San Juan de Dios
summary: On January 28, 1789, Lieutenant Colonel of Cavalry Don Luis Méndez, a single man and legitimate son of the deceased Don Luis Méndez and Doña Tomasa de Molina, all from Málaga, made his will. He bequeathed $30 to his orderly Don Francisco Albín, $30 to Don Gregorio García, and $40 plus service items to his servant Petronila. He left the remainder of his estate to the Hospital de San Juan de Dios upon its legal establishment. The will was executed in the Agua Caliente or Marte neighborhood of Cartago, before notary Don José Romualdo Zamora.

people_involved: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco
summary: On January 28, 1789, Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco, general representative for Don Agustín de Gana (a merchant from Panama), and Don Lorenzo Guillen, also from Panama, agreed to submit their dispute over account rendering to arbitration. They appointed Don Francisco de Echeverría and Don Manuel Torre y Romero, both merchants, as arbitrators; Echeverría resided in the province, and Torre y Romero was a local resident.

On January 30, 1789, Doña Josefa Rosalía Alvarado and her daughter, Doña Josefa Dominga Galeano (over 25 years old), granted power of attorney to Don Manuel José Ortiz and, secondarily, to Don Juan Ansuatigui, both residents of Panama. Their purpose was to collect a legacy left to them by the deceased Doña Ana Manuela Alvarado, formerly a resident of Chiriquí and widow of Don José Medina, with Doña Josefa Rosalía being her sister and Doña Josefa Dominga her niece.

On January 30, 1789, Juan Tomás Martínez granted power of attorney to Royal Ensign Don Antonio de la Fuente to collect $140 from Doña Joaquina del Corral, which Martínez had paid as a down payment for a slave named Encarnación, sold extrajudicially by Doña Joaquina. Alternatively, de la Fuente was authorized to sell the slave, who had been left with Don José Peralta over a year ago, and in that case, complete the payment to Doña Joaquina for the slave's full value of $200.
On January 31, 1789, Doña María Francisca del Corral took charge of something (the sentence is incomplete).

people_involved: Sargento Mayor don Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla
summary: Don Joaquín de Oreamuno took responsibility for $250 from a $1500 fund belonging to the San Francisco Convent and a chaplaincy established by Sargento Mayor don Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla after Juliana Bonilla's death. He mortgaged his house in Cartago, which was bordered by properties owned by Doña María Bolívar, Presbítero don Félix García, Doña Manuela Pastora, and Doña Rosa Madriz.

Doña María del Carmen Medina granted power of attorney to her husband, Don Nicolás Gutiérrez, to collect her inheritance. This inheritance was due to her as the legitimate daughter of the late Don Valerio Medina, a former resident of Chiriquí.

Don Tomás Umaña, a resident of Villa Nueva de San José, took charge of $80 in silver from a chaplaincy founded by Francisco de Paz, secured by lands in the Murciélago area. Umaña mortgaged his house on these lands, which were later redeemed by neighbors on September 4th, and the obligation was cancelled.

Cristóbal Moya, a free mulatto, leased a canoe for transport across the Reventazón River to Matina. He agreed to pay three sacks of cacao, each valued at $25, from the $300 in cacao that hacendados owed him annually.

Don Tomás Benito Hidalgo took responsibility for $525 in cacao, secured by a pasture and lands in the Felipe Díaz area, which previously belonged to Doña Florentina de Aragón and the San Francisco Convent. On March 4, 1807, Don Manuel Marchena, a Regidor and Alcalde Provincial, cancelled the obligation after $350 in silver was deposited into the consolidation fund.

Don Francisco Ulloa and his wife, Doña Dominga Robredo, took charge of $150 in silver from a chaplaincy belonging to Presbítero don Francisco Antonio Robredo. This fund was previously managed by the late Don Nicolás Cleto Chavarría and his wife Doña Eufemia Pacheco. The obligation was cancelled on June 29, 1796, having passed to Don Miguel Guzmán.

Beneficiado don Ramón de Azofeifa and Don Esteban Venegas, acting as executors for the late Governor Don José Perié, granted power of attorney to Licenciados don Juan Manuel and don José Tomás Zelaya, residents of Nueva Guatemala.

Beneficiado don Ramón de Azofeifa and Don Esteban Venegas, as executors for the late Governor Don José Perié, granted power of attorney to Don Mateo Mantilla, a resident of León (Nicaragua). Mantilla was authorized to collect Perié's salaries from the Royal Coffers, up to January 7th, the date of his death.

Antonia Romero Catalán obligated herself for $272 in silver, which her minor children, José Antonio and Rafaela, inherited from their deceased uncle Juan Romero. This sum was received in cacao trees in Matina, the deceased's house, and an enclosure in Cartago.

Capitán don Mateo Mora, a resident of Villa Nueva, was appointed Receiver of Alcabalas for the Cartago Province by the Principal Administrator of León. He provided Don José Antº García as his guarantor for when he would take possession of the Receivership.

people_involved: Capitán don Simón Escalante y Paniagua
summary: Don Esteban Venegas, the interim Receiver of Alcabalas for the Cartago Province, was upheld by the Royal Judge in his right to the Receivership, despite the Principal Administrator having given it to Don Mateo Mora. Venegas continued in his post and provided Capitán don Simón Escalante y Paniagua, a resident of Villa Vieja, as his guarantor.

people_involved: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco
summary: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco, general attorney for Don Agustín de Gana, both residents of Panamá, partially substituted Licenciado don Santiago Moreno, a lawyer of the Royal Audiencia. Moreno was tasked with handling an appeal regarding the sale of a ship to Don Antonio de la Fuente and representing Gana's interests in the estate of the intestate Don Domingo Endana.

people_involved: Capitán de pardos José Miguel Cárdenas
summary: Capitán de pardos José Miguel Cárdenas, acting as guardian for Esteban and Ana Céspedes (children of the late Ramón Céspedes), sold a half-lot house to Juana María Iglesias for $167 in silver. The property was bordered by houses of Don Manuel Guzmán, Presbítero don Gregorio Bonilla, Don Santiago Bonilla, and Doña Ana Sancho. The sale was later cancelled on March 16, 1793.

people_involved: Alférez Real don Antonio de la Fuente
summary: Alférez Real don Antonio de la Fuente sold a dark-skinned slave named Manuel Acosta to Beneficiado don Luis Demetrio Coronado, the Cura of Nicoya, for $300 in silver. Acosta was previously owned by Don José Acosta, who acquired him from Don Francisco Medina in Buenos Aires in 1783 as part of a convoy of 23 slaves.

Don Antonio de la Fuente, acting as a substitute attorney for Don Manuel Galisteo of León, sold a house in Villa Nueva to Don José Norberto Alpízar, a resident of Villa Nueva, for $300 in money. The house was bordered by the Tobacco Administration, a royal street, and the house of Alejandro Méndez.

people_involved: Capn. de milicias don Salvador Cuende
Capitán don Juan Francº de Bonilla
summary: Capitán de milicias don Salvador Cuende, residing in Cartago and acting as the testamentary executor for his deceased mother Doña Manuela Ibarra, sold a 45-year-old black slave named Miguel Antonio Ibarra to Capitán don Juan Francº de Bonilla for $128 in silver. The sale was later rescinded on October 10th of the same year.

This entry details the testament of María Antonia Badilla, legitimate daughter of the late Antonio Badilla and Manuela Salas. She was the widow of José Toribio López, with whom she had four surviving children, and was also married to Felipe Santiago Medina, who abandoned her and died absent.
