Don Antonio de la Fuente was named as her executor, or José Manuel García in his absence, and her children were her heirs.

This entry lists a group of individuals including Francisco Irola, Ventura Moya, Hipólito Morales, José Antonio Calderón, Marcos Morales, Miguel Irola, José Antonio Quesada, Rafael Irola, Juan José Bonilla, Don Nicolás Castillo, Sebastián Quesada, Juan Pablo Morales, Joaquín Molina, José Antonio Salas, Simón Coto, Pedro Moya, José Manuel Solano, José de Jesús Moya, and Esteban Quesada, without further context in this snippet.

A group of Ujarraz residents, including Santos Meza, Manuel Palacios, Justo Picado, Jorge Matamoros, Tomás Valerín, Ignacio Calderón, and Juan de Dios Rojas, granted power of attorney to José Antonio de Alvarado. This was to represent them in a lawsuit initiated by their parish priest, Fray Antonio de la Concepción, who sought to classify them as 'indios' and impose tributary status. The case stemmed from a report by a former Gobernador's predecessor denying the existence of such people in the region, and the Intendente of León had forwarded the matter for proof.

Captain Gregorio de Oreamuno sold José Manuel Oreamuno, a 23-year-old enslaved 'mulato blanco,' to Captain Bruno de Alvarado for $200 plata. José Manuel was the son of Juana María, an enslaved woman who had been inherited by Gregorio from his father, who in turn inherited her from Gregorio's grandfather, José Antonio Oreamuno.

Doña Ana Rita Gómez, daughter of the late Manuel José de Gómez and Juana María Barahona, granted power of attorney to her husband, Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla, to draft her will. She designated her husband and Presbítero Don Juan José Benito Bonilla as executors, with her unborn child as the universal heir, or her husband if the child were to die.

Doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho de Castañeda, daughter of the late Juan Sancho de Castañeda and Juana de Alvarado y Girón, made her will. She mentioned her marriage to Rafael de Mier Cevallos and the loss of their two children, and named several relatives including her nephew José Miguel Sancho and nieces Bárbara García and Ana Teresa Fierro. She also specified bequests to Mónica Sancho and María Aragón, and listed four enslaved individuals she owned: Cecilia, Ana María de Jesús, María del Sacramento, and José del Rosario, appointing Presbítero Juan José de Oreamuno and Manuel José García as her executors.

Doña Josefa Rosalía de Alvarado sold a solar (plot of land) situated at the corner of the main plaza in Cartago to Presbítero Don Gregorio Bonilla for $50. The property was bordered by the houses and solares of Don Santiago Bonilla and Doña Narcisa Bonilla, the parish church, and the royal Cabildo.

Doña María Francisca del Corral acknowledged a debt of $192 to Pedro José Lizondo for 12 tercios of cacao, due in December. She stipulated that if the monetary payment was not made, she would settle the debt with an enslaved 'mulatilla' named Tomasa, with any excess value of Tomasa to be returned.
Doña Estefanía Pacheco sold an enslaved woman named Manuela Pacheco, described as 'color loro' and approximately 16 years old, to Doña Cecilia Castillo, a resident of Villa Nueva, for $250 plata.

people_involved: María Gertrudis de Laya y Bolívar
summary: Doña María Gertrudis de Laya y Bolívar, a widow, and Don Santiago Bonilla committed to an obligation of $200 plata. This sum was designated for the alms of Patriarch San Joaquín, with an annual interest payment of 8%.

people_involved: Maximiliano Antonio de Alvarado y Girón
summary: Don Rafael de Alvarado y Girón assumed an obligation for $200 plata, received from his sister Doña María del Carmen Alvarado. This sum originated from the estate of their deceased brother, Presbítero Don Maximiliano Antonio de Alvarado y Girón, specifically from properties he had leased in Nicoya, which his heirs had redeemed. Rafael committed to paying 5% interest annually to María del Carmen, with Don Bruno de Alvarado serving as guarantor.

Presbítero Don Gregorio Bonilla undertook an obligation for $80 plata, connected to a chaplaincy originally instituted by Francisco de Paz in the mid-18th century and previously managed by Don Tomás Umaña. The principal of this chaplaincy was linked to a plot of land acquired by Doña Laureana de Chaves, which had since been redeemed by residents of the Aserrí valley. Bonilla secured this obligation by mortgaging a house and solar.
Beneficiado Don Nicolás Carrillo, who served as the priest of Esparza, granted a general power of attorney to Pedro José Lizondo.

Buenaventura Lizondo sold a 'cerco de pita' on his property in Ujarraz to Cayetano Meneses for $32 plata. The land, originally purchased from Pedro Machado, was bordered by the royal road to Matina, lands belonging to Machado, and the fence of María Venegas.

Juana María Castillo and Teodora Castillo, acting as heirs of the late Diego Castillo, sold his house, a 100-vara solar, surrounding walls, a bench, and a small table to Nicolás Gómez for $81 and 4 reales plata.

Nicolás Gómez, stating he had no children, formally donated the properties acquired in the September 26th sale, along with any other assets he might own at his death, to his wife, María Dolores Sancho, should he die intestate.

Isidro López assumed an obligation for $94 and 7 reales concerning the guardianship of his minor brother, Esteban. This sum represented Esteban's inheritance from the estate of their deceased mother, María Antonia Padilla.

Don Salvador Cuende, a Captain from Nicaragua residing locally and acting as executor for his deceased mother Doña Manuela Ibarra, granted freedom to Benito, an enslaved Black man, in exchange for $300.
Doña Joaquina López del Corral leased her cacao plantation, Chirropo, located in the Matina Valley, to Don Esteban Herdocia for a period of five years, with an annual rent of 10 tercios of cacao.

Doña Joaquina López del Corral formally canceled Don Esteban Herdocia's obligation, acknowledging that he had punctually fulfilled the terms of the lease for the initial five years and an additional three years.

Doña Antonia Manuela de Alvarado sold two pieces of land in Cuaginiquil, near Cartago, to Pedro José Lizondo for $110 plata. One parcel was situated between the pasture of her son-in-law, Don Rafael de Alvarado, and that of the buyer.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Rafael José de la Rosa
summary: Don José Romualdo Zamora, acting for himself and his brother-in-law Don Pablo Coronado, sold a house in Cartago to Presbítero Don Rafael José de la Rosa for $450 plata. The house, inherited from Doña María Josefa de Soto, was bordered by properties belonging to the San Francisco Convent, Doña Ignacia de la Rosa, Doña María del Carmen Pacheco, and Doña Gertrudis Zabaleta. The transaction was granted before Capitán Don Francisco Carazo.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Rafael José de la Rosa
summary: An Escribano cancelled a $300 obligation charged to Presbítero Don Rafael José de la Rosa, which pertained to a chaplaincy previously held by the deceased Presbítero Don Francisco Robredo. This cancellation was made in virtue of an order from Vicario Don Ramón de Azofeifa, confirming its redemption.

Don Bruno de Alvarado, a Lieutenant of the militias in Nicaragua residing in Cartago, incurred a debt of $225 plata to Pedro José Lizondo. This amount was a loan that Don Bruno de Alvarado committed to repay in the following month.

Don Sebastián Fernández de Urrutia, a former judge appointed by the Juez de residencia in Nicoya, was summoned to appear before the court. He granted power of attorney to Francisco José Vega, a resident of Nicoya, to represent him in the proceedings.

people_involved: Don Pedro Tiburcio Machado y Ugarte
summary: Don Pedro Tiburcio Machado y Ugarte and his wife Doña María Mercedes Soto Mayor received a house in Cartago through a cession from Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla. The house, located in the same block as properties of Don José Antonio and Don Manuel José García and Doña Ana Sancho, was encumbered with $300 for chaplaincies, with $200 for the San Francisco Convent and $100 for Ntra. Sra. del Rosario.

Presbítero Don José Ramón Machado presented an order from the Ecclesiastical Court, which was added to the record, confirming the oblación of the property. This order mandated the cancellation of the obligation deed that secured the principals, which had been granted by the deceased owner.

Manuel José Sáenz and his wife Doña Cayetana Ulloa took on an obligation of $300 plata for the chaplaincy of Nuestra Señora de los Ángeles. This obligation was secured by a farm in the Barrio del Agua Caliente, which they received along with some furniture from the chaplaincy. The obligation was previously held by Nicolás Araya and had been imposed by Doctor Don Pedro Jiménez.
Manuel José Sáenz and Doña Cayetana Ulloa declared that the obligation for the chaplaincy of Nuestra Señora de los Ángeles had been transferred to Doña Manuela Baeza.

Doña Antonia Manuela de Alvarado leased a cacao plantation named 'la Lacayo', consisting of 1000 trees in Matina, to José Antonio Solano y Barrantes. The lease agreement was for three years at an annual price of $125 cacao.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Rafael José de la Rosa
Don Pedro Tiburcio Machado y Ugarte
summary: Presbítero Don Rafael José de la Rosa took on a $300 obligation, representing one of three chaplaincy branches previously held by Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla in a house in Cartago, which Bonilla had ceded to Don Pedro Tiburcio Machado y Ugarte. Don Pedro immediately delivered the $300 to de la Rosa, which belonged to a chaplaincy of the deceased Presbítero Don Francisco Robredo, and de la Rosa hypothecated his house and lot in Cartago as security.

Don Nicolás Gutiérrez, acting for himself and his wife Doña María del Carmen Medina, granted general power of attorney to Don Ignacio Llórente, a resident of Cartago, and secondarily to Don Manuel José Ortiz, a resident of Panamá. He also revoked a previous power of attorney that had been given to Escribano Juan José Vázquez of Chiriquí.

Don Manuel Torre y Romero and his wife Doña Antonia Jiménez committed to an obligation of $425 plata at 5% interest, in favor of Nuestra Señora del Pilar de los Tres Ríos. They received this amount in 100 heads of cattle located in the Garavito area.

Pedro José Lizondo took on an obligation for $500 plata, which Don José Antonio de Oreamuno, as guardian of Doña Micaela de Alvarado (who was declared inept), delivered to him. Lizondo was obligated to pay 5% interest on this amount.
Don Sebastián de Guevara, as the new guardian of his mother-in-law Doña Micaela de Alvarado, cancelled the $500 obligation previously held by Pedro José Lizondo, having received the principal amount.

Pedro José Lizondo, acting as attorney for Presbítero Don Alejandro Paniagua, leased a cacao plantation named 'la Paniagua' in the Matina valley, consisting of 600 trees, to Blas de la Candelaria Solano. The lease duration was to be mutually agreed upon, and the annual price was $50.

people_involved: Capitán Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla
summary: Doña Antonia Manuela Alvarado sold a piece of land in Cuaginiquil, near Cartago, to Capitán Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla for $60 plata. The land, measuring 800 varas from North to South, was bordered by the Coris River and the Salitral River to the East and West, with the measurement starting from the bridge where Prudencio Picado's fence was located.

people_involved: Don Benito de Alvarado y Girón
Don Francisco Nicolás de Alvarado y Girón
Don José Francisco Santana de Alvarado y Girón
Presbítero Don Rafael José de la Rosa
summary: This entry records the will of Don Rafael de Alvarado, legitimate son of the deceased Don Benito de Alvarado y Girón and Doña Leonida de Ocampo. He was married to Doña Ana Josefa de Ulloa and named his wife and Presbítero Don Rafael José de la Rosa as executors, with his sons Don Francisco Nicolás and Don José Francisco Santana de Alvarado y Girón as heirs.

Doña Antonia Manuela de Alvarado sold a piece of land for pasture in Cuaginiquil to Don José Antonio del Campo for $96 dinero. This land, acquired from her deceased husband's estate, was contiguous with another parcel her husband, Don Romualdo de Oreamuno, had previously sold to del Campo.

people_involved: Doña María Gertrudis de Laya y Bolívar
summary: Doña María Gertrudis de Laya y Bolívar grants power to her son, don Santiago Bonilla, to administer her estates located in the jurisdiction of Bagaces and Río Grande.
Teniente Coronel don Juan Pinillos, the interim Governor, grants power to don Francisco Icaza, the Postmaster in León, to collect his salaries as Governor and Commander from the Royal Treasury.

people_involved: Doña Mercedes del Villar y Gutiérrez
summary: Doña Mercedes del Villar y Gutiérrez, a native and resident of the town of Rivas, grants general power to her husband, Capitán don Salvador Cuende.

Mateo Ibarra and his wife María Nicolasa Calvo assume a debt of $1672 in cacao for a chaplaincy previously managed by Felipe Hernández, which belongs to the San Francisco Convent in Cartago. They mortgage a cacao plantation in Barbilla, Matina, as security.
Agustín Blas Rodríguez, who is in a lawsuit with Joaquín Trejos, grants power to Cristóbal de Ocampo Golfín to represent him in the legal proceedings.

people_involved: Capitán don José Gregorio de Oreamuno
doña Juana Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Capitán don José Gregorio de Oreamuno and his wife doña Juana Muñoz de la Trinidad incur a debt of $200 at 5% interest to the San Francisco Convent of Esparza, previously managed by Silvestre Chacón. They mortgage their house, which is bordered by properties of doña Joaquina Miranda, doña Micaela de Alvarado, and heirs of don Félix Meneses.

Francisco Esteban Jiménez, a native of Cartago and resident of Villa Nueva, incurs a debt of $300 in silver at 5% interest to Pedro José Elizondo. His father, Manuel Antonio Jiménez, acts as his guarantor.

Residents of Ujarrás grant power to don José Asenjos to represent them in León, Nicaragua, for a pending lawsuit against their former priest, Fray Antonio de la Concepción. The lawsuit concerns their racial status, as they claim not to be indigenous.

José Francisco Oreamuno and his wife María Antonia Pacheco incur a debt of $200 in silver at 5% interest to the San Francisco Convent of Cartago, previously managed by don Joaquín de Oreamuno. They mortgage their house, bordered by properties of José Antonio González, Pedro Lobo, and Mateo Molina. This obligation was cancelled on Dec 22, 1778, having passed to Félix Caniaño, and later cancelled by don Pablo Rejas, Cura of Esparza, on Dec 16, 1814.

people_involved: don Juan de Alvarado y Girón
summary: Don Juan de Alvarado y Girón grants power to don Antonio de la Fuente to manage his affairs and those of his minor ward, doña María Alvarado, for whom he is a tutor.

people_involved: Doña Baltasara de la Madriz Linares
Presb" don José Miguel Sancho de Castañeda
summary: Doña Baltasara de la Madriz Linares grants power to Presbyter don José Miguel Sancho de Castañeda and Capitán don Mateo Mantilla, both residing in León, to collect $200 owed to her by don Antonio Soto Mayor.
Don José Antonio de Oriamuno grants general power to Capitán don Mateo Mantilla, who resides in León.

people_involved: Dwña María de Alvarado y Girón
summary: Doña María de Alvarado y Girón and her son don Nicolás form a company for cattle breeding.

José Romualdo Zamora and his wife doña Juana Rita Coronado incur a debt of $200 in silver at 5% interest, secured by five caballerías of land in La Ancheta, Esparza, belonging to the Benefice of that city. This debt was previously managed by don Sebastián Fernández de Urrutia and was cancelled on Dec 16, 1814, by the Beneficiado don Pablo Rejas, Cura of Esparza.
Don Antonio de la Fuente grants power to don José Ignacio Rucavado to collect a debt from don Francisco Ramo, a merchant in Rivas, for silk goods he held on commission.
Félix Sanabria receives 106 "cortos bienes" belonging to his minor relative, José Rafael Sánchez, for whom he is a tutor.
Félix Sanabria, acting as tutor for José Rafael Sánchez, sells a house located by the Reventado River to Pedro Elias Valverde for $44 in silver.

Francisco Javier Mayorga, a mulatto official of the pardos corps in Cartago, promises $1000 in silver as arras to his future wife, doña Francisca González de Villalón. Despite the social inequality, Francisca's mother, doña Manuela Almandos y Zabaleta, consents to the marriage under the condition of the arras promise.

Doña Dominga Zabaleta sells an enslaved woman named María Josefa Zabaleta, described as "color loro" and about 26 years old, born and raised in her house, to don Francisco Antonio de Echavarría, a native of Spain, for $200.
Pedro José Elizondo grants power to don Bernardo Gómez, Subdelegate Judge in Bagaces, to collect $225 owed to him by don Bruno de Alvarado, a Sublieutenant of militias in Nicoya.

Presbyter don Félix García owes doña Dominga Zabaleta $150. Doña Dominga declares that this principal belongs to one of her two daughters, doña Juana Nazaria, as proceeds from an enslaved woman named Josefa Catalina, who was given to her by a benefactor and whom she sold to Pedro Fuentes. This obligation was cancelled on Oct 21, 1796.

Don Juan María Masís, having learned of the death of his son Cayetano Lumbides in Condega, grants power to don Mateo Mantilla, Captain of militias in León, to represent him in the succession proceedings.
Doña Manuela Gertrudis Sancho sells a mulatto girl named Ana María de Jesús, about 15 years old, born and raised in her house, to Presbyter don Félix García.

Don Francisco Antonio de Echavarría, a native of Spain, granted freedom to his white-skinned slave, María Josefa Zabaleta, who was approximately 26 years old. He had purchased her from Doña Dominga Zabaleta on April 22 of the same year.

people_involved: Doña Manuela Clemencia Almandos y Zabaleta
summary: Doña Francisca González de Villalón, with her mother Doña Manuela Clemencia Almandos y Zabaleta's consent for her marriage to Francisco Javier Mayorga, renounced her inheritance from Doña Manuela. This renunciation was made in favor of her sister Doña Bárbara Jiménez, citing her mother's financial scarcity and other just motives.

people_involved: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco
summary: Don José Acosta, acting on behalf of Don Luis Fernández, sold a slave named Rafael García, described as white/mulatto and about 26 years old, to Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco for $200. Rafael García, who had been purchased by Fernández from Presbítero Don Juan Antonio Chamorro, was noted as a fugitive who had stolen a mule and its tack.

Don Benito Bonilla, a native of Cartago and resident of León, who had secured the rights to collect tithes from Cartago parishes for three years at 1000 pesos annually, ceded these rights to Pedro José Elizondo. The sub-lease covered the territory from Quebrada Honda to the Matine valley, with Elizondo obligated to pay $1750 annually in León.

José Francisco Arleguí, a resident of Santa Ana, assumed guardianship of the minor Pedro, who is the son of Don Carlos Portocarrero and Doña Benita Arleguí. This event was noted as 'No corrió' (not executed).

Don José Ruperto Prieto, acting as the executor for the deceased Lieutenant Colonel Don Luis Méndez, granted power of attorney to Don Domingo Ubico, a resident of Guatemala City. This power enabled Ubico to collect debts owed to Méndez by Don Juan del Barrio and from the Royal Coffers.

people_involved: Don Francisco Nicolás Santana de Alvarado y Girón
Don José Francisco Santana de Alvarado y Girón
summary: Doña Ana Josefa de Ulloa, a widow, formally obligated herself to her minor sons, Don Francisco Nicolás and Don José Francisco Santana de Alvarado y Girón. She committed to providing each son with $367 and 3/4 reales as their paternal inheritance.

Gertrudis Rodríguez, a childless widow of Francisco Granados, while ill in bed, declared her modest assets. She then donated these assets to her nephew José Narciso Rodríguez, and to María del Pilar Rodríguez and Gabriela Rodríguez.

María Josefa González de Araujo granted power of attorney to her husband, Don Mateo Hernández. This power allowed him to collect her inheritance from the estate of her deceased natural father, Don Andrés González de Araujo.

locations: Quebrada Honda del Monte del Aguacate
summary: Don José Gregorio Oreamuno obligated himself to Don Fermín de Eva for $150 annually for three years. This commitment was made as Oreamuno took on the sub-lease of tithes in the Bagaces territory, specifically from the Abangares river to Quebrada Honda del Monte del Aguacate.

Luisa Chaves, a resident of Ujarrás, granted freedom to her very old black slave, Carmen Flor, and Carmen's 20-year-old mulatto son, José Benito Chaves. Luisa declared that José Benito was the son of her deceased son, Cayetano Mateo, who had requested his freedom in a letter before his death. Luisa also stated that her other children, Antonia Tomasa, Lorenza, and María del Rosario, were emancipated and each received a slave.

Don José Antonio Jiménez and Doña Petronila Robredo made their testament, detailing their lineage, children, and properties, including three slaves. They also recounted a debt owed by Don Manuel Antonio Sandoval, Don José Antonio's half-brother, for a slave, mules, and money. The testators freed their slave Pedro Antonio.

Doña Joaquina López del Corral sold Encarnación Corrales, a 22-year-old mulatto shoemaker of 'loro' color who was born and raised in her house, to Don José Ignacio Rucavado for $250. Don José Ignacio Rucavado was a merchant and resident of Cartagena de Indias.

people_involved: Beneficiado Don José Antonio de Alvarado
summary: Pedro José Elizondo obligated himself for $114 and 3/4 reales belonging to Matías Cordero, an absent individual whose whereabouts are unknown, with his father Buenaventura Elizondo acting as guarantor. This obligation followed proceedings where Beneficiado Don José Antonio de Alvarado, Cura of Villa Nueva, transferred guardianship of Matías, who is married in Lajuela de Villa Vieja, to the court.

Doña Petronila Mora, a resident of Villa Nueva and widow of Esteban Cervantes, sold a piece of land to Ramón Montero, also from Villa Nueva. The land's boundaries were meticulously described, referencing the María Aguilar and Tiribí rivers, as well as former properties of José Miguel Cervantes and the deceased Don Miguel Jiménez.

Don José Vázquez y Téllez, Governor of the province, granted power of attorney to Don Juan José Medina and Don Gabriel José Estrada, both Procuradores in the Royal Audiencia of Guatemala, to obtain the official 'pase' for his Governor title and to handle general litigation.

Don José Vázquez y Téllez granted general power of attorney to Capitán de granaderos Don Mateo Mantilla and Don José Asenso, Procurador of Nicaragua, both residents of León. This power was for obtaining a record of his Governor title from the Royal Officials in Nicaragua and for managing all his legal disputes.

people_involved: Capitán Don Pedro Tiburcio Machado y Ugarte
summary: Don José Vázquez y Téllez named ten individuals as guarantors for his 'juicio de residencia' (judicial review of his term as governor). Each guarantor was responsible for 250 pesos plata.

Don José Antonio de Oriamuno, Capitán Don Joaquín de Oriamuno, and Teniente Don Manuel Hidalgo each paid 250 pesos of their fianza before Don Tomás de Acosta. This payment was made in compliance with a mandate from the Real Audiencia, and their respective guarantees were subsequently cancelled.

Don Buenaventura Lizondro, Don Pedro José Lizondro (who also signed as Elisondo), and Don Bernardo Gómez acted as guarantors for Governor Don José Vázquez y Téllez. This guarantee enabled him to take charge of the Court of Intestate Estates and Goods of the Deceased.

Don Joaquín de Arguedas sold a plot of land on the 'calle real' to José Antonio Carrillo for 16 pesos. The property, which included a stone fence and was originally owned by Valentín Barrio, bordered houses belonging to Francisco Barros, Doña Francisca Madriz, Gregoria Barros, and Doña Francisca Hidalgo.

people_involved: Doña María Gertrudis de Laya y Bolívar
Doña María del Rosario de Bonilla
Presbítero Don José Antonio de Bonilla
summary: Doña María Gertrudis de Laya y Bolívar issued a codicil to her will from 1783, declaring debts for chaplaincies. She detailed distributions to her daughters Doña Juana Bonilla and Doña María del Rosario de Bonilla, noting 65 pesos collected by Tomás Alvarado from Juan Bonilla in Bagaces. She also provided for her sons, Presbítero Don José Antonio de Bonilla, Presbítero Don Miguel Bonilla, and Don Santiago Bonilla, and improved the inheritance for her daughters Doña Juana, Doña María Cruz, and Doña Justa.

Doña María Francisca Velasco Estrada, a native and resident of Cartago, made her will. She was the legitimate daughter of the deceased Don Francisco Velasco and Doña Josefa de Estrada, and the widow of Don Marcos Alvarado, with whom she had no children. She named Doña Luz Aguilar and her stepdaughter Doña Ana María de Alvarado as legatees, mandated the founding of a chaplaincy, and appointed Presbítero Don Pablo José Molina and Don José Ruperto Prieto as her executors.

Capitán Don Joaquín de Alvarado sold an enslaved woman named Juana Antonia de Alvarado, described as 'negra' and approximately 28 years old, to Jerónimo Flores, a resident of Villa Vieja. The sale price was 325 pesos plata.

Doña Ana Solano sold a house with a walled plot to Javier Mayorga for 200 pesos. Mayorga, along with his wife Doña Francisca González de Villalón, declared that the house belonged to his three sisters, María Antonia, Ramona, and Micaela Chavarría, as a donation in recompense for their share in their mother María Bartola Ancheta's house.

Doña Rita Coronado, widow of Don Romualdo Zamora, obligated herself to her six minor children for 1789 pesos 7 reales, representing their inheritance portions ('hijuelas'). Her children were Don Juan Manuel, Don José María, Don Julián, Doña Irene, Doña Joaquina, and Doña Cecilia.
Doña Manuela Pastora confessed to owing Don Ángel Núñez del Arco 204 pesos 5 reales, which he had lent her. The repayment was due by May 1791.
Don Joaquín de Oreamuno, acting as the attorney for Don Agustín de Gana (who was also represented by Don Ángel Núñez del Arco), officially cancelled the debt owed by Doña Manuela Pastora.

people_involved: El Beneficiado Don José Antonio de Alvarado
summary: El Beneficiado Don José Antonio de Alvarado, Cura of Villa Nueva and testamentary executor of Don José Blanquezer, founded a perpetual chaplaincy of recited masses. Don José Blanquezer's will was granted in Esparza in 1777 before Teniente de Gobernador Don Julián Daniel. Alvarado himself was designated as the patron and chaplain, with the closest ordained relative to succeed him.

people_involved: Don José Antonio Bustos y Santiago
summary: Don José Alvarez, a resident of León and merchant in Cartago, granted power of attorney to Don José Antonio Bustos y Santiago, Regidor of the town of Nicaragua. This power was for collecting outstanding debts owed to Alvarez in the town of Nicaragua.

Doña Joaquina Pastora, widow of Joaquín Romero Catalán, committed to her four children, Vicente, Nazario, Domingo, and María Romero, for 654 pesos 6 reales from their paternal inheritance. This act secured their rightful share of the inheritance.

Paula Sancho, in her third marriage to Marcelino Calvo (who was absent in Matina), committed to her five children from her first marriage to Sebastián Camaño for 891 pesos 3 reales. Fernando Masís acted as her guarantor for this obligation.
Doña Paula González, a widow, sold half a house plot without walls in Cartago to don Nicolás Gutiérrez for 40 pesos. The property bordered the house of Doña Margarita González to the West.

Don Francisco Javier Navarro, a resident and Colonel of infantry militias in the province of Conchaco in the Kingdom of Peru, granted general power of attorney to don Manuel Martínez de Pinillos. Don Manuel Martínez de Pinillos was a resident in Madrid.

Felipe Barrios leased a cacao plantation for seven years in the Matina valley, at a place called La Pontezuela, next to José Nicolás Camaño's property. The plantation belonged to the confraternity of Nuestra Señora de Matina, whose steward was Juan Carranza, and the annual price was 50 pesos.
Doña Josefa Rosalía Alvarado granted general power of attorney to don Juan José Medina, a procurator from Guatemala. This power of attorney would allow Medina to act on Alvarado's behalf.

people_involved: Don Manuel Guzmán (son of Teresa Galindo)
Don Miguel Guzmán (son of Teresa Galindo)
Doña Tomasa Guzmán (daughter of Teresa Galindo)
Doña Francisca Guzmán (daughter of Teresa Galindo)
Doña María Guzmán (daughter of Teresa Galindo)
summary: Doña Teresa Galindo, a widow, with permission from her present children, granted freedom to her slave, Manuel Antonio Guzmán. This act was in recognition of his extensive service to her and her children, especially to her deceased son, Don Ramón.

Pedro Elizondo, having a pending lawsuit against don Joaquín Alvarado for 243 pesos 4 reales and needing to travel to his Landecho hacienda, granted power of attorney to don José Antonio de Oriamuno. This power allowed Oriamuno to continue the litigation on Elizondo's behalf.

people_involved: Don Manuel Guzmán (husband of María Teresa Garlín)
Doña Francisca Guzmán (daughter of María Teresa Garlín)
Doña María Guzmán (daughter of María Teresa Garlín)
Doña Tomasa Guzmán (daughter of María Teresa Garlín)
Don Manuel Guzmán (son of María Teresa Garlín)
Don Miguel Guzmán (son of María Teresa Garlín)
Don Manuel Antonio Guzmán (son of María Teresa Garlín)
summary: Doña María Teresa Garlín, legitimate daughter of don Bartolomé Garlín and Doña Angela Sáenz, made her will. She was married to don Manuel Guzmán, with whom she had twelve children, eight of whom were alive. Among her assets was a cacao hacienda called La Robleda, for which she owed 300 pesos to the heirs of Padre Robledo, and she named don Antonio de la Fuente and her son don Miguel Guzmán as executors.

people_involved: Capn. don Juan Francisco de Bonilla
summary: Captain don Juan Francisco de Bonilla granted power of attorney to don Benito de Bonilla and don Carlos Portocarrero, residents of León, to petition the Intendente. He sought to exchange his suppressed position of Depositario General for a simple Regidor position in Cartago, valued at 150 pesos, for which he had paid a higher amount.

people_involved: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco
summary: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco, a merchant from Panama residing in Cartago, sold a 26-year-old white slave named Rafael García to don Pedro Antonio Solares, a merchant from Villa Vieja and native of Asturias. The seller had acquired the slave from don José Acosta, who was the agent for don Luis Fernández, for 200 pesos.

people_involved: Don Manuel de la Torre y Romero
summary: Beneficiado don Ramón de Azofeifa and don Esteban Venegas, as testamentary executors of don José Perié, granted special power of attorney to don Juan Palles. They needed him to solicit the judgment in a lawsuit that their deceased party had pursued against don Manuel de la Torre y Romero regarding a company matter, in order to finalize their accounts.

people_involved: Capn. don Juan Francisco de Bonilla
Capn. don José Antonio de Bonilla
summary: Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla, legitimate son of the deceased Captain don José Antonio de Bonilla and Doña Gabriela Morales, granted power of attorney to his wife, Doña Ana Rita Gómez, to make a will on his behalf, as he was about to travel to Guatemala. He named his wife and don Pablo José de Molina as executors and instituted Doña Ana Rita as his universal heir.

Don Isidro de Oreamuno took charge of two chaplaincy branches, one for 915 pesos belonging to the Barba convent and another for 150 pesos for the Santa Iglesia parroquial. These were situated on a cedar wood house, a boiler, a sugar mill, and four caballerías of land in Murciélago, jurisdiction of Villa Nueva, transferred to him by don Tomás de Alvarado and his wife Doña María del Rosario Bonilla. He also mortgaged over 1200 pesos of his paternal inheritance, with ecclesiastical license from Cura Azofeifa.

people_involved: Capitán de granaderos don Francisco Carazo
summary: Don Francisco Antonio de Echavarría, a Spanish-born merchant, granted freedom to his mulatto slave, José Antonio Zabaleta, who was about 21 years old. This act followed Captain de granaderos don Francisco Carazo's payment of 250 pesos for Zabaleta's rescue and freedom, whom Echavarría had purchased from Doña Eufemia Pacheco.

Presbítero don Francisco Falcón, a native of the Bishopric of Panama and legitimate son of the deceased don Juan de Dios Falcón and Doña Tomasa Girón, made his will. He declared among his assets a mulatto slave named Eusebio Avendaño, who was a fugitive in Nicaragua. He instituted Doña María Valeria Samudio as his universal heir, excepting his hereditary rights from his parents' succession, which he had ceded to his sister Doña Petronila Falcón. Presbítero don Juan José Oreamuno was named executor.
Don Joaquín de Oreamuno is identified as a Notario Eclesiástico on this date.
An unnamed Costa Rican grants general power of attorney to Don Mariano Ezeta, Secretary of the Presidency, and Licdo. Don Santiago Moreno, both residents of Nueva Guatemala.

Don Antonio Ramón de Azofeifa, holding multiple ecclesiastical titles including Cura Rectoral of Cartago and Comisario del Santo Oficio, grants general power of attorney to Don Andrés Lindón, an agent of business in the Indies, and Don Manuel de Ayala, Director General of Temporalidades of America and Secretary of the Supreme Council, both residents of Madrid.

Siblings José Miguel Alvarez and María Antonia Alvarez, with her husband José Joaquín Coronel's permission, sell half a house and half a plot of land for 200 pesos to Captain of Pardos José Miguel Cárdenas. The property is described by its boundaries, including adjacent properties owned by José Antonio Vázquez, Dominga Guzmán (deceased), Captain Cárdenas himself, Petronila Cárdenas, and Ana Micaela Calvo, near the church of San Nicolás.

The Governor, Captain Don José Vázquez y Téllez, a knight of the Order of Alcántara, grants general power of attorney for lawsuits to Don Juan Antonio de la Peña, a merchant and resident of Nueva Guatemala.
Don José Antonio Oreamuno, appointed collector of tobacco tithes and required to provide a 6,000 peso guarantee, presents Pedro José Elizondo as his guarantor.
Don Pedro Tiburcio Machado y Ugarte, the auctioneer for the city's tobacco monopoly and obligated to guarantee 200 pesos annually, names Pedro José Elizondo as his guarantor.
Don Esteban Corti, a medical practitioner residing in the city, grants general power of attorney for lawsuits to Don Felipe Marchena, a resident of Cádiz.

The Governor, having learned that Ventura Moya of Ujarrás is seriously injured and wishes to make a joint will with his wife, commissions Don Joaquín de Oreamuno, Alcalde of the Santa Hermandad, to travel to Ujarrás and receive the testament.

Ventura Moya and his wife Juana de la Trinidad Rojas make their joint will before Alcalde Don Joaquín de Oreamuno in Ujarrás. They name their parents and three children, along with their children's spouses. José Bernardo Moya and Don José Antonio de Alvarado are appointed as executors.

A lawsuit between Don Manuel Torre y Romero and the late Governor Don José Perié was resolved through arbitration, with Torre ordered to pay Perié 1181 pesos and 7/4 reales. Don Joaquín de Oreamuno acted as guarantor for Torre, mortgaging his property. The debt was cancelled on May 28, 1794, by Don Esteban Venegas, Perié's executor.
Don Manuel Marchena y Vargas Machuca acknowledges a debt of 6,000 pesos to Don José Alvarez, a resident of León, for merchandise. He agrees to pay within 18 months, and the debt was later cancelled.

Don Felipe Arburola makes his will, naming his deceased parents Don Manuel de Arburola and Doña María Lorenza Fajardo, and his deceased wife Doña Manuela Estrada. He designates his natural children with Dolores Campos (Manuela, Antonia, and José María) as heirs, and mentions his cousins Doña Joaquina and Doña María Francisca López del Corral. Don Antonio de la Fuente and Don Manuel Arburola are named as executors.

Doña Micaela de Arleguí makes her will, identifying her deceased parents Don Manuel Antonio Arleguí and Doña Engracia de Oses, and her deceased siblings Doña Juana María and Don Francisco. She bequeaths assets to her servant Jacoba Arleguí and Jacoba's daughter Francisca Josefa, whom she raised. Don José Antonio Jiménez and Don Manuel de la Torre are appointed as executors.
Don José Miguel de Ocaña grants general power of attorney to Don José de Corona.

Don Manuel Marchena y Vargas Machuca, general attorney for Don Francisco Díaz Catalán (a merchant from Spain residing in Cartagena de Indias), substitutes his power to Don José Corona. Corona is tasked with collecting debts owed by Don Francisco Ramo to Díaz Catalán in the provinces of this Kingdom.

Don Antonio de la Fuente, Alférez Real and Síndico General for the convents and religious of San Francisco in this province, grants power of attorney to Don José Asenjo, Procurator of the Intendancy of Nicaragua, and Don Manuel Galisteo, a merchant from León, to collect synods due to the doctrinal and reductor priests of this province.

Pedro José Elizondo acknowledges a debt of 5,000 pesos to Don Luis de Cueto, a resident of León, for the balance of an account for merchandise sold on consignment. He agrees to pay in two annual installments.

Don Felipe Gallegos, Ayudante Mayor de Milicias and Teniente, makes his will, detailing his parentage (Pascual Gallegos and Arcadia de Trigo) and his marriage to Guadalupe de Alvarado, with whom he had three children (Arcadia, María, and Rafael). He also mentions his stepson, Santos Lombardo, from Guadalupe's previous marriage to Pedro Lombardo, who is due an inheritance from his deceased paternal grandparents, Francisco Javier Lombardo and his wife, from Panamá.

Don Francisco Javier, now deceased, had raised and educated his grandson Don Santos, spending his limited assets on him, his own burial, and Royal Justice expenses. He left only a hand mill, which was lent to the physician Don Esteban Corti. Don Francisco Javier was married a second time to Doña Ramona Noguera, who is also deceased, and they had no children. Don Antonio de la Fuente and Don Francisco Carazo were named as his executors.

people_involved: Don Pedro Tiburcio Machado y Ugarte
summary: Don Pedro Tiburcio Machado y Ugarte, the postmaster, was required to provide a 200 pesos bond. Don Mateo José García presented himself as guarantor, offering to mortgage a cacao hacienda located in Matina.
Don José Antonio del Campo granted general power of attorney to Don Gabriel Estrada, a procurator and resident of Nueva Guatemala.

Doña Juana Guevara, widow of Don Cayetano de Alvarado, granted power to her son, Bdo. don José Antonio Alvarado, to make her will. She named her children, Bdo. don José Antonio (current priest of Villa Nueva), Don Joaquín, Don Tomás, and Doña Marcelina de Alvarado, as her heirs. The executors were the said priest and Presbítero don Pablo José Molina.

Doña Manuela Baeza, a widow, sold a 15-year-old mulato blanco slave named Juan Manuel Ulloa to Don Manuel Sánchez Duque for 200 pesos. Don Manuel Sánchez Duque was represented by Don Pedro José Elizondo, and Doña Manuela Baeza's son, Don Juan Manuel de Alvarado, signed on her behalf.

Fernando Masís took responsibility for a capellanía branch worth 150 pesos, belonging to Nuestra Señora de la Concepción, which was previously managed by Antonio Segura and his wife. He mortgaged a cacao hacienda with 1500 trees in Matina and his residence as collateral.

people_involved: Doña Encarnación Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Don José Antonio Oriamuno and his wife, Doña Encarnación Muñoz de la Trinidad, took charge of a capellanía branch worth 2066 pesos 5 reales, belonging to the San Francisco convent, previously managed by Don Ruperto Pérez and his wife, Doña Rita Alvarado. They mortgaged a tiled house, various tools, furniture, livestock, lands in Río Grande, their residence, and a ranch in Esparza.

Doña Ana Rita Coronado, as the widow of the deceased Escribano Don Romualdo Zamora, granted power of attorney to Licenciado don Pantaleón del Águila, a lawyer of the Royal Audiencia in Guatemala, to collect sums owed to her late husband there.

people_involved: Don Manuel Marchena y Vargas Machuca
Don Pedro Gómez de la Peña
summary: Don Manuel Marchena y Vargas Machuca, acting as attorney for Don Francisco Díaz Catalán of Cartagena de Indias, who had sums owed to him in Guatemala, substituted his power of attorney to Don Pedro Gómez de la Peña.

people_involved: Don José Antonio Alvarado (son of Benito)
Teniente Coronel don Manuel Diez Gallo
summary: Don Antonio de la Fuente, representing the absent siblings Don José Antonio, Don Juan, Don Isidro Alvarado, and Doña Ana Josefa Ulloa (widow of Don Rafael Alvarado), and defending the minor Doña María Josefa Alvarado, sold 20 caballerías of land in Las Piedras de Bagaces to Teniente Coronel don Manuel Diez Gallo for 600 pesos. The land, inherited from their parents Don Benito Alvarado and Doña Leonida de Ocampo, bordered the buyer's property.

Doña Manuela Baeza took charge of a capellanía branch worth 300 pesos, founded by Dr. don Pedro Jimena in favor of Nuestra Señora de los Angeles, previously managed by Manuel Sáenz and his wife Doña Cayetana Ulloa. She mortgaged her residence and a cattle and horse ranch in El Carmen, Bagaces valley, with her son, Juan Manuel de Alvarado, signing for her.

Don Juan Francisco Bonilla, Depositario and Regidor, and his wife Doña Ana Rita Gómez, presented several individuals as guarantors for Don Juan Francisco's 2000 pesos bond required for his office. The guarantors included Don Joaquín de Oreamuno, Don Tomás Hidalgo, Don Sebastián Fernández de Urrutia, Don Fernando Chavarría, Don Santiago Bonilla, Don Juan de Dios Brenes, Doña María Francisca Corrales, Capitán de pardos Miguel Cárdenas, Doña Cecilia Escalante, and Don Tomás Alvarado. Doña Cecilia's son, Manuel García Escalante, signed for her.
Doña Manuela Viveros, Doña Rosa Madriz, Doña Baltasara Madriz, and Doña Ana Rita Madriz granted general power of attorney for lawsuits to Presbítero don José Miguel Sancho, who resided in León.

people_involved: Doña María de la Luz Aguilar
summary: Doña María de la Luz Aguilar, a native of León, granted general power of attorney to Presbítero don Félix Galarza, a resident of the same city.

people_involved: R. P. Guardián Fr. Pablo Chacón
Síndico de los Conventos y Regidor don Juan Guidiori
summary: Several friars, including R. P. Guardián Fr. Pablo Chacón, Padre Reductor Fr. Nazario Gallo (Boruca), Fr. Juan Francisco de Arburola (Pacaca), Fr. Juan Luís de Soto (Barba), Fr. José Francisco de Alvarado (Aserrí and Curridabat), Fr. Manuel Sáenz (Quircó, Cot, and Tobosi), Fr. Joaquín Hidalgo (Ujarrás), and Fr. José Gil Solís (Atirro and Tucurrique), granted power of attorney to Don Juan Guidiori (Síndico de los Conventos and Regidor, resident of León) and Don Domingo Galarza (resident of León) to collect their synods for the current year.

Don José Aballe, Captain of the ship Malambruno anchored in Matina, granted power of attorney to Don José Ignacio de Rucavado to continue a pending lawsuit against Don Mateo José García regarding freight charges for eight loads transported by his mules from the Matina valley.

Don Francisco Nicolás Gutiérrez and his wife Doña María del Carmen Medina took charge of a capellanía branch worth 200 pesos, established on the assets of Juliana de Bonilla, which was previously managed by Don Joaquín de Oreamuno. They mortgaged their adobe house with a tiled roof as collateral.

Doña María del Carmen Medina requested the cancellation of the capellanía deed from October 1, 1791, stating that she had delivered its value to Don Rafael Arnesto de Troya, who was the new tenant of the capellanía.

people_involved: Doña Juana Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Don Gregorio de Oreamuno and his wife, Doña Juana Muñoz de la Trinidad, took charge of a chaplaincy worth 200 pesos, belonging to the convent. They mortgaged their house as security for this obligation.

Don Manuel de Arburola and his wife, Doña Josefa Prudenciana Hidalgo, took charge of a chaplaincy founded by Juliana de Bonilla, valued at 200 pesos and belonging to the convent. They mortgaged their house as security.

Don José Ignacio Rucavado transferred the power of attorney, originally granted by Don José Aballe to Don Francisco Antonio Echavarría, to Don Francisco Antonio Echavarría for a lawsuit against Don Manuel José García.
Pedro José Elizondo granted a general power of attorney to Don Luis Cueto de Landa, who was a Regidor and Alguacil Mayor of the city of León.

Don Manuel Guzmán and his wife, Doña Juana Andrea Ugalde, took charge of 315 pesos from the tutelages of Doña Fermina, Doña Anacleta, Don Gabriel, and Doña Lorenza de Ugalde, who are minor children of Don Faustino de Ugalde and Doña Rita de Alvarado. Previously, Don Ruperto Granados and his wife, Doña Rita (in her second marriage), were in charge. They mortgaged their house. A marginal note from July 28, 1798, indicates Don Ignacio Miguel Llórente, as attorney for Don Clemente Pérez Granados of Panamá, gave a receipt to Don Manuel Guzmán, and Don Manuel Antonio Guzmán received for his wife, Doña Fermina Ugalde.

people_involved: Don Manuel Marchena y Vargas Machuca
summary: Don José Ignacio Rucavado, a merchant and resident of Cartagena de Indias, transferred an enslaved mulatto boy named Encarnación Corrales to Don Manuel Marchena y Vargas Machuca. This slave was given to Rucavado by Doña Joaquina López del Corral, acting as attorney for Don Francisco Diez Catalán, in payment of 250 pesos. The transfer to Marchena occurred because Marchena was now the attorney. A marginal note from March 8, 1792, states that Rucavado, due to Marchena's absence, delivered the slave to Don José Aballe, who was recommended by Diez Catalán to take his assets.

Don José Ignacio Rucavado sold a small farm (chacrarilla) in a place called La Arenilla, near the city, to Captain Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla for 80 pesos. Rucavado had acquired this property from Don Alejandro Lampar and José Ramos.

people_involved: Don José Sebastián Fernández de Urrutia
Licenciado Don Juan José de la Madriz Linares
summary: Several heirs, including Don José Sebastián Fernández de Urrutia and the daughters of Doña Bárbara Madriz and Doña Francisca Madriz, granted power to Don Carlos Portocarreño. They sought to claim the inheritance of Licenciado Don Juan José de la Madriz Linares, a deceased Canon of the León Cathedral and brother to Doña Bárbara and Doña Francisca, who also passed away intestate on October 15th. José Ant° de Oreamuno signed as tutor for Doña Micaela.

people_involved: Doña María Elena López de la Flor
summary: Luisa Chaves, widow of Juan Francisco Solano, made her will in Ujarrás, naming her children and detailing the inheritance of an enslaved woman, Josefa del Carmen, and her children. She granted freedom to Josefa del Carmen and her son José Benito. Her executors were José Ant° Mora and Don José Antonio de Alvarado, and her heirs included her children and granddaughter Catalina de los Dolores.
Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla leased a cacao plantation named Las Viejas, located in the Matina valley, to Felipe Moya, a resident of Ujarrás, for three years at an annual price of 75 pesos.

Don José Ruperto Prieto, as testamentary executor for the deceased Lieutenant Colonel Don Luis Méndez, granted his general power of attorney to Don Gabriel de Estrada, a Procurator of the Royal Audience of Guatemala.

people_involved: Don Manuel Marchena y Vargas Machuca
Don Pedro Gómez de la Peña
summary: Don Manuel Marchena y Vargas Machuca, a native of Spain, granted general power of attorney to Don Pedro Gómez de la Peña and Don Agustín Zabala, both residents of Guatemala.

Doña Juana Rita Coronado, widow of the Scribe Don José Romualdo Zamora, obligated herself to her six minor children for 254 pesos and half a real each, which they inherited from their paternal inheritance.

José Antonio Monge, a resident of Villa Nueva, provided a prison bond for José Jacinto Gamboa, who was facing criminal charges for allegedly stealing a mule from Felipe Santiago Delgado. A marginal note from May 18, 1792, states that the Alcalde notified Monge to pay the value of the mule, as Gamboa had already been sentenced, and upon payment, Gamboa was released.

Gabriela Josefa Alvarez, natural daughter of the deceased Don José Nicolás Alvarez and Efigenia Machuca, made her will. She ordered masses for the souls of her sister Casilda Azofeifa and for José Antonio and Juan Antonio Azofeifa y Machuca. She declared herself single with no forced heirs, naming her soul as the heir and Presbítero Don Pablo José Molina and Presbítero Don Rafael Rosas as executors.

Doña Juana Rita Coronado, widow of the Scribe Don José Romualdo Zamora, granted general power of attorney to Don Cristóbal de Ocampo Golfín, a resident of the neighborhood, to collect outstanding debts owed to her deceased husband.

Don José Alejandro Lampar was appointed as Lieutenant of Villa Vieja, with the obligation to provide a residency bond for the year he would serve as proprietor. The notary for this record was Gobernador Vázquez y Téllez.

An unnamed official, who had been serving temporarily in replacement of José Corona for several months, presented José Antonio Oreamuno, Joaquín Oreamuno, and Tomás Hidalgo as his guarantors. The specific reason for the guarantee is not detailed.

On February 6, José Ignacio Rucavado gave power of attorney to Pedro Gómez de la Peña, a tobacco interventor residing in Guatemala. This power was granted so Gómez de la Peña could respond to charges in a case of embezzlement being pursued against Manuel José de Zea.

On February 6, Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco was notified by the Audiencia to post bail and not leave the province, in connection with the ongoing case against Manuel José de Zea. He presented Captain José Miguel Cárdenas as his guarantor to fulfill this requirement.

On February 6, José Ignacio Rucavado presented Baltasar de Echavarría as his guarantor. This action was taken for a similar reason as Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco, implying a connection to the legal proceedings against Manuel José de Zea.

On February 6, Antonio de la Fuente was ordered by the Regente de la Audiencia to present himself as a prisoner in Guatemala within 60 days to answer charges. He provided Rafael de Alvarado as his guarantor for this obligation.

On February 6, Pedro José Elizondó presented Buenaventura Elizondó as his guarantor. This was done for the same reason as Antonio de la Fuente, indicating he was also obliged to appear as a prisoner in Guatemala.

On February 6, José María Peralta provided Gregorio Ramírez, a resident of Villa Nueva, and José Miguel Ocaña, a local resident, as his guarantors. This action was taken for the same reason as the previous individuals, likely related to an obligation to appear in Guatemala.

On February 6, Manuel Morales presented José Selopis, a resident of Villa Nueva, as his guarantor for the same reason as others, implying an obligation to appear in Guatemala. The record notes that this document was not signed.

On February 6, Pedro Antonio de Iribarren, who was the Administrator of the Tobacco Factory, granted general power of attorney to Diego Montiel. Montiel was identified as the Adelantado of Costarrica and a resident of the city of Granada.

On February 6, Pedro Antonio de Iribarren further granted general power of attorney to Rafael Díaz Cabeza de Vaca. Díaz Cabeza de Vaca held the position of Captain of the militia battalion in the city of León.
On February 8, Benito Fajardo posted bail for Antonio Pao, who was a prisoner. Pao was required to travel to Guatemala within 60 days as part of his obligation.
On February 8, Juan Francisco de Bonilla provided bail for Francisco Antonio de Echavarría. This bail was of the same nature as the one provided for Antonio Pao, suggesting a similar obligation.
On February 11, Pedro Antonio de Iribarren granted general power of attorney to Licenciado José del Barrio. José del Barrio served as the Relator of the Royal Audiencia of Guatemala.

On February 11, Francisco Antonio de Echavarría granted general power of attorney to his brother, Baltasar de Echavarría. This transfer of authority was a general one, covering various legal or administrative matters.

On February 13, José María de Peralta, preparing for a trip to Guatemala, granted general power of attorney to his wife, Ana Benita Corrales. Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco was designated as the secondary recipient of this power.

On February 13, Pedro José Elizondó, who was about to leave for Guatemala, granted general power of attorney to his wife, Manuela Masís. Bernardo Gómez was named as the secondary recipient of this power.
On February 13, Ana Benita Corrales granted general power of attorney to her husband, José María de Peralta. The record indicates that this particular document was not signed.

On February 22, numerous residents from Villa Nueva and Villa Vieja, including Manuel Fernández and Juan Manuel Solís who signed, granted power of attorney to Ramón Vererio. Their purpose was to have Vererio petition in Guatemala for a reduction of the tobacco tithe from ten percent to five percent, arguing it was an arbitrary crop.

On April 14, Felipe Sancho assumed the tutelage of his minor nephews, Nicolás and Josefa de Oreamuno, children of Encarnación Sancho, involving a sum of 6840 pesos. He secured this obligation by presenting five guarantors: his mother Baltasara Madriz, José Manuel García, Nicolás Castro, María Arlegui, and José Sebastián Fernández de Urrutia, who collectively hypothecated properties and assets across several locations including Cartago, La Candelaria, Matina, Villa Nueva, and Santa Ana.

On May 2, Pedro Antonio de Iribarren, the Administrator of Tobacco, granted general power of attorney to three individuals: Domingo José de Yribarren, who was the accountant for the salt revenue in Ecija, and Juan Pedro Barraneche Yribarren and Antonio Barraneche de Yribarren, both residents of Madrid.

On May 16, José Ignacio Rucavado sold a mulatto slave named Encarnación Corrales to José Aballe for 263 pesos and 4 reales. Encarnación Corrales was described as being about 24 years old and an official shoemaker.

On May 22, Bernardo Gómez assumed the tutelage of the minor children of the late José León de Bonilla. He committed to a sum of 216 pesos, representing the value of 50 cattle, 2 horses, and 1 mare located in Bagaces, and agreed to pay 5% annual interest on this amount.

On June 11, Claudio Castro and his wife Josefa Quesada, residents of Villa Nueva, took possession of a 75-pound copper pot valued at 75 silver pesos. The pot, offered by Isidro Zamora, belonged to the Confraternity of the Conception in the Cartago convent, and they agreed to pay an annual rent of 3 pesos and 6 reales.

On July 4, Francisco Navarro, a Spanish Colonel of Peru militias and a merchant in Cartago, granted complete freedom to Juana María Martínez. He had previously purchased her as a slave from José Baca, a merchant from Rivas de Nicaragua, and she secured her liberty by paying him 250 pesos.

people_involved: Doña María del Carmen de Medina
summary: Don Bernardo Gómez incurred a debt of 200 pesos to Doña María del Carmen de Medina for livestock, structured as a censo of 5,010.

Doña Florentina de Aragón and Doña Ana Ángulo sold two plots of land in the city's main plaza to Presbítero Don Ramón de Azofeifa, the local parish priest. The first plot was previously owned by Doña Manuela, Doña Joaquina, and Doña Ana de Ángulo, and the second was adjacent to Doña Mariana de Alvarado's house.
Francisco Carrasco granted a general power of attorney to Don José Antonio de Oreamuno.
Don Santiago de Bonilla granted a general power of attorney to Licenciado Don Santiago Moreno, an attorney residing in Guatemala.

Don Miguel Alfaro, Don Cayetano Gutiérrez (as heir of Don Lorenzo Ruiz), Don Julián Alfaro (as heir of Don Antonio Rodríguez), José Santiago Bermúdez, and Teresa Quesada (widow of Miguel Piedra) jointly granted general power of attorney to Don Juan José de Aguilar, a prosecutor and resident of Guatemala.

people_involved: Don Manuel Marchena y Vargas Machuca
Don Pedro Gómez de la Peña
summary: Don Manuel Marchena y Vargas Machuca, acting as the attorney for Don Francisco Diez Catalán of Cartagena, granted power to Don Pedro Gómez de la Peña, the postal revenue comptroller, to collect outstanding debts in Guatemala.

people_involved: Presbítero Don José Francisco de Alvarado
Presbítero Don Juan José de Oreamuno
summary: Presbítero Don José Francisco de Alvarado made his will in Los Tres Ríos, detailing his extensive property including a house, an oratory with numerous religious artifacts, and a cattle ranch. He declared seven enslaved individuals, granting freedom to Gregorio, and made various donations to his niece, overseer, sisters (who are also his executors), and nephews.

people_involved: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco
summary: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco, a native of the Kingdom of Panama, granted general power of attorney for lawsuits to Don Santiago Moreno and, secondarily, to Don Pantaleón del Águila, both attorneys in Guatemala.

people_involved: Don Manuel Marchena y Vargas Machuca
summary: Captain Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla sells a small farm in La Arenilla to Don Manuel Marchena y Vargas Machuca for 80 pesos. Bonilla had previously acquired this property from Don José Ignacio Rucabado.

people_involved: Manuela de Jesús de la Fuente
summary: The Royal Ensign Don Antonio de la Fuente grants general power of attorney to his son-in-law Don Ignacio Llorente, his wife Doña María Francisca Alvarado, and Don Juan Manuel Alvarado. Preparing for a trip to Guatemala City, he also authorizes them to make a will on his behalf, declaring himself the legitimate son of the deceased Don Ignacio de la Fuente and Doña María Mendaña from Astorga, and naming his children as heirs.
Captain of Grenadiers Don Francisco Carazo, who also serves as provincial Mayor and Alderman, grants general power of attorney to Don Juan Payés y Font, a resident and merchant of Guatemala.

Doña Nicolasa Cabral sells a 50-vara front plot of land to Don Francisco Carazo for 100 pesos. The plot, inherited from her parents, is bordered by the Parish Church, Don Joaquín de Alvarado's house, another house of Carazo, and Doña Manuela Baeza's property.

Don José Ignacio de Rucabado, a merchant, transfers the mulatto slave Encarnación Corrales, a 22-year-old shoemaker, to Don José Aballe, a resident of Cartagena. Rucabado received Corrales as a 250-peso payment from Doña Joaquina López del Corral for a debt owed to his principal, Don Francisco Díaz Catalán.
José Antonio Calderón, a resident of Ujarrás, sells a complete, walled plot of land to Francisco Céspedes for 50 pesos. Calderón had obtained this property from his sister, Cecilia Calderón.

Doña Antonia Manuela de Alvarado, widow of Colonel Don Romualdo de Oriamuno, sells a piece of land to Ensign Don Manuel Hidalgo for 56 pesos. She inherited the land from her father-in-law, Don Antonio de Oriamuno, and her son Manuel Oreamuno signs on her behalf.

people_involved: Doña Ana Teresa de Alvarado y Girón
Doña Ana Dionisia Josefa de Alvarado
Presbítero Don José Francisco de Alvarado
summary: Doña Ana Teresa de Alvarado y Girón, a single woman, makes her will, naming Doña Ana Dionisia Josefa de Alvarado as her natural daughter and heir. She grants freedom to the mulatto slave Petronila, who was part of a legacy from her deceased brother, Presbítero Don José Francisco de Alvarado, and makes bequests to her niece Doña Ramona Fallas and her grandchildren Doña María del Carmen Medina and Don Lorenzo Arnesto de Troya.

Don Joaquín de Arguedas and his wife Doña Manuela Conejo assume responsibility for two chaplaincy funds, totaling 300 pesos, and mortgage their home. A marginal note indicates these chaplaincies were later transferred to Don Esteban Herdocia in 1794.

Ignacio Céspedes, a mestizo, acknowledges receipt of 700 pesos worth of goods belonging to his wife, María de Jesús Salazar, natural daughter of Polonia Salazar. These goods were received from Doña María Francisca de Alvarado and Don Ignacio Llorente, who held them on behalf of Don Antonio de la Fuente, by disposition of a benefactor of María de Jesús.

Juan Andrés Acuña, a widower from La Puebla de Los Angeles, makes his will, naming his five grandsons as heirs. He mentions his deceased wife, María Francisca Calderón, and their four deceased children, as well as his son Nicolás's children with Antonia Fernández. He also states he raised Juan José Acuña, an orphan, since birth.

people_involved: Doña María Feliciana de la Fuente
summary: The Reverend Don Ramón de Azofeifa, Parish Priest, sells a house to Don Ignacio Llorente and his wife Doña María Feliciana de la Fuente for 700 pesos. The buyers pay 400 pesos and assume responsibility for three chaplaincies, including one founded by Don Francisco de Ocampo and another linked to houses in Villa Nueva where Don Manuel Antonio Chapuí resided. Marginal notes mention a transfer in 1794 and a cancellation in 1819.
Doña Antonia Mario, a native and resident of Cartago, makes her will. She is identified as the legitimate daughter of the deceased Doña Josefa Chivarría and Don Nicolás de Mario.

people_involved: Unnamed Widow of José Francisco Rojas
summary: The estate of an unnamed widow of José Francisco Rojas, who had no children with him, is being managed. Her sisters, Ramona Mario and Benita, and her nephew, Don José Antonio Mora (Teniente Gobernador de Ujarrás), are mentioned. Don Joaquín de Oreamuno and Don José Antonio Mora are named as the executors of her will, with her soul designated as the heir.

people_involved: Don José Sebastián Fernández de Urrutia
summary: Don José Sebastián Fernández de Urrutia and his wife, Doña Antonia de Arlegui, took charge of a capellanía worth 200 pesos, which belonged to N. Sra. del Rosario parish and was previously managed by Don Tomás Hidalgo. They hypothecated their house as security for this responsibility.

people_involved: Don José Antonio de Oreamuno (Sargento Mayor)
summary: Doña Antonia Manuela de Alvarado, widow of Coronel don Romualdo de Oreamuno, sold a piece of land she inherited from her father-in-law, Don José Antonio de Oreamuno (Sargento Mayor), to Teniente don Rafael de Alvarado for 25 pesos. The land, measuring 320 varas by 670 varas, bordered Sabana Grande, the seller's chácara, her potrero, and Pedro Elizondo's potrero.

Don Juan Manuel de Alvarado received 400 pesos from his mother, Doña Manuela Baeza, as his inheritance from his deceased father, Don Pedro de Alvarado. This inheritance included a mulatillo named Miguel Francisco, valued at 200 pesos.

people_involved: Don José Antonio de Oreamuno (Sargento Mayor)
summary: Doña Antonia Manuela de Alvarado, widow of Coronel don Romualdo de Oreamuno, sold a piece of hill and land named El Cuajiniquil, which she inherited from her father-in-law Don José Antonio de Oreamuno (Sargento Mayor), to Bernardo Calvo for 350 pesos. Her son, Capn. don Gregorio de Oreamuno, signed the document on her behalf.

Manuel Soto sold a plot of land without walls, inherited from his parents, to Doña María Trinidad de Alvarado for 15 pesos. The plot measured 36 varas long and 21 varas wide, bordering streets, the house of the indigenous José llama, the solar and house of the deceased Josefa Alegría, the solar of Buenaventura Lizondro, and the house of Paula Sancho.

people_involved: Don José Antonio de Oreamuno (Sargento Mayor)
Presb. Don José Antonio de Oreamuno
summary: Capn. don Gregorio de Oreamuno and his wife, Doña Juana de la Trinidad, took charge of an 800-peso capellanía founded by the late Don José Antonio de Oreamuno (Sargento Mayor). The capellanía was linked to a cattle ranch and chácara near Cartago, including various buildings, livestock, and equipment. Doña Antonia Manuela de Alvarado, Gregorio's mother, delivered the assets and provided an additional potrero to compensate for missing items. A marginal note indicates a cancellation in 1827 by Presb. Don José Antonio de Oreamuno, with the debt transferred to C. Isidro Oreamuno.

people_involved: Don José Antonio de Oreamuno (Sargento Mayor)
summary: Doña Antonia Manuela de Alvarado, widow of Coronel don Romualdo de Oreamuno, formally ceded an 800-peso capellanía, instituted by her father-in-law Don José Antonio de Oreamuno (Sargento Mayor), to her son Capn. don Gregorio de Oreamuno and his wife. This capellanía was tied to a cattle ranch and chácara in La Lima, near Cartago. To replace missing assets, she provided a potrero she inherited from her father-in-law, bordering Diego Chavarria's potrero and Teniente don Rafael de Alvarado's potrero. Her son Manuel Oreamuno signed on her behalf.

Capn. don Francisco Carazo and his wife, Doña Ana Jacoba de Alvarado, obligated themselves to Don Luis Castillo, a minor under 14 years old and son of Doña Cecilia del Castillo from Villa Nueva, for 1000 pesos at 5% interest. They hypothecated a hacienda named Tenorio in the valley of Bagaces, which included 1000 cattle, 100 mares, and a donkey. A marginal note indicates Don Luis cancelled the obligation on January 30, 1799.

people_involved: Alférez Juan de la Rosa Maitín
summary: Capn. José Miguel Cárdenas and Alférez Juan de la Rosa Maitín became guarantors for José Antonio Cárdenas, who was imprisoned for a debt of 76 pesos and 5.5 reales of cacao owed to Doña Antonia de Arlegui. José Antonio Cárdenas was a guarantor, along with Matías Carmona and Fernando Masís, for Miguel Antonio Cuende.

Rafaela Granados sold a very deteriorated small house made of round wood, covered with tiles, located on common land in Cartago, to José Fernando Leandro for 25 pesos. The property, inherited from her father Pedro Granados, was in El Llano de Quircot and bordered her sister Antonia Granados's fence, the buyer's fences, the royal road, and Cristóbal Aguilar's old possession.

María de la Rosa Hernández sold an entire 50-vara square plot with an old house, inherited from her deceased daughter Ana Gertrudis Alegría, to Don Isidoro Sánchez for 75 pesos. The property bordered streets, houses of Paula Sancho and Don Manuel Quesada, and houses of Doña María Fernández and Don León de Bonilla.

Unnamed individuals received a loan of 350 pesos in money and cattle from Presbítero don Nicolás Carrillo, Cura de Esparza, at 5% interest. They pledged their hacienda 'Mateo' in Bagaces, a pasture, and their residence in Cartago as collateral, which had a 400-peso pension to the Convento de S. Francisco.

Presbítero don Juan José de Oreamuno, as the executor of the late Presbítero don José Francisco de Alvarado, sold three enslaved individuals to fulfill the will. Antonia (30 years old) and her daughter Fulgencia (1 year old) were sold to don José Antonio del Campo for 250 and 75 pesos respectively, while Antonia's other daughter, Andrea (6 years old), was sold to doña María Manuela de Miranda for 125 pesos.

Don Bernardo Gómez granted power of attorney to don Vicente Frutos to represent him in the residency trial concerning his tenure as Lieutenant Governor in Bagaces. He had been appointed to this role by Coronel don Juan Pinillos, who was the interim Governor of the Province.

María Mercedes Aguilar and her guarantor Miguel Rojas, both residents of Villa Nueva, committed to pay 16 pesos 7 reales to José Emigdio Duran. This sum was his share of the inheritance following the death of José Alejo Duran, who was María Mercedes Aguilar's son-in-law and died in the Bagaces valley.

Don Manuel Marchena y Vargas Machuca, attorney for don Francisco Díaz Catalán, substituted his power of attorney to don José Ruperto Prieto. This substitution was made because Marchena y Vargas Machuca was preparing to depart for Guatemala.
Don Manuel Marchena y Vargas Machuca granted his personal power to don José Ruperto Prieto.
Teniente de caballería don José Corona granted his general power of attorney to don Manuel Marchena y Vargas Machuca.
Presbítero don Félix Antonio Alvarado y Girón granted his general power of attorney to don Manuel Salmón Pacheco. Pacheco is a native of Cartago and resides in the Bishopric of Durango.

people_involved: Children of José Francisco de Bonilla
summary: Don José Joaquín de Alvarado, acting for himself and his sister doña Marcelina Alvarado (both heirs of doña Juana Antonia de Guevara), sold a house in Cartago to don José Francisco de Bonilla for his children. The 300-peso payment, plus a 100-peso chaplaincy, was to be satisfied by Presbítero don Sebastián Jiménez using funds provided by the children's godfathers and uncles as a donation.

Don Francisco Javier Quijano obligated himself to his three children, José, Manuel José, and María Dominga Quijano, for a total of 351 pesos 4 3/4 reales. This sum, received from his mother-in-law doña Teresa Garlín, belonged to his deceased wife doña Antonia Guzmán and was due to their children as her heirs.

Presbítero don Gregorio Bonilla and his sister doña María Petronila Bonilla (widow of don Carlos Ruiz) donated a house and other goods to their niece and daughter doña María Josefa Ruiz Fernández, wife of don José Ruperto Prieto. The house, previously acquired from doña Josefa de Alvarado, was valued at 800 pesos and had an 80-peso pension to the Mitra, with additional donations from the siblings.

locations: Plaza de la iglesia de San Nicolás
summary: Don Manuel Torre y Romero took charge of a 200-peso chaplaincy, previously held by Presbítero don Francisco Robredo. He mortgaged his residence, a 1500-peso house with 9 rooms and a fenced lot, located near the Plaza de la iglesia de San Nicolás and other named neighbors, as collateral.

Don George Salazar, a resident of Villa Vieja, substituted the general power of attorney to don Antonio de la Fuente. This power had originally been conferred by the residents of Quebrada Seca, first to don Mariano Zamora and then to Salazar.

Doña María Casimira Pacheco, daughter of the late doña Francisca Pacheco, made her will. Being single and without forced heirs, she named several legatees including her godchildren, nieces, and nephews. Beneficiado don José Antonio de Alvarado, Cura de Villa Nueva, and Presbítero don Pablo José Molina were named as executors.
Doña María Cecilia Escalante and her son don Manuel José García Escalante entered into an obligation.
A loan of 200 pesos at 5% interest was made to Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla. This loan was later cancelled in 1810.
Clemencia Astorga, the widow of Felipe Hernández, received the inventoried assets from her deceased husband's estate, which were valued at 1611 pesos and 1 real.

José Nicolás Camaño, a native of Cartago, made his will in Los Tres Ríos, detailing his family, including his deceased parents and wife, and his six children. He also listed properties, including a chácara in Taras, and named Félix and Antonia as his executors.
Don Juan Francisco Bonilla and Don Francisco Carazo granted power of attorney to Procurador Don José Ignacio Martínez, who resided in Guatemala.
Don Manuel Marchena granted power of attorney to retired Captain Don Luis de Aguilar, a resident of Nicaragua.

people_involved: Doña María Francisca Marchena y Vargas Machuca
summary: Gobernador Don José Vázquez y Téllez granted general power of attorney to his wife, Doña María Francisca Marchena y Vargas Machuca, who resided in Granada, Andalucía.

Santos Rivera acted as guarantor for Don Pedro José Elizondo, who had won the provincial tithe auction in León for 1205 pesos. Elizondo mortgaged a house and hacienda in Taras, managed by his slave José Antonio Ulloa, while Rivera mortgaged three houses and a hacienda in Toyogres.

Don Bernardo Gómez, Doña Josefa Izaguirre, and Don Blas Masís also acted as guarantors for Don Pedro José Elizondo for the same tithe auction. Elizondo mortgaged two houses, while the guarantors mortgaged various properties including cattle, mules, horses, houses, and haciendas in Cucuilapa, El Reventado river, and Taras.
María Manuela González granted power of attorney to her grandson, Paulino Castillo, to collect the assets left by her deceased son, Vicente Castillo, in the jurisdiction of Nicoya.

people_involved: Don Pedro Tiburcio Machado y Ugarte
summary: Captain Don Pedro Tiburcio Machado y Ugarte, Administrator of Correos, granted power of attorney to Don Jerónimo de la Vega, a resident of Granada, to collect a debt of 438 pesos 6 reales from Captain Don Luis Tije.

Don José Antonio Arana, a resident of Villa Vieja, became guarantor for Don José Francisco Taboada for 1200 pesos that Taboada held in deposit from Don Ángel Núñez, which Don Lorenzo Guillen had taken without judicial order.

Don Ignacio Miguel Llórente, representing Don Antonio de la Fuente, and Doña Florentina de Aragón settled a lawsuit concerning house rent. Doña Florentina paid 300 pesos cash and 150 pesos via a one-month note.

people_involved: Doña María Francisca López del Corral
summary: Doña María Francisca López del Corral granted power of attorney to Benito Simón Chavarría to manage and cultivate her cacao haciendas in Matina and to assist in her maintenance.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Félix de Jesús García
summary: Don José Antonio Bonilla and his wife, Doña Antonia Manuela Meneses, obligated themselves to Presbítero Don Félix de Jesús García for a 100-peso loan, mortgaging a pasture near the Agua Caliente river.

Doña Antonia Manuela Alvarado granted power of attorney to Licenciado Don Santiago Moreno, a lawyer from Guatemala, to defend her in a lawsuit with the City Council regarding land ownership. Her son, Don Juan José Oreamuno, signed on her behalf.
Petronila Cárdenas sold a tiled room, described by its boundaries, to Miguel de Cárdenas for 50 pesos. The room bordered a street, Clara González's property, and the buyer's property.

people_involved: Teniente Coronel Don Manuel Diez Gallo
summary: Don Joaquín Oreamuno, a procurator, obligated himself for the value of 121 cattle and proceeds from previously sold cattle received from Teniente Coronel Don Manuel Diez Gallo, Presbítero Don Manuel Orozco, and Doña Engracia Aguilar, residents of Nicaragua, whose cattle were embargoed for debts to the city.
José Ramos provided bail for Juan Pereira, who was being judged for cohabitation and being a neighborhood troublemaker.
Doña Margarita Pacheco leased a cacao hacienda in the Matina valley to José Antonio Solano for three years at 100 pesos annually. This lease was cancelled by Doña Margarita in 1802.
José Mateo Calderón provided bail for José Gabriel Calderón, who was being judged for assaulting his brother Félix de Jesús with a knife and sticks, and for throwing stones at his captors.

Procurador Síndico Don Manuel José García, with the approval of Regidores Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla and Don Francisco Carazo, granted power of attorney to Licenciado Don Pantaleón del Águila, a lawyer from Guatemala, to defend the city in a lawsuit against Doña Manuela Antonia Alvarado concerning ejido lands. This occurred during the absence of Alférez Real Don Antonio de la Fuente.
Doña Florentina de Aragón grants general power of attorney to Don Marian i Ezeta, a resident of Guatemala.
Don Pedro Antonio Solares, a native of Spain and merchant in the province, grants general power of attorney to Don Miguel Ángel Núñez, a native of Panama.
Doña María Arlrguí grants power to her husband, Don Mateo Camacho, to represent her in the inheritance proceedings of her uncle, the Prebendado Don Francisco Madriz, as she is an intestate heir.

Don José Antonio Oreamuno, acting as curator for Doña Micaela de Alvarado, sells a house in Cartago to Jacinto García for 172 pesos 6 reales. The house is bordered by properties belonging to Don Joaquín Arguedas, Don Rafael Arnesto de Troya, Doña Águeda Madriz, and José Antonio Sáenz.

Don Rafael Arnesto de Troya and his wife Doña Dionisia de Alvarado take charge of a 200-peso chaplaincy belonging to the San Francisco convent in Cartago, previously managed by Doña María del Carmen Medina, widow of Don Nicolás Gutiérrez. Doña Ana Teresa de Alvarado acts as guarantor, and they mortgage their house.

María Antonia Ortiz, a native of Cartago, makes her will. She is the daughter of Pantaleón Ortiz and Juana Manuela Pacheco, widow of Manuel Pacheco, and wife of José Francisco Oreamuno. Her legatees are Petronila Pacheco and her niece Francisca, and her mother is her heir. Don Joaquín de Oreamuno and her husband José Francisco Oreamuno are named as executors.

José Ventura Lizondro, a resident of Cartago, makes his will. He was widowed from Margarita de la Cruz Izaguirre, with whom he had eight children, most of whom died young. He orders a chaplaincy for his grandson José Santana Lizondro to be ordained, with his son Pedro José Lizondro as patron. His executors are Pedro José Lizondro and his sister-in-law María Josefa Izaguirre, and his heirs are his son and three grandsons.

people_involved: Gobernador Don José Vázquez y Téllez
summary: Doña Joaquina Corrales sells a 6-year-old mulatto slave named Fernando, son of her slave, to Governor Don José Vázquez y Téllez for 120 pesos.

Don José Antonio Jiménez, executor of the deceased Presbítero Don Andrés Fernández, establishes a chaplaincy of masses for the souls of the Presbítero and his parents, Don Andrés Fernández and Doña María Trejos, in favor of the San Francisco convent in Cartago. This chaplaincy is linked to a cacao hacienda called La Trejo in the Matina valley and was later cancelled in 1797 by Don José Antonio with the license of Don Ramón de Azofeifa.

people_involved: Gobernador Don José Vázquez y Téllez
summary: Don Tomás Alvarado and his wife Doña María del Rosario Bonilla sell six 'caballerías' of land in Santa Ana, Bagaces, to Don Juan José Granados, a resident of Nicaragua, for 180 pesos. Governor Don José Vázquez y Téllez accepts the sale on behalf of Granados.
Don José Miguel Ocaña posts bail for Francisco Guevara, who was imprisoned for drunkenness and for confronting the Mayor with a drawn sword.
Doña Joaquina López del Corral emancipates her 33-year-old son, Don José Miguel Ocaña, and advances him 315 pesos 4 reales against his inheritance.
Don José Miguel Ocaña posts bail for Joaquín Gorgona, who is being judged for suspected complicity in the homicide of José Cayetano Zamora in Escasú.

Doña María Petronila de Bonilla, a widow, grants power to her son Don Manuel Ruiz Fernández to collect debts owed to her deceased son, Presbítero Don Eusebio Ruiz Fernández, in the town of Guanacaste.

Presbítero Don Félix Alvarado takes charge of a 228-peso chaplaincy belonging to the San Francisco convent in Cartago, previously managed by Doña Ana Micaela Carazo. He mortgages his right to a house, which is bordered by properties of Presbítero Don Félix García, Ana María Escalante, Doña Gabriela Sarmiento, and Angela Molina.
