Don Manuel Antonio Jiménez posts bail for his son Don Francisco Esteban Jiménez, who was arrested for disrespect and insubordination to the Royal Justice.

Doña Joaquina López del Corral, with the consent of her legitimate sons Don José Miguel Ocaña and Don José Corona, recognizes the ownership of donated goods for her spurious daughters Doña Francisca, Doña Catalina, and Doña Manuela, who are represented by their special curator Don Joaquín de Oreamuno. The parties were disputing the ownership of children of slaves, as Doña Joaquina was the usufructuary of the donated property.

Don Manuel José García, Procurador Síndico of Cartago and Mayordomo of the Cofradía de Animas, sells one 'caballería' of land in Villa Vieja to Don Cayetano Gutiérrez. The land is bordered by properties of the Rodríguez family and Juan Manuel Arguedas, and features landmarks like Paso del Guayabo, Quebrada Seca, and Bermúdez.
Doña María Francisca Corrales sold an enslaved black boy named Juan Crisóstomo, 12 years old and son of her enslaved woman Ramona Corrales, to don Esteban Cortis for 200 pesos.
Doña María Francisca Corrales sold an enslaved mulatto girl named Justa, 15 to 16 years old and daughter of her enslaved woman Manuela, to don Manuel Marchena for 200 pesos.
Doña María Francisca Corrales granted general power of attorney to don Manuel Marchena.

people_involved: M. R. P. Fr. Gil Solís
summary: Jerónima Garro, widow of Francisco Delgado, made her will, naming her three children Félix de la Rosa, Marcos Antonio, and Rita Josefa as heirs. She directed her "quinto" to be used for sacrifices for souls, with alms distributed to Fr. Francisco Mondragón and Fr. Gil Solís, and appointed don Francisco Carazo as executor.

Don Cayetano Gutiérrez, a resident of Villa Vieja, granted power of attorney to don Joaquín Oreamuno to defend him in a lawsuit against the residents of Villa Vieja concerning the collection of 200 pesos for the rebuilt cabildo.
Doña Joaquina del Corral granted general power of attorney to her sons-in-law, don Manuel Marchena and don José María Peralta.

Don José Francisco Bonilla, Lieutenant of Villa Nueva, granted power of attorney to his brother don José Antonio Bonilla to pursue a lawsuit against Esteban Jiménez regarding his social status, asserting that he is not noble and therefore enjoys no privileges.

Doña Joaquina del Corral granted general power of attorney to don Manuel Marchena and don José Corona. A special clause in this power, which would have prohibited Governor don José Vázquez y Téllez from entering her house, was subsequently crossed out.

people_involved: Daughters of Doña Joaquina del Corral
summary: Doña Joaquina del Corral formally revoked a specific clause from a previous power of attorney, declaring it null and void. This clause, which would have prohibited Governor don José Vázquez y Téllez from entering her house, was deemed by her to cause irreparable harm to her honor and that of her daughters.

Manuel González, a resident of Bagaces, granted general power of attorney to don Joaquín Oreamuno. This power specifically authorized Oreamuno to defend González in a lawsuit filed by Juana Cordero concerning child support for a son she claims is his.

Verification proceedings for the nuncupative will of doña Juana Rita Gordo, initiated by her widower don Basilio Urtecho, were approved by the Governor on April 20, 1793, and by the Audiencia in Guatemala on June 1. Governor Vázquez ordered these proceedings and the will to be added to the protocol on August 21. The will itself was made in Esparza on January 22, 1793, where Juana Rita Gordo, 37, a resident of León, declared her marriage to Basilio Urtecho, her three natural children (Tomás, Eustaquio, Potenciana), and her natural mother (doña María Antonia Gordo), and distributed her assets among her husband and natural children.

Doña Mariana Alvarado, a widow of don José Cruz and don Manuel Cuentas, granted power to testate to don José Ruperto Prieto. She named Presbítero don Gregorio Bonilla and Prieto as executors, and her three children from her first marriage, doña Rafaela, don Manuel, and don Pedro, as her heirs.
Don Pedro José Elizondo posted bail for Juan Alonso Centeno, who was imprisoned and facing charges for disrespect and insubordination to justice.

Don Manuel Marchena, acting as attorney for his brother-in-law don José Corona, sold an enslaved white man named Pedro Salguero, 30 years old, to don Juan Francisco Bonilla for 250 pesos. Pedro Salguero had previously been purchased by Corona from don Ángel Núñez.
Don Rafael de Alvarado, a Lieutenant of Grenadiers, granted general power of attorney to Licenciado don Santiago Moreno.

José Miguel Monje, acting for himself and on behalf of Cristóbal Aguilar, Félix Calvo, Matías Méndez, Manuel Calderón, and Felipe Zúñiga, granted power to don Mariano Iglesias. This power authorized Iglesias, a supernumerary procurator of the Intendencia de León, to attend the auction of the Banderilla lands, which had been measured in favor of the grantors.

people_involved: don José Antonio de la Huerta y Caso
summary: Presbítero don Gregorio Bonilla granted power to don Francisco Gavarrete, Prosecretary of the Ecclesiastical Curia. This power was to request canonical approval from don José Antonio de la Huerta y Caso, Dean and Provisor of León and Judge of chaplaincies, for a chaplaincy founded by Bonilla's great-aunt, doña Francisca Bonilla.
Don Francisco Navarro, a Colonel from South America, grants general power of attorney to Don José Ignacio Rucabado, a native of Vizcaya and resident of Cartago.

Don José Miguel de Ocaña assumes responsibility for a 600-peso chaplaincy branch belonging to the San Francisco Convent in Cartago, previously held by Doña María Francisca del Corral. The funds are received in five rooms of Doña Francisca's house, which Ocaña then mortgages.
Doña Joaquina Corrales sells her enslaved woman, Petronila, and Petronila's one-year-old son, Mercedes, to Don Juan Francisco Bonilla for 300 pesos.
Don Joaquín Oreamuno sells nine and a half 'caballerías' of land located in the Río Grande area to Don Pedro José Elizondo for 200 pesos.

Several priests from various towns, including Barba, Pacaca, Aserrí, Cot, Ujarrás, Atirro, Tucurri, and Buruca, grant power of attorney to Don Domingo Galarza and Don Mateo Mantilla, both Regidores from León, to collect outstanding synods from the previous year (1792) and future years.

people_involved: Don Juan Antonio de la Peña
summary: Don Manuel José García, the Procurador Síndico, with the approval of the 'capitulares' (Don Antonio de la Fuente, Don Juan Francisco Bonilla, and Don Francisco Carazo), grants power of attorney to Don Juan Antonio de la Peña, a resident of Guatemala, to handle a lawsuit between Cartago and Doña Manuela Antonia Alvarado concerning common lands (ejidos).
Don Juan Francisco Bonilla obligates himself for 100 pesos to Doña Nazaria Jinesta. The money was delivered by Doña Dominga Jinesta on Doña Nazaria's behalf.

Don José Mª Peralta, having been allowed to return to Cartago from Guatemala after legal proceedings against Don Manuel José de Zea, mortgages his house in Villa Nueva and other previously embargoed assets as a legal guarantee. Doña Joaquina Corrales and Doña María Francisca Corrales also act as his guarantors, mortgaging their respective properties, including haciendas in Matina and enslaved people.

Don Antonio de la Fuente, Regidor Alférez Real, and his wife, Doña María Francisca Alvarado, mortgage their residence, the house occupied by Governor Don José Vázquez y Téllez, 200 head of cattle in Bagaces, and four cacao haciendas in Matina.

Don Manuel Antonio Guzmán assumes responsibility for a 600-peso chaplaincy branch belonging to the San Francisco Convent in Cartago, linked to the El Puente cacao hacienda in Matina. This chaplaincy was previously managed and redeemed by Doña Manuela Fernández Pastora.

Don Roque Ibáñez takes charge of a 100-peso chaplaincy branch belonging to the Dolores brotherhood in Cartago, previously held by Don Miguel Guzmán. He mortgages several animals, and this obligation was cancelled in 1794.

Don Joaquín Oreamuno acts as guarantor for his father, Don José Antonio Oreamuno, for 150 pesos, which was the price for the office of Regidor Alguacil Mayor of the Cartago Ayuntamiento, awarded to his father.

Don José Antonio Jiménez grants power of attorney to Licenciado Don José Tomás Zelaya, a lawyer in Guatemala, to defend him in a lawsuit brought by Doña Ana Rita Madriz. Madriz claims to have been dispossessed of her house, which was adjudicated to Jiménez as a guarantor for her past debts.
Doña Joaquina Corrales grants general power of attorney to her son-in-law, Don Manuel Marchena.

people_involved: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco
summary: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco, a resident of Panama, grants power of attorney to Captain Don Luis de Aguilar and, secondarily, to his brother Don Romualdo Aguilar, both residents of Rivas, Nicaragua. They are tasked with demanding payment of 1030 pesos that Don Francisco Ramo collected from Don Domingo Oroc in San Miguel on behalf of Don Antonio de la Fuente and remitted to Don Antonio.

Don Juan Francisco Bonilla, the Depositario General, obligates himself to Don Manuel Marchena, attorney for Don José Plazaola of León, for 876 pesos and 3 reales from the assets of the deceased Don Francisco Javier de Benavides. This debt was later cancelled in 1796 by Don José Ignacio Rucabado, Plazaola's attorney.

Don Tomás de Castañeda, a native of Spain, confesses to owing Don Juan Francisco Bonilla 184 pesos. This debt originated from Don José Aballe to Don Pedro Antonio Iribarren, who then endorsed it to Bonilla. Castañeda was condemned to pay due to his partnership with Aballe and for taking over Aballe's mercantile assets.
Incomplete entry mentioning Doña Micaela Alvarado and Doña Antonia.

Andrea, doña María Arleguí, and the heirs of the late doña Francisca Madriz (doña Manuela Viveros, don Sebastián Fernández de Urrutia, doña Josefa Boniche, doña Baltasara Madriz, doña Ana Benita, and doña Rosa Madriz) grant freedom to José Bruno Madriz, a 60-year-old Black man. José Bruno Madriz was inherited by them from their ancestors.

Fr. Juan Francisco de Arburola, former priest of Pacaca since 1789 and current priest of Curridabat, grants power to don Domingo Galarza, a resident and Regidor of León. This power is for Galarza to collect outstanding synods owed to Arburola.

Doña Teresa Alvarado, her daughter doña Ana Josefa Dionisia Alvarado, and her granddaughter doña María del Carmen Medita grant freedom to the enslaved woman Petronila, 27, and her three children with Cayetano Calvo: Josefa Toribia (7), Josefa Isabel (2), and María de Jesús (1.5). They also free Fernando, 9, another son Petronila had before marriage.

José Miguel González, a resident of Iscasú and general representative for the entire neighborhood, commits to constructing a church. The church will be 30 varas long and include all necessary ornaments, chalice, cruets, missal, and other utensils and jewels.

Captain don José María de Peralta declares that he has received all the assets awarded to doña Catalina Corrales. A marginal note indicates that a deed from November 27, 1794, was canceled because Peralta renounced the guardianship of the minor.
A transaction takes place between Miguel, Felipe, Manuel, Jerónimo, and Florencio Arias, who are the sons and heirs of Juan José Arias. The transaction concerns the division of assets.

Doña Joaquina Corrales declares a debt of 6,000 pesos to don Manuel Marchena for goods from Castile, including debts from other individuals for the same effects. The payment is due within 18 years, in money or cacao at 32 pesos per load delivered in this city.
The debt declared by doña Joaquina Corrales to don Manuel Marchena on December 30, 1793, was canceled on July 30, 1795, as noted in the margin.

Doña Antonia Pacheco, a widow, sells her tiled house with an entire plot of land to don José María de Peralta for 500 pesos. The property is located immediately next to the plaza, bordering doña Joaquina Corrales' house to the East, the priest's house to the West (across a street), don Fermín Mondragón's house to the South, and the Parish cemetery to the North (across a street).
A marginal note indicates that the debt related to the sale of the house from doña Antonia Pacheco to don José María de Peralta was canceled on January 20, 1795.

Santiago Corrales and his wife Rosa Castillo, residents of Villa Nueva, take charge of a chaplaincy branch worth 400 pesos belonging to the Convent and Presbyter don Pedro José Alvarado. Don José Antonio Chavarria redeems this, and they mortgage 8 tame horses, 11 mares, a house, and an enclosure.

Doña Paula González, a widow, grants power to don Agustín Gastiasoro to collect any sums belonging to her deceased son, don Casimiro Alvarado, who died in the Kingdom of Lima. The collected funds are to be placed in the care of don José Vicente Icaza, a resident of León.
Doña Petronila Carazo, a widow, grants freedom to the enslaved man Juan José Carazo, approximately 40 years old and of "loro" color, to take effect after her death.

Don Benito Fajardo sells a house, inherited from his deceased father don Miguel Fajardo, to don Benito García. The house, valued at 300 pesos and divisible among Benito and his sisters doña Antonia and doña Ana María, is described by its neighbors: Presbyter don Pablo Molina, Presbyter don Félix Alvarado, don José Francisco Bonilla, and don Esteban Herdocia.

Don José María de Peralta, acting as guardian for doña Catalina Corrales, grants power of attorney to don José Antonio Jiménez. This is due to Peralta's impending absence as he plans to travel to the city of León.

Doña Manuela Josefa Rodríguez, a resident of Villa Vieja, grants power of attorney to her brother, don Mariano Rodríguez. He is to defend her against the mandated exhibition of residence for her deceased husband, don Joaquín Zamora, as Zamora left her no assets to support herself and her children.
Dionisio Villalobos posts bail for Cayetano Fernández, who is imprisoned for the crime of larceny.

Presbyter don Félix Alvarado takes charge of a chaplaincy worth 100 pesos belonging to the city's convent, which Paula Cantillo redeems. He mortgages his 18-year-old enslaved man, José Sebastián, as security.
A marginal note indicates that the chaplaincy debt was canceled on August 21, 1795, because the debt had been transferred to don José Antonio de Alvarado.

Don Pedro Antonio Solares, a native of Spain, grants power of attorney to don Hilario Parodi, Perpetual Regidor of Rivas de Nicaragua. Parodi is authorized to collect 1014 pesos owed to Solares by don Francisco Ramo, a resident of the same town, for a commercial transaction.

Don Juan Francisco Bonilla, General Depositary and Mayor, grants power of attorney to Licenciado don José Tomás de Zelaya, a lawyer of the Royal Audience of this Kingdom. Zelaya is to defend Bonilla's Royal jurisdiction against the Vicar Forane, Ecclesiastical Judge, and Priest of this city, who have attempted to assert jurisdiction over a temporal case against laypeople initiated in 1793.
Don Joaquín de Oriamuno declares that he holds 160 pesos, which is the value of lands formerly belonging to don Juan Mejía.

Property including a cattle ranch, sugar mill, houses, and an oratory, belonging to Doña Micaela Sáenz and the Oriamuno family, is burdened by two capellanías. Don José Antonio Oriamuno ratifies a mortgage on this property. Don José Antonio Jiménez, Doña Petronila Robredo, Don Tomás Hidalgo, and Doña Rita Oriamuno act as guarantors for the mortgage.

Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla, the Alcalde Depositario General, acknowledges a debt of 300 pesos to Don Carlos Portocarrero, a former resident of Cartago now living in León. This debt is for lands and cattle that Portocarrero's attorney, Presbítero Don Félix Alvarado, sold on his behalf. The debt was later cancelled on September 15, 1794.

José Antonio Brenes takes responsibility for 91 pesos and 1/4 reales belonging to the three minor children of the deceased Juan Vega: Raimundo, Bernarda, and Joaquín. As security for this responsibility, Brenes mortgages two mules, four cows, and a yoke of oxen.
Cura Don Ramón de Azofeifa grants general power of attorney to Doctor Don José del Barrio, who is a resident of Guatemala.

Don Miguel Ignacio Llórente acknowledges holding various embargoed assets, including gold and silver jewelry, merchandise, clothing, and papers, that belonged to Don Juan Rodríguez de León and Don Antonio Artiles. These goods were seized due to a requisition from Don José Rodolfo, a merchant in Panamá. The embargo was subsequently cancelled on April 23 and August 20, 1794.

people_involved: Gobernador Don José Vázquez y Téllez
Doña María Francisca Marchena y Vargas Machuca
summary: Gobernador Don José Vázquez y Téllez grants general power of attorney to his wife, Doña María Francisca Marchena y Vargas Machuca. She is noted as a resident of Granada in Andalucía.

José Antonio Redondo receives the inheritance left by his deceased father, Santiago Redondo, which is designated for his minor siblings, José de la Encarnación and Ana Redondo. His brother, Félix José Redondo, acts as a guarantor for this transaction.

people_involved: Gobernador Don José Vázquez y Téllez
Presidente Don José Domas y Valle
summary: Colonel Don José Antonio Molina, who is traveling to Panamá to find a ship to his destination, receives a significant amount of gold dust, diamond jewelry, earrings, gold buttons, and gold chains from Gobernador Vázquez y Téllez. These valuables are to be delivered to the Gobernador de Panamá, to be held at the disposal of Presidente Don José Domas y Valle of the Kingdom.

Don Antonio Artiles, a native of Santa Cruz de Tenerife, formerly residing in Santiago de Veragua and currently imprisoned in Cartago, grants power of attorney to Don Juan Rodríguez de León. Rodríguez de León, also a prisoner and native of Asturias, is traveling to Panamá to demand indemnification from Don José Rodolfo, a merchant in Panamá, and to clear Artiles' name regarding alleged embezzlement and his conduct.

people_involved: Alférez Real Don Antonio de la Fuente
summary: Don Ignacio Miguel Llórente acts as guarantor for Alférez Real Don Antonio de la Fuente, who is permitted by the judge in the cases against Don Manuel José de Zea to return to Cartago. De la Fuente must leave an instructed and funded attorney and provide an 800-peso bond upon his arrival to cover any civil and criminal liabilities.

Don Francisco Carazo, serving as Regidor Alcalde Provincial, resigns his position in favor of his son, Don Lorenzo Carazo. He formally requests His Majesty to issue the appropriate title for his son to assume the role.

Don Francisco Carazo makes his will, detailing his and his wife Doña Ana Jacoba de Alvarado's assets, including haciendas, cattle, and several slaves. He declares holding 2000 pesos from Doña María Cecilia Castillo, half for her son Rafael and half for her son Luis, and orders the freedom of his slaves Francisco and José Antonio Zavaleta. His wife, his son Don Lorenzo, and Presbítero Pablo Molina are named as executors, and his 15 named children, plus one unborn, are his heirs.

Juan de Ocampo makes his will, having been widowed twice. His first marriage to Rafaela Cascante produced a deceased son, José Antonio, and a living daughter, Estéfana, residing in Espíritu Santo de Esparza. His second marriage to Juana de la Trinidad Fonseca resulted in three deceased children. He notes his deceased son José Antonio served eight years in the Matina valley troops, including time as a prisoner of the Mosca Nation, and names Antonio García as his executor and Estéfana as his heir.

Don Ignacio Miguel Llórente provides a jail bond for Don Antonio Artiles, who is imprisoned on charges of embezzlement. Artiles is accused of committing this crime in complicity with Don Juan Rodríguez.
Don Bernardo Gómez grants general power of attorney to Don Joaquín de Oreamuno.

Juan de Ocampo, through a codicil to his will, appoints Don Sebastián Fernández as his new executor. This change occurs because Antonio García, who was initially named, declined to accept the position.

people_involved: Don Manuel José Gómez de Barahona
summary: Don Pedro Antonio Solares, a native of Spain residing in Villa Vieja, grants power to Don Manuel José Gómez de Barahona, a resident of Rivas de Nicaragua, to collect 1,014 pesos owed by Don Francisco Ramo.

people_involved: Don José de los Santos Lombardo
summary: Don José de los Santos Lombardo, with his curator's license, empowers Don Vicente Robles, a merchant from Panama, to collect 1,000 pesos from Don José Lazo, the Guarda Mayor of the Plaza in Panama. This debt is for a house sold by Don José Huertas, who acted under power from Don Francisco Javier Lombardo, the grantor's grandfather.

people_involved: El R. P. Fr. Domingo Arias
summary: Father Fray Domingo Arias, the reducing priest of Buruca, grants power to Don Domingo Galarza, a perpetual councilman of León, to collect the synod due to him for the year '93.
Numerous residents from Villa Nueva and Villa Vieja, acting on their own behalf and for other neighbors, grant power to Don Juan Zavala, a resident and merchant of Guatemala, for legal disputes.

José Francisco Oreamuno, widower of María Antonia Ortiz, and his mother-in-law, Juana Manuela Pacheco, acknowledge receiving funds related to the marriage. Oreamuno received 319 pesos he contributed, and Pacheco received 104 pesos 6 reales that her deceased daughter contributed.

Don Francisco Carazo's codicil is recorded, naming Don José Antonio Oreamuno and Don Joaquín Oreamuno as arbiters, and Don Ignacio Llórente and Don José Ruperto Prieto as accountants. His slave, Francisco Solano Carazo, is to receive several animals.

Cristóbal Aguilar obliges himself for 136 pesos from the inheritance of the deceased children of Miguel Aguilar and María Dolores Martínez: Ramona, Cosme, María de los Angeles, and Cayetano. A marginal note from April 30, 1800, indicates Ramona and Cosme Aguilar, and Alfonso Aguilar as tutor for María de los Angeles and Cayetano Aguilar, cancel the obligation.

Don Juan Francisco Bonilla leases a cacao plantation called Chirripó in Matina to Don Sebastián Guevara for three years at 175 pesos per year. Don Sebastián Fernández, who partly owns the plantation, gives his consent.

people_involved: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco
summary: Don Joaquín de Alvarado sells his 18-year-old mulatto slave, Gregorio Alvarado, to Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco for 200 pesos. Gregorio was born to one of Alvarado's slaves.

people_involved: Alférez Real Don Antonio de la Fuente
summary: Matías Román acts as guarantor for 500 pesos for Alférez Real Don Antonio de la Fuente, who is in Guatemala. This guarantee is to allow de la Fuente to come to Cartago and cover any outcomes of a future sentence.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Juan Manuel del Corral
Presbítero Don Rafael Agustín de Ayesta
summary: Presbyter Don Juan Manuel del Corral, priest of Villa Vieja, empowers Presbyter Don Rafael Agustín de Ayesta, Rector of the Seminary of León, to negotiate a benefice exchange with Priest Don Ramón de Azofeifa.

people_involved: Maestrescuela Don Albino López de la Plata
summary: Priest Don Ramón de Azofeifa, priest of Cartago, grants power to Maestrescuela Don Albino López de la Plata, a resident of León, for the same purpose of negotiating a benefice exchange.

locations: Santuario de N. S. de los Angeles
people_involved: Presbítero Don Juan Manuel del Corral
summary: Presbyters Azofeifa and Corral formalize an agreement to exchange their benefices. Azofeifa, priest of Cartago, cites health reasons and improvements he made in his current parish, while Corral, priest of Villa Vieja, seeks peace and rest among his own, noting his benefice is vast and dispersed. They agree that if one party fails to uphold the agreement, they will pay the other's expenses.
Don Esteban Cortis, a professional physician from the Italian States of the Roman Empire residing in Cartago, grants power, first to Don Basilio Urtecho and second to Don Ignacio Rucabado.

Don Gregorio de la Rosa and his mother, Doña Ignacia de la Rosa, took charge of a chaplaincy of one hundred pesos, previously held by the deceased Don Joaquín Isidro Quesada. Don Ignacio Llórente redeemed this chaplaincy. Doña Ignacia mortgaged her house as a guarantor for the transaction.

people_involved: R. P. Fray Juan Luis de Soto
summary: The Reverend Father Fray Juan Luis de Soto, parish priest of San Bartolomé de Barba, granted power of attorney to Don Domingo Gilarza. Don Domingo, a councilman and resident of León, was empowered to collect the synod due to Fray Juan Luis from the year 1793.
Don Pedro José Elizondo granted general power of attorney to Don Joaquín de Oreamuno. The specific purpose of this general power was not detailed in the record.

Don José María de Peralta, acting as tutor for the minor Doña Catalina Corrales, granted power of attorney to Don José Tomás de Zelaya, a lawyer before the Royal Audience. This power was for defending Doña Catalina in a lawsuit concerning her right to patria potestad, as she was an illegitimate daughter and not living with her mother, Doña Joaquina del Corral. The condition for her to live with her mother was that Doña Joaquina separate from her son-in-law, Don Manuel Marchena, who had allegedly offended her life and honor.

Don José de Robles, a resident of Panamá, made an agreement with Don Santos Lombardo regarding a debt of one thousand pesos owed by Don José Lazo to Lombardo. Lombardo was to endorse the debt document to Don Vicente Robles, Don José's brother. Don José de Robles, about to return to Panamá, committed to transferring the sum to Don Agustín de Gana if his brother received payment, or endorsing the documents to Gana for collection otherwise.

Don José Ruperto Prieto, Síndico of the Convento de San Francisco, granted power of attorney to his colleague in Nicaragua, Don Juan Antonio Muñoz, and Don Luis de Aguilar. This power was for collecting principal and interest debts from Doña Manuela Ibarra, totaling 550 pesos in cacao and 140 pesos in silver.

Don José Antonio del Campo sold an enslaved woman named Antonia, approximately 29 years old, and her 3-year-old daughter Fulgencia, both of black color, to Don Juan Francisco Bonilla. Bonilla acted as the agent for Don Manuel Gómez Barahona, a resident of Nicaragua. Antonia was sold for 250 pesos and Fulgencia for 100 pesos, having been previously purchased from Bachiller Don Juan José Oriamuno.

Doña Antonia Arley, a widow, granted power of attorney to her son, Don Félix Cuende, who resided in Nicaragua. This power enabled him to litigate for the freedom of two enslaved women previously freed by Doña Manuela Ibarra. This specific power did not revoke the general power of attorney she had already conferred upon Don Manuel Bonilla.

people_involved: Teniente Don José Antonio de Alvarado
summary: In Bagaces, before Teniente Don José Antonio de Alvarado, Don Juan Manuel de Alvarado, a native of Cartago, acted as guarantor for Don Antonio de la Fuente for 800 pesos. This sum was related to Don Manuel José de Zea, a former Administrator. Don Juan Manuel mortgaged 100 cattle, 4 caballerías of land, 8 mules, and 10 horses located at El Carmen.
Notary Urtecho issued a testimony of a deed, dated May 13, 1794, by order of the Governor. This testimony was to be added to his protocol, ensuring the official record of the transaction.

people_involved: Don José de los Santos Lombardo
summary: Don José de los Santos Lombardo acknowledged a debt of 200 pesos to Don Juan Francisco Bonilla. This money had been lent to Lombardo to finance his upcoming trip to the Kingdom of Panamá.

people_involved: Don Albino López de la Plata
summary: A transaction was made between Don José Ruperto Prieto, acting as agent for Don Benito Bonilla (son-in-law and heir of Don Luis Cueto), and Don Pedro José Elizondo, who owed 5,000 pesos to Cueto. Elizondo agreed to provide a draft of 400 pesos to Don Albino López de la Plata in León for Bonilla, and by December 1st of this year, he would transport 20 mules loaded with cacao from Cartago to León at his own cost, with Bonilla having the right of first refusal. The remaining balance would be paid by Elizondo in August 1795, concluding the lawsuit with costs borne by the debtor.

María Francisca Castillo, widow of Juan Manuel Solano, made her will. She named Presbítero Don Pablo Molina as her executor. She had three children with Juan Manuel Solano: José Miguel, Pedro José, and Juana María Solano, with the latter two being married.

Don Santos Lombardo, preparing for a voyage to Panamá, granted power of attorney to Don José Antonio Oreamuno to dictate his will. He appointed Presbítero Don Pablo Molina and his wife, Doña Micaela Conejo, as executors, and designated his unborn child with Doña Micaela as his heir.

people_involved: Presbítero Don José Antonio de Alvarado
summary: Presbítero Don José Antonio de Alvarado established a chaplaincy for recited masses, endowing it with 100 pesos owed by Don José Francisco Bonilla, secured by his house, and 50 pesos held by his brother, Don Joaquín de Alvarado, a resident of León. He stipulated that two masses would be said by the chaplain, each endowed with 3 pesos and 6 reales, and entrusted the chaplaincy to the Convento de San Francisco, with its guardian serving as patron and chaplain.

Doña Ana Jacoba de Alvarado, widow of Don Francisco Carazo, and her son Don Lorenzo Carazo, acting as testamentary executors, granted power of attorney to Don José Asenjo, a procurator and resident of León. Don Lorenzo also tasked Asenjo with seeking confirmation of his title as Regidor and Provincial Mayor, which his father had previously renounced in his favor.
In Villa Vieja, Don José Antonio Arana and his wife Doña María Francisca Zamora were involved in an unspecified transaction or event. The record of this entry is incomplete.

Doña Bárbara Zamora redeems a chaplaincy of 185 pesos. She mortgages her house, other properties in El Carbonal, three fences, and 16 mules. Don Miguel Ziinnra and Don Miguel Vargas act as guarantors for Don Miguel Ulate.
In Villa Vieja, Doña Manuela Josefa Reyes, a widow, grants power of attorney to Don Juan Ramos.
In Villa Nueva, Don Basilio Urtecho acknowledges a debt of 50 pesos to Don Esteban Venegas. This debt is to be paid in January 1795.

Don Esteban Herdocia and Doña Josefa Alfeirán take charge of a 300-peso chaplaincy, redeemed by Don Joaquín Arguedas. They mortgage their house, which borders properties of Doña María Manuela Miranda, Padre Don Félix García, Don Benito García, and Doña Cecilia Galarza Escalante. Don Juan Francisco Bonilla later took over this debt in June 1800.

A lawsuit transaction occurs between Doña María Francisca Corrales and Don Francisco Taboada, who acts as agent for Don Lorenzo Guillen. Don Francisco Taboada acknowledges a debt of 246 pesos 7 reales to Guillen, payable in March 1795.

Presbítero Don Benito de Bonilla and his sister Doña Bernardina de Bonilla take a 100-peso chaplaincy for the Cofradía de N. Señora de los Dolores, with permission from Mayordomo Presbítero Don Pablo Molina. Doña Bernardina mortgages her house as guarantor, and Don Miguel Guzmán previously held this chaplaincy.

Félix Camaño takes charge of two chaplaincies totaling 200 pesos, previously held by his deceased father, Nicolás Camaño. A cacao plantation named San José, with 1800 trees, was adjudicated to Félix Camaño from his father's estate and was obligated for this debt.

Don José María de Peralta pledges to pay a 500-peso fine to the Santísimo Sacramento if he ever accepts deposited goods from any tribunal in his house. However, on September 8, 1795, Peralta annuls this agreement, stating that accepting such deposits is a civic duty and he does not wish to expose himself to legal trouble.

people_involved: Gobernador Don José Vázquez y Téllez
summary: Gobernador Don José Vázquez y Téllez grants power of attorney to Don Joaquín de Oreamuno. This power is for Oreamuno to pursue lawsuits against Don Manuel Marchena and Doña Joaquina Corrales.
Francisco Carmona owes Pedro Manuel Salguero 461 pesos, which was lent in the valley of Malina. Carmona agrees to repay the debt through his personal labor in mule driving and other tasks.

people_involved: Alguacil Mayor Don José Antonio Oriamuno
summary: Alguacil Mayor Don José Antonio Oriamuno emancipates his son, Salvador Oreamuna. Salvador had turned 25 years old in the preceding March.

people_involved: Teniente Coronel Don Juan Francisco Bonilla
Gobernador Don José Vázquez y Téllez
summary: Teniente Coronel Don Juan Francisco Bonilla, also a Regidor, Depositario General, and Alcalde ordinario, donates an enslaved woman named Petronila to Gobernador Don José Vázquez y Téllez. Bonilla had purchased Petronila, who is 30 years old, from Doña Joaquina Corrales for 300 pesos.

people_involved: Don Pedro Tiburcio Machado y Ugarte
Capitán de pardos José Miguel Cárdenas
summary: Don Manuel José García, Don Pedro Tiburcio Machado y Ugarte (as agent for Don Joaquín Arguedas), Capitán de pardos José Miguel Cárdenas (for himself and as agent for Teniente de pardos Miguel Arburola), and Bernardo Calvo act as guarantors for Machado y Ugarte, who manages the Real Estanco de tabaco and stamped paper. The 600-peso guarantee is for Administrator Don Mariano Valenzuela, with various properties mortgaged by the guarantors, including houses and pastures in Cartago and its outskirts.
Francisco Santiago Fonseca obliges himself to Manuel Fonseca and María Josefa Fonseca for 95 pesos each. This amount represents their inheritance from their deceased father, José Antonio Fonseca.

Don Manuel Antonio Jiménez, who received 100 cordadas of land from the Purires river as payment for a 25-peso quota, sells 32 cordadas of this land to Don Joaquín de Oreamuno for 40 pesos. The land borders the pasture of Miguel Arias and Prudencio Picado.

José Acuña murdered Esteban López, and Rafaela García, Esteban's legitimate wife, is considered an accomplice. Esteban López left an infant daughter, Juana López, who was awarded some small assets. This event is under the order of Alcalde Don Joaquín.

Don Gregorio de Oreamuno sold his hacienda and hato, 'San Jerónimo,' located in El Andecho, to Francisco Javier Mayorga for 797 pesos. The property's boundaries were described by various natural features including the Ho Grande river and several ravines.

Josefa Nicolasa Quesada, following an Alcalde's order, apprenticed her 8-year-old son, Manuel Francisco Bonilla, to master carpenter Jesús Morales for six years. The purpose of this arrangement was for Manuel to learn the carpentry trade.

Doña Justa Bonilla, authorized by her husband Don Isidro Oreamuno, sold the enslaved person José Francisco Oreamuno, described as 'moreno' and around 40 years old, to Francisco Javier Mayorga for 200 pesos.

In Villa Nueva, Presbítero Don Antonio Cayetano Chacón, the parish priest of Jinotepe, granted power to Jerónimo Flores to locate and apprehend his enslaved person, José Manuel Oreamuno, who had escaped. Flores was also authorized to sell José Manuel if apprehended.

In Villa Nueva, the heirs of Santos Fernández, who was the universal heir of Manuel de Jesús Román (who made a will in 1787), agreed to fulfill Román's wish to establish a capellanía de misas. Santos Fernández had died intestate, and her assets reverted to these heirs. After inventorying and valuing the assets, 230 pesos 4 reales were designated for the capellanía.

The heirs of Santos Fernández and Manuel de Jesús Román, some from Cartago and some from Villa Nueva, formally established the capellanía de misas rezadas as per Román's will. The endowment, valued at 230 pesos, included cacao trees in Malina and a plantain farm in Ujarrás, currently held by Félix Várela. Don Antonio Ramón de Azofeifa, the Cura of Cartago, was designated as its patron and chaplain.

In San Luis de Aserrí, Don Bernardo Gómez, a resident of Cartago, committed to paying 2,300 pesos if a court case with Francisco de Jesús Navarro required it. This obligation was a condition for him to be allowed to leave the province.

In Villa Nueva, Don Nicolás Castro acted as a guarantor for Don Mariano Valenzuela, Administrator of the Royal Tobacco Monopoly, for 500 pesos to secure the sealed paper branch. Castro mortgaged his house in Villa Nueva, along with 23 mules and 200 cattle, as collateral.

Governor Vázquez y Téllez granted ownership of a house to Don Pedro Ulloa for 62 pesos in Villa Nueva. This transaction resulted from an execution and auction of assets belonging to Don Nicolás Astúd and Doña María Mora, who owed 233 pesos 7 reales in costs.
Francisco de Jesús Navarro received and took into deposit the inventoried assets belonging to the estate of the deceased Manuel Rodríguez.

people_involved: Don José Albino López de Plata
summary: Don Antonio Ramón de Azofeifa, Comisario del Santo Oficio, executed orders from the Holy Tribunal in Mexico (dated March 18, 1794) concerning the arrest and asset seizure of Don Esteban Curti. As part of this, the enslaved person Juan Corrales, aged 13-14, was auctioned and sold for 205 pesos to Doña Francisca Leonarda del Corral, representing Don José Albino López de Plata. The formal transfer was then executed by several officials.

people_involved: R. P. Fray Luis de Soto
summary: Don José Ruperto Prieto, Síndico of the Franciscan Convent in Cartago, granted power to Don José Antonio de Alvarado. Alvarado was tasked with collecting any assets left by the late R. P. Fray Luis de Soto, which were currently in the possession of Doña Cecilia Castillo, a resident of Villa Nueva.

Don Manuel Antonio Jiménez sold 32 'cordadas' of land in the Purues area to Presbítero Don Gregorio Bonilla for 32 pesos. This land had been previously awarded to Jiménez as payment for his share in acquiring lands near the Purire river.

Various 'curas doctrineros y de reducciones' from different towns, including Fray Pablo Chacón, Fray Eugenio del Valle, and Fray José Francisco Alvarado (representing Fray Nazario Gallo), granted power to Regidor Don Domingo Galarza and Don Mateo Mantilla, residents of León. Their mandate was to collect outstanding synods owed to the priests.

Doña Manuela Pastora, a widow, granted power to her son, Presbítero Don Juan Sierra, who is the Cura of Teustepet. This authorization was for Don Juan Sierra to defend both himself and his mother in a lawsuit initiated against them by Don Antonio Ramón de Azofeifa, the Cura of Cartago.
Doña Ana Josefa Ulloa granted power to Don José Antonio de Alvarado to represent and defend her in an ongoing executive lawsuit.
Presbítero José Antonio de Bonilla, the parish priest of El Viejo in the jurisdiction of León, granted general power of attorney to Tomás Alvarado.

María Josefa Alvarado sold a 16-cordada plot of land, planted with 'can i blanca', to her son Gabriel Lizondro. The land bordered properties of Javier Mayorga and Manuel Antonio Jiménez, and the price was two-thirds of cacao.

Salvador Oreamuno took charge of 372 pesos from a chaplaincy, which Joaquina del Corral redeemed. These funds belonged to the Convent of San Francisco in Esparza, with Joaquín de Oreamuno acting as guarantor, and were secured by a mortgage of 300 heads of cattle in El Andecho.

Antonio de la Fuente, as executor for Luisa de Guzmán y Echavarría, declared the establishment of a 200-peso chaplaincy, funded by a small house near the Soledad church. The chaplaincy was for four masses for the souls of Luisa and her husband, Miguel de Alvarado, with Antonio de la Fuente as patron and Pedro de Alvarado as chaplain. José Antonio de Alvarado and Antonia de Alvarado, who had taken over the chaplaincy after 1782, now formally recognized it, mortgaging a newly built, substantial house.

Luisa de Guzmán y Echavarría established a 200-peso chaplaincy, secured by a small house, for masses for her soul and that of her husband, Miguel de Alvarado. Antonio de la Fuente was designated as the patron and Pedro de Alvarado as the chaplain.
Antonio de la Fuente stated that canonical collation of the chaplaincy was given to his son, Baltasar de la Fuente.
Matías Román and María de los Ángeles Valverde took on the debt associated with the chaplaincy.
María Francisca del Corral, a widow, took charge of a 150-peso chaplaincy branch, for which Presbítero Nicolás Hidalgo served as chaplain. She mortgaged her residential house as security.

Alejandro Lampar declared that he had offered the house he held as part of a chaplaincy, with a principal of 820 pesos belonging to chaplain Francisco Robledo. Lampar had made significant improvements to the house, costing over 400 pesos, which he sold to Joaquín de Oreamuno and his wife Florencia Jiménez for 100 pesos. The Oreamunos took on the house with the 820-peso chaplaincy obligation and mortgaged their own house for security.

María Dolores Cubero, widow of Francisco Carrasco and guardian of their children, leased her deceased husband's farm in Esparza to Diego Soto, a resident of Villa Vieja, for seven years. The lease included livestock and tools, with an annual rent of 18 pesos for the first two years and 30 pesos thereafter. Soto mortgaged his house in Quebrada Seca, along with horses and cattle, as security.

José Antonio de Alvarado and his wife Antonia de Alvarado took responsibility for two chaplaincy branches: one for 100 pesos previously held by Presbítero Félix de Alvarado, and another for 200 pesos previously held by Ana Benita Núñez. Both chaplaincies belonged to the Convent of San Francisco, and the couple mortgaged their house on Calle de la Soledad and animals in Bagaces as security.
Manuel José Soto sold a plot of land in Cerro Grande, bordering the Río de Paz, to José Antonio de Alvarado for 37 pesos.

Presbítero Nicolás Hidalgo, Lieutenant Priest of Guanacaste, took charge of a 228-peso chaplaincy branch from the city's convent, previously held by Presbítero Félix Alvarado. He mortgaged a herd of 200 cattle, 60 mares, and 2 donkeys in La Barranca, Esparza, as security.

Manuel Antonio Jiménez, a widower of Ignacia Nicolasa Gutiérrez, made his will. He listed his nine children, noting that three had passed away, with Manuel Felipe leaving four children and Manuel Antonio (son) leaving one child who survived only six months. Jiménez was remarried to María Dolores Camacho, with whom he had no children, and also mentioned his grandchildren Rafael García and Ignacia, and his son-in-law Florencio Arias.
Santos Rivera posted bail for Joaquín and Blas Quirós, who were being prosecuted for clandestine tobacco planting.

María Dolores Cubero, widow of Francisco Carrasco, formalized an agreement made with her husband and the executors of her brother Pablo Cubero's estate (Miguel Cárdenas and Antonio García). She committed to paying the costs of Pablo Cubero's estate and the guardianships of her siblings within two years, in exchange for taking possession of Pablo's house.

José Antonio Carrillo granted power to his mother, María Josefa de Aguirre, and his brother, Presbítero José Nicolás Carrillo (Parish Priest of Bagaces), to make his will. He was married to Manuela Valverde, and his heirs were their four children: Vicenta Joaquina, Ambrosio Joaquín, Juan Agustín, and Ildefonso Joaquín.
Rosa Madriz, a widow, leased two cacao plots in Matina to José del Bago for five years. The annual rent was five tercios of cacao.
Juan Francisco Bonilla sold an enslaved woman named Petronila to Manuel Marchena.
Silvestre Fernández, representing the heirs of Santos Fernández, sold a house previously owned by Manuel de Jesús Román to Manuel Ortiz for 100 pesos. The property was located on the edge of Puebla.

Don Juan Francisco Bonilla received 96 pesos in deposit. This money was generated from the auctioned goods of José Acuña and Catarina Castillo, who were identified as 'reos' (criminals or defendants). The document for this transaction was not signed.

A transaction was made between Don José Ruperto Prieto, as Syndic of the Convent, and Don José Antonio Oreamuno, as attorney for Doña Cecilia Castillo, to settle a lawsuit over assets left by the deceased Fray Juan Luis de Soto. The Convent received 400 pesos and revoked the power of attorney previously held by Don José Antonio de Alvarado. Franciscan friars advised settling the dispute to avoid scandal and protect the order's honor.

people_involved: Don Manuel Marchena y Vargas Machuca
Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral
summary: Don José Miguel Corona sold his 14-year-old mulatto slave, José de Jesús Corral, to Don Manuel Marchena y Vargas Machuca for 200 silver pesos. Corona had inherited the slave through his paternal legitimate inheritance, which was delivered by his mother, Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral.

Antonia Gertrudis Quirós, owner of her 15-year-old mulatto slave José Santiago Cayetano Quirós, granted him permission to work independently for five years. The slave, who was adjudicated to her for 150 pesos from her mother Brígida Valverde's estate, was to pay 165 pesos 4 reales to gain his freedom.

Félix Camaño, acting as the executor for his deceased father José Nicolás Camaño, committed to paying 107 pesos 6 reales to the estate's creditors by the following March. The creditors included Don Antonio de la Fuente, Maestro José Antonio Sáenz, Don José Antonio Jiménez, and the local Convent. Félix Camaño mortgaged half a house he inherited to secure this payment.

Don Sebastián de Guevara, appointed as curator for Doña Micaela de Alvarado to manage her estate and assets, named Pedro Garda as his guarantor. This arrangement ensured the proper administration of Doña Micaela's finances.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Juan José de Oreamuño
summary: Doña Antonia Manuela de Alvarado granted power of attorney to her son, Presbítero Don Juan José de Oreamuño. This authorization allowed him to represent her in an ongoing legal dispute concerning land.

Doña Florentina de Aragón, the widow of Governor Don Juan Fernández de Bobadilla, granted freedom to her slave, Antonia Barrios, who was over 50 years old. Antonia Barrios had been purchased from Don Antonio de la Fuente, who at the time was the tutor of Doña Micaela de Alvarado.

Juan Manuel Salas, acting for himself and his wife María Catarina Ulloa, sold their 19-year-old white slave, José Manuel Ulloa, to Don José María Peralta for 100 pesos. The slave was described with specific physical characteristics including brown eyes, little beard, and black curly hair.

Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla and his wife Doña Ana Rita Gómez exchanged 1345 pesos from two chaplaincy funds, one dedicated to San Francisco de Paula and the other to Nuestra Señora de Malina. They received the sum in various goods including cattle, mares, and field horses, and mortgaged their houses, slaves, and estates as security.

Doña Dominga Jiménez sold a deteriorated small farm (chácara) to Don José María Peralta for 150 silver pesos. The property, which included cane fields, a pasture, a corn fence, a house, and a sugar mill, belonged to her minor children and bordered the Molino River. Her son, Pedro José de Jesús, signed the document on her behalf.

locations: Campos de sabana de esta ciudad
summary: Doña Manuela Pastora sold a small farm (chácara) to her son, Don Esteban Herdocia, for 150 pesos. The property included fences, a living house, and a sugar mill house, bordering the city's savanna fields to the North. Don Esteban Herdocia, being 24 years old and married, was considered outside paternal authority, and his brother José Gordiano Herdocia signed for their mother.

people_involved: Presbítero Don José Francisco de Alvarado
summary: In her codicil, Doña Ana Teresa de Alvarado directed that a fifth of her cattle from Tres Ríos be given to each of her nieces, Doña Ramona Fallas and Doña María Arlegui, with the remainder going to her heir. She also donated the enclosure where Félix Calvo, a free mulatto, lived, in recognition of his service to her deceased brother, Presbítero Don José Francisco de Alvarado. Her daughter, Doña Dionisia de Alvarado, and Don Manuel Conejo were named as executors.

Doña Micaela Valverde, widow of José Solano, made her will, listing her children as María Josefa, Gertrudis, and Félix, whose whereabouts were unknown. Her sons-in-law were Gregorio Calvo and Prudencio Picado, and her grandson was José Vicente. Don Andrés Polandij served as a witness to the will.

people_involved: R. P. Fray José Joaquín Hidalgo
summary: The Reverend Father Fray José Joaquín Hidalgo, Parish Priest of Ujarrás, granted power of attorney to Don Domingo Galarza, a resident of León. This authorization allowed Don Domingo Galarza to collect the stipends owed to Father Hidalgo since the year 1790.

Don Pedro José Elizondo acknowledged a debt of 1856 pesos 4 reales to Don Benito Bonilla, whose attorney was Don José Prieto. Elizondo had received this sum in 619 head of cattle, which he left in Bonilla's possession.

Martín González, son of the deceased Miguel González and Efigenia Alvarado, made his will. He was first married to Benita Carranza, with whom he had María, Lorenzo, and Nicolás, the latter reportedly deceased in Bagaces and Nicoya. His second marriage was to Juana Antonia Masís, with whom he had Isidro, Eduardo, Gregoria, Antonia, and Juana.
Isidro González, son of Martín González and the deceased Juana Antonia Masís, received the inventoried goods from his mother's estate in deposit.

Don Manuel García Escalante, acting as tutor for doña María Catarina del Corral, the minor daughter of doña Joaquina del Corral, granted power of attorney to Licenciado don Santiago Moreno, a lawyer from Guatemala.

Doña Juana Rita de Coronado, legitimate daughter of the deceased don Sebastián de Coronado and doña María de Soro, and widow of don José Romualdo Zamora, granted power to testate to Presbítero don Pablo José Molina. Her albaceas were Pablo José Molina and don Juan Manuel Zamora, and her heirs were her six children.
Agustín Núñez provided bail for Isidro Barahona, who was facing criminal charges in an investigation concerning the death of Juana María Solano.

Doña Juana Rita Coronado, whose deceased husband, don José Romualdo Zamora (a former escribano), had a pending lawsuit between don José Perié and don Manuel Torre y Romero, granted power to don Joaquín de Oreamuno to collect outstanding legal costs owed to her husband from that case.

Don Rafael de Alvarado and his wife doña Bartola de Oreamuno obligated themselves to doña Ignacia de la Rosa, a native of Panama and resident of Cartago, for a loan of 800 pesos. This obligation was later cancelled in 1798 by the creditor.

Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco provided bail for don Basilio Urtecho, a public and government escribano of the province, who was suspended and imprisoned in the Royal prison for misconduct in his office. Núñez later withdrew from this bail on April 20 of the same year due to an upcoming trip to Panama.

people_involved: Ana Teresa de Soto y Barahona
summary: Doña Petronila Carazo, legitimate daughter of the deceased Captain don Pedro Carazo and doña Ana Teresa de Soto y Barahona, made her will. She was the widow of don Juan Teruel, a native of Spain, and had a son, don Juan Diego, who was in Lima. Among her assets was a cattle ranch in El Zapote, Esparza, and she granted freedom to its manager, Juan José Carazo.
Don Pedro José Elizondo granted general power of attorney to don Pedro Agüero, a merchant and resident of León.

Doña Petronila Rodríguez Robledo made a codicil to the will she had executed in 1790 with her husband, don José Antonio Jiménez, before the escribano don José Romualdo Zamora. She named don Juan Francisco and don José Francisco Bonilla as arbiters, don José Antonio Bonilla as curator for her minor children, and don Manuel José García and don Ignacio Llórente as accountants.
Don Basilio Urtecho, who was imprisoned in a dungeon, granted general power of attorney to Licenciado don José Tomás de Zelaya, a lawyer from Guatemala.

Don José Ruperto Prieto and don Sebastián Fernández de Urrutia provided bail for don Manuel Marchena, who was imprisoned for the crime of challenging Cavalry Officer don José Corona. Marchena was declared free of the charge on December 10, 1796, and the bail was cancelled.
Don Pedro José Elizondo granted general power of attorney to don Francisco Javier Navarro, a Colonel from another Kingdom.
Don José Ignacio de Rucabado and don Nicolás de Oreamuno granted their general power of attorney to don Manuel de Jesús Zea, who resided in Guatemala.

The escribano Basilio Urtecho protested the proceedings against him, alleging that Alcalde 2nd don Juan Francisco Bonilla had adulterated an investigation by examining unpresented witnesses and conducting a secret inquiry into his conduct. Urtecho claimed he was suspended, imprisoned, and his assets embargoed without proper examination of his witnesses, and that the case was consulted with Licenciado don Pantaleón de Águila without his knowledge, preventing him from recusing Águila as he had done with Licenciados don Severino Ramírez and don José del Barrio.

An unnamed petitioner (otorgante) appealed a legal decision, requesting freedom from imprisonment and denying charges, stating he could not find guarantors. The Gobernador denied the appeal but offered release under house arrest with three guarantors, which the petitioner claimed he could not secure, mentioning Juan de Dios Brenes had previously refused to be a guarantor again. The petitioner also cited a threat from the Gobernador in March and concerns about biased witnesses in the plenary trial.

Joaquín Quirós, son of the deceased María Josefa Quirós and married to María de los Angeles Mora, made his testament. He had 12 children with María de los Angeles Mora, of whom 5 died young, Blas died married, and 6 were living. He owned lands in Chircagres, Chures, and Pirrís, and named his wife and Juan de Dios Brenes as executors.

people_involved: Capitán don Pedro Tiburcio Machado y Ligarte
summary: Don Santana Jiménez, a resident of Villa Nueva, granted power of attorney to Capitán don Pedro Tiburcio Machado y Ligarte. This power was for Machado y Ligarte to represent Jiménez in the estate proceedings of his deceased father, don Manuel Antonio Jiménez.

Don Francisco Esteban Jiménez, a resident of Villa Nueva and son and executor of the deceased don Manuel Antonio Jiménez, received the inventoried goods from his father's estate. The total value of these goods amounted to 2,415 pesos and 6 reales.

José Francisco Vega, legitimate son of the deceased Pedro José Vega and María Efigenia Sanabria, made his testament. He was married to María Candelaria Salas, with whom he had three living children: Pedro Nicolás, Gertrudis Lucía, and Isabel María. Isabel María married Fermín Monge, Gertrudis Lucía married Cipriano Bonilla, and Pedro Nicolás married Manuela Rosalía Núñez, with Félix Calvo named as his executor.

people_involved: Doña Ana Rita de la Madriz Linares
Doña Rosa de la Madriz Linares
Canónigo don Juan José de la Madriz Linares
Presbítero don José Miguel Sancho de Castañeda
summary: Don Sebastián Fernández de Urrutia, doña Ana Rita de la Madriz Linares, and doña Rosa de la Madriz Linares, as heirs of the deceased Canónigo don Juan José de la Madriz Linares, granted power of attorney to don José Asenjo, a Procurador from León. This power was to enable Asenjo to collect their respective inheritances from Presbítero don José Miguel Sancho de Castañeda.

people_involved: Presbítero don Juan de Dios Sáenz
summary: Don Bernardo Gómez, son of the deceased don Bernardo Gómez and doña María Josefa Altamirano, granted power to his son, don José Luis Gómez, to make his will. He named Presbítero don Juan de Dios Sáenz and his wife, doña Ana Elizondo, as executors, and instituted his four children as heirs: don José Luis and don Serapio (from his first wife doña Juana Garro), and doña María and doña Francisca Nicolása (from doña Ana Elizondo).
Don Bernardo Gómez modified his previous will, changing his desired burial location from the Convent to the church of Los Ángeles.

people_involved: Doña María de la Cruz Jinesta
summary: Doña Dominga Jinesta declared that she had 5 mule beasts belonging to her daughter, doña María de la Cruz Jinesta, which were under a 4-year administration contract with don Manuel Arburola. The contract stipulated that if her daughter married during this period, Arburola would return the beasts or pay 20 pesos plata for each, to which Arburola agreed.

locations: Villa de los Santos del Reino de Tierra Firme
people_involved: Doña Clara Josefa de las Mercedes Osejo
Doña Francisca Javiera Castro y Gordillo
Don Blas de Laya y Bolívar
summary: Doña Clara Josefa de las Mercedes Osejo, a resident of Esparza and daughter of the deceased don Esteban Osejo and doña Francisca Javiera Castro y Gordillo, made her testament. She was first married to don Blas de Laya y Bolívar, with whom she had children who died in infancy, and was now married to don Carlos José Pérez. Her first husband, don Blas, had served as Alcalde de la Santa Hermandad and Teniente de Gobernador of Esparza, with related financial obligations handled by his half-brother and executor, don José Francisco Taboada, during the Government of Perié. She named her current husband and her brother, don Alejandro Osejo, as heirs.

María Arias, widow of don Felipe Jiménez, obligated herself to her four children, Manuel José, Carlos José, Rafaela, and Florencio, for 315 pesos and 2.5 reales. This amount represented their inheritance from the estate of their grandfather, don Manuel Antonio Jiménez.

Don José Antonio García leased his cacao hacienda, Santa Gertrudis, located in Sarmiento of the Matina valley, to don Bartolomé González, a native of Spain, for five years. The hacienda contained 1,500 fruit-bearing cacao trees and 700 cotton plants, with the annual rent set at 5 tercios of cacao (125 pesos), and González also agreed to cultivate the cotton on a shared basis.
Don Joaquín Arguedas and his wife, doña Manuela Conejo, took charge of a chaplaincy valued at 250 pesos, which belonged to the Convent.

Don José Ruperto Prieto, acting as attorney for Doña Antonia Flores (wife of Don Blas Espinosa, residents of Rivas de Nicaragua), sells a house in Cartago to Don Joaquín de Arguedas for 200 silver pesos. The house is located near the Plaza Mayor and borders properties of several other individuals.

Don José Francisco de Bonilla grants power of attorney to Licenciado Don Santiago Moreno, a lawyer from Guatemala, to collect debts owed to him by the Audiencia. These debts are related to his past role as a Judge of Residence during the governorship of Don Juan Pinillos in the province.

Don Pedro José Elizondo grants power of attorney to his son, Don José Santana Elizondo, a cleric, to represent him in the estate proceedings (mortuoria) of Buenaventura Elizondo, who was the grantor's father.

Doña Antonia Marín, widow of Don José Miguel Velazco, grants power of attorney to Licenciado Don Santiago Moreno. This is to represent her in a lawsuit filed by Don Antonio de la Fuente, who claims her deceased husband owed him a sum of pesos, a case currently under appeal.

people_involved: Presbítero Don José Cayetano de Arleguí
summary: Don Miguel Guzmán and his wife Doña Antonia García take charge of 150 silver pesos belonging to a chaplaincy. This money was previously held by Don Francisco Ulloa and his wife Doña Dominga Robredo, and the chaplaincy was last served by Presbítero Don Francisco Robredo and instituted by Presbítero Don José Cayetano de Arleguí. They mortgage their house as security.

Juan de la Rosa Martín, a Sublieutenant of Pardos, posts bail for José Jerónimo Moya, who was imprisoned by court order during an investigation into the death of Juana María Solano. A marginal note from June 1798 indicates Martín later delivered Moya and cancelled his bail.
Luis Chavarría posts bail for Trinidad Pacheco, who was imprisoned by court order in the same case mentioned previously (the death of Juana María Solano).
Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla receives 63 pesos from the auctioned assets of the prisoner José Acuña. The remaining pesos were used to transport Acuña to the Royal Court Prison.

Doña Antonia Arlegui, widow of Don Romualdo Cuende and mother/guardian of Doña Ramona Cuende, as well as heir to Don Félix and Don Isidro Cuende, grants power of attorney to Don José Manuel Bonilla, Alguacil Mayor of Rivas, Nicaragua. This is to represent her in the estate proceedings of her mother-in-law, Doña Manuela Ibarra.
Doña Antonia Arlegui obligates herself to her daughter, Doña Ramona Cuende, for the inheritance Ramona is due from the estate of her grandmother, Doña Manuela Ibarra.
Don Sebastián Fernández de Urrutia and his wife Doña Antonia Arlegui take charge of 112 pesos and 4 reales from a Vera Cruz chaplaincy. They mortgage two properties in Santa Ana as security.

people_involved: Don Manuel Marchena y Vargas Machuca
summary: Don Manuel Marchena y Vargas Machuca, having experienced great ingratitude from his mother-in-law Doña Joaquina López del Corral and her children, obligates himself to pay a 500 silver peso fine to the effigy of San Juan de Dios in the church of La Soledad if he visits their houses or communicates with them. He reserves the right to collect debts and pursue judicial matters against them.

Presbítero Don Benito Bonilla, regretting his past attendance at prohibited gambling houses, obligates himself to avoid such places and games of cards and dice. He promises to pay a 100 peso fine to the Purísima Concepción venerated in the parish church if he is found to have handled prohibited game cards or dice.

Don Sebastián Guevara, acknowledging the harmful consequences of prohibited card and dice games, promises to abstain from them for three years. If he fails, even by playing non-prohibited games like truco or malilla, he will pay a 150 peso fine to the Santísimo Sacramento of Cartago.

Don Manuel Oreamuno and Comandante José Joaquín Coronel are appointed defenders for Antonia Josefa Cerdas, Emidia Cerdas, María Dolores Benítez, and Ignacia Benítez, who are daughters, stepdaughters, and heirs of León José Benítez. This is in response to a lawsuit by Don Ignacio Miguel Llórente demanding 250 pesos he gave in Matina, plus an additional 25 pesos.

A cacao hacienda with a thousand trees in La Portezuela was sold for 400 pesos to Don Sebastian Guevara. This sale was made to cancel a debt owed to Don Antonio de la Fuente, who was the father-in-law of an unnamed party.

Padre don José Santana Elizondo, acting as attorney for the successions of his grandfather Buenaventura Elizondo and his father Pedro José Elizondo, acknowledged a 100-peso debt. This debt was owed to the cofradía del Santísimo of the parish church in Cartago.

Margarita Izaguirre, widow of Buenaventura Elizondo, and Leonarda Granados, widow of José Joaquín Elizondo, accepted an obligation to the Royal Treasury. This obligation arose because Buenaventura had guaranteed fines against his son Pedro José Elizondo in cases involving Don Manuel José de Zea. Margarita received 473 pesos 5 reales for her marital gains, and Leonarda received 190 pesos 4 reales for her three minor children (Félix Nazario, José de los Angeles, and José Antonio), under the condition that they would be liable if Pedro José could not pay.

people_involved: Don Pedro Tiburcio Machado y Ugarte
summary: Don Pedro Tiburcio Machado y Ugarte, a native of Baranlis, Vizcaya, made his will in Cartago. He was married to Doña María Mercedes Soto Mayor and had seven children. He held several public offices including the tobacco tercena, postal administration, and alcabala collection in Cartago, and had served as steward of city revenues for about six years. He named his wife and Don Antonio de la Fuente as executors, Don Joaquín Oreamuno as arbiter, Don Ignacio Llórente as accountant, and Don Sebastián Fernández de Urrutia as defender of minors, with his children as heirs.

people_involved: Don Manuel de la Torre y Romero
Don Pedro Tiburcio Machado y Ugarte
summary: Don Manuel de la Torre y Romero was appointed to administer the tobacco tercena and stamped paper in Cartago, a role previously held by the late Don Pedro Tiburcio Machado y Ugarte. His widow, Doña María Mercedes Soto Mayor, handed over the administration. Don Manuel provided Don Juan Francisco Bonilla and his wife Doña Ana Rita Gómez as guarantors.

Antonio Molina, a resident of the outskirts of Cartago, made his will. He was the natural son of the deceased Águeda Molina. He was widowed from María del Rosario Rojas, with whom he had one son, Manuel José Molina (also deceased), who had three children with Josefa de la Cruz Martínez. Antonio then married Josefa Petronila Jiménez, with whom he had two children. His wife was named executrix, and his two living children and three grandchildren were his heirs.

Padre don José Santana Elizondo, a deacon, personally assumed the 100-peso debt that his grandfather Buenaventura Elizondo owed to the Santísimo Sacramento cofradía of the parish church in Cartago. He mortgaged a house he owned in the city center as security for this debt.

Manuel Antonio Barrantes, 47 years old and the legitimate son of Lorenza Valerino, sold a 'cerco de poro' (a type of enclosure or fence) located next to the boundary marker of La Puebla to José Antonio Solano for 48 silver pesos.

Deacon Don José Santana Elizondo granted general power of attorney to Captain Don Mateo Mantilla, a resident of León. This power was for lawsuits and to request dimissory letters for his ordination as a Presbyter in any bishopric he found convenient, as his Bulls had not arrived from his elected Prelate of this Bishopric.

people_involved: Presbítero don Antonio Ramón de Azofeifa
summary: Don Antonio de la Fuente, acting as attorney for Doña María Irene Delgado (widow of Don José María Paz, resident of León, and mother/guardian of her four heirs), and also representing Doña María Irene's children as heirs of Ana Jiménez (who died intestate in Cartago), sold a 20-year-old mulatto slave named José Ceferino Jiménez to Presbyter Don Antonio Ramón de Azofeifa, the local priest, for 200 silver pesos. José Ceferino was born to Rosa, a slave of Ana Jiménez (wife of Paz), who was a slave of another Ana Jiménez (mother of María Irene Delgado's mother-in-law).

people_involved: Doña Antonia Petronila Arnesto de Troya
Doña María Josefa Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Doña Antonia Petronila Arnesto de Troya made her will. She was the legitimate daughter of Don Luis Arnesto de Troya and Doña María Josefa Muñoz de la Trinidad. She was married to Don José Santiago Valverde of Villa Nueva, with whom she had no children. Before her marriage, she had two daughters, Doña Juana and Doña Dionisia Troya, for whom a benefactor had given her 500 silver pesos. Her mother was named executrix, and her daughters were her heirs.

Don Antonio de la Fuente, using the same legal representation as on December 23rd, sold a 15-year-old white mulatto slave named Josefa Felipa to Don Juan Francisco Bonilla for 175 silver pesos. Josefa Felipa had been raised in the house of Ana Jiménez, who was the mother-in-law of Doña María Irene Delgado.

people_involved: Presbítero don Felipe de Jesús García
summary: Francisco Quesada, as the husband of Doña Santos Jiménez (daughter and heir of Ana Jiménez), sold a 52-year-old mulatto slave named Rosa Jiménez to Don Juan Francisco Bonilla for 150 silver pesos. From this amount, 6 pesos for alcabala and 35 pesos 1 real for court costs of the estate of another Ana Jiménez (said to be the sister of Quesada's wife, though disputed) were to be paid. The remaining 108 pesos 7 reales were held in deposit by the buyer until the lawsuit concluded. A later note from November 11, 1817, indicates Presbyter Don Felipe de Jesús García received this sum from Bonilla's executors and delivered it to Francisco Quesada's heirs.

people_involved: Don Pedro Tiburcio Machado y Ugarte
summary: Don Sebastián Guevara and the heirs of Don Manuel Antonio Jiménez (Don Francisco Esteban Jiménez, Don Santana represented by Don Pedro Tiburcio Machado y Ugarte, and minors represented by Don José Antonio de Oreamuno and Machado) reached an agreement to settle a lawsuit. Guevara had sued for lands in Rosales (Puás) that Doña Isabel Fernández clandestinely sold to Don Manuel Antonio Jiménez in 1770. To avoid further litigation, the Jiménez heirs gave Guevara a 49-cordada pasture called La Cucaracha in Purires for 200 silver pesos.

An unnamed individual, acting as curator for his mother-in-law Micaela de Alvarado and as heir to the Rosales lands, transferred these lands to the Jiménez family. The transaction was for 200 pesos, which was the value of La Cucaracha.

Don Sebastián Guevara granted general power of attorney to Don Joaquín de Oreamuno. This power specifically authorized Oreamuno to collect 400 pesos plus interest from Pedro Elizondo, a debt owed to Guevara's mother-in-law, Doña Micaela de Alvarado.

Doña Joaquina Corrales acted as guarantor for her son-in-law, Don Manuel Marchena, who was the successful bidder for the city's tithes at 1,200 pesos. She mortgaged two houses, a small farm in the common lands (ejidos), and two herds of mules as collateral.
Don José Ignacio Sáenz made his will, stating he was married to Doña Juana Josefa Meoño and had one son, Manuel José, aged 14. His wife and Don José Antonio Sáenz were named as his executors.

Juan de Dios Brenes posted bail for the scribe Basilio Urtecho, who was imprisoned for alleged abuses in his office. On June 15 of the same year, Brenes cancelled the bail after Urtecho was ordered and returned to prison.

Cayetano Fernández and his wife María del Carmen Guzmán sold a house in Cartago, originally given to María del Carmen by her father José Manuel Guzmán, as they were moving to Ujarrás. María del Carmen Chavarría purchased the house for 100 pesos, which was bordered by properties of María Francisca Arguello, María Masís, Tomás Arburola, and the widow of Mateo Román.
Don Manuel García Escalante granted general power of attorney to his wife, Doña Manuela Petronila del Corral.

people_involved: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco
summary: Don Manuel Segundo Lombardo, a native of Panamá, acknowledged a debt of 1,394 pesos and 6 reales to Don José Santos Lombardo, who was the assignee of Don Raimundo Carranza. Don Manuel Segundo paid 20 pesos and was granted an extension for the remainder, with the condition that he could be compelled to pay if assets were found. Don José Santos Lombardo, being under 25, signed with his tutor Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco.
Doña Ana Jacoba Alvarado, widow of Don Francisco Carazo, declared that she had received the inheritance corresponding to her 15 children.

Don José Luis Gómez made a will on behalf of his deceased father, Don Bernardo Gómez, who had died on March 6 of the same year. The will detailed his father's possessions, including clothing, silver items, riding gear, and livestock at the Cucuilapa ranch and lands.

Several Franciscan fathers, including parish priests and 'reductores' from various locations, granted power to Don Domingo Galarza and Don Mateo Mantilla, residents of León. This power was to collect outstanding synods owed to them from the year 1795 and the current year, 1796.

Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla and his wife Doña Ana Rita Gómez granted freedom to their enslaved girl, María Manuela Bonilla, who was about six years old. María Manuela was the daughter of another enslaved woman belonging to the grantors, named Ventura Gómez.

Doña Carmen Medina granted power of attorney to her husband, Don Francisco Idiarte, who was preparing to travel to Panamá. The power was specifically for him to collect various sums of money owed to her in that city.

Don Pablo Reyes, a resident of Villa Nueva, and his wife Doña Isabel Alvarado, acknowledged a debt of 211 pesos and 7.5 reales to Don Francisco Javier Navarro. This debt was for goods from the land and from Castile, and they committed to repaying it by April 1797.

The Most Reverend Father Guardian Fr. José Joaquín Hidalgo granted power of attorney to Don Domingo Galarza, a resident of León. This power was to collect synods owed to Fr. Hidalgo as Cura of Ujarrás, covering the period from January 7, 1790, until April 15 of the current year, 1796.

Doña Manuela Baeza, Don José Antonio García, Don Miguel Ignacio Llórente, and Don Matías Román acted as guarantors for Don Antonio de la Fuente. This guarantee enabled him to hold the aguardiente (liquor) monopoly for three years.
Don Joaquín Arguétías posted bail for Don Juan de Luna, who was being prosecuted for allegedly writing a document that Pedro Elizondo presented to the Government Court in Cartago.

Don Juan Francisco Bonilla, acting as executor for Doña Petronila Carazo, acknowledged holding 4,163 pesos and 5.5 reales. This money belonged to Don Juan Riego Teruel, who was absent in Perú, and represented the liquid portion of his maternal inheritance.

Don José Ruperto Prieto and Don Nicolás Oreamuno posted bail for the Major Assistant, Don Juan Manuel de Cañas. He was arrested in the chapter house and was being prosecuted for being considered the author of an anonymous letter and for other crimes detailed in the legal proceedings.

Don José Luis Gómez, Mateo Molina, Ramón Molina, and Blas Marín posted bail for Pedro Elizondo. Elizondo was imprisoned and being prosecuted for presenting a disrespectful, insulting, and impertinent document to the Governor.

Doña María Francisca del Corral, a widow, granted power of attorney to Don Pedro Antonio Iribarren. This power was to represent her in legal proceedings concerning the offering of a chaplaincy, which was under her charge and belonged to the Parish of Esparza, valued at 450 pesos.

José Vega, Miguel Lobo, and Manuel Granados were involved in a situation concerning Don José Antonio Alvarado, who was imprisoned for alleged crimes. The specific action they took is not fully detailed in the provided text.

Don José Vázquez y Téllez was accused of no longer being Governor and was to be taken to Guatemala. Alvarado, an Alcalde, committed "estelionatos" and had an association with Escribano Basilio Urtecho, leading to their release on bail. Juan Barrantes later replaced Miguel Lobo as guarantor on June 7, 1797.

Don José Miguel Corana was arrested in his house by the Military Court for breaking his house arrest, going to Pedro Lizondro's house, and attempting to hit Ana Lizondro. Don Manuel García Escalante and Don José Miguel Ocaña posted bail for him.

Don José Vázquez y Téllez, Governor of the province and elected Commander of La Guaira port, granted general power of attorney to Don Ildefonso Antonio de Gereda, Don Juan Francisco Bonilla, Don José Ignacio Rucabado, and Don José Antonio del Campo. This power was for his business and lawsuits, and to defend him in future lawsuits related to his governorship.

Pedro Manuel Salguero granted power of attorney to Don Pedro Antonio de Iribarren, an auditor of tobacco revenue in León, to represent him in a lawsuit. The lawsuit concerned the resignation of 1,900 pesos and properties belonging to the Convent of Cartago.

Don Manuel Diez Dobles and his mother, Doña Mariana de Alvarado, took responsibility for a chaplaincy branch of 105 pesos, belonging to the Purísimo Misterio de la Concepción de María Santísima in the Convent of Cartago. Doña Ana Jacoba de Alvarado had redeemed this chaplaincy, and Don José Antonio de Oreamuno, the mayordomo, consented. Doña Mariana mortgaged her house, and Don Manuel mortgaged six mules.

Don Juan Francisco Bonilla, as executor of Doña Petronila Carazo's will, and with the consent of the defender of Doctor Don Juan Diego Teruel (her absent son and heir in Lima), leased the "El Zapotal" cattle estate to Don José Lorenzo Carazo. Don José Lorenzo Carazo's mother, Doña Ana Jacoba de Alvarado, guaranteed the lease and mortgaged her "Tenorio" estate in Bagaces.
Pascual Bejarano granted power of attorney to Don Antonio de la Fuente to collect ninety pesos owed to him by the succession of Don Bernardo Gómez.

people_involved: Don José Antonio Rivas de Neira
summary: Doña María del Carmen Alvarado granted power of attorney to her son, Don Felipe Gutiérrez, to collect 700 pesos from the estate of the deceased Don Francisco Bellido, or from his widow or guarantors. This debt originated from Don Miguel de Alvenda, Bellido's father-in-law, and was secured by the "La Chocolata" estate.

Don Felipe Gutiérrez obligated himself to his mother, Doña María del Carmen Alvarado, for 700 pesos, to be paid at 5% interest if he collected the debt from the previous power of attorney. He also committed to founding a chaplaincy for the souls of his mother, his eldest son, and his deceased maternal uncle, Presbítero Don Maximiliano Antonio de Alvarado. Don Nicolás de Oreamuno guaranteed this obligation, mortgaging his "Paso Hondo" cattle ranch in Bagaces, next to Don José Ignacio Rucabado's property.

locations: La Puebla de pardos y morenos
people_involved: Presbítero Licenciado Don Miguel de Bonilla
Doña María de Laya y Bolívar
summary: Presbítero Licenciado Don Miguel de Bonilla sold a Creole slave named Juan José de Bonilla, a tailor who could read, to the Cofradía de María Santísima, Reina de Los Angeles, for 250 silver pesos. The slave had been a donation from his mother, Doña María de Laya y Bolívar. Don Manuel José García, the Mayordomo of the Cofradía, received the slave.

locations: Villa Nueva del valle de Aserrí
people_involved: Don Manuel Marchena y Vargas Machuca
summary: Don Manuel Marchena y Vargas Machuca and his wife, Doña Francisca Leonarda López Corral, acted as guarantors for Don Mariano Valenzuela, the tobacco administrator, for his role as post office administrator in Villa Nueva del valle de Aserrí. They mortgaged their house in Cartago, located on Calle del Calvario, which bordered properties of Don Rafael de Alvarado, Doña María Catalina López Corral, Doña Manuela Pastora, and Doña Antonia Arlegui.

people_involved: Don José Antonio García y Ramírez
Teniente Coronel Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla
summary: Don José Antonio García y Ramírez took over two pious works totaling 1,230 pesos, previously held by Teniente Coronel Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla. He mortgaged cattle and horses at Los Robles, with his father, Don Manuel José García, and mother-in-law, Doña Ana Micaela Carazo, acting as guarantors by mortgaging their houses. The obligation was later cancelled by Mayordomo Don Nicolás Castro on April 19, 1803.

people_involved: Don José Sebastián Fernández de Urrutia
Juan de Jesús Fernández de Urrutia
summary: Don José Sebastián Fernández de Urrutia, natural son of Don Domingo Urrutia and Doña Tomasa Viveros, made his will. He was married to Doña Antonia Arlegui and had four children. His assets included land in Santana and a cacao plantation in Chirripó. He named Padre Don Ramón de Azofeifa and Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla as executors, and Don Antonio de la Fuente as arbiter and accountant.
