Don Manuel García y Escalante was appointed postmaster for the province, replacing the deceased Don Pedro Tiburcio Machado. His wife, Doña Manuela Petronila del Corral, mortgaged her house as collateral for his good performance. The house's boundaries are described, mentioning several neighbors.

Manuel Sáenz, representing the residents of Agua Caliente, granted power of attorney to Don Antonio de la Fuente. This was to defend them in a lawsuit against the heirs of Don Félix Meneses concerning the preference of two 'caballerías de tierra' in that neighborhood.

people_involved: Don José Antonio Conde de la Peña
summary: Don Manuel García y Escalante granted power of attorney to Don José Antonio Conde de la Peña, a merchant from León. The purpose was to collect 1,184 pesos from the Royal Coffers, which Don Manuel had supplied to Don José Vázquez y Téllez for his salary drafts.

María Antonia Inza, widow of Tomás Alvarado, committed to her two minor sons, Rafael Mauricio (12 years old) and Ensebio (5 years old). She obligated herself for 249 pesos 4 reales, which each son inherited from their father.

Don Tomás de Acosta, appointed Governor of Costa Rica by a Royal Decree from Aranjuez dated June 22 of the previous year, took an oath of office. His representative, Don Blas Rodríguez de Zea, had already paid homage. Don Tomás swore before Lieutenant Colonel Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla to faithfully perform his duties, maintain the province in the King's name, and not surrender it to any enemy.

Don Antonio de la Fuente, acting as the representative for Doña María Irene Delgado, sold an enslaved mulatta named María Ignacia Jiménez to Don Francisco Javier Navarro, a Colonel in Conchuco, Peru. María Ignacia, 22 years old and creole, was born and raised in the house of Doña Ana Jiménez, who was the mother-in-law of Don Antonio's principal. The sale price was 200 silver pesos.

Manuel José Calvo formally transferred a piece of land to Magdalena Segura, widow of Francisco Ramírez. Calvo had sold this land, inherited by his wife Manuela Gómez from her parents, to Francisco Ramírez 14 years prior but had not yet formalized the deed. The land is located in Chures and was sold for 14 pesos.
Don Salvador Oreamuno posted bail for José Silverio Quirós, who was facing charges of robbery.

Félix Camaño and his wife Trinidad Ángulo took possession of 200 pesos paid by José Francisco Oreamuno, which belonged to the Convent. They received the money in a house that was José Francisco Oreamuno's residence in the city.

people_involved: Bachiller Don Antonio María de la Fuente
summary: Don Antonio de la Fuente, holding multiple prominent roles, revoked a power of attorney previously given to Don José Ignacio Martínez, a Procurator from Guatemala. He then granted this power to his son, Bachiller Don Antonio María de la Fuente, who was a Presbyter and Grammar Master at the Seminary in Guatemala.

Alférez Don Lorenzo Carazo, acting as the general representative for Maestro Don José Antonio Carazo, sold an enslaved mestiza woman named Emidia Carazo (25 years old) and her mestiza daughter Joaquina Carazo (5 years old) to Don Mariano Gorozabel, a resident of Peru living in the city. Don José Antonio Carazo had acquired the enslaved individuals through maternal inheritance. The price was 350 pesos.

people_involved: Doña María de la O Céspedes
summary: Doña Ana Victoria Morales made her will, declaring no forced heirs. She stated that five enslaved individuals in her possession belonged to her nephew, Don Manuel Porcio, who had been absent for 40 years. Her legatees were the children of her brother, Don Justo Ventura Morales, and Don Tomás Hidalgo and Don Antonio de la Fuente were appointed executors.

people_involved: Don José Antonio García y Ramírez
summary: Don Manuel José García and José Brenes were appointed as custodians for the seized assets of Pedro Elizondo. Don Manuel José García provided Don José Antonio García y Ramírez and his wife Doña Bárbara Conejo as guarantors.

Don Ildefonso Antonio Gereda, a native of Spain, issued a receipt to Don Manuel José García for 207 pesos 4 reales. This amount was the proceeds from the auction of some of Pedro Elizondo's assets, which were purchased by Don José Ignacio Rucabado.
Juan Alvarez, a resident of Villa Vieja, posted bail for the scribe Basilio Urtecho, who was being prosecuted for abuses committed in his office.
Don José Miguel Corona, a Cavalry Lieutenant, granted his general power of attorney to Doña Joaquina Corrales.

Don José Vázquez y Téllez acknowledged a debt of 1,400 pesos to Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla. This money had been supplied to Vázquez y Téllez for his urgent needs and travel expenses to his new post as Commander of the Port of La Guaira. The protocol was closed on the same day by Vázquez y Téllez.

Don Joaquín de Arguedas, Miguel Cárdenas, Miguel Arburola, and Bernardo Calvo granted power to Don Manuel José García. This power was to defend them in a lawsuit against Don Pedro Machado's assets. The plaintiffs sought to recover money they were forced to pay as guarantors for Machado's administration of tobacco and sealed paper revenue.

Don Manuel Marchena guaranteed 900 pesos to the Royal Treasury for the repair of weapons, a task being undertaken by Don José Miguel Ocaña. To secure this guarantee, Marchena mortgaged four enslaved individuals: Justa, Petronila, Joaquina, and José de Jesús, all bearing the surname del Corral.

Pascual Bejarano, legitimate son of the deceased Manuel Bejarano and María Antonia Méndez, and a resident of 'this city,' granted power to his master, Pedro Lizondro, to make a will. Bejarano, who was preparing for a journey to the capital of the Kingdom, stated he had no forced heir and wished for his assets to be used for a chaplaincy.

people_involved: Teniente Coronel Don Ignacio de Acosta
summary: Heirs of Don Félix Joaquín de Meneses and Doña Gabriela Josefa de Arleguí, including Don José Antonio Bonilla and the Meneses siblings, granted power to Lieutenant Colonel Don Ignacio de Acosta, Alderman Don Luis Ignacio Caballero, and Doctor Don José Agustín Caballero. This power was for collecting their inheritance from Don Félix, who died in 'this city' in 1781, having been a native of Havana and leaving 318 pesos in inheritance, with 150 pesos put to interest as noted by his brother-in-law Don José Murillo.

Doña María del Carmen Medina, having married Don Francisco Idiarte, initially granted him power to collect her paternal inheritance in Santiago Alanje, Tierra Firme. Upon learning he was mismanaging 200 pesos already collected and was also collecting 593 pesos and 2 reales owed by Don José Beitia from a deal with her previous husband, Don Nicolás Gutiérrez, she revoked Idiarte's power. She then granted power to Don Francisco de Paula Romero, a resident of Santiago Alanje, to reclaim her papers and money.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Rafael José de la Rosa
summary: María Francisca Castillo, widow of Juan Manuel Solano, made her will, naming Presbítero Don Rafael José de la Rosa and her son Pedro José as executors. She detailed her children with Juan Manuel Solano: Juana María (deceased, married twice, no succession), José Miguel (married to Leonarda Quesada), and Pedro José.

people_involved: Gobernador Don José Vázquez y Téllez
summary: Several guarantors for Governor Don José Vázquez y Téllez, including Don José Antonio de Oreamuno and Don Joaquín Arguedas, granted power to Licenciado Don Santiago Moreno, a lawyer in Guatemala. They sought defense in the Governor's upcoming judicial review (residencia), arguing their guarantee deed was invalid due to lack of registration, despite being ordered to pay 400 pesos for the transport of notary José María España for the review.

A large group of residents from Villa Nueva, including Captain Don Mateo de Mora, Don Hilario Zeledón, and many others, granted general power. This power was given primarily to Don Joaquín de Oreamuno and secondarily to Don Mateo de Mora.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Joaquín Isidro de Quesada
summary: Don José Antonio Jiménez granted power to Don Pedro Antonio de Iribarren, a resident of León. This power was to represent his son, Don Anselmo Jiménez, born from his marriage to Doña Petronila Robredo, in claiming the chaplaincy branches left after the death of Presbítero Don Joaquín Isidro de Quesada.

Don Manuel Marchena, a native of Spain and gravely ill, granted power to his wife, Doña Francisca Leonarda del Corral, to make a will. He named her as his first executor and universal heir, with Don Joaquín de Oreamuno as his second executor.

people_involved: Bdo. Don Antonio Ramón de Azofeifa
summary: Don José Onofre García, over 25 years old and recently married to Doña Ventura Esquivel, received assets worth 1105 pesos from the Blessed Don Antonio Ramón de Azofeifa. These assets included a house in 'this city,' gold and pearl items, a gold reliquary, a 4-year-old mulatto boy named Ramón, and a 1.5-year-old mulatto girl named María de los Dolores, among other items.
Don Sebastián Guevara leased a cacao plantation named La Calle, located in Matina and containing approximately 1500 fruit trees, to Buenaventura Chavarría for a period of six years.
Ramón Céspedes, acting for himself and his wife Francisca Ruiz, sold a house owned by his wife in the San Francisco neighborhood of Cartago to Juan Francisco Chavarría for 125 pesos of cacao.

people_involved: Presbítero don Juan Salvador de Laya y Bolívar
Doña María Gertrudis de Laya y Bolívar
Bdo. don José Antonio de Bonilla
summary: Don Isidro de Oreamuno formally recognized the assets his wife, Doña Justa Josefa de Bonilla, brought into their marriage. These assets, totaling 844 pesos, included donations from her uncle Presbítero don Juan Salvador de Laya y Bolívar, inheritances, a donation from Bdo. don José Antonio de Bonilla, and a 14-year-old mulatilla named María Petronila.

Don Francisco Esteban Jiménez, acting for himself and as the testamentary executor for his deceased father Don Manuel Antonio Jiménez, sold two connected pieces of land in the La Rueda area to Don Salvador Oriamuno for 43 pesos. The land bordered the royal road leading to the town of Tobosi.

Nicolás Ramírez sold a piece of land he inherited from his parents, Juan Rafael Ramírez and Micaela Chinchilla, to Manuel Vega for 10 pesos plata. The land was located towards the volcano mountain range near Cartago and bordered the road to Cot.

Don José María de Peralta granted power of attorney to the Marqués de Ayzinena and Don José Francisco de Ayzinena, both from Guatemala, to collect payments from the Royal tobacco revenue for his past work and period of suspension.

people_involved: Capitán de pardos José Miguel Cárdenas
summary: Capitán de pardos José Miguel Cárdenas and his wife Ana Catalina Carrillo borrowed 100 pesos belonging to the Cartago curacy, which had been under the charge of the deceased José Miguel Barrios. The loan was secured by the debtors' residence and a stone-fenced pasture.

Gobernador Acosta placed Julián, a 12-year-old son of imprisoned Manuel Fallas and Nicolasa Mora from Villa Nueva, as an apprentice with Don José Miguel de Ocaña to learn armory and blacksmithing from his officials, Juan Bautista Meléndez and Reyes Bonilla, for five years. However, the document was not executed because Julián reportedly escaped.
José Vega and Manuel Granados renewed the jail bond they had provided for Don José Antonio de Alvarado. Juan Barrantes joined as a new guarantor, replacing Miguel Lobo who had withdrawn his bond.

Don Manuel Marchena was awarded a five-year contract to provision 50 soldiers stationed at the Matina detachment. He was responsible for transporting daily rations of meat and biscuit/totoposte, with payment occurring every six months, and the contract outlined conditions for changes in troop numbers.
José Miguel Alvarado provided bail for Benito Alvarado, who was facing criminal charges and was gravely ill in jail, a condition confirmed by a certificate from physician José Antonio Rosales.

Don Juan Francisco Bonilla, responsible for pupilary usury funds belonging to the natural children of Don Felipe Arburola and Dolores Campos, and also holding his own funds, ceded a total of 260 pesos to José María Valle. This sum was secured on Arburola's former house in El Ojo de Agua, and Valle agreed to continue paying the interest and took possession of the house.

Don José Miguel Ocaña requested that Ramón Quesada, who was imprisoned, be released into his custody to assist with cleaning and conditioning the King's weapons entrusted to Ocaña. Ocaña subsequently became Quesada's jail guarantor.

people_involved: Teniente Coronel don Juan Francisco Bonilla
summary: Teniente Coronel don Juan Francisco Bonilla took charge of two chaplaincy funds, totaling 1040 pesos, previously managed by Doña María Francisca del Corral. He mortgaged a ranch in Santana, including over 200 cattle and an enslaved mulatto named Pedro Salguero, and the cacao hacienda 'El Guanacaste' in Matina, which Doña María Francisca had delivered. (Later, parts of the debt were cancelled by Don Manuel Marchena in 1806 and Don Joaquín Hidalgo in 1808).

Don Joaquín Arguedas and Doña Manuela Conejo borrowed 200 pesos from a chaplaincy, previously managed by Don José Antonio Bonilla and founded by the late Presbítero Don Francisco Robredo. They mortgaged their house located by the city plaza, opposite the Parish, as collateral for the loan.

Don José María de Peralta provided a bond to Don Francisco Javier Navarro for 4,886 pesos and one real, mortgaging various properties including houses, land, mules, and goods. This action was taken to secure Navarro's larger debt to the Marqués and Don José de Ayzinena.

Don José Ignacio de Rucabado and his wife, Doña Josefa de Oriamuno, acknowledged a debt of 700 silver pesos to Governor Don Tomás de Acosta. The loan was provided with a repayment deadline set for August 1798.

Doña Antonia Marín, a widow, leased her cacao plantation, 'La Velasco,' located in the Matina valley and Chirripó, to Emigdio Rojas for a period of seven years. The hacienda, which contains 1,600 fruit-bearing trees, was leased for an annual price of 160 pesos in cacao.

Doña Ana Victoria de Morales executed a codicil to her will, stipulating that her five slaves be granted freedom upon her death. She also immediately granted freedom to Petronila, who is identified as Mónica's daughter, and named Doña Catalina Carrillo, wife of Capitán José Miguel Cárdenas, as a legatee.
Cayetano Ramírez and Santiago Otárola, a resident of Villa Nueva, provided bail for José Quirós. Quirós had been imprisoned for more than a year as a result of a criminal legal process.

Don Félix de Bonilla, widower of Doña Rafaela Herdocia, committed to his minor children, Don Juan José, Don José María, Don Mateo, and Don Manuel Tranquilino, for their inheritance. Each child was due 596 pesos, 4 reales, and a half from their inheritance.

people_involved: Gobernador Don Diego de Artiaga Chirino
Licenciado Don Antonio de Guevara Sáenz
summary: Don José Antonio Bonilla, representing his wife Doña Antonia Manuela Meneses, along with Don Paulino, Doña Antonia, Doña Engracia, and Doña Juana Meneses, sold two caballerías of land to Manuel Sáenz for 550 pesos. The land, located between the Agua Caliente river and the Cobre mines, had a long history of ownership, tracing back to grants made by Governor Don Diego de Artiaga Chirino in the 1500s to the first conquistadors.
Manuel Miguel Lobo drafted his will, naming his wife, María Antonia Coto, and his son, Antonio Leonardo Lobo, as his executors. His son Antonio Leonardo Lobo is married to Rafaela Gómez.

Joaquín Quirós committed to his grandchildren, Felipe and Ambrosia, who are the children of the late Blas Quirós and Ana María Rojas. He obligated himself for 31 pesos, 2 reales, and a half, representing each grandchild's inheritance.

Miguel Mora and his wife, María Catalina Calvo, with the approval of Miguel's son Antonio Mora, donated a property in the city's common lands to Pedro Antonio Mora. Pedro Antonio, whom they raised as their own son, received a plot in El Tejar containing approximately 200 plantain trees and a small house.

Doña Josefa García, inheriting a cacao plantation in Matina from her parents Don Gabriel García and Doña Candelaria Jiménez, leased the estate to José Antonio Solano for three years at an annual rate of 150 pesos cacao. She acted on behalf of herself and her minor siblings, who are from various marriages of her parents.

Don José Santana Jiménez, a resident of Villa Nueva, reached an agreement with Don Joaquín de Oreamuno, who represented the villa's residents, regarding the 'Chocó' lands. Jiménez, who initiated the land survey, agreed that despite the title being in his name, the lands would belong to the residents, provided he was included among them and his expenses were reimbursed.

people_involved: Don Manuel de la Torre y Romero
summary: Don Manuel de la Torre y Romero, a native of Lumbreras, drafted his will, identifying his deceased parents as Don Domingo Torre and Doña Angela Romero. He named his wife, Doña Antonia Jiménez, and their children, Francisco Manuel, Tomás Ramón, and María Josefa de la Torre. He appointed Don José Antonio del Campo and Don José Ruperto Prieto as arbiters, Don Anselmo Jiménez as accountant, and his wife and Don José Antonio Jiménez as executors.

Don José Santana Jiménez, a resident of Villa Nueva, granted power of attorney to Don Mateo Mantilla. This authorization allows Mantilla to auction the Chocó lands, situated north of the Virilla river, on Jiménez's behalf.

Martín González sold a caballería of land in the area known as El Aguacate to José Miguel Monje for 50 pesos cacao. The property is located adjacent to lands that previously belonged to the deceased Juan Fonseca.

people_involved: Comandante de pardos José Joaquín Coronel
summary: Doña María Antonia Alvarez, the legitimate daughter of Don Nicolás Alvarez, drafted her will. She is married to Comandante de pardos José Joaquín Coronel, and they have a daughter named Ana Josefa. She appointed Presbítero Don Juan José Oreamuno and Don Joaquín de Oreamuno as her executors.
José Manuel Lizano sold a parcel of land in Chircagres, located northeast of the city, to Felipe Jiménez for 14 pesos. Lizano had inherited this land from his aunts.
José Manuel Lizano sold a second parcel of land in Chircagres to Mauricio Zúñiga for 14 pesos. This transaction occurred the day after his previous land sale in the same area.

José Manuel Lizano sold a third parcel of land in Chircagres to Gregorio Andrade for 22 pesos. This property, bordering the Chures river to the east, was inherited by Lizano from his aunts, who were the daughters of his great-grandfather, Juan Gómez.

Don Juan Martín de Echandy and his wife, Doña María Francisca Hidalgo, acknowledged receipt of a house located opposite Doña Rosalía de Alvarado's residence. The house, which belonged to a chaplaincy in Esparza, was acquired by them as tenants after being publicly auctioned for 450 pesos cacao, and they committed to paying a 5% annual rent.
Don Santiago de Bonilla and his wife, Doña María Josefa de Oreamuno, assumed responsibility for 100 pesos that had been redeemed by Don José Antonio de [incomplete name].

people_involved: Presbítero don Juan Manuel de Casasola
summary: A capellanía of 200 pesos cacao was founded by the deceased Presbítero don Juan Manuel de Casasola for Nuestra Señora de los Dolores of this Parish, with Presbítero don Francisco Robredo reciting it.
Another capellanía of 250 pesos plata was founded by Juliana Bonilla, which belongs to the Convento.
A house and a ranch (hato) with 900 cattle, located in the jurisdiction of Bagaces in El Peñón, were mortgaged, likely in relation to the mentioned capellanías.

Don Alejandro Lampar, Notary of the Holy Office, and his wife Doña Ana María de Oreamuno took charge of a 250-peso capellanía branch founded by Presbítero don Juan José Camacho, mortgaging their house. This obligation was partially cancelled by Presbítero don Joaquín García on November 29, 1817.

José Antonio Sáenz, a master carpenter, agreed to take José Santana Alvarado, a minor under 14 and son of the deceased Francisco Javier de Alvarado and Elena Guerrero, as an apprentice for 5 years. However, Sáenz later refused to take the contract.

people_involved: Presbítero don Antonio Maximiliano de Alvarado
R. P. Fray Francisco Antonio de Jesús
summary: Doña Juana Andrea de Ugalde, daughter of deceased Don Faustino de Ugalde and Doña Rita de Alvarado, and wife of Don Manuel José Guzmán, made her will. She mentioned her deceased uncle Presbítero don Antonio Maximiliano de Alvarado, her stepfather don Ruperto Pérez, and her siblings, appointing her husband as executor and her brothers Joaquín and Juan Pérez as legatees.

people_involved: Presbítero don Antonio Ramón de Azofeifa
summary: Don Sebastián de Guevara sold a house in Cartago, previously acquired from Don Manuel Guzmán, to Presbítero don Antonio Ramón de Azofeifa for 250 pesos. The house was bordered by specific neighbors.

people_involved: Presbítero don Antonio Ramón de Azofeifa
summary: Cura don Antonio Ramón de Azofeifa sold a 19-year-old mulatto slave named Ceferino Jiménez or Luna to Gobernador don Tomás de Acosta for 200 pesos. This sale was later cancelled on December 7, 1798.

people_involved: Unnamed wife of Don Miguel Guzmán
summary: José Antonio Fernández obligated himself for 57 pesos to María de los Angeles, a 6-year-old orphan, for a fence and house in the Agua Caliente neighborhood. This obligation was cancelled in 1803 after Don Miguel Guzmán and his wife received the money.

people_involved: Doña María Francisca López del Corral
Don José Antonio López del Corral
Don Joaquín de Alvarado y Jirón
Unnamed infant daughter of Doña María Francisca López del Corral
Presbítero don José Francisco de Alvarado
summary: Doña María Francisca López del Corral, widow of Don Joaquín de Alvarado y Jirón and Don Pedro Aymerich, made her will. She detailed her properties, including haciendas in Matina and a mill, and listed her slaves, granting freedom to Manuela and Joaquín. She appointed Don Joaquín Oreamuno and Don Manuel Marchena as executors, and Don José Antonio Oreamuno and Don José Ruperto Prieto as arbitrators.

José Francisco de Oreamuno took charge of 100 cattle, valued at 425 pesos, from a capellanía belonging to Nuestra Señora del Pilar de los Tres Ríos, which Don Manuel Torre redeemed. He mortgaged the cattle, land, mules, and a pasture in the ejidos.

Don Antonio de la Fuente, as executor for Ana Victoria de Morales, freed Petronila, a slave who was the daughter of Mónica (another slave of Morales). As Petronila actually belonged to Morales's nephew, Don Manuel Porcio, the executor reserved 200 pesos for Porcio.

Don Sebastián de Guevara and his wife Doña Juana Lacalle took charge of 126 pesos from a capellanía belonging to the Beneficio de Esparza. They mortgaged a pasture in Purires called Cucaracha, valued over 500 pesos.

people_involved: Ana de los Santos Ocaña y García
María de la Candelaria Ocaña y García
Andrea de los Angeles García y Chaves
summary: Don José Miguel de Ocaña donated a house and lot in Cartago's El Fatal neighborhood to his three natural daughters, Ana de los Santos, María Nicolasa, and María de la Candelaria Ocaña y García, whom he had with Andrea de los Angeles García y Chaves. The donation included conditions for their cohabitation and protection from potentially abusive husbands.

Juan José Arlegui reported the death of his father-in-law, Javier Alvarado, who left a house valued at 110 pesos. The house was to be divided among his widow, María Elena Guerrero, and their seven children.

José Maroto, natural son of María Josefa Palomino and widower of Juana Madrigal, made his will. He had children Josefa (married to José de la Rosa Villavicencio), Manuel, and Ambrosia with Juana Madrigal. His wife, Juana Madrigal, was previously married to José Antonio Acosta, with whom she had a daughter, María Antonia Acosta. José Maroto also bequeathed half of his fifth to his illegitimate son, José Bruno.
María Josefa Gómez, widow of Antonio Raimundo Guzmán, sold a stone fence located in Ujarrás, at the foot of the hill known as 'de los Madrices,' to Félix Bogarín for 25 pesos.

Doña Encarnación Sancho sold a mulatta named Marcela Oreamuno, approximately 20 years old, to Presbítero don Felipe de Jesús García for 200 pesos. Marcela was born and raised in the house of Encarnación Sancho's first husband, don José Francisco Oreamuno.

Don Francisco de Ulloa and his wife, doña Dominga Robredo, made their wills. They named their only remaining son, don José de la Trinidad, as their heir. Francisco de Ulloa contributed a mulatillo named José Antonio, a small enslaved woman named María de la Encarnación, and another mulatta named María Josefa, who married don José de Dios Ulloa. Dominga Robredo contributed a house, various goods, 80 pesos inherited from her brother don Nicolás Robredo, and a cacao plantation inherited from her brother Presbítero don Francisco Robredo. They appointed don Manuel de la Torre and don Joaquín de Oreamuno as arbiters.

José Hermenegildo Navarro, married to Isabel Piedra, made his will. They had nine minor children: Antonio Reyes, Josefa Cornelia, Gertrudis, María de los Angeles, María Ascensión, María Manuela, José María del Carmen, Ana Cleta, and Sebastiana de la Trinidad. His wife and his compadre, Felipe Arias, were named as executors.

Petronila Mesa sold a piece of land in Los Cerrillos de Toyogres to don Francisco Ruiz y Santiago for 18 pesos. An attached private document shows that Juana Salguero, widow of José Manuel Barrios, also sold a fence in Toyogres to Ruiz, which she and her husband had previously bought from Petronila Mesa for the same price.
Don José Nicolás Oreamuno granted general power of attorney to his brother-in-law, don José Ignacio de Rucabado, who was a Lieutenant of grenadiers in the militia battalion of this city.

María Antonia Barros, widow of Tomás Alvarado, leased a cacao plantation with over 900 trees to José Manuel Maroto for five years. The plantation is located in the Matina valley, in the area called Bonilla, for an annual rent of 90 pesos in cacao.

Don Tomás Hidalgo and his wife, doña Rita de Oreamuno, took charge of 130 pesos from a chaplaincy of Nuestra Señora del Pilar de los Tres Ríos. They mortgaged their dwelling house, which bordered don Antonio de la Fuente's house to the South.

Several priests, including Fr. Pablo Chacón (Cura of Barba), Fr. Manuel Sáenz (Cura of Quircó, Cot, and Tobosi), Fr. Domingo Arias (Cura of Aserrí and Curridabat), Fr. Joaquín de Rodríguez (Reductor of Atirro and Tucurrique), Fr. Sebastián Leitón, and Fr. Jacinto Maestre (Curas of Pacaca), granted power of attorney to don Domingo Galarza and, secondarily, to don Mateo Mantilla, both residents of León, to collect outstanding synods.

Juana Rita Ramírez sold a 50-vara square plot of land with a small gallery to José Céspedes for 16 pesos. The property, which she acquired from don Ramón Puchi, was bordered by the former house of María del Carmen Alvarado to the North, don Joaquín Arguedas's house to the South, the Madriz ladies' plot to the East (across a street), and Lorenzo Montes's plot to the West.

Manuel José Calvo, who four years prior sold a quarter cavalry of land inherited by his late wife Manuela Gómez to don Manuel Antonio Jiménez for 22 pesos, now granted the deed to the buyer's heirs. The land, located in Chures and bordering don Cleto Ulloa's fence and Roque Aguilar's fence, was transferred to Josefa García, an heir of Jiménez.

Don Rafael de Alvarado acted as guarantor for don Manuel Marchena, who had successfully bid 150 pesos in silver for the office of Regidor and Provincial Mayor. Alvarado mortgaged his house, valued at 500 pesos, to secure Marchena's obligation to the Public Treasury until he obtained the necessary titles for his position.
Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla and his wife, doña Ana Rita Gómez, obligated themselves to doña Ignacia de la Rosa for a loan of 400 pesos, borrowed for one year at 5% interest.

Don José Santos Lombardo sold a house he inherited from his grandfather, don Francisco Javier Lombardo, to don Juan Francisco de Bonilla for 375 pesos in silver. The house, located on Calle de la Soledad, was bordered by María Alvarado's house to the East, José Antonio Alvarado's house to the West, Alejandro Lampar's house to the North, and José Antonio del Campo's house to the South.

Don Tomás Alvarado, a resident of Villa Nueva, acted as guarantor for don José Santana Jiménez regarding the measurement and value of lands in Chocó, pending the issuance of the property title. Alvarado mortgaged his house in Villa Nueva, 10 mules, a sugar mill, and sugarcane fields.

Doña María Bolívar, having been informed of the death of her son, Presbítero don José Antonio Bonilla, who was the Cura of Pueblo del Viejo, granted power of attorney to Presbítero don Jerónimo Guerrero and don José Plazaola to represent her in the respective inheritance proceedings. Her other son, Presbítero don Miguel de Bonilla, signed on her behalf.
Presbítero don Félix de Jesús García grants general power of attorney to Presbítero don José Miguel Sancho. José Miguel Sancho is noted as residing in León.

Don Manuel de la Torre Romero, acting as executor for Presbítero don Francisco Robredo, sells a caballeria of land to don Juan Francisco Bonilla for 45 pesos. The land, located in Santana within the jurisdiction of Villa Nueva, was originally acquired by Robredo from don Francisco Ulloa.

Don Miguel Martín Celedón and his wife Clemencia Astorga commit to pay 513 pesos 2.5 reales of cacao to the seven minor children of Felipe Hernández. Felipe Hernández was Clemencia Astorga's first husband.

Don Miguel Martín Celedón and Clemencia Astorga sell a pasture, measuring over 100 varas square and featuring a stone fence, to José Maroto for 85 pesos. The property is situated by the Taras River and borders the royal road to the East.

Doña Joaquina Corrales grants freedom to her enslaved woman, Dominga Corral. Dominga is described as a mestiza, about 50 years old, with curly hair and short stature, and is the daughter of another enslaved woman named Ubalda.

Don Pedro Ramírez, a native and resident of Cartago, makes his will in Tres Ríos. He details his two marriages, children from each, and their spouses, and names his sons José Onofre and Vicente as executors. He is unable to sign due to illness and advanced age.

Doña Antonia Marín, as principal, and don Juan Francisco Bonilla, as guarantor, commit to pay 570 pesos 2.5 reales of silver to José Ruperto Prieto. This debt was originally owed by Antonia's deceased husband, José Miguel Velasco, to Antonio de la Fuente, and the credit was transferred to Prieto, who is an agent for Juan Payes y Font of Guatemala.
Don José Antonio del Campo and don Juan Francisco de Bonilla grant general power of attorney to don Francisco Paniagua. Francisco Paniagua is identified as a procurator and resident of Guatemala.
Don Manuel Marchena grants general power of attorney to don Blas Rodríguez de Zea. Blas Rodríguez de Zea is described as a merchant from Guatemala.

Doña Lucía de Alvarado, widow of José Nicolás Bonilla, makes her will, detailing her children and assets, including three enslaved people. Her son, Presbítero don Gregorio, supported her for 16 years. She names José Ruperto Prieto and Juan Manuel Alvarado as executors.
José Francisco and Nicolás Vega post bail for Ramón Araya. Ramón Araya is facing criminal charges for assaulting Pedáneo Francisco Sánchez.

Doña María Francisca del Corral sells a 25-year-old light-skinned mulata named María Isabel to Presbítero don Félix Alvarado for 200 pesos silver. María Isabel is the daughter of an enslaved woman previously bought from doña Francisca Miranda.

Don Juan Alvarado commits to his sister, doña María Josefa de Alvarado, for 1739 pesos 2 reales, which he received in various assets. A marginal note from April 10, 1822, indicates that don Nicolás Castro, a resident of San José, took over this guardianship after Juan Alvarado's death.

Juan Antonio Rojas, Lorenza Quirós Valverde, María de Jesús Quirós, and Antonia de Jesús Quirós, as heirs of the deceased Josefa Brígida Valverde, grant freedom to their enslaved woman Manuela Valverde and her minor daughter María de los Angeles. The act was performed before Antonio de la Fuente on December 15 and ordered to be added by Gobernador Tomás de Acosta on December 22.

Doña Angela María Bergañea, a native and resident of Cartago, makes her will. She was the natural daughter of the deceased Joaquín de Bergañea (from Spain) and Luisa Masís (from Cartago). Her European husband, Lorenzo Lares, disappeared about 40 years ago. She authorizes her cousin Andrea Guerrero to declare her assets and names her cousins Teodora and María Castillo, and her sister María Carranza as legatees, with Presbítero don Rafael de la Rosa as executor.

Presbítero don Rafael José de la Rosa, as testamentary executor for doña Angela María Bergañea, sells a small house and its plot in Cartago to Subteniente de pardos Francisco Javier Mayorga for 65 pesos silver. The property borders the former house of doña Rafaela Herdocia to the North.
Doña María Catarina Alarcón, a native and resident of Cartago, makes her will. She is identified as the legitimate daughter of don Sal... (name incomplete).

Details are provided about a testadora, daughter of deceased Cayetano Alarcón and Dionisia Meléndez, and her marriage to don Santiago Solís, with whom she had four children: Juana, Manuela, Rafaela, and José Gil. Her deceased brother, Presbítero don José Joaquín Alarcón, and her uncle, Presbítero don Manuel Meléndez, had previously donated property to her, including a pasture in Las Cóncavas.

Capitán don Joaquín Oreamuno, acting as interim political governor in the absence of the Gobernador, grants general power of attorney. The primary power is given to Capitán don Mateo Mantilla, a resident of León, and the secondary power to don Anselmo Jiménez, a resident of Cartago, who is traveling to León.

Don Joaquín Oreamuno, in partnership with don Santiago de Bonilla, secured the tithes of Bagaces for three years, at 1105 pesos annually. Oreamuno obligates himself for half of this annual sum and offers don José Antonio Jiménez, don Tomás Hidalgo, and don Santana Jiménez as guarantors.

Doña María del Carmen Alvarado, widow of don Juan Gutiérrez and daughter of deceased don Juan Manuel de Alvarado and doña Juana María Galarza, makes her will. She names her sons Dámaso, Nicolás, Felipe, Evaristo, and Maximiliano as heirs, and mentions a house donated by her deceased brother, Presbítero don Maximiliano de Alvarado. She appoints don Silvestre Ugalde as an arbiter judge and Presbítero don Juan José Oreamuño and her son don Evaristo Gutiérrez as executors.

people_involved: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco
summary: Antonia González, widow of Pedro Guzmán, sells a fenced plot of common land in the Agua Caliente neighborhood to don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco for 60 pesos plata. Additionally, she donates a cedar wood house on the property to Núñez del Arco, with the condition that he pays for her burial.

Don José Antonio Jiménez, don Tomás Hidalgo, don Santana Jiménez, don Gregorio Oreamuno, Juan de Dios Brenes, and Bernardo Calvo act as guarantors for don Joaquín Oreamuno and don Santiago de Bonilla. Oreamuno and Bonilla had been awarded the tithes of 'la Pila de la ciudad de Esparza,' encompassing the area from Río del Salto to Quebrada Honda, for 1105 pesos annually over three years.

The same guarantors (José Antonio Jiménez, Tomás Hidalgo, Santana Jiménez, Gregorio Oreamuno, Juan de Dios Brenes, and Bernardo Calvo) guarantee the payment of the Royal Ninths due to His Majesty from the tithes of Esparza. These tithes were awarded to Señores Oreamuno and Bonilla.
Don Santiago de Bonilla grants general power of attorney to don José de Asenjo, a resident of León, and secondarily to don Mariano Iglesias, also from León.
Don Tomás Hidalgo confesses to owing don Joaquín Oreamuno 400 pesos, and Antonio Delgado confesses to owing him 200 pesos, both at an interest rate of 5%.

people_involved: Doña María Josefa de la Trinidad
summary: Doña María Manuela de Alvarado, widow of don Manuel Hidalgo and daughter of deceased don José de Alvarado and doña Josefa Úrsula Conejo, makes her will. She names her five adult children: Presbítero don Nicolás, don Manuel, doña Juana, doña Rosa, and doña Prudenciana, and details their marital statuses.

people_involved: Don Manuel de la Torre y Romero
summary: Don José Antonio de Bonilla obligates himself to don Manuel de la Torre y Romero for 287 pesos in cacao.

people_involved: Doña María Ignacia de la Rosa
summary: Doña María Ignacia de la Rosa grants her mulato slave, Benito Zavaleta, who is about 30 years old, permission to work freely and buy his freedom until May 1801. Benito provides doña Dominga Jinesta and María Josefa Zavaleta as guarantors, who mortgage their houses in the San Francisco neighborhood. A marginal note indicates the debt was canceled in 1803.

Juan María de Orocú, Judge of Esparza and Commander of the detachment or Vigía in Caravallo on the South coast, grants power to don Manuel Marchena. This power allows Marchena to collect wages from the Royal Coffers for individuals who have served or will serve His Majesty in the Vigía.

José Antonio Solano takes Bartolomé, about 12 years old, and Francisca, 6 years old, as pupils. They are the children of Juan Acuña, who is imprisoned and being prosecuted for theft. Solano commits to teaching them Christian doctrine, raising, educating, and maintaining them as his own children.

people_involved: Doña Ana Rita de la Madriz Linares
Doña Rosa de la Madriz Linares
Doña Bárbara de la Madriz Linares
Doña Francisca de la Madriz Linares
Licenciado don Juan José de la Madriz Linares
Don Francisco de la Madriz Linares
Licenciado don José Miguel Sancho Castañeda
summary: Several heirs of the deceased Licenciado don Juan José de la Madriz Linares, who died intestate in León, grant power to don Manuel Marchena to collect their inheritances. The heirs, including Ana Rita and Rosa de la Madriz Linares, and the children of Bárbara de la Madriz Linares and Francisca de la Madriz Linares, acknowledge receiving their share of 3,500 pesos from a house sale. They revoke previous powers given to Licenciado don José Miguel Sancho Castañeda and don José de Asenjo.

people_involved: Doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral
summary: Manuel Rodríguez takes charge of 52 pesos from the guardianship of María de los Dolores Lobo, the minor daughter of Manuela Lobo and stepdaughter of Rodríguez. This sum was previously held by doña Joaquina Tomasa López del Corral. Rodríguez mortgages his house in the arrabal of the city, adjacent to Eugenio Cantillo's property.

people_involved: Don Manuel Marchena y Vargas Machuca
summary: Don Sebastián de Guevara, Lieutenant of Cavalry and Commander of the Matina Detachment, granted power to Don Manuel Marchena to collect salaries from the Royal Coffers for the individuals serving in the detachment.

people_involved: Don Manuel Marchena y Vargas Machuca
Gobernador Don José Joaquín de Nava
summary: Doña María Catarina del Corral sold a 10-year-old pardo slave named Blas Fulgencio del Corral to Don Manuel Marchena y Vargas Machuca for 100 silver pesos. Blas Fulgencio was the son of Manuela Corral, a slave previously donated to Doña María Catarina by Governor Don José Joaquín de Nava.

Numerous individuals, including Don José Antonio de Oreamuno, granted power to Capitán Don Joaquín Oreamuno, Hermenegildo Navarro, José Francisco Piedra, and Félix Delgado to manage affairs concerning lands in Purires. José Francisco Piedra and Félix Delgado were specifically noted to have rights to these lands as sons of the deceased Miguel Piedra and Francisco Delgado.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Joaquín Isidro de Quesada
summary: Don José Miguel Barros, a resident of Villa Vieja, assumed responsibility for 100 pesos belonging to Don Anselmo Jiménez. These funds were associated with a house in Villa Vieja that previously belonged to Presbítero Don Joaquín Isidro de Quesada.

Doña María Fernández, widow of Don Pedro José Corrales and daughter of deceased Don Juan Fernández Martínez and Doña Cayetana de Acosta, made her will. She named several nieces as legatees, including Doña Bartola Elizondo and various Fernández, Marín, and García women. Presbítero Don Rafael Rosa and Capitán Don Mateo de Mora were appointed as her executors.

Doña Tomasa López Leitón, daughter of deceased Don Fernando López de Castro and Doña Catarina Leitón, and widow of Manuel Antonio Navarro, made her will. She listed her surviving children as María Salomé, María Magdalena, José Hermenegildo, Josefa, Nicolás de Bari, Pablo José, Antonio Bernardino, and Rafael Navarro, and appointed her sons Pablo and Rafael as executors.

Joaquín Trejos, son of deceased Juan Miguel Trejos and María Manuela Maroto, made his will. He detailed his family, including his first wife Antonia Arias and their daughter María de los Angeles (who married Juan José Bustamante), and his current wife Rafaela Josefa Vásquez and their son José Francisco. Benito Carranza and Francisco Lobo were named as his executors.

Don Antonio de la Fuente, a Royal Ensign originally from Astorga, Spain, granted general power of attorney to three business agents in Madrid: Don Francisco Javier de Subisarreta, Don Santiago Sáenz, and Don Francisco Gómez de Coz.

Capitán Don Rafael de Alvarado and his wife Doña Bartola de Oreamuno assumed responsibility for 200 pesos cacao from a chaplaincy. This chaplaincy was founded by Don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín, previously tenanted by Don José Antonio Lara, and currently has Don Santana de Alvarado as its chaplain.

people_involved: Doña Juana Nicolasa de Vida Martel
Presbítero Don Juan José de Oreamuno
summary: Don Antonio Fernando Carrillo, a single man and son of deceased Don Manuel Carrillo and Doña Juana Nicolasa de Vida Martel, made his will. He named numerous relatives as legatees, including his siblings Don Benito Carrillo and Doña María Antonia Carrillo, and several nieces and nephews. Presbítero Don Juan José de Oreamuno and Don Benito Carrillo were appointed as executors.

people_involved: Doña María de las Mercedes Guerrero
summary: A dowry letter was issued for Subteniente Don José Nicolás Oreamuno and his wife Doña María Josefa del Campo, who married on August 18th. The dowry, valued at 954 silver pesos, included a detailed list of clothing, household goods, and jewelry. Doña María Josefa was the daughter of Don José Antonio del Campo, a native of Burgos, and Doña María de las Mercedes Guerrero.

Eulalia Fonseca, widow of Ramón Alvarado and daughter of the deceased Juan Fonseca and Francisca Bonilla, makes her will. Her children are listed as Nicolás, Manuel, Ana, Manuel de Jesús, María Josefa, and Antonia Alvarado. Her son Manuel Alvarado and José Francisco Oreamuno are named as her executors.

An account of the partition of goods belonging to the deceased José Francisco Carmona and his wife María de los Angeles Alfaro is made. The partition is distributed among two of María de los Angeles Alfaro's children, José Nicolás Garita and Ana de la Asunción Carmona.

people_involved: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco
summary: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco and Domingo Brenes (representing his wife Juliana Guzmán and brothers-in-law Eugenio and Miguel Guzmán) settle a lawsuit. The Guzmáns had sued Núñez over a farm that belonged to their grandmother, Antonia González. Brenes agrees to pay Núñez 80 silver pesos in August 1800, mortgaging his house in Agua Caliente as guarantee, covering previous payments Núñez made to González and Francisco Quesada for work on the farm.

Don Santiago Bonilla acknowledges a debt of 2,200 pesos to Don Manuel Marchena, which Marchena paid on his behalf. Bonilla pledges to repay within 22 months, mortgaging his hacienda 'El Peñen' and his credit against the estate of the deceased Don Julián Azofeifd, related to a payment Bonilla made in a case against Gobernador Perié.

Don Gregorio Ulloa, representing his grandfather Don Alfonso Ulloa's heirs, sells the enslaved woman Tomasa Ulloa to Don José Antonio del Campo for 200 silver pesos. Tomasa, daughter of Cayetana, was known to abandon her children, such as Francisca and Manuel, who were recovered by the heirs through legal means, confirming Tomasa's status as an enslaved person.

Don Manuel García y Escalante grants power of attorney to Don Mariano José Iglesias, a resident of León, to bid for the office of 'escribano de cabildo y Gobierno'. García y Escalante has already made a bid of 500 silver pesos and authorizes Iglesias to take necessary steps to secure the position.

This entry is the heading of a power of attorney to make a will, granted by Don José Manuel García, legitimate son of Don Julián García and Doña Ana de Sancho. The subsequent pages of the document are missing.

Doña Joaquina del Corral acts as a guarantor for Don Manuel Marchena, who is the successful bidder for the tithes of Cartago. She mortgages two houses and two cacao haciendas as collateral for this agreement.

Doña Joaquina del Corral again acts as a guarantor for Don Manuel Marchena, this time in favor of the Royal Treasury for the 'novenos'. She uses the same properties (two houses and two cacao haciendas) as collateral for this obligation.

Don Juan Francisco Bonilla, Don Joaquín Oreamuno, Don José Miguel Ocaña, and Don José Antonio Jiménez act as guarantors for Don Manuel de la Torre, who is administering the Royal Treasury of Cartago (subordinate to León), for two thousand pesos. Each guarantor mortgages specific properties in Cartago. An annotation from 1802 states that Presbítero Don Ramón de Azofeifa and Juan de Dios Brenes replaced Bonilla and Ocaña as guarantors.

José Ramón Palacios, a native of Nicaragua and resident of Villa Nueva, describes how he was asked in 1793 to care for dilapidated properties in San Antonio belonging to two chaplaincies. These properties were previously managed by Presbítero Don Pedro de Alvarado and Don José Antonio Chavarría (for the Cartago Convent), who had abandoned them. Palacios worked to restore and cultivate the properties and now constitutes himself as a tenant of these chaplaincies.

Don José Antonio García and his wife Doña Romualda Ramírez take charge of 100 pesos from a chaplaincy belonging to the Cartago Convent. These funds were previously managed by Benito Carrillo. They mortgage their residence as collateral for this responsibility.

Doña Margarita Aguirre agrees to act as a guarantor for her son, Don Pedro Elizondo, who faces arrest unless he provides a bond. This is in agreement with Don José Antonio de Oreamuno, who is commissioned to execute a sentence against a former tobacco factor and his accomplices, and has proceeded to auction Elizondo's assets for 1249 pesos and 5 reales.

Don Antonio Alfaro, representing the neighborhood of Lajuela, leases the common pasture lands (ejidos) of Cartago, specifically 'El Tambor' and 'El Carrizal', with detailed geographical boundaries. He will pay 32 silver pesos annually for these lands, which were previously leased by Don Francisco López and Rafael Pacheco.
Don Rafael Alvarado, appointed Commander of the Matina garrison, grants power to Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla to collect his salaries from the Royal Coffers.
Don Manuel José García and Manuel Sáenz act as guarantors for Don Antonio de la Fuente, allowing him to continue administering the aguardiente branch.

Don Sabastián de Guevara, acting as tutor for his mother-in-law Doña Micaela de Alvarado, sells a chácara (farm) with sugarcane, plantains, and a mill in Agua Caliente to José Antonio Solano for 528 pesos 4 reales cacao. The property, inherited by Doña Micaela from her grandfather Don Miguel de Alvarado, will be possessed by Santos Rivera.
José Antonio Solano receives 320 pesos cacao at 5% interest from Don Sabastián de Guevara, who is acting as tutor for Doña Micaela de Alvarado. This transaction was later cancelled in 1801.
Presbítero Fray Nazario Gallo, a Franciscan friar and parish priest of Pacaca, grants power to Don Domingo Galarza, or in his absence, Don Mateo Mantilla, to collect his corresponding stipends.

locations: Ojos de Agua del llano de Ujarras
summary: José Nicolás Ramírez, Pedro Várela, Trinidad Pérez, and José Joaquín Chaves sell two 'caballerías' of land in Ojos de Agua del llano de Ujarras to Don Juan Francisco Bonilla for 80 pesos. The land was inherited by their respective wives, Joaquina, Ramona, and Rita Ramírez, and Pérez's portion borders land owned by Cot.
Don Tomás Alvarado and his wife Doña María del Rosario Bonilla commit to a 400-peso chaplaincy in favor of the parish of Esparza, mortgaging their house on San Francisco street in Cartago.

people_involved: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco
summary: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco grants freedom to his 18-year-old enslaved man Gregorio, whom he had purchased about 5 years prior from Don Joaquín de Alvarado for 200 pesos, with the condition of freeing him at the end of his days.

Doña Baltasara Madriz, acting with power from her son Don José Miguel Sancho (a Beneficiado residing in León), sells the 25-year-old enslaved man Ciríaco García to Don Manuel Marchena for 300 pesos plata. Ciríaco, acquired from the estate of Presbítero Don Juan José Madriz, is sold due to his history and risk of escape.

Di° Romero, a native of Sevilla and legitimate son of Di° Romero and Doña M de Guzmán, grants a dowry of 1506 pesos to his wife Doña Mariana Flores de Miranda, a native of Cartago and legitimate daughter of Ayudante Juan de Morales Miranda and Doña Beatriz Méndez.

people_involved: Presbítero Licenciado Don Diego de Campos
summary: Doña Inés de Benavides Moreno, a widow of José García Merinero (native of Spain), makes her will, mentioning her deceased daughter Andrea and her enslaved woman Juana. Her nephew, Presbítero Licenciado Don Diego de Campos, is a legatee, and Capitanes Sebastián de Aguirre and José Marín are her executors.

An obligation is granted in favor of José de Quesada, legitimate son of the deceased Juan de Quesada and the grantor, for 86 pesos 3 reales from his inheritance. Capitán Juan Gómez acts as guarantor, and the obligation was granted before Don Diego de Carvajal, Lieutenant General of Cartago.
A will is granted before Capitán Antonio Alvarez de Ulate, Alcalde of the Santa Hermandad, in the Valle de Barba. The will mentions the husband as tutor of goods and the children as heirs.

Alférez Diego Morera and his wife María de Segura are debtors, and Sargento Antonio de Ocampo and his wife María Morera are guarantors, for an obligation in favor of a chaplaincy. This was done before Francisco Montero de Espinosa, Lieutenant General of the Valleys.

Magdalena de Piedra, a resident of Cartago, leases a cacao plantation in the Matina valley to Domingo de los Santos, a corporal of the squad. The three-year lease, for a property bordering the Hacienda del Coco and the mountain, is set to begin on January 1, 1723.

people_involved: Capitán Don José Lebrón Cortés de Monroy
Capitán Don Juan Antonio de Villarevia
Teniente General Don Pedro José Sáenz
summary: Don José de Mier Cevallos and Doña Catalina González Camino make an obligation before witnesses Capitanes Don José Lebrón Cortés de Monroy, Don Juan Antonio de Villarevia, and Don Bernardo Marín, and before Teniente General Don Pedro José Sáenz.

people_involved: Capitán Don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno
Capitán Don Miguel de Laya y Bolívar
Beneficiado Don Juan de Rivas y Chaverri
summary: Capitán Don Francisco Javier de Oriamuno and his wife Doña Ana Efigenia García commit to a chaplaincy founded by Doña Cecilia Vázquez de Coronado for 300 pesos, delivered by her executor Don Fernando de Moya. The chaplaincy is owned by the sons of Capitán Don Miguel de Laya y Bolívar and José de Miranda (residents of Esparza), with Beneficiado Don Juan de Rivas y Chaverri (parish priest of Esparza) as interim owner, and they mortgage houses in Cartago.

people_involved: Gobernador Don Baltasar Francisco de Valderrama
Teniente General Don Pedro José Sáenz
summary: A power of attorney is granted by Gobernador Don Baltasar Francisco de Valderrama, Sergeant Major of the Royal Armies of Europe. This was done before Teniente General Don Pedro José Sáenz and witnesses José de Mier Cevallos, Don Juan Antonio de Villarevia, and Don Félix Vicente Galarza.

Juan Fernández Martínez and his wife Doña Cayetana de Acosta commit to a chaplaincy of 200 pesos cacao, founded by Francisco de Ocampo, which belongs to Presbítero Licenciado Don Manuel Guzmán. The chaplaincy is charged upon a hacienda.

A cacao hacienda in Matina, previously recognized for Presbíteros Don Manuel de Guzmán and Don José Camacho, was now granted solely to Don Manuel de Guzmán. This decision was made by an Ecclesiastical Judge's sentence.
A marginal note indicates that Gobernador Valderrama granted power of attorney to Alférez Don Carlos Galarza.

people_involved: Don Antonio de Guevara y Sáenz
summary: Presbítero Don Antonio de Guevara y Sáenz founded a chaplaincy of recited masses with a capital of 1,500 pesos, situated on a farm in the Barba valley. He stipulated that his two slaves, Juan de Chaves and Antonio de Oviedo, would be freed upon his death, and his nephew, Don Esteban de Alvarado, would become the chaplain.

people_involved: Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría
summary: Doña Antonia de Echavarría Navarro leased two haciendas in the Matina valley to José Cayetano Prado for three years, at a price of 200 pesos of cacao. Her son, Don José Miguel de Guzmán y Echavarría, signed on her behalf, and the transaction was witnessed by Teniente General Don Pedro José Sáenz.

people_involved: Capitán Don José de Mier Cevallos
summary: Capitán Don José de Mier Cevallos sold a plot of land and walls to Presbítero Don José de Chaves for 50 pesos. This plot had been acquired by the natives of Boruca pueblo as payment for a debt owed by the deceased Teniente de Gobernador Francisco de Aguirre, whose family had also died in Tierra Firme.

people_involved: Capitán Don Francisco Javier de Onamuno
General Don Diego de La Haya Fernández
summary: Capitán Don Francisco Javier de Onamuno revoked a power of attorney previously given to his deceased uncle, General Don Diego de La Haya Fernández, concerning chaplaincies in Panama. He then granted new power to Licenciado Don Francisco Javier, a cleric from Panama, to invalidate any interim chaplain appointments made by his uncle. This was done before Teniente General Don Pedro José Sáenz, who was governing due to Gobernador Valderrama's censure.

people_involved: Licenciado Presbítero Don Antonio Raimundo de Estrada
Don Luis Fernando de Liendo y Goicoechea
summary: An unnamed woman's testament details her two marriages, her four daughters from her first marriage to Alférez Juan Ginés, and the distribution of her assets. Her estate was to be divided among Licenciado Presbítero Don Antonio Raimundo de Estrada, her daughter Josefa Ruiz, Miguel Matamoros, and the children of Juan Matamoros (her grandchildren). The will was executed before escribano Don Luis Fernando de Liendo y Goicoechea in her daughter Catalina's house near Ujarrás.

people_involved: José Cayetano de la Madriz Linares
Cura Don José Miguel de Guzmán
Don Luis Fernando de Liendo y Goicoechea
summary: Juana Calderón and her son José Cayetano de la Madriz Linares obligated themselves for 900 pesos in chaplaincies, allocated to Cura Don José Miguel de Guzmán, Licenciado Don Antonio de Guevara, and Licenciado Don Manuel Sáenz. These funds were charged against a house formerly owned by Capitán Cayetano Jiménez, and the deed was prepared by escribano Goicoechea but did not pass.

people_involved: Don Juan Francisco de la Fons Vidor
Licenciado Don Manuel José González Coronel
Licenciado Don José Hermenegildo de Arlegui
Don Luis Fernando de Liendo y Goicoechea
summary: Don Juan Francisco de la Fons Vidor, a physician and surgeon, and his wife Doña María Leonor de Miranda, obligated themselves for 700 pesos charged as a chaplaincy on their house in the public plaza. This amount included 500 pesos for a chaplaincy founded by Alférez Antonio Machado and 200 pesos for one founded by Doña Eugenia de Abarca, with specific chaplains assigned to each. The transaction was recorded by escribano Goicoechea.

people_involved: Capitán Don Francisco de la Riba
summary: In Matina, Capitán Don Francisco de la Riba leased a cacao hacienda to Don Juan Bonilla for seven years at 100 pesos cacao per year. Don Juan Bonilla agreed to pay 484 pesos in Cartago and 100 pesos in Matina to Don Ventura Barraganes as part of the rent, with the agreement made provisionally before Teniente Gobernador Don Lucas Antonio de Arlegui.

In Bagaces, Don Antonio Paniagua granted power of attorney to Capitán Don Simón Paniagua, Teniente Gobernador of Villa Vieja, to represent him in a residency trial. This trial concerned charges against Don Antonio Paniagua for his service as Alcalde de la Santa Hermandad in 1783, and the power was granted before Teniente Julián Navarro.

people_involved: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco
summary: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco granted general power of attorney to Licenciado Don Santiago Moreno, a lawyer from Guatemala.

people_involved: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco
summary: An amplification of the previously granted power of attorney was made, explicitly including the faculty to substitute and revoke. Both the original and amplified documents were executed before Alcalde 1° Don Tomás Alvarado.

people_involved: R. P. Fray José Joaquín Hidalgo
summary: The R. P. Fray José Joaquín Hidalgo, Cura of Ujarrás, granted power of attorney to Don Domingo Galarza, or in his absence, to Don Mateo Mantilla, both residents of León. This power was for collecting the synod due to him from the Royal Coffers, and the document was notarized by Gobernador Acosta.

people_involved: Fray José Rafael de Jesús Jiménez
summary: Fray José Rafael de Jesús Jiménez, Cura of Atirro and Tucurrique, and Fray José Francisco de Alvarado, guardian of the city's convent, acting on behalf of Fray Sebastián Leitón, Cura of Boruca, grant power to Galarza and Mantilla for an unspecified purpose.

Governor don Tomás de Acosta establishes a chaplaincy for recited masses to be said annually for his soul and those of his wife, parents, daughter, and other relatives. He allocates 700 pesos held by don José Ignacio Rucabado and doña Josefa de Oreamuno as capital, who in turn mortgage their house and 500 cattle in Paso Hondo. Don José Ruperto Prieto is named patron until one of his legitimate sons with doña María Josefa Ruiz Fernández is ordained, with interim patrons being Presbyters don Benito Bonilla, don Juan José Oreamuno, and don José María Esquivel. A marginal note from 1802 indicates Acosta canceled this foundation due to Bonilla's death and established a new one.

Don José Nicolás de Oreamuno acknowledges a debt of 2,570 pesos to don José Ignacio Rucabado and doña Josefa de Oreamuno, which he received in the form of livestock and tools. This debt was later cancelled in 1807.

Doña Salvadora Ramírez executes the will for her deceased husband, don Manuel José García, according to a power granted on September 23, 1799. Don Manuel José García was the son of don Julián García and doña Ana de Sancho, and he had ten children with doña Salvadora.

Don Nicolás de Oreamuno acts as a guarantor for don José Antonio del Campo and don Juan Francisco de Bonilla, who are auctioneers of the aguardiente branch, for 1,130 pesos to be paid annually for five years. He mortgages 500 cattle, 50 mares, 20 horses, 10 mules, a house, corrals, and other annexes located in Paso Hondo.
Captain don Nicolás Astúa, the appointed Commander of the Matina Detachment, begins to grant power to don Juan Francisco de Bonilla. The document, however, was not concluded.

Juana Solano, widow of José Vega, makes her will in Ujarraz before Alcalde don Manuel Hidalgo. She names her common children and their spouses, as well as her grandchildren and a great-granddaughter, as her heirs.

Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla grants freedom to his slaves, Rosa Luna and her daughter Felipa Luna, whom he acquired from the estate of doña Ana Jiménez. They obtained their freedom by paying 325 pesos for their rescue.

people_involved: Teniente don José Antonio de Alvarado
summary: Lieutenant don José Antonio de Alvarado, the appointed Commander of the Malina Detachment, grants power to don Juan Francisco de Bonilla to collect funds from the Royal Coffers for the individuals of the said Detachment at the appropriate time.

Don Pedro and don Miguel Elizondo receive 1447 pesos and 4 reales from don Cornelio Fernández, which belong to a chaplaincy branch associated with the city's convent. The sum is represented by a house, various furniture, tools, and cattle located at Río Grande. The document was not signed.

Doña Antonia Arlegui, widow of don Romualdo Cuende, grants power to Miguel Ángel Marín, a resident of the town of Nicaragua, to collect the assets belonging to her children from the estate of her mother-in-law, doña Manuela Ibarra.

Santiago and Andrés Cayetano Cruz, acting for themselves and their brothers Juan Ramón and Eusebio Cruz, all residents of Villa Nueva, enter into a transaction with Captain don Mateo Mora. They commit to having two recited masses said annually by the Cura of Villa Nueva and to establishing a chaplaincy worth 100 pesos (5 pesos annually) on a cattle ranch beyond Las Amoladeras.

Doña María de Alvarado, legitimate daughter of don Pedro de Alvarado and doña Angela Guevara, makes her will. She had several natural children, including Micaela, Ramona, Guadalupe, Dominga, and Manuel Francisco (all deceased), as well as Ana Rita and María de la Luz. Guadalupe and Dominga were married and left children, and her executors are don José Santos Lombardo and doña Ana Rita de Alvarado.
Don Manuel Marchena grants freedom to his white-skinned slave, Justa, who is about 16 years old. He had purchased her in 1793 from doña María Francisca Corral.

Don Cornelio Fernández, a resident of Villa Nueva, renews his recognition of a debt of 1447 pesos and 4 reales, owed since 1796 for a chaplaincy belonging to the city's convent. He secures this debt with the same property (a house, furniture, cattle, and accessories in Río Grande, along with 3 caballerías of land) and adds an obraje on the same lands (valued at 500 pesos) and a house in Villa Nueva next to the tobacco factory (valued at 1000 pesos).
Don José Santos Lombardo obligates himself for 60 pesos and 2.5 reales in favor of three minors: doña Arcadia, doña María, and don Rafael Gallegos, who are the children of doña Guadalupe Alvarado.

A sum of 58 pesos 3 reales was adjudicated to the minor children, Don Cayetano and Doña Silvestre Ordóñez. This payment was made in representation of their deceased mother, Doña Dominga Alvarado, from the estate of Doña María Alvarado.

Don Nicolás López de Castro, a Captain and owner of the schooner 'El Paisano' from Havana, which arrived in Matina due to damage, granted power to Licenciado don Pantaleón del Águila, a lawyer from Guatemala. This power allowed Águila to seek a license from the Captaincy General to sell goods originally destined for Portobelo and San Juan.

people_involved: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco
summary: Don José Lorenzo Carazo provided a guarantee for Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco, who had won a lawsuit against Domingo Brenes for 180 pesos. This guarantee ensured that the judgment could be executed despite any potential appeal.

people_involved: Capellán Presbítero don José Antonio Carazo
Presbítero don Félix de Jesús García
summary: Doña Manuela Pastora, a long-standing debtor of a 500-peso capellanía, renewed her recognition of this debt following the death of the Capellán Presbítero don José Antonio Carazo. She acknowledged Don Manuel Carazo as the new Capellán, though a marginal note indicates that by 1802, Presbítero don Manuel Carazo had also died, and Presbítero don Félix de Jesús García was serving the capellanía.

Don Nicolás López de Castro, acting on behalf of his business partner Don Manuel Chicoy from Havana, sold an 18-year-old enslaved man named José Solano to Governor Don Tomás de Acosta for 250 pesos. José Solano was described as a tailor, literate, and of 'trigueño' complexion.

people_involved: Presbítero don Félix de Jesús García
summary: María de Jesús Quirós sold a 27-year-old mulata enslaved woman, Dominga Josefa, and her 3-year-old son, José de la Encarnación, to Presbítero don José Nicolás Carrillo, the Cura of Bigaces. The mother and son, inherited from Quirós's parents, were sold for 250 pesos and 65 pesos respectively, with Presbítero don Félix de Jesús García accepting on behalf of the buyer.

people_involved: Presbítero don Félix de Jesús García
summary: Doña Tomasa López Leitón, a widow, made a codicil to her will, declaring she had sold land in Purires to her son, Pablo José Navarro. She named her granddaughter, Gabriela Navarro, daughter of Francisca Josefa Navarro, as a legatee. Her executors were Presbítero don Félix de Jesús García and her son, Pablo Navarro.

Don Tomás de Alvarado sold a house in Villa Nueva, inherited from his deceased brother Presbítero don José Antonio Alvarado, to Don Manuel Marchena for 300 pesos. The house was encumbered with a 300-peso charge to the curacy of Villa Nueva, the annual income of which was used for religious services, a responsibility the buyer assumed.

people_involved: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Don Manuel Marchena and his wife, Doña Francisca del Corral, leased the assets of the Confraternity of Nuestra Señora de la Concepción from Mayordomo Don José Antonio Oreamuno for eight years. The assets, valued at 1,536 pesos 6 reales, included land, livestock, and a house. They agreed to pay 5% annual interest and mortgaged the leased property, with Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora acting as guarantor, mortgaging her house and a hacienda in Matina.

people_involved: Sr. Vicario don Ramón de Azofeifa
summary: Don Joaquín de Oreamuno took charge of two capellanías: one for 600 pesos cacao founded by Don Alonso de Porras, with Sr. Vicario don Ramón de Azofeifa as capellán, located in Poás; and another for 320 pesos founded by Don Francisco de Ocampo Golfín and Doña Magdalena Pérez de Luna, with Don Santana de Alvarado as capellán, previously held by Don Ramón Esquivel. Oreamuno mortgaged a small ranch in Los Horcones with 100 cattle.

Manuel Justo Chavarría, a resident, made his will, identifying his deceased parents as Joaquín Chavarría and Baltasara Trejos. He was married to María Francisca Portugués, with whom he had two sons, Francisco Santos (10) and Juan Bautista (7). He noted his wife inherited half their home from her mother, María Portugués, and declared an unfulfilled promise to visit Nuestra Señora del Pueblo del Viejo. His executors were his wife and his brother, Diego Chavarría.

María Micaela Valverde made her will, identifying her deceased parents as Francisco Valverde and Francisca Granados, and her deceased husband as José Solano. She had three living children: Félix José, who had been absent for over twenty years and was reportedly in Ciudad Real; María Josefa, a widow of Gregorio Calvo; and Gertrudis, married to Prudencio Picado. Her executors were Don Pedro Elizondo and her son-in-law, Don José Luis Gómez.

Manuel de la Trinidad Rojas, a resident of La Arenilla, made his will, identifying his deceased parents as José de Rojas and Doña Catalina Leitón. He was married to Luisa Navarro, and they had three children: Juan Esteban (deceased, married to Cecilia Cordero, leaving a 19-year-old son Antonio Abad), Ubaldo Cayetano (married to Rosa Liz), and Ana Micaela Rojas (married to Nicolás Barahona).

people_involved: Doña Antonia de Arlegui y Madriz
summary: Doña Antonia de Arlegui y Madriz, widow of don Sebastián Fernández, leased her 3000-tree cacao hacienda named Chirripó in the Matina valley to Juan Bautista Ríos. The lease was for three years, with an annual payment of 200 pesos of cacao.

Ramona Aguilar and Cosme Aguilar reported the estate of their deceased parents, Miguel Aguilar and María de los Dolores Martínez, which included four legitimate children. In 1794, their paternal uncle Cristóbal Aguilar received these goods, valued at 136 pesos cacao. Due to his advanced age, Cristóbal requested to be relieved, leading to a new appraisal of the estate at 82 pesos plata, with Ramona and Cosme receiving their shares, and Alfonso Aguilar, their cousin and tutor, receiving the shares for María de los Angeles and Cayetano.

Antonia Gertrudis Quirós, a single woman and legitimate daughter of deceased Francisco Quirós and Josefa Brígida Valverde, made her will in the barrio of Chircagres. She named her nephew Juan Carlos Barrantes and Manuel Antonio Barquero as executors, and her granddaughter María de los Dolores Martínez (wife of José Manuel Maroto, and daughter of her deceased natural son Juan de Jesús Martínez and María de los Dolores Monestel) as her universal heir. Her assets included an enslaved man, José Santiago Quirós, and an enslaved mulatilla, Antonia Josefa.

José Miguel Sánchez, a native of Pueblo del Laborío and resident of arrabal del Molino, made his will. He was the legitimate son of José Sánchez and Lorenza de la Trinidad Morales, and married to Juana de Dios López, with whom he had no children. He named his brother Manuel Nicolás Sánchez and José Antonio García as executors, his wife and his soul as heirs of a fifth part, and his mother as universal heir, also mentioning his deceased mother-in-law María Antonia Badilla and a house in Villa Nueva.

Presbítero don Félix Alvarado, acting as attorney for don Esteban Herdocia, sold a house in Cartago to don Juan Francisco Bonilla for 600 pesos. The property was bordered by houses belonging to doña María Cecilia Escalante, don Benito García, Presbítero don Félix García, and doña María Manuela Miranda. The buyer also assumed a 200-peso debt to the Archicofradía del Santísimo and Nuestra Señora del Rosario.

Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla, don Manuel Marchena, and don Lorenzo Carazo acted as guarantors for don Manuel José García Escalante, who was awarded the office of escribano for 500 pesos, payable over 5 years. Bonilla secured 200 pesos with a mortgage on a house bought from don Esteban Herdocia, Marchena secured 200 pesos with his slave Ciríaco and a pasture in Toyogres, and Carazo secured 100 pesos with 100 cattle in Sagaces.

people_involved: Alférez Real don Antonio de la Fuente
summary: Doña María Manuela Baeza, widow of don Pedro de Alvarado, made her will, listing her living children (don Juan Manuel, Beneficiado don Pedro, don Miguel Zenón, doña María Francisca, doña Ana Jacoba, doña Antonia) and her deceased son Capitán don José Rafael. She detailed her children's marriages and mentioned that don Antonio de la Fuente financed Beneficiado don Pedro's studies in 1791, and don Miguel Zenón went to Nicaragua. She left 50 pesos to María de los Dolores Alvarado, a girl she raised, and appointed don Juan Francisco Bonilla as arbiter judge, Capitán don José Ignacio Rucabado and don Baltasar de Echavarría as accountants, and her sons don Pedro and don Juan Manuel, along with don Ignacio Miguel Llórente, as executors.

people_involved: Doña María Francisca López del Corral
summary: Doña María Francisca López del Corral granted freedom to her enslaved woman, Manuela Petronila Miranda, who was about 50 years old and of mixed white and brown complexion. Doña María Francisca had purchased Manuela Petronila from doña Francisca de Miranda.

María de Jesús Valverde, a widow, sold an enslaved man named José Isidro Valverde to don Manuel Marchena for 200 pesos plata. José Isidro, 18 years old, of brown complexion with distinct facial features, was inherited by María de Jesús from her mother, Josefa Valverde.

people_involved: Cura don Antonio Ramón de Azofeifa
summary: Cura don Antonio Ramón de Azofeifa sold an enslaved man named José Solano to don Manuel Chicoy and don Nicolás López de Castro, merchants from Havana, for 250 pesos. José Solano, 18 years old, a tailor's official who could read and write a little, had been purchased by the Cura from Tomasa Solano, a resident of Ujarrás.

people_involved: Doña María Francisca López del Corral
summary: Doña María Francisca López del Corral sold a 4-year-old mulatilla named Nicolasa to don Manuel Marchena for 100 pesos. Nicolasa was the daughter of another enslaved woman belonging to Doña María Francisca, named María de Jesús, and was described as having a white complexion, black eyes, and straight hair.

Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla sold a house and its walled lot to don José Nicolás de Oreamuno for 450 pesos, with a payment deadline in 1801 (later cancelled in 1803). The property, which Bonilla had acquired from don José Santos Lombardo, bordered properties of don Alejandro Lampar, don José Antonio del Campo, the deceased doña María de Alvarado, and don José Antonio Alvarado.

Doña Ana Jacoba de Alvarado, a widow, sold an enslaved man named Diego Carazo to don José Nicolás de Oreamuno for 190 pesos. Diego Carazo, of advanced age and pardo complexion, had a contracted right hand from syphilis and a healed fractured right thigh, and was acquired by Doña Ana Jacoba through adjudication in her deceased husband don Francisco Carazo's estate.

people_involved: don José Rafael de la Rosa
summary: Doña Antonia Micaela de Segura made her will, detailing her two marriages, her legitimate children (Presbítero Roque Jacinto, Presbítero don José Antonio Valentín, and don Manuel Bernardino), and two natural children (Pablo and Rosa Josefa). She left 100 pesos to Rosa Josefa and named her sons José Antonio and Bernardino de la Cueva as heirs, with Presbítero don Benito Bonilla and don José Rafael de la Rosa as executors.

locations: Nuestra Señora de la Concepción de Matina
people_involved: Doña Isidora de la Madriz Linares
don Manuel de la Torre y Romero
Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero
summary: Doña Isidora de la Madriz Linares sold two 'caballerías' of land in Santana to the cofradías and pious works of San Nicolás de Tolentino, San Francisco de Paula, Nuestra Señora de la Concepción de Matina, and Señor San José, represented by their mayordomo don Manuel de la Torre y Romero. This land was part of a legacy from Licenciado don Manuel Francisco Martínez Cubero for her and her three siblings.
Antonia Gertrudis Quirós, residing in Churuca, sold an enslaved mulata named Antonia Josefa Quirós, aged 20, to Miguel Marín, a resident of the villa of Nicaragua, for 200 pesos plata.

Juan Antonio Matamoros made his will, identifying his deceased natural mother María Estéfana Calvo and his wife María Francisca Chavarría. He listed their children: Mariano, Rita, Hipólita, María Antonia (all adults), and José Julián (16 years old), and mentioned the husbands of his daughters. His wife and son José Mariano were named executors.

people_involved: Doña Minucia Josefa Fernández de la Pastora
Beneficiado don Juan José de Sierra
summary: Doña Minucia Josefa Fernández de la Pastora granted general power of attorney to her sons, don Esteban and don José Gordiano Herdocia, residing in Nicaragua, specifically to collect assets from the estate of her deceased legitimate son, Beneficiado don Juan José de Sierra, of whom she is the sole heir.

people_involved: Doña Baltasara de la Madriz Linares
Beneficiado don José Miguel Sancho de Castañeda
Presbítero don Juan José de la Madriz Linares
summary: Doña Baltasara de la Madriz Linares, widow, granted power of attorney to don José Antonio Polonio Carazo to represent her in the estate of her legitimate son, Beneficiado don José Miguel Sancho de Castañeda, who died on August 19th of this year in Pueblo del Viejo, Nicaragua, and named her as his heir. The power also included participating in the sale of a house that belonged to the deceased Presbítero don Juan José de la Madriz Linares.

Juan Antonio Rojas, on behalf of himself and his wife Lorenza Valverde, sold an enslaved mulata named Juana Rojas, 23 years old, to don Joaquín de Oreamuno for 250 pesos plata. Juana Rojas was inherited by Lorenza from her mother, Josefa Valverde.

Tomás Granados, from Toyogres, made his will, identifying his deceased parents and his wife, María de las Nieves Ulloa. He listed their children, including those who died without marrying (Joaquín de Jesús and Polonia), and the spouses of his living children. He also mentioned two grandsons and named Teniente Pedro José Carvajal and his daughter Tomasa Josefa as executors.

people_involved: don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco
summary: A judicial sale by auction was made to don José María de Peralta for 255 pesos for a 'chácara' (small farm), house, and fences in the barrio del Aguacaliente. This sale was the result of an execution pursued by don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco against Domingo Brenes.

Don Joaquín de Alvarado emancipated his 27-year-old legitimate son, don Manuel Alvarado, and donated to him a quarter share of his residence, another property in Las Piedras, and a share in the enslaved woman Paula Alvarado.

Presbítero don Benito Bonilla sold a walled plot of land, 75 varas square, near La Puebla, on the main street of Nuestra Señora de Los Angeles, to Agustín Núñez for 66 pesos plata. The land was acquired in two lots, one from doña María García and another from don Andrés Bolante, with a portion previously ceded to Micaela Valverde.

Agustín Núñez, a master tailor, took on Santiago Otárola as an apprentice for 6 years, and Jesús Arcia as an apprentice for 5 years. Santiago is the son of Ventura Bejarano, and Jesús is the son of Micaela Arcia.
Doña Joaquina Miranda, a widow, sold an enslaved mulato named Damasio Miranda, approximately 25 years old, to don Juan Francisco de Bonilla.
A record describes a male slave, son of Benita Barahona, with specific physical features including a 'roma' nose and 'azambado' color. His price was 200 pesos plata.

Don José Ruperto Prieto, acting on a power of attorney from 1793, granted the will of the deceased Doña Mariana Alvarado. She was the legitimate daughter of Don Pedro de Alvarado and Doña Angela de Guevara, and had passed away on December 12th of the previous year. She was first married to Don José Cruz, with whom she had three children (Rafaela, Manuel, and Pedro, all over 25), and later married Don Manuel Cuestas without having more children. Don José Ruperto Prieto was named executor after the death of Presbítero Don Gregorio Bonilla.

people_involved: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco
summary: Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla and Don Manuel Marchena owed Don Ramón Palacio, a merchant from Peru residing in Cartago, 2948 pesos for goods, with payment due the following June. A marginal note indicates this obligation was cancelled on April 20, 1803, by Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco, acting with power from Don Nicolás López de Castro, to whom the debt had been endorsed.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Antonio María de la Fuente
Presbítero Don Rafael Baltasar de la Fuente
