summary: Don Antonio de la Fuente, Alférez Real of the Cartago Ayuntamiento and son of deceased parents from Astorga, granted power to his wife, Doña María Francisca de Alvarado, to make his will while he was ill in bed. He renounced the value of his positions as Alférez Real and Anotador de hipotecas for Cartago and Nicoya, ceding these values to the King due to a debt related to a case against Don Manuel de Zea. He named his wife and two absent priest sons as executors, and listed twelve children as his heirs, with Don Juan Manuel de Alvarado also appointed as an agent.

Several residents of Aguacaliente, who had purchased land from the succession of Don Félix Meneses, agreed upon rules for land use to resolve ongoing disputes. The agreement stipulated specific periods for animal grazing, designated areas for planting, and regulations for wood cutting, requiring non-residents to pay the community. It also outlined responsibilities for barrio celadores to maintain fences and penalties for neighbors who intentionally damaged enclosures.

people_involved: Unnamed wife of Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla
summary: Teniente Coronel Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla, acknowledging the harmful effects of games of chance, pledged on his honor to abstain from prohibited gambling for one year to avoid upsetting his wife. He specified exceptions for certain card games played purely for diversion and agreed to a 500-peso fine to San Joaquín in the Parish if he broke his promise.

Fray Jacinto Maestre, cura doctrinero for Cot, Quircot, and Tobosi, and Fray Juan López, cura doctrinero for Atirro and Tucurrique, granted power to Don Domingo Galarza and Don Mateo Mantilla, residents of León, to collect outstanding synods.

José Antonio Calderón, a resident of Ujarrás, sold a slave named Mariano Solano for 250 pesos to Don Nicolás López de Castro, a resident of Cartago preparing to depart for León, and his partner Don Manuel Chicoy, who resided in La Habana. Mariano Solano was described as approximately 18 years old, 'azambado' in color, with specific facial features and hair.

people_involved: Cofradía de Nuestra Señora de los Angeles
summary: Don Antonio de la Fuente, acting with power of attorney from Don Sebastián José de Robles, a resident of Santa María in Panama, sold a runaway slave named Ambrosio for 200 pesos to the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora de los Angeles and its Mayordomo, Don Joaquín de Oreamuno. Ambrosio was described as about 20 years old, 'zarabo' in color, with an ugly face and a distinctive limp caused by a 'clavo de buba' on his heel.

Don Máximo Guindos, a resident of Acoyapa, Nicaragua, granted power of attorney to Don Pedro Ruiz, or alternatively to Don Eusebio Chavarría, to represent him in the estate proceedings of his deceased mother, Doña Francisca Meza.

María Jerónima Gairo, widow of Francisco Delgado, made her will, naming her children from that marriage: Rita Josefa, who was married to Cayetano Meneses; Félix de la Rosa, who was married to María Josefa Alfaro; and Marcos Antonio.

Francisco Polanro and his wife Micaela Alfaro sold an enslaved boy named Juan de Jesús, 6 years old, for 100 pesos to José Lorenzo Carazo. Juan de Jesús was the son of Ana Josefa, another enslaved person previously sold by Polanro to Pedro Solares.

people_involved: José Antonio Valentín de la Cueva
summary: José Antonio Valentín de la Cueva, Manuel Bernardino de la Cueva, and Josefa Ro-a Segura, acting as heirs of the late Antonia Micaela de Segura, sold a house on Calle de la Soledad for 300 pesos to José Francisco de Oreamuno. The property was bordered by houses belonging to Antonia Mario, the late María de Alvarado, Tomasa Gómez, and the late Feliciana Rojas Guzmán.

Joaquín de Oreamuno, as Mayordomo of the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora de los Angeles, sold the enslaved man Ambrosio Robles to Presbítero Pedro José Alvarado for 200 pesos. Oreamuno had previously purchased Robles from Antonio de la Fuente, noting that Robles no longer had a heel mark or limp.

José Francisco Quesada made his will, stating he is married to María de los Santos Jiménez, widow of Juan Cayetano Calvo, and has no children of his own. He raised his 6-year-old nephew Ignacio de Quesada (son of his brother Sixto) and his stepson José de las Mercedes Calvo (son of his wife and her first husband), who uses the Quesada surname. His executors are Presbítero José Rafael de la Rosa and Salvador de Oreamuno, and his heir is his father Jacinto de Quesada.

Ana Tacoba de Alvarado, widow of Francisco Carazo and guardian of their children, sold a piece of land measuring 18 caballerías and 4 cuerdas in Santa Ularia, across the Río Grande, to José Miguel González for 450 pesos.

Antonia Masís, a widow, sold an enslaved man named Francisco de Borja, 25 years old and son of her enslaved woman Manuela, to Presbítero Rafael Arnesto de Troya for 300 pesos. Her son, Pedro García, signed the document on her behalf.

Mateo Camacho sold a house in El Fatal, which he inherited from his deceased wife María de Arlegui, to José María del Valle for 100 pesos. José María del Valle is a resident of the city and captain of the pardo company in the Aserrí valley.
The year 1801 began with Francisco Luis Ruiz serving as the First Mayor and Notary, a role later taken over by José Ruperto Prieto.

Subteniente Juan de la Rosa Maitín and Jesús Ruiz posted bail for José de la Trinidad Pacheco and José Jerónimo Moya, who were imprisoned as suspected accomplices in the homicide of Juana María Solano. The case was cancelled in 1805 due to their acquittal.

Antonia Josefa Mondragón made her will, mentioning a pasture called La Quinta in El Cangrejal that she had sold to Félix Bonilla for 600 pesos without a formal deed. She appointed José González Cuadra as executor, left one-third of her assets to her granddaughter María del Carmen Mondragón, and named her son José Fermín Mondragón as universal heir.

Cura Antonio Ramón de Azofeifa leased 100 head of cattle, valued at 400 pesos, to Manuel Marchena for two years at a 5% interest rate. The cattle belonged to the pious works of San Nicolás de Tolentino and Nuestra Señora de la Soledad.

people_involved: Manuel Antonio Guzmán Portocarrero y Garlín
José Manuel Guzmán Portocarrero y Garlín
José Miguel Guzmán Portocarrero y Garlín
summary: María Teresa Garlín, widow of Manuel Guzmán, made her will, listing her children and grandchildren. Her husband had drowned in Matina port approximately 30 years prior. Among her assets was an enslaved mulatto named Manuel Antonio.
Sebastián de Guevara vowed to abstain from all games of chance, agreeing to pay a 200-peso fine to the church of San Pedro, which was to be rebuilt in the city, if he broke his vow.
Francisco and Mateo Ramírez, along with Juan José and Francisco Aguilar, sold a piece of land belonging to the Ramírez family in Laguna de Birrís to José de los Angeles Loaiza for 20 pesos.

Nicolás de Oreamuno sold an enslaved woman named Marcela González, 36 years old and inherited from his parents, to Mateo Mantilla, a resident of León, for 200 pesos. Joaquín de Oreamuno accepted the sale on behalf of the buyer.

Pedro José Elizondo granted general power of attorney to Manuel García Escalante. Elizondo cited his inability to stay in the city due to illness from the climate and his need to personally oversee his indigo hacienda, located over 14 leagues away.
Presbítero Félix de Jesús García began a transaction, though the details are incomplete in the record.

people_involved: Don José Antonio Conde de la Peña
summary: Don José Antonio Conde de la Peña, a resident of León, sold a 13-year-old enslaved girl named Gabriela García for 250 pesos. Don José María de Peralta acted as the commissioner for the unnamed buyer.
Juan de Dios Brenes granted jail bail to Nicolás Cárdenas, who was undergoing criminal proceedings.

people_involved: Don Juan Francisco Sáenz Vázquez Coronado y Quintanilla
summary: Don José Antonio Sáenz, son of the deceased Don Juan Francisco Sáenz Vázquez Coronado y Quintanilla and Doña Francisca Martínez, made his will. He was married to Doña Ana Teresa Monestel, daughter of Francisco Monestel and Doña Micaela Zamdra, and had three children: Antonia Rudesinda (married to Fernando Marcelino Valverde), María Magdalena, and Manuela Josefa (both single). He also named his stepson, Don Juan Antonio Segura, and appointed his wife and José Joaquín Coronel as executors.
Ubaldo Quirós, acting as the tutor for the minor children Agustín and Laureara, received 135 pesos and 2.5 reales from the inheritance of their deceased father, Gregorio Quirós.
Don Felipe Sancho y Castañeda granted general power of attorney to Don Francisco Albert, a resident of Guatemala.

people_involved: Doña María Francisca López del Corral
Presbítero Don José Alejandro Escalante y Paniagua
summary: Doña María Francisca López del Corral sold a 4-year-old enslaved mulatto boy named Joaquín, son of her enslaved woman Tomasa, to Presbítero Don José Alejandro Escalante y Paniagua for 100 pesos. The sale was not accepted by the Presbítero, and Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla subsequently took possession of Joaquín for the same price in 1802.

Residents of El Tejar granted power of attorney to Félix Solano to petition the Bishop. They sought to prevent the sale of lands belonging to Nuestra Señora de la Concepción, currently held by Don Manuel Marchena, and proposed that the lands remain with the Virgin or benefit the barrio, offering to cover Marchena's outstanding interest payments.

Doña Joaquina Corrales guaranteed Don Manuel Marchena, the auctioneer of the city's tithes for the current triennium (1529 pesos 4 reales annually), by mortgaging two houses, a hacienda in Matina, and another in the ejidos of Cartago.

Doña Joaquina Corrales provided a further guarantee for Don Manuel Marchena, covering 180 pesos 4 reales corresponding to the Royal Ninths from the tithes, using the same previously mortgaged properties.
José Antonio Rojas sold a fenced property in Agua Caliente, which included a house, a sugar mill, a sugarcane field, and a plantain grove, to Don Manuel Sáenz for 100 pesos.

people_involved: Doña Rosa de la Madriz Linares
summary: Doña Rosa de la Madriz Linares, a widow, sold half a building plot in the city to Doña Ana Elizondo for 50 pesos.

Doña Juana Solís sold her rights to lands in Las Cóncavas to Mariano Matamoros for 100 pesos. These lands had previously belonged to her deceased brother Manuel Meléndez and before that to Doña Micaela Chinchilla, and were bounded by the Blanquillo and Cañas rivers and the Ujarrás road.

people_involved: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora, Doña Ana Jacoba de Alvarado, Don José María Peralta, and Don Félix de Bonilla each provided a guarantee of 750 pesos for Don Manuel José García Escalante, who was appointed Lieutenant of Royal Officials for the province.

people_involved: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora
Don Antonio de Soto y Barahona
Presbítero Don Félix de Jesús García y Muñoz
Spouse of Don Félix de Bonilla
summary: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora, a tenant of a chaplaincy founded in 1731 by Don Antonio de Soto y Barahona, recognized Presbítero Don Félix de Jesús García y Muñoz as her creditor. This recognition followed the death of previous chaplains and the appointment of García y Muñoz, a great-grandson of the founder, as the new chaplain. Her house was mortgaged. (A marginal note indicates Don Félix de Bonilla and his spouse became new tenants in 1805).

José de la Rosa Loaiza made his will in his house in Agua Caliente. He was the legitimate son of the deceased Domingo Quirós and Juina Loaiza. He was married to María Francisca Solano, with whom he had four children: Manuel Gregorio (married to Antonia Sáenz), José de los Angeles (married to Juana González), Josefa Liberata (married to Hilario Bolívar), and Rosa Joaquina (who died as a minor).

people_involved: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora granted power of attorney to Don Juan Vicente Villacorta, a merchant from the villa of Nicaragua, to sell a cacao hacienda in that villa. The hacienda was inherited from her deceased son, Presbítero Don Juan de Sierra, and she instructed Villacorta to prioritize her other two sons, Don Esteban and Don José Gordiano Herdocia, in the sale.

Don José Manuel Guzmán made his will. He was the legitimate son of the deceased Don Manuel Guzmán and Doña Teresa Garlín. He was married to Doña Juana Andrea Ugalde, daughter of Don Faustino Ugalde and Doña Rita de Alvarado, and they had no children. He raised Juan Pérez, his wife's half-brother, and left him some assets. He also named Cornelio, son of Águeda Guzmán, as a legatee. His mother was named heir, and his brother Don Miguel Guzmán and Don Manuel Anastasio Conejo were named executors.

people_involved: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora sold her cacao hacienda named La Chaquira, located in the villa of Nicaragua and comprising over 12,000 cacao trees, to her sons Don Esteban and Don José Gordiano Herdocia for 4000 pesos. She had inherited this hacienda from her deceased son, Beneficiado Don Juan de Sierra.

Don Joaquín de Oreamuno granted general power of attorney to Don Mateo Mantilla, a resident of León, and in his absence, to Don Anselmo Jiménez, a resident of 'this city' (likely Cartago) who also resides in León.

Presbítero don Juan José Oreamuno grants power to don Rafael Agustín de Ayesta, Secretary of the Episcopal Curia of León, to take possession of a chaplaincy founded by Governor don Tomás de Acosta, which has a principal of 800 pesos.

people_involved: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora agrees with her sons, don Esteban and don José Gordiano Herdocia, to return 1000 pesos received for a hacienda she sold them. In return, they must pay her one peso daily for life. Doña Manuela does not sign due to illness.

people_involved: doña Luisa de Guzmán y Echavarría
Bachiller don Baltasar de la Fuente
summary: Matías Román and his wife María de los Angeles Valverde take charge of 200 pesos from a chaplaincy founded by doña Luisa de Guzmán y Echavarría, for which Bachiller don Baltasar de la Fuente is the Chaplain. This sum was previously held by doña Antonia de Alvarado and her husband don José Antonio de Alvarado. Román and Valverde mortgage their house and corresponding plot, which borders doña Dionisia Fallas's house, maestro José Antonio Sáenz's plot, and the Plaza de San Nicolás.

José Hermenegildo Navarro, from the barrio of Purires, makes his will. He is the legitimate son of deceased Manuel Antonio Navarro and doña Tomasa López Leitón, and is married to María Isabel Piedra. He names his ten children, appoints don Joaquín de Oreamuno as arbiter, don Lorenzo Carazo as accountant, and don Alejandro Lampar as defender of minors. His wife and son Antonio de los Reyes are named executors.

Don Manuel Oreamuno sells a piece of land in Rincón de la Laguna to Pablo Calderón for 50 pesos. The land is located on the road from Cartago to Los Valles and has no specific boundaries as it is in the middle of the savanna.

Doña Antonia de Alvarado, with judicial license due to her husband don José Antonio de Alvarado's long absence from Guatemala City, sells a pasture in Cetro Grande to José Antonio Solano for 372 pesos. Her son, don Joaquín de Alvarado, signs on her behalf.

Don Santiago Bonilla assumes a debt of 750 pesos to the executors of the deceased don Juan José Granados. Granados, a resident of Nicaragua and lessee of the tithes of Esparza, had ceded the tithes of the Andecho district to Bonilla for 250 pesos annually for three years. Don Nicolás Castro, a resident of Villa Nueva, had collected the tithes for Granados since January 1st of this year, and is now obligated to render accounts to Bonilla.

people_involved: doña María de Laya y Bolívar
summary: Doña María de Laya y Bolívar sells her share and right in 2.5 caballerías and 7 cordadas of land in Río Grande to don Juan José Acosta, a resident of Cubujuquí de Heredia, for 62 pesos and 4 reales.

people_involved: Presbítero don José Rafael Arnesto de Troya
summary: Doña Jacoba de Alvarado, don Lorenzo Carazo (as tutor for doña Gertrudis Carazo), and don José Antonio García (as agent for doña Micaela Carazo), all heirs of doña Petronila Carazo, sell a house in Cartago to Presbítero don José Rafael Arnesto de Troya. The house is located on the main street leading to the Soledad church and borders properties of a chaplaincy, doña Josefa Oreamuno, doña Antonia Masís, and doña Bartola Oreamuno. The price is 700 pesos.

Nicolás Araya sells a pasture in Llano de Ujarrás to Miguel Antonio Matamoros for 40 pesos. Araya had acquired the land from the deceased Felipe Jiménez. The pasture measures 520 varas long and 220 varas wide, is fenced by a ditch, and borders Río Blanquillo, lands of the Ramírezes, Francisco Araya's fences, and the grantor's own fences.

Manuel Jiménez, son of the deceased Felipe Jiménez and María Arias, acknowledges receipt of his share of 310 pesos left by his grandfather Manuel Antonio Jiménez. This money was for him and his siblings Carlos, Rafaela, and Florencio. His mother, María Arias, had already satisfied Carlos and Rafaela's shares. Manuel takes charge of Florencio's share as his tutor, with his brother Carlos Jiménez acting as guarantor.

people_involved: doña María Gertrudis de Laya y Bolívar
summary: Alcalde don Isidro de Oreamuno and his wife doña Justa de Bonilla grant freedom to their 19-year-old mulatto slave, Petronila. Petronila was inherited by doña Justa from her parents, don Andrés de Bonilla and doña María Gertrudis de Laya y Bolívar, and is the daughter of another slave named Marcelina de Bonilla. The value of Petronila, 200 pesos, falls within the fifth of the grantors' assets, which exceeds 1000 pesos.

Don Nicolás López de Castro, a merchant from Havana, grants power of attorney to don Ángel Núñez del Arco, and failing him, to don Manuel García Escalante, for all his lawsuits and business in "this province."

Capitán don Joaquín de Oreamuno, majordomo of the factory of the Holy Parish Church in Cartago, grants power to don Mateo Mantilla, a resident of León, and don Apolonio Carazo, who is soon departing for León, to collect Royal Ninths and chaplaincies belonging to the Parish.

people_involved: R. P. Fray José Francisco de Alvarado
summary: R. P. Fray José Francisco de Alvarado, the doctrinal priest of the town of Barba, grants power.

Don José Lorenzo Carazo, acting as tutor for Doña Gertrudis Carazo, sold the slave Juan Antonio, described as 35-40 years old and son of Rita Barahona, to Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla for 200 pesos plata. The sale included all defects except 'gota coral' or 'mal de corazón'.

people_involved: Don Manuel de la Torre y Romero
summary: Cura Don Ramón de Azofeifa and Juan de Dios Brenes replaced Don Juan Francisco Bonilla and Don José Miguel Ocaña as guarantors for Don Manuel de la Torre y Romero, the Lieutenant of the Royal Subordinate Treasury, each for 500 pesos. Azofeifa mortgaged 4 slaves and their rents, while Brenes mortgaged his house, 6 caballerías of land, and 12 mules.

people_involved: Doña Ana Rita Gómez de Lara
summary: Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla and Doña Ana Rita Gómez de Lara fulfilled a promise made at the marriage of their grandniece, Doña Paulina Fajardo, to Coronel Don Francisco Javier Navarro. They delivered assets valued at 4717 pesos 7 reales, including houses, land, cacao trees, cattle, and other goods. Navarro acknowledged receipt and offered two slaves, Pedro Guzmán and Juana Guerrero, and 1000 pesos plata as arras.
Coronel Don Francisco Javier Navarro granted general power of attorney to Don José Asenjo, a procurador of the Intendencia de León.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Juan José de Oreamuno
Presbítero Don Rafael de la Rosa
summary: Don Tomás de Acosta founded a capellanía for masses for the souls in purgatory, including his family members. The principal of 700 pesos was held by Don José Ignacio de Rucabado and Doña Josefa de Oreamuno, who guaranteed it with a mortgage on their house and 500 cattle in Pasohondo. Don José Ruperto Prieto was named patron and chaplain, with interim chaplains until his son, Don Joaquín Prieto (then 10 years old), could be ordained. In 1816, Acosta added the city's cura as an interim chaplain, with his wife signing for him due to his poor eyesight.

Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla acted as guarantor for Coronel Don Francisco Javier Navarro, who had been awarded the office of Regidor and Fiel Ejecutor for 150 pesos. Bonilla mortgaged his house opposite the San Francisco church, valued at 2500 pesos.

Don Nicolás Castro, a resident of San José, owed Doña Manuela Baeza 200 pesos at 5% annual interest. He mortgaged his house in San José and a cattle ranch with 12 caballerías of land called Aranjuíz in the jurisdiction of Esparza.

Don Tomás de Acosta sold the slave José Solano to Don Ángel Núñez del Are, acting as attorney for Don Nicolás López de Castro (resident in León), for 250 pesos. Payment was made via a draft against Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla.

Pedro Alpízar, a resident of San José, became guarantor for José Manuel Solera for the cost of 12 caballerías of land in Turrúcares and the expenses for its title and possession. Alpízar mortgaged a sugar mill, sugarcane, a pot, oxen, and his dwelling house, all valued over 500 pesos.
José Manuel Solera, a resident of Alajuela, granted general power of attorney for lawsuits to Don José Asenjo, or in his absence, to Don Carlos Portocarrero.

Fray Sebastián Leitón, Cura of Atirro and Tucurrique, and Fray Rafael de Jesús Jiménez, Cura of Pacaca, granted power of attorney to Don Domingo Galarza, or in his absence, to Don Mateo Mantilla (residents of León), to collect synods owed to them as curas.

Subteniente Don José Lorenzo Carazo, appointed tutor of the mentally ill Doña Gertrudis Carazo, received all her assets, totaling 4313 pesos 5.5 reales. These assets included a house, a cattle ranch (El Zapotal), a cacao plantation in Matina, and slaves. He committed to fulfilling his duties.

Teniente Don Manuel Hidalgo and his wife Doña María García took charge of two capellanía branches: one for 915 pesos cacao belonging to the convent of San Bartolomé de Barba, and another for 150 pesos plata belonging to the parish church, founded by Tomás de Chaves and located in Murciélago. Don Isidro de Oreamuno previously held these capellanías.
Doña Paulina Fajardo leased two cacao plantations to Bartolomé Guerrero.

Gertrudis Cecilia Calderón, a single legitimate daughter of deceased parents, made her will. She designated her assets for masses for her soul and those of her parents and other relatives. Don Joaquín de Oreamuno was named as her executor.

Manuel Quirós and his wife María Encarnación Brenes committed to pay 443 pesos 2 reales to the three minor children of the deceased Andrés Soto. These children, José Joaquín, José Cayetano, and Toribio del Carmen, were from María Encarnación Brenes's first marriage to Andrés Soto.

people_involved: Presbítero don Félix de Jesús García
summary: Presbítero don Félix de Jesús García granted a general power of attorney to don Francisco Javier Navarro. This legal action transferred broad authority to Navarro on behalf of García.

Manuel Antonio Morales and his wife María Josefa Montoya committed to pay 83 pesos 6 reales to the minor Rafael. This payment represented the value of Rafael's inheritance from his father, Rafael Carlos Fuentes, who was María Josefa Montoya's first husband.

José Marcito, natural son of Josefa Palomino and widower of Juana Madrigal, made his will. He named his current wife Rita Feliciana Pacheco and Capitán José Miguel Cárdenas as executors, and a 7-year-old boy named Brunf as a legatee. The will detailed his children from his first marriage and appointed a judge-arbitrator and accountant.

Don José Antonio García, legitimate son of deceased parents, made his will. He listed his wife, Doña Romualda Ramírez, and their children, including Don Onofre who was married to Doña Ventura Esquivel. His son Don Onofre and Don José Antonio García Ramírez were named as executors.

people_involved: Presbítero don José Rafael Arnesto de Troya
summary: Don Pedro José Elizondo sold a pasture located in Sabana Grande to Presbítero don José Rafael Arnesto de Troya for 375 pesos. This transaction had occurred four and a half years prior to this record.

people_involved: Presbítero don José Rafael Arnesto de Troya
summary: Presbítero don Rafael Arnesto de Troya granted a general power of attorney to don Antonio de la Fuente. This legal instrument empowered de la Fuente to act on behalf of the Presbítero.
The Procurador Síndico, don Manuel Alvarado, granted a general power of attorney to Coronel don Joaquín de Arechavala. Don Joaquín was noted as a resident of León.

Doña Juana de Alvarado sold a quarter of a solar (plot of land) in Cartago to doña Jacoba de Alvarado for 92 pesos 7 reales. Don Joaquín Alvarado later approved this sale in October 1803, exercising his right to the property.

Don Manuel Hidalgo sold a pasture in Sabana Grande to don Félix Bonilla for 750 pesos. The property was described as being fenced with stone and wood, bordering the royal road of Las Amoladeras to the South.

Ana Águeda Guzmán provided a receipt to don Miguel Guzmán for 50 pesos, which was a legacy from the deceased don Manuel Guzmán to Cornelio, Ana Águeda's son. She committed to deliver the funds to Cornelio upon his majority, with Juan de Dios Brenes acting as guarantor.
Don Francisco Javier Navarro granted a general power of attorney to don Félix Machado. Don Félix Machado was noted as residing in the town of Rivas de Nicaragua.

Doña María Francisca del Corral sold an enslaved girl named Joaquina Raimunda to don Manuel Marchena for 140 pesos plata. Joaquina Raimunda was described as being about 9 years old, light-skinned, with large eyes and a slight lisp.

people_involved: Don Juan Francisco de la Madriz
summary: Doña Rosa Madriz, daughter of deceased parents and widow of don Tomás del Corral, made her will. She listed her deceased and living children, including Don Vicente and Doña Venancia, who were named as heirs along with her granddaughter Doña Ángela del Corral. Her assets included two cacao plantations in San Miguel, Matina valley, and she bequeathed 25 pesos to her granddaughter Joaquina.

people_involved: Doña María Ignacia de la Rosa
Presbítero don Rafael de la Rosa
summary: Doña María Ignacia de la Rosa, a native of Panama, made a codicil to her will. She mentioned her two sons, Don Gregorio and Don José Lino, and left 130 pesos for her minor grandson José Joaquín, to be managed by Presbítero don Rafael de la Rosa. Doña Gertrudis Zavaleta was a legatee, and Presbítero don Juan José Oreamuno was named as executor.

people_involved: Don Manuel de la Torre y Romero
summary: Don Manuel de la Torre y Romero and his wife doña Antonia Jiménez, who were responsible for the administration of tobacco, stamped paper, playing cards, and gunpowder, named don Joaquín de Oreamuno and Juan de Dios Brenes as guarantors for their administration.

Don José Antonio del Campo, a native of Spain and resident of Cartago, granted a general power of attorney to don Francisco Panlagua. Don Francisco Panlagua was identified as a Procurador in Guatemala.

María Sabina González, legitimate daughter of deceased parents from Cartago and widow of Benito Picado, made her will. She listed her children, noting that several were deceased, and identified Juan Picado as a living son.

Don Miguel Guzmán and Doña Antonia García declared receiving 69 pesos 4 reales from José Antonio Fernández, related to the guardianship of María de los Angeles, daughter of the deceased José Antonio Mata and María Cayetana. They committed to holding the money at 5% annual interest and mortgaged their house. A later document from October 19, 1815, shows Yg lacia Bonilla (widow of José Antonio Fernández) and Manuel José Pereira (husband of María de los Angeles Mata) canceling this obligation. Ramón Guzmán signed for his mother, Doña Antonia.
Don Francisco Javier Navarro received in deposit the assets that were embargoed from Don Tomás Alvarado the previous day.

María Micaela Valverde made a codicil to her will. She had previously sold a house to Félix Camaño and had given certain assets to her daughter Gertrudis after the will, which are to be included in her legitimate inheritance.
María Micaela Valverde sold a house in Cartago to Félix Camaño for 150 silver pesos.

José Francisco Oreamuno sold a house to Presbyter Don Félix de Jesús García for 188 pesos. The house was inherited by Oreamuno's wife, Manuela Badilla, from her parents, and its boundaries were described in relation to houses owned by Félix Camaño, María Dolores Pacheco, Rafael Pacheco, and Francisca Pacheco.

Don José Antonio Jiménez made a codicil to his 1790 will, augmenting his assets with two enslaved children, Joaquín and Nicolasa, and other items. He granted freedom to his enslaved woman, Manuela, and specified that some goods given to his son, Don Ramón, should not be part of his legitimate inheritance, but 206 pesos he delivered to him should be. Don Lorenzo Carazo and Don Felipe Sancho were named as arbiters.

Juan Antonio Rojas sold an enslaved woman named María Juliana Valverde, 17 years old, of 'aindiado' color and straight hair, to Don Joaquín de Oreamuno for 225 pesos. Juan José Rodríguez, Rojas's son-in-law, signed for the seller.

Don Antonio de la Fuente, Don Joaquín de Oreamuno, and Don Francisco Javier Navarro granted general power of attorney to Presbyter Don Antonio María de la Fuente, an attorney of the Royal Audiencia, or failing him, to Procurator Don Francisco Albar. This power concerned a barracks to be built in the city and a pending lawsuit against the Procurator Síndico for alleged injuries.

Don Joaquín de Oreamuno posted bail for Don Tomás de Alvarado, who was being prosecuted for allegedly revealing the secrecy of two dispatches from the Superiority. The case was sent to the Intendente of León for sentencing, and Alvarado was allowed to leave prison for his home under bail due to serious illness, following an examination by Juan de la Rosa Maitín.

Don Miguel Guzmán, as executor for Don Manuel Guzmán, gave a receipt to Presbyter Don Ignacio Ramírez for 152 pesos owed. In turn, several Ugalde siblings (Juana Andrea, Fermina, Anacida, Guadalupe, and Silvestre via his attorney Fermín García) and José Ángel Pérez (husband of Guadalupe) gave a receipt to Don Miguel for their share of their guardianships and those of their deceased siblings, Lorenza and Gabriel Ugalde.

Don Pedro José Elizondo took charge of a chaplaincy branch belonging to the Benefice of Bagaces, valued at 122 pesos, with permission from Don Lorenzo Carazo, attorney for the Bagaces priest, Presbyter Don Manuel Joaquín Núñez. Don Luis Arias, as guarantor for the deceased Don Rafael Morales, redeemed this sum. Elizondo mortgaged land in San Bernardo and provided Pascual Bejarano as an additional guarantor.

Doña Bárbara Jiménez, natural daughter of Don José Antonio Jiménez and Doña Manuela Clemencia Almandos, made her will. She was single and named her nieces María de Jesús and Josefa Mayorga, and her servants Paula and María Inza as legatees. Presbyter Don Juan José Oreamuno was named as executor.
Doña Josefa Boniche, residing in San José, granted general power of attorney to Captain Don Santiago Bonilla.
Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla granted general power of attorney to Don José Ruperto Prieto.
Doña María Josefa González Araujo, widow of Don Mateo Hernández, granted general power of attorney to Don José Francisco Madriz, a resident of Bagaces.
Don Manuel Marchena sold an enslaved man named Ciríaco García, approximately 25 years old, to Don Joaquín de Oreamuno for 300 pesos. Marchena had acquired Ciríaco from Doña Baltasara Madriz.

people_involved: José Antonio de Alvarado y Bonilla
summary: Don Tomás Alvarado granted general power of attorney to his son, Don José Antonio de Alvarado y Bonilla, who resided in Guatemala.

Francisco Lobo, Manuel Mauricio Montoya, Nicolás Molina, Gregorio and Jesús Jiménez, Manuel Mata, Jerónimo Hernández, Manuel Francisco Brenes, Francisco Camacho, and Juan Calderón, all residents of Tejar, granted general power of attorney to José Miguel Fernández. This power did not invalidate a previous one given to Félix Solano, who was absent.

Don José Ana Jiménez, a resident of San José, sold an enslaved woman named Ana Benita Fajardo, 35 years old, and her 4-year-old son, Juan José, to Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla for 200 and 60 pesos respectively. Jiménez had purchased them from Doña María Chacón, also from San José.

Don Félix Bonilla and Doña Catarina del Corral, with Don Manuel Alvarado as guarantor, obligated themselves for 1581 pesos 6 reales to Nuestra Señora de la Concepción, a debt originating from land and cattle bought by Don Manuel Marchena. They mortgaged two houses in Cartago and a pasture in Agua Caliente, while Alvarado mortgaged two houses in Valle Hermoso. The debt was later cancelled in 1805 by Mayordomo Núñez del Arco.

Don Manuel Alvarado, with Don Nicolás Castro as his guarantor, committed to pay Don Félix Bonilla 808 pesos 1/2 reales, with an annual interest rate of 5%. Both Alvarado and Castro were residents of Valle Hermoso.

Antonia Gertrudis Quirós made a codicil, revoking a bequest to her slave Antonia Josefa Quirós because the slave had left her service and found a new master in Nicaragua. The funds were reallocated for Antonia Gertrudis's soul and burial expenses.

Don Manuel García Escalante, Administrator of Posts and Lieutenant of Royal Officials, empowered Don José Asenjo of León to transfer the public scribe office, which Escalante had acquired for 500 pesos, to Don José Santos Lombardo.
Don José Santos Lombardo granted power to Don José Asenjo to formally accept the transfer of the public scribe office, as outlined in the preceding legal document.
Don Juan de Alvarado provided a guarantee for Don Manuel Alvarado, who served as the alcabala collector for the province, by mortgaging 200 head of cattle located in Bagaces.

To ensure the payment of 500 pesos for the public scribe office, Don José Santos Lombardo presented Don Lorenzo Carazo, Don Sebastián Guevara, Don Félix Bonilla, and Don Manuel Sáenz as his guarantors.

Don José María Peralta sold two houses and a 50-vara square lot on the public plaza to the city, represented by the Procurador Síndico, for 1555 pesos 1/2 real. The property, previously bought from Doña Antonia Pacheco, was intended for a barracks and bordered properties owned by Doña Luz Pacheco, Doña Joaquina del Corral, and priest Don Ramón de Azofeifa, as well as the parish cemetery.
Fray Manuel García, the priest of Atirro and Tucurrique, authorized Colonel Don Joaquín Arechavala, a resident of León, to collect any stipends due to him.
Fray José Gregorio Osorno, the priest serving Cot, Quircut, and Tobosi, granted power to Don Mateo Mantilla to collect outstanding stipends on his behalf.
Fray José Francisco Delgado, the priest of Pacaca, authorized Don Tomás Toruno, a resident of León, to collect any stipends owed to him.

Upon learning of her husband Patricio Gómez's death in Masaya and the goods he left behind from a trip to León, María Nicolasa Molina empowered her brother, Marcelino Gómez, who was traveling to Masaya, to claim her husband's estate.

María Bermúdez, daughter of deceased Bernardo Bermúdez and Juana Josefa Quesada, made her will. She had three children with her first husband, José de los Angeles Ramírez, and no children with her subsequent husbands. Her deceased daughter María had two daughters, María Josefa and María de la Cruz, and Juan de Dios Brenes was named her executor.

Don Juan Manuel de Alvarado, married for approximately eight years to Doña Trinidad Ruiz Fernández, acknowledged receiving 714 pesos in dowry goods for his wife from her mother, Doña María Petronila Bonilla. Doña Trinidad's father, Don Carlos Ruiz Fernández, was deceased.
Don Fermín Mondragón granted general power of attorney to Don Jerónimo de Escarpeta, a merchant residing in the city.

The estate of the deceased Manuel Fernández was divided among his widow, María Josefa Gutiérrez (now married to Bernardo Monje), and their three children: Antonia, Manuel, and Ana María. The widow and Bernardo Monje committed to pay Manuel, a minor, his inheritance of 35 pesos 7 reales.

The children of the deceased Félix Camacho and Antonia Brenes—Antonio, Félix, Jesús, Micaela (with husband Ceferino Alvarado), and Dolores (with husband José Francisco Piedra)—collectively agreed to donate a house in El Tejar to their unmarried sisters, Soledad and Josefa Camacho, fulfilling their late mother's wishes.
Don Francisco Javier Navarro granted general power of attorney to Don Félix Machado, who resided in Nicaragua.
Doña María Francisca del Corral committed to a chaplaincy associated with Don Pedro Portocarrero, obligating herself for 300 pesos.
Don Carlos Portocarre-ro, through his attorney Don Lorenzo Carazo, mortgaged his house and slaves. The specific details of the mortgage are not provided, only the act of hypothecation.

María Josefa González, a widow, leased a cacao plantation named La Cubero, located in the Matina valley and adjacent to another called Foto, to Rafael Salguero. The lease was for 5 years at an annual rent of 130 pesos in cacao.

people_involved: Doña María de la Encarnación Muñoz de la Trinidad
Presbítero don José Rafael de la Rosa
summary: Don José Antonio de Oreamuno, a Regidor and Alguacil Mayor, made his will, detailing his lineage, marriage to Doña María de la Encarnación Muñoz de la Trinidad, and their six children. He also listed his properties, including lands in Esparza and two slaves, and named his executors, including his son Don Joaquín.
Don Vicente del Corral received the inventoried assets from the estate of his deceased mother, Doña Rosa Madriz. The total value of the inheritance was appraised at 1650 pesos and 5 reales.
Nicolás Araya sold a house and an enclosed plot of land in the plain of Ujarrás to his son-in-law, Simón Bonilla. The transaction was completed for a sum of 125 pesos.

people_involved: Doña María de las Mercedes Guerrero
summary: Doña María de las Mercedes Guerrero, widow of Don José Antonio del Campo, granted power of attorney to Doña María del Campo and Don José de la Randi to collect her deceased husband's inheritance from his late father, also named Don José Antonio del Campo. The collected funds were intended for her eight minor children.

people_involved: Presbítero don Félix de Jesús García
summary: Doña Teresa Garlín made her will, outlining her family, including her deceased husband Don Manuel Guzmán, and their children, some deceased and some living. She bequeathed a slave named Benita and Benita's son Julián to her single daughter Doña Tomasa, and named her executors and heirs, including grandchildren.

people_involved: Coronel don Juan Francisco de Bonilla
summary: Don Isidro de Oreamuno sold a plot of land in El Espinal to Don José Nicolás Oreamuno for 475 pesos. The land, acquired partly by inheritance and partly by purchase from his brother Don Manuel Oreamuno, was described by its boundaries, including a pasture owned by Coronel Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla and lands of the indigenous people of Laborío.
Don Sebastián de Guevara granted general power of attorney to Don Francisco Albert, who is identified as a procurator.

people_involved: Presbítero don Félix de Jesús García
summary: Presbítero Don Félix de Jesús García, acting as the executor for Presbítero Don Ramón de Azofeifa, sold two slaves, Vicenta (16 years old) and Marcos (13 years old), to Presbítero Don Félix de Alvarado, the Ecclesiastical Judge of Nueva and Vieja. Vicenta was sold for 250 pesos and Marcos for 210 pesos.

people_involved: María de la Asunción del Corral
summary: Don Manuel Marchena sold a 24-year-old white slave named María de la Asunción del Corral to Presbítero Don Félix de Alvarado for 250 pesos. The slave was described as tall, stout, with black hair and eyes.
Josefa Quirós received the inventoried assets from the estate of her deceased husband, Juan Calvo. The total value of these assets was appraised at 400 pesos and 1 real.

people_involved: Presbítero don Juan de la Cruz Pérez
summary: Don José Nicolás Oreamuno sold a 10-year-old slave named José Joaquín to Presbítero Don Juan de la Cruz Pérez, the Lieutenant Priest of the city. The slave, described as light-skinned with straight hair and a scar on his fontanelle, was sold for 180 pesos.

people_involved: Presbítero don Félix de Jesús García
summary: Presbítero Don Félix de Jesús García received the inventoried assets from the estate of Doña Teresa Garlín. The total value of these assets was appraised at 2752 pesos and 4.5 reales.
María Josefa Alfaro, widow of Félix Delgado, received the inventoried assets from his estate. The total value of these assets was appraised at 990 pesos and 2 reales.
Don José Nicolás Oreamuno sold a pasture located in the outskirts of the city to José Céspedes for 160 pesos. The pasture was bordered by a royal road to the south and the Río Seco to the west.
Don José Francisco Madriz, a resident of Valle Hermoso, granted general power of attorney to Don Francisco Albert, who is identified as a procurator of this Kingdom.

Miguel de Jesús Abarca made his will, identifying his deceased parents and his first deceased wife, María Francisca Jiménez, with whom he had two children, Joaquín and Joaquina, who were in puberty. He also mentioned his second wife, Josefa Francisca Villar, whom he married approximately one year and ten months prior, and named Antonio de Jesús Jiménez as his executor.
Doña Manuela Baeza, widow of Don Pedro de Alvarado, sold six caballerías of land located in El Carmen, within the jurisdiction of Bagaces, to the Confraternity of Nuestra Señora de la Concepción.

Doña Antonia Conejo, a resident of Orosi, donates a piece of land in Tres Ríos to Francisco Antonio Conejo. She had raised and educated Francisco Antonio as her own son, and the land was inherited from her parents.

Don Manuel Marchena sells a house and lot in San José to Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla for 150 pesos silver, in addition to a 300-peso charge for the San José parish's septenary of the Blood of Christ. The property, previously acquired from Don Tomás de Alvarado, is bordered by the parish cemetery, Agustina Mora's property, Mateo Castro's lot, and Jerónimo Flores' house.

Don Manuel Sáenz, appointed Mayordomo de propios for the city of Cartago, guarantees his position by mortgaging his residence and a small farm with a sugar mill in Agua Caliente. This mortgage was later cancelled in 1806.

Ana María Valerino, legitimate daughter of José Cayetano Valerino and María Bernarda Escalante, makes her will. She names her natural son, José Francisco, who is about 13 years old, and appoints Don Manuel Escalante as his tutor, with Félix Monje as her executor.

Antonio de Jesús Jiménez, acting as tutor for the minors Joaquín and Juan de Jesús, declares that he has received 100 pesos for each minor. He commits to paying their mother, the widow Vicenta Méndez, 5% annually.

Don Nicolás Oreamuno, Doña Josefa Oreamuno, and her husband Don Ignacio Rucabado assume a debt of 780 pesos cacao. This debt is associated with a chaplaincy founded by Don José Pérez del Muro, which was charged to the house of their deceased mother, Doña Encarnación Sancho, when it was auctioned years prior.

Don Juan Manuel de Alvarado grants power to Don Blas Rodríguez de Zea to sell his runaway mulatto slave, Miguel Francisco Alvarado. Miguel Francisco escaped 12 days prior and is reportedly traveling with Don Antonio de la Fuente towards Guatemala to find a new master.
Doña Mercedes Guerrero, widow of Don José Antonio del Campo, receives inventoried goods in deposit. The total value of these goods amounts to 3514 pesos and 2 reales.

Doña Bartola Oreamuno, widow of Don Rafael de Alvarado, sells a piece of land in Ciénaga Grande, near Cartago, to Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla for 91 pesos and 2 reales. The land, inherited from her parents, is bordered by the royal road of Las Amoladeras, El Espinal, and the Salitral river.

people_involved: Presbítero don Rafael de la Rosa
summary: Presbítero don Ramón de Azofeifa, the priest of Cartago, makes his will, listing various books and seven slaves. He stipulates that two slaves, José Nicolás and María de los Angeles, are to be freed after his death. He names Don Alejo Ramírez and Don Ramón Jiménez to manage his cattle and debts, respectively, and appoints Dolores Sancho and Rita Madriz as legatees, Don Joaquín Oreamuno as arbitrator, and Presbítero don Félix García, Presbítero don Rafael de la Rosa, and Don Alejo Ramírez as executors.

Juan Ramírez, legitimate son of the deceased Juan Ramírez and María de la Trinidad Ortega, makes his will. He is married to María Manuela Carrillo, with whom he has five living children and two deceased children. His living children are married to Ana Gertrudis Granados, Antonia Abarca, Dolores Chinchilla, and Trinidad Damas, respectively, with Lucas also married. Juan de Dios Brenes and Francisco Lobo are named as executors.

Don Juan Manuel de Alvarado, whose mulatto slave Miguel Francisco Alvarado ran away, has learned through a letter from Presbítero don José Ignacio Ramírez in San Miguel that the priest has the slave. Miguel Francisco sought out the priest to buy him and become his master, offering 200 pesos silver. Don Juan Manuel de Alvarado grants power to Coronel don Joaquín de Arechavala, a resident of León, for this purpose.
Don Vicente del Corral grants general power for lawsuits to Don Manuel Marchena.

people_involved: Doña María de la Encarnación Muñoz de la Trinidad
summary: Doña María de la Encarnación Muñoz de la Trinidad, widow of Don José Antonio Oreamuno, delivers assets from her husband's estate to her son, Don Salvador Oreamuno. He is to administer and exploit these assets, valued at 1714 pesos, and in return, provide food and clothing for her and her family. This contract is terminable at will by either party.

people_involved: Don Luis de la Barrera y Negreiro
summary: Doña Jacoba de Alvarado, widow of Don Francisco Carazo, grants power to Don Domingo Iturralde, Don Antonio Jiménez, and Don Luis de la Barrera y Negreiro, all residents of Panamá, to collect the assets of her son, Don Apolonio Carazo. Don Apolonio died intestate in Chagres while in transit to Panamá from La Habana, where he conducted business. Don Pedro José Carazo signs on behalf of Doña Jacoba.
José Francisco Araya sells to Antonio José... (The entry is incomplete).

Granados inherited a piece of land in Chircagres, bordering the royal road to Ujarrás and the Barquero river. The land measures 100 varas on the South, East, and West sides, and 250 varas on the North, valued at 18 pesos 6 reales.

María Josefa Aguirre, widow of José Cayetano Carrillo, made her will. She had six children with Carrillo, including José Francisco, José Antonio, Presbítero don Nicolás, Catalina, María Josefa, and José Miguel (who died over 25). She was previously married to José Miguel Solano, with whom she had no children. Her children Presbítero don Nicolás and María Josefa were named as executors.
Doña Dominga Robledo sold a mulatto slave named María Ulloa to Don Manuel Sáenz for 250 pesos plata. María Ulloa, described as about 30 years old, was born to another of Robledo's slaves.

Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla sold a mulatto slave named Miguel Zenón Bonilla to Don Gordiano Herdocia, a resident of Nicaragua, for 250 pesos. Miguel Zenón, about 22 years old and son of another slave named Ventura Bonilla, was sold with all his faults, and Don Nicolás Carazo accepted the sale on behalf of the buyer.

people_involved: Presbítero don Rafael Ernesto de Troya
summary: Presbítero don Félix Alvarado, the priest of Heredia, sold a house he inherited from his parents in Cartago to Presbítero don Rafael Ernesto de Troya for 500 pesos. The house was located near properties belonging to Presbítero don Félix García, Doña Antonia Pacheco, Don Benito García, and a former property of Doña Ángela Molina.

Mateo Araya, husband of Juana Arburola (natural daughter of the late Don Felipe Arburola), received 31 pesos 6 reales from Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla. This sum represented his wife's inheritance, and also included the shares belonging to Juana's siblings, Antonia and José María Arburola.

Juan José Aguilar, widower of Catarina Ramírez, made his will, naming his eleven legitimate children and their spouses. He left some lands in a place called Cervantes. His sons Juan Francisco and Manuel Francisco Aguilar were named as executors.

Don Miguel Guzmán sold the La Pontezuela hacienda, located in the Matina valley and containing 1500 fruit trees, to Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla for 300 pesos. Guzmán had inherited the hacienda from his parents.

Felipa Neri Quesada, widow of Manuel del Villar, made her will. She had five children with del Villar, and their spouses are mentioned. She later married Juan de la Rosa Maitín, with whom she had no children, and he was named her executor.
Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla and Don Manuel Marchena granted a general power of attorney for lawsuits to Don José Asenjo, a resident of León.

Don Salvador Oreamuno took on an obligation to the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora del Rosario for 150 pesos (in cacao) and to the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora de la Concepción for 150 pesos (in cacao) and 100 pesos (silver). These sums were previously managed by his deceased father, Don José Antonio de Oreamuno, and Salvador committed to paying 5% annual interest.

Doña Lucía de Alvarado made a codicil to her will, stating she had sold some jewels for her maintenance. She owed her grandson Don Nicolás Ruiz income from a chaplaincy and had sold land in La Palma to her grandson Don Manuel Ruiz. She also detailed the inheritance of a slave, Juana Lebrón, and her children Anselmo and María Dolores, from her deceased daughter Doña Águeda de Bonilla, who had received Juana from her husband Don Pedro Lebrón.
Doña Jacoba de Alvarado, widow of Don Francisco Carazo, sold the enclosures where Pedro Barahona resided in Ujarrás to Pedro Barahona for 100 pesos.

Don José Ruperto Prieto (representing Don Pedro Diez Dobles), Don Tomás Hidalgo (representing Doña Rafaela Diez Dobles), and Don Juan Manuel de Alvarado (representing Don Manuel Diez Dobles) sold two houses in Cartago to Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla for 525 pesos. These houses, inherited from their mother Doña Mariana Alvarado, were located on a 50-vara square plot on one of the four corners of the city plaza, bordering properties of the late Don Tomás Corral, the late Presbítero don Ramón de Azofeifa, and Don Miguel Guzmán. One house was encumbered with 105 pesos for Nuestra Señora de la Concepción, which Don Manuel Diez Dobles took responsibility for.

Don José Ignacio Rucabado noted that Don Francisco Javier Villasanta, from Cartago, had requested an indulto (pardon) granted by the King (due to the Prince of Asturias' marriage) for a smuggling charge in Cartagena. The Captain General of the Kingdom declared that the indulto was to be granted by the Governor of Cartagena, and Villasanta was to remain imprisoned until he could appeal there.

Francisco Javier Mayorga, married to Francisca Villalón, made his will. He named his six legitimate children as heirs, along with his three sisters and three nieces as legatees. He appointed Manuel Sáenz as tutor for his children and Rafael de la Rosa and Francisca Villalón as executors.

Doña Ramona Carranza, having learned of the death of her son, Presbítero Juan Andrés Fonseca, in Villa del Sauce, granted power of attorney to her brother, Benito Carranza, to collect her inheritance from her son's estate. Juan Andrés Fonseca had named Presbítero José Eugenio de Herrera as his executor.

Doña Dionisia Fallas, despite her husband Rafael Troya's absence and her own financial hardship, sold a property she inherited from her mother, Ana Teresa de Alvarado, to Presbítero José Rafael Arnesto de Troya for 400 pesos. The property, located in Los Tres Ríos, included two houses and a 'caballería de tierra' with specific boundaries.

Don Manuel Alvarado owed Gobernador Tomás de Acosta 2250 pesos, which he had borrowed with a payment deadline in August. He mortgaged his house in San José as collateral. The debt was cancelled in 1806.

Fray Bernardo Roldan, the cura of Cot, Quircot, and Tobosi, granted power of attorney to Domingo Galarza, and failing him, Mateo Mantilla, both residents of León, to collect the synod due to him as cura.

Presbítero Félix de Jesús García, acting as executor for the late Presbítero Ramón de Azofeifa, granted power of attorney to Rector Rafael Agustín de Ayesta, residing in León, to collect the synod for the first five months of the previous year from the Royal Coffers, which was due to Azofeifa as cura of 'this parish' and the doctrines of Laborío and Pueblo Nuevo.

Presbítero Rafael de la Rosa, acting as interim cura, granted power of attorney to Rafael Agustín de Ayesta, and failing him, Bdo. Juan Onofte Oconor, both residing in León, to handle any matters that might arise for him in that city.

Capitán Santiago de Bonilla and his wife María Josefa Oreamuno committed to a capellanía branch of 150 pesos for the Beneficio de Esparza, and 200 pesos in silver for the same Beneficio, which was part of a capellanía founded by Antonio Hidalgo. They mortgaged their house, located one block north of the parish and cabildo, as collateral.

Fray Miguel España, former cura of Currirabá and Aserrí, granted power of attorney to Domingo Galarza, a resident of León and Síndico of that convent, to collect the synod due to him for the months he served as cura.

Juan Manuel Alvarado and his wife María Trinidad Ruiz sold an enslaved mulatto named Miguel Francisco, 30 years old, for 200 pesos. María Trinidad Ruiz had inherited Miguel Francisco from her father. Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco accepted on behalf of the buyer, Pedro Antonio Solares.

José Madrigal, son of deceased Tomás Madrigal and Teresa Cárdenas, made his will. He was first married to Josefa Segura, with whom he had three daughters: Nicolasa, Joaquina, and the deceased Juana. He was then married to Josefa Clemencia Muñoz, with whom he had María de los Ángeles (born before marriage). He appointed his son-in-law Lorenzo Rodríguez and Isidro Badilla as executors.

Don Sebastián de Guevara and his wife Doña Juana de la Calle committed to a capellanía branch of 72 pesos, secured by the house of the late Doña Manuela Pastora, which their son Gordiano Herdocia had 'oblado'. The capellán is Presbítero José Ana Alvarado, residing in Villa de Nicaragua, and his agent is Ramón Jiménez. They mortgaged their house.

Félix Camaño, son of deceased José Nicolás Camaño and María Rivas, made his will. He was married to Trinidad Ángulo and had no children. His assets included his personal cabriolé. He named his wife as his sole heir and first executor, with Simón Gutiérrez as the second executor.

Manuel Quesada, Juana Bustamante (siblings), and Gertrudis Morales (sister-in-law) of the late Presbítero José de los Reyes Quesada, who died as cura in Chocollos, initially gave power of attorney to José María Zamora to collect their inheritance. Now, with Benito Carranza traveling to León, they granted him power to receive their inheritance from José María Zamora or the executors.
Mateo Molina, son of deceased Francisco Molina and Andrea González, made his will.
Don José Miguel Ocaña, unable to sign due to an accident, granted power to the Alcalde Provincial to draft his will, naming his mother, doña Joaquina del Corral, as his universal heir and albacea.

Don Pedro Elizondo assumed a debt of 1447 pesos 4 reales from doña Josefa Salazar, widow of don Cornelio Fernández, for a chaplaincy. The debt was secured by various properties and guaranteed by don Juan Francisco de Bonilla and don Pedro Solano, and later cancelled in 1807 when don Antonio Figueroa took responsibility for it.
Mateo Molina's codicil instructed the payment of a debt owed to his sisters, María Antonia Molina and Roberta Molina.

José Antonio Solano, son of José Nicolás Solano and Antonia Baltasara Barrantes, made his will. He named his wife, Antonia Rosa Rivera, and his father-in-law, Santos Rivera, as albaceas, and appointed don José Ruperto Prieto as arbiter judge and don Roque Sáenz as defender for his minor son, José Joaquín.

people_involved: Don José Antonio García y Ramírez
summary: Don José Antonio García y Ramírez granted general power of attorney to his brother, don Fermín García.

Doña Joaquina del Corral acted as guarantor for don Juan Francisco de Bonilla and don Manuel Marchena, who were collecting tithes and Royal Ninths. She secured this obligation by mortgaging two houses in Cartago, a sugar cane hacienda, a slave, livestock, and a cacao hacienda in Malina.

On the same date, doña Joaquina del Corral further guaranteed don Juan Francisco de Bonilla and don Manuel Marchena for the annual sum of 1252 pesos 2 reales for the tithes, utilizing the same properties previously mortgaged.

On March 18, proceedings began for the opening of the will of doña Manuela Pastora, who had passed away the previous night. The sealed will, dated December 6, 1802, was discovered within her personal trunk, and witnesses included don José Ruperto Prieto, don José Lorenzo Carazo, don Pedro José Carazo, and don Manuel Oreamuno.

people_involved: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora
Don Francisco Fernández de la Pastora
Presbítero don Rafael de la Rosa
summary: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora's will, dated December 6, 1802, detailed her family and estate. She was the legitimate daughter of Francisco Fernández de la Pastora and Francisca de Arburola, and had been married to Juan José Sierra. She also had four illegitimate children: Joaquina, Rafaela (deceased, leaving four children with Félix de Bonilla), Esteban, and Gordiano. The will also mentioned three slaves, with Rosa being granted freedom, and named her sons José Gordiano and Esteban Herdocia, along with Presbítero Rafael de la Rosa, as albaceas.

Don Manuel Marchena sold a 21-year-old zambo slave named Isidro Valverde to don Lorenzo Carazo for 220 pesos. Isidro, described with specific physical features, had been previously acquired by Marchena from María de Jesús Valverde.
R. P. Fray Domingo Arias, the Reductor of Boruca, granted power to don Domingo Galarza to collect the synods owed to him for his past service.

people_involved: Doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora
summary: Don Juan Francisco Bonilla became a guarantor for don Manuel García Escalante, Teniente de Oficiales Reales, for 750 pesos owed to the Royal Treasury. This action replaced doña Manuela Fernández de la Pastora, who had passed away, and Bonilla mortgaged his house as security.

people_involved: Don Manuel de la Torre y Romero
summary: Don Joaquín de Oreamuno provided a guarantee for doña Antonia Jiménez, enabling her to continue managing the city's tercena, a responsibility her husband, don Manuel de la Torre y Romero, was no longer able to fulfill.

people_involved: Don José Antonio García y Sancho
summary: Doña Romualda Ramírez, widow of don José Antonio García y Sancho and daughter of Felipe Ramírez and Juana Otárola, made her will. She listed her six children, including don Onofre (married to Buenaventura Esquivel), and her grandchildren Jacinto and Matea (children of Onofre), and niece Isabel Ramírez. Her son don Onofre and don Fermín García were named albaceas.

people_involved: Presbítero don José de los Reyes Quesada
summary: Don Manuel Quesada, doña Gertrudis Morales, and doña Juana Bustamante, heirs to their deceased brother Presbítero don José de los Reyes Quesada, granted power to don José María Zamora in León. This power allowed Zamora to collect their inheritances and represent them in the estate proceedings, as their brother had named other individuals as albaceas.

Don Manuel Marchena and his wife, doña Francisca del Corral, assumed a 340-peso debt for a chaplaincy, previously held by don Juan Francisco de Bonilla, and mortgaged their house. A later note indicates that this debt was transferred to don Juan José Bonilla in 1822, with doña Francisca del Corral (also referred to as Franca. Nava y Corral) involved in the cancellation.

Doña Joaquina Corrales acted as a guarantor for don Juan Francisco Bonilla and don Manuel Marchena, who were auctioneers of the city's tithes. The guarantee was for 1113 pesos 1 real and was secured by a previously established mortgage.

Doña Joaquina Corrales provided a guarantee for the Royal Ninths, amounting to 131 pesos 2.5 reales, and for an additional 155 pesos 4.5 reales due to a new consolidation establishment. This guarantee was secured by the same mortgage mentioned previously.

A judicial sale took place for a 2-caballería pasture in the El Rio Blanco neighborhood, which belonged to don Pedro José Elizondo, to cover liabilities in a case against don Manuel José de Zea. Don Manuel Sáenz purchased the land for 300 pesos. The property had previously been bought by Manuel Aguilar in 1778 and its boundaries were described, mentioning adjacent sites of Simón Chacón and a former property of Diego Guillen.

Don Manuel Marchena, acting with power of attorney, granted the will of don José Miguel Ocaña, who had passed away on February 5th. Don José Miguel Ocaña was the legitimate son of the deceased don Gabriel de Ocaña and doña Joaquina del Corral, who was named as the sole heir and executor of his estate, which included silverware.
Captain don Manuel Hidalgo granted general power of attorney to don Joaquín de Oreamuno.

Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla and his wife, doña Ana Rita Gómez, took responsibility for 600 pesos from a chaplaincy of the Confraternity of Nuestra Señora de los Angeles, which belonged to don José Miguel Porras, a resident of Heredia. They mortgaged their house, which was later cancelled in 1810 by doña María Sandoval, the widow of the patron don José Miguel Porras.

Don Manuel Marchena and his wife, doña Francisca del Corral, took on 320 pesos in 80 head of cattle from a chaplaincy branch under the care of the Confraternity of Nuestra Señora de los Angeles. The chaplain, Presbyter don José Ana Alvarado, residing in Nicaragua, was represented by his attorney, don Ramón Jiménez, and they mortgaged their house.

people_involved: don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco
summary: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco granted general power of attorney to don Vicente Icaza, who was the Postmaster of León.

Don Juan Manuel de Cañas, a Sergeant Major and resident of San José, acted as a guarantor for don Manuel García Escalante for 750 pesos, replacing don Félix de Bonilla, who had requested to be exempted from his guarantee. Don Juan Manuel de Cañas mortgaged 30 marks of worked silver, his house, and a pasture in San José.

Doña Antonia Marín, the legitimate daughter of the deceased don Agustín Marín and doña Catarina Masís, and widow of don Miguel Velasco, made her will. She had children with don Miguel Velasco: doña Ana (who was married to the deceased don Pedro del Corral and had a daughter named Angela), doña Antonia, don Francisco, and don Manuel. Her children don Manuel and doña Antonia were named as executors.

Don Juan Manuel Alvarado was the successful bidder for the assets of Nuestra Señora de Ujarrás, located in the jurisdiction of Bagaces, which included land, cattle, horses, mares, branding irons, a house, and various tools, totaling 2282 pesos. He took these assets under an annual 5% annuity. Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla and don Manuel Marchena acted as guarantors, and all mortgaged their houses.

Don Nicolás Carazo was the successful bidder for the assets of the Confraternity of Nuestro Amo and Nuestra Señora del Rosario, located in Alajuela, totaling 2117 pesos 2 reales, primarily consisting of livestock. He took these assets under an annual 5% annuity. Doña Joaquina Corrales, don Salvador Oreamuno, don Manuel Ruiz, and José Solera acted as guarantors, each mortgaging their own assets including houses and cattle in La Palma and Turrúcares.

Doña María Francisca del Corral sold a 34-year-old mulatto woman named María de Jesús, who was the daughter of another enslaved woman named Manuela, to don José María Peralta. María de Jesús had two children, Joaquina (4 years old) and José Sacramento (6 months old). All three were sold together for 330 pesos.
Don Joaquín de Oreamuno granted general power of attorney to don Francisco Javier Navarro.

Don Manuel Marchena sold a 9-year-old light-skinned mulatto girl named Nicolasa Corrales to don Lorenzo Carazo for 150 pesos. Marchena had acquired Nicolasa through purchase from doña María Francisca Corrales.
Nicolás Araya, José del Carmen Cartín, and Francisco Molina sold a piece of land in the plain leading to Ujarrás to don Manuel Sáenz for 50 pesos. The land bordered the road to Ujarrás on the North.

Don José Ignacio Rucabado and his wife, doña Josefa Oreamuno, sold a house and pasture on common lands in the area called El Reventado to veteran Sergeant Agustín Núñez for 150 pesos. The house was situated within the pasture, which bordered the Reventado River to the East.

people_involved: Presbítero don Félix de Jesús García
summary: Doña Bárbara, doña Mónica, doña Isabel, and doña Micaela Sancho, all legitimate daughters of don José Manuel Sancho and doña Baltasara Madriz, and all over 25 years old, made their wills. Doña Bárbara was married to don José Antonio Oreamuno but had no children, while the others were single. They wished for their house to become a perpetual chaplaincy after the last sister's death, requiring two annual masses. Their brother, don Felipe, and his descendants were designated as patrons and chaplains, with don Felipe and Presbyter don Félix de Jesús García named as executors.
Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla granted general power of attorney to Don Gordiano Herdocia, a resident of the town of Nicaragua.
Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla and Don Manuel Marchena granted general power of attorney to Don Pedro López, a Procurator and resident of Guatemala.

Presbítero don Félix Alvarado, who purchased assets of the Animas brotherhood for 1534 pesos 6 reales, received the deed from mayordomo don José Ruperto Prieto. The assets included a pasture, livestock, a house, corrals, and a plantain grove, all acquired through alms and donations.

Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla acted as guarantor for Don Manuel García Escalante for 750 pesos, replacing Don Juan Manuel de Cañas who requested exemption. Bonilla extended his guarantee to 1500 pesos.

Capitán don Mateo de Mora and don José Ana Jiménez, who purchased assets of the Animas brotherhood of San José for 1900 pesos, received the deed from mayordomo don Hilario Zeledón. The assets included livestock and an iron brand, all located in a pasture called La Uruca, bordering Presbítero don Cayetano Chacón's pasture.

people_involved: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco
summary: Don Pedro Antonio Solares, through his attorney Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco, received the deed for assets of the Nuestra Señora de la Soledad brotherhood of Barba, which he purchased for 995 pesos 3 reales. The assets included livestock, a house, furniture, corrals, and lands, bordering Presbítero don Félix Alvarado's pasture.

people_involved: Coronel don Juan Francisco de Bonilla
summary: Coronel don Juan Francisco de Bonilla, who purchased 20 cattle from the Nuestra Señora de la Soledad brotherhood for 828 pesos, took them as a redeemable annuity. He mortgaged his house in Cartago and a property in Escasú. The debt was later cancelled in 1817, as the mayordomo Santos Rivera exempted the deceased Coronel due to a guarantee provided by Subteniente don Manuel Sáenz and Presbítero don Ana Ulloa.

Don Salvador Oreamuno and Don Ramón Jiménez, who purchased assets of the Santísimo and Nuestra Señora del Rosario brotherhoods for 694 pesos and 404 pesos respectively, took them as an annuity. The debt was cancelled in 1829.

people_involved: Presbítero don José Rafael de la Rosa
summary: Doña Ana Rita Coronado, widow of Don Romualdo Zamora, granted power to her son, Presbítero don Juan Manuel Zamora, to make a will. She named her children Juan Manuel, Julián, José María, Joaquina, María Cecilia, and Irene (married to Don Carlos Volio) as heirs, with Juan Manuel or Presbítero don José Rafael de la Rosa as executors.

people_involved: Presbítero don José Rafael de la Rosa
summary: María de la Candelaria Carranza, a widow from the Taras neighborhood, made her will. She named her eight children as heirs, all married except María del Carmen, and appointed Presbíteros don José Rafael de la Rosa and don Juan José Oreamuno as executors.

Don José Onofre García and his wife Doña Ventura Esquivel incurred a debt of 150 pesos to Don Tomás de Acosta, which was lent for a year. They mortgaged a 14-year-old mulatto boy named Ramón Azofeifa as collateral.
P. Fray José Francisco Delgado, the priest of Pacaca, granted power to Presbítero don Pedro Solís, residing in León, to collect his stipend.

locations: calle de la factoría de tabacos
people_involved: Presbítero don Félix de Jesús García
summary: Don Félix Bonilla and his wife Doña Catalina del Corral, residents of Valle Hermoso, took responsibility for 500 pesos cacao from a chaplaincy belonging to Presbítero don Félix de Jesús García, previously held by Doña Manuela Pastora. They mortgaged their house on the tobacco factory street.
Rafael Pacheco and his wife Juana de Dios Erenes made their wills. They had no children and named each other as reciprocal heirs.
Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla donated a house in Ojo de Agua to Rita Chavarría, where she currently resides.

locations: calle que va para el convento
summary: Don Gordiano Herdocia, acting for himself and as attorney for his brother Don Esteban, sold a house in Cartago to Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla for 666 pesos 5.5 reales. The house, inherited from Doña Manuela Pastora, is located on the street leading to the convent.

María Francisca Pacheco, widow of Juan José Romero, made her will. She had two daughters, Cayetana and Antonia, with Antonia (deceased and married to Nicolás Delgado, also deceased) having four children: Félix, Francisco, Juliana, and María Delgado. Her daughter Cayetana and grandson Francisco Antonio Delgado were named as executors.

people_involved: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco
summary: Don José Francisco Gómez granted power to Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco to marry Doña Rafaela Chavarría, a native of Cartago, on his behalf.

people_involved: Presbítero don Pedro José de Alvarado
summary: Presbítero don Pedro José de Alvarado granted power to his nephew Don Lorenzo Carazo to make a will. Lorenzo, along with Presbítero don Nicolás Carrillo and Don Pedro Carazo, would serve as executors, with his soul named as the heir.

Don Santiago González, mayordomo of the Nuestra Señora de la Asunción brotherhood of Barba, granted a deed to Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco, general attorney for Don Pedro Antonio Solares, a resident of Heredia. This deed was for assets in Quebrada Seca belonging to the brotherhood, which Solares purchased on November 11th for $636 as the sole bidder.

A Royal Order was issued in San Lorenzo on December 26, 1804, mandating the sale of all properties belonging to 'obras pías'. The proceeds from the subsequent auction were deposited in the Real Caja Subalterna. The auctioned assets included a house, an effigy, furniture, tools, livestock, and a pasture with a corral located in the llano del Arbolito, bordering lands of several individuals.

Doña María Arleguí y Alvarado sold a 51-cordada piece of inherited land in the Quercuá area to Félix Calvo for $100. The property bordered lands belonging to Doña Andrea Arleguí, Doña Antonia Arleguí, the indigenous people of Quircot, and the late don Francisco Carazo.

people_involved: Capitán de Granaderos don Joaquín de Oreamuno
summary: José and Miguel López, residents of San José, leased properties from the Cofradía de los Angeles in Sabegre for a term of five years. The leased assets, valued at $1665.6 reales, included livestock, a house, corral, and various tools, with Capitán de Granaderos don Joaquín de Oreamuno serving as their guarantor.

Doña Romualda Ramírez, a widow, leased a pasture located in El Reventado on ejido lands to Sargento Agustín Núñez for six years. The property bordered the Camino Real del Paso de la Carreta, Núñez's own pasture, the Peña del Río Reventado, and Rafael Valverde's house and lot, with an annual rent of six pesos.

people_involved: Capitán de Granaderos don Joaquín Oreamuno
summary: Fray Juan López, a Franciscan friar and appointed 'reductor' for the town of Boruca, granted power of attorney to Capitán de Granaderos don Joaquín Oreamuno. This authorization was for all his affairs, specifically for collecting his stipend from the Royal Treasuries in León.

Don Gregorio Castro y Alvarado, a resident of San José, leased properties from the Cofradía de Mercedes y del Santísimo in Escasú. The leased items, totaling $113, included cattle, mares, a colt, and a branding iron, with an agreement to pay 5% interest and provide a mortgage.
Don Lorenzo Carazo, a lieutenant in the local battalion, granted general power of attorney to don Manuel Marchena.

people_involved: Coronel don Juan Francisco de Bonilla
summary: Capitán don Joaquín de Oreamuno, acting as majordomo for the Cofradía de los Angeles, sold properties of the cofradía in Las Guacas to Coronel don Juan Francisco de Bonilla for $954. The sale included structures, fences, livestock, and approximately 24 caballerías of land on the volcano hill, with the proceeds deposited in the Real Caja Subalterna as per the Royal Order of December 26, 1804.

Doña Salvadora Ramírez, a widow and resident of Cartago, executed her will. She was the daughter of the late don Felipe Ramírez and doña Juana Otárola, and widow of don José García. She named her ten children and appointed her sons don José Antonio and don Fermín as executors.

Magdalena Quirós sold a house, which she and her late husband had built, to José Antonio Solano for $54. The house was located on a street near the cross dividing La Puebla, bordering properties of José Antonio Ramos, Santos Rivera, and Manuela Meza.

Lorenza Lis y Ríos, upon learning of her son Manuel Lis's death in Nicoya, where he left her as his heir, granted power of attorney to Cabo veterano Tomás Sánchez. Sánchez, who was traveling to Nicoya, was authorized to represent her and collect her inheritance, while the deceased Manuel Lis had appointed the priest don Nicolás Hidalgo as his executor.

Presbítero don Pedro Alvarado, acting as attorney for don Juan Pablo Jiménez, sold a 42-year-old enslaved woman named Efigenia Jiménez to doña Cecilia Jiménez. Don Juan Pablo Jiménez had inherited Efigenia from his father.

Capitán José María Peralta guaranteed Coronel Juan Francisco de Bonilla, the auction winner of five aguardiente stalls in Cartago. The auction was for two years at ten pesos monthly per stall. Peralta mortgaged a sugar mill and cane fields near the city, valued over a thousand pesos, as security.

Félix Calvo, a resident of Cartago, made his testament. He identified his parents, his wife Lucía Monge, and their eleven children. He also named the spouses of three of his children and his executors, Bernardo Calvo and José Miguel Monge.

Subteniente Manuel de las Mercedes Sáenz granted power to his wife, Cayetana de Ulloa, to make a will. He designated Beneficiado Rafael José de la Rosa and his brother-in-law José de Ulloa as executors, and their nine children as heirs.
Capitán Sebastián de Guevara, while ill in bed, granted power to his wife, Juana de la Calle, to make a will. He named her and Tomás Alvarado as executors, and their five children as heirs.
Josefa Boniche, a native of Cartago residing in San José, granted general power to her son, José Fco. Pérez, who was a resident of Nicaragua.

María Gertrudis Bolívar sold a mulata slave named Marcelina, approximately 50 years old, to Coronel Juan Francisco de Bonilla for $100. Marcelina had previously been acquired from María del Rosario Bonilla.
Ana María Valerino y Escalante made a codicil to her will, which was originally executed on March 20, 1804, before Alcalde 1° José Ruperto Prieto. The codicil primarily addressed her debts.

Capitán Manuel Hidalgo, a resident of San José, sold a piece of land in Cerro Chiquito to Coronel Juan Francisco de Bonilla for $150. The land, originally from Hidalgo's mother-in-law Dominga Trinidad, was described with boundaries including lands of Roque Aguilar, the town of Ujarrás, and a path from Ujarrás to Cartago.

Coronel Juan Francisco de Bonilla and Dolores Arnesto de Troya exchanged houses. Bonilla's house in Ojo de Agua, valued at $200, was exchanged for Dolores's house in Heredia, valued at $350, which she received as a donation from her brother Fray Miguel España. Bonilla paid the $150 difference, and detailed boundaries for both properties were recorded.

Julián Sáenz, a widower from Ujarrás, made his testament. He named his deceased parents, his deceased wife Feliciana Rojas, and his five children as heirs. He also mentioned his son-in-law Manuel Gregorio Loaiza and Coronel Joaquín Arechavala, for whom two of his sons worked in León.

Manuel Marchena, Salvador Oreamuno, and Nicolás Oreamuno guaranteed Juan José Bonilla, an enslaved person, who was auctioned by Santiago de Bonilla for $250 and 4 reales. Santiago de Bonilla granted Juan José freedom to earn this sum within two years.

Salvador Oreamuno, Nicolás Oreamuno, and Francisca Nava del Corral presented a certification to Alcalde 2° Manuel María de Peralta. This certification, based on a resolution from León dated November 3, 1820, declared that Manuel Marchena's estate was not liable for the enslaved person he guaranteed, leading to the cancellation of the obligation.

Capitán Santiago Bonilla, acting as general agent for Mateo Mantilla of León, sold an 18-year-old mulata slave named Gabriela Oreamuno to Félix Machado y Ligarte, a resident of Nicoya, for $200. Gabriela, previously owned by José Peña Conde, was imprisoned in Cartago for her involvement in a robbery committed by her aunt, Marcela Oreamuno.
Colonel Juan Francisco de Bonilla posted bail for Benito Zavaleta, who was imprisoned for complicity in a robbery. The robbery was committed by Marcela Oreamuno against her master, Mateo Mantilla.

Doña Cecilia Jiménez sold a 40-year-old mulatto slave named Ana Efigenia to Doña Antonia Jiménez for $200. Cecilia had acquired Ana Efigenia from her brother, Juan Pablo Jiménez, who inherited her from their deceased father, José Antonio Jiménez.

Doña Martina Barraganes, widow of Francisco Ruiz, granted power of attorney to Bachiller Don José María Zamora. Zamora, a resident of Guatemala, was empowered to collect assets left by her deceased husband in Sonsonate.

María de las Mercedes Bermúdez, daughter of deceased Bernardo Bermúdez and Juana Josefa Quesada, made her testament. She detailed her four marriages and children, including Gregoria, María Josefa, and Mateo Ramírez from her first marriage to José Ramírez.
