Her deceased daughter, María Josefa, will be represented in the inheritance by her two daughters, María Josefa and María de la Cruz Chinchilla.

Diego Chavarría, son of deceased Joaquín Chavarría and Baltasara de los Reyes Trejos, made his testament. He was married to Doña Dolores Frutos, and they had seven children. His wife and son Carlos Germán were named as executors.

The testament of Doña Rita Coronado, who died on March 7 of the current year, was granted by her son, Presbyter Don Juan Manuel Zamora, using a power of attorney. She was the widow of Don José Romualdo Zamora and had six children, including Irene, who was married to Carlos Volio.

Captain Don Joaquín de Oreamuno sold a 35-year-old black slave named Ciriaco Madrid to Captain Don Manuel Hidalgo, a resident of Valle Hermoso, for $300. Oreamuno had previously acquired Ciriaco Madrid from Colonel Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla.

Doña Bartola Navarro, daughter of Don Juan Navarro and Doña Dionisia Guerrero y Arcos, made her testament. She was married to Miguel Jerónimo Pacheco, and they had four children: Basilia, Pantaleón, Dolores, and Onofre. Her husband and Beneficiado Don Félix de Alvarado were named as executors.

Andrea Josefa Guerrero y Arcos, single daughter of deceased José Miguel Guerrero y Arcos and María Josefa Masís, made her testament. She mentioned her nieces Basilia Pacheco and Dominga Navarro, and stated she raised her niece Ana María del Pilar Pérez. Bachiller Don Rafael José de la Rosa was named as executor.

people_involved: Pedro José de Alvarado y Jirón
summary: Doña Cecilia Jiménez, single daughter of deceased Don José Antonio Jiménez and Doña Petronila Rodríguez Robredo, made her testament. She declared that her young slave, María Nicolasa, whom she is raising, would be freed upon her death if she served faithfully. She also bequeathed part of her assets to her brother, Don Ramón Jiménez, and named Beneficiado Don Pedro José de Alvarado y Jirón as executor.

Jacinto Segura made his testament, detailing his three marriages and numerous children. He had children with María Rita Leitón, Antonia Navarro, and María de las Nieves Hernández. The testament also outlined the marital status of several of his children, and named Antonio Delgado and Rafael Navarro as executors.

Francisco Lobo, widower of Luisa Cecilia de Ocampo, made his testament. He had two children, Cesáreo (who died in infancy) and the deceased María de la Asunción, who was married to José Rafael Navarro. His eight grandchildren, children of María de la Asunción, were named as heirs, and he also bequeathed a third of his assets to Rafael del Carmen Segura and his mother, Juana Segura. Beneficiado Don Rafael José de la Rosa and José Miguel Lobo, the testator's brother, were named as executors.
Manuel Francisco Robles and his wife Antonia de la Concepción Valverde made their joint testament. They named their two children, María Manuela and José María Robles.

José de Jesús Navarro, widower of María de la Asunción Lobo, made his will. He named his eight children, all under 14, and appointed Rafael de la Rosa, Manuel Francisco Robles, and Bernardo Calvo as his executors. María de la Asunción Lobo was the legitimate daughter of Francisco Lobo and Luisa Cecilia Ocampo.
Manuel de Alvarado owed Tomás de Acosta 1789 pesos at 6% interest, to be paid by August 1807. He mortgaged his house in Valle Hermoso as collateral. The mortgage was cancelled on May 29, 1809.

Nicolás de Bari Navarro and his wife Juana Rosa Alvarado made their will. Their single sons, José Francisco, José, and Blas Antonio, are mentioned as children, with José Francisco and José also named as executors.

people_involved: María Josefa de la Concepción Monge
summary: José Miguel Monge and his wife Manuela Josefa Guzmán, residents of Taras, made their will. They had several children who died in infancy, and one living daughter, María Josefa de la Concepción. Manuela Josefa Guzmán was previously married to Vicente Soto and had a daughter, Dolores, who also passed away. They also raised a child named Cayetano de los Angeles Montoya. Rafael de la Rosa and the surviving testator were named executors.

people_involved: María Soledad de los Reyes Zeledón
summary: Juan Agustín Astúa, a resident of San José, made his will. He was married to Mercedes Vargas and had no children. His parents, Cayetano Astúa and María Soledad de los Reyes Zeledón, were named as his heirs, and his wife and father-in-law, Bruno Vargas, were appointed as executors.

Colonel Juan Francisco de Bonilla sold a property known as "el Potrero del burro" in Púas, located at the junction of the Vigía and Sarchí rivers, for $400. The buyers were Carlos Barrantes (from Cartago), Manuel Isidro Barrantes, Efigenio González, José Manuel Arguedas, and María Martina Barrantes (from Heredia). The buyers' obligation for $200 of the price was cancelled on December 7, 1807.

Ana Elizondo, a widow, sold half a plot of land in Cartago for $50.00 to Cecilia Jiménez. The property was previously acquired by Ana Elizondo from the deceased Rosa Madriz and was bordered by properties of Rosa Madriz, Dominga Sancho, the deceased Mariana Alvarado, the Guevara ladies, and Ana Elizondo herself.

Captain Joaquín de Alvarado's will was granted on August 16, 1806, by Mateo de Mora, who had been given power of attorney on July 16, 1806. Joaquín de Alvarado had died on July 20, 1806. His children, Manuel, Antonia, Catarina, and Benito, were named as heirs, and among his assets was a 16-year-old enslaved mulatto girl named Paula. The will also mentions assets from his deceased wife Rita Alvarado, inherited from her parents Benito Alvarado and Leonida de Ocampo.

Prudencio Picado sold a pasture in Piirires for $550 to Beneficiado Félix de Alvarado. The property was bordered by pastures belonging to Salvador Oreamuno, Colonel Juan Francisco de Bonilla, Joaquín Oreamuno, and Hermenegildo Navarro.
Presbyter Florencio Castillo, Lieutenant Priest of La Majuela, granted general power of attorney to Juan Manuel Zamora.

María Josefa Arias of Heredia, with her husband Bernardo Rodríguez's permission, granted power of attorney to Cacique Marcelino Romero of Chinandega. This power was for Romero to collect debts owed to her deceased husband, Reyes Alfaro, who had been a merchant in those provinces and died there.

Juan Antonio Arias and his wife Ramona Masís made their will in the Arenilla neighborhood. They were the legitimate children of Juan José Arias and Micaela Navarro, and Francisco Masís and the deceased Micaela Bonilla, respectively. Their children were Antonio Fernando, Juana María, Julián del Sacramento, and María Francisca, with the latter three being married. They also had grandchildren, José Nazario and María Gertrudis. Their sons Antonio Fernando and Julián del Sacramento were named executors.

José Ana Jiménez and his wife Antonia Carranza made their will in San José. They had six children together. Antonia Carranza was previously married to Juan Fernández, a native of Spain, with whom she had four children. Josefa Martina Fernández, one of Antonia's children, was married to Juan Castro. Their assets included several houses in San José, one previously owned by the deceased José Miguel Peralta, and another by the deceased Miguel Sánchez, an indigenous person from Cartago's Laborío, which they were in the process of selling to Juan de Dios Ramírez.

Tomás Altamirano formally obliges himself for the guardianship of his nine minor children, who inherited 122 pesos, 2 reales, and 2 décimos from their deceased mother, María de los Angeles Venegas. This obligation was granted in San José, de Valle Hermoso.

Doña María de la Luz Castro, daughter of deceased Isidro Castro and Isabel González, grants power to her son Eusebio Rodríguez to make her will. Her executors are Eusebio and her other son, Pedro Rodríguez, and her six children from her marriage to Manuel Cayetano Rodríguez are named as heirs.

Doña Ramona Fallas, a single woman and legitimate daughter of deceased Jacinto Fallas and Narcisa Conejo of Cartago, makes her will in San José. She leaves legacies to her three grandnieces and names Manuel Flores and Nicolás Castro as executors, with her brother-in-law Pedro Flores as an heir.
Don Mariano Valenzueja grants general power to Don José Tomás de Zelaya, a lawyer of the Royal Audience of this Kingdom. The document was granted in the town of San José.

Don Nicolás Castro acts as a guarantor for Don José de los Angeles Elizondo, a resident of Bagaces, for the administration of tobacco, stamped paper, and gunpowder in that district, up to $800. He mortgages two pastures in Mojón and Salitralillo as collateral, with the document granted in San José.

Doña María Josefa Rojas, a single woman and resident of Heredia, makes her will, naming her living children Juan Telésforo and Josefa Salvadora as heirs. She details her assets, including a 7-year-old slave named Joaquín, and appoints Félix de Alvarado and Presbyter Pedro Vicente González as executors.

The will of Juan José Muñoz, a resident of Heredia, granted on September 9th, 1806, is protocolized on October 20th. Juan José Muñoz, who died on September 19th, named his brother Elías Muñoz and his wife Antonia Murillo as executors, and his granddaughter Antonia Ugalde as his heir.

Doña María Arias, a widow, sells a pasture in Mata Redonda to Don Gregorio Ulloa for $200. The property, previously acquired from Baltasar Echavarría, borders lands owned by Presbyter Cayetano Chacón, María Jiménez, and Pedro Flores, and is near the María Aguilar river.

Don Gregorio Ulloa acts as a guarantor for Don José Antonio García for $400, related to the administration of the "tercena" of tobacco, stamped paper, and gunpowder. A mortgage is provided as security for this obligation, which was granted in San José.

Don Juan José Valverde obliges himself for $247, representing the inheritance of his sisters, Josefa Dionisia and Manuela Antolina Valverde, from their deceased parents, Pío Valverde and Ana María Chacón. Damasio Alpízar acts as guarantor for Juan José and also for José and José Norberto Valverde, who are under 25, to receive their inheritance.

Cayetano Meneses, a resident of Ujarrás, makes his will, detailing his two marriages and children. His first marriage was to Petronila Valerín, with whom he had María Ascensión, now married to Manuel Moya; his second is to María Bernarda Montoya, with whom he has Carlos de los Santos, María de la Encarnación, and Gabriela. His wife María Bernarda and son Carlos are executors, and all living children are heirs.

Ramona Carranza, daughter of deceased José Antonio Carranza and María Nicolasa Morales, makes her will in 1807, detailing her three marriages and children. Her executors are her son-in-law José Miguel Monge and her son Atanasio Solano, and her four living children are named as heirs.

Micaela Rojas, a single woman from La Arenilla, makes her will in 1807, naming her sister-in-law Juana Josefa Quesada and her nieces and nephew, María Josefa Rojas, Antonia Rojas, and Juan José Rojas, as legatees. Nicolás de Bari Navarro and his son Francisco Navarro are appointed as her executors.

In 1807, Presbyter Don Pedro José Alvarado sells a 39-year-old mulata slave named Manuela to Don Nicolás Oreamuno for 150 pesos. Alvarado had acquired Manuela from Don Félix Bonilla and his wife Doña Catalina Corrales.
The will granted by Juan (name incomplete) in San José on December 17, 1806, is protocolized on January 15, 1807.

Cornelio Monge and Rudesindo Chacón, as albaceas, requested the opening of the estate of Juan de Jesús Ureña before Alcalde 2° Hilario Zeledón in San José. Several individuals, including Manuel Rivas and José Manuel Monge, provided declarations regarding the estate.

Doña Encarnación Muñoz de la Trinidad, daughter of the deceased Tomás Muñoz de la Trinidad and Antonia Josefa de Arburola, and widow of Alguacil Mayor José Antonio Oreamuno, made her will. She named her two sons, Joaquín and Salvador Oreamuno, as albaceas.

Manuel Antonio Obando, son of the deceased Juan José Obando and Rita Ramírez, made his will in the Zapote neighborhood of San José. He was married to Manuela Josefa Brenes and had one daughter who died in infancy. His brother Juan José Obando and Pedro Morales were named as albaceas.

José Antonio Monge and José Manuel Monge, residents of San José, obligated themselves to Factor Don Mariano Valenzuela for 600 pesos with 5% annual interest for 4 years. They mortgaged 300 cattle in La Candelaria, a house, and a pasture in the San Antonio neighborhood.
Don José Nicolás Oreamuno sold a piece of land in El Espinal, bordering the Camino Real de Las Amoladeras, to Don Juan Francisco Bonilla for 300 pesos.

José Antonio Solano sold a 'chácara' (small farm) in Agua Caliente, bordering the Toyogres River, to Don Nicolás Carazo for 425 pesos. The property had previously belonged to Doña Micaela de Alvarado.

Manuel Cordero, son of the deceased Enrique Cordero and Josefa Micaela Araya, and his wife María del Rosario Salazar, daughter of the deceased Mateo Salazar and Tomasa Alpízar, made their joint will in San José. They had no children and named Juan José Méndez, whom they had raised, as a legatee. They also named each other as reciprocal heirs and Don Félix de Bonilla as an alternate albacea.

Doña Rosa Sáenz, widow of José Antonio Badilla, obligated herself in San José to her three minor daughters, Gabriela, María Josefa, and Josefa Romualda, for 165 pesos and 6 reales, which they inherited from their father.

Don Antonio Vargas, widower of Doña Atanasia Fernández, obligated himself in San José to his five minor children, José Manuel, Miguel Cipriano, Josefa Rufina, Josefa Margarita, and José Tomás Vargas, for 370 pesos and 1 real, which they inherited from their mother.

Don Pedro José de Rueda, a native of Esparza, granted his will in San José. He was the son of the deceased Miguel Rueda and María Damiana Morera, and widower of Doña Felipa Barquero, with whom he had six children. His son-in-law Manuel Flores and Nicolás Castro were named as albaceas.

The albaceas of Pedro José de Rueda's will requested information from witnesses before Alcalde Hilario Zeledón. Declarations were made by Manuel Fernández, Eusebio Rodríguez, Félix Fernández, José Antonio Castro, and Manuel Rivas. The Alcalde approved the information and ordered the protocolization of the nuncupative will.
María Magdalena Alvarado, widow of Juan de Jesús Ureña, obligated herself in San José to her minor son Miguel Ureña for 89 pesos and 1 real, which he inherited from his father.

Rafael Flores, son of Micaela Monge, made his will in San José. He was married to Josefa Flores and had a son, Cayetano Flores, who was married for a second time. His granddaughters, María Josefa and Gertrudis Flores, inherited a fence from their mother, Ana Rumero. His wife and Francisco Piedra were named albaceas, and his son was the heir.
The encabezamiento (beginning) of Pedro Alpízar's will was recorded, but the process was not continued due to his strong delirium.
Don Manuel Oreamuno granted freedom to his enslaved woman, Juana Antonia Oreamuno, who was about 36 years old and had specific physical characteristics. He had inherited her from his parents.

Don José Francisco Bonilla, Alcalde 1° of Heredia, granted a power of attorney before Governor Don Tomás de Acosta to his wife, Doña Juana de Alvarado, to make a will on his behalf. He named his wife, Don Juan Francisco Bonilla, and Presbítero Don Félix de Alvarado as albaceas, and his six legitimate children as heirs.
Protocolization of the power of attorney granted by Don José Francisco Bonilla to his wife, Doña Juana de Alvarado, to make a will on his behalf.

people_involved: Juan José López de la Rea
R. P. Fr. Juan José López
summary: Don Francisco Javier López, a native and resident of Alajuela, made his will. He was the son of the deceased Juan José López de la Rea and Josefa Jiménez, and was married to Doña Benita de la Cruz Herrera, with whom he had four married children. Doña Benita had two children from a previous marriage with Antonio Rojas.

people_involved: R. P. Fr. Juan José López
summary: R. P. Fr. Juan José López, the priest of Boruca, granted power to Mateo Mantilla, a resident of León, to collect the synod owed to him from the year 1806.

In San José, Hermenegildo Zeledón, son of the deceased Bernarda Zeledón, made his will. He was first married to Tomasa Calderón, with whom he had a married daughter, Feliciana, and is currently married to Manuela López, with whom he has living children Antonio, Rafaela, and Nicolás, and his wife is pregnant. Pedro and Antonio Vargas are named as his executors.

In San José, José Antonio García, legitimate son of the deceased Antonio García and Antonia Paniagua (former residents of Cartago), granted power to his wife, Ana Sáenz, to make his will. His four legitimate children, José Gregorio, Josefa Gordiana, José Nicolás, and José Rafael García, are named as heirs. Captain Mateo Mora and Ana Sáenz are named as executors.
María Francisca Alvarado, widow of Antonio de la Fuente, received in deposit the inventoried goods from her husband's estate, which were valued at 3352 pesos and had been inventoried on March 20th.

In San José, Lorenzo Sequeira, legitimate son of Felipe Sequeira and Antonia González, and his wife Micaela Rojas, legitimate daughter of Francisco Rojas and María Francisca Ramírez, made their will. They have eight common children, with the first three being married. Félix Bonilla is named as an arbiter judge, and the survivor and Juan José Bonilla as executors.

In San José, Juana María de Sala, legitimate daughter of the deceased José de la Sala (native of Spain) and Juliana Monga, made her will. She is the widow of José Casimiro Chaves, with whom she had seven children. Her grandson is Juan Vargas, and her son Pedro Chaves and son-in-law Cayetano Vargas are named as executors.

In Lajuelita de San José, Matías Rojas and his wife Angela Mesen made their will, detailing their children and grandchildren. They also left some assets to Manuel Trinidad Rojas, whom they raised. Mateo Mora and Hilario Zeledón are named as arbiter judges, and their sons Manuel Antonio and Francisco as executors.

The power of attorney granted on April 8th in Heredia by Ramona Pérez, widow of Patricio Alvarado (who died in Santiago de Veragua), was protocolized before Alcalde 1° José Francisco Bonilla. This power allows her brother, Antonio Pérez, to collect the goods left by her deceased husband.

The assets of Juan Antonio Molina were partitioned among his widow, Apolinaria Calderón, and his children. The widow received 131 pesos, and each heir received 25 pesos, 4 reales, and 13 maravedís, with Antonio Piedra representing the younger children.

Fernando Marín granted power to his son, Pedro Marín, to make a will. Fernando was first married to Joaquina Muñoz de la Trinidad, with whom he had eight children, and is now married to Justa Chavarría, with whom he has a son, José Luis. His children Simón and María Josefa are named as executors.

Presbítero Juan José Oreamuno, as the testamentary executor of Bárbara Jiménez, sold her former residence to Francisco Javier Mayorga for 300 pesos. The property bordered lands of Joaquín Coronel, Félix Bonilla, Juan Vázquez, and Miguel Pacheco, with 150 pesos of the sale designated for the buyer's children as inheritance.

The will of Lorenzo Gutiérrez, legitimate son of the deceased Martín Gutiérrez and Petronila Barrientos, was protocolized in Heredia. He was married to María Micaela García, with whom he had eight children, two of whom are married. Mariano Villalobos is named as executor.

In Heredia, Antonio González, legitimate son of the deceased Gaspar González and María Trinidad Villalobos, made his will before Alcalde 1° José Francisco Bonilla. He is married to María de las Mercedes Rojas, with whom he has seven children, and owns 90 heads of cattle in Siquiares. His wife and son Ciríaco are named as executors.

In San José, Justo Zamora, legitimate son of the deceased José Nicolás Zamora and Antonia Josefa de Castro, made his will. He is married to Rosa Mora, with whom he has children Ubalda de la Trinidad (widow of Jerónimo Umaña) and José (married). His son José and Nicolás Castro are named as executors.

In San José, Juan Manuel Quirós and his wife Teresa Castro made their will, listing their seven children. Their assets included a house, land in La Uruca and Tibás, and a loom. They were also responsible for 200 pesos belonging to the minor children of Juan Manuel's deceased brother, Tomás Quirós.

Manuel Rojas and his wife Jacoba Badilla made their testament in the Uruca neighborhood of San José. Manuel is the legitimate son of José Rojas and Cayetana Estrella, and Jacoba is the legitimate daughter of Eduardo Badilla and Nicolasa Jiménez. They have four children: José Eduardo, Luisa, Juan José, and Pedro, with Luisa already married. Don Gregorio Ulloa and don José Ulloa are named as albaceas (executors).

Doña María Francisca del Corral sold an enslaved person named Carmen to don José María Peralta for 180 pesos. Carmen is described as about 13 years old, light-skinned, slender, with black eyes and straight hair, and is the daughter of another enslaved person named María de Jesús.

Doña Juana Suárez granted power of attorney to Presbítero don Pedro Solís, Promoter Fiscal of the Ecclesiastical Curia of León. This is to pursue a divorce case against her husband, don Benito Cervantes, who is imprisoned in Nicoya, due to his excessive rigidity and other justified reasons.

The testament of don Elías Muñoz and his wife doña Isidora Ugalde, originally made on May 13th in Río Segundo before Alcalde 1° don José Francisco Bonilla of Heredia, was protocolized on June 3rd. A codicil was also granted on May 27th in Río Segundo before the same Alcalde, naming don Joaquín Oreamuno of Cartago as Juez arbitro, don Blas Pérez as defender of minors, and don Juan Ramos as second albacea.

The testament of Pedro Chaves, made on the 1st day of the month in San José before Alcalde 2° don Hilario Zeledón, was protocolized on June 3rd. Pedro Chaves is the legitimate son of the deceased José Casimiro Chaves and doña Juana María de la Sala, and is married to doña Ángela Paniagua with three children. Don Juan Sáenz and don José Antonio Sáenz are named as albaceas.

Presbítero don Rafael Arnesto de Troya sold a cattle and horse ranch in Miravalles, jurisdiction of Bagaces, to Presbítero don José de la Encarnación Fernández for 15,117 pesos 6 reales. This transaction was part of a permuta (exchange) with Presbítero don Manuel Joaquín Núñez. The document notes that the deed was not finished or executed.

The testament of don Pioquinto Arias, made on the 10th day of the month in Heredia before Alcalde 1° señor Bonilla, was protocolized on June 12th. Pioquinto Arias, son of José Manuel Arias and Clara Rodríguez, was married first to Gabriela Rojas, with whom he had six children, and is now married to María Antonia Flores without succession. His brother don José Arias and don Juan José Quesada are named as albaceas.

Florencio Jiménez received an inheritance valued at 77 pesos 4 reales from his grandfather, Manuel Antonio Jiménez, from his tutor and brother, Manuel Jiménez. His brother, Carlos Jiménez, acted as a guarantor for this receipt.

María del Rosario Alcázar, widow of Pedro Alpízar, obligated herself to her six minor children for their paternal inheritance. Each child, named Damiana, Manuel, José Francisco, María Francisca, Antolino de Jesús, and Prudencia Alpízar, was due 67 pesos 3 reales and 3/16.

Don Manuel Flores, tutor of the minor children of the deceased don Pedro Rueda and doña Felipa Barquero, obligated himself to them for their inheritance. The children, named Josefa, Trinidad, Felipa, Ildefonsa, and Francisco, were due 268 pesos 4 reales and 3 cuartillos, with don Nicolás Castro serving as his guarantor.

Gregorio Piedra, tutor of the minor children José Hilario and Trinidad, obligated himself to them for their inheritance. The children, whose parents were the deceased José Piedra and Juana Valenciano, were due 84 pesos 4 reales and two-fifths.

Don Francisco Castro made his testament in San José. He is the legitimate son of the deceased don José Antonio Castro and doña Petronila Alvarado, and a widower of doña María Trinidad Ramírez, with whom he had four minor children. Don Mateo de Mora was named Juez arbitro, and his brother don Gregorio Castro and don Tomás Ramírez were named as albaceas.

Doña Ramona Porras, widow of don José Reyes, obligated herself to her three minor daughters for their inheritance. Her daughters, doña Ana María, doña Ana Josefa, and doña Juana de Jesús, were due 1613 pesos and 1/2 real.

Don Vicente Paniagua, widower of doña Mercedes Pérez, obligated himself to his three minor daughters for their maternal inheritance. His daughters, Felipa, María Salomé, and Isabel, were due 246 pesos 5 reales.
Don Pedro Antonio Solares, a native of Spain, Administrator of Correos, and Alcalde 2°, granted general power of attorney to señores Retes and Aqueche in the city of Guatemala.
Presbítero don Juan Manuel Zamora granted general power of attorney to don Ramón Jiménez.

Don José Ulloa, rematario (bidder) of four aguardiente stalls in San José, obligated himself to pay 40 pesos per month for one year to the Receptor de Alcabalas. Don Gregorio Ulloa served as his guarantor, and don José Ulloa hypothecated the products as security.
Don Félix José Fernández, widower of Doña Petronila Chacón, obligates himself to his minor son, Don Manuel, for 774 pesos and 6 reales. This sum represents Don Manuel's maternal inheritance.

Don Bernardino Alvarado of San José sells a quarter caballeria of land in Churris to José Antonio Solano of Cartago for 50 pesos plata. This land was inherited by Alvarado's wife, Doña Josefa García, from her grandfather, Don Manuel Antonio Jiménez.

Doña Mariana Vanegas, a widow, sells a piece of land in the Río Segundo plain, Heredia jurisdiction, to Presbítero Don Emidio Umaña for 50 pesos plata. The property borders lands of the late Don Cayetano Ugalde, the seller, the buyer, and Don Mariano Rodríguez and his brothers.

José Bogantes and León Salas, residents of Heredia, are awarded the lease of two aguardiente estanquillos in Heredia and one in Alajuela. They are to pay ten pesos per month for each during the year and provide Don Mauricio Salinas as guarantor to the Receptor de Alcabalas.

people_involved: Coronel Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla
summary: Casimiro Rojas sells a house with its enclosed lot in San José to José Antonio García for 250 pesos. The property borders houses of Juan Antonio Alpízar, Doña Juana Reyes, Domingo Méndez, and Coronel Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla.

people_involved: Juana de la Cruz de Ocampo
summary: José Miguel Peraza, son of Francisco Peraza and Petronila Fernández, makes his will. He is married to Juana de la Cruz de Ocampo and they have eight children. His albaceas are Don Antonio Zamora and Pablo Vargas, and he resides in the barrio of María Aguilar.

Don Manuel Segundo Lombardo, a native of the Kingdom of Panama and resident of San José, donates the excess of a small house and fence to his servant, José Reyes Sibaja. This property had been exchanged between them in San José.

Coronel Don Juan Francisco Bonilla bails Cadete Don Manuel Antonio Cañas from jail at the Cuartel de San José. Cañas was imprisoned at the request of Alcalde Don Hilario Zeledón for committing injuries and disrespect against his person and office.

Don Félix José Fernández receives the inventoried assets from the estate of Doña Joaquina Reyes, valued at 720 pesos, in deposit. Doña María Josefa Reyes, for whom Fernández is a tutor, claims rights to these assets. Fernández mortgages his house in San José.
Don Manuel García Escalante grants general power of attorney to Don Tomás Toruno, a procurator and resident of León.

Don José María Peralta, who leased five aguardiente estanquillos in 'this city' for a year, obligates himself to pay 50 pesos per month to the Receptor de Alcabalas. Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla acts as his guarantor.

Presbítero Don Félix de Alvarado, the priest of Heredia, sells an enslaved man named José de Jesús to Don Lorenzo Carazo for 200 pesos plata. José de Jesús, described as being about 22 years old, was inherited by Alvarado from his parents.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Rafael José de la Rosa
Presbítero Don Félix de Jesús García
summary: Presbítero Don Rafael José de la Rosa and Presbítero Don Félix de Jesús García, as testamentary executors for the late Presbítero Don Ramón de Azofeifa, sell his former residence to Don Juan Francisco Bonilla for 827 pesos and 5 reales. The house is located on a corner of the city's Plaza and borders the Cuartel, the Guevara ladies' house, the buyer's house (formerly Doña Mariana Alvarado's), and the Plaza.

Doña Ana Jacoba de Alvarado, widow of Don Francisco Carazo, makes her will, listing her parents, deceased husband, twelve living children, and three deceased children. Her assets include land and three enslaved people, one of whom, Juana Antonia, she mandates to be freed. Her executors are her son Don Lorenzo Carazo and her brother Presbítero Don Pedro de Alvarado, and she also holds inheritance money for her children from Doctor Don Juan Diego Teruel.

Don José Ulloa, who leased an aguardiente estanquillo in Heredia and another in Alajuela for a year, obligates himself to pay 20 pesos per month to the Receptor de Alcabalas. Don Gregorio Ulloa acts as his guarantor.

Don Francisco Javier Navarro bails Don Antonio Figueroa, a native of Spain, who was summoned in this province by order of the Captain General of the Kingdom. Figueroa intends to travel to Guatemala to appear before that Tribunal.

Doña Manuela Petronila del Corral acts as guarantor for her husband, Don Manuel García Escalante, who is the Lieutenant of Royal Officials in 'this city.' She replaces Doña Jacoba de Alvarado in the general bond, as Doña Jacoba is gravely ill and wishes to be excused from the obligation.

Don Manuel Marchena, as mayordomo of the Confraternity of Nuestra Señora del Carmen, executes a deed of sale to Don Joaquín de Oreamuno. Oreamuno purchased the confraternity's assets, mostly cattle located in Alajuela, for 2305 pesos and 5 reales, which he had previously paid into the Royal Treasury.

people_involved: Don José de la Cruz González
summary: On August 26, a testament made on June 24 by Don Mariano Rodríguez and Doña Ana Sancho was protocolized before Alcalde 1° Don José Francisco Bonilla in Heredia. The testament detailed their parentage, their thirteen children (some married), their properties in Ojo de Agua, Heredia, and Alajuela, and named their executors and an arbitrator judge.

On August 26, a deed made on July 24 before Don José Francisco Bonilla in Heredia was protocolized. Don Gaspar González sold a fenced pasture in La Pitahaya for 300 pesos to his three sons, his stepson, and his three sons-in-law. The land was originally acquired by Gaspar González as a contributor to a communal land purchase through Don Francisco Antonio Pérez.

locations: Plaza de la ermita de San Nicolás
summary: On August 29, Matías Román, with judicial permission from Gobernador Acosta, sold a house and lot in Cartago near the Plaza de la ermita de San Nicolás to Don Joaquín Hidalgo for 200 pesos. The house was embargoed due to Román's bond for Don Antonio de la Fuente in a case against Factor Don Manuel José de Zea, and permission to sell was granted because the house was deteriorating. Marginal notes indicate Román received 100 pesos in 1809 and another 100 in 1810.

On September 7 in Heredia, Don Manuel Isidoro Barrantes and his wife Doña Luisa Rodríguez received 781 pesos 4 reales as part of the assets belonging to the minor María de los Dolores Barrantes. Manuel Isidoro Barrantes became the minor's tutor after her mother, Doña Tiburcia Ulloa, lost the tutorship by remarrying, and Don Juan Carlos Barrantes served as guarantor. A marginal note indicates these assets later passed to Don Francisco Borbón and Doña Tiburcia Ulloa in 1816.

people_involved: Doña María de los Dolores Barrantes
summary: On September 9 in Heredia, Don Francisco Borbón and his wife Doña Tiburcia Ulloa obligated themselves for 599 pesos 2.5 reales in various goods to the minor Doña María de los Dolores Barrantes. María de los Dolores is Tiburcia's daughter from her first marriage to the late Don Juan Antonio Barrantes. Don Francisco Ramírez and Don Trinidad Borbón served as guarantors.

On September 9 in Heredia, Juan Manuel Sánchez and his wife Angela Jiménez made their testament. They were children of deceased parents and had one child who died in infancy. They named Pantaleón Sánchez, a boy they raised, as a legatee, and designated José Miguel Bolaños and José María Jara as executors, with reciprocal inheritance for the surviving spouse and then for the souls of the testators.

On September 9 in Heredia, Germán Salazar, widower of María Petronila Rodríguez, obligated himself to his four legitimate children (Lorenzo, Bernarda, Joaquina, and María Manuela) for 32 pesos 3.5 reales each. This amount represented their inheritance from their deceased mother.

On September 10 in Heredia, Doña Antonia Pacheco, a widow from Cartago whose parents and husband were all deceased, made her testament. She had no succession and appointed her nephew, Presbítero Don Félix de Alvarado, and Don José Francisco Bonilla as executors to distribute her assets according to her instructions without needing to render accounts.

On September 11 in Heredia, Presbítero Don Pedro Vicente González sold a fenced pasture with a house and two enclosures to Presbítero Don José Nereo Fonseca for 230 pesos. The property was located near a street leading to Don Gaspar González's pasture, another street leading to La Rivera, and the Quebrada Seca.

On September 19, José Miguel Monge, Mayordomo of the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora de la Concepción in Quircot, granted a deed in favor of Doña Antonia Jiménez. Doña Antonia Jiménez was the successful bidder for the cofradía's livestock, for which she paid 262 pesos 5 reales.

On September 22, Rudesindo Zúñiga, Mayordomo of Nuestra Señora de las Mercedes and Nuestro Amo de Escasú, transferred assets to Don Gregorio Castro y Alvarado. Don Gregorio Castro y Alvarado was the successful bidder for the goods of these entities, for which he paid 104 pesos 2 reales.

On September 28, before Gobernador Acosta, Doña Manuela Conejo sold a part of a house, including a corner room, another facing it, and two lean-to rooms, to Don José Santos Lombardo for 150 pesos, with 100 pesos due in one year. The property was located near the Plaza Real and houses owned by Doña Antonia Arleguí and Don Tomás Hidalgo. Her son, José Arguedas, signed on her behalf, and a marginal note indicates the payment was cancelled in 1808.

On October 5, Don Gregorio Oreamuno sold a piece of land on the hill named El Caracol to Félix Monge for 80 pesos. Don Gregorio Oreamuno had inherited this land from his parents, and it bordered a stream running alongside the hill.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Félix de Jesús García
summary: On October 6, Juan José Aguilar made a codicil to his 1804 testament. In this codicil, he left the value of some lands in Cervantes to Presbítero Don Félix de Jesús García to fulfill specific instructions that had been communicated to him.

On October 12, Félix Ramón Monge and his wife Nieves Chavarría made their testament. Félix Ramón Monge is the legitimate son of José Nicolás Monge and Antonia Manuela González, and Nieves Chavarría is the legitimate daughter of Joaquín Chavarría and Baltasara Trejos.

Four sisters, María de los Angeles, Ramona, Juana de la Cruz, and María Dominga de los Angeles, have raised a boy named Manuel Ramón Monge since he was small. Don Félix de Jesús García is named as the arbiter, with Don Joaquín Oreamuno as the alternate.

Don José Antonio García, who was the rematario of goods belonging to the cofradía de Nuestro Amo de Esparza, offers Don Nicolás Castro as a guarantor. This guarantee is for 537 pesos 2 reales, to be paid in four annual installments with a 5% interest rate.

people_involved: Presbítero don Rafael Arnesto de Troya
summary: Don Juan Francisco Bonilla sells an enslaved person named Esteban to Presbítero don Rafael Arnesto de Troya for 250 pesos. Esteban, described as about 20 years old, short, 'loro' colored, with a flat nose, curly hair, and thick lips, is a silversmith and the son of Bonilla's enslaved woman, Ventura.

Don Silverio Ocampo and his wife Doña Narcisa Molina obligate themselves for 537 pesos and a quarter real. This obligation is made in favor of Doña Narcisa's three minor children from her previous marriage to Ignacio Oviedo: Ramón Esteban, María Rafaela, and María Francisca.

Ramón Segura and his wife Ana Navarro obligate themselves for 233 pesos 3 and a half reales to Ana Navarro's two minor daughters, Francisca Felipa and Saturnina del Carmen, from her previous marriage to Pascual Bejarano, representing their paternal inheritance. Joaquina Quiteria Chacón is provided as the guarantor for this obligation.

people_involved: Doña María de la Luz Pacheco
summary: Doña María de la Luz Pacheco makes her will, detailing her lineage as the legitimate daughter of Don Dionisio Pacheco and Doña Francisca Serrano de Reyna, both deceased. She was widowed twice, first from Don Joaquín Montoya of Popayán, with whom she had a daughter named Doña Juana, and then from Don Fermín Mondragón, with whom she had four children: Doña María del Carmen, Presbítero don José Francisco, Doña Máxima, and Doña Antonia. She also mentions her deceased mother-in-law, Doña Antonia Mondragón, and an enslaved mulata named Manuela, appointing her son Presbítero don José Francisco and Presbítero don Juan José Oreamuno as her executors.
Luis Martín Chacón receives in deposit the goods that were embargoed from Rafael Mora and his wife Ignacia García. The couple is currently facing criminal proceedings for the crime of theft.

In San José, Don José Mariano Valenzuela, Factor de tabacos, and his wife Doña Rosa Morales, grant power of attorney to Don Pedro Pórtela. This is to represent them in the estate proceedings of Doña Rosa Morales's father, Don José Mariano Morales, who recently passed away in Guatemala.

Don Pedro Antonio Solares, a native of Spain and resident of Heredia, becomes the guarantor for Don José Mariano Valenzuela, Factor de tabacos, for two thousand pesos owed to the Royal Treasury. This action replaces Don José Mariano Morales, the previous guarantor, who died in Guatemala. Solares mortgages two large pastures with houses, over 600 animals (cattle and horses), 150 mules, and three additional houses he owns in Heredia.

Julián Arias and his wife María Josefa Alfaro obligate themselves for 137 pesos, 6 reales, and 28 maravedís. This sum is for María Josefa's three minor children from her previous marriage to Félix Delgado: Nicolasa Florentina, Jesús María, and Francisca de los Angeles, representing their paternal inheritance.

Bernardino Alvarado, mayordomo of the cofradía de Nuestra Señora de la Concepción de Ujarrás and the cofradía del Santísimo Sacramento of the same place, grants a deed to Don Juan Francisco Bonilla. Bonilla was the rematario in 1805 of the goods belonging to these cofradías, and the deed is for 356 pesos 2 reales.
Don José Ana Jiménez, a resident of the town of Valle Hermoso, grants general power of attorney. The power is given to Don Carlos Portocarrero, a procurador and resident of León.
Doña Antonia Arleguí, a widow, receives in deposit the goods that were inventoried as part of the estate of her deceased sister, Doña María Arleguí.

Don Juan Manuel González, a resident of Heredia, having married Doña María Josefa Reyes, grants power of attorney to Don Félix Fernández. This power is to reclaim 800 pesos, gold and silver jewelry, and other goods belonging to his wife, which were under the care of her deceased mother, Doña Joaquina Reyes.

Doña Dominga Robredo gives an enslaved person named Manuel Ulloa to Don Anselmo Jiménez as payment for a 200 peso debt owed by her deceased son, Don José Ulloa. Manuel Ulloa is described as about 18 years old, stout, tall, dark-skinned, with black, curly hair and little beard. Don Anselmo Jiménez is a native of Cartago and a resident and merchant of Masaya.

Doña Feliciana de la Fuente, a widow, sells a small house and half a plot of land to Doña Irene Zamora, also a widow, for 100 pesos. The payment is on installment with a 5% interest rate; Doña Feliciana could not sign, while Doña Irene signed as Josefa Irene Zamora.

Luis Martín Chacón makes his will, identifying himself as the legitimate son of the deceased Luis Chacón and Antonia Quirós. He was previously widowed from Benita Josefa Montoya, with whom he had ten children, and is currently married to Lucía Solano without succession. He names his deceased son Isidro, who left three children, and appoints Juan de Dios Brenes and Eduardo González as his executors.

Inventory and partition proceedings are conducted before Alcalde 2° Don Lorenzo Carazo for the estate of the deceased María de los Angeles Mora. Her widower is Joaquín Quirós, and her six heirs are identified, including their spouses and children, some of whom are deceased and represented by their own offspring.
In San José, Don José Ana Jiménez provides a jail bond before Don Hilario Zeledón, who is the Alcalde 2°.
Criminal proceedings were initiated against the soldier don Nicolás Rojas for the crime of incest. The specific date and year for this proceeding are not explicitly mentioned in the text.

Francisco Javier Chinchilla, widower of María Cayetana Chaves, executed his will in San José before escribano don Hilario Zeledón. He named his son Juan de Dios Chinchilla and José Gregorio Fernández as executors, and listed his deceased parents and ten children, noting that only Juan de Dios was married.

Don Paulino, Doña Antonia Manuela, Doña Engracia, and Doña Juana Meneses sold a house in Cartago to don Juan Francisco Bonilla for 200 pesos. The property was bordered by the buyer's house, the late José María del Valle's property, Manuel Palma's property, and don Mateo Camacho's property.

Don Nicolás Oreamuno sold a piece of land in El Espinal to don Juan Francisco Bonilla for 300 pesos. The land was bordered by the buyer's pasture, a stream, lands of the natives of Laborío, a road, and the Salitral river.

Félix Mora posted bail for his son Rafael Mora and his wife Ignacia García, who were being prosecuted for theft against don Simón Marín. The bail was later cancelled on October 1, 1808, after the accused were acquitted.

Don José Antonio García sold a stone-fenced pasture in El Guarco, located on common lands, to Presbítero don Félix Alvarado for 150 pesos. The property was bordered by common lands, a royal road, the Molino river, don José María Peralta's pasture, and doña Joaquina del Corral's farm.
Doña Ana Rita Alvarado sold half a plot of land, which she inherited from her mother Doña María Alvarado, to don Nicolás Oreamuno for 35 pesos.

Don Eusebio Rodríguez, Mayordomo of the Cofradía del Señor San José of San José, Valle Hermoso, transferred cattle belonging to the confraternity, located in La Candelaria, to Presbítero don Félix Valverde for 254 pesos.

Don Ramón Gutiérrez and don Manuel José Bogantes, Mayordomos of the Asunción and Soledad confraternities of Barba, transferred 372 heads of cattle to don Miguel González for 1116 pesos. The cattle were located between the Siquiares stream and Itiquís river in Alajuela.

Don Ramón Gutiérrez and don Manuel José Bogantes, Mayordomos of the Asunción and Soledad confraternities, transferred 300 cattle, a pasture with a house and corral belonging to the same confraternities, to don José Mariano Valenzuela for 961 pesos and 4 reales.

Don Ramón Gutiérrez and don Manuel José Bogantes, Mayordomos of the Asunción and Soledad confraternities, transferred 50 cattle belonging to the same confraternities to don Francisco Javier Navarro for 150 pesos.

Don José Ignacio Rucabado, a native of Spain, acted as guarantor for don Francisco Javier Villasanta, also from Spain, who was arrested in Cartago by order of the Captain General of the Kingdom. Villasanta was allowed to travel freely within the Kingdom if he provided satisfactory bail.
Don Nicolás Oreamuno, who acquired goods from the Archicofradía de Nuestro Señor San José de las Cañas for 1087 pesos, committed to paying this sum in installments with a 5% interest rate.

Don Manuel Marchena, Mayordomo of San Juan de Dios venerated in the Soledad church, transferred 12 heads of cattle and a branding iron belonging to the saint to Presbítero don Emidio Umaña for 48 pesos, which Umaña paid to the Royal Treasury.

people_involved: don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco
summary: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco, Mayordomo of Nuestra Señora del Rosario of Cartago parish, transferred various cattle belonging to the confraternity to don Joaquín Oreamuno for 295 pesos, which Oreamuno paid to the Royal Treasury.
Don Manuel Marchena, Mayordomo of San Juan de Dios of Cartago, transferred goods located in Ujarrás to don Juan Francisco Bonilla for 79 pesos and 3 reales. These goods included 1900 roof tiles.

Nicolás Quirós, a resident of Cerro Grande, made his will. He was married to Josefa Quiteria Soto, with whom he had six children, and named his wife and son-in-law Juan José Chinchilla as executors. His parents, Diego Quirós and María Francisca Sáenz, were deceased.

Juan Francisco Guillen, married to Josefa Vicenta Méndez, acknowledged a debt related to the inheritance of Josefa's two sons, Juan and Joaquín Porras, from her first marriage to Jesús Porras. Josefa had taken charge of the debt after her second husband, Rafael Araya, died, and Guillen received 105 pesos 6 reales, obliging himself to return it.

people_involved: Presbítero Rafael José de la Rosa
summary: María Cayetana Carmona, a single woman from La Puebla with no succession, made her will, naming Presbítero Rafael José de la Rosa as her executor and her soul as the heir. Her parents, Juan Matías Barrantes (a) Carmona and Candelaria Taulera, were deceased.

Basilio Peraza, widower of María Ascención Arias, made his will in San José. He named his brother Miguel Peraza as executor and listed his four children with María Ascención Arias, as well as María Josefa Castillo, his wife's daughter from her first marriage to Miguel Castillo.

The mayordomos of the Asunción and Soledad confraternities of San Bartolomé de Birba transferred 333 heads of cattle to José de la Luz and José Miguel Ureña, residents of Valle Hermoso, for 333 pesos. The cattle were grazing in the areas known as Aserrises and Verbena.
Two testaments were officially recorded (protocolized) before Don Hilario Zeledón, the First Mayor of San José.

Rudesindo Cordero, legitimate son of the deceased José Miguel Cordero and María Francisca Alvarado, made his will. He was married to Micaela Morales, with whom he had nine children. Pedro Morales was named as his executor.

people_involved: José Miguel (natural son of Rita Aguilar)
Juana María (natural daughter of Rita Aguilar)
summary: Rita Aguilar, legitimate daughter of the deceased José Antonio Aguilar and Juana María Chavarría, made her will. She was the widow of Amaro de Jesús Mora, with whom she had five children (only one surviving), and later had three natural children. Miguel González was named as her executor, and Francisca de la Cruz Segura was her aunt.

José Antonio García committed to pay 169 pesos 2 3/4 reales to the children of the deceased Julián Sáenz (José Miguel, Joaquín, María, José Francisco, and Ana Benita). This payment was for the value of goods he received as the tutor for the four minor children.
This entry notes the official recording (protocolization) of five subsequent testaments.

people_involved: Juana María González de León (spouse of Matías Antonio Sandoval)
summary: In Heredia, before Alcalde 2° Matías Sandoval, José Miguel Porras and his wife María Sandoval made their wills. They detailed their parentage and their eight children, including the deceased Rita Porras and her seven children. José Francisco Porras was named arbiter judge, and Presbítero Pedro Vicente González and their son José María Porras were named executors.

people_involved: José Francisco Porras (son of Juan Agustín Porras)
Juana María González de León (spouse of Juan Agustín Porras)
summary: In Heredia, before Alcalde Matías Sandoval, José Francisco Porras, legitimate son of the deceased Juan Agustín Porras and Juana María González de León, made his will. Being single, he instructed his executors to distribute his assets and noted funds held for the estate of the deceased Presbítero Joaquín de Quesada. Presbíteros Pedro Vicente González, José Nereo Fonseca, and Emidio Umaña were named as executors.

In San José, before Alcalde 2° Gregorio Ulloa, Juan José Blanco made his will. He was the legitimate son of Manuel Hipólito Blanco and María Gertrudis Rojas, married to María Trinidad Valverde, with whom he had a daughter and another child expected. His father and his uncle, Rafael Blanco, were named as executors.

In Heredia, before Alcalde Sandoval, Juana de Dios Gutiérrez, a widow from barrio de los Targuaces, made her will. She was the widow of Juan José Acosta and had two children. She ordered the freedom of her slave, José Antonio, and named her son as her executor.

In San José, at Los Cedros, before Alcalde Zeledón, José Francisco Acuña made his will. He was married to Juana María Cervantes and had eight children, with the first four being married. Manuel Salazar and his son Francisco Antonio were named as executors.
Manuel José Bogantes and Ramón Gutiérrez, mayordomos of the Asunción and Soledad confraternities of Barba, transferred 243 heads of cattle to Cornelio Monge, a resident of San José, for 729 pesos.
Mateo Castro, mayordomo of the Soledad confraternity of San José, transferred various animals belonging to the confraternity to Gregorio Ulloa, who was the buyer, for 501 pesos 4 reales.

José Ruperto Prieto, mayordomo of the Animas confraternity of this parish (implied Cartago), transferred various cattle belonging to the confraternity to Felipe Sancho, who was the buyer, for 198 pesos.

Manuel Marchena, Síndico of the Convent of Cartago, sold lands in Rincón de Tibás to Juan Antonio Salazar and Juan Francisco Solís, residents of Heredia, for 66 pesos 5 1/2 reales. The lands were bordered by quebrada de Turis, lands of the Zamoras, lands of the Chacones, and an old road, with the sum paid into the Royal Treasury for a chaplaincy.

Manuel Marchena, the Síndico, issued a receipt to Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco, attorney for Pedro Antonio Solares, for 214 pesos deposited in the Royal Treasury. This sum belonged to the curacy of Barba and was a charge on Solares' house in Heredia.

María Bolívar, a widow, sought to reclaim her belongings embargoed by Provisor Juan Francisco de Vilches, which were held in trust by her son, Presbítero José Antonio Bonilla, as executor of her deceased husband, Andrés de Bonilla. She granted power of attorney to Procurators Pedro Miguel López and Joaquín Mariscal of Guatemala, with her son Santiago Bonilla signing on her behalf due to her illness.
Juan de Jesús Navarro, a resident of barrio de Sabana Grande, made his will. He was the legitimate son of the deceased Alfonso Navarro and Bárbara Zamora, and married to Rita Josefa Monge.
An unnamed testator's children are listed as Benito, María, Joaquina, Eusebio, Francisco, Petronila, and Ignacio. Their son, José Benito, is named as the executor of the will.
Don Ramón de Palacios, a native of Spain and resident of San José, granted general power of attorney to Don Félix Bonilla.
Doña Rita Oreamuno, the widow of Don Tomás Hidalgo, received inventoried goods from his estate. The assets were valued at 4851 pesos 3 reales.

people_involved: Doña María de la Luz Pacheco
summary: Presbítero don José Francisco Mondragón received inventoried goods from the estate of his deceased mother, Doña María de la Luz Pacheco. The assets were valued at 1875 pesos 5 reales.

José Francisco Rojas, a resident of Heredia, replaced José Arias in a bond for Silverio Ocampo and Doña Narcisa Molina, concerning the guardianship of the late Ignacio Oviedo's children. A marginal note from 1818 indicates Presbítero don Nicolás Carrillo, as ad litem curator for the minor Doña Rafaela Oviedo, delivered her assets to Manuel Chaves, whom she chose as her tutor.
This entry records the formal protocolization of eight testaments that follow in the registry.

Jerónimo Flores made his testament in San José before Alcalde 1° Don Hilario Zeledón. He detailed his two marriages and the children from each, including deceased children and a granddaughter. Capitán don Mateo de Mora was the arbiter judge, and Don Gregorio Ulloa and Don José Ana Jiménez were named as executors.

Doña Catarina Tenorio, widow of Don Pedro Fernández, made her testament in San José before Alcalde 2° Don Gregorio Ulloa. She listed her parents and eight children, detailing their marital statuses and mentioning deceased children and their offspring. Her sons, Presbítero Don Encarnación and Don Félix, were appointed as executors.

Don Ramón Esquivel, a native of Heredia, made his testament in San José before Alcalde Señor Ulloa. He detailed his two marriages, listing children from his first marriage and his stepson from his second wife's previous marriage. Don Gregorio Ulloa and Capitán don Mateo de Mora were named as executors.

José Antonio León, a resident of Escazú, made his testament in San José, detailing his two marriages and numerous children and stepchildren. He also listed his deceased daughter's children and appointed his sons Manuel de Jesús (the younger) and Narciso as executors.

Doña Francisca Zamora, widow of Don Antonio Cayetano Mora, made her testament in San José before Alcalde Señor Zeledón. She listed her parents and six children, detailing their marital statuses. Her sons Pablo Antonio and Miguel Jerónimo were appointed as executors.

José Benito Duran made his testament in San José, detailing his parentage and his marriage to Juana Ramona León, who was a widow. He had no children with his current wife, and his wife and stepson, Francisco Dolores Mata, were named as executors, with his wife as the sole heir.

Don Norberto Alpízar and his wife Doña Antonia Chacón made a joint testament in San José before Alcalde Señor Zeledón. Due to their advanced age and lack of children, they named each other as reciprocal heirs, with specific conditions for the disposition of their assets. The surviving spouse and Presbítero don Antonio Cayetano Fernández were named as executors.

María Josefa Aguilar, a single woman and legitimate daughter of the deceased Manuel Aguilar and Antonia Rodríguez, made her will in San José before an Alcalde. She named her uncle, Don Anselmo Aguilar, as her executor, and her soul as her heir.

people_involved: Wife of Rafael José de la Rosa
summary: Félix Gutiérrez, son of the deceased Josefa Gutiérrez and a former resident of Cartago, made his will. He is married to María Simona Aguirre, with whom he has a son, Joaquín, currently in Guatemala. He also raised a boy named Venancio Bravo. His executors are Presbítero Don Rafael José de la Rosa and his wife.

Tomás Camaño sold a house and its entire lot to Manuel Román for 100 pesos, payable in 1810. The property, which Camaño had previously purchased from Pedro and Miguel Solano, bordered the slaughterhouse to the East.

Don José María Peralta and Don Pedro Carazo, who are leaseholders of two of the five liquor stalls in the city, committed to paying the Royal Treasury 20 pesos monthly. They also mutually guaranteed each other's obligations.
Francisco Raimundo Calvo committed to Bartolo Masís for 214 pesos, representing Masís's inheritance. Bartolo Masís is the grandson and heir of Calvo's deceased sister, María Francisca Calvo.

In Heredia, Presbítero Don Félix Alvarado, the interim priest, canceled a debt of 266 pesos and 5.5 reales owed by Don Pedro Antonio Solares. This debt was for a chaplaincy belonging to the curacy and was recognized by Solares's residence. Solares had paid the amount into the Royal Treasury as per government orders.

In Heredia, León Salas, a leaseholder of one of the four established liquor stalls, committed to paying the Royal Treasury 10 pesos monthly. Don Mauricio Salinas served as his guarantor for this obligation.
In Heredia, Juan Alvarez posted bail for his son, Ramón Alvarez, who was imprisoned and charged with cattle rustling. Ramón Alvarez was accused alongside Justo Coto.
In Heredia, Don Ángel Castro sold a piece of land in El Coyol to Vicente Rojas, a resident of San José, for 85 pesos. The land bordered the Virilla River to the South.

In Heredia, Don Pedro Arias, a resident of Alajuela and leaseholder of one of the two liquor stalls in his neighborhood, committed to paying the Royal Treasury 10 pesos monthly. Andrés Espinoza served as his guarantor.
On June 18th, four documents that had been granted in Heredia before the First Alcalde, Don José Francisco Bonilla, were officially added to the protocol.

In Heredia, Doña María de Soto, widow of Francisco de Ocampo, sold a pasture of 8 to 10 caballerías in Rincón del Padre Ocampo to Presbítero Don Félix Alvarado for 1000 silver pesos. The property, which she had purchased from Don Ventura Sáenz de Bonilla, bordered José Solera's pasture to the North, the Virilla River to the South, Ignacio Oviedo's former pasture (now Isidro Soto's) to the East, and "Nuestro Amo" enclosure with the Segundo River in between to the West.

In Heredia, Doña Juana Saborío, a widow of Fermín Zamora and legitimate daughter of the deceased Don Juan José Saborío and María Leonor Vareas, made her will. She had three children with Fermín Zamora: Juan Antonio (married), Antonia (married to Antonio Solano, both deceased, leaving four daughters), and José Miguel (who died in Nicaragua). Her executors are her son Juan Antonio and José Antonio González.

In Heredia, Don Miguel González, legitimate son of the deceased Don José González and Doña Ana María Alfaro, made his will. He was first married to Ramona Salazar, with whom he had six children, and is currently married to Doña María González, who is pregnant. His extensive properties included houses, a forge, a sugar mill, pastures, land in Santa Olaria with various structures and livestock, and a house near the Río Grande. His executors are his son Don Juan Antonio and his son-in-law Antonio Rodríguez, with Francisco Chaverri or Mariano Rodríguez as arbiter judge.

Doña Ramona Porras, widow of Don José Reyes, ratified the sale of a pasture with a house, plantain grove, and fences to Presbítero Don Félix Alvarado. This property, located in the town's lands, bordered Don Pedro Antonio Solares's and Don Gaspar González's pastures to the North (with a royal road in between) and lands of Quebrada Seca residents to the East. The sale was for 450 pesos and had originally been made by her husband.

In Heredia, Doña Josefa Salas, widow of Don Ramón Arguedas, committed to her minor daughter, Doña Patricia Arguedas, for 122 pesos and 6.5 reales. This amount represented Patricia's paternal inheritance.

In Heredia, Doña Gordiana González, widow of Don Antonio Quesada, committed to her five minor children: María Josefa, Manuel Melchor, Leandro, María Dominga, and Antonia Hilaria (posthumous). This obligation was for 205 pesos and 5.5 reales, which they received as paternal inheritance.

In Heredia, Doña María de los Santos Moya, widow of Cristóbal Orozco, committed to her two minor children, José Ana and Francisca Joaquina Orozco. This obligation was for 161 pesos and 5.5 reales from their paternal inheritance, plus an additional 247 pesos and 12.3 reales from the inheritance of their grandmother, Doña Ramona Hidalgo, who was Cristóbal Orozco's mother.

Pedro Soto obligated himself to his granddaughters, Ciriaca and María Manuela Murillo, for 70 pesos 2 reales from their inheritance. Their mother, Manuela Soto, lost guardianship after remarrying José Antonio Quesada, leading to Pedro Soto being appointed as their sole grandfather and guardian.

Pedro Espinosa and Margarita de Jesús Bonilla, residents of Alajuela, made their wills in Heredia, detailing their legitimate parents and common children. Margarita also specified her previous marriage to Rafael Salazar and their children, including their marital statuses and offspring. Arbitrators and executors were named for their estate.

Micaela García, widow of Lorenzo Gutiérrez, obligated herself for 82 pesos 7 reales from their paternal inheritance to her six minor children: María Magdalena, Juan, Manuel, Julián, María del Pilar, and María Ramona. The document was noted as not having been completed or signed.

José de la Rosa Valerio obligated himself for 100 pesos 2 reales from their paternal inheritance to his four minor siblings: Rafael Antonio, Pablo José, Juan de Jesús, and José de la Trinidad. All five are children of the deceased José Manuel Valerio, with Benito Camacho serving as guarantor.

Don Juan Sandoval sold a piece of land in Tibás to Santos Contreras for 67.5 pesos. The property was bordered to the North by the royal road leading to La Bermúdez and to the South by lands belonging to the Zamoras.

Don Timoteo Soto and his wife Doña Gordiana González obligated themselves for 41 pesos 1.1 reales each to Gordiana's five minor children from her first marriage to Don José Antonio Quesada. The funds represent their paternal inheritance, and Don José Ángel Soto acted as guarantor.

Don Anselmo Aguilar and Doña Gertrudis Hidalgo, residents of San José, made their wills, detailing their parents (from San José and Heredia respectively) and their common children. Anselmo Aguilar also mentioned his previous marriage to Doña Ramona Rodríguez and their two sons. Arbitrators and executors were designated.

José Cayetano Gamboa, widower of Manuela Villalobos, obligated himself for 108 pesos 7.5 reales from their maternal inheritance to his five minor children. The children are José Félix, Antonia, Sabina, Joaquín, and José María.

José Ángel Chinchilla obligated himself for 164 pesos from their paternal and maternal inheritances to his four minor siblings: José Concepción, José Antonio, María del Pilar, and María Calixta. All five are children of the deceased Francisco Javier Chinchilla, with Juan de Dios Chinchilla and Rafael Chinchilla acting as guarantors.

Santos Contreras, a resident and native of Heredia, made his will in San José. He is the legitimate son of Cristóbal Contreras and Josefa Salas, and is married to Josefa Ramírez, with whom he has ten children. He named his wife and Pedro López as executors, and José Francisco Porras as arbitrator.

Narciso Badilla obligated himself for 146 pesos and half a real to his minor grandsons, Félix and Antonio, who are the children of his deceased son, José Antonio Badilla. His son, José María Badilla, signed the document on his behalf.

The will of Doña Micaela Aguilar, dated May 31st, was added to the protocol on June 22nd. She was the legitimate daughter of Juan José Aguilar and Juana María Solano, and widow of José Chacón. Her will detailed her children with José Chacón, their marital statuses, and her grandchildren, naming her son-in-law, Presbyter Aguilar, and Félix Fernández Carranza as executors.

Antonio Bernardino Murillo and his wife María Berrocal made their wills in San José. Antonio was the natural son of Juana Murillo, and María was the legitimate daughter of Juan Berrocal and Francisca Sáenz. They listed their children and their marital statuses, naming Félix Bonilla as arbitrator (or Eusebio Rodríguez in his absence) and the survivor and José de la Ascensión Mora as executors.

Andrés Bermúdez sold approximately 500 varas of land in Las Dos Cercas to Manuel Antonio Aguilar for 200 pesos. The land was bordered by the property of his deceased father, Santiago Bermúdez de la Cruz, to the East, the Tinbí River to the North, and the royal road to Palo Grande and Patarra to the West and South.
Félix Cerdas, Antonio Acuña, and Ramón Arguedas, who were co-heirs of Domingo Chinchilla and Cayetana Delgado, sold a piece of land to Don Anselmo Aguilar.

A piece of land in El Mojón, bordered by the Mojón road, Quebrada de los Negros, lands of Polonia Chinchilla and María de los Angeles Aguilar, and fences of Francisco Félix Delgado, was sold for 110 pesos. The transaction was signed by Félix José Cerda.

In San José, José Bogantes, a resident of Heredia and rematario of aguardiente stalls in Heredia and Alajuela, committed to paying 20 pesos monthly to the Receptor de alcabalas. Don Matías Sandoval served as his guarantor for this obligation.
In San José, Gregorio Piedra, son of the late José Piedra and Juana Valenciano, committed to paying 84 pesos 45 reales to his minor siblings, José Hilario and Trinidad, as part of their inheritance.

Cayetano Madriz, a veteran corporal and rematario of an aguardiente stall in Ujarrás, committed to paying ten pesos monthly to the Royal Treasury. Juan José Bonilla, also a resident of Ujarrás, served as his guarantor.

José Nicolás Quesada, son of the late José Quesada and María del Rosario Sánchez, committed to paying 90 pesos, 6 reales, and 29 maravedís to his six minor siblings (Juan Pablo, Antonio, José Concepción, Juana Francisca, Nicolás de Jesús, and María Micaela) as their inheritance. José Antonio González acted as his guarantor.

Don Ramón Jiménez was appointed tutor for his minor sister-in-law, Doña María Cecilia Zamora, at her request. Ramón, along with his wife Doña Joaquina Zamora, received María Cecilia's inheritance of 950 pesos, which included 167 cattle, 2 mules, 4 mares, 1 horse, 2 colts, and 200 pesos in a house, from her deceased mother Doña Rita Coronado. An earlier record from 1814 notes that Jiménez delivered these assets to Don Pedro Marín, who became María Cecilia's husband.
Governor Acosta officially confirmed the appointment of Don Ramón Jiménez as the tutor for the minor Doña María Cecilia Zamora.

Presbítero Don José de la Encarnación Fernández, the priest of Bagaces, transferred the hacienda of the San José de Las Cañas confraternity to Don Nicolás Oreamuno, his rematario. The hacienda, valued at 1087 pesos, included a house, corral, branding irons, 185 cattle, 11 mares, and 13 tame horses. Oreamuno paid 362 pesos 3 reales upfront, with the remainder to be paid in two annual installments with 5% annual interest.

Presbítero Don Rafael Arnesto de Troya sold a cattle and horse hacienda in Afiravalles to Presbítero Don José de la Encarnación Fernández for 15110 pesos 6 reales. The hacienda, previously acquired from Don Pío Arguello and Doña Engracia Aguilar, included a house, utensils, salt, an oratory, various livestock, and plantain groves. Don Cipriano Fernández received the hacienda on behalf of the buyer on April 21, 1807, and a 1812 note indicates Arnesto cancelled the debt upon full payment.
Don Benito de Alvarado, residing in San José, granted general power of attorney to his brother, Don Manuel de Alvarado. This power was later cancelled in 1816 at the request of both brothers.
Don Manuel Alvarado granted general power of attorney to his brother, Don Benito de Alvarado. This power was later cancelled in 1816 at the request of both brothers.
Don Marcos Ángulo, Captain and master of the brigantine San José y Las Animas, which was anchored in the port of Punta de Arenas, granted general power of attorney to Don Manuel García Escalante.

Doña Joaquina Pastora sold an enslaved mulata named Mónica Pastora, 32 years old, to Presbítero Don Pedro José Alvarado for 200 pesos. Mónica, described with dark skin, curly black hair, pockmarks, and a large flat nose, had been inherited by Joaquina from her mother, Doña Manuela Pastora.

Don Ramón Jiménez, Mayordomo of the Confraternity of Nuestro Amo, sold the confraternity's assets located in the jurisdiction of Heredia, within lands of Alajuela residents, to Presbítero Don Félix Alvarado for 1300 pesos 7 reales.

Don Juan Francisco Bonilla sold a house situated on a corner of the public plaza to Presbítero Don Félix Alvarado for 827 pesos 5 reales cash. Bonilla had acquired the house from the executors of the late Presbítero Don Ramón Azofeifa.

Don José Antonio García, rematario of the assets of the Confraternity of Nuestro Amo in Esparza, and his wife Doña Bárbara Conejo, committed to paying 537 pesos 2 reales over 8 years with 5% annual interest. Don Nicolás Castro, a resident of San José, served as their guarantor, with their son Joaquín García signing on behalf of Doña Bárbara.

Presbítero Don Félix de Jesús García sold an enslaved mulato named Hilario, 17 years old and son of his enslaved woman Manuela Guzmán, to Don Nicolás Castro, a resident of San José, for 250 pesos. Castro was to pay this amount, along with an additional 100 pesos loaned to him, within one year with 5% annual interest.
Manuel José Quesada, Mayordomo of the Confraternity of Nuestra Señora de Ujarrás, transferred the confraternity's assets to Presbítero Don Pedro José Alvarado.

Four caballerías of land, two houses, a pigsty, corrals, various furniture, 7442 cattle, and 9 mares were sold for 1480 pesos and 2 reales, with the payment made to the Royal Treasury. The property was located in the jurisdiction of Bagaces.

Don Elias Muñoz, a resident of Heredia, committed to paying 322 pesos 4 reales and 3 maravedíes to Rafael, Gertrudis, and Josefa Joaquina, representing their inheritance from their deceased parents, Don Cayetano Ugalde and Doña Ignacia Arias. Payments for Gertrudis and Josefa Joaquina were to be given to their grandmother, Doña Micaela Alfáro, and for Rafael to Don Fernando Ugalde, who was caring for the minors. Don Juan Luis Muñoz and Juan Barrantes served as guarantors.

María Francisca Romero, legitimate daughter of the deceased Diego Romero and Manuela Camacho, and widow of Francisco Quesada, made her will. She named her children José Manuel, José Antonio, José Francisco, María de la Trinidad, Rita Josefa, Francisca Josefa, and Josefa Rosalía, with the first five being married. Her sons José Antonio and José Francisco were appointed as executors, and her grandson Antonio Bernardo Cerdas was also mentioned.

Don Nicolás Oreamuno, who also signed as José Nicolás de Oreamuno, granted general power of attorney to Don Pablo de Alvarado. Don Pablo was described as a native of Cartago and a resident in the capital of the Kingdom.

Don Juan Francisco Bonilla sold a house with its enclosed plot to Don Francisco Javier de Villasanta for 600 pesos. The property had been acquired from the succession of Doña Manuela Pastora and was bordered by the properties of Doña María Francisca Corrales, Francisco Javier Mayorga, Don Manuel Marchena, and Doña Ana Elisondo.

Don Elias Muñoz, a resident of Heredia and testamentary executor of Don Juan José Muñoz, sold three caballerías of land to Félix Solano for 75 pesos. The land was located in the area of La Boca del Monte and bordered properties belonging to Don Ramón Gutiérrez and Juan José Acosta, as well as natural features like the Cacao stream, Aguacate mountain, and Guanacaste stream.

José Fermín Monge, legitimate son of the deceased Nicolás Monge and Antonia González, made his will. He was married to Isabel Vega, with whom he had children: Juan José, José Feliciano, María Josefa, José de los Angeles, and José Ignacio. His wife, Isabel Vega, was appointed as his executor.

people_involved: María de los Angeles (daughter of Piedra)
summary: María de la Concepción Piedra, legitimate daughter of the deceased Miguel Piedra and María Teresa Quesada, and widow of Felipe Arias, made her will. She named her living children José Joaquín, José Miguel, María de los Angeles, and Juan del Carmen. Don Joaquín Oreamuno was designated as the arbiter judge, and her son José Joaquín and her brother José Miguel Piedra were appointed as executors.

José Antonio Brenes sold a piece of land in the area named Paíz to Josefa Quiteria Soto for 30 pesos. The land had previously belonged to Manuel Lizano and before him to Manuela Martínez, and it bordered the royal road to the North.

José Francisco Rojas, legitimate son of the deceased José Rojas and Cayetana Estrella, all residents of San José, made his will. He was married to Doña Francisco Blanco, with whom he had children: Ana de la Luz, Miguel, María Josefa, and Manuela de los Reyes, all of whom were married. He also raised an abandoned girl named María de Jesús, to whom he bequeathed half of his quinto. Don Gregorio Ulloa was named arbiter judge, and his wife and son Miguel were appointed as executors.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Luis Demetrio de Coronado
summary: Don Ramón Jiménez, as husband of Doña Joaquina Zamora and guardian of Doña María Cecilia Zamora, along with Don Julián Zamora and Doña Irene Zamora, all heirs ab intestato and first cousins of the deceased Presbítero Don Luis Demetrio de Coronado, granted general power of attorney to Presbítero Don Juan Manuel Zamora. Don Juan Manuel was a native of Cartago and resided in the jurisdiction of Masaya.

Don Manuel Sáenz and Don Pedro José Carazo, who won the auction for two of the five aguardiente stalls in Cartago, committed to paying 20 pesos jointly and severally each month to the Alcabalas Collector.
José Trinidad Pacheco, who won the auction for an aguardiente stall in Cartago, committed to paying 10 pesos monthly to the Alcabalas Collector and provided Don José María Peralta as his guarantor.

Don Juan Manuel Alvarado, who won the auction for the aguardiente stall established in Ujarrás, committed to paying 10 pesos monthly to the Alcabalas Collector and provided Don José Ruperto Prieto as his guarantor.

Matías Méndez, natural son of the deceased Blas de Jesús and Rosa Méndez, and being single and without succession, made his will. His assets included carpentry tools and various small pastures. He named his niece Margarita Solano and his first cousin Juan Manuel Marín as legatees, and Presbítero Don Félix García as his executor.
Don Manuel Marchena and Don Joaquín Oreamuno, acting as testamentary executors for Doña María Francisca del Corral, received inventoried assets totaling 1167 pesos for deposit.

In Heredia, Santiago González and Anselmo Arias, who won the auction for an aguardiente stall established in Bagaces, committed to paying 10 pesos monthly for one year to the Alcabalas Collector. José Bermúdez and Mariano Ruiz served as their guarantors.

In Heredia, Presbítero Don José Emigdio Umaña received assets valued at 324 pesos from Don Elias Muñoz, which belonged to the minors Rafael, Josefa Joaquina, and Gertrudis, children of the deceased Don Cayetano Ugalde and Doña Ignacia Arias. Don Elias Muñoz had replaced some missing assets with a pasture near the Guayabo pass in Río Segundo, and the transaction was approved by the First Alcalde, Don José Francisco Bonilla.

In Heredia, Manuel González, husband of Doña Ramona Ugalde (daughter of the deceased Don Cayetano Ugalde and Doña Ignacia Arias), received 108 pesos from his wife's guardian, Don Elias Muñoz, representing her inheritance.
In Heredia, León Salas was the auction winner for one of the four aguardiente stalls. The entry is incomplete.
An unnamed individual commits to paying 10 pesos monthly for a year to the Receptor de Alcabalas, with Don Mauricio Salinas acting as guarantor.
Doña Josefa Micaela Arias, widow of Don Miguel Cabezas, obliges herself to her six minor children for 270 pesos and 1.5 reales, representing their paternal inheritance.

Doña María Sandoval, widow of Don José Miguel Porras, obliges herself to her three minor children for 452 pesos and 3.5 reales from their inheritance. She also obliges herself to her six grandchildren, children of her deceased daughter Doña Rita Porras and Don José Bonilla, for 54 pesos and 5.5 reales from their inheritance.

Spouses Don Gregorio Ulloa and Doña Ramona Hernández, natives of Cartago and residents of San José, make their wills. They list their parents and five legitimate children, mention properties in several locations, and leave goods to Silvestre Ulloa, whom they raised. Don José Ulloa is named as an executor.

Juan Manuel Soto obliges himself to his eight minor siblings for 807 pesos from their inheritance, as their parents Joaquín Soto and Rosaura Chaves are deceased. Juan de Jesús Castillo acts as guarantor for this obligation.
A testament is added to the registry.

people_involved: María Felipa de la Cruz Castillo
summary: Nicolás Rojas, legitimate son of Javier Rojas and Mariana Fallas, makes his will before Alcalde 1st Don Hilario Zeledón. He is married to María Felipa de la Cruz Castillo, widow of Gregorio Reyes, and has no children, but mentions his stepdaughter María Gertrudis Reyes. His parents are named as heirs, and his wife and Presbítero Don Félix Velarde are executors.
The testament of Juan Pablo Chaves, natural son of the deceased Ignacio Chaves and Manuela Estrella, is initiated but suspended due to the testator's delirium.

Ángel de Jesús Bustamante, tutor of the minor children Vicente and Antonia Toribia Bustamante, receives 106 pesos and 2 reales from their deceased parents' inheritance. Luis Antonio Bustamante provides a guarantee for the administration.

Don José Ulloa, a resident of Cartago and auctioneer of aguardiente distilleries in San José, Heredia, and Alajuela, obliges himself to pay 60 pesos monthly for a year to the Receptor de Alcabalas, with Don Gregorio Ulloa as his guarantor.

Capitán Don Sebastián de Guevara and his wife Doña Juana de Lacalle take charge of 100 pesos from a chaplaincy belonging to Presbítero Don José Ana Alvarado, which was redeemed by Doña Feliciana de la Fuente, widow of Don Ignacio Llórente. They mortgage a pasture in Purires as security.

Don José Ana Jiménez, a resident of San José, transfers the assets of the Santísimo Cofradía, primarily livestock, to Don Félix Bonilla for 1123 pesos and 4.5 reales, a sum already paid to the Royal Treasury.
Coronel Don Juan Francisco Bonilla grants general power of attorney to Presbítero Don Andrés Carranza, who is the Cura of Usulután.

Proceedings initiated by Don José Antonio García, tutor of Don Julián Sáenz's minor children, for the sale of a house are protocolized. García had requested authorization on November 9 to sell a dilapidated house, which the Governor authorized on November 11 after hearing witnesses.

locations: Santuario de Nuestra Señora de la Soledad
summary: Don José Antonio García, tutor of the minor children of the deceased Don Julián Sáenz and Doña Feliciana Rojas, sells a house and half a plot inherited by the minors to Rafael de Mata for 133 pesos and 2.5 reales, payable in two years. The property is located near the Santuario de Nuestra Señora de la Soledad and other named neighbors. The sale was cancelled in 1811.

Coronel Don Juan Francisco Bonilla sells a 20-year-old mulatto slave named José de Jesús María, son of his slave Ventura, to Don Ramón Palacios for 300 pesos. José de Jesús María is described as literate and skilled in various trades including bleeding, weaving, and music.
Leandro Matamoros receives goods embargoed from Félix Bogarín, who is facing legal action for constructing a house poorly for Doña Ana Elizondo.
