Don Juan Andrés García and Rosa Rivera obligate themselves for 552 pesos 5 reales from the inheritance of Joaquín Solano. Joaquín is the minor son of Rosa Rivera and her first husband, José Antonio Solano. Another daughter, Ana de Jesús, died after her father.

Don Francisco Javier Navarro, acting as attorney for Don Pedro Elisondo, sold a piece of land named Santa Lucía in the Río Grande area to Félix Gutiérrez. The land measured 1x8 cordadas in perimeter and was sold for 105 pesos.

people_involved: Presbítero don Rafael José de la Rosa
summary: Spouses José Bernardo Calvo and María Manuela Rosales made their wills, listing their legitimate children and their parents. María Manuela Rosales also declared a natural son, Cayetano, born before her marriage. They appointed Presbítero don Rafael José de la Rosa as arbiter judge and the surviving spouse and Presbítero Hipólito as executors.

Doña Fermina Ugalde, widow of Don Manuel Antonio Guzmán, placed her 13-year-old son, Joaquín Eufrasio Guzmán, as an apprentice with merchants Don Mateo Ibarra and Don Sebastián Melón. The agreement stipulated that the merchants would transport him to San Miguel or Guatemala, instruct him in their trade, and provide for him until he turned 25, without his earnings being claimed by his family.

Doña Feliciana de la Fuente, widow of Don Ignacio Llórente, delivered her 13-year-old son, Domingo de Jesús, to Don Mateo Ibarra and Don Sebastián Melón. This apprenticeship was under the same conditions as the previous agreement for Joaquín Eufrasio Guzmán.

María Antonia Molina, a single woman, made her will, naming her natural daughter, Ana Josefa, as her heir. She also mentioned owning a house with her sister Roberta, inherited from their deceased brother Presbítero Pablo Molina. Presbítero don Pedro Alvarado and Presbítero don Florencio del Castillo were appointed as executors.

Don Manuel Marchena and Doña Francisca del Corral granted freedom to their two slaves, Petronila del Corral (about 50 years old) and her son José de Jesús Marchena (about 28 years old). José de Jesús paid 200 pesos for his freedom and promised to pay 100 pesos for his mother's freedom within a year. A marginal note from 1813 indicates the 100-peso debt was cancelled.

people_involved: Presbítero don Rafael José de la Rosa
summary: Don Joaquín Oreamuno, Mayordomo de fábrica of the Holy Church, granted power to Presbítero don Rafael José de la Rosa. This power allowed him to collect capellanía income owed to his Mayordomía in Nicaragua.

In San José, spouses Pedro Montero and Manuela Josefa Guzmán made their wills, listing their parents and eight children. They specified the marital status of some daughters and appointed Don Mateo Mora (or Don Eusebio Rodríguez) as arbiter judge, with the surviving spouse and two eldest children as executors.

In San José, Don Mateo Bertora, a merchant and former artilleryman originally from Arvenga, Genoa, made his will. He declared himself a widower of Catalina Rusi and named his natural daughter, María Catalina, born with Francisca Jerónima Castro, as his sole heir. He appointed Don José Ana Jiménez, Doña Antonia Carranza, and Don José Miguel Jiménez as executors and guardians for his daughter.

In San José, before Mayor Don Hilario Zeledón, Don Pedro Umaña made his will, listing his parents, his wife Doña Manuela de Jesús Fallas, and their six children. He mentioned the marriages of four daughters and that his son Cecilio was studying for the priesthood, for whom he made a special provision. Don Pedro also acknowledged having raised an unnamed bastard son and appointed Don Eusebio Rodríguez as executor.
In Heredia, Juan Francisco Rodríguez made his will. He is the legitimate son of the deceased José Gabriel Rodríguez and Bárbara Josefa Oviedo and is married.

A family record details Paula León's children with an unnamed partner (María Francisca, Rafaela, Antonia, Manuel José, Antonio de los Dolores) and her previous marriage to José Fonseca, with whom she had Sotero and María. The record also mentions her residence in La Sabanilla, lists Juan Antonio Salazar and Manuel Villalobos as arbiters, and Juan José Rodríguez as an executor for an unnamed testador.

Don Anselmo Gutiérrez and Doña Manuela Gertrudis Flores were designated by Factor de Tabacos Don José Mariano de Valenzuela to manage the 'tercena' of Heredia, including stamped paper and gunpowder. They committed to the Royal Treasury for 500 pesos, with Don Ramón Gutiérrez acting as their guarantor.

Don Feliciano Salinas, son of Anastasio Salinas and Ramona Ulloa, and his wife Doña Ramona Paniagua, daughter of Simón Paniagua and Bárbara Zamora, made their will in Heredia. They named their children Ana Joaquina and Ana Micaela, and appointed the survivor, Don Mauricio Salinas, and Don Blas Pérez as executors.

Manuela Silvestra Sáenz, natural daughter of Ana Morales and widow of Juan Pablo Morales, made her will in Ujarrás. She listed her living children and several deceased children, including Antonia who left three children. Her son Marcos and Manuel Morales were named as executors.
Three testaments were added in 1809, all made in Alajuela before Alcalde 2° Don Matías Sandoval.

Cipriano Rojas and his wife María de Jesús Hernández made their will, listing their seven children and properties near Alajuela. Cipriano had previously served as executor for his brother Tomás Solera, and they had raised José Ricardo Rojas. Presbítero Don Nereo Fonseca, Don Miguel Alfaro, and Don Pedro Monje were appointed as their executors.

Miguel Cruz and his wife María Villegas made their will, listing their eight children and two 'caballerías' of land in Tacares. Don Matías Sandoval, Don Silvestre Ramos, and Don José Francisco Saborío were named as executors.

Don Patricio González and his wife Doña Bibiana Alfaro made their will, listing their common children Francisco de la Trinidad and Inés Anselma. Patricio had a previous daughter, María de la Asunción, with María del Rosario Rodríguez, while Bibiana had no children with her previous husband, Enrique Alfaro. Their home was in Río Segundo, and Don Valentín Arias, Don Ramón Quesada, and Don Rafael Alfaro were appointed as Juez arbitro, defensor de menores, and executor, respectively.
The Factor de Tabacos, Don José Mariano de Valenzuela, granted general power of attorney to Don José Ruperto Prieto for his lawsuits in San José.

Santos Rivera, legitimate son of Antonio Rivera and Teresa Santiago, and his wife María de Jesús, made their will. They listed their three married children: Rosa, Cornelio, and Pedro. The surviving spouse and Don Vicente Frutos were named as executors.

Inventories and partition of the estate of María Francisca Romero, widow of Francisco Quesada, were conducted. All her children and heirs were adults, and her grandson Antonio Bernardo, son of María Trinidad, was included as a legatee.

Don Miguel de Jesús Carranza, a resident of San José, confessed to owing Presbítero Don Félix de Jesús García 200 pesos, borrowed for 3 years at 5% annual interest. He mortgaged 90 cattle located in 8 'caballerías' in PuAs. The debt was cancelled in 1811.

Doña Cecilia Jiménez sold a house and its plot, inherited from her father, to Rafael Ciríaco Guerrero for 350 pesos. The payment was to be made at 15 pesos monthly from Guerrero's salary as a master armorer in the Royal Treasury. The sale was cancelled in 1811.

María Jerónima Garro, widow of Francisco Miguel Delgado and resident of Purires, made a codicil to her will. She declared some advances made to her children Félix Delgado (deceased), Antonio, and Rita.

Don Manuel García Escalante, acting as attorney for Don Marcos Ángulo, acknowledged various advances from Don Manuel Alvarado totaling 1945 pesos 6 reales. These funds were for the repair of the brigantine 'San José y Las Animas' in Punta de Arenas, sailor support, and payments made in Panama. The brigantine was mortgaged and committed to be ready in August for a new cargo and subsequent voyage.

Don Ramón Jiménez, Mayordomo of several confraternities, transferred their assets in Bagaces (286 cattle and various furniture) to Don Lorenzo Carazo for 839 pesos, which Carazo had paid to the Royal Treasury.
Governor Don Tomás de Acosta granted power of attorney to Don Juan Domingo Iturraide, a resident and merchant of Panama, to sell an unspecified item.

A slave named Constancia, daughter of Feliciana, is being sent to an agent on the brigantine San José. Feliciana is described as being about 24 years old, light-skinned, with curly hair, and skilled in embroidery, sewing, and cooking.

Prudencio Picado received 118 cattle, 11 mares, and 6 horses, valued at 552 pesos, from Ramón Jiménez, which belonged to the Confraternities of Nuestro Amo and Nuestra Señora del Rosario. Picado agreed to pay 5% annual interest, mortgaging his livestock and house, with Antonio Delgado and his wife Gertrudis Navarro acting as guarantors. The debt was cancelled in 1814 by payment to Presbítero Félix Alvarado, the Mayordomo.
Atanasio Solano, José Antonio Solano, and Miguel Monge, as the husband of Manuela Guzmán, who are all heirs of the deceased Ramona Carranza, provided a receipt for their inheritances.

Pablo Martínez, also known as Calderón, made his will. He is the legitimate son of the deceased Tiburcio Martínez y Calderón and Bernarda Núñez, and is married to Teresa de Jesús García, with whom he has seven children. He appointed Capitán José Miguel Cárdenas as the defender of minors and his wife and Félix Jiménez as his executors.

José Julián Matamoros and his wife Josefa Joaquina Lobo took charge of 200 pesos from a chaplaincy belonging to the city's Convent, which Josefa Prudenciana Hidalgo redeemed. They secured the debt with a house and plot of land, valued at 140 pesos, and agreed to pay 5% interest. The debt was cancelled in 1818, with the principal later passing to María Concepción Ocaña, as manifested by Nicolás Carazo, Síndico del Convento.

The City Council, including Governor Tomás de Acosta, Alcaldes Ordinarios José Marín Peralta and Nicolás Oreamuno, and other officials, granted power of attorney to José María Zamora. Zamora, a lawyer of the Kingdom, was authorized to handle all matters concerning the City Council in the capital city of Guatemala.

people_involved: Presbítero José de los Reyes Quesada
summary: Manuel José Quesada, Gertrudis Morales (widow of Nicolás Quesada), and Manuel Morales (husband of Juana Antonia Bustamante), as heirs of the deceased Presbítero José de los Reyes Quesada, former Cura of Chocollos, granted power of attorney. They authorized Presbítero Florencio del Castillo, residing in León, to claim their inheritances. The grantors are residents of Ujarrás.

Francisco Chavarría, a merchant from San José, owed Adrián Zavala, a merchant from Granada, 2500 pesos for various Castilian and local goods. Chavarría agreed to pay the debt over five years, with Juan Francisco Bonilla and Nicolás Oreamuno each guaranteeing 1000 pesos, and Camilo de Mora, a resident of San José, guaranteeing 500 pesos.

Presbítero Rafael Arnesto de Troya granted power of attorney to Presbítero Nicolás Carrillo, who resides in Bagaces. This power was for Carrillo to represent him in a pending matter with Lorenzo Arnesto.

Joaquín Hidalgo, Mayordomo of the Confraternity of Nuestra Señora de los Angeles, transferred the Confraternity's assets located in Savegre to Juan Francisco Bonilla, who was the highest bidder. Bonilla paid 1245 pesos and 4.5 reales into the Royal Treasury for these assets, which included 500 cattle, 6 mares, 6 tame horses, a house, corrals, pigsty, banana plantations, and tools.

In San José, José Manuel Guerrero sold a piece of land in Los Dos Ríos to Manuel Antonio Aguilar for 50 pesos. This land was inherited by Guerrero from his deceased father-in-law, Santiago Cruz, and bordered properties belonging to José Aria Jiménez, Justo Picado, and his sister-in-law Juana Gertrudis Bermúdez.

In San José, Eufemia Pacheco and María Echevarría, who are the mother and sister of Francisco Echevarría, respectively, obligated themselves as guarantors for him to Camilo de Mora. They guaranteed up to 1000 pesos and mortgaged their houses, in case Mora's existing guarantee for Francisco became effective.
Manuel Antonio Aguilar, a resident of San José, granted general power of attorney to Camilo de Mora. This power was for Mora to handle all of Aguilar's lawsuits.

people_involved: Presbítero Rafael José de la Rosa
summary: Dolores Siles, wife of Eusebio Cantillo, sold a piece of land in Chircagres to Josefa Quiteria Soto, widow of Nicolás Quirós, for 30 pesos. Dolores had inherited this land from her first husband, Manuel Sito. The property bordered land belonging to the deceased José Antonio Solano, Presbítero Rafael José de la Rosa, the Ramírezes, and Benito Contreras.

In San José, Nicolasa Reyes, legitimate daughter of the deceased Ángel Reyes and Josefa Valverde, made her will. She was married first to Antonio Roldan, with whom she had a son, Fray Bernardo, and second to José Rodríguez, with whom she had a daughter who died in infancy. She named several legatees, including Cruz Arburola, Irene Reyes, Cristóbal de Jesús Mondragón, Rita, María, and Joaquina, and appointed Hilario Zeledón and Anselmo Aguilar as arbitrators, and Camilo de Mora and Eusebio Rodríguez as executors.

Pedro Manuel Brenes, widower of Josefa Leonarda Aguilar and now married to María Apolinaria Ulloa, acknowledged a debt of 89 pesos and a half real to his daughter, María de la Trinidad. This debt included the inheritance his first wife received upon the death of her father, Juan José Aguilar. Pedro Manuel Brenes provided José Brenes, a warden from the barrio of Churruca, as a guarantor for this debt.

Ramona Benita Villalobos, a widow, sold 300 varas of land in Serrogre to Gregorio Brenes for 34 pesos. This land was inherited from her late husband, Juan Mauricio Zúñiga, and bordered the Ibirrís river to the South and West.

people_involved: Doña Tomasa Joaquina López del Corral
summary: Don Nicolás Oreamuno and his wife, Doña María Josefa del Campo, took responsibility for 200 pesos from a capellanía (chaplaincy) belonging to the Convento de Esparza. Doña Tomasa Joaquina López del Corral had previously redeemed these funds.

The escribano, Don José Santos Lombardo, took responsibility for 200 pesos from a capellanía associated with Presbítero don Pedro Portocarrero, who resided in León. Doña Manuela Conejo had previously held these funds, and Lombardo mortgaged his house as security.

Presbítero don Nicolás Carrillo, the Sacristán Mayor of this city, granted general power of attorney to Presbítero don Francisco Cha^arría, and in his place, to Presbítero don Francisco Mayorga. Both Cha^arría and Mayorga resided in León.

people_involved: Don José de la Rosa Sáenz
summary: Doña María García y Masís, widow of Don José García, sold a house with its entire lot to Patricio Rivera for 100 pesos. She had previously purchased the property from Don José de la Rosa Sáenz. The property bordered houses belonging to Presbítero don Hipólito Calvo, María Cubero, Clemente González, and José Antonio Sánchez.

people_involved: Presbítero don Rafael José de la Rosa
summary: Presbítero don Rafael José de la Rosa, the interim Cura of this city, granted power to Bachiller don Florencio del Castillo, and in his absence, to Rector don Francisco Mayorga of the Colegio Seminario. This power was for them to take canonical collation of the Curate Benefice of this city or any other benefice conferred upon him.

José Emiliano Alfaro, son of the late Narciso Alfaro and María Francisca Céspedes, obligated himself to his five younger siblings for their inheritance of 18 pesos and 1.5 reales each. He also stated that he, along with his sisters María Josefa and Josefa Joaquina, and their husbands Julián Arias and Benito Martínez, had already received their shares.

Don Salvador Oreamuno, along with Don Manuel Marchena and Don Nicolás Oreamuno, had acted as guarantors for Juan José Bonilla, a mulatto slave belonging to the Cofradía de los Angeles, who was auctioned to Don Santiago Bonilla. The Gobernador ordered the three guarantors to pay the principal and interest or become tenants of the sum. Don Salvador Oreamuno took responsibility for one-third of the principal and interest, amounting to 96 pesos and 5.5 reales, at 5% annual interest.
Don Manuel Marchena acknowledged a debt of 96 pesos and 5.5 reales to the Cofradía de los Angeles, for reasons explained in the previous document regarding the guarantor situation.

Don Nicolás Oreamuno acknowledged a debt of 96 pesos and 5.5 reales to the Cofradía de los Angeles. This debt was due to the reasons explained in the previous documents concerning his co-obligors, Don Salvador Oreamuno and Don Manuel Marchena.

Doña Antonia Jiménez, widow of Don Manuel de la Torre, sold her mulatto slave, Ana Efigenia, to Gobernador don Tomás de Acosta for 200 pesos. Ana Efigenia was described as 40 years old, of regular stature, white-skinned, and black-haired, and Doña Antonia had purchased her from Doña Cecilia Jiménez.

Presbítero don Pedro Vicente González, the Teniente Cura of Heredia, took responsibility for 200 pesos from a capellanía belonging to Presbítero don José Antonio Bonilla, the current Cura of El Viejo. The funds were previously held by the late Doña María Francisca del Corral, and González mortgaged his house in Heredia as security.

Don Joaquín Oreamuno and Don Manuel Marchena, acting as executors for Doña María Francisca Corrales, sold a mill with a house in the El Fatal neighborhood to Presbítero don Félix Alvarado for 133 pesos and 3.5 reales. The property bordered houses of Tomás Arburola and the heirs of Félix Batista, the royal road, and the buyer's pasture.

In San José, Don José Ulloa, the auction winner for four aguardiente stalls in the town, obligated himself to pay 40 pesos monthly to the Receptor de Alcabalas. Don Gregorio Ulloa served as his guarantor.

In San José, Santiago González, a resident of Heredia and the auction winner for the aguardiente stall in the Bagaces valley, obligated himself to pay 10 pesos monthly to the Receptor de Alcabalas. Anselmo Arias, also from Heredia, acted as his guarantor.

In San José, Micaela Rojas, widow of Lorenzo Sequeira, obligated herself to her minor children (María de la Encarnación, Hilaria, Pascuala, and José Trinidad) for 46 pesos and 2.5 reales each, representing their inheritance.

In San José, Juan Manuel Borbón sold a piece of land in El Espinal to Don Félix Fernández Carranza for 112 pesos. Borbón had acquired the land from Doña Rosa Sáenz and Don Anselmo Aguilar. The property bordered the Quebrada de los Salazares to the East and the royal road to the North.

In Heredia, Manuel Carvajal, the auction winner for one of the four aguardiente stalls in the town, obligated himself to pay 10 pesos monthly for one year to the Receptor de Alcabalas. Ramón Carbonero served as his guarantor.

In Heredia, Cayetano Orozco and María de los Santos Moya sold a piece of land in La Lagunilla to Presbítero don Pedro Vicente González for 100 pesos. They had acquired the land from Doña Francisca Antonia de Sierra, a widow. The property bordered the seller's fence and pasture, the late Don Manuel González's pasture, and the buyer's pasture.

In Heredia, José María Ramos, the auction winner for an aguardiente stall in Esparza, obligated himself to pay 10 pesos monthly for one year to the Receptor de Alcabalas. Juan Barrantes served as his guarantor.
In Heredia, Doña Francisca Antonia de Sierra, a widow, sold a piece of land in La Lagunilla to Doña María González for 120 pesos. The property bordered the Quebrada de La Bermúdez to the North.

In San José, Don Anselmo Aguilar and Doña Gertrudis Hidalgo executed a codicil, changing their arbiters. They appointed Don Mateo de Mora, and in his absence, his son Don Joaquín de Mora, as the new arbiters.

Don José Ulloa, a concessionaire for aguardiente stalls in Heredia and Alajuela, committed to paying 20 pesos monthly for one year to the Receptor de Alcabalas. Don Gregorio Ulloa served as his guarantor for this obligation.

Francisco Barquero, a resident of Heredia, sold a piece of land in Los Hornos to Francisco Rodríguez, also from Heredia, for 20 pesos. Barquero had previously acquired this land from Ana María Micaela Quirós. The property was bordered by the royal road to Monte and a water ditch.

people_involved: Presbítero don Rafael Arnesto de Troya
summary: Don Camilo Mora, acting as the attorney for Don Manuel Antonio Aguilar, acknowledged a debt of 500 pesos to Presbítero don Rafael Arnesto de Troya. The loan was for one year at 6% annual interest, secured by a mortgaged pasture in San Antonio. This debt was noted as cancelled in 1810.

Don José María Peralta, a concessionaire for one of the city's five aguardiente stalls, committed to paying 10 pesos monthly for one year to the Receptor de Alcabalas. His wife, Doña Ana Benita del Corral, acted as his guarantor.

Don Manuel Sáenz, a concessionaire for an aguardiente stall in the city, committed to paying 10 pesos monthly for one year to the Receptor de Alcabalas. His wife, Doña Cayetana Ulloa, served as his guarantor.

Presbítero don Félix Alvarado, the interim priest of Heredia, granted power of attorney to Don José Alba, an Agent of the Indies residing in the Court of Seville. The purpose was for Alba to seek one of the Prebends of the Bishopric of León for Alvarado.

Isabel Vega, the widow of Fermín Monge, committed to her minor children, José Feliciano, María Josefa, José de los Angeles, Juan José, and José Ignacio. This obligation was for 20 pesos 3.5 reales each, representing their paternal inheritance.

people_involved: Presbítero don Rafael Arnesto de Troya
summary: Don Nicolás Oreamuno sold a mulatto slave named Nicolás to Presbítero don Rafael Arnesto de Troya for 100 pesos. Nicolás was described as being about 20 years old, of regular stature, white-skinned, with reddish curly hair, a dry left leg, and working as a tailor.

Doña Joaquina del Corral sold a piece of her house's lot to Don Manuel García Escalante for 50 pesos. The lot was bordered by her own lot, Doña Antonia Arlegui's lot (with a royal street in between), Doña Gertrudis Carazo's house, and Don Ignacio Rucabado's lot and the Governor's house.

Doña Josefa Oreamuno committed to paying 5% annual rent for four years for cattle leased by her husband, Don Ignacio Rucabado, from the Cofradía de Nuestro Amo de Bagaces. The lease included 137 cattle, 13 mares, and 16 horses, valued at 8.5 pesos 4 reales, along with possession of the hacienda. She mortgaged her own free cattle hacienda in Bagaces jurisdiction as security.

Antonio Bogantes, a concessionaire for one of the four aguardiente stalls in Heredia, committed to paying 10 pesos monthly for one year to the Receptor de Alcabalas. Félix Paniagua acted as his guarantor.

Alejo Aguilar, as husband of Joaquina Cubero and guardian of María de los Santos Cubero, granted power of attorney to Don Carlos Machado, a native of Cartago residing in Rivas. This was to represent him in the inventory of assets left by his deceased father-in-law, Vicente Cubero, in Rivas, Nicaragua, due to Aguilar's poor health.

people_involved: Presbítero don Rafael Arnesto de Troya
summary: Presbítero don Rafael Arnesto de Troya donated a house in the city to his niece-in-law, Doña Rafaela Fajardo. He had previously purchased this house from Presbítero don Félix de Alvarado. The property was bordered by houses belonging to Trinidad Pacheco and Presbítero don Félix García, and lots owned by Doña María Manuela Miranda and Doña Antonia Pacheco.

José Bernardo Monge and María Josefa Gutiérrez, a married couple, made their wills. They named their common children as Bernardo de Jesús, José Manuel, and Francisco Fulgencio. María Josefa's previous marriage to Manuel Fernández produced Antonia Calixta, Ana María (deceased), and Manuel. The surviving spouse and Juan Calvo were appointed as executors.

José Francisco Oreamuno, natural son of María Francisca Mayorga, made his will. He was married for a second time to Manuela Badilla, with whom he had Josefa Nicolasa, Manuel Francisco, and José de Jesús. Manuela Badilla had three children from a previous marriage to Pedro Lobo: Antonio Cayetano, Antonio Vicente, and Josefa Joaquina, who was married to Julián Matamoros. Don Joaquín Oreamuno was named arbiter judge, and his wife and Julián Matamoros were named executors, with his three children with Manuela as heirs.

Don Juan Manuel de Cañas leased cattle (500 cattle, 30 mares, 20 horses) from the Cofradía de Nuestro Amo de Bagaces, valued at 2530 pesos. Don Santiago Bonilla delivered the cattle to Don Manuel Antonio Cañas, son and representative of the lessee. Don Juan Manuel de Cañas committed to paying 5% annual interest until 1817, with Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla and Don Joaquín de Oreamuno initially as guarantors, though Señor Bonilla later became the sole guarantor.
In San José, José Joaquín Coronel posted bail for Manuel Maroto, who was facing criminal charges. Maroto was accused of having wounded the deceased Félix Cárdenas in the Matina valley.

In San José, Rudesindo Salazar and Don José Manuel Chaves, as husband of María del Rosario Salazar, sold a piece of land in the Escasú neighborhood to Don Hilario Zeledón for 50 pesos. The land's boundaries were extensively described, referencing natural features and landmarks such as a ditch made by Juan Delgado and a pass named after Capitán Juan Astúa.

Don Alejo Ramírez, as the testamentary executor of the deceased Presbítero don Ramón Azofeifa, granted freedom to two slaves: Ceferino Quesada and his wife Dominga Solano. Ceferino was described as 29 years old, brown-skinned, and having a speech impediment, while Dominga was about 40 years old and darker-skinned.
Ceferino Quesada received 375 pesos for a mulatto slave and 200 pesos for a black slave with straight black hair. In return for these sums, he granted freedom to both slaves.

Don Miguel Fernández, legitimate son of the deceased Don Pedro Fernández and Doña Catalina Tenorio, made his will in San José before Alcalde 2° Don Félix Fernández. He is married to Doña Bárbara Valverde, with whom he has six children, all under 25 years old, and named his brother Don Cipriano Fernández and Don Camilo Mora as executors.

Don Juan Sáenz, legitimate son of the deceased Don Gregorio Sáenz and Doña Francisca de Castro, made his will in San José before Alcalde Félix Fernández. He is a widower of Francisca Josefa Mata, with whom he had seven children, and is currently married to Josefa Matilde Hernández, who is pregnant. The will details the marital status of his children and mentions his deceased sons León and Silverio, with Silverio leaving two children, and names Don Cristóbal Sáenz as an executor.

Don José Ana Jiménez and his wife Doña Antonia Carranza entered into a contract with the tobacco factor Don José Mariano de Valenzuela before Alcalde 1° Don Gregorio Ulloa. Jiménez is obligated to transport 100 bales of tobacco from Punta de Arenas to the Factoría de León in his brigantine 'San Benito,' captained by Don Francisco Castro, for a freight price of 3 pesos per bale, with all risks borne by the conductor. The brigantine is preparing for a voyage to Realejo.

Cristóbal Quirós, legitimate son of the deceased Juan Vicente Barquero (alias Quirós) and Antonia Josefa Rodríguez, made his will. He is married to Francisca Josefa Molina, with whom he has eight children, all married except Francisco. His wife and son Manuel are named as executors.
This entry records the closure and index of a registry, noting that documents were added in 1812.

Don José Antonio Zumbado and his wife Doña María González made their wills in Heredia before Alcalde 2° Santiago González. They are the parents of seven children: Florencia, José de los Santos, Joaquín, María Mercedes, Matías, Ramón, and Nicolás. Presbítero Don Vicente González (brother of María) and Don Julián Zamora are named as executors.

Nicolás Camacho, legitimate son of the deceased Benito Camacho and Josefa Valerio, made his will in Heredia before Alcalde Santiago González. He is married to Doña Antonia Alfaro and has no children, stating his wife would be the heir if not pregnant, and his mother a legatee. His wife and brother-in-law Ambrosio Alfaro are named as executors, and the will was granted in the barrio of Quebrada Seca.

Antonio Bogantes and his wife Sabina Víqüez made their wills in Quebrada Seca before Alcalde Santiago González. They have seven children, including Francisca, who is married to Manuel Ugalde. The surviving spouse and Miguel Chaverri are named as executors, with Mariano Rodríguez and José Cruz González appointed as arbiters.

Captain Don Santiago Bonilla and his wife Doña María Josefa Oriamuno sold a pasture and an open piece of land in Coris to Colonel Don Juan Francisco Bonilla. The pasture was inherited by María Josefa, and the open land was previously purchased by Santiago from Manuel Oreamuno. The properties, valued at 400 and 100 pesos respectively, are described with boundaries including the Coris river, the royal road to Amoladeras, and lands of Antonio Piedra, Cruz Bonilla, and Juana Bonilla.

Don Vicente Ramírez, a resident of Pueblo Nuevo, donated a piece of land to José Francisco Quesada. The land was inherited by Vicente from his deceased father, Don Pedro Ramírez, and is bounded by the Chiquito river, a mountain road, and lands belonging to Vicente and his brothers, including Don Alejo Ramírez.

Rosa Rivera sold a house with its plot in the arrabal of the city to Felipe Romero for 40 pesos. The property is bordered by houses and plots belonging to the deceased Miguel Ramos, José Antonio Ramos, Manuela Meza, and Santos Rivera.

Don Nicolás Carazo and his wife Doña Escolástica Peralta took on an obligation of 300 pesos for a chaplaincy of Nuestra Señora de los Angeles, previously held by the deceased Doña Manuela Baeza. This obligation is secured by Baeza's former residence, which the Carazos have now taken, and they will pay 5% interest. The house is described with boundaries including the parish cemetery and properties of Antonia, Jacoba, and Lucía Alvarado.

Don Tomás de Acosta donated 128 pesos to his godchild, Doña Margarita Hidalgo. Her father, Captain Don Manuel Hidalgo, a resident of Valle Hermoso, accepted the donation on his daughter's behalf and received the money.
Don Manuel Marchena leased 118 heads of cattle, eleven mares, and five horses.

Miguel Obando, a resident of Valle Hermoso, sold a piece of land in the area called los Anonos to Simón Mena for 25 pesos. The land was bordered by properties of Marcos Jiménez, Manuel Jiménez, Francisco Madriz, and the royal road leading to Escasú.

Miguel Obando sold another piece of land in los Anonos to Manuel Pascual Mena for 15 pesos. This property was adjacent to lands of Nicolás Castro, Eusebio Sáenz, the Pavas, and the road to Escasú, with a ravine in between.

Miguel Obando sold a third piece of land in los Anonos to Candelario Salazar for 30 pesos. The boundaries included Eusebio Sáenz's fence, the Barranca de las Pavas, the Tiribí River, and the royal road leading to Escasú.

Doña Antonia Jiménez, a widow, sold a city plot she inherited from her father to Ceferino Quesada for 90 pesos. The plot was bordered by properties of Ana Micaela Carazo, Francisca Miranda, Juan Pablo Jiménez, and the royal street.

Presbítero Juan José Oreamuno assumed guardianship for his nine nephews and nieces, children of the deceased Bartola Oreamuno, with each child inheriting 65 pesos and 3 cuartillos. He also acknowledged existing obligations on a pasture and a house, totaling 208 pesos and 3 reales, previously held by Bartola.

Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco granted freedom to his mulatto slave, Gregorio, who was approximately 27 years old. Gregorio had been purchased from the deceased Joaquín Alvarado in 1794 or 1795 for 200 pesos, and his freedom was granted for 100 pesos received from Gregorio, who obtained the money from a benefactor.

The testament of the unmarried sisters Manuela Simona, Manuela Feliciana, and Josefa Gertrudis Valverde, legitimate daughters of the deceased Santiago Valverde and Gregoria Ramírez, was recorded. They named each other as heirs and appointed Cura Rafael José de la Rosa and Manuel García Escalante as their executors.

The Ayuntamiento of Cartago, following a Royal Order from January 22 of the previous year (1809), elected Manuel Pavón y Muñoz as the deputy for the Kingdom and Vocal of the Supreme Central Junta of Spain and Indies. The Ayuntamiento then granted him general power to represent the province.

Rudesindo Zúñiga, a resident of Escasú, sold a piece of land in the barrio of Escasú, specifically in the area called los Anonos by the Tiribí River, to Cipriano Fernández for 500 pesos. The land was bordered by properties of Pablo Vargas, Juan Herrera, the Tiribí River, and the royal road from San José to Escasú.

María Leonida Oviedo, widow of Pablo Vargas, undertook obligations for the inheritance of her minor children Joaquín, Domingo, and Telésfora, each receiving 16 pesos, 3 reales, and 3 novenos. Hilario Chaves also undertook obligations for José Indalecio, Manuel Buenaventura, and Ciríaco de los Angeles, each receiving 19 pesos and 4 7/9 reales, with Juan José Herrera acting as his guarantor.

María Leonida Oviedo, widow of Pablo Vargas, sold a piece of land on the other side of the Tiribí River to Romualdo Saborío for 120 pesos. The land was bordered by the Tiribí River to the North and East, the road to Escasú to the South, and land previously sold by Rudesindo Zúñiga to the heirs of Pablo Vargas to the West.

The testament of Manuel Vargas, granted on February 26, 1810, in San José de Valle Hermoso, was protocolized. Manuel Vargas, a natural son of Andrés Mesen and Gabriela Coto, detailed his two marriages to Ana Vargas and Antonia Josefa Valverde, listing all his children from both unions and appointing Mateo de Mora as his executor.

Doña Eulalia Fernández, widow of Hermenegildo Aguilar, undertook an obligation in favor of her seven minor children, Blas, Tiburcio, Josefa, Calixto, Alejo, Pedro, and Rafael. Each child was due 58 pesos and 4 1/11 reales from their paternal inheritance.

locations: en medio de los dos ríos
summary: Miguel Obando, from Valle Hermoso, sold a piece of land in the area named 'en medio de los dos ríos' to José Francisco Piedra for 20 pesos. The land was bordered by properties of Nicolás Obando, 'los Bermúdez', the royal road to San Antonio, and common lands.
Antonio Gregorio Roldan emancipated his son, José Miguel Roldan, who was over 25 years old.

The Cabildo of Cartago was in session, composed of Governor Tomás de Acosta, Regidor and Alcalde 1° Juan Francisco de Bonilla, Alcalde 2° Hermenegildo Bonilla, Alcalde Provincial Manuel Marchena, Alguacil Mayor Joaquín de Oreamuno, and Síndico General Joaquín García.

Don Manuel Pavón is granted power to represent "this province" for the roles of Deputy of this Kingdom and Vocal of the Supreme Central Governing Junta of Spain. The power explicitly restricts him from binding the province or alienating its domains to foreign powers, emphasizing the Nation's right to resist surrender until defeated by superior forces and after extreme sacrifice for religion, King, and Country.

people_involved: Coronel Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla
Doña María de la Cruz Bonilla
summary: Coronel Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla sells Marcelina Bonilla, a "mulata blanca" over fifty years old with black hair and pockmarks, to Doña Juana and Doña María de la Cruz Bonilla. Marcelina was previously acquired by Bonilla from Doña María Bolívar, who is the mother of the buyers. The sale price is 100 pesos, to be paid within one year.

Rafaela Jiménez, widow of Lorenzo Guzmán, sells two and a half caballerías and half a quarter of land in the area named Púas to Efigenio González for 25 pesos. She inherited this land from her father, Don Manuel Felipe Jiménez. The property is described with specific boundaries including Zanja Vieja, río del Cuajiniquil, and quebrada de la Ceiba.

Don Ramón Zamora and Doña Juana Antonia Rodríguez, residents of Heredia living in Barba, execute their will. They have no children together. Doña Juana Antonia was previously married to Don Agustín Moya, with whom she had a son, Vicente, who had children from two marriages: Juan Agustín and José with Doña Petronila Saborío, and María de los Santos and Juana with Doña Petronila Arguello. Their son Agustín (from the first marriage) passed away, leaving a daughter, Francisca Paula. Don Mariano Zamora is the testator's brother, and Don José Moya (grandson of Doña Juana Antonia) and Don Tomás González are named executors.

people_involved: Sargento Mayor Don Juan Manuel de Cañas
Presbítero Don Juan de la Cruz Pérez
summary: In San José, Sargento Mayor Don Juan Manuel de Cañas, representing the absent Juan Antonio Espinosa, sells a house and lot to Don José Rafael de Gallegos for 140 pesos 1 real. The property belonged to Juan Antonio Espinosa through the death of his mother, Gertrudis Castro, widow of José Espinosa. Don Camilo de Mora provides a guarantee for the buyer, and Juan Antonio Espinosa, a soldier in the Granada Regiment, later cancelled the obligation in Cartago on October 1, 1810.

In San José, Don Gregorio Ulloa and Doña Ramona Hernández, his wife, make a codicil to their will from October 30, 1808. They revoke a donation previously intended for Silvestre Ulloa because he "took state" (likely meaning he married or entered a religious order).

In San José, Doña Bárbara Valverde, widow of Don Miguel Fernández, obligates herself to her minor children (Antonio, Santana, Tomás, Jesús, María, and Ana) for 837.5 reales each. This amount represents their paternal inheritance from their deceased father, Don Miguel Fernández.

people_involved: Doña María de la Rosa Soto
summary: In San José, José de la Ascensión Ortiz and his wife Doña María de la Rosa Soto obligate themselves to four of Doña María's minor children from her previous marriage to Don Francisco Esteban Jiménez (Cayetana, José Ana, Félix José, and Juan José). These children, under their care, are owed 204 pesos 1 real each as inheritance from Don Francisco Esteban. Don Antonio Vargas and Juan Manuel Quirós act as guarantors for this obligation.

In San José, Don Nicolás Castro obligates himself to the four minor children of his deceased brother, Don Francisco Castro (Don José de Jesús, Doña María del Rosario, Don Ramón, and Don Joaquín). They are owed 324 pesos 3 reales for the first child and 299 pesos 3 reales for each of the other three, as their paternal inheritance. Don Pío Castro acts as guarantor for this obligation.

people_involved: Don Juan de Dios de Ayala
summary: Don Juan de Dios de Ayala grants general power of attorney to Don Joaquín Arechavala, a Colonel of militias in León.

people_involved: Don Juan de Dios de Ayala
summary: Don Juan de Dios de Ayala grants general power of attorney to the Marqués de Aycinena.

Francisca Molina sells a 47-vara square lot to José de los Angeles Pérez for 20 pesos. The lot is located three blocks from the "plaza real" and is bounded by properties belonging to Don Juan Pablo Jiménez, Doña Nicolasa Meléndez (former owner), María Molina, and Benita Molina (sister of the seller).

Félix Antonio de Quesada and his wife Josefa de la Ascensión Araya, residents of Alajuela, make their will. Félix Antonio is the legitimate son of the deceased José de Quesada and María Francisca Hidalgo, who were residents of Heredia. Their children are Leandro, María (married to Lorenzo Sancho), Gertrudis, Micaela, José Francisco, Pedro Rafael, and Josefa Brígida. The executors are the surviving spouse and Don Julián Rodríguez.

people_involved: Beneficiado Don Rafael Arnestó de Troya
summary: Don Tomás de Acosta sells a 24-year-old "mulata" named Constancia, described as light-skinned with regular stature and curly black hair, to Beneficiado Don Rafael Arnestó de Troya for 250 pesos. Constancia is the daughter of another "mulata" named Feliciana. However, on the same date, they desist from the transaction because Constancia pleaded with her master not to be taken from his possession.

people_involved: Doña María de la Cruz Zavaleta
Coronel Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla
summary: Doña María de la Cruz Zavaleta and Doña Nazaria Zavaleta owe 50 pesos to Coronel Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla. The debt is to be paid within two years at a 5% interest rate.

Don Félix de Alvarado, acting as executor for the deceased Juan Antonio Barrantes (a former resident of Heredia), sells a piece of land measuring 500 by 200 varas in the area of La Bermúdez to Atanasio Araya for 52 pesos. The land's boundaries are described, including the Bermúdez stream and a royal road.

Benita Miranda sold a piece of land measuring 56 varas from East to West and 23 varas from North to South in Cartago to Nicolás Pérez for 18 pesos. The property was bordered by the houses and lots of Ceferino Luna, Joaquina Molina, Bruno Andrade, and José Pérez.

The estate of the deceased Joaquín Quirós was partitioned among his heirs. These included his widow Antonia, his children Rosa, Petronila, and Josefa (represented by their husbands), and his grandchildren José Felipe, Ambrosia, José de Dios Quirós, and Joaquina Quirós. The assets included a piece of land in Churis, at Ojo de Agua, bordered by the Churis and Ibiris rivers, and land belonging to Gregorio Andrade and Joaquina Molina.

Doña Bárbara and Doña Isabel Sancho sold two enslaved mulatas to Beneficiado don Félix de Alvarado, who was acting as a representative for don Manuel Taboada, a resident of León. The enslaved individuals were Petronila, aged 35, and her 18-year-old daughter, María de la Cruz, sold for 250 and 300 pesos respectively.

Beneficiado don Félix de Alvarado sold an enslaved mulata named María de la Asunción, aged 34, and her two sons, Raimundo (five months old) and Francisco (five years old), to don Félix Bonilla. Alvarado had previously acquired María de la Asunción from don Manuel Marchena. The sale prices were 150 pesos for María de la Asunción, 50 pesos for Raimundo, and 100 pesos for Francisco.

Francisco Salazar, legitimate son of the deceased José Salazar and Doña Eugenia Rivera, made his testament in San José. He was married to María de los Angeles Prado and named his six surviving children as heirs, also leaving a legacy to his nephew Hilario Salazar. Don Nicolás Castro and don Ensebio Rodríguez were appointed as his executors.

Don Juan Luis Lizano, a resident of Bagaces and vecino of León, assumed an obligation for a 500 pesos chaplaincy principal. This principal was previously held by the deceased Pedro Sarmiento and pertained to the Beneficio of Bagaces, under the jurisdiction of Esparza, where Padre don Miguel Aguilar served as interim priest. Beneficiado don Joaquín Lizano, the parish priest of Alajuela, acted as guarantor.

Trinidad Pacheco and his wife Joaquina Arias undertook an obligation for a 400 pesos silver chaplaincy principal, previously held by the deceased José Francisco Oreamuno, belonging to Nuestra Señora del Pilar in Tres Ríos. They received the principal in 80 heads of cattle and committed to an annual interest payment of 5%, with don Salvador de Oreamuno as guarantor. Don Manuel José Conejo was the Mayordomo.

people_involved: Beneficiado don Rafael Arnesto de Troya
summary: Beneficiado don Rafael Arnesto de Troya acquired the enslaved woman Francisca Tomasa Alvarez, aged 39, from Doña María Mercedes Guerrero for 21.5 pesos and half a real, and subsequently granted her freedom. Doña María Mercedes, widow of don José del Campo, had purchased Francisca Tomasa from don Gregorio Ulloa of Valle Hermoso for the same price, noting her 'agreste e indómita' nature when acquired at 27 years old.

José Miguel Cárdenas, natural son of the deceased Josefa Petronila Cárdenas, made his testament. He was married to Catalina Carrillo, with whom he had a son, José Gregorio, and named him as his heir. Catalina Carrillo had previously been married to Ramón Céspedes, with whom she had children Esteban and Ana Céspedes. Beneficiado don Nicolás Carrillo and Catalina Carrillo were named as executors.
Don José María Peralta, who won the bid for one of the five aguardiente stalls in Cartago, committed to paying 10 pesos monthly for one year. His wife, Ana Benita del Corral, served as his guarantor.
Don Manuel Sáenz, who won the bid for one of the five aguardiente stalls in Cartago, committed to paying 10 pesos monthly for one year. His wife, Doña Cayetana Ulloa, served as his guarantor.

Don José Arias, a resident of Alajuela and bid winner for the second aguardiente stall in his vicinity, committed to paying 10 pesos and 4 reales monthly for one year. Don Manuel Guzmán, also a resident of Alajuela, served as his guarantor.

José María Ramos, who won the bid for the aguardiente stall in Esparza and the first of four stalls in Heredia's jurisdiction, committed to paying 10 pesos monthly for each stall for one year. José Sáenz and José Antonio Salas served as his guarantors.
Manuel Carvajal, who won the bid for the third of four aguardiente stalls in Heredia, committed to paying 10 pesos monthly for one year. Ramón Carbonero served as his guarantor.

Anselmo Arias, who won the bid for the fourth of four aguardiente stalls in Heredia and the stall in Bagaces, committed to paying 10 pesos monthly for each stall for one year. Guadalupe Víquez served as his guarantor.
Antonio Bogantes, who won the bid for the second of four aguardiente stalls established for Heredia, committed to an obligation for the term of one year.

Don José Antonio Sáenz, a native of Cartago and resident of Heredia, sold a house and its plot in Cartago to Bernardo Calvo, a resident of Cartago, for 350 pesos. The property was bordered by land belonging to Don Joaquín Hidalgo, Doña Petronila Alvarado, José de la Rosa Sáenz (his son), and José Miguel Cárdenas.

people_involved: Teniente Coronel don Juan Agustín Porras
summary: Doña Ramona Porras, legitimate daughter of the deceased Teniente Coronel don Juan Agustín Porras and doña Juana de León, made her will in Heredia. She was the widow of don José Reyes and had three daughters: doña Juana (married to don Cipriano Pérez), doña Ana José, and doña Ana María. Her assets included her dwelling house, a pasture with a house in La Pitahaya, and a sixth part of a pasture called El Cuajiniquil in El Agualote, also with a house. Don José María Porras, don Joaquín Flores, and don Manuel José Bogantes were named as executors.
Doña Manuela Petronila Porras, widow of don Manuel Antonio Paniagua, granted power of attorney to don Benito Lardizabal, a resident of Nicaragua, to collect debts owed to her deceased husband.

Don Avelino Alfaro and his wife doña Gertrudis Godínez made their will in Heredia. They had eight children, and their assets included their dwelling house in Quebrada Seca. Mateo Alfaro had received a calf from his uncle Juan Antonio Godínez. The surviving spouse and Ambrosio Alfaro were named as executors.
Doña Simona Ulate, widow of Antonio José Arroyo, committed to her minor children regarding their paternal inheritance.

Hermenegildo Villalobos, widower of Antonia Concepción Bolaños, committed to his ten minor children (Jerónimo, Andrés, Cecilia, Dolores, María Luisa, Manuel de Jesús, María de los Ángeles, Manuela, Ramón, and Matea del Pilar) regarding their maternal inheritance.

Don José Antonio Sáenz, natural son of the deceased doña Ana de Morales, made his will in Heredia. He was married to doña María Gertrudis de Alvarado and had four children: Tomás, José de la Rosa, María Estéfana, and Hilaria. His son José de la Rosa and don Valentín Anas were named as executors.

Don José Miguel Zamora sold a 10-cuadra piece of land in El Huís to José Antonio Bolaños, a resident of Heredia, for 30 pesos. The land was bordered by the seller's lands, other owners, doña Manuela Rodríguez's lands, and the road to the mountain.

Doña Juana María Zamora, widow of don Cayetano Castro, committed to her four minor children (María, Manuela, Antonio, and Ramón) for 25 pesos, 6 reales, and one cuartillo each, as their paternal inheritance.

Don Pioquinto Rodríguez, widower of doña María Ugalde, committed to his seven minor children (María Demetria, Bernardo, Feliciana, Guadalupe, Francisco, Nicolás, and Casimiro) for 20 pesos, 5 reales, and 6 novenos each, as their maternal inheritance.

Don José Antonio Gutiérrez committed to the five minor children of doña Juana Antonia Gutiérrez (Mariano, Pablo, Rafaela, Manuel, and José Flores) for 176 pesos and 2 reales, with each child receiving 35 pesos and 2 reales from their paternal and maternal inheritance. Don Juan Soto served as guarantor.

María Ambrosia Villegas, widow of Miguel Cruz, committed to her five minor children (Gordiana, Francisco, Juan, María, and Isidro) for 35 pesos, 4 reales, and 3 octavos each, as their paternal inheritance.

Don Fabiano Jiménez committed to the minor children Serafina and Juan de Dios Ramírez for 129 pesos and 2.5 reales, corresponding to their paternal inheritance from their deceased father Cayetano Ramírez. Their mother, Rufina Oses, is now married to the grantor. José Jiménez and Javier Alvarado served as guarantors.

Don Pedro Arias sold a piece of land in Los Targuaces to don Juan Pablo Lara for 55 pesos. Arias had acquired the land from don José Ángel Pérez, who in turn had acquired it from don Vicente Paniagua. The land was bordered by lands of don Vicente Paniagua, don José Manuel Herrera, don Juan Soto, don Manuel Zumbada, and don Sebastián Ulate.

Francisco Venegas, acting as tutor for his nephews and nieces (Juana, Benito, Francisca, Josefa, Francisca, Felipe, María de la Asunción, José Felipe, Josefa Francisca, and Miguel Julián), committed for their inheritance of 308 pesos, 3 reales, and 8 décimos from the estate of their deceased parents, Juan Venegas and María Dolores Oviedo. Santos Venegas served as guarantor.

Don Juan de Jesús Alfaro committed for 108 pesos and 2.5 reales belonging to the heir Gabriel, son of don Juan Francisco Arias. Don Miguel Alfaro served as guarantor. There is another minor heir, Ignacia, for whom don Manuel Solórzano will be responsible.

José Pío Rojas, acting as tutor for his siblings Julián, Ramón Pablo, Francisco, José Cayetano, and Bárbara, committed for the inheritance they received from their deceased father, Juan Esteban Rojas. Lorenzo Murillo served as guarantor.
Marcelo Oviedo and his wife Ramona Aguilar committed to an obligation. The details of the obligation are not fully provided in the text.

The children of the deceased Juan Esteban Rojas, María Candelaria, Juan Casimiro, Cipriana, and José Marta, each received 35 pesos and one real as inheritance from their father. The grantor, Juan Esteban Rojas's widow, is involved in this obligation, with Francisco Javier Alfaro as guarantor.

Juan Miguel Alfaro granted freedom to his 3-year-old slave, María Isabel, who was the daughter of his other slave, Manuela. Manuela had acquired 25 pesos through her own industry and paid it to Juan Miguel Alfaro for her daughter's liberty.

Don José Manuel Murillo made his testament in Heredia, detailing his family and property. He was the legitimate son of the deceased Don Manuel Murillo and Doña Mariana Rodríguez, and had children from two marriages: Manuel José and José Francisco with Micaela González, and nine children with his current wife Francisca Herrera. He also mentioned a property in Púas, within the ejidos of Cartago.

Doña Manuela Rodríguez, a widow, sold a piece of land measuring 608 by 300 varas in Tibás, Heredia, to Don Juan Antonio Vargas for 76 pesos. The land bordered the royal road to Valle Hermoso, fences belonging to Pedro Rodríguez, and the buyer's house.

Doña Manuela Rodríguez, a widow, sold another piece of land in Tibás, Heredia, measuring 350 by 320 varas, to Eustaquio León for 32 pesos. This property bordered a road to Quintana, fences of José Ramírez, a water channel, and the fence of Don José Arias.

Don Juan Sandoval sold two contiguous pieces of land in Tibás, Heredia, to Francisco Zúñiga and Ventura Chaves, widow of Joaquín Zúñiga, for 28 and 21 pesos respectively. The properties bordered Manuel Oviedo's land and other lands belonging to the grantor.

Presbítero Don José Emigdio Umaña, acting as tutor for his minor siblings Don Juan Antonio and Doña Antonia, obligated himself for 45 pesos, 6 reales, and seven eighths that each inherited from their deceased mother, Doña Antonia Josefa Pérez. He had already delivered the inheritance of his sister Doña Paula to her husband, Don Paulino Fonseca, with Don Francisco Fonseca serving as guarantor.

Doña Manuela Rodríguez, a widow, sold a piece of land in Tibás, Heredia, measuring 500 by 450 varas, to Ignacio Bolaños for 50 pesos. The land bordered properties of José Antonio Bolaños, the buyer's fence, Eustaquio León, and Antolino Méndez.

Don Gregorio Ulloa, as former Alcalde of San José, ratified the sale of the deceased Juana Méndez's house to Reyes Quesada for 50 pesos. The house, which was Juana Méndez's only asset, was sold to cover her debts and bordered properties belonging to Gregorio Carapos, Jacoba Castro, Don Manuel Elizondo, and María Sandí.

José de la Trinidad Ulloa, a resident of Cartago, obligated himself as the successful bidder for four aguardiente stalls in San José, each at a monthly rent of ten pesos. Don Gregorio Ulloa served as his guarantor for this obligation.

The testament of Juan Granados, originally granted on July 27 in Valle Hermoso, was protocolized on September 24. The testament detailed his family, including his mother Manuela Josefa Granados, wife María del Carmen Astúa, and eleven children, with his son Hilario and son-in-law Miguel Prado named as executors.

Damián Barrantes, widower of Juana de Jesús Retana, obligated himself to his six minor children: Juan, José Manuel, María Isabel, Juana Josefa, José Matías, and María Barrantes. Each child received 35 pesos and 6 reales as their maternal inheritance from their deceased mother.

María de la Concepción Rojas, widow of Francisco Miguel Céspedes, obligated herself to her five minor children: Esteban de la Trinidad, María Dolores, Vicente de Jesús, Juan José de Dios, and José de Jesús. Each child received 38 pesos and 4 reales as their paternal inheritance from their deceased father.

Don José del Resano Carrillo and his wife Doña María Josefa Fernández, residents of Alajuela, obligated themselves to Beneficiado Don Félix de Alvarado for a 400 pesos loan. They agreed to pay 6% annual interest and mortgaged their house and farm in their neighborhood.

people_involved: Presbítero Don José de la Encarnación Fernández
summary: Presbítero Don José de la Encarnación Fernández, a resident of Valle Hermoso, incurred a debt of 2000 pesos to Presbítero Don Pedro de Alvarado, to be paid within two years with 6% interest. He mortgaged his cattle ranch named Miravalles, located in the jurisdiction of Bagaces, as security.

people_involved: Presbítero Don José de la Encarnación Fernández
summary: On November 9, 1819, Presbítero Don Pedro de Alvarado, the creditor, canceled the debt owed by Presbítero Don José de la Encarnación Fernández. The cancellation noted that the interest charged was 5% instead of the originally agreed 6%.

Rafael Navarro, a widower who had remarried, obligated himself to his five minor children for their maternal inheritance from their deceased mother, María Lobo, each receiving 2 pesos and 7 reales. His father-in-law, Francisco Lobo, requested security for the minors' assets, and Don Manuel Marchena served as guarantor.

A record notes a mulata named Constancia, daughter of Feliciana, described as 24 years old with light skin and curly black hair, with a price of 250 pesos. The entry is marked 'No corre', indicating the transaction was not finalized or was cancelled.

Juan de Dios Brenes made his will, identifying himself as the legitimate son of the deceased José Gregorio Brenes and María Efigenia Segura. He detailed his two marriages, first to María Francisca Umaña (widow of Miguel Coto, who died in '87') and then to María de las Nieves Guzmán, listing all his children and step-children, and appointing Cura Rafael de la Rosa and his son Juan Francisco as executors.

Antonio García and his wife, Juliana Oreamuno, committed to an obligation of 127 pesos for a chaplaincy previously managed by the deceased Elias Muñoz, a resident of Heredia. They agreed to pay 5% interest and mortgaged their house in Cartago as collateral.

Captain Salvador de Oreamuno sold a pasture located in the Purires neighborhood, specifically at 'la rueda', to Alejo Aguilar for 450 pesos. The property was bordered by lands belonging to Manuel Portugués, Manuel Francisco Robles, Miguel Cárdenas, and Joaquín Oreamuno, as well as the royal road leading from Cartago to Tobosi.

The Cabildo, Justicia y Regimiento of Cartago confirmed the election of Bachiller don Florencio del Castillo as a deputy for the upcoming Cortes Generales, following an election held on October 1 as per a Royal Order from February 14. Castillo, a native of the province and a distinguished academic and ecclesiastical official in León, was granted general power for his functions, with the document signed by several prominent citizens.

Colonel Tomás de Acosta sold a mulata slave named Constancia, daughter of Feliciana, to Presbítero Félix de Alvarado for 250 pesos plata. Constancia was described as 24 years old with light skin and curly black hair. The sale was later rescinded on January 5, 1811, at Constancia's request to remain with her mother and siblings who were leaving the province.

Marcos Ruiz, acting for himself and his mother-in-law Venancia del Corral, along with Antonia Velazco (widow of Pedro del Corral), sold a house to Colonel Juan Francisco de Bonilla for 300 pesos. The house was inherited from the deceased Rosa Madriz and bordered properties of the buyer, the deceased María Francisca del Corral, Ana Elizondo, and Cecilia Jiménez.

Juan Antonio Castro, preparing for a trip to Panama, obtained a 200-peso loan from Juan de Dios de Ayala, guaranteed by Presbítero José de la Encarnación Fernández, and an additional 100 pesos from Joaquín de Oreamuno. To secure these debts, Castro and his wife, Irinea Hidalgo, mortgaged their home for a one-year term with 5% interest.

A partition of assets was conducted following the deaths of spouses Juan Antonio Pereira and Josefa Fuentes. Their surviving children, Cayetano, Juan, and María, along with the descendants of their deceased children Francisco, Trinidad, Tomasa, and Loreta, were named as heirs. Each heir received 37 pesos.

Juana Antonia Ramírez, widow of José de la Trinidad Fernández, made her will, listing her nine children and their marital statuses, noting several had died. Her surviving children and grandchildren were designated as heirs, and her sons José Miguel and José Antonio were appointed as executors. Her residence was in the arrabal of Cartago.

Manuel de Rivas y Bejar, Mayor of Valle Hermoso and a native of Panama, granted power of attorney to Vicente López, a resident of La Chorrera. López was tasked with investigating a chaplaincy principal imposed on the former house of Marcelina de Arechua, which was founded by her ancestors for their relatives, and to which Rivas y Bejar's eldest son was entitled as a direct descendant and grandson of Ventura de Bejar.

Doña María Francisca Velazco y Estrada, daughter of the deceased Francisco Velazco and Luisa Estrada, and widow of Marcos de Alvarado, made her will. Having no children, she named María Campos y Molina, who had lived with her for many years, as her sole heir. The executors appointed were Beneficiado don Nicolás Carrillo and María Campos y Molina.

Coronel don Juan Francisco de Bonilla, don Manuel Marchena, and don Ramón Palacios (a native of Spain) granted general power of attorney to don José Priat. José Priat was a resident and merchant of León.

people_involved: Presidente Gobernador y Capitán General del Reino
summary: Coronel don Juan Francisco de Bonilla, acting on commission from the President Governor and Captain General of the Kingdom, received the oath from don Juan de Dios de Ayala. Ayala, a Knight of the Order of Santiago and Captain of the Royal Armies, was the Governor and Commander General of the province of Costa Rica, taking an oath prescribed by his royal title issued in the Alcázar de Sevilla on August 23 of the previous year.

Don José María Peralta and his wife doña Ana Benita del Corral obligated themselves for 600 pesos to the Royal Treasury. This obligation was for the expenditure of tobacco, stamped paper, and gunpowder in this city, which was under their charge. Coronel don Juan Francisco de Bonilla served as their guarantor.

Numerous residents from Valle Hermoso, Heredia, and Alajuela, who owned mules and transported tobacco to Puntarenas and León de Nicaragua, granted power to don Manuel de Alvarado, a resident of Valle Hermoso. This power authorized Manuel de Alvarado to contract on their behalf for future transport services, aiming to prevent losses from others making low-price agreements.

Don José Manuel Flores, a resident of Valle Hermoso, ratified the sale of three caballerías of land in 'el Mundito' (beyond the Río Grande) that his deceased father, Jerónimo Flores, had made to don José Solera. The land was part of what José Manuel and his siblings possessed, and José Solera had paid 75 pesos to Jerónimo Flores the previous year.

José María Carbonero, a resident of Alajuela, sold a piece of land in 'la Guácima' to don José Solera for 50 pesos. The seller had acquired this land through an exchange with don Cayetano Gutiérrez. The property was bordered by lands of Pedro Monje, Cayetano Gutiérrez, Gregorio Hernández, and the Ciruelas River.

Don Joaquín Solera obligated himself to the heirs of the deceased don Cristóbal Orozco, namely don José Ana Orozco and doña Joaquina Orozco, for 309 pesos and 1 real. This amount represented the value of goods stipulated in an inventory. Don Juan Manuel González served as the guarantor for this obligation.

Doña Francisca Antonia de Sierra, a widow, sold two pieces of land in 'La Lagunilla' to José Miguel González for 100 pesos. One piece, 600 varas long, was already enclosed by the buyer, and the other, 900 varas in circumference, was located between doña María González's pasture and the royal road.

Pedro Nolasco Salguero obligated himself to his siblings, Manuela, Manuel Marcelino, and José María Salguero, for 117 pesos and 7.25 reales. This amount represented their share of the inheritance from their parents, José Antonio Salguero (widower of Ramona Azofeifa). Ambrosio Zamora acted as the guarantor for Pedro Nolasco Salguero.

Tomás Ramírez and his wife María del Rosario Sosa made their will in Heredia. They listed their parents and several living children, as well as a deceased son, Juan, who had two daughters from two marriages. Their daughters María de la Rosa, María de la Trinidad, Basilia, and María Trinidad were married to Pedro Antonio Camacho, Policarpo Valerio, Joaquín Vargas, and Dionisio Chacón, respectively. The surviving spouse and their son-in-law Policarpo Valerio were named executors.
Tomás Ramírez and María del Rosario Sosa, his wife, made a codicil to their will. In this codicil, they named don Mariano Rodríguez and don Julián Zamora as arbiters.

Don Francisco Ocampo, a resident of Heredia, ratified the sale of half a caballería of land in 'Ojo de Agua' (specifically 'el Rincón del Padre Ocampo') that his deceased father, don Francisco Ocampo, had made to the also deceased don Antonio Murillo, a former resident of Alajuela. The land was part of what the grantor and his siblings possessed, and the price was 15 pesos.

Juan Inocente Martínez, a single man and natural son of the deceased Micaela Martínez, both residents of Valle Hermoso, made his will. Don Camilo Mora and don Francisco (last name incomplete) were named as executors for his estate.

An unspecified estate, likely belonging to Castro y Pacheco, distributed 100 pesos to María de la Luz Martínez and 25 pesos to Juan Antonio Martínez. María de la Luz Martínez is identified as the sister, and Juan Antonio Martínez as the nephew of the implied testator.

José Antonio Herrera and Josefa Castro, widow of Agustín Jiménez and residents of Valle Hermoso, obligated themselves to Pablo, Dolores, and Romualda, children of Josefa and the late Agustín Jiménez, for 47 pesos 4 reales from their paternal inheritance. Julián Castro served as guarantor for this obligation, and another son, Jesús, had passed away.

The will of Francisco Miguel Céspedes, son of deceased Tomás Céspedes and Tomasa Castillo, was protocolized. He was married to María de la Concepción Rojas and had five minor sons, and the will, granted on April 28 in Valle Hermoso before Alcalde Manuel de Rivas, named José Antonio García and Nicolás Montero as executors.

Manuel Francisco Mora, a single man and son of deceased Juan Francisco Mora and Francisca Jiménez, made his will in San José before Alcalde José Rafael de Gallegos. He acknowledged a natural daughter, Benita, who was over 25 and a widow, and named his siblings Juan de Mora, Juana Paula Mora, and Angela María Mora as his heirs, with Juan de Mora and Manuel Guzmán as executors.

Juan de la Rosa Maitín, a native of Panamá, made his will in Cartago before Alcalde José Nicolás de Oriamuno. He was married to Felipa Neri de Quesada, widow of Manuel del Villar, and had no children with her. His five stepdaughters, daughters of Manuel del Villar, were named as his heirs, and José Ruperto Prieto and José Miguel Cárdenas were appointed as executors.

Josefa Arias, daughter of Manuel Arias and Micaela Alfaro and widow of Miguel Cabezas, made her will in her home in Quebrada Seca, Heredia, before Alcalde Blas Pérez. She had six children, and her son Ramón and Manuel Hidalgo were named as executors. Her son Pedro was married to Mercedes González.

Juan Zúñiga and his wife Gertrudis Víquez made their joint will in their home in San Juan, Heredia, before Alcalde Blas Pérez. They had four children, and named the survivor of them, Mariano Zamora, and his son José Antonio Zamora as executors.

José Ángel Guevara and his wife Micaela Cubero, natives of Cartago and residents of Heredia, made their joint will in Quebrada Seca, Heredia, before Alcalde Blas Pérez. They had no children, but José Ángel left a legacy to Juan Ventura Guevara, whom he had raised, and Micaela left legacies to Andrés Guevara and Encarnación Cubero.
Don Nicolás de Oreamuno granted general power of attorney to Presbyter Don Félix de Jesús García.

Don Manuel García Escalante granted power to Don Tomás de Acosta, Governor-elect of Santa Marta, to collect 1363 pesos from Don José Vázquez y Téllez. This debt arose from money supplied by Escalante, for which Vázquez y Téllez, a former Governor, had drawn against the Royal Coffers of León, which subsequently refused payment.

Manuel Marchena, Syndic of San Francisco convents, and María Francisca de Alvarado were involved in a lawsuit over a house formerly owned by Governor Diego de la Haya, which had a chaplaincy founded on it. The case, pending since August 1808, led to the house being auctioned due to deterioration, with Presbyter Félix de Alvarado purchasing it for 750 pesos. A marginal note from 1812 indicates that Juan Francisco Bonilla later took responsibility for the chaplaincy funds, cancelling Alvarado's obligation.

Captain Manuel Hidalgo granted power to Don Joaquín Hidalgo, residing in Reino de Tierra Firme, to sell his 35-year-old mulatto slave, Ciríaco Madriz. Manuel Hidalgo had previously purchased Ciríaco from Salvador Oreamuno.
Manuel Fernández sold a house with an enclosed plot of land in Cartago to Antonio Rojas for 40 pesos.
Don Lucas Estévez, a transient merchant in Cartago, granted power of attorney to Sergeant Don Antonio García to handle all his lawsuits.

Don Lucas Estévez declared a debt of 1433 pesos 7 reales to the Royal Treasury for import duties on goods. He paid 400 pesos to Don Manuel Alvarado, and his attorney, Don Antonio García, was to pay the remaining balance. Estévez needed to travel to León de Nicaragua to investigate an embargo on his merchandise, and the debt was later cancelled in June 1811 when Don Joaquín de Oreamuno paid for him.

Numerous residents of Alajuela, who owned 325 caballerías of land in Turrúcares, granted power of attorney to Don Pedro Monge and Don Juan de Jesús Alfaro. This was to ensure the lands were administered for the common benefit of all residents, preventing private profit.
Don José Vargas, widower of Doña María Mercedes Zamora, obligated himself to his three minor daughters, Doña María Josefa, Doña Bárbara, and Doña Isidora, for 218 pesos 4 reales as their inheritance.

Don Juan Francisco Bonilla became a guarantor for Don Juan Manuel de Cañas, replacing Don Joaquín Oreamuno, for 2530 pesos. This sum represented the value of cattle leased by Cañas from the brotherhood of Nuestro Amo de Bagaces. The Cura of Bagaces, Presbítero Don Miguel Aguilar, agreed to this arrangement, which was later cancelled in 1817.

José de la Trinidad Guillen, a resident of San José, sold a house with its plot in Cartago to José Miguel Brenes for 70 pesos. The property bordered lands belonging to Presbítero Don Rafael Troya, Doña Dolores Frutos, Doña Tomasa Guzmán, Alejandro García, and Don Vicente Frutos.

Don Manuel Marchena declared that Don Francisco Montoro, a resident of Portobelo, had imported various clothing items. As Montoro needed to return to the 'Reino de Tierra Firme', Marchena became guarantor for the Royal duties on the goods that reached Cartago.

Don Francisco Montoro, along with his brother Don José Montoro, obligated themselves to pay 225 pesos to Don Manuel Ortiz in Panama on behalf of Don Manuel Marchena. This was in repayment for Marchena having acted as guarantor for import duties and for providing hospitality and sustenance.

Antonia Barrantes, daughter of Francisco Barrantes and Doña María Hidalgo, and widow of José Nicolás Godínez, made her testament in Heredia before Alcalde 2° Don Mauricio Salmas. She had five children with Godínez, and her son Juan Antonio and grandson Pedro Salazar were named as executors.

Don Marcos Ángulo sold an unserviceable brigantine named 'San José de las Ánimas', docked in the port of Punta de Arenas, to Don Antonio Figueroa for 150 pesos. The transaction took place before Alcalde 1° Don Juan Francisco Bonilla due to the absence of a scribe.

Manuel Antonio Barrantes, son of Luis Barrantes and Josefa Says (Sáenz), made his testament in Heredia before Alcalde Señor Salinas. He was married to María Manuela Jiménez, with whom he had four married children. Juana Teresa Arroyo was a legatee, and Juan Barrantes and his wife were named as executors.
Don Felipe Fernández, a resident of San José, emancipated his son Tomás, who was over 26 years old. Governor Ayala approved the emancipation.

Don Manuel García Escalante received a cargo in deposit that was being transported from Panama to Costa Rica by the brigantine 'San Pedro Nolasco', captained by Don Lucas Chamorro. The cargo had been embargoed by order of the Governor in Punta de Arenas and subsequently sent to Cartago.

María Venegas sold a piece of land in Cerro Grande to Don José Antonio Sáenz for 70 pesos. The land bordered the Ibirrís river and properties belonging to Francisco Gutiérrez and Manuel Trinidad Brenes.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Félix de Jesús García
summary: Don Pedro Monge, a resident of Alajuela, granted power of attorney to Presbítero Don Félix de Jesús García for all his affairs.
Rosa Rivera, a widow, sold a cacao plantation named 'La Solano' in the Matina valley to Pedro Cásasela for 100 pesos.

Juan María Orocú, a resident of Santiago Alange who had lived in Esparza for 20 years, made a nuncupative testament in Esparza on February 3, 1811, before Cura Don Miguel Aguilar and other witnesses. He was a widower of Teodora Rosario Cordero, with whom he had children.

Don Buenaventura Umaña presented a testament, and several individuals including don José Antonio García, don Camilo Mora, don Pedro José Carazo, don Salvador Oreamuno, and don Nicolás Carazo made declarations regarding it.
Gobernador Ayala, through an official decree on May 20, approved the testament and ordered its protocolization.

Four residents of San José (don Ramón Palacios, don Manuel Antonio Aguilar, don Rafael Gallegos, don Hilario Zeledón) acted as guarantors for don Camilo Mora, don Rafael Tabeada, don Ascensión Mora, and don Carmen Salazar (a resident of León). This guaranty was for import duties on goods brought by the brigantine San Pedro Ñolasco, allowing the goods to be sold while import permits were verified. The transaction was cancelled in 1812.
Doña Ana Jacoba de Alvarado acted as guarantor for don Nicolás Carazo for import duties under similar circumstances as the previous entry. This transaction was cancelled in 1812.
Don Joaquín de Oreamuno acted as guarantor for don Juan Pablo Jiménez, don Ramón Jiménez, and don Juan Antonia Castro for import duties, similar to the preceding transactions.

In San José, don José Ana Jiménez sold a plot of land in Poás to don Pedro Antonio Solares, a resident of Heredia, for 250 pesos. The land's boundaries were precisely defined by the royal road, Cuajiniquil River, Sarchí River, and La Vigía stream.
In San José, don José Ana Jiménez granted general power of attorney to don Joaquín Oreamuno, a resident of Cartago.

In San José, Juan de Dios Quesada sold a piece of land in El Salitral to don Manuel Antonio Aguilar for 75 pesos. The property's boundaries included the Tiribí River, the royal road to Palo Grande, the buyer's pasture, and the Cascajal road.

María Josefa Zavaleta, a single woman and natural daughter of the deceased María Manuela Zavaleta, made her will. She named her cousin, Leonardo Zavaleta, as her sole heir and executor, as she had no succession.

Mariano Solano of Alajuela acknowledged a 375-peso overdue debt to don Basilio Carrillo, a merchant from León. Carrillo granted an extension until the next January, contingent on Solano providing a satisfactory guarantee to Presbítero don Juan Manuel Zamora, the priest of Heredia. Don Matías Sandoval of Alajuela provided the guarantee, and Solano also mortgaged his lands in La Ceiba, livestock, a pasture, and two plots.

people_involved: Coronel don Juan Francisco de Bonilla
summary: Coronel don Juan Francisco de Bonilla acknowledged receiving 666 pesos 5 reales from Presbítero don Félix de Alvarado. These funds were held by Alvarado for the winner of a lawsuit concerning a house formerly owned by don Diego de la Haya, and Bonilla committed to pay the current total of 683 pesos 2.5 reales on Alvarado's behalf when due.

Angela Vargas, a widow from Villavieja, formally recognized that the preservation of her deceased husband José Julián González's assets was due to the diligent work and efforts of their son, Juan María González, who was over 25 years old.

Presbítero don Cipriano Gutiérrez acknowledged a debt of 2700 pesos to Presbítero don Félix de Alvarado, Comisario del Santo Oficio. To secure the payment, Gutiérrez mortgaged a 7-caballería hacienda in Río Grande, which included cattle and horses. The debt was cancelled in 1821 by don Juan José Bonilla, Alvarado's executor.
Don José Arias sold a piece of land in Tibás to Pascual Zamora for 60 pesos.
María Venegas, a widow, sold a piece of land in Chircagres to Pedro Coto for 10 pesos. The land was bordered to the west by the royal road.

Don José María Peralta posted bail for don Juan Francisco Valenzuela, who was imprisoned for illegally importing goods from Jamaica through Puerto de Matina. Valenzuela was granted freedom under bail due to his illness.

Don Joaquín Oreamuno posted bail for don Miguel Ramírez de Zaragoza, who was imprisoned for illegally importing goods from Jamaica through Puerto de Matina. Ramírez de Zaragoza was granted freedom under bail due to his illness.

people_involved: Coronel don Juan Francisco de Bonilla
summary: Coronel don Juan Francisco de Bonilla acted as guarantor for don Antonio Figueroa, who owed 192 pesos 3 reales in import duties for mercantile goods. Figueroa had refused to pay, citing various exceptions, and the Governor ordered him to provide a bond for the outcome while the matter remained unresolved.

locations: En medio de los Dos Híos
summary: José Gregorio Andrade, a native of Cartago and resident of Alajuela, sold a piece of land in "En medio de los Dos Híos" to brothers José and Manuel Gregorio Loaiza for 58 pesos. The land, previously acquired from Manuel Lizano, bordered lands of Ujarraz to the east, with the Churris River in between.

Presbítero don Pedro José Alvarado paid don Félix de Bonilla 150 pesos to grant freedom to a 6-year-old slave named Francisco. Francisco was the son of María de la Asunción, another slave, and both had previously been owned by Presbítero don Félix de Alvarado.

Don Francisco Javier Navarro, acting as agent for don Pedro Elizondo, sold a house and its walled plot to don Esteban García for 300 pesos, with half paid upfront and half on credit. The property was bordered by houses belonging to Alejandro Jesús García, the former property of doña Teresa Garlín, Clemencia Ramírez, and doña María Alvarado.
An escritura (deed/document) was cancelled at the margin due to a payment appearing at the foot of the document. This cancellation occurred in 1814.

Presbítero don Félix de Alvarado sold a 25-year-old mulato named Julián, described as dark-skinned and slender, to don Gregorio Ulloa for 200 pesos. Félix de Alvarado had previously purchased Julián from doña Tomasa Guzmán.
Doña María García, widow of don José García, sold a house and solar to José Antonio Ramos for 38 pesos. The property was bordered by Rafaela Ramos, Loreta Quirós, Nicolás Rivera, and Felipe Romero.

Don José María Peralta, who won the bid for one of the five aguardiente stalls in the city, committed to paying 10 pesos monthly for a year to the Receptor de Alcabalas. His wife, doña Ana Benita del Corral, served as his guarantor.

Don José Ulloa, who won the bid for the four aguardiente stalls in the San José district, committed to paying 65 pesos 3 reales monthly for a year to the Receptor de Alcabalas. Don Gregorio Ulloa acted as his guarantor.

An engagement contract was formalized in Heredia between don Manuel Flores y Jiménez, a natural son from Guayaquil, and doña María Josefa Taboada, a legitimate daughter. Both parties were over 25 years old, and ecclesiastical procedures were underway.

José María Ramos, who won the bid for one of the four aguardiente stalls in Heredia, committed to paying 10 pesos monthly for a year to the Receptor de Alcabalas. Liberato Fonseca served as his guarantor.

Anselmo Arias, who won the bid for one of the four aguardiente stalls in Heredia and one of the two in Alajuela, committed to paying 20 pesos monthly for a year to the Receptor de Alcabalas. Nicolás Benavides acted as his guarantor.

Antonio Bogantes, who won the bid for one of the four aguardiente stalls in Heredia, committed to paying 10 pesos monthly for a year to the Receptor de Alcabalas. Manuel Ugalde served as his guarantor.
