Don Cayetano Gutiérrez sold a piece of land in Cabecera de la guácima to Antonio Bogantes for 50 pesos. This land was part of a larger purchase made by Gutiérrez from don Trinidad Arias and was bordered by various landmarks and properties belonging to Pedro Monge, Juan Zúñiga, and the Castillos.

Don Efigenio González and his wife doña María Josefa Barrantes made their will in Heredia, listing nine surviving children and three who died in infancy. Their daughter María Mercedes was married to Pedro Cabezas, and they owned a house in Quebrada Seca and a cattle ranch in Puás. The surviving spouse and their son José Miguel were named executors.
José Bermúdez, who won the bid for the aguardiente stall in Esparza, committed to paying 10 pesos monthly for a year to the Receptor de Alcabalas. José de la Luz Ureña served as his guarantor.

Don Juan José Ulloa sold a chácara (farm) in Palo Grande to don Gregorio Ulloa for 190 pesos. The property included two houses, a sugar mill (trapiche), and various fences, bordered by the street to Patarra, the royal road to Aserrí, Angela López's property, and the Jorco river.

Mónica López, widow of Santiago Bermúdez, committed to her five minor children—Manuel, María Concepción, Antonio de Jesús, Eugenio de Jesús, and Ciríaco de Jesús—for 284 pesos 4 reales, representing their paternal inheritance.

Andrés and Eusebio Bermúdez sold a piece of land in El Salitral, inherited from their father Santiago de la Cruz Bermúdez, to don Nicolás Castro for 200 pesos. The property was bordered by the royal road, a hill also called Salitral, and the land designated for their sister María Manuela Bermúdez.

María del Carmen Astúa, widow of Juan Granados, committed to her five minor children—José Hilario, Manuel de la Trinidad, José Fernando, María Francisca, and Nicolasa—for 168 pesos 3 reales, representing their paternal inheritance.

Don Cristóbal Sáenz, executor for don Juan Sáenz, confirmed the sale of a piece of land in El Espinal to don Miguel Carranza for 60 pesos. Juan Sáenz had originally purchased this land from his brother, don José Antonio Sáenz. The property was bordered by Ramón Mena's pasture, a spring, a stream, the road to Mata Redonda, and Ramón Esquivel's pasture.

Don Nicolás de Oreamuno and his wife doña María Josefa del Campo took charge of a capellanía (chaplaincy) belonging to the Beneficio of the city, valued at 225 pesos cacao, which translated to 150 pesos 1/2 reales in silver. Doña Jacoba de Alvarado, a widow, had redeemed the capellanía, which carried a 5% census, and they mortgaged their hacienda in Paso Hondo.

Don Blas Pérez, a resident of Heredia, who won the bid for one of the four vacant aguardiente stalls in that town, committed to paying 10 pesos monthly for a year to the Receptor de Alcabalas. Don Ignacio Ugalde served as his guarantor.
Presbítero don José Nicolás Bonilla was fined 10 pesos, with the proceeds benefiting the Fábrica (church works/fabric).
Señor Lombardo, an escribano, grants general power of attorney to Don Juan José de León, a resident of Guatemala City.

Don Francisco Javier López, 1st Mayor of Alajuela, grants power of attorney to Don Pablo Alvarado to represent him in a lawsuit. Felipe Alvarado filed the suit, accusing López of injustice for ordering a street opened at Baltasar Sánchez's request.
Antonia Gertrudis Quirós grants freedom to her mulatto slave, José Santiago Quirós, who is approximately 30 years old. José Santiago Quirós paid 200 pesos for his manumission.

María de Jesús Vanegas, widow of Roque Aguilar, makes her will. She names her legitimate sons Pedro Nicolás and the deceased Nicolás Antonio, and her natural children José Trinidad, Antonia Petronila, and the deceased María Antonia. Her executors are Pedro Nicolás and José Trinidad.

Don Rafael Gallegos and Don Rafael Taboada, residents of San José, acknowledge a debt of 1000 pesos to Presbítero Don Félix de Alvarado. The debt is for a two-year term at 6% annual interest, and they mortgage their houses as security. This debt was cancelled in 1817.

Miguel Herrera and his wife María Gertrudis Alfaro, residents of Alajuela, make their will in San José. They list their seven children, including four married daughters, and name the surviving spouse and Don Julián Rodríguez as executors. Their home is in Turrúcares.

Rafaela Artavia, widow of Candelario Salazar, sells fences of poro and piñuela in Los Anonos to Don Romualdo Saborío for 210 pesos. The property is bordered by Don Eusebio Sáenz's fences, a road, the Tiribí River, and Las Pavas ravine.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Félix de Jesús García
summary: Don Manuel Antonio Aguilar, a resident of San José, owes Presbítero Don Félix de Jesús García 250 pesos, with a three-year term at 6% interest. Don Camilo Mora acts as guarantor for this debt, which was cancelled in 1818.
The beginning of the will of Gabriel Mejías, natural son of María Mejías, is recorded. The process is interrupted because the testator is out of his senses.

Don Ramón Palacios, originally from Spain and Vizcaya, donates a 146-pound metal cauldron and a house in San José to María de los Angeles Ramírez. This donation is in recognition of her good services, and the house borders properties belonging to Don Lorenzo Zumbado, Pablo Chaves, and a house being built by Manuel Antonio Aguilar.

Don Ramón Fallas, legitimate son of deceased Juan Antonio Fallas and Francisca Calderón, makes his will in San José before Mayor Don Hilario Zeledón. He is married to Paula Monje and lists their four children, naming José Antonio and Cornelio Monje as his executors.

Juana María, Luisa Josefa, and Ildefonsa Chaves ratify a land donation made by their deceased father Francisco to the late Joaquín Soto. The land is located at the royal pass of Virilla, and the ratification is made in favor of Soto's heirs, Juan Manuel Soto and Ignacio Jiménez.

Francisco Javier Aguilar, widower of Doña Nicolasa Mesen, makes his will in San José. He had no children with Nicolasa, who had a natural daughter named Rosa Mesen, and has no children with his current wife, Doña Manuela Rojas. He names Don Joaquín Oreamuno and his wife as executors, with his wife also being his heir.

Juan Manuel Quirós sells a 600x200 vara piece of land in La Uruca for 148 pesos to the heirs of Joaquín Soto and Rosaura Chaves. The land, previously negotiated with Soto, borders the royal pass road, the Torres River, Don Cipriano Fernández's pasture, and Las Animas.

Simona Guzmán, whose husband Pedro Acuña has been absent in Nicaragua for eleven years, sells a house and half a lot in San José to Pedro Montero for 200 pesos. This sale, authorized by the Justice, is to pay her husband's creditors. Don Nicolás Castro, Don Mateo de Mora, and Don Gregorio Ulloa provided declarations during the authorization process.
Doña Manuela Rodríguez sells a piece of land in Puás to Vicente Rojas for 100 pesos. The property borders the royal mountain, Las Cañas ravine, and lands belonging to Don Blas Pérez.

Faustino Herrera obligates himself to the minor daughters of the late Don Vicente Panlagua and Doña Mercedes Pérez, Felipa and María Salomé, for their inheritances. The inheritances include paternal, maternal, and from their deceased sister Isabel, with Don Félix Panlagua and Encarnación Herrera acting as guarantors.

Don Juan Rafael Rodríguez, widower of Doña Antonia Soto, obligates himself in favor of his nine minor children. These children are José María, Diego, María de Jesús, two named Ramona, and Ber... (name incomplete).
Encarnación, Juan Francisco, and Rafaela received 144 pesos and 5 reales as part of their inheritance.

Jerónimo Villalobos, son of the late Hermenegildo Villalobos, committed to his younger siblings for 43 pesos and 5 1/2 reales. This amount was combined with 33 pesos, 6 reales, and 5 1/2 reales each received from their mother Antonia Concepción Bolaños's inheritance. José de la Rosa Sáenz and Juan Solís acted as guarantors.

Ramón Cabezas, son of Josefa Arias, committed to his four younger siblings (José Miguel, Cayetano, Dolores, and Manuel del Pilar) for 23 pesos and 4 reales from their maternal inheritance. An additional 45 pesos and 5 reales were added from their father Miguel Cabezas's inheritance. Antonio Alfaro and Juan Antonio Godínez served as guarantors.

José Ángel Monge committed to the two minors, María del Carmen and María Gabriela Badilla, for 90 pesos and 7 reales. This amount was their inheritance from their mother, Josefa Sáenz. Manuel Agüero acted as guarantor.

Tomás Romero sold a piece of land in El Salitral to Francisco Miguel Arguedas for 60 pesos. The land was part of what Romero's wife, María Francisca Bermúdez, inherited from her father, and its boundaries were described in detail.
Don Félix José Fernández emancipated his son, Don Manuel José, who was over 25 years old. This act was approved by Gobernador Ayala.

José Ángel Hernández, a widower of Antonia Josefa de Ocampo, made his will in Heredia before Alcalde 1° Julián Rodríguez. He had five children with his first wife and was remarried to Josefa Ocampo, with whom he had no children. Jesús Villalobos and his second wife were named as executors.

Before Alcalde 1° Hilario Zeledón in San José, several officials and citizens consented to invest funds from the Cofradía de Nuestro Amo into the ongoing construction of the church's facade. These funds, originally redeemed by Félix Bonilla and others, were intended for the benefit of the church and were to be delivered to Ecónomo Juan Manuel de Cañas.

Luis Cruz and his wife Antonia Josefa Alvarado made their will in Alajuela before Alcalde 1° Francisco Javier López. They had five children together, and Luis Cruz had three children from a previous marriage to Manuela Josefa Carvajal. Juan Agustín Lara and Félix Quesada were named as executors.

Doña Mónica Cervantes, widow of Don Juan Buenaventura Castro, made her will in Alajuela. She had four children: Pablo, Juana, Salvador, and Ramón. Miguel Alfaro and Matías Sandoval were named as executors, and José Francisco Saborío as the arbiter judge.

Don Pedro Monge and his wife Doña María Gertrudis Soto made their will in Alajuela before Alcalde 2° José Francisco Saborío. They had ten children, with some already married. They owned land in La Guácima, and Antonio Vargas was named as arbiter judge, with the surviving spouse, Pedro Vargas, and Victoriano Vargas as executors.

Doña María Arias, legitimate daughter of the late José María Arias and Clara Rodríguez, made her will in Heredia before Alcalde 2° Mauricio Salinas. She was the widow of José Manuel Núñez and had no children. Valentín Arias was named as executor, and her soul was designated as the heir.

Toribio Espinosa, legitimate son of the late Francisco Espinosa and Ramona Barrantes, made his will in Heredia before Alcalde Mauricio Salinas. He was married to María Trinidad Zamora and had no children. His wife and José Murillo were named as executors, and his wife was designated as the heir.
Don Anselmo Gutiérrez and his wife Doña Manuela Gertrudis Flores, residents of Heredia, committed to Don José Francisco Fonseca, also a resident, for a loan of 100 pesos at 5% annual interest.
Don Lucas Estévez, a transient merchant, granted general power of attorney to Don Joaquín Oreamuno.

Ascensión Ortiz and his wife María de la Rosa Soto made their will. They had no children together, but María de la Rosa Soto had seven children from a previous marriage to Esteban Jiménez. Mariano Rodríguez was named as arbiter judge, and Francisco Castro and Antonio Vargas were named as executors.
Don Antonio Figueroa, a native of the Kingdoms of Spain, granted general power of attorney to Don Felipe Sancho.

José Dolores Madrigal, a widower of Josefa Andrea Segura and Clemencia Muñoz, and currently married to María Sánchez, made his will. He detailed his children from his previous marriages and his current marriage, including an unborn child. His current wife, María Sánchez, and José Gregorio Cárdenas were named as executors.

Don Antonio Figueroa was accused by Don Manuel de Alvarado, the Receptor de Alcabalas, of improperly trying to avoid import duties for goods from San Andrés and of mismanaging funds. The Gobernador ordered Figueroa not to leave for Tierra Firme without posting a bond against calumny, which Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla provided.
José Bernardo Carvajal, heir of the late José Manuel Carvajal, received 374 pesos from Presbítero don Pedro Vicente González. The money was part of the inheritance that González had been holding.

Don Juan Francisco Valenzuela and Don Miguel Ramírez Zaragoza imported goods from Jamaica via Matina, which were embargoed and deposited with Don Manuel García Escalante by order of the Gobernador. Due to delays and damage to the goods, the importers requested their release under bond, which the Gobernador granted. Don Manuel Marchena and Don Joaquín Oreamuno (and Bonilla for Valenzuela) provided guarantees, and later the President ordered the full release of the goods and the freedom of Valenzuela and Ramírez.

Don Rafael Barroeta, along with Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla, Don Manuel de Cañas, and Don Manuel de Alvarado, proposed to the Gobernador to lift the tobacco monopoly in Cartago and surrounding towns to prevent an insurrection similar to Nicaragua's. They offered to guarantee 2126 pesos 6 reales for one year if the King did not approve the lifting of the monopoly. The proposal was accepted 'for now' on January 16 by a junta, and it was decided to consult S.M. immediately, bypassing the Presidente due to the insurrection.
Don Gregorio Antonio Campos, a resident of San José, granted general power of attorney to Don Eusebio Rodríguez, who was also from San José.

Cayetana de la Trinidad Romero, single and without succession, made her will. She was the legitimate daughter of the deceased Juan José Romero and María Francisca Pacheco. Her nephews Félix and Francisco Antonio Delgado were named executors, and her heirs included her nephews, her goddaughter María de la Trinidad Pacheco (whom she raised and married to José Francisco Navarro), Jesús María Navarro (whom she also raised), and Feliciana Martínez.

people_involved: Gobernador don Juan de Dios de Ayala
summary: Don Nicolás Carazo received a draft of 1000 pesos from Gobernador don Juan de Dios de Ayala, drawn against Don Vicente Robles of Panamá, which Carazo is to collect during his upcoming trip to that city. Carazo committed to repay the sum with 6% interest within a year, with Licenciado don Rafael Barroeta acting as his guarantor.

Francisco de la Trinidad Ramírez, son of the deceased Miguel Ramírez and Catalina Gómez, made his will in Chircagres on January 11, 1812. He was a widower of Joaquina Portugués, with whom he had four children, and had five more children from a second, unnamed marriage. Don Tomás Ulloa and Cecilio Calderón were named executors, and the will was legalized on February 21 with several witnesses.

José Antonio Quesada and his wife Concepción Brenes took on a debt of 290 pesos for chaplaincies belonging to the Convent, which had been redeemed by Doña Rosa Soto (widow of Don Esteban Jiménez) and Lucas Araya. They mortgaged their house as security for this debt. A marginal note indicates that Cayetano and Ponciano Madrigal took over this debt in 1817.
Doña Ana Rita de Oreamuno, legitimate daughter of the deceased Don José Antonio Oreamuno and Doña Encarnación Trinidad, made her will.

people_involved: Cura Presbítero don Rafael José de la Rosa
summary: The estate of the widow of don Tomás Hidalgo is being managed. Her children and sons-in-law are mentioned, with Fulgencio Hidalgo, Eulalia Hidalgo, and don Félix Fernández serving as executors. The estate includes a cattle ranch in La Trinidad, Esparza, and Cura Presbítero don Rafael José de la Rosa is the arbitrator judge.

Doña Vicenta, doña Juana, and don José Arnesto de Troya sold a piece of land to don Juan Pablo Jiménez for 70 pesos. The land, measuring 20 varas by 43 varas, was bordered by houses belonging to doña Rita de Oreamuno, doña Josefa de Oreamuno, and doña Antonia Masís, with a street in between.

Don Juan Francisco Bonilla was awarded the tithes (diezmos) for the province, covering areas from Alajuela to the Matina valley, for a term of 3 years at a cost of 6750 pesos. Don Joaquín Oreamuno and don Manuel Marchena served as his guarantors for this agreement.

Don Mateo de Mora, a retired Captain, made his testament in San José. He was married to doña Lucía Fernández and had 15 living children, including Antonia Mercedes, Feliciana, and Josefa Gertrudis, who were married to don Hilario Zeledón, don Ensebio Rodríguez, and don Juan Esquivel respectively. His assets included various lands, a house, cotton, and three enslaved women, and he detailed expenses for his son Juan José's studies in León. His nephew don Camilo Mora was the arbitrator judge, and his son José Joaquín and son-in-law don Hilario Zeledón were executors.

Miguel Pacheco made his testament, identifying his deceased mother as Rosa Pacheco. He had children Basilia, Pantaleón, Dolores, and Onofre with his first wife, doña Bartola Navarro, and disinherited Pantaleón for denying him as father. With his second wife, Jacoba Morales, he had José de la Cruz, Gertrudis, and Joaquín. Presbítero don Félix de Alvarado served as both arbitrator judge and executor, along with Jacoba Morales.

locations: Pueblo Nuevo de los Tres Ríos
summary: Don Francisco Ramírez sold a piece of land in Pueblo Nuevo de los Tres Ríos to don Manuel García Escalante for 210 pesos. The land, measuring 21 cordadas in circumference, was bordered by the seller's own lands, the Río Chiquito, lands of don Alejo Ramírez, and the Quebrada de Limón.

Don Manuel Segundo Lombardo made his testament in San José. He was the legitimate son of deceased residents of Santiago de Veragua, don Rafael Lombardo and doña María Antonia Gálvez, and was married to doña María Ninfa Franco, with whom he had no children. He named Reyes Sibaja as a legatee and his niece, doña María de Jesús Campos, as his heiress. Don Anselmo Aguilar and don José Pimental were appointed as executors.

people_involved: Don Joaquín José Díaz de Rivera
Doña Rudesinda de los Dolores Mora
summary: Doña María Ninfa Franco made her testament in San José. She was the legitimate daughter of deceased residents of Villa de los Santos, don Francisco Franco and doña Antonia Amoros, and was married to don Manuel Segundo Lombardo without children. She named numerous legatees, including her brother don Juan Franco, her godchildren, and children she was raising. Presbítero don Félix Velarde and her brother don Juan Franco were appointed as executors.

Don Telésforo Sandoval, a resident of Heredia, sold a piece of land in Llano de Tibás to Trinidad Castro for 60 pesos. The land measured 325 varas square and was bordered by properties belonging to Juan Antonio Salazar, Juan Antonio Zamora, don Mauricio Salinas, and Juan Torres.

people_involved: Cura Presbítero don Rafael José de la Rosa
summary: Raimundo Montoya made his testament, identifying his father as José Cayetano Montoya and his deceased mother as Francisca Ramona Hernández. He was married to María Dolores Ruiz, with whom he had a daughter named Juana de Dios. Don Francisco Javier de Villasanta was the arbitrator judge, and his wife María Dolores Ruiz and Cura Presbítero don Rafael José de la Rosa were appointed as executors.

locations: San Sebastián del Señorío de Vizcaya
summary: Don Francisco Javier de Villasanta made his testament. He was the legitimate son of the deceased don Juan de Villasanta and doña Josefa Antonia Berriarza, both natives of San Sebastián del Señorío de Vizcaya. He was married to doña Ambrosia de la Fuente, with whom he had four daughters: María Petronila, María Ramona, Agustina Josefa, and María Hipólita. Presbítero don Pedro Alvarado, don Pedro Carazo, and his wife doña Ambrosia de la Fuente were named as executors, with don José Ruperto Prieto as the arbitrator judge.

people_involved: Cura Presbítero don Rafael José de la Rosa
summary: Tomás Arburola made his testament, identifying his deceased mother as María Arburola. He was a widower of Dorotea Molina, with whom he had three daughters: Dominga, married to Francisco Villalobos; Rosa, widow of Francisco Luna; and Paula Josefa. Don Manuel García Escalante and Presbítero don Félix García were appointed as executors, and Cura Presbítero don Rafael José de la Rosa was the arbitrator judge.
Bartolo Rojas sold a piece of land in San José to Matías Rojas.

The will of Presbítero don Cayetano Chacón, who died on June 15 at midnight, was legalized and protocolized in San José. The process was initiated by Presbítero don Félix Velarde and approved by Alcalde don Camilo Mora, with declarations from witnesses don Eusebio Rodríguez, don Cipriano Fernández, don Félix Bonilla, and don José Ana Jiménez.

Presbítero don Antonio Cayetano Chacón made his will on September 1, 1806, with codicils in 1809 and 1812. He left legacies to churches and the poor in Jinotepe and Diriamba, donated to the Catholic Monarch, and ordered the freedom of his enslaved woman Sebastiana, while her daughters Sebastiana and María Carlos were to be freed upon his sister Antonia Chacón's death. He also distributed properties and money among his siblings, half-siblings, and other beneficiaries, including his raised son José Lorenzo and godson José Antonio Sandino.

In a codicil to his will, Antonio Cayetano Chacón revoked the legacy for six blandones for the Main Altar of his home church in San José, stating that he had already had them made during his lifetime and they were currently in use.

In a codicil to his will, Antonio Cayetano Chacón redirected a 500-peso legacy originally intended for José Antonio Sandino, who had since died. The sum was to be distributed among his nieces: 200 pesos to Antolina Valverde, and 100 pesos each to Josefa Valverde, Dolores Valverde, and Luz Chacón, all described as orphans or quasi-orphans and single.

José María Bonilla granted power of attorney to Doctor don Miguel Barroeta, the Cura of San Miguel, to collect 200 pesos. This money was a legacy left to Bonilla by the late Presbítero don José Andrés Carranza, former Cura of Usulután, and was to be received from Carranza's albacea, don Benigno Becerrín.

Eduardo Picado and Antonia Francisca Arburola, residents of Ujarrás, made their wills. They had no children. Antonia, previously married to Juan de Dios Rojas (also without children), named her father Manuel Francisco Arburola as her heir, or her husband if her father was absent. Eduardo named Antonia as his sole heir. The surviving spouse and Joaquín García were appointed as albaceas.

Gobernador don Juan de Dios de Ayala granted power of attorney to don Lorenzo Jurado, Teniente de Chiriquí, to sell an enslaved person named Victoria Medina. Victoria, approximately 16 years old, was a musician and shoemaker, and had been purchased by Ayala from doña María José Medina.

Joaquín Carazo and his wife Ana Francisca Bonilla took responsibility for 150 pesos in cacao from a capellanía belonging to the Cofradía del Santísimo in this city, a debt previously redeemed by don Francisco Javier Villasanta. They mortgaged their house as security. A marginal note indicates this debt was cancelled in December 1817, having been taken over by Rafael Escalante.

Manuel Marchena granted his enslaved mulato, Vicente, three years to purchase his freedom for 300 pesos. Vicente, a 25-year-old tailor who was acquired as part of Marchena's wife's dowry when he was 5, secured guarantors for the payment: José Gregorio Cárdenas, Ramón Ortiz, Alejo Aguilar, José Marchena and his wife Feliciana Salas, and Alejo Salazar and his wife Josefa Núñez. A marginal note from 1816 indicates Marchena cancelled the debt after receiving 225 pesos from Vicente, with Alejo Salazar assuming the remaining 75 pesos.

Doña Francisca Sierra (also known as Francisca Antonia de Sierra), a resident of Heredia, granted power of attorney to her son, don José León Taboada, a cleric residing in Guatemala. The purpose was to collect 250 pesos from don Anselmo Reina, also from Heredia, who owed 450 pesos but had already paid 200 pesos to Francisca's other son, don Luis Taboada.
Don Juan Alfaro, a resident of Alajuela, sold property to don Miguel Carranza, a resident of San José.

A transaction involving 31 caballerías of land in Puás and Rincón del Tigre for 140 pesos. The land is described by its boundaries, including properties of Don Juan Carranza and Don José Ana Jiménez, and natural features like Quebrada de la Pila and Río de Rosales.

people_involved: Don Juan de Dios de Ayala
summary: Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla confessed to owing Gobernador Don Juan de Dios de Ayala 3000 pesos, which was supplied in León via a draft against Coronel Don Joaquín Arechavala. Bonilla agreed to pay 6% annual interest, with repayment due upon Ayala's promotion or departure from the province. A marginal note indicates the debt was cancelled by Araya in 1817.

Juana Manuela Peraza, widow of Gabriel Cubillo and resident of San José, granted power of attorney to Félix Solís and Miguel Avendaño. This power was to collect debts from José María Salazar related to her deceased husband's estate, which occurred in Santa Teresa, Masaya, for the benefit of herself and her five children.

In San José, Don Félix Fernández Carranza sold 2 caballerías of land in Sarchí de Puás to Don Tomás González for 50 pesos. This land was inherited by Don Félix from his deceased wife and was part of a large pasture belonging to the Porras family.

In San José, José Ramón Parajeles sold a piece of land in the Barrio del Murciélago to the heirs of José Antonio Segura. The land, bordering the Virilla River, had been previously sold to the deceased for 280 pesos, which his widow, María de los Dolores Rojas, had just finished paying.

In San José, Doña María Josefa Chacón, a single woman, made her will. She ordered the liberation of her slaves, José Prudencio and María Manuela, and designated her brother-in-law, Don Romualdo Saborío, as the preferred buyer for her house. She named several nieces and nephews as legatees and appointed Don Félix Fernández and Don Romualdo Saborío as her executors.

In San José, Don Félix Fernández Carranza owed Doña Antonia Chacón, a widow, 800 pesos. This money was a loan from the assets left by Presbítero Don Cayetano Chacón to José Lorenzo Castro. Don Félix recognized an annual interest of 5% and provided Don Nicolás Castro (for 500 pesos) and Don Manuel Flores (for 300 pesos) as guarantors.

Juan Antonio Arias, son of the deceased Juan José Arias and Micaela Navarro, made his will in 'this city'. He was a widower of Ramona Masís, with whom he had four children, and was currently married to Catalina Araya, with whom he had three children. His executors were Nicolás de Bari Navarro and his son Antonio Fernando Arias.

Don Joaquín Hidalgo and his wife, Doña Ana Oreamuno, took on a capellanía debt of 133 pesos 2 reales (equivalent to 200 pesos cacao) belonging to Presbítero Don Félix de Alvarado. They mortgaged their house, located in front of the San Nicolás plaza, as security.

Don José María de Peralta sold a 12-year-old mulatto slave named Joaquina to Doña Mercedes Guerrero for 200 pesos. Joaquina, described as light-skinned with black hair and a flat nose, had been previously purchased by Peralta from Doña María Francisca del Corral.

people_involved: Don Juan de Dios de Ayala Gudiño Medina y Calderón
summary: Gobernador Don Juan de Dios de Ayala Gudiño Medina y Calderón, a Knight of the Order of Santiago, granted power of attorney to his brother, Don Francisco de Ayala, who was the Lieutenant of the King in Panamá. This power allowed Don Francisco to petition the Court for honors and favors for the Gobernador.
Don Juan Francisco Bonilla sold a 17-year-old mulatto slave named Manuel Francisco to Don Ramón Palacios for 280 pesos. Manuel Francisco was the son of Bonilla's other slave, Ventura.

Bernardino Navarro obligated himself to his grandchildren, Francisca Felipa and Saturnino, for 233 pesos 3 reales from their paternal inheritance. Their father was the deceased Pascual Bejarano, and their mother was Ana Navarro, who later married Ramón Segura. Quiteria Romero, Bernardino Navarro's mother, was named as a guarantor, but the transaction was not concluded.

Jesús Méndez obligated himself to Rafael, Juan, and Joaquina, the minor children of the deceased Reyes Bonilla and Feliciana Ramírez (Méndez's sister-in-law), for 13 pesos 1 real each from their inheritance. The older children, Gabriela and Yaruaria (widow of Juan), had already been paid their shares. Méndez also sold a small house from the inheritance assets to Cayetano Sánchez for 50 pesos.

José Dolores Madrigal formalized the sale of a piece of land in Purires, which he had sold 'last year' to the now-deceased Don José Antonio del Campo for 30 pesos. The land's boundaries included a street to Candelaria, the buyer's land, Quebrada de Cabrera, Isabel Piedra's land, and land of the natives of Tobosi. The formalization was done at the request of the buyer's widow, Doña Mercedes Guerrero.

Don Juan Francisco Bonilla took responsibility for a debt of 707 pesos 2 reales that was previously owed by Presbítero Don Félix de Alvarado. This debt originated from the sale of a house formerly owned by Don Diego de la Haya. A marginal note indicates the debt was cancelled in 1817, having been taken over by Señora Coronela Doña Sinforosa Prieto.

Don Manuel García Escalante, owner of the 21-year-old slave José Joaquín Hermenegildo Corrales (a weaver and bloodletter, son of slave Ana), granted him three years to pay 250 pesos for his freedom. Don Juan Francisco Bonilla, Presbítero Don Félix de Alvarado, Licenciado Don Rafael Barroeta, Don Manuel de Alvarado, and the present notary each acted as guarantors for 50 pesos. A marginal note indicates this was cancelled in 1815.

Francisco Quirós, married to Rosario Aguirre, made his will. He had three daughters with Rosario: María de Jesús, Antonia Francisca, and Ana Josefa. Rosario Aguirre had previously been married to Manuel José Chaves, with whom she had a daughter named Trinidad, who was the widow of Francisco's brother, Rafael Quirós.

people_involved: Presbítero don Félix de Jesús García
summary: Don Manuel Segundo Lombardo, a resident of San José, grants power of attorney to Presbítero don Félix de Jesús García, or failing him, don Anselmo Aguilar, to sell a house he owns on a corner of the Plaza.

José Manuel Rojas makes his will. He is the legitimate son of the deceased José Rojas and Cayetana Estrella. He was widowed from Jacoba Badilla, with whom he had four children: José, Luisa, Juan, and Pedro. He is currently married to Petronila Rojas, with whom he has two daughters: Josefa and Micaela de la Soledad. His executors are his current wife and don Gregorio Ulloa.

In San José, Raimundo Morales, a resident of Heredia, sells a piece of land in La Uruca to Pantaleón Rivera for 50 pesos. The land borders properties of Don Francisco Alvarado, María Rojas, the 'potrero de las Animas', and Juan Manuel Quirós. Part of this land was previously sold by Raimundo, and another part by his father, Francisco Morales.

In San José, Pantaleón Rivera makes his will. He is the legitimate son of the deceased Nicolás Rivera and Manuela Suárez. He is married to María Cayetana Barquero, with whom he has seven children. His home is in the Murciélago neighborhood. Don Antonio Vargas is the arbiter judge, and his executors are Presbítero don José Francisco Mondragón and his son Juan de los Dolores.

people_involved: Don José Francisco Guerrero de Arcos
Presbítero don José María del Campo
summary: Doña María Mercedes Guerrero, legitimate daughter of the deceased Don José Francisco Guerrero de Arcos and Doña María Manuela Miranda, and widow of Don José Antonio del Campo, grants power to make her will to her son Presbítero don José María del Campo, or failing him, her son Don José Gabriel, or failing both, Presbítero don Nicolás Carrillo. Her heirs are her children, and the same appointed individuals are her executors.

people_involved: Gobernador don Juan de Dios de Ayala
summary: Don Joaquín Hidalgo owes Gobernador don Juan de Dios de Ayala 300 pesos at 6% interest, with a one-year term.

In Alajuela, before Alcalde 2° Don Antonio Alfaro, Don Pioquinto Rodríguez makes his will. He was widowed from Doña María Apolonia Ugalde, with whom he had eight children. He is currently married to Doña Candelaria Sáenz, with whom he has no children. His executors are Don Matías Sandoval and Don Santiago González.

In Alajuela, before Alcalde 2° Don Antonio Alfaro, Cipriano Arguello and his wife Sabina Avendaño make their will. They have one son, José León. Their executors are Don Manuel Jiménez and Don Anselmo Zumbado.

people_involved: Doña Juana María de Soto y Barahona
summary: A sealed will, dated June 19, 1806, by Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla and his wife Doña Ana Rita Gómez, was legalized on December 9. The cover was made on June 20, 1806, before Gobernador Acosta. They have no children and own extensive properties across various locations, including houses, pastures, cattle, and cacao haciendas, some of which are managed by their mulato slaves Pedro Salguero and Juan Antonio. They also designate land in Ujarrás for the benefit of the poorest women of the village.

people_involved: Presbítero don Rafael José de la Rosa
summary: Unnamed testators made provisions in their testament, including granting freedom to slaves Ventura and María Cayetana, and naming several legatees and albaceas. The testament detailed extensive personal property and listed eleven slaves located in Santa Ana and Ujarrás.

people_involved: Señora Coronela doña Ana Rita Gómez
summary: The accidental Commander, in the absence of the Governor, opened the testament of the deceased Coronela doña Ana Rita Gómez at the request of Bonilla, after she was found dead.

Doña Joaquina López del Corral sold three caballerías of land in the Río Grande area, specifically 'En medio de las quebradas,' to Pedro Espinosa for 60 pesos. The land's boundaries are detailed by various streams.
Don José Francisco Saborío, acting with power of attorney for Don Romualdo Rodríguez, issued a receipt to Don Ramón Esquivel for 150 pesos that Esquivel held from Rodríguez's guardianship.

people_involved: Presbítero don Rafael José de la Rosa
Presbítero don José María del Campo
summary: Doña María Manuela Miranda, natural daughter of the deceased Doña Juana Josefa Miranda and widow of Don Francisco Guerrero de Arcos, made her testament. She named her daughters Doña María Mercedes and Doña María Lisarda, and appointed Presbítero don Rafael José de la Rosa, or in his absence, her grandsons Presbítero don José María del Campo and Don José Gabriel del Campo, as albaceas.
Cruz Navarro and his wife Doña Antonia Ramírez incurred a debt of 200 pesos to Don Juan Francisco Bonilla, with a 4-year term and 6% interest.

Domingo Contreras and Lino Rodríguez, residents of Heredia, committed to pay 72 pesos and 2 reales as inheritance to five minors (Juan, Petronila, José, Natividad, and Manuel del Espíritusanto), who are the children of the deceased Santos Contreras and Josefa Ramírez.

María Magdalena Navarro, legitimate daughter of the deceased Manuel Antonio Navarro and Tomasa Leitón, and being single and without succession, made her testament. She named her niece Gabriela Navarro (wife of José Antonio Solano) as legatee and appointed José Francisco Navarro and José Antonio Solano as albaceas.

Don Fulgencio and Doña Eulalia Hidalgo took responsibility for 100 pesos redeemed by their deceased mother, Doña Rita de Oreamuno, which belonged to Nuestra Señora del Pilar de los Tres Ríos. They mortgaged their inheritance shares in their mother's former house located in the Plaza Real of the city.

In San José, Doña Antonia Chacón, a widow, sold a pasture in Mata Redonda to Don Gregorio Ulloa for 300 pesos. She had acquired this land from Don Hilario Zeledón, and it bordered the María Aguilar river and Miguel Peraza's pasture.

Doña María Petronila Bonilla, legitimate daughter of the deceased Don José Nicolás Bonilla and Doña Lucía de Alvarado, and widow of Don Carlos Ruiz Fernández, made her testament. She named her living children, mentioned her deceased son and other children, detailed her relationships with her children's spouses, and listed her deceased brothers and grandchildren. She also mentioned a hacienda in La Palma and her servant, appointing her son Don Manuel and son-in-law Alvarado as albaceas, and Don Juan Francisco Bonilla as judge arbiter.
Tomás Loaiza emancipated his legitimate son Marcos, who was over 25 years old. The Governor approved this act.

Doña Lorenza Ruiz, a resident of Heredia, granted power of attorney to her son, Don José Antonio Carvajal, to collect goods in the villa of Rivas that belonged to her as the sole sister and intestate heir of the deceased Doña Paula Zamora.
Don José Ignacio Rucabado and his wife Doña Josefa Oreamuno sold a house with a walled plot in the city to Coronel don Tomás de Acosta. The property bordered the house of Presbítero don Rafael.

Señor Acosta founded a chaplaincy on a property, benefiting the lineage of Don José Ruperto Prieto. Don Tomás concurred and accepted the arrangement, which involved 900 pesos, of which 300 had been received.

Francisco Lobo, legitimate son of the deceased Fernando Lobo and Manuela Josefa Rodríguez, made his will. He was married to María Josefa Montoya, with whom he had five children. Don Salvador Oreamuno and his wife, María Josefa Montoya, were named as albaceas.

Don Juan José Zamora, acting with power from his mother Doña Manuela Rodríguez, sold a 450-vara square piece of land in Tibás to Pedro Rodríguez for 67 pesos. The land bordered the Quintana road, a royal street, and lands of Ignacio Bolaños.

Don Pedro José Zamora, a resident of Heredia, acting on behalf of his mother Doña Manuela Rodríguez, sold a piece of land in Tibás to Manuel Rodríguez for 67 pesos. The land measured 750 varas long by 450 varas wide and bordered Don Pedro Antonio Solares' pasture, the seller's lands, Juan José Cantillano's fence, and Cayetano Araya's fence.
Manuel Rodríguez, a resident of Heredia, sold a 450-vara square piece of land to Don Miguel González for 105 pesos. Manuel Rodríguez had originally acquired this land from Doña Manuela Rodríguez.

Licenciado Don Rafael Barroeta granted power to Don Benito Alvarado to collect 280 pesos from any holder of the ship 'San Benito.' This sum was owed to Barroeta by the deceased Don Antonio Espinosa, as Barroeta had paid it as a guarantor to Don José Ana Jiménez for part of the ship's price.

Don Pedro José Zamora, acting on behalf of his mother Doña Manuela Rodríguez, sold a piece of land in Tibás to Felipe de Jesús Chacón for 35 pesos. The land bordered the royal road, and an additional quarter of land also bordered the royal road of Montano.

Don Manuel Alvarado, Don Benito Alvarado, and Don Juan Aluma formed a partnership for a ship named 'Nuestra Señora de la Concepción' (alias 'el Costarrica'), built in Puerto del Coyolito. The ship, currently anchored at Isla de San Lucas with a cargo, cost 15890 pesos 2 reales, with the Alvarados contributing 14490 pesos 2 reales and Aluma 1400. Aluma would serve as Captain and Benito as Maestre without salary, and after the ship's cost is covered, they would share equal rights and profits.

Doña Casimira Pacheco made a codicil to her 1792 will. She revoked legacies to Doña Joaquina and Doña Teresa Quesada, amplified a legacy to Juan José Brenes, and made new legacies to Presbítero Don José Machado and her servant Cayetana, wife of Pedro Ramírez.
Doña Nicolasa Reyes made a codicil to her 1809 will, revoking a legacy previously made to Doña Cruz Arburola, daughter of Doña Rafaela Arburola.

Presbítero Don Félix Alvarado, Comisario del Santo Oficio and Sacristán Mayor of the city, granted power to Don Manuel Anduaga, Agent of the Indies in Cádiz, to solicit favors for himself and his ward, Don Nicolás Ulloa.
Licenciado Don Rafael Barroeta granted power to Don Manuel Anduaga to request honors, graces, and favors from the Crown on his behalf.
Licenciado Don Rafael Barroeta granted power to Don Pedro Beteta, and in his absence, to Don Pantaleón de la Águila, an attorney of the Audiencia, to request all necessary documents on his behalf.

Doña Tomasa Guzmán, single and without succession, made her will. She was the legitimate daughter of the deceased Don Manuel Guzmán and Doña Teresa Garlín. She ordered her slave, Benita, to be freed and named Don Manuel Sáenz and Don Gregorio Ulloa as albaceas, with her soul as the heir.

Bernardino Navarro obligated himself for 386 pesos in favor of his two minor grandchildren, Francisca Felipa and Saturnino del Carmen, children of his deceased son-in-law Pascual Bejarano and his daughter Ana Navarro. Ramón Segura, Ana's second husband, had previously managed the minors' assets with his mother Juana Quiteria Chacón as guarantor, but was removed as tutor at Bernardino's request.
Dámaso Martínez, acting as tutor for his brother-in-law Saturnino, provided a receipt to Ramón Navarro for 193 pesos, which was Saturnino's share.

people_involved: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco
summary: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco, acting as attorney for Don Pedro Antonio Solares, sold a 14-year-old mulatto slave named Águeda to Presbítero Don Félix Alvarado for 200 pesos. Águeda was described as zambo with straight black hair, born and raised in Solares' household.
Don Rafael Taboada granted power to Don Carlos Machado, a resident of Nicaragua, to collect any sums owed to him.
María Josefa Montoya, widow of Ambrosio Núñez, obligated herself for 187 pesos in favor of her minor sons, Antonio de los Dolores Núñez and Antonio del Espíritusanto Núñez.
Lombardo renounced his position as escribano (notary) in favor of the Public Treasury. This act led to the closure of the protocol he was managing.
Doña Rita Ruiz granted power of attorney to Don Joaquín Carazo. He was authorized to represent her in the estate proceedings related to her deceased mother, Doña María Petronila Bonilla.

Don Manuel Sáenz, a leaseholder of an aguardiente stall in the city, committed to paying 10 pesos monthly for 13 months to the Receptor de Alcabalas. Regidor Rafael de la Mata served as his guarantor for this obligation.

Don José María Peralta, a leaseholder of an aguardiente stall in the city, committed to paying 10 pesos monthly for 13 months to the Receptor de Alcabalas. Don Nicolás Carazo served as his guarantor for this obligation.

Juan Rafael Céspedes, a leaseholder of an aguardiente stall in the city, committed to paying 10 pesos monthly for 13 months to the Receptor de Alcabalas. Don Juan Antonio Castro served as his guarantor for this obligation.

Manuel Román, José Miguel Brenes, and the Chavarría siblings (Carlos, José María, Félix, and Joaquín) sold a house and its plot to Félix Monge for 150 pesos. The property, previously owned by the deceased Diego Chavarría, was bordered by houses belonging to Rosario Chavarría, José Trejos, Dolores Calvo, and Hilario Zúñiga.

Don Juan Antonio Castro formally took charge of the tutelage for the minor sisters, Doña Juana Hidalgo and Doña Paula Hidalgo. This entry marks the beginning of his responsibility for their care and assets.

Rudesindo Picado and his wife Gertrudis Solano obligated themselves for 353 pesos, which was adjudicated to the seven minor children of the deceased José Picado and María Josefa Arias. Prudencio Picado, the minors' grandfather, had chosen Rudesindo as their tutor due to being the closest relative.

Joaquín García, a leaseholder of the aguardiente stall in Ujarraz, committed to paying 10 pesos monthly for 13 months to the Receptor de Alcabalas. Don Juan Francisco Bonilla served as his guarantor for this obligation.
Don Antonio Figueroa granted a general power of attorney to Don Víctor Zavala. The document does not specify the exact nature of the powers granted.

Don Juan Francisco Bonilla granted power of attorney to Don Joaquín de Arechavala, a resident of León. Arechavala was authorized to bid for the tithes encompassing the districts of Alajuela, Villa Vieja, Villa Nueva, and Cartago.
Don Nicolás Orearauno granted power of attorney to Capitán Don Pedro César, a resident of León. César was authorized to request any necessary documents on behalf of Orearauno.

Don Juan Antonio Castro, having been appointed tutor for the minors Doña Juana and Doña Paula Hidalgo, provided a receipt. This receipt acknowledged his reception of the assets that constituted their inheritances from both their father and mother.

Ana Panlagua, also known as Coronel, made her will. As the single, legitimate daughter of the deceased Capitán de pardos Joaquín Coronel and Doña Antonia Alvarez, and having no succession, she named Juana Francisca (a girl she raised) and her daughters, along with Doña Manuela de Nava, as legatees. Doña Manuela de Nava and Don Joaquín García were appointed as executors, with Don Manuel Escalante serving as the arbiter judge.
Eusebio Molina confessed to owing his mother, María del Carmen González, 300 pesos. This sum had been lent to him by his mother to finance his marriage.

Presbítero Don Félix de Alvarado sold a pastureland named Sarchi de Puás in Rincón Largo to Don Patricio González, a resident of Heredia, for 300 pesos. This land, totaling 6 1/2 caballerías, was acquired by Alvarado from Don Miguel González, Don José Reyes (co-heir of Don Juan Agustín Porras), and Don Mariano Rodríguez.

Sebastián Ramos, José Antonio Quirós, Francisco Aguilar, and Mateo Araya, residents of the Arrabal and Chircagres neighborhoods, granted power of attorney to Eduardo González. He was authorized to request any necessary documents on behalf of all their neighbors.

Don Fulgencio Hidalgo, the legitimate son of the deceased Don Tomás Hidalgo and Doña Rita Oreamuno, made his will. He listed a sword and dagger, pawned to Padre Fray Francisco Moncada for 13 pesos, among his assets, and named his sister Doña Eulalia as legatee. Capitán Don Félix Fernández and Juan Rafael Céspedes were appointed as executors.

María Francisca Chavarría, widow of Juan Matamoros, made her will. She had five children with Juan Matamoros: Mariano, Julián, Rita, Hipólita, and Antonia. Her son-in-law was José de la Luz Brenes, and her granddaughter was María Mercedes Duran. Her daughter Rita was noted as the widow of Pantaleón Calvo, and her male children were named as executors.

Don Manuel Marchena granted power of attorney to Don Carlos Portocarrero, a notary residing in León, and to Don Juan Manuel Carazo, who also resided in León. The specific purpose of this power was not detailed.

Juan Francisco Aguilar, Cayetano Brenes, José Manuel Ulloa, Agustín Granados, and Manuel Francisco Aguilar sold a piece of land in Laguna de Horres to Don Rafael de la Mata for 14 pesos and 6 reales. The payment was delivered to Joaquín Ramírez, who was also an heir to these lands and had ordered the sale.
The entry begins with Brigadier Don Tomás de Acosta and his spouse, but the text is cut off before the event details are completed. No further information is available for this specific event.
Doña Margarita Grondel grants freedom to her enslaved mulata, Feliciana, who is approximately 60 years old.
Don José Mariano Valenzuela, a tobacco factor from León, grants general power of attorney to Don Pedro Antonio Solares of Heredia, or to Don Miguel Ángel Núñez if Solares is unavailable.

Doña Braulia Conejo, unmarried and childless, makes her will, leaving a pasture in La Lima and lands in Tres Ríos. Her soul is named as the heir, and Don Joaquín Oreamuno and Don Manuel Sáenz are appointed as executors.

María Dolores Sancho, widow of Nicolás Gómez and childless, makes her will, naming María Trinidad, a girl she raised, as a legatee. Don Lorenzo Carazo and Doña Hipólita Carazo are appointed as executors.

Don Manuel Ruiz grants power of attorney to Don Nicolás Carazo to represent him in the estate proceedings of his deceased mother, Doña María Petronila de Bonilla, as Ruiz needs to be absent at his hacienda.

Félix Solís obligates himself to his stepsons, Antonio de los Dolores Núñez and Antonio del Espíritu Santo Núñez, for 374 pesos from their inheritance. Manuel María Núñez and Tomás Sánchez act as guarantors, and the obligation was cancelled in 1827.

Don Ramón Jiménez and his wife Doña Joaquina Zamora take on a 550-peso loan from the Cofradía del Santísimo Sacramento, mortgaging their cattle ranch 'El Chapernal' in Bagaces and their house. The loan was cancelled in 1822 by Presbítero Don Juan Manuel Carazo.

Presbítero Don Félix Alvarado, the interim priest, sells an enslaved man named Marcos, approximately 22 years old, to Don Antonio Figueroa for 250 pesos. Marcos had previously belonged to Presbítero Don Ramón de Azofeifa.
Don Nicolás Carazo and his wife Doña Escolástica Peralta secure a 230-peso loan from the Esparta parish at 5% interest, mortgaging various properties including a sugar kettle, pasture, and house.
Don Antonio Figueroa grants general power of attorney to Don Tomás Herrera, a resident of Panama.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Rafael del Carmen Calvo
summary: Presbítero Don Félix Alvarado donates 100 pesos to his godson, Pedro del Sacramento Valerín, to be held by Presbítero Don Hipólito Calvo at 6% interest. In 1829, Valerín received the money and interest from Presbítero Don Rafael del Carmen Calvo, acting for his deceased brother.
Don Felipe Sancho and his wife Doña Ramona Alvarado acknowledge a 232-peso debt to the city's priest, secured by their house, which was formally mortgaged. The debt was cancelled in 1825.

Santos Rivera, acting as executor for José Antonio Solano and guardian for the minor Joaquín Solano, sells a piece of land in Churris to Felipe Romero for 60 pesos. The land had been previously bought from Bernardino Alvarado.

María Josefa Romero y Sibaja, a widow from Heredia and guardian of her two daughters, grants power of attorney to Don Sebastián Melón of Guatemala to collect 200 pesos left to her daughters by her deceased husband, José Antonio Amores.

Juan Rafael Céspedes and his wife Doña María Francisca Hidalgo take responsibility for a 300-peso debt owed to Chaplain Presbítero Don Pedro Portocarrero, previously held by Don José Ignacio Rucabado. They mortgage their house and a pasture, with Don José Antonio Echandi signing for Doña María Francisca Hidalgo.

people_involved: Presbítero Don José Ramón Machado y Ugarte
summary: Don Nicolás Oreamuno sells a house in Cartago to Presbítero Don José Ramón Machado y Ugarte for 500 pesos. The property is bordered by houses belonging to Doña Ana María Oreamuno, Doña Mercedes Guerrero, Manuela Badilla, and Doña Antonia Alvarado.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Rafael José de la Rosa
summary: Francisco Javier Mayorga and his wife Doña Francisca Villalón make their wills, listing their children and properties in Andecho, San Jerónimo, and Cartago. Their legatees include their sisters Micaela and Ramona Chavarría, and nieces María Josefa, Antonia Josefa, and María Josefa Chavarría. The surviving spouse and Presbítero Don Rafael José de la Rosa are named as executors.

José Felipe Romero makes his will, detailing his family, including his wife Francisca Estéfana Corrales, son José Vicente, and stepson José de la Cruz Corrales. Brigadier Don Tomás de Acosta is the arbiter, and his wife and Simón Bonilla are the executors.

María Cubero, widow of Francisco Carrasco, makes her will, listing her parents, her daughter Joaquina with Carrasco, and two other children named José and María Dolores. Her sister Ana Cubero and Alejo Aguilar are named as executors.
An attempt to issue a prison bail bond by Doña Ventura Jiménez for her son, Don Policarpo Soto, accused of cattle rustling, was suspended because Doña Ventura was a married woman.
Don José Francisco Jiménez, a resident of Ala- (likely Alajuela), is mentioned in an incomplete entry.
Ceferino Quesada posted bail for Don Policarpo Soto, a resident of this city, who was criminally prosecuted for allegedly being guilty of cattle rustling.
Antonio de la Trinidad Leitón posted bail for María Dorotea Leitón, who was criminally prosecuted for allegedly attempting to poison her husband.

people_involved: Presbítero don Félix de Jesús García
summary: Presbítero don Félix de Jesús García sold an enslaved person named Antonio, approximately 16 years old and son of an enslaved woman he bought from Doña Tomasa Guzmán, to Presbítero don José Francisco Mondragón for 250 pesos.
Don Lorenzo Carazo sold an enslaved person named José de Jesús, 25 years old, whom he had purchased from Presbítero don Félix Alvarado, to Don Francisco Castro, a resident of San José, for 250 pesos.

Rafael Navarro sold a house and its lot in this city to Pablo Navarro. The property was bordered by Felipe Castillo's lot to the North, Esteban Venegas's house to the South, Benita Molina's house to the East, and Miguel Roldan's house to the West.

Doña Cecilia Jiménez, single and daughter of the deceased Don José Antonio Jiménez and Doña Petronila Robledo, made her will. She granted freedom and some goods to her enslaved woman Nicolasa, and named her brother Don Ramón Jiménez and his children Don Eustaquio, Doña Ana Bernabela, and Doña Juaná de Dios, along with several churches, as legatees. Her brother Don Ramón and Don Pedro Carazo were appointed as executors.

Eugenio Cantillo, legitimate son of the deceased Juan José Cantillo and Josfa Padilla, made his will. He was married to Antonia Josefa Calvo and had children Narciso, Agustina, and María Josefa, also mentioning an unnamed stepson and his nieces María Sacramento Cantillo and Antonia. Don Manuel García Escalante and Gregorio Cárdenas were named as executors.

Félix Mariano Solís lent 100 pesos to Feliciano Monge for 10 years at 53% interest. Feliciano Monge's mother, Isabel Vega, guaranteed the loan by mortgaging two houses in El Arrabal. The loan was cancelled in 1825.

Simona Quesada, legitimate daughter of Benito Quesada and Teresa Rojas, made her will. She was the widow of Nicolás Sánchez, with whom she had children Ramón, María, José, and Antonia, all married except José. Sargento Esteban González and Miguel Arburola were appointed as executors.

people_involved: Presbítero don José de la Encarnación Fernández
summary: Doña María Gertrudis Bolívar agreed to sell her livestock, mares, horses, lands, and other assets from her hacienda in Mateo, jurisdiction of Bagaces, to Presbítero don José de la Encarnación Fernández. The buyer would pay 200 pesos upfront, and matters concerning chaplaincy on the hacienda would be handled with her son, Presbítero don José Antonio Bonilla, as Chaplain. Don Isidro Oreamuno, her father-in-law, signed on her behalf.

people_involved: Presbítero don José de la Encarnación Fernández
summary: Doña María Gertrudis Bolívar, widow of Don Andrés Bonilla, sold the Mateo hacienda to her son, Presbítero don José Antonio Bonilla, with the consent of Presbítero Fernández, due to improved pricing. Her son would pay 1000 pesos upfront, and the delivery would be made in the coming December by her son Presbítero don Miguel and Don Manuel Flores.

Don Ramón López and his wife Doña Ana Jacoba Quesada received 160 pesos as a censo from Don Manuel García Escalante, which belonged to the minor children of the deceased Doña Ana Jacoba Quesada. They mortgaged a house on the outskirts of this city that previously belonged to the late Matías Román.

Juan Manuel Marín made his will. He was a widower of Juana Cortés, with whom he had sons Luis Antonio and Juan José. He was currently married to Manuela Josefa Bejarano, with whom he had living children Antonia de Jesús, María Policarpa, Manuel de Jesús, and María Trinidad. His wife and son Manuel de Jesús Marín were named as executors.

people_involved: José de los Angeles Vargas Blanco
summary: Rudesindo Vargas and his wife Doña María Josefa Blanco made their wills. Rudesindo was the legitimate son of José Antonio Vargas and María Josefa Arias, while Doña María Josefa Blanco was the legitimate daughter of Don Juan Francisco Blanco and Doña María Josefa Castro, residents of San José. Their children were José, Antonio, Rafaela, José, Jesús María, Jacinto de los Angeles, and José de los Angeles. Don Miguel Rojas and Don Eusebio Rodríguez were appointed as executors.

Miguel Lobo and his wife Manuela Coto made a codicil to their will, mentioning a decrease in assets and debts. Their grandson Manuel Lobo was also mentioned. Don Joaquín Carazo and Ildefonso Alfaro were named as executors.

Don José María de Peralta received the inventoried assets from the estate of Doña Bartola Elizondo in deposit. This was due to the absence of Don Luis Gómez, who, as the legitimate guardian of the minors, should have received the deposit.

people_involved: María de la Encarnación Ulloa (enslaved woman)
María de la Encarnación Ulloa's husband
summary: Don Manuel Sáenz granted freedom to his enslaved woman María de la Encarnación Ulloa. This was made possible by 150 pesos from Doña Dominga Robredo, 60 pesos donated by Don Manuel Sáenz, a 10-peso discount from María de la Encarnación Ulloa's husband, and a commitment from her husband to pay 40 pesos, totaling her price of 260 pesos.
María Josefa Solano, legitimate daughter of José Antonio Solano and Micaela Valverde, made her will.

Doña Juana Meoño sold a house and its adjoining lot to Casimiro Arrióla for 176 pesos. The property was bordered by the house of José Corrales, the Church of Soledad, the former house of Agustín Núñez, and the house of Carlos Chavarría.

people_involved: Coronel don Juan Francisco de Bonilla
Teniente Coronel don Juan Manuel de Cañas
summary: Don Salvador Oreamuno became a new guarantor for Teniente Coronel don Juan Manuel de Cañas, replacing Coronel don Juan Francisco de Bonilla. Bonilla had declared in his will that he was withdrawing from all guarantees, including one for Cañas related to 2530 pesos from the Brotherhood of the Most Holy of Bagaces. The new guarantee was accepted by Presbítero don Pablo Rojas, the priest of Bagaces. This fianza was later cancelled in 1817.

Miguel Arburola and his wife María Nicolasa Chavarría made their will. They had no children together, but Miguel recognized Juana Alvarado as his natural daughter and had two sons, Juan and Marcos Rodríguez, after marriage. María Nicolasa was previously married to Juan José Rodríguez, with whom she had a son, Pablo Rodríguez, who recognized two natural sons, José María Hernández and José María Acuña. They also raised an orphan, Joaquín Arburola.

people_involved: Padre Cura don Rafael José de la Rosa
summary: Rafael Pacheco and his wife Juana de Dios Brenes made their will. They had no surviving children, and named Padre Cura don Rafael José de la Rosa as an arbiter judge. Their nieces, María Joaquina and María Francisca Pacheco, were legatees, as were José Francisco Corrales, José Pacheco, and Antoni Valerín, who had been raised by Juana de Dios Brenes.

Captain don Juan de Alvarado made his will, mentioning his wife doña Ana Josefa Carazo and their children don José Cayetano and doña María. His assets included the Tenorio hacienda, and his mother-in-law doña Jacoba de Alvarado and sister doña María de Alvarado were noted. His brothers-in-law, don Lorenzo and don Pedro Carazo, were named albaceas, and don Ramón Jiménez was named arbiter judge.

Félix Esteban Calvo and his wife Lucía Monge made their will, listing their nine children and their spouses. Their son Marcos de la Trinidad had moved to Nicaragua and married in El Viejo. Sargento Esteban González was named arbiter judge.
Cayetano Granados provided bail for José María Rivera, who was imprisoned on suspicion of involvement in the death of Nicolás Vega's wife.

José de Jesús and Cruz Fuentes, as debtor and guarantor, obligated themselves to the children of the deceased Bernardo Garro, María Baltasara and José Valentín, for 226 pesos from their inheritance. This obligation was cancelled in 1817 by a receipt from Miguel Arias, who took over these guardianships.

Doña Antonia Arlegui, a widow, granted power of attorney to Presbítero don Nicolás Hidalgo to collect the remaining sum from don Manuel Gómez, the testamentary executor of the deceased don Manuel Bonilla. This sum was received by Bonilla, as Arlegui's attorney, from the estate of doña Manuela Ibarra.

people_involved: María Josefa de los Dolores Brenes
summary: Juan José Abarca and his wife María Josefa de los Dolores Brenes made their will. They had no children of their own but had raised José María Abarca since his infancy. Don Manuel García Escalante and Captain Juan Chavarría were named albaceas.

José Antonio Piedra, a resident of El Tejar, made his will. He was married to Andrea Jinesta and had five children: Juan, Antonio de la Encarnación, Antonio Baltasar, Francisco Ignacio, and María Rafaela. His wife and José Francisco Navarro were named albaceas.
Doña Juana Andrea Ugalde, a widow, made her will. Her assets were to be distributed according to instructions given to her albacea, don Pedro Carazo.

people_involved: Presbítero don Félix de Jesús García
summary: Presbítero don Félix de Jesús García sold two enslaved women, Manuela (approx. 42 years old) and her daughter Micaela (approx. 21 years old), to don Francisco Castro, a resident of San José, for 500 pesos. Manuela had been purchased from don Pedro Elizondo.

Manuela Aguilar, widow of José Vega, granted general power of attorney to Juan Chinchilla, specifically to collect any amount due from her deceased husband's estate that remained in the possession of her two minor daughters residing in Nicaragua.

Doña Antonia Clemencia Astorga, a native and resident of Cartago in the Taras neighborhood, made her will. She was a widow in her first marriage to Pedro González, with whom she had a daughter, Jacinta González, and a widow in her second marriage to Felipe Hernández, with whom she had a daughter, Josefa Catarina.

An unnamed woman, married for the third time to don Martín Zeledón, makes her will. She lists her children, including Josefa Matilde, José del Rosario, José Nicolas, Juana Ventura, Juan Bautista, and José Bernardo Hernández. Her daughter Catarina is married to José Navarro, Matilde to don Trinidad Zeledón, and José del Rosario Hernández to Rita Navarro. Her husband, don Martín Zeledón, and don José Antonio García are named as executors.
Don Antonio Sánchez, a merchant from this Kingdom, grants general power of attorney to don José María Peralta.

The Mayor, who was the highest bidder for an aguardiente stall in this city, commits to paying the Tax Collector 25 pesos monthly for one year for the rights to the stall. Don Nicolás Carazo acts as his guarantor.

locations: Paso de la Carreta del Arrabal
summary: Don Manuel García Escalante sells a mill, a house, two small pastures, and a plot of land in Paso de la Carreta del Arrabal to José Céspedes for 400 pesos. This sale was later rescinded in 1820 by both parties.

people_involved: Capitán Don Juan Manuel de Alvarado
summary: Captain don Juan Manuel de Alvarado, acting as executor for doña Lucía de Alvarado and on behalf of his sister-in-law doña María Josefa Ruiz, sells 8 caballerías of land in La Palma to Presbítero don Félix Alvarado for 237 pesos. The land titles were originally granted to don José Nicolás Bonilla, his grandfather-in-law.

Brigadier don Tomás de Acosta grants power of attorney to Colonel don Pablo de Arosemena, a resident of Panama, to collect outstanding salaries from the Royal Coffers for his service in the Government of Santa Marta. Don Tomás de Acosta's wife, doña Margarita Grondel, signs on his behalf due to his poor eyesight, referencing documents held by his previous attorney, don Juan Jiménez.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Félix de Jesús García
summary: Cristóbal Cayetano Aguilar and María Leonida Otárola, husband and wife, make their wills. They list their parents, nine children (Ignacio and José Diego are deceased), and two grandchildren (María Josefa and José María). The surviving spouse, Presbítero don Félix Alvarado, and Presbítero don Félix de Jesús García are named as executors.

people_involved: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco
summary: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco, acting as attorney for don Pedro Antonio Solares, who in turn represents the Vicar of Veragua, don Fernando Solís, sells a 23-year-old mulata named Francisca Javiera to Presbítero don Félix Alvarado for 200 pesos.

people_involved: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco
summary: Don Miguel Ángel Núñez del Arco, acting with the same authority as in the previous entry, sells a 24-year-old mulato named José Antonio to don Pedro Sobenes, a resident of Nicoya, for 200 pesos.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Rafael Baltasar de la Fuente
summary: Presbítero don Rafael Baltasar de la Fuente, the parish priest of the town of Nicaragua, grants power of attorney to Ramón Cubero, a resident of Nicaragua, to collect all debts owed to him in that province.

Residents of the Taras and El Arrabal neighborhoods, represented by several individuals including León Calvo and Miguel Montoya, grant power of attorney to Hilario Salas to request the demarcation of lands belonging to the Hidalgo family (known as Felipe Díaz lands) and the Chavarría family.

Doña Dolores Frutos, a widow, and her adult children (Carlos, José María, Félix Chavarría), along with her sons-in-law Miguel Brenes (husband of Feliciana Chavarría) and Manuel Román (husband of Ana María Chavarría), sell a pasture located on Oreamuno lands to her son and brother, Presbítero don Fernando Chavarría, for 271 pesos and 4 reales.

Don Nicolás Castro, a resident of San José, leases 426 cattle, 20 mares, and 16 horses, valued at 2103 pesos, from doña María Alvarado. He will pay 5% annually for 6 years, with the livestock located in the jurisdiction of Engaces.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Juan de la Cruz Pérez
summary: Don Juan Antonio Castro and Juan Rafael Céspedes, acting on their own behalf and for several Hidalgo family members (including minors Doña Paula and Don Lorenzo), sell a site and livestock in Landecho and La Trinidad, including ten caballerías of land, to Presbítero don Juan de la Cruz Pérez, a resident of San José, for 784 pesos. Judicial authorization for the sale of the minors' shares is attached, with witnesses Don Felipe Sancho (54), Don Salvador Oreamuno (45), and Don Hermenegildo Bonilla (over 25).

Juana Cascante, legitimate daughter of deceased Andrés Cascante and María Cabezas of Villa Vieja, makes her will. She has a daughter named Juana Josefa. Among her assets are livestock left by the late doña Rita Coronado, located on the El Chapernal hacienda of her master, don Ramón Jiménez. Don Ramón Jiménez and don Pedro José Carazo are named as executors.

José Brenes, a resident of Agua Caliente and highest bidder for two aguardiente stalls in this city, commits to paying the Tax Collector 50 pesos and 4 reales monthly for one year. Don José María Peralta, Manuel Sáenz, Venancio Madriz, Rafael Ulloa, Julián Brenes, Manuel Loaiza, Manuel Molina, Jesús Coto, Miguel Arrieta, Cecilio Calderón, and Cleto Rojas act as his guarantors.

Don Mariano Rodríguez, a resident of Heredia, and Trinidad Pacheco redeem 200 pesos from a chaplaincy that burdened the Oricuajo site, which they declare to own in halves. They agree not to sell without mutual consent, preferring the co-owner.

Don Vicente Fábrega and his wife doña Irene Zamora commit to the minor José María, son of doña Irene and her first husband don Carlos Volio, for 1436 pesos and 2 reales. This amount represents the minor's paternal inheritance, received in various goods. The obligation was cancelled in 1823 by Volio.

Rafael Ciríaco Guerrero and his wife Felipa Coronel made their will, listing their children José Joaquín, José Nicolás, Ramón, Antonio, Mercedes, and Ignacia. Rafael also detailed his previous marriage to María de la Cruz Cedeño, with whom he had Vicente, Joaquín, Francisco, José María, Baltasar, and Agustín. The will mentioned a forge and blacksmith accessories among their assets, and named Manuela del Corral and Manuel Escalante as executors/arbiters.

Don José María de Peralta assumed responsibility for a 420-peso chaplaincy belonging to the Cura of Heredia, Don José Antonio Bonilla, which was previously held by the deceased Doña Joaquina López del Corral. Peralta mortgaged his house and a small farm in Agua Caliente as security. An 1816 deed related to this was later cancelled.

people_involved: Juan Salvador de Laya y Bolívar
summary: Doña María de Laya y Bolívar, widow of Don Andrés Bonilla, sold a cattle ranch in Mateo, Bagaces, to her son, Presbítero Don José Antonio Bonilla, Cura of Heredia. The ranch, inherited from her brother Juan Salvador de Laya y Bolívar, included 27 caballerías of land, 393 cattle, 22 mares, and 11 horses, for 3535 pesos. The price was reduced by several chaplaincies, and her son remained indebted for the balance.

Doña María de Laya y Bolívar, legitimate daughter of Don Miguel de Laya y Bolívar and Doña Isabel de Miranda, and widow of Sargento Mayor Don Andrés de Bonilla, made her will. She listed her children: María del Rosario (widow of Tomás Alvarado), Presbítero José Antonio, Santiago, Presbítero Miguel, Juana (single), María Cruz (single), and Justa (married to Isidro Oreamuno). Her husband's estate proceedings were in 1785, and she named Presbítero Don Juan José Oreamuno and Don Manuel García Escalante as executors.

Doña Joaquina López del Corral made a closed will on January 3, 1811, before Notario Lombardo. This will detailed her family, including her deceased parents, two marriages, and children, as well as her financial situation and assets.

Doña Joaquina López del Corral, who died on October 9, 1815, had her closed will opened on October 17, 1815. The will detailed her two marriages, children, and financial struggles, including debts incurred from her husbands and expenses for her children's studies and travels, such as her son's trip to La Guaira. Her assets included two forges, a silver chest, and three enslaved women, Antonia and her daughters María Mercedes and Nicolasa. Her four daughters were named as heirs, and several clerics and officials were present for the opening.

Miguel Lobo granted power of attorney to Miguel Antonio Matamoros, a resident of Masaya, to collect 72 pesos from Manuel de Jesús Arguello, a resident of Heredia. This amount was for the freight of two mules that Arguello had in his possession for four and a half years without Lobo's consent. Matamoros was instructed to claim the debt from Arguello's executors or heirs if he had passed away.

Alcalde Juan Francisco de Bonilla, acting on his own behalf, granted power of attorney to Lieutenant Don Nicolás Carazo to sell an enslaved mulatto named Miguel Bonilla. Miguel Bonilla was described as tall, 'azambado,' hairless, with curly black hair, turned eyes, and large heels.

Alcalde Juan Francisco de Bonilla took responsibility for 156 pesos and 6.5 reales from a chaplaincy belonging to the minor cleric Don Tomás Prieto. He mortgaged a sugar mill estate located in Ujarrás as security for this amount.
José Francisco Piedra, a resident of San José, provided bail for Mateo Alvarado, who was facing charges of larceny. Alvarado had been granted temporary release from jail due to illness.

Don Francisco Castro, a resident of San José, sold two enslaved mulatto women, Manuela de la Asunción and Micaela, to Governor Don Juan de Dios de Ayala. Manuela was 46 years old, described as 'fine black' and tall, while Micaela was 18 years old, 'pardo' in color and 'metida en carnes' (fleshy).

María Vanegas, Pedro Vanegas, Dolores Céspedes, and José Antonio Araya sold a piece of land called El Común del Cerro grande, measuring 13 'coniadas' of 100 varas, to Alejo Aguiar for 75 pesos. The land was bordered by properties of Pedro Coto, Manuel de Jesús Pacheco, Pedro Vanegas, Domingo Coto, Lucas Araya, Francisco Vanegas, and the Cachimba stream.

Captain Lorenzo Carazo sold three slaves, Isidro, his wife Josefa, and their son Joaquín, to Vicente Fábrega for 550 pesos. Isidro and Josefa were inherited from Lorenzo's mother, Jacoba Alvarado, and Joaquín, 1 year and 8 months old, was born in Lorenzo's house. Isidro and Josefa are described as being around 33 years old.

Juan Francisco de Bonilla granted power of attorney to Antonio Figueroa to sell two of his mulatto slaves: Juan José, about 20 years old, and Miguel Bonilla, who was a fugitive in 'the other Kingdom'.

Antonia Arlegui sold an adobe-walled shop with cedar wood and its plot to Narciso Esquivel for 150 pesos, with 80 pesos due in 6 months. The property was bordered by houses of Félix de Alvarado, Juana Calle, and Manuela Conejo. The sale was cancelled in 1817, with Antonia's son, José Antonio Urrutia, signing on her behalf.
Manuel Marchena granted power of attorney to Nicolás Carazo, Antonio Figueroa, and Vicente Fábrega, in that order, to sell his 24-year-old mulatto slave named Blas, who was a tailor.

people_involved: Presbítero don Félix de Jesús García
summary: Manuel Peralta received the dowry goods of his wife, Ana Josefa Chavarría, valued at 1243 pesos and 1 real. They had married on November 30, 1815. The dowry included 573 pesos and 6 reales in cash, delivered by Presbyter Félix de Jesús García, who was Paulina Fajardo's tutor. The goods were appraised by tailor José María Meneses and silversmith Ramón Ortiz.

people_involved: clérigo minorista don Francisco de Paula Campos y Pérez
Presbítero don Rafael del Carmen Calvo
summary: Mateo Rojas and Manuel José Pérez, along with their wives Cruz Pérez and Juana Ramona Monge, took on a debt of 200 pesos from a chaplaincy founded by Micaela Duran, for which Francisco de Paula Campos y Pérez was the chaplain. They mortgaged their houses, one in the city limits and another in Taras, plus some cattle. This debt was cancelled in 1850 by Presbyter Rafael del Carmen Calvo.

people_involved: Presbítero don Félix de Jesús García
summary: Presbyter Félix de Jesús García, Judge of Capellanías, granted power of attorney to Carlos Machado y Ugarte to collect interest on 800 pesos owed by Juan José Villar and 370 pesos owed by Pedro Muñoz.

people_involved: don Juan de Dios de Ayala
summary: Juan Francisco de Bonilla, acting as military governor in the absence of Juan de Dios de Ayala, sold a slave named Juan José, 18 years old, to Lucas Estévez, a resident of Panama and native of Ragusa, for 300 pesos. Juan José was described as a musician with basic tailoring skills.
Jerónima Garro, widow of Francisco Delgado, sold 30 'cordadas' of land in Purires and a place called Las Barrancas to Captain Joaquín Oreamuno for 60 pesos.

Brigadier Tomás de Acosta sold a 19-year-old slave named Mercedes, daughter of Feliciana, to Presbyter Pedro José Alvarado for 200 pesos. Due to vision impairment, Tomás de Acosta's wife, Margarita Grondel, signed on his behalf.

José Madrigal made his will, detailing his three marriages and children. He was widowed from Andrea Josefa Segura, with whom he had Juana. He then married Clemencia Muñoz, having María de los Angeles. His third marriage was to María Sánchez, with whom he had José Francisco, Juana María, Juana de Jesús, Marcos (all living), and Juan Manuel (deceased). His executrix was his wife María Sánchez and Jerónima Moya.

Tomasa Solano, daughter of deceased Francisco Solano and Luisa Chaves, made her nuncupative will in Ujarrás. She was first married to Gregorio García, with whom she had a deceased son, Joaquín. Her second husband was the deceased Bernardino Alvarado, with whom she had eight children, five of whom were married, one deceased as a child, and two single. Her executors were her children José del Patrocinio and Margarita.

José Alvarado requested the legalization of Tomasa Solano's will on May 8. Witnesses, including Cayetano Madriz, Manuel Morales, Braulio Román, Valentín Alvarado, Reyes Rivera, Luis Alarcón, and Roque Solano, declared, and the Alcalde approved the information on May 14.
Nicolás Carazo stated that Colonel Pablo Arosemena had sent him something via the pailebot 'Reina de los Angeles,' also known as 'El Costarrica,' which belonged to Antonio Figueroa.

Goods belonging to a resident of Panama were opened in the presence of Figueroa, revealing items requested by the owner's sisters and others. These goods were subsequently embargoed by order of the Governor, pending a decision from the Captain General. Don José María Peralta, a retired Captain, served as the guarantor for the value of the embargoed effects.
Doña Antonia Arlegui, the widow of don Romualdo Cuendi, sold 56 cordadas of land located in Quercua to Silvestre Masís for 45 pesos.

Don Antonio Sánchez, a single, retired veteran corporal from Guatemala province, originally from Colunga, Asturias, made his will. He left various religious legacies, funds for don Tomás Gómez's studies, and bequests to Tomás's sisters Eduviges and Regina, as well as to doña Nicolasa Elizondo and her daughter doña María Soledad for their service. He also bequeathed money to his sisters María Ramona and María Bernarda Sánchez y García in Colunga, with the remainder of his estate designated for masses at the Colegio de Cristo de la Nueva Guatemala. Presbítero don Nicolás Carrillo and Capitán don Juan Dengo were named as his executors.

Don Juan Francisco de Bonilla sold a pasture in the common lands of Cartago to Presbítero don Evaristo Gutiérrez for 900 pesos. The property, located in La Pólvora and bordering the Reventado river, included land belonging to the indigenous people of Quircot, to whom Bonilla paid 3 reales monthly. A street leading from Cartago to Felipe Díaz crossed the pasture.

people_involved: Presbítero don Manuel Orozco y Ayala
summary: Don José Aranda, military commander of Nicaragua, and his wife doña Isabel Muñoz, ceded 2,000 pesos in livestock and land from their San Jerónimo hacienda in Nicoya to their son, don José María Aranda. This advance on his future inheritance was to support his pursuit of sacred orders, as his chaplaincy rights, inherited from Presbítero don Manuel Orozco y Ayala and his deceased cousin don José Tomás de Gamero (both grandsons of don Juan Antonio Muñoz), were complicated and required their personal attention in Nicaragua.

Don José Santos Lombardo and his wife doña Micaela Conejo made their wills, naming each other as reciprocal heirs since they had no children. Don José Santos Lombardo was the son of the deceased don Pedro Lombardo and doña Guadalupe Alvarado, while doña Micaela Conejo was the daughter of the deceased don Diego Conejo and doña María Guzmán. The surviving spouse and don Rafael Gallegos were appointed as executors.

Don Vicente Fábrega granted freedom to his 2-year, 5-month-old slave, Joaquín Valverde, who was described as white with brown hair. Fábrega had purchased Joaquín along with his parents, Isidro and Josefa, from don Lorenzo Carazo. The manumission occurred after doña María Hipólita Carazo, Joaquín's godmother, paid 50 pesos for his freedom.

Doña Florencia Jiménez, legitimate daughter of the deceased don José Antonio Jiménez and doña Petronila Robredo, made her will.
