She was married to don Joaquín Oreamuno, with whom she had twelve living children, including Ana Josefa (married to don Joaquín Hidalgo), Juliana (married to the deceased don Antonio García), and Félix (married to doña Ramona Carazo). Her husband and son Félix were named as executors.
In the year 1816, don José Santos Lombardo served as the First Mayor of the city.
Presbítero don Pablo Rojas, the priest of Esparza, granted general power of attorney to don Joaquín Carazo and don Nicolás Carazo. This power was later revoked in 1824.

Don Tiburcio Sáenz and his wife doña Juana Alvarado made their wills. They had several children, including Teniente don Manuel, don Roque, doña Tomasa, doña Paula Josefa, doña María Manuela, and Fray Juan de Dios, who had died as a religious. Fray Juan de Dios had previously made his will in March 1801 in Guatemala, naming his parents as heirs and leaving a third of his 2100 pesos estate to his sisters doña Paula Josefa and doña María Manuela. The surviving spouse, their son don Manuel, and their grandson don Anselmo Sáenz were appointed as executors.

Don Juan Francisco Bonilla guaranteed to the Royal Treasury that don Juan Antonio Castro would fulfill his contract with the tobacco factor. The contract stipulated the transport of 200 petacas of tobacco to the León factory on Castro's ship, named San José alias El Milagro, at a rate of 8 pesos per two-tercio load.
Presbítero don José Ana Ulloa, Sacristán mayor of the rectoral church in Cartago, granted general power of attorney to don Juan García, a resident of León.

Doña Dominga Robredo, a widow, sold a house in Cartago to doña María Josefa Madriz for 231 pesos. The property was bordered by land belonging to don Manuel Marchena, don Gregorio Oreamuno, the widow of Antonio Piedra, and don Joaquín Oreamuno. Don Ramón Jiménez, her nephew, signed on behalf of the seller.
Rita Solano, widow of Pedro Barahona, committed to pay 58 pesos and 6 reales to her two minor sons, Francisco Antonio and Felipe Nicolás, as their paternal inheritance.

José Corrales and his wife María Gregoria Acosta took responsibility for 230 pesos from a chaplaincy belonging to the convent in Cartago, which was founded by doña Josefa de Oses Navarro. Don Manuel Marchena had previously held these funds. They mortgaged their house near Cartago as security.

Don Pedro Carazo, don Antonio Figueroa, don José Antonio Pérez, don Lorenzo Zumbado, Cosme Castro, and Manuel Rojas granted power of attorney to don Nicolás Carazo. This was to address the embargoed clothes they had introduced to Costa Rica from Panama on the ship 'N. S. de los Angeles' (also known as 'El Costarrica'), which were held at the Receptoria de Alcabalas.

people_involved: Don Juan de Dios de Ayala
summary: Gobernador don Juan de Dios de Ayala sold two enslaved mulatta women, Manuela de la Ascensión Guzmán (46) and her daughter Micaela (20), to Presbítero don Baltasar de la Fuente, Teniente Cura of Heredia, for 500 pesos. Don Juan de Dios de Ayala had previously purchased them from Presbítero don Félix de Jesús García.

Don Pedro José Carazo and his wife doña Anacleta Ugalde made their wills, stating they had no children and naming each other as reciprocal heirs. Legatees included don Pedro José Carazo's seven sisters, and the albaceas were the surviving spouse, don Lorenzo Carazo, and subdiácono don Juan Manuel Carazo.

Don Alejo Ramírez, a resident of Pueblo Nuevo and widower of doña Trinidad Madriz, committed to provide 141 pesos of inheritance to each of his seven minor children: María del Filar, Blas, Concepción, Margarita, Nicolás, María de Jesús, and Estanislao.

Don José María Peralta sold a house and its solar to Presbítero don Pedro Alvarado for 700 pesos. The property was located near a house owned by doña Feliciana Fuentes and don Vicente Fábrega, a solar of the señoras Chavarrías, the Cuartel, and the cemetery.

Don Ramón Jiménez, acting on behalf of his brother-in-law don Vicente Fábrega, sold an enslaved woman named Josefa, approximately 33 years old, to Presbítero don Félix Alvarado for 250 pesos. Josefa had previously been owned by don Lorenzo Carazo.

Don Manuel Sáenz and his wife doña María Cayetana Ulloa made their wills, listing their ten children and mentioning their cattle ranch in Paquita, camino de Panamá. They named Ana Rita Sáenz, whom they raised, as a legatee, and appointed the surviving spouse and Presbítero don José Ana Ulloa as albaceas.
Don Santiago Bonilla emancipated his son, don Joaquín Bonilla, who was over 25 years old, and provided him with 600 head of cattle and horses, along with 5 new mules, for his independent use.

Don Joaquín Bonilla assumed responsibility for 420 pesos from a chaplaincy belonging to Presbítero don José Antonio Bonilla, Cura of the villa de Nicaragua, which had previously been held by don José María Peralta. He mortgaged the livestock received from his father and named his parents, don Santiago Bonilla and doña María Josefa Oreamuno, as guarantors.

Brigadier don Tomás de Acosta granted freedom to his enslaved man, Esteban, who was about 27 years old and the son of an enslaved woman named Feliciana. Don Tomás de Acosta's wife, doña Margarita Grondel, signed the document on his behalf due to his impaired vision.

Don Juan José Bonilla acknowledged receipt of his wife doña María Teodora Ulloa's dowry, totaling 7156 pesos 5 reales. The dowry included valuable jewelry, household items, and a house in the plaza of Cartago, valued at 1300 pesos, which bordered properties of Presbítero don Félix Alvarado, the deceased doña María Petronila Bonilla, the Cabildo, don Joaquín Carazo, and the deceased don Sebastián Urrutia.

Don Juan José Bonilla was appointed tutor to don Nicolás Ulloa, a minor cleric. On December 24, 1816, Bonilla and his wife, María Teodora Ulloa, acknowledged receiving 1089 pesos 3 reales belonging to the minor from Presbítero don Félix de Alvarado.
In September 1824, don Nicolás Ulloa acknowledged receipt of the sum previously mentioned and cancelled the debt.

On January 31, 1817, Coronel don Juan Francisco de Bonilla made his will. He was a widower of Ana Rita Gómez and married to Sinforosa Prieto, with whom he had two children, María Petronila and Adriano María. He bequeathed land to the city's residents, named several legatees including family and servants, and appointed his children as heirs.

On February 5, 1817, don Narciso Esquivel sold a shop, which he had purchased from doña Antonia de Arlegui, to don José Santos Lombardo and company for 150 pesos. The debt for this sale was cancelled in 1817.

On February 15, doña Margarita Frutos sold a pasture in the Chircagres neighborhood, specifically in the Laguna de Orres area on lands belonging to the Ramírezes, to Rafael Mata for 150 pesos. Don Manuel Sáenz, the buyer's agent, paid the sum.

On March 4, doña Gertrudis Robledo, widow of don Juan Pablo Jiménez, granted power of attorney to don Carlos Portocarrero (or don Gordiano Herdocia in his absence) to collect 193 pesos 3 reales and a half from don Pedro Carrillo, which he owed to her deceased husband. Her son, don Joaquín Jiménez, signed for her.
On March 13, Francisco Javier Mayorga sold a site named San Jerónimo in the Valle del Andecho to don Joaquín Oreamuno for 150 pesos.

On March 17, don Juan Antonio Castro and his wife, doña Irinea Hidalgo, received 300 pesos from Brigadier don Tomás de Acosta with 6% annual interest and a one-year term, mortgaging their house next to don Juan José Bonilla's.

In 1829, the executors of doña Margarita Grondel, Presbíteros don Juan de Jesús Urrutia and don Joaquín García, cancelled doña Irinea Hidalgo's bond, as resolved by arbitrators Licenciados don Agustín Gutiérrez and don Manuel Aguilar in a lawsuit.

On March 24, don Juan Antonio Castro sold a pasture, which he had acquired from the heirs of his in-laws don Tomás Hidalgo and doña Rita Oreamuno, to don Joaquín Oreamuno for 200 pesos. The pasture was contiguous to the town of Laborío.

On April 9, don Ramón Molina made his will. He was the legitimate son of Francisco Molina and Andrea González, and married to Antonia Rojas. He had twelve surviving children and three who died in infancy. He owned a house in La Arenilla and lands in Avatice, partly inherited and partly bought from his nephews Manuel and Narcisa Molina.

On April 16, doña Feliciana Lampar, wife of don José de la Trinidad Ulloa, granted power of attorney to don José Jurado, a resident of Chiriquí, to collect notes and 24 pesos that Gavino Aparicio owed to her husband.
On April 24, don Juan José Bonilla granted general power of attorney to don Gordiano Herdocia, a resident of León.

On April 29, Hermenegildo Patulla, a resident of San José, confessed to owing Luz Brenes 220 pesos, received as 8 mules leased for 4 years, with a 5% interest rate. Manuel Antonio Mora served as his guarantor.
In 1821, Luz Brenes provided a receipt for the debt.
On May 16, Presbítero don Félix de Alvarado granted general power of attorney to don Juan José Bonilla.
On June 11, Alcalde don Joaquín Carazo and his brothers...

Lorenzo, Nicolás, Juan Manuel, Ana, Hipólita, Jacoba, Loreto, Carmen, and Lucía Carazo, along with their brother-in-law Félix Oreamuno (husband of Ramona Carazo), sold a property in Ujarrás to Sergeant 1st Class Cayetano Madriz, Ponciano Madriz, and Esteban Morales for 260 pesos. The property included a house, fences, lands, poroses, and water rights, and was located at Puente de Fajardo.

Santiago Bonilla (arbitrator judge) and Manuel Oreamuno (substitute executor for Manuel Ruiz's estate), along with Juan Manuel Alvarado and Rita Ruiz, sold 12 caballerías of land in Santa Lucía (La Palma), Bagaces, to Presbyter Félix de Alvarado. The land was inherited from Lucía Alvarado and María Petronila Bonilla, and a private sale document from 1810 was added as Nicolás Ruiz did not appear. This sale, combined with a previous one, adjusted the total to 20 caballerías under a 1762 title for José Nicolás de Bonilla.

Juan Francisco de Bonilla made a codicil to his will, appointing Juan Manuel de Cañas as arbitrator judge due to Tomás de Acosta's blindness. He named his wife, Sinforosa Prieto, as the third executor and left legacies to his brothers-in-law, godchildren, mother-in-law, Regina Prieto, Joaquina Prieto, and Rafael Fajardo.

Juan José Bonilla, as the contractor for the diezmos (tithes) of the province from Quebrada Honda to Matina for three years and 6900 pesos, obligated himself to the Real Hacienda for the 'novenos Reales.' Juan Francisco de Bonilla and Joaquín Oreamuno served as his guarantors, with Nicolás Carazo signing on behalf of an ill Juan Francisco de Bonilla.

Juan José Bonilla subleased the diezmos of the city's collection points and their annexes from Tres Ríos to Matina, as well as those of Villa de Alajuela, to José Santos Lombardo. Lombardo agreed to pay 700 pesos annually for the first and 500 pesos for the latter for three years, with Rafael Gallegos acting as his guarantor.

people_involved: María Gertrudis de Laya y Bolívar
summary: María Gertrudis de Laya y Bolívar, widow of Sergeant Major Andrés de Bonilla, granted power of attorney to Presbyter Joaquín Machado y Ugarte or Miguel Matamoros. This was to allow them to collect her inheritance as the sole heir to two-thirds of the assets of her deceased son, Presbyter José Antonio Bonilla, who died on August 4th in Nicaragua. Her son, Miguel Bonilla, signed on her behalf.

Presbyter Pedro José Alvarado, son of the deceased Pedro Alvarado and Manuela Baeza, made his will, including two slaves (Santiago and Mercedes) among his assets. He established two chaplaincies, naming his godson and grand-nephew Julián Carazo and his godson and grand-nephew Cayetano Alvarado as chaplains, with various Carazo relatives as interim chaplains and patrons. He also left legacies to his siblings, nephews, and nieces, and named Deacon Juan Manuel Carazo and Presbyter José Gabriel del Campo as executors.

Manuel Marchena and his wife Francisca del Corral (who signed as Francisca Nava y Corral) became guarantors for José María Peralta, who was in charge of the tobacco, stamped paper, and gunpowder 'tercena.' They replaced the deceased Colonel Juan Francisco de Bonilla as guarantors for 1000 pesos.

José María Peralta, Ramón Jiménez, and Vicente Fábrega provided a guarantee to the Real Hacienda for Nicolás Carazo, Pedro Carazo, Antonio Figueroa, Lorenzo Zumbado, and Cosme Castro. This guarantee allowed them to receive certain embargoed clothes, as ordered by the Governor based on the opinion of Assessor Licenciado Rafael Barroeta.

Manuel Núñez and his wife Rita Vega received a censo (annuity/loan) of 70 pesos belonging to San Antonio Murillo, originating from alms of the church of Nuestra Señora de los Angeles. They mortgaged their house as security for this transaction.

Juan Manuel de Cañas, responsible for 2530 pesos belonging to the Cofradía del Santísimo de Bagaces, presented Rafael Barroeta as a guarantor. This action was taken to replace the deceased Colonel Juan Francisco de Bonilla, who had previously served as guarantor.
José Francisco de Bonilla emancipated his son, Policarpo Bonilla, who was over 25 years old and residing in the city of León at the time of the emancipation.

Sinforosa Prieto, widow of Juan Francisco Bonilla, took charge of a chaplaincy branch worth 707 pesos and 2.5 reales, previously held by her deceased husband and belonging to the Convent of this city. She mortgaged her Coris pasture as security. A marginal note from 1839 indicates the cancellation of this obligation by Sinforosa's payment and a new tenancy by Presbyter José Antonio Oreamuno, José Oreamuno, and Félix Vicente Fábrega.

Manuel María Peralta and his wife Ana José Chavarría took charge of 140 pesos belonging to Nuestra Señora del Pilar de los Tres Ríos, which had been previously held by Trinidad Pacheco. Their guarantor was Paulina Fajardo, Ana José Chavarría's mother-in-law, who mortgaged her house as security.

Doña Tomasa Alvarado, a single woman without succession, made her will. She ordered the freedom of her mulata slave, Vicenta, and bequeathed her a loom, a corn grinding stone, and a cacao grinding stone. Don Joaquín Iglesias was named her executor.

Don José María Peralta sold a stone-fenced pasture in Los Cerrillos for 800 pesos to his son, Don Manuel Peralta, and his son-in-law, Don Tranquilino Bonilla. The sale was complicated by a previous deal with Presbítero Don Evaristo Gutiérrez and the need for a community retracto due to the undivided assets of Don José María's deceased wife, Doña Ana Benita del Corral, as advised by Licenciado Barroeta.

Presbítero Don José Ana Ulloa and Don Manuel Sáenz took charge of 800 pesos belonging to the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora de la Soledad de Cartago, previously held by Don Juan Francisco Bonilla, and secured in a pasture called El Cangrejal. They mortgaged their house as collateral. An annotation from 1829 indicates the debt was cancelled by Mayordomo José María Frutos.

Doña Joaquina Alvarado sold 6 caballerías of land in El Carmen, Bagaces, to Don Manuel José Flores, a resident of San José, for 135 pesos. She stipulated that a chaplaincy, previously charged to her deceased mother Doña Bartola Oreamuno and her house, should now be understood to apply to this land, with 100 pesos of the sale price allocated to it and charged to Flores. An annotation from 1841 indicates this debt was cancelled.

people_involved: Presbítero Don Rafael José de la Rosa
summary: Presbítero Don Rafael José de la Rosa, the Cura of Cartago, granted general power of attorney to Presbítero Don Juan Onofre Oconor, the Sacristán Mayor of the Cathedral of León.

Don Benito García took charge of the tobacco, gunpowder, stamped paper, and utensils tercena, replacing Don José María Peralta who had resigned. Don Joaquín Oreamuno, the Alcalde 1° and Teniente de Gobernador, acted as his guarantor for a sum of one thousand pesos.

people_involved: el señor Cura de esta ciudad
summary: Capitán Don Hermenegildo Bonilla took charge of 200 pesos in cacao from the Cofradía de Nuestra Señora del Rosario and 100 pesos in cacao from the Cofradía del Santísimo, both previously held by Don Juan Francisco Bonilla. He mortgaged his house and three pastures donated by his brother, the Cura of Cartago, as collateral. An annotation from 1824 indicates this debt was cancelled.

Presbítero Manuel Antonio Sáenz, legitimate son of Don José Antonio Sáenz and Doña María Josefa Alvarez, made his will. He owned a house in San José and land with cattle near Las Cañas, Bagaces, and was owed two years' synods from his time as Sacristán Mayor of Esparza. He named his sisters Ramona, Candelaria, and Bibiana, and his servants Eulogia and Jesús as legatees, and Presbítero Don Nicolás Carrillo and his brother-in-law Don Sotero Ramírez as executors.

Lucas Araya, legitimate son of José Antonio Araya and Petronila Vanegas, made a nuncupative will on November 1st. He was married to María Francisca Oreamuno, with whom he had two sons, José Nicolás and José María. On November 19th, his widow requested information, and several witnesses declared, leading to the Alcalde's approval for protocolization.

Don Joaquín de Jesús Bonilla, a single man over 30 years old, made his will, naming his parents as executors and heirs. His uncle, Presbítero Don José Antonio Bonilla's estate, owed him 4 years of personal service at his Hacienda Mateo, at 5 pesos per month.

people_involved: Coronel Don Juan Manuel de Cañas
su esposa (Brigadier Don Tomás de Acosta's wife)
summary: Brigadier Don Tomás de Acosta, unable to handle affairs related to his ongoing residencia (review of his governorship) due to blindness and other ailments, granted general power of attorney to Coronel Don Juan Manuel de Cañas. His wife signed on his behalf. Licenciado Barroeta was the commissioner for the residencia.

Presbítero Don Manuel Antonio Sáenz made a codicil to his will, bequeathing money to his sister-in-law Doña Manuela Valverde and her three children: Doña María Manuela, Doña María Josefa, and Don Antonio María Sáenz. He also donated something to Doña Bernardina Sáenz and his nephew Don Saturnino Astúa.

Eduardo González and his wife María de los Angeles Brenes took charge of 165 pesos in silver belonging to the Convent of Cartago, previously held by Doña Antonia Alvarado. They mortgaged their house, lands, and other possessions in Río Grande, which they had purchased from Don Ramón Gutiérrez.

Alcalde Don Joaquín Carazo paid a debt of 125 pesos to Don Joaquín Iglesias by giving him a truco (billiards table) with its balls and utensils. This truco had been donated by Presbítero Don Félix Alvarado to Don Joaquín Carazo's wife, Doña Ana Francisca Bonilla, who also appeared.

Cayetano Madriz and his wife Gregoria Picado, along with Ponciano Madriz and his wife María Nicolasa Quesada, all residents of Ujarrás, took charge of 290 pesos in silver belonging to the Convent of Cartago. They mortgaged their houses and lands, which previously belonged to the Carazos. An annotation from 1825 indicates the debt was cancelled.
Manuela Josefa Araya, a resident of Villavieja, acting for herself and her deceased husband Alejo Moya, sold land to Don Rosario Carrillo.

An unnamed woman and her husband acquired land in Alajuela through purchases made in 1803, 1805, and 1808. The land, totaling 1000 varas and half a street, was located near Alajuela, bordering the Itiquís river at Los Cerrillos, and was originally bought by the husband from Benita Solórzano. The woman later ratified the sale.

Vicente Granados, a native of Villa Nueva and resident of Esparza, granted his will at Hacienda Chomes. He was married to Josefa Fonseca and had two children, Antonia and Cristóbal. José Antonio García notarized the will, authorized by Gobernador Ayala, and Ramón Jiménez and Jesús Castro were named executors.

people_involved: Presbítero don Rafael José de la Rosa
summary: Eusebio Molina, son of Manuel Molina and María del Carmen González, granted his will. He was married to María de las Mercedes Quesada and had two minor children, María del Espíritusanto and José Francisco. Presbítero don Rafael José de la Rosa was the arbitrator judge, and Manuel Escalante and Joaquín Oreamuno were named executors.

José María Meneses, as husband of Rita Velasco, granted power of attorney to Atanasio Gutiérrez, who resided in Usulután, to represent them in the estate proceedings of his deceased father-in-law, Manuel Velasco.

people_involved: Presbítero don Rafael de la Rosa
Presbítero don Rafael de la Fuente
summary: Presbítero don Félix de Alvarado and Alcalde don Joaquín Oreamuno committed to paying Bachiller don Rafael Francisco Osejo 300 pesos annually for three years to teach a philosophy course, aiming to improve youth instruction. Various individuals also subscribed to contribute to the project, which included provisions for scribes, notebooks, and fees for students, with exceptions for the poor.

María Josefa del Carmen González, daughter of Martín González and Ana Benita Carranza, granted her will. She was married to Manuel Molina and had two sons, Onofre (deceased without succession) and Eusebio. Her son Eusebio and Salvador Oreamuno were named executors.
Don Manuel de la Torre received a loan of 573 pesos 5 reales from doña Juana Ignacia García for two years or more. Doña Antonia Jiménez and don Joaquín Oreamuno (the Alcalde) acted as his guarantors.

Don Juan Antonio Castro obligated himself to don Manuel Palm., a resident of Panamá, for 277 pesos owed by don Lorenzo Díaz of San José. Castro needed Díaz to build his ship in Punta de Arenas and pledged to pay Palm. upon the ship's first return voyage, estimated for November 1818. He mortgaged his house with his wife, doña Irinea Hidalgo.

Don Nicolás Oreamuno, who won the auction for tithes from El Salto to Quebrada Honda, and from Bagaces, Esparza, and Las Cañas for 1588 pesos annually over three years, obligated himself to the Royal Treasury. He presented Alcalde don Joaquín Oreamuno as his guarantor.

Antonio Luciano Gutiérrez, son of the deceased Miguel Gutiérrez and Petronila Chacón, granted his will. He was a widower of Francisca Nicolasa Estrada, with whom he had no children, and was currently married to doña Carmen Medina, with whom he also had no succession yet. His wife and don Félix Oreamuno were named executors, and his mother was the heir.

José Brenes, who won the aguardiente monopoly for one year for 679 pesos 4 reales (56 pesos 5 reales per month), obligated himself to pay this sum to the Royal Treasury. He offered Alcalde don Joaquín Oreamuno as his guarantor.

Juan José Bonilla, a resident of Ujarraz and winner of the aguardiente monopoly for that town, obligated himself to pay the Royal Treasury 11 pesos 7 reales monthly for one year. He offered Francisco Brenes, a resident of 'esta ciudad,' as his guarantor.

people_involved: Presbítero don Pedro José de Alvarado
summary: Presbítero don Pedro José de Alvarado sold his 15-year-old mulatto slave, Santiago Alvarado, to don Juan José Bonilla.

Antonia de la Rosa Rivera, widow of José Antonio Solano, made her will. She had one son, Joaquín Solano, from her first marriage, and two children, Anacleta and Sinforosa, from her second marriage to Venancio Madriz. Her executors were her husband and her brother, Pedro Rivera.

Presbíteros don Nicolás Carrillo and don Rafael José de la Rosa, acting as executors for Colonel don Juan Francisco de Bonilla, sold the land site named Las Huacas to Juan de Dios Brenes. The property, including a house, corrals, and fences, was sold for 630 pesos to Brenes, who represented the neighborhood of Chircagres.

Alcalde don Joaquín Oreamuno sold an enclosure of land in La Isla to don Gregorio Ulloa for 600 pesos, which Oreamuno had previously acquired from Bartolomé de Rojas. Gregorio Ulloa also purchased six shares from various individuals. The land's boundaries were extensively described, mentioning properties of Mercedes Torres, Joaquín Díaz, Rosario Mesa, Francisco Villavicencio, Rafael Meléndez, and Manuel Mora, and extending to the Jorco and Tiribí rivers.

Don Félix Oreamuno and his wife doña Ramona Carazo took charge of a principal of 300 pesos cacao from a chaplaincy. This chaplaincy was founded by Francisco Aguirre for Pedro Martínez Colina and now belongs to the chaplain don Nicolás Oreamuno. They mortgaged a pasture in Purires, specifically in Cucaracha, along with 4 mules and 50 cattle.

Presbítero don Rafael Arnesto de Troya sold a pasture in La Lima to don Ramón Jiménez for 600 pesos. Arnesto de Troya had purchased this pasture from the deceased don Pedro Elisondo. The property was fenced and bordered by the properties of doña Bartola Oreamuno, doña Mercedes Guerrero, and the Sabana Grande.
The parish priest don Joaquín Isidro Lizano granted general power of attorney to don Manuel Oreamuno.

Doña Ana María Oreamuno sold a pasture in Retana to Presbítero don Evaristo Gutiérrez for 500 pesos. The land was in litigation between the heirs of don Antonio Oreamuno and the city, but Ana María had been paying annual dues and had fenced it with Cabildo permission.

people_involved: María Gertrudis de la Aya y Bolívar
summary: Doña María Gertrudis de la Aya y Bolívar, daughter of the deceased Miguel de la Aya Bolívar and Isabel de Miranda, made her will. She was the widow of Andrés de Bonilla and had seven children, including Presbítero José Antonio who recently died in Nicaragua, and grandchildren Joaquín and María Joaquina Bonilla. Her executors were her son, Father Miguel Bonilla, and Presbítero don Félix de Jesús García.

people_involved: María Gertrudis de la Aya y Bolívar
summary: Doña María Gertrudis de la Aya y Bolívar granted power to her son, Presbítero don Miguel Bonilla.

Don Félix Oreamuno took charge of 200 pesos cacao from a chaplaincy belonging to Presbítero don José María del Campo. Don Joaquín Oreamuno acted as guarantor for this transaction. The 200 pesos cacao were equivalent to 133 pesos and 2.5 reales of silver.

Ambrosio Zamora, a resident of Villa Vieja, declared that about 20 years prior, he sold four 50-vara square lots in Villa de Alajuela to don Rosario Carrillo for 56 pesos. The lots, inherited from his mother, were described by their boundaries, mentioning properties of Cura don Joaquín Lizano, Josefa Saborío, Lorenzo López, Manuel Jinesta, Josefa Chavarría, Cipriano Rojas, Ramón García, Juan Mariano Rodríguez, and Rafael Carrillo.

Lorenzo González, legitimate son of the deceased Martín González and Benita Carranza, made his will. He was married to Josefa Fuentes and had six children, including José de la Encarnación who was married. His executors were his wife and don Félix Oreamuno.

Prudencio Picado, natural son of the deceased Juana Efigenia Picado, made his will. He was a widower of Mónica Trejos, with whom he had nine children, and later married Gertrudis Solano, with whom he had eight more children. Several of his children were married, and some from his first marriage died without succession, while one from his second marriage, José Domingo, also died. His executors were his current wife and don Félix Oreamuno.

Miguel Arias and his wife Joaquina Carranza took on an obligation for 216 pesos and 1.5 reales to the minors María Baltasara and José Valentín. These funds were their inheritance from their mother Joaquina Carranza's first husband, Bernardo Garro, and were to be delivered from the estate of Jesús Fuentes, Joaquina's second husband. Joaquín Trejos acted as guarantor for this obligation.

Presbítero don Félix de Alvarado sold a mulata named Josefa Carazo to Presbítero don Joaquín Isidro Lizano for 250 pesos. Josefa Carazo was described as being about 30 years old, red-skinned, curly-haired, short, and stout.
Juan de Dios Brenes declared the individuals who contributed to pay for the Las Huacas land site. This land had been purchased for the neighborhood for 630 pesos.

A detailed record lists numerous individuals and the specific amounts of pesos associated with them, ranging from 25 pesos to 4 reales. These entries likely represent financial contributions, debts, or other monetary obligations within the community of Cartago.
Rafael Escalante and his wife, Segunda Granados, assumed responsibility for 100 pesos belonging to the Confradía del Santísimo. They secured this obligation by hypothecating their house.

José Nicolás Barahona, son of the late Tomás Barahona and Ana Josefa Rodríguez, made his will. He was a widower of Ana Micaela Rojas and named his nine children, two of whom were married, and appointed Francisco Abarca and Juan Jiménez as executors.

The residents of the Chircagres barrio granted power to don Joaquín Oreamuno (the Mayor), don Félix Oreamuno, Juan de Dios Brenes, and José Antonio Mora. This authority was designated for the defense of the 'Huacas' and for the economic governance of the community.
